Others block the tiny machines bacteria use to make proteins, or interfere with how they copy their DNA. They can also affect helpful gut bacteria, which is why they sometimes upset the stomach.

Viruses are different. They have no cell walls or protein-making machinery of their own; they hijack your cells instead. So antibiotics do nothing against colds, flu, COVID-19 or most sore throats and coughs. Taking them for a cold won't help you recover faster, and it exposes your body's bacteria to the drug, which can help resistance develop. Antivirals and vaccines are the tools for viruses.

sections.key: Overusing antibiotics lets resistant bacteria survive and spread, producing superbugs that kill over a million people a year.
sections.b:
Every time antibiotics are used, bacteria that happen to survive can multiply and spread their resistance, even swapping resistance genes with other bacteria. Overuse in humans and animals speeds this up. The result is superbugs: infections that some or most antibiotics can no longer treat.

A major study estimated that in 2019, drug-resistant bacterial infections directly caused about 1.27 million deaths worldwide. Fleming himself warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse could lead to resistance.

sections.key: Take antibiotics only when prescribed, exactly as directed and never shared, while scientists search for new ones.
sections.b:
Everyone can help. Only take antibiotics when a doctor prescribes them, and don't pressure doctors for them for colds or flu. Take them exactly as directed. Never share them or use leftovers; return unused medicines to a pharmacy. Keep your vaccinations up to date and wash your hands well, since preventing infections is the best protection.

Very few new classes of antibiotics have been found in recent decades, partly because they're less profitable than drugs taken daily. Scientists are searching soil, oceans and even the human body for new compounds, and using AI to screen millions of molecules. They're also exploring bacteriophages, viruses that kill specific bacteria, used experimentally on otherwise untreatable infections.

quiz.q: Why was penicillin not a medicine straight after its discovery in 1928?
o: Its inventor kept the mould secret
The mould only worked in London
It was too dangerous to give to patients
It was hard to purify, so it remained a laboratory curiosity
quiz.e: Turning a lucky discovery into a usable drug took years of further work.

quiz.q: What did Florey's team do around 1940?
o: Purified penicillin and showed it could cure infections
Found the first virus-killing drug
Discovered that mould causes infections
Replaced penicillin with a vaccine
quiz.e: They purified penicillin and tested it on mice and then people, making it a real medicine.

quiz.q: Why won't antibiotics cure a cold?
o: Colds are too mild to treat
Colds are caused by viruses, which lack the structures antibiotics target
The usual dose is too small to work
Colds are caused by allergies
quiz.e: Antibiotics target bacterial features, so they do nothing against viruses.

quiz.q: What drives antibiotic resistance?
o: Washing hands too often with ordinary soap
Vaccination programmes against common infections
Overuse that lets surviving bacteria multiply and spread
Cold weather that weakens the immune system
quiz.e: Each use gives surviving bacteria the chance to multiply and pass on resistance.

quiz.q: What should you do with leftover antibiotics?
o: Keep them at home for the next illness
Return them to a pharmacy for safe disposal
Offer them to a friend with similar symptoms
Take them early at the next sign of a cold
quiz.e: Sharing or reusing leftovers encourages resistance; pharmacies dispose of them safely.

LESSONS.push: A holiday and a mouldy dish changed medicine. Why is that progress now at risk?

LESSONS.title: DNA: your body's instruction manual
LESSONS.hook: Two metres of code in every cell, written in a four-letter alphabet.

sections.key: DNA carries the instructions for building and running living things, and its double-helix structure was revealed in 1953.
sections.b:
DNA, short for deoxyribonucleic acid, carries the instructions for building and running almost every living thing, from bacteria to blue whales. It's found inside nearly every cell in your body. Unwound and laid end to end, the DNA in a single human cell would stretch about two metres, yet it's packed into a nucleus too small to see without a microscope.

In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick published its structure: a double helix, like a twisted ladder. Their model relied heavily on X-ray images by Rosalind Franklin, especially 'Photo 51', and on data from Maurice Wilkins. Watson, Crick and Wilkins won the 1962 Nobel Prize. Franklin had died of cancer in 1958, aged 37, and her crucial role is now widely recognised.

sections.key: DNA's code uses four bases, and because A pairs with T and C with G, each strand is a template for copying the other.
sections.b: The rungs of the DNA ladder are made of four chemical bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. That means each strand is a complementary template for the other, so a cell can copy its DNA by unzipping the ladder and building new partner strands. The human genome contains about 3 billion of these base pairs.

sections.key: Cells copy a gene into messenger RNA, then read it three letters at a time to string amino acids into a protein.
sections.b:
To use a gene, a cell first copies it into messenger RNA, which carries the instructions out of the nucleus to protein-building machines called ribosomes. Ribosomes read the message three letters at a time. Each three-letter 'word', called a codon, calls for one of 20 amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, or signals where to stop.

Four letters give 64 possible codons, so most amino acids have several, which means some spelling changes make no difference to the protein. In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei decoded the first codon, starting a race that cracked the whole code by the mid-1960s.

sections.key: Mutations are changes in DNA, most are harmless, and they create the small differences between people.
sections.b:
Every time a cell divides, it copies its 3 billion letters and occasionally makes a mistake. Radiation, like UV from the sun, and chemicals, like those in tobacco smoke, can also damage DNA. These changes are mutations. Most are harmless or quickly repaired. Some cause disease, including many cancers, which is one reason sun protection matters in Australia. Occasionally a mutation is useful, and over generations such changes are the raw material for evolution.

Any two people share about 99.9% of their DNA. The remaining 0.1%, around 3 million letters, accounts for differences in appearance and some disease risks. There's more genetic variation within any so-called racial group than between groups, so scientists consider race a social idea rather than a clear biological category.

sections.key: Cheap genome sequencing and DNA fingerprinting let doctors and investigators read and compare individual DNA.
sections.b:
The Human Genome Project, an international effort to read an entire human genome, finished in 2003 after 13 years at a cost of about US$2.7 billion. Today a genome can be sequenced in about a day for a few hundred dollars. Doctors can diagnose rare genetic diseases in babies, match cancer treatments to a tumour's mutations and track viruses in real time, as in the COVID-19 pandemic.

In 1984, Alec Jeffreys found that repeated stretches of DNA vary so much between people they form a pattern almost unique to each person, identical twins aside. DNA fingerprinting settled a 1985 immigration case, cleared an innocent man who had confessed and, in 1988, helped convict the real killer. Modern profiles compare short repeated sequences at around 20 places in the genome.

quiz.q: What does DNA do in a living cell?
o: It stores and carries the instructions for building and running the organism
It provides the main energy supply for the cell
It digests food inside the cell
It carries oxygen around the body
quiz.e: DNA is the instruction manual for almost every living thing.

quiz.q: Why can a cell copy its DNA by unzipping the ladder?
o: The two strands are exact copies of each other
Each base has a fixed partner, so each strand templates the other
Special enzymes copy it without reading the strands
The rungs are made of four identical bases
quiz.e: A pairs with T and C with G, so each strand dictates its partner.

quiz.q: Why can some spelling changes in DNA make no difference to a protein?
o: Proteins are built without ever reading the gene
Most amino acids are coded by several different codons
Cells ignore every change that occurs in a gene
Every error is repaired before the gene is read
quiz.e: Four letters give 64 codons for only 20 amino acids, so the code has built-in redundancy.

quiz.q: Why does sun protection matter for your DNA?
o: UV radiation can damage DNA, and the resulting mutations can cause cancers
Sunlight makes DNA copy itself too slowly
Sunscreen repairs old mutations
UV changes the order of the codons in every cell
quiz.e: Damaged DNA can mutate, and some mutations lead to cancer.

quiz.q: Why can DNA fingerprinting tell people apart?
o: It reads all 3 billion letters of a person's genome
It looks for a single gene that everyone else lacks
It compares repeated stretches that vary almost uniquely
It measures how long the DNA is inside a cell
quiz.e: Variable repeated stretches form a pattern almost unique to each person.

LESSONS.push: Unwound, the DNA in one cell would stretch about two metres. How does it fit?

LESSONS.title: How black holes work
LESSONS.hook: Places where gravity wins completely, time slows down and even light can't escape.

sections.key: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
sections.b:
A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Every object has an 'escape velocity': about 11 kilometres per second for Earth. For a black hole it exceeds the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second, and since nothing travels faster than light, nothing gets out.

In 1783, English clergyman John Michell imagined 'dark stars' that light couldn't escape. The modern idea came from Einstein's general relativity (1915), which describes gravity as the bending of space and time by mass. Karl Schwarzschild soon found that the equations allowed such regions. For decades many physicists, including Einstein, doubted they existed. The name 'black hole' was popularised in the late 1960s.

sections.key: Stellar black holes form when a very massive star's core collapses, and supermassive ones sit at galaxy centres.
sections.b:
A star of roughly 20 or more times the Sun's mass eventually runs out of fuel. Without the outward push of nuclear fusion, its core collapses under its own gravity in a fraction of a second, often triggering a supernova that blasts away the outer layers. What remains is crushed into a black hole. The Milky Way probably contains millions of these stellar black holes, most of them invisible.

Most large galaxies also have a supermassive black hole at their centre, weighing millions to billions of Suns. Gas falling into one can heat up and shine brighter than a whole galaxy, creating a quasar.

sections.key: The event horizon is the boundary beyond which nothing can escape, and tidal stretching can tear apart anything near a small black hole.
sections.b:
The boundary around a black hole is the event horizon. Outside it, a powerful enough rocket could still escape. Inside, every possible path leads further in. A black hole with the mass of our Sun would have an event horizon only about 6 kilometres across, and Earth squeezed into one would be about the size of a marble. At the centre, general relativity predicts a 'singularity', where our current physics breaks down.

Gravity strengthens closer to a mass. Near a small black hole, the pull on your feet would far exceed the pull on your head, stretching you like a noodle. Scientists really do call this spaghettification. Near a supermassive black hole the stretching at the horizon is gentler, so you could cross it unaware, but you'd never come back.

sections.key: General relativity says time passes more slowly in stronger gravity, an effect GPS satellites must correct for.
sections.b:
Einstein's general relativity predicts that time passes more slowly in stronger gravity. It isn't only theory: clocks on GPS satellites, high above Earth in weaker gravity, tick slightly faster than clocks on the ground, and the system must correct for it.

Near a black hole the effect becomes extreme. To a distant observer, a clock falling towards a black hole would appear to tick slower and slower as it neared the event horizon, its light growing dimmer and redder.

sections.key: Black holes can't be seen directly, but orbiting stars, gravitational waves and radio images reveal them.
sections.b:
Black holes can't be seen directly, but their surroundings can. Astronomers proved our galaxy's supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, is there by tracking stars whipping around an invisible object at enormous speeds. It weighs about 4 million Suns and lies around 26,000 light-years away. That work won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

In 2015, the LIGO detectors in the US picked up gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space itself, from two black holes colliding more than a billion light-years away. In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio telescopes working as one Earth-sized dish, released the first image of a black hole's shadow, in galaxy M87. In 2022 it imaged Sagittarius A*.

quiz.q: Why can nothing escape from a black hole?
o: Its escape velocity is greater than the speed of light
It is made of dark matter
It absorbs all heat from nearby objects
It is too distant for light to reach us
quiz.e: Nothing can travel faster than light, so nothing can beat that escape velocity.

quiz.q: How do stellar black holes usually form?
o: Two planets collide and merge
A galaxy runs out of gas
Dark energy condenses in space
The core of a very massive star collapses after its fuel runs out
quiz.e: Without fusion's outward push, the core collapses under its own gravity.

quiz.q: What happens once something crosses the event horizon?
o: It slows down and is eventually pushed back out
Every path leads further in, so escape is impossible
It is converted into pure light and radiated away
It reaches the singularity at the same instant
quiz.e: The event horizon is the boundary beyond which nothing can escape.

quiz.q: What do GPS satellites show about gravity and time?
o: Weaker gravity high above Earth makes their clocks tick slightly faster
Their clocks stop working in orbit
Their clocks run backwards at night
Time is unaffected by gravity
quiz.e: The system corrects for this real effect of general relativity.

quiz.q: How did astronomers show a supermassive black hole sits at the centre of our galaxy?
o: They photographed it in visible light in 1990
They tracked stars whipping around an invisible object
They watched it swallow a whole planet
They measured its heat with a space thermometer
quiz.e: The stars' speeds revealed a huge unseen mass, work that won a 2020 Nobel Prize.

LESSONS.push: Time runs slower near a black hole, and GPS already corrects for a version of it.

LESSONS.title: The life and death of stars
LESSONS.hook: How stars are born, why their mass decides their fate, and why many of them don't shine alone.

sections.key: Stars form in nebulae when gravity pulls gas together until the core ignites nuclear fusion.
sections.b:
Stars form inside giant, cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, made mostly of hydrogen. Something, perhaps a nearby supernova or a collision between clouds, disturbs the gas. Gravity pulls denser clumps together, and as they shrink they heat up. When the core reaches about 10 million degrees, nuclear fusion ignites and a star is born.

The Orion Nebula, a fuzzy patch in Orion's 'sword' (the handle of the Saucepan in Australian skies), is a stellar nursery you can see with the naked eye.

sections.key: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium, and a star's colour reveals its temperature.
sections.b:
In a star's core, hydrogen nuclei are squeezed so hard they fuse into helium, converting a little mass into a lot of energy. The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of matter into energy every second. That outward push balances gravity pulling inwards, and for most of a star's life the two stay locked in balance. The Sun is a fairly ordinary star, 4.6 billion years old and roughly halfway through its life. Its surface is about 5,500°C, its core about 15 million °C. Energy can take tens of thousands of years to leave the core, then about eight minutes to reach Earth.

Colour shows temperature: reddish Antares is cooler, blue-white Rigel hotter.

sections.key: Small stars live longest and massive stars burn out fast; the Sun will end as a white dwarf.
sections.b:
A star's mass decides its colour, brightness and lifespan. Small, cool red dwarfs use fuel so slowly they can shine for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed. Most stars in the galaxy are red dwarfs, too faint to see by eye. Massive blue stars burn hot and fast and last only a few million years: more fuel means a shorter life.

In about 5 billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant, perhaps engulfing Mercury, Venus and possibly Earth. Long before then, in about a billion years, its growing brightness will have boiled away Earth's oceans. It will puff off its outer layers as a planetary nebula, leaving a white dwarf: a dense, Earth-sized ember that cools over trillions of years.

sections.key: Massive stars explode as supernovae because fusing iron releases no energy, leaving neutron stars or black holes.
sections.b: Massive stars end far more violently. They fuse heavier and heavier elements in their cores, up to iron. Fusing iron doesn't release energy, so the core collapses in less than a second and rebounds in a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine a galaxy of billions of stars. The collapsed core becomes a neutron star, so dense that a teaspoon would weigh billions of tonnes, or, if massive enough, a black hole.

sections.key: Close to half of Sun-like stars have a companion, and exploding white dwarfs in pairs work as cosmic measuring sticks.
sections.b:
Our solitary Sun is a little unusual: close to half of Sun-like stars have at least one companion. Algol, in Perseus, dims noticeably every 2.9 days as a fainter partner crosses in front of it. Sirius is circled by a small, faint white dwarf, Sirius B.

When a white dwarf pulls enough gas from a close partner, or merges with another white dwarf, it can blow apart in a type Ia supernova. These reach a predictable peak brightness, so astronomers use them to measure distances across the universe, work that earned ANU's Brian Schmidt a share of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. Starlight is also old: light from Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky, left it about 8.6 years ago. Warrumbungle National Park in NSW became Australia's first Dark Sky Park in 2016.

quiz.q: What balances the pull of gravity inside a star like the Sun?
o: The push of energy released by hydrogen fusion
The star's rotation alone
Outward pressure from surrounding nebula gas
Magnetic fields from nearby stars
quiz.e: Fusion energy pushes outwards while gravity pulls in, holding the star stable.

quiz.q: What does a star's colour tell you?
o: How far away it is
How old the universe is
Its temperature, with blue-white stars hotter than reddish ones
How fast it spins
quiz.e: Colour reveals temperature, such as cooler reddish Antares and hotter blue-white Rigel.

quiz.q: Why do massive stars live shorter lives than small stars?
o: They are younger when they first form
They burn their large fuel supply far faster
They contain much less hydrogen to start with
They are cooled down by their great size
quiz.e: Heavier stars burn fuel so fast that more fuel still means a shorter life.

quiz.q: Why does the core of a massive star collapse?
o: The surrounding nebula pulls it apart
It cools suddenly to absolute zero
Fusing iron releases no energy to hold it up
It runs out of heavy elements to fuse
quiz.e: Without energy from fusion to resist gravity, the core collapses and a supernova follows.

quiz.q: Why are type Ia supernovae useful to astronomers?
o: Their predictable peak brightness lets them measure distances
They produce all the Sun's energy
They are the only supernovae visible from Earth
They show where nebulae are forming
quiz.e: Because they reach a predictable brightness, how dim they look reveals how far away they are.

LESSONS.push: The more fuel a star has, the shorter its life. Here's the odd logic behind that.

LESSONS.title: The Big Bang
LESSONS.hook: 13.8 billion years ago, everything you can see was packed into a space smaller than an atom. How do we know?

sections.key: The Big Bang was the expansion of space itself, everywhere at once, not an explosion into existing space.
sections.b: The Big Bang theory describes how the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. The name is misleading. It wasn't an explosion in one place, flinging matter outwards into empty space. It was the expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once. There's no centre and no edge to point to. The name was coined, somewhat mockingly, by astronomer Fred Hoyle in a 1949 radio broadcast; he preferred a rival theory.

sections.key: Distant galaxies are receding faster the further away they are, showing that space itself is stretching.
sections.b:
In the 1920s, astronomers still argued about whether other galaxies even existed. Edwin Hubble settled that and then, in 1929, showed that nearly all galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the faster they recede. That's what you'd expect if space itself is stretching. Picture raisins in rising bread dough: every raisin moves away from every other, and distant ones separate faster. Run the film backwards and everything converges.

Because space expanded while light travelled, the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across, though only 13.8 billion years old.

sections.key: The cosmic microwave background is light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, and it is strong evidence for the theory.
sections.b:
If the universe began hot and dense, some of that heat should still be around, stretched into faint microwaves by billions of years of expansion. In 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs found a mysterious hiss in their radio antenna, coming from every direction. At first they suspected pigeon droppings. It was the cosmic microwave background, and it won them a Nobel Prize.

For its first 380,000 years, the universe was a glowing fog of charged particles that scattered light. When it cooled enough for atoms to form, the fog cleared and light travelled freely. After a long 'dark age', gravity pulled gas into the first stars and galaxies within a few hundred million years. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, is spotting galaxies from this early era.

sections.key: The Big Bang correctly predicts the universe's hydrogen and helium, yet ordinary matter is only about 5% of what exists.
sections.b:
In the first fraction of a second, the universe was too hot for atoms. As it cooled, within about three minutes protons and neutrons fused into the nuclei of the lightest elements. The theory predicts about three-quarters hydrogen and a quarter helium by mass, with a trace of lithium, which is what astronomers see in the oldest stars and gas clouds.

Everything we can see, including stars, planets and people, is only about 5% of the universe's contents. About 27% is dark matter, detected only through its gravity. The other 68% or so is dark energy, which is speeding up the expansion, discovered in 1998. We don't yet know what either is.

sections.key: The theory describes what happened after the early hot, dense state, not what caused it or whether anything came before.
sections.b:
The Big Bang theory describes how the universe evolved from an early hot, dense state. It doesn't explain what caused that state or whether anything came 'before'. Time itself may have begun with the Big Bang, making 'before' meaningless, like asking what's north of the North Pole.

Some physicists explore ideas such as cosmic inflation, a brief burst of extreme expansion in the first instant, or even multiple universes. These are active areas of research, not settled science. The universe beyond what we can observe may be much larger, possibly infinite.

quiz.q: What was the Big Bang?
o: An explosion at a single point in empty space
The expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once
A collision between two earlier universes
The birth of the first stars
quiz.e: There was no centre or edge; space itself expanded.

quiz.q: What does it tell us that distant galaxies recede faster than nearby ones?
o: Galaxies repel each other
Earth sits at the centre of the universe
Space itself is stretching
Distant galaxies are lighter
quiz.e: Stretching space carries distant galaxies away faster, like raisins in rising dough.

quiz.q: What is the cosmic microwave background?
o: Radiation from distant black holes
Early light, stretched into faint microwaves by expansion
Noise from our own planet's atmosphere
Light given off by the very first stars
quiz.e: It is a leftover glow from the early universe and strong evidence for the theory.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the universe's contents is ordinary matter?
o: About 5%
About 27%
About 50%
About 95%
quiz.e: The rest is dark matter and dark energy, neither of which we yet understand.

quiz.q: What does the Big Bang theory explain?
o: What caused the universe to begin
How the universe evolved from an early hot, dense state
What existed before time began
Why there are multiple universes
quiz.e: It describes what happened afterwards; causes and 'before' remain open questions.

LESSONS.push: The Big Bang had no centre and wasn't an explosion. So what actually happened?

LESSONS.title: The Moon: our strange companion
LESSONS.hook: It was born in a collision, it's slowly drifting away, and it controls the tides at your local beach.

sections.key: The Moon most likely formed when a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth, and its dark seas are ancient lava plains.
sections.b:
The leading explanation is the giant-impact hypothesis. About 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body, sometimes called Theia, smashed into the young Earth. The collision flung molten rock into orbit, which clumped together to form the Moon. Evidence includes the Moon's small iron core and the remarkable similarity between Apollo Moon rocks and rocks on Earth.

The dark patches you can see are called maria, Latin for 'seas', because early astronomers thought they were oceans. They are plains of solidified lava that flooded huge impact basins roughly 3 to 3.9 billion years ago. With no wind, rain or moving plates, craters last billions of years. Binoculars show bright rays spreading from young craters like Tycho.

sections.key: The Moon is tidally locked, so we always see the same side, and phases come from seeing different amounts of its lit half.
sections.b:
The Moon spins once in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth, about 27 days, so the same side always faces us. Earth's gravity gradually slowed its spin until it locked into step, a process called tidal locking. The far side isn't permanently dark; it gets just as much sunlight. Humans first saw it in 1959, in photos from a Soviet probe.

The Moon makes no light of its own; half of it is always lit by the Sun. As it orbits, we see different amounts of that lit half, giving the phases in a cycle of about 29.5 days. From Australia, the Moon appears 'upside down' compared with northern hemisphere pictures, so a waxing crescent is lit on the left.

sections.key: The Moon's gravity raises two tidal bulges, and it is slowly drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 centimetres a year.
sections.b:
The Moon's gravity pulls hardest on the ocean facing it, creating a bulge, and least on the far side, where another bulge forms. As Earth rotates through the two bulges, most coasts get two high tides a day. When Sun and Moon line up at full and new moon, we get extra-large spring tides. Australia's north-west has some of the world's largest tides, over 10 metres.

Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Lasers fired at them show it is drifting away by about 3.8 centimetres a year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow. Tidal forces are also lengthening Earth's day: hundreds of millions of years ago, a day was around 22 hours.

sections.key: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks the Sun, a lunar eclipse when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
sections.b:
By a remarkable coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away, so they look almost the same size in our sky. When the Moon passes directly in front of the Sun, it can block it completely in a total solar eclipse.

When Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, its shadow falls on the Moon, often turning it red, in a lunar eclipse. Eclipses don't happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted slightly. As the Moon drifts away, it will look too small to cover the Sun, and total solar eclipses will end.

sections.key: Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty no country can claim the Moon, but plans to mine it raise new questions.
sections.b:
Officially, nobody owns the Moon. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, joined by Australia and more than 100 other countries, says no nation can claim the Moon or any other celestial body, and that space should be used for peaceful purposes. But plans to mine lunar water ice raise a new question: can a company own what it digs up?

In 2020, Australia was one of eight founding signatories of the Artemis Accords, US-led principles that support using space resources and call for protecting historic sites such as the Apollo landing areas. Dozens more countries have since signed, while China and Russia are planning their own lunar research station instead.

quiz.q: What evidence supports the idea that a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth?
o: The Moon is made of the same material as the Sun
The Moon has a huge iron core
Moon rocks closely resemble rocks on Earth
The Moon has no craters
quiz.e: Similar rocks and a small iron core fit a Moon built from debris of Earth and the impactor.

quiz.q: Why does the Moon always show the same face to Earth?
o: It does not spin at all
Its spin matches its orbit, locked by Earth's gravity
Its far side is always in darkness
Earth's atmosphere blocks the view
quiz.e: Tidal locking slowed its spin until one rotation equals one orbit.

quiz.q: Why do most coasts have two high tides a day?
o: Waves are pushed by two steady winds each day
The Sun heats the water twice during a day
Earth rotates through two bulges raised by the Moon
Rivers fill the sea twice during each day
quiz.e: One bulge faces the Moon and another forms on the far side.

quiz.q: Why don't eclipses happen every month?
o: The Moon's orbit is tilted slightly
The Moon is too small
The Sun moves out of the way
Earth's shadow is too thin
quiz.e: The tilt means the Sun, Earth and Moon rarely line up exactly.

quiz.q: What does the 1967 Outer Space Treaty say about the Moon?
o: Whoever lands first owns it
Only the United States may use it
It belongs to the United Nations
No nation can claim it
quiz.e: The treaty bans national claims, though mining plans raise new questions.

LESSONS.push: The Moon is leaving us at about the speed your fingernails grow.

LESSONS.title: How the internet works
LESSONS.hook: What actually happens in the second between tapping a link and seeing a page.

sections.key: The internet is a global network of networks with no single owner, and it grew from ARPANET in 1969.
sections.b: The internet is a global network of networks: billions of computers, phones and servers owned by millions of organisations, linked by cables, fibre optics, radio and satellites. Nobody owns it as a whole. It grew from ARPANET, a US research network that sent its first message in October 1969. The system crashed after two letters, so the first message was 'lo'. Australia's first international internet connection came in 1989, linking the University of Melbourne to Hawaii.

sections.key: Data is split into packets, each with a destination IP address, that routers pass along by different routes.
sections.b:
When you send a photo or make a video call, the data is chopped into small packets, typically around 1,500 bytes each. Each carries addressing information, like an envelope, and travels independently, possibly by different routes. At the destination they're reassembled in order. If one goes missing, only that piece is resent. This packet switching makes the network resilient: if one route fails, packets take another.

Every device has an IP address. The older IPv4 system, with addresses like 203.0.113.42, allows about 4.3 billion combinations, which ran out as the internet grew. The newer IPv6 allows an almost unimaginable number. Routers read each packet's address and pass it on hop by hop, often across a dozen or more routers.

sections.key: DNS translates names into IP addresses, and shared protocols such as TCP/IP keep everything arriving correctly.
sections.b:
People remember names like abc.net.au, but computers need numbers. The Domain Name System, or DNS, translates names into IP addresses. Your device asks a DNS server, sometimes passing through a chain of others, and gets an answer in a fraction of a second. If DNS fails, websites seem to vanish even though they're still running, which is behind some major outages.

The internet also works because everyone follows shared rules, called protocols. Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed the two most important in the 1970s: IP handles addressing and routing, and TCP makes sure data arrives complete and in order. ARPANET adopted TCP/IP on 1 January 1983, often called the internet's birthday. HTTP and SMTP, for web pages and email, sit on top.

sections.key: About 99% of international traffic crosses the sea in fibre-optic cables, and your last-mile connection is often the slowest link.
sections.b:
It's easy to imagine data flying through space, but around 99% of international internet traffic travels through undersea fibre-optic cables. Hundreds of them cross the ocean floors, many only about as thick as a garden hose, carrying data as pulses of light. Australia's cables land in places including Sydney and Perth. Ship anchors, earthquakes and even shark bites occasionally damage them.

The link from your home to the wider network is called the last mile, and it's often the slowest part. Most Australian homes connect through the NBN by fibre, fibre and copper, cable or fixed wireless. Mobile networks use radio to nearby towers. Remote areas increasingly use low-Earth-orbit satellites, which sit much closer than older ones, reducing delay.

sections.key: The World Wide Web is one service running on the internet, alongside email, video calls and streaming.
sections.b: The internet and the web aren't the same thing. The internet is the network. The World Wide Web, proposed by Tim Berners-Lee at the physics lab CERN in 1989, is one service running on it, made of web pages linked together and viewed in a browser. Email, video calls, online games and streaming are other services using the same network. Berners-Lee chose not to patent the web, making it free for anyone to use, which helped it spread worldwide.

quiz.q: Why is the internet called a 'network of networks'?
o: It links many separately owned networks, with no single owner
One company runs a single giant network
It is made only of undersea cables
It is limited to one country's computers
quiz.e: Millions of organisations' networks are joined together, and nobody owns the whole.

quiz.q: Why does sending data as packets make the internet resilient?
o: Packets are encrypted so they can never be lost
Packets can reroute if a path fails, and only lost ones are resent
Packets always follow the same fixed path
Packets wait in storage until the network is quiet
quiz.e: Independent packets can route around damage.

quiz.q: What does DNS do when you type a web address?
o: Blocks viruses from the site
Stores a copy of the web page
Translates the name into an IP address
Chooses the fastest cable
quiz.e: Computers need numbers, so DNS turns names into addresses.

quiz.q: How does most international internet traffic travel?
o: Through satellites
Through undersea fibre-optic cables
Through radio towers
Through copper phone lines
quiz.e: Around 99% crosses the sea in cables carrying pulses of light.

quiz.q: How does the World Wide Web relate to the internet?
o: They are two names for exactly the same thing
It is one service running on the internet, like email
It is the physical network of cables and satellites
It replaced the older internet in the year 1989
quiz.e: The internet is the network; the web is one of the things that runs on it.

LESSONS.push: Nearly all international data crosses the ocean floor, not the sky.

LESSONS.title: How encryption keeps secrets
LESSONS.hook: The maths behind the padlock in your browser, and why it protects nearly everything you do online.

sections.key: Encryption uses a key to turn readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext that only the key holder can reverse.
sections.b:
Encryption turns readable information, called plaintext, into scrambled data, called ciphertext, using a key. Only someone with the right key can turn it back. It quietly protects your messages, passwords, banking, medical records and card payments. Without it, anyone who could intercept internet traffic, such as someone on the same public Wi-Fi, could read what you send.

Secret codes are ancient. Julius Caesar is said to have shifted each letter three places along the alphabet, so A became D. Such ciphers fall to frequency analysis: E is the most common letter in English, so the most common symbol probably stands for E. The Arab scholar al-Kindi described this in the 9th century.

sections.key: Breaking Germany's Enigma cipher in World War II helped the Allies and laid foundations for modern computing.
sections.b:
In World War II, Germany used the Enigma machine. Its rotating wheels scrambled each letter differently, creating an astronomical number of possible settings, and the settings changed daily.

Building on earlier work by Polish mathematicians, British codebreakers at Bletchley Park, including Alan Turing, built machines to find those daily settings. The intelligence helped the Allies win the Battle of the Atlantic and is thought to have shortened the war. The effort also helped lay the foundations for modern computing.

sections.key: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key and is fast but hard to share safely, while public-key encryption uses a public lock and a private key.
sections.b:
In symmetric encryption, the same key locks and unlocks the data. Ciphers like the widely used AES standard are fast and extremely secure, so they protect files, phones and most internet traffic. The problem is sharing the key. For centuries, keys had to be delivered physically, by couriers or in person.

In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a revolutionary idea, and in 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman created RSA. Public-key encryption uses two linked keys. Your public key can be shared with anyone to lock messages to you. Only your private key unlocks them. Think of a padlock anyone can snap shut, but only you can open.

sections.key: HTTPS uses public-key encryption to agree on a secret key, then fast symmetric encryption, but the padlock doesn't prove a site is trustworthy.
sections.b:
When you see HTTPS and a padlock, a protocol called TLS is protecting the connection. Your browser checks the site's digital certificate, issued by a trusted authority, to confirm it's the real site. The two then use public-key techniques to agree on a shared secret key, and switch to fast symmetric encryption for the rest of the session.

The padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the website is trustworthy. Scam sites can have padlocks too.

sections.key: Modern encryption rests on maths that is easy one way and extremely hard to reverse, so attackers usually target people and software instead.
sections.b:
Modern encryption relies on maths that is easy to do one way and extremely hard to reverse. Multiplying two huge prime numbers is easy for a computer. Working out which two primes made the result is enormously hard. Guessing a 256-bit key by brute force would take longer than the age of the universe.

So attackers rarely break the maths. They steal passwords, trick people or exploit software bugs. Apps like Signal, WhatsApp and iMessage use end-to-end encryption, so only sender and recipient can read messages. Future quantum computers could break some public-key systems, so new post-quantum standards were published in 2024.

quiz.q: Why can't someone on the same public Wi-Fi read your encrypted messages?
o: They don't have the key that turns the scrambled data back
Public Wi-Fi never carries any messages
Encrypted messages travel by a separate network
Scrambled data can only be read once
quiz.e: Without the right key, ciphertext is just scrambled data.

quiz.q: What did Bletchley Park's codebreaking machines have to find each day to read Enigma messages?
o: The meaning of each word
The position of each radio sender
The machine's daily settings
The names of the operators
quiz.e: Enigma's astronomical number of possible settings changed daily, so finding them was the key to reading its messages.

quiz.q: What problem did public-key encryption solve?
o: Making symmetric ciphers run faster
Sharing a secret key safely with someone far away
Storing passwords on a phone
Stopping messages being copied
quiz.e: A public key can be shared openly, so no secret key has to be delivered in advance.

quiz.q: What does the browser padlock actually tell you?
o: The website is trustworthy and legitimate
The site is free of any scam content
The site has been checked by police
Your connection to the site is encrypted
quiz.e: The padlock protects the connection, but scam sites can have one too.

quiz.q: How do attackers usually get around modern encryption?
o: Guessing every possible key one at a time
Running the prime number maths backwards
Stealing passwords, tricking people or exploiting software bugs
Waiting for the encryption key to expire
quiz.e: The maths is rarely the weak point; people and software are.

LESSONS.push: Your bank's padlock rests on a maths trick that took centuries to find.

LESSONS.title: How GPS knows where you are
LESSONS.hook: Your phone finds you to within a few metres by listening to ultra-precise clocks orbiting high above the Earth.

sections.key: GPS works by timing signals from satellites, with your phone listening only and never transmitting.
sections.b:
The Global Positioning System is run by the US and uses a constellation of around 31 satellites orbiting about 20,200 kilometres above Earth. Each one constantly broadcasts, in effect, "I'm this satellite, here's my position, and this is the exact time."

Your phone doesn't send anything back. It only listens. By measuring how long each signal took to arrive, it works out how far away each satellite is. That distance is the starting point for everything else GPS does.

sections.key: Distances to at least four satellites fix your position and correct your phone's clock error.
sections.b:
If you're exactly 20,500 km from one satellite, you could be anywhere on a giant sphere around it. A second satellite narrows that to a circle. A third narrows it to two points, one of which is usually far out in space. This process is called trilateration.

A fourth satellite is needed because your phone's clock isn't perfectly accurate. Your device usually uses many more satellites for better accuracy.

Timing matters enormously. Signals travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second, so an error of one millionth of a second would put you out by about 300 metres. That's why each satellite carries atomic clocks accurate to billionths of a second.

sections.key: The US deliberately degraded civilian GPS until May 2000, and removing that blur made positions about ten times more precise.
sections.b:
GPS began as a US military project. The first satellite launched in 1978, and the full system was declared operational in 1995. For years the military deliberately added errors to the civilian signal, a feature called Selective Availability. Ordinary receivers were accurate to only about 100 metres, while military users got precise positions.

In May 2000, on the orders of President Bill Clinton, it was switched off. Civilian accuracy improved roughly tenfold overnight, helping spark the boom in car navigation, fitness trackers and smartphone maps. The US later announced that newer satellites would be built without the ability to degrade the signal at all.

sections.key: Phones combine several satellite systems with Wi-Fi, mobile towers and downloaded data to find you quickly.
sections.b:
GPS isn't the only system. Russia runs GLONASS, the European Union runs Galileo, and China runs BeiDou. Together they're called GNSS, global navigation satellite systems. Most phones use several at once, seeing more satellites and getting faster, more accurate fixes. Australia is building SouthPAN, which improves accuracy across Australia and New Zealand for farming, mining, aviation and emergency services.

A standalone receiver can be slow to lock on, because it downloads satellite data slowly from space. Your phone downloads it over the internet and also estimates your location from mobile towers and Wi-Fi networks. That's why it can find you almost instantly, even indoors.

sections.key: GPS signals are weak and can be blocked or bounced, yet the system underpins navigation, farming, emergency services and precise timing.
sections.b:
GPS signals are weak by the time they reach Earth and can't pass through buildings or ground. In city centres they bounce off tall buildings, making your blue dot jump around; this is the urban canyon effect. Tunnels and dense forest can block them entirely. Phones are typically accurate to about five metres under open sky, while surveying and farming equipment can reach centimetre accuracy.

GPS guides planes and ships, helps emergency services find people and lets tractors drive straight lines to save fuel and fertiliser. Its timing keeps mobile networks, power grids and stock exchanges in sync. The US opened GPS to civilian use after a Korean Air Lines plane strayed into Soviet airspace and was shot down in 1983.

quiz.q: How does your phone work out its distance from a GPS satellite?
o: By sending a signal and timing the reply
By measuring how long the satellite's signal took to arrive
By reading the satellite's brightness
By asking a mobile tower to measure it
quiz.e: Satellites broadcast their position and the time, and your phone calculates distance from the signal's travel time.

quiz.q: Why does a GPS fix need a fourth satellite?
o: To work out which hemisphere you are in
To boost the signal strength
To double-check the satellite's orbit
To correct for your phone's imperfect clock
quiz.e: The fourth signal lets the receiver solve for its own clock error as well as its position.

quiz.q: What happened to civilian accuracy when Selective Availability was switched off?
o: It improved roughly tenfold
It stayed the same
It got slightly worse
It improved only for the military
quiz.e: Removing the deliberate error let ordinary receivers get far more precise positions, which fuelled consumer navigation.

quiz.q: Why can your phone usually find you almost instantly, even indoors?
o: It also uses downloaded satellite data, Wi-Fi and mobile towers
It carries its own atomic clock inside
It sends a signal up to the satellites
It remembers where you were last time
quiz.e: Phones combine satellite signals with internet data and nearby networks for fast fixes.

quiz.q: Why does your blue dot jump around in a city centre?
o: Satellites move away from cities at night
Phones switch GPS off in built-up areas
Signals bounce off tall buildings and confuse the receiver
Mobile towers jam the satellite signals
quiz.e: This is the urban canyon effect: reflected signals make the receiver misjudge distances.

LESSONS.push: Your phone never talks to a satellite, yet it knows where you are.

LESSONS.title: Blockchain, simply
LESSONS.hook: What a blockchain actually is, what it's good for, and what it isn't, without the crypto hype.

sections.key: A blockchain lets strangers agree on a shared record without a central authority in charge.
sections.b:
Normally, when you send money online, a trusted middleman such as your bank keeps the official record of who owns what. Digital files are easy to copy, so without that middleman, how would anyone stop you spending the same digital dollar twice?

A blockchain is a way for many people who don't know or trust each other to agree on a shared record, with no central authority. It's a list of records, usually transactions, that thousands of computers keep identical copies of, often called a distributed ledger. Anyone can check it, and no single person or company controls it.

sections.key: Each block holds a fingerprint of the one before it, so changing old data breaks every later link and is quickly noticed.
sections.b:
Transactions are grouped into blocks. Each block includes a hash of the block before it. A hash is a digital fingerprint: a short code calculated from the data, which changes completely if even one character changes.

Because each block holds the previous block's fingerprint, the blocks link into a chain. Change anything in an old block and its fingerprint changes, breaking every link after it. Because so many copies exist, you can't quietly rewrite history in one place, and everyone else would immediately notice.

sections.key: Networks agree on new blocks through proof of work or proof of stake, and Bitcoin and Ethereum took different paths.
sections.b:
The network needs a way to decide who adds the next block. Bitcoin uses proof of work: computers called miners compete to solve a hard mathematical puzzle, and the winner adds the block and earns new bitcoin. It's deliberately expensive, which makes cheating costly.

Ethereum switched in 2022 to proof of stake. Participants lock up their own coins as a guarantee of good behaviour and risk losing them if they cheat. That cut Ethereum's energy use by more than 99%.

Bitcoin, launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, was the first blockchain, with supply capped at 21 million coins. Ethereum, launched in 2015, added smart contracts: programs on the blockchain that carry out an agreement automatically when set conditions are met.

sections.key: Blockchains suit shared, tamper-resistant records without a trusted middleman, but can be slow, energy-hungry and irreversible.
sections.b:
Blockchains are genuinely useful when many parties need a shared, tamper-resistant record and don't want to trust one middleman: sending money across borders, tracking supply chains or proving ownership of a digital item. But many proposed uses would work as well, or better, with an ordinary database run by a trusted organisation. A good question is: why does this need a blockchain?

Removing the middleman has costs. Public blockchains can be slower and more expensive than card networks. Bitcoin's electricity use has been estimated to be comparable to that of a mid-sized country. Transactions generally can't be reversed, and if you lose your wallet's private key, there's no customer service. Your coins are gone.

sections.key: Cryptocurrency prices are highly volatile and crypto is a common vehicle for scams, so only risk money you can afford to lose.
sections.b:
Thousands of other cryptocurrencies exist. Many have collapsed, and some were outright scams. Prices are extremely volatile; a coin can lose most of its value within weeks, and money held on a crypto exchange isn't protected by the government's Financial Claims Scheme the way bank deposits are.

In 2025, AUSTRAC, Australia's financial crime regulator, limited cash transactions at crypto ATMs to $5,000 after finding they were heavily used by scam victims, many of them older Australians. Crypto is also a favoured scam payment because transfers are fast and hard to reverse.

If you choose to invest, use only money you can afford to lose, use reputable Australian-registered exchanges, and be deeply sceptical of anyone promising guaranteed returns. This is general information only.

quiz.q: What problem does a blockchain solve?
o: Making bank accounts safer from online hackers
Letting strangers agree on a shared record with no central authority
Speeding up every kind of online payment
Storing files more cheaply than any database
quiz.e: A blockchain replaces a trusted middleman with many computers holding matching copies.

quiz.q: Why is it so hard to quietly alter an old blockchain record?
o: Old blocks are locked by a government agency
Each block is stored on one secure central server
Hashes stay the same even if the data changes
Changing a block breaks the fingerprint links in every later block
quiz.e: Each block contains the previous block's hash, so tampering is quickly noticed.

quiz.q: What did Ethereum's switch to proof of stake change?
o: It capped the supply at 21 million coins
It made transactions reversible
It cut energy use by more than 99%
It replaced miners with a central bank
quiz.e: Locking up coins as a guarantee replaced the energy-hungry puzzle race of proof of work.

quiz.q: What is a sensible test for any blockchain project?
o: Check how many coins it has issued so far
Ask why it needs a blockchain rather than a database
Count how many computers are mining it
Look at how new the technology is
quiz.e: Many uses work as well with a database run by a trusted organisation.

quiz.q: Why is crypto a favoured payment method for scammers?
o: Exchanges are insured by the government
Prices stay steady so losses are small
Banks refuse to investigate crypto payments
Transfers are fast and hard to reverse
quiz.e: Once a crypto transfer is sent, getting the money back is very difficult.

LESSONS.push: Why does a database nobody owns need so much electricity to stay honest?

LESSONS.title: How AI chatbots work
LESSONS.hook: They can write essays and code, yet they sometimes invent facts with total confidence. Understanding how they work explains both.

sections.key: AI chatbots generate text by repeatedly predicting the most likely next token, based on everything before it.
sections.b:
Chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are built on large language models, or LLMs. At their core they do something that sounds simple: given some text, they predict what text is likely to come next.

They generate replies one small piece at a time, called a token, which is often part of a word. Each token is predicted from everything before it. Done extremely well, at enormous scale, this produces surprisingly capable writing, reasoning and conversation.

sections.key: Models learn patterns from vast amounts of text by tuning billions of parameters, and the transformer design made that practical.
sections.b:
A model is trained on a huge collection of text, such as books, websites and code. It repeatedly tries to predict missing or next words and adjusts itself when it's wrong, tuning billions of internal numbers called parameters. Over trillions of examples it picks up grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and writing styles. Nobody writes explicit rules; the patterns are learned from data.

Modern models use the transformer, introduced by Google researchers in a 2017 paper, 'Attention Is All You Need'. Its key idea, attention, lets the model weigh how every word relates to every other, so it can track context, like what 'it' refers to several sentences back. ChatGPT's release in November 2022 brought this technology to the public.

sections.key: After initial training, models are fine-tuned with human feedback to be helpful, honest and harmless.
sections.b:
A model trained only to predict text isn't automatically a helpful assistant. It might just continue your question with more questions.

So developers fine-tune it on examples of good conversations. They also use feedback, often from people rating different answers, to reward responses that are helpful, honest and harmless. This technique is known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, along with variations of it. It's also how developers try to reduce harmful or biased outputs.

sections.key: Models produce plausible text rather than looking up facts, so they can state falsehoods fluently and can stumble on simple tasks.
sections.b:
Because language models generate what sounds plausible, they can give confident, fluent answers that are simply wrong, including made-up facts, quotes, statistics or references. This is called hallucination. Unless connected to search tools, a model isn't looking things up in a database of facts. Newer systems hallucinate less and can cite sources, but errors still happen, especially on obscure topics, precise numbers and recent events.

Models also don't read letters as you do. Text is chopped into tokens, so 'strawberry' may arrive as a couple of chunks, which is one reason chatbots famously miscounted its r's. Newer 'reasoning' models work step by step and have improved greatly at maths and logic, but fluency in one area says little about reliability in another.

sections.key: A model's knowledge stops at its training cut-off and its context window is limited, so check answers and use it wisely.
sections.b:
A language model doesn't update its knowledge while you chat. What it knows comes from data collected up to a cut-off date, so without a search tool it may not know recent news or prices. It can also only consider a limited amount of text at once, its context window. Modern windows hold hundreds of pages, but very long chats can still lose early details. Some apps add 'memory' features, which can usually be viewed and switched off in settings.

AI also raises big questions: jobs, convincing fake images and video, energy and water use, responsibility for harm, and safety. Governments, including Australia's, are developing rules. Understanding the basics helps you use these tools wisely.

quiz.q: What is the core task of a large language model?
o: Predicting what text is likely to come next
Looking up facts in a database
Following a long list of written rules
Translating words into pictures
quiz.e: Everything a chatbot writes comes from repeated next-token prediction.

quiz.q: How does a model learn grammar, facts and writing styles?
o: By adjusting billions of parameters as it predicts text from data
By being given explicit rules by programmers
By copying answers from a stored list
By reading each user's chats and memorising them
quiz.e: Patterns are learned from examples rather than written by hand.

quiz.q: Why are models fine-tuned with human feedback after initial training?
o: To increase the amount of text they have seen
To give them access to live search
To make them helpful, honest and harmless assistants
To stop them using tokens
quiz.e: A model that only predicts text isn't automatically a helpful assistant.

quiz.q: Why can a chatbot state a false fact so confidently?
o: It deliberately tries to mislead users
It generates plausible text from patterns rather than checking facts
It copies errors from the user's question
It only repeats the last thing it read
quiz.e: Plausible-sounding is not the same as true, so important answers need checking.

quiz.q: Why might a chatbot without search get a recent news question wrong?
o: It forgets everything each second
It can't read numbers
Recent news is blocked by law
Its knowledge stops at a training cut-off date
quiz.e: A model doesn't learn while you chat; its knowledge ends at its cut-off.

LESSONS.push: A chatbot can write a flawless essay, then miscount letters in one word.

LESSONS.title: Correlation vs causation
LESSONS.hook: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together. Does ice cream kill? The most useful idea for reading any headline.

sections.key: A correlation means two things change together, which doesn't mean one causes the other.
sections.b:
A correlation means two things tend to change together. As ice-cream sales rise, so do drownings. Countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel Prizes per person. People who carry lighters get lung cancer more often. All of these correlations are real. But in none of them does the first thing cause the second.

'Correlation doesn't imply causation' is one of the most important phrases in science, and one of the most ignored in headlines and advertising.

sections.key: A hidden third factor may drive both things, or the cause may run the opposite way to what you'd assume.
sections.b:
Often a third factor, called a confounding variable, drives both things. Hot weather makes people buy ice cream and go swimming, so drownings rise. Wealthier countries eat more chocolate and also fund more research. Smoking causes people to carry lighters and causes lung cancer. Ask: is something causing both?

Sometimes the arrow points the other way. People who use walking sticks tend to be less mobile, but the sticks don't cause it; poor mobility leads people to use sticks. Do diet soft drinks cause weight gain, or are people already worried about their weight more likely to choose them? Always consider whether the effect might be the cause.

sections.key: With enough data, unrelated things line up by chance and mean nothing.
sections.b:
With enough data, some things line up by pure chance. For about a decade, the number of films Nicolas Cage appeared in each year closely tracked the number of people who drowned by falling into US swimming pools. Per capita cheese consumption tracked the number of people who died by becoming tangled in their bedsheets.

The writer Tyler Vigen collects these 'spurious correlations'. If you compare enough random things, some will match beautifully while meaning nothing.

sections.key: Observational studies can find links but struggle to prove cause, while randomised controlled trials balance hidden factors and can show it.
sections.b:
Many health headlines come from observational studies, where researchers observe what people do rather than assigning treatments. They're valuable and sometimes the only ethical option: you can't randomly assign people to smoke. But people who choose to do something differ in other ways. Good studies adjust for known confounders like age, income and smoking, but unknown ones can still mislead.

The gold standard for cause and effect is the randomised controlled trial. Participants are randomly assigned to groups, such as a new drug or a placebo. Randomisation makes the groups similar in every way, including factors nobody measured, so the treatment is the only systematic difference. Blinding, where people don't know their group, further reduces bias.

sections.key: Causation can be established without trials through strong, consistent evidence, and headlines deserve three sceptical questions.
sections.b:
Sometimes causation can be shown without trials. The link between smoking and lung cancer was proven by overwhelming evidence: it was very strong, appeared in study after study and different populations, more smoking meant more risk, quitting reduced it, smoking came first, and laboratory research showed how smoke damages cells. Epidemiologist Austin Bradford Hill set out such criteria in 1965, and they're still used.

Headlines often turn correlations into causes: 'Coffee makes you live longer!' when coffee drinkers merely lived longer. Watch for 'causes', 'boosts', 'prevents'. Ask: Was this an observational study or a randomised trial? What else could explain the link? Could the cause run the other way?

quiz.q: What does 'correlation doesn't imply causation' mean?
o: Correlations are never real
Causes can't be found through science
Two things can change together without one causing the other
Only strong correlations are meaningful
quiz.e: A real link between two things doesn't show that one produces the other.

quiz.q: Why do ice-cream sales and drownings rise together?
o: Ice cream makes swimmers tired
Hot weather drives both
Drownings make people buy ice cream
Ice-cream sellers work near pools
quiz.e: A confounding variable, hot weather, increases both buying ice cream and swimming.

quiz.q: What does the Nicolas Cage and pool drownings match show?
o: Film releases directly affect public safety
Pool drownings are easy to predict
Actors can influence official statistics
With enough data, unrelated things can line up by chance
quiz.e: Compare enough random things and some will match beautifully while meaning nothing.

quiz.q: Why can a randomised controlled trial show cause when observational studies struggle?
o: Random assignment makes groups alike, even in unmeasured ways
It always uses a much larger sample size
Participants choose their own preferred treatment
It only studies people who are already healthy
quiz.e: Because randomisation balances hidden factors, the treatment is the likely cause of any difference.

quiz.q: A headline says 'Coffee makes you live longer!' based on an observational study. What should you ask?
o: What else could explain the link, and could the cause run the other way?
How much the coffee cost per cup
Whether the study was published this year
Which cafe the participants used to visit
quiz.e: Observational studies show links, so check for confounders and reversed causes before accepting a cause.

LESSONS.push: Ice cream and drownings rise together. So what's actually going on?

LESSONS.title: Logical fallacies
LESSONS.hook: The tricks that make weak arguments sound strong. You'll hear at least three of these in the next news bulletin.

sections.key: A logical fallacy is a reasoning flaw that makes an argument seem stronger than it is, and ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument.
sections.b:
A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument seem more convincing than it is. Fallacies appear in politics, advertising, social media and family dinners. Sometimes they're deliberate manipulation; often they're honest mistakes. Naming them helps you think clearly, argue fairly and resist manipulation.

An ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument: 'Why listen to her views on the economy? She's never run a business.' Whether she has run one doesn't decide if she's right. A related trick is whataboutism, answering criticism by pointing to someone else's faults, which dodges the actual issue.

sections.key: A straw man attacks a distorted version of someone's view, and a false dilemma hides the other options.
sections.b:
A straw man misrepresents someone's position as weaker or more extreme, then knocks that version down. Someone says, 'We should reduce sugar in school canteens,' and the reply is, 'So you want to ban birthday cake!' The fairer opposite is the steel man: restating the other side's argument in its strongest form before responding.

A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist. 'You're either with us or against us.' 'Either we build this road or the town dies.' Real life usually offers a range of options and trade-offs. When someone gives you just two choices, especially when one is obviously bad, ask what has been left out.

sections.key: Chains of consequences need evidence at every link, popularity isn't proof, and authority counts only within real expertise.
sections.b:
A slippery slope claims one small step will inevitably end in disaster, without showing why each step follows. 'If students use phones for research, soon they'll be on TikTok all lesson.' Some chains are real, but each link needs evidence.

The bandwagon fallacy says something is true or good because many people believe it: 'Millions use this remedy.' Popularity isn't evidence, and plenty of widely held beliefs have been wrong.

An appeal to authority is reasonable only when the person is a genuine expert in the relevant field and reflects expert consensus. A famous actor's opinion on vaccines, or a single doctor contradicting thousands of others, isn't strong evidence.

sections.key: Circular reasoning assumes its conclusion, and hasty generalisation leaps from too few examples.
sections.b:
Circular reasoning assumes what it's trying to prove: 'This news site is trustworthy because it says it only reports the truth.' The conclusion is hidden inside the premise.

A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too little evidence: 'I got a rude driver twice, so all rideshare drivers are rude.'

Both are easy to fall into when we already believe the conclusion, which is exactly when we should check our own reasoning most carefully.

sections.key: A fallacy shows that one argument is weak, not that its conclusion is false.
sections.b:
Pointing out a fallacy doesn't prove the conclusion is false. It only shows that this particular argument for it is weak. Someone can argue badly for something true.

Assuming a claim is false because it was argued badly is itself an error, sometimes called the fallacy fallacy. And shouting 'Straw man!' in an argument rarely changes minds.

The real value of knowing fallacies is checking your own reasoning and asking better questions of others.

quiz.q: Why is 'She's never run a business, so ignore her economic views' a fallacy?
o: It gives two options only
It assumes its own conclusion
It attacks the person rather than the argument
It relies on too few examples
quiz.e: Whether someone has run a business doesn't decide whether their argument is right.

quiz.q: What is the fairer opposite of a straw man?
o: Repeating your own argument louder
Restating the other side's argument in its strongest form first
Quoting an expert who agrees with you
Pointing out the other side's past mistakes
quiz.e: A steel man engages with the best version of an argument before responding.

quiz.q: When is citing an expert a reasonable argument?
o: Fame and a large public following
A senior job title in any industry
Having many people share their opinion
Genuine expertise in the field and agreement with expert consensus
quiz.e: Authority counts only within real expertise, and one contrarian doesn't outweigh thousands of experts.

quiz.q: Why is 'I got a rude driver twice, so all rideshare drivers are rude' a fallacy?
o: It offers only two possible options
It attacks the person instead of the claim
It draws a broad conclusion from too few examples
It misrepresents the other side's view
quiz.e: A hasty generalisation leaps from too little evidence to a sweeping conclusion.

quiz.q: What does spotting a fallacy in an argument show?
o: That the conclusion must be false
That the argument is weak, not that the conclusion is false
That the speaker is deliberately lying
That the topic is not worth discussing
quiz.e: A true claim can be argued badly, so assuming it's false is the fallacy fallacy.

LESSONS.push: Spotting a bad argument doesn't prove its conclusion wrong. Why not?

LESSONS.title: How to judge a claim
LESSONS.hook: 'Scientists say…', 'A study found…'. A practical checklist for deciding what to believe.

sections.key: Evidence has a hierarchy, and small studies can produce dramatic results by chance, so the weight of evidence matters more than any single study.
sections.b:
Anecdotes, expert opinions, single studies and large reviews all count as 'evidence', but they're not equally reliable. Personal stories and opinions sit near the bottom. Above them come observational studies, then randomised controlled trials. Near the top are systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which combine many good studies. One study rarely settles a question.

Small studies can also produce dramatic results by chance. Getting 7 heads in 10 coin flips isn't unusual; 7,000 heads in 10,000 flips would be astonishing. A treatment that 'worked for 8 of 10 people' is far less convincing than one tested on thousands. Surprising small-study findings often shrink in larger studies, the decline effect.

sections.key: Without a fair comparison group you can't separate a treatment's effect from placebo or natural recovery.
sections.b:
Without a comparison group, you can't tell whether an improvement came from the treatment, the placebo effect or people simply getting better on their own.

The choice of comparison matters too. A new drug that beats a sugar pill may still be worse than the treatment doctors already use, so the most useful trials test new options against standard care. Be wary of comparisons with patients from years earlier, or with people who chose not to take part, since they may differ in many ways.

When you read about a study, ask: compared with what?

sections.key: Ask 'out of how many?', because relative risks can hide tiny absolute changes and accurate tests for rare conditions give many false alarms.
sections.b:
'Doubles your risk' sounds alarming, but if risk goes from 1 in 100,000 to 2 in 100,000, the absolute change is tiny. Headlines prefer relative numbers because they sound bigger. 'Cuts risk by 50%' might mean 2 in 1,000 falling to 1 in 1,000. Always ask: out of how many people?

Rarity also matters. Imagine a disease affecting 1 in 1,000 people and a test that's 99% accurate. Test 1,000 people: about 1 has the disease and tests positive, but about 10 of the 999 healthy people also test positive by mistake. A positive result means only about a 1 in 11 chance of having it. That's why doctors often confirm with a second test.

sections.key: Check who is making a claim and what they gain, and demand extraordinary evidence for extraordinary claims.
sections.b:
Ask who's making the claim and what they gain if you believe it. Research funded by companies with a stake isn't automatically wrong, but it's more likely to favour the sponsor, so independent confirmation matters. Be wary of claims that appear only on sites selling a product. Is the source a peer-reviewed journal, a reputable organisation like the CSIRO or a university, or a press release, blog or social post?

Astronomer Carl Sagan popularised the principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. Be alert to miracle breakthroughs, 'what they don't want you to know', testimonials instead of data, attacks on mainstream experts and pressure to buy now. Real breakthroughs are usually cautious and replicated by independent teams.

sections.key: Check the source, the type and size of study, the comparison, the absolute numbers and what experts think.
sections.b:
Next time you meet a claim, run through six questions.

What's the source, and could they be biased? What kind of evidence is it: anecdote, observational study or trial? How many people were studied? Compared with what? What are the absolute numbers? And what do most experts in the field think?

You won't always have time to check everything, but even asking two or three of these questions will make you far harder to fool.

quiz.q: Which kind of evidence is generally the most reliable?
o: A vivid personal story
A single expert's opinion
One small study with striking results
A systematic review combining many good studies
quiz.e: Combined results from many good studies carry more weight than any single study or anecdote.

quiz.q: Why does a trial need a comparison group?
o: To separate the treatment's effect from placebo and natural recovery
To make the study larger and more impressive
To stop participants dropping out early
To get the results back more quickly
quiz.e: Without a comparison, you can't tell what caused any improvement.

quiz.q: Why might someone with a positive result on a 99% accurate test for a rare disease probably not have it?
o: Among many healthy people, a small error rate gives more false positives than true ones
The test is only accurate the first time
Rare diseases can't be reliably detected
Positive results usually disappear later
quiz.e: When a condition is rare, false alarms can outnumber real cases.

quiz.q: What does 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' mean?
o: Experts should never be questioned
Surprising claims are usually correct
The more a claim overturns established science, the stronger its evidence must be
Only famous studies deserve attention
quiz.e: Miracle cures and secret knowledge need a very high bar of proof.

quiz.q: Which question belongs on a quick checklist for judging a claim?
o: How many times has it been shared?
Compared with what, and out of how many people?
How confident does the author sound?
Is the headline written in capitals?
quiz.e: Checking the comparison and the absolute numbers makes you much harder to fool.

LESSONS.push: A test is 99% accurate and you test positive. Why are you probably fine?

LESSONS.title: Probability for everyday life
LESSONS.hook: Why the pokies always win, why a streak of heads means nothing, and how to think clearly about risk.

sections.key: Independent events have no memory, so a streak never makes the opposite result 'due'.
sections.b:
Probability measures how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A 50% chance is 0.5; a 1 in 4 chance is 0.25. A 70% chance of rain means that on days with similar conditions, it rained about 70% of the time.

A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. What are the odds of heads next? Still 50%. The coin has no memory. Believing tails is now 'due' is the gambler's fallacy. In 1913 at the Monte Carlo casino, a roulette ball landed on black 26 times in a row, and gamblers lost millions betting that red must come next. The same applies to lotto numbers, poker machine spins and the sex of a family's next baby.

sections.key: Gambling has negative expected value, and jackpot odds are far longer than our brains can picture.
sections.b:
Expected value is the average result if you repeated something many times. If a game costs $1 and gives a 1 in 10 chance of winning $5, you'd spend $10 to win $5 about once: an expected loss of 50 cents a play. Casino games, poker machines and lotteries are designed this way. NSW poker machines must return at least 85% of money wagered over time, so players lose around 15% on average.

The odds of winning division one in Australia's Powerball are about 1 in 134 million. Buying one game a week, you'd expect to wait around 2.5 million years. A ticket is entertainment, not a financial plan.

sections.key: Surprising coincidences are likely when there are many chances for them to happen.
sections.b:
How many people need to be in a room for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday? Just 23. With 70 people, it's over 99%.

The birthday paradox surprises us because we think about our own birthday matching someone's, rather than any pair matching. With so many possible pairs, coincidences become likely.

In a country of 27 million people, a 'one in a million' event happens to around 27 people. Unlikely things happen all the time. They just don't happen to any particular person often.
