Other Japanese scientists later found inosinate in dried bonito and guanylate in dried shiitake. Combined with glutamate, these nucleotides multiply umami rather than adding to it. Japanese dashi pairs kombu with bonito. Western cooks pair tomatoes or parmesan with meat.

sections.key: Dedicated taste receptors confirmed umami as the fifth basic taste, probably a signal for protein.
sections.b:
For decades many Western scientists doubted that umami was a separate taste. They argued it was a blend of other tastes, or an effect of smell. The debate shifted in the early 2000s, when researchers identified taste receptors on the tongue that respond specifically to glutamate, giving umami a clear biological basis. Today it is widely accepted as the fifth basic taste, alongside sweet, sour, salty and bitter.

Why would we evolve to detect it? A common explanation is that umami signals protein. Glutamate is released when protein-rich foods are cooked or aged, so a taste that rewards it steers us towards nourishing food. Sweetness signals energy from sugars, bitterness may warn of toxins, and sourness of unripe or spoiled food.

sections.key: A 1968 letter started decades of fear about MSG, but the evidence does not support it.
sections.b:
For its first half-century MSG drew few complaints. In 1968 a doctor wrote to a prominent medical journal describing numbness and palpitations after eating at Chinese restaurants in the United States, wondering whether cooking wine, sodium or MSG was to blame. The term 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' spread through newspapers, and restaurants posted 'no MSG' signs. Many now see the panic as tinged with prejudice, since parmesan, tomatoes and stock were rarely blamed.

Since the 1970s, many studies, including double-blind trials, have generally failed to find consistent reactions at normal food amounts. Food Standards Australia New Zealand considers MSG safe for the general population. In Australia it appears on labels by name or as flavour enhancer 621, and 'no added MSG' products may still contain natural glutamate. This is general information, so speak with a doctor about any concerns.

sections.key: A little umami adds depth and can even help cut the salt in a dish.
sections.b:
Today MSG is mostly made by fermentation. Bacteria feed on sugars from crops such as sugarcane, corn or cassava and produce glutamate, which is purified and crystallised. It looks like fine white salt, tastes mild on its own, and lifts soups, stir-fries, stews and dressings. MSG has roughly a third as much sodium as table salt, so swapping some salt for a little MSG can reduce sodium without losing flavour.

You do not need the crystals to cook with umami. A splash of soy or fish sauce, a spoonful of tomato paste, a grating of parmesan, a few dried mushrooms or a dab of Vegemite in gravy all deepen flavour in the same way.

quiz.q: What did Kikunae Ikeda's discovery show about savoury taste?
o: It is just a blend of salty and sweet
It is a distinct taste linked to glutamate
It comes only from seaweed
It is an effect of smell alone
quiz.e: Ikeda isolated glutamic acid from kombu and named its savoury taste umami, separate from the four known tastes.

quiz.q: Why does dashi, made with kombu and bonito flakes, taste so strongly savoury?
o: The two ingredients cancel out any bitterness
Bonito flakes contain added MSG
Boiling releases sugar from the seaweed
Glutamate and inosinate multiply each other's umami
quiz.e: Nucleotides such as inosinate multiply glutamate's umami effect rather than simply adding to it.

quiz.q: Why might humans have evolved to detect umami?
o: It signals protein-rich food
It warns of spoiled food
It signals sugary food
It marks foods high in salt
quiz.e: Glutamate is released when protein-rich foods are cooked or aged, so umami may steer us towards nourishing food.

quiz.q: What does the evidence say about MSG at normal food amounts?
o: Studies show it causes serious harm
Double-blind trials found no consistent reactions
It is banned in Australia
Natural glutamate is safe but MSG is not
quiz.e: Trials have generally failed to find consistent reactions, and Food Standards Australia New Zealand considers MSG safe.

quiz.q: How can a cook add savoury depth while cutting salt?
o: Use more salt and less umami
Add a lot of sugar to mask saltiness
Swap some salt for MSG, with a third of the sodium
Boil the dish for much longer
quiz.e: MSG has roughly a third of table salt's sodium, so a small swap can lower sodium without losing flavour.

LESSONS.push: A chemist tasted his soup in 1908 and found a taste nobody had named.

LESSONS.title: Why chillies burn: the science of heat
LESSONS.hook: Chilli heat is not a taste at all. It is a clever chemical trick that fools your pain sensors, and the story of how it conquered the world's kitchens is just as surprising.

sections.key: Chillies are American plants that spread around the globe within a century of Columbus's voyages.
sections.b: Thai, Indian, Sichuan and Korean food all learned to use chillies only in the last five centuries. Chillies belong to the genus Capsicum, originated in the Americas and were domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago. After Columbus's voyages, Spanish and especially Portuguese traders carried them around the world. Unlike many crops, they were easy to grow from seed, thrived in warm climates and offered a cheap, intense flavour. Within about a century they grew in India, Africa and South-East Asia, where local cooks made them their own, often replacing or supplementing black pepper.

sections.key: Capsaicin triggers the nerve receptor that detects painful heat, so chilli burns without any actual heat.
sections.b:
The burn comes mainly from capsaicinoids, chiefly capsaicin. Taste buds do not detect it. Instead it binds to TRPV1, a protein on pain-sensing nerve endings. TRPV1 normally detects dangerous heat, switching on above roughly 43 degrees Celsius. Capsaicin flips the same switch, so your brain concludes your mouth is burning though the temperature has not changed. That is why chilli can make you sweat and flush. Work on how such receptors sense temperature and pain earned David Julius a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

In 1912 pharmacist Wilbur Scoville measured heat by diluting extract until tasters felt none. Labs now measure capsaicinoids directly and convert to Scoville units. A bell pepper scores zero, a jalapeno a few thousand, and the hottest bred varieties exceed two million.

sections.key: Capsaicin deters mammals but not seed-spreading birds, and we enjoy the burn as a safe thrill.
sections.b:
Why would a plant make something that burns? One explanation is directed deterrence. Mammals chewing chillies crush the seeds, while birds swallow them whole and spread them in droppings. Birds' TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin, so they eat the hottest chillies in comfort. Capsaicin may also protect fruit from fungi: wild chillies in wetter parts of Bolivia, where fungal attack is more common, tend to be hotter. Scientists still debate how much each factor matters.

Humans are among very few animals that seek out the burn. Psychologist Paul Rozin calls it benign masochism, like enjoying a roller coaster while your brain knows you are safe. Endorphins may add pleasure, though how much is uncertain. Tolerance builds, since repeated exposure makes nerve endings less responsive for a while.

sections.key: Most capsaicin sits in the pale ribs, not the seeds, and it dissolves in fat rather than water.
sections.b:
Many people think the seeds are the hottest part. In fact capsaicin is made mostly in the pale, spongy ribs, or placenta, that hold the seeds. Seeds taste hot because they press against it. Removing the ribs and seeds tames a chilli considerably.

Capsaicin is oily. It dissolves poorly in water but well in fats and alcohol, so gulping water mostly spreads it around. Dairy such as milk and yoghurt helps, probably because its fat and a protein called casein help carry capsaicin away. Starchy foods like rice or bread can also give some relief by mopping up the oil. Handle very hot chillies with gloves, avoid touching your eyes, and take extreme chilli challenges cautiously. Capsaicin is also the active ingredient in some pain-relief creams and in pepper spray.

sections.key: Pepper, wasabi and Sichuan pepper each trigger different sensations from chilli's burn.
sections.b:
Not every pungent spice works like chilli. Black pepper gets its bite from piperine, which also activates TRPV1 and a related receptor, though more mildly. Wasabi, horseradish and mustard rely on isothiocyanates, which are volatile, so the heat rushes up the nose and fades quickly. They activate a different receptor, TRPA1, which also responds to irritants such as the fumes from cut onions.

Sichuan pepper, from the dried husks of a prickly ash shrub unrelated to chillies or black pepper, does something stranger. A compound called hydroxy-alpha-sanshool produces a tingling, buzzing numbness that researchers have compared to a mild vibration on the lips. Sichuan cooking pairs this numbing sensation with chilli heat in mala, meaning 'numbing and spicy'.

quiz.q: Why did chillies spread so quickly after 1492?
o: They grew easily from seed, thrived in warmth and tasted intense
They were rare and kept as royal luxuries in Europe
They could only be grown in cool regions
They were used as a replacement for sugar
quiz.e: Chillies grew easily from seed in warm climates and offered a cheap, intense flavour, so cooks everywhere adopted them.

quiz.q: How does capsaicin make your mouth feel hot?
o: It raises the temperature of the tongue
It switches on TRPV1, the receptor that detects painful heat
It destroys the sweet taste buds
It dissolves the lining of the mouth
quiz.e: Capsaicin flips the same TRPV1 switch as real heat, so the brain gets a burning message though nothing is hotter.

quiz.q: Why can birds eat very hot chillies without discomfort?
o: They have no taste buds
They only eat the seeds
Their stomach acid destroys capsaicin instantly
Their version of TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin
quiz.e: Birds' TRPV1 does not respond to capsaicin, so they eat chillies and spread the seeds intact.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to ease a burning mouth after chilli?
o: Drink a large glass of cold water
Eat more chilli
Drink milk or eat yoghurt
Rinse with fruit juice
quiz.e: Capsaicin dissolves in fat, so dairy's fat and casein help carry it away, while water mostly spreads it around.

quiz.q: How does the heat of wasabi differ from chilli's?
o: It lingers longer on the tongue
Volatile compounds rush up the nose and fade quickly
It comes from the same compound as chilli
It numbs the lips instead of burning
quiz.e: Wasabi's isothiocyanates are volatile and activate TRPA1, so the heat hits the nose and fades fast.

LESSONS.push: Chilli heat isn't a taste at all. Your mouth is being tricked.

LESSONS.title: Uluru and Kata Tjuta: the rocks at the heart of Australia
LESSONS.hook: A single rock rising out of a flat red plain looks like it was dropped from the sky. The real story involves vanished mountains, half a billion years and a culture that has known this place for tens of thousands of years.

sections.key: Uluru is a huge, isolated sandstone monolith whose red colour is only a thin coat of rust.
sections.b:
Stand on the plain at sunset and Uluru seems to catch fire, shifting from ochre to orange to deep red, then purple. It rises about 348 metres, higher than the Eiffel Tower, in the south of the Northern Territory, about 450 kilometres by road from Alice Springs. It is striking because the land around is almost flat, covered in red sand, spinifex and desert oaks. The base walk is roughly ten kilometres and takes most people about three hours.

The red is only a thin skin. Inside, the rock is dull grey. Its iron-bearing minerals oxidise in air and rain, so the surface has rusted. The low sun at dawn and dusk scatters away blue light, leaving warm reds. After rare heavy rain, Uluru turns silvery and waterfalls pour down its gullies.

sections.key: Uluru is sandstone made from long-vanished mountains, then tilted almost upright by movements of the Earth's crust.
sections.b:
More than 500 million years ago, a mountain range in central Australia was being worn down. Rivers dumped the debris in great fans of sand and gravel, which a shallow sea buried. The weight pressed the grains into solid rock. The coarse sand became Uluru's sandstone, rich in feldspar.

The faint parallel lines up Uluru's sides are the original sand layers, which should lie flat. Hundreds of millions of years ago, movements of the crust squeezed central Australia and tilted Uluru's layers by close to 90 degrees. Erosion then stripped away the softer rock around the tougher stone. Geologists think much of Uluru continues underground, so what we see may be only a fraction of the whole.

sections.key: Kata Tjuta is made of the same ancient mountains as Uluru, but it is taller and broken into many domes.
sections.b:
Kata Tjuta, once called the Olgas, lies about 30 kilometres west of Uluru. The pebbles and boulders from the same ancient mountains became its conglomerate, so the two are siblings, sorted by the rivers into different sizes of stone. Many visitors are surprised that it is taller: its highest dome rises around 546 metres above the plain.

Kata Tjuta means 'many heads' in the local language, and there are 36 rounded domes separated by deep valleys and narrow gorges. Conglomerate, a jumble of pebbles and boulders cemented together, weathers differently from sandstone, which is why it has broken into many separate shapes. The Valley of the Winds walk winds between the domes, where the temperature drops and sounds echo strangely.

sections.key: For Anangu, Uluru and Kata Tjuta are living places of law, family and responsibility, shaped by ancestral beings.
sections.b: Long before any geologist arrived, the Anangu knew this country intimately. Anangu are the Traditional Owners, and Aboriginal people have lived in central Australia for many tens of thousands of years. For Anangu, the landscape is explained through Tjukurpa, a body of law, knowledge and story that describes how ancestral beings travelled across the land and created its features. Marks, caves and waterholes around Uluru are linked to these stories and to rules for living. Some places are sacred and are not to be photographed or visited by outsiders, which is why certain parts of the base walk carry signs asking visitors to respect them. To Anangu, Uluru is not a scenic backdrop.

sections.key: Ownership returned to Anangu in 1985, and the climb closed in 2019 after years of discussion.
sections.b: In 1873 the explorer William Gosse saw the rock and named it Ayers Rock after Sir Henry Ayers, a South Australian politician. For about a century tourism grew, and many visitors climbed a steep route up one side, despite Anangu asking people not to. On 26 October 1985 ownership of the national park was formally handed back to Anangu, who leased it to the federal government for joint management. The park is World Heritage listed for both natural and cultural values, and the Anangu name Uluru now comes first in official use. After years of discussion, the park board decided to end the climb, and it closed permanently on 26 October 2019, exactly 34 years after the handback.

quiz.q: What gives Uluru its red colour?
o: Red algae growing on the surface
A thin coating of oxidised iron, essentially rust
Red sand permanently glued on
Rock that is red all the way through
quiz.e: The inside is grey; only the surface has rusted to red.

quiz.q: Why do the faint lines on Uluru's sides run almost vertically?
o: Wind carved them that way
Rain cut grooves down the rock
Earth movements tilted the original layers by close to 90 degrees
Ancient people carved them
quiz.e: The sand layers were once flat but were tipped nearly upright by movements of the crust.

quiz.q: How are Uluru and Kata Tjuta related?
o: Both are sandstone formed in the same river
Same ancient mountains, different sizes of stone
Kata Tjuta is a broken-off piece of Uluru
They formed in unrelated eras and places
quiz.e: Rivers sorted the debris of the same mountains into sand for Uluru and pebbles and boulders for Kata Tjuta.

quiz.q: What is Tjukurpa for the Anangu?
o: Law, knowledge and story explaining how ancestral beings shaped the land
The name for the red sand of the desert plains
A ceremony held only at sunset each day
The name given to the walk around the base
quiz.e: Tjukurpa links the landscape to law and story, which is why Uluru is a place of law, family and responsibility.

quiz.q: Why did the climb on Uluru close in 2019?
o: The rock became too weathered to climb safely
The park board chose to end it after years of discussion
A rockfall permanently blocked the route
The Northern Territory banned all tourism
quiz.e: Anangu had long asked visitors not to climb, and the board closed the climb permanently on 26 October 2019.

LESSONS.push: Uluru is red on the outside only. Find out what's underneath.

LESSONS.title: Lightning: how storms make electricity
LESSONS.hook: Somewhere on Earth, lightning strikes dozens of times every second. Here is how a cloud builds up enough electricity to light the sky, why thunder follows, and how to stay safe.

sections.key: A lightning bolt heats a narrow channel of air to several times the Sun's surface temperature, and it strikes constantly.
sections.b: In an instant, a channel of air only a few centimetres wide is heated to roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius, about five times hotter than the visible surface of the Sun. Satellites suggest 40 to 50 flashes every second worldwide, over a billion a year. Most are over tropical land, where warm, moist air rises fastest. Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, where lake air meets cool mountain winds, is one of the most lightning-rich spots on Earth. Central Africa's Congo basin is another, and Australia's tropical north has spectacular storms before the wet season, with Darwin famous for its evening light shows. Lightning also helps life: its heat joins nitrogen and oxygen into compounds that rain carries into soil for plants to use.

sections.key: Collisions between ice particles in a storm cloud separate electric charge, much like a giant battery.
sections.b: A thunderstorm is a giant vertical engine. Warm, humid air rushes upward, cools and condenses into droplets, and near the top they freeze. Inside, powerful updrafts throw around tiny ice crystals, supercooled water and soft ice pellets called graupel. When crystals and graupel collide, electric charge is transferred. The lighter crystals, generally positive, are swept to the top, while the heavier graupel, usually negative, gathers lower down. The cloud becomes a giant battery, with opposite charges separated by kilometres of air. Air is a good insulator, so charge keeps building until the insulation finally breaks down. Exactly how a flash begins is still an active area of research.

sections.key: A faint leader reaches down, a brilliant return stroke races up, and the heated air's shock wave is thunder.
sections.b:
Most lightning never reaches the ground. When a bolt does, it begins with a faint, branching channel of charged air, the stepped leader, zigzagging down. Near the ground, tall objects send up streamers. When they meet, the circuit is complete and the return stroke, the blinding flash we see, surges up into the cloud. Several strokes often follow the same channel, making lightning flicker.

Thunder is the sonic boom. The channel heats so fast that the air expands explosively, sending out a shock wave. Distant thunder rumbles because sound from a long, twisting channel arrives at different times and echoes. Sound travels about a third of a kilometre per second, so count the seconds from flash to thunder and divide by three for the distance in kilometres.

sections.key: Lightning can strike the same place twice, and a car protects you because of its metal body, not its tyres.
sections.b: Several popular beliefs about lightning are wrong. It does strike the same place twice. Tall buildings are hit again and again, and the Empire State Building is struck many times every year. Rubber tyres do not make a car safe. A hard-topped car protects you because its metal body carries the current around the outside and into the ground, keeping the people inside out of its path. Lying flat on the ground is poor advice, because current can spread across the surface. Sheltering under a lone tree is one of the worst choices of all: the tree is a likely target, and the current can jump sideways to anyone standing beneath it.

sections.key: If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck, so go inside and stay there.
sections.b: The simplest rule is 'when thunder roars, go indoors'. If you can hear thunder, the storm is close enough for lightning to reach you, because strikes can land many kilometres from the main storm. The safest places are solid buildings with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped vehicle with the windows up. Inside, avoid corded phones, running water and touching plugged-in appliances, since current can travel through wiring and pipes. Experts generally suggest waiting around 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back outside. This is general information, not personal advice. In severe weather, check Bureau of Meteorology warnings and follow your state emergency service's instructions.

quiz.q: Where is lightning most common?
o: Over polar ice caps
Over tropical land, where warm air rises
Over cold oceans in winter
Over dry deserts with little moisture
quiz.e: Warm, moist air rises fastest over tropical land, so storms and flashes are most frequent there.

quiz.q: What separates electric charge inside a storm cloud?
o: Wind rubbing against the cloud
Sunlight heating the cloud top
Electricity rising from the ground
Ice crystals colliding with soft ice pellets (graupel)
quiz.e: Collisions between ice particles transfer charge, and updrafts separate the light and heavy particles.

quiz.q: You count 9 seconds between a flash and its thunder. Roughly how far away is the strike?
o: 9 kilometres
3 kilometres
27 kilometres
1 kilometre
quiz.e: Sound travels about a third of a kilometre per second, so divide the seconds by three.

quiz.q: Why is a hard-topped car fairly safe in a lightning storm?
o: The rubber tyres insulate it from the ground
Lightning cannot hit moving objects
The metal body carries current around the outside to the ground
Cars are too low to be struck
quiz.e: It is the metal shell, not the tyres, that steers current around the occupants.

quiz.q: When should you head indoors in a storm?
o: Only once rain begins to fall
As soon as you hear thunder
When lightning is directly overhead
Once the wind picks up
quiz.e: If you can hear thunder, lightning can reach you, so go inside and wait about 30 minutes after the last rumble.

LESSONS.push: A lightning bolt is hotter than the Sun's surface. Here's how a cloud makes one.

LESSONS.title: Rainforests: Earth's richest places
LESSONS.hook: Rainforests cover only a small slice of the planet's land, yet they are home to a huge share of its living things. Australia has some of the oldest on Earth.

sections.key: A rainforest is a wet forest with a closed canopy, built in layers like a tall apartment building.
sections.b:
In the Daintree in far north Queensland, sunlight drips through layer after layer of leaves, and everything grows on something else. A rainforest is a forest with heavy, reliable rainfall and a closed canopy, where the treetops join to shade the ground. Tropical rainforests grow near the equator. Temperate ones grow in cool, wet places such as Tasmania and New Zealand. Together they cover a small fraction of the Earth's land, yet hold a large share of its species.

Think of a tall apartment building. Emergent giants poke above the canopy, the leafy roof where most life lives. Below sit the dim understorey and a forest floor that gets only a few per cent of the sunlight.

sections.key: Many tropical rainforests grow on thin soil because nearly all their nutrients are stored in living plants.
sections.b:
You might expect lush forests to need deep, rich soil. Often the opposite is true. In many tropical rainforests, constant heat and rain break down fallen leaves within weeks, and heavy downpours wash nutrients out of the ground. The forest survives by recycling at speed. Fungi and roots spread through the leaf litter and grab nutrients almost as soon as they are released, so most of the forest's wealth sits in living plants, not the soil.

That is why clearing rainforest for farming can disappoint. Once the trees are cut and burned, the land may grow good crops for a few years before the thin soil is exhausted. A forest that took centuries to build is very hard to bring back.

sections.key: Rainforests release water into the air and store carbon, so clearing them can change rainfall and add to climate change.
sections.b:
Rainforests do not just receive rain. They help make it. Trees draw water from the soil and release it as vapour through tiny pores in their leaves, a process called transpiration. Moist air rising from the canopy forms clouds that drop rain further inland, where the water is drawn up and released again. Scientists call these moving streams of moisture 'flying rivers'. Research suggests much of the Amazon's rainfall is recycled this way. If too much forest is cleared, parts of the system could dry out and struggle to sustain rainforest at all.

Rainforests also hold vast amounts of carbon in trunks, roots and soil. Clearing and burning them releases carbon dioxide and adds to climate change.

sections.key: Some Australian rainforests are remnants of the forests that covered the supercontinent Gondwana.
sections.b:
Australia is famous for deserts, but it also holds some of the oldest rainforests on Earth. The Wet Tropics of Queensland, including the Daintree, were World Heritage listed in 1988, partly for their exceptional record of plant evolution. Many early flowering plant families still grow there.

Further south, the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia stretch across parts of New South Wales and southern Queensland. They are remnants of forests that once covered the supercontinent Gondwana, which joined Australia, Antarctica, South America, Africa and India. As Australia drifted north and dried out over millions of years, rainforest retreated to moist pockets along the east coast and the ranges, where it survives like a living museum.

sections.key: Rainforest plants depend on animals such as the cassowary, and protecting the forest protects foods and medicines too.
sections.b:
In Queensland, one of the key gardeners is a bird taller than many people. The southern cassowary swallows fallen fruit whole, including fruits too large for any other native animal, and deposits the seeds in dung, often far from the parent tree. Some plants appear to rely heavily on it. Fig trees need tiny wasps to pollinate their hidden flowers, and fruit bats carry seeds and pollen at night. Every species is tangled up with others.

The forests matter to people too. Coffee, cocoa, bananas and vanilla have origins in tropical forests, and some medicines come from rainforest plants. The macadamia comes from rainforests of south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales. Large areas are still cleared each year, mostly for farming and grazing, but protection works when enforced.

quiz.q: Which part of a tropical rainforest is the dense leafy roof where much of the forest's life is concentrated?
o: The forest floor
The understorey
The canopy
The emergent layer
quiz.e: The canopy is the dense roof of leaves and branches that shelters birds, insects, possums and many plants.

quiz.q: Why are many tropical rainforest soils surprisingly poor?
o: The trees release chemicals that poison the soil
Nutrients are recycled quickly into living plants and washed out by rain
It is too cold for fallen leaves to decompose
Rainforests grow mainly on bare rock and gravel
quiz.e: The forest stores most of its nutrients in living plants, so the soil beneath holds little.

quiz.q: What is transpiration?
o: Plants releasing water vapour through pores in their leaves
Rain washing nutrients out of the soil
Fallen leaves breaking down into soil
Trees falling and opening gaps in the canopy
quiz.e: Transpiration returns water to the air, feeding the clouds that bring rain further inland.

quiz.q: Why are the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia scientifically important?
o: They are remnants of forests that once covered an ancient supercontinent
They are the largest rainforests left on Earth
They grew back after the last ice age ended
They are planted forests restored in the 1900s
quiz.e: As Australia drifted north and dried, rainforest survived only in moist pockets, preserving ancient plant families.

quiz.q: Why is the southern cassowary important to Queensland's rainforest?
o: It eats harmful insects that attack trees
It spreads the seeds of large fruits through its dung
It pollinates the hidden flowers of fig trees
It digs up the soil to release nutrients
quiz.e: Cassowaries carry seeds far from parent trees, including fruits no other native animal can swallow.

LESSONS.push: Rainforests help make their own rain, yet often grow on poor soil. How?

LESSONS.title: How beaches and coastlines are made
LESSONS.hook: A beach looks permanent, but it is really a river of sand that never stops moving. Here is how waves build, shift and carve Australia's coastlines.

sections.key: A beach is a temporary store of sand that waves, tides, currents and wind constantly rearrange.
sections.b:
Picture your favourite beach on a calm summer morning, then again after a big winter storm, with the sand stripped back to a steep scarp and rocks exposed. Both are the same beach. Coastlines are among the most active landscapes on Earth, reshaped daily by waves, tides, currents and wind. Sand that seems solid underfoot is in transit. It arrives from rivers and cliffs, is pushed along the shore, and is sometimes lost offshore or blown inland.

Most waves start as wind blowing over the sea, often far away. Wave size depends on wind strength, how long it blows and the open water it crosses, called the fetch. Southern Ocean storms send long, powerful swells to Australia's southern and western coasts.

sections.key: Beach sand is worn-down rock, mostly quartz on many Australian beaches, sometimes mixed with shell.
sections.b:
Scoop up a handful of sand and you hold a sample of the land behind it. On many Australian beaches the grains are mostly quartz, a hard mineral that survives long after softer minerals have been ground away. Rivers carry it down from eroding mountains, and waves sort it by size.

Other beaches tell different stories. Some tropical beaches are made largely of broken shell and coral, pale and crunchy underfoot. Black sand forms where waves wear down dark volcanic rock. Whitehaven Beach in the Whitsundays is famously white and fine because the sand is extremely pure silica. Heavy minerals can collect in darker streaks, and some Australian beaches have been mined for minerals such as rutile and zircon.

sections.key: Waves arriving at an angle move sand along the coast in a process called longshore drift.
sections.b:
Waves rarely hit a beach dead straight. They usually arrive at a slight angle and push sand up the beach on a slant, while the backwash drags it straight back down the slope. Each wave moves grains a little further along the shore, and over months and years enormous volumes of sand travel along the coast. This is longshore drift.

On much of Australia's east coast the overall drift runs northward, from New South Wales towards Queensland. Where that river of sand meets a headland or a change in the coast, it can pile up into sand spits and huge dune systems. K'gari, formerly Fraser Island, is widely described as the largest sand island in the world, built in part from sand delivered this way.

sections.key: Waves carve rocky headlands into caves, then arches, then stacks.
sections.b:
On rocky coasts, waves act like a slow chisel. They pound weaknesses such as cracks and softer layers, and hurl sand and pebbles against the rock. A crack becomes a sea cave. If caves form on both sides of a narrow headland, they may meet to make an arch. Eventually the arch roof falls, leaving a pillar of rock called a stack, which is slowly worn down to a stump.

Victoria's Twelve Apostles, limestone stacks along the Great Ocean Road, are a famous example. Nearby, London Bridge was a double arch until its inner span collapsed in 1990, leaving two startled tourists stranded on the outer section until a helicopter rescued them.

Beaches also change with the seasons. Big winter storms drag sand offshore into bars, and gentler summer swells push it back.

sections.key: Rips are the everyday hazard, so swim between the flags; and building too close to a moving shore invites erosion.
sections.b:
The biggest everyday hazard on Australian beaches is not sharks but rip currents. Water pushed up the beach often flows back through a channel between sandbars, forming a narrow, fast current away from shore. Rips can look deceptively calm: a darker, flatter gap in the breaking waves. The safest choice is to swim between the red and yellow flags at a patrolled beach. If caught, stay calm, float, raise an arm for help, and swim parallel to shore if you can. Surf Life Saving Australia has detailed guidance.

Problems also arise when we build too close to the moving edge. Storms in 1974 and 2016 badly eroded Collaroy and Narrabeen in Sydney. Seawalls can starve neighbouring beaches of sand, and rising seas are expected to push shorelines inland. Healthy dunes act as a natural sand bank.

quiz.q: What does the 'fetch' of a wave refer to?
o: The height of the wave when it breaks
The distance of open water the wind blows across
The speed of the incoming tide
The angle at which a wave meets the beach
quiz.e: Wave size depends on wind strength, how long it blows and the fetch, or the open water it crosses.

quiz.q: Which mineral makes up most of the sand on many Australian beaches?
o: Salt
Quartz
Gold
Coal
quiz.e: Quartz is hard enough to survive long after softer minerals have been ground away.

quiz.q: What is longshore drift?
o: Sand blown inland by strong winds
A narrow current that flows out to sea
The movement of sand along the coast by waves arriving at an angle
The tide covering and uncovering the beach
quiz.e: Waves push grains up the beach on a slant and the backwash pulls them straight down, so sand creeps along the shore.

quiz.q: In what order do waves usually erode a rocky headland?
o: Stack, arch, cave, stump
Arch, cave, stump, stack
Stump, stack, arch, cave
Cave, arch, stack, stump
quiz.e: A crack becomes a cave, then an arch, then a stack that is finally worn to a stump.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to avoid rip currents at the beach?
o: Swim where the water looks flattest
Swim beside rocks
Swim at dawn
Swim between the red and yellow flags
quiz.e: Patrolled flagged areas are chosen by lifesavers to be the safest place to swim, because rips can look calm.

LESSONS.push: A beach looks permanent. Why is it really a river of sand that never stops moving?

LESSONS.title: Tropical cyclones: anatomy of a monster storm
LESSONS.hook: Cyclones, hurricanes and typhoons are the same storm with different names. Learn how warm oceans power them, why they spin, and what Cyclone Tracy taught Australia.

sections.key: Cyclone Tracy destroyed most of Darwin and led to much stronger building codes in cyclone regions.
sections.b:
On Christmas Eve 1974, Darwin went to bed expecting a stormy night. Cyclone Tracy was small, but in the early hours of Christmas Day it struck with ferocious winds. By morning most of the city's homes were destroyed or badly damaged, and around 66 to 71 people had been killed, according to commonly cited figures. Most of the population was evacuated in the following days, one of the largest peacetime airlifts in Australian history.

Tracy was a turning point. Investigations found that many houses had simply come apart in the wind, and building codes in cyclone-prone regions were strengthened dramatically. Northern Australian homes are now built to hold together under forces that once would have torn them apart.

sections.key: Cyclones, hurricanes and typhoons are the same kind of storm; the name depends on where it forms.
sections.b:
A storm is called a hurricane, a typhoon or a cyclone depending on where it forms, not what it is. In the North Atlantic and north-east Pacific it is a hurricane. In the north-west Pacific, near Japan and the Philippines, it is a typhoon. In the Indian Ocean and around Australia it is a tropical cyclone.

All are rotating storm systems that form over warm tropical seas, with a calm centre and spiralling bands of thunderstorms. In Australia the Bureau of Meteorology names cyclones from a rotating list. When a storm is especially deadly or destructive, its name is retired, which is why there will never be another Cyclone Tracy.

sections.key: Cyclones run on heat from seas above about 26 degrees, and Earth's rotation makes them spin clockwise in the south.
sections.b:
A tropical cyclone is a heat engine fuelled by the ocean. It needs sea surface temperatures of roughly 26 to 27 degrees Celsius or more, through a fairly deep layer of water. Warm water evaporates, the moist air rises and cools, and the vapour condenses into cloud and rain. Condensation releases heat, which makes the air rise faster and draws in more moist air. This feedback loop organises thunderstorms into a cyclone. Over land or cooler water the storm is cut off from its fuel and weakens, though its rain can still cause severe flooding.

Earth's rotation deflects air flowing towards the low-pressure centre, to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. So Australian cyclones spin clockwise. Near the equator the effect is almost zero, so cyclones rarely form there.

sections.key: A cyclone has a calm eye surrounded by the eyewall, where the strongest winds and heaviest rain are found.
sections.b:
From a satellite, a mature cyclone is a vast pinwheel of cloud, often several hundred kilometres across. At its centre is the eye, typically a few tens of kilometres wide, where air sinks, skies may be clear and winds are light. People caught as the eye passes sometimes think the storm is over, only for the winds to return suddenly from the opposite direction.

Around the eye is the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms where the most violent winds and heaviest rain are concentrated. Beyond that, spiral rainbands bring bursts of squalls. Australia rates cyclones from category 1 to 5 by their strongest wind gusts. Category 5 storms can produce gusts well over 280 kilometres per hour.

sections.key: Storm surge and flooding often kill more people than wind, so follow official warnings.
sections.b:
Wind grabs the headlines, but water is often the greatest danger. As a cyclone nears land, its winds pile seawater against the coast, and the low pressure lets the sea bulge upward. This storm surge can push the ocean far inland, especially at high tide over low-lying land. Some of the deadliest cyclones in history, including disasters in Bangladesh and Myanmar, killed most of their victims through surge. Heavy rain is the other hazard, and flooding can continue for days as the storm's remains drift inland.

Climate change is a nuanced story. Cyclone numbers in the Australian region have declined somewhat, but warmer oceans are expected to make a larger share intense, and rising seas lift surges higher.

This is general information: in a cyclone area, follow Bureau of Meteorology warnings and emergency service instructions, including evacuation orders.

quiz.q: What did investigations after Cyclone Tracy find, and what changed as a result?
o: Many houses had come apart in the wind, so building codes were strengthened
Most damage came from flooding, so homes were raised on stilts
The warnings were ignored, so evacuation became compulsory
The storm was unusually large, so Darwin was relocated
quiz.e: Tracy showed how poorly houses held together, leading to far tougher building codes in cyclone regions.

quiz.q: What is a tropical cyclone called in the north-west Pacific, near Japan?
o: A hurricane
A typhoon
A tornado
A monsoon
quiz.e: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same kind of storm; the name depends on the ocean where it forms.

quiz.q: Why do cyclones weaken quickly after crossing the coast?
o: They are cut off from the warm ocean water that fuels them
Mountains on the coast break up the eye
The air over land is far too humid
The Coriolis effect stops them from spinning
quiz.e: Warm seas are the fuel supply, so a cyclone over land or cooler water loses its energy.

quiz.q: Where are the strongest winds in a cyclone found?
o: In the eye
In the eyewall
At the outer edge of the rainbands
Far ahead of the storm
quiz.e: The eyewall is a ring of towering thunderstorms around the calm eye.

quiz.q: What is a storm surge?
o: A sudden burst of hail and lightning
A cyclone that moves unusually fast
A rise in sea level pushed onto the coast by the storm
Lightning inside the cyclone's eyewall
quiz.e: Winds and low pressure raise the sea against the coast, and surge is often more deadly than wind.

LESSONS.push: Cyclone, hurricane, typhoon: one storm, three names, and a reason it spins as it does.

LESSONS.title: Glaciers: rivers of ice
LESSONS.hook: Glaciers look frozen in place, but they flow, grind and carve like slow-motion rivers. They shaped many of the world's most beautiful landscapes, including some in Tasmania.

sections.key: A glacier is a large mass of ice that flows downhill under its own weight.
sections.b:
Stand beside a glacier in New Zealand or Alaska and you will hear it creak, groan and sometimes crack like a gunshot, because it is moving. A glacier is a large body of ice that forms on land and flows downhill or outward under its own weight. Most move perhaps tens of centimetres to a few metres a day, though some outlet glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica race along at many kilometres a year.

Glaciers and ice sheets together hold most of the planet's fresh water, around two thirds by common estimates. Glaciers exist on every continent except mainland Australia, from tropical peaks in South America and Africa to the polar regions.

sections.key: Buried snow is squeezed into dense ice, which creeps downhill by deforming and by sliding on its bed.
sections.b:
Every glacier begins as snow. Where more falls in winter than melts in summer, it builds up year after year. As new layers pile on, older snow is compressed into rounded grains called firn. Over years to centuries the firn is squeezed until the air spaces close off as tiny bubbles and it becomes solid glacier ice. Thick ice absorbs red light, which is why deep crevasses glow blue, and the trapped bubbles preserve samples of ancient air.

Under enough pressure, solid ice behaves a little like stiff toffee. Its crystals slowly deform and slide past one another, and many glaciers also slide on meltwater at their base. The brittle surface cracks into crevasses, which can be tens of metres deep and hidden under snow bridges.

sections.key: Glaciers carve broad U-shaped valleys, bowl-shaped cirques, sharp peaks and fjords.
sections.b:
As a glacier moves, it plucks rocks from its bed and drags them along like sandpaper. A river usually cuts a narrow V-shaped valley, but a glacier widens and deepens it into a broad U with steep walls. At the head of a glacier, ice gouges a bowl-shaped hollow called a cirque, which often holds a lake after the ice melts. Where several cirques eat into a mountain from different sides, they leave a sharp pyramid peak, as with the Matterhorn in the Alps.

When glaciers carve valleys below sea level and the ice later retreats, the sea floods in, creating fjords like those of Norway and Fiordland in New Zealand.

sections.key: Moraines and erratic boulders reveal where ice once lay, and rock flour turns glacial lakes turquoise.
sections.b:
Glaciers are messy. Everything they carry, from fine rock flour to boulders the size of houses, is dumped where the ice melts. Ridges of this debris are called moraines, and they mark the sides and furthest reach of old glaciers. Huge lone boulders sitting far from any matching rock are glacial erratics. In the 1800s, scientists such as Louis Agassiz used clues like these to argue that much of Europe had once been buried under ice, an idea that was startling at the time.

Meltwater is milky with fine rock flour, which is why glacier-fed lakes often glow turquoise, as at Lake Tekapo in New Zealand and Lake Louise in Canada.

sections.key: Tasmania's landscapes were carved by ice, and most of the world's glaciers are now shrinking.
sections.b:
Mainland Australia has no glaciers today, and saw only small ones in the Snowy Mountains during the last ice age. Tasmania tells a different story. Ice caps and glaciers once covered parts of the Central Highlands and West Coast ranges. Dove Lake, beneath Cradle Mountain, sits in a basin carved by ice, and Lake St Clair, Australia's deepest freshwater lake, was also shaped by glaciers. Heard Island, an Australian territory in the Southern Ocean, still has active glaciers.

Worldwide, most mountain glaciers are losing ice, linked to rising temperatures. Their meltwater feeds rivers that supply many millions of people, and shrinking glaciers may mean lower summer flows. Melting ice also adds to sea level rise. In 2019 Iceland held a memorial for Okjokull, a glacier that had lost so much ice it was no longer considered one.

quiz.q: What makes a glacier move?
o: Its own weight, which makes the ice flow downhill
Tides pulling on the ice
Wind pushing it along the valley
Meltwater carrying it like a river
quiz.e: A glacier is a mass of ice heavy enough to flow under its own weight.

quiz.q: What is firn?
o: A deep crack in the surface of the ice
Compressed, granular snow that becomes glacier ice
A lake that forms below a glacier
A floating iceberg that broke off
quiz.e: Buried snow is squeezed into firn, then into dense ice as the air spaces close off.

quiz.q: What shape of valley does a glacier typically carve?
o: V-shaped
W-shaped
Flat and shallow
U-shaped
quiz.e: Rivers cut narrow V-shaped valleys, but glaciers widen and deepen them into broad U shapes.

quiz.q: What is a glacial erratic?
o: A glacier that moves unusually fast
A turquoise lake fed by meltwater
A boulder dropped by ice far from its source
A type of crevasse hidden by snow
quiz.e: Lone boulders far from matching rock are clues that ice once carried them there.

quiz.q: Why is the Tasmanian high country dotted with cirques, moraines and small lakes?
o: Glaciers carved it during the last ice age
Volcanoes shaped it
Ancient seas left them behind
Glaciers still cover it today
quiz.e: Ice caps and glaciers once covered parts of Tasmania, leaving features such as the basin of Dove Lake.

LESSONS.push: Solid ice flows like a river and carved Tasmania. How does something frozen move?

LESSONS.title: Caves: the hidden world beneath our feet
LESSONS.hook: Under quiet paddocks and plains lie vast cave systems, sculpted drop by drop over hundreds of thousands of years. Here is how rain dissolves rock, and what caves preserve.

sections.key: Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, opening up caves over hundreds of thousands of years.
sections.b:
Drive across the Nullarbor Plain and you see almost nothing: a flat, treeless expanse. The name comes from the Latin for 'no tree'. Yet beneath it lies one of the largest areas of limestone on Earth, riddled with caves, some holding long underground lakes explored by divers. Such landscapes are called karst, after a limestone region in Slovenia.

Most caves are made by dissolving rock. Rain absorbs a little carbon dioxide from the air, and much more as it soaks through soil full of decaying plants. This forms a weak carbonic acid, the same acid that fizzes in soft drinks. It slowly dissolves limestone, widening cracks over tens to hundreds of thousands of years into passages and chambers. When the water table drops, air fills the passages.

sections.key: Cave formations grow as dripping water leaves behind tiny amounts of calcite.
sections.b:
Once a cave fills with air, a new kind of sculpture begins. Water dripping from the ceiling carries dissolved limestone. When it reaches the cave air, it releases some of its carbon dioxide, and a tiny amount of the mineral calcite is left behind. Drip by drip, a thin hollow straw forms, which can thicken into an icicle-like stalactite hanging from the roof. Where drops land, calcite builds upward into a stalagmite. A memory aid: stalactites hold 'tight' to the ceiling, while stalagmites 'might' reach up one day. When the two meet they form a column.

Growth is usually a fraction of a millimetre a year, so touching formations is discouraged because skin oils can stop them growing.

sections.key: Jenolan, Naracoorte and the Undara lava tubes show how varied and valuable Australian caves are.
sections.b:
Australia's best-known show caves are the Jenolan Caves in New South Wales, where visitors have explored lit chambers since the 1800s. Scientific dating suggests the caves are very old, possibly hundreds of millions of years, making them among the oldest known open caves in the world.

In South Australia, the Naracoorte Caves act as natural traps. For hundreds of thousands of years animals fell through openings in the ground and could not climb out, leaving a remarkable fossil record that includes Australia's extinct megafauna. With Riversleigh in Queensland, Naracoorte was World Heritage listed in 1994. In north Queensland, the Undara lava tubes are a different kind of cave, formed by flowing lava rather than water.

sections.key: When a cave roof collapses a sinkhole opens, and some caves are among the largest spaces on Earth.
sections.b:
As caves grow, their roofs can thin and collapse, opening a hole called a sinkhole or doline. Some form slowly as the ground sags. Others appear suddenly, swallowing roads, cars and occasionally buildings. Mount Gambier in South Australia is famous for its water-filled sinkholes, including the Umpherston Sinkhole's sunken garden. On Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, sinkholes called cenotes open into water-filled caves. The ancient Maya relied on them for fresh water, and some were sacred places for offerings. Divers explore flooded passages linking them that stretch for hundreds of kilometres.

Caves also set records. Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known system, with more than 600 kilometres of mapped passages. Vietnam's Son Doong is so vast that parts of its main passage could hold city buildings, and a jungle grows where the roof has collapsed.

sections.key: Cave animals often lose eyes and colour, and cave formations preserve records of past climates.
sections.b:
Deep caves are dark, damp and short of food, yet life has moved in. Over many generations, many cave animals have lost their eyes and pigment, since neither helps in total darkness, and developed long antennae or legs and sharp senses of touch and smell. The olm, a pale salamander from the caves of south-eastern Europe, can live for many decades and survive for years without eating. Australia has its own hidden cave fauna, including blind fish and shrimp in the underground waters of Cape Range in Western Australia.

Caves also preserve climate records in their formations, helping scientists read the past. Many remain unexplored, and volunteers are still finding new passages around the world, including in Australia. They are fragile places worth protecting.

quiz.q: Which acid is mainly responsible for dissolving limestone to form caves?
o: Sulfuric acid
Hydrochloric acid
Carbonic acid
Citric acid
quiz.e: Rain that absorbs carbon dioxide becomes weakly acidic and slowly dissolves limestone.

quiz.q: Which cave formation grows upward from the cave floor?
o: Stalagmite
Stalactite
Straw
Cenote
quiz.e: Stalagmites build up where drops land, while stalactites hang from the ceiling.

quiz.q: Why are the Naracoorte Caves so valuable to scientists?
o: They hold the world's longest underground river system
They trapped animals for ages, preserving a rich fossil record
They were formed by flowing lava, not water
They contain the world's largest known stalactite
quiz.e: Animals fell in and could not escape, leaving a record that includes Australia's extinct megafauna.

quiz.q: What are cenotes?
o: Caves formed by volcanic activity
Caves formed inside glaciers
Water-filled sinkholes, famously in Mexico's Yucatan
Sea caves cut by crashing waves
quiz.e: When a cave roof collapses it can expose water below, as with cenotes that the Maya used for fresh water.

quiz.q: Why have many cave animals lost their eyes and colour?
o: Eyes and pigment are useless in total darkness
Cave water slowly bleaches their bodies
They lose them to hide from predators
They are simply born without them by accident
quiz.e: Over generations, features that do no good in the dark are lost while other senses sharpen.

LESSONS.push: Under the empty Nullarbor lies a hidden world that rain carved. How does water eat stone?

LESSONS.title: Jet streams: the rivers of wind above us
LESSONS.hook: High above the clouds, narrow bands of wind race around the planet at hundreds of kilometres an hour. They steer our weather, speed up flights and once carried balloon bombs across an ocean.

sections.key: Jet streams are narrow, fast bands of high-altitude wind that mostly blow west to east and speed up eastbound flights.
sections.b:
Every so often a long-haul flight lands well ahead of schedule, and the pilot mentions a strong tailwind. That boost comes from a jet stream, a narrow, fast-flowing band of air high in the atmosphere. Jet streams usually sit about 9 to 16 kilometres up, near the top of the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere. Core winds commonly exceed 100 kilometres per hour, and strong winter jets can pass 300.

They mostly blow from west to east. That is why flights heading east across the Pacific or North Atlantic are often noticeably quicker than the return trip, and why airlines plan routes each day to ride the jet one way and avoid it the other.

sections.key: A Japanese meteorologist measured the jet stream in the 1920s, and Japan later used it to send balloon bombs across the Pacific.
sections.b:
In the 1920s the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi released weather balloons near Mount Fuji and tracked them as they rose. He found remarkably strong westerly winds high above Japan. He published largely in Esperanto, and his work attracted little attention outside Japan.

In the Second World War, American B-29 bomber crews flying high over Japan met fierce headwinds that slowed them almost to a crawl, and the jet stream became widely known. Japan had already used Oishi's findings. From late 1944 it launched thousands of hydrogen balloons carrying bombs, designed to ride the jet stream across the Pacific to North America. Most failed or landed harmlessly, but one killed six people on a picnic in Oregon in 1945.

sections.key: Temperature contrasts and Earth's spin create jet streams, which meander in Rossby waves that steer our weather.
sections.b:
Jet streams are born from temperature differences. The tropics receive far more heat than the poles, so the atmosphere keeps trying to move heat poleward. Where warm air sits beside cold, the contrast creates a steep pressure difference at altitude, and air flows. Earth's rotation deflects that flow into a mostly west-to-east path. The sharper the contrast, the faster the wind. Each hemisphere generally has a polar front jet and a higher, subtropical jet closer to the tropics.

A jet rarely runs straight. It snakes around the globe in meanders thousands of kilometres long, called Rossby waves after the meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby. Where the jet bulges poleward, warm air follows. Where it dips towards the equator, cold air follows. The jet tends to steer storms along its path, so forecasters watch it closely.

sections.key: A stalled jet can lock weather in place, and Australian winter rain depends on the jet and the westerlies.
sections.b:
Usually the jet's waves travel steadily east, carrying weather systems with them. Sometimes the pattern stalls. A large high can wedge in place and force the jet to loop around it, called a blocking pattern. The same weather can then sit over a region for days or weeks: one area bakes in a heatwave while another floods. In Australia, a related feature is the cut-off low, a pocket of cold air that breaks away and lingers, sometimes bringing very heavy rain to the south-east.

The subtropical jet often crosses Australia in winter, carrying moisture from the Indian Ocean in long northwest cloud bands that can bring valuable rain inland. Further south, the polar front jet sits over the westerlies sailors called the Roaring Forties. In winter this belt shifts north, sending cold fronts and rain to Perth, Adelaide and Melbourne.

sections.key: Jet streams cause clear-air turbulence that radar cannot see, and how climate change affects them is still debated.
sections.b:
Jet streams are a headache as well as a help for aviation. Where fast air shears past slower air, it can create clear-air turbulence. These invisible bumps do not show on weather radar because there is no cloud. Pilots rely on forecasts and reports from other aircraft to avoid the worst patches, which is one reason it is sensible to keep your seatbelt fastened while seated.

Scientists are also studying how a warming climate affects the jets. Some research suggests clear-air turbulence over the North Atlantic has increased in recent decades. Other researchers have argued that rapid Arctic warming could make the northern jet wavier and more prone to blocking, but this idea is still debated and the evidence remains mixed.

quiz.q: Why is an eastbound flight across the Pacific often quicker than the return trip?
o: It rides a jet stream that mostly blows from west to east
The Earth spins faster at higher altitudes
Airlines fly lower on eastbound routes
Aircraft engines work better in one direction
quiz.e: Jet streams blow mostly west to east, so eastbound flights gain a tailwind and westbound flights avoid it.

quiz.q: How did Japan use the jet stream in the Second World War?
o: It launched balloon bombs to drift towards North America
It sped up its navy with high-altitude winds
It scattered leaflets over Australia
It forecast typhoons for its fleet
quiz.e: Japan used the strong westerly winds to carry hydrogen balloons across the Pacific.

quiz.q: What mainly drives the formation of jet streams?
o: Strong ocean tides near the coast
Earthquakes deep in the ocean floor
Temperature contrasts between air masses, plus the Earth's rotation
The Moon's gravity pulling on the air
quiz.e: Temperature differences create pressure differences, and Earth's rotation turns the flow west to east.

quiz.q: What is a blocking pattern?
o: A storm that blocks out the Sun for days
A wall of dust moving over a continent
A stalled pattern that holds the same weather in place
Mountains physically stopping the wind
quiz.e: When a high wedges in place and the jet loops around it, heatwaves or floods can persist.

quiz.q: Why can clear-air turbulence be hard for pilots to avoid?
o: It only happens at night over the oceans
It occurs only close to busy airports
It cannot be seen on radar because there is no cloud
It is caused by wake from other aircraft
quiz.e: Without cloud there is nothing for radar to detect, so pilots rely on forecasts and reports from other aircraft.

LESSONS.push: A Japanese scientist found a river of wind in the sky, and a war put it to use.

LESSONS.title: The Spanish Armada, 1588
LESSONS.hook: The most powerful empire on Earth sent a giant fleet to conquer England. Fireships, bad maps and brutal storms decided what happened next.

sections.key: The Armada grew from a religious and political feud between Catholic Spain and Protestant England.
sections.b:
Picture two rulers who had once been in-laws. Philip II of Spain had been married to Mary I of England, Elizabeth I's older half-sister. After Mary died, Elizabeth steered England firmly towards Protestantism, while Philip saw himself as the champion of Catholic Europe. The quarrel deepened for decades. English privateers such as Francis Drake raided Spanish treasure ships and colonies, and Elizabeth sent soldiers to help Dutch Protestants rebelling against Spanish rule.

The breaking point came in 1587, when Elizabeth allowed the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, the Catholic cousin many hoped would replace her. To Philip, invading England now looked like a matter of faith, security and honour all at once.

sections.key: The Armada was meant to escort an invasion army across the Channel, not conquer England alone.
sections.b:
The Armada that sailed in 1588 numbered around 130 ships, carrying sailors, soldiers, priests, horses and enormous supplies. Its commander, the Duke of Medina Sidonia, was a wealthy nobleman with little experience at sea who had reportedly tried to decline the job. The fleet could not conquer England by itself. Its task was to sail up the English Channel, link up with the Duke of Parma's veteran army in the Spanish Netherlands, and protect the barges carrying those troops to Kent.

The flaw was plain in hindsight. No deep-water port existed where the big ships and Parma's barges could safely meet, and messages between the two dukes moved slowly. Coordinating them under enemy fire would prove almost impossible.

sections.key: The English could not break the Armada's formation until fireships scattered it off Calais.
sections.b:
In late July 1588 the Armada was sighted off Cornwall and beacons flared along the coast. It moved up the Channel in a disciplined crescent, with strong warships guarding the supply vessels at the centre. The English, led by Lord Howard of Effingham with Drake as a senior captain, had faster ships and longer-range guns. Spanish tactics relied on boarding, so the English kept their distance. The Armada stayed largely intact and anchored off Calais.

On the night of 7 to 8 August, by the modern calendar, the English sent eight burning ships, packed with tar and pitch, drifting towards the anchored fleet. Many Spanish captains cut their cables and scattered. At Gravelines the English attacked closer, wrecking or capturing several ships and pushing the rest away from Parma.

sections.key: Storms, hunger and disease on the voyage around Scotland and Ireland cost Spain more than English guns did.
sections.b:
With the wind from the south and the English behind them, the Spanish could not return down the Channel. Medina Sidonia sailed north around Scotland and down the west coast of Ireland, a huge detour through unfamiliar, stormy waters. The ships were battered and short of water and food, and their charts of those coasts were poor. Autumn gales drove many onto the rocks of Ireland and Scotland. Thousands of men drowned, and many who reached shore were killed or captured.

Historians think roughly a third or more of the fleet never made it back to Spain, and a far larger share of the men died. Most of those losses came from weather, disease and hunger rather than from battle.

sections.key: The Armada did not end Spanish power, but it became a founding story of English defiance.
sections.b:
While the danger was still real, Elizabeth travelled to Tilbury on the Thames to review her troops. Accounts record her saying she had the body of a weak and feeble woman, but the heart and stomach of a king. Historians debate her exact words, because the best-known version was written down years later. English propaganda presented the victory as God's favour and called the storms a Protestant wind.

The reality was messier. The war dragged on until 1604. An English counter-attack in 1589 failed badly, and Philip's later armadas in the 1590s were scattered by storms. Spain stayed dominant in Europe for decades. Yet the failure kept Protestant England independent, encouraged the Dutch revolt and gave English sailors confidence. Its biggest legacy was a story of plucky defiance, retold in 1805, 1940 and beyond.

quiz.q: What finally pushed Philip II to treat an invasion of England as a matter of faith, security and honour?
o: The death of Mary I
Elizabeth allowing the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots
The founding of an English colony in Virginia
Drake's voyage around the world
quiz.e: Years of raids and rebellion culminated in the 1587 execution of the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots.

quiz.q: What was the Armada's main job?
o: To blockade London and starve it into surrender
To capture Ireland as a base for attack
To escort the Duke of Parma's army across the Channel to England
To seize the English treasure fleet at sea
quiz.e: The fleet was meant to protect the barges carrying Parma's troops, not to conquer England alone.

quiz.q: What broke up the Armada's formation off Calais?
o: A sudden fog
A mutiny on the flagship
A night attack with fireships
Cannon fire from the French shore
quiz.e: Burning ships drifting into the anchored fleet terrified Spanish captains, who cut their cables and scattered.

quiz.q: What caused most of the Armada's losses?
o: Storms, shipwrecks, hunger and disease on the way home
English boarding parties in close combat
Dutch privateers attacking stragglers
A plague outbreak in the Spanish ports
quiz.e: The detour around Scotland and Ireland in autumn gales killed far more men than battle did.

quiz.q: What happened after 1588?
o: Spain surrendered and signed peace immediately
England invaded and conquered Spain in 1589
The war continued until 1604, and Spain remained a dominant power
Spain never built another large fleet
quiz.e: The Armada's defeat did not end Spanish power; the myth of a decisive victory is simpler than the reality.

LESSONS.push: The mightiest fleet in Europe was beaten, but not mainly by English guns. By what?

LESSONS.title: The Great Fire of London
LESSONS.hook: In September 1666 a small fire in a bakery grew into a firestorm that swallowed a medieval city. What rose from the ashes still shapes London today.

sections.key: A small bakery fire in 1666 spread because London's timber houses, narrow lanes and warehouses were perfect fuel.
sections.b:
Sometime after midnight on Sunday 2 September 1666, a fire started in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane, near London Bridge. Farriner insisted he had put out his oven, but the house was soon ablaze. The Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bludworth, reportedly decided the blaze was not worth demolishing neighbouring houses for. It was a costly misjudgement.

London was still largely medieval. Houses were timber and plaster, with overhanging upper storeys that almost touched across narrow streets. Rubbish, hay and firewood lay everywhere. Firefighting meant leather buckets, axes, hand pumps and hooks for pulling buildings down, with no organised brigade. The summer had been dry and a strong east wind was blowing. When the fire reached warehouses on the Thames full of oil, tallow, coal and brandy, it grew too hot to approach.

sections.key: The fire raged until Wednesday and was stopped by firebreaks, and diaries preserve vivid human details.
sections.b:
For about four days the fire swept west and north. People fled with what they could carry, piling belongings into carts and boats. St Paul's Cathedral, covered in wooden scaffolding for repairs, caught fire, and its lead roof reportedly ran down the streets. King Charles II and his brother James, Duke of York, helped create firebreaks by pulling down or blowing up houses. When the wind eased on Tuesday night, the firebreaks held, and the fire was under control by Wednesday and Thursday.

We know much of this from Samuel Pepys and John Evelyn. Pepys watched from a boat, noting pigeons that hovered around their homes until their wings caught fire. He also buried his wine and parmesan cheese in his garden. Evelyn described the ground so hot it was hard to walk on.

sections.key: The fire destroyed most of the old city, and fear led to scapegoating.
sections.b:
About 13,000 houses were destroyed, along with 87 parish churches, St Paul's Cathedral, the Guildhall and many other public buildings. Tens of thousands of people were homeless, camping in the fields north of the city. Only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, but historians think the true number was higher, since the poor, or anyone consumed by intense heat, may never have been counted.

People wanted someone to blame. Foreigners and Catholics were attacked in the streets. A French watchmaker named Robert Hubert confessed to starting the fire and was hanged, even though evidence later suggested he had not been in London when it began. Fear ran high: London had lost perhaps a fifth of its people to the Great Plague of 1665. An inquiry eventually concluded the fire was an accident.

sections.key: London was rebuilt on its old street pattern, but with brick and stone and new safety rules.
sections.b:
Within days, Christopher Wren and John Evelyn presented plans for a new London with wide boulevards and open piazzas. None was adopted. Property owners wanted their land back quickly, and sorting out who owned what was hard enough already. The city was rebuilt largely along its old street pattern, with important changes. New laws required buildings of brick or stone, set limits on heights and widened some streets.

Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral with its famous dome, which took decades to complete, and dozens of new city churches. A special Fire Court settled disputes between landlords and tenants so rebuilding could get moving.

sections.key: The fire left a monument, helped launch fire insurance and shaped modern fire safety.
sections.b:
Near Pudding Lane stands the Monument, a stone column designed by Wren and Robert Hooke. It is 202 feet, roughly 61 metres, high, and stands about 202 feet from where the bakery was. The fire also helped launch modern property insurance: in the following years businesses began offering cover against fire, and some ran their own teams of firefighters to protect insured buildings.

A popular story says the fire ended the plague by burning the rats, but historians doubt it. The plague was already declining and also faded in areas the fire never touched. What is certain is that the disaster changed how cities thought about fire safety, building materials and planning, lessons that later shaped building codes around the world, including in Australia.

quiz.q: Why did flames spread so easily between London's houses?
o: The houses were timber, with upper storeys that nearly touched across narrow lanes
Most houses had thatched roofs and stone walls
The streets were paved with wooden blocks and tar
Gas lamps exploded along the main streets
quiz.e: Timber buildings, close-packed lanes and a strong wind let the fire leap from one side of a street to the other.

quiz.q: How was the fire finally brought under control?
o: Heavy rain fell on the city for two days
Houses were pulled down or blown up as firebreaks, and the wind eased
The Thames was diverted into the burning streets
A trained fire brigade pumped water from the river
quiz.e: Demolishing buildings created gaps the flames could not cross once the wind dropped.

quiz.q: Why was Robert Hubert's confession doubtful?
o: Evidence suggested he was not in London when it began
He later recanted his confession before a jury
He was a trained baker with no clear motive
The fire had actually begun on a different street
quiz.e: Fear led to scapegoating, and an inquiry later concluded the fire was an accident.

quiz.q: What did new building rules require after the fire?
o: Wooden houses with fire buckets
Thatched roofs soaked in water
Houses no taller than one storey
Buildings made of brick or stone
quiz.e: London was rebuilt largely on its old street plan, but with brick and stone and limits on heights.

quiz.q: Why do historians doubt that the fire ended the plague?
o: The plague was already declining and also faded in areas the fire never reached
The fire spread the plague even further
The plague had already ended years before 1666
Records show the fire killed all the rats in London
quiz.e: A tidy story is not good evidence; the plague faded in places the fire never touched.

LESSONS.push: A single oven started it. Why was a medieval city so ready to burn in 1666?

LESSONS.title: The East India Company: a business that ruled
LESSONS.hook: It began as a group of London merchants chasing pepper. Within two centuries it had its own army and ruled millions of people across India.

sections.key: The East India Company began in 1600 as a monopoly trading venture and turned to Indian textiles after losing the spice islands.
sections.b:
On the last day of 1600, Elizabeth I granted a charter to a group of London merchants, giving them the sole English right to trade with Asia. Their target was spices, especially pepper. The Company was an early joint stock venture: investors pooled money to fund risky voyages and shared the returns. The richer, more aggressive Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, soon pushed the English out of the most lucrative spice islands in what is now Indonesia.

So the English turned to India, where they found something more valuable than pepper: cotton textiles. Indian calicoes and chintzes became a fashion craze at home. Its fortified trading posts, called factories, grew into Madras (now Chennai), Bombay (Mumbai) and Calcutta (Kolkata). At first it depended on the favour of the Mughal Empire.

sections.key: In 1757 Robert Clive won Bengal for the Company largely through intrigue, because key commanders had already switched sides.
sections.b:
As Mughal power weakened in the 1700s, the Company began to use soldiers and money to play politics. Bengal was among India's richest provinces. In 1756 its young ruler, the Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah, captured Calcutta after the Company strengthened its fortifications without permission. Robert Clive, an ambitious and ruthless Company officer, sailed north to retake it.

He found allies among Bengal's elite who wanted the Nawab gone, including his army commander Mir Jafar. At the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Clive's much smaller force faced the Nawab's army, but much of it never fought because its commanders had already agreed to switch sides. Siraj ud-Daulah was later killed and Mir Jafar installed as a puppet ruler. Huge sums flowed to the Company and to Clive personally.

sections.key: In 1765 the right to collect Bengal's taxes turned the Company from a trader into a government.
sections.b:
The real turning point came in 1765. The weakened Mughal emperor granted the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa: the right to collect land revenue across a vast, populous region. Instead of bringing silver from Britain to buy Indian goods, the Company could now use Indian taxes to pay for them, and for its growing army.

Poorly supervised officials often grew rich through private trade and bribes, earning the nickname 'nabobs' back in Britain. In 1770 a devastating famine struck Bengal. Millions died, possibly as much as a third of the population in the worst areas, and critics accused the Company of making things worse by keeping up harsh tax collection while people starved.

sections.key: Britain's Parliament stepped in as the Company's power and debts became a national problem.
sections.b:
By the early 1770s the Company was both mighty and in financial trouble, and Parliament grew alarmed that a private business was running an empire. The Regulating Act of 1773 began bringing it under government oversight, and later laws created a government board to supervise its political decisions. The 1773 Tea Act, meant to help the Company sell surplus tea in America, led to the Boston Tea Party. Warren Hastings, the first Governor General of Bengal, was impeached in a seven-year trial and acquitted, but it showed British unease.

Meanwhile the Company fought wars against Mysore and the Marathas. Most of its soldiers were Indian sepoys led by British officers, and its armies reached hundreds of thousands, larger than Britain's own. It also grew opium for smuggling into China, to pay for Chinese tea.

sections.key: After the 1857 uprising the British Crown took direct control, and the Company was dissolved.
sections.b:
In 1857 a mutiny by sepoys at Meerut spread into a widespread rebellion across northern India, fuelled by grievances from annexations and taxes to fears of religious interference. The fighting was brutal on both sides, and the British response was savage. Afterwards, Parliament decided the Company could no longer be trusted with India. In 1858 the Crown took direct control, beginning the period known as the Raj, and the Company was formally dissolved in 1874.

By the 1850s it ruled much of the subcontinent directly or through treaties with princely states, with its trading monopolies stripped away. Its legacy is debated. It left cities, railways planned in its final years and words such as 'loot', borrowed from Hindi. It also warns of a profit-seeking corporation holding unchecked political and military power.

quiz.q: Why did the East India Company shift its focus to India?
o: The Dutch pushed it out of the most lucrative spice islands, and Indian textiles proved valuable
Spices had stopped selling in Europe by 1610
The Mughal emperor ordered it to relocate
The charter forbade any trade in Indonesia
quiz.e: After losing the spice trade to the Dutch, the Company found cotton textiles were more valuable than pepper.

quiz.q: How did Robert Clive win at Plassey in 1757?
o: With a much larger and better-armed army
Using new rifles that the Nawab lacked
Because key commanders in the Nawab's army had switched sides
By a sea bombardment of the fort alone
quiz.e: Plassey was won more through intrigue than fighting, since much of the Nawab's army never fought.

quiz.q: What was the diwani the Company gained in 1765?
o: The right to collect land revenue in Bengal and nearby regions
A monopoly on all Indian cotton exports
Ownership of the port of Bombay
A permanent seat at the Mughal court
quiz.e: Collecting taxes turned a trading company into a government with its own revenue.

quiz.q: Which American event was linked to the Company's troubles?
o: The Salem witch trials
The Louisiana Purchase
The Boston Tea Party
The California gold rush
quiz.e: The 1773 Tea Act tried to help the struggling Company sell surplus tea in the colonies and led to the Boston Tea Party.

quiz.q: What happened to India after the 1857 rebellion?
o: It became independent
France took control
The Mughal Empire was restored
The British Crown took direct control
quiz.e: Parliament decided the Company could not be trusted, and the Crown began the Raj in 1858.

LESSONS.push: A pepper-trading firm ended up with its own army. How does a business come to rule?

LESSONS.title: Meiji Japan: the great makeover
LESSONS.hook: In about forty years, Japan went from a closed realm of samurai and shoguns to an industrial power that defeated a European empire. How did it happen so fast?
