They are always fixed rate loans
The government subsidises their interest
quiz.e: Security lowers the lender's risk, but it means you could lose the asset if you default.

quiz.q: What is a balloon payment?
o: A monthly account fee
A refund at the end of the loan
A large lump sum due at the end of the loan
A penalty for paying early
quiz.e: Balloons shrink repayments but raise total interest, and the lump sum still has to be found later.

quiz.q: What is a smart step before accepting car yard finance?
o: Agree to all add-ons
Sign the same day to lock in the deal
Focus only on the weekly repayment
Get your own quote or pre-approval to compare
quiz.e: A benchmark from your own bank lets you judge whether the dealer's offer is actually good.

quiz.q: Under responsible lending laws, what must licensed lenders do?
o: Approve every application that meets a minimum
Make reasonable inquiries and not offer unsuitable loans
Offer the lowest rate available in the market
Avoid looking at your credit report
quiz.e: Lenders must check your income, expenses and needs, which is why truthful applications protect you.

LESSONS.push: A cheap-looking loan can cost more than a dearer one. The advertised rate hides why.

LESSONS.title: Getting out of debt: a practical plan
LESSONS.hook: Debt can feel like a fog where every bill blurs into one. The way out starts with turning that fog into a list, then using free help that many people never know exists.

sections.key: Write down every debt, then protect housing, utilities and other high-consequence debts first.
sections.b:
People in debt often avoid opening envelopes, and that is human. But you can't plan around numbers you haven't seen. Set aside an hour and log in to every account. For each debt, write who you owe, the balance, the interest rate, the minimum repayment and the due date. Include credit cards, loans, buy now pay later, overdue bills, money owed to family, and any ATO or Centrelink debt.

Then sort them. Priority debts carry the most serious consequences: rent or mortgage, energy and water, and a car loan if you need the car for work. Fines and tax debts can escalate too. Cover these first. Never take out a new high-cost loan to keep up with another debt. This is general information, not financial advice.

sections.key: Contact lenders early and ask for a hardship variation, and get any agreement in writing.
sections.b:
If you can't meet repayments, contact the lender before you fall far behind. Under the National Credit Code, you can ask for a hardship variation if illness, job loss or other changed circumstances make repayments hard. Options can include a pause, reduced repayments for a period or a longer loan term. Lenders must consider the request and respond.

Energy, water and phone companies have hardship programs too. Ask for the hardship team, explain what happened and what you can realistically afford, and get any agreement in writing. Hardship arrangements can be noted on your credit report, but that is generally far less damaging than missed payments and defaults.

sections.key: Pay minimums on everything, then put all spare money on one debt, using whichever method you will stick with.
sections.b:
With essentials covered and minimums being paid, direct any extra money at one debt at a time. There are two popular methods.

The avalanche method targets the highest interest rate first, which usually saves the most money. The snowball method targets the smallest balance first, whatever the rate, giving a quick win that builds momentum.

When one debt is cleared, roll its repayment into the next, so the amount you throw at debt keeps growing. Mathematically the avalanche usually wins, but the snowball can suit people who need motivation. The best method is the one you will actually stick with.

sections.key: Combining debts helps only if the new loan is cheaper and you stop adding new debt.
sections.b:
A consolidation loan rolls several debts into one, ideally at a lower rate. A balance transfer moves credit card debt to a card with a low or zero rate for a promotional period. Both can work, but there are traps.

Promotional rates end, and the balance often reverts to a high rate. New purchases on a balance transfer card may attract full interest. A longer loan can lower repayments but raise the total cost. And if you keep using the old cards, you can end up with the new loan plus fresh debts.

If you consolidate, consider cancelling or lowering the limits on old cards, and plan to clear the balance before any promotional period ends.

sections.key: Free financial counsellors can help; debt agreements and bankruptcy are serious last resorts.
sections.b:
The free, independent National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007 or at ndh.org.au, connects you with counsellors who can explain options and negotiate with creditors. Some private debt management and credit repair businesses charge large fees for things you can often do free, like requesting hardship. Speak to a free counsellor before signing anything. You can also complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority, also free.

When debts are truly unmanageable, federal law offers debt agreements and bankruptcy, administered by the Australian Financial Security Authority (afsa.gov.au). They can stop collection action but are recorded on public registers and your credit report, and can limit borrowing. Get independent advice first. Afterwards, build a small emergency fund so the next repair doesn't go on a card.

quiz.q: Which is usually considered a priority debt?
o: A store card balance
A credit card with a low limit
Money owed to a streaming service
Rent or mortgage repayments
quiz.e: Falling behind on housing or utilities has the most serious consequences, so they come first.

quiz.q: Under the National Credit Code, what can you ask a lender for if you are struggling?
o: A higher credit limit
A hardship variation
A cash refund of interest
A new credit card
quiz.e: Asking early for a hardship variation gives you options such as a pause or reduced repayments.

quiz.q: What does the avalanche method target first?
o: The debt with the highest interest rate
The smallest balance
The newest debt
The debt owed to family
quiz.e: Clearing the highest-rate debt first usually saves the most interest overall.

quiz.q: What is a common trap with balance transfers?
o: The new card is always more expensive
The promotional rate ends and the balance reverts to a high rate
Old cards are cancelled automatically
They always shorten the loan term
quiz.e: Promotional rates end, so plan to clear the balance before then and stop adding new debt.

quiz.q: What is the National Debt Helpline?
o: A paid credit repair service
A government-owned lender
A free service linking you to counsellors
A private debt collection agency
quiz.e: Free, independent counsellors can explain your options and negotiate with creditors, so try them before any paid service.

LESSONS.push: Debt feels like fog. One hour and one page can start to clear it.

LESSONS.title: Buying big things without the debt trap
LESSONS.hook: A new fridge, a laptop, a couch: big purchases often come with a tempting offer to pay later. Here is how buy now pay later, interest-free deals and rent-to-own really work, and a better way to buy.

sections.key: Pay-later offers make big prices feel small, and the risks come from stacking plans and missing payments.
sections.b:
At checkout, a friendly line appears: four easy payments, no interest. A thousand-dollar purchase suddenly looks like a few hundred. That shift in feeling is the point. Splitting a cost makes it easier to say yes, and research suggests people tend to spend more when paying feels less painful.

Buy now pay later typically means four payments over about six weeks, the first upfront. Many charge no interest, earning money from retailers' fees and customers' late or account fees. Since mid-2025, BNPL has been regulated as credit, so providers need a credit licence and must check the product isn't unsuitable for you. The risks are several plans across providers, missed-payment fees and credit report problems. This is general information, not financial advice.

sections.key: Interest-free deals are only free if you clear the balance in time, because afterwards high interest and fees apply.
sections.b:
Furniture and electronics stores often advertise long interest-free periods, perhaps a year or more, through a store card or finance partner. These can be useful if you pay the full amount within the period.

The trap is what happens if you don't. Any remaining balance usually starts attracting a high rate, often similar to a credit card. Many of these products also charge a monthly account fee, and some an establishment fee, so the deal isn't truly free. The account may stay open for future purchases.

Before signing, ask three questions: what is the rate after the interest-free period, what are the fees, and what is the minimum repayment?

sections.key: Consumer leases can cost far more than the item's price, so look at the No Interest Loan Scheme first.
sections.b:
Some businesses offer appliances, furniture or electronics on a weekly lease, sometimes promoted to people on Centrelink payments with deductions taken straight from their payments. These leases can cost much more than the retail price, and at the end you may not own the item. ASIC has repeatedly warned about the high cost of some leases.

If you need an essential like a fridge or washing machine and can't afford it, look at alternatives first. The No Interest Loan Scheme, run by Good Shepherd with community partners, offers loans for essential goods to eligible people on low incomes, with no interest or fees. Services Australia may also offer an advance payment if you receive certain payments.

sections.key: Wait before big purchases, and judge the total cost, not the instalment.
sections.b:
A simple habit stops most regretful purchases: wait. For anything over an amount you choose, perhaps a few hundred dollars, give yourself 48 hours, or a week for bigger items. If you still want it, it's probably a considered decision rather than an impulse.

Next, work out the total cost, not the instalment. Add up every payment and fee if you use credit. Then ask a blunt question: if I had to pay the full price today from my own money, would I still buy it? If not, the payment plan is making the decision for you. Check that your existing repayments plus this one still leave room for rent, bills and food.

sections.key: Saving first through a sinking fund avoids interest and gives you bargaining power.
sections.b:
The cheapest way to buy something big is usually to save first. A sinking fund is money set aside regularly for a known future cost, such as a laptop, car registration or a replacement fridge. Divide the expected price by the pay cycles until you need it, and automate a transfer into a separate account on payday. You earn a little interest instead of paying it, and cash can give you bargaining power. Ask politely whether paying upfront gets a better price.

Compare prices across retailers, and be wary of 'sale' prices that aren't real bargains. Consider quality secondhand goods. New goods come with automatic consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law, which can matter more than an extended warranty.

quiz.q: Since mid-2025, how is buy now pay later regulated in Australia?
o: It is unregulated
As a form of credit requiring a licence
Only by the retailer
As a type of insurance
quiz.e: BNPL providers need a credit licence and must check the product isn't unsuitable for you.

quiz.q: What usually happens to a store finance balance left after the interest-free period?
o: It is forgiven
It is converted into a gift card
It is paid by the retailer
It starts attracting a high interest rate
quiz.e: The deal is only free if you clear the balance in time, and account fees may apply as well.

quiz.q: What is a cheaper alternative to rent-to-own for essential goods on a low income?
o: A payday loan
A second consumer lease
The No Interest Loan Scheme
A store card
quiz.e: The No Interest Loan Scheme offers loans for essentials with no interest or fees to eligible people.

quiz.q: Which question helps test whether a payment plan is driving a decision?
o: How small is the weekly payment?
Would I buy it if I had to pay the full price today?
Is the store open tomorrow?
Does the product come in another colour?
quiz.e: If you wouldn't pay the full price from your own money, the instalments are doing the persuading.

quiz.q: What is a sinking fund?
o: A failing super fund
A type of buy now pay later account
A government grant for appliances
Money set aside regularly for a known future cost
quiz.e: Saving a little each payday lets you buy outright, avoid interest and sometimes negotiate a better price.

LESSONS.push: A $1,000 price tag can be made to feel like $250. Here's the design behind it.

LESSONS.title: Building an emergency fund from scratch
LESSONS.hook: A blown tyre, a vet bill, a sudden gap between jobs: life sends invoices without warning. An emergency fund turns those moments from a crisis into an inconvenience, and you can start with very little.

sections.key: An emergency fund stops surprise costs becoming high-interest debt, and about three months of essentials is a common target.
sections.b:
Two people face the same expensive car repair. One pays from savings, feels annoyed and moves on. The other uses a credit card, pays interest for months, and when the next surprise hits, the debt grows. The difference is not income or intelligence; it is a buffer.

A common target is about three months of essential expenses: rent or mortgage, bills, groceries, transport and minimum debt repayments. Casual workers, freelancers and single-income households may want more. Starting from zero, break it down: first enough for one surprise bill, then one month of essentials, then two, then three. Add up essentials from bank statements or use Moneysmart's budget planner. This is general information, not financial advice.

sections.key: Keep the fund separate, reachable within a day or so, and earning some interest.
sections.b:
An emergency fund needs to be accessible quickly, but not so close that you dip into it for takeaway. A separate high-interest savings account, ideally not linked to a card, is a common choice. Many pay bonus interest only if you meet conditions, such as a monthly deposit and no withdrawals, so read the terms. Losing the bonus in a month you use the fund is fine.

If you have a home loan with an offset account, money held there reduces your interest. Deposits in authorised banks, building societies and credit unions are protected by the government's Financial Claims Scheme up to a limit; check the current limit at fcs.gov.au.

sections.key: Automate a small transfer on payday, then add windfalls and savings from cut costs.
sections.b:
The most reliable way to save is to make it automatic. Set up a regular transfer to your emergency account on payday, before you can spend the money. Start with an amount that doesn't hurt, even a small sum each pay, and raise it when you can.

Add windfalls such as a tax refund, a bonus or money from selling things you no longer use. When you cut a cost, like cancelling an unused subscription or switching to a cheaper phone plan, redirect that saving straight into the fund so it doesn't disappear into everyday spending. Some banks offer round-up features that move small change from each purchase into savings, which can help build the habit.

sections.key: Decide in advance what counts as an emergency, and refill the fund promptly after using it.
sections.b:
An emergency fund only works if it survives until an emergency. Decide in advance what counts: unexpected, necessary and urgent things, like a failed hot water system, an urgent dental bill, a car repair you need for work, or essentials after losing your job. Holidays, gifts and planned bills like car registration or insurance are not emergencies. Predictable costs belong in a separate sinking fund. Frequent raids may mean your budget needs adjusting, not that you lack willpower.

Using the fund is not failure; it did its job and you avoided debt. Then restart your automatic transfers and set a realistic timeframe to refill it. Review your target yearly, as your essential costs change.

sections.key: If an emergency arrives first, ask for payment plans and use cheaper help than payday loans.
sections.b:
Sometimes the emergency arrives before the fund does. Avoid the most expensive options first, such as payday loans and some consumer leases. Ask the business you owe about a payment plan; many tradespeople, vets, utilities and hospitals offer them.

If you receive certain Centrelink payments, Services Australia may give you an advance payment, which you repay from future payments, and there are crisis payments for specific severe situations; check eligibility at servicesaustralia.gov.au. The No Interest Loan Scheme can help eligible people with essential costs. The National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007, offers free financial counselling. Once the problem is handled, start your fund, even with a tiny first deposit.

quiz.q: What is the main job of an emergency fund?
o: To invest in shares for growth
To replace your superannuation
To stop surprise costs becoming high-interest debt
To pay for holidays and gifts
quiz.e: A buffer lets you absorb surprises without borrowing, and about three months of essentials is a common target.

quiz.q: What protects deposits in authorised Australian banks up to a limit?
o: The Financial Claims Scheme
AFCA
The National Credit Code
The Fair Work Act
quiz.e: The government's Financial Claims Scheme protects eligible deposits up to a limit, which you can check at fcs.gov.au.

quiz.q: What is the most reliable way to build savings?
o: Saving whatever is left at month's end
Waiting for a windfall
An automatic transfer on payday
Checking your balance daily
quiz.e: Automating the transfer moves money before you can spend it, so saving doesn't depend on willpower.

quiz.q: Which of these is best paid from a sinking fund rather than an emergency fund?
o: A burst hot water system
Annual car registration
An urgent dental bill
Essentials after a job loss
quiz.e: Predictable, planned costs belong in a separate sinking fund so they don't drain your buffer.

quiz.q: If you receive certain Centrelink payments, what might Services Australia offer in a pinch?
o: A free credit card
A cash grant for a holiday
A low-rate home loan
An advance repaid from future payments
quiz.e: An advance payment is cheaper than payday loans, though it reduces your later payments.

LESSONS.push: The same car repair can cost two people very different amounts. Why?

LESSONS.title: Income protection: insuring your pay
LESSONS.hook: Your ability to earn may be worth more than your house or car, yet many people insure those and not their income. Here is how income protection works, and the questions to ask before you buy or keep it.

sections.key: Income protection replaces part of your income, typically a monthly benefit of up to about 70 percent, if illness or injury stops you working.
sections.b:
Ask people for their most valuable asset and they name their home or car. But for a working adult, the pay they expect to earn over coming decades is often worth far more. Illness or injury that stops you working for months can drain savings fast while bills keep arriving.

Income protection pays a regular monthly benefit while you can't work because of a covered illness or injury. It replaces only part of your income, commonly up to around 70 percent in many current policies, which keeps an incentive to return to work. It differs from life insurance, which pays on death, and total and permanent disability cover, which pays a lump sum. Definitions of being unable to work vary, so read the product disclosure statement. This is general information, not financial advice.

sections.key: The waiting period sets when payments start, and the benefit period sets how long they can last.
sections.b:
Two choices shape both the cost and usefulness of a policy. The waiting period is how long you must be unable to work before benefits start, often 30, 60 or 90 days, or longer. A longer wait usually means a cheaper premium, which can suit you if you have sick leave or an emergency fund to bridge the gap.

The benefit period is how long payments can continue once they start, such as two years, five years or until a set age. Longer periods cost more but protect against long-term illness, which does the most financial damage. Think about how long your savings and leave could realistically carry you, then compare combinations.

sections.key: Cover inside super is convenient but often more limited than a standalone policy.
sections.b:
Many people already have income protection through their super fund without realising it. Check your fund's website or annual statement. Cover inside super is paid from your super balance, which spares your weekly budget but reduces your retirement savings. It often has shorter benefit periods and stricter definitions than standalone policies. Default cover can be switched off if your account has been inactive for a period, or for some younger members and low balances, unless you opt in.

A standalone policy, bought directly or through an adviser, can usually be tailored more closely. You can hold both, but benefits may be offset so you can't claim more than the limits allow. Compare before you add or cancel anything.

sections.key: Premiums for cover held outside super are generally tax-deductible, and benefits are generally taxable.
sections.b:
The tax treatment surprises some people. If you pay premiums for income protection held outside super, the ATO generally lets you claim them as a deduction, because the policy replaces taxable income. The flip side is that benefit payments are generally taxable income too.

Premiums paid from within super aren't claimed in your personal return. If a policy bundles income protection with other cover, such as life insurance, only the income protection part is usually deductible, and your insurer should show the split.

Premiums can be stepped, rising with age, or level, starting higher but rising more slowly. Both generally increase over time. Check the ATO website for the rules that apply to you.

sections.key: Answer application questions honestly, and know where sick leave, workers compensation and government support end.
sections.b:
When applying, you'll be asked about your health, job, income and lifestyle. Answer fully and honestly. Under Australian law you must take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation, and inaccurate answers can let the insurer reduce a payout, refuse a claim or cancel the policy. Get quotes from more than one insurer or speak to a licensed adviser, and compare disability definitions, benefit amounts, waiting and benefit periods and exclusions, not just price.

Income protection is one layer. Paid personal leave covers short absences. Workers compensation may cover work-related injury or illness. Services Australia income support is means-tested and usually far below a working wage. Knowing where these end helps you choose how much private cover makes sense.

quiz.q: How does income protection differ from life insurance?
o: It pays a lump sum only if you die
It replaces part of your income when you can't work
It covers damage to your home or car
It pays only your super contributions
quiz.e: Income protection replaces part of your income while you can't work, whereas life insurance pays on death.

quiz.q: What usually happens to premiums if you choose a longer waiting period?
o: They double
They are not affected
They become tax-free
They are usually cheaper
quiz.e: A longer wait means you cover the gap yourself, with sick leave or savings, so the premium is lower.

quiz.q: How are premiums for income protection inside super usually paid?
o: From your weekly pay
By the government
From your super balance
By your employer on top of super
quiz.e: Cover inside super spares your weekly budget but reduces your retirement savings.

quiz.q: What is the general tax treatment of income protection held outside super?
o: Premiums are generally deductible and benefits generally taxable
Premiums and benefits are both tax-free
Premiums are taxed and benefits deductible
Neither is relevant to tax
quiz.e: The policy replaces taxable income, so premiums are generally deductible and benefits generally taxable.

quiz.q: Why must you answer application questions honestly?
o: It guarantees you a lower premium
Otherwise a claim can be reduced or refused
It removes the waiting period
It is only a formality
quiz.e: Inaccurate answers can let the insurer reduce a payout, refuse a claim or cancel your policy.

LESSONS.push: Your future pay may be your biggest asset, and most people leave it uninsured.

LESSONS.title: Writing a resume that gets read
LESSONS.hook: A recruiter might give your resume less than a minute on the first pass. Here is how to make those seconds count, step by step.

sections.key: Your resume is skimmed first, so tailor it to each job ad, using the ad's language honestly.
sections.b:
Picture a hiring manager with sixty applications, a cold coffee and a meeting in twenty minutes. They glance at the top of page one, scan your latest job title, look for words that match the ad and decide whether to keep going. At many larger employers, software also sorts applications first. Both reward a clear layout, plain headings, relevant words near the top and evidence you can do the job.

Print the job ad and highlight every skill, tool and duty. Keep a master document, then copy it for each application. Put the most relevant experience first and use the ad's phrases where honest. Reorder skills and trim unrelated roles to a line. Don't stuff in words you can't back up. Aim for twenty focused minutes.

sections.key: Use a predictable order, with a short summary that says who you are and what you offer.
sections.b:
Australian resumes follow a familiar pattern, and familiar is good because readers know where to look. Start with your name, phone, email, suburb and state, and a LinkedIn link if it's current. You don't need your street address, a photo, date of birth or marital status; leaving them out also helps protect you from unconscious bias.

Next, a two or three sentence summary, then work history, most recent first, then skills, then education and licences or tickets, such as a white card or RSA. Two to three pages is common for experienced workers. 'Hospitality supervisor with six years in busy venues, strong at rostering and training' beats 'hard-working team player seeking new challenges'.

sections.key: Show what changed because you were there, with numbers you can honestly explain.
sections.b:
Most resumes read like job descriptions: 'responsible for customer service'. That tells the reader the role, not how well you did it. Swap duties for achievements, using action, task and result. Instead of 'handled customer complaints', try 'resolved escalated complaints for a busy retail store, helping lift our customer survey score over six months'.

Numbers make claims concrete: how many customers, how big a budget, how much time saved, how many people trained. Only use figures you can explain in an interview, because good interviewers will ask. If you can't measure something, describe the scale or outcome. Start lines with strong verbs such as led, built, reduced, organised or trained.

sections.key: Typos and vague or stretched claims sink more applications than missing experience.
sections.b:
Recruiters often say the fastest route to the 'no' pile is a typo in the first few lines. Read your resume aloud, slowly, then ask someone else to read it. Watch for inconsistent dates, mixed tenses and an unprofessional email address. Short lines with clear headings are easier to scan than long blocks.

Leave out reasons for leaving jobs, salary history and unrelated personal details. Don't exaggerate titles or qualifications: employers can and do check, and a stretched claim can cost you the job later. Gaps in your history are normal; a brief line such as 'career break, caring for family' or 'travel and study' is enough. Send a PDF unless the employer asks otherwise.

sections.key: Keep the cover letter specific and short, and line up referees before you apply.
sections.b:
If the ad asks for a cover letter, keep it to about a page. Open with the role and one genuine reason you want it. In the middle, pick two or three requirements and give a brief example of how you meet each. Close by welcoming a chat. Address it to a real person if the ad names one, and never leave another company's name in.

Most employers check references by phone before an offer. Choose two or three people who have recently supervised you, not friends or family. Ask permission, confirm their contact details and tell them which jobs you're applying for. 'Referees available on request' is acceptable. Then track where you applied and when, so you can follow up.

quiz.q: Why mirror the job ad's language when it is honest to do so?
o: It helps software and skimming humans see the match
It is a legal requirement for applicants
It makes the resume look longer
Recruiters only read the last page
quiz.e: Matching the ad's terms helps screening software and busy humans see quickly that you fit.

quiz.q: Which of these is generally best left off an Australian resume?
o: Your suburb and state
Your licences and tickets
Your date of birth
Your LinkedIn link
quiz.e: Personal details like date of birth are unnecessary, and omitting them helps protect you from unconscious bias.

quiz.q: What turns a duty into an achievement?
o: Listing more duties
Using longer sentences
Showing the result you produced
Adding a photo
quiz.e: Achievements show what changed because you were there, ideally with numbers you can explain.

quiz.q: How should you handle a gap in your work history?
o: Hide it by changing dates
Note it briefly and honestly
Write a full page explaining it
Leave the whole job history off
quiz.e: Gaps are normal, and a short honest line is enough.

quiz.q: What should you do before listing someone as a referee?
o: Nothing, employers rarely call
Choose a close friend
Give their details only to a competitor
Ask permission and tell them about the role
quiz.e: Referees who know the role can speak to what matters, and most employers do check.

LESSONS.push: Your resume may get less than a minute. What happens in that time?

LESSONS.title: Reading your payslip
LESSONS.hook: That little document on payday tells you whether you are being paid correctly. Most people never really read it. Here is how.

sections.key: Your payslip is your best everyday check that you are being paid what you are owed.
sections.b:
Imagine working the same Saturday shifts for a year, only to discover your weekend penalty rate was never applied. Underpayment is more common than many people realise, and it is not always deliberate. Payroll errors, wrong award classifications and outdated rates all happen, and your payslip is where they show up first.

In Australia, employers generally must give employees a payslip within one working day of payday, on paper or electronically. Reading it takes two minutes each pay and can save you hundreds or thousands of dollars. This is general information, not legal or financial advice. The Fair Work Ombudsman (fairwork.gov.au) is the official place to check your situation.

sections.key: The law sets out what a payslip must show, and gross and net pay are the two figures to understand first.
sections.b:
A compliant payslip names your employer, including their ABN, and names you. It shows the pay period and the date you were paid. Gross pay is your total before tax. Net pay is what lands in your bank account.

It should also list deductions such as tax or salary sacrifice, plus any bonuses, loadings, allowances or penalty rates. If you are paid by the hour, it shows your hourly rate and the hours paid at that rate. It shows the superannuation your employer is paying and the fund it is going to. If any of this is missing, politely ask your payroll team why.

sections.key: Check that the right tax is withheld and that super is paid, at the right rate, into your chosen fund.
sections.b:
Under the pay as you go system, your employer withholds tax and sends it to the Australian Taxation Office. The amount depends on your earnings, how often you are paid and your tax file number declaration. Most people claim the tax-free threshold from one employer only. If you claim it from two jobs at once, too little tax may be withheld and you could face a bill at tax time.

Super is paid on top of your wages. The super guarantee is a percentage of your ordinary time earnings and has risen in steps, so check the current rate on the ATO website. A payslip shows what your employer says it will pay, not what arrived. Every few months, check your fund's app, website or myGov to confirm contributions are landing.

sections.key: Your base rate and penalty rates usually come from an award or agreement, and you can look them up.
sections.b:
Many Australian workers are covered by a modern award, a legal document that sets minimum pay and conditions for an industry or occupation. Others are covered by an enterprise agreement negotiated at their workplace. These set your minimum base rate and extras such as casual loading, overtime and penalty rates for evenings, weekends and public holidays.

To check yours, use the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator or download your award's pay guide. You will need your award, your classification level and whether you are full time, part time or casual. Minimum rates are usually reviewed each year, with changes commonly starting from the first full pay period on or after 1 July. A rate that was right last year might be wrong now.

sections.key: Spend two minutes each payday checking your hours, rate and super, and raise any error calmly and in writing.
sections.b:
Keep a note of your hours each week, including start and finish times and breaks. When your payslip arrives, compare the hours with your record and check that each type, such as overtime or Sunday work, has the right rate. Glance at the year to date totals and your leave balance. Save every payslip as a PDF in one folder, because records are your best evidence.

If something looks wrong, write to your manager or payroll. Say what you noticed, what you believe is correct and how you worked it out, and keep a copy. If it is not fixed, the Fair Work Ombudsman offers free help, and the ATO handles unpaid super. Time limits apply to recovering wages, so act early. Employers must not punish you for raising a genuine concern.

quiz.q: Why is it worth reading your payslip every pay?
o: It proves your employer has followed every award rule correctly
It is where pay errors, such as a missing penalty rate, show up first
It replaces the need to ever check your hours or super elsewhere
It is only useful at tax time, when you lodge your return
quiz.e: A two-minute check each pay catches mistakes early, before they add up.

quiz.q: What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?
o: Gross is the total before tax, and net is what reaches your bank account
Gross is your hourly rate, and net is your annual salary
Gross includes super only, and net includes your wages only
Gross is what you earn at work, and net is what you save
quiz.e: Gross pay is before tax and deductions; net pay is what you actually receive.

quiz.q: A payslip shows super calculated for the period. What should you also do?
o: Nothing, because the payslip proves the money was paid
Ask the ATO to pay it directly into your fund each month
Wait until retirement to look at your balance
Check your fund occasionally to confirm the money actually arrived
quiz.e: A payslip shows what your employer says it will pay, not what has landed in your fund.

quiz.q: Where do your minimum base rate and penalty rates usually come from?
o: Whatever your employer decides each year
Your tax file number declaration
A modern award or an enterprise agreement that covers your job
The ATO, which sets pay rates for each industry
quiz.e: Awards and agreements set minimum rates, and you can look them up with the Fair Work Ombudsman's tools.

quiz.q: You think your pay is wrong. What is a sensible first step?
o: Wait a few years in case it corrects itself
Write to your manager or payroll with what you noticed and keep a copy
Stop working until the error is fixed
Post about it publicly before speaking to anyone
quiz.e: Raising errors calmly and in writing, early, usually fixes them and creates a record.

LESSONS.push: A document you receive every payday could be hiding an error. Do you know where to look?

LESSONS.title: Asking for a pay rise
LESSONS.hook: Many people wait years to be offered more money. Here is how to prepare for, start and handle the pay rise conversation yourself.

sections.key: Silence rarely gets you paid more, and most managers expect the question at some point.
sections.b:
Sam has been in the same role for three years. She has trained two new starters, taken on the rostering and quietly fixed the ordering system. Her pay has only moved when the award minimum went up.

Plenty of people never ask, because it feels awkward, greedy or risky. Yet to a manager, a well prepared request from a valued employee is a normal part of running a team, and far better than that person resigning without warning. Asking does not guarantee a yes. But a clear, evidence based conversation usually leads somewhere useful: a rise now, a plan for one later or honest feedback about what is standing in the way.

sections.key: Before asking for more, check the legal minimum for your role, then research what similar roles pay.
sections.b:
If an award or enterprise agreement covers you, it sets minimum rates for your classification. Use the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator or pay guides, and check your classification level, since duties often grow faster than job titles. If you are paid below the minimum, that is an underpayment to be fixed, not a pay rise conversation. This is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Your market value is roughly what another employer would pay for your skills, location and work. Job sites, job ads that list pay, industry surveys and professional associations all help. You are generally free to discuss your pay with colleagues too. Look for a range, then pick a specific amount near the upper end of what you can justify, plus the lowest outcome you would happily accept.

sections.key: Make your request about the value you add, not about your personal expenses.
sections.b:
The strongest case focuses on what you contribute. Gather evidence: projects you delivered, problems you solved, money or time you saved, new responsibilities and positive feedback from customers or colleagues. Write it down in one or two pages. Be specific: 'took over weekly rostering for a team of twelve' beats 'helped out with admin'.

Avoid leading with personal reasons such as rent or the cost of living. They are real pressures, but they are not reasons your employer should pay you more than someone else in the same role. If you have been given a bigger job without a bigger title or pay, say so plainly, and show how your role has changed since your pay was last set.

sections.key: Ask when your value is visible and the budget is still open, and book a proper meeting.
sections.b:
Good moments include your annual review, soon after a clear win, when you take on new responsibilities, or a few months before budgets are set for the next financial year, which starts on 1 July for many Australian organisations. Bad moments include the middle of a crisis, straight after redundancies or late on a Friday.

Do not ambush your manager in a corridor. Ask for a meeting: 'I would like to book half an hour to talk about my role and pay. Would next week work?' That gives them time to prepare and signals you are serious. If there is a formal review cycle, find out when decisions are made, because by the review meeting the money may already be allocated.

sections.key: State your request clearly, back it with evidence, listen, and turn any no into a plan.
sections.b:
Open warmly, saying you enjoy the role and want to talk about pay given how your work has grown. Share two or three strong examples, make a specific request and briefly explain how you arrived at it. Then pause. Silence feels uncomfortable, but it gives your manager space to respond. Stay calm, and avoid ultimatums unless you are truly prepared to leave.

If the answer is no, ask what would need to change, and agree specific, measurable goals and a date to revisit, perhaps in three or six months. Put it in writing. You can also ask for training, a study allowance, flexible hours or a better title. Then follow up with a short email, and track your progress. If promises are repeatedly broken, that is useful information too.

quiz.q: Why is asking for a pay rise often better than staying silent?
o: Managers always say yes to a prepared request
Pay only changes when employees ask in writing
It is the only way an employer will ever notice your work
It usually leads to a rise, a plan or honest feedback about what is blocking one
quiz.e: Even without an immediate yes, a clear conversation produces something useful.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are paid below your award minimum?
o: Ask for a pay rise and accept whatever is offered
Wait for the next annual review
Treat it as an underpayment to fix, not as a pay rise negotiation
Quit before raising it with anyone
quiz.e: Legal minimums are owed to you; a rise is a separate conversation about pay above that floor.

quiz.q: Which approach makes the strongest case for a pay rise?
o: Explaining that rent and living costs have gone up
Specific evidence of the value you add and how your role has grown
Listing how long you have been in the job
Pointing out that a colleague earns more than you
quiz.e: Your employer pays for the value you add, so lead with concrete contributions.

quiz.q: What is the best way to arrange a pay conversation?
o: Book a meeting in advance so your manager has time to prepare
Raise it in a corridor so it feels casual
Bring it up in the middle of a busy crisis
Wait until your manager asks you about it
quiz.e: A booked meeting signals you are serious and gives your manager time to prepare.

quiz.q: After you make your request, what helps most?
o: Keep talking until your manager agrees
Threaten to resign to speed up the decision
Drop the subject and never raise it again
Pause and listen, and if it is a no, agree goals and a date to revisit
quiz.e: Listening, then turning a no into a clear plan keeps a future yes possible.

LESSONS.push: Many people wait years for a rise nobody offers. What actually helps you get one?

LESSONS.title: Running a meeting worth attending
LESSONS.hook: Most of us have sat through a meeting that should have been an email. Here is how to run one people are glad they came to.

sections.key: A meeting uses everyone's time at once, so its cost is multiplied by the number of people in the room.
sections.b:
Picture eight people in a one hour meeting. That is not one hour of work. It is eight hours, nearly a full working day. If the meeting drifts, ends without a decision and needs a follow up, the cost doubles.

Bad meetings also drain energy, interrupt focused work and teach people that their time does not matter. Good ones can settle in thirty minutes a question that would take two weeks of emails, and get everyone moving in the same direction. The difference is rarely luck. Good meetings are designed, and anyone can learn how, whether you lead a team or are organising your first catch up.

sections.key: Check a meeting is the right tool, state its purpose in one sentence and invite only the people who need to be there.
sections.b:
If you only need to share information, an email, short document or recorded update is often better. Meetings suit things that need live conversation: decisions, tricky problems, building agreement, brainstorming and sensitive issues. Finish this line: 'By the end of this meeting, we will have...' If you cannot, you are not ready to book. Put that sentence at the top of the invitation.

Invite only people who must decide, hold information you cannot get elsewhere or must carry out the outcome. Others can read a summary. But leaving out a key person often means redoing the meeting. Respect different working hours, and consider twenty five or fifty minutes instead of an hour, leaving a buffer between calls.

sections.key: A useful agenda lists questions to answer, not just topics to talk about.
sections.b:
An agenda that says 'budget, rosters, other business' tells nobody what to prepare. Turn each item into a question with a time: 'Which of the two venue quotes do we accept? Ten minutes. Read the attached comparison first.'

Put the most important item first, while energy is high, and send the agenda and any reading at least a day ahead. Ask people to come prepared, and say so plainly. Some teams start with a few quiet minutes to read the key document together, which levels the playing field and means nobody bluffs. If someone wants to add an item, ask them to tell you beforehand. An agenda is a promise about how you will use people's time.

sections.key: Start on time, keep the discussion on track and make sure every voice is heard.
sections.b:
Begin on time, even if someone is late, and restate the purpose in a sentence. As chair, your job is to guide, not dominate. Watch the clock and gently steer drifting conversations: 'Good point, let us park it.' Keep a visible parking lot list so people know side issues have not been ignored.

Draw out quieter people by asking them directly, and politely rein in those who speak at length. In hybrid meetings, make sure remote attendees can hear, see shared material and get a fair turn, perhaps by calling on them first. If the discussion is going in circles, summarise where things stand and ask what is needed to decide.

sections.key: End with decisions, named owners and due dates, then send a short written summary the same day.
sections.b:
The last five minutes matter most, so protect them. Read back what was decided in plain words. List the actions: what, who and by when. An action without a name next to it usually does not happen. Check nobody disagrees, then finish a few minutes early. A good test: could every attendee tell a colleague, in a sentence or two, what was decided and what they must do next?

Within a few hours, send a brief note covering decisions, actions with owners and dates, and open questions. Store it where the team can find it. Check on actions when due. Review regular meetings now and then, and be willing to shorten or cancel them.

quiz.q: Why is a one hour meeting with eight people costly?
o: It always runs over by an hour
It uses eight hours of people's time, nearly a full working day
It costs the same as a one person meeting
The cost only counts if the meeting makes a decision
quiz.e: Meeting cost is multiplied by the number of people in the room.

quiz.q: What is a good test that you are ready to book a meeting?
o: You can finish the line: 'By the end, we will have...'
You have a long list of topics to cover
Everyone in the team has been invited
You can fill a full hour
quiz.e: If you cannot state the purpose in one sentence, the meeting is not ready.

quiz.q: What makes an agenda genuinely useful?
o: It lists broad topics such as 'budget' and 'other business'
It is handed out at the start of the meeting
It leaves the order of items to be decided on the day
Each item is a question with a time, sent with reading a day ahead
quiz.e: Questions tell people what to prepare and what must be answered.

quiz.q: A discussion drifts off topic. What should the chair do?
o: Let the conversation run until it ends naturally
Cancel the meeting and rebook it
Note the point on a parking lot list and steer back to the agenda
Ask the quietest person to leave
quiz.e: A visible parking lot keeps focus while showing side issues are not ignored.

quiz.q: Why should a meeting end with named owners and due dates?
o: It lets the meeting run longer to cover everything
An action without a name beside it usually does not happen
It replaces the need for a written summary
It shows who talked the most
quiz.e: Clear owners and dates turn talk into action, and a same-day summary locks it in.

LESSONS.push: Eight people, one hour, and a whole working day gone. How do good meetings avoid it?

LESSONS.title: Giving and receiving feedback at work
LESSONS.hook: Feedback can lift a team or wreck a week. A few practical techniques make it clearer, kinder and far more useful.

sections.key: Most feedback fails because it is vague, late or delivered in a way that triggers defence.
sections.b:
Think of the last time someone said 'Can I give you some feedback?' Your heart probably sped up. Feedback feels personal because work is tied to our sense of competence and belonging. Delivered badly, it makes people stop listening and start defending.

The common problems are easy to spot. Vague feedback, such as 'be more professional', gives nothing to act on. Feedback saved for an annual review arrives months too late. Feedback mixed with frustration sounds like an attack. And generic praise like 'great job' feels hollow. The good news is that giving and receiving feedback are both skills, and a few simple structures make conversations shorter, clearer and less painful.

sections.key: Describe when it happened, what the person did and the effect it had, then ask for their view.
sections.b:
One widely used structure, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership, has three steps. Name the situation: 'In Tuesday's client meeting'. Describe the specific behaviour you saw or heard, without guessing at motives: 'you interrupted the client twice'. Explain the impact: 'they seemed frustrated and we did not get the full picture'.

This keeps the conversation on facts rather than character judgements like 'you are rude'. Then pause and ask, 'How did it look from your side?' There may be context you missed. The same structure works for praise: 'When you stayed calm with that upset customer this morning, the whole queue relaxed, and she thanked us on the way out.'

sections.key: Give feedback soon, in private for criticism, and end with what to do next, agreed together.
sections.b:
Feedback is most useful within a day or two, but not in the heat of the moment. If you are angry, wait. Give criticism in private, never in front of colleagues or customers. Ask first: 'Have you got ten minutes?' Avoid important feedback by text or chat, where tone is easily misread.

Once you have heard their view, shift forward. Ask 'What could we try next time?' People commit more to solutions they helped shape. Make any request clear, such as 'please let clients finish before you jump in', and agree on one or two changes, not ten. Then follow up and notice improvement. Think of feedback as coaching: the goal is not to win an argument about the past but to make next week better.

sections.key: Listen, ask questions and thank the person, even when it stings.
sections.b:
When feedback lands, your instinct may be to explain, justify or counter attack. Try to resist, at least at first. Breathe, listen to the whole message and ask clarifying questions: 'Can you give me an example?' or 'What would good look like?' Summarise what you heard to check you understood. Then thank them, even if you disagree, because giving feedback takes effort and some courage.

You do not have to accept every point on the spot. It is fine to say, 'I want to think about that and come back to you.' Later, sort what you heard into three piles: useful and true, partly true and simply not right. Act on the first pile.

sections.key: Ask for specific feedback regularly, and if you lead others, thank people for honesty so they keep offering it.
sections.b:
Waiting for feedback means getting it on someone else's schedule, often when something has gone wrong. Ask instead, and be specific, because 'Any feedback?' usually produces 'No, all good'. Try 'What is one thing I could do to make my reports more useful?' Ask a mix of people, including those who report to you, who may need reassurance that honesty is safe.

Leaders shape feedback culture more than any policy. If you get defensive, people stay quiet and you lose early warnings. If you thank people for raising concerns, they learn it is safe. Hold regular one to ones, and keep a light record so reviews hold no surprises. Keep feedback separate from formal performance or disciplinary processes, which have their own rules. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes free guides for managers and employees.

quiz.q: Which of these is the most useful kind of feedback?
o: Saved up for the annual review so it covers everything
Delivered quickly while you are still feeling frustrated
General praise that is friendly, such as 'great job'
Specific and timely, so the person knows what to change
quiz.e: Vague or late feedback gives nothing to act on, so specific and timely beats both.

quiz.q: In the situation, behaviour, impact structure, what does 'behaviour' mean?
o: Your opinion of the person's character
How the person usually behaves at work
What you saw or heard the person do, described without guessing motives
The effect the action had on the team
quiz.e: Sticking to observable behaviour keeps feedback factual rather than personal.

quiz.q: Where is the best place to give critical feedback?
o: In front of the team so everyone learns from it
In private, soon after the event, once you are calm
By text, so the message is clear and recorded
At the next annual review
quiz.e: Private, calm and soon keeps the other person able to listen.

quiz.q: Someone gives you feedback you disagree with. What is a good response?
o: Listen, ask for examples, thank them and think about it later
Explain why they are wrong straight away
Agree with everything to end the conversation
Ignore it unless your manager repeats it
quiz.e: You can thank someone and take time to decide what is true without being defensive.

quiz.q: How do leaders make honest feedback more likely?
o: They ask 'any feedback?' once a year
They respond to challenges by explaining why they were right
They avoid asking so no one feels pressured
They thank people for raising concerns, even uncomfortable ones
quiz.e: People speak up when they see that honesty is welcomed, not punished.

LESSONS.push: The word 'feedback' makes most of our hearts race. A simple structure can calm it.

LESSONS.title: Burnout and the right to disconnect
LESSONS.hook: Burnout is more than a bad week. Learn the warning signs, what you can change and what Australian workplace rules say about switching off.

sections.key: Burnout is a work related pattern of exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness, not simple tiredness.
sections.b:
Jess used to love her job. Now Sunday nights bring a knot in her stomach, she snaps at colleagues and tasks that once took an hour drag on all afternoon. She is not lazy. She may be burning out.

The World Health Organization describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition, resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It has three features: energy depletion or exhaustion, increased mental distance from your job or feelings of negativity or cynicism about it, and reduced professional effectiveness. Because burnout is about work specifically, solutions often involve how work is organised, not just personal resilience. This lesson is general information, not medical, legal or professional advice.

sections.key: Burnout builds slowly and is driven mostly by working conditions, not personal weakness.
sections.b:
Early signs include trouble switching off, poor sleep, tiredness that rest does not fix, irritability, dreading work, getting sick more often and uncharacteristic mistakes. You might feel numb about things that used to matter. Others may notice first, so take it seriously if a partner or friend says you seem different. These signs overlap with depression and anxiety, so do not self diagnose. Speak with your GP. Healthdirect and Beyond Blue offer free information and phone support around the clock.

Researchers point to mismatches between people and work: too heavy a workload for too long, little control, too little recognition, conflict or isolation, unfairness, and clashing values. Long hours alone do not always cause burnout. The danger zone is high demands, low control and little support. That reduces self blame and points to practical changes.

sections.key: Australian work health and safety laws cover psychological health, not just physical safety.
sections.b:
Under work health and safety laws, employers must, so far as is reasonably practicable, ensure the health and safety of workers, and health includes psychological health. In recent years, most Australian jurisdictions have introduced regulations on managing psychosocial hazards, which are aspects of work that can cause psychological harm. Examples include excessive job demands, poor support, low role clarity, bullying, harassment and poor workplace relationships.

This means a sustained, unmanageable workload is not just your personal problem. It is a workplace risk your employer should identify and control. Safe Work Australia and your state or territory regulator publish guidance. Many employers also offer an Employee Assistance Program, which typically provides free, confidential short term counselling, so it is worth asking whether yours does.

sections.key: Many Australian employees can now refuse unreasonable contact outside working hours.
sections.b:
In 2024, Australia added a right to disconnect to the Fair Work Act. It began applying to employees of non small business employers in August 2024 and was extended to small business employees in August 2025.

In broad terms, an employee can refuse to monitor, read or respond to contact, or attempted contact, from their employer or a third party such as a client outside their working hours, unless that refusal is unreasonable. Whether it is unreasonable depends on factors such as the reason for the contact, how it is made, whether you are paid to be available, your role and your personal circumstances. Emergencies and genuine on call arrangements are treated differently. Check the Fair Work Ombudsman website for how this applies to you.

sections.key: Protect your time with daily habits, and raise workload with your manager early, with specifics and options.
sections.b:
Set a clear end to your workday and mark it with a small ritual, such as closing the laptop or writing tomorrow's top three tasks. Turn off work notifications outside hours. If you manage others, avoid late night emails, or schedule them for morning. Take your leave and switch off fully. None of this fixes a broken workload, but it helps you recover.

Many people wait until they are close to collapse before saying anything. Book a private conversation and describe the situation concretely: what is on your plate, how many hours it takes and what is slipping. Frame it as a resourcing problem to solve together, and bring options for what could be paused, delegated or simplified. Follow up in writing. If nothing changes, consider HR, a union, your health and safety representative or the Fair Work Ombudsman.

quiz.q: How does the World Health Organization describe burnout?
o: A medical condition caused by personal weakness or poor coping
An occupational phenomenon from chronic workplace stress that has not been managed
Ordinary tiredness that a long weekend cures
A mood disorder that only affects managers
quiz.e: Burnout is linked to work itself, so solutions involve how work is organised.

quiz.q: Which combination is most likely to lead to burnout?
o: High demands, low control and little support
Long hours spent on work you care about and enjoy
Short hours with plenty of recognition and praise
A varied job with supportive, friendly colleagues
quiz.e: Working hard is not the problem by itself; demands without control or support are.

quiz.q: What does Australian work health and safety law say about psychological health?
o: It is entirely the worker's own responsibility
It only applies to physical injuries
It applies only to large companies
Employers must manage risks to it, so far as reasonably practicable
quiz.e: An unmanageable workload is a workplace risk, not just a personal problem.

quiz.q: What does the right to disconnect allow?
o: Ignoring any message from your employer at any time
Working only the hours you prefer
Refusing contact outside working hours, unless the refusal is unreasonable
Refusing contact only during paid leave
quiz.e: The right is broad but depends on factors such as your role, pay and the reason for contact.

quiz.q: What is the best way to raise a heavy workload with your manager?
o: Only once you are close to collapse, to show how serious it is
Early and concretely, with specifics and options for what could change
As a confession that you personally cannot cope
By email only, without ever having a conversation
quiz.e: Framing workload as a shared resourcing problem, with options, makes it easier to fix.

LESSONS.push: A bad week and burnout can feel alike. A law passed in 2024 may help you tell them apart.

LESSONS.title: Working on an ABN: contractor or employee?
LESSONS.hook: More Australians are picking up work as contractors. Here is how to tell if it is genuine, and what to sort out if you go it alone.

sections.key: Contracting can offer freedom, but it shifts tax, super, leave and risk from the business to you.
sections.b:
Liam is offered a job building websites. The pay is good, but the business asks him to get an ABN and send invoices instead of going on the payroll. It sounds simple. Yet the difference between employee and independent contractor changes almost everything: who pays your tax and super, whether you get paid leave, whether an award covers you and what happens if the work dries up.

Plenty of people contract happily, from tradies and consultants to designers, and enjoy the flexibility. But the label is not just paperwork. This lesson is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, so check your own situation with official sources.

sections.key: The real nature of the working relationship matters more than what the contract calls it.
sections.b:
There is no single test. Courts and tribunals look at the whole relationship, including how it works in practice. Following 2024 changes to the Fair Work Act, the law makes clear that the real substance of the arrangement counts.

Signs of employment include the business controlling how, when and where you work, being paid for your time rather than a result, using their equipment, working only for them, being part of their team and being unable to send someone else. Signs of genuine contracting include running your own business, choosing how to do the job, taking on financial risk, using your own tools, working for several clients and being able to delegate.

sections.key: Calling an employee a contractor to avoid obligations is illegal.
sections.b:
Sham contracting is when a business falsely presents employment as independent contracting. It can be deliberate, to avoid paying super, leave and award rates, or a genuine misunderstanding. It is against the law to misrepresent employment as contracting, to dismiss an employee in order to re engage them as a contractor doing much the same work, or to pressure someone into becoming a contractor with a false statement.

If you are really an employee, you may be entitled to back pay, super and leave even if you signed a contractor agreement and hold an ABN. If you are unsure, the Fair Work Ombudsman explains the difference, and the ATO offers an employee or contractor decision tool on its website.

sections.key: An ABN is free, but you must be running a business, and no one withholds tax for you.
sections.b:
If you genuinely carry on a business, you can apply for an Australian Business Number at abr.gov.au. It is free, though many websites charge to do it for you. You will need your tax file number. Employees and hobbyists do not qualify. Quote it on invoices, as businesses may have to withhold tax from suppliers who do not.

As a contractor, the full invoice usually lands in your account with no tax taken out. That money is not all yours. Include it in your tax return, and the ATO may place you on pay as you go instalments. Many contractors move a set share of each payment into a separate tax account. You must register for GST once turnover reaches the threshold, or immediately in some industries, such as ride sourcing. Check current thresholds on the ATO website.

sections.key: Contractors build their own safety net, so set rates that cover real costs and put agreements in writing.
sections.b:
Genuine contractors often get no paid leave, employer super or workers compensation automatically. Many make voluntary super contributions, though some contractors paid mainly for their labour can still be entitled to super guarantee payments, so check ATO guidance. Consider public liability, professional indemnity and income protection insurance, and plan time off.

A common mistake is setting a rate by dividing an employee salary by working hours. You must also cover super, unpaid leave, insurance, equipment, accounting fees and quiet periods, which is why contract rates often exceed the equivalent wage. Agree in writing on scope, price, payment terms, who owns the work and how either side can end the deal, and send clear invoices with your ABN. If a deal feels lopsided, get independent legal advice before signing.

quiz.q: What changes when you work as a contractor rather than an employee?
o: Your employer withholds tax but pays no super
You are automatically covered by an award
You no longer need to pay any tax
You handle your own tax and super, and paid leave is not automatic
quiz.e: Contracting shifts tax, super, leave and risk from the business to you.

quiz.q: What matters most in deciding whether someone is an employee?
o: What the signed contract calls the arrangement
Whether the worker has an ABN
The real substance of how the working relationship operates
Whether the worker is paid by invoice
quiz.e: Courts look at the whole relationship, not just the label on the paperwork.

quiz.q: What is sham contracting?
o: Any contract between a business and a freelancer
Falsely presenting what is really employment as contracting
Contracting that pays less than an award
Working for several clients at once
quiz.e: It is illegal, and a worker who is really an employee may be owed back pay, super and leave.

quiz.q: Which statement about an ABN is correct?
o: It is free to apply for, but you must be carrying on a business
It is available to every employee on request
It must be bought through a registration service
It removes the need to include income in your tax return
quiz.e: You can apply for free at abr.gov.au, but only if you are genuinely running a business.

quiz.q: Why do contract rates usually need to be higher than an equivalent wage?
o: Clients are legally required to pay a premium
Contractors work longer hours than employees
Tax is not charged on contract income
The rate must cover super, leave, insurance, costs and quiet periods
quiz.e: Dividing a salary by hours leaves out the costs an employer would normally carry.

LESSONS.push: One line on your invoice can change your tax, super and rights. Which side are you on?

LESSONS.title: Leaving a job the right way
LESSONS.hook: How you leave a job can shape your references, your final pay and your reputation for years. Here is how to resign well.

sections.key: How you leave can shape your references, final pay and reputation, because industries are smaller than they look.
sections.b:
The manager you leave behind may one day interview you, become your client or be called as your referee. The colleague who covered your workload after a messy exit may turn up at your next workplace. A good exit protects your references, makes sure you receive everything you are owed and leaves the door open.

A bad exit, such as walking out mid shift, posting complaints online or vanishing without a handover, can follow you for years. Leaving well does not mean pretending everything was perfect. It means being clear, professional and fair, even if you are glad to be going. This is general information, not legal advice. The Fair Work Ombudsman has details for your situation.

sections.key: Check your required notice, tell your manager in person first, then confirm in writing.
sections.b:
Your notice period is usually set by your award, enterprise agreement or contract, so check all three. One to four weeks is common, often depending on how long you have worked there. Casual employees often have different rules. If you do not give the required notice, some awards and agreements allow your employer to deduct an amount from your final pay.

Your manager should hear the news from you, not the grapevine. Ask for a short private meeting, say you have decided to leave, give your last day and thank them. You need not explain where you are going or air every grievance. An exit interview suits that better. Then send a short resignation letter or email with the date, your role, a clear statement that you are resigning, your last day and a thank you. Keep a copy.

sections.key: Think carefully before accepting a counter offer, and stay calm if the reaction is tough.
sections.b:
An employer may respond to your resignation with more money, a new title or a promise that things will change. It can be flattering, and occasionally it is exactly what you wanted. But ask why you started looking in the first place. If the reasons were pay alone, a counter offer might solve it. If they were culture, management, workload or growth, money rarely fixes those for long. Consider, too, why it took a resignation to get the offer.

Some managers react badly, with anger or guilt. Stay polite, firm and brief. The decision is yours. You must not be threatened or punished for exercising workplace rights, and the Fair Work Ombudsman can give information if things go wrong.

sections.key: A clear handover is the best way to protect your reputation on the way out.
sections.b:
Use your notice period to make life easy for whoever takes over. Write a handover document covering current projects, where key files and passwords are stored through approved channels, upcoming deadlines, regular tasks and important contacts. Note what is half finished and what happens next. Offer to train a colleague or your replacement. Be honest about what you cannot finish.

Keep working properly until your last day, because coasting is noticed. Return laptops, phones, keys and uniforms. Do not take confidential information, client lists or company files, which could breach your contract or the law. Say goodbye to colleagues and swap personal contact details with those you want to stay in touch with.

sections.key: Make sure your final pay includes everything you are owed, then leave on good terms.
sections.b:
Final pay should include wages to your last day and other outstanding amounts. Under the National Employment Standards, unused annual leave is paid out, including leave loading if your award, agreement or contract provides for it. Unused personal or carer's leave generally is not. Long service leave depends mostly on your state or territory and sometimes your award. Check your final payslip against your leave balance, confirm your final super is paid, and download your payslips before system access ends. Raise anything missing in writing, then contact the Fair Work Ombudsman if needed.

Ask a manager or senior colleague to be a referee. Give constructive exit feedback, update LinkedIn only after telling your manager, send a farewell message and avoid criticising your old employer publicly. Many people return later.

quiz.q: Why does the way you leave a job matter?
o: It changes how much notice you must give
Past managers and colleagues may become future referees, clients or coworkers
Your old employer must publish a reference
It affects only your final payslip
quiz.e: Industries are small, so a professional exit protects your reputation and references.

quiz.q: Where is your required notice period usually set?
o: In your award, enterprise agreement or employment contract
By your manager on the day you resign
By the Fair Work Ombudsman for each person
By a single national rule of two weeks
quiz.e: Check all three documents, because some let employers deduct pay if you give short notice.

quiz.q: You receive a counter offer after resigning. What is a wise first step?
o: Accept at once, because the offer proves you are valued
Refuse without thinking, because counter offers never work
Accept it, then keep job hunting in secret
Ask why you wanted to leave and whether money would fix it
quiz.e: If your reasons were culture, workload or growth, extra money rarely solves them.

quiz.q: What should a good handover include?
o: Copies of client lists to keep for your records
A list of colleagues' faults for the replacement
Current projects, deadlines, regular tasks, key contacts and next steps
Only a verbal summary on your last day
quiz.e: A written handover makes life easy for your replacement and protects your reputation.

quiz.q: Which is generally included in your final pay?
o: Unused personal or carer's leave, but no annual leave
Unused annual leave, but not usually unused personal leave
Neither type of leave, which lapses when you resign
All leave types, including sick leave
quiz.e: Annual leave is paid out under the National Employment Standards; personal leave generally is not.

LESSONS.push: The last two weeks of a job can matter more than the last two years. Here is why.

LESSONS.title: The people who wrote the dictionary
LESSONS.hook: Somebody had to decide what every word means. Meet the stubborn, eccentric and occasionally imprisoned people who built the English dictionary.

sections.key: For most of its history, English had no dictionary of everyday words at all.
sections.b:
Shakespeare wrote his plays with no dictionary of ordinary English on his desk. That was normal. For centuries, English speakers simply used words and argued about them. The first English dictionaries appeared around 1600 and were modest. Robert Cawdrey's A Table Alphabeticall, published in 1604, listed only about 2,500 'hard words', mostly borrowed from Latin, French and Greek, for readers who found them puzzling.

Nobody thought ordinary words like 'dog' or 'run' needed defining. These early books were glossaries for the newly educated, not records of the whole language. The idea of capturing every word, common or rare, and how it was really used took another century and a half to arrive.

sections.key: Samuel Johnson built a landmark dictionary on evidence: quotations showing how good writers really used words.
sections.b:
In 1746 a group of London booksellers hired Samuel Johnson, a brilliant but often broke writer, to produce a proper dictionary. The French Academy had taken decades with dozens of scholars. Johnson, with a handful of assistants in a house off Fleet Street, took about nine years. His Dictionary of the English Language appeared in 1755 with roughly 42,000 entries.

Its real innovation was evidence. Johnson read widely, marked passages showing words in action and used more than 100,000 quotations to illustrate meanings. That method became the foundation of serious dictionary making in English. A few entries let his wit show, such as 'lexicographer: a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge', and his teasing definition of 'oats' as a grain 'which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people'.

sections.key: Noah Webster used his dictionary to give the United States its own, simpler spelling.
sections.b:
Across the Atlantic, the schoolteacher Noah Webster believed the new United States deserved its own version of English. He published An American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828 and used it to push spelling changes he thought simpler and more logical.

That is why Americans write 'color', 'center' and 'defense' while Australians, following British habits, write 'colour', 'centre' and 'defence'. Most of his more radical ideas never caught on, but his choices stuck in schools, newspapers and printing houses. One determined dictionary maker helped split English spelling into two traditions, which is why spellcheckers ask whether you want Australian or American English.

sections.key: The OED set out to trace the history of every English word, with help from an army of volunteer readers.
sections.b:
In 1857 the Philological Society in London called for a dictionary recording every English word since around the 12th century and how its meaning had changed. Scottish schoolmaster James Murray became editor in 1879 and worked in a corrugated iron shed, the Scriptorium, lined with pigeonholes for slips of paper. The first part appeared in 1884, covering only 'A' to 'Ant'. Murray died in 1915. The dictionary was finished in 1928, in ten volumes, roughly 70 years after it was proposed.

Murray appealed to the public to post in word examples on slips, and thousands of volunteers in Britain, America and Australia sent millions. One of the most productive was William Chester Minor, an American former army surgeon confined to Broadmoor, a hospital for the criminally insane, after killing a man in London in 1872.

sections.key: Modern dictionaries describe how people really speak rather than lay down the law.
sections.b:
Australia got its own major dictionary, the Macquarie, in 1981, recording words like 'arvo', 'doona' and 'ute' with Australian meanings and pronunciations. That reflects a bigger change in thinking. Early dictionary makers often wanted to fix the language and decide what was correct. Most modern lexicographers are descriptive instead: they observe how people actually use words and record it, including slang and new coinages.

When a dictionary adds a word, it is not approving it, only noting that enough people use it. Today editors search huge digital text collections to spot new words and shifting meanings, and online dictionaries are updated several times a year. Johnson's paper slips have become databases, but the goal is the same.

quiz.q: Why did the first English dictionaries only list 'hard words'?
o: Printers could not fit more words in a book
Ordinary words had not yet been invented
Governments restricted books about everyday speech
Ordinary words seemed obvious, so only unusual ones needed explaining
quiz.e: Early dictionaries were glossaries for newly educated readers, not records of the whole language.

quiz.q: What was Johnson's key innovation in dictionary making?
o: Choosing the correct meaning of each word by committee
Listing words in order of how often they were spoken
Defining words using quotations showing how good writers really used them
Copying the French Academy's method
quiz.e: Evidence from real use became the foundation of serious dictionary making in English.

quiz.q: Why do Americans write 'color' while Australians write 'colour'?
