sections.key: Before storm season, clear gutters, trim branches, check the roof and plan to secure loose items.
sections.b:
Much storm damage comes from flying debris and falling trees. Before the season, clean gutters and downpipes, trim overhanging branches (use a qualified arborist for large trees) and check the roof. List loose items such as trampolines, outdoor furniture, bins and pot plants to secure or bring inside when a warning is issued.

In cyclone areas, residents often fit shutters or protect windows, and learn whether their home was built to modern cyclone standards. Keep your emergency kit stocked, fill vehicles with fuel, and charge phones and power banks when a warning comes. Park cars under cover or away from trees if hail is forecast. For storm damage that is not life-threatening, call the SES on 132 500.

sections.key: Shelter in the strongest, windowless part of the building, beware the calm eye, and go indoors when you hear thunder.
sections.b:
In a severe storm or cyclone, the safest place is usually indoors in the strongest part of the building, often a small internal room such as a bathroom, laundry or hallway, away from windows. If the building breaks up, protect yourself under a sturdy table or mattress. In a cyclone, be wary of the calm eye: the wind drops and the sky may clear, then the winds return, often from the opposite direction and just as strong. Stay in until authorities say it has passed.

Lightning can strike many kilometres from the rain, so if you can hear thunder, you are in range. Go indoors or into a hard-topped car, and avoid open ground, water and isolated trees. It is safe to touch a lightning victim; call 000 and start CPR if they aren't breathing normally.

sections.key: Treat fallen power lines as live, avoid damaged buildings and floodwater, and be cautious with clean-up tasks.
sections.b:
The clean-up brings its own risks. Always assume fallen power lines are live. Stay well clear, at least 8 metres according to many electricity networks, and remember that water, fences and wet ground near a line can be electrified too. Report them to your electricity distributor, or call Triple Zero (000) if there is immediate danger.

Don't enter badly damaged buildings, and watch for broken glass, exposed nails and asbestos in older homes. Avoid driving through floodwater or under damaged trees. Chainsaw and ladder injuries are common after storms, so be cautious or leave big jobs to professionals and the SES. Photograph damage before clearing it, for insurance. This is general information; follow official advice for your area.

quiz.q: What does a cyclone's category describe?
o: Wind strength only, so low categories can still be deadly
Total danger including flooding and surge
Rainfall totals
How far inland it will travel
quiz.e: Weaker cyclones can still kill through flooding rain or storm surge.

quiz.q: Why might people in a storm surge zone be told to evacuate even from well-built homes?
o: Their homes will be blown over
Roads will be closed
Power will fail
The threat is rising water, not wind
quiz.e: Surge is a rise in sea level that building strength can't protect against.

quiz.q: Which is a sensible pre-season home task?
o: Cut the power at the mains
Park under overhanging trees
Clean gutters, trim branches and plan to secure loose items
Remove the roof gutters
quiz.e: Flying debris and falling trees cause much damage, and clear gutters help heavy rain drain.

quiz.q: What should you remember about the calm eye of a cyclone?
o: The cyclone is over, so go outside
The winds return, often from the opposite direction
It lasts for hours
It means the danger is lower
quiz.e: The calm is temporary and the winds return just as strong.

quiz.q: How should you treat a fallen power line?
o: Assume it is live and keep well clear
Move it with a stick
Touch it if it's dead
Ignore it
quiz.e: Lines and nearby wet ground or fences can be electrified.

LESSONS.push: A cyclone's category tells you about wind. It leaves out the bigger danger.

LESSONS.title: Staying alive on long drives
LESSONS.hook: Australia's long, empty roads are beautiful, but fatigue, wildlife and remote breakdowns catch out even experienced drivers. Here is how to make every road trip end safely.

sections.key: Country roads carry a disproportionate share of Australia's road deaths, and fatigue and distraction are the quiet killers on long drives.
sections.b:
There is something hypnotic about a long Australian highway: straight bitumen, red dirt, a horizon that never gets closer. That is part of the danger. Most Australians live in cities, yet a large share of road deaths happen on rural and regional roads, often in single-vehicle crashes where a car leaves the road or hits a tree. Speeds are higher, roads may be narrow or unsealed, and help can be hours away.

Road safety campaigns talk about the 'fatal five': speeding, drink and drug driving, not wearing a seatbelt, fatigue and distraction. On long drives the last two matter most, because they creep up on people who felt fine when they set out.

sections.key: Tired driving can be as dangerous as drink driving, and only sleep can fix it.
sections.b:
Being awake for a long time impairs reactions and judgement in a way research has compared to having alcohol in your blood. The scariest part is the microsleep: a few seconds when your brain switches off, often without you realising.

At 100 kilometres per hour a car covers nearly 28 metres every second, so a four-second microsleep carries you well over 100 metres with nobody in control. Warning signs include yawning, heavy eyes, drifting in your lane, missing signs and not remembering the last few kilometres.

Opening the window or turning up the music does not fix tiredness. The only real cure is sleep, so pull over somewhere safe for a rest or a power nap.

sections.key: Start well rested, take a break at least every two hours and share the driving.
sections.b:
Fatigue is far easier to prevent than to fight. Start a long drive well rested, and avoid setting out after a full day of work or when your body normally sleeps, such as late at night and in the mid-afternoon slump.

Road safety agencies commonly recommend a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours. Get out, walk around, and have a drink and a snack. Look for Driver Reviver sites, which often operate on major highways in holiday periods and offer free tea, coffee and a chat. If you can, share the driving with another licensed driver.

Be honest about how far you can go. An extra night in a motel is a small price compared with the cost of a crash.

sections.key: Brake firmly in a straight line rather than swerving hard for an animal, and give road trains and gravel plenty of respect.
sections.b:
Kangaroos, wallabies, wombats, emus and livestock are a real hazard, especially at dawn, dusk and night. Slow down where wildlife signs appear and scan the verges for eyes reflecting your headlights. If an animal jumps out, brake firmly in a straight line. Many serious crashes happen when drivers swerve, lose control and hit a tree or oncoming vehicle. Kangaroos can change direction suddenly, and where there is one there are often more.

Road trains, trucks towing several trailers, can stretch beyond 50 metres. Pass only with a long, clear view ahead. If one approaches on a narrow road, slow down and move left. On gravel, drive slower, avoid harsh braking and steering, and keep your headlights on in dust. Check road conditions first, as roads may close after rain.

sections.key: If you break down in remote country, stay with your vehicle, and know how to call Triple Zero (000) with your exact location.
sections.b:
Before heading remote, tell someone your route and arrival time. Carry far more water than you think you need, plus food, a first aid kit, a spare tyre and tools. Mobile coverage vanishes across much of Australia, so many travellers carry a satellite device or personal locator beacon.

If you break down, stay with your vehicle. It is far easier for searchers to spot than a person, and it gives shade. People have died walking away in extreme heat.

After a crash, get clear of traffic and turn on your hazard lights. Call Triple Zero (000) if someone is hurt or trapped, a vehicle is on fire or the road is blocked. The free Emergency+ app shows your GPS location to read to the operator. A first aid course will prepare you to help.

quiz.q: Why are long country drives especially risky?
o: Rural roads are always closed after dark
Higher speeds, distant help and monotonous scenery make lapses costly
Rural drivers are not required to wear seatbelts
Most country crashes involve overseas visitors
quiz.e: Speed, remoteness and a lulling landscape combine so that small lapses in attention can have severe consequences.

quiz.q: What makes a microsleep so dangerous at highway speed?
o: It always gives a long and obvious warning
It only affects drivers who have been drinking
It gives the driver a few seconds of rest
The car can travel over 100 metres with nobody in control
quiz.e: A few unnoticed seconds at 100 kilometres per hour covers a huge distance with no one driving.

quiz.q: How often do road safety agencies commonly recommend a break on a long drive?
o: Every two hours, for at least 15 minutes
Every six hours, for about five minutes
Only once you start to feel sleepy
Once at the halfway point of the trip
quiz.e: Regular breaks prevent fatigue building up, which is much easier than fighting it once it arrives.

quiz.q: A kangaroo leaps out in front of your car. What is the general advice?
o: Swerve hard to miss it
Speed up to get past it
Turn off your headlights
Brake firmly in a straight line
quiz.e: Swerving often causes the worst crashes, so braking in a straight line is usually safer.

quiz.q: Why is it usually best to stay with your vehicle if you break down in remote country?
o: A car is far easier for searchers to find and gives shade
Mobile coverage is better inside a vehicle
Walking at midday is the safest option
Search teams only look near roads at night
quiz.e: A vehicle is easy to spot and gives shelter, whereas people who walk away in the heat have died.

LESSONS.push: A four-second blink at 100 km/h covers over 100 metres. Here is how drivers lose them.

LESSONS.title: Heart attack and stroke: spotting the signs
LESSONS.hook: Heart attacks and strokes are medical emergencies where every minute counts. Recognising the warning signs, and calling for help fast, can save a life or prevent lifelong disability.

sections.key: In heart attacks and strokes, delay causes damage, so calling for help quickly matters more than anything.
sections.b:
A man feels heavy pressure in his chest while mowing the lawn and tells himself it is indigestion. A woman notices her husband's speech is slurred at dinner, but he says he is just tired. Scenes like these happen in Australian homes every day, and the delay can be devastating.

In a heart attack, part of the heart muscle is starved of blood. In most strokes, part of the brain is. The longer the blockage lasts, the more tissue dies, so doctors say 'time is muscle' for the heart and 'time is brain' for strokes. Modern hospital treatments can open blocked vessels, but many work best when given early, which only happens if someone calls for help quickly.

sections.key: A heart attack is a blocked artery starving the heart muscle, while a cardiac arrest is the heart's rhythm failing so it stops pumping effectively.
sections.b:
Your heart muscle is fed by its own blood vessels, the coronary arteries. Over years, fatty plaque can build up inside them. If a plaque cracks, a clot can form on top and block the artery. The heart muscle beyond the blockage is starved of oxygen and begins to die. Doctors call this a myocardial infarction, or heart attack.

It is different from a cardiac arrest, though the two are often confused. In a cardiac arrest, the heart's electrical rhythm goes haywire and it stops pumping effectively, so the person collapses, stops breathing normally and becomes unresponsive.

A heart attack can trigger a cardiac arrest, which is one reason it must never be ignored or treated as something to wait out.

sections.key: Warning signs vary and can be subtle, so if symptoms are severe, worsening or last more than 10 minutes, call Triple Zero (000).
sections.b:
The Heart Foundation describes warning signs such as pain, pressure, heaviness or tightness in the chest, which may spread to the arm, shoulder, neck, jaw or back. Others include shortness of breath, nausea, a cold sweat and feeling light-headed. Women, older people and people with diabetes may have less typical symptoms, such as unusual tiredness or breathlessness. Symptoms can come and go.

If you have warning signs, stop and rest. If they are severe, get worse quickly or last longer than 10 minutes, call Triple Zero (000) for an ambulance. Do not drive yourself, because paramedics can start treatment straight away. Follow the operator's advice, including any about aspirin. If the person collapses and is not breathing normally, start CPR and send for a defibrillator. Untrained bystanders can use one by following its spoken instructions.

sections.key: A stroke cuts blood supply to part of the brain, and if the Face, Arms or Speech are affected, it is Time to call Triple Zero (000).
sections.b:
Most strokes are ischaemic, caused by a clot or plaque blocking an artery to the brain. Others are haemorrhagic, where a blood vessel bursts and bleeds. Either way, brain cells lose oxygen and die. Researchers estimate that in a typical large stroke the brain can lose close to two million nerve cells every minute without treatment. Hospitals can now dissolve or remove many clots, but only if the person arrives quickly.

The Stroke Foundation's F.A.S.T. test is a simple check. Face: has the mouth drooped? Arms: can they lift both? Speech: is it slurred? Time: if you see any sign, call Triple Zero (000) straight away. Other signs include sudden one-sided weakness, vision loss, dizziness or a severe headache. Note when symptoms began. Give no food or drink, and stay with them.

sections.key: Stroke symptoms that vanish quickly still need urgent medical attention, and many risk factors can be reduced.
sections.b:
Sometimes stroke symptoms appear and then disappear within minutes or hours. This is often a transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, sometimes called a mini stroke. It can be a warning that a major stroke may follow, so it needs urgent medical attention even if the person feels fine.

For both heart attack and stroke, many risk factors can be reduced: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, physical inactivity, excess weight and heavy drinking. Regular health checks with a GP help find problems early.

This lesson is general information, not medical advice. For more, see the Heart Foundation, the Stroke Foundation and healthdirect. In an emergency, always call Triple Zero (000), and consider a first aid course, which teaches CPR and defibrillator use hands on.

quiz.q: Why do doctors say 'time is muscle' for heart attacks?
o: The heart grows stronger the longer it is blocked
Hospitals only treat heart attacks in the morning
The longer a blockage lasts, the more heart muscle dies
Muscle tissue repairs itself after a few minutes
quiz.e: Heart tissue starved of blood keeps dying, so quick treatment saves more of it.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a heart attack and a cardiac arrest?
o: A heart attack is a blocked artery; a cardiac arrest is the heart failing to pump
They are two names for exactly the same event
A cardiac arrest is a blocked artery; a heart attack is a stroke
A heart attack happens only to people who collapse
quiz.e: A heart attack is a plumbing problem, an arrest is an electrical one, and the first can trigger the second.

quiz.q: Why should someone with heart attack symptoms call an ambulance rather than drive?
o: Hospitals refuse patients who arrive by car
Ambulances are always faster than cars
Paramedics can start treatment at once and manage a cardiac arrest
It is illegal to drive with chest pain
quiz.e: Treatment starts as soon as paramedics arrive, and they can respond if the heart stops.

quiz.q: In the F.A.S.T. test, what does the A stand for?
o: Airway
Arms
Alertness
Ambulance
quiz.e: Checking whether the person can lift both arms is one quick way to spot a stroke.

quiz.q: Stroke symptoms vanish after 15 minutes. What should happen next?
o: Nothing, because it has passed
Wait a week and see if it returns
Seek urgent medical attention, as it may be a TIA
Rest until the next morning
quiz.e: A mini stroke can warn of a major stroke, so it still needs urgent care.

LESSONS.push: Some heart attack symptoms look nothing like the movies. Know the signs that count.

LESSONS.title: Lost in the bush: how to be found
LESSONS.hook: Every year in Australia, bushwalkers, campers and tourists get lost, and most are found alive. The ones who do best usually prepared before they left and stayed calm once things went wrong.

sections.key: Getting lost usually starts with small, ordinary mistakes, and the urge to keep moving often makes it worse.
sections.b:
Few people set out for an adventure that ends in a police search. More often it starts small. A walker follows a faint side trail that looks like a shortcut. A day hike runs late and the light fades. Mist rolls over a ridge and every gum tree looks the same. A tired walker takes a wrong turn at an unmarked junction and keeps going, hoping the track will reconnect.

Search and rescue teams know these patterns well. People rarely realise they are lost straight away, and the urge to keep moving and fix the problem quickly often carries them further from where searchers will look.

sections.key: Leave a trip plan, check conditions and carry a personal locator beacon, because a phone alone is not enough.
sections.b:
The most important safety step happens before you leave home. Tell a reliable person your route, when you expect to be back and when to raise the alarm. Check the weather, fire danger ratings and park alerts. Carry extra water and food, warm and waterproof layers, a torch, a first aid kit, and a map and compass or GPS, and know how to use them.

Do not rely on a phone alone, since coverage is patchy and batteries die. A personal locator beacon sends a distress signal by satellite to the Australian Maritime Safety Authority. Most include GPS, work almost anywhere with a clear view of the sky and need no subscription. Register yours with AMSA for free, and only activate it in a genuine life-threatening emergency.

sections.key: If you realise you are lost, stop moving, stay calm and make a plan, which is usually to stay where you are.
sections.b:
The moment you realise you do not know where you are, the most useful thing you can do is stop. Many outdoor organisations teach STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Sit down, have a drink of water and let the first rush of panic pass.

Think about when you last knew for certain where you were. Observe the time of day, the weather and how much water, food and battery you have. Then plan. If you can confidently retrace your steps to a known point, that may be sensible. If not, the best plan is usually to stay where you are, especially if someone knows your trip plan. Wandering further makes you harder to find, burns energy and water, and can lead into steep or dangerous country.

sections.key: Protecting yourself from the weather is more urgent than finding food.
sections.b:
Survival instructors use a rough rule of threes: around three hours in harsh conditions without shelter, around three days without water and around three weeks without food. The numbers vary greatly, but the order is useful.

In hot conditions, find shade, rest through the heat of the day and ration your effort rather than your water, drinking what you need. In cold, wet or windy conditions, which occur in alpine areas and Tasmania even in summer, hypothermia is a serious danger. Put on all your layers, get out of the wind, and insulate yourself from the cold ground with leaves, a pack or anything dry.

Food matters least. Most people can go several days without eating and still be found in reasonable health.

sections.key: Make yourself big, bright and noisy, stay near open ground, and call Triple Zero (000) if you have any signal.
sections.b:
Move to a clearing, track or open ridge if it is safe, as thick canopy hides you from the air. Lay out bright clothing or a space blanket. Three of anything, such as three whistle blasts, three flashes of light or three piles of rocks, is widely recognised as a distress signal. A whistle carries much further than a voice and uses less energy. A small mirror or phone screen can flash sunlight at aircraft.

If you have reception, call Triple Zero (000) and ask for police, who coordinate land searches. Your call can connect through another carrier's network, and the Emergency+ app shows your GPS coordinates. Then stay put, follow instructions and keep your phone in low power mode. A text to family may get through when a call will not.

quiz.q: What often carries lost walkers further from where searchers will look?
o: Staying in one spot and waiting
Wearing bright clothing in open ground
Carrying a whistle for signalling
The urge to keep moving to fix things fast
quiz.e: Moving on in a hurry usually takes you further from your planned route and from searchers.

quiz.q: Why carry a personal locator beacon rather than rely only on a phone?
o: It works beyond mobile coverage and sends your location by satellite
It replaces the need for a trip plan
It needs a monthly subscription to work
It can be used for any minor problem
quiz.e: A beacon can still raise the alarm where phones have no coverage or flat batteries.

quiz.q: What does the STOP approach stand for?
o: Sprint, Travel, Observe, Pause
Signal, Track, Orient, Proceed
Stop, Think, Observe, Plan
Stay, Talk, Open, Pray
quiz.e: Pausing to think and plan stops panic from driving you further into trouble.

quiz.q: According to the rule of threes, which need becomes urgent first?
o: Food
Finding a road
Lighting a large fire
Shelter from harsh conditions
quiz.e: You can last only hours in harsh weather, days without water and weeks without food.

quiz.q: Which is widely recognised as a distress signal?
o: Three whistle blasts, flashes or piles of rocks
One long, loud shout
Two waves of the arm
A single bright flash
quiz.e: Groups of three are widely recognised as a call for help and are easy to make.

LESSONS.push: Most people who get lost in the bush are found. What did the survivors do first?

LESSONS.title: Magnetism: the invisible pull
LESSONS.hook: A fridge magnet, a compass needle and the southern lights are all showing you the same hidden force at work.

sections.key: People used magnetic rocks and compasses for thousands of years before anyone could explain why they work.
sections.b:
Long before anyone understood it, people noticed that certain dark rocks pulled iron towards them. These lodestones are made of magnetite that has become naturally magnetised, possibly by lightning strikes. In China, lodestone spoons were said to swing round to point in a fixed direction, and by around the eleventh century Chinese sailors steered with magnetised needles. The compass later spread to the Arab world and Europe, where it helped make the great ocean voyages possible.

For centuries, nobody could say why a sliver of iron should care which way north was. The answer lay deep inside atoms, and deep inside the Earth itself.

sections.key: Every electron acts like a tiny magnet, and a material is magnetic when enough of them line up.
sections.b:
Each electron acts like a tiny bar magnet, thanks to a property called spin. In most materials, including wood, plastic, water and your body, electrons pair up and their effects cancel. In a few, unpaired electrons add together, and when enough point the same way, the object is magnetic.

Iron, nickel and cobalt are the classic magnetic metals. Their atoms group into domains, each already magnetised. In a nail the domains point every which way and cancel. Bring a strong magnet near and they swing into line, so the nail becomes a magnet for a while. Permanent magnets keep their domains aligned. Aluminium is barely magnetic, so a magnet ignores a soft drink can but grips a steel tin.

Heat scrambles the order. Above the Curie point, about 770 degrees Celsius for iron, the magnetism disappears.

sections.key: Moving electric charges make magnetism and moving magnets make electricity, which is why generators, motors and scanners work.
sections.b:
In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted saw a compass needle twitch when current flowed in a nearby wire: electricity can create magnetism. In 1831 Michael Faraday showed the reverse. Moving a magnet near a coil makes a current flow: electromagnetic induction. In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell showed electricity and magnetism are one force, and predicted waves travelling at the speed of light. Light, radio waves and X-rays are all electromagnetic waves.

Faraday's discovery powers your life. Nearly every power station spins a magnet and a coil past each other so induction pushes current through the coil. Motors run the trick backwards, in your fridge, washing machine and car windows. Speakers move a cone with a magnet and coil. MRI scanners line up hydrogen atoms in your body, then listen to their faint radio signals.

sections.key: Swirling molten iron deep underground makes Earth a giant magnet that deflects the solar wind.
sections.b:
The Earth behaves like a huge magnet, which is why compasses work. Its field is generated about 3,000 kilometres below your feet, in the outer core, where molten iron churns and flows like a natural dynamo. The field reaches far into space and deflects most of the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun.

Some particles are funnelled towards the poles, where they hit gases in the upper atmosphere and make them glow. In the Southern Hemisphere that glow is the aurora australis, sometimes seen from Tasmania.

The field is restless. The magnetic poles wander, and every so often the whole field flips. The last full reversal happened roughly 780,000 years ago.

sections.key: Many animals sense Earth's magnetic field to navigate, although exactly how is still being worked out.
sections.b:
Humans need a compass, but many animals seem to carry one inside them. Experiments show that migratory birds, sea turtles, salmon and even some insects use Earth's magnetic field to find their way. Young loggerhead turtles appear to read the field's strength and angle to stay on course across thousands of kilometres of ocean.

How they sense it remains one of biology's lingering puzzles. One leading idea is that light-sensitive proteins in birds' eyes react to magnetism, perhaps letting them 'see' the field as a faint pattern over their vision. Another is that tiny grains of magnetite in some animals' bodies act like compass needles. Both may be true in different species.

quiz.q: What are naturally magnetic rocks called?
o: Moonstones
Lodestones
Flintstones
Bloodstones
quiz.e: Lodestones are naturally magnetised magnetite, and they led to the compass.

quiz.q: Why is a nail not normally a magnet, even though iron is magnetic?
o: Its atoms contain no electrons
Heat has destroyed its magnetic properties
Aluminium in the nail cancels the effect
Its magnetic domains point in all directions and cancel out
quiz.e: Magnetism appears only when enough tiny magnets line up in the same direction.

quiz.q: What happens when you move a magnet near a coil of wire?
o: Nothing, unless the wire is hot
A current flows through the wire
The wire becomes a permanent magnet
The magnet loses its strength
quiz.e: This is electromagnetic induction, the principle behind nearly every power station.

quiz.q: What causes the aurora australis?
o: Sunlight reflecting off polar ice
Lightning high above the clouds
Solar particles funnelled to the poles making gases glow
Moonlight scattering through ice crystals
quiz.e: Earth's magnetic field steers the solar wind towards the poles, where it lights up the sky.

quiz.q: Which statement about animals and magnetism is accurate?
o: Only birds can sense the field
It works only at night
It was disproved in the 1990s
The sensing mechanism is still being worked out
quiz.e: Many animals use the field to navigate, but the sensing mechanism is still debated.

LESSONS.push: A rock that points north, and a force that links light to your fridge door.

LESSONS.title: How sound travels
LESSONS.hook: Every voice, song and thunderclap is just air being squeezed and stretched, and the physics explains everything from echoes to sonic booms.

sections.key: Sound is a travelling ripple of pressure, not a stream of air rushing from the source to your ear.
sections.b:
Clap your hands and you shove the air between them outwards. Those molecules bump their neighbours, which bump theirs, and a ripple of squashed and stretched air spreads in every direction. That ripple is sound. It is a pressure wave, and the air itself barely moves: each molecule nudges back and forth and passes the push along, like a ripple running down a slinky.

When the wave reaches you, it pushes and pulls on your eardrum, which vibrates in step. Tiny bones in your middle ear pass the vibration to the fluid-filled cochlea, where thousands of hair cells turn it into nerve signals. Your brain turns those signals into a friend's laugh or a favourite song.

sections.key: Sound travels about 343 metres per second in air, and much faster through water and solids.
sections.b:
In air at about 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels about 343 metres every second, roughly a kilometre in three seconds. Light is nearly a million times faster, which is why you see lightning before you hear thunder. Count the seconds between flash and rumble, then divide by three to estimate the storm's distance in kilometres.

Sound is faster in warm air than cold, and much faster through liquids and solids, where closely packed particles pass the push along. In seawater it travels at roughly 1,500 metres per second, and in steel several times faster again. That is why you can hear an approaching train through the rails before you hear it through the air.

sections.key: Pitch depends on how many times per second a wave vibrates, while loudness is measured in decibels on a scale where every 10 more means ten times the sound energy.
sections.b:
Pitch depends on frequency, the number of waves passing each second, measured in hertz. The A above middle C, used to tune orchestras, is 440 hertz. Young people typically hear about 20 to 20,000 hertz, shrinking with age. Elephants use infrasound below our range, while dogs, bats and dolphins hear ultrasound above it. Overtones make instruments sound different on the same note.

Loudness is measured in decibels on a logarithmic scale: every 10 decibels means ten times more sound energy, which we hear as roughly twice as loud. A library is around 30 to 40, conversation around 60 and a loud concert well over 100. Long or repeated exposure above roughly 85 decibels can permanently damage the hair cells in your inner ear. Healthdirect can help with ringing or muffled hearing.

sections.key: Returning echoes let animals and machines see with sound, and a moving source's pitch rises as it approaches and falls as it leaves.
sections.b:
Shout across a valley and the sound bounces back as an echo. Many bats send out rapid, high-pitched calls and judge the distance, size and texture of insects from the echoes, in total darkness. Dolphins use clicks underwater. This is echolocation. Ships use sonar to map the seafloor, and medical ultrasound builds an image from echoes off organs, which is how many parents first see their baby.

An ambulance siren drops in pitch as it passes, though the siren has not changed. As it approaches, waves bunch up and arrive more often; as it leaves, they stretch out. This is the Doppler effect, described by Christian Doppler in 1842. It works for all waves: police radar measures car speed, weather radar tracks wind in storms, and astronomers measure how fast galaxies move away.

sections.key: Sound needs something to travel through, and anything that outruns it creates a sonic boom.
sections.b:
Films are full of roaring explosions in space, but real space is silent. Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, and the near vacuum between planets has almost none to carry it. Astronauts on a spacewalk talk by radio, which uses electromagnetic waves that need no medium.

Back on Earth, something interesting happens when an object travels faster than sound. A supersonic jet outruns its own pressure waves, which pile up into a cone-shaped shock wave. When it sweeps over you, you hear a sudden sonic boom. The first officially confirmed supersonic flight was made by American pilot Chuck Yeager in the Bell X-1 rocket plane in 1947. A cracking whip makes a tiny sonic boom too.

quiz.q: What actually travels from a sound source to your ear?
o: A stream of air rushing towards you
A pressure wave passed between molecules
Tiny particles of sound
Light that your ears detect
quiz.e: The air itself barely moves; the pressure ripple does the travelling.

quiz.q: Thunder arrives six seconds after the lightning. Roughly how far away is the storm?
o: About 600 metres
About six kilometres
About twenty kilometres
About two kilometres
quiz.e: Sound covers about a kilometre every three seconds, so six seconds is roughly two kilometres.

quiz.q: An increase of 10 decibels means about how much more sound energy?
o: Twice as much
Ten per cent more
A hundred times as much
Ten times as much
quiz.e: The decibel scale is logarithmic, so small increases in the number are big jumps in energy.

quiz.q: Why does an ambulance siren drop in pitch as it passes you?
o: The driver changes the siren setting
Waves bunch up on approach and stretch out as it leaves
Sound slows down after passing you
Your ears get tired of the sound
quiz.e: The motion of the source changes how often waves reach you, which shifts the pitch.

quiz.q: Why would an explosion in space be silent?
o: Space is too cold for any vibration
Light travels too fast for sound to form
Almost no particles exist to carry the vibration
Astronauts' helmets block all noise
quiz.e: Sound is a vibration passed between particles, and the near vacuum has almost none.

LESSONS.push: You see lightning first for a reason. Count the gap and you can measure the storm.

LESSONS.title: Photosynthesis: how plants eat sunlight
LESSONS.hook: A towering gum tree is built mostly from thin air, and the process that does it also made the oxygen you are breathing.

sections.key: A tree's mass comes mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.
sections.b:
In the 1600s, the Flemish scientist Jan Baptist van Helmont planted a small willow in carefully weighed, dried soil and gave it nothing but water for five years. The willow gained a great deal of weight, yet the soil had barely changed. He concluded the tree was made from water. He was partly right, but he missed the most surprising ingredient.

Most of a plant's dry mass is carbon, and that carbon comes from carbon dioxide drawn out of the air. A huge gum tree is, in a very real sense, built from thin air, stitched together with water and powered by sunlight. The process that does this is called photosynthesis.

sections.key: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, and the oxygen they release comes from the water, not the carbon dioxide.
sections.b:
A plant draws water up from its roots and takes in carbon dioxide through tiny leaf pores called stomata. Using the energy in sunlight, it rearranges these into glucose, a sugar, and releases oxygen. In shorthand, six carbon dioxide plus six water become one glucose and six oxygen. Glucose is the plant's food and building material: burned for energy, stored as starch, or linked into cellulose for cell walls and wood. Almost every food you eat traces back to this reaction.

It seems natural that the oxygen comes from the carbon dioxide. But 1940s experiments with a traceable heavy oxygen showed it comes from water, which plants rip apart using light. Plants do this at ordinary temperatures, and researchers are still trying to copy it to make clean fuels such as hydrogen.

sections.key: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, which is the colour we see.
sections.b:
The green of leaves comes from chlorophyll, a pigment packed inside structures called chloroplasts. Chlorophyll is very good at absorbing red and blue light, which powers photosynthesis. It is poor at absorbing green, so much of that light bounces back towards our eyes.

Leaves also contain yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids. In many deciduous trees, autumn reveals them. As days shorten, the tree stops making chlorophyll and breaks down what it has, and the hidden yellows and oranges show through. Red autumn colours are different: they often come from new pigments made in the leaf at that time of year.

Most Australian native trees, including eucalypts, are evergreen, so our famous autumn displays usually come from introduced species.

sections.key: Light reactions capture energy and a second stage builds sugar, and some plants adapt the process to cope with heat and drought.
sections.b:
Photosynthesis has two linked stages in the chloroplast. First, chlorophyll absorbs light, splits water, releases oxygen and charges two energy-carrying molecules, ATP and NADPH, like freshly charged batteries. Second, in the Calvin cycle, those batteries power the building of sugar. An enzyme called RuBisCO grabs carbon dioxide from the air and fixes it into an organic molecule. RuBisCO is slow and sometimes grabs oxygen by mistake, so plants make vast amounts of it. It is probably the most abundant protein on Earth.

Opening stomata lets water escape, a problem in hot, dry places. Sugarcane, maize and Australia's spinifex grasses use C4 photosynthesis, concentrating carbon dioxide around RuBisCO. Cacti, pineapples and many succulents use CAM, opening their stomata only at night, storing carbon dioxide as an acid and using it by day with pores shut.

sections.key: Microbes that learned to photosynthesise filled the air with oxygen and transformed Earth.
sections.b:
Photosynthesis is far older than plants. Microbes developed it first, and one group, the cyanobacteria, worked out how to split water and release oxygen. Over hundreds of millions of years that oxygen built up, and around 2.4 billion years ago the atmosphere changed dramatically in the Great Oxidation Event.

Some early oxygen reacted with iron dissolved in the oceans, helping to form banded iron formations. Western Australia's Pilbara holds spectacular examples, and they supply much of the iron ore the country exports.

Today, tiny ocean plankton are thought to produce around half of the world's oxygen, with land plants providing much of the rest. Even the coal, oil and gas we burn are stored sunlight, captured by photosynthesis millions of years ago.

quiz.e: Plants build their bodies mainly from carbon taken from carbon dioxide in the air.

quiz.e: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects the green light it does not absorb.

LESSONS.push: A giant gum tree is mostly made of something you cannot see. What is it?

LESSONS.title: The cell: life's building block
LESSONS.hook: You are a walking city of tens of trillions of cells, each one a busy factory with its own power stations, post office and instruction library.

sections.key: Cells were first seen in the 1600s, and cell theory says all living things are made of cells and every cell comes from an existing cell.
sections.b:
In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through his microscope and saw rows of tiny empty boxes. They reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in, so he called them cells. He was seeing the walls of dead plant cells. Soon after, the Dutch draper Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who ground his own lenses, found pond water and tooth scrapings swarming with tiny living creatures: bacteria and other single-celled organisms nobody had seen before.

In the late 1830s Schleiden and Schwann argued that plants and animals are built from cells. In the 1850s Rudolf Virchow popularised the key addition: every cell comes from another cell. This overturned the belief that life springs from mud or rotting meat, and it let medicine understand disease as something going wrong in cells.

sections.key: An adult has roughly 30 trillion cells, each wrapped in a thin membrane that controls what gets in and out.
sections.b:
Recent estimates put an adult human at around 30 trillion cells, thousands of times more than the number of people on Earth. Most, by count, are red blood cells: tiny discs with no nucleus, built to carry oxygen. Some nerve fibres run a metre from spine to foot. You also carry a similar number of bacteria, mostly in your gut.

Every cell is wrapped in a membrane only a few billionths of a metre thick. It is a double layer of fatty molecules called phospholipids, with water-loving heads outside and water-avoiding tails inside. But a cell needs food in and waste out, so the membrane is studded with proteins that act as gates, pumps and messengers. Some let only certain substances through. Others receive signals from hormones or other cells.

sections.key: Cells contain specialised parts that store instructions, build proteins and supply energy.
sections.b:
A typical animal or plant cell is crowded with specialised parts called organelles. The nucleus is the control centre, holding the DNA with instructions for building proteins. Those instructions are copied and sent out, where ribosomes, tiny molecular machines, read them and assemble proteins one building block at a time.

A folded network called the endoplasmic reticulum helps make and transport many proteins, and the Golgi apparatus packages and labels them for delivery, a bit like a post office. Mitochondria release energy from food, producing ATP, a molecule that powers almost everything the cell does.

Plant cells also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a stiff wall for support. Bacteria are simpler cells with no nucleus; their DNA simply floats inside.

sections.key: Mitochondria are descended from free-living bacteria that were swallowed by another cell long ago.
sections.b:
One of biology's most surprising ideas is that parts of your cells were once separate living things. The theory, championed by Lynn Margulis from the late 1960s, says mitochondria began as free-living bacteria. More than a billion years ago, one cell engulfed another but did not digest it. The two formed a partnership: the guest supplied energy and the host supplied shelter and food. Over time the guest became a permanent part of the cell.

The evidence is strong. Mitochondria have their own small loop of DNA, similar to bacterial DNA, and they divide on their own, much as bacteria do. Chloroplasts in plants appear to have the same kind of origin, from captured cyanobacteria. You inherit your mitochondria from your mother.

sections.key: Cells constantly divide to grow and repair the body, and cancer happens when mutations break the controls on that division.
sections.b:
You began as a single fertilised egg, and every one of your trillions of cells came from that cell dividing again and again. Before dividing, a cell copies its DNA, then splits so each new cell gets a full set. This continues throughout life. The lining of your gut is renewed every few days, and red blood cells last about four months. Most nerve cells in your brain, however, are thought to last most of your life.

Division is tightly controlled by signals telling a cell when to grow, stop or die. Cancer is what happens when mutations break those controls, so cells keep dividing when they should not. Understanding the cell is why modern cancer treatments can target specific faults.

quiz.q: Which idea is part of cell theory?

quiz.e: Cells arise only from existing cells, which overturned the idea of spontaneous generation.

o: It controls what enters and leaves the cell

quiz.e: The membrane is a flexible border that lets in food, removes waste and receives signals.

quiz.q: What do ribosomes do?
o: Store DNA

quiz.e: Ribosomes read copied instructions and assemble proteins one building block at a time.

quiz.e: Having their own loop of DNA and dividing independently points to a bacterial ancestry.

quiz.q: What happens in cancer?
o: Cells stop copying their DNA
Cells die faster than the body can replace them
Nerve cells begin dividing normally
Mutations break division controls, so cells keep dividing
quiz.e: Cancer is a failure of the signals that tell cells when to grow, stop or die.

LESSONS.push: You carry about as many bacteria as human cells, and some live inside your cells.

LESSONS.title: Radioactivity: the restless atom
LESSONS.hook: Some atoms are quietly falling apart all around you, and learning to understand them gave us carbon dating, cancer treatment and nuclear power.

sections.key: Radioactivity was discovered in 1896 when uranium fogged photographic plates, and Marie Curie went on to name it and find two new elements.
sections.b:
In 1896 Henri Becquerel was testing whether uranium salts, after soaking up sunlight, gave off X-rays. Cloudy Paris weather interrupted him, so he put the salts and wrapped photographic plates in a drawer. When he developed the plates anyway, they showed clear images. The uranium was giving off invisible, penetrating radiation all on its own.

Marie Curie found the rays' strength depended on the amount of uranium, not its chemical form, so it came from inside the atom. She coined the word radioactivity. With her husband Pierre she discovered polonium, named for her homeland, and radium in 1898. She won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics and the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, the first person to win two. She died in 1934 of an illness linked to radiation exposure; her notebooks are still radioactive.

sections.key: Unstable atoms release three main kinds of radiation, each with very different penetrating power.
sections.b:
An atom is radioactive when its nucleus has an unstable mix of protons and neutrons. To settle down, it throws off energy or particles, called decay. In the early 1900s Ernest Rutherford and others identified three main types.

Alpha particles are clumps of two protons and two neutrons. They are heavy and slow, and a sheet of paper or the outer layer of your skin stops them, though they are harmful if breathed in or swallowed. Beta particles are fast electrons, stopped by a thin sheet of aluminium. Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves, like extremely powerful X-rays, and need thick lead or concrete to block them.

Alpha or beta decay turns an atom into a different element.

sections.key: No one can predict when a single atom will decay, but a large group decays at a perfectly regular rate called its half-life.
sections.b:
Radioactive decay is truly random. There is no way to predict when any particular unstable atom will break down. Yet in a large collection of atoms, the pattern is beautifully regular. The half-life is the time for half the atoms in a sample to decay. After one half-life, half remain; after two, a quarter; after three, an eighth.

Half-lives range from tiny fractions of a second to billions of years. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, roughly the age of the Earth. Carbon-14, constantly made in the atmosphere and absorbed by living things, has a half-life of about 5,730 years. Measuring how much is left in old bones, wood or charcoal lets scientists date them back roughly 50,000 years.

sections.key: Splitting heavy atoms releases enormous energy, which can power cities or, in weapons, destroy them.
sections.b:
In late 1938, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium, a much lighter element. Their former colleague Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out why: the nucleus had split in two. They called it fission.

The pieces weigh slightly less than the original atom, and the missing mass becomes a huge amount of energy, as Einstein's E equals mc squared predicts. Each split also frees more neutrons, which can split more atoms in a chain reaction. Controlled, the heat boils water to drive turbines in a nuclear power station. Uncontrolled, it is the basis of the atomic bomb.

Australia holds some of the world's largest known uranium resources, and whether it should have nuclear power remains a lively debate.

sections.key: Everyone receives low levels of natural background radiation, and carefully controlled radiation is one of medicine's most valuable tools.
sections.b:
Everyone receives low-level natural background radiation from rocks and soil containing uranium, thorium and potassium, from radon gas seeping out of the ground, and from cosmic rays, which is why long-haul flights add a little extra. Even bananas and your own body contain slightly radioactive potassium. The doses are tiny. In Australia, ARPANSA oversees radiation safety and publishes clear information.

The same property that makes radiation dangerous also makes it useful. Aimed radiotherapy beams destroy cancer cells while sparing as much healthy tissue as possible. Short-lived radioactive tracers reveal how the heart, bones or thyroid work. Technetium-99m has a half-life of about six hours and is made from materials produced at the OPAL reactor at Lucas Heights in Sydney. Talk to your doctor about any specific scan or treatment.

quiz.e: Natural background radiation is everywhere, including in food and in your own body, at very low doses.

LESSONS.push: A cloudy day in Paris in 1896 revealed a hidden property of matter. What was it?

LESSONS.title: Heat and temperature: what 'hot' really means
LESSONS.hook: Why does a tiled floor feel colder than carpet in the same room? The answer reveals what heat and temperature really are.

sections.key: Tiles feel colder than carpet at the same temperature because they pull heat away from your skin faster, and heat is energy flowing, not the same thing as temperature.
sections.b:
Step barefoot from carpet onto bathroom tiles on a winter morning and the tiles feel icy, though a thermometer would show both at the same temperature. Your skin does not sense temperature directly. It senses how quickly heat flows out of it. Tiles conduct heat well, so they pull warmth from your feet fast. Carpet traps air, a poor conductor, so it feels warmer. The same trick makes metal playground equipment burn in summer while a wooden bench feels merely warm.

Everything is made of moving atoms and molecules. Temperature measures how vigorously they move, on average. Heat is energy flowing from a hotter object to a cooler one. A bathtub of warm water holds far more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water, because it has vastly more molecules.

sections.key: Nothing can be colder than absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, where particle motion is at its minimum.
sections.b:
If temperature is jiggling, there must be a point where the jiggling is as small as it can be: absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. The Kelvin scale, named after Belfast-born Lord Kelvin, starts there, with steps the same size as Celsius degrees, so water freezes at about 273 kelvin. Atoms have been cooled to within billionths of a degree of it, where some metals become superconductors and some liquids flow without friction.

In the early 1700s Daniel Fahrenheit built accurate mercury thermometers, with water freezing at 32 degrees and boiling at 212. Anders Celsius proposed 100 degrees between the two; his original ran upside down, until it was flipped. Australia switched from Fahrenheit to Celsius in the early 1970s, which is why older Australians still talk of a 'century' for a 100 degree day.

sections.key: Heat travels by conduction through materials, by convection in moving fluids and by radiation through space.
sections.b:
Conduction is heat passing directly through a material, particle bumping particle, like a metal spoon warming in hot soup. Convection happens in liquids and gases, which can flow. Warm fluid is less dense and rises, cooler fluid sinks, and the circulation carries heat around. That is how a heater warms a room.

Radiation needs no material at all. Every warm object gives off infrared light, and that is how the Sun's warmth crosses 150 million kilometres of empty space to reach your face.

A vacuum flask blocks all three: the vacuum between its walls stops conduction and convection, and shiny surfaces reflect radiation back where it came from.

sections.key: Water needs a lot of energy to warm up, which moderates coastal weather and helps sweat cool your body.
sections.b:
Put a metal saucepan and the water inside it on the stove, and the pan gets hot long before the water does. Water has an unusually high heat capacity: it takes a lot of energy to raise its temperature, and it releases that energy slowly as it cools.

This shapes weather. Oceans warm and cool far more slowly than land, so coastal cities such as Perth and Sydney have milder swings in temperature than inland towns such as Alice Springs. On a hot afternoon, land heats faster than the sea, warm air rises over the land, and cooler air flows in from the ocean as a sea breeze.

Water's thirst for energy also cools you: as sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from your skin.

sections.key: A fridge does not make cold: it pumps heat from inside to outside using a fluid that evaporates and condenses.
sections.b:
Heat naturally flows from hot to cold, never the other way on its own. A fridge pushes it uphill, from the cold inside to the warmer kitchen, and pays for this with electricity.

The trick is a refrigerant circulating in a closed loop of pipes. Inside the fridge, it evaporates at low pressure, and evaporating soaks up heat, just as sweat cools your skin. A compressor then squeezes the vapour, making it hot, and it releases that heat through coils at the back or sides, which is why they feel warm. The fluid condenses back to a liquid and the cycle repeats.

Reverse-cycle air conditioners and heat pumps work the same way, often moving several units of heat per unit of electricity.

quiz.e: Your skin senses the rate heat leaves it, not the temperature itself.

quiz.e: Water's high heat capacity soaks up and releases heat slowly, which steadies nearby weather.

quiz.q: What does a refrigerator actually do?

quiz.e: A fridge moves existing heat uphill using a fluid that evaporates and condenses.

LESSONS.push: A tiled floor and a carpet sit in the same room. Why does one feel colder?

LESSONS.title: Enzymes: life's tiny machines
LESSONS.hook: Reactions that would take millions of years on their own happen in your cells in a split second, thanks to molecules called enzymes.

sections.key: Most of the reactions life depends on are far too slow without help, and enzymes are proteins that speed up specific reactions without being used up.
sections.b:
Your cells break down sugars, copy DNA, build proteins and clear waste every second. Left alone at body temperature, most of these reactions would crawl along at a hopeless pace, some taking millions of years. A lab chemist might use strong acids, high pressure or fierce heat, but none are options inside a cell. Life solved the problem with enzymes: large molecules, nearly all proteins, that make specific reactions happen enormously faster without being used up. Such molecules are called catalysts.

People used enzymes for thousands of years in brewing, baking and cheesemaking. In 1897 Eduard Buchner showed that juice from ground-up yeast, with no living cells, could still ferment sugar. In 1926 James Sumner crystallised the enzyme urease and showed it was a protein.

sections.key: Enzymes lower the energy hurdle a reaction must clear, so many more molecules make it over.
sections.b:
Picture a reaction as a ball that must be pushed over a hill before it can roll down the other side. That hill is the activation energy. Even if the products are more stable than the starting materials, few molecules have enough energy to get over the top, so the reaction is slow.

An enzyme provides an easier route, effectively lowering the hill. It can hold reacting molecules close together in exactly the right orientation, stretch or strain chemical bonds so they break more easily, and position charged parts of itself to stabilise the awkward arrangement at the top of the hill.

An enzyme does not change where the reaction ends up, only how quickly it gets there, and it emerges unchanged, ready to work again.

sections.key: An enzyme works because of its precisely folded shape, so heat or acidity that unravels the fold stops it working.
sections.b:
Enzymes are choosy. Most work on one molecule, or a small family, called substrates. An enzyme is a chain of amino acids folded into a precise shape, with a pocket called the active site. In 1894 Emil Fischer likened the fit to a key in a lock. In 1958 Daniel Koshland refined this with induced fit: the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate, like a glove tightening around a hand.

Disturb the fold and the enzyme stops working. Warming speeds an enzyme up at first, but beyond a point heat shakes the fold apart, called denaturation. You see it in a cooked egg: the white turns solid as its proteins unravel, for good. Most human enzymes work best near body temperature. Pepsin thrives in strong stomach acid; small-intestine enzymes prefer milder conditions.

sections.key: Cells control their enzymes with feedback and inhibitors, and many medicines work by blocking enzymes.
sections.b:
A cell cannot leave all its enzymes running at full speed, or it would waste resources and overproduce some products. So enzymes are regulated. Often the end product of a chain of reactions binds to an enzyme near the start and slows it down, a neat feedback that keeps supplies in balance. Other molecules act as inhibitors, either jamming the active site or binding elsewhere and changing the enzyme's shape.

Medicine makes heavy use of this. Aspirin works partly by blocking enzymes involved in making substances that cause pain and inflammation. Penicillin blocks enzymes bacteria need to build their cell walls. Many other drugs target specific enzymes too. This is general information only, so ask a doctor or pharmacist about any particular medicine.

sections.key: Enzymes quietly work in washing powders, food production and research, and scientists now design new ones.
sections.b:
Biological laundry powders contain enzymes that break down protein, fat and starch stains, so they work well in cooler water. Cheesemakers have long used rennet, which contains an enzyme that curdles milk. Enzymes help clarify fruit juice, make sweet syrups from starch and tenderise meat. Papaya and pineapple contain such enzymes, which is why fresh pineapple can stop jelly setting.

In research, an enzyme from a hot spring bacterium, able to survive repeated heating, made possible the PCR technique used to copy DNA. Scientists are now improving enzymes and designing new ones. Frances Arnold shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using directed evolution to breed better enzymes in the lab.

quiz.e: Enzymes make specific reactions happen far faster and are left unchanged to work again.

quiz.e: Enzymes in fruit such as pineapple and papaya break down the proteins that make jelly set.

LESSONS.push: Reactions that should take millions of years happen in your cells in a blink. How?

LESSONS.title: The secret life of soil
LESSONS.hook: The ground beneath your feet is not dirt: it is a living, breathing system that took thousands of years to build and feeds almost everything on land.

sections.key: Healthy soil teems with life, from bacteria and fungi to worms and insects.
sections.b:
A handful of healthy soil is one of the most crowded habitats on Earth. Soil scientists often note that a single teaspoon can hold more microorganisms than there are people on the planet. Bacteria, fungi, single-celled protists and microscopic nematode worms share the space with mites, springtails, beetle larvae, ants and earthworms. Most of these organisms have never been studied, and many have not been named.

The earthy smell after rain comes partly from geosmin, a compound made by certain soil bacteria. People are remarkably sensitive to it. Far from lifeless dirt, soil is a busy underground city where life is recycled day and night.

sections.key: Soil takes centuries to form from rock, so soil lost to erosion is effectively gone for good.
sections.b:
Soil begins as rock. Heat and cold, freezing water, plant roots and rainwater slowly break it apart. Lichens and mosses colonise the surface and add organic material as they die. Microbes and small animals mix it with mineral grains, and layers form: dark, humus-rich soil near the top, paler mineral layers below, then the parent rock.

This is extremely slow. A few centimetres of new soil can take hundreds of years or more, so soil lost to erosion is effectively lost for good. In the 1930s, drought and poor farming on the American Great Plains caused the Dust Bowl, when dust storms stripped away topsoil and forced many families off their farms. Soil is also estimated to hold more carbon than the atmosphere and all living plants combined.

sections.key: The mix of sand, silt and clay controls how soil holds water, air and nutrients.
sections.b:
The mineral part of soil comes in three particle sizes. Sand is the largest and feels gritty. Silt is finer and smooth, a bit like flour. Clay is tiny and sticky when wet. Their balance gives a soil its texture, and texture matters enormously.

Sandy soil drains fast and warms quickly but holds little water or nutrients. Clay holds plenty of both but can become waterlogged, and sets hard when dry. Gardeners prize loam, a mix of all three, which holds moisture while still letting air reach the roots. A simple test: roll a moist pinch between your fingers. Clay forms a ribbon, and sand falls apart.

sections.key: Fungi trade water and nutrients for plant sugars, while worms and decomposers recycle dead material.
sections.b:
Most land plants partner with fungi in relationships called mycorrhizae. The plant supplies sugars from photosynthesis. In return, fungal threads called hyphae spread far beyond the roots and bring back water and nutrients, especially phosphorus. The partnership is ancient and may have helped the first plants colonise land. Claims that forests share food and warnings through a 'wood wide web' are debated, so treat them with caution.

Earthworms swallow soil and decaying matter, leave nutrient-rich castings, and open tunnels for air and water. Darwin devoted his last book, in 1881, to them. Bacteria and fungi break dead material into substances plants can absorb again. Victoria's giant Gippsland earthworm can reach about a metre long.

sections.key: Many Australian soils are old and low in nutrients, and native plants have adapted in clever ways.
sections.b:
Australia's soils are often very old and very poor. Much of the land has been stable for a long time, without recent glaciers grinding up fresh rock or widespread volcanoes spreading mineral-rich ash. Over millions of years, rain has leached out many nutrients, and phosphorus is often scarce.

Native plants have adapted. Banksias, grevilleas and their relatives grow dense mats of fine cluster roots that release chemicals to free up tightly bound phosphorus. Some natives are even harmed by the phosphorus in ordinary garden fertiliser. Farmers have long added fertilisers such as superphosphate, and scientists study how to farm these soils without degrading them or causing salinity. Serious erosion and dust storms have happened here too. The community Landcare movement began in Victoria in the late 1980s and now has thousands of local groups repairing land.

quiz.q: Why does the ground smell earthy after rain?
o: Rain releases chlorophyll from the roots of grass
Soil bacteria make geosmin, which people detect easily
Methane bubbles up from wet soil
Humus dissolves into the rainwater
quiz.e: Geosmin, made by certain soil bacteria, is a key part of that earthy smell.

quiz.q: Why is soil lost to erosion effectively lost for good?
o: A few centimetres of new soil can take hundreds of years to form
New soil forms within a single growing season
Rock can no longer break down into soil
Farmers cannot grow crops in new soil
quiz.e: Soil forms extremely slowly, so on a human timescale eroded soil does not come back.

quiz.q: Why do gardeners prize loam?
o: It drains water faster than any other soil
It is made entirely of fine clay particles
It sets hard so roots stay anchored
It holds moisture while still letting air reach the roots
quiz.e: Loam mixes sand, silt and clay, balancing water retention with airflow.

quiz.q: What is the trade in a mycorrhizal partnership?
o: The plant supplies water and the fungus supplies sugars
The plant supplies seeds and the fungus supplies oxygen
The plant supplies sugars and the fungus supplies water and nutrients
The plant supplies nitrogen and the fungus supplies sunlight
quiz.e: Plants pay in photosynthesis sugars, and fungi return water and nutrients such as phosphorus.

quiz.q: How have banksias adapted to phosphorus-poor soil?
o: They grow only in swamps
They grow cluster roots that free up bound phosphorus
They absorb phosphorus from the air
They trap insects to digest for phosphorus
quiz.e: Cluster roots release chemicals that unlock scarce phosphorus from the soil.

LESSONS.push: Soil scientists say one teaspoon can hold more life than there are people.

LESSONS.title: Hammurabi's Code: law carved in stone
LESSONS.hook: Nearly 4,000 years ago a Babylonian king had his laws carved into a towering black stone for everyone to see. It is one of the oldest legal texts we can still read, and it is far stranger and more human than 'an eye for an eye' suggests.

sections.key: The best-known copy of Hammurabi's laws was found in Iran in 1901, far from Babylon, where it was made.
sections.b:
In the winter of 1901 to 1902, French archaeologists at Susa, in what is now south-western Iran, unearthed three pieces of polished black stone. Fitted together, they formed a pillar over two metres tall, covered in tiny wedge-shaped cuneiform writing in the Akkadian language. It was a law code issued by Hammurabi, king of Babylon, who ruled from about 1792 to 1750 BCE. But Susa is not in Babylon. Scholars think an Elamite king carried the stone off as war plunder in the 12th century BCE. It now stands in the Louvre in Paris.

Hammurabi began as ruler of one city among several competing ones in Mesopotamia. Over about four decades, diplomacy, alliances and war brought much of the south and centre under his control.

sections.key: The stone presents the king's laws as justice backed by the gods, meant to protect the weak from the strong.
sections.b:
Running a large kingdom meant managing canals, taxes and disputes between people with different local customs. Letters from Hammurabi's reign show a hands-on ruler, writing to officials about everything from flood repairs to a single stolen field. His law collection, probably set up late in his reign, was meant to show that he had brought order and fairness.

At the top of the stone, a carving shows Hammurabi standing before a seated god, usually identified as Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. A prologue lists the king's achievements, then come the laws, then an epilogue. In it he says he set up the laws so the strong would not oppress the weak, and invites any wronged person to have the stone read to them.

sections.key: The roughly 282 laws cover ordinary life, from farming and trade to marriage and medicine.
sections.b:
Scholars count about 282 laws, though a section near the end was deliberately rubbed away in antiquity and has been partly recovered from other copies. Most follow a simple pattern: if someone does this, then this happens.

The subjects are surprisingly ordinary. There are rules on renting fields and boats, interest on loans, wages for workers, fees for doctors, inheritance, divorce and the care of children. A builder whose badly built house collapsed and killed its owner could be put to death. A tavern keeper who cheated customers over beer could be punished. Reading the laws is like looking through a window at the worries of ordinary Babylonians: debts, floods, unpaid bills and family quarrels.

sections.key: Punishments depended heavily on the social rank of both victim and offender.
sections.b:
The code's most famous principle is retaliation: if a man destroys the eye of another man, his own eye will be destroyed. But this applied mainly between people of the same high status. Babylonian society had roughly three ranks: free citizens, a middle group of commoners or dependants, and enslaved people.

If a free man blinded a commoner, he paid a fine in silver instead. If he injured an enslaved person, he paid compensation to the owner. Women's rights depended on their family position, and some laws protected wives and widows. The code is both fair-minded and deeply unequal, a reminder that every legal system reflects the values of its time.

sections.key: Older law codes existed, historians debate how the code was used, and its lasting idea is public, written law.
sections.b:
Hammurabi is often called the first lawgiver, but older collections survive, including one linked to Ur-Nammu of Ur, roughly three centuries earlier. His stone stands out because it is so complete.

Historians also debate its purpose. Thousands of Babylonian contracts and court records survive, yet they rarely cite the code. Many scholars think it was less a statute book than a royal showcase of wise judgments for judges and scribes to learn from. Scribes copied it for centuries.

Its big ideas still matter: laws should be written down and public, punishment should be proportionate, judges should not change decisions once made, and false accusers should be punished. They resurface from Roman law to modern Australian courts.

quiz.q: Why was the best-known copy of the code found in Iran rather than Babylon?
o: Hammurabi ordered it carved at Susa
Babylonian merchants traded it to Susa
Scholars think an Elamite king took it as war plunder
French archaeologists moved it there in 1901
quiz.e: It was made in Babylon and carried to Susa centuries later as plunder.

quiz.q: What did Hammurabi say his laws were meant to achieve?
o: That the strong would not oppress the weak
That every citizen would pay equal taxes
That foreign kingdoms would pay tribute
That priests would hold all legal power
quiz.e: The epilogue presents the laws as protection for the weak, backed by the sun god of justice.

quiz.q: What kind of matters do most of the laws cover?
o: Religious rituals
Military strategy
Royal ceremonies
Everyday matters such as trade, wages, debts and family
quiz.e: The laws are full of ordinary concerns such as loans, fees, inheritance and building.

quiz.q: What usually happened if a free man blinded a commoner?
o: He lost his own eye
He paid a fine in silver
He was banished from Babylon
He faced no consequence
quiz.e: Exact retaliation applied mainly between equals, while injuring a lower-ranked person usually meant a payment.

quiz.q: Why do many historians doubt the code worked like a modern statute book?
o: It was destroyed soon after it was made
It contained only a handful of laws
Surviving contracts and court records rarely cite it
It was kept secret from judges
quiz.e: Babylonian legal documents seldom refer to it, so it may have been a model of royal justice instead.

LESSONS.push: Why the same injury could cost a fine or an eye in ancient Babylon.

LESSONS.title: Trial by jury: twelve ordinary people
LESSONS.hook: Somewhere in Australia today, twelve strangers are sitting in a small room deciding whether someone is guilty of a serious crime. Why do we hand such power to ordinary citizens, and what actually happens if your name is drawn?

sections.key: Jurors are drawn at random from the electoral roll, and answering a summons is a legal duty.
sections.b:
An envelope from the sheriff's office or court tells you that you have been selected for possible jury service. It is a normal part of being enrolled to vote: in every state and territory, potential jurors are chosen at random from the electoral roll. Not everyone summoned serves. Some people are ineligible, such as many lawyers, police officers and politicians, and others can be excused for good reasons, like caring duties or serious hardship.

Respond by the deadline, because ignoring a summons can lead to a fine. Employers generally cannot penalise you for serving, and jurors receive an allowance, though amounts and wage top-ups vary by state. This is general information, not legal advice, so check your state or territory court's juror pages.

sections.key: Juries replaced trial by ordeal in England, and a 1670 case made jurors free from punishment for their verdicts.
sections.b:
In early medieval England, guilt could be tested by ordeal: carrying a red-hot iron or being lowered into water, with the outcome believed to reveal God's judgment. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council banned priests from taking part, which made ordeals unworkable. Courts turned to groups of local men already asked about crimes in their area, who gradually became neutral judges of evidence.

In 1670 the jury trying Quakers William Penn and William Mead refused to convict, even after the judge locked the jurors up and fined them. Juror Edward Bushel challenged his imprisonment. In Bushel's Case, Sir John Vaughan ruled that jurors cannot be punished for a verdict the judge dislikes. The principle travelled with English law to Australia.

sections.key: Juries mainly hear serious criminal trials, usually with twelve members.
sections.b:
Most legal matters in Australia do not involve a jury. Minor offences and most civil disputes, such as contract claims, are decided by a magistrate or judge alone. Juries mainly decide serious criminal cases, such as murder, sexual offences, serious assault and large-scale fraud, and criminal juries usually have twelve members.

Section 80 of the Constitution says a trial on indictment for a Commonwealth offence must be by jury, though the High Court has read that protection fairly narrowly. In some states an accused person can choose a judge-alone trial in certain circumstances. Civil juries are rare, but some states still allow them in particular cases, such as some defamation claims.

sections.key: Jurors decide the facts from the evidence presented in court, while the judge explains the law.
sections.b: The judge controls the courtroom, rules on evidence and explains the law. The jury decides what actually happened. In a criminal case, jurors must be satisfied of guilt beyond reasonable doubt, a high standard designed to protect innocent people from wrongful conviction. They must decide only on evidence presented in court. Doing your own research, searching online about the case or visiting the scene can be a criminal offence, because it can lead to an unfair trial. Jury room discussions stay confidential even after the case ends. Verdicts traditionally had to be unanimous, but most states now allow majority verdicts in some circumstances after long deliberation. Some trials involve distressing evidence, and courts in most states offer free, confidential counselling to jurors afterwards.

sections.key: Supporters value juries as a democratic check on the state, while critics question their consistency and cost.
sections.b:
Supporters say juries bring community values into the courtroom and check the power of the state, since a government cannot imprison someone for a serious crime without convincing ordinary citizens. Juries also spread responsibility for grave decisions across many people and give citizens a direct role in justice. Many jurors find the experience absorbing and meaningful.

Critics raise real concerns. Complex fraud or scientific evidence can be hard for non-experts to follow, jury trials take longer and cost more, and jurors may be swayed by media coverage or personal impressions. Some countries, such as Japan, use mixed panels of judges and citizens instead. Most Australian legal experts accept the system is imperfect, and debate about how to improve it continues.

quiz.q: Where do Australian courts draw potential jurors from?
o: Tax office records
The electoral roll
Driver licence databases
Online volunteers
quiz.e: Jurors are chosen at random from people enrolled to vote.

quiz.q: What did Bushel's Case in 1670 establish?
o: Jury verdicts must always be unanimous
Women could serve on juries
Jurors cannot be punished for a verdict the judge dislikes
Judges could overrule any verdict
quiz.e: The ruling made a jury's verdict its own, free from official pressure.

quiz.q: Which cases do juries mainly decide in Australia?
o: Serious criminal cases such as murder and serious assault
Most civil disputes, such as contract claims
Minor offences such as parking fines
Appeals heard by the High Court
quiz.e: Minor offences and most civil matters go to a magistrate or judge alone.

quiz.q: Why must jurors avoid researching a case online?
o: Court websites block such searches
It is allowed but frowned upon
It only matters in civil trials
It can be a criminal offence and cause an unfair trial
quiz.e: Jurors must decide only on the evidence presented in court.

quiz.q: What is one common criticism of jury trials?
o: Juries always favour the prosecution
Complex evidence can be hard for non-experts to follow
Juries are chosen by politicians
Jurors never get to hear any evidence
quiz.e: Critics worry about complex cases, cost, delays and outside influence.

LESSONS.push: Ordinary people can decide a murder trial. How that works, and why.

LESSONS.title: Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys
LESSONS.hook: Who makes the laws, who carries them out, and who decides what they mean? Keeping those three jobs apart is one of the oldest safeguards against tyranny, and Australia does it in its own distinctive way.

sections.key: Government power splits into three jobs, and keeping them apart makes abuse of power harder.
sections.b:
Imagine a vault that needs three keys turned at once, held by three different people. No one can empty it alone. That is the idea behind the separation of powers. The legislature makes laws; in Australia, that is Parliament. The executive runs the country day to day, including the Prime Minister, ministers and the public service. The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes: the courts. If one group controlled all three, it could write any rule, enforce it however it liked and judge its own case.

The French thinker Montesquieu made the case in The Spirit of the Laws (1748): liberty is at risk when one body both makes and enforces laws, or when judges are not separate from rulers. His reading of England was imperfect, but his argument shaped modern democracies.

sections.key: The United States separates its three branches strictly and builds in checks and balances.
sections.b:
The framers of the United States Constitution in 1787 took Montesquieu seriously.
