quiz.e: Viewing from opposite sides of Earth's orbit makes nearby stars shift against distant ones, and geometry gives the distance.

quiz.q: What did Henrietta Leavitt discover about Cepheid variables?
o: The slower they pulse, the more brightly they truly shine
They are all the same distance from Earth
They are planets orbiting distant stars
They only appear in the Southern Hemisphere
quiz.e: A Cepheid's pulse rate reveals its true brightness, and comparing that with its apparent dimness gives distance.

quiz.q: Why are Type Ia supernovae useful for measuring distance?
o: They never fade
They explode consistently, so their peak brightness is known
They are the closest stars to Earth
They always occur in our own galaxy
quiz.e: A known brightness lets astronomers work out distance from how dim the explosion looks.

quiz.q: What is the Hubble tension?
o: Redshift not being linked to distance at all
Cepheids failing to pulse regularly
Disagreement between the expansion rate from the ladder and from the Big Bang afterglow
The universe slowing down faster than predicted
quiz.e: Two good methods give different expansion rates, which might point to an error or to missing physics.

LESSONS.push: Nobody has stretched a tape measure to a star. So how do we know how far?

LESSONS.title: First Nations astronomy
LESSONS.hook: Long before telescopes, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples read the night sky as a calendar, a map, a law book and a library of stories.

sections.key: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have read the night sky for many thousands of years, with knowledge that differs between nations.
sections.b:
Australia's First Peoples have lived on this continent for at least 50,000 years, and many researchers think longer. For all that time they have looked up at the same southern sky, and their knowledge of it is woven through culture, law and daily life.

There is no single "Aboriginal astronomy". Australia has hundreds of distinct nations and language groups, each with its own stories and ways of reading the sky, though some stories are shared across vast distances. The stars were used to tell the seasons, find food, navigate, mark ceremonies and pass on rules for living. Some of this knowledge is sacred and not for public sharing.

sections.key: Many groups see an emu in the dark dust lanes of the Milky Way, and its changing position tracks the emu breeding season.
sections.b:
Western constellations join up bright stars. Many Aboriginal traditions also look at the spaces between them. The best known example is the Emu in the Sky. Its head is the Coalsack, a dark dust cloud beside the Southern Cross, and its neck, body and legs stretch along dark lanes in the Milky Way.

On autumn evenings, after dark, the emu appears to be running across the sky. For a number of groups this coincides with the time emus are mating and laying eggs, a signal for when eggs could be collected. Later in the year the emu's shape appears to change position, reflecting different stages of the breeding cycle.

sections.key: The Pleiades star cluster is the heart of the Seven Sisters story, which links sites across thousands of kilometres of desert.
sections.b:
The Pleiades, a small, tight cluster of stars, has inspired stories in cultures from ancient Greece to Japan. In Australia it is the heart of the Seven Sisters, one of the most widespread and important Aboriginal stories.

In many desert versions, sisters are pursued across the country by a man, often linked to stars in the constellation Westerners call Orion. As they flee, their journey creates and names features of the landscape, forming songlines: routes that link sites over thousands of kilometres and carry knowledge, law and ceremony.

In 2017 the National Museum of Australia staged Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, developed with Anangu, Martu and Ngaanyatjarra communities and sharing parts of the story through paintings, song and dance.

sections.key: Star figures such as Tagai, and the seasonal appearance of particular stars, guide when to plant, fish, hunt and expect weather changes.
sections.b:
For Torres Strait Islanders, the most important sky figure is Tagai, a great fisherman standing in his canoe. In common descriptions, his left hand holds a fishing spear, the Southern Cross, and his right hand holds a sorbi fruit, the stars of Corvus. His canoe and crew are made of other stars. Tagai teaches the importance of following rules and sharing, and his position guides when to plant, fish and hunt turtle and dugong.

Across Australia, stars appearing at dawn or dusk signal events on the ground. In the 1850s William Stanbridge recorded Boorong knowledge in north-western Victoria, including a star linked to when malleefowl build nesting mounds. These calendars are tailored to local country, since seasons differ across Australia.

sections.key: First Nations sky knowledge includes careful observations of tides, eclipses and variable stars, and it belongs to specific communities.
sections.b:
Sky knowledge was not only stories; it recorded careful observations. The Yolngu of north-east Arnhem Land link the tides to the Moon, describing the Moon filling with water as tides rise, which captures a real connection. Several groups have stories explaining eclipses, often as the Sun woman and Moon man coming together. Researchers have found traditions that appear to describe changing brightness in stars such as Betelgeuse and Antares, which astronomy recognises as variable. Some scholars think stories about Wolfe Creek Crater may preserve memories of real events, though that is hard to prove.

To learn more, seek sources made by or with communities, such as Aboriginal-run tours and museum resources. Stories differ between nations, and some knowledge is restricted.

quiz.q: Why is there no single 'Aboriginal astronomy'?
o: The sky looks different in every state
Hundreds of distinct nations each have their own stories and ways of reading the sky
Most knowledge was lost long ago
Only a few groups ever observed the stars
quiz.e: Knowledge is held by specific nations, so stories from one group should not be assumed to apply everywhere.

quiz.q: What forms the Emu in the Sky?
o: The brightest stars of Orion
The planets along the ecliptic
The dark dust lanes of the Milky Way
The Magellanic Clouds
quiz.e: Many traditions read the dark spaces between stars, with the Coalsack forming the emu's head.

quiz.q: What do songlines in the Seven Sisters story do?
o: Predict when comets will return
Link sites across the land and carry knowledge, law and ceremony
Show the dates of eclipses
Measure the distances between stars
quiz.e: The sisters' journey creates and names landscape features that connect country across thousands of kilometres.

quiz.q: How did many communities use the appearance of particular stars?
o: To measure how far away stars were
To predict earthquakes
To tell the time of day
As seasonal calendars for food, breeding and weather
quiz.e: Stars at dawn or dusk signalled events on country, so calendars are tailored to local seasons.

quiz.q: What do the Yolngu understand about tides?
o: They are caused by the wind
They are linked to the Moon
They happen only at night
They are caused by whales
quiz.e: Yolngu knowledge connects the Moon to the tides, matching the real cause.

LESSONS.push: Long before telescopes, the dark gaps between stars told people when to hunt.

LESSONS.title: How touchscreens feel your finger
LESSONS.hook: Your phone screen has no buttons, yet it knows exactly where you tapped, swiped or pinched. The secret is that your finger is part of an electrical circuit.

sections.key: A touchscreen is a transparent sensor over a display, and older resistive screens work when pressure pushes two conductive layers together.
sections.b:
Pick up your phone and tap an app. The glass does not move or click, yet the phone responds instantly. A touchscreen is really two things stacked together: a display that shows pictures, and a transparent sensor on top that works out where your fingers are, measuring tiny electrical changes many times a second.

The first touchscreens most people met were resistive, on early handheld organisers, GPS units, some ATMs and signature pads. Two thin, flexible conductive layers sit separated by a tiny gap. When you press, the top layer touches the bottom one, completing a circuit at that spot. Resistive screens work with a fingernail, a gloved hand or a stylus. But they need a firm press, feel spongy and traditionally handled one touch at a time.

sections.key: Modern capacitive screens detect how your conductive fingertip disturbs a small electric field in a grid of transparent electrodes.
sections.b:
Almost every modern smartphone uses a capacitive screen. Your body conducts electricity, mainly because it is full of salty water. Beneath the glass sits a fine grid of transparent electrodes, usually made from indium tin oxide, which conducts electricity while letting light through. The grid holds a small electric field.

When your fingertip comes close, it disturbs that field and changes the capacitance, the ability of nearby conductors to store electric charge, at the points nearest your finger. You do not need to press at all; a light brush is enough. That is why capacitive screens feel so responsive, and why they are covered by tough, smooth glass rather than soft plastic that has to bend.

sections.key: A controller chip scans a grid of electrodes many times a second to pinpoint every finger, and software works out what you meant.
sections.b:
The electrodes are laid out in rows and columns, like lines on graph paper. A controller chip rapidly tests each crossing, measuring how much its capacitance has shifted. Where a finger rests, a cluster of crossings changes, and the chip calculates the cluster's centre. Because each crossing is measured separately, the screen tracks several fingers at once. This projected capacitance is what makes multi-touch gestures such as pinch to zoom possible.

The sensor only reports where fingers are; software decides what you meant. It tells a tap from a long press by timing, a swipe from a scroll by speed, and a pinch by tracking two points. Tablets use palm rejection to ignore your hand, and some phones add haptic feedback, a tiny vibration that fools your fingertip into feeling a click.

sections.key: Gloves insulate your fingertip so the screen cannot sense it, while water droplets can mimic a touch.
sections.b:
Capacitive screens explain some everyday frustrations. Ordinary woollen or leather gloves insulate your fingertip, so the screen cannot sense it. That is why touchscreen gloves have conductive thread woven into the fingertips. A standard plastic stylus does nothing for the same reason, so styluses for phones have conductive tips.

Water is the opposite problem. Droplets on the glass conduct enough to disturb the field, so a wet screen may register phantom taps or ignore real ones. Manufacturers use software to tell the small, steady signal of a raindrop from the moving signal of a finger, and some phones have a wet touch mode. Even so, using your phone in heavy rain or underwater remains unreliable for most people.

sections.key: Capacitive touchscreens date back to the 1960s, but the 2007 iPhone made them universal.
sections.b:
Touchscreens are older than many people assume. In the mid 1960s British engineer E. A. Johnson, at the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, described a capacitive touchscreen intended for air traffic control displays. In the early 1970s engineers at CERN, the European physics laboratory near Geneva, built capacitive touchscreens to control a particle accelerator. Resistive screens developed around the same era and spread through industry, kiosks and handheld gadgets.

The big leap into everyday life came in 2007, when Apple launched the first iPhone with a multi-touch capacitive screen designed for fingers rather than a stylus. Within a few years, physical keyboards on phones had largely disappeared, and swiping had become something even toddlers attempt on picture books.

quiz.q: What makes a resistive touchscreen register a touch?
o: Heat from your fingertip
Pressure pushing two conductive layers together
Light blocked by your finger
Sound waves crossing the glass
quiz.e: Pressing completes a circuit between two layers, which is why a stylus or gloved hand works.

quiz.q: Why can your finger operate a capacitive screen?
o: Your skin is slightly magnetic
Your fingertip reflects infrared light
Your fingerprint ridges grip the glass
Your body conducts electricity and disturbs the screen's electric field
quiz.e: A conductive fingertip changes the capacitance at the points nearest it.

quiz.q: What does projected capacitance make possible?
o: Tracking several fingers at once for multi-touch
Screens that work through thick gloves
Charging the phone through the screen
Brighter display colours
quiz.e: Each electrode crossing is measured separately, so multiple touches can be told apart.

quiz.q: Why do touchscreen gloves work when ordinary gloves do not?
o: They are thinner than ordinary gloves
They warm the screen as you touch
They have conductive thread in the fingertips
They contain tiny magnets
quiz.e: Conductive fingertips let the electrical effect of your finger reach the screen.

quiz.q: What was different about the 2007 iPhone's screen compared with many earlier ones?
o: It needed a firm press from a stylus
It used a multi-touch capacitive screen designed for fingers
It only worked with a gloved hand
It was the first touchscreen ever built
quiz.e: Multi-touch capacitive screens designed for fingers made touch interfaces mainstream.

LESSONS.push: Your phone feels your finger without a single button. It is borrowing from you.

LESSONS.title: How Wi-Fi works (and an Aussie connection)
LESSONS.hook: Every time you stream a show on the couch, your devices are holding a fast, invisible radio conversation. Part of the technology that makes it reliable came from Australian radio astronomers.

sections.key: Wi-Fi is a set of shared rules for sending data by radio, mainly on the 2.4 and 5 gigahertz bands.
sections.b:
Sit in a café and you are surrounded by conversations you cannot hear. Phones, laptops and smart speakers all talk to wireless routers by radio. Wi-Fi is simply a set of agreed standards that let devices from different companies exchange data through the air. The name is a brand, coined in 1999, and it does not officially stand for anything; "wireless fidelity" is a popular myth.

It is the same basic physics as FM radio, just at higher frequencies. Most Wi-Fi uses around 2.4 gigahertz and 5 gigahertz, and newer gear can use 6 gigahertz where allowed. Each band is divided into channels, like motorway lanes. The 2.4 gigahertz band travels further and passes through walls better, while higher bands carry more data but fade faster, so modern routers usually offer both.

sections.key: Your router links your devices to the internet, and devices sharing a channel take turns, which is why crowded networks feel slow.
sections.b:
The box in your hallway is several devices in one. A modem part connects to your internet service, such as the NBN. A router part gives each device a local address and directs traffic. An access point part converts data to Wi-Fi signals and back.

A channel is shared space, like a room where only one person can speak clearly at a time. Devices listen before they transmit, and if the channel is busy they wait a short, random time. Data travels in packets, the receiver confirms each one, and lost ones are resent. When many devices and neighbouring networks crowd the same channel, everyone waits longer. That is why an apartment block in the evening can feel sluggish even on a fast plan.

sections.key: Distance, brick, concrete, metal, water and interference all weaken Wi-Fi signals, and echoes cause trouble too.
sections.b:
Radio waves spread out and weaken with distance, and lose strength passing through obstacles. Brick, concrete and metal block Wi-Fi especially well, which is why a router in one corner of a double brick house may struggle to reach the far bedroom. Water absorbs these frequencies too, so fish tanks and even crowds of people can dampen a signal. Mirrors and metal appliances reflect it.

There is also interference. Microwave ovens work at roughly the same frequency as 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi, so heating leftovers can briefly disrupt a nearby connection. And signals bounce off walls and furniture, arriving several times with slight delays, a problem that turned out to be crucial in Wi-Fi's history.

sections.key: CSIRO scientists helped solve the indoor echo problem, and their patent earned Australia hundreds of millions of dollars.
sections.b:
In the early 1990s a CSIRO team led by radio astronomer John O'Sullivan set out to make fast wireless networking work indoors. The obstacle was echoes: signals bouncing around a room smeared into each other and scrambled the data.

Drawing partly on techniques for sharpening faint signals in radio astronomy, the team developed a way of spreading data across many frequencies and correcting for the echoes. CSIRO patented the approach, and it became important to fast Wi-Fi standards. CSIRO later took legal action against major technology companies over the patent, and the settlements brought in hundreds of millions of dollars. Many Australians proudly call Wi-Fi an Aussie invention, though in truth it combined work from many people and countries.

sections.key: Place the router centrally and in the open, update it, and secure it with a strong password.
sections.b:
A few habits improve most home networks. Put the router somewhere central and elevated, out in the open rather than in a cupboard, behind the television or on the floor. Keep it away from microwaves and large metal objects.

In bigger or multi-storey homes, a mesh system uses several units that talk to each other to blanket the house, which usually works better than a single powerful router. Restart and update your router occasionally, since manufacturers fix bugs and security holes. Protect your network with a strong password and the newest security option your devices support, typically WPA3 or WPA2.

Finally, Wi-Fi only covers the last few metres. If your internet plan itself is slow, no router can fix that.

quiz.q: What is true about the 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi band compared with higher bands?
o: It always carries more data
It cannot pass through walls
It travels further and passes through walls better
It is only used by microwave ovens
quiz.e: Lower frequencies reach further, while higher bands carry more data but fade faster.

quiz.q: What do Wi-Fi devices do before transmitting on a shared channel?
o: Raise their power to drown out others
Listen to check whether the channel is busy
Switch to a cable connection
Ask the internet provider for permission
quiz.e: Listening and waiting a random time avoids collisions, but crowded channels still slow everyone down.

quiz.q: Why can a microwave oven interfere with Wi-Fi?
o: It uses the same electrical circuit
It permanently blocks all radio waves
It resets nearby routers
It operates at roughly the same frequency as 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi
quiz.e: Overlapping frequencies mean a running microwave can briefly disrupt nearby connections.

quiz.q: What problem did the CSIRO team help solve?
o: Signal echoes scrambling data indoors
Batteries draining too quickly
Viruses spreading over networks
Routers overheating
quiz.e: They found a way to spread data across many frequencies and correct for echoes.

quiz.q: Where is the best place for a home router?
o: Inside a cupboard to hide it
Somewhere central and elevated, out in the open
Behind the television on the floor
Next to the microwave oven
quiz.e: Open, central, raised placement avoids obstacles and sources of interference.

LESSONS.push: Heating leftovers can briefly disrupt your Wi-Fi. Here is the physics.

LESSONS.title: Where the cloud really lives
LESSONS.hook: Your photos, emails and streamed shows are not floating in the sky. They live in giant, humming buildings full of computers, and those buildings are some of the most carefully guarded places on Earth.

sections.key: The cloud means using computers owned by someone else, kept in warehouse-sized data centres full of servers.
sections.b:
Take a photo and a copy may be backed up to the cloud within moments. The word suggests something weightless, but the reality is metal, cables and electricity. The cloud simply means using computers that belong to another company, reached over the internet. When you check email in a browser, stream a show or save to an online drive, the work and storage happen in a data centre, possibly thousands of kilometres away.

A large data centre looks like a library where the shelves are computers. Tall racks hold servers, computers without screens or keyboards, stacked like pizza boxes. Fibre optic lines, often from several providers, link it to the internet. Hyperscale sites can hold tens of thousands of servers, protected by fences, guards, mantraps and biometric checks.

sections.key: Servers turn electricity into heat, so cooling is one of a data centre's biggest engineering jobs.
sections.b:
Every server turns electricity into heat, and thousands packed together could quickly cook themselves. Many data centres arrange racks in alternating hot and cold aisles: cool air is pushed through the front of the servers and hot air is captured from the back. Large chillers, fans and cooling towers then remove the heat.

Some facilities use water to cool, which raises concerns in dry regions. Others pump liquid directly to the hottest chips, an approach that has become more common as artificial intelligence hardware runs hotter. Some companies build in cold climates, such as the Nordic countries, to use chilly outside air, and a few have experimented with reusing waste heat to warm nearby homes.

sections.key: Backup power keeps data centres running through blackouts, and multiple copies of your data mean one failure does not lose it.
sections.b:
A data centre cannot switch off during a storm. If the grid supply flickers, banks of batteries in an uninterruptible power supply take over instantly. Within seconds to minutes, large diesel or gas generators start and carry the load for as long as their fuel lasts. The system is tested regularly.

Hard drives fail all the time, and in a building with thousands of them, some fail every day. So an uploaded photo is typically stored as several copies, or split into pieces with extra error-correcting information, across different drives and machines. Important services also copy data to separate buildings or regions. This redundancy is why a cloud backup is generally safer than one external drive in a drawer. Still, accounts get hacked and services shut down, so keep precious files in more than one place.

sections.key: Content delivery networks keep copies of popular content on servers near users so it loads faster.
sections.b:
When you press play on a popular show, the video probably does not travel from a central data centre overseas. Streaming services and many websites use content delivery networks, which keep copies of popular content on servers close to where people live, including in Australian cities and inside some internet providers' networks.

Your request is quietly directed to the nearest suitable server, so the video starts faster and long international links are not clogged with millions of identical streams. The same trick speeds up news sites, software updates and online games.

This matters in Australia, which is far from many of the world's big data hubs, so every round trip to the United States or Europe adds a noticeable delay.

sections.key: Data centres use roughly one to two percent of the world's electricity, and where your data is stored can matter legally.
sections.b:
Convenience has a footprint. Estimates from bodies such as the International Energy Agency suggest data centres use somewhere around one to two percent of the world's electricity, and demand is rising quickly as artificial intelligence grows. Big cloud companies have signed deals to buy large amounts of renewable energy, though how green any particular data centre is can be complicated.

In Australia, Sydney and Melbourne host most data centres, and new projects compete for grid connections and land. Location also matters legally. Data stored in another country may be subject to that country's laws, so governments, banks and health services often require sensitive information to stay onshore. As a user, delete things you no longer need, and check where and how a service stores your data, especially anything personal or confidential.

quiz.q: What does 'the cloud' really refer to?
o: Data stored in satellites
Wireless signals in the air
A special part of your phone's memory
Computers owned by another company, reached over the internet
quiz.e: Your files sit on physical machines in data centres that you will probably never see.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of hot and cold aisles in a data centre?
o: To manage airflow so servers stay cool
To separate staff from visitors
To store spare parts
To divide different customers' data
quiz.e: Cool air enters the front of the servers and hot air is captured from the back.

quiz.q: Why do cloud services keep multiple copies of your data?
o: To charge you more for storage
So a failed drive or building does not lose it
To make files load in colour
Because the law forbids single copies
quiz.e: Redundancy protects against drive failures, fires and outages.

quiz.q: Why do streaming services use content delivery networks?
o: To encrypt passwords
To block advertising
To cool their servers
To store copies of popular content close to viewers
quiz.e: Nearby copies start faster and avoid clogging long international links.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the world's electricity do data centres use, according to estimates?
o: About one to two percent
About ten percent
About a third
Less than one hundredth of one percent
quiz.e: The share is modest but rising quickly as artificial intelligence grows.

LESSONS.push: Your photos are not floating in the sky. Here is where they actually sit.

LESSONS.title: Inside the battery in your pocket
LESSONS.hook: Lithium-ion batteries power your phone, laptop, cordless drill and maybe your car. Knowing how they work explains why they slowly fade, and how to make them last longer.

sections.key: A lithium-ion battery works by shuttling lithium ions between two electrodes while electrons do useful work through your device.
sections.b:
Every time you unplug your phone, you carry a small chemical machine. A lithium-ion battery has an anode, usually graphite, and a cathode made from a lithium compound with metals such as cobalt, nickel, manganese or iron. Between them sit an electrolyte, which lets lithium ions pass, and a thin porous separator that stops the electrodes touching.

When the battery powers your phone, lithium ions travel through the electrolyte from anode to cathode. Electrons take the long way round, through the phone's circuits. That flow of electrons is the current doing useful work. Charging pushes everything back the other way.

sections.key: Lithium is the lightest metal and gives up electrons easily, so it stores a lot of energy for its weight.
sections.b:
Lithium is the lightest metal, and it is eager to give up an electron. Together, those traits let a battery store plenty of energy without much weight.

Compared with older rechargeables such as nickel cadmium, lithium-ion batteries hold far more energy for their size and lose little charge sitting on a shelf. They also avoid the memory effect that once led people to drain batteries fully before recharging. That combination made truly portable electronics possible.

Australia has a direct stake in this story. It is one of the world's largest miners of lithium, much of it dug from hard rock deposits in Western Australia and shipped overseas for processing.

sections.key: The lithium-ion battery took decades and many researchers, and three of them shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
sections.b:
In the 1970s, during the oil crisis, British chemist M. Stanley Whittingham built an early rechargeable lithium battery. It used pure lithium metal and could be dangerous.

Around 1980, American physicist John Goodenough, working at Oxford, found a cobalt oxide cathode with much higher voltage. In the mid 1980s, Japanese chemist Akira Yoshino swapped the reactive lithium metal for a carbon-based anode, creating a far safer design.

Sony sold the first commercial lithium-ion batteries in 1991, in a video camera. The three scientists shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Goodenough was 97, the oldest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize.

sections.key: Batteries fade through chemistry that heat speeds up, so keep devices cool and avoid long stretches at completely full or completely empty.
sections.b:
Your battery holds less charge after a couple of years because of chemistry, not a conspiracy. Each cycle swells and shrinks the electrodes, and side reactions use up lithium. A crust grows on the anode and traps lithium that can no longer carry charge. Heat speeds this up, so a hot car dashboard in an Australian summer is especially bad. Long periods at completely full or empty add stress.

Phones charge fast to about 80 percent, then slow down on purpose to avoid damage. Partial top-ups are fine. Keeping charge roughly between 20 and 80 percent helps, and optimised charging settings do this for you. Use reputable chargers. Cold only reduces performance temporarily.

sections.key: A damaged lithium-ion battery can overheat and catch fire, so stop using swollen or hot batteries and never put used ones in household bins.
sections.b:
Lithium-ion batteries are generally very safe, but they pack a lot of energy and a flammable electrolyte. If one is crushed, punctured, badly made or overcharged without protection, an internal short circuit can heat it. That heat triggers more reactions in a spiral called thermal runaway, which can cause fire. These fires are hard to put out and can reignite. Warning signs are swelling, hissing, unusual heat or a strange smell. Stop using and charging the device, and check your fire service's advice.

Crushed batteries cause fires in garbage trucks and recycling centres. Keep them out of kerbside bins. Use a drop-off point, such as the B-cycle scheme's supermarket and hardware store collection points, and tape the terminals first.

quiz.q: What happens inside the battery as it powers your phone?
o: Lithium ions move from the anode to the cathode while electrons travel through the circuits
Electrons travel through the electrolyte while lithium ions travel through the circuits
The lithium is burned off gradually to release heat that becomes electricity
The separator slowly dissolves and releases stored charge into the phone
quiz.e: Ions move through the electrolyte and electrons take the outside route, and that flow of electrons is the current.

quiz.q: Why is lithium so well suited to portable batteries?
o: It is very light and gives up electrons easily
It is very dense and holds charge by sheer weight
It is cheap and never needs to be mined
It reacts slowly, so it loses charge on a shelf
quiz.e: Being the lightest metal and an eager electron donor lets lithium store lots of energy for little weight.

quiz.q: Why was replacing lithium metal with a carbon-based anode important?
o: It made the battery much safer
It doubled the voltage of the cell
It let the battery charge in seconds
It removed the need for an electrolyte
quiz.e: Pure lithium metal is reactive and could be dangerous, so a carbon anode produced a far safer design.

quiz.q: Which habit is most likely to help your phone battery last longer?
o: Keeping it out of heat and avoiding long spells fully flat or fully charged
Draining it to zero every time before recharging
Leaving it on a car dashboard to stay warm
Only ever charging it when it is completely empty
quiz.e: Heat and long stretches at the extremes stress the battery, and partial charges are fine.

quiz.q: What should you do with a used lithium-ion battery?
o: Take it to a battery drop-off point, with the terminals taped
Put it in the kerbside recycling bin with other items
Put it in the general rubbish if it looks undamaged
Keep it in a hot place until the charge runs out
quiz.e: Batteries crushed in bin trucks can ignite, so use a drop-off point such as the B-cycle scheme.

LESSONS.push: Your phone's battery is fading, and heat is the quiet culprit. Here's the chemistry.

LESSONS.title: The internet lives under the sea
LESSONS.hook: When you video call someone overseas, your voice almost certainly travels as flashes of light through a cable lying on the ocean floor. These hidden lines carry the vast majority of the world's international data.

sections.key: Almost all international internet data travels through cables on the sea floor, not satellites.
sections.b:
Ask people how the internet crosses oceans and many guess satellites. Satellites matter for remote areas, ships and planes, but the overwhelming majority of data between continents travels through cables on the sea floor.

Several hundred submarine cables are in service, stretching well over a million kilometres in total. When you email London, join a meeting with colleagues in Singapore or watch an overseas video that isn't cached locally, your data races through them. Cables are faster, carry vastly more data and cost far less per bit than satellites, which is why they dominate.

sections.key: Submarine cables carry data as pulses of laser light along hair-thin glass fibres, boosted along the way by repeaters.
sections.b:
At the heart of a cable are a handful of optical fibres, strands of extremely pure glass about as thin as a human hair. Lasers send pulses of light down each one, and the light stays inside by reflecting off the glass boundary. Modern systems send many colours down the same fibre at once, each carrying its own stream.

Layers of protection surround the fibres: gel, steel wires, a copper layer to carry power and plastic insulation. In the deep ocean, a cable may be only as thick as a garden hose.

Light fades over distance, so repeaters spaced roughly 50 to 100 kilometres apart boost it with optical amplifiers. Power reaches them along the copper layer from shore stations.

sections.key: Cables are laid by specialised ships along a surveyed route, and are armoured and buried near shore where anchors and fishing gear pose a risk.
sections.b:
Before laying, surveyors map the seabed and avoid steep slopes, rocky ridges, undersea volcanoes and busy anchorages. Specialised cable ships then carry thousands of kilometres of cable coiled in huge tanks.

In deep water, the ship slowly pays out the cable, which sinks to rest on the sea floor, sometimes more than eight kilometres down. Closer to shore, where fishing and anchors pose dangers, the cable is thicker and more heavily armoured, and a plough often buries it in a trench. It comes ashore at a landing station.

A long cable can take many months to lay, and projects often cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

sections.key: Cables break often, mostly from human activity rather than sharks, and traffic is rerouted while repair ships fix them.
sections.b:
Cables do break. Industry groups estimate well over a hundred faults worldwide each year. Most come from people, particularly fishing trawlers dragging gear and ships dropping or dragging anchors. Earthquakes and underwater landslides cause others. Sharks have been filmed biting cables, but they are not a significant cause of damage.

When a fault occurs, traffic is usually rerouted over other cables, so users may only notice slower speeds. A repair ship then finds the break, lifts the cable with a grappling hook or a remotely operated vehicle, splices in a new section on deck and lowers it back. Many countries protect cable zones near their coasts.

sections.key: Undersea cables are older than the internet: telegraph cables cut message times between Australia and Britain from weeks to hours, and Australia still depends on them.
sections.b:
In 1858, a telegraph cable across the Atlantic let Queen Victoria and US President James Buchanan exchange messages. It failed within weeks, partly because operators applied too much voltage. In 1866, the steamship Great Eastern laid a durable one. Insulation was gutta percha, a natural latex.

Australia joined the network in 1872, when the Overland Telegraph from Adelaide to Darwin linked to an undersea cable north toward Java. Messages that took weeks by ship now arrived within hours.

Today almost all of Australia's international traffic still depends on cables, landing mainly near Sydney and Perth, plus Darwin and the Sunshine Coast. Protection zones restrict anchoring and some fishing. Tech giants now help fund new cables, and governments treat them as critical infrastructure.

quiz.q: How does most international internet traffic cross the oceans?
o: Through cables laid on the sea floor
Through satellites orbiting above the Earth
Through radio towers on ships
Through cables strung between islands above water
quiz.e: Cables are faster, carry far more data and cost less per bit than satellites, so they dominate.

quiz.q: Why do long submarine cables include repeaters?
o: Light fades over distance, so the signal needs boosting
The glass fibres cannot carry any light more than a few metres
They convert the signal into radio waves for the final stretch
They stop sharks from biting the cable
quiz.e: Even pure glass dims the light gradually, so powered repeaters amplify it every 50 to 100 kilometres or so.

quiz.q: Why is a cable thicker and often buried near the shore?
o: Fishing gear and anchors are a danger in shallow water
The water is colder there and the glass would crack
Ships need to lift it for inspection each year
Waves would otherwise wash it into the open ocean
quiz.e: The deep sea is relatively undisturbed, so protection is added where human activity is heavy.

quiz.q: What causes most submarine cable faults?
o: Human activity such as trawlers and anchors
Sharks biting through the cable
Overheating of the glass fibres
Solar storms disrupting the light
quiz.e: Fishing gear and anchors cause most breaks, while sharks are not a significant cause.

quiz.q: What changed for Australia when the 1872 telegraph link opened?
o: Messages to Britain arrived within hours instead of taking weeks or months
Australia gained its first radio broadcasts
Letters to Britain were no longer sent by ship at all
The first satellite link connected Darwin and Java
quiz.e: Telegraph cables cut communication times between Australia and Britain from weeks to hours.

LESSONS.push: Your video call to London doesn't go through space. It goes through the ocean floor.

LESSONS.title: Babbage, Lovelace and the first computer
LESSONS.hook: In the 1830s, long before electricity was in homes, a cranky English mathematician designed a programmable computer made of brass gears. A young countess saw what it could become.

sections.key: Babbage wanted machines to calculate error-free mathematical tables, because human 'computers' and typesetters let mistakes creep in.
sections.b:
In the early 1800s, sailors, engineers, astronomers and bankers relied on thick books of mathematical tables: logarithms, tide times, star positions and interest calculations. People called 'computers', a job title long before it meant a machine, worked them out, and typesetters copied them by hand. Errors crept in at every stage, and a wrong digit in a navigation table could put a ship on the rocks.

Charles Babbage, a brilliant and famously argumentative English mathematician, was frustrated. By his own later story, while checking tables with his friend John Herschel, he wished steam could do the calculations.

sections.key: The Difference Engine turned table-making into repeated addition that gears could do, but it was never completed in Babbage's time.
sections.b:
In the 1820s, Babbage designed a machine to produce tables mechanically. It used the method of differences, which turns many formulas into repeated addition, something gears can do reliably. It would even print results, removing copying errors.

The British government funded it, and Babbage hired a skilled engineer, Joseph Clement. A small working section impressed visitors. But the machine needed thousands of precisely machined parts, and disputes over money and tool ownership plagued the project. Work stopped in the early 1830s.

By then Babbage had become distracted by a far more ambitious idea.

sections.key: The Analytical Engine was a general-purpose design with memory, a processor, punched-card instructions and decision-making, which makes it the first design for a computer.
sections.b:
The Analytical Engine could do any calculation. It had a 'store' for holding numbers and a 'mill' for arithmetic, roughly what we now call memory and a processor. Instructions came on punched cards, an idea borrowed from the Jacquard loom, which wove complex patterns into silk.

Crucially, the machine could choose what to do next based on its own results, and repeat sets of instructions. Those features mean it could follow programs, the defining trait of a computer.

Babbage refined the design for decades, but the Analytical Engine was never built.

sections.key: Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes gave the clearest account of the Analytical Engine, including a step-by-step method often called the first published computer program.
sections.b:
Augusta Ada Byron was born in 1815, the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron, who left when she was a baby. Her mother ensured she had an unusually strong education in mathematics and science. Around seventeen, Ada met Babbage and saw part of the Difference Engine. She was captivated, and later, as Countess of Lovelace, kept up a lively correspondence with him.

In 1842, Luigi Menabrea published a paper describing the Analytical Engine. Lovelace translated it and added notes about three times longer. In Note G she set out a method to calculate the Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program. Historians debate how much was Babbage's, but her notes were the clearest account of the time.

sections.key: Lovelace saw that a computer could work on any symbols, not just numbers, and in 1991 a working Difference Engine proved Babbage's design sound.
sections.b:
Babbage mostly saw a powerful calculator. Lovelace saw more: the engine could manipulate any symbols whose relationships follow rules. If musical sounds could be captured that way, she speculated, it might compose music. She also cautioned that it could only do what it was instructed to do. In 1950, Alan Turing called this 'Lady Lovelace's objection'. She died in 1852, aged 36.

Was Babbage too far ahead of his time, or were his designs flawed? The Science Museum in London built his Difference Engine No. 2 from his drawings, using tolerances achievable in his era. Finished in 1991, it worked. A programming language, Ada, is named for her.

quiz.q: What problem was Babbage trying to solve?
o: Human errors in hand-calculated and hand-copied mathematical tables
A shortage of mathematicians to teach navigation
The high cost of printing books of tables
Slow postal delivery of astronomical data
quiz.e: Errors crept in at every stage of making tables, and mistakes could have serious consequences such as shipwrecks.

quiz.q: Why were gears able to calculate tables in the Difference Engine?
o: The method of differences turns many formulas into repeated addition
It used steam to solve equations directly
It stored every possible answer in advance
It relied on punched cards to guess results
quiz.e: Repeated addition is something gears can do reliably, which made mechanical table-making possible.

quiz.q: What made the Analytical Engine a design for a true computer?
o: It could follow programs, with decisions and repeated instructions
It could print tables faster than the Difference Engine
It was powered by steam rather than by hand
It was built from more gears than any earlier machine
quiz.e: Being able to choose what to do next and repeat instructions means a machine can follow programs.

quiz.q: Why are Lovelace's notes so significant?
o: They gave the clearest account of the engine, including a step-by-step method for it to run
They proved the machine was impossible to build
They were a translation without any new ideas
They replaced Babbage's designs with her own machine
quiz.e: Note G set out a detailed method for the engine, often called the first published computer program.

quiz.q: What was Lovelace's most remarkable insight?
o: Machines could manipulate any rule-based symbols, not only numbers
Engines would one day be powered by electricity
Computers would always need punched cards
A machine could think and originate ideas by itself
quiz.e: She saw that computing could extend beyond arithmetic to anything expressible in rules, such as music.

LESSONS.push: A countess saw a use for the first computer that its own inventor missed.

LESSONS.title: How files get squeezed: the art of compression
LESSONS.hook: A whole CD's worth of music can shrink to about a tenth of its size, so thousands of songs fit on your phone. Compression works by finding patterns, and by cleverly throwing away what your eyes and ears will not miss.

sections.key: Compression stores the same information in fewer bits, either perfectly rebuilt (lossless) or close enough (lossy).
sections.b:
One minute of uncompressed CD-quality stereo audio takes about ten megabytes. Uncompressed high definition video would need hundreds of megabytes every few seconds, far more than a typical home connection could carry. Yet you stream films on a train and store thousands of photos on a phone.

The trick is compression: representing the same information, or something close enough, in fewer bits. Lossless compression shrinks a file so it can be rebuilt perfectly, bit for bit. Lossy compression goes further by discarding details people are unlikely to notice. Most media you enjoy relies on clever lossy methods built on top of lossless ideas.

sections.key: Lossless compression exploits repetition and gives common symbols shorter codes, but it cannot shrink truly random data.
sections.b:
Picture a clear blue sky, where a row holds a thousand identical blue pixels. Instead of storing blue a thousand times, store 'blue, repeated 1,000 times'. This is run length encoding. A more powerful method from Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv in the late 1970s replaces repeated sequences with a short pointer: 'go back this far and copy this many characters'. Variations power ZIP files, PNG images and web page transfers.

Morse code already used another idea: the common letter E is one dot, while rare Q gets a long pattern. In 1952, David Huffman, then an MIT student, published a method for building the best such code. Truly random data cannot be shrunk at all.

sections.key: JPEG saves space by discarding fine detail and colour precision that human vision barely notices.
sections.b:
Lossy image compression exploits quirks of human vision. JPEG, a standard from the early 1990s, first separates brightness from colour. Our eyes are far more sensitive to brightness differences than colour ones, so JPEG usually stores colour at lower resolution.

Next it splits the image into small blocks, typically eight by eight pixels, and describes each as a mix of smooth patterns, from broad gradients to fine stripes. The fine, busy patterns matter least to our eyes, so they are rounded off heavily or thrown away. Lossless coding then packs what remains.

Push the quality setting down and the trick shows: blurry edges, smudged colours and visible square blocks.

sections.key: MP3 and AAC shrink audio by dropping or skimping on sounds your hearing would mask or miss.
sections.b:
Audio formats such as MP3, developed in Germany in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and the later AAC, use psychoacoustics, the science of how we perceive sound. We cannot hear very high or very low frequencies well, and a loud sound masks quieter sounds at nearby frequencies.

An encoder analyses music in short slices, works out which parts would be masked or inaudible, and spends fewer bits on them or drops them. The result can be roughly a tenth the size of the original CD audio while sounding very similar to most listeners.

At low bit rates, you may hear swirly, watery artefacts, particularly in cymbals and applause.

sections.key: Video codecs send only what changes between frames, and repeated lossy saving degrades quality, so keep an original copy.
sections.b:
Consecutive video frames are usually very similar. In a newsreader shot, the background barely changes. Codecs such as H.264, H.265 and AV1 store full keyframes only occasionally, and describe how blocks have moved since an earlier frame, plus small corrections. When data goes missing, streams turn into smeared blocks because movement is applied to the wrong picture until the next keyframe. Confetti, rain and fast panning are hard to compress.

Lossy formats also cause generation loss. Each time you edit and re-save a JPEG, or share a photo through apps that recompress it, more detail is lost. Keep an original of anything important, and make compressed copies from that master.

quiz.q: What is the difference between lossless and lossy compression?
o: Lossless can be rebuilt perfectly, while lossy discards details people are unlikely to notice
Lossless discards detail, while lossy keeps every bit
Lossless is used only for video, while lossy is used only for audio
Lossless makes files bigger, while lossy makes them smaller
quiz.e: Lossless rebuilds the original bit for bit, whereas lossy accepts small, hard-to-notice changes for smaller files.

quiz.q: How does run length encoding shrink a row of a thousand identical blue pixels?
o: It stores 'blue, repeated 1,000 times'
It keeps one blue pixel and deletes the rest
It converts the blue to grey to save space
It stores the row twice and compares them
quiz.e: Describing a repetition instead of storing each copy is the core idea behind many lossless methods.

quiz.q: Why can JPEG store colour at lower resolution than brightness?
o: Our eyes are far more sensitive to brightness than to colour differences
Cameras record colour less accurately than brightness
Colour takes more bits than brightness, so it is always cut
Screens cannot display fine colour detail
quiz.e: JPEG exploits human vision by spending its bits where our eyes notice most.

quiz.q: What does an MP3 encoder do to make audio smaller?
o: Drops or skimps on sounds that would be masked or inaudible
Removes every quiet sound from the recording
Lowers the volume of the whole track
Stores the track at half speed
quiz.e: Psychoacoustics tells the encoder which parts you won't hear, so those get fewer bits or none.

quiz.q: Why do photos grow blurrier when shared through several messaging apps?
o: Each app recompresses the image and discards more detail
The apps gradually shrink the image's pixel count to save battery
Photos weaken when they travel over the internet
Each share adds a layer of noise to the original
quiz.e: Repeated lossy compression is generation loss, so make copies from the original master.

LESSONS.push: A whole CD fits in a tenth of the space, and you can't hear what was thrown away.

LESSONS.title: From sand to silicon: how microchips are made
LESSONS.hook: The chip in your phone holds billions of switches, each smaller than most viruses. Making one is arguably the most precise manufacturing humans have ever attempted.

sections.key: A chip's transistors are microscopic switches, and a modern phone processor packs over ten billion into a fingernail-sized chip.
sections.b:
Every app you open and message you send is processed by transistors, microscopic switches that turn current on and off. Combine enough of them in the right patterns and they can add numbers, compare values, store data and run any program.

The first transistor, built at Bell Labs in 1947, was big enough to see and handle. Today a high end phone processor packs well over ten billion onto a chip roughly the size of a fingernail. The features are only tens of atoms across, layered with astonishing accuracy across a whole silicon disc at once. The process can take a few months from bare wafer to finished chip.

sections.key: Chips begin as sand refined into silicon of extraordinary purity and grown into a single giant crystal, then sliced into wafers.
sections.b:
Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, found in quartz sand and rock. But chips need silicon purer than almost anything else people make, with impurities around one atom in a billion.

Purified silicon is melted. A seed crystal is dipped in and slowly drawn upward while rotating, so the silicon solidifies into one perfect crystal called an ingot, a technique named after Polish scientist Jan Czochralski. Modern ingots can be as wide as a dinner plate and around two metres long. Diamond saws slice them into wafers less than a millimetre thick, polished until flatter than almost any other surface.

sections.key: Photolithography prints circuit patterns onto a wafer with light, then etches, adds or alters material, layer after layer in a dust-free cleanroom.
sections.b:
The key technique is photolithography. The wafer is coated with a light sensitive chemical, photoresist. Light shines through a mask carrying the circuit pattern and is focused through lenses onto the wafer. Wherever light hits, the photoresist changes, so it can be washed away. The exposed areas can then be etched, have material added, or be bombarded with other atoms to change how they conduct electricity, called doping. The machine steps across the wafer, printing the pattern for hundreds of chips.

A chip has hundreds or even over a thousand such steps. One dust particle can destroy a chip, so fabs use cleanrooms with air thousands of times cleaner than a hospital operating theatre. Not every chip works. The share that does is the yield.

sections.key: The most advanced chips are printed with extreme ultraviolet light, made by firing lasers at tin droplets, in machines only one company builds.
sections.b:
The smaller the wavelength, the finer the patterns that can be printed. For years, chipmakers used deep ultraviolet light and tricks such as exposing the same layer several times. The most advanced chips now use extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, at 13.5 nanometres.

Making it is extraordinary. A powerful laser hits tiny droplets of molten tin tens of thousands of times a second, creating a plasma that emits EUV light. Air and glass absorb EUV, so the beam travels in a vacuum and is steered by ultra smooth mirrors rather than lenses.

Only one company, ASML in the Netherlands, makes these machines. Each is about the size of a bus and costs hundreds of millions of dollars.

sections.key: Chip progress is slowing past Moore's law, and no single country makes a modern chip from start to finish.
sections.b:
In 1965, Gordon Moore, later a co-founder of Intel, noticed the number of components on a chip was doubling regularly. In 1975 he revised this to roughly every two years. Moore's law held for decades, but the pace has slowed. Names like '3 nanometre' are now mostly labels for each generation, not real measurements, so chipmakers stack components and redesign transistors instead.

No single country makes a modern chip alone. Designs often come from the United States, the most advanced manufacturing is concentrated in Taiwan, especially at TSMC, EUV machines come from the Netherlands, and specialised materials from Japan, South Korea and Europe. The shortages after 2020 showed how fragile this chain is, and governments are now spending heavily on local factories.

quiz.q: What does a transistor do?
o: Acts as a microscopic switch that turns current on and off
Stores electricity like a tiny battery for later use
Converts heat from the chip into light
Amplifies Wi-Fi signals to the phone's antenna
quiz.e: Billions of switches arranged in the right patterns can add, compare, store data and run programs.

quiz.q: Why must the silicon used for chips be so pure?
o: Even tiny impurities would disrupt the precise structure of the crystal
Sand is too coarse to be used in electronics
Pure silicon is cheaper to slice into wafers
Impurities make the wafer too heavy to polish
quiz.e: Chips need silicon purer than almost anything else people make, with impurities around one atom in a billion.

quiz.q: Why do chip factories use cleanrooms?
o: A single dust particle can destroy a chip
Workers need protection from harmful chemicals only
Light would otherwise make the wafers glow
Robots cannot work in normal air
quiz.e: Features are so small that one speck of dust can ruin a chip, so cleanroom air is thousands of times cleaner than a theatre.

quiz.q: Why does EUV light travel in a vacuum and bounce off mirrors?
o: Air and glass absorb EUV light
Mirrors make the light brighter than lenses do
Vacuums let the tin droplets stay molten
Lenses would melt in the laser's heat
quiz.e: Because EUV is absorbed by air and glass, machines use a vacuum and ultra smooth mirrors.

quiz.q: What does a chip labelled '3 nanometre' actually tell you?
o: It names a generation of technology, not a measurement of any feature
Every feature on the chip is exactly three nanometres wide
The chip is three nanometres thick
The chip was printed with three nanometre light
quiz.e: These names once related to real dimensions but are now mostly labels for each new generation.

LESSONS.push: Your phone's chip is made with light, molten tin and the cleanest air on Earth.

LESSONS.title: Philosophical razors: shaving away bad explanations
LESSONS.hook: Your car won't start. Is it a flat battery, or sabotage by a jealous neighbour? A handful of simple rules called 'razors' can save you from chasing the wrong answer.

sections.key: A razor is a rule of thumb that shaves away unlikely explanations to show where to look first, without proving anything.
sections.b:
Picture a detective with ten suspects and one afternoon. She needs a way to decide where to look first. Thinkers have long used short rules for exactly this job, nicknamed 'razors' because they shave away explanations that are possible but improbable.

A razor never proves anything. It doesn't tell you the answer is definitely the simple one. It tells you where the smart money is, so you can spend your attention sensibly. Think of razors as tie breakers and starting points, not verdicts. Used well, they stop you getting lost in elaborate theories. Used badly, as a way to end every conversation, they become a lazy excuse not to think.

sections.key: When two explanations fit the facts equally well, favour the one that needs fewer assumptions.
sections.b:
The most famous razor is named after William of Ockham, an English friar and philosopher who lived around 1287 to 1347. The slogan 'entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity' was written by later scholars, but the idea runs through his work.

In plain terms: when two explanations fit the facts equally well, favour the one that asks you to assume less. If your biscuits vanish, a hungry teenager requires one assumption. A burglar who ignored your laptop and took only the Tim Tams requires several.

Notice the key phrase: equally well. Occam's razor doesn't say simple explanations are always true. Complexity has to earn its place by explaining something the simpler version can't.

sections.key: Don't assume bad intent when a mistake, busyness or ignorance would explain things, unless a pattern says otherwise.
sections.b:
A colleague leaves you off an important email chain. You might think they are freezing you out. Hanlon's razor suggests a gentler first guess: they probably forgot.

The usual wording is 'never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity', credited to a man named Robert Hanlon, who submitted it to a joke book about Murphy's Law around 1980. A kinder version: don't assume bad intent when busyness, ignorance or a simple mistake would do.

It helps because our brains are quick to see enemies, and it saves friendships and wasted anger. It isn't naive, though. If the 'mistakes' keep happening in one direction, the pattern itself becomes evidence.

sections.key: Claims need supporting evidence from the person making them, and common explanations should be ruled out before rare ones.
sections.b:
Someone says a celebrity is secretly a lizard. You ask for evidence, and they reply, 'Prove they're not.' Christopher Hitchens's answer: 'What can be asserted without evidence can also be dismissed without evidence.' The person making a claim should supply reasons. You can set it aside until they do. That doesn't mean it is false.

Medical students learn: when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras. A headache and runny nose is most likely a cold, not an exotic disease. If your internet drops, a tired router is a horse and a targeted hack is a zebra. This is about base rates, how often each explanation occurs. Zebras do exist, so rule out the horses first.

sections.key: Razors set your starting odds, not your conclusion, so follow the evidence when it points to the complicated answer.
sections.b:
By the 1840s, astronomers knew Uranus wasn't moving quite as the maths predicted. The simple response would have been small measurement errors. Instead, some argued for a more complicated answer: an unseen planet tugging on it. In 1846, Neptune was found close to where the calculations said it would be. The elaborate explanation was right because it explained what the simpler one couldn't.

That is how to treat every razor. People are sometimes genuinely malicious, and zebras sometimes turn up. When something surprising happens, ask what simple explanation fits all the facts, could it be a mistake, and who is making the claim. Treat your first answer as a working hypothesis. A razor that stops you looking becomes a blindfold.

quiz.q: What is a philosophical razor best used for?
o: Deciding which explanation to investigate first
Proving which explanation is correct
Ending a debate by picking the simplest answer
Showing that complicated explanations are always wrong
quiz.e: A razor shows where the smart money is, but it never proves an explanation.

quiz.q: According to Occam's razor, when should you favour the simpler explanation?
o: When it fits the facts as well as a more complex one
Whenever it is easier to understand
Whenever it was proposed first
When it has more supporters
quiz.e: Simplicity only wins when explanations fit equally well, since complexity must earn its place.

quiz.q: Why is Hanlon's razor useful?
o: It guards against jumping to the conclusion that someone meant harm
It proves other people are always well intentioned
It tells you to ignore repeated mistakes
It shows that other people are usually careless
quiz.e: Our brains are quick to see enemies, though a repeated one-sided pattern is still evidence worth noticing.

quiz.q: Under Hitchens's razor, who must supply the evidence for a claim?
o: The person making the claim
The person doubting the claim
An independent expert chosen by both sides
Nobody, as claims can't be tested
quiz.e: What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence, so the burden sits with the claimant.

quiz.q: What does the discovery of Neptune teach about razors?
o: Follow the evidence even if it points to a more complicated explanation
The simplest explanation is usually right
Measurement errors explain most odd results
Unseen causes should never be considered
quiz.e: The elaborate explanation was right because it explained something the simple one couldn't.

LESSONS.push: A simple rule can stop you chasing the wrong explanation, until it stops you thinking.

LESSONS.title: Why conspiracy theories feel so convincing
LESSONS.hook: Real conspiracies happen, yet most grand theories about secret plots fall apart. Learn why they grip clever people, and how to tell a real cover-up from a story.

sections.key: Real conspiracies happen, but they are uncovered through documents, whistleblowers and court cases, not by theories that never produce solid evidence.
sections.b:
In 1972, burglars were caught inside the Democratic Party's offices in the Watergate building in Washington. Over two years, journalists and investigators uncovered a cover-up that reached the White House, and President Richard Nixon resigned in 1974. For decades, tobacco companies also played down what their own scientists knew about smoking's harms.

So powerful people sometimes collude and lie. That is what makes conspiracy theories plausible. The question isn't whether conspiracies ever happen. It is how to tell real ones, uncovered through documents, whistleblowers and court cases, from the many theories that never produce solid evidence however long people look.

sections.key: Conspiracy theories appeal because we expect big events to have big causes, over-detect patterns, and find comfort in a world someone controls.
sections.b:
When something shocking happens, a small, random cause feels insulting. Psychologists call this proportionality bias: a big effect seems to need a big explanation. The 1963 assassination of John F. Kennedy is a classic case. A lone gunman changing history feels wrong, so a grand plot seems fitting. Recognise when an explanation appeals mainly because it feels emotionally right.

Our ancestors who assumed a predator in a rustle in the grass were safer than those who assumed wind. Many researchers think this shaped minds that over-detect patterns and intentions. Conspiracy theories turn chaos into a story with villains and a plan. That can be comforting, since someone is in charge. People are more drawn to them when anxious, powerless or uncertain.

sections.key: A theory that no evidence could ever disprove tells you nothing about the world.
sections.b:
Here is a warning sign worth memorising. Ask a believer what evidence would change their mind. If the answer is 'nothing', or every piece of contrary evidence is explained away as part of the plot, the theory has become self-sealing. Missing evidence proves the cover-up. Official denials prove the cover-up. Experts who disagree are in on it.

This structure feels powerful because it can't be refuted, but that is exactly its weakness. A claim that survives every possible observation tells you nothing about the world.

Real investigations work the other way. Journalists who exposed Watergate could point to money trails, tapes and witnesses. When a theory's main evidence is the absence of evidence, be cautious.

sections.key: Large conspiracies are hard to keep secret because the more people involved, the faster someone talks.
sections.b:
The Apollo programme employed hundreds of thousands of people across government agencies, universities and private companies. A hoax would have needed all of them, plus rival scientists in the Soviet Union who tracked the missions, to stay silent for over fifty years.

In 2016, physicist David Grimes published a model estimating how quickly large conspiracies would be likely to leak. His rough conclusion was that secrets involving thousands of people tend to come out within a few years.

You don't need the maths to see the logic. People talk, change jobs, write memoirs, fall out with their bosses and seek fame. Real conspiracies usually involve small groups, and even those are often exposed eventually.

sections.key: Ask who benefits from you believing a story, and when talking with a believer, use curiosity and keep the relationship.
sections.b:
Ask not only who benefits from the alleged plot but who benefits from you believing it. Some promoters sell supplements, courses or subscriptions. Others earn advertising money, and outrage keeps people watching. Some foreign governments have spread divisive stories to weaken trust in other countries' institutions. None of this proves a claim false, but apply scepticism evenly, to governments and corporations and to influencers telling you what they are hiding.

If someone you care about is deep in a rabbit hole, mockery backfires. Ask genuine questions: what first made you think this, and what would change your mind? Find common ground and share your own uncertainty. Prebunking, such as Cambridge's online games, teaches manipulation tricks in advance. People rarely leave a belief by losing an argument, but often return through trusted friends.

quiz.q: How are real conspiracies usually uncovered?
o: Through documents, whistleblowers and court cases
Through anonymous online rumours
Through repeated claims that they must exist
Through the absence of any official records
quiz.e: Real cover-ups such as Watergate were exposed with specific evidence, unlike theories that never produce any.

quiz.q: What is proportionality bias?
o: The sense that a big event needs a big explanation
The tendency to trust small groups over large ones
The belief that most events are caused by chance
The habit of favouring official explanations
quiz.e: A random or small cause can feel inadequate for a shocking event, which makes grand plots appealing.

quiz.q: Why is a self-sealing theory a warning sign?
o: Nothing could ever count against it, so it tells you nothing
It is always based on an outright lie
It is always spread by governments
It cannot be explained to other people
quiz.e: A claim that survives every possible observation can't be tested, so it tells you nothing about the world.

quiz.q: Why does the number of people involved matter for a conspiracy?
o: The more people who know, the more likely the secret leaks
Larger groups are more careful with secrets
Big projects are always too complex to hide
Only small groups can be investigated
quiz.e: People talk, change jobs and write memoirs, so secrets held by thousands tend to come out within years.

quiz.q: What is a better way to talk with someone who believes a conspiracy theory?
o: Ask genuine questions and keep the relationship
Mock the claims until they back down
Win the argument with a long list of facts
Avoid the subject and cut contact
quiz.e: Mockery confirms the story that outsiders are closed-minded, while trusted friends are how people often return.

LESSONS.push: Some conspiracies are real. Here's how to tell which ones, and why the others stick.

LESSONS.title: Cold reading: how psychics seem to know you
LESSONS.hook: 'You have a great deal of unused potential.' Sounds just like you, doesn't it? Discover the simple tricks that make strangers seem to read your mind.

sections.key: We accept vague, general statements as uniquely true of ourselves, a tendency called the Forer or Barnum effect.
sections.b:
In 1948, psychologist Bertram Forer gave his students a personality test, then handed each a supposedly personal analysis. On average they rated it above four out of five for accuracy. Then came the twist: every student had received exactly the same text, assembled largely from astrology material. It included lines such as 'you have a great need for other people to like and admire you' and 'at times you are extroverted, affable, sociable, while at other times you are introverted, wary, reserved'.

This tendency to accept general statements as uniquely true of ourselves is called the Forer effect, or the Barnum effect, after the showman P. T. Barnum. Later studies have repeated it many times.

sections.key: Barnum statements sound insightful because they are nearly impossible to get wrong, often covering both sides of a trait.
sections.b:
Look closely at a typical 'reading' and you find statements that are nearly impossible to get wrong. 'You can be your own worst critic.' 'You have a secret you haven't told many people.' 'Though you seem confident, you sometimes doubt yourself.' Each sounds insightful, but try thinking of one adult it doesn't describe.

Some cover both sides at once, a trick British mentalist Ian Rowland called the 'rainbow ruse': 'You are generally easygoing, but when someone crosses a line, you can be fierce.' Whatever you are like, you hear yourself. Add flattery, such as hidden talents or a big heart, and most people agree. Agreement then feels like proof the reader is gifted.

sections.key: Cold readers throw out broad guesses and watch your reactions, so you supply most of the information yourself.
sections.b:
Imagine a medium on stage: 'I'm getting an older man, a father figure, maybe a grandfather or uncle. There's a name with a J, or perhaps an M.' In a room of two hundred, almost everyone has lost an older male relative, and many know a John, James, Mary or Michael. This scattershot approach is called shotgunning. When someone nods, the medium narrows in.

Readers also fish with questions dressed as statements, such as 'Who is the person with the heart problem?' You supply the answer and may later recall the medium telling you. Skilled readers watch faces, posture, clothing, jewellery and accents. It feels like revelation, but you do most of the work.

sections.key: We remember a reader's hits and forget the misses, and some 'psychics' secretly gather real information beforehand.
sections.b:
After a reading, people say the psychic knew things no stranger could. Yet when researchers record sessions, they find plenty of wrong guesses. We remember the astonishing hit and forget the dozen misses. Misses get rescued too: 'Keep that name, it will make sense later,' or the water sensed was a bath, a beach holiday or a leaky tap. This is confirmation bias with flexible meanings.

Hot reading means gathering real information beforehand. Today a glance at social media can reveal someone's pets, hometown and children. In the 1980s, sceptic James Randi showed that faith healer Peter Popoff was receiving details about audience members through a hidden earpiece, fed by his wife backstage. When a reader knows something impossible, ask first whether the information was available.

sections.key: To test a psychic claim, remove every ordinary source of information, and watch for readings used to win trust and then money.
sections.b:
A horoscope or tarot reading can be harmless fun. The danger comes when the same techniques win trust and then money. Some scams begin with a 'psychic' who senses a curse and offers to lift it for a fee, then another fee. Grieving people are especially vulnerable. If you think you have been targeted in Australia, Scamwatch, run by the ACCC, explains how to report it. This is general information, so seek proper advice for your situation.

To test psychic powers, the reader shouldn't see or hear the person, know anything in advance, or get feedback. Then compare accuracy with chance. Such tests have generally not supported psychic claims, and James Randi's foundation long offered a large prize that was never claimed. Ask: what could they have seen, heard, guessed or looked up?

quiz.q: What did Forer's students discover about their personality analyses?
o: Every student had received exactly the same text
Each analysis had been written from their own test results
The analyses were drawn at random from a hat
The analyses were the opposite of their real personalities
quiz.e: Students rated a generic analysis as highly personal, showing how readily we accept general statements about ourselves.

quiz.q: Why does the 'rainbow ruse' work on almost everyone?
o: It describes both sides of a trait, so you hear yourself in it
It uses private details about each person
It relies on rare, unusual personality traits
It is delivered faster than people can think
quiz.e: A statement that covers opposite possibilities can't be wrong, so it feels accurate whatever you are like.

quiz.q: Why does shotgunning work in a large audience?
o: Broad guesses fit many people, and reactions show where to narrow in
The medium has researched each person in advance
Names starting with J or M are very rare
People rarely react to what a stranger says
quiz.e: In a big room almost every guess fits someone, and their reaction guides the next one.

quiz.q: Why do people leave readings convinced the psychic was accurate?
o: They remember the hits and forget the misses
The psychic only makes guesses that are always right
Researchers find psychics are mostly correct
People rarely discuss readings afterwards
quiz.e: Selective memory and flexible meanings turn an ordinary hit rate into an apparent miracle.

quiz.q: What is needed to test a psychic claim fairly?
o: Remove every ordinary source of information and compare accuracy with chance
Let the reader chat with the person to build trust
Ask the psychic whether they feel the test was fair
Test only believers who are open to the result
quiz.e: If the reader can't see, hear or learn anything about the person, only real ability could beat chance.

LESSONS.push: A 1948 classroom trick still explains why strangers seem to know you so well.

LESSONS.title: Why you understand less than you think
LESSONS.hook: You use a zip every day. Could you explain how it actually works? Most people are surprised by how quickly their confidence collapses.

sections.key: We feel we understand everyday things deeply until we try to explain how they work.
sections.b:
Try a quick experiment. On a scale of one to seven, how well do you understand how a zip works? Now explain, step by step, how the teeth lock together and how the slider separates them. Most people start confidently and stall within a sentence or two.

In a well-known 2002 study, Yale psychologists Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil asked people to rate their understanding of everyday objects such as zips, flush toilets and locks, then write detailed explanations. After trying, people's ratings dropped noticeably. The researchers named this the illusion of explanatory depth. We feel we understand things deeply because we know what they look like and how to use them.

sections.key: Knowing how to use something is a different skill from knowing how it works.
sections.b:
Picture a bicycle. Now imagine drawing one accurately: frame, pedals, chain and wheels. Easy, surely. British psychologist Rebecca Lawson tested this in the mid 2000s by asking people to draw or complete diagrams of bicycles. Many made errors that would make a real bike impossible to ride, such as attaching the chain to the front wheel or joining the frame in ways that would stop the handlebars turning. Regular cyclists did better, but even some of them slipped.

The point isn't that people are foolish. Using something is a different skill from knowing how it works. Our everyday knowledge is mostly useful shortcuts, not a detailed blueprint.

sections.key: Our minds keep rough outlines and lean on the world and other people, so borrowed knowledge feels like our own.
sections.b:
One reason is efficiency. Storing the full workings of every gadget would waste mental effort. You don't need to understand a toilet's valve to flush it. The mind keeps a rough outline and leans on the world as a reference. When you look at a bicycle, the details are right there, so it feels as if they are in your head too. Explanations also come in layers, and each can hide the next. You know a car burns fuel to move, but not how that turns the wheels. We stop at the first layer and mistake it for the bottom.
