The Victoria, captained by Basque navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano, sailed on across the Indian Ocean and around Africa, avoiding Portuguese ports. Men kept dying of scurvy and hunger, and at Cape Verde 13 crew were detained ashore. In September 1522, three years after leaving, the Victoria reached Spain with 18 of the original crew. The cloves covered much of the expedition's cost, and Elcano received a coat of arms showing a globe.

The voyage proved the oceans are connected, the Americas were separate from Asia, and Earth was far bigger than Columbus believed. Their log was a day behind Spain's calendar, because sailing west they saw one fewer sunrise, an early hint of the International Date Line.

quiz.q: What was Magellan trying to reach by sailing west?
o: The western coast of India
The Spice Islands in modern Indonesia
The unexplored coast of Australia
A passage to the North Pole
quiz.e: He argued the Moluccas might lie on Spain's side of the Tordesillas line.

quiz.q: What did the fleet find at the southern tip of South America?
o: A winding passage into a new ocean
A frozen sea that blocked every route
A land bridge to Antarctica
A harbour rich in fresh supplies
quiz.e: The Strait of Magellan, about 570 kilometres long, led into the Pacific.

quiz.q: What caused scurvy among the crew crossing the Pacific?
o: Drinking too much salty seawater
The cold, wet weather at sea
Disease carried by the ship's rats
Months without fresh food, so a lack of vitamin C
quiz.e: Scurvy bleeds the gums and weakens the body, and fresh food prevents it.

quiz.q: Why did Magellan die at Mactan?
o: He was poisoned at a feast by his allies
His own captains mutinied and killed him
His ships could not cross the reef to help his small party
A storm wrecked his flagship
quiz.e: About 50 men faced a much larger force led by Lapulapu, now a Philippine national hero.

quiz.q: What odd discovery did the survivors make on returning to Spain?
o: Their food supplies had not spoiled
Their log was a day behind the calendar
Their clocks had run faster than Spain's
The stars looked different from before
quiz.e: Sailing west with the Sun, they saw one fewer sunrise, a hint of what the Date Line handles today.

LESSONS.push: Five ships left. Three years on, one came back with 18 men. Why did it matter?

LESSONS.title: James Cook's voyages
LESSONS.hook: A farm labourer's son became the Pacific's greatest mapmaker. His voyages changed science, and the fate of the peoples he met.

sections.key: James Cook, a farm labourer's son, taught himself navigation, astronomy and surveying and became a brilliant chart maker.
sections.b:
James Cook was born in Yorkshire in 1728, the son of a farm labourer. He learned seamanship on coal ships out of Whitby, joined the Royal Navy in 1755 and rose quickly. During the Seven Years' War he helped chart the St Lawrence River, then made his name mapping Newfoundland with remarkable precision. Largely self-taught, he was a skilled mathematician and astronomer, rare for someone without a privileged education.

In 1768 he was chosen to command a scientific voyage to the Pacific aboard the Endeavour, a converted Whitby coal ship.

sections.key: Cook's first voyage observed the transit of Venus from Tahiti, then charted New Zealand and Australia's east coast.
sections.b:
The official purpose of the first voyage (1768 to 1771) was to watch Venus cross the Sun from Tahiti on 3 June 1769. Transits come in pairs about eight years apart, with over a century between pairs, and astronomers hoped to calculate the Earth-Sun distance. Cook also carried secret orders to seek the great southern continent, Terra Australis. Aboard was the wealthy young botanist Joseph Banks, who collected thousands of plants with Daniel Solander.

Cook mapped both islands of New Zealand, partly seen by Abel Tasman in 1642. Early encounters with Māori ended in bloodshed. In April 1770 he reached Australia's east coast at Kamay (Botany Bay), named for Banks's new plants, where Gweagal men opposed the landing. On Possession Island in August 1770, Cook claimed the east coast for Britain without its peoples' consent.

sections.key: The Endeavour survived hitting the Great Barrier Reef, and Cook's voyages worked as floating laboratories.
sections.b:
In June 1770 the Endeavour ran aground on the Great Barrier Reef. The crew threw cannons, ballast and supplies overboard and, once afloat, slowed the leak by drawing a sail packed with oakum and wool under the hull: fothering. They limped to the Endeavour River, near Cooktown, where repairs took about seven weeks. There they had extended contact with the Guugu Yimithirr people and recorded the word 'kangaroo', from gangurru.

Banks and Solander brought back many plants new to European science, and artist Sydney Parkinson made hundreds of drawings before dying on the voyage home. The first voyage was still deadly: over a third of the crew died, mostly of disease caught at Batavia (Jakarta). Cook later fought scurvy with fresh food, sauerkraut and strict cleanliness, and lost very few men to it.

sections.key: Cook disproved a temperate southern continent on his second voyage and was killed in Hawai'i in 1779.
sections.b:
On the second voyage (1772 to 1775), Cook carried a copy of John Harrison's marine chronometer, accurate enough to calculate longitude at sea, and praised it. He crossed the Antarctic Circle, showing any southern continent must lie in the icy far south, not the temperate latitudes Europeans imagined.

On the third voyage (1776 to 1780), searching for a Northwest Passage above North America, he became the first European known to reach Hawai'i, in 1778. He sailed north through the Bering Strait until ice blocked the way. Back in Hawai'i, amid rising tensions over a stolen boat, he was killed in a confrontation at Kealakekua Bay on 14 February 1779. His crew completed the voyage without him.

sections.key: Cook's charts led Britain to found a colony at Sydney, and his legacy is celebrated by some and mourned by others.
sections.b:
Cook's charts and Banks's enthusiasm for Botany Bay influenced Britain's decision to send convicts to New South Wales. The First Fleet arrived in January 1788, but Captain Arthur Phillip found Botany Bay unsuitable, with poor soil and little fresh water, and moved about 12 kilometres north to Sydney Cove in Port Jackson, a harbour Cook had noted but not entered. The founding, on 26 January, is now Australia Day, which many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people mourn as the beginning of invasion.

Cook's maps were so accurate that some were used for over a century, and his voyages advanced botany, astronomy and knowledge of the Pacific. Yet for many Aboriginal Australians, Māori and Pacific peoples, his arrival marks dispossession and disease. Both views reflect real history, and holding both is part of understanding the past honestly.

quiz.q: What does Cook's early career show?
o: Only wealthy men could command Navy ships
Navy officers trained at university in surveying
Skill and self-teaching took a farm labourer's son to command
Cook began his career as a botanist
quiz.e: He rose from Whitby coal ships and mapped Newfoundland with remarkable precision.

quiz.q: What was the official purpose of Cook's first voyage?
o: To claim a colony for Britain
To observe the transit of Venus from Tahiti
To rescue stranded whalers
To map the Arctic coast
quiz.e: Astronomers hoped it would help calculate the distance from Earth to the Sun.

quiz.q: How did the crew slow the leak after the Endeavour struck the reef?
o: They drew a sail packed with oakum and wool under the hull
They poured hot tar over the damaged planks
They nailed empty barrels across the hole
They packed the hold tightly with sand
quiz.e: This technique, called fothering, let them limp to the Endeavour River for repairs.

quiz.q: What did Cook's second voyage show about a southern continent?
o: It lay just east of New Zealand
It was joined to Australia
It was a vast desert
Any such land must lie in the icy far south
quiz.e: He crossed the Antarctic Circle and found no temperate southern land.

quiz.q: Why did Captain Phillip move the First Fleet from Botany Bay?
o: Local people welcomed the move
Storms had wrecked part of the fleet
Botany Bay had poor soil and little fresh water
Cook had ordered the move before leaving
quiz.e: He chose Sydney Cove in Port Jackson, a harbour Cook had noted but not entered.

LESSONS.push: A farm labourer's son mapped the Pacific. Why do we still argue about him?

LESSONS.title: The race to the poles
LESSONS.hook: Frostbite, starvation and extraordinary endurance. The early 1900s 'heroic age' of polar exploration produced triumph and tragedy.

sections.key: Between about 1897 and 1922, explorers raced to the poles in conditions that killed many of them.
sections.b:
By 1900, the North and South Poles were among the last great unreached places on Earth. The Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, usually dated from about 1897 to Shackleton's death in 1922, brought expeditions from Britain, Norway, Australia, Japan, Germany and elsewhere.

Explorers faced temperatures below minus 40 degrees, blizzards, hidden crevasses and months of darkness. They had wool and fur clothing, sledges, and little or no radio contact. Expeditions often lasted two or three years, and many men didn't return.

sections.key: Amundsen reached the South Pole first because his dogs, skis and careful planning suited the ice, while Scott's team died on the return.
sections.b:
Roald Amundsen had learned polar techniques from Inuit people: fur clothing, dog sledging and careful pacing. He secretly switched his plans from the North Pole to the South. From the Bay of Whales he laid supply depots, marked so they could be found in poor visibility, and used sled dogs, some killed to feed the others and the men. His five-man team, on skis, reached the pole on 14 December 1911 and returned safely.

Britain's Robert Falcon Scott relied on ponies and motor sledges, which failed, then man-hauled heavy sledges. His five men reached the pole on 17 January 1912 to find Amundsen's tent. They all died on the return, about 18 kilometres short of a major depot. Scott also faced unusually cold weather, and his team hauled about 16 kilograms of rock samples to the end.

sections.key: Careful preparation and the right tools, not courage alone, decided who survived.
sections.b:
Lawrence Oates, crippled by frostbite, walked out into a blizzard to avoid slowing the others, reportedly saying, 'I am just going outside and may be some time.' Scott and his last two companions died in their tent.

Historians still debate Scott's choices, but some differences are clear. Amundsen's dogs travelled fast over snow and ice and could be eaten along the way. Scott's ponies suffered in the cold and his men exhausted themselves hauling. Amundsen's team were expert skiers and dog drivers. He later wrote that victory awaits the one who has everything in order.

sections.key: Mawson survived alone for weeks and Shackleton's whole crew survived after their ship was crushed by ice.
sections.b:
Adelaide geologist Douglas Mawson led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition (1911 to 1914) from Cape Denison, one of the windiest places on Earth at sea level. In December 1912, Belgrave Ninnis fell into a crevasse with the sledge carrying most of their food. Mawson and Xavier Mertz turned back, eating their dogs. Mertz died, probably partly from vitamin A poisoning from dog liver. Mawson struggled on alone for about a month, fell into a crevasse himself, and reached base just after his ship had left. He survived another winter.

In 1915, Ernest Shackleton's Endurance was crushed by sea ice in the Weddell Sea. His 28 men camped on the ice, then reached Elephant Island. Shackleton and five others sailed the James Caird about 1,300 kilometres to South Georgia. Every man was rescued. The wreck was found in 2022, 3,000 metres down.

sections.key: The North Pole is hard to prove you reached, and Antarctica is now protected for peace and science.
sections.b:
The North Pole sits on drifting sea ice, which makes it hard to reach and harder to prove. American Robert Peary claimed it in 1909 with Matthew Henson and four Inuit men, Ootah, Egingwah, Seegloo and Ooqueah, and Frederick Cook claimed 1908. Both claims are widely doubted. In 1926, Amundsen, Lincoln Ellsworth and Umberto Nobile flew over the pole in the airship Norge, generally regarded as the first verified visit.

The 1959 Antarctic Treaty set Antarctica aside for peaceful science, banning military activity and, under a later protocol, mining. Australia claims about 42%, the largest share, though claims are held in abeyance. It runs stations such as Mawson, Davis and Casey, supplied from Hobart. Ice cores there hold air bubbles hundreds of thousands of years old. The Arctic's shrinking summer sea ice is one of the clearest signs of warming.

quiz.q: What was the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration?
o: A Norwegian whaling boom lasting a century
A war between nations over Antarctic territory
A series of Arctic rescue missions
A period of dangerous polar expeditions from about 1897 to 1922
quiz.e: Expeditions from many nations went south, and many men didn't return.

quiz.q: What gave Amundsen a decisive edge over Scott?
o: A larger team of strong ponies
Motor sledges that worked in the cold
Dogs, skis, experience and careful planning
A much shorter route to the pole
quiz.e: Amundsen learned techniques from Inuit people and marked his depots so they could be found.

quiz.q: What does Scott's expedition teach about preparation?
o: Courage alone is enough to survive polar travel
Courage could not make up for unsuitable transport and planning
Ponies are better than dogs in deep snow
Man-hauling is the fastest way to cross ice
quiz.e: Scott's ponies suffered and his men exhausted themselves hauling, while Amundsen's dogs and skis suited the ice.

quiz.q: What happened to Shackleton's crew after Endurance was crushed?
o: Every man was eventually rescued
Half the crew died on Elephant Island
The crew sailed home without help
They all reached the South Pole on foot
quiz.e: Shackleton's boat voyage to South Georgia led to the rescue of the whole crew.

quiz.q: Why are early North Pole claims disputed?
o: No one wrote about the trips afterwards
The pole lies on solid land and is easy to check
Both explorers turned back before reaching it
The pole is on drifting sea ice, and the reported records seem implausible
quiz.e: The first verified visit was the 1926 airship flight of the Norge.

LESSONS.push: Two teams raced for the South Pole. One planned for dogs, one for ponies.

LESSONS.title: Mesopotamia: where civilisation began
LESSONS.hook: Between two rivers in modern Iraq, people built the first cities, the first written laws and some of the first empires. You still use their ideas every time you check the time.

sections.key: Controlling river water produced a farming surplus, and that surplus made specialised jobs and civilisation possible.
sections.b:
Mesopotamia means 'land between rivers', the Tigris and Euphrates in modern Iraq. It sat in the Fertile Crescent, an arc of good farmland from the eastern Mediterranean down to the Persian Gulf, where farming began more than 10,000 years ago with wheat, barley, sheep and goats.

The southern plain was hot and dry, and the rivers flooded unpredictably. So people dug canals, dykes and irrigation ditches to control the water and grow a surplus. With a surplus, not everyone had to farm, and some became priests, craftspeople, soldiers and rulers. That shift from everyone feeding themselves to specialised jobs is the seed of civilisation.

sections.key: Sumerian cities like Uruk were among the first true cities, run through temples that paid workers in barley, bread and beer.
sections.b:
In southern Mesopotamia, the Sumerians built cities such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash. By around 3000 BC, Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people inside walls about 9 kilometres long. Each city had its own ruler and patron god, worshipped in a temple on a stepped mud-brick platform called a ziggurat. Cities traded grain and woollen textiles for timber, metals and stone, and fought each other over land, borders and water.

Temples and palaces owned land and herds and paid weavers, brewers and farm workers in rations of barley, bread, oil and beer. Society was layered, from rulers and priests down to enslaved people, often war captives or debtors. Boys from wealthier families could train for years in scribal schools.

sections.key: The Sumerians gave us early writing, the wheel and the base-60 counting behind our minutes and hours.
sections.b:
Sumerians developed cuneiform, one of the first writing systems, around 3200 BC. They were among the first to use the wheel, first for making pottery and then for carts. They counted in base 60, a handy number because it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. Their Babylonian successors carried it on, which is why we still have 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle.

Sumerians also recorded the movements of the sky. Their poems about the hero-king Gilgamesh became the Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

sections.key: Sargon built the first empire, and Hammurabi's code showed that written, public laws make rules predictable.
sections.b:
Around 2334 BC, Sargon rose to power. Legend says he was found as a baby in a reed basket. He conquered the Sumerian cities and built the Akkadian Empire, often called the world's first, ruling many peoples from Akkad, a capital whose ruins have never been found. Akkadian stayed the region's main written language for centuries, though the empire lasted under two.

Hammurabi ruled Babylon for about 40 years. Around 1754 BC he had 282 laws carved on a tall black stone pillar, now in the Louvre. They covered trade, wages, loans, marriage, property, medical fees and crime. Many followed 'an eye for an eye', but punishments depended on whether the victim was a noble, commoner or enslaved. Its importance lay in laws being written and publicly displayed, so rules applied predictably, not at a ruler's whim.

sections.key: Assyria and Babylon rose and fell, and Mesopotamian ideas still shape our time, mathematics and law.
sections.b:
In the first millennium BC, the Assyrians built a feared military empire. From Nineveh, near modern Mosul, King Ashurbanipal gathered a great library of clay tablets, many now in the British Museum. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, and Babylon rose again under Nebuchadnezzar II, who built huge walls and the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate, now in a Berlin museum. The Hanging Gardens are described by later Greek writers, but no clear trace has been found. In 539 BC, Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon.

Mesopotamian astronomy and mathematics influenced Greek scholars, and the flood story in Gilgamesh parallels the story of Noah. The seven-day week may also draw on it. Much was forgotten until archaeologists in the 1800s dug up tablets and deciphered cuneiform. Today, looting and conflict threaten Iraqi sites.

quiz.q: Why did irrigation help start civilisation in Mesopotamia?
o: It created a food surplus, so some people could do other jobs
It made the rivers flood more often and fertilise more land
It meant everyone had to farm full time
It let people avoid trading with neighbours
quiz.e: A surplus freed people to become priests, craftspeople, soldiers and rulers.

quiz.q: What was a ziggurat?
o: A royal tomb outside the city walls
A walled marketplace beside the river
A flat-bottomed boat for carrying grain
A stepped mud-brick platform for a city's temple
quiz.e: Each Sumerian city had a patron god worshipped in a temple on a ziggurat.

quiz.q: Why does an hour have 60 minutes?
o: The Romans chose 60 for their calendar
It matches the length of the Moon's orbit
Sumerian base-60 counting, carried on by Babylonians
Egyptian sundials fixed the number
quiz.e: Sixty divides evenly in many ways, and the same system gives a circle 360 degrees.

quiz.q: Why was Hammurabi's code important?
o: It abolished punishment for all crimes
Laws were written and publicly displayed, so rules applied predictably
It gave every person equal rights
It was the first collection of religious texts
quiz.e: Punishments still depended on social class, but written law limited a ruler's whim.

quiz.q: Which of these is a legacy of Mesopotamia?
o: Astronomy and mathematics that Greek scholars inherited
The invention of paper
The Roman alphabet
The printing press
quiz.e: Its ideas in astronomy, mathematics, law and story spread far beyond the region.

LESSONS.push: Why does an hour have sixty minutes? The answer is 5,000 years old.

LESSONS.title: The invention of writing
LESSONS.hook: Writing was invented from scratch only a handful of times in history. It began with accountants, not poets.

sections.key: Writing began as bookkeeping, when growing cities needed records that didn't depend on anyone's memory.
sections.b:
For most of history, knowledge passed through speech, song and memory. People used tally marks, knotted cords and pictures, but these couldn't record language itself. Oral cultures kept vast bodies of knowledge. Aboriginal Australian songlines, for example, carry knowledge of country, law, navigation and seasons across many generations through song, story and dance. Oral knowledge isn't inferior, but it depends on living people.

As farming villages grew into cities, administrators had to track taxes, trade, rations and debts across thousands of people. In Mesopotamia, small clay tokens stood for goods such as sheep or jars of oil. A leading theory says tokens were sealed in clay envelopes and marked outside, until people realised the marks alone would do.

sections.key: Writing in Uruk began as accounts and receipts on clay, then grew into cuneiform that served for about 3,000 years.
sections.b:
By around 3200 BC in Uruk, scribes drew signs for objects and numbers on clay tablets to record grain, livestock and labour. Most earliest tablets are accounts and receipts. Poems, letters, laws and stories came later, as signs came to stand for spoken words.

Scribes pressed a cut reed into damp clay, making wedge-shaped marks. The name comes from Latin cuneus, wedge. Pictures became abstract symbols standing for words or syllables, and learning hundreds of signs took years of schooling. Cuneiform was adapted for Akkadian, Hittite and, in simplified form, Old Persian. Hundreds of thousands of tablets survive, because clay lasts, especially when fires baked it hard, as when Nineveh was sacked. Scholars in the 1800s deciphered it partly using a trilingual inscription at Behistun in Iran.

sections.key: Writing was invented independently only a few times, in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably Egypt.
sections.b:
Egyptian hieroglyphs appear around 3200 BC, about when Mesopotamian writing did, and may have developed independently. They mixed signs for sounds and for whole ideas. Scribes used faster scripts, hieratic and later demotic, in ink on papyrus. After the last inscription in AD 394 the knowledge was lost. The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carries one decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, and Champollion announced the decipherment in 1822.

In China, writing on animal bones and turtle shells to question ancestors dates to around 1200 BC, and modern characters descend directly from it, making it the oldest system still in use. The Maya created a full system of several hundred signs. Nearly every other writing system was borrowed from these few, or inspired by the idea.

sections.key: The alphabet used a small set of signs for individual sounds, so far more people could learn to read.
sections.b:
Early systems needed hundreds or thousands of signs, so only trained scribes could write. Around 1800 BC, Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai borrowed hieroglyph shapes to make a small set of signs for consonant sounds. The Phoenicians, seafaring traders from modern Lebanon, spread their version around the Mediterranean. It also gave rise to scripts such as Hebrew and Arabic.

The Greeks added vowels. The Romans adapted a Greek-derived alphabet, partly via the Etruscans, into the Latin alphabet used for English today. With only a couple of dozen letters, far more people could learn to read. The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta.

sections.key: Writing materials shaped who could write, and writing made history, law and cumulative knowledge possible.
sections.b:
Mesopotamians used clay, cheap and durable but heavy. Egyptians made papyrus from Nile reeds. Europeans later used parchment from animal skin, while early Chinese scribes wrote on bamboo strips and silk. Paper was developed in China during the Han dynasty, about 2,000 years ago, and spread west through the Islamic world. The Chinese also pioneered printing, and Gutenberg's press, around 1450, made books far cheaper in Europe.

Writing made history possible, which is why historians distinguish prehistory from history. It fixed laws, enforced contracts and let knowledge build across generations. Lists, tables and long arguments are easier on a page than in the head. It also concentrated power, as for thousands of years only a small elite could read. Every message you type stands on this 5,000-year-old invention.

quiz.q: Why did writing develop as cities grew?
o: Poets wanted to preserve their songs
Administrators needed records that didn't depend on memory
Kings wanted lasting monuments to themselves
Priests wanted to hide their knowledge
quiz.e: Taxes, trade, rations and debts across thousands of people were too much to hold in memory.

quiz.q: What were the earliest Mesopotamian tablets mostly about?
o: Accounts and receipts for goods
Love poetry and songs
Religious prayers and hymns
Royal histories and battles
quiz.e: Writing began as bookkeeping, and poems and letters came later.

quiz.q: How often was writing invented independently, according to most scholars?
o: In almost every ancient culture
Once only, in Mesopotamia
Dozens of times across the world
Only a few times; nearly all others were borrowed
quiz.e: Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably Egypt, are the accepted independent cases.

quiz.q: Why did the alphabet let more people learn to read?
o: It used a picture for every word
It was written only on paper
It used only a couple of dozen signs for sounds
Only priests were allowed to teach it
quiz.e: Earlier systems needed hundreds of signs, so only trained scribes could write.

quiz.q: What distinguishes history from prehistory?
o: The use of fire
The existence of written records
The start of farming
The growth of cities
quiz.e: Writing let people record events, so history became possible.

LESSONS.push: The first writing wasn't poetry or prayer. It was something far more ordinary.

LESSONS.title: The Indus Valley civilisation
LESSONS.hook: Five thousand years ago, cities in modern Pakistan and India had grid streets and covered drains. We still can't read their writing.

sections.key: The Indus civilisation was as old as Egypt's pyramids and larger in area, yet it was forgotten until the 1920s.
sections.b: Along the Indus River and its neighbours, in today's Pakistan and north-west India, a major civilisation arose around the same time as Egypt's pyramids. It is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site excavated. It was forgotten for thousands of years until archaeologists recognised it in the 1920s, at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. At its height it covered a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia, with more than a thousand known settlements, from small villages to big cities such as Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Population estimates vary widely, but some scholars suggest several million people at its peak.

sections.key: Indus cities were laid out on a plan and had covered drains and wells, which suggests organisation across whole cities.
sections.b:
Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had streets in a rough grid, with wide main roads and smaller lanes. Bricks came in consistent proportions, roughly 1:2:4 for thickness, width and length, across hundreds of kilometres. That suggests shared rules. Many cities had a raised citadel with public buildings above a lower residential town. Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath, about 12 metres long, was sealed with bitumen.

The water engineering was remarkable. Mohenjo-daro may have had hundreds of brick-lined wells. Many houses had bathing areas and toilets draining into covered brick sewers with inspection holes. Dholavira, in a drier area, built large reservoirs for rainwater. Few places had anything comparable for thousands of years.

sections.key: Most Indus people farmed, but skilled crafts and standardised weights fed a trade network reaching Mesopotamia.
sections.b:
Most Indus people were farmers and herders, growing wheat, barley, peas and sesame. They were among the earliest to grow cotton and weave it into cloth. Craftspeople drilled long, polished carnelian beads, so prized that similar ones turn up in Mesopotamian royal tombs. They also made painted pottery, copper and bronze tools, and clay toys.

Merchants traded cotton, beads, gems and timber by land and along the Arabian coast. Mesopotamian texts mention a land called Meluhha, probably the Indus region. Standardised cube-shaped stone weights, following a consistent system, suggest organised trade. The port of Lothal had a large brick basin that many think was a dockyard.

sections.key: The Indus script remains undeciphered because the inscriptions are short and there is no bilingual key.
sections.b:
Thousands of small square seals, often showing bulls, elephants or a one-horned beast, were probably pressed into clay to mark goods and their owners. The one-horned animal, sometimes called a unicorn, is the most common image, and its meaning is unknown.

The seals carry short inscriptions. Several thousand inscribed objects survive, using around 400 different signs, but most inscriptions are only about five signs long. There is no long text and no bilingual inscription to act as a key, as the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian. Many decipherments have been proposed, but scholars accept none. Most agree it was usually written right to left. Until it is read, we don't know their language or any names.

sections.key: No palaces or royal tombs have been found, and the cities faded as the climate and rivers changed.
sections.b:
Unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, Indus sites show no obvious palaces, grand royal tombs or monuments glorifying rulers. A small stone bust nicknamed the 'Priest-King' may not show a king at all. The gap between rich and poor seems smaller than elsewhere, and there are few signs of large-scale warfare. Some scholars suggest power was shared, though absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence.

Over a few centuries, the big cities were gradually abandoned as people moved to smaller villages, especially eastward. Leading explanations include a weakening monsoon, shifting rivers and less trade with Mesopotamia. The old idea of a sudden invasion is no longer widely accepted. Mohenjo-daro is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, threatened by salt and erosion.

quiz.q: What was remarkable about the Indus civilisation's place in history?
o: It was the first civilisation to use iron tools
It was as old as Egypt's pyramids but forgotten until the 1920s
It was a small river kingdom with few settlements
It was always well known to later historians
quiz.e: Despite covering a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia, it was forgotten for thousands of years.

quiz.q: What suggests Indus cities were organised on a large scale?
o: Giant royal palaces at the centre of each city
Detailed written laws carved into stone
Walls of stone that surrounded every house
Grid-like streets, standard bricks and covered drains
quiz.e: Planned streets, matching brick proportions and citywide drains point to shared rules and coordination.

quiz.q: What does the discovery of standard stone weights suggest?
o: Trade was organised and followed a consistent system
Each village made up its own measures
Trade was only local and informal
Weights were used only in religious rituals
quiz.e: Consistent weights point to organised trade, backed by finds like Indus seals in Mesopotamia.

quiz.q: Why has the Indus script never been deciphered?
o: All the inscriptions were deliberately destroyed
The script was read only from left to right
Inscriptions are very short and there is no bilingual key
It was never used for writing at all
quiz.e: With only about five signs per inscription and no Rosetta Stone equivalent, scholars have little to work with.

quiz.q: What is the leading view on why the big Indus cities declined?
o: One sudden invasion destroyed every city
Climate and river changes, with trade decline
A single volcanic eruption buried them
A civil war between rival kings
quiz.e: Weaker monsoons and shifting rivers likely drove people to smaller villages; the invasion idea has been dropped.

LESSONS.push: Their drains were covered 5,000 years ago, yet no one can read their words.

LESSONS.title: Ancient China and the first emperor
LESSONS.hook: One ruler united China, standardised its writing, linked its first great walls and was buried with an army of clay soldiers.

sections.key: The Shang left China's earliest writing, and the Zhou introduced the Mandate of Heaven, which justified rebellion against bad rulers.
sections.b:
Chinese civilisation grew along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, where people farmed millet and rice. The Shang dynasty (about 1600–1046 BC) left the earliest known Chinese writing, on oracle bones: priests carved questions to ancestors onto bones and shells, heated them and read the cracks. The Shang were also masters of bronze casting.

The Zhou dynasty that overthrew them introduced the Mandate of Heaven: the idea that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler and withdraws it from a bad one. Floods, famines and revolts could be read as signs a dynasty had lost the mandate, which justified rebellion.

sections.key: Constant war between seven states produced a burst of ideas, from Confucian duty to Daoist harmony to Legalist strict law.
sections.b: As Zhou power faded, China split into competing states, and by the end seven major powers were fighting for survival. Constant war drove new ideas in the age of the Hundred Schools of Thought. Confucius, who lived slightly earlier, taught respect, duty, family loyalty and government by virtuous example. Daoism, traditionally traced to the possibly legendary Laozi, emphasised harmony with nature. Legalists argued that strict laws, rewards and harsh punishments made a state strong. Military thinking flourished too, including The Art of War, traditionally credited to Sun Tzu. Iron tools and crossbows also changed farming and warfare.

sections.key: Qin Shi Huang united China using Legalist methods and one script, one currency and one set of measures.
sections.b:
King Ying Zheng of Qin, using Legalist ideas and a ruthless army, conquered the other states and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, 'First Emperor of Qin'. The name China likely comes from Qin. He replaced hereditary lords with officials appointed and paid by the centre, a system later dynasties kept. He was also brutal: according to the historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later, he ordered books burned and scholars executed, though some details may be exaggerated.

To bind the empire together, he imposed one script, one currency and standard weights and measures. He even fixed cart axle widths so wagons could use the same ruts. Roads and canals moved troops and goods quickly. He died in 210 BC, and his dynasty collapsed within four years.

sections.key: The Great Wall mostly dates from the Ming, while the Terracotta Army guarded the First Emperor's tomb.
sections.b:
Several Warring States had built walls against rivals and northern nomads. Qin Shi Huang joined and extended the northern ones, using rammed earth and forced labour. Most of the stone and brick wall tourists visit dates from the Ming dynasty, over 1,500 years later. All its branches together stretch more than 20,000 kilometres. It is not visible from the Moon with the naked eye, a popular myth.

In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an found the Terracotta Army: an estimated 8,000 life-size soldiers, with horses and chariots, guarding the emperor in the afterlife. Each face looks individual, and they were once brightly painted. The emperor's own burial mound has never been opened. Sima Qian described rivers of mercury inside, and soil tests have found unusually high mercury levels there.

sections.key: The Han softened Qin's system, opened the Silk Road and developed paper, creating foundations that outlasted them.
sections.b:
The Han dynasty kept Qin's centralised system but softened it, adopting Confucian ideas and choosing officials partly by recommendation and examination rather than birth alone. That grew into the imperial civil service examinations, used for over a thousand years. The emperor system lasted until 1912.

Around 138 BC, the envoy Zhang Qian travelled deep into Central Asia, and his reports helped open trade routes later called the Silk Road. Silk, spices, horses, glass, ideas and religions moved along them, and Buddhism reached China from India this way. Han China also developed paper, which Cai Lun improved around AD 105, and early lodestone direction-finders, ancestors of the compass. China's majority ethnic group still calls itself the Han.

quiz.q: What was the Mandate of Heaven?
o: A law code that fixed the rights of every farmer
A calendar used by priests to predict floods
A rule that only the eldest son could rule
The idea that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler
quiz.e: Disasters and revolts could signal that a ruler had lost the mandate, which justified rebellion.

quiz.q: Which Warring States school argued that strict laws and harsh punishments made a state strong?
o: Legalism
Daoism
Confucianism
Mohism
quiz.e: Legalism favoured strict laws and punishments, and the Qin used it to conquer rival states.

quiz.q: Why did a single standard script matter so much to the empire?
o: It was much easier to carve than older scripts
It reduced the number of characters to a few dozen
People speaking different languages could read the same characters
It replaced spoken language across the empire
quiz.e: A shared script bound the empire together, and Chinese writing still works this way today.

quiz.q: What is true of the Great Wall tourists visit today?
o: It was built in one go by the First Emperor
Most of its stone and brick dates from the Ming dynasty
It can be seen from the Moon with the naked eye
It was built to stop the Silk Road trade
quiz.e: Qin walls were mostly earth; the famous stone and brick sections are about 1,500 years younger.

quiz.q: How did the Han change the way officials were chosen?
o: Entirely by a lottery among adult men
Only by military rank won in battle
Only by inheriting a father's post
Partly by recommendation and examination
quiz.e: Han examinations grew into the civil service exams used for more than a thousand years.

LESSONS.push: One ruler fixed the width of cart axles. Why that mattered to an empire.

LESSONS.title: The Maya, Aztecs and Inca
LESSONS.hook: Pyramids, floating gardens and a road network across the Andes. The Americas produced great civilisations with no contact with Europe or Asia.

sections.key: Without any contact with Eurasia, Americans domesticated crops that now feed the world and built cities and states.
sections.b:
People reached the Americas at least 15,000 years ago, most likely from Asia. Without contact with Eurasia, they domesticated crops that now feed the world: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, chillies, squash and many beans.

In Mesoamerica (modern Mexico and Central America) and the Andes, complex societies arose with cities, monumental architecture and states. The Olmecs, from around 1200 BC, are often called Mesoamerica's first civilisation, famous for colossal carved stone heads. In the Andes, Caral in Peru was building large ceremonial mounds nearly 5,000 years ago, around the time of Egypt's early pyramids.

sections.key: The Maya were rival city-states with the most complete writing system and an advanced zero-based maths.
sections.b:
The Maya flourished especially between about AD 250 and 900, in city-states such as Tikal, Palenque and Copán. They were never one empire: rival kingdoms formed alliances and fought wars. Kings recorded their deeds on carved stone stelae. Their writing, using several hundred glyphs, was the most complete in the ancient Americas, and scholars have largely deciphered it since the 1970s and 1980s.

Maya mathematics counted in base 20 using a dot for one, a bar for five and a shell for zero. They were among the few ancient peoples to develop zero independently. Priests tracked the Sun, Moon and Venus and could predict eclipses. Their Long Count calendar began at 3114 BC. The 2012 'end of the world' was a modern myth: a cycle simply rolled over, like an odometer.

sections.key: The Aztecs built Tenochtitlan on a lake, fed it with chinampas and ruled central Mexico through tribute.
sections.b:
The Mexica, or Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325. It grew into one of the world's largest cities, with perhaps 200,000 people, connected to the shore by causeways and fed partly by chinampas: farm plots built up from the lake bed with mud and plants.

From 1428 the Aztecs led an alliance of three cities that conquered much of central Mexico, demanding regular tribute of maize, cloth, cacao, feathers and gold. They practised human sacrifice on a large scale, believing it helped keep the Sun moving and the world in balance. Modern Mexico City stands on the ruins.

sections.key: The Inca ruled a vast empire without writing, using roads, runners, knotted khipu and labour tax.
sections.b:
In the 1400s, especially under Pachacuti, the Inca expanded from Cusco to an empire of about 4,000 kilometres, from modern Ecuador to Chile. They built roughly 40,000 kilometres of roads with rope bridges, and relay runners called chasquis carried messages hundreds of kilometres in a day or two. Their tight stonework at Machu Picchu and Cusco has survived major earthquakes.

The Inca had no written script as we know it. Officials recorded numbers, and possibly more, on knotted cords called khipu, where knot type and position showed values in base 10. Instead of money, people paid tax in labour, called mit'a, and the state stored food, cloth and weapons in storehouses. Farmers built terraces and freeze-dried potatoes into chuño.

sections.key: Disease killed most of the people, and these civilisations live on in their descendants, languages and foods.
sections.b:
Hernán Cortés arrived in Mexico in 1519 with a few hundred Spaniards. Allied with tens of thousands of Indigenous people who resented Aztec rule, he took Tenochtitlan in 1521. Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532, as a civil war split the empire. The biggest killer was disease: smallpox and other illnesses, to which Indigenous Americans had no immunity, killed a huge share of the population.

These were not 'lost' civilisations. Millions still speak Mayan languages, Nahuatl and Quechua. English words like chocolate, tomato, avocado and chilli come from Nahuatl. Potatoes transformed European diets, and Indigenous communities now lead efforts to protect their languages, sites and stories.

quiz.q: What is notable about the crops the early Americans domesticated?
o: They were developed without contact with Eurasia and now feed the world
They were all brought from Asia by later traders
They were used only for religious ceremonies
They were abandoned once Europeans arrived
quiz.e: Maize, potatoes and tomatoes came from the Americas, developed independently of Eurasia.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Maya is correct?
o: They were ruled as one empire from a single capital
They had no writing system at all
They were rival city-states, not one empire
They predicted the world would end in 2012
quiz.e: The Maya were separate kingdoms, and the 2012 claim is a modern myth about a calendar cycle rolling over.

quiz.q: How did the Aztecs feed a city built on a lake?
o: By importing all food from Europe by ship
With chinampas, farm plots built up from the lake bed
By hunting herds on the island itself
By farming only on the steep mountains
quiz.e: Chinampas were built from mud and plants and helped feed Tenochtitlan.

quiz.q: How did the Inca keep records without a written script?
o: Clay tablets pressed with a reed stylus
Painted books made from bark paper
Carved wooden boards covered in glyphs
Knotted cords called khipu, using base 10
quiz.e: The type and position of knots on khipu showed numerical values.

quiz.q: What killed the largest share of Indigenous Americans after the conquest?
o: Battles with Spanish soldiers
Earthquakes that struck the cities
Diseases like smallpox
Famines caused by crop failure
quiz.e: Indigenous Americans had no immunity to European diseases, which killed many more than battles did.

LESSONS.push: They had no iron or wheeled transport, yet built roads, cities and calendars.

LESSONS.title: Athens and Sparta: the Greek city-states
LESSONS.hook: Ancient Greece was never one country. It was hundreds of fiercely independent cities, and two of them couldn't have been more different.

sections.key: Greece was never one country but many independent cities, each called a polis, linked by shared culture.
sections.b:
Greece's mountains and islands split people into small communities. From around 800 BC, these grew into city-states, each called a polis (the root of words like politics and police). A polis was a city plus its farmland, with its own government, laws, army, coins and gods. Scholars have counted roughly a thousand, most with only a few thousand people. Greeks shared a language, religion, the oracle at Delphi and the Olympic Games, and called non-Greek speakers 'barbarians'. Yet they fought each other constantly.

Farmland was scarce, so from the 700s BC cities sent settlers to found independent colonies. Marseille began as Massalia, Naples as Neapolis and Istanbul as Byzantium.

sections.key: Athens grew rich from trade, silver and a navy, then became a democratic centre of philosophy, drama and art.
sections.b:
Athens, built around the rocky hill of the Acropolis, grew rich from trade, the silver mines at Laurion and its powerful navy. In the 400s BC it became the cultural capital of the Greek world.

Athenian citizens governed themselves in an early democracy, debating in the Assembly and trading in the agora, the bustling marketplace and meeting ground. The city produced philosophers like Socrates and Plato, playwrights like Sophocles, and the historian Thucydides. Its most famous building, the Parthenon, a marble temple to the goddess Athena, was completed in 432 BC and still stands above the modern city.

sections.key: Sparta organised everything around war, and depended on a huge enslaved population, the helots.
sections.b:
Sparta, in the southern Peloponnese, took a very different path. At about age seven, boys left home for the agoge, a harsh state-run training system that taught endurance, discipline and fighting. Adult men lived and ate with their army messes and were banned from trade, so their full-time job was war. Spartan women had unusual freedom: they exercised outdoors, owned land and ran estates.

All this rested on the helots, a huge enslaved population who did the farming and outnumbered Spartan citizens many times over. Fear of a helot revolt shaped Spartan life.

sections.key: Sparta's reputation for few words is partly legend, and its mixed government shared power among kings, elders and ephors.
sections.b:
Spartans were famous for saying a lot in few words. According to ancient writers, when Philip II of Macedon threatened, 'If I invade Laconia, I will destroy you', they replied with one word: 'If.' That's where laconic comes from. Most of what we know comes from outsiders, so some is myth.

Sparta's government was unusual too. Two kings from two royal families led the army and performed religious duties. A council of elders, the gerousia, had 28 men over 60 plus the kings, and prepared laws. Five ephors, elected every year, could supervise and even put the kings on trial. An assembly of adult Spartan men approved major decisions by shouting. Greeks admired this balance.

sections.key: A 27-year war between Athens and Sparta ended in Athenian defeat, and Greek city-states soon fell to Macedon.
sections.b:
As Athens built an empire of allied cities, Sparta and its allies grew alarmed. War broke out in 431 BC and lasted, on and off, 27 years. Athens had the stronger navy, Sparta the stronger army. A plague in 430 BC killed perhaps a quarter of Athens' population, and a disastrous invasion of Sicily cost thousands of lives. With Persian money, Sparta built a fleet, and in 404 BC a starving Athens surrendered.

The city-states kept fighting, and Thebes broke Sparta's army at Leuctra in 371 BC, freeing many helots. Philip II of Macedon then defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BC. The age of independent city-states was over, but their ideas about citizenship, law and debate have lasted thousands of years.

quiz.q: What was a polis?
o: A temple built to honour a Greek god
A body of soldiers in the Spartan army
An independent Greek city-state with its own laws and army
A Greek colony ruled directly from Athens
quiz.e: Greece was never one country; it was hundreds of self-governing city-states.

quiz.q: What helped make Athens rich and powerful in the 400s BC?
o: Vast farmland and a huge army
Trade, silver mines and a strong navy
Gold mines in the northern mountains
Tribute from the whole Persian empire
quiz.e: Trade, the Laurion silver mines and the navy funded Athens' cultural golden age.

quiz.q: What did Spartan society depend on?
o: Wealthy merchants who funded the army
Foreign workers hired from Athens
Spartan women who worked the farms
Enslaved helots who did the farming
quiz.e: Helots farmed so that Spartan men could train for war, but Sparta always feared their revolt.

quiz.q: Why does the Spartan reply 'If' show why we call speech laconic?
o: It said a lot in a single word
It was a long speech in reply
It was a written treaty
It was a battle cry
quiz.e: Laconic comes from Laconia, the Spartan homeland, where brevity was admired.

quiz.q: What was the outcome of the Peloponnesian War?
o: Athens surrendered to Sparta after 27 years
Athens defeated Sparta with its stronger army
Persia conquered both rivals
The war ended in a peace treaty with no winner
quiz.e: Starving and weakened by plague and defeat in Sicily, Athens surrendered in 404 BC.

LESSONS.push: Ancient Greece was never one country. Two of its cities nearly destroyed each other.

LESSONS.title: The birth of democracy
LESSONS.hook: Around 2,500 years ago, the citizens of Athens tried something radical: letting ordinary people make the decisions.

sections.key: Athenian democracy began with Cleisthenes' reforms in 508 BC, shifting power from noble families to citizens.
sections.b: Demokratia combines demos, the people, and kratos, power or rule. Before democracy, Athens was ruled by aristocrats and, at times, by tyrants: strongmen who seized power. Around 594 BC the lawmaker Solon eased debt slavery and gave poorer citizens a voice. Then in 508 BC the reformer Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian society into ten new tribes that mixed people from the city, coast and countryside, so power flowed from citizens across the whole region rather than a few noble families. This is usually counted as the birth of Athenian democracy, though it kept developing over the following decades.

sections.key: Athens was a direct democracy where citizens voted themselves and most officials were chosen by lot, not elected.
sections.b:
Athens had a direct democracy: citizens didn't elect representatives, they decided themselves. The Assembly met about 40 times a year on the Pnyx hillside. Any citizen could attend, speak and vote, usually by show of hands, on war and peace, laws, taxes and treaties. Imagine Australians gathering in person to vote on every new law.

Athenians thought elections favoured the rich, famous and persuasive, so most public jobs were filled by lot. A council of 500 citizens, 50 from each tribe, was chosen randomly each year to prepare business for the Assembly. Most people could serve only twice in a lifetime. Only jobs needing expertise, like the ten military generals, were elected.

sections.key: Athenian juries were huge, chosen by lot and made up of ordinary citizens, which made bribery and capture hard.
sections.b:
Athens had no police force, public prosecutors or professional judges. Ordinary citizens brought cases themselves, and each side spoke in person, although they could pay a speechwriter. Speeches were timed with a water clock, the klepsydra.

Juries were enormous, often 201, 501 or more citizens aged over 30, chosen by lot on the day to make bribery hard. They voted by secret ballot using bronze discs and gave no reasons. Socrates was tried by a jury of about 500. Modern juries echo the same idea of ordinary citizens judging cases.

sections.key: Pay for jurors and Assembly members let ordinary workers participate, not just the wealthy.
sections.b:
Democracy only works if ordinary people can afford to show up. A labourer who spent a day on a jury lost a day's wages. So in the mid-400s BC, the statesman Pericles introduced pay for jurors, and around 400 BC Athens began paying citizens to attend the Assembly as well. The amounts were modest, roughly enough to live on for a day. Critics grumbled that it encouraged idle crowds, but it meant farmers, craftsmen and rowers could genuinely take part. Paying politicians and public servants today follows the same logic: public office shouldn't be only for the wealthy.

But who counted as a citizen was another matter.

sections.key: Athenian democracy excluded most residents, could banish powerful men, and still inspired later democracies.
sections.b:
'Rule by the people' really meant rule by a minority of free men. Women couldn't vote or hold office. Enslaved people had no political rights. Foreign residents, called metics, couldn't vote even after generations, and from 451 BC citizenship required both parents to be Athenian.

Once a year, citizens could vote to banish someone who seemed too powerful, scratching a name on a pottery shard called an ostrakon. If enough votes were cast, probably at least 6,000, the person named most often was exiled for ten years, without a trial. That gave us the word ostracise.

Plato distrusted democracy, and a jury sentenced Socrates in 399 BC. Yet when modern democracies emerged, their founders studied Athens, and juries, referendums and citizens' assemblies chosen by lot still echo it.

quiz.q: Why is Cleisthenes' reform of 508 BC counted as the birth of Athenian democracy?
o: It made one strongman the permanent ruler
It shifted power from a few noble families to citizens across the region
It abolished the Assembly in favour of a king
It gave every resident the right to vote
quiz.e: Mixing the new tribes spread power across all citizens rather than leaving it with noble families.

quiz.q: Why did Athenians fill most public jobs by lot?
o: They had no way of counting votes
Few citizens were willing to take part
The gods insisted it be done that way
They thought elections favoured the rich, famous and persuasive
quiz.e: Lotteries gave ordinary citizens a real turn and reduced the advantage of wealth and charm.

quiz.q: Why were Athenian juries chosen by lot on the day of the trial?
o: To make bribing jurors difficult
To make sure only experts judged cases
To finish trials faster than usual
To let the wealthy sit on every jury
quiz.e: Large juries picked by lot at the last minute made bribery hard.

quiz.q: Why did Athens begin paying jurors and Assembly members?
o: To make public office more prestigious
To raise money for the navy
So working people could afford to take part
To keep foreigners out of politics
quiz.e: Without pay, a day in the Assembly or on a jury cost poorer citizens a day's wages.

quiz.q: Who was excluded from Athenian citizenship and voting?
o: All men over thirty years of age
Women, enslaved people and foreign residents
Farmers who lived outside the city
Anyone with a criminal record
quiz.e: Democracy belonged to a minority of free men; ideas about who counts have changed a great deal.

LESSONS.push: Athenians picked most officials by lottery, not votes. They had a reason.

LESSONS.title: Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis
LESSONS.hook: In the 400s BC the mighty Persian Empire invaded Greece twice. Three battles decided whether Greek civilisation would survive.

sections.key: Persia's punishment of Athens for helping a revolt set up a clash between an empire and quarrelsome city-states.
sections.b:
By 500 BC, the Achaemenid Persian Empire ruled millions of people across three continents, linked by royal roads and governed through provinces called satrapies. Greek cities on the coast of Ionia, in modern Turkey, were under Persian control. When they rebelled in 499 BC, Athens and Eretria sent ships to help, and rebels burned the provincial capital of Sardis. King Darius I crushed the revolt and resolved to punish Athens.

The wars that followed pitted a vast, well-organised empire against a handful of quarrelsome Greek city-states, and the outcome shaped the history of Europe.

sections.key: Greek hoplites fought as a disciplined phalanx, while triremes gave the navy its power.
sections.b:
A Greek hoplite was a citizen-soldier who bought his own armour: a bronze helmet, a large round shield and a long thrusting spear. Hoplites fought shoulder to shoulder in a phalanx, each man's shield partly protecting his neighbour, so discipline mattered more than individual heroics.

At sea, the key weapon was the trireme, a sleek warship rowed by about 170 oarsmen on three levels, with a bronze ram at the bow for smashing enemy hulls. Rowers were often poorer citizens, and their importance to the navy later strengthened their political voice in Athens.

sections.key: Athenians charged across the plain at Marathon and defeated a larger Persian force.
sections.b:
In 490 BC a Persian fleet landed at Marathon, about 40 kilometres from Athens. The Athenians, joined by the small city of Plataea, were outnumbered but charged across the plain and won a decisive victory. Herodotus says about 6,400 Persians died against 192 Athenians, figures that may be inflated.

He also tells of a runner, Pheidippides, who ran roughly 240 kilometres to Sparta to ask for help before the battle. The more famous story, of a messenger running from Marathon to Athens and dying after announcing victory, appears in later writers. It inspired the marathon race at the 1896 Olympics.

sections.key: Xerxes invaded with a vast force, and a small Greek rearguard at Thermopylae bought time before it fell.
sections.b:
Darius died before he could strike again, so his son Xerxes planned a far bigger invasion. His engineers built bridges of boats across the Hellespont and dug a canal through the Athos peninsula. In 480 BC a vast army and navy moved into Greece. Many Greek cities submitted. Others, led by Sparta and Athens, formed an alliance.

A Greek force of several thousand, including King Leonidas and 300 Spartans, blocked the narrow pass of Thermopylae. For three days they held off the Persians, including the elite Immortals. Then a local Greek, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass. Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with a rearguard of Spartans and several hundred Thespians, who were killed. It was a defeat, but it bought time.

sections.key: Greek victories at Salamis and Plataea ended the invasion, and Herodotus recorded the wars.
sections.b:
The Persians burned an evacuated Athens. Themistocles had earlier persuaded the city to spend a silver strike on around 200 triremes. Now he lured the bigger Persian fleet into the narrow straits near Salamis, reportedly with a false message that the Greeks were about to flee. Crowded together, the Persian ships couldn't manoeuvre, and the Greek triremes rammed and sank many.

In 479 BC, the Greeks defeated Mardonius's army at Plataea, and the invasions were over. Had Persia won, Athens' democracy and golden age might never have happened.

Herodotus, writing a generation later, is called the father of history. But he included myths and rumours, so his numbers, such as Xerxes' army of millions, are almost certainly exaggerated.

quiz.q: Why did Darius I resolve to punish Athens?
o: Athens had refused to pay a yearly tax
Athens had invaded Persian territory in Egypt
Athens had insulted a Persian ambassador
Athens had sent ships to help the Ionian Greek revolt
quiz.e: Athens and Eretria helped the rebels who burned Sardis, so Persia targeted them.

quiz.q: Why did discipline matter so much to a hoplite phalanx?
o: Each man's shield partly protected his neighbour
Soldiers fought alone in separate duels
Spears were too light to use as a group
Armour was provided by the state
quiz.e: The phalanx only worked if soldiers held the line shoulder to shoulder.

quiz.q: What should we remember about the Marathon story?
o: Persian records confirm every detail
Herodotus gave exact numbers historians trust
Some famous details come from later writers
The messenger story is the earliest source
quiz.e: Ancient accounts mix evidence with later legend, so numbers and famous stories need caution.

quiz.q: Why is Thermopylae remembered even though the Greeks lost?
o: The Greeks destroyed the Persian navy there
A small force held a narrow pass and bought precious time
Xerxes was killed in the fighting
The Persians withdrew from Greece afterwards
quiz.e: The stand showed courage, and delaying the Persians gave the Greeks time to prepare.

quiz.q: Why did the Persian fleet struggle at Salamis?
o: Their ships were slower than the Greek ones in open water
A storm scattered their fleet before battle
Their rowers refused to fight
Their ships were crowded in narrow straits and couldn't manoeuvre
quiz.e: Themistocles lured the bigger fleet into a space where its numbers became a weakness.

LESSONS.push: A few thousand Greeks held a pass against an empire. Then a message tricked a fleet.

LESSONS.title: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle
LESSONS.hook: Three thinkers, teacher to student to student, laid the foundations of Western philosophy, science and politics.

sections.key: From around 600 BC, Greek thinkers sought natural explanations for the world and argued about them openly.
sections.b: Around 600 BC, thinkers in Greek cities began asking what the world was made of, without appealing to gods. Thales of Miletus thought everything came from water, and is said to have predicted a solar eclipse. Pythagoras and his followers found mathematical patterns in music and the cosmos. Heraclitus said everything is always changing: you can't step into the same river twice. Democritus, building on his teacher Leucippus, proposed that all matter is made of tiny indivisible particles, which he called atoms. They were often wrong in the details, but the method mattered: seeking natural explanations and arguing about them openly.

sections.key: Socrates claimed to be wise only because he knew how little he knew, and he questioned people until their confident definitions failed.
sections.b:
Socrates (about 470–399 BC) wrote nothing down. We know him through his students, mainly Plato and Xenophon. A stonemason's son who served as a hoplite, he wandered Athens barefoot, questioning people who claimed to know about justice, courage or goodness, until their confident definitions fell apart. He said he was wise only because he knew how little he knew.

In 399 BC, a jury convicted him of corrupting the youth and disrespecting the city's gods, and he was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock. He refused his friends' offer to help him escape.

sections.key: Asking probing questions exposes hidden assumptions and leads to better definitions, even without a final answer.
sections.b:
The Socratic method starts with a claim, such as 'courage is standing firm in battle', then asks questions that reveal exceptions and contradictions, forcing a better definition. Many dialogues end without a final answer, but everyone understands the problem more clearly.

At his trial, as Plato records it, Socrates declared that 'the unexamined life is not worth living'. The method lives on in tutorials, law school classes where students are questioned on cases, and coaching and therapy that help people examine their own assumptions. Its core habit, asking 'how do you know?', is useful anywhere.

sections.key: Plato argued the real world is an imperfect copy of perfect Forms, and imagined a state ruled by trained philosopher-kings.
sections.b:
Plato (about 428–348 BC) wrote around 35 dialogues, most starring Socrates, and founded the Academy in Athens around 387 BC. He argued that the things we see are imperfect copies of perfect, eternal Forms: every circle you draw is slightly flawed, but the Form of a circle is perfect. In his allegory of the cave, prisoners chained in the dark mistake shadows on a wall for reality, and philosophy is the journey out into the light.

In The Republic, he imagined a city of workers, guardians and rulers, ruled by philosopher-kings trained for decades to know the Good. He argued suitable women could be guardians too. He distrusted democracy, partly because it had executed Socrates. Critics, from Aristotle to Karl Popper, argue his ideal state would be authoritarian.

sections.key: Aristotle built knowledge from observation and defined the good life as flourishing through virtue, and their ideas survived through Byzantium and Baghdad.
sections.b:
Aristotle (384–322 BC) studied at Plato's Academy for about 20 years, tutored Alexander the Great, then founded the Lyceum. Unlike Plato, he believed knowledge starts with careful observation. He dissected animals, noted that dolphins breathe air, and developed the first formal system of logic. Some of his science was wrong, like heavier objects falling faster, but his method endured.

In ethics, he said a good life is eudaimonia, flourishing through practising virtue. Each virtue is a balance between extremes: truthfulness sits between boastfulness and false modesty.

Greek learning survived in the Byzantine Empire and the Islamic world, where scholars in Baghdad translated Aristotle. It returned to Europe through Latin translations. Whitehead called European philosophy 'a series of footnotes to Plato'.

quiz.q: What was new about the first Greek philosophers' approach?
o: They sought natural explanations without appealing to gods
They relied on priests to explain the world
They avoided arguing about their ideas
They wrote only about politics and law
quiz.e: Their conclusions were often wrong, but openly arguing for natural explanations was the lasting breakthrough.

quiz.q: What did Socrates mean by saying he was wise because he knew how little he knew?
o: He believed no one could learn anything
He had read more than anyone else in Athens
Recognising the limits of your knowledge is the start of wisdom
He thought knowledge was only for the young
quiz.e: Admitting ignorance lets you question confident claims, which is the core of Socratic thinking.

quiz.q: What is the main habit the Socratic method builds?
o: Memorising answers from respected teachers
Asking 'how do you know?' to test assumptions
Winning arguments by speaking longer
Avoiding disagreement to keep the peace
quiz.e: Questioning exposes exceptions and contradictions, leading to a clearer understanding.

quiz.q: What does Plato's allegory of the cave show?
o: The best cities should be built underground
Knowledge comes only from observing nature
Sunlight is dangerous to untrained eyes
People can mistake shadows for reality until they leave the cave
quiz.e: For Plato, philosophy is the hard journey from illusion towards real understanding.

quiz.q: How did Aristotle's approach to knowledge differ from Plato's?
o: He denied that anything could be known
He relied on myths and stories of the gods
He started from careful observation of the real world
He studied only mathematics and music
quiz.e: Aristotle dissected animals and gathered evidence, grounding knowledge in the real world.

LESSONS.push: He wrote nothing down, yet shaped how we think. Why he drank the hemlock.

LESSONS.title: Alexander the Great
LESSONS.hook: Before he turned 33, he built one of the largest empires in history. Then it fell apart almost overnight.

sections.key: Philip II built Macedon into a military power, and his son Alexander became king at 20.
sections.b:
Macedon, north of Greece, was seen by many Greeks as half-barbarian. Philip II turned it into a military power, reorganising its army around the phalanx: dense blocks of soldiers with pikes called sarissas, around five to six metres long. His son Alexander was educated by Aristotle, who taught him philosophy, medicine and literature. Alexander reportedly slept with a copy of Homer's Iliad under his pillow and saw himself as a new Achilles. At 18 he commanded cavalry at Chaeronea. When Philip was assassinated in 336 BC, Alexander became king at 20 and quickly crushed rivals and rebellious Greek cities.

Legend adds that he tamed the wild horse Bucephalus by noticing it feared its own shadow.

sections.key: In ten years Alexander defeated the Persian Empire, winning battles at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela.
sections.b:
In 334 BC Alexander crossed into Asia with around 40,000 soldiers. He defeated Persian forces at the Granicus River, then beat King Darius III himself at Issus in 333 BC. After a seven-month siege of the island city of Tyre, he took Egypt, where he founded Alexandria and was welcomed as pharaoh. In 331 BC he crushed Darius again at Gaugamela, in modern Iraq, and marched into Babylon and the Persian capitals. Darius was killed by his own nobles in 330 BC. Alexander now ruled the old Persian Empire.

At Gordium in 333 BC, legend says he sliced through a tangled knot that only Asia's future ruler could undo. 'Cutting the Gordian knot' now means solving a hard problem boldly.

sections.key: Alexander's exhausted army refused to march further east, so he turned back after eight years of campaigning.
sections.b:
Alexander kept marching east through modern Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Pakistan, fighting difficult guerrilla campaigns in the mountains. In 326 BC he defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes River in a hard-fought battle that included war elephants. Impressed, he let Porus keep ruling as an ally.

Alexander wanted to push on to what he believed was the edge of the world, but at the Hyphasis River his soldiers, who had marched thousands of kilometres over eight years, refused. He turned back, leading part of the army through the Gedrosian desert, a brutal crossing that cost many lives.

sections.key: Alexander never lost a major battle, but he died young in 323 BC and his empire fractured among his generals.
sections.b:
Alexander never lost a major battle. He combined infantry, cavalry and siege engineering and often charged at the head of his Companion cavalry. He tried to blend Greek and Persian rule, adopting Persian dress and marrying Roxana and later Persian princesses. He could also be brutal: he razed Thebes, killed or enslaved thousands at Tyre, and killed his friend Cleitus in a drunken rage.

In 323 BC, he fell ill in Babylon and died after about two weeks, aged 32. The cause is still debated: fever, typhoid, malaria, heavy drinking and poison have all been suggested. Asked who should inherit, he supposedly said, 'To the strongest.' His generals fought for decades, and the empire broke into kingdoms, including Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucid Empire.

sections.key: Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture, and how we know him shows why to check sources.
sections.b:
The three centuries after Alexander are called the Hellenistic period. A common form of Greek, koine, became a shared language from Egypt to Afghanistan. Alexandria grew into the intellectual capital of the ancient world, with its famous Library and scholars like Euclid. Greek art mixed with local traditions, producing Greek-influenced Buddhist statues in Gandhara.

Those who marched with Alexander wrote about him, but their works are lost. The surviving histories, by Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus, Quintus Curtius and Justin, were written between about 300 and 500 years later. Some portray him as a hero, others as a tyrant ruined by power and drink. So when you meet a vivid Alexander story, ask who told it, when, and why.

quiz.q: How did Philip II turn Macedon into a military power?
o: By building the largest navy in the Mediterranean
By hiring Persian soldiers to fight for him
By reorganising its army around the phalanx with long pikes
By conquering Athens in a single campaign
quiz.e: The phalanx with five to six metre sarissas was the core of Macedon's army, which Alexander inherited.

quiz.q: What did the Gordian knot story come to mean?
o: Waiting patiently for the right moment
Solving a hard problem boldly
Following ancient prophecy exactly
Untangling a problem step by step
quiz.e: Alexander supposedly sliced through the knot, so cutting it means taking a bold shortcut.

quiz.q: Why did Alexander turn back from India?
o: He was defeated by King Porus
His empire had run out of money
His generals had been plotting against him
His exhausted army refused to go further
quiz.e: After eight years and thousands of kilometres, his soldiers refused to march on.

quiz.q: What happened to Alexander's empire after his death?
o: His generals fought each other and it split into kingdoms
His son ruled it peacefully for decades
It stayed united under Ptolemy
Persia quickly won it back
quiz.e: With no strong heir, his generals divided the empire into rival kingdoms.

quiz.q: Why should we treat vivid Alexander stories with caution?
o: Accounts were written centuries later
No ancient writer ever described him
His army kept no records at all
Coins and inscriptions disprove them
quiz.e: The main histories were written 300 to 500 years later, so it pays to ask who told a story and why.

LESSONS.push: He never lost a major battle, yet died at 32 with no clear heir. What followed.

LESSONS.title: What the Greeks gave us
LESSONS.hook: Theatre, the Olympics, geometry, medicine and thousands of everyday words. You use Ancient Greece every day without noticing.

sections.key: The Greeks gave us the Olympics and theatre, along with words like stadium, drama and chorus.
sections.b:
Every four years, athletes from across the Greek world gathered at Olympia to honour Zeus. A sacred truce allowed safe travel. The earliest event was a sprint of about 190 metres, the stadion, which gave us the word stadium. Winners received an olive wreath. The games ended around AD 393 and were revived in Athens in 1896.

In Athens, plays were performed at festivals for the god Dionysus in huge open-air theatres; the one at Epidaurus seated around 14,000. Tragedies by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides explored fate, pride and suffering. Comedies, especially by Aristophanes, mocked politicians and celebrities. Actors, all men, wore masks, while a chorus sang and commented. Drama, scene, chorus, tragedy, comedy and theatre are all Greek.

sections.key: Homer's epics and Greek myths still supply our stories and everyday phrases.
sections.b:
The Iliad and the Odyssey, epic poems credited to Homer, were probably written down in the 700s BC after generations of oral performance. The Iliad tells of the rage of Achilles during the Trojan War; the Odyssey follows Odysseus' ten-year struggle to get home. Greeks memorised and quoted them as we might quote Shakespeare.

Greek myths of gods and heroes, from Zeus and Athena to Heracles and Medusa, still fill films, novels and games. Phrases like Achilles' heel, a Trojan horse, Pandora's box and a herculean task all come from these stories.

sections.key: Greek thinkers proved results step by step and treated disease as natural, shaping mathematics and medicine.
sections.b:
Euclid's Elements, written in Alexandria around 300 BC, organised geometry into proofs built from a few simple starting assumptions. It was a textbook for over 2,000 years. Archimedes showed that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 and worked out the principle of buoyancy. Eratosthenes estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing noon shadows in two Egyptian cities, getting surprisingly close. Aristarchus even suggested the Earth orbits the Sun.

Hippocrates of Kos, born around 460 BC, taught that illnesses have natural causes, not divine punishment, and that doctors should carefully record symptoms. His followers' theory of four humours was wrong, yet it dominated Western medicine for about 2,000 years. The Hippocratic Oath inspired modern pledges such as the Declaration of Geneva.

sections.key: Greek temples used set column styles and clever optical tricks, and still shape public buildings today.
sections.b:
Greek temples followed strict proportions and used three main column styles, called orders. Doric columns are plain and sturdy, Ionic columns have scroll-shaped tops, and Corinthian columns are topped with carved acanthus leaves.

Builders even used subtle tricks: the Parthenon's columns swell slightly and lean inwards so the building looks perfectly straight from a distance. The Romans copied these styles, and they spread again during the Renaissance and the Greek Revival of the 1700s and 1800s. Look at courthouses, banks and museums, including many in Australian cities, and you'll often see Greek-style columns and triangular pediments.

sections.key: The Greek alphabet added vowels, led to Latin and Cyrillic, and gave English thousands of root words.
sections.b:
Around the 800s BC, Greeks adapted the alphabet of the Phoenicians, seafaring traders from modern Lebanon. Phoenician writing recorded only consonants, so the Greeks turned some unneeded letters into vowels. The Greek alphabet then passed to the Etruscans and Romans, becoming the Latin alphabet used for English, and later inspired Cyrillic. Greek letters are everywhere in science: pi for circles, delta for change, alpha, beta and gamma for radiation.

English is packed with Greek: democracy, philosophy, biology, telephone and alphabet itself. Cardiology comes from kardia, heart, and -itis means inflammation. An odyssey is a long journey, after Odysseus. Learning roots like tele (far), graph (write) and bio (life) helps you decode unfamiliar words.

quiz.q: What do the words stadium, drama and chorus have in common?
o: They all come from Latin
They all come from Greek
They were all invented by Shakespeare
They all originate in Phoenician
quiz.e: Many English words for sport and performance trace back to Greek Olympic and theatre traditions.

quiz.q: What does the phrase 'Achilles' heel' mean?
o: A great warrior's strength
A hard journey home
A gift hiding a threat
A person's one weak point
quiz.e: It comes from Achilles, whose vulnerable heel became a symbol of one fatal weakness.

quiz.q: Why is the Greek approach in Euclid's Elements still important?
