It governed Russia alongside the soviets for years
The Bolsheviks shut it after one day
quiz.e: Lenin would not share power with a body his party did not control, so one-party rule began almost immediately.

quiz.q: What was the main cause of the famines of 1932-33?
o: A foreign naval blockade
Floods across Ukraine
Forced collectivisation of farms under Stalin
The loss of territory at Brest-Litovsk
quiz.e: Stalin's drive to force peasants onto collective farms disrupted food production, killing millions.

quiz.q: Why did the Soviet Union dissolve in 1991?
o: It lost a direct war with the United States
Gorbachev's reforms let the system unravel and it broke up
Its army overthrew the Communist Party leadership
Its space programme ran out of funding for years
quiz.e: Reform meant to renew the system instead loosened the state's control, and it broke into 15 countries.

LESSONS.push: In 1917 Germany helped send Lenin home to Russia. Here's why, and what followed.

LESSONS.title: The Roman Republic
LESSONS.hook: For nearly 500 years Rome had no king. Its system of checks and balances inspired the founders of modern republics.

sections.key: Rome expelled its last king around 509 BC and built a republic where power was shared, short-term and checked.
sections.b:
According to Roman tradition, Rome was founded in 753 BC and ruled by seven kings. The last, Tarquin the Proud, was overthrown in about 509 BC after his son assaulted a noblewoman, Lucretia. How much is legend is debated, but Romans came to hate the idea of a king, or rex. They created a res publica, 'the people's affair', the origin of our word republic.

Instead of a king, Rome elected two consuls each year. They commanded armies and led government, but each could veto the other, and after a year they stepped down and could be prosecuted for abuses. The Senate, mostly former officials sitting for life, controlled public money and foreign affairs. In a real emergency, a dictator could be appointed, but only for six months.

sections.key: Citizens voted in assemblies weighted towards the rich, and plebeians won rights through collective action.
sections.b:
Adult male citizens voted in assemblies, but votes were counted by group. In the assembly that elected consuls, groups were arranged by wealth and the richest voted first, so the result was often settled before poorer citizens were asked. Ambitious men climbed a ladder of offices, the cursus honorum, from quaestor to praetor to consul. Campaigning was costly, so a career needed money, famous ancestors or powerful friends.

Early Rome was dominated by patricians, a few old families. Everyone else was a plebeian. In the Conflict of the Orders, plebeians repeatedly walked out together, a kind of general strike. They won officials called tribunes, who could veto harmful actions, and the Twelve Tables (about 450 BC), which put the laws on public display. In 367 BC they won the right to become consul.

sections.key: Rome conquered Italy by turning defeated peoples into allies, then crushed Carthage in the Punic Wars.
sections.b:
Rome gradually took over Italy, often making defeated peoples allies who kept local self-government but supplied soldiers. That gave it huge reserves of manpower. Then it clashed with Carthage, a wealthy trading city in modern Tunisia. In three Punic Wars between 264 and 146 BC, Rome built its first serious navy and eventually won.

The most famous moment came in 218 BC, when the Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army, with war elephants, over the Alps into Italy. At Cannae in 216 BC he destroyed a much larger Roman army. But Rome refused to negotiate and fought on. In 146 BC it destroyed Carthage completely, the same year it sacked Corinth in Greece.

sections.key: Conquest made the rich richer and made soldiers loyal to their generals instead of the Republic.
sections.b:
Conquest brought enormous wealth, but mostly to the rich, who bought up land and built large estates worked by enslaved captives. Small farmers, away fighting for years, lost their farms and drifted to Rome. The brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus tried to give public land to the poor and were killed in 133 and 121 BC, a shocking break with custom.

Around 107 BC the general Marius is traditionally credited with opening the army to poor volunteers. These soldiers depended on their commanders for pay and for land when they retired. Their loyalty shifted from the Republic to the generals who led them.

sections.key: Rival generals used armies to seize power, ending the Republic, but its ideas shaped modern government.
sections.b:
In 88 BC the general Sulla marched his army on Rome itself, later becoming dictator with no six-month limit. Pompey, Crassus and Julius Caesar then competed for power. Caesar's dictatorship ended with his assassination in 44 BC. His heir Octavian became sole ruler and took the name Augustus in 27 BC. The institutions survived on paper, but real power sat with one man.

The Republic's ideas lived on. The founders of the United States studied Rome closely, creating a Senate, dividing power between branches and writing as 'Publius'. Australia's Senate has a Roman name, though its design owes more to the American model. Fixed terms, vetoes, published laws and legal process all have Roman roots, as does 'candidate', from the Latin for 'dressed in white'.

quiz.q: Why did Rome limit each consul to one year and give each a veto over the other?
o: So that the Senate could be avoided
So that wars would be shorter
So that elections would cost less
So that no single man could rule alone as a king had
quiz.e: The republic spread power among short-term officials who checked one another.

quiz.q: How did plebeians win rights from the patrician elite?
o: By raising their own army and marching on Rome
By paying heavy taxes to the patrician families
By walking out of the city together in a general strike
By electing one of their own as king of Rome
quiz.e: Collective action left Rome without workers or soldiers, forcing concessions such as tribunes and written laws.

quiz.q: What helped Rome recover after crushing defeats like Cannae?
o: The elephants Hannibal had left behind in Italy
Italian allies supplied huge reserves of manpower
A peace treaty that Carthage offered after Cannae
Mercenary fleets hired from the Greek cities
quiz.e: Allies who kept local self-government but supplied soldiers gave Rome a deep reserve, so it could fight on.

quiz.q: Why did armies become a threat to the Republic?
o: Soldiers depended on generals for pay and land
The army grew too small to fight abroad
The Senate began commanding every legion directly
Soldiers refused to serve outside Italy any longer
quiz.e: Once troops looked to their commanders for their future, generals could use them to seize power.

quiz.q: What lasting lesson did the Republic's collapse offer?
o: Republics cannot survive once they conquer others
Dictators always step down when asked politely
Senates should hold all the power in a state
Leaders ignoring rules can slide into one-man rule
quiz.e: Rome's story, and its borrowed ideas of divided power, still warn what happens when checks fail.

LESSONS.push: Rome threw out its kings and built a system to stop any one man ruling. It failed. Why?

LESSONS.title: Julius Caesar and the end of the Republic
LESSONS.hook: A brilliant general, a gifted writer, a reckless gambler. Caesar's rise and murder turned Rome from republic into empire.

sections.key: Caesar rose through debt, charm and a private deal with Pompey and Crassus, which won him an army.
sections.b:
Gaius Julius Caesar was born around 100 BC into an old but not wealthy family. He was charismatic and ambitious, deep in debt from spending on public games and, said his enemies, bribes. Captured by pirates as a young man, he reportedly joked he would crucify them and, once ransomed, did. In 63 BC he was elected pontifex maximus, the chief priest, in his thirties. Even his rival Cicero praised his speaking.

In 60 BC Caesar formed a private alliance with Crassus, Rome's richest man, and Pompey, its most famous general, later called the First Triumvirate. It was a deal, not an office. As consul in 59 BC he forced through laws, then secured a five-year command in Gaul, giving him an army of his own.

sections.key: Conquering Gaul made Caesar rich and loved by his army, and his own writing made him famous.
sections.b:
From 58 to 50 BC Caesar conquered all of Gaul, roughly modern France and Belgium. He bridged the Rhine and crossed to Britain twice. His greatest victory was Alesia in 52 BC, where he trapped Vercingetorix inside a ring of walls, with another facing outward against a huge relief army. Ancient writers claimed around a million Gauls died and another million were enslaved. Historians treat the figures cautiously, but the toll was enormous.

Caesar also wrote about it. His Commentaries on the Gallic War use plain Latin and call him 'Caesar', so they read like neutral reports. They were not. Circulating in Rome, they kept his name in the news and made every war look necessary.

sections.key: In 49 BC Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army, started a civil war and beat Pompey.
sections.b:
By 50 BC Crassus was dead and Pompey's bond with Caesar had weakened. The Senate ordered Caesar to give up his army and return as a private citizen, when he would likely face prosecution. Governors were banned from leading armies into Italy. In January 49 BC he led a legion across the Rubicon, reportedly saying 'The die is cast.' Today 'crossing the Rubicon' means passing a point of no return. In 48 BC he defeated Pompey at Pharsalus.

Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered. Caesar backed Cleopatra in her struggle with her brother Ptolemy XIII, and she took the throne. In 47 BC he beat King Pharnaces so quickly he wrote, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.

sections.key: Caesar's reforms, including the Julian calendar, were lasting, but his rule alarmed senators.
sections.b:
After further wins in Africa and Spain, Caesar pardoned many former enemies. This won admiration but left opponents alive and resentful. He gave land to veterans, founded colonies, extended citizenship and enlarged the Senate. He also replaced Rome's drifting calendar with a 365-day year and a leap day every four years, the Julian calendar, the basis of ours. July is named after him.

But in early 44 BC he was named dictator for life, sat on a golden chair and put his portrait on coins, a first for a living Roman. To many senators, he looked like a king.

sections.key: Caesar's murder on 15 March 44 BC did not save the Republic; it led to more civil war and to Rome's first emperor.
sections.b:
On 15 March 44 BC, senators led by Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius stabbed Caesar to death at a Senate meeting, claiming to save the Republic. More than 60 men were said to be in the plot, and he suffered 23 wounds.

Instead of restoring the old order, the murder triggered more civil wars. Caesar's adopted heir Octavian joined Mark Antony to defeat the assassins at Philippi in 42 BC, then beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC. In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus. He never called himself king, but he was Rome's first emperor, and the Republic was over.

quiz.q: What was the First Triumvirate?
o: A council of three elected consuls in Rome
A private alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus
A Senate committee created to govern Gaul
A legion that served under Caesar in Gaul
quiz.e: The three combined wealth, fame and ambition in an informal deal that won Caesar an army.

quiz.q: Why did Caesar write his Gallic War commentaries in the third person?
o: It made them read like neutral reports
Roman law required generals to write that way
He wanted to hide that he was the author
Latin had no first-person form for generals
quiz.e: Calling himself 'Caesar' gave his publicity an air of objectivity.

quiz.q: What does 'crossing the Rubicon' mean today?
o: Winning a decisive victory
Breaking a promise
Retreating from a battle
Passing a point of no return
quiz.e: By leading an army into Italy, Caesar made civil war unavoidable.

quiz.q: Which of Caesar's reforms still shapes our lives?
o: The Roman alphabet used across Europe
The network of paved Roman roads
The 365-day calendar with a leap year
The Senate and its voting rules
quiz.e: The Julian calendar was the basis of the one we use today.

quiz.q: What did Caesar's assassination achieve?
o: It restored the Republic to full health
More civil war and Rome's first emperor
It made Brutus the new Roman dictator
It ended Rome's wars across the empire
quiz.e: The killers wanted to save the Republic, but the power struggle ended with Augustus ruling alone.

LESSONS.push: Caesar's killers wanted to save the Republic. Why did the murder end it instead?

LESSONS.title: Daily life in ancient Rome
LESSONS.hook: Apartment blocks, fast food, public toilets and traffic jams. Life in Rome was surprisingly familiar.

sections.key: Most Romans lived in cramped, fire-prone apartment blocks in a city of around a million.
sections.b: By the time of Augustus, Rome may have held around a million people, probably the largest city in the world, though numbers are debated. Most lived in insulae, apartment blocks several storeys high, often cheaply built and prone to fire and collapse. The poorest lived on the top floors, farthest from water and hardest to escape, while shops filled the ground floor. Augustus capped building height at about 20 metres and set up a firefighting force, the vigiles. Wealthy families lived in a domus, a private house around an open courtyard. Traffic was so bad that Julius Caesar banned most wheeled carts from the city in daylight.

sections.key: Roman life depended on a household hierarchy: fathers held legal power, slaves did much of the work and schooling depended on wealth.
sections.b:
The paterfamilias, the oldest living male, held legal power over his children and grandchildren, including their property, though custom usually softened it. Women could not vote or hold office, but wealthy women could own property and wield influence. Slavery was central to the economy, in homes, fields and mines. Lives could be brutal, yet many urban slaves were freed and could rise, sometimes becoming very rich.

Many babies did not survive infancy. Children whose parents could pay went from about age seven to a teacher, learning to read, write and count on wax tablets. Beatings were common. Richer boys moved on to Greek and Latin literature and rhetoric, the art of persuasion.

sections.key: Romans ate out at street counters and spent afternoons at public baths with shared latrines.
sections.b:
Many apartments had no proper kitchen, and cooking upstairs risked fire, so ordinary Romans bought hot food at thermopolia, an ancient fast food. Pompeii had dozens. One excavated around 2020 still held traces of duck, pork, goat, fish and snails. The staple diet was bread, porridge, olive oil, beans and wine mixed with water, flavoured with garum, a fermented fish sauce.

Many Romans visited the baths daily. A big bathhouse had cold, warm and hot rooms, the hot ones heated by furnaces sending air under raised floors and through walls. Many also had gardens, snack sellers and libraries, and entry was cheap. Public latrines had long stone benches with running water beneath.

sections.key: Rome kept its people entertained with chariot races and gladiator shows.
sections.b:
The Circus Maximus, a huge chariot-racing track, may have held around 150,000 spectators. Fans passionately followed four racing teams known by their colours: Reds, Whites, Greens and Blues. Top charioteers became celebrities and earned fortunes. The Colosseum, opened in AD 80, held about 50,000 people for gladiator fights, animal hunts and public executions. Gladiators were mostly slaves or prisoners, though some volunteered, and not every fight ended in death.

The state also handed out free or cheap grain to poorer citizens. The poet Juvenal complained that the people now cared only about 'bread and circuses', a phrase still used for distracting people with food and entertainment instead of real political power.

sections.key: Religion filled Roman homes, and Pompeii, buried by Vesuvius, preserved daily life.
sections.b:
Religion was part of daily routine. Many homes had a small shrine, the lararium, where families offered food or incense to household spirits. Public temples honoured Jupiter, Juno and Mars, and Romans readily adopted foreign gods such as Isis. Saturnalia, held in December, involved feasting, gifts and role reversals in which masters might serve their slaves.

In AD 79, Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii, near modern Naples, under several metres of ash and pumice. Excavations have revealed streets, shops and bakeries with carbonised loaves still in the ovens, plus wall paintings and thousands of pieces of graffiti, from election slogans to love notes. Plaster poured into hollows left by decayed bodies produced casts of victims' final moments.

quiz.q: Why were Roman apartment blocks dangerous for the poor?
o: They were built beside the flooding Tiber river
They were taxed heavily by the number of floors
They were owned by the city's legions
Cheap, fire-prone buildings with the poor on top
quiz.e: Cheap construction and open flames made fires common, and the top floors were hardest to escape.

quiz.q: Who held legal power over a Roman household?
o: The eldest child once he reached adulthood
The mother, as head of the household
The oldest living male, the paterfamilias
A local priest assigned by the Senate
quiz.e: In law the paterfamilias controlled even adult descendants and their property, though custom softened this.

quiz.q: Why did ordinary Romans often buy hot food from thermopolia?
o: Home cooking was banned within the city walls
Many flats had no kitchen and cooking risked fire
Street food was provided free by the state
Most families could not afford to buy bread
quiz.e: Cramped, fire-prone housing made street food the practical choice.

quiz.q: What does 'bread and circuses' mean?
o: Distracting people with food and entertainment
A Roman recipe served at festivals
Paying soldiers with grain and games
A school of public speaking in Rome
quiz.e: Juvenal's complaint is still used for politics that trades spectacle for substance.

quiz.q: Why does Pompeii tell us so much about Roman life?
o: It was the capital city of the Roman Empire
Its people left detailed diaries behind
It was never excavated and remains untouched
Ash buried it quickly and preserved everyday life
quiz.e: The eruption of AD 79 froze a working Roman town, so we see bakeries, graffiti and homes as they were.

LESSONS.push: Fast food and traffic jams in ancient Rome. What did a Roman day really look like?

LESSONS.title: Roads, aqueducts and concrete
LESSONS.hook: Roman engineers built so well that some of their bridges, roads and domes are still in use two thousand years later.

sections.key: Roman roads, built in layers and cambered, linked the empire and many still shape European routes.
sections.b: Romans built around 80,000 kilometres of paved roads so armies, officials, traders and messages could move quickly. They were built in layers of stone, gravel and sand, topped with fitted paving stones and cambered so rain ran off into ditches. They ran as straight as the landscape allowed, cutting through hills and crossing marshes on embankments. Milestones marked distances, and relay stations let official messengers change horses. The Via Appia, begun in 312 BC, survives in long stretches, some with its ancient paving. Many modern European roads follow Roman routes, which is partly why the saying 'all roads lead to Rome' stuck.

sections.key: Aqueducts used only gravity and a gentle slope to supply cities, while great sewers carried waste away.
sections.b:
By the early 200s AD, Rome had eleven aqueducts delivering hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of water a day to fountains, baths and wealthy homes. They relied on gravity alone, keeping a steady downhill gradient over tens of kilometres, sometimes well under a metre of drop per kilometre. Most of each channel ran underground. The arches mainly crossed valleys, as at the Pont du Gard in France. The Aqua Virgo, finished in 19 BC, still feeds the Trevi Fountain.

Water had to flow out again. The Cloaca Maxima, traditionally begun in the 500s BC, drained the marshy Forum valley. Overflow flushed waste into the Tiber, keeping streets cleaner but polluting the river, and many homes were not connected. Parts of it still carry water today.

sections.key: An arch carries weight around its curve, letting Romans span wide gaps and build bridges, vaults and domes.
sections.b:
Romans did not invent the arch, but they used it on a massive scale. An arch is built from wedge-shaped stones, held by a wooden frame until the central keystone goes in, after which it supports itself. It carries weight around its curve and down into its supports, so it can span wider gaps than a flat stone beam, which would crack.

Line up arches and you get a bridge or aqueduct. Extend an arch and you get a vault, a curved ceiling. Rotate it and you get a dome. Triumphal arches, such as the Arch of Constantine beside the Colosseum, celebrated victories and inspired later monuments like the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.

sections.key: Roman concrete made with volcanic ash lasted for two thousand years, allowing the vast Pantheon dome.
sections.b:
Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash called pozzolana, and rubble, to make concrete. It let them build quickly, in almost any shape, with less skilled labour than carved stone, and some mixes set underwater. Roman harbour structures have survived 2,000 years of pounding by the sea. Researchers found that seawater reacted with the ash to grow new minerals that strengthened the concrete. A 2023 study suggested lime lumps could also help seal cracks.

The Pantheon, rebuilt under Hadrian around AD 125, has a dome about 43 metres across, as high as it is wide. An open oculus, about 8 metres wide, lets in light. Lighter volcanic stone near the top and sunken panels reduce weight. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

sections.key: Roman engineering served power: soldiers built forts and walls, and Roman ideas shaped buildings for centuries.
sections.b:
Legionaries carried tools as well as weapons and built a fortified camp each night on campaign. In 55 BC Caesar's engineers bridged the Rhine in about ten days. Many European cities began as Roman military bases. Hadrian's Wall, begun around AD 122, ran about 117 kilometres across northern Britain, and stretches still stand.

Roads moved legions, aqueducts made big cities possible, and grand buildings displayed Rome's wealth. Surveyors used the groma to lay out straight lines and the chorobates to level. The architect Vitruvius argued that buildings should be strong, useful and beautiful. His Ten Books on Architecture inspired Renaissance architects, and its influence shows in the domes, arches and columns of parliaments, banks and museums worldwide, including many in Australia.

quiz.q: Why were Roman roads built in layers and cambered?
o: So they could float over marshes
So they lasted and rain ran off into ditches
So horses could run faster uphill
So they were cheaper to maintain
quiz.e: Layered foundations and a curved surface kept water from wrecking the road.

quiz.q: What made water flow through Roman aqueducts?
o: Gravity along a gentle, steady downhill slope
Pumps worked by slaves
Windmills along the route
Water pressure from steep drops
quiz.e: Engineers kept a slight, continuous gradient over tens of kilometres, so no power was needed.

quiz.q: Why can an arch span wider gaps than a flat stone beam?
o: It is made from lighter stone than a beam
It is held together by iron clamps inside
It spreads all its weight onto the keystone
It carries weight around its curve to its supports
quiz.e: The curve redirects weight down through the supports, so the stone is not cracked by bending.

quiz.q: What made Roman concrete so durable, especially in seawater?
o: Steel bars cast inside the concrete
A coating of lead on all the surfaces
Volcanic ash reacting with seawater to form minerals
A thick outer layer of polished marble
quiz.e: Reactions between seawater and volcanic ash grew new minerals over time.

quiz.q: How did engineering serve the Roman Empire's power?
o: It made war with neighbours unnecessary
Roads moved armies and aqueducts fed cities
It replaced the need for a standing army
It lowered the taxes paid by the provinces
quiz.e: Infrastructure held the empire together and displayed its permanence.

LESSONS.push: Some Roman bridges and domes still stand after 2000 years. What was their secret?

LESSONS.title: Why Rome fell
LESSONS.hook: Historians have offered hundreds of reasons for the fall of Rome. The truth is a slow, complicated unravelling, and half the empire didn't fall at all.

sections.key: After two peaceful centuries, a chaotic crisis in the AD 200s led to the empire being split in two.
sections.b:
The first two centuries of the empire, the Pax Romana, brought relative stability and trade from Britain to Syria. Then, from AD 235 to 284, Rome had over 20 emperors, most murdered or killed in battle. Invasions, civil wars, plague and runaway inflation, as emperors debased silver coins to pay soldiers, battered the empire. In 260 the Persians captured Emperor Valerian. Aurelian reunited the empire by 274.

Diocletian decided the empire was too big for one ruler and shared power among four emperors in 293. Constantine emerged from the civil war that followed and founded Constantinople in 330. After Theodosius died in 395, the empire was permanently divided into a Western Empire and a richer, more populous Eastern Empire.

sections.key: A costly army and heavy taxes weakened the West just as migrating peoples pressed on its borders.
sections.b:
The late empire needed a larger army, probably several hundred thousand soldiers, and paying it was a constant struggle. Diocletian's price controls in 301 largely failed. Taxes rose, and laws tied farmers to their land so taxes could be collected. Rome relied more on Germanic recruits and allied groups, called foederati, whose loyalty was never guaranteed.

In the late 300s the Huns pushed Germanic peoples such as the Goths west. Allowed across the Danube in 376, the Goths were mistreated and rebelled, crushing a Roman army at Adrianople in 378. Visigoths, Vandals, Burgundians and Franks settled inside the empire. In 410 Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome, the first time in about 800 years.

sections.key: Blows from Attila and the Vandals left puppet emperors, and in AD 476 the last Western emperor was deposed.
sections.b:
The Vandals captured Carthage in 439, seizing some of the West's richest provinces and their grain and taxes. Attila, who led the Huns from 434 until 453, extracted huge payments of gold from the East. In 451 he invaded Gaul and was stopped at the Catalaunian Plains by a Roman and Visigothic army. He turned back from Italy the next year, though famine and disease probably mattered more than Pope Leo I. In 455 the Vandals sacked Rome.

Western emperors were by then puppets of powerful generals. In 476 Odoacer deposed the teenage Romulus Augustulus and ruled Italy as king. Life did not change overnight: new kingdoms often kept Roman laws, Latin, towns and the church.

sections.key: Rome fell from a combination of military pressure, political instability and economic weakness.
sections.b:
The historian Alexander Demandt collected more than 200 proposed causes, from lead poisoning to moral decay. Edward Gibbon partly blamed Christianity, a view most historians now see as too simple. Most point to a mix. Constant civil wars wasted soldiers and money. Taxes rose, and the loss of rich provinces cut revenue. Plagues, and possibly climate shifts, played roles. Meanwhile, migrating peoples found an empire less able to resist.

Some historians prefer to speak of a 'transformation' as Roman and Germanic cultures blended. Others stress a real collapse in living standards.

sections.key: The Eastern, or Byzantine, Empire survived for nearly a thousand years more, until 1453.
sections.b: The Eastern half, called the Byzantine Empire by historians, was ruled from Constantinople. Its people mostly spoke Greek but called themselves Romans. Under Justinian in the 500s it reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of Spain, built Hagia Sophia and produced a law code, later called the Corpus Juris Civilis, that shaped legal systems across Europe. Byzantine scholars preserved many ancient Greek texts, and scholars who moved west helped feed the Renaissance. Constantinople finally fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, an event often treated as the true end of the Roman Empire.

quiz.q: Why did Diocletian share power among four emperors?
o: He wanted to end the Senate
He hoped to create a republic
He planned to give up the West
He judged the empire too big for one ruler
quiz.e: The division of rule eased defence of a vast empire, though it collapsed into civil war after he retired.

quiz.q: Why did the Goths rebel against Rome after crossing the Danube in 376?
o: They wanted Rome's gold
They were ordered to fight the Huns
Local Roman officials badly mistreated them
Rome refused them land
quiz.e: Mistreatment turned refugees into enemies, and they crushed a Roman army at Adrianople.

quiz.q: What did 476 actually mean for people living in the West?
o: Cities were abandoned and fell into ruin
Little changed at first as new kingdoms kept Roman ways
The Christian church disappeared overnight
All Roman law was banned by the new rulers
quiz.e: The date marks a political end, but Roman institutions and culture continued under new rulers.

quiz.q: What do most modern historians say about why Rome fell?
o: A mix of military, political and economic problems
Christianity alone destroyed its will to fight
Lead poisoning weakened every Roman leader
Attila single-handedly conquered the empire
quiz.e: Civil wars, heavy taxes, lost provinces, plague and migrating peoples combined.

quiz.q: Why is the Byzantine Empire called the empire that did not fall?
o: It conquered the West and ruled from Rome
It moved its capital back to Rome in 476
It was ruled by Odoacer from Ravenna
The East lasted until 1453 from Constantinople
quiz.e: The East survived nearly a thousand years longer and kept Roman law and learning alive.

LESSONS.push: Historians have named over 200 reasons Rome fell. Why most are probably wrong.

LESSONS.title: Zeno and the painted porch
LESSONS.hook: A shipwrecked merchant walked into an Athens bookshop, and a philosophy was born that would guide emperors and slaves alike.

sections.key: Zeno lost his fortune in a shipwreck, turned to philosophy, and taught in a painted colonnade that gave Stoicism its name.
sections.b:
Zeno was a merchant from Citium, on Cyprus. According to the biographer Diogenes Laertius, a shipwreck near Athens, traditionally dated around 312 BC, cost him a cargo of purple dye. In an Athens bookshop he heard about Socrates and asked where men like that could be found. The bookseller pointed to the philosopher Crates and said, 'Follow that man.' Zeno later joked, 'I made a prosperous voyage when I was shipwrecked.' The details may be embroidered, but the moral stuck: disaster can start something better.

Around 300 BC, Zeno began teaching in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, a public colonnade by the Athenian marketplace. His followers became known as Stoics, 'the porch people'.

sections.key: From the Cynics, Zeno took the idea that virtue is enough for a good life, and the Stoics made virtue the only true good.
sections.b:
Crates was a Cynic, one of Athens' most provocative groups. Their best-known figure, Diogenes, reportedly lived in a large storage jar, owned almost nothing and mocked wealth and fame. Crates gave away his fortune to live likewise. From them Zeno learned that happiness doesn't depend on possessions or status. The Stoics kept the core but dropped the shock tactics: you could live virtuously while marrying, working and taking part in public life.

The Stoics said the only true good is virtue: wisdom, justice, courage and self-control. Health, wealth, reputation and even life are 'indifferent'. Not worthless: they are 'preferred indifferents', sensible to pursue, but they do not decide whether your life goes well. What matters is how you use what you're dealt.

sections.key: Stoics aimed to live by reason and in community, and to correct the mistaken judgements behind destructive emotions.
sections.b:
Zeno taught that the goal is to live in agreement with nature. The universe is ordered by reason, which Stoics called logos. Humans are rational, social beings, so living naturally meant using reason well and serving the human community. Stoics were early cosmopolitans, 'citizens of the world', picturing concern spreading outward from self and family to all of humanity.

A common myth is that Stoics wanted to feel nothing. They targeted the passions: fear, craving, distress and excessive pleasure, which grow from false judgements, such as thinking a loss of money is a genuine catastrophe. Correct the judgement and the passion weakens. They welcomed good feelings such as joy and goodwill.

sections.key: Cleanthes and Chrysippus built Stoicism into a full system of logic, physics and ethics.
sections.b:
Zeno's successor Cleanthes, a former boxer, reportedly carried water at night to pay for his studies. He wrote the Hymn to Zeus, one of the few early Stoic works to survive in full. The third head, Chrysippus, was so influential that a saying went, 'If there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa.' Ancient sources credit him with more than 700 works, nearly all lost.

Stoic philosophy had three parts: logic (how to reason), physics (how the world works) and ethics (how to live). They compared it to a field: logic is the fence, physics the soil, ethics the fruit.

sections.key: Rome's love of duty and self-control made Stoicism popular, and the best-known Stoic writings are Roman.
sections.b:
In 155 BC Athens sent three philosophers to Rome as ambassadors, including the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon, and their lectures caused a sensation. Stoicism's focus on duty, self-control and public service suited Roman values. Cato the Younger, who resisted Julius Caesar, became a Stoic hero.

The best-known surviving writings are from the Roman era: Seneca's letters, the teachings of Epictetus, recorded by his student Arrian, and the private notebook of Emperor Marcus Aurelius. After about AD 200 the school faded, but its ideas lived on in Christian thought, a Renaissance revival and today's popular books, podcasts and cognitive therapies.

quiz.q: What did Zeno mean by joking that he had made a prosperous voyage when shipwrecked?
o: He sold his cargo for a handsome profit
Losing his cargo led him to philosophy
He had planned the wreck to escape debt
He found treasure washed up on the shore
quiz.e: Misfortune can open a better path.

quiz.q: According to the Stoics, what is the only true good?
o: Virtue
Wealth
Pleasure
Fame
quiz.e: Health, wealth and reputation are 'indifferent': preferable, but they do not make a life good.

quiz.q: What did Stoics think about emotions?
o: All feelings must be suppressed completely
Emotions cannot be changed by thinking
Only joy should be avoided by the wise
Destructive ones come from false judgements
quiz.e: They aimed to remove destructive passions, not feeling itself, by correcting mistaken beliefs.

quiz.q: In the Stoic picture of philosophy as a field, what was ethics?
o: The fence
The soil
The fruit
The harvest tools
quiz.e: Logic guards, physics nourishes, and ethics, how to live, is the result.

quiz.q: Why was Stoicism so popular in Rome?
o: It rejected public life and politics
Its stress on duty and self-control suited Roman values
It was adopted as the state religion
It opposed service in the army
quiz.e: Stoic ideals matched Roman ideals, and Roman writers gave us the best-known texts.

LESSONS.push: A shipwreck, a bookshop and a joke about luck. How Stoicism began.

LESSONS.title: Epictetus: freedom in the mind
LESSONS.hook: Born enslaved, lame in one leg, exiled by an emperor. Epictetus taught that no one can take away your freedom to choose your response.

sections.key: Epictetus was born enslaved, gained his freedom and taught philosophy, first in Rome and then in Nicopolis.
sections.b:
Epictetus was born around AD 50 in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, and enslaved from childhood. His name means 'acquired'. His owner, Epaphroditus, a secretary to Emperor Nero, allowed him to study Stoicism under Musonius Rufus. He walked with a limp. One story says his master twisted his leg until it broke while he calmly warned him it would; another says illness. After gaining his freedom, he taught in Rome.

Around AD 93, Emperor Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome, and Epictetus opened a school at Nicopolis in Greece. He lived simply: when a thief stole his iron lamp, he reportedly replaced it with a clay one. He wrote nothing. His student Arrian recorded his talks in the Discourses and the short Enchiridion, or handbook.

sections.key: Focus on what is up to you, and remember that your judgements, not events, disturb you.
sections.b:
The Enchiridion opens with its central idea. Within our control are our judgements, intentions, desires and actions. Outside it are our bodies, property, reputation, other people and events. Suffering comes from treating what we can't control as ours to command, like demanding traffic clear. This isn't passivity: you still prepare and act, but you judge yourself by effort and character, not outcome.

Epictetus taught that 'it is not things that disturb us, but our judgements about things.' If someone insults you, your interpretation of the insult hurts. This idea inspired Albert Ellis and Aaron Beck as they developed rational emotive behaviour therapy and cognitive therapy. Cognitive behavioural therapy, which grew from their work, is now among the most widely used talking therapies.

sections.key: Train your desires, actions and judgements, and play your life's roles well.
sections.b:
Epictetus said anyone who wants to be good must train in three areas. The first is desire: wanting only what is up to us, so we are never frustrated or afraid. The second is action: carrying out our duties to others thoughtfully and fairly. The third is assent: not accepting any impression as true until we've examined it, especially when tired, angry or excited.

He compared life to a play: you don't choose your role, but you can play it well. Our duties come from our relationships as son, brother, citizen, neighbour or friend. If your brother wrongs you, remember your role as a brother and act well anyway. His philosophy was less abstract theory than how to behave at dinner, at work and in a family argument.

sections.key: The Enchiridion uses short images to teach acceptance of loss and moderation.
sections.b: The Enchiridion is full of memorable images. Never say about anything, 'I have lost it,' Epictetus advised, but rather, 'I have given it back': possessions and even people are on loan to us. Behave in life as at a banquet: when a dish comes round, take a modest portion politely; if it hasn't reached you yet, don't reach for it. And don't ask for events to happen as you wish, but wish for them to happen as they do, and your life will go smoothly. These lines are demanding, but they aim at a calm that doesn't depend on luck.

sections.key: Real freedom is freedom of the mind, which no tyrant can take away.
sections.b:
For Epictetus, a formerly enslaved man, freedom meant something deep. A tyrant could chain your leg, he said, but not even Zeus could overpower your will.

Centuries later, US Navy pilot James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam in 1965. He'd been introduced to the Enchiridion while studying at Stanford, and he credited it with helping him endure more than seven years as a prisoner of war, including torture and long periods in solitary confinement. As he parachuted down, he later wrote, he told himself he was leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus.

quiz.q: What did Epictetus's life show about his philosophy?
o: Only the free can become truly wise
Wealth is essential to a virtuous life
Philosophy requires holding public office
Freedom of mind does not depend on circumstances
quiz.e: A man born enslaved became a respected teacher, living what he taught.

quiz.q: Which of these is within your control, according to Epictetus?
o: Your reputation
Other people's behaviour
Your own judgements and choices
Whether the traffic clears
quiz.e: Only our judgements, intentions and actions are truly ours; the rest is outside our control.

quiz.q: What should you do with a first impression, according to Epictetus's discipline of assent?
o: Act on it immediately
Examine it before accepting it as true
Ignore all impressions
Ask others to judge it
quiz.e: Pausing to test your reactions stops anger and fear from running your decisions.

quiz.q: What did Epictetus advise saying instead of 'I have lost it'?
o: I have given it back
It was never mine
It will return
Fate took it
quiz.e: Seeing possessions and people as on loan makes loss easier to accept.

quiz.q: Why did Epictetus think no tyrant could take away your freedom?
o: Tyrants cannot enforce laws
Freedom is guaranteed by law
Only Zeus can imprison
Others can bind your body, but not your will
quiz.e: Freedom lies in how you choose to respond, which no one else can seize.

LESSONS.push: A man born enslaved taught that nobody can take his freedom. How did that help a POW?

LESSONS.title: Seneca: time, anger and wealth
LESSONS.hook: Playwright, statesman, millionaire, adviser to Nero. Seneca wrote brilliantly about living well, and struggled to live up to it.

sections.key: Seneca was a Roman philosopher and adviser to Nero who admitted falling short of his own ideals.
sections.b: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (about 4 BC to AD 65) was born in Córdoba, Spain, and became a leading Roman writer, orator and senator. In AD 41 Emperor Claudius exiled him to Corsica, accused of adultery with the emperor's niece, and he spent eight years there. Recalled in 49, he became tutor and then chief adviser to the young Nero. For several years he helped steer the empire, and he grew enormously rich. Critics, then and now, call him a hypocrite: a Stoic preaching simplicity while living in luxury and serving a tyrant. Seneca himself admitted he fell far short of his ideals.

sections.key: Life is not short; we waste much of it, and Seneca's letters to Lucilius offer practical guidance on living well.
sections.b:
In On the Shortness of Life, Seneca argued: 'It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it.' People guard their money carefully but give their time to anyone who asks. They postpone living until retirement, as if they were guaranteed to reach it. His remedy: treat time as your most precious possession, spend it deliberately and live fully today.

Late in life, Seneca wrote 124 surviving letters to his friend Lucilius, a Roman official in Sicily. Each tackles a practical theme: friendship, grief, fear, old age, wealth, even noisy neighbours. They are personal and warm, often starting with something from his day. They read like advice from a wise, flawed friend.

sections.key: Seneca called anger a brief madness and gave practical ways to prevent it.
sections.b:
In On Anger, Seneca called anger a brief insanity that harms the angry person more than its target. His strategies sound strikingly modern. Delay your response, since time cools anger. Notice the early warning signs. Avoid provoking people and situations when you're tired or hungry. Imagine how you look when furious. And consider that the other person may not have meant harm, or that you've done the same yourself.

He praised Plato, who, furious with a slave, asked his nephew Speusippus to deal with the man instead, because he was angry, and so in no state to judge.

sections.key: Practising simple living removes fear of loss, and grief is natural but should not be endless.
sections.b:
In one letter, Seneca advised setting aside a few days now and then to live on the cheapest food and roughest clothing, then asking, 'Is this what I feared?' The point was freedom, not self-punishment. Once you know you can cope with little, the fear of losing things loosens, and you can enjoy what you have without clinging to it. Modern versions include a week of simple meals or a spending freeze.

Seneca also wrote consolations, comforting the bereaved. One went to Marcia, still mourning her son three years on. Another went to his mother, Helvia, from exile. He did not urge suppressing grief: our eyes should be neither dry nor overflowing. We may weep, but not wail. Be grateful for the time you had, and gradually return to life.

sections.key: Seneca wrote influential tragedies and science, then died calmly after Nero ordered him to kill himself.
sections.b:
Seneca also wrote tragedies, including Medea, Phaedra, Oedipus and Thyestes, full of revenge and overwhelming passion, perhaps showing what happens when emotions go unchecked. They influenced Elizabethan dramatists such as Thomas Kyd and William Shakespeare. His Natural Questions investigated earthquakes, comets and thunder. For Seneca, studying nature lifted the mind above petty worries.

In AD 65 Nero accused Seneca of involvement in the Pisonian conspiracy and ordered him to take his own life. According to the historian Tacitus, he faced it calmly, told weeping friends to remember the philosophy they had studied and left them 'the image of his life'. His composure became a famous model of Stoic courage.

quiz.q: Why do critics call Seneca a hypocrite?
o: He taught Stoicism but never wrote it down
He preached simplicity yet lived in luxury
He refused to advise Nero on any matter
He lived in poverty while praising wealth
quiz.e: Seneca admitted he fell far short of the ideals he taught.

quiz.q: What did Seneca say about the shortness of life?
o: Life is long enough if we do not waste it
Life is too short to plan
Only the rich have enough time
Time can be saved for later
quiz.e: The problem is not the supply of time but how carelessly we spend it.

quiz.q: Which of these did Seneca recommend for dealing with anger?
o: Respond immediately while it is fresh
Suppress it completely
Confront the person while tired
Delay your response, because time cools anger
quiz.e: Pausing gives judgement time to return and prevents regret.

quiz.q: Why did Seneca recommend practising poverty?
o: To punish himself for his riches
To save money
To lose the fear of losing wealth
To impress others
quiz.e: Learning you can cope with little loosens fear and lets you enjoy what you have.

quiz.q: What made Seneca's death a model of Stoic courage?
o: He escaped Nero's orders
He faced it calmly and comforted his friends
He denied the charges loudly
He asked Nero for mercy
quiz.e: His composure under a forced death showed the philosophy he had taught.

LESSONS.push: He advised an emperor, grew rich, and wrote about living simply. Was Seneca a hypocrite?

LESSONS.title: Marcus Aurelius: the philosopher emperor
LESSONS.hook: The most powerful man in the world wrote private notes to himself about staying humble, patient and good. They became one of history's most-read books.

sections.key: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from AD 161 to 180 and is remembered chiefly as a philosopher.
sections.b:
Marcus was born in AD 121 into a wealthy Roman family. Emperor Hadrian noticed him and arranged for his chosen successor, Antoninus Pius, to adopt Marcus and prepare him for power. Marcus studied intensely and loved philosophy. His Stoic tutor Junius Rusticus lent him his own copy of the teachings of Epictetus, a gift Marcus recorded with gratitude.

He became emperor in 161 and insisted on sharing power with his adoptive brother, Lucius Verus, until Verus died in 169. Historians count Marcus as the last of the 'Five Good Emperors', a period of relative stability. He is the only Roman emperor remembered mainly as a philosopher.

sections.key: Marcus longed for a quiet life of study but faced war, plague and betrayal.
sections.b: Despite his wish for a quiet life, Marcus spent much of his reign at war. Rome fought the Parthian Empire in the east, then he spent years on the Danube frontier fighting Germanic peoples such as the Marcomanni. The Antonine Plague, probably smallpox, was brought back by returning troops and spread through the empire, killing millions by many estimates. In 175 a trusted general, Avidius Cassius, rebelled after a false rumour of Marcus's death. Several of Marcus's children died young. His writings show a man constantly trying to stay calm and decent amid pressure, loss and exhaustion.

sections.key: The Meditations was a private journal of reminders, never meant for publication.
sections.b:
Marcus wrote notes to himself in Greek, many during military campaigns. One section is headed 'Among the Quadi', a tribe he fought. We call the collection the Meditations, but the title in the manuscripts means something like 'To Himself'. These are not a polished book. They are reminders, repeated in different words, of principles he struggled to live by. That is part of their power: we're reading an emperor's honest efforts to be better.

Book 2 opens by telling yourself at the start of the day that you'll meet meddling, ungrateful, arrogant people. They act this way because they don't know good from bad. We are made for cooperation, like hands or the two rows of teeth, so you can't be harmed by them or angry with them.

sections.key: Impermanence, the present moment, duty and acceptance run through the Meditations.
sections.b:
Marcus returns again and again to a few ideas. Everything is temporary: even emperors and empires are soon forgotten, so don't chase fame. Focus on the present task, doing it as if it were the last act of your life. Accept what happens as part of nature's order. Do your duty to others, since we are made to work together.

And look at things as they are, stripped of grand labels: fine wine is fermented grape juice, and a purple imperial robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish. Seeing plainly takes the heat out of craving and envy.

sections.key: Marcus's son Commodus ended Rome's golden age, but the Meditations became one of history's most-read guides to living.
sections.b:
Marcus died in AD 180 on the Danube frontier, probably of illness. Unlike the four emperors before him, he had a surviving son, and he made Commodus his heir. Commodus proved erratic and cruel, fought as a gladiator and was assassinated in 192. Historians often mark Marcus's death as the end of Rome's golden age.

Only a few manuscripts of the Meditations survived the Middle Ages. The first printed edition appeared in 1559, and the book has been in print ever since. Readers have included Frederick the Great, Theodore Roosevelt and Bill Clinton, along with countless ordinary people. Its appeal is simple: if the man who ruled the Roman Empire struggled with anger, grief and self-doubt, and kept trying anyway, so can the rest of us.

quiz.q: What made Marcus Aurelius unusual among Roman emperors?
o: He refused to hold power for himself
He was the very first Roman emperor
He fought no wars during his reign
He is remembered chiefly as a philosopher
quiz.e: A devoted Stoic learner, he is the only emperor remembered mainly for philosophy.

quiz.q: What did Marcus's writings reveal about his reign?
o: A man who enjoyed war and conquest
A ruler uninterested in his duties
A man trying to stay calm amid war and plague
A leader who avoided hardship
quiz.e: The notes show a constant effort to stay steady under pressure.

quiz.q: What was the Meditations originally?
o: A set of speeches given to the Senate
A private journal of reminders to himself
A legal code issued for the provinces
A series of letters written to his son
quiz.e: Never meant for publication, it records his honest efforts to live well.

quiz.q: Why did Marcus tell himself to see things 'as they are'?
o: Plain seeing removes the pull of craving
It lets him judge other people harshly
It proved luxury was evil in itself
It helped him avoid his public duties
quiz.e: Calling wine fermented grape juice strips away glamour that fuels desire.

quiz.q: Why has the Meditations appealed to readers for centuries?
o: It gives rules for governing an empire
It records Marcus's military victories
It predicts events in the future
It shows a powerful man struggling and trying again
quiz.e: If an emperor wrestled with the same flaws, ordinary readers can keep trying too.

LESSONS.push: The most powerful man in Rome wrote notes to himself about anger and doubt. Why?

LESSONS.title: Stoic practices for modern life
LESSONS.hook: Stoicism was always meant to be practised, not just studied. Eight exercises you can start today, most taking less than five minutes.

sections.key: Preview the day's likely difficulties each morning, decide how you will respond, and hold your plans lightly.
sections.b:
Like Marcus Aurelius, spend a few minutes each morning previewing the day. What might go wrong? A late train, a tense meeting, a child who won't get ready for school? How do you want to act if it does? This isn't pessimism. It's rehearsal, the same reason athletes visualise a race and pilots practise emergencies in simulators. Two or three situations is plenty.

Add what modern Stoics call the reserve clause. Seneca's wise person says, 'I will sail, unless something prevents me.' Commit fully to the goal, but silently add 'fate permitting'. If a storm cancels the flight, you haven't failed at what was in your control.

sections.key: Imagining loss, or your problem seen from far above, restores gratitude and perspective.
sections.b:
The Stoics practised premeditatio malorum: briefly imagining the loss of your health, a loved one or your home. It sounds grim, but it often brings a rush of appreciation, pushing back against hedonic adaptation, our habit of getting used to good things. Keep it brief and gentle. If it triggers real anxiety, drop it and focus on gratitude instead.

Marcus Aurelius also pictured life from above: cities, armies, weddings and funerals, all small against vast time. Try seeing your problem from a plane, then from orbit. Research led by Ethan Kross suggests that self-distancing, even talking to yourself as 'you' or by name instead of 'I', can reduce emotional reactivity and help people reason more wisely about conflicts.

sections.key: Picture a respected witness and say less, so you act on your better instincts.
sections.b:
In his 11th letter to Lucilius, Seneca passed on a tip he borrowed from Epicurus: choose a person of fine character and live as though they were always watching. He suggested Cato, or the gentler Laelius if Cato seemed too stern. The point isn't fear of judgement. It's that a respected witness helps you act on your better instincts. When you're about to snap or cut a corner, ask what they'd do.

Talk less, too. Zeno said we have two ears and one mouth so we can listen more than we speak. Epictetus urged saying only what's needed, and avoiding gossip. Before speaking, ask whether it needs saying.

sections.key: An insult only wounds if you accept it as a harm, so test it for truth or answer with humour.
sections.b:
Epictetus advised that if you're told someone has been speaking badly of you, don't defend yourself. Say, 'He obviously didn't know my other faults, or he'd have mentioned those too.' Seneca tells how Cato was struck in a public bathhouse by a man who didn't recognise him. When the man later apologised, Cato replied, 'I don't remember being hit.'

The idea is that an insult only harms you if you accept it as harm. Next time you're criticised, ask whether any of it is true. If it is, learn from it. If it isn't, it says more about them. Humour often ends the fight.

sections.key: A calm nightly review of what went well and what to change builds the self-awareness every other practice needs.
sections.b:
Seneca reviewed each day before sleep, asking: What bad habit did I cure today? What fault did I resist? In what way am I better? He did it without harshness, like a kind teacher, forgiving himself while noting what to change.

Try writing three lines each night: one thing you did well, one thing you'd do differently, and one thing you're grateful for. It takes about five minutes. Over weeks, patterns appear, such as which situations reliably set you off. That self-awareness is the foundation of every other Stoic practice.

quiz.q: Why preview the day's likely problems each morning?
o: It trains you to expect that everything goes wrong
It helps you avoid every difficult person
It lets you choose your response in advance
It replaces the need to plan the day at all
quiz.e: Rehearsal means that when the difficult moment arrives, you've already decided how to act.

quiz.q: What does negative visualisation usually produce when done briefly and gently?
o: Deeper appreciation of what you have now
Constant fear of loss
Indifference to loved ones
A firm prediction of misfortune
quiz.e: Imagining loss counters our tendency to stop noticing the good things we have.

quiz.q: Why picture a person you admire watching you?
o: It teaches you to fear public judgement
It lets you borrow their opinions on issues
It removes the need for self-control entirely
It helps you act on your better instincts
quiz.e: A respected witness prompts better conduct, not fear.

quiz.q: What is the Stoic view of an insult?
o: It must always be answered at once
It only harms you if you accept it as a harm
It proves the speaker is right
It should be ignored without any reflection
quiz.e: Ask whether it's true: learn from it if so, and let it go if not.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of the evening review?
o: A record you can use against other people
Proof that you were right all day long
Self-awareness of your patterns over time
A detailed plan for the next day's meals
quiz.e: A gentle nightly review reveals patterns you can then change.

LESSONS.push: Stoics rehearsed bad days on purpose. Why that made them calmer.

LESSONS.title: The Socratic method
LESSONS.hook: The most powerful tool Socrates left us wasn't an answer. It was a way of asking questions.

sections.key: Socrates questioned confident beliefs to test them, aiming at truth rather than victory.
sections.b:
Socrates didn't give lectures. He asked questions. He'd find someone confident about a big idea, like justice, courage or piety, and ask them to define it. Then he'd test the definition against examples until contradictions appeared. The method is called elenchus, meaning cross-examination or testing.

The aim was not to win an argument but to get closer to the truth. Socrates said he was just as eager to be refuted as to refute, because being shown a mistake rid him of a false belief, which he saw as a benefit.

He wrote nothing himself. We know him mainly through Plato and Xenophon, and scholars still debate how much of Plato's 'Socrates' is the real man.

sections.key: A counterexample can break a definition, and each failure forces a better one.
sections.b:
At the start of Plato's Republic, the elderly Cephalus suggests that justice means telling the truth and paying back what you owe. Socrates asks: if a friend lent you a weapon, then went mad and asked for it back, would returning it be just? Clearly not. So the definition fails as stated.

Others try new definitions, such as 'helping friends and harming enemies', and each is tested in turn. Each counterexample forces a better definition. Often the dialogue ends without a final answer, but everyone understands the question more deeply than before.

sections.key: Wisdom begins with recognising the limits of your own knowledge.
sections.b:
In Plato's Apology, Socrates says his friend Chaerephon asked the Oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer was no. Puzzled, Socrates questioned politicians, poets and craftsmen. He found they believed they knew things they didn't. The craftsmen really did know their trades, but assumed this made them experts on everything else.

He concluded he was wiser in one way only: he didn't think he knew what he didn't know. This humility is the starting point of the method. You can't learn what you think you already know.

sections.key: Reasoning your way to an insight is uncomfortable but builds deeper, longer-lasting understanding.
sections.b:
In Plato's Theaetetus, Socrates compares himself to a midwife, like his mother. He didn't implant ideas. He helped others bring out their own, then checked whether each 'newborn' was sound. When you reason your way to an insight, you understand it more deeply and remember it longer. Teachers use Socratic questioning to help students think rather than memorise, and law schools, especially in the United States, use it to grill students about cases.

Many early dialogues end in aporia, or puzzlement. In the Meno, Socrates questions an enslaved boy about doubling a square's area. The boy gives a confident wrong answer, sees it's wrong, then finds the right one. Being shown you don't know is uncomfortable, but it makes you want to find out.

sections.key: Ask for meaning, evidence, assumptions, alternatives and consequences, with curiosity rather than hostility.
sections.b:
Useful Socratic questions include: What exactly do you mean? What's your evidence? What are you assuming? Could there be another explanation? What would follow if that were true? What would someone who disagrees say? They work on news stories, workplace decisions and family debates alike. Cognitive behavioural therapists use similar questions to test anxious thoughts: 'What's the evidence this will go badly? What would I tell a friend?'

Questioning can feel like an attack if done to score points. Socrates annoyed powerful Athenians by exposing their ignorance in public, and in 399 BC he was tried and executed. Used with curiosity, it is a fine tool. Turn it on your own beliefs first.

quiz.q: What is the point of Socratic questioning?
o: To win debates by trapping opponents
To test ideas and get closer to the truth
To make others agree with you
To teach facts by repetition
quiz.e: The method values being shown a mistake, because it removes a false belief.

quiz.q: Why did the example of returning a weapon to a friend who had gone mad matter?
o: It proved that justice does not really exist
It showed that friends should never lend things
It settled once and for all what justice is
'Paying back what you owe' isn't always just
quiz.e: A counterexample exposes a flaw in a definition and forces a better one.

quiz.q: What made Socrates wiser than the people he questioned?
o: He didn't think he knew what he didn't know
He knew more than every expert
He had memorised the oracle's teachings
He had trained as a craftsman
quiz.e: Recognising the limits of your knowledge is where learning begins.

quiz.q: Why is reasoning your way to an insight better than being told the answer?
o: It is always quicker
It avoids any confusion along the way
You understand it more deeply and remember it longer
It means you never make mistakes
quiz.e: Working it out, even through puzzlement, builds lasting understanding.

quiz.q: Which question is Socratic in spirit?
o: Why are you so wrong?
Who told you that nonsense?
Can we stop talking about it?
What evidence is there for that?
quiz.e: Socratic questions seek clarity and evidence, not victory.

LESSONS.push: Socrates never wrote a word, yet changed how we think. His method is one skill.

LESSONS.title: Eastern philosophy: sages of India and China
LESSONS.hook: At the same time Greek philosophy was flourishing, thinkers in India and China were asking similar questions, and reaching different answers.

sections.key: Between roughly 800 and 200 BC, major philosophical traditions arose independently across several civilisations.
sections.b:
In 1949 the German philosopher Karl Jaspers noticed that in roughly the same period, independent traditions arose that still shape billions of lives: Greek philosophy, the Hebrew prophets, Buddhism and Jainism in India, and Confucianism and Daoism in China. Some accounts add Zoroastrianism, though its founder's dates are very uncertain.

Jaspers called it the Axial Age, a pivot in human history. Historians debate how tidy the idea is, and some say it overstates the coincidence. Still, across the world, thinkers began asking systematically how to live, what makes a good ruler and how to deal with suffering.

sections.key: Jain many-sidedness and Carvaka scepticism show Indian thought valuing humility and evidence.
sections.b:
Mahavira, Jainism's great teacher, lived in north-eastern India around the time of the Buddha. Jain thinkers developed anekantavada, or many-sidedness: reality is so complex that any single statement is only partly true. The parable of the blind men and the elephant illustrates it. One feels the trunk and says it's a snake, another the leg and says it's a tree. Each is partly right; none sees the whole. For Jains, it is a reason for humility and tolerance.

Not all Indian thinkers were spiritual. The Carvaka, or Lokayata, were materialists. They trusted only what we perceive directly, so they rejected the soul, rebirth, karma and the gods. Almost none of their writings survive. We know them mostly through rivals who quoted them to refute them.

sections.key: Confucius taught that a good society rests on virtuous people and mutual duty, and his followers debated human nature.
sections.b:
Confucius, traditionally dated 551 to 479 BC, was a Chinese teacher and minor official in an age of war between rival states. He taught ren, humaneness, and li, proper conduct. Society works when relationships, such as ruler and subject, parent and child, and friends, are carried out with mutual responsibility. His version of the golden rule, from the Analects: 'Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.'

His followers disagreed on human nature. Mencius held it is basically good: anyone seeing a child about to fall into a well feels compassion. Xunzi held people are naturally selfish and need education and ritual, as a craftsman straightens wood. Confucianism later became China's official state philosophy under the Han dynasty. Exams on the Confucian classics shaped government posts for centuries, until 1905.

sections.key: Daoism teaches living in harmony with the Way, acting without forcing, like water.
sections.b:
Daoism is traditionally traced to Laozi, a legendary sage whose historical existence is uncertain, and the short, poetic Dao De Jing, only about 5,000 Chinese characters. Its opening line says the Dao that can be spoken of is not the eternal Dao. The Dao, or 'the Way', is the underlying flow of the universe.

Daoism values simplicity, humility and wu wei, often translated as 'effortless action': acting in harmony with things rather than forcing them, like water, which is soft yet wears down stone. The later sage Zhuangzi famously dreamt he was a butterfly, then wondered whether he was a butterfly dreaming he was Zhuangzi.

sections.key: These traditions share ideas with Stoicism and still shape cultures and practices like mindfulness.
sections.b:
Despite big differences, these traditions share threads with each other and with Stoicism. Many warn that endless desire causes suffering and that compassion is central to a good life. Buddhism's attention to the mind resembles the Stoic focus on judgements: how we interpret events shapes how we suffer. Scholars caution against making them sound identical, since their views of the self and universe differ.

Their influence endures. Confucian values shaped government, education and family life across East Asia for over two thousand years. Buddhism is practised by hundreds of millions, including many Australians, and its meditation inspired Jon Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based stress reduction in the late 1970s. Daoism shaped Chinese painting, poetry, medicine and tai chi.

quiz.q: What did Karl Jaspers notice about the period 800 to 200 BC?
o: One empire came to unify all philosophy
Philosophy gradually disappeared from Asia
Greece alone produced the major thinkers
Independent traditions emerged in several civilisations
quiz.e: He called it the Axial Age, though historians debate how tidy the idea is.

quiz.q: What does the parable of the blind men and the elephant illustrate?
o: Elephants are dangerous animals
Any single viewpoint captures only part of a complex truth
The senses are always unreliable
The loudest person is usually right
quiz.e: Many-sidedness encourages intellectual humility and tolerance of other views.

quiz.q: What did Xunzi believe about human nature, in contrast to Mencius?
o: People are naturally good and need no guidance
Human nature cannot be shaped at all
People are naturally selfish and need education and ritual
Only rulers have a nature worth studying
quiz.e: Mencius saw natural compassion; Xunzi saw a need for shaping, like straightening wood.

quiz.q: What does wu wei, or 'effortless action', mean?
o: Acting in harmony with things, not forcing them
Doing absolutely nothing at all in life
Obeying rulers without ever questioning them
Avoiding every form of effort and work
quiz.e: Like water, which is soft yet wears down stone.

quiz.q: What do Buddhism and Stoicism have in common?
o: Both worship the same gods
Both teach that how we interpret events shapes how we suffer
Both deny that ethics matters
Both hold identical views of the self and universe
quiz.e: Scholars note the parallels are real, but the traditions are not identical.

LESSONS.push: Greece wasn't alone. Why great thinkers arose across the world at about the same time.

LESSONS.title: The Enlightenment
LESSONS.hook: In the 1700s, thinkers argued that reason, not tradition or kings, should guide human life. Their ideas built the modern world.

sections.key: The Enlightenment championed reason, evidence and individual rights over tradition and unquestioned authority.
sections.b:
In 1784 the German philosopher Immanuel Kant answered the question 'What is Enlightenment?' with a motto borrowed from the Roman poet Horace: sapere aude, 'dare to know'. He meant having the courage to use your own understanding without being guided by someone else.

Building on the Scientific Revolution, thinkers across Europe and its colonies argued that reason and evidence, not tradition or superstition, should guide how we understand the world and organise society. Isaac Newton's Principia (1687) showed a few laws explaining both falling apples and orbiting planets. If nature followed rational laws, why not society too? The movement is usually dated from the late 1600s to around 1800.

sections.key: Coffee houses, salons and the Encyclopédie carried Enlightenment ideas, despite repeated bans.
sections.b:
Ideas spread through coffee houses, scientific societies, Parisian salons often hosted by women, and a booming trade in books. The great project was the Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert and published from 1751. It aimed to gather all human knowledge, including practical trades, and French authorities repeatedly banned it.

Voltaire (1694 to 1778) used wit and satire to attack intolerance and censorship. His novel Candide (1759) mocks the idea that we live in the best of all possible worlds. He was jailed in the Bastille, spent years in exile, and in 1765 helped clear Jean Calas, a Protestant wrongly executed in 1762.

The famous line 'I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it' wasn't his. His biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall wrote it in 1906.

sections.key: Locke argued governments exist to protect natural rights and rule by the consent of the governed.
sections.b:
The English philosopher John Locke (1632 to 1704) argued that people are born with natural rights, including life, liberty and property, and that governments exist to protect them. Government rests on the consent of the governed. If it violates those rights, people may replace it.

In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), he argued that the mind at birth is like a blank slate, shaped by experience rather than inborn ideas. He also made an influential case for religious toleration. His ideas deeply influenced the American Declaration of Independence, with its 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness', and later democratic constitutions.

sections.key: Montesquieu and Rousseau shaped modern ideas about checking power and grounding authority in the people.
sections.b:
In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued liberty is safest when power is divided: one body makes laws, another carries them out, and an independent judiciary interprets them. Each checks the others, so no one becomes all-powerful. This separation of powers became central to the US Constitution. Australia's Constitution also separates legislative, executive and judicial power, and the High Court guarded judicial independence in the 1956 Boilermakers' case.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau opened The Social Contract (1762) with: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' He argued legitimate authority comes from the collective will of the people, not kings or force. Critics note his claim that dissenters can be 'forced to be free' could justify authoritarianism. Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) extended these arguments to women.

sections.key: Enlightenment science and ideals shaped the modern world, yet many thinkers accepted injustices.
sections.b:
The Scottish Enlightenment produced David Hume, Adam Smith (The Wealth of Nations, 1776) and James Hutton, who argued the Earth was far older than most believed. Enlightenment science reached Australia too: James Cook's voyage, backed by the Royal Society, observed the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, then charted the east coast in 1770. Joseph Banks collected thousands of plant specimens.

Free speech, tolerance, democracy and equal rights are Enlightenment legacies, running through the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights. But many thinkers accepted slavery, colonialism or the exclusion of women. British colonisation of Australia began in 1788, with devastating effects on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Many argue the answer is to apply Enlightenment principles more consistently, not abandon them.

quiz.q: What did Kant mean by 'dare to know'?
o: Having the courage to use your own understanding
Accepting what authorities teach
Studying only the natural sciences
Rejecting all earlier knowledge
quiz.e: Enlightenment thinkers put reason and evidence ahead of unquestioned authority.

quiz.q: Why was the Encyclopédie significant?
o: One author wrote the whole work alone
The French church sponsored and supported it
Authorities repeatedly banned its knowledge project
It covered only the natural sciences
quiz.e: Spreading knowledge widely was seen as a threat by those in power.

quiz.q: According to Locke, what is the purpose of government?
o: To enforce a single official state religion
To protect natural rights, with consent
To make citizens obey a hereditary monarch
To decide what the people may believe
quiz.e: If a government violates those rights, people may replace it.

quiz.q: Why did Montesquieu favour dividing government power among branches?
o: So decisions can be made faster
So the monarch keeps full control
So voters have fewer choices
So each branch can check the others and prevent tyranny
quiz.e: Separated powers keep any one person or group from becoming all-powerful.

quiz.q: What is a fair criticism of the Enlightenment's legacy?
o: Many accepted slavery or excluded women
It rejected science and reason entirely
It opposed free speech and tolerance
It had no lasting influence on later law
quiz.e: The ideals were broader than the people who first stated them.

LESSONS.push: A famous defence of free speech is usually credited to Voltaire. He never wrote it.

LESSONS.title: Do we have free will?
LESSONS.hook: If every event has a cause, including every thought in your brain, are your choices really yours? One of philosophy's oldest puzzles.

sections.key: If every choice has prior causes, it is unclear how any choice can be free.
sections.b:
It feels obvious that you choose freely: this morning you could have had tea instead of coffee. But science describes the world as a chain of causes. Your brain is physical matter following physical laws, shaped by genes, upbringing and experiences you didn't choose. If every decision was caused by earlier events, stretching back before you were born, in what sense could you have done otherwise?

This is the problem of free will and determinism. It matters because praise, blame, pride, guilt and justice all seem to assume that people could have chosen differently.

sections.key: Hard determinists deny free will, while libertarians say some choices are not fully caused.
sections.b:
Hard determinists say every choice is fully caused by earlier events, so free will in the deep sense doesn't exist. The feeling of choosing is real, but produced by brain processes we don't control. In 1814 Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intellect that knew every particle's position and could predict the entire future. Neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky, in his 2023 book Determined, argues this should make us rethink blame and favour prevention and rehabilitation over retribution.

Philosophical 'libertarians', nothing to do with the political kind, hold that some choices aren't fully determined and we originate our actions. Some point to quantum randomness. Critics reply that randomness gives no control: a choice caused by a random neuron event isn't more 'yours'.

sections.key: You act freely when you act on your own reasons without coercion, even if those reasons were caused.
sections.b:
Most professional philosophers are compatibilists: in the large 2020 PhilPapers survey, a clear majority leaned that way. They argue free will doesn't require escaping cause and effect. You act freely when you act on your own desires, reasons and values, without being forced, manipulated or compelled. If you choose coffee because you want coffee, that's free, even if your wanting was caused. If someone holds a gun to your head, it isn't.

David Hume in the 1700s, and more recently the late Daniel Dennett, defended versions of this view. The ancient Stoics were early compatibilists. Chrysippus said a pushed cylinder rolls because of its own shape: events prompt us, but our response comes from our own character.

sections.key: Responsibility may not require that you could have done otherwise.
sections.b:
In 1969 Harry Frankfurt challenged a common assumption: that you're only responsible if you could have done otherwise. Imagine a scientist secretly places a device in Jones's brain. If Jones is about to decide not to vote for a certain candidate, the device will make him vote for them anyway. But Jones decides to vote for them entirely on his own, and the device never activates.

Jones couldn't have done otherwise, yet he seems fully responsible, because the choice came from his own reasons. Frankfurt's cases gave compatibilists a powerful argument, though debate continues.
