sections.key: Libet's experiments are debated rather than decisive, and views on free will shape how we treat responsibility.
sections.b:
In the early 1980s, Benjamin Libet asked people to flex a wrist whenever they felt like it and note when they felt the urge. A build-up of brain activity, the readiness potential, began several hundred milliseconds before people reported deciding. Some concluded the brain decides before 'we' do. A 2012 study led by Aaron Schurger suggested it may partly reflect random background fluctuations instead. Libet himself argued people could still 'veto' an action. The experiments are debated, not decisive.

The debate matters in practice. Courts already weigh age, mental impairment and duress. If choices are shaped by circumstances we didn't choose, perhaps we should be more compassionate and humbler about success. Yet most people think it still makes sense to hold ourselves responsible. Build habits and surroundings that make good choices easier.

quiz.q: Why does determinism threaten the idea of free will?
o: Science proves that people never make decisions
Laws forbid people from choosing anything freely
Earlier causes make 'doing otherwise' unclear
Brains are unable to process real choices
quiz.e: Our ideas of blame and praise assume we could have chosen differently.

quiz.q: Why do critics say quantum randomness doesn't rescue libertarian free will?
o: Quantum effects never occur in nature
Random events are fully predictable
Randomness is the same as determinism
A random event gives you no more control over the choice
quiz.e: A choice caused by chance isn't any more 'yours' than one caused by earlier events.

quiz.q: According to compatibilists, when do you act freely?
o: Only when your choice has no prior cause at all
When you act on your own reasons, uncoerced
Only when you have unlimited options to pick from
Whenever you simply feel that you want something
quiz.e: Free will doesn't need escaping cause and effect, only freedom from force or manipulation.

quiz.q: What does Frankfurt's thought experiment suggest about Jones?
o: He is responsible, because the choice came from his own reasons
He is not responsible, because he couldn't have done otherwise
He is not responsible, because the device exists
He can't be judged either way
quiz.e: Being able to do otherwise may not be required for responsibility.

quiz.q: What do Libet's experiments show about free will?
o: That conscious choice is a complete illusion
That people can never veto an action
Nothing decisive: interpretations of the brain activity are debated
That decisions take exactly one second
quiz.e: Later research questioned the original interpretation of the readiness potential.

LESSONS.push: Your brain may start a movement before you feel you chose it. What that means.

LESSONS.title: Existentialism
LESSONS.hook: No script, no predetermined purpose. Existentialists argued we're free to create meaning, and responsible for what we make of ourselves.

sections.key: Humans have no preset purpose: we exist first, then create ourselves through our choices.
sections.b:
In a famous 1945 lecture in Paris, Jean-Paul Sartre summed up existentialism as 'existence precedes essence'. A paper knife has a purpose in the craftsman's mind before it is made, so its essence comes first. Humans, Sartre argued, have no pre-set purpose. We exist first, then create who we are through our choices and actions. For Sartre, an atheist, this followed from the absence of a creator.

So we're 'condemned to be free': we can't escape choosing, and even refusing to choose is a choice. With freedom comes total responsibility, and anxiety. Many flee through 'bad faith', blaming their job, upbringing or society. In Being and Nothingness (1943), Sartre described a café waiter whose movements are a little too perfect, as if hiding his freedom behind a role.

sections.key: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche laid the foundations, and postwar Paris made existentialism a cultural movement.
sections.b:
Søren Kierkegaard (1813 to 1855) focused on the individual facing anxiety and choice, and on a passionate commitment that reason can't justify, for him Christian faith: a 'leap of faith'. Friedrich Nietzsche (1844 to 1900) declared in 1882 that 'God is dead', meaning belief in God was fading in Europe and leaving a crisis of values. He feared nihilism and urged people to create their own values and affirm life, even its suffering.

After the war and the occupation of France, Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir and their circle held court in Left Bank cafés like the Café de Flore and founded the journal Les Temps modernes in 1945. Sartre was offered the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature and declined it, saying a writer shouldn't become an institution.

sections.key: Camus argued life is absurd, but we can rebel by living fully anyway.
sections.b:
Albert Camus, a French writer born in Algeria in 1913, rejected the existentialist label but is closely linked to it. He described the absurd: the clash between our longing for meaning and a silent, indifferent universe. His novel The Stranger (1942) follows a man who refuses to pretend to feelings he doesn't have.

In The Myth of Sisyphus, published the same year, he retold the Greek myth of a man condemned to push a boulder uphill forever. Camus concluded: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' Embracing life in full awareness of the absurd is a kind of rebellion. He won the Nobel Prize in 1957.

sections.key: De Beauvoir applied existentialism to women's lives and argued that true freedom means willing freedom for others.
sections.b:
Simone de Beauvoir, a philosopher, novelist and Sartre's lifelong partner, wrote The Second Sex (1949), a founding text of modern feminism. She argued that women had been defined as 'the Other' in relation to men, treated as secondary rather than as free subjects, and that ideas of femininity are shaped by society, not fixed by nature. Her famous line, 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', applied the existentialist idea that we're not bound by a fixed essence.

In The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), she argued that true freedom requires willing freedom for others too.

sections.key: Existentialism had critics and bitter quarrels, but its practical message is authenticity and responsibility.
sections.b:
Religious thinkers objected to Sartre's atheism, Marxists thought it too individual, and others found it gloomy. Its leaders quarrelled too. Sartre and Camus were friends until 1952, when a harsh review of Camus's The Rebel in Sartre's journal caused a bitter split. Camus had condemned political violence and Soviet labour camps, while Sartre, for a time, defended the Soviet Union. They never reconciled before Camus died in a car accident in 1960.

The practical message is demanding but empowering. Live authentically, by values you've chosen rather than what others expect. Take responsibility instead of hiding behind 'I had no choice'. Accept that some anxiety comes with freedom. Create meaning through commitments to people, work and causes. Viktor Frankl's logotherapy and modern existential psychotherapy draw on these ideas.

quiz.q: What does 'existence precedes essence' mean?
o: We are all born with one fixed purpose
Our essence is decided in advance by a creator
We exist first, then define ourselves
Nothing really exists beyond our thoughts
quiz.e: With no preset human nature, we are what we make of ourselves.

quiz.q: What is 'bad faith' in Sartre's sense?
o: Pretending you have no choice
Doubting your own religious beliefs
Telling a lie to a close friend
Breaking a promise made to someone
quiz.e: Blaming job, upbringing or society hides our freedom.

quiz.q: What did Nietzsche mean by 'God is dead'?
o: God's non-existence had been scientifically proven
Religion ought to be banned from public life
People had become more virtuous and moral
Belief in God was fading, creating a values crisis
quiz.e: He feared nihilism and urged people to create their own values.

quiz.q: How does Camus suggest we respond to the absurd?
o: Search for a hidden cosmic meaning behind it
Live fully, aware of it, as a kind of rebellion
Give up on life because nothing matters
Pretend the universe has a plan for us
quiz.e: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.'

quiz.q: What does de Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' express?
o: Biology fully determines a woman's role in life
Gender has no real effect on social life
Femininity is shaped by society, not nature
Women should avoid defining themselves at all
quiz.e: It applies the existentialist idea that we are not bound by a fixed essence.

LESSONS.push: Sartre turned down a Nobel Prize. His reason says a lot about the man.

LESSONS.title: A short history of AI
LESSONS.hook: AI did not arrive overnight. It is a 70-year story of bold promises, bitter winters and a few moments that stunned the world.

sections.key: In 1950 Turing proposed a conversation test of machine intelligence, and in 1956 the field was named.
sections.b:
In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing, famous for wartime code-breaking, published 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', asking: can machines think? Because 'thinking' is hard to define, he proposed the imitation game, now the Turing test. If a judge chatting through text could not reliably tell a machine from a person, we should take its intelligence seriously. He also predicted machines might one day learn, not just be programmed step by step.

The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined by John McCarthy in a proposal for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, organised with Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester. It produced no single breakthrough, but gave the field a name, a community and an ambitious agenda.

sections.key: Early AI used hand-written rules, and its pioneers' predictions proved far too optimistic.
sections.b:
The first decades of AI were dominated by symbolic AI: programs built from hand-written rules and logic. They proved maths theorems, played draughts and solved puzzles. In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA mimicked a therapist using simple pattern matching, and some users became emotionally attached to it, which alarmed its creator.

Confidence ran high. In 1965 Herbert Simon predicted that within twenty years machines would be capable of doing any work a person can do. Meanwhile, Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 perceptron, an early learning machine loosely inspired by brain cells, hinted at a different path that was largely sidelined for years.

sections.key: Overhyped promises led to funding cuts, twice, because hype outran what the technology could do.
sections.b:
Real-world problems proved far messier than puzzles. Programs that worked in tidy demonstrations failed on everyday language and vision, and computers were too slow and data too scarce. In the early 1970s, critical reviews such as Britain's 1973 Lighthill report led governments to cut funding, beginning the first 'AI winter'.

The 1980s brought a boom in expert systems, rule-based programs that captured specialist knowledge for businesses. They proved expensive and brittle, and by the late 1980s and early 1990s the market collapsed into a second winter. The lesson: hype can outrun what the technology can actually do.

sections.key: Deep Blue won by narrow brute force, while the 2012 deep learning breakthrough revived learning machines.
sections.b:
In May 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5 in New York, after he had beaten an earlier version the year before. Yet it did not learn as people do. Specialised hardware evaluated around 200 million positions per second, combined with chess knowledge programmed by experts. It was superb at chess and could do nothing else.

Learning machines never died. Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio kept refining neural networks through the lean years. By the 2010s huge internet datasets, fast graphics chips (GPUs) and better training methods had arrived. In 2012 AlexNet, from Hinton's Toronto group, won the ImageNet image-recognition competition by a striking margin. 'Deep learning' soon transformed speech, translation and image analysis. The trio shared the 2018 Turing Award.

sections.key: Learning-based systems beat Go champions and, with transformers, produced today's large language models.
sections.b:
Go has vastly more positions than chess, so brute force alone could not master it. In March 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat top professional Lee Sedol four games to one in Seoul. It combined deep neural networks, search and reinforcement learning, improving partly by playing itself. In game two it played Move 37, which experts first thought a mistake but later saw as brilliant. Many had expected this milestone to be years away.

In 2017 Google researchers introduced the transformer, which made it practical to train on enormous amounts of text. This led to large language models, and ChatGPT's release in November 2022 made them mainstream. Past predictions were often wildly optimistic, yet deep learning has also surprised sceptics. Treat confident forecasts in either direction with caution.

quiz.q: What was the idea behind the Turing test?
o: A machine passes if it beats a human at chess
A machine passes if a judge can't tell it from a person in chat
A machine passes if it solves hard maths theorems
A machine passes if it performs a physical task like a person
quiz.e: Turing replaced the vague question 'can machines think?' with a practical test.

quiz.q: What was the problem with early AI predictions?
o: They underestimated how fast computers would get
They ignored rule-based programs altogether
They predicted that AI would never be built
They were far too optimistic about timing
quiz.e: Early confidence ran well ahead of what the technology could do.

quiz.q: What caused the 'AI winters'?
o: Overhyped promises and then funding cuts
A government ban on all AI research
Computers overheating in the early labs
A shortage of trained mathematicians
quiz.e: Hype outran what the technology could actually do.

quiz.q: Why was Deep Blue's victory over Kasparov a narrow kind of intelligence?
o: It learned chess by playing millions of games itself
It read thousands of chess books to learn
It used fast search and programmed chess knowledge only
It could talk about any subject like a person
quiz.e: It was superb at one task but helpless outside it.

quiz.q: Why did AlphaGo's 2016 win surprise many experts?
o: Go has far fewer positions than chess does
It won every single game of the match
It was built without using neural networks
Experts thought it was still years away
quiz.e: A learning system, not brute force, mastered a game thought to be out of reach.

LESSONS.push: AI went through two deep freezes. Why the field went cold, and how it thawed.

LESSONS.title: How machines learn
LESSONS.hook: Nobody wrote the rules that let your phone recognise your face. The machine worked them out from examples. Here's how.

sections.key: Machine learning finds patterns in data instead of following hand-written rules.
sections.b:
Traditional software follows rules a programmer writes by hand: if this, then that. That suits payroll or calculators, but try writing rules to recognise a cat in a photo or tell spam from real email. There are too many exceptions.

Machine learning takes a different approach. You give the computer many examples and let it find the patterns itself. Show a spam filter millions of emails marked 'spam' or 'not spam', and it learns which features, such as certain phrases, links or senders, tend to signal junk. The result is called a model.

There are two stages. Training is the learning phase: the model makes predictions, measures how wrong they are and adjusts, over and over. Inference is using the finished model on new inputs. Most models don't keep learning while you use them.

sections.key: In supervised learning, a model learns from examples labelled with the correct answers.
sections.b:
The most common kind of machine learning is supervised learning. The training data comes with labels, the right answers. To predict house prices, you might feed a model thousands of past sales with details like suburb, land size and bedrooms, along with what each sold for. It learns how those features relate to price, then estimates prices for homes it has never seen.

The same approach powers medical image tools trained on scans labelled by specialists, and bank fraud detectors trained on transactions marked genuine or fraudulent. The catch: good labels are slow and expensive to create, and the model can only be as good as they are.

sections.key: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data, and reinforcement learning learns by trial and error.
sections.b:
Sometimes you have plenty of data but no labels. Unsupervised learning looks for structure itself. Clustering groups similar items: a supermarket might find distinct groups in loyalty card data, such as busy families or bargain hunters, without anyone defining them. Anomaly detection spots things that don't fit, like an odd reading from a machine about to fail. People still have to interpret the results.

Reinforcement learning works a bit like training a dog with treats. An agent takes actions and gets rewards or penalties, learning which strategies earn the most reward. AlphaGo improved by playing millions of games against itself. Feedback from human raters helps make chatbots more helpful. Designing the right reward is tricky: systems can find unexpected shortcuts.

sections.key: Neural networks are layers of simple units whose connection weights are adjusted during training.
sections.b:
Many modern models are artificial neural networks, loosely inspired by the brain. A network is made of layers of simple units, sometimes called neurons. Each unit takes in numbers, weights them, adds them up and passes a result to the next layer.

The weights, the strength of each connection, are what the network learns. During training, a method called backpropagation works out how each weight contributed to an error and nudges it slightly in a better direction. Repeat that billions of times and useful patterns emerge. 'Deep' learning simply means networks with many layers. Despite the name, they work very differently from real brains.

sections.key: Models can memorise their training data or absorb its biases, so how they are tested and trained matters.
sections.b:
A student who memorises last year's exam answers aces the practice paper but fails when the questions change. Models can do the same, called overfitting: fitting training data so closely, including its noise, that they do poorly on new examples. Developers hold back a test set the model never sees and judge performance on that. The goal is generalisation: working well in the real world.

A model also learns whatever its data shows, including past biases. In 2018 Reuters reported that Amazon scrapped an experimental recruiting tool that penalised CVs mentioning women's activities, having learned from mostly male applicants. Some facial analysis systems made more errors on darker-skinned faces, largely because of unrepresentative training photos. When an automated system judges a loan, job application or medical image, ask what data it learned from and how it was tested.

quiz.q: What is the key idea of machine learning?
o: Programmers write every single rule by hand
Computers copy the human brain exactly
Data is collected but never actually used
The computer finds patterns from examples
quiz.e: The result of the learning is called a model.

quiz.q: Predicting house prices from past sales with known prices is an example of what?
o: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Overfitting
quiz.e: The known sale prices are the labels.

quiz.q: How does reinforcement learning work?
o: By grouping similar items into clusters
By copying answers that are already labelled
By trial and error, guided by rewards
By memorising a whole textbook of facts
quiz.e: AlphaGo improved by playing against itself.

quiz.q: What does a neural network actually learn during training?
o: The weights of the connections between its units
A list of rules written by programmers
The names of the training examples
A copy of the brain's wiring
quiz.e: Backpropagation nudges each weight to reduce errors.

quiz.q: Why do developers test a model on data it never saw in training?
o: To make the training process run faster
To catch a model that memorises instead of generalising
To strip the labels out of the data
To give the model more examples to learn from
quiz.e: A held-back test set shows whether the model works on new data.

LESSONS.push: Nobody wrote the rules your phone uses to recognise a face. So who did?

LESSONS.title: AI images and deepfakes
LESSONS.hook: Type a sentence, get a photo that never existed. Understanding how image generators work is the first step to not being fooled by them.

sections.key: Image generators learn word-to-image patterns from vast caption pairs and generate new pixels, not stored photos.
sections.b:
AI image generators turn a text prompt into a new picture. Type 'a kookaburra in a raincoat, watercolour style' and seconds later you get an image no one has ever painted. These systems are trained on enormous collections of images paired with captions, often billions of pairs gathered from the internet. They learn statistical links between words and visual features: what 'watercolour' looks like, the shape of a kookaburra, how light falls on wet fabric.

The model doesn't paste together pieces of stored photos. It generates new pixels based on the patterns it has learned.

sections.key: Diffusion models turn random static into an image step by step, steered by the prompt.
sections.b:
Many leading generators use diffusion. In training, you take a real image and add random noise a little at a time until it becomes pure static, like an old TV with no signal. Then you train a neural network to reverse each small step. After enough practice, the model can start from static and remove noise step by step until a clear image emerges. Starting from different noise each time, the same prompt gives different pictures.

The prompt steers each step. The text is converted into numbers that capture its meaning, nudging the image towards the description. Because the model has learned associations, not rules about the world, it has struggled with finger counts and legible signs. Newer systems do better, but mistakes slip through.

sections.key: Deepfakes make real people appear to say or do things they never did, and the harms are serious.
sections.b:
A deepfake is synthetic media that makes a real person appear to do or say something they never did. The term emerged around 2017 from face-swapping videos. Today, tools can clone a voice from a short recording and generate realistic video. Some uses are harmless, such as film effects or clearly labelled satire. The harms include non-consensual sexual images, political fakes and scams.

In a widely reported 2024 case in Hong Kong, an employee at an engineering firm transferred roughly US$25 million after a video call in which the 'executives' were deepfakes. Criminals also use cloned voices to impersonate family members.

sections.key: Visual clues are fading, so check the source and context before believing or sharing.
sections.b:
Older fakes gave themselves away with warped hands, mismatched earrings, garbled text, odd shadows or overly smooth skin. Those clues are worth checking, but they are becoming less reliable as the technology improves.

Better habits focus on context. Who posted this first, and are they credible? Is a reputable news outlet reporting it? Look for the same moment from other angles: a real event is usually captured by many people, while a fake often exists as a single striking image. Some companies add invisible watermarks or 'content credentials' to AI images, but these aren't universal. If a clip provokes strong emotion, slow down and check where it came from before sharing.

sections.key: Australian law now targets sexual deepfakes, copyright questions remain open, and wise use means openness and consent.
sections.b:
In 2024 Australia made it a federal criminal offence to share sexually explicit deepfakes of adults without consent. Defamation, fraud and harassment laws can also apply. The eSafety Commissioner can help remove image-based abuse, and you can report it at esafety.gov.au. If you are targeted, keep evidence such as screenshots and links, report it, and consider legal advice.

Copyright is unsettled. Generators were largely trained on web images, often without artists' permission. Developers say learning patterns is lawful; creators call it unfair copying, and cases, including by Getty Images, are under way. In Australia, copyright generally requires a human author, so purely AI-made images may not be protected.

Use image AI openly. Don't depict real people without consent, and check a tool's terms before commercial use.

quiz.q: How does an AI image generator produce a picture?
o: It generates new pixels from learned patterns
It pastes together pieces of stored photos
It searches the web for a matching photo
It traces the outline of a stock image
quiz.e: The model learns links between words and visual features, rather than storing photos to copy.

quiz.q: Why have image generators struggled with things like fingers or text?
o: They are deliberately programmed to avoid them
They have no training images that show hands
They learn associations, not rules about the world
Prompts are almost always far too short
quiz.e: Newer systems are better, but errors still happen.

quiz.q: What is a deepfake?
o: Any holiday photo that has been edited lightly
Synthetic media showing a real person doing or saying what they didn't
A blurry or low-quality photo of a person
A computer virus that hides inside image files
quiz.e: Voices can be cloned too, and scams use both.

quiz.q: Why are clues like warped hands a weak test for AI fakes?
o: AI images no longer show people
Phones remove them automatically
They were never useful
Newer generators make far fewer of these mistakes
quiz.e: Check the source and context instead.

quiz.q: What does Australian copyright law generally require for protection?
o: A human author
A registration fee
Publication online
A signed licence
quiz.e: Purely AI-made images may not be protected.

LESSONS.push: A video call full of familiar faces cost one company about US$25 million. None were real.

LESSONS.title: Using AI well
LESSONS.hook: AI assistants can save you hours or quietly lead you astray. The difference usually comes down to how you use them.

sections.key: Treat an AI assistant as a fast, well-read helper whose work you must still check.
sections.b:
Think of an AI chatbot as a very fast, widely read assistant who is eager to please and sometimes confidently wrong. It can draft an email in seconds, explain a tricky concept five ways and summarise a long document. But it doesn't know your situation unless you tell it, it can misunderstand you, and its errors can sound completely convincing.

People who get the most from AI stay in charge. They give clear direction, review everything important and treat the output as a draft, not a final answer. You remain responsible for what you do with it.

sections.key: Give the goal, audience, format and details, then refine through conversation.
sections.b:
AI can't read your mind, and vague requests get generic answers. Compare 'Write a letter to my landlord' with 'Write a polite but firm email to my landlord in Brisbane asking for a leaking tap to be repaired. I reported it three weeks ago. Keep it under 150 words.' The second gives goal, situation, tone and length. You can also ask it to take a role, such as a patient maths tutor, or show an example of the style you want.

Your first prompt rarely gives the perfect result, so treat it as a conversation. Say what to change: 'shorter', 'less formal', 'more Australian examples'. Break big tasks into steps. A powerful trick is to ask the AI to interview you first: 'Before you write my CV summary, ask me five questions about my experience.'

sections.key: Chatbots can 'hallucinate' fluent, plausible falsehoods, so important facts need checking.
sections.b:
Language models generate text that sounds right from patterns, which isn't the same as checking it is right. Lacking reliable information, they can fill the gap with fluent inventions: a fake statistic, a book that doesn't exist, a made-up quote. This is called hallucination.

In 2023, New York lawyers were fined for filing a court document citing cases a chatbot had invented. Similar incidents have occurred elsewhere, including in Australia. Web-searching tools reduce the problem but don't eliminate it.

The costlier a mistake, the more checking it deserves. For a birthday poem, errors hardly matter. For medication doses, tax rules or a contract, they matter a lot. Confirm that cited sources exist and say what is claimed, cross-check key facts with trusted sources such as government agencies, and confirm advice applies in Australia.

sections.key: What you type is sent to the company running the tool, so keep sensitive details out.
sections.b:
What you type into an online AI tool is sent to the company that runs it. Depending on the service and your settings, conversations may be stored, reviewed by staff or used to improve future models. So treat a chatbot like any online service.

Never share passwords, full card or bank details, or identity documents. Think twice before pasting in medical records, legal disputes or anything about other people, such as a client's details or a friend's private message. Check the privacy settings, which often let you limit how your data is used. At work, follow your employer's AI policy, because putting confidential information into public tools can breach privacy obligations.

sections.key: AI shines at drafts and practice where you can judge the result, but it is no substitute for professionals or people.
sections.b:
AI earns its keep where a good first draft saves time and you can judge the result. Paste in a confusing insurer's letter, with personal details removed, and ask what it means. Turn a brain dump into a to-do list, rehearse asking for a pay rise with the AI playing the boss, or ask it to quiz you on a topic. Use it to get started or unstuck, then add your own judgement.

Be careful with very recent events unless it can search the web. For health, finances or legal rights, use it to prepare questions, then talk to a doctor, licensed financial adviser or lawyer. Leaning on it too heavily can stop you building a skill. Chatbots are no substitute for friends, family or professional support. If you are struggling, Lifeline is on 13 11 14.

quiz.q: How should you treat an AI assistant's output?
o: As a final answer from an expert
As unreliable and therefore useless
As a draft to review, since it can be confidently wrong
As accurate whenever it sounds confident
quiz.e: You remain responsible for what you do with it.

quiz.q: Which prompt is likely to get the most useful result?
o: A single keyword with no other detail
A one-line request such as 'Write a letter'
The single word 'Help' typed on its own
A request stating goal, audience, tone and length
quiz.e: Context beats vague requests.

quiz.q: Why can a chatbot cite a court case that doesn't exist?
o: It deliberately lies to users who ask
It generates plausible text without checking facts
Its sources are always badly out of date
It copies cases from a secret legal database
quiz.e: Fluent, confident inventions like these are called hallucinations.

quiz.q: Which of these should you avoid pasting into a public AI tool?
o: Your bank details and passwords
A recipe you want adapted
A poem draft
A holiday packing list
quiz.e: Conversations may be stored or reviewed.

quiz.q: How should you use AI for a serious health or money decision?
o: Follow its advice without checking it first
Let it make the final decision for you
Use it to prepare questions for a professional
Avoid reading about the topic altogether
quiz.e: It shouldn't be your only source for high-stakes decisions.

LESSONS.push: Lawyers were fined for citing cases that never existed. How chatbots invent.

LESSONS.title: AI's risks and debates
LESSONS.hook: Some experts call AI the most important technology in history. Some think the fears are overblown. Here's what they actually disagree about.

sections.key: Informed experts disagree about AI's risks, so ask of any claim what the evidence is and what timeframe it covers.
sections.b:
Debates about AI can sound like boosters against doomsayers, but the real picture is more interesting. Serious researchers, economists and policymakers disagree about how fast AI will improve, how much it will change society and which risks matter most. Some focus on harms happening now, such as bias, scams and privacy breaches. Others worry most about future systems far more capable than today's. Many care about both. These views compete for attention and funding rather than conflict.

Be wary of confident predictions from any side, and notice who benefits from a story: companies may overstate their products, while headlines reward alarm. Ask what the evidence is, and what timeframe is being discussed.

sections.key: Automated decisions can harm many people at once, so they need human oversight, transparency and a way to challenge them.
sections.b:
When AI helps decide who gets a loan, a job interview or extra scrutiny from a government agency, errors and biases can affect huge numbers of people at once. Models trained on historical data can absorb past discrimination. A 2016 ProPublica investigation reported that a US tool used to predict reoffending wrongly flagged Black defendants as high risk far more often than white defendants.

Australia has its own cautionary tale. Robodebt wasn't modern AI, but it was automation: it used averaged income data to raise welfare debts, many of them wrong. A 2023 Royal Commission called it crude and cruel. The lesson is that automated decisions need human oversight, transparency and a clear way to challenge them.

sections.key: AI makes convincing fakes cheap and personal data easy to mine, so verify surprising content and guard your data.
sections.b:
Generative AI makes persuasive fakes cheap: realistic images, cloned voices and armies of automated accounts. Scammers already use them. Researchers still debate how much AI fakes have swayed voters. A subtler risk is the 'liar's dividend': once anything could be faked, someone caught on a genuine recording can claim it's fake.

AI is also very good at finding patterns in personal data, which helps detect fraud but enables surveillance. The Privacy Commissioner found in 2021 that Clearview AI breached Australians' privacy by scraping online photos, and in 2024 that Bunnings breached it with in-store facial recognition, a finding Bunnings challenged at a tribunal. Verify surprising content before sharing it, and watch for voice and video scams.

sections.key: AI will change tasks within many jobs, and while the long-run outcome is contested, skills and retraining will matter.
sections.b:
Earlier automation mostly affected routine physical work. Today's AI can also draft text, write code, analyse documents and produce images, so it touches office and creative jobs too. What happens next is genuinely contested.

Optimists point out that past technologies, from tractors to computers, eliminated some jobs but created new ones and raised living standards over time. Others argue AI could change work faster and more broadly than before, leaving some people worse off even if the economy grows. Most economists agree that tasks within jobs will change, that transitions can be painful, and that skills and retraining will matter. Keep building skills that complement AI.

sections.key: Making AI pursue intended goals is an open problem, and governments are still choosing how to regulate it.
sections.b:
The alignment problem is the challenge of making AI reliably pursue the goals people actually intend. Today it shows up as chatbots tricked into harmful answers, or systems that find loopholes in their instructions. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio have warned of extreme risks from future systems, and in 2023 hundreds of experts signed a statement calling extinction risk from AI a global priority. Yann LeCun argues these fears are overblown and distract from present harms.

The EU's 2024 AI Act is risk-based: a few uses are banned, high-risk uses face strict rules, lower-risk uses lighter ones. Australia's 2025 National AI Plan relies mainly on existing laws, voluntary guidance and an AI Safety Institute. How AI develops is a choice, shaped by laws, businesses and the public.

quiz.q: What is a useful way to judge any claim about AI?
o: Trust whichever expert sounds most sure
Favour the most alarming prediction
Check the evidence and the timeframe
Assume companies understate their products
quiz.e: Confident predictions from any side deserve scrutiny, so check the evidence and the timeframe.

quiz.q: What lesson did Australia's Robodebt scheme offer about automation?
o: Automated decisions need human oversight and a right of challenge
Automation is always accurate when it uses averaged data
Welfare payments are best decided entirely by machines
Only modern AI systems can cause errors like these
quiz.e: Robodebt showed that automated decisions without oversight or a right of challenge can harm many people.

quiz.q: What is the 'liar's dividend'?
o: Profit made from selling AI detection software
A tax proposed on the spread of fake news
Dismissing real evidence as fake once fakes are common
A reward for spotting deepfakes
quiz.e: When anything could be faked, genuine evidence becomes easier to deny.

quiz.q: What do most economists agree about AI and jobs?
o: Tasks within many jobs will change, and transitions can hurt
Only factory jobs will be affected by it at all
Nearly every job will vanish within five years
New technology has never created any new jobs
quiz.e: The size of the effect is contested, but task change and painful transitions are widely expected.

quiz.q: What approach does the EU's AI Act take?
o: It bans every use of AI across Europe
It relies only on voluntary company promises
It sets stricter rules for higher-risk uses
It regulates only chatbots and nothing else
quiz.e: A risk-based approach matches the strength of the rules to the potential for harm.

LESSONS.push: Experts agree AI matters. What they dispute is which risks, and how soon.

LESSONS.title: Marsupials: life in the pouch
LESSONS.hook: Born the size of a jellybean, finished in a pouch. Australia's marsupials took a very different path to the rest of the mammal world.

sections.key: Marsupials give birth to tiny, barely formed young that finish developing attached to a teat, usually in a pouch.
sections.b:
A red kangaroo's pregnancy lasts only about 33 days. The newborn joey is pink, hairless and under a gram, about the size of a jellybean. Using its strong front legs, it crawls through its mother's fur to the pouch, latches onto a teat and stays for months. That is the marsupial way: a short pregnancy with no long placental feeding, then development outside the body. Some small species have no true pouch and carry young clinging underneath.

A mother kangaroo can pause a new embryo's development, called embryonic diapause, until the pouch is free. She can also feed a joey at foot and a newborn at once, with two kinds of milk from two teats. Of about 330 marsupial species, around two-thirds live in Australia and New Guinea.

sections.key: Kangaroos hop efficiently because their leg tendons store and release energy like springs.
sections.b:
Kangaroos and wallabies are macropods, meaning 'big feet', a family of around 60 species. The red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial; big males standing upright can be as tall as a person. Hopping looks tiring, but long leg tendons store and release energy like springs, so once a kangaroo is moving, going faster costs surprisingly little extra effort. Reds can briefly reach around 50 kilometres per hour. Moving slowly, kangaroos use their strong tail as a fifth leg.

Kangaroos are most active around dawn and dusk, when collisions are most common, so take extra care driving then.

sections.key: Koalas and wombats are specialists: koalas live on low-energy leaves, and wombats dig and make cube-shaped droppings.
sections.b:
Koalas are not bears. They eat almost only eucalyptus leaves, which are low in nutrients, high in fibre and toxic to most animals. A long gut and specialised microbes help, and young koalas eat a soft faeces called pap from their mother to gain those microbes. The diet gives so little energy that koalas rest or sleep 18 to 22 hours a day. In 2022, koalas in Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT were listed as endangered, mainly through habitat loss, disease, dogs and cars.

Wombats are the only animals known to make cube-shaped poo, dozens of cubes a night, left on rocks and logs as territory markers. A 2018 study found that regions of differing stiffness in the last stretch of intestine shape the drying droppings. It won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2019.

sections.key: Tasmanian devils face a contagious cancer, while the thylacine was hunted to extinction by 1936.
sections.b:
The Tasmanian devil is the largest living carnivorous marsupial, with one of the most powerful bites for its size of any mammal. Devils vanished from the mainland about 3,000 years ago. Since the mid-1990s, devil facial tumour disease, a rare cancer spread by biting, has caused severe declines. Insurance populations are bred in captivity, and since 2020 some devils have been released into a fenced sanctuary in New South Wales.

The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was the largest carnivorous marsupial of modern times, a dog-like hunter with dark stripes across its back. Seen as a threat to sheep, it was targeted by a government bounty from 1888 to 1909, with more than 2,000 paid. The last known thylacine died at Beaumaris Zoo, Hobart, on 7 September 1936, now National Threatened Species Day.

sections.key: Isolation let Australian marsupials evolve into roles that placental mammals fill elsewhere, and you can help injured ones.
sections.b:
Australia's marsupial richness is a story of isolation. After Australia separated from Antarctica tens of millions of years ago and drifted north, its marsupials evolved on their own, filling roles that placental mammals fill elsewhere. The results show striking convergent evolution: sugar gliders resemble flying squirrels, the marsupial mole resembles golden moles, and the thylacine looked remarkably like a wolf.

The practical side is simple. Drive slowly at dawn and dusk in the bush. If you find an injured animal, or a dead kangaroo or wombat by the road, call a local wildlife rescue service, because a living joey may still be in the pouch.

quiz.q: How do marsupials differ from other mammals in reproduction?
o: They lay soft-shelled eggs in a nest
A long pregnancy nourished by a placenta
A short pregnancy, then a tiny newborn on a teat
They produce young without any milk
quiz.e: Marsupials deliver tiny, barely formed young that complete development attached to a teat.

quiz.q: What makes fast hopping efficient for kangaroos?
o: Hollow bones that keep the body light
Springy tendons that store and release energy
A very large heart that pumps faster
Air sacs in the tail that add lift
quiz.e: Tendons act like springs, so extra speed costs little extra effort.

quiz.q: Why do koalas rest for up to 22 hours a day?
o: They are nocturnal hunters that tire
They hibernate through the winter
Eucalyptus leaves give very little energy
Their pouches make movement hard work
quiz.e: A low-energy, toxic leaf diet leaves koalas little fuel for activity.

quiz.q: What drove the thylacine to extinction?
o: A cancer spread between animals by biting
A bounty and hunting, as it was seen as a sheep threat
A long drought that dried up Tasmania
Competition for food from kangaroos
quiz.e: Persecution, including a bounty scheme, ended the thylacine by 1936.

quiz.q: Why do sugar gliders resemble flying squirrels?
o: They are close relatives that split recently
Similar roles evolved independently in isolation
Humans introduced them from North America
They share exactly the same diet as squirrels
quiz.e: Convergent evolution produces similar body plans in unrelated animals that fill similar roles.

LESSONS.push: A newborn kangaroo weighs less than a gram. How does it reach the pouch?

LESSONS.title: Platypus and echidnas: the egg-laying mammals
LESSONS.hook: When the first platypus reached Britain, scientists checked it for stitches. It was real, and it was even stranger than it looked.

sections.key: Only five living mammals lay eggs, and they are specialised animals, not primitive leftovers.
sections.b:
Only five living mammal species lay eggs: the platypus and four species of echidna. Together they are the monotremes, a group that split from the ancestors of all other mammals more than 160 million years ago. The name means 'single opening': like birds and reptiles, they have one opening, the cloaca, for waste and reproduction.

The platypus lives only in eastern Australia, including Tasmania. The short-beaked echidna lives across Australia and New Guinea, while the three long-beaked echidnas live only in New Guinea. They are not 'primitive' leftovers but highly specialised animals with a very long, separate evolutionary history.

sections.key: Monotremes are true mammals with fur and milk, but they have no nipples and lay leathery eggs.
sections.b:
Monotremes have fur, a single lower jawbone and the three tiny middle ear bones typical of mammals, and they feed their young on milk. The twist: they have no nipples. Milk seeps out through pores on patches of belly skin, and the young lick or suck it up. They are warm-blooded but run cooler than most mammals, at around 32 degrees Celsius compared with our 37. Adult platypuses have no teeth and grind food with hard pads; echidnas never have teeth.

A female platypus seals herself in a riverbank burrow and incubates one to three soft, leathery eggs for roughly ten days. An echidna lays one egg into a temporary belly pouch. It hatches after about ten days, and the baby, called a puggle, stays until its spines begin to grow.

sections.key: A platypus hunts by sensing electric fields with its soft bill, and males carry a painful venomous spur, so never handle one.
sections.b:
The platypus bill is soft, rubbery and packed with sensors. Diving, the platypus closes its eyes, ears and nostrils, so it hunts almost blind. Tens of thousands of electroreceptors detect the faint electric fields from prey muscles, and touch receptors help too. Sweeping its head side to side, it finds larvae, worms and yabbies in the mud, stores them in cheek pouches and chews at the surface.

Males carry a sharp spur on each hind ankle, joined to a venom gland. Venom production rises in the breeding season, which suggests it is mainly used in fights between males. A spur injury isn't known to be fatal to humans but causes severe pain and swelling that ordinary painkillers barely touch, sometimes for weeks. Never handle a wild platypus.

sections.key: The short-beaked echidna is a widespread, spiny ant-eater with its own electric sense and defences.
sections.b:
The short-beaked echidna lives in almost every habitat in Australia, from deserts and forests to the snowy high country, making it the most widespread native mammal on the continent. Its spines are modified hairs. It laps up ants and termites with a long, sticky tongue, and its snout carries electroreceptors too, though far fewer than a platypus bill.

When threatened, an echidna digs straight down or curls into a spiky ball. In winter, several males sometimes follow a female in a line called an 'echidna train'. Male echidnas also have ankle spurs, but they don't deliver venom; a gland on the spur appears to produce a secretion in the breeding season, possibly for communication. Echidnas are long-lived for their size, surviving for decades.

sections.key: Europe doubted the platypus was real and that monotremes laid eggs, and today the platypus needs our protection.
sections.b:
First Nations peoples had known these animals for tens of thousands of years, but European naturalists were baffled. When a preserved platypus reached Britain in the late 1790s, George Shaw, who described it in 1799, wondered if it was a fake, a duck's bill stitched onto a mammal. Scientists argued for decades over whether monotremes laid eggs, as Aboriginal informants said. In 1884, William Caldwell, working in Queensland, found proof and telegraphed that they were 'oviparous', or egg-laying.

Today the platypus is listed as Near Threatened globally. Threats include dams, drought, land clearing, pollution, foxes, dogs and drowning in enclosed yabby traps, banned in several states. To see one, visit a quiet creek at dawn or dusk, stay still and watch for ripples. Pick up fishing line and hair ties.

quiz.q: Which statement about monotremes is correct?
o: They are specialised animals with a long, separate evolutionary history
They are the primitive ancestors of all other mammals
There are about a dozen egg-laying mammals alive today
They are reptiles that grow fur
quiz.e: Monotremes are not primitive leftovers; they have evolved separately for over 160 million years.

quiz.q: How do monotreme babies get milk?
o: From nipples inside a pouch
Through pores in patches of belly skin
The mother regurgitates it for them
They do not drink milk at all
quiz.e: Monotremes have no nipples, so milk seeps through skin pores and the young lap it up.

quiz.q: How does a platypus find prey underwater?
o: By sight, using large eyes
By echolocation, using clicks
By smell, using sensitive nostrils
By sensing electric fields with its bill
quiz.e: Its bill detects the faint electric fields from prey muscles while its eyes, ears and nostrils are shut.

quiz.q: How does the short-beaked echidna feed?
o: It laps up ants and termites with a long, sticky tongue
It hunts fish with its spines
It filters plankton from creeks
It grinds plants with strong teeth
quiz.e: A long sticky tongue suits echidnas to a diet of ants and termites, and they have no teeth.

quiz.q: What helps protect platypuses near waterways?
o: Feeding them bread at dawn
Picking up line and ties that entangle them
Handling them to check their health
Building more dams along rivers
quiz.e: Rubbish, altered river flows and enclosed traps all threaten platypuses, so small actions matter.

LESSONS.push: Scientists once suspected the platypus was a hoax. Then a telegram arrived.

LESSONS.title: Australia's remarkable birds
LESSONS.hook: Nearly half the world's bird species descend from ancestors that sang in ancient Australia. The birds here are older, louder and cleverer than you might think.

sections.key: Songbirds, nearly half of all birds, first evolved in Australia and New Guinea.
sections.b:
Songbirds, including robins, finches, crows and sparrows, number roughly 5,000 species, close to half of all birds. Scientists long assumed they began in the Northern Hemisphere. DNA studies from the early 2000s showed the oldest songbird lineages, including lyrebirds, scrub-birds, bowerbirds and treecreepers, live in Australia and New Guinea. The strong consensus is that songbirds evolved here tens of millions of years ago, then spread worldwide. So a European blackbird singing in London carries an Australian inheritance.

The superb lyrebird takes song to an extreme. A male's song is largely near-perfect copies of kookaburras, whipbirds and rosellas, woven with his own calls as he displays his lacy tail. Some captive birds have copied camera shutters and machinery.

sections.key: Cockatoos and magpies show intelligence and culture, learning from and cooperating with each other.
sections.b:
Australia has more than 50 parrot species, including cockatoos, galahs, lorikeets and budgerigars. Cockatoos are exceptionally intelligent and long-lived: Cookie, a Major Mitchell's cockatoo, reached about 83 in a US zoo. In Sydney, sulphur-crested cockatoos learned to lift wheelie-bin lids. A 2021 study tracked the skill spreading across suburbs as birds learned by watching, a rare example of animal culture in a city. Residents respond with bricks and gadgets, and the birds keep testing them.

Australian magpies are closer to butcherbirds than to European magpies. They live in cooperative family groups and sing together to announce territory. In a 2022 study, magpies fitted with tracking harnesses were apparently helped out of them by others. Swooping happens in spring and only some males do it; calmly walk away.

sections.key: Emu fathers incubate the eggs, and cassowaries are vital seed-spreaders of the rainforest.
sections.b:
The emu is the world's second-tallest bird after the ostrich, up to about 1.9 metres. It can't fly but runs at around 50 kilometres per hour and swims well. The female lays large, dark green eggs, then often leaves. The male incubates them for about eight weeks, barely eating or drinking, then guards the striped chicks for months. The emu and the kangaroo appear on Australia's coat of arms.

The southern cassowary, Australia's heaviest bird, lives in far north Queensland rainforest, with a helmet-like casque and a dagger-like claw on each foot. It swallows fruit whole and passes the seeds intact, often far away, so some rainforest plants rely on it. The Australian population is endangered. Cassowaries are shy but can kick hard when cornered or fed. Never feed one.

sections.key: In 1932 soldiers failed to cull crop-raiding emus because they scattered and ran fast; bounties and fencing worked better.
sections.b:
In late 1932, a large number of emus, often estimated at around 20,000, moved onto wheat farms in Western Australia's Campion district. Farmers, many of them former soldiers, asked the federal government for help. Defence Minister George Pearce sent Major G.P.W. Meredith with a small group of soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition.

The emus scattered into small groups, ran fast and proved very hard to hit. After two attempts, the military withdrew. Meredith claimed 986 kills for 9,860 rounds fired, a figure historians treat cautiously. Later bounty schemes and better fencing did more to protect crops. The 'war' became a famous piece of Australian folklore.

sections.key: You can help Australia's birds by joining citizen science, planting natives and keeping cats indoors.
sections.b:
More than 800 bird species have been recorded in Australia, and a large share are found nowhere else. You don't need to travel to enjoy them: a local park, wetland or backyard can host dozens. Taking part in citizen science, such as BirdLife Australia's Aussie Backyard Bird Count each October, turns your observations into useful data.

To help birds, plant local native shrubs that provide food and shelter, offer a shallow bird bath with clean water and keep cats indoors, especially at night. Avoid feeding wild birds bread or mince, which can make them sick and create dependence. A pair of binoculars and a field guide app go a long way.

quiz.q: Where did songbirds originally evolve?
o: Northern Europe
South America
Australia and New Guinea
Africa
quiz.e: The oldest songbird lineages live in Australia and New Guinea, pointing to an origin there.

quiz.q: How did bin-opening spread among Sydney's cockatoos?
o: Birds learned it by watching others
Each bird worked it out alone
It is an inherited instinct
Residents taught the birds
quiz.e: Social learning spread the skill across suburbs, a rare case of animal culture in a city.

quiz.q: Why are cassowaries important to rainforests?
o: They eat invasive insects
They dig waterholes for others
They pollinate rainforest flowers
They spread seeds by eating fruit whole
quiz.e: Seeds pass through cassowaries intact and are deposited far away, so some plants depend on them.

quiz.q: Why did the military struggle in the 1932 Emu War?
o: The emus were too few to find
Emus scattered into small groups and ran fast
Farmers refused any military help
The soldiers had no firearms at all
quiz.e: The emus' speed and dispersal made them hard to hit, and fencing and bounties worked better.

quiz.q: Which action helps Australia's backyard birds?
o: Planting native shrubs and keeping cats in at night
Feeding them bread and mince every day
Letting pet cats roam freely at night
Removing bird baths from backyards
quiz.e: Native plants, clean water and indoor cats provide food and shelter without harm.

LESSONS.push: Where did the world's songbirds first evolve? Not where scientists once assumed.

LESSONS.title: Australia's reptiles, up close
LESSONS.hook: Australia is a reptile superpower, home to giant crocodiles, dinosaur-like lizards and some of the world's most venomous snakes. Here's how to appreciate them safely.

sections.key: Australia has more than 1,000 reptile species, mostly found nowhere else, and the dry interior suits them.
sections.b:
Australia has more than 1,000 described reptile species, one of the richest reptile faunas of any country, and new ones are still being named. Most are found nowhere else on Earth. Lizards dominate: skinks alone make up several hundred species, joined by geckos, dragons, legless lizards and monitors.

The dry interior is especially rich, because warm, sunny conditions suit animals that rely on outside heat to regulate body temperature. Reptiles also need far less energy than mammals or birds of the same size, so they cope with scarce food and water. Many are small, shy and active at night. Six of the world's seven sea turtle species occur in Australian waters, along with dozens of sea snake species.

sections.key: Australia's venomous snakes rarely kill, because most bites are avoided, treated or dry.
sections.b:
Most Australian land snakes are elapids, including taipans, brown snakes, tiger snakes and death adders. The inland taipan has the most toxic venom of any land snake in laboratory tests, yet it is shy, lives in remote inland Australia and has no recorded human deaths. Brown snakes cause the most deaths, largely because they are common near farms and towns.

Even so, Australia averages only around two snakebite deaths a year. Some bites are 'dry', delivering little or no venom, and effective antivenoms, fast ambulance services and good first aid mean nearly everyone who is bitten survives.

sections.key: Saltwater crocodiles recovered strongly under protection, and Australia has more goanna species than any other continent.
sections.b:
The saltwater crocodile is the world's largest living reptile. Big males commonly reach about five metres and around a tonne; females are much smaller. 'Salties' live in rivers, billabongs, estuaries and coastal waters across northern Australia and can travel long distances by sea. Hunting for skins reduced them to a fraction of their former numbers by the 1970s. After protection began in the early 1970s they recovered dramatically, and the Northern Territory now has around 100,000. Nest temperature helps decide whether hatchlings are male or female.

Goannas are monitor lizards. Australia has around 30 species, more than any other continent, from pygmy monitors shorter than a ruler to the perentie, which can exceed two metres. Many monitors seem to have venom glands, though their role in hunting is debated.

sections.key: Australian reptiles have clever defences, from bluffing frills to skin that drinks.
sections.b:
When threatened, the frill-necked lizard of northern Australia opens its mouth wide, hisses and flares its frill into a startling disc, looking far bigger than it is. If the bluff fails, it sprints away upright on its hind legs, often to the nearest tree. It appeared on the two-cent coin.

Other species have tricks of their own. The thorny devil, a spiky desert lizard, has tiny grooves between its scales that draw water from damp sand or dew towards its mouth by capillary action, so it can drink through its skin. The blue-tongue lizard flashes a bright blue tongue when threatened, and is a welcome garden visitor because it eats snails. The shingleback, a close relative, often returns to the same partner year after year.

sections.key: Give snakes and crocodiles space, and know the correct first aid for a snakebite.
sections.b:
Snakes bite in self-defence, often when someone tries to catch, move or kill one. Keep still, then back away slowly. Keep grass short, clear rubbish and control mice. In the bush, wear boots and long pants, and use a torch at night. For a snake indoors, call a licensed snake catcher; most native reptiles are protected.

For a suspected snakebite, call 000, keep the person still and calm, apply a pressure immobilisation bandage over the bite and up the whole limb, then splint it. Don't wash, cut or suck the bite, and don't use a tourniquet. In crocodile country, obey warning signs, never swim where crocodiles may live, stand well back from the water, don't clean fish near it, and camp well away; Queensland advises at least 50 metres.

quiz.q: Why are reptiles so well suited to Australia's dry interior?
o: They need large amounts of water
Sunny conditions suit animals that use outside heat
They are mostly active in winter
They store water in their tails
quiz.e: Reptiles use outside heat and need little energy, so they thrive where food and water are scarce.

quiz.q: Why do brown snakes cause the most snakebite deaths?
o: They have the most toxic venom of any snake
They are common near farms and towns
They are the largest elapids of all
They bite without any warning every time
quiz.e: Exposure matters more than toxicity: the inland taipan is more venomous but lives remotely and is shy.

quiz.q: What happened to saltwater crocodile numbers after protection in the 1970s?
o: They kept falling
They stayed the same
They disappeared from the Northern Territory
They recovered dramatically
quiz.e: Protection reversed the decline caused by hunting for skins.

quiz.q: What does a frill-necked lizard do when threatened?
o: Changes colour to blend in
Plays dead on the ground
Flares its frill and hisses
Sheds its tail
quiz.e: Bluffing by looking bigger is its first defence, with a sprint to a tree as the backup.

quiz.q: What first aid is advised for a suspected snakebite?
o: Cut the bite and suck out the venom
Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite
Wash the bite and let it bleed freely
Call 000 and bandage the bitten limb firmly
quiz.e: Keeping the person still and bandaging the whole limb slows venom spreading while help comes.

LESSONS.push: Australia's most toxic land snake has no recorded human deaths. Here's why.

LESSONS.title: How clever are animals?
LESSONS.hook: Crows that craft tools, dolphins with names, elephants that cooperate. Animal minds are far richer than we once assumed, and harder to measure.

sections.key: Intelligence is hard to compare across species, so tests need careful controls and fair design.
sections.b:
Comparing intelligence across species is hard. Each animal evolved to solve its own world's problems: a squirrel remembers thousands of buried nuts, a bat navigates by echoes, a bee learns which flowers pay off. Tests designed around human strengths can make other species look dull.

Scientists also learned caution from Clever Hans, a German horse in the early 1900s that seemed to do arithmetic. In 1907, psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed Hans was reading tiny, unconscious cues from his questioner. Today researchers use careful controls and look at abilities like problem-solving, memory, learning from others and understanding what other individuals know.

sections.key: Crows and chimpanzees make and use tools, showing that tool use is not uniquely human.
sections.b:
New Caledonian crows make tools in the wild, shaping hooked sticks and cutting stepped strips from pandanus leaves to extract grubs. In a famous 2002 Oxford experiment, a crow named Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a food basket from a tube. Crows also drop stones into water to reach floating food. American researchers who wore a mask while trapping crows found the birds scolded that mask for years, and taught other crows to do the same.

In 1960, Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees at Gombe strip leaves from twigs to fish termites from mounds, a shock when tool-making was seen as uniquely human. Chimpanzee communities have different traditions, which young animals learn over years, and orangutans and bonobos also use tools. Whether apes can learn human language is debated.

sections.key: Dolphins and elephants pass on knowledge and cooperate, which makes their societies cultural.
sections.b:
In Shark Bay, Western Australia, some bottlenose dolphins tear off marine sponges and wear them over their beaks while probing the seafloor for fish, protecting themselves from scrapes. Mothers pass 'sponging' mainly to their calves, especially daughters, which makes it a form of culture. Each dolphin also develops a signature whistle. Others copy it to call that individual, and the dolphin responds, so the whistles work much like names.

Elephant families are led by an older female, the matriarch, whose knowledge of water, dangers and routes can be vital in droughts. In Kenya, families with older matriarchs were better at telling familiar from unfamiliar calls and at reacting to male lion roars. In experiments, pairs of elephants learned to pull two ends of a rope together, and waited for a partner before pulling.

sections.key: Passing the mirror test suggests self-recognition, but failing proves little because the test is narrow.
sections.b:
In 1970, psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr developed the mirror test. An animal gets time with a mirror, then a coloured mark is placed where it can only see it in the reflection. If it uses the reflection to touch or inspect the mark, it may recognise the image as itself. Great apes passed, along with some bottlenose dolphins, an Asian elephant and Eurasian magpies. Humans usually pass at around 18 months to two years.

But the test relies on vision, so it may be unfair to animals that experience the world through smell or sound. Dogs usually fail, yet a 2017 study found they spent longer sniffing their own urine when its scent was altered. Some gorillas may avoid eye contact. In 2019 a cleaner wrasse apparently passed, sparking debate about what the test measures.

sections.key: Complex minds have evolved many times in very different bodies, which matters for how we treat animals.
sections.b:
Complex minds have evolved many times, in very different bodies. Birds' brains are wired differently from ours but can pack in large numbers of neurons, and octopuses, bees, parrots, rats and pigs all show impressive learning. In 2012, a group of scientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, stating that many animals possess the brain systems that support conscious experience.

You can see animal smarts yourself: watch local magpies, crows or cockatoos solve problems, or try puzzle feeders with a dog. Recognising animal minds has practical weight too, informing debates about farming, zoos, research and wildlife protection.

quiz.q: What did the Clever Hans case teach scientists?
o: Horses can do arithmetic
Animals cannot be tested
Careful controls must rule out unconscious cues
Larger brains always mean cleverer animals
quiz.e: Hans was reading his questioner's cues, so good experiments must rule out unintended signals.

quiz.q: What did Jane Goodall's chimpanzee observations challenge?
o: That only humans make and use tools
That apes live in social groups
That termites build large mounds
That tools can only be made with hands
quiz.e: Seeing chimpanzees shape twigs to fish for termites overturned the view that tool-making was uniquely human.

quiz.q: What is 'sponging' in Shark Bay dolphins?
o: A cleaning ritual between mates
A learned habit of wearing sponges to forage
Eating sponges for nutrients
Hiding from predators in sponge beds
quiz.e: Learned and passed between generations, sponging is an example of animal culture.

quiz.q: Why can failing the mirror test be misleading?
o: Mirrors frighten all animals equally
Only humans can see their reflections
The mark is always visible without a mirror
It relies on vision, and animals may ignore the mark
quiz.e: Passing suggests something interesting, but failing proves little because the test is narrow.

quiz.q: What does the spread of complex minds across species suggest?
o: Only primates can learn complex tasks
Intelligence evolved once and was inherited
Complex minds evolved many times, in different bodies
Brain size alone predicts intelligence
quiz.e: Birds, octopuses and mammals all show clever learning despite very different brains.

LESSONS.push: A horse once seemed to do arithmetic. What it was really doing changed science.

LESSONS.title: Senses beyond our own
LESSONS.hook: Bats see with sound, turtles read the Earth's magnetism and sharks feel your heartbeat's electricity. Every animal lives in a different sensory world.

sections.key: Each animal senses only a slice of reality, its umwelt, and ours is just one of many.
sections.b:
In the early 1900s, the German biologist Jakob von Uexküll used the word umwelt, meaning 'surrounding world', for the slice of reality each animal can sense. A tick responds to warmth and the smell of butyric acid in mammal sweat; a bee lives in a world of ultraviolet patterns; a dog in a world of scent trails. Our own umwelt is narrow. We can't hear the ultrasonic calls of bats, see ultraviolet light or feel electric fields.

Understanding other animals' senses helps explain their behaviour, and has inspired technologies from sonar to medical ultrasound. It is also a reminder that our view of reality is just one of many.

sections.key: Bats read echoes and dogs read scent, each with senses far beyond ours.
sections.b:
Insect-hunting bats make rapid, mostly ultrasonic calls and listen to the echoes, judging the distance, size, direction and texture of objects well enough to snatch insects in total darkness. Dolphins echolocate with clicks, and some blind people learn to navigate with tongue clicks. Australia's large flying foxes mostly don't echolocate; they use good eyesight and smell.

A dog's nose is another marvel: an estimated 200 to 300 million scent receptors, against roughly five or six million in humans, with much of the brain devoted to smell. Sniffed air goes to a special smelling region, and exhaled air leaves through side slits so it doesn't blow away incoming scent. Dogs smell many thousands of times better than we do. Biosecurity detector dogs sniff out undeclared food and plants at airports.

sections.key: Some animals sense Earth's magnetism and sharks sense weak electric fields to navigate and find hidden prey.
sections.b:
Many animals detect Earth's magnetic field to navigate, including migratory birds, sea turtles, salmon and some insects. Caged European robins oriented in their migratory direction, and changed it when the field was altered. Young sea turtles appear to learn their home coastline's magnetic signature and use it years later to return to nest. How they sense it is debated: light-sensitive cryptochrome proteins in birds' eyes, tiny iron particles, or both.

Sharks and rays have jelly-filled pores on their snouts, the ampullae of Lorenzini, that detect extremely weak electric fields, such as those from the muscles and heartbeat of a fish buried in sand. A hammerhead's wide head spreads these sensors to sweep the seabed. Popular claims that sharks smell one drop of blood from kilometres away are exaggerated.

sections.key: Many animals see ultraviolet, and having more colour receptors does not guarantee better colour vision.
sections.b:
Our lens blocks most ultraviolet light, but bees, butterflies, many birds, fish and reptiles see it. To a bee, flowers that look plain to us carry bold UV patterns called nectar guides that point to pollen and nectar. Many birds have four types of colour receptor rather than our three. Reindeer see some UV, which may help them spot lichen and predators against Arctic snow.

Mantis shrimp are often said to see unimaginable rainbows, with up to 16 photoreceptor types, around 12 for colour. But a 2014 study led by University of Queensland researchers found they are worse than humans at telling similar colours apart. They may recognise colours quickly and directly, like a barcode scanner. They can also see circularly polarised light, which is extremely rare.

sections.key: Several popular ideas about animal senses are wrong, so ask what an animal might be sensing.
sections.b:
Goldfish don't have three-second memories; they can learn and remember tasks for months. Bulls don't charge at red; they are colour-blind to red and react to the movement of the matador's cape. Other senses are real but under-appreciated: pythons and pit vipers detect body heat with infrared-sensing pits, and many birds hear infrasound far below our range.

The practical lesson: when an animal's behaviour seems strange, ask what it might be sensing. Your dog may be reading a scent story, and a bird may be seeing colours on a flower that you can't.

quiz.q: What does the word 'umwelt' describe?
o: An animal's habitat
An animal's diet
The slice of reality an animal can sense
A migration route
quiz.e: Each species senses only part of the world, and ours is just one version.

quiz.q: Which statement about Australian flying foxes is true?
o: They are blind
They use echolocation to find fruit
They sense magnetic fields to find nectar
They mostly rely on sight and smell
quiz.e: Bats are not blind, and large flying foxes find food mainly with eyesight and smell.

quiz.q: How do sharks and rays detect a fish buried in sand?
o: They sense weak electric fields from its muscles and heart
They smell a single drop of its blood from kilometres away
They listen for echoes bouncing off its body
They see an ultraviolet glow from its skin
quiz.e: Jelly-filled pores on the snout detect extremely weak electric fields.

quiz.q: What did a 2014 study find about mantis shrimp colour vision?
o: They see millions more colours than we do
They are completely colour-blind to everything
They are worse than humans at telling similar colours
They see only in ultraviolet light
quiz.e: More receptor types did not make their colour discrimination better; they seem to use a different system.

quiz.q: Why do bulls charge at a matador's cape?
o: They react to its movement, being colour-blind to red
They see the colour red as a threat
They smell the dye in the fabric
They hear the cape rustling in the wind
quiz.e: Bulls are colour-blind to red, so movement, not colour, provokes them.

LESSONS.push: Mantis shrimp have 16 photoreceptor types. So why are they worse at telling colours apart?

LESSONS.title: The great animal migrations
LESSONS.hook: A young bird flies from Alaska to Tasmania without landing. Moths navigate by the stars. Migration is one of nature's most astonishing feats.

sections.key: Animals migrate to reach resources that come and go, accepting a costly, dangerous journey for abundant food or safe breeding.
sections.b:
Migration is a regular, usually seasonal movement between places, often a round trip repeated every year. Animals migrate to take advantage of resources that come and go: summer insects in the Arctic, fresh grass after rain, safe breeding beaches or warmer winter refuges. It is a gamble, because the journey is costly and dangerous, but the reward is abundant food or safer places to raise young.

The Arctic tern holds the distance record. It flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, tracked at roughly 70,000 kilometres or more, and sees more daylight than any other animal.

sections.key: The bar-tailed godwit flew nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania, and shorebirds on this route depend on protected stopovers.
sections.b:
In October 2022, a five-month-old bar-tailed godwit tagged in Alaska flew about 13,500 kilometres to Tasmania in around 11 days, without landing to feed, drink or rest. It was its first journey, and the longest nonstop bird flight recorded. Beforehand, godwits eat until fat is a large share of their weight, while organs they won't need, such as parts of the gut, shrink.

Millions of shorebirds travel the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, breeding in Siberia and Alaska and spending the rest of the year on Australian and New Zealand coasts, such as Roebuck Bay and Moreton Bay. They refuel on the Yellow Sea's tidal mudflats, where large areas have been lost to reclamation. Several species have declined sharply, and the far eastern curlew, the world's largest shorebird, was listed as critically endangered in Australia in 2015.

sections.key: Australia hosts mass migrations of Christmas Island red crabs and bogong moths, both triggered by seasons and guided by nature.
sections.b:
On Christmas Island, tens of millions of red land crabs live in the forest. With the first heavy rains of the wet season, usually October to December, they march to the coast to breed. Females release eggs into the sea at high tide before dawn, near the last quarter moon. Rangers close roads and build crab bridges; invasive yellow crazy ants are a serious threat.

Each spring, billions of bogong moths fly up to about 1,000 kilometres from the plains of southern Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria to cool caves in the Australian Alps, returning in autumn. Research published in 2025 showed they use the starry sky, including the Milky Way, as a compass, plus magnetism. Long a food for Aboriginal peoples, they crashed in the 2017 to 2019 drought and are now endangered.

sections.key: Monarch butterflies migrate across several generations, while wildebeest follow the rains in a huge loop.
sections.b:
In North America, eastern monarch butterflies fly up to around 4,000 kilometres to overwinter in fir forests in the mountains of central Mexico. No single butterfly makes the whole round trip. The migrating 'super generation' lives for many months, while summer generations carrying the journey north live only a few weeks each. Monarchs navigate by a sun compass, correcting for the sun's movement with an internal clock in their antennae. They reached Australia in the 1870s, where they are called wanderers.

In East Africa, more than a million wildebeest, with zebras and gazelles, loop through the Serengeti and Masai Mara following the rains. Hundreds of thousands of calves are born within a few weeks, which overwhelms predators. Mara River crossings usually happen from around July to October. The herds feed lions, hyenas and crocodiles, and fertilise the grasslands.

sections.key: Migrants navigate using the sun, stars, magnetism, landmarks and smell, and light pollution and habitat loss threaten them.
sections.b:
Migrating animals use a toolkit of cues. Many birds use a sun compass by day and star patterns by night; in the 1960s, planetarium experiments showed that indigo buntings learn to orient using the stars around the pole. Magnetic sensing, landmarks such as coastlines and mountains, and smell also play roles: salmon return to home streams partly by scent. Many young birds make their first migration alone, guided by inherited directions.
