If cash runs out in between, it may be unable to pay its debts on time, even though the order is profitable. Growth that outpaces available cash is sometimes called overtrading.

The length of this loop is the cash conversion cycle: cash goes into stock or labour, becomes a sale, then waits to be paid. A cafe paid at the counter has a short cycle. A builder who invoices weeks later needs far more cash to keep going. Many small business advisers cite cash flow as a common reason small businesses struggle or close.

sections.key: Invoice promptly, follow up late payers, and set aside tax so cash stays in the business.
sections.b:
Late payments are a common drain. Invoice as soon as work is done, not at month's end. Make invoices clear: what was delivered, the amount, the due date and easy payment options. If you're registered for GST, invoices must meet tax invoice requirements, which the ATO explains. Consider shorter terms, deposits for large jobs or progress payments, and follow up politely but promptly.

Outflows matter too. Pay suppliers on time, but there's usually no need to pay weeks early. Avoid tying up cash in excess stock. The classic trap is tax: GST you collect isn't your money, and neither is income tax you'll owe later. Many owners move a set percentage of each payment into a separate account.

sections.key: Runway is how many months your cash will last, and a rolling forecast shows shortfalls before they arrive.
sections.b:
Runway is vital for new businesses not yet profitable. Divide your cash by your monthly net cash outflow, or burn rate. With $60,000 in the bank and $10,000 more going out than coming in each month, you have about six months. Knowing this early gives you time to cut costs, raise prices, chase sales or find funding.

A forecast can be a simple spreadsheet. List cash coming in, based on when customers will realistically pay, not when you invoice. List cash going out: wages, rent, suppliers, loans, super, GST and tax. The difference gives a running balance. Many businesses keep a rolling 13-week forecast, updated weekly. The goal isn't perfect prediction; it's spotting dips in time to act.

sections.key: Check your cash position weekly, keep a buffer and seek professional advice early when things look tight.
sections.b:
A few habits make a big difference. Look at your bank balance and unpaid invoices every week. Build a cash buffer, with many advisers suggesting enough to cover at least a few months of fixed costs. Keep business and personal money in separate accounts. Use accounting software to track who owes you and what you owe.

If cash is getting tight, act early. Talk to your accountant, your bank and, if needed, the ATO about payment arrangements. This is general information only; a registered tax agent or accountant can advise on your situation.

quiz.q: How can a business record a profit yet have no cash?
o: Profit is recorded when a sale is made, but payment may arrive months later
Profit only counts once the bank balance rises
Cash is always larger than profit under accounting rules
Expenses are only recorded after customers pay
quiz.e: Profit is booked at the sale, while cash arrives when the customer actually pays.

quiz.q: Why might a manufacturer with a profitable big order still fail?
o: Big orders are never profitable
Customers always cancel large orders
It must fund materials and staff for months before being paid
The tax office takes the order's value
quiz.e: Growth can outrun available cash, so a profitable order can still leave a business unable to pay bills.

quiz.q: What is a sensible way to handle tax and GST?
o: Spend GST collected, then pay it from later sales
Move a set percentage of each payment into a separate account
Wait until the end of the year to think about it
Ask customers to pay it directly to the ATO
quiz.e: GST collected and income tax owed aren't your money, so setting it aside avoids a nasty surprise.

quiz.q: What does a runway figure tell you?
o: How much profit you will make next year
How long invoices take to be paid
How many months your cash lasts at the current spending rate
How much stock you should hold
quiz.e: Runway is cash divided by monthly net outflow, giving you time to act before money runs out.

quiz.q: What should you do if cash is getting tight?
o: Act early and speak to your accountant, bank or the ATO
Wait and see whether sales improve
Stop checking balances to reduce stress
Use personal savings without telling anyone
quiz.e: Early action and professional advice leave far more options than waiting until cash is nearly gone.

LESSONS.push: A business can be profitable on paper and still go broke. How does that happen?

LESSONS.title: Starting a business in Australia
LESSONS.hook: ABN, ASIC, GST, sole trader or company: the paperwork sounds daunting, but the basic steps are simpler than most people think.

sections.key: The ATO looks at intention to profit, regularity and business-like behaviour to decide whether you're in business.
sections.b:
Not every side activity is a business. The ATO considers whether you intend to make a profit, whether the activity is repeated and regular, whether it's organised in a business-like way, and its size. Selling a few of your own paintings each year may be a hobby; producing them regularly for sale, marketing them and keeping records looks like a business.

The distinction matters for tax: business income is generally taxable and business expenses may be deductible. The ATO and business.gov.au both have guidance to help you decide.

sections.key: Sole traders and partners are generally personally liable for business debts, while companies offer limited liability with more obligations.
sections.b:
Your structure affects your tax, legal duties and personal risk. A sole trader is the simplest and cheapest: you and the business are legally the same, you use your own tax file number, and profit is taxed at personal rates. A partnership is two or more people sharing profits. A company is a separate legal entity. Trusts are often used for family businesses. You can change structure later, though it may cost money.

The biggest difference is liability. A sole trader is personally responsible for all business debts, so a house and savings could be at risk. Partners are generally liable for the whole partnership's debts. A company offers limited liability, though directors can still be personally liable in some situations, such as trading while insolvent. Companies cost more and need ASIC registration.

sections.key: An ABN is a free 11-digit number, and trading under any name other than your own generally means registering it with ASIC.
sections.b:
Most people starting out apply for an Australian Business Number, an 11-digit number that identifies your business. Applying is free through the Australian Business Register, reachable via business.gov.au. Beware of third-party sites charging fees for the same thing. You need an ABN to register a business name and for GST. Without one, businesses paying you may have to withhold tax at the top marginal rate.

If you trade as Sarah Nguyen, you needn't register a name. If you trade as 'Northside Dog Walking', you generally must register it with ASIC, for one or three years, for a fee. It doesn't give you exclusive ownership; a trade mark through IP Australia does. Check the name and a matching domain are available first.

sections.key: You must register for GST once your GST turnover reaches $75,000 a year, and many choose to register earlier.
sections.b:
Goods and services tax is a 10% tax on most goods and services in Australia. You must register when your annual GST turnover reaches $75,000, or $150,000 for non-profit organisations. Taxi and ride-sourcing drivers must register regardless of turnover.

Once registered, you generally add GST to your prices, lodge a business activity statement, or BAS, and pass the GST you collect to the ATO, minus GST credits on your business purchases. You can register voluntarily below the threshold; whether that's worthwhile depends on your customers and costs.

sections.key: Check which licences and insurance you need, keep records for five years, and get professional advice on key decisions.
sections.b:
Depending on your industry and location, you may need licences or permits, from food handling to building work. ABLIS, on business.gov.au, helps you find them. If you employ staff, workers' compensation insurance is compulsory and you must pay super. Public liability and professional indemnity insurance aren't always required, but are common. The ATO generally requires business records to be kept for five years.

A sensible order: check you're really in business, choose a structure, get an ABN, register a name if needed, consider GST. Open a separate business bank account from day one and set up simple accounting software. Business.gov.au is a free, reliable starting point. This is general information only: rules change, so talk to a registered tax agent, accountant or lawyer.

quiz.q: Which activity is most likely to look like a business rather than a hobby?
o: Selling a few paintings a year with no records
Painting occasionally and giving the works away
Regularly producing paintings for sale, marketing them and keeping records
Painting only when you feel inspired
quiz.e: Intent to profit, regular activity and business-like organisation point towards a business.

quiz.q: What is the main personal risk of being a sole trader?
o: You must pay a higher rate of GST
You cannot change structure later
You need an ASIC registration for your own name
You are personally responsible for all business debts
quiz.e: A sole trader and the business are legally the same, so personal assets may be at risk.

quiz.q: When do you generally need to register a business name?
o: When you trade under a name other than your own
Whenever you earn any income
Only if your turnover exceeds $75,000
Never, if you have an ABN
quiz.e: Trading as 'Northside Dog Walking' needs a registered name, while trading under your own name does not.

quiz.q: When must a business register for GST?
o: Once it has any employees
As soon as it gets an ABN
When annual GST turnover reaches $75,000
Only when it becomes a company
quiz.e: The standard threshold is $75,000 a year, though you can register voluntarily earlier.

quiz.q: Which step is recommended from day one?
o: Keeping receipts in one personal account
Opening a separate business bank account
Waiting a year before setting up accounting
Skipping insurance until you have staff
quiz.e: Separating business finances makes records, tax and decisions much simpler.

LESSONS.push: ABN, ASIC, GST: what you actually need to start a business here, and what you don't.

LESSONS.title: Lessons from startup wins and flops
LESSONS.hook: Canva was rejected by investors again and again. Juicero raised over $100 million and vanished. What separates them is rarely luck alone.

sections.key: Canva and Atlassian solved real, widespread problems, and Atlassian grew by letting a good product sell itself.
sections.b:
In 2007, Melanie Perkins, then a Perth university student, noticed how hard design software was to learn. With Cliff Obrecht she started Fusion Books, an online tool for school yearbooks, run from her mother's lounge room. Pitching a broader platform, Perkins has said she was rejected by around 100 investors. With Cameron Adams, she launched Canva in 2013. It is now one of the world's most valuable private tech companies.

Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar met at UNSW and founded Atlassian in Sydney in 2002, reportedly with about $10,000 on a credit card. Their early product Jira helped software teams track bugs. They grew for years without a traditional sales team, relying on transparent prices and word of mouth. Atlassian listed on Nasdaq in 2015.

sections.key: Product-market fit means being in a good market with a product that market strongly wants.
sections.b:
Investor Marc Andreessen popularised the term in a 2007 essay, describing it as being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market. You can often feel it: customers use the product eagerly, tell others and complain loudly when it breaks.

Growth marketer Sean Ellis proposed a simple test. Ask users how they'd feel if they could no longer use your product. If around 40% or more say 'very disappointed', you may be close. Before fit, focus on learning; after it, on growing.

sections.key: Juicero and Quibi spent heavily before proving demand, and money and famous names cannot replace customers who want the product.
sections.b:
Juicero launched in 2016 with a Wi-Fi-connected juice press that initially sold for about US$700, later cut to about US$400, and used proprietary juice packs. It raised roughly US$120 million. In 2017, Bloomberg reporters showed the packs could be squeezed by hand to produce much the same juice. It shut down that year. A sophisticated solution must deliver real value beyond the simplest alternative.

Quibi, a phone streaming service led by Jeffrey Katzenberg, raised about US$1.75 billion, launched in April 2020 and shut down about six months later. Observers cited COVID-19 lockdowns, hard-to-share clips and free rivals like YouTube and TikTok. Money can't substitute for testing whether customers want the product.

sections.key: Failed startups often cite no market need and running out of cash, and running out of money is usually a symptom.
sections.b:
Research firm CB Insights has analysed post-mortems written by founders of failed startups. In its widely cited reports, 'no market need' and 'ran out of cash' rank among the most common reasons, alongside being outcompeted, pricing problems and team issues. The reasons are self-reported, so the data isn't perfect.

Still, the pattern fits experience. Building something people don't need is the most common and most avoidable mistake. Running out of money is often the final symptom rather than the root cause.

sections.key: Test demand early, watch your cash, follow customer behaviour and be willing to change direction when evidence says so.
sections.b:
A pivot is a structured change of strategy that keeps what you've learned. Slack emerged from a company building an online game called Glitch; the game failed, but its internal chat tool became the product. Instagram began as Burbn, a check-in app, before its founders focused on the photo-sharing people actually used. YouTube's founders have said it was first pitched as a video dating site.

The hard judgement is when to persist and when to pivot. Let customer behaviour, not pride or sunk costs, decide. Talk to customers early, launch small, and watch your runway. Remember survivorship bias: for every famous success, many similar companies failed. Success stories show what's possible, not what's guaranteed.

quiz.q: What did Atlassian do unusually in its early years?
o: Spent heavily on a large sales team
Grew for years without a traditional sales team
Sold only to Australian customers
Gave its software away to avoid competitors
quiz.e: Transparent prices and word of mouth among developers let the product sell itself.

quiz.q: What does the Sean Ellis test measure?
o: How many users would be 'very disappointed' to lose your product
How many investors have rejected your pitch
How quickly your sales are growing
How cheaply you can make the product
quiz.e: If around 40% or more of users would be very disappointed, you may be near product-market fit.

quiz.q: What did Juicero's story show about expensive solutions?
o: Hardware start-ups can never succeed
Investors will always back a good idea
Customers prefer products that connect to Wi-Fi
A sophisticated product must beat the simplest alternative
quiz.e: When the packs could be squeezed by hand, customers saw the product added little real value.

quiz.q: Why is 'ran out of cash' often not the true root cause of failure?
o: It is usually a symptom of building something people don't need
Cash problems are unrelated to business results
Founders rarely mention money in post-mortems
Banks refuse to lend to start-ups
quiz.e: Without real demand, revenue never arrives, so running out of money is often the final symptom.

quiz.q: What should decide whether to pivot or persist?
o: The founder's confidence in the original idea
How much money has already been spent
Evidence from customer behaviour
The advice of competitors
quiz.e: Evidence from how customers actually behave should outweigh pride and sunk costs.

LESSONS.push: One start-up was rejected around 100 times. Another raised $120 million for a juicer.

LESSONS.title: What code really is
LESSONS.hook: Every app on your phone is just a very long, very precise recipe. Once you see the five ingredients, software stops being magic.

sections.key: Code is a set of precise instructions that a computer follows exactly, step by step.
sections.b:
At its heart, code is a list of instructions written for a computer. Think of a recipe: preheat the oven, mix the flour and eggs, bake for 30 minutes. A computer follows instructions the same way, one step at a time, in order.

The difference is that a computer has no common sense. A human cook will notice if the recipe forgets to say 'crack the eggs first'. A computer will happily throw the eggs in whole. Programming is the craft of writing instructions so clear that something with zero judgement can still get them right.

sections.key: Ada Lovelace published what is often called the first computer program in 1843, long before electronic computers.
sections.b:
The idea is older than electronic computers. In 1843 the English mathematician Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer that was designed but never completed. Her notes included a step-by-step method for calculating a sequence called the Bernoulli numbers, often described as the first published computer program.

She also saw that such a machine might one day work with music or symbols, not just numbers. Today a modern car runs on millions of lines of code, but each line is still an instruction in the spirit of hers.

sections.key: Variables hold values the program can change, and conditions let it choose what to do using 'if this, then that'.
sections.b:
Programs remember things with variables. Picture a pantry of labelled jars: 'sugar', 'flour', 'eggs left'. A variable is a labelled jar holding a value, such as a number, a word or a list. A banking app might keep a variable called balance holding 250. Buy a coffee and the program takes the value out, subtracts 5, and puts 245 back in the same jar.

Recipes also contain decisions: if the cake is still wet in the middle, bake it five more minutes. Code does this with conditions, usually written with 'if'. A thermostat program might say: if the temperature is above 24 degrees, turn on cooling; otherwise, leave it off. Rejecting a wrong password is a condition at work.

sections.key: Loops repeat instructions, and functions are named, reusable blocks of instructions called whenever needed.
sections.b:
Nobody writes a recipe that says 'stir, stir, stir' 200 times; they write 'stir until smooth'. That is a loop: repeating a block of steps a set number of times, or until a condition is met. A music app loops through every song in a playlist. An email program loops through thousands of messages looking for a search word. Computers never get bored or tired.

Many recipe books have a basic white sauce on one page, and other recipes just say 'make one quantity of white sauce'. In code that is a function: a named bundle of instructions you can call whenever needed, taking inputs and handing back a result. A shopping app might have one that takes a price and a postcode and returns the delivery cost. Write it once, test it once, use it everywhere.

sections.key: Real programs combine variables, conditions, loops and functions in layers, and free tools like Scratch let anyone try them.
sections.b:
These few building blocks make everything from calculators to video games. In a step counter, a variable stores today's steps. A loop keeps checking the motion sensor. A condition asks whether the phone moved in a walking pattern, and if so adds one. A function turns steps into kilometres, and another condition checks whether you've hit your goal. Large programs work the same way, organised into layers so teams can each work on one part.

To try it yourself, Scratch is a free tool from MIT where you snap together coloured blocks labelled 'repeat', 'if' and 'set variable' and watch a cartoon character obey. Next time you use an app, try spotting where it remembers, decides or repeats.

quiz.q: Why must programming instructions be so precise?
o: Computers are too slow to handle general instructions
A computer has no common sense and does exactly what it is told
Programming languages only accept numbers
Computers fix mistakes in instructions automatically
quiz.e: A computer has no judgement, so unclear instructions produce wrong results.

quiz.q: Why is Ada Lovelace's 1843 work significant?
o: She built the first electronic computer
She completed Babbage's Analytical Engine
She published a step-by-step method for a machine, often called the first program
She invented the Bernoulli numbers
quiz.e: Her notes set out a step-by-step method for a machine to calculate, decades before electronic computers.

quiz.q: What does a variable do in a program?
o: Repeats a set of steps until finished
Holds a named value that the program can read and change
Chooses between two possible actions
Translates code for the computer
quiz.e: A variable is a labelled jar: the label stays the same while the contents change.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a function?
o: It makes a program run forever
It lets you write a set of steps once and reuse it
It removes the need for any variables
It decides whether a password is wrong
quiz.e: A function is a named, reusable block, so you write and test it once and use it everywhere.

quiz.q: How do large programs handle many pieces of code?
o: They avoid using loops or conditions
They are written as one long list of steps
They organise the same building blocks into layers
They use entirely different ideas from small programs
quiz.e: Large programs use the same few building blocks, organised in layers so teams can work on separate parts.

LESSONS.push: Every app is a recipe followed by something with zero common sense. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: Algorithms, explained
LESSONS.hook: The word sounds futuristic, but it comes from a scholar in 9th-century Baghdad, and you use algorithms every time you look up a word or take the fastest route home.

sections.key: An algorithm is a clear, step-by-step method for solving a problem, and the idea exists apart from any code.
sections.b:
An algorithm is a precise method for getting something done. School long division is one: follow the steps and you get the answer every time. So is the way you find a name in a phone book. Code is how an algorithm is written for a computer, but the algorithm is the idea behind it. A good one must be unambiguous, must finish, and must produce the right result.

The word comes from al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician working in Baghdad in the 9th century, whose books on calculation spread through Europe in Latin. Around 300 BC, Euclid described a method for finding the largest number dividing two others. It is still taught and used inside some encryption that protects online banking.

sections.key: Binary search halves the possibilities each step, and a smarter sorting method can be tens of thousands of times faster.
sections.b:
Guess a number from 1 to 100, told 'higher' or 'lower' each time. Guessing 1, 2, 3 could take 100 tries. Guessing 50, then 25 or 75, halves the possibilities each time. This is binary search, and it always finds the number within seven guesses. Among a million sorted items, it needs only about 20 steps. It only works if items are in order, so computers spend much effort sorting.

Bubble sort swaps neighbouring items that are out of order, repeating until none remain. It works but is painfully slow on big lists. Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, then merges them, like combining two sorted piles of exam papers. On a million items, it can be tens of thousands of times faster.

sections.key: Efficiency is how an algorithm's work grows as data grows, so the right algorithm often beats a faster computer.
sections.b:
Computer scientists care less about speed on ten items than about how the work grows as the data grows. Some algorithms double their work when the data doubles. Others quadruple it, and some grow so explosively that even the fastest supercomputer could not finish before the sun burns out.

This is why choosing the right algorithm often matters more than buying a faster computer. A clever method on an old laptop can beat a clumsy method in a data centre. Programmers describe this growth with a notation called 'Big O'.

sections.key: Map apps use shortest-path algorithms, while social feeds use ranking algorithms that predict what will keep you engaged.
sections.b:
When a map app plots the fastest drive from Parramatta to Bondi, it solves a shortest-path problem. Roads become a network of points and connections, each with a travel time. In 1956 the Dutch computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra devised a method for this, reportedly in about 20 minutes at a cafe in Amsterdam. Modern apps use faster descendants, plus live traffic from other phones, to reroute you around a crash.

By 'the algorithm', people usually mean ranking systems on social media, video and shopping sites. They use signals such as what you watched, liked, shared or lingered on to predict what you'll engage with. Early Google search used PageRank, which treated links as votes of importance. Because feeds optimise for engagement, they can favour content that provokes strong emotions, which is a real and debated concern.

sections.key: You can shape feed algorithms with your choices, and algorithmic thinking helps with everyday problems.
sections.b:
Knowing how algorithms work gives you some control. Feed algorithms learn from your behaviour, so deliberately following, muting and choosing 'not interested' changes what you see. Pausing on outrage teaches the system to show more of it.

Algorithmic thinking also helps offline. Looking for a lost item? Search systematically, room by room, rather than randomly. Packing a car boot? Big items first is a simple algorithm that usually works well. Breaking a messy task into clear, repeatable steps is exactly what programmers do, and it works just as well in a kitchen or an office.

quiz.q: What three things must a good algorithm do?
o: Be fast, be short and use no memory
Be unambiguous, finish eventually and give the right result
Use code, use loops and use a database
Run on any computer, in any year, at any speed
quiz.e: An algorithm must be clear, must end, and must be correct, whatever language it is written in.

quiz.q: Why does binary search find an item so quickly?
o: It checks every item in order
It guesses at random until it succeeds
It halves the remaining possibilities with each step
It works on lists in any order
quiz.e: Halving the possibilities each step means about 20 steps for a million sorted items.

quiz.q: Why can choosing the right algorithm beat buying a faster computer?
o: Faster computers cannot run clever methods
Algorithms are free to run on any machine
Modern computers cannot sort lists
How the work grows with the data can outweigh raw hardware speed
quiz.e: A clever method on an old laptop can beat a clumsy method in a data centre.

quiz.q: Why can engagement-optimising feeds be a concern?
o: They can favour content that provokes strong emotions
They delete posts that people like
They only show content from friends
They stop working when traffic is heavy
quiz.e: Optimising for engagement can promote emotionally charged content, which is a real and debated concern.

quiz.q: How can you influence what a feed shows you?
o: Watching more of the content you dislike
Deliberately following, muting and choosing 'not interested'
Pausing on outrage to understand it
Nothing, because feeds ignore your choices
quiz.e: Feeds learn from your behaviour, so your deliberate choices change what they show.

LESSONS.push: A word from 9th-century Baghdad now decides what lands in your feed. How?

LESSONS.title: Why there are so many programming languages
LESSONS.hook: There are thousands of programming languages, from Python to COBOL. Here's why, and which ones actually run your world.

sections.key: Programming languages let people write instructions in readable form that are translated into the machine code a processor runs.
sections.b:
A processor only understands machine code: long strings of ones and zeros representing basic operations such as adding two numbers. Writing that by hand is slow and error-prone. Programming languages sit in the middle. They let people write with words and symbols closer to human thinking, then translate them into machine code.

The earliest programmers in the 1940s worked almost directly with machine instructions. FORTRAN, released by IBM in 1957 and led by John Backus, was one of the first widely used high-level languages, built for heavy maths. COBOL followed in 1959 for business record-keeping, influenced by Grace Hopper. It still runs many banks, insurers and agencies, because rewriting decades of reliable code is risky and expensive.

sections.key: Languages differ because they make different trade-offs between speed, safety, ease and purpose.
sections.b:
Thousands of languages have been created, though only a few dozen are in wide everyday use. Why not one for everything? For the same reason there isn't one tool in a shed. A hammer and a screwdriver both help you build, but suit different jobs.

Some languages are designed for raw speed, giving close control over memory and hardware. Others prioritise safety, catching mistakes before the program runs. Some are easy to read and quick to write. Others specialise in one domain, such as databases or statistics. Every design choice is a trade-off, and new languages appear when people want a different balance.

sections.key: Compiled languages are translated ahead of time, interpreted languages as the program runs, and many mix both.
sections.b:
There are two broad ways to turn code into something a computer can run. A compiled language, such as C, C++, Rust or Go, is translated in full before it runs, like translating a whole book before publishing. The result usually runs very fast.

An interpreted language, like Python, is translated while the program runs, more like a live interpreter at a meeting. That makes experimenting easier, but it often runs more slowly. In practice the line has blurred, and many modern languages, including JavaScript in web browsers, use clever mixtures of both.

sections.key: Python suits data and AI, JavaScript runs the web, Swift and Kotlin build phone apps, SQL queries databases, and C underpins operating systems.
sections.b:
Python, created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991, is named after Monty Python, not the snake. It has readable code and is widely used in data analysis, science, automation and AI. JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995, famously in about ten days. Despite the name, it has little to do with Java; the name was largely marketing. It runs in every major browser.

Swift, from Apple in 2014, builds iPhone and Mac apps. Kotlin is Google's preferred language for Android, alongside the older Java, also common in large business systems. SQL asks questions of databases, such as 'show all customers in Victoria'. C, created in the early 1970s at Bell Labs, remains the foundation of operating systems like Linux. C# suits business software and Unity games.

sections.key: Languages share the same core ideas, so pick one beginner-friendly language and build small projects you care about.
sections.b:
Languages are more alike than they look. Nearly all have variables, conditions, loops and functions. Once you understand these in one, a second is mostly new spelling and grammar, like learning Spanish after Italian. Employers generally care more about problem-solving than any single language. The hard part isn't memorising commands but breaking problems into small, precise steps.

If you want to try coding, pick one language and stick with it. Python is a common first choice because it reads almost like English. For websites, start with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Free courses are plentiful, and Australian public libraries often run coding sessions. Build small things you care about, like a budget calculator. Expect to feel stuck often; that is simply what programming feels like.

quiz.q: Why do programming languages exist?
o: Processors can only run English text
They let people write readable instructions that get translated to machine code
They make every program run at the same speed
They remove the need for a processor
quiz.e: Languages sit between human thinking and the machine code a processor actually understands.

quiz.q: Why are there so many programming languages?
o: Each makes different trade-offs between speed, safety, ease and purpose
Old languages stop working after a few years
Governments require each country to have its own
Nobody has tried to improve the early ones
quiz.e: Every design choice is a trade-off, and new languages appear when people want a different balance.

quiz.q: How does an interpreted language differ from a compiled one?
o: It is translated in full before it ever runs
It is translated as the program runs
It never gets turned into machine instructions
It can only be used for websites
quiz.e: Interpreted languages are translated as they run, which eases experimenting but often means slower speed.

quiz.q: Which language is the main one that runs in web browsers?
o: Swift
SQL
C
JavaScript
quiz.e: JavaScript runs in every major web browser, which is why it is one of the most used languages.

quiz.q: Why does learning a second language usually get easier?
o: Employers hand out the code for you
Languages mostly share variables, conditions, loops and functions
The second language is always simpler than the first
Computers translate your first language automatically
quiz.e: The core ideas carry over, so a new language is mostly new spelling and grammar.

LESSONS.push: COBOL is over 60 years old and still handles money. Why won't it go away?

LESSONS.title: How websites work
LESSONS.hook: Type a web address and a page appears in under a second. Behind that blink is a relay race across the planet.

sections.key: A browser on your device requests files from a server, a computer that stores and sends out the website.
sections.b:
Every website visit is a conversation between two computers. Your browser, such as Safari, Chrome, Firefox or Edge, is the client: it asks for things. A server is a computer, usually in a data centre, that stores a website's files and sends them out when asked. Servers are simply computers built to run all day and answer many requests at once. Big sites run on thousands of them around the world.

The first web server was a NeXT computer in Tim Berners-Lee's office at CERN, with a handwritten label warning colleagues not to switch it off. The first website, info.cern.ch, went live in 1991. In 1993 the Mosaic browser displayed pictures alongside text, and public interest exploded.

sections.key: Domain names read from right to left, from a top-level ending like .au down to the name its owner registered.
sections.b:
Computers find each other with numeric IP addresses, but people use domain names, which have a structure. Read abc.net.au from right to left: .au is Australia's country-code ending, .net.au is a category within it, and abc is the name its owner registered. Australian names are overseen by auDA, a not-for-profit body. Since 2022, anyone with an Australian connection can register directly under .au, such as example.au.

Domain names are rented, not owned outright. You pay a registrar for one to five years at a time, and if you forget to renew, someone else can grab the name.

sections.key: HTML gives a page its structure, CSS controls how it looks, and JavaScript makes it interactive.
sections.b:
Web pages use three main languages. HTML, HyperText Markup Language, describes what is on the page: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, here is an image, this text links to another page. It is the frame and rooms of a house. Tags wrap around content to mark where each element begins and ends. Links, the feature that makes the web a web, are part of HTML.

CSS, Cascading Style Sheets, is the paint and furniture: colours, fonts, spacing and layout, rearranged to fit a phone or a big monitor. JavaScript is the wiring and plumbing. When a menu slides open or a form warns you've missed your postcode, JavaScript is at work. Keeping the three separate makes sites easier to build and redesign.

sections.key: Loading a page involves a DNS lookup, a secure connection, a request, a response and rendering, and the work is split between front end and back end.
sections.b:
When you type an address and press enter, your browser first uses DNS to find the server's numeric address. It opens a connection and, for secure sites, agrees on encryption, shown by the padlock. It sends a request using rules called HTTP. The server responds with HTML. The browser discovers it also needs images, fonts, CSS and JavaScript, requests those, and assembles the page, often within a second.

Developers split the work in two. The front end runs in your browser: layout, buttons and animations. The back end runs on servers, handling things you don't see, like checking your password or storing your order. At checkout, the front end collects your details while the back end processes payment, updates stock and triggers a confirmation email.

sections.key: HTTPS protects your connection but not a site's honesty, so check addresses carefully and manage your cookies.
sections.b:
HTTPS and the padlock mean your connection to a site is encrypted, so others on the network can't read it. They do not mean the site is honest; scam sites use HTTPS too. Always check the domain name carefully, since scammers register look-alike addresses, such as an extra letter or a different ending.

Cookies are small files that sites store in your browser to remember logins and preferences, and sometimes to track you across sites. Your browser settings let you view and clear them. Knowing how the web works is one of the simplest ways to stay safe on it.

quiz.q: What is a web server?
o: A browser that asks for web pages
A computer that stores a website's files and sends them when asked
A cable linking your device to the internet
A program that designs web pages
quiz.e: The browser is the client that asks; the server stores the files and answers.

quiz.q: What does it mean that domain names are 'rented'?
o: You must renew it or someone else can grab the name
You can only use it at home
Your browser charges a fee every visit
Only the government can use .au names
quiz.e: You pay a registrar for one to five years at a time and lose the name if you forget to renew.

quiz.q: Which job does CSS do on a web page?
o: Stores customer orders in a database
Describes headings, paragraphs and links
Controls colours, fonts, spacing and layout
Checks passwords on the server
quiz.e: HTML is the structure, CSS is the paint and furniture, and JavaScript is the wiring.

quiz.q: Which task belongs to the back end of a website?
o: Animating a button when you tap it
Showing the layout on your phone
Choosing the fonts for headings
Processing your payment and updating stock levels
quiz.e: The back end runs on servers and handles unseen jobs such as payments, passwords and databases.

quiz.q: What does the padlock icon (HTTPS) tell you?
o: The site is honest and safe to trust
Your connection to the site is encrypted
The site was checked by the government
The site stores no cookies
quiz.e: HTTPS protects the connection, but scam sites can use it too, so still check the domain name.

LESSONS.push: A web page arrives in under a second. Here's the relay race behind it.

LESSONS.title: Bugs and debugging
LESSONS.hook: A moth in a relay, a rocket lost in under a minute, and a rubber duck on a desk: the surprising story of how software goes wrong and gets fixed.

sections.key: A bug is a mistake in software that makes it behave in ways its creators didn't intend.
sections.b:
A bug is an error that makes a program crash, freeze, show the wrong number or open a security hole. Most bugs are not the computer's fault: it did exactly what it was told, and the instructions were wrong or incomplete. Large programs are enormously complex and people make mistakes, so bugs are unavoidable. Debugging, tracking them down, is one of the most important skills in programming.

On 9 September 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II traced a fault to a moth trapped in a relay and taped it into the logbook: 'First actual case of bug being found.' The joke worked because engineers already called faults 'bugs'; Thomas Edison used the word in the 1870s. The page is held by the Smithsonian.

sections.key: Bugs include syntax errors, logic errors and edge cases the programmer didn't anticipate.
sections.b:
Syntax errors are like spelling or grammar mistakes, such as a missing bracket, and the computer usually refuses to run until they're fixed. Logic errors are sneakier: the program runs happily but gives the wrong answer, like a discount that subtracts 10 dollars instead of 10 percent.

Then there are edge cases, unusual situations the programmer didn't think of. What if a surname has an apostrophe, a customer orders zero items, or a date falls on 29 February? Many real-world bugs live at these edges.

sections.key: Good debugging means reproducing the bug, narrowing down where it happens, forming a theory and testing one change at a time.
sections.b:
Effective debugging is closer to detective work than guesswork. First, reproduce the bug reliably: exactly what actions make it happen? Next, narrow down where it occurs by checking the program's values at different points. A handy trick is halving: if the problem is somewhere in 1,000 lines, check the middle, then keep halving.

Then form a theory about the cause, change one thing, and test again. Changing many things at once may make the bug vanish without revealing why, and it may come back.

The 1999 book The Pragmatic Programmer tells of a programmer who explained code line by line to a rubber duck. Explaining forces you to state what each step actually does, rather than what you assume, and the gap is often where the bug hides.

sections.key: The Ariane 5 failure and Y2K show how small software assumptions can have huge consequences, and how hard work can prevent them.
sections.b:
On 4 June 1996, the first Ariane 5 rocket veered off course and was destroyed about 40 seconds after launch, with four scientific satellites aboard. Guidance code reused from Ariane 4 tried to squeeze a large number, related to horizontal speed, into a space too small. Ariane 5 was faster, so it overflowed and the system shut down. The backup ran identical software and failed the same way. The loss is often estimated at several hundred million US dollars.

For decades, many programs stored years as two digits to save memory, so 1999 was just 99. The worry was that 00 would be read as 1900. Governments and businesses, including in Australia, spent enormous sums fixing code. Problems were mostly minor. Some argue the threat was exaggerated, but many experts credit the repair effort.

sections.key: Update your software, report problems clearly, and apply debugging habits to everyday troubles.
sections.b:
Bugs affect everyone, not just programmers. Software updates often fix bugs, including security flaws, so installing them promptly is one of the simplest ways to stay safe.

When reporting a problem to a company or IT help desk, describe it like a debugger would: what you did, what you expected, what actually happened, and whether you can make it happen again. The same mindset works for a car that won't start or a recipe that failed. Reproduce the problem, change one thing at a time, and explain it out loud. Sometimes the duck knows best.

quiz.q: Why are most software bugs not the computer's fault?
o: Computers randomly change the code
The computer did exactly what it was told, and the instructions were wrong
Bugs are caused by insects in the hardware
Computers refuse to follow long instructions
quiz.e: Computers follow instructions exactly, so bugs come from mistakes or gaps in those instructions.

quiz.q: Which describes a logic error?
o: A missing bracket that stops the program running
A program that crashes when switched on
The program runs but gives the wrong answer
A website that loads slowly
quiz.e: Logic errors run without complaint but give wrong results, like subtracting 10 dollars instead of 10 percent.

quiz.q: Why change only one thing at a time when debugging?
o: It makes the program run faster
The bug may vanish without you learning why, and then return
Changing several things is not allowed
It removes the need to reproduce the bug
quiz.e: Single changes reveal the cause, while many changes can hide it.

quiz.q: What caused the Ariane 5 failure in 1996?
o: Reused guidance code overflowed on a larger number
A launch crew entered the wrong date
Two-digit years confused the guidance computer
A moth was trapped in a relay
quiz.e: Ariane 5 was faster than Ariane 4, so a number from the reused code overflowed.

quiz.q: What is good practice when reporting a problem to IT support?
o: Describe only how annoyed you are
Say it broke without further detail
Describe what you did, expected, saw, and whether it repeats
Wait until it fixes itself
quiz.e: Clear, reproducible details help the person fixing it find the cause.

LESSONS.push: A moth, a rocket lost in seconds, and a rubber duck. How software goes wrong.

LESSONS.title: Mental models: a toolkit for thinking
LESSONS.hook: The best thinkers don't know everything. They carry a handful of reliable ways of seeing, and reach for the right one at the right moment.

sections.key: A mental model is a simplified picture of how something works, and having several beats relying on one.
sections.b:
A mental model is a simplified picture of how something works, like supply and demand or compound interest. Everyone uses them, mostly without noticing. Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's long-time partner, argued in a 1994 talk that you need a 'latticework' of models from many fields: economics, psychology, physics, biology and more.

His warning was the saying 'to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail'. If you only know one way of seeing, you'll force every problem into it. A few broadly useful models, practised until they become habits, can sharpen almost any decision.

sections.key: First principles rebuilds a problem from basic truths, and inversion asks what would guarantee failure so you can avoid it.
sections.b:
Mostly we reason by analogy, doing what others do. First-principles thinking, an idea going back to Aristotle, strips a problem back to what is fundamentally true, then reasons up. Ask what we are sure of and what is merely assumed. If a bathroom renovation quote seems huge, list the parts: materials, labour, waterproofing, plumbing, permits. You may find which are negotiable. It's slower, so save it for problems that matter.

Inversion, 'invert, always invert', often credited to mathematician Carl Jacobi, flips the question. Instead of 'how do I succeed?', ask 'what would make this fail?' and avoid it. Imagine a project failed a year from now and ask why; Gary Klein calls this a pre-mortem.

sections.key: Second-order thinking asks 'and then what?', tracing consequences beyond the immediate effect.
sections.b:
First-order thinking stops at the immediate result: this price cut wins customers. Second-order thinking keeps asking 'and then what?' Competitors may cut prices too, and everyone earns less.

A widely told story, possibly exaggerated, describes a bounty on cobras in colonial Delhi that led people to breed cobras for the reward. Whether or not it happened exactly that way, the 'cobra effect' names a real pattern: well-meant rules that create the opposite of what was intended. Before acting, sketch the likely reactions of the people and systems affected, over months, not just days.

sections.key: Build in a buffer for error, because estimates of time, money and risk are usually too optimistic.
sections.b:
Engineers don't design a bridge to carry exactly the heaviest expected truck; they build it for several times that load. Investor Benjamin Graham, Warren Buffett's teacher, borrowed the idea for finance as a 'margin of safety': buy only when the price is well below your estimate of value, in case you're wrong.

It works in everyday life too. Leave 20 minutes spare for the airport run. Add a contingency of 10 to 20% to a renovation budget. Borrow less than the bank says you can. We're reliably over-optimistic about how long things take and what they cost, so a buffer isn't pessimism; it's realism. The less reversible the decision, the bigger the margin you want.

sections.key: Know where your competence ends, remember that every model simplifies reality, and use models as questions, not answers.
sections.b:
Buffett and Munger describe a 'circle of competence': areas where you truly understand how things work. Outside it, confidence is dangerous, because you don't know what you don't know. What matters is knowing where its edge is. Outside it, slow down, seek real expertise and prefer small, reversible bets.

'The map is not the territory', a phrase from Alfred Korzybski in the early 1930s, reminds us that budgets, forecasts and dashboards leave things out. When map and ground disagree, trust the ground. Related is Chesterton's fence: before removing a rule that seems pointless, find out why it was put there.

Use models as questions: what's true here, what would guarantee failure, and then what? Practise on small decisions, and use several.

quiz.q: What risk does 'to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail' describe?
o: Forcing every problem into the one way of seeing you know
Spending too much on tools
Using too many models at once
Asking experts for help too often
quiz.e: With only one mental model, you'll misapply it, so build a latticework of several.

quiz.q: What is the point of inversion?
o: Copying what everyone else does
Asking what would make something fail, then avoiding it
Doing the opposite of every piece of advice
Reasoning only from the immediate result
quiz.e: Avoiding obvious mistakes is often easier and more valuable than finding brilliant moves.

quiz.q: What does the 'cobra effect' describe?
o: A rule that is too strict to be followed
A bounty that always reduces the problem
A decision made in a hurry
A well-meant rule that produces the opposite of what was intended
quiz.e: Second-order thinking looks past the first result to the reactions it causes.

quiz.q: Why add a buffer to time and budgets?
o: Estimates are usually too optimistic
Banks require it by law
It guarantees projects finish early
Bridges are built the same way
quiz.e: We reliably underestimate time and cost, so a margin of safety is realism rather than pessimism.

quiz.q: What should you do when deciding outside your circle of competence?
o: Trust your confidence, because experience transfers
Place one large bet to learn quickly
Slow down, seek real expertise and prefer small, reversible bets
Ignore the maps and trust your instincts
quiz.e: Outside your circle you don't know what you don't know, so keep bets small and get expert advice.

LESSONS.push: The best thinkers don't know more. They carry a few ideas. Which ones?

LESSONS.title: Understanding risk
LESSONS.hook: People fear sharks and plane crashes, then drive home tired without a second thought. Our risk radar is badly calibrated, and it can be fixed.

sections.key: We judge risk by how vivid and emotional it feels, not by how likely it is.
sections.b:
Humans didn't evolve to read statistics. We judge danger with fast, emotional shortcuts. Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic: we rate something as more likely when examples spring easily to mind. Shark attacks and plane crashes get saturation news coverage, so they feel common. Heart disease, falls at home and car crashes rarely make headlines, so they feel ordinary.

Paul Slovic and other researchers found we also fear risks that feel uncontrollable, unfamiliar or imposed on us far more than risks we choose. Australia records a handful of fatal shark bites a year, yet around 300 or more people drown, many in rivers, lakes and backyard pools.

sections.key: Fear of a rare, dramatic event can push us into a bigger, quieter risk, and per kilometre flying is far safer than driving.
sections.b:
A 'dread risk' is a rare event that kills many people at once, such as a plane crash or terrorist attack. It triggers fear far beyond its statistical danger. After the September 11 attacks in 2001, many Americans avoided flying and drove instead. Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer estimated the extra driving caused roughly 1,500 additional road deaths in the following year, more than the passengers killed on the four hijacked planes.

Australia's road toll runs at roughly 1,100 to 1,300 deaths a year, plus tens of thousands of serious injuries. Qantas has never had a fatal jet accident, and per kilometre, flying on a major airline is many times safer than driving. The riskiest part of a trip is often the drive to the airport.

sections.key: 'Doubles your risk' can mean going from 1 in a million to 2 in a million, so always ask for the absolute numbers.
sections.b:
Headlines love relative risk: 'X doubles your risk of Y'. But doubling a tiny risk still leaves a tiny risk. In 1995, UK authorities warned that newer contraceptive pills doubled the risk of a type of blood clot. The absolute increase was roughly from 1 in 7,000 women to 2 in 7,000. Many women stopped taking the pill, and researchers later linked the scare to a rise in unplanned pregnancies and abortions, which carry their own risks.

Whenever you hear 'increases risk by 50%', ask: 50% of what? How many people out of 1,000 or 10,000 are actually affected?

sections.key: The base rate is how common something is to begin with, and ignoring it in favour of a good story leads to wildly wrong conclusions.
sections.b:
The base rate is how often something happens in the first place, and we routinely ignore it when a good story comes along. Kahneman and Tversky described 'Steve': shy, tidy and helpful, with a passion for detail. Is he more likely a librarian or a farmer? Most people say librarian, because he fits the stereotype. But in the United States there were more than 20 male farmers for every male librarian, so Steve is far more likely to farm.

The same trap catches us with a 'sure thing' share tip, a start-up that looks like the next big success, or a stranger who 'looks suspicious'. Before judging by fit, ask how common it is.

sections.key: Ask how likely, how bad, compared with what, and whether you can reduce it, then focus on common, controllable risks.
sections.b:
Good risk thinking asks four questions. How likely is it, in absolute terms? How bad would it be, and is it reversible? Compared with what, including the risk of the alternative? Can I cheaply reduce it? Say '3 in 1,000' rather than '0.3%', and notice when a vivid story is doing the work data should.

The biggest killers are slow and familiar: heart disease, dementia, cancers, smoking and inactivity, plus falls among older Australians. Put effort into seatbelts, not driving tired, pool fences, sun protection and health checks. Zero risk doesn't exist; doing nothing carries risk too. Researchers compare activities in 'micromorts', a one-in-a-million chance of death. For medical choices, ask your doctor to explain the numbers in plain terms.

quiz.q: What does the availability heuristic lead us to do?
o: Trust the figures that experts publish
Rate risks as more likely when vivid examples come easily to mind
Fear only the risks we choose to take
Ignore dangers that affect other people
quiz.e: Vivid, memorable examples make a risk feel more common than it really is.

quiz.q: What did the road deaths after September 11 show about fear of dread risks?
o: Fear of a vivid risk can push us into a larger, quieter one
Driving is safer than flying per kilometre
Dramatic risks are always overestimated by experts
People ignore risks that kill many at once
quiz.e: Fear of flying sent many onto the road, where the extra deaths exceeded the number killed on the hijacked planes.

quiz.q: A headline says a drug 'doubles your risk' of a clot. What should you ask first?
o: Which newspaper reported the study
How many people were surveyed in total
Whether the drug is popular in other countries
How big the risk was to begin with, in absolute numbers
quiz.e: Doubling a risk of 1 in 7,000 still leaves a very small risk.

quiz.q: Why is a shy, tidy man more likely to be a farmer than a librarian?
o: Farmers are usually shy and tidy
Librarians are rarely tidy
There are far more farmers than librarians, so the base rate outweighs the stereotype
Surveys show shy people prefer farming
quiz.e: How well someone fits a stereotype shouldn't override how common each group is.

quiz.q: Where does the lesson suggest putting your safety effort?
o: Avoiding rare, dramatic dangers like shark attacks
Common, controllable risks such as seatbelts, pool fences and sun protection
Risks that make the loudest headlines
Eliminating every risk completely
quiz.e: The biggest harms are common and familiar, and many are cheap to reduce.

LESSONS.push: People fear sharks, then drive home tired. Why our risk radar is off.

LESSONS.title: Game theory for everyday life
LESSONS.hook: Why rivals end up in price wars, why cooperation survives among strangers, and what a 1950s puzzle reveals about neighbours, workmates and nations.

sections.key: Game theory studies strategic situations, where your best move depends on what others do, so think about their response before you act.
sections.b:
Game theory is the study of strategic decisions: situations where the outcome for you depends not only on your own choice but also on the choices of others. The 'games' can be chess, poker, business competition, wage negotiations, elections or arms races. Modern game theory was launched by mathematician John von Neumann and economist Oskar Morgenstern in their 1944 book 'Theory of Games and Economic Behavior'. It's now used across economics, politics, biology and computer science.

You don't need the maths to benefit. The core habit is simple: before acting, think about how others will respond, and what each person gains or loses from each choice. They're doing the same.

sections.key: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player's self-interest leads both to a worse result than cooperating, and a Nash equilibrium shows why that bad outcome is stable.
sections.b:
The most famous game was developed at the RAND Corporation around 1950, and mathematician Albert Tucker gave it its prison story. Two suspects are questioned separately. If both stay silent, each gets one year. If one betrays, the betrayer walks free and the other gets ten years. If both betray, each gets five. Whatever your partner does, betraying looks better, so two rational players betray and get five years each.

This is a Nash equilibrium, an idea John Nash described in 1950 and shared a 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize for. It is a set of choices where no player can do better by changing only their own choice. Bad situations can be stable: everyone may want change, but no one gains by moving first.

sections.key: Price wars, doping, overwork and overfishing share a prisoner's dilemma structure, but communities can often escape it with shared rules.
sections.b:
Once you recognise the pattern, you see it everywhere. Two petrol stations on the same corner would both profit if prices stayed high, but each is tempted to undercut. Athletes may dope because they fear rivals do. If everyone stays back late to look committed, no one gains an edge, yet everyone loses their evenings. The problem often isn't bad people. It's bad incentives.

Ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised the 'tragedy of the commons' in 1968: on a shared pasture, each herder gains from one more cow while overgrazing is everyone's cost. Overfishing and pollution follow the same logic. Yet Elinor Ostrom, the first woman to win the economics Nobel (2009), showed communities often manage shared resources for centuries using local rules, monitoring and fair penalties.

sections.key: In repeated games, cooperating first and then copying the other player often does very well, because repetition and reputation make cooperation rational.
sections.b:
Real life is rarely a one-off. Around 1980, political scientist Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments where strategies played the prisoner's dilemma against each other many times. The winner was the simplest entry, 'tit-for-tat', submitted by Anatol Rapoport: cooperate on the first move, then copy whatever the other player did last time.

Axelrod concluded that successful strategies were nice (never betray first), retaliatory (respond to betrayal), forgiving (return to cooperation quickly) and clear (easy to read). Later research found that slightly more forgiving variants can do better when mistakes happen. Most relationships, at work, with neighbours or with a co-parent, are repeated games, so reputation and trust are worth more than a one-off win.

sections.key: Coordination, credible commitment and positive-sum thinking let you change the game rather than just play it.
sections.b:
Not every game is a conflict. In coordination games, everyone wins by choosing the same option. Which side of the road to drive on matters little, as long as everyone agrees; Australians drive on the left. Economist Thomas Schelling, a 2005 Nobel laureate, showed people often coordinate on obvious 'focal points' without talking. He also studied credible commitment: limiting your own options can strengthen your position. A union that publicly commits to a strike, or a seller with a firm 'no discounts' policy, changes what others expect. A threat only works if people believe you'll follow through.

When stuck in a dilemma, change the game: agreements, contracts, shared rules or clear communication. Look for positive-sum options too. Many negotiations are about making the pie bigger.

quiz.q: What is the core habit of thinking with game theory?
o: Always assume other people will cooperate
Ignore what others do and focus on your own goals
Think about how others will respond before you act
Learn the full mathematics before deciding
quiz.e: Strategic situations are ones where your result depends on other people's choices as well as your own.

quiz.q: In the prisoner's dilemma, what happens when both players act in narrow self-interest?
o: Both end up worse off than if they had cooperated
Both go free
One player always wins
The game has no outcome
quiz.e: Betrayal is individually tempting, but mutual betrayal leaves both worse off.

quiz.q: What did Elinor Ostrom's research on shared resources show?
o: Only private ownership can protect resources
Governments must control all shared resources
Communities can often manage commons well using local rules and monitoring
The tragedy of the commons is inevitable
quiz.e: The tragedy is a risk, not a certainty, because people can build rules to manage shared resources.

quiz.q: Why does cooperating first, then copying the other player, work well in repeated games?
o: Repetition and reputation reward cooperation while discouraging betrayal
It guarantees the other player cooperates forever
It ensures you win every single round
It works only when the other player is unaware
quiz.e: Tit-for-tat is nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear, so it builds trust and punishes betrayal.

quiz.q: When does a seller's firm 'no discounts' policy strengthen their position?
o: When it is hidden from customers
When customers believe the seller will stick to it
When it applies only to large orders
When competitors set the same price
quiz.e: A commitment only changes what others expect if it is credible.

LESSONS.push: Why rivals slide into price wars, and why cooperation still survives.

LESSONS.title: Insurance without the confusion
LESSONS.hook: Most of us pay for insurance for years without reading a word of the policy. Here's how it actually works, and how to avoid a nasty surprise at claim time.

sections.key: Insurance pools many people's premiums to pay large losses, so insure what you couldn't afford to lose and self-insure the rest.
sections.b:
Thousands of people each pay a small, predictable premium into a pool. In any year, only a few suffer a big loss, like a house fire or serious car crash, and the pool pays. Insurers use statistics to set premiums and add costs and profit, so on average customers pay in more than they get back. That's fine: you're buying protection, not an investment.

The golden rule is to insure what you can't afford to lose: your house, a year of income, or liability for injuring someone. Cheap phones and extended warranties are often poor value, because Australian Consumer Law already gives you a repair, replacement or refund for major faults. An emergency fund lets you 'self-insure' small losses and choose higher excesses.

sections.key: Medicare covers public hospital care, private cover adds choice, and life and income protection guard your ability to earn.
sections.b:
Medicare gives free public-patient treatment in public hospitals. Private hospital cover lets you choose your doctor, and extras cover pays towards dental and physio. Since 2019, hospital policies are grouped as Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic. The Medicare Levy Surcharge taxes higher earners without appropriate hospital cover, and Lifetime Health Cover adds 2% to premiums for each year over 30 before you first join, up to 70%, removed after ten continuous years.

Your income is often your biggest asset. Income protection commonly pays up to around 70% of income if illness or injury stops you working. Life cover pays your beneficiaries a lump sum; TPD pays if you can never work again; trauma cover pays on diagnosis of serious illness. Super funds often provide some by default, but premiums reduce your balance.

sections.key: Building, contents and car covers protect big assets, and CTP covers injuries to people, not damage to cars.
sections.b:
Home building insurance covers the structure; contents covers your belongings, and renters usually need only contents. Check whether flood, storm and bushfire are covered, as these matter hugely in Australia.

For cars, Compulsory Third Party (CTP) insurance, generally tied to your registration, covers injuries you cause to other people, but not damage to cars or property. Third-party property cover pays for damage you do to other people's cars and property. Adding fire and theft covers your own car for those events, and comprehensive cover also pays for damage to your own car. Crashing into a luxury car without property cover can be very costly.

sections.key: The excess is what you pay towards a claim, and a higher excess usually means a lower premium.
sections.b:
The excess is the amount you pay out of your own pocket when you make a claim. If your car repair costs $4,000 and your excess is $800, the insurer pays $3,200. Choosing a higher excess usually lowers your premium, which can make sense if you have savings to cover it and rarely claim. Some policies have different excesses for different situations, such as young or unlisted drivers.

Premiums also depend on your address, claims history and what's being insured. Don't just auto-renew. Premiums often rise each year, so compare at renewal and ask your current insurer for a better price.

sections.key: Read the PDS for exclusions and limits, and check your sums insured so you aren't underinsured when you need to claim.
sections.b:
Every policy has a Product Disclosure Statement (PDS), and home insurance also has a shorter Key Facts Sheet. A few minutes on the right sections can save thousands. Check exclusions, limits such as caps on jewellery or laptops, and definitions like 'flood'. Answer questions honestly, because misleading information can void a claim. If the insurer's complaints process fails, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) offers a free dispute service.

Being underinsured means your cover can't replace what you lose. After bushfires and floods, many households found their sum insured couldn't cover a rebuild, as costs had risen or demolition and code upgrades weren't counted. Use a building cost calculator, tally contents room by room, and review cover yearly. This is general information only; talk to a licensed adviser.

quiz.q: What is the golden rule for deciding what to insure?
o: Insure everything you own, however small
Insure losses you couldn't afford to cover yourself
Insure only what the law requires
Insure whatever the insurer recommends
quiz.e: Insurance suits losses that would wreck your finances, while small losses can be covered from savings.

quiz.q: How does the Lifetime Health Cover loading work?
o: A flat $500 a year for everyone
10% for each year over 25
Nothing if you earn under $100,000
2% for each year over 30 before you first take out hospital cover
quiz.e: The loading is capped at 70% and removed after ten continuous years of cover.

quiz.q: What does Compulsory Third Party (CTP) insurance cover?
o: Damage to your own car
Injuries you cause to other people
Damage to other people's cars
Theft of your car
quiz.e: CTP covers injuries to people, not damage to vehicles or property.

quiz.q: What does choosing a higher excess usually do?
o: Lowers your premium
Increases your premium
Removes exclusions
Doubles your cover
quiz.e: Taking on more of each claim yourself generally reduces what you pay the insurer.

quiz.q: What does being underinsured mean?
o: You have too many policies
Your premium is too high
Your cover isn't enough to replace what you lose
You didn't read the PDS
quiz.e: Rising rebuild costs and extra expenses often leave people short when disaster strikes.

LESSONS.push: You may pay for it for years. Do you know what it covers at claim time?

LESSONS.title: Planning for retirement in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Retirement could last 25 years or more. How super, the Age Pension and your own savings fit together, and how to work out what 'enough' looks like.

sections.key: Many Australians will spend 20 to 30 years in retirement, and many stop work earlier than planned, often for health reasons.
sections.b:
A 65-year-old today can expect, on average, to live roughly another 20 years or more, and many will reach their 90s. Retirement may last a quarter or even a third of your adult life, so starting early gives compound growth decades to work.

It doesn't always go to plan. A recent ABS survey found recent retirees stopped work at an average age of about 64, while workers aged 45 and over planned to retire at around 65 or 66. Reaching retirement age or qualifying for super was the most common reason, but illness, injury or disability came second, and those who retired for health reasons stopped at about 57. Build a buffer for finishing early. Many people now cut back hours gradually.

sections.key: Retirement rests on super, the Age Pension and your own savings, and super can be taken as a lump sum or an account-based pension.
sections.b:
Australia's system has three pillars: compulsory superannuation paid by employers, the means-tested Age Pension as a safety net, and voluntary savings, including your home and extra contributions.

At retirement you can take super as a lump sum, a regular income, or both. A common choice is an account-based pension: your money stays invested and you draw regular payments, with a minimum percentage that rises with age. For most people, payments from a taxed super fund are tax-free from age 60, and earnings inside a retirement pension account are generally untaxed too, within limits. An annuity or lifetime income product trades flexibility for guaranteed payments. The right mix depends on your health, needs and other income.

sections.key: The Age Pension is a means-tested payment from age 67, and whichever of the income test or assets test gives the lower amount applies.
sections.b:
The Age Pension is paid through Services Australia. Pension age has been 67 since July 2023, and you generally need ten years of Australian residency. It isn't based on tax paid. It's means-tested, and around 60% of Australians of pension age receive a full or part pension, often alongside super.

Two tests apply, and the lower result is the pension you get. The income test counts earnings, including 'deemed' income that assumes your financial assets earn a set rate. The assets test counts investments, retirement-phase super, cars, caravans and investment property. Your family home is exempt. Couples are assessed together. Even a small part pension can be valuable, as it usually brings a Pensioner Concession Card. Rates change regularly, so check Services Australia for current figures.

sections.key: The ASFA Retirement Standard sets 'modest' and 'comfortable' budgets as a starting point, but your own spending plan matters more.
sections.b:
The most quoted benchmark is the ASFA Retirement Standard, from the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia. It estimates yearly budgets for a 'modest' and a 'comfortable' lifestyle for singles and couples, and the super balance needed at retirement to fund them. It assumes you own your home and receive a part Age Pension.

The figures are updated regularly, so look up the current edition. Treat them as a starting point, not a verdict. Renters generally need considerably more, because rent is a big ongoing cost. The best estimate is your own: sketch what you expect to spend, including travel, health and home repairs.

sections.key: Many retirees spend too cautiously, so check your super, use free planning tools and get licensed advice for big decisions.
sections.b:
Saving is only half the job. The federal Retirement Income Review (2020) found many retirees draw only the legal minimum from super and die with most of their wealth intact, having lived more frugally than they needed to. Fear of running out is understandable, but it can mean missing travel and comforts while you're healthy. Spending tends to be highest in the active early years and eases later, though health and aged care costs can rise near the end. Since July 2022, super funds must have a retirement income strategy for members, so ask yours what help it offers.

Check your balance, fees, investments and insurance. Try Moneysmart's free retirement planner or Services Australia's Financial Information Service. This is general information only; for your situation, see a licensed financial adviser.

quiz.q: Why build a buffer for finishing work earlier than you expect?
o: Many people stop earlier than planned, often because of illness or injury
Super cannot be accessed before 65
Employers must stop employing people at 60
Pension age falls as you get older
quiz.e: Workers planned to stop around 65 or 66, but recent retirees averaged about 64, and health reasons pushed some out much earlier.

quiz.q: For most people, how are payments from a taxed super fund treated from age 60?
o: Taxed at 30%
Generally tax-free
Taxed at your marginal rate
Taxed only above $50,000
quiz.e: Super income from a taxed fund is generally tax-free from 60, within limits.

quiz.q: How is the Age Pension means-tested?
o: Only on the value of your home
Only on your super balance
On how much tax you paid while working
An income test and an assets test apply, and the lower result is paid
quiz.e: Both tests are applied, and whichever gives the lower pension is used.

quiz.q: What does the ASFA Retirement Standard provide?
o: The legal minimum super balance
Budgets for 'modest' and 'comfortable' retirement lifestyles
The maximum pension you can receive
The amount employers must contribute
quiz.e: ASFA estimates yearly budgets and the lump sums needed to fund them, as a starting point.

quiz.q: What did the Retirement Income Review find about many retirees?
o: They overspend and run out of money early
They invest too heavily in shares
They draw only the minimum from super and often live more frugally than needed
They retire before they qualify for super
quiz.e: Fear of running out can mean missing comforts while you're healthy enough to enjoy them.

LESSONS.push: Many retirees spend far less than they could. The reason may surprise you.

LESSONS.title: Inside the Earth
LESSONS.hook: Nobody has ever drilled even halfway through the crust, yet we know the Earth has a solid metal heart as hot as the surface of the Sun. Here's how.

sections.key: Earth is layered like a peach: a thin crust, a thick mantle of solid rock that slowly flows, and a metal core.
sections.b:
The Earth has a radius of about 6,371 kilometres and is built in layers. Picture a peach: the skin is the crust, the flesh is the mantle and the stone is the core. The layers formed early, when heavy metals sank towards the centre and lighter rock floated to the top.

The mantle makes up roughly 84% of the planet's volume and reaches down about 2,900 kilometres. It is often drawn as molten lava, but it is almost entirely solid. Under enormous heat and pressure it creeps a few centimetres a year, rather like a glacier or very stiff toffee. Hotter rock rises and cooler rock sinks in slow convection currents that carry heat out of the planet and help drive the plates.

sections.key: Oceanic crust is thin, dense and young, while lighter continental crust is thicker and holds the oldest rocks.
sections.b:
There are two kinds of crust. Oceanic crust is usually only 5 to 10 kilometres thick and made of dense, dark basalt. It is created at mid-ocean ridges and destroyed where it sinks into the mantle, so almost none is older than about 200 million years.

Continental crust is typically 30 to 50 kilometres thick, and up to about 70 under ranges like the Himalayas. It is lighter, so it floats higher and rarely sinks. That is why continents hold Earth's oldest rocks, including zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia dated to about 4.4 billion years. The crust and top of the mantle form the rigid lithosphere, broken into tectonic plates that ride on the softer asthenosphere beneath.

sections.key: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel, while the inner core stays solid at 5,000 to 6,000 degrees because of immense pressure.
sections.b:
The core begins about 2,900 kilometres down. The outer core, roughly 2,200 kilometres thick, is liquid metal: mostly iron with some nickel and lighter elements. The inner core is a solid ball about 1,220 kilometres in radius, roughly two-thirds the size of the Moon.

Its temperature is estimated at around 5,000 to 6,000 degrees Celsius, similar to the surface of the Sun. It stays solid despite that heat because the pressure at the centre, millions of times the air pressure at the surface, squeezes the atoms together.
