The inner core is slowly growing as the planet cools and the liquid metal around it freezes onto it.

sections.key: Earthquake waves bend, speed up and vanish as they cross different layers, which revealed a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.
sections.b:
The deepest hole ever drilled, Russia's Kola Superdeep Borehole, stopped at about 12 kilometres, a tiny scratch. Almost everything we know about the deep Earth comes from earthquake waves. P-waves are push-pull waves that travel through solids and liquids. S-waves are side-to-side waves that cannot pass through liquid. Waves speed up, slow down and bend at layer boundaries. In 1909 Andrija Mohorovičić found the base of the crust, now called the Moho.

After a large quake, S-waves never arrive across a broad shadow zone on the far side, showing the outer core is molten. In 1936 Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann explained puzzling faint P-waves by proposing a solid inner core. Earth's average density, about 5.5 times water, also says heavy metal lies deep inside.

sections.key: Churning liquid iron in the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field, which shields us from the solar wind and flips over long periods.
sections.b:
The swirling liquid iron in the outer core acts like a giant dynamo. As the electrically conducting metal moves, driven by heat and Earth's rotation, it generates electric currents that produce a magnetic field. It makes a compass point roughly north and deflects most of the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun. Some particles are funnelled towards the poles, making the upper atmosphere glow: the aurora australis, sometimes seen from Tasmania and southern Victoria.

The field isn't fixed. The magnetic poles wander, and the north magnetic pole has moved hundreds of kilometres over the past century. The whole field has flipped many times, as volcanic rock records the field as it cools. The last reversal was about 780,000 years ago. Reversals are irregular and take thousands of years, with no good evidence they caused mass extinctions.

quiz.q: Which best describes the mantle?
o: An ocean of molten lava
A layer of liquid iron
A thin skin of basalt
Solid rock that flows very slowly
quiz.e: The mantle is almost entirely solid, but under heat and pressure it creeps a few centimetres a year.

quiz.q: Why do continents hold the oldest rocks on Earth?
o: Continents formed before the oceans
Continental crust is lighter, so it rarely sinks back into the mantle
Continental crust is thinner
Oceanic rocks dissolve in seawater
quiz.e: Oceanic crust is recycled within about 200 million years, but buoyant continental crust survives for billions.

quiz.q: Why does the inner core stay solid despite temperatures similar to the Sun's surface?
o: It is cooled by the oceans
The magnetic field freezes it
It is made of rock, not metal
Immense pressure squeezes the atoms together
quiz.e: The pressure at the centre is so great that the iron stays solid even at around 5,000 to 6,000 degrees.

quiz.q: What showed scientists that Earth's outer core is liquid?
o: Drilling samples from deep boreholes
Volcanoes that erupt liquid iron
S-waves cannot pass through it, leaving a shadow zone
Satellite photographs of the interior
quiz.e: S-waves cannot travel through liquid, so the S-wave shadow zone revealed a molten outer core.

quiz.q: What generates Earth's magnetic field?
o: Moving liquid iron in the outer core
The solid inner core acting as a bar magnet
Iron deposits in the crust
The solar wind hitting the atmosphere
quiz.e: The churning, electrically conducting liquid iron of the outer core works like a dynamo.

LESSONS.push: We have never drilled past 12 km. So how do we know the centre?

LESSONS.title: Volcanoes, earthquakes and tsunamis
LESSONS.hook: Australia feels rock-solid, yet in 1989 an earthquake killed 13 people in Newcastle. Here's what makes the ground shake and mountains explode.

sections.key: Runny magma makes gentle, flowing eruptions, while thick, gassy magma makes explosive ones.
sections.b:
Whether a volcano oozes or explodes depends on its magma. Runny, low-silica basalt lets gas escape and builds broad shield volcanoes like Hawaii's. Thick, silica-rich magma traps gas like a shaken soft drink until pressure blasts it apart, building steep stratovolcanoes such as Mount Fuji.

Explosive eruptions can be huge. Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 AD. Tambora in 1815 was the largest in recorded history, and its ash and sulfur haze cooled the climate, making 1816 the 'year without a summer'. Krakatoa in 1883 was heard across the Indian Ocean, including parts of Western Australia, and its tsunamis killed tens of thousands. Australia has volcanoes too: Mount Gambier, last erupted roughly 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, is thought dormant, not extinct.

sections.key: The Ring of Fire around the Pacific hosts most active volcanoes and the biggest earthquakes, where locked plates slip all at once.
sections.b:
The Pacific is ringed by a horseshoe of subduction zones about 40,000 kilometres long. This Ring of Fire holds roughly three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes and most earthquakes, including nearly all the largest. Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country, and New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu are often shaken. Australia sits mid-plate, far from the edges.

The biggest quake recorded was Chile in 1960, at magnitude 9.5. The 2004 Sumatra quake (about 9.1) generated tsunamis that killed roughly 230,000 people in 14 countries. In 2011 a magnitude 9.0 to 9.1 quake off Japan caused a tsunami that killed around 18,000 and the Fukushima accident. At subduction zones, plates lock for centuries then slip at once. Scientists cannot predict the exact time and place of a quake.

sections.key: Each whole step on the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy, and intensity depends on where you are.
sections.b:
In 1935 seismologist Charles Richter created a scale to compare California earthquakes. Today scientists mainly use the moment magnitude scale, which suits very large quakes, though news reports still often say 'Richter'.

The scale is logarithmic: each whole number up means about ten times more ground shaking and roughly 32 times more energy. So a magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times the energy of a magnitude 5.

Magnitude measures the size of the quake itself. Intensity describes how strongly shaking was felt in a particular place, which depends on distance, depth and local soil. A moderate quake directly under a city can do more damage than a huge one far offshore.

sections.key: Australia's largest quakes struck sparsely populated areas, while the smaller 1989 Newcastle quake killed 13 because it hit a city.
sections.b:
Australia is not immune. Stress transmitted through the plate still cracks its interior. On 14 October 1968, a quake of about magnitude 6.5 wrecked much of the Wheatbelt town of Meckering in Western Australia and tore open a fault scarp tens of kilometres long. On 22 January 1988, three quakes, the largest about magnitude 6.6, struck near Tennant Creek in the Northern Territory within 12 hours, the biggest recorded on the mainland. Because both hit sparsely populated areas, no one died.

The magnitude 5.6 Newcastle quake of 28 December 1989 was far smaller, yet it killed 13 people, nine in the collapse of the Newcastle Workers Club, because it struck a city partly built on soft ground. It led to tougher building standards.

sections.key: Tsunamis are fast, long waves that grow in shallow water, so after strong shaking or a retreating sea, drop, cover and then head for high ground.
sections.b:
A tsunami is usually caused when an undersea earthquake lifts or drops the sea floor, moving the whole column of water above it. Landslides and eruptions can also cause them. In deep ocean it travels around 800 kilometres an hour yet is under a metre high, so ships barely notice. In shallow water it slows and piles up into a wall of water. Often the first sign is the sea drawing back from shore.

In an earthquake, drop, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on. Most injuries come from falling objects, so avoid windows and don't run outside past falling masonry. Near the coast, strong or long shaking, or a retreating sea, means move to high ground without waiting for an alert. Australia's Joint Australian Tsunami Warning Centre monitors the region.

quiz.q: Why do some volcanoes erupt explosively while others ooze lava?
o: Thick, gassy magma traps pressure until it blasts apart, while runny magma lets gas escape
Explosive volcanoes are always much taller
Oozing volcanoes sit only under the ocean
Explosive volcanoes contain no gas at all
quiz.e: Runny basalt lets gas escape gently, while thick, silica-rich magma traps it like a shaken soft drink.

quiz.q: Why do most of the world's biggest earthquakes occur around the Pacific Ring of Fire?
o: The Pacific is the deepest ocean
Plates there lock at subduction zones and then slip all at once
The Sun heats the Pacific more strongly
It is the oldest part of the crust
quiz.e: Huge areas of plate can lock together for centuries at subduction zones before slipping suddenly.

quiz.q: Roughly how much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?
o: About 2 times
About 10 times
About 1,000 times
About 32 times
quiz.e: Each whole step on the magnitude scale means roughly 32 times more energy.

quiz.q: Why did the 1989 Newcastle quake kill 13 people when larger Australian quakes killed no one?
o: It struck a city partly built on soft ground
It triggered a tsunami
It was actually the largest
It happened at night
quiz.e: Meckering and Tennant Creek hit sparsely populated areas, while Newcastle hit a city.

quiz.q: Why do ships in the deep ocean barely notice a passing tsunami?
o: Tsunamis only form near the coast
In deep water it is very fast but under a metre high
Tsunamis travel underwater, below ships
Tsunamis are too slow to feel
quiz.e: A tsunami only grows tall when it slows and piles up in shallow water.

LESSONS.push: A magnitude 5.6 quake killed 13 people in Newcastle. Why so deadly?

LESSONS.title: How weather works
LESSONS.hook: Every forecast you check is the result of sunlight, spinning air and some of the most powerful computers on the planet.

sections.key: Weather is driven by the Sun heating the Earth unevenly, with the atmosphere and oceans moving heat around.
sections.b:
All weather begins with sunlight. The Sun heats the tropics far more strongly than the poles, because near the equator its rays hit the ground almost head-on, while at high latitudes the same energy is spread over a larger area. Land also heats and cools faster than water.

The atmosphere and oceans constantly try to even out these differences, moving warm air towards the poles and cold air towards the equator. That restless movement of air, heat and moisture is what we call weather. Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term average, usually measured over 30 years or more.

sections.key: High pressure usually brings settled, dry weather, low pressure brings cloud and rain, and cold fronts bring the southern 'cool change'.
sections.b:
Air has weight, pressing at sea level with an average of about 1013 hectopascals, the unit on weather maps. Sinking air forms a high; it warms and dries, so highs usually bring clear skies, light winds and frosty winter nights. Rising air forms a low; it cools, its moisture condenses into cloud, and lows bring wind and rain. In the Southern Hemisphere, winds circle anticlockwise around highs and clockwise around lows.

A front is the boundary between air masses, such as hot interior air and the cold Southern Ocean. In southern Australia, cold fronts sweep in from the west every few days. Ahead of one, hot, dry northerlies raise summer fire danger. Then the wind swings south-west and the temperature can drop ten degrees within an hour: Melbourne's 'cool change'.

sections.key: Clouds form when rising air cools and its water vapour condenses, and a raindrop holds roughly a million cloud droplets.
sections.b:
Air always contains invisible water vapour. When air rises, it expands and cools, and cool air holds less vapour. The vapour condenses into tiny droplets or ice crystals around specks of dust, salt or smoke. Billions make a cloud. Air rises when heated from the ground, forced up by mountains, or lifted by fronts. Cumulus are puffy fair-weather clouds, stratus flat grey sheets, cirrus wispy high ice clouds, and towering cumulonimbus bring lightning, hail and heavy rain.

To fall as rain, droplets must grow enormously; a raindrop holds around a million cloud droplets. In ice clouds, crystals grow at the expense of supercooled water. Hail forms as updrafts carry ice up and down, adding onion-like layers. Raindrops are not teardrop-shaped; large ones flatten like a hamburger bun.

sections.key: Forecasts come from supercomputers solving the physics of the atmosphere, and a 70% chance of rain means a 70% chance of at least 0.2 millimetres at that location.
sections.b:
Modern forecasting feeds observations from weather stations, balloons, ships, aircraft, radar and satellites, including Japan's Himawari, into supercomputers. They divide the atmosphere into a 3D grid and use physics to calculate how it will change. Because tiny errors grow, forecasters run the model many times with slightly different starting conditions, called an ensemble. Forecasts improve by roughly a day of useful accuracy per decade, but detailed forecasts beyond about 10 days remain unreliable.

In BOM forecasts, 'chance of rain' means the chance of at least 0.2 millimetres at that location, not the share of the area or day that will be wet. Check expected amounts too: a 90% chance of 1 millimetre differs from a 40% chance of 30 millimetres. For severe weather, rely on official BOM and emergency service warnings.

sections.key: Tropical cyclones form over seas warmer than about 26.5 degrees Celsius and, in the Southern Hemisphere, spin clockwise.
sections.b:
Tropical cyclones, called hurricanes or typhoons elsewhere, form over tropical oceans warmer than about 26.5 degrees Celsius. Warm, moist air rises, its vapour condenses and releases heat, and that heat powers a spiralling storm that can be hundreds of kilometres across. Like other lows in the Southern Hemisphere, they spin clockwise.

Australia's cyclone season runs from November to April, with around ten forming in our region in a typical season. The Bureau of Meteorology rates them from category 1 to 5; a category 5 brings gusts above 280 kilometres an hour. Storm surge and flooding rain often do more harm than wind. Cyclone Tracy flattened much of Darwin on Christmas Day 1974, leading to far stronger building codes across the north.

quiz.q: Why does the Sun heat the tropics more strongly than the poles?
o: The tropics are closer to the Sun
Near the equator the Sun's rays hit almost head-on, while at high latitudes the same energy is spread over a larger area
Land at the poles reflects all sunlight
The poles are covered in cloud all year
quiz.e: This uneven heating drives the air and ocean movements we call weather.

quiz.q: What typically happens when a cold front passes through southern Australia?
o: The wind swings north and temperatures rise
Humidity stays the same and skies clear
The wind swings south-west and temperatures can drop ten degrees or more
A tropical cyclone forms
quiz.e: After a cold front the wind turns south-westerly and the temperature falls: the 'cool change'.

quiz.q: What is the main reason clouds form?
o: The Sun heats water droplets in the sky
Wind blows sea spray upwards
Cold air pushes moisture down
Rising air cools and its water vapour condenses
quiz.e: As air rises it cools, and its vapour condenses onto tiny particles to form cloud droplets.

quiz.q: In a BOM forecast, what does a 70% chance of rain mean?
o: A 70% chance of at least 0.2 mm falling at that location
It will rain on 70% of the area
It will rain for 70% of the day
70% of forecasters expect rain
quiz.e: The figure is the probability of at least 0.2 millimetres falling at the location, so check expected amounts too.

quiz.q: Roughly how warm must the sea be for a tropical cyclone to form?
o: About 15 degrees Celsius
About 26.5 degrees Celsius
About 20 degrees Celsius
About 35 degrees Celsius
quiz.e: Warm seas supply the heat and moisture that power the storm.

LESSONS.push: A 70% chance of rain does not mean what most people think.

LESSONS.title: Ice ages
LESSONS.hook: Twenty thousand years ago you could have walked from Melbourne to Hobart, and on to New Guinea. The reason lies in a slow wobble in Earth's orbit.

sections.key: Technically we live in an ice age, in a warm interglacial period that began about 11,700 years ago.
sections.b:
To geologists, an ice age is any long period when large ice sheets exist on Earth. By that definition we are living in one now, because Antarctica and Greenland are covered in ice. The current ice age began about 2.6 million years ago.

Within it, the climate has swung between cold glacial periods, when ice sheets spread across North America and northern Europe, and shorter warm interglacial periods like today's. Our interglacial, the Holocene, began about 11,700 years ago. When people say 'the Ice Age', they usually mean the most recent glacial period, which peaked around 20,000 years ago.

sections.key: Slow, regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt pace the ice ages, and feedbacks such as carbon dioxide amplify the small nudge.
sections.b:
Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković calculated how small orbital changes alter the sunlight reaching different latitudes. Eccentricity, the shape of Earth's orbit, varies over about 100,000 years. Obliquity, the axis tilt, varies between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over 41,000 years. Precession, the axis wobble, takes roughly 23,000 years. Together they change how much summer sunshine reaches the far north, where ice sheets grow and melt. In 1976, deep-sea sediment cores confirmed this rhythm.

The nudges are small, but feedbacks amplify them. Spreading ice reflects more sunlight, and colder oceans absorb more carbon dioxide. Antarctic ice cores, going back about 800,000 years, show carbon dioxide at roughly 180 parts per million in glacial periods and about 280 in warm ones.

sections.key: At the Last Glacial Maximum, ice sheets covered the northern continents while Australia was colder, drier, windier and dotted with small glaciers.
sections.b:
The Last Glacial Maximum, roughly 26,000 to 19,000 years ago, was the coldest part of the last glacial period. Ice sheets up to about 3 kilometres thick covered Canada, the northern United States and much of northern Europe. Global temperatures were around 6 degrees Celsius colder than before the industrial era, though figures vary. Woolly mammoths and cave lions roamed Europe's cold steppes.

Australia had no large ice sheets, but it was colder, drier and windier, and desert dunes expanded. Glaciers carved Tasmania's highlands, including Cradle Mountain's lakes, and small glaciers formed near Mount Kosciuszko. Willandra Lakes, including Lake Mungo, held water at various times. Aboriginal people had already lived here for tens of thousands of years and adapted to these harsh conditions.

sections.key: With so much water locked in ice, seas were about 120 metres lower, joining Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania, until rising water separated them.
sections.b:
At the Last Glacial Maximum, so much water was locked up in ice that global sea levels were roughly 120 metres lower than today. Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania formed a single landmass scientists call Sahul. The Bass Strait region was a broad plain of lakes and low hills that could be walked across, and a land bridge joined Cape York to New Guinea. A similar landmass, Sunda, joined Indonesian islands to Asia.

As the ice melted, seas rose, at times by more than a metre per century. Tasmania was cut off roughly 12,000 years ago and New Guinea roughly 8,000 years ago, though estimates vary. Seas reached near present levels about 7,000 years ago. Some researchers suggest certain Aboriginal oral traditions may preserve memories of rising seas, an idea taken seriously but still debated.

sections.key: Ice ages show how sensitive climate is: small nudges, amplified by feedbacks, changed sea levels by over 100 metres.
sections.b:
A modest change in sunlight, amplified by ice and carbon dioxide feedbacks, was enough to shift global temperatures by several degrees and sea levels by over 100 metres.

Today, carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 parts per million before industry to well over 400, higher than at any time in the ice-core record and far faster than natural glacial cycles. On orbital grounds alone, scientists expect the next glacial period is many tens of thousands of years away, and human emissions may delay it further. The coastlines we know, and the Aboriginal history written into them, are a reminder that the map is never permanent.

quiz.q: Why do geologists say we are still in an ice age?
o: Global temperatures are falling
Glaciers are advancing worldwide
Large ice sheets still cover Antarctica and Greenland
The last glacial period never ended
quiz.e: An ice age is any period with large ice sheets; we are in a warm interglacial within one.

quiz.q: How do feedbacks strengthen the effect of Milankovitch cycles?
o: Volcanoes erupt more often during glacial periods
Spreading ice reflects sunlight and colder oceans absorb carbon dioxide
The Moon moves closer to Earth
Ocean salt levels rise
quiz.e: Bright ice reflects sunlight and lower carbon dioxide reduces greenhouse warming, amplifying the orbital nudge.

quiz.q: How did the ice-age climate affect Australia?
o: Large ice sheets covered the interior
It was colder, drier and windier, with small glaciers in Tasmania and the Snowy Mountains
It was warmer and wetter than today
Nothing changed on the mainland
quiz.e: Australia was never covered by large ice sheets, but its climate was very different.

quiz.q: About how much lower were sea levels at the Last Glacial Maximum?
o: About 5 metres
About 30 metres
About 500 metres
About 120 metres
quiz.e: So much water was locked in ice sheets that seas were roughly 120 metres lower, joining Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania.

quiz.q: What do ice-age sea level changes teach us about climate?
o: Small nudges, amplified by feedbacks, can cause large changes
Climate always changes slowly and gently
Orbital changes alone cause all warming
Coastlines stay roughly the same over time
quiz.e: Modest changes in sunlight, amplified by feedbacks, shifted temperatures by several degrees and seas by over 100 metres.

LESSONS.push: You could once walk from Melbourne to Hobart. Where did that land go?

LESSONS.title: Renewable energy
LESSONS.hook: Australia has more rooftop solar per person than almost anywhere on Earth. Here's how renewables work, and what makes the switch hard.

sections.key: Renewable energy comes from naturally replenished sources and produces almost no emissions while running.
sections.b:
Renewable energy comes from sources that are constantly replenished: sunlight, wind, flowing water and heat from the Earth. Fossil fuels like coal and gas release carbon dioxide stored over millions of years when burned, and electricity generation has long been one of Australia's largest sources of greenhouse emissions.

Renewables produce almost no emissions while running, although making and installing them has a footprint. Across their whole lifetime, solar, wind and hydro emit only a small fraction of the carbon of coal per unit of electricity. They also use free fuel, a big reason the cost of renewable electricity has fallen so sharply over the past two decades.

sections.key: Solar panels turn sunlight directly into electricity using silicon cells, and Australia has one of the highest rates of rooftop solar in the world.
sections.b:
Solar photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity. When light hits a cell of specially treated silicon, it knocks electrons loose and the cell's structure pushes them one way, creating direct current. An inverter converts this to the alternating current used in homes. A University of New South Wales team led by Martin Green developed the PERC cell design in the 1980s, which became the world's dominant solar cell technology for years. Panel prices fell by around 90% during the 2010s as mass production scaled up, largely in China.

Sunshine, rebates and falling prices helped more than a third of Australian houses install panels, around four million systems by the mid-2020s, among the highest rates per person in the world.

sections.key: Wind turbines complement solar because wind often blows at night, and hydro can start within minutes as backup.
sections.b:
Wind turbines capture the energy of moving air, spinning a generator. Modern towers can exceed 100 metres, with blades longer than an Olympic swimming pool. Wind speeds rise with height and power rises steeply with speed, so taller turbines produce much more. The best resources are along the southern coast and in elevated areas, and South Australia gets well over half its electricity from wind and solar combined. Wind suits solar because it often blows at night and in winter, when solar output is low.

Hydroelectric power, Australia's oldest large-scale renewable, uses water flowing downhill through turbines and can ramp up within minutes, a valuable backup when solar and wind dip. Tasmania gets most of its electricity from hydro, and the Snowy Mountains Scheme is the mainland's biggest.

sections.key: Batteries and pumped hydro store surplus renewable energy, with batteries responding to grid problems in fractions of a second.
sections.b:
At midday, rooftop solar can flood the grid, and wholesale prices sometimes go negative. Then the sun sets and the wind drops. Storage solves both problems.

In 2017, after a statewide blackout the year before, the Hornsdale Power Reserve was built near Jamestown in South Australia. At 100 megawatts, it was then the world's largest lithium-ion battery, built in under 100 days. It stabilises the grid, responding to faults in fractions of a second, faster than traditional power stations. Home batteries store daytime solar for the evening.

Snowy 2.0 is pumped hydro: it links two reservoirs, Tantangara and Talbingo, pumping water uphill when power is cheap and releasing it when needed, storing energy for days rather than hours. Its cost has blown out from about $2 billion to more than $12 billion.

sections.key: Renewables need storage, transmission, land and mined minerals, but they supply a rising share of Australia's electricity.
sections.b:
Solar and wind are variable, so the grid needs storage, backup such as gas, and smarter demand management. Good sites are often far from cities, so thousands of kilometres of new transmission lines are needed, which can face strong opposition. Wind and solar farms use large areas of land, and turbines can affect birds and landscapes. Panels, turbines and batteries need mined minerals, and recycling at scale is still developing.

Still, renewables supplied roughly 40% of electricity in the main eastern and southern grid by the mid-2020s, up from under 10% in the early 2000s, and in 2022 the federal government set a target of 82% by 2030, though progress is debated. For a home system, get several quotes from accredited installers and check rebates.

quiz.q: Why has the cost of renewable electricity fallen so sharply?
o: Renewables use free fuel and have scaled up
Fossil fuels are banned
Renewables are subsidised so heavily they cost nothing
Renewables need no equipment
quiz.e: Sunlight and wind cost nothing to use, and mass production has made equipment far cheaper.

quiz.q: What does an inverter do in a solar system?
o: Stores electricity for night-time
Cools the panels
Tracks the Sun across the sky
Converts direct current into alternating current
quiz.e: Panels produce direct current; the inverter converts it to the alternating current used in homes.

quiz.q: Why is wind a useful partner for solar?
o: Wind turbines need sunlight to work
Wind often blows at night and in winter, when solar output is low
Wind is completely constant
Solar panels power wind turbines
quiz.e: Wind often picks up when solar output is low, smoothing total renewable supply.

quiz.q: What makes Snowy 2.0 different from a regular hydro power station?
o: It pumps water uphill to store energy for later
It uses seawater
It runs only in winter
It burns gas when water is low
quiz.e: Pumped hydro stores energy by pumping water uphill when power is cheap and releasing it when needed.

quiz.q: Which is a genuine challenge of expanding renewables?
o: They produce large emissions while running
Their fuel is expensive
They need new transmission lines, storage and mined minerals
They cannot work in Australia's climate
quiz.e: Renewables have free fuel and low emissions, but need transmission, storage, land and materials.

LESSONS.push: Why South Australia's giant battery was built in under 100 days.

LESSONS.title: GDP: measuring an economy
LESSONS.hook: One number gets quoted every quarter as the scorecard for an entire nation. Here's what it actually counts, and what it quietly leaves out.

sections.key: GDP, gross domestic product, is the market value of final goods and services produced in a country over a period, and can be measured by production, income or spending.
sections.b:
GDP is the market value of all the final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a set period, usually a quarter or a year. 'Final' matters: a loaf of bread counts, but the baker's flour is not counted again, or it would be double counted. 'Domestic' means inside the country, whoever owns the business. The Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes GDP every three months. In the mid-2020s Australia produced roughly $2.5 to $2.7 trillion a year.

Every dollar spent is someone's output and someone's income, so GDP can be measured three ways: production (value added by industries), income (wages and profits), and expenditure: C + I + G + (X − M). They never match perfectly, so statisticians reconcile them, and revisions are normal.

sections.key: Real GDP strips out price rises, and GDP per person shows whether average living standards are improving.
sections.b:
If prices rise 4% and output stays flat, the dollar value of GDP still rises about 4%. That is nominal GDP. Real GDP adjusts for inflation by valuing output at constant prices, and it is what 'the economy grew 0.5% last quarter' means. Australia's real GDP has typically grown around 2 to 3% a year, and 3% growth doubles an economy in roughly 24 years.

A country can also grow GDP simply by adding people. Australia's population has grown quickly, largely through immigration, so total GDP can rise even when output per person is flat. That is why economists watch GDP per capita, in the order of $100,000 in the mid-2020s. In 2023 and 2024 several quarters saw total GDP grow while per person GDP fell, a 'per capita recession'. Averages say nothing about how income is shared.

sections.key: GDP leaves out unpaid work, counts some harm as growth, and measures activity rather than whether the activity is wise.
sections.b:
GDP only counts activity with a market price. Cooking dinner at home, raising children, caring for an ageing parent and volunteering with the local fire brigade add nothing, even though the ABS has estimated unpaid work would be worth a very large sum if paid.

Meanwhile some bad events raise GDP. Rebuilding after a bushfire or flood adds output, but the community is no better off than if the disaster had never happened. Running down a forest or mineral deposit counts as income, with no deduction for what is used up. GDP measures activity, not whether that activity is wise.

sections.key: Even GDP's pioneers warned it doesn't measure welfare, so alternatives such as the Human Development Index try to fill the gap.
sections.b:
Modern national accounts grew out of work in the 1930s by economists including Simon Kuznets, who himself warned that a nation's welfare can hardly be inferred from its national income. In 1968 US senator Robert Kennedy said gross national product, GDP's close cousin, measures everything 'except that which makes life worthwhile'.

GDP ignores leisure, health, pollution, inequality and how safe people feel. Alternatives include the United Nations' Human Development Index, which adds life expectancy and education, and the OECD's Better Life Index. In 2023 the Australian Government released 'Measuring What Matters', a framework tracking around 50 indicators of wellbeing alongside traditional economic figures.

sections.key: Treat GDP as one dashboard light: check whether it is real or per person, what drove it, and pair it with other signals.
sections.b:
Like most rich countries, Australia is mainly a services economy: health care, education, finance, retail, construction and professional services produce most output and employ most workers. Mining contributes roughly a tenth of GDP in many years and much more of exports, yet employs only around 2% of workers. Manufacturing has shrunk since the mid-20th century and agriculture is a few per cent of GDP, though both remain important exporters. Household consumption is around half of GDP.

When figures come out, ask: real or nominal? Quarterly or annual? What happened per person? Which parts drove the change? One weak quarter is not a crisis, and first estimates are often revised. Pair GDP with unemployment, wages, inflation and household income. Some of the most valuable things in your life will never appear in the national accounts.

quiz.q: Why isn't the flour a baker buys counted separately in GDP?
o: Flour is exempt from tax
It would be double counted, since its value is already in the bread
Only services are counted
Food is excluded from GDP
quiz.e: GDP counts final goods and services only.

quiz.q: How could total GDP rise while average living standards fall?
o: If exports fall
If inflation is zero
If population grows faster than output
If the dollar rises
quiz.e: That is why economists watch GDP per capita, not just the total.

quiz.q: Which of these adds nothing to GDP?
o: Rebuilding homes after a flood
Digging up iron ore
Buying a new car
Caring for an ageing parent unpaid
quiz.e: GDP only counts activity with a market price.

quiz.q: Why is GDP a poor measure of wellbeing on its own?
o: It ignores leisure, health, pollution and inequality
It counts only exports
It is published too infrequently
It includes only government spending
quiz.e: GDP measures economic activity, which is why alternatives such as the Human Development Index exist.

quiz.q: Which statement about mining in Australia's economy is true?
o: It employs most Australian workers
It is only a few per cent of exports
It has a large share of exports but employs only about 2% of workers
It makes up about half of GDP
quiz.e: Services dominate output and jobs, while mining is capital intensive.

LESSONS.push: GDP can rise while the average person gets poorer. How?

LESSONS.title: Interest rates and the RBA
LESSONS.hook: A decision made in a Sydney boardroom can change your mortgage repayment within weeks. Here's how the cash rate works and why it moves.

sections.key: The cash rate is the overnight rate banks charge each other, and the RBA sets a target for it to keep inflation between 2 and 3%.
sections.b:
Every day, banks lend each other money overnight to settle payments. The interest on those loans is the cash rate. The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) sets a target for it and holds the rate there by adjusting the interest it pays and charges banks on money held with it. The RBA doesn't set your mortgage or savings rate, but the cash rate is the base cost of short-term money, so most other rates move with it.

The RBA sets rates independently of the government of the day, which keeps election-year politics out of it. Since 1993 it has targeted inflation of 2 to 3% on average over time, while supporting full employment. Since 2025 a Monetary Policy Board has made the decisions, at eight scheduled meetings a year.

sections.key: The RBA raises rates to cool an overheating economy and cuts them to support a weak one.
sections.b:
When strong demand pushes prices up faster than the target, the RBA raises the cash rate. Borrowing costs more, so mortgage holders spend less and businesses hold back on expanding. Saving becomes more attractive, demand slows and price rises ease, though slower demand can also cost jobs. From May 2022 to November 2023 the RBA lifted the rate from a record low of 0.1% to 4.35%, one of its fastest rises.

When the economy is weak, it cuts instead, and cheaper loans encourage spending and investment. It cut sharply in the 2008 financial crisis, and in 2020 it also bought government bonds to push longer-term rates down. But rates can't fall far below zero, and very cheap money can inflate house prices and encourage risky borrowing.

sections.key: Most Australian home loans are variable, so a change in the cash rate reaches repayments within weeks.
sections.b:
Most Australian mortgages have variable rates, which lenders usually adjust soon after an RBA decision, though they can move by more or less than the cash rate. That makes Australian households more sensitive to rate changes than Americans, who mostly hold 30-year fixed loans.

The numbers add up fast. On a $500,000, 30-year loan, a rise of 0.25 percentage points lifts monthly repayments by roughly $80. The 2022 to 2023 rises added well over $1,000 a month to many such loans. Borrowers on fixed rates are shielded until their fixed term ends, when they face the new rates all at once.

sections.key: Rate rises usually help savers and tend to lift the Australian dollar, while cuts do the opposite.
sections.b:
Rate changes cut both ways. When rates rise, banks generally lift what they pay on savings accounts and term deposits, though often more slowly and by less than loan rates, so it pays to compare accounts. Retirees living off deposits welcome higher rates; borrowers don't.

Rates also affect the exchange rate. Higher Australian rates, relative to other countries, can attract foreign money and lift the dollar. That makes imports and overseas holidays cheaper and exporters less competitive. Rates influence share and property prices as well, because they change what investors can earn elsewhere and how much buyers can borrow.

sections.key: Rate changes take a year or more to work fully, so plan for a range of outcomes and keep a buffer.
sections.b:
Economists say monetary policy works with 'long and variable lags', a phrase from Milton Friedman. A rate change can take a year or two to reach spending, jobs and inflation, so the RBA must steer by forecasts. Move too slowly and inflation becomes entrenched, as in the 1970s, when it topped 15% and took years to bring down. Move too hard and the economy can tip into recession.

No one predicts rates reliably, so build in a buffer. Lenders test whether you could cope with rates about 3 percentage points higher, and it's wise to use a similar margin in your own budget. Extra repayments or an offset account help, as does comparing your rate with what new customers are offered. For decisions about your loans, talk to a licensed financial adviser or broker.

quiz.q: What is the cash rate?
o: The interest rate every bank must charge on home loans
The rate banks charge each other for overnight loans
The rate of inflation the RBA wants to reach
The rate banks pay on every savings account
quiz.e: The cash rate is the base cost of short-term money for banks, so most other rates move with it.

quiz.q: Why would the RBA raise the cash rate?
o: To cool demand when prices are rising too fast
To make borrowing cheaper for households
To help the economy grow faster
To push the price of housing higher
quiz.e: Higher rates slow spending and borrowing, which eases price rises, though it can cost jobs.

quiz.q: Why do rate changes reach Australian households so quickly?
o: Rates are fixed by law each year
Most home loans have variable interest rates
Banks must match the cash rate exactly
Most mortgages are fixed for 30 years
quiz.e: Variable-rate loans are usually adjusted soon after an RBA decision, so repayments change within weeks.

quiz.q: How do higher Australian rates tend to affect the dollar?
o: They push the dollar down and make imports dearer
They have no link to the exchange rate
They lift the dollar and make imports cheaper
They make exporters more competitive overseas
quiz.e: Higher rates can attract foreign money, lifting the dollar, which helps importers and hurts exporters.

quiz.q: Why must the RBA act on forecasts rather than current data?
o: Rate changes take a year or more to have full effect
Economic data is kept secret from the RBA
Rate decisions only take effect once a year
Banks refuse to pass on changes for months
quiz.e: Because of long and variable lags, today's decision shapes the economy a year or two ahead.

LESSONS.push: A decision in Sydney can change your repayments within weeks. Here is the lever behind it.

LESSONS.title: Why countries trade
LESSONS.hook: Australia digs, ships and teaches its way to prosperity. The idea behind it, comparative advantage, is one of economics' most surprising insights.

sections.key: Trade lets people and countries specialise in what they do best and swap for the rest.
sections.b: Imagine growing your own food, sewing your own clothes and building your own phone. You would be poor, busy and badly dressed. Instead, you specialise in a job and trade your earnings for things others make better or cheaper. Countries do the same. Australia has vast iron ore deposits and good farmland but a small population and high wages, so it makes sense to export resources and farm products and import cars, electronics and clothing. Specialisation lets workers get very good at a few things, and trade lets everyone enjoy a far wider range of goods than they could produce alone.

sections.key: Even a country that is better at everything gains by focusing on the goods it gives up least to produce.
sections.b: In 1817 British economist David Ricardo showed something counterintuitive. Suppose Portugal can make both wine and cloth more efficiently than England. Trade still benefits both, provided each specialises in the good with the lowest opportunity cost, meaning the least given up elsewhere. A top lawyer may type faster than her assistant, but her time is worth far more on legal work, so she hires the assistant to type. Both are better off. This is comparative advantage, as opposed to absolute advantage. It explains why even highly productive countries import things they could make themselves.

sections.key: Exports bring money in and imports are what we get in return, with iron ore and education among Australia's biggest earners.
sections.b:
Exports are goods and services sold to foreigners; imports are bought from abroad. Politicians often treat exports as wins and imports as losses, but most economists see imports as the point of trade: they are what we get in return. A trade deficit isn't automatically bad, and Australia ran deficits for much of its history while growing rich.

Services count too. A tourist visiting the Great Barrier Reef or a foreign student in Melbourne is an Australian export. Iron ore, mostly from the Pilbara and used to make steel, is usually the largest export, often worth over $100 billion a year, followed by coal and liquefied natural gas. International education is the largest services export. China buys around a third of Australia's goods exports.

sections.key: Tariffs protect some local jobs but raise prices for everyone else, which is why countries negotiate trade agreements.
sections.b:
A tariff is a tax on imports. It protects local producers, but consumers pay higher prices and businesses pay more for inputs. From 1973, starting with a 25% across-the-board cut, Australian governments dismantled most of the protection they had given manufacturers. Some industries shrank, and car manufacturing ended in 2017, but prices fell and more efficient industries grew. The US Smoot-Hawley tariffs of 1930 are a warning: they triggered retaliation that worsened the collapse of world trade in the Great Depression.

The World Trade Organization has set global rules since 1995. Australia also signs free trade agreements, with the US (2005), China (2015) and the UK (2023), and joins regional pacts like the CPTPP and RCEP. These lower tariffs, though benefits are often smaller than governments promise.

sections.key: Trade makes nations richer overall, but gains are uneven, costs are easy to overlook and reliance on one buyer is risky.
sections.b:
Economists broadly agree that trade raises national income, but not everyone wins. Workers facing new import competition can lose jobs, often concentrated in particular towns, so good policy offers retraining and support rather than blocking trade. Dependence is a risk too. From 2020 China restricted Australian goods including barley, wine, coal and lobster during a diplomatic dispute. Exporters were hit hard, though many found other markets and most restrictions were lifted by 2024.

Much of what you use daily was probably made overseas, and many Australian jobs depend on exports. When you hear tariff debates, ask who gains, who pays and by how much. Protection has visible winners, while its costs are spread thinly across millions of consumers.

quiz.q: Why does it make sense for Australia to import cars and clothing?
o: Australia is not allowed to make them
Exporting resources and importing other goods leaves everyone with more
Imports are always cheaper than local goods
Australia has no workers able to make them
quiz.e: Specialising in what you do best and trading for the rest gives a far wider range of goods.

quiz.q: What does comparative advantage say?
o: Only the most efficient country should make anything
Imports always harm the importing economy
Countries should aim to be fully self-sufficient
Even a country better at everything gains by specialising
quiz.e: Gains come from focusing on what costs you least to give up, not from being best at everything.

quiz.q: Why is a foreign student studying in Melbourne counted as an Australian export?
o: They pay income tax in Australia
A foreigner is paying for a service Australia provides
Universities are owned by the government
Students are never counted in trade figures
quiz.e: An export is anything a foreigner pays Australia to provide, including services like education.

quiz.q: Who bears the costs of a tariff?
o: Only the foreign producers who export
Local consumers and businesses through higher prices
No one, because tariffs raise government revenue
Only the workers in protected industries
quiz.e: Tariffs shelter some producers but make imports dearer for consumers and for businesses buying inputs.

quiz.q: What does the China trade dispute from 2020 show?
o: Exporters can never find other markets
Trade restrictions are always permanent
Relying heavily on one buyer is risky
Trade deficits cause diplomatic disputes
quiz.e: Heavy dependence on a single buyer leaves exporters exposed when relations sour.

LESSONS.push: Why a country that is better at everything still gains from trade.

LESSONS.title: Recessions: when economies shrink
LESSONS.hook: Australia once went almost 30 years without one, a record for a rich country at the time. What exactly is a recession, and what can governments do about it?

sections.key: A recession is a significant, widespread fall in economic activity, often measured as two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.
sections.b: A recession is a significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months. In Australia, the media usually applies a rule of thumb: two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP, known as a 'technical recession'. Economists prefer a broader view. In the United States, a committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research dates recessions by weighing employment, incomes, spending and production together. An economy can dip without a technical recession, and a sharp rise in unemployment can hurt more than GDP figures suggest. A very deep, long recession is called a depression.

sections.key: Recessions start when spending drops sharply, and fear can then deepen the downturn into a vicious circle.
sections.b:
Recessions usually start when spending drops sharply across the economy. Common triggers include financial crises, when banks stop lending; central banks raising rates hard to fight inflation; supply shocks like the oil price spikes of the 1970s; the bursting of share or property bubbles; and wars or pandemics.

Once spending falls, a vicious circle can take hold. Businesses sell less, so they cut staff and investment. Newly unemployed people spend less, which hurts other businesses. Fear spreads too: worried households save rather than spend, even if their own jobs are safe, deepening the downturn.

sections.key: The Great Depression pushed Australian unemployment to about 30%, and the 1990-91 recession followed a borrowing boom and very high rates.
sections.b:
The Great Depression began around 1929, marked by the Wall Street crash that October, and lasted much of the 1930s. World trade collapsed. Australia, dependent on wool and wheat exports and overseas borrowing, was hit hard, with unemployment peaking at around 30% in 1932 by union estimates. Devaluing the Australian pound in 1931 made exports cheaper for foreign buyers and gave farmers some relief, but recovery was slow.

The 1990-91 recession followed a late-1980s boom in borrowing, property and shares. The RBA lifted rates sharply, with mortgage rates reaching about 17% in 1989. Several banks and building societies ran into trouble, and unemployment rose to about 11% in 1992. Paul Keating called it 'the recession we had to have'. It locked in lower inflation, and the RBA adopted its inflation target in 1993.

sections.key: Australia avoided a technical recession from 1991 to 2020, including through the 2008 global financial crisis.
sections.b:
After 1991, Australia went nearly 29 years without a technical recession, the longest run of any advanced economy at the time. Helping factors included floating the dollar in 1983, tariff cuts, an independent central bank, strong population growth and booming Chinese demand for minerals. Critics note that population growth flattered the figures, since GDP per person fell in some periods.

In the 2008 global financial crisis, much of the world suffered its worst recession since the 1930s after Lehman Brothers collapsed. Australia recorded one negative quarter but avoided a technical recession, thanks to a well-regulated banking system, rapid RBA rate cuts, a deposit guarantee, stimulus including cash payments of up to $900 and school building, and China's own massive stimulus.

sections.key: Governments fight recessions with lower rates, extra spending and automatic stabilisers, and households can build buffers.
sections.b:
The pandemic ended the run. Real GDP fell about 7% in the June quarter of 2020, the largest quarterly fall on record. Unlike most recessions, it was caused deliberately by health measures. JobKeeper paid employers $1,500 a fortnight per eligible worker, JobSeeker payments were temporarily boosted, and the RBA cut rates to 0.1%. The rebound was quick, though the stimulus is widely thought to have added to the inflation that followed.

Governments have two main tools: monetary policy (the RBA cutting rates) and fiscal policy (extra spending, tax cuts and payments). Automatic stabilisers help too: when unemployment rises, welfare payments rise and tax revenue falls. Households can keep an emergency fund of a few months' expenses, manage debt and maintain their skills. For personal decisions, talk to a licensed financial adviser.

quiz.q: What is a 'technical recession'?
o: Any fall in the share market
Unemployment rising above 10%
A year of unusually high inflation
Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP
quiz.e: It is a simple rule of thumb, while economists also weigh jobs, incomes, spending and production.

quiz.q: Why can a downturn feed on itself?
o: Falling spending leads to job cuts, which cut spending further
Banks always lend more when sales fall
Households spend more when they feel worried
Governments raise taxes automatically
quiz.e: Less spending means less business, fewer jobs and even less spending, and fear deepens the circle.

quiz.q: What set the scene for the 1990-91 recession?
o: A collapse in wool and wheat exports
A global pandemic and lockdowns
A borrowing boom followed by sharply higher interest rates
The floating of the Australian dollar
quiz.e: A late-1980s borrowing and property boom led the RBA to raise rates sharply, and the economy contracted.

quiz.q: What helped Australia avoid a technical recession in the GFC?
o: Raising interest rates quickly to curb spending
Strong banking rules, rate cuts, stimulus and Chinese demand
Closing banks for a year to stop losses
Leaving global trade until the crisis passed
quiz.e: Policy responses and China's stimulus kept demand for Australian resources strong.

quiz.q: What are automatic stabilisers?
o: Laws that freeze prices during a downturn
RBA decisions to cut interest rates sharply
Welfare and tax changes that cushion downturns automatically
Tariffs that protect local industries from imports
quiz.e: When unemployment rises, welfare payments rise and tax revenue falls, cushioning the blow automatically.

LESSONS.push: Australia once avoided recession for almost 30 years. What that streak was built on.

LESSONS.title: Writing work emails people read
LESSONS.hook: Most work emails get skimmed in seconds. A few simple habits make yours the ones that get read, understood and acted on.

sections.key: Assume your reader is busy and skimming, so make the subject line and opening say what the email is and what you need.
sections.b:
Your reader is probably on a phone between meetings, deciding from the subject line and first couple of lines whether to act now, deal with it later or ignore it. Before writing, ask: what do I want this person to know, and what do I want them to do? If you can't answer both in a sentence, you're not ready to write.

Treat the subject line as a headline. 'Quick question' or 'Update' says nothing and is hard to find later. Try 'Approval needed: Q3 marketing budget by Friday'. Prefixes like 'Action:' or 'FYI:' help people triage. If the topic changes, change the subject line. A very short message can go entirely in the subject, followed by 'EOM' (end of message).

sections.key: Put your main point or request in the first sentence or two, then the detail.
sections.b:
Many of us were taught to write chronologically: background, then reasoning, then the point. At work, flip it. Put the bottom line up front, a habit known as BLUF, borrowed from military writing. Start with the conclusion, decision or request, then add context for anyone who wants it.

Compare 'Following our discussion last week, and after reviewing the supplier quotes, I've looked at our options...' with 'I recommend we go with Supplier B; it's $4,000 cheaper and can deliver two weeks sooner. Details below.' The second version can be understood and acted on even if the reader stops after one sentence.

sections.key: Keep emails short, one topic each, and say exactly what you need, from whom and by when.
sections.b:
Aim for an email that fits on a phone screen. Cut warm-up phrases like 'I just wanted to reach out to touch base regarding'. Stick to one topic per email, or one of them gets forgotten, and use short paragraphs. Number multiple questions so the reader can reply 'Yes to 1, no to 2'. If it needs pages of explanation, attach a document or book a meeting.

Vague requests get vague results. 'Thoughts?' invites delay; 'Can you confirm by Thursday 5 pm whether the venue booking for 40 people is okay?' gets an answer. Name the person when writing to several, because a request addressed to everyone is often done by no one. Offer options ('Does 10 am or 2 pm suit?'), and say 'No reply needed' when it applies.

sections.key: Email strips out tone, so write a little warmer than feels necessary, and talk instead when the matter is urgent or emotional.
sections.b:
Without voice and facial expression, readers tend to read neutral messages as more negative than intended. A clipped 'Fine.' or 'Per my last email' can land as irritation. In Australian workplaces, 'Hi Sam' and 'Thanks' or 'Kind regards' are standard. Avoid sarcasm, excessive exclamation marks and ALL CAPS, and match your reader's formality.

Email is poor for some jobs. If it's urgent, call. If it's emotional, such as feedback, conflict or bad news, talk in person or by video. If a chain goes back and forth three or four times, have a quick conversation, then send a short summary of what was agreed. Never send an email while angry: save it as a draft and reread it later. Work emails can be forwarded and may be used in legal disputes.

sections.key: Run a quick final check of recipients, attachments, the ask and the tone before sending.
sections.b:
A thirty-second check prevents most email embarrassments. Are the right people in To (who must act) and Cc (who just need to know)? Use Reply All only when everyone genuinely needs your reply. Did you attach the file you mentioned? Is your key point in the first lines, with any request and deadline clear? Are names spelt correctly? Read anything sensitive aloud and imagine how it sounds to someone having a bad day.

Many email programs let you delay or schedule sending. That gives you a window to catch mistakes and avoids late-night emails that pressure colleagues to reply outside hours. Then send, and move on.

quiz.q: Which subject line is most effective?
o: Quick question
Update
Hi
Approval needed: Q3 budget by Friday
quiz.e: A good subject line tells the reader what the email is about and what is needed.

quiz.q: Which opening best follows 'bottom line up front'?
o: Following last week's discussion, I have reviewed the quotes...
I recommend Supplier B: it is $4,000 cheaper and delivers sooner.
I hope you are well and having a good week...
As you know, we have been looking at suppliers...
quiz.e: Leading with the conclusion lets the reader act even if they stop after one sentence.

quiz.q: Why should you name a specific person when making a request to a group?
o: Email programs require a named recipient
It shortens the email
A request to everyone is often done by no one
It is more polite than using first names
quiz.e: Naming the person makes clear who is responsible, so the request actually gets done.

quiz.q: What should you do when an email chain has gone back and forth three or four times?
o: Have a quick conversation, then summarise what was agreed
Add more people to the thread
Reply in capital letters to stress the point
Wait a week and send a longer reply
quiz.e: Talking resolves it faster, and a short written summary keeps the record.

quiz.q: Who belongs in the To line rather than Cc?
o: People who just need to know
Your manager, on every email
People who must act on the email
Anyone mentioned by name
quiz.e: To is for people who must act, and Cc is for those who only need to be informed.

LESSONS.push: Most work emails are judged in seconds. What decides whether yours gets read?

LESSONS.title: Acing a job interview
LESSONS.hook: Interviews reward preparation far more than charisma. Here's how to research, structure your stories and follow up like a pro.

sections.key: Interviewers want evidence you can do the job, will want to do it and will fit the team, so prepare examples and research the organisation.
sections.b:
Interviewers want to know three things: can you do the job, will you want to do it, and will you work well with the team? Your task is to give clear evidence for all three. Start with the position description, highlight the key skills and selection criteria, and pick a real example for each. Sort out the practical details: time, location or video link, and who you're meeting. Arrive about ten minutes early, or test your technology beforehand.

Then research the organisation: its website, news coverage and the LinkedIn profiles of your interviewers. Don't just recite facts; connect them to yourself: 'I saw you're expanding into Queensland; I managed a similar regional rollout in my last role.'

sections.key: Answer behavioural questions with STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
sections.b:
Behavioural questions ask how you handled real situations: 'Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer.' The idea is that past behaviour is a reasonable guide to future behaviour. The STAR method gives your answer a clear shape.

Situation: briefly set the scene. Task: what you needed to achieve. Action: what you did, the heart of the answer, so use 'I' rather than 'we'. Result: what happened, ideally with a number, and what you learnt. Aim for one to two minutes per answer. Prepare six to eight STAR stories in advance, since each can usually be adapted to several different questions.

sections.key: Prepare for classic questions, and when stumped, pause, ask for clarification and be honest.
sections.b:
'Tell me about yourself' invites a one to two minute professional summary: your current role, relevant experience and why this job, not your life story. 'What's a weakness?' calls for a genuine but manageable weakness and what you're doing about it, not a disguised boast like 'I'm a perfectionist'. If asked why you're leaving, stay positive and never criticise a former employer.

Nerves are normal. If stumped, say 'Good question, let me think.' If unsure what's being asked, ask. If you don't know something, say so and explain how you'd find out. For salary, research typical pay beforehand and give a range. In Australia, anti-discrimination laws generally stop employers basing hiring decisions on attributes such as age, pregnancy, race or disability, so you can politely steer back to your ability to do the job.

sections.key: Practise answers out loud, let enthusiasm show and always have thoughtful questions ready for them.
sections.b:
First impressions form early: arrive on time, greet people warmly, dress slightly more formally than the workplace's everyday standard, and be polite to everyone, including the receptionist. On video, check lighting, framing, sound and background, and look at the camera. The most useful habit is practising answers out loud, with a friend or by recording yourself, because things that sound fine in your head often come out rambling. Employers often choose the capable candidate who clearly wants the job over a slightly stronger but indifferent one.

When asked 'Do you have any questions for us?', don't say no. Try 'What would success look like in the first six months?' The answers help you decide if you want the job. Save leave and pay for later.

sections.key: Send a brief thank-you, prepare your referees, and reflect on what to improve.
sections.b:
Within a day, consider sending a short email thanking the interviewer and briefly restating your interest. It won't rescue a poor interview, but it's courteous and keeps you front of mind. In Australia, reference checks with previous managers are common, so give your referees a heads-up and tell them about the role.

Write down the questions you were asked and how you answered while it's fresh; it's valuable practice for next time. If you haven't heard back by the date they mentioned, a polite follow-up email is fine. If you miss out, it's reasonable to ask for feedback, though not every employer will provide it.

quiz.q: What are most interviewers trying to find out?
o: Your age, address and salary history
Your hobbies, school and family life
Whether you can do the job, want it and will fit the team
Whether you have any weaknesses at all
quiz.e: Your job is to give clear evidence for all three, using real examples.

quiz.q: What does the 'A' in STAR stand for, and why does it matter most?
o: Action: what you did, which is the heart of the answer
Attitude: how you felt about the situation
Answer: the final reply to the question
Ability: the skills listed in the job ad
quiz.e: The Action step shows what you personally did, so say 'I' rather than 'we'.

quiz.q: What is a good answer to 'What's a weakness?'
o: A disguised boast such as being a perfectionist
A genuine, manageable weakness and what you are doing about it
Saying you have no weaknesses
A weakness that makes you unfit for the role
quiz.e: Honesty plus a plan for improvement is more convincing than a disguised boast.

quiz.q: Why practise your answers out loud?
o: Answers that sound fine in your head often come out rambling
It lets you memorise a script word for word
It removes the need to research the employer
Interviewers expect rehearsed speeches
quiz.e: Speaking aloud shows where answers ramble, so you can tighten them before the day.

quiz.q: Which is a sensible step after the interview?
o: Call daily for an update on the decision
Post about the interview on social media
Apply again for the same job next day
Brief your referees and note your answers for next time
quiz.e: Preparing referees and reflecting on your answers helps this application and the next.

LESSONS.push: Every interviewer is trying to answer three questions. Do you know them?

LESSONS.title: Genes and inheritance
LESSONS.hook: Why do you have your mother's eyes but your grandfather's chin, and why can two siblings look like strangers?

sections.key: A gene is a stretch of DNA carrying instructions for a protein, and you inherit two copies of most genes.
sections.b: A gene is a section of DNA that holds instructions, usually for building a particular protein. Proteins do most of the work in your body, from carrying oxygen to colouring your eyes. Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes, packed into 23 pairs of chromosomes inside almost every cell. One chromosome in each pair came from your mother and one from your father, so you carry two copies of most genes. Different versions of the same gene are called alleles. One allele might produce more pigment, another less, and the combination you inherit shapes the result.

sections.key: Mendel found by breeding peas that traits don't blend, and that dominant alleles show with one copy while recessive ones need two.
sections.b:
Gregor Mendel, a monk in what is now the Czech Republic, crossed thousands of pea plants between about 1856 and 1863, tracking traits like flower colour and plant height. Traits didn't blend: tall crossed with short gave tall, not medium. Some versions mask others. A dominant allele shows with one copy; a recessive allele needs two, one from each parent.

Purple crossed with white peas gave all purple. But when those plants bred together, white flowers returned in about one in four offspring, roughly three to one. The white allele was hidden, not lost. Mendel published in 1866 and was largely ignored; around 1900 three scientists independently rediscovered his work.

sections.key: People can carry a recessive allele without knowing, and two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance per child of passing on two copies.
sections.b:
Because recessive alleles can hide, many people carry one copy of a gene variant linked to a genetic condition without any sign of it. Cystic fibrosis is a well-known example: roughly 1 in 25 Australians carries a cystic fibrosis variant.

If two carriers have a child, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of the child inheriting two copies, a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier, and a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting neither. This is why reproductive carrier screening is offered in Australia; a GP or genetic counsellor can explain the options.

sections.key: Most traits are shaped by many genes plus environment, and random shuffling makes every child a unique mix.
sections.b:
Mendel chose traits controlled mainly by one gene. Most human traits are messier. Height involves thousands of genetic variants, each with a tiny effect, plus childhood nutrition and health. Eye colour involves several genes, which is why two blue-eyed parents can occasionally have a brown-eyed child. Environment matters too: genes load the dice, but diet, experience and chance help decide the roll.

Siblings differ because each egg or sperm carries one chromosome from each of 23 pairs, chosen at random, allowing over 8 million combinations. Crossing over, where chromosomes swap segments, shuffles genes further. Full siblings share about half of the DNA that varies between people, on average. Identical twins share almost all of it.

sections.key: Recessive variants on the X chromosome show up more often in men, and genes are influences rather than destiny.
sections.b:
Genes on the X chromosome behave unusually. Most females have two X chromosomes; most males have one X and a much smaller Y. If a male inherits a recessive variant on his single X, no second copy masks it. That is why red-green colour blindness affects roughly 1 in 12 men of northern European ancestry but only about 1 in 200 women. Haemophilia follows the same pattern, usually passing from carrier mothers to sons.

If a condition appears in several relatives, mention it to your GP, who may suggest screening or a genetic counsellor. A gene variant linked to disease often raises risk rather than guaranteeing illness, and lifestyle matters for conditions like heart disease. Consumer DNA tests vary in accuracy for health claims.

quiz.q: What does a gene usually contain?
o: A copy of your whole genome
Instructions for building a protein
The memories you inherit
A fixed prediction of your health
quiz.e: A gene is a stretch of DNA that holds instructions, usually for a protein.

quiz.q: Why did white flowers reappear when Mendel bred the purple first-generation peas together?
o: The white allele had been hidden, not lost
The purple allele weakened over time
The plants blended into a paler colour
White flowers mutate in the second generation
quiz.e: A recessive allele can be carried silently until two copies meet.

quiz.q: If both parents are carriers of a recessive condition, what is the chance a child inherits two copies?
o: 1 in 2
1 in 10
1 in 4
Certain
quiz.e: Each child of two carriers has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting two copies.

quiz.q: Why can full siblings look quite different?
o: They have different numbers of chromosomes
Only one sibling inherits the father's genes
DNA changes after birth to match the environment
Each child gets a random shuffle of each parent's DNA
quiz.e: Random chromosome selection and crossing over make each child a unique mix.

quiz.q: Why is red-green colour blindness more common in men?
o: Men have one X, so a recessive variant isn't masked
It is carried on the Y chromosome
Testosterone damages colour vision
Men have more colour genes to go wrong
quiz.e: With only one X chromosome, a male has no second copy to mask a recessive variant.

LESSONS.push: Two blue-eyed parents can have a brown-eyed child. The textbook story is too simple.

LESSONS.title: The human story
LESSONS.hook: For most of the last few hundred thousand years, we weren't alone: several kinds of human shared the planet, and some of them are in your DNA.

sections.key: Humans didn't descend from chimpanzees; we share an ancestor from 6 to 7 million years ago, and upright walking came long before big brains.
sections.b:
Humans didn't evolve from chimpanzees. Both lineages descend from a shared ancestral ape that lived in Africa roughly 6 to 7 million years ago, and both have kept evolving since. Species on our side of the split are called hominins. Their family tree is a bushy shrub, not a ladder, with several branches living at once and most ending in extinction. We are the only surviving twig.

In 1974 in Ethiopia, Donald Johanson's team found about 40% of a skeleton they named Lucy, after the Beatles song playing in camp. She was an Australopithecus afarensis who lived about 3.2 million years ago, around a metre tall with a chimp-sized brain, yet her hips and legs show she walked upright. Footprints at Laetoli, Tanzania, about 3.6 million years old, confirm it.

sections.key: Stone tools and bigger brains came first, then Homo erectus became the first hominin known to spread beyond Africa.
sections.b:
The oldest known stone tools, from Lomekwi in Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, older than our genus, Homo. From around 2.5 million years ago, sharp flakes become common across East Africa, and early Homo species such as Homo habilis appear, though exactly which species belong where is debated. Better tools gave access to meat and marrow, which probably fuelled larger brains.

Homo erectus appeared about 2 million years ago, with long legs and a body much like ours, and made shaped stone hand axes. It was the first hominin known to leave Africa: fossils about 1.8 million years old have been found in Georgia, and the species reached China and Java, where it may have survived until around 110,000 years ago. When hominins learned to control fire is debated.

sections.key: Homo sapiens arose in Africa about 300,000 years ago and later met Neanderthals and Denisovans, whose DNA many of us still carry.
sections.b:
Our species evolved in Africa. The oldest fossils generally assigned to it, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, are about 300,000 years old. Many researchers think modern humans emerged across Africa, with regional populations exchanging genes, rather than in one small cradle.

When modern humans spread out of Africa, they met other humans. Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia from roughly 400,000 until about 40,000 years ago, and were skilled toolmakers who buried some of their dead. Denisovans are known mainly from DNA, first read in 2010 from a finger bone in Siberia. Both interbred with our ancestors. People with ancestry from outside Africa typically carry 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA, and many Papua New Guineans and Aboriginal Australians carry several per cent Denisovan DNA.

sections.key: Modern humans spread across the world from about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago and reached Australia at least 50,000 and possibly 65,000 years ago.
sections.b:
The main dispersal of modern humans out of Africa happened roughly 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. People moved along coasts and across Asia with remarkable speed, and reaching Australia required sea crossings even when sea levels were low.

Excavations at Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land have produced dates of about 65,000 years, though some researchers argue for closer to 50,000; the range is still debated. At Lake Mungo in New South Wales, the burials of Mungo Lady and Mungo Man are around 40,000 years old. Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples also hold that they have always been on this land.

sections.key: Every living person belongs to one young, closely related species, and the human family tree is a bush, not a chain.
sections.b:
The human story has a few big lessons. First, all living people belong to one young species, and genetically we are very similar; there is more genetic variation within Africa than between Africa and the rest of the world. Second, being the only human species is unusual. For most of hominin history, several kinds of human lived at once.

Third, the story keeps changing as new fossils and ancient DNA emerge, so treat any date as a best current estimate. When you read a headline about a 'missing link', remember the family tree is a bush, not a chain. Other species, like the small Homo floresiensis of Indonesia, also survived until relatively recently.

quiz.q: What did Lucy's skeleton show about human evolution?
o: Big brains came before walking upright
Early hominins already used fire
Walking upright came long before big brains
Hominins first evolved outside Africa
quiz.e: Lucy had a chimp-sized brain but upright-walking hips and legs.

quiz.q: Why is Homo erectus significant?
o: It was the first hominin known to spread beyond Africa
It was the first to make any stone tools
It evolved directly from modern humans
It never left Africa
quiz.e: Fossils in Georgia, China and Java show Homo erectus travelled widely.

quiz.q: How much Neanderthal DNA do people with ancestry from outside Africa typically carry?
o: None at all
About 25%
About 1 to 2%
About 50%
quiz.e: Modern humans interbred with Neanderthals, so most people today carry a small share of their DNA.

quiz.q: How should we treat the date humans first reached Australia?
o: As settled at exactly 40,000 years ago
As a debated range, from about 50,000 to 65,000 years
As unknowable, since no evidence exists
As recent, within the last 10,000 years
quiz.e: Dates are best current estimates, and the range for first arrival is still debated.

quiz.q: Why is the idea of a 'missing link' misleading?
o: The human family tree is a bush with many branches, not a chain
Humans evolved from chimpanzees in a straight line
Fossils have been found for every ancestor
Evolution only happened once
quiz.e: Several hominin species lived at once, so evolution wasn't a single line from ape to human.

LESSONS.push: For most of our history, we shared Earth with other kinds of human. Some live on in us.

LESSONS.title: Extinction
LESSONS.hook: Over 99% of all species that have ever lived are gone. What wiped them out, and are we living through the next great loss?

sections.key: More than 99% of all species that ever lived are extinct, so what matters is how fast species are being lost.
sections.b:
Extinction is the permanent loss of a species, and it is a normal part of life's history. More than 99% of all species that have ever existed are now extinct. A typical species lasts around one to ten million years in the fossil record, though some survive far longer. What matters is the rate.

Most of the time, species vanish slowly, called background extinction. One widely used estimate is roughly one extinction per million species per year. Occasionally something far more dramatic happens: a mass extinction, often defined as the loss of at least three-quarters of Earth's species in a geologically short time, perhaps thousands to a few million years. These events reshape life, clearing space for new groups.

sections.key: Five mass extinctions are known, and rapid environmental change, such as huge volcanism or an asteroid, is the common thread.
sections.b:
Scientists recognise five mass extinctions. The end-Ordovician, about 445 million years ago, struck as ice ages dropped sea levels. The Late Devonian, around 372 million, hit reefs and marine life. The end-Permian, about 252 million, was the worst, wiping out roughly 90% of marine species. The end-Triassic, 201 million, cleared the way for dinosaurs. The end-Cretaceous, 66 million years ago, killed the non-bird dinosaurs and around three-quarters of all species.

The Permian and Triassic events coincide with enormous volcanic eruptions that released carbon dioxide, causing warming, ocean acidification and oxygen-starved seas. The Cretaceous is linked to an asteroid about 10 kilometres wide striking near Chicxulub in Mexico, as huge Indian eruptions also ran. Change faster than species can adapt or move is what kills.

sections.key: Human activity is driving extinctions far above the background rate, with around a million species threatened.
sections.b:
