Today, extinctions are running far above the background rate. A major 2019 global assessment by the scientific body IPBES estimated that around one million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades. The main drivers are habitat destruction, especially clearing land for farming, overhunting and overfishing, invasive species, pollution and climate change.

Whether this already counts as a 'sixth mass extinction' is debated: the losses so far are well short of three-quarters of species. But many scientists warn that, at current rates, we could be heading that way.

sections.key: Australia has lost more than 30 native mammals since 1788, mostly to feral predators, land clearing and changed fire patterns.
sections.b:
Australia has one of the world's worst records for mammal extinctions. Since 1788, more than 30 native mammals have been lost, including the lesser bilby and the pig-footed bandicoot. The main culprits are feral cats and foxes, along with land clearing and changed fire patterns. Small ground-dwelling mammals fared worst, and many survivors cling on in small pockets or on islands.

Some losses unfolded in plain sight. The Christmas Island pipistrelle, a bat weighing a few grams, declined steeply through the 2000s. A rescue was approved in July 2009, but searchers found only one bat. Its last call was recorded on 26 August 2009. The Bramble Cay melomys, a rodent on a tiny Torres Strait cay, was flooded repeatedly by rising seas and declared extinct in 2019, widely described as the first mammal lost to human-driven climate change.

sections.key: Controlling feral predators, protecting habitat and creating safe havens have already brought Australian species back from the brink.
sections.b:
The news isn't all bad. Conservation works when it tackles the real causes. In Australia, fenced predator-free sanctuaries and islands cleared of cats, foxes and rats have allowed species like bilbies, bettongs and numbats to recover in places. Lord Howe Island's rodent eradication, carried out in 2019, has helped native birds and insects rebound.

Individuals can help too: keep cats indoors or contained, choose native plants, support habitat protection, and report sightings of threatened species to citizen science programs. Every species kept alive keeps options open for the future.

quiz.q: Since extinction is normal, what matters when judging today's losses?
o: Whether any species has ever vanished
How fast species are disappearing compared with the usual pace
Whether the lost species were large animals
How long ago the first extinction happened
quiz.e: The concern is the rate of loss, which is now far above the background pace.

quiz.q: What is the common thread behind mass extinctions?
o: Slow cooling over hundreds of millions of years
Disease spreading among large animals
Competition from newly evolved mammals
Rapid environmental change faster than species can adapt
quiz.e: Whether volcanism, an asteroid or ice ages, fast change is what kills.

quiz.q: Is today's loss of species already a sixth mass extinction?
o: Yes, because three-quarters of species have gone
Debated, because losses so far are well short of three-quarters
No, because current extinction rates are normal
Yes, because 99% of species have gone
quiz.e: Rates are far above background, but a mass extinction means losing about three-quarters of species.

quiz.q: What are the main causes of Australia's mammal extinctions since 1788?
o: Drought alone
Feral cats and foxes, land clearing and changed fire patterns
Asteroid impacts and disease from zoos
Overhunting by tourists
quiz.e: Introduced predators plus habitat change hit small ground-dwelling mammals hardest.

quiz.q: What has helped Australian species recover?
o: Predator-free sanctuaries and islands cleared of feral pests
Releasing more cats and foxes into the wild
Clearing more land for new farms
Leaving threatened species alone to recover
quiz.e: Conservation works when it tackles the real causes, such as feral predators.

LESSONS.push: More than 99% of species that ever lived are gone. The real question is how fast.

LESSONS.title: Gene editing and CRISPR
LESSONS.hook: A tool borrowed from bacteria now lets scientists rewrite DNA letter by letter. It has already cured patients, and caused a scandal.

sections.key: CRISPR is a bacterial immune system that scientists reprogrammed in 2012 to cut chosen DNA, winning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
sections.b:
CRISPR began in bacteria. Many store short snippets of viral DNA in a region of their genome called CRISPR. If the virus returns, the bacterium makes RNA copies that guide cutting proteins, such as Cas9, to the matching viral DNA. In the 2000s scientists realised that reprogramming the guide could direct the cut to almost any sequence.

In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed CRISPR-Cas9 could be programmed to cut chosen DNA in a test tube, and within months teams including Feng Zhang's showed it worked in human cells. Earlier tools, such as zinc finger nucleases and TALENs, were slow and costly to redesign for each target. CRISPR was cheap, fast and flexible. Doudna and Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

sections.key: A guide RNA leads Cas9 to a matching DNA sequence, where it cuts, and the cell's repair either disables the gene or inserts a new sequence.
sections.b: The system has two main parts. A short guide RNA, designed to match about 20 letters of target DNA, leads the Cas9 protein to the right spot in the genome. Cas9 then cuts both strands of the DNA. The cell rushes to repair the break. Often the repair is sloppy, adding or deleting a few letters, which usually disables the gene. If scientists also supply a template, the cell can sometimes copy it in, inserting a corrected sequence. Newer versions, called base editing and prime editing, can change individual letters without fully cutting the DNA, making edits more precise.

sections.key: Casgevy, approved in 2023, uses CRISPR on a patient's own stem cells to treat sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia.
sections.b: The first approved CRISPR medicine, Casgevy, was approved in the United Kingdom in November 2023 and in the United States soon after. It treats sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia, inherited blood disorders caused by faulty haemoglobin. Doctors collect a patient's blood stem cells and edit them to switch back on a form of haemoglobin normally made only before birth. After chemotherapy clears the old bone marrow, the edited cells are returned. Many trial patients became free of severe pain crises or regular transfusions. The treatment is gruelling and extremely expensive, costing millions of dollars per patient.

sections.key: Somatic edits affect only one patient, while germline edits would pass to future generations, which is why they are so controversial.
sections.b:
Where the change is made matters. Somatic editing changes cells in one patient, such as blood or liver cells, and isn't passed to children, like any other medical treatment. Germline editing changes embryos, eggs or sperm, so every cell of the resulting person, and all their descendants, would carry the edit. That raises deep questions of safety and consent, and Australia, like many countries, prohibits heritable changes to the human genome.

In November 2018, Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced the birth of twin girls from embryos edited to disable the CCR5 gene, aiming at HIV resistance. A third edited child followed. The edits were medically unnecessary and imprecise, and consent was a serious concern. He was sentenced to three years in prison in 2019, and the case prompted calls for stronger oversight.

sections.key: Gene editing offers real hope, from crops to inherited disease, but raises questions of safety, cost and where to draw the line.
sections.b:
Genetic modification of crops long predates CRISPR; the first GM food, a slow-softening tomato, went on sale in the US in 1994. In Australia nearly all cotton is GM, and GM canola has been grown in several states since 2008, though Tasmania keeps a moratorium. Since 2019, simple CRISPR edits that add no new DNA are not treated as GMOs.

Trials are testing treatments for inherited blindness, high cholesterol and rare liver diseases, and gene drives could spread edits through pests like malaria-carrying mosquitoes. Questions remain: unintended edits, who can afford treatment, and where treating disease ends and enhancement begins. When you read about a 'breakthrough', check whether it was in cells, animals or human trials, and whether it was peer reviewed.

quiz.q: Where did the CRISPR system originally come from?
o: A bacterial defence against viruses
Chemists designing it from scratch
Human white blood cells
Plants capturing sunlight
quiz.e: Bacteria store viral DNA snippets as a memory, and scientists reprogrammed that system.

quiz.q: What role does the guide RNA play in CRISPR-Cas9?
o: It repairs the cut afterwards
It copies the whole genome
It leads Cas9 to a matching DNA sequence
It switches off the cell
quiz.e: The guide RNA is programmed to match the target, so Cas9 cuts in the right place.

quiz.q: What does the approved CRISPR therapy Casgevy treat?
o: Cystic fibrosis and HIV
Sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia
Type 1 diabetes
Inherited blindness
quiz.e: It edits a patient's own blood stem cells so they make a form of haemoglobin normally made before birth.

quiz.q: What makes germline editing especially controversial?
o: It only affects skin cells in one person
It is cheaper than somatic editing
The edits can be passed on to future generations
It is legal and unregulated everywhere
quiz.e: A germline edit would be carried by all of a person's descendants, raising deep safety and consent questions.

quiz.q: How should you judge a gene-editing 'breakthrough' headline?
o: Trust it if it mentions the word CRISPR
Assume it will reach patients within months
Check if it involved cells, animals or humans, and peer review
Ignore any result that involves animal studies
quiz.e: Most advances take years to reach patients, so the stage of the research matters.

LESSONS.push: Bacteria invented a way to cut DNA. Humans borrowed it, with remarkable results.

LESSONS.title: The first life on Earth
LESSONS.hook: Some of the oldest evidence of life on Earth is in Western Australia, and you can still see its living relatives at Shark Bay.

sections.key: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, yet zircon crystals from Western Australia suggest liquid water existed within a few hundred million years.
sections.b: Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago from dust and rock orbiting the young Sun. Early on, a Mars-sized body is thought to have smashed into it, flinging out the debris that became the Moon. The surface was bombarded by space rocks and the air had no oxygen. Yet it may have cooled faster than once thought. Tiny zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, about 4.4 billion years old, are the oldest known pieces of Earth, and their chemistry suggests liquid water, perhaps even oceans, existed remarkably early.

sections.key: No one knows exactly how life began, but all living things descend from a single ancestral population called LUCA.
sections.b:
How non-living chemistry became life is a great open question. In 1952, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey passed sparks through gases and water and made amino acids, showing life's ingredients can form naturally. Leading ideas include deep-sea hydrothermal vents and shallow ponds that dry out and refill, concentrating chemicals, an echo of Darwin's 'warm little pond'. Many researchers think early life used RNA, which can both store information and speed up reactions, before DNA and proteins took over.

All living things share the same basic genetic code, pointing to LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. It wasn't the first life, but the population all survivors descend from, probably single-celled microbes in a warm, oxygen-free place. One 2024 study estimated about 4.2 billion years ago; the timing is debated.

sections.key: The oldest widely accepted evidence of life, about 3.5 billion years old, is in Western Australia, and living versions survive at Shark Bay.
sections.b:
Some of the oldest widely accepted evidence of life comes from the Pilbara in Western Australia. Rocks about 3.5 billion years old contain stromatolites, layered structures built by microbial communities, and the 3.4 billion-year-old stromatolites at Strelley Pool are well studied. Older claims exist, including possible 3.7 billion-year-old stromatolites in Greenland, but they are contested because non-living processes can mimic life.

You can see living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, a World Heritage Area. The water is about twice as salty as seawater, which keeps away snails and other grazers. Microbial mats trap and bind sediment into domes, often growing a fraction of a millimetre a year. Some are thought to be a few thousand years old. They offer a glimpse of what coastlines may have looked like for much of Earth's history.

sections.key: Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen from photosynthesising cyanobacteria began building up in the air, transforming the planet.
sections.b: For its first two billion years, Earth's air had almost no oxygen. That changed when cyanobacteria began photosynthesising, using sunlight to split water and releasing oxygen as waste. At first the oxygen was absorbed by iron dissolved in the oceans, which rusted and settled to form banded iron formations. The Pilbara's huge iron-ore deposits in the Hamersley Range formed in this era, so Australia's iron exports partly owe their existence to ancient microbes. Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen began building up in the atmosphere, an event called the Great Oxidation Event. It was toxic to many microbes but opened the way for complex life.

sections.key: Complex cells arose when one microbe engulfed another, and most major animal groups appeared rapidly in the Cambrian.
sections.b:
The complex cell, or eukaryote, has a nucleus and internal compartments, and plants, animals and fungi are all built from them. A key event was when one microbe engulfed another without digesting it, and the swallowed partner became the mitochondrion, the cell's power station. Plants gained chloroplasts by absorbing cyanobacteria. This idea, endosymbiosis, was championed by Lynn Margulis in the 1960s and is widely accepted. Complex cells appear in the fossil record at least 1.6 billion years ago.

Soft-bodied multicellular life appeared in the Ediacaran from about 635 million years ago. From around 538 million years ago, most major animal groups appear within perhaps 20 million years, the Cambrian explosion, bringing eyes, shells, legs and jaws. Sites include the Emu Bay Shale on Kangaroo Island.

quiz.q: What are the Jack Hills zircons in Western Australia known for?
o: Containing dinosaur fossils
Being the oldest known pieces of Earth
Having been made by bacteria
Having come from Mars
quiz.e: Their age and chemistry suggest liquid water existed very early in Earth's history.

quiz.q: What was LUCA?
o: The very first living cell
A dinosaur ancestor
The most recent population all living things descend from
A kind of ancient RNA molecule
quiz.e: LUCA wasn't the first life; it is the shared ancestor of everything alive today.

quiz.q: Why do stromatolites survive at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay?
o: The salty water keeps away many grazing animals
The water there is extremely cold
They are protected by fences and rangers
Scientists feed them every season
quiz.e: Water about twice as salty as seawater keeps out snails and other grazers that would eat the microbial mats.

quiz.q: What caused oxygen to build up in the air around 2.4 billion years ago?
o: Huge volcanic eruptions
Photosynthesising cyanobacteria
A large asteroid impact
The first land plants
quiz.e: Cyanobacteria released oxygen as a waste product of photosynthesis, and once the oceans' iron was used up it built up in the air.

quiz.q: How did mitochondria originate, according to endosymbiosis?
o: They evolved from plant leaves
They formed after the Cambrian explosion
They are viruses that live inside cells
One microbe engulfed another, which lived on inside it
quiz.e: The swallowed microbe wasn't digested and became the cell's power station.

LESSONS.push: You can still see relatives of Earth's earliest life on a Western Australian shore.

LESSONS.title: Fossils
LESSONS.hook: Almost nothing that dies becomes a fossil. The few that do are messages from deep time, and Australia holds some of the most important.

sections.key: Fossilisation is rare: an organism usually needs quick burial, so the record favours hard parts and watery places.
sections.b: Most living things vanish after death. Scavengers eat them, bacteria break them down and weather scatters the rest. To become a fossil, an organism usually needs to be buried quickly in mud, sand, volcanic ash or sediment, which cuts off oxygen and scavengers. Hard parts such as bones, teeth and shells survive best, so the record is dominated by shelled sea creatures. Only a tiny fraction of all species are thought to be preserved, mostly those living in or near water where sediment builds up. Gaps are expected, not suspicious, and predictions still work: in 2004, researchers searched rocks of the right age and found Tiktaalik, a transitional fish with limb-like fins.

sections.key: Minerals can turn buried bone into stone, while trace fossils such as footprints record what animals did.
sections.b:
Once buried, minerals such as silica or calcite can seep into bone or wood and gradually turn it to stone, keeping fine detail. Sometimes the original dissolves, leaving a mould that fills to form a cast. Soft tissue is rare: insects in amber, mammoths in Siberian permafrost, animals in tar pits.

Trace fossils record behaviour instead of bodies: footprints, burrows, bite marks, nests and coprolites, the polite name for fossilised dung. They can show how fast an animal moved or what it ate. At Lark Quarry near Winton, Queensland, thousands of dinosaur footprints about 95 million years old were once read as a stampede. Some researchers now think the animals were wading or swimming.

sections.key: Fossils are dated from rock layers and radiometric dating of volcanic rock, and carbon dating only reaches back about 50,000 years.
sections.b:
Scientists date fossils in two main ways. Relative dating uses superposition: in undisturbed layers, deeper rock is older. Widespread index fossils help match layers across regions.

For actual ages, scientists use radiometric dating, measuring the steady decay of radioactive elements such as uranium or potassium in volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil.

A common myth is that dinosaurs are carbon dated. Radiocarbon dating only works back to about 50,000 years, so it suits mammoths and early human sites, not dinosaurs.

sections.key: Landmark finds, from Mary Anning's marine reptiles to South Australia's Ediacara fossils, repeatedly forced a rethink of the history of life.
sections.b:
In the early 1800s, Mary Anning, a working-class woman from Lyme Regis in England, found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be recognised scientifically and one of the first plesiosaurs. Her finds helped establish that extinction was real, yet she was largely denied credit in her lifetime. Megalosaurus (1824) and Iguanodon (1825) were the first dinosaurs named, and early reconstructions got a lot wrong: Iguanodon's thumb spike was first placed on its nose like a rhino's horn.

In 1946, geologist Reg Sprigg noticed strange impressions in the Ediacara Hills of the Flinders Ranges. They were soft-bodied sea-floor creatures over 550 million years old, among the oldest large, complex life known. The Ediacaran period, named in 2004, was the first new geological period in over a century.

sections.key: Fossil collecting is restricted in parks and many sites, so check the rules and report significant finds to a museum.
sections.b:
Fossil hunting can be a rewarding hobby, but rules matter. Collecting is generally banned in national parks and many protected sites, and important fossils, such as those at Ediacara, are protected by law. Rules vary between states, so check before you dig, and always get landholder permission on private land.

If you find something that looks significant, photograph it where it lies, note the location and contact your state museum. Many major Australian finds, including dinosaurs around Winton, were first spotted by farmers and members of the public. Museum fossil days and guided digs are a great way to start.

quiz.q: What usually has to happen for an organism to become a fossil?
o: It dies slowly in a warm, dry place
It is covered in leaves and left in the open
It is eaten and then preserved in the predator
It is buried quickly, cutting off oxygen and scavengers
quiz.e: Quick burial protects remains from scavengers and decay, which is why fossilisation is so rare.

quiz.q: What do trace fossils such as footprints and burrows tell us?
o: How animals behaved, such as how fast they moved
Exactly what colour the animal was
Only how big the animal's skeleton was
Which rock layer is oldest
quiz.e: Trace fossils record behaviour that bones alone cannot show.

quiz.q: Why can't carbon dating be used to date dinosaur fossils?
o: Dinosaur bones contain no carbon at all
Radiocarbon dating only works back about 50,000 years
The method only works on volcanic rock
Dinosaurs lived too recently for it
quiz.e: Dinosaurs are dated with radiometric methods applied to volcanic layers, because radiocarbon fades out after about 50,000 years.

quiz.q: Why are the Ediacara fossils of South Australia significant?
o: They are the first dinosaur bones ever found
They prove that mammoths lived in Australia
They are some of the oldest large, complex organisms known
They are the youngest fossils in the world
quiz.e: Ediacara preserves soft-bodied creatures over 550 million years old, earlier than the Cambrian explosion.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a fossil that looks significant?
o: Dig it out quickly before anyone else finds it
Take it home and keep it somewhere safe
Leave it where it is and tell nobody
Photograph it where it lies, note the spot and tell a museum
quiz.e: Recording the find in place preserves its scientific value, and many major Australian finds began this way.

LESSONS.push: Almost nothing that dies becomes a fossil. Here's what it takes.

LESSONS.title: Cardio fitness
LESSONS.hook: Your heart is a muscle that answers to training. How fit it is may say more about your future health than almost any other number.

sections.key: Cardio trains your heart, lungs, blood vessels and muscles to deliver and use oxygen more efficiently.
sections.b:
Cardiovascular exercise is any sustained activity that raises your heart rate and breathing: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, running, rowing, even vigorous gardening. It trains a whole delivery system. With regular training, the heart pumps more blood with each beat, so it can beat less often. Muscles grow more tiny blood vessels, called capillaries, and more mitochondria, the structures inside cells that turn oxygen and fuel into energy.

That's why a trained person's resting heart rate is often lower. A typical adult rests somewhere between 60 and 100 beats per minute, and many endurance athletes rest in the 40s or 50s.

sections.key: Regular cardio lowers the risk of heart disease and other illnesses, and higher fitness is linked with a longer life.
sections.b:
Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Australia, and regular aerobic exercise is one of the most reliable ways to reduce the risk. It lowers blood pressure, improves cholesterol and makes the body more sensitive to insulin. Active people also have lower rates of stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression and some cancers, including bowel and breast. Benefits start within a week or two.

VO2 max is the most oxygen your body can use in hard exercise. Labs measure it with a mask; smartwatches estimate it. Large observational studies link higher fitness with longer life, and low fitness carries a risk comparable to smoking. VO2 max declines with age, but training slows the fall, and the biggest gains come when an inactive person starts moving.

sections.key: Most cardio can be easy and conversational, with a smaller share of hard intervals to lift fitness.
sections.b:
Trackers divide effort into zones of your maximum heart rate. A rough estimate of maximum is 220 minus your age, though real maximums vary by 10 or more beats. Easy, conversational effort, zone 2, sits at about 60 to 70% of maximum. Moderate intensity runs up to about 76%; vigorous is above. Wrist readings can lag or jump, so many coaches also use a 0 to 10 effort scale, where zone 2 feels like a 3 or 4.

Many endurance coaches use polarised training: about 80% of sessions easy, 20% hard. Hard intervals, such as four bouts of four minutes at high effort, raise fitness efficiently, and HIIT suits people short on time. The best ratio is debated, but mostly easy with some hard is well supported.

sections.key: Australia's 2026 guidelines ask adults for 30 minutes or more of moderate to vigorous activity on most days, plus 7,000 or more steps if they track them.
sections.b:
In March 2026, Australia replaced its physical activity guidelines with 24-hour movement guidelines covering activity, sitting and sleep. Adults of all ages should do 30 minutes or more of moderate to vigorous activity on most days, adding up to about two and a half hours a week, plus several hours of light activity, such as pottering around the house or garden.

For adults aged 18 to 64 who track their steps, the target is 7,000 or more a day. Muscle strengthening on two or more days, and balance and mobility work on three or more, round out the week.

sections.key: Start gently, build gradually, see your GP first if you have symptoms or a heart condition, and choose activity you will repeat.
sections.b:
For most people, moderate activity like walking is very safe, and the risks of staying inactive are far greater. If you have a heart condition, chest pain, dizziness, unexplained breathlessness or other chronic health issues, speak with your GP first. Exercise & Sports Science Australia publishes a short pre-exercise screening questionnaire. Stop and seek medical help if you feel chest pain or pressure, severe breathlessness or faintness.

Begin with sessions you can finish comfortably and add a little each week. The best cardio is what you keep doing: brisk walking, swimming, cycling, walking part of your commute, or parkrun, which welcomes walkers. Tracking minutes rather than distance keeps beginners patient. A GP or accredited exercise physiologist can tailor a plan.

quiz.q: Why is a trained person's resting heart rate often lower?
o: The heart muscle has become smaller and weaker
The blood vessels have narrowed
The lungs take over part of the work
The heart pumps more blood with each beat, so it beats less often
quiz.e: Training makes each beat more efficient, so fewer beats are needed.

quiz.q: What does the research say about low cardiorespiratory fitness?
o: It is linked with a mortality risk comparable to smoking
It only matters for professional athletes
It has no link to how long people live
It cannot be improved after middle age
quiz.e: Higher fitness is associated with longer life, and people can improve it at any age.

quiz.q: In polarised training, how is effort usually split?
o: Half easy and half hard
About 80% easy sessions and 20% hard sessions
Almost all sessions at maximum effort
About 20% easy and 80% hard
quiz.e: Mostly easy work builds an aerobic base, and a smaller dose of hard work lifts fitness.

quiz.q: How much activity do the 2026 guidelines ask of adults on most days?
o: 10 minutes of any movement
Two hours of vigorous exercise
30 minutes or more of moderate to vigorous activity
One hour of light stretching only
quiz.e: That adds up to about two and a half hours a week, alongside light activity, strength and balance work.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel chest pain or faintness during exercise?
o: Slow down slightly and push through
Drink water and keep going
Finish the session, then rest
Stop and seek medical help
quiz.e: Chest pain, severe breathlessness or faintness are reasons to stop and get medical help.

LESSONS.push: Why a lower resting heart rate is usually a sign of a stronger heart.

LESSONS.title: Strength training
LESSONS.hook: Muscle is not vanity. It is what lets you climb stairs, carry shopping and get up off the floor at 85.

sections.key: Strength training slows age-related muscle loss and protects bone, blood sugar control and independence at every age.
sections.b:
From around your 30s, you gradually lose muscle mass and strength unless you act, and the loss speeds up after about 60. Severe age-related muscle loss is called sarcopenia. It raises the risk of falls, fractures and losing independence. Strength training is the most effective way to slow or reverse it. It also improves blood sugar control, supports healthy bones and joints, and makes everyday tasks easier.

People in their 80s and 90s can still build meaningful strength with supervised training. Grip strength, a simple measure of overall strength, is linked with longer life in large studies.

sections.key: Muscle and bone adapt to load, and muscle also helps the body manage blood sugar.
sections.b:
Muscle and bone both respond to load. When you lift something challenging, muscle fibres are stressed, then rebuild stronger. Bones adapt to the forces placed on them too, which is why resistance and impact exercise help prevent osteoporosis. An Australian trial at Griffith University, called LIFTMOR, found that carefully supervised heavy resistance and impact training improved bone density in postmenopausal women with low bone mass.

Muscle is also the body's biggest store for glucose from food, so more muscle helps keep blood sugar steady. The metabolism boost is often overstated, though: each kilogram of muscle burns only slightly more energy at rest than fat.

sections.key: To keep getting stronger, gradually increase the challenge, using compound lifts that work many muscles at once.
sections.b:
The core principle is progressive overload. Your body adapts to the demands you place on it, then stops once a load feels easy. To keep improving, add challenge gradually: a little weight, an extra rep or set, a slower movement, or less rest. If you can do 10 good squats with a 10 kg dumbbell, aim for 12 next week, then move to 12 kg. Muscles can grow across loads from about 6 to 30 repetitions, if sets finish close to fatigue.

Compound lifts give the most return: the squat, deadlift or hip hinge, bench press or push-up, overhead press, and row or pull-up. Machines, dumbbells, bands and bodyweight all work. Learn technique with light weights first, ideally with a qualified coach.

sections.key: Aim for muscle-strengthening on at least two days a week, and remember that muscles get stronger during recovery.
sections.b:
Australia's 24-hour movement guidelines, updated in 2026, recommend muscle strengthening on at least two days a week for adults, plus balance and mobility work on three or more days, which matters most later in life for preventing falls. Two full-body sessions of 30 to 45 minutes are enough for most beginners. Start with one exercise per major movement pattern, two or three sets each, stopping with one to three reps in the tank.

Training is the stimulus; recovery is when you get stronger. Many plans leave about 48 hours before hitting a muscle group hard again, and sleep matters because repair is active overnight. Soreness a day or two later is normal and no measure of a good session. Sharp, joint or persistent pain is worth checking with a physiotherapist or doctor.

sections.key: Eat enough protein from ordinary food, and drop the myths: lifting won't make women bulky by accident, fat can't be spot-reduced, and supervised lifting is safe for teens.
sections.b:
Muscles are built from protein. Australia's baseline is about 0.84 grams per kilogram of body weight a day for men and 0.75 for women, rising for people over 70. For people who lift, benefits for muscle growth tend to level off near 1.6 grams per kilogram. A serve of 20 to 40 grams at each meal seems helpful. Eggs, meat, fish, dairy, tofu, legumes and nuts all count; protein powder is convenient, not essential.

Several myths keep people out of the weights room. Building large muscles takes years of deliberate training, so women won't get bulky by accident. You can't burn fat from one spot, so crunches alone won't flatten a stomach. Supervised strength training is safe for teens and doesn't stunt growth. If you have a health condition, talk to your doctor first.

quiz.q: Why does strength training matter as we get older?
o: It stops the skin from visibly ageing
It replaces any other kind of exercise
It only helps people who already lift
It slows muscle loss, lowering the risk of falls
quiz.e: Muscle declines from our 30s, and strength training is the most effective way to slow or reverse that.

quiz.q: How do bones respond to resistance and impact exercise?
o: They adapt to the load, which helps prevent osteoporosis
They become more brittle over time
They stop changing after childhood
They are unaffected by exercise
quiz.e: Bone, like muscle, strengthens in response to the forces placed on it.

quiz.q: What is progressive overload?
o: Lifting the heaviest weight possible every session
Gradually increasing the challenge as your body adapts
Doing the same routine until it feels hard
Adding rest days each week
quiz.e: Once a load feels easy, adding weight, reps, sets or tempo keeps the body adapting.

quiz.q: When do muscles actually get stronger?
o: Only while you are lifting
Only if you feel very sore afterwards
During recovery, after training, with food and sleep
Once you stop training for several weeks
quiz.e: Training is the stimulus, but repair and growth happen during recovery.

quiz.q: What does the evidence say about protein for people who lift?
o: Everyone needs powder to meet their needs
More than 3 g per kilogram builds the most muscle
Protein only matters once a day
Muscle-growth benefits tend to level off at around 1.6 g per kilogram
quiz.e: Most people can meet their needs from food, so protein powder is convenient, not essential.

LESSONS.push: Muscle quietly declines from your 30s. The fix is simpler than you think.

LESSONS.title: Alcohol and your body
LESSONS.hook: It's Australia's favourite social drug. Here's what actually happens after that first sip, and what 'a standard drink' really means.

sections.key: Alcohol reaches every organ within minutes, and the liver clears roughly one standard drink an hour whatever you do.
sections.b:
Alcohol is ethanol, a small molecule that dissolves in water and fat, so it spreads through the body easily. Most passes into the blood from the small intestine, and food in the stomach slows this. Within minutes it reaches the brain and every organ. People with less body water, on average smaller people and women, reach a higher blood alcohol concentration from the same drink. It also carries about 29 kilojoules per gram, nearly as much as fat, with no nutritional value.

The liver does most of the clearing, converting ethanol to toxic acetaldehyde, then to acetate. It works at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink an hour for many people. Coffee, cold showers and exercise don't speed it up, so you can still be over the limit the morning after.

sections.key: An Australian standard drink holds 10 grams of pure alcohol, and the NHMRC advises no more than 10 a week and 4 on any one day.
sections.b:
One standard drink contains 10 grams of pure alcohol, whatever the drink, and serves rarely line up neatly. A 375 mL can of full-strength beer is about 1.4, mid-strength about one. A 150 mL glass of wine is about 1.5, and a 750 mL bottle around 7 to 8. A 30 mL nip of spirits is about one, but pre-mixed cans are often 1.5 to 2 or more. Labels must state the number.

The NHMRC's 2020 guidelines advise healthy adults to drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day. The less you drink, the lower your risk. People under 18, and women who are pregnant, planning a pregnancy or breastfeeding, are advised not to drink. The guidelines describe a level of risk, not a safe threshold.

sections.key: Alcohol slows the brain, impairs judgement and reaction time, and disrupts sleep.
sections.b:
Alcohol is a depressant: it slows communication in the brain. A drink or two can bring relaxation and lower inhibitions, but also slower reactions and poorer judgement, which is why the blood alcohol limit for fully licensed drivers across Australia is 0.05. At higher levels come slurred speech, poor coordination, vomiting and memory blackouts, and very high levels can suppress breathing.

Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it disrupts sleep later in the night, especially REM sleep. Hangovers come from dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation and the effects of acetaldehyde. Alcohol is also a factor in many injuries, falls and assaults.

sections.key: Regular drinking raises the risk of at least seven cancers, liver disease, heart problems and dependence.
sections.b:
The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen, its highest category of evidence. Alcohol is linked with at least seven cancers: mouth, throat, voice box, oesophagus, liver, bowel and breast. Risk rises with the amount you drink over time.

Long-term heavy drinking can cause fatty liver, hepatitis and cirrhosis, high blood pressure, irregular heart rhythms and a weakened heart muscle. It can also affect mood, memory and sleep, and lead to dependence. The older idea that a daily drink protects the heart is now contested, as newer research suggests earlier studies overstated the benefit.

sections.key: Look honestly at your own drinking pattern, and use simple steps like alcohol-free days and counting drinks to cut back.
sections.b:
Alcohol is woven into Australian celebrations, sport and work, and most people drink for ordinary reasons: to relax, celebrate or fit in. There's no shame in looking honestly at your habits. Notice patterns, such as drinking when stressed or bored, or sessions well past four drinks. Signs worth taking seriously include drinking more than you meant to, needing more for the same effect, or feeling unwell without it.

To cut back, plan several alcohol-free days, count standard drinks from labels, alternate with water, eat first, and try mid-strength or zero-alcohol options. If you're worried, talk to your GP or call the National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline on 1800 250 015. Heavy drinkers should not stop suddenly without medical advice, as withdrawal can be dangerous.

quiz.q: What speeds up how quickly your body clears alcohol?
o: Drinking strong black coffee
Taking a long cold shower
Nothing; only time lowers it
Exercising before bed
quiz.e: The liver works at a fairly fixed pace, so coffee or showers only make you feel more alert.

quiz.q: What do the NHMRC alcohol guidelines describe?
o: A completely safe amount to drink daily
The amount needed to feel relaxed
A limit that applies only to men
A level of risk, not a safe threshold
quiz.e: Staying within 10 a week and 4 a day reduces risk, but no amount is completely risk-free.

quiz.q: How does alcohol affect sleep?
o: It aids falling asleep but disrupts later sleep
It deepens sleep through the whole night
It has no effect on sleep quality
It only affects the sleep of heavy drinkers
quiz.e: Alcohol can make sleep feel easier to start but poorer in quality.

quiz.q: What does newer research say about the idea that a daily drink protects the heart?
o: It has been proven true for everyone
It is contested; earlier studies may overstate it
It only applies to red wine drinkers
It is certain for all adults over 40
quiz.e: Alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen, and any heart benefit looks smaller than once thought.

quiz.q: What should a heavy drinker do before cutting down sharply?
o: Stop suddenly and avoid seeing a doctor
Switch to spirits only for a month
Get medical advice first, as withdrawal can be dangerous
Drink only on weekends from then on
quiz.e: A GP can help plan a safe reduction, and the National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline is available.

LESSONS.push: Your wine glass probably holds more than one standard drink. Here's the maths.

LESSONS.title: Knife skills
LESSONS.hook: One good knife, used well, makes cooking faster, safer and far more enjoyable.

sections.key: A chef's knife, paring knife and bread knife cover almost everything, and a well-kept knife matters more than a costly one.
sections.b:
You don't need a block of 15 knives. A chef's knife, 20 to 25 centimetres long, does most of the chopping, slicing and dicing. A paring knife, around 8 to 10 centimetres, handles peeling and hulling strawberries. A serrated bread knife saws through crusty bread and ripe tomatoes without squashing them. Hold a chef's knife before buying: it should feel balanced, with knuckle clearance above the board.

Western, especially German-style, knives use tougher steel and a thicker curved blade suited to rocking. Japanese-style knives, such as the gyuto and santoku, use harder steel that holds a finer edge, often around 15 degrees per side versus roughly 20, but thin edges can chip on bones or frozen food. Neither is better overall. A mid-priced knife kept sharp beats an expensive neglected one.

sections.key: Pinch the blade with your cutting hand and curl your guiding fingertips under, so the blade can never reach them.
sections.b:
Most chefs use a pinch grip: thumb and the side of the index finger pinch the flat of the blade just in front of the handle, with the other three fingers around the handle. This gives far more control than a pointing finger on top. Stand square to the board and let the knife do the work, with a smooth forward or rocking motion rather than pushing straight down, which crushes food.

Your guiding hand uses the claw grip. Curl your fingertips under, behind your knuckles, with the thumb tucked back. The flat of the blade rests against your knuckles as a guide, and you walk the claw back as you cut. It feels awkward at first, so practise slowly on a cucumber or carrot. Professional chefs are fast because the motion is automatic, not because they rush.

sections.key: Learn to slice, dice, mince, julienne and chiffonade, because even pieces cook evenly.
sections.b:
Uniform pieces cook at the same rate, which is the main reason cuts matter. Slicing means cutting across into even pieces. Dicing means cutting into cubes: large, medium or small. Mincing is chopping very finely, used for garlic, ginger and herbs. Julienne is thin matchsticks, around 3 millimetres wide, and brunoise is tiny cubes cut from those matchsticks.

Chiffonade suits leafy herbs like basil: stack the leaves, roll them tightly and slice across to make fine ribbons. To dice an onion, halve it through the root, peel, make horizontal and vertical cuts toward the root without cutting through it, then slice across.

sections.key: Most knife injuries come from movement, so steady the board, cut food flat, and treat a sharp knife with care.
sections.b:
Most knife injuries happen when something moves unexpectedly. Put a damp tea towel or non-slip mat under your board. Before cutting something round, like a potato, slice a thin piece off one side so it sits flat. Use wooden or plastic boards; glass, marble and stone blunt knives and are slippery. Keep a separate board for raw meat, or wash it thoroughly after use.

A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, because a blunt blade needs more force and is more likely to slip. Wash knives by hand and dry them straight away; dishwashers dull edges. Store knives in a block, on a magnetic strip or with guards. Carry a knife point down, and if you drop one, step back and never try to catch it.

sections.key: Honing realigns a bent edge, while sharpening removes metal to create a new one.
sections.b:
Honing and sharpening are different jobs. A honing steel, the rod that often comes with knife sets, doesn't really sharpen. It realigns an edge that has bent slightly with use, and a few light strokes before cooking keep a knife performing well.

Sharpening grinds away a little metal to form a fresh edge. Whetstones give the best results: a medium grit around 1,000 for regular sharpening, and a finer stone of 3,000 or more for polishing. Pull-through sharpeners are easier but can remove more metal. Many kitchen shops offer sharpening services. A simple test: a sharp knife slices a tomato skin cleanly without pressing.

quiz.q: What is the main trade-off of hard, thin Japanese-style knife edges?
o: They hold a finer edge but can chip
They are softer and never need sharpening
They are heavier and slower to cut
They can never be sharpened at home
quiz.e: Harder steel stays sharper, but thin edges are more brittle than tougher Western blades.

quiz.q: Why does the claw grip keep your fingers safe?
o: It holds the food more tightly than any other grip
Tucked fingertips sit behind your knuckles, which guide the blade
It keeps your fingers further from the board
It lets you cut faster with less control
quiz.e: The blade rests against your knuckles, so it can never reach your fingertips.

quiz.q: Why do cooks cut ingredients into uniform pieces?
o: So they look larger on the plate
So they absorb more salt
So they cook at the same rate
So they last longer in the fridge
quiz.e: Even pieces finish cooking together instead of some burning while others stay raw.

quiz.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a blunt one?
o: A sharp blade is lighter in the hand
A sharp blade cuts only soft foods
A blunt knife cannot cut at all
A blunt blade needs more force and is more likely to slip
quiz.e: Less force means more control, so a sharp knife is less likely to slip.

quiz.q: What does a honing steel do?
o: Realigns a slightly bent edge
Grinds off metal to create a new edge
Polishes the handle and the bolster
Hardens the blade over time
quiz.e: Honing maintains an edge between sharpenings, while sharpening creates a new one.

LESSONS.push: Why the sharpest knife in your kitchen is also the safest one.

LESSONS.title: The science of flavour
LESSONS.hook: Taste happens on your tongue, but flavour happens mostly in your nose. Knowing the difference turns good cooks into great ones.

sections.key: Taste is what receptors on the tongue detect, while flavour combines taste with smell, texture, temperature and more.
sections.b:
In everyday speech taste and flavour are interchangeable, but scientists separate them. Taste is what receptors in the tongue and mouth detect: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. Sweet signals energy, salty signals sodium and sour signals acidity. Bitter may have evolved as a warning, though we learn to love it in coffee, dark chocolate and beer. The old tongue map is a myth: every area with taste buds detects all five. Fat is a candidate for a sixth taste, still debated.

Flavour is the bigger experience: taste plus aroma, texture, temperature and sensations like chilli burn or fizz. Even sound counts, as people rate crisps as fresher when the crunch is louder. Knowing which sense each element hits shows what a dish is missing.

sections.key: Most of the variety in flavour comes from smell, and ingredients that share aroma compounds often pair well.
sections.b:
Your tongue reports a handful of tastes, but your nose tells apart a vast range of aromas. As you chew, aroma travels from the back of your mouth up into your nasal cavity, called retronasal smell. That's why food seems bland with a blocked nose. Pinch yours while eating a jellybean and you notice only sweetness until you let go. The claim that 80% of flavour is smell isn't precise, but smell supplies most of the variety.

The food pairing hypothesis says ingredients that share key aroma compounds go well together, like tomato and basil. A 2011 analysis of about 56,000 recipes found Western cuisines often follow this, while East Asian cuisines, such as Korean, tend to avoid it. Shared aromas create harmony; clashing ones create excitement.

sections.key: Umami is the savoury taste of glutamate, and it grows much stronger when glutamate is combined with compounds found in meat, fish and dried shiitake.
sections.b:
In 1908, Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda identified glutamate as the source of the deep savoury taste of kombu seaweed broth and named it umami, roughly 'pleasant savoury taste'. It was accepted internationally as a basic taste after its receptors were found around 2000.

Glutamate is abundant in parmesan, ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce, fish sauce, anchovies and Vegemite. Umami gets a big boost from synergy: combining glutamate with compounds in meat, fish and dried shiitake intensifies it far more than either alone. MSG is purified glutamate. Food regulators including FSANZ consider it safe, and controlled studies haven't confirmed 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'.

sections.key: Chilli burn is a pain signal from heat-sensing nerves, not a taste, and fat soothes it better than water.
sections.b:
Chilli heat comes from capsaicin, which switches on a nerve receptor called TRPV1, whose normal job is detecting painful heat. So the burn is a pain signal rather than a taste, and your body reacts as if your mouth were genuinely hot, with sweating, flushing and watering eyes. American physiologist David Julius used capsaicin to track down that receptor, work that earned a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Menthol tricks cold-sensing nerves in a similar way, which is why mint feels cool.

Capsaicin dissolves in fat, so milk, yoghurt or coconut milk soothe a burning mouth better than water. Birds barely feel capsaicin, so they eat chillies happily and spread the seeds.

sections.key: Cold dulls flavour and contrast keeps food interesting, so taste as you cook and fix problems with salt, acid, sweetness or fat.
sections.b:
Cold dulls sweetness and aroma, which is why ice cream mix tastes cloyingly sweet when warm, and why chilled dishes like gazpacho need more seasoning. Contrast matters too, because senses adapt to constant sensations: crunch on soft food, a sharp pickle beside rich meat, or salt flakes on caramel.

Season to taste means taste, adjust and taste again, at each stage. Flat? Add salt first, then acid. Too salty? Dilute with more unsalted base, or balance with acid, fat or a little sweetness; the idea that a potato draws out salt is largely a myth. Too sour? Add sweetness or fat. Too sweet? Add acid or salt. Too bitter? Salt, sweetness and fat help. Too hot? Add dairy, more base or a touch of sugar. Adjust in small amounts.

quiz.q: What is the difference between taste and flavour?
o: Taste is detected on the tongue; flavour adds aroma and texture
They mean exactly the same thing in science
Taste comes from the nose and flavour from the tongue
Flavour is limited to chilli burn and fizz
quiz.e: Taste is a small set of basic qualities, while flavour is the wider experience built from several senses.

quiz.q: Why does food seem bland when your nose is blocked?
o: Your tongue stops detecting any sweetness
Aroma can't reach the nasal cavity from the mouth
Saliva production stops while you eat
Taste buds switch off whenever you have a cold
quiz.e: Retronasal smell supplies most of the variety in flavour.

quiz.q: What happens when glutamate is combined with compounds found in meat, fish or dried shiitake?
o: The savoury taste is cancelled out entirely
The food turns noticeably bitter
Umami is intensified far beyond either alone
Nothing at all changes in the dish
quiz.e: This synergy is why combinations like mushroom and meat taste so deeply savoury.

quiz.q: Why does milk soothe chilli burn better than water?
o: Milk cools the mouth below normal
Milk destroys the TRPV1 receptor
Water makes capsaicin stronger
Capsaicin dissolves in fat, not water
quiz.e: Chilli heat is a pain signal from capsaicin, which fat can carry away.

quiz.q: A dish tastes flat. What should you try first?
o: Add salt, then acid if needed
Add more of every ingredient
Add chilli
Serve it colder
quiz.e: Salt and acid lift a flat dish, so taste and adjust in small amounts.

LESSONS.push: Pinch your nose and a jellybean loses its flavour. Here's why.

LESSONS.title: Food safety at home
LESSONS.hook: Australians get food poisoning millions of times a year, and much of it starts in home kitchens. A few habits prevent most of it.

sections.key: Food poisoning is common in Australia, and bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 60°C.
sections.b:
Food Standards Australia New Zealand estimates Australians have around 4 to 5 million cases of food poisoning each year, with tens of thousands of hospitalisations. Many are never diagnosed and are dismissed as a '24-hour bug'. Causes include Campylobacter, Salmonella, Listeria, toxin-producing E. coli and norovirus. Pregnant women, babies, young children, older people and anyone with a weakened immune system face a higher risk, especially from soft cheeses, deli meats and raw eggs.

Most bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 60°C, the danger zone, and some can double every 20 minutes or so. Keep the fridge at 5°C or below, ideally 3 to 4°C, the freezer at about minus 18°C, and hot food above 60°C. Some bacteria make toxins that cooking doesn't destroy, so prevention matters more than reheating.

sections.key: Food left in the danger zone for under 2 hours can be used or refrigerated, 2 to 4 hours must be used now, and over 4 hours goes in the bin.
sections.b:
The 2-hour/4-hour rule guides ready-to-eat food that has been left out. It counts the total time between 5°C and 60°C. Under 2 hours, use it or refrigerate it. Between 2 and 4 hours, use it straight away. Over 4 hours, throw it out. On a hot Australian day, bring an esky with ice bricks to picnics and barbecues.

Leftovers are safe if handled well. Refrigerate cooked food once it stops steaming, and divide large batches into shallow containers so they cool faster. Eat within 2 to 3 days or freeze. Reheat until steaming hot throughout, ideally 75°C, and only once. Rice needs extra care: spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking and produce toxins if rice sits at room temperature, so cool and refrigerate it quickly.

sections.key: Keep raw meat apart from ready-to-eat food, cook high-risk meats to 75°C, and take extra care with raw-egg dishes.
sections.b:
Cross-contamination spreads bacteria from raw meat, poultry or seafood to food that won't be cooked again. Store raw meat in sealed containers on the bottom shelf. Use separate boards for raw meat and salads, or wash boards and knives in hot soapy water between uses, and wash your hands with soap for about 20 seconds. Don't wash raw chicken: splashing spreads Campylobacter around the kitchen, and cooking kills it anyway.

Cook chicken, mince, sausages, burgers and rolled or stuffed meats to 75°C in the thickest part, because mincing and rolling mix surface bacteria inside. A cheap meat thermometer removes guesswork. Dishes with raw or lightly cooked eggs, such as homemade mayonnaise, aioli and eggnog, are a leading cause of Salmonella outbreaks in Australia. Use pasteurised egg products and keep raw-egg sauces in the fridge for no more than a day.

sections.key: Symptoms can start hours to weeks after eating, so see a doctor if they are severe or persistent, or if you are in a high-risk group.
sections.b:
Food poisoning usually causes nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes fever, headache or aches. Symptoms can start within a few hours of eating or take several days, depending on the cause; Listeria can take weeks. That means the last meal you ate isn't always the culprit.

Most cases pass within a few days. The main priority is fluids: sip water or oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy. See a doctor if you have blood in your stool, signs of dehydration such as dizziness or very little urine, a high fever, or symptoms lasting more than a few days. Seek help early if you are in a high-risk group.

sections.key: Clean, chill, separate and cook: four habits prevent most home food poisoning, and when in doubt, throw it out.
sections.b:
Most home food poisoning can be prevented with four habits. Clean: wash hands before cooking and after handling raw meat, and keep benches, boards and tea towels clean. Chill: refrigerate food promptly and check your fridge with a cheap thermometer. Separate: keep raw and ready-to-eat foods apart. Cook: cook high-risk foods thoroughly.

Also avoid cooking for others while you have vomiting or diarrhoea, and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop. Don't use cracked or dirty eggs. When in doubt, throw it out: a smell test can't detect many harmful bacteria. This is general information, not medical advice.

quiz.q: Why is the temperature range of 5°C to 60°C called the danger zone?
o: All bacteria die at those temperatures
Most food poisoning bacteria multiply fastest in it
Food spoils only outside it
It is the range used to cook meat safely
quiz.e: Keep cold food at 5°C or below and hot food above 60°C to slow bacterial growth.

quiz.q: Ready-to-eat food has spent a total of 3 hours in the danger zone. What should you do?
o: Put it back in the fridge for later
Reheat it and then refrigerate it
Use it straight away and don't refrigerate it
Throw it out
quiz.e: Between 2 and 4 hours the food should be used immediately, and after 4 hours it should be thrown out.

quiz.q: Why is it recommended not to wash raw chicken?
o: Washing makes the meat tough and dry
Water washes the flavour out of it
Cold water makes the bacteria multiply
Splashing spreads Campylobacter and cooking kills it
quiz.e: Proper cooking is what makes chicken safe, and washing only spreads bacteria around the kitchen.

quiz.q: Why isn't your last meal always the cause of food poisoning?
o: Symptoms can take hours, days or weeks to appear
Food poisoning only comes from drinks
Symptoms always begin within minutes
It only ever comes from restaurant meals
quiz.e: Different bacteria and viruses have different incubation times, and Listeria can take weeks.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you rely on a smell test to check if food is safe?
o: Safe food has no smell
Smell can't detect many harmful bacteria
Bacteria always smell sour
Smell only detects dairy
quiz.e: Food can look and smell fine and still carry bacteria, so when in doubt, throw it out.

LESSONS.push: Some bacteria can double every 20 minutes. Know the temperatures that matter.

LESSONS.title: The science of baking
LESSONS.hook: A cake is a chemistry experiment you get to eat. Understand the reactions and your baking stops being luck.

sections.key: Baking is a set of chemical reactions, and you control gluten through flour, mixing, resting and fat.
sections.b:
A stir-fry forgives a heavy hand with the garlic. A cake doesn't: once batter is in the oven, you can't taste and adjust. Flour, water, fat, sugar, eggs and raising agents react together as proteins bond, gases expand, starches set and sugars brown. Change one quantity and the structure changes, so swapping butter for oil or skipping an egg can give a dense or collapsed bake.

Gluten is the stretchy protein network formed when wheat flour is wetted and worked. You control it four ways. Flour: bread flour has around 12% protein or more, plain around 10%, so bread flour is chewier. Mixing: overmixed muffin batter turns tough. Resting: time relaxes gluten, so pastry and pizza dough roll out more easily after a rest in the fridge. Fat: it coats proteins, which is why pastry fat is called shortening.

sections.key: Yeast ferments sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, raising dough slowly and building flavour.
sections.b:
Baker's yeast is a single-celled fungus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Given warmth, moisture and food, it ferments sugars from the flour into carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol. The gluten network traps the gas and the dough rises.

Fermentation also builds flavour, which is why slow, cool rises, even overnight in the fridge, often make tastier bread. Yeast likes lukewarm conditions; very hot water can kill it, and it dies in the oven as the loaf heats through. Salt slows yeast and helps control the rise, but don't dump it directly onto yeast. Sourdough uses wild yeasts and bacteria instead.

sections.key: Bicarb soda is far stronger than baking powder, and air, steam and eggs also shape how a bake rises and sets.
sections.b:
Chemical raising agents work faster than yeast but are easy to get wrong. Bicarb soda is roughly three to four times as powerful as baking powder, so swapping spoon for spoon can ruin a bake. Both weaken with age, especially in humid kitchens. Test baking powder in hot water (lively fizzing means it's good) and bicarb with a splash of vinegar. Out of self-raising flour? Sift two teaspoons of baking powder into each cup of plain flour. Dutch-processed cocoa is alkalised, so it won't react with bicarb like natural cocoa.

Air and steam raise bakes too: creaming butter and sugar, whisked egg whites, and water turning to steam in choux and Yorkshire puddings. Eggs set structure, add richness, and their lecithin emulsifies fat and water.

sections.key: Crust colour depends on sugar, protein, moisture and heat, and glazes, ingredients and rack position let you steer it.
sections.b:
Crust colour comes mainly from browning reactions between sugars and proteins. They need a dry surface and temperatures well above boiling point, so the moist crumb inside stays pale. An egg wash adds shine and colour: yolk alone gives a deep golden finish, whole egg a golden gloss, and milk a softer, less shiny brown.

Doughs rich in sugar, milk or eggs brown faster, which is why brioche darkens quickly. Alkaline conditions speed browning, so traditional pretzels are dipped in an alkaline bath for a glossy mahogany crust. If tops darken before the middle is cooked, lay a loose sheet of foil over them. A lower oven rack gives a browner base; a higher one browns the top.

sections.key: Weigh ingredients, know your oven, and change one thing at a time when fixing a bake.
sections.b:
A cup of flour can vary by 20% or more depending on whether you scoop or spoon it. Professional bakers weigh everything on digital scales. An Australian cup is 250 millilitres and tablespoon 20 millilitres, while a US cup is about 240 and most countries use a 15 millilitre tablespoon, so check where a recipe comes from, especially for bicarb and salt.

Ovens often run hotter or cooler than the dial says, so an oven thermometer helps. Fan-forced ovens cook faster; lower the temperature by about 20°C. Opening the door early can sink a cake. A peaked, cracked cake usually means the oven was too hot; a dense one, old raising agent or overmixing; a pale crust, a cool oven. Bake a new recipe exactly as written, then change one variable at a time.

quiz.q: Why does fat limit gluten in pastry?
o: It dissolves the flour into the water
It coats the proteins so gluten strands stay short
It makes the dough rise much faster
It pulls water out of the dough
quiz.e: Fat is why pastry fat is called shortening: it keeps gluten strands short and the bake tender.

quiz.q: Why do slow, cool rises often make tastier bread?
o: The yeast cooks the flour
Cold water adds sweetness
Fermentation builds flavour over time
The dough absorbs more air
quiz.e: Longer fermentation develops flavour as well as raising the dough.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to swap bicarb soda for baking powder spoon for spoon?
o: They are exactly the same strength
Baking powder is much stronger
Bicarb only works in yeast dough
Bicarb is roughly three to four times as powerful
quiz.e: Using the wrong one at the same quantity can give a flat, soapy or collapsed bake.

quiz.q: What mainly produces the golden-brown colour of a crust?
o: Sugars and proteins browning on a hot, dry surface
Steam building up inside the dough
The yeast dying as the loaf bakes
The flour drying out in the packet
quiz.e: Sugars, proteins, dryness and heat all affect how quickly a crust browns.

quiz.q: Why do professional bakers weigh ingredients rather than use cups?
o: Scales are quicker than measuring spoons
A cup of flour can vary by 20% or more
Cups are always far too large
Weighing ingredients changes the chemistry
quiz.e: Weighing removes the guesswork that can turn a moist cake dry.

LESSONS.push: The same cup of flour can differ by 20%. Why bakers trust their scales.

LESSONS.title: Meal planning that works
LESSONS.hook: Twenty minutes of planning on the weekend can save you money, waste and the nightly 'what's for dinner?' dread.

sections.key: Planning meals ahead saves money, cuts waste and removes daily decision fatigue, and it starts with your calendar and what you already have.
sections.b:
Australian households throw away a lot of food: national estimates put it at around 2.5 million tonnes a year, commonly estimated at over $2,000 per household. Much of it is fresh produce forgotten in the crisper. Planning means you buy what you will cook, avoids the nightly scramble that leads to expensive takeaway, and makes healthy eating easier because the decision is made while you're calm and not hungry. Even three or four planned dinners a week helps.

Begin with the week, not recipes. Which nights are busy with sport, late shifts or visitors? Match meals to the night: a 15-minute stir-fry for Tuesday training, a slow roast for Sunday. Then check your fridge, freezer and pantry. 'Shop your kitchen first' cuts both waste and your grocery bill.

sections.key: Choose meals that share ingredients, plan for leftovers, then write a list grouped by supermarket section and stick to it.
sections.b:
Look for overlap. A bunch of coriander can go into Monday's tacos and Wednesday's curry; a roast chicken on Sunday becomes Monday's wraps and Tuesday's soup. Theme nights, such as pasta Monday and fish Friday, remove decision fatigue. Keep ten or so reliable favourites, add one new recipe a week if you enjoy variety, and leave a gap night for leftovers or unexpected plans.

Then write down every ingredient you don't already have, with quantities, grouped by section: produce, meat, dairy, pantry. Keep a running list for staples as they run low, ideally shared so no one buys three jars of the same thing. Stick to it. Supermarkets are designed to encourage impulse buys, and a list is your best defence.

sections.key: Compare unit prices, buy in season, use frozen and tinned staples, and stretch meat with legumes.
sections.b:
Larger Australian supermarkets must display unit prices, such as the price per kilogram or per 100 grams, on shelf labels. Use them: the larger pack isn't always cheaper, and specials sometimes aren't special. Fruit and vegetables in season are usually cheaper and tastier.

Frozen vegetables are picked and frozen quickly, keeping their nutrients and never going limp in the fridge. Tinned tomatoes, beans, lentils and chickpeas are cheap, nutritious and last for ages. Stretch meat with legumes, or use eggs and cheaper cuts like chuck steak or chicken thighs, which suit slow cooking. Home brands are often made to similar standards. And never shop hungry.

sections.key: Cool batch-cooked food quickly and label it, and remember that use-by dates are about safety while best-before dates are about quality.
sections.b:
Batch cooking means making a big pot of bolognese, curry or soup and portioning it for later. Cool food quickly in shallow containers and get it into the fridge within about two hours; you don't need to wait until it is cold. Keep the fridge at 5°C or below and the freezer at about minus 18°C. Label everything with contents and date. Eat refrigerated leftovers within two to three days, reheat until steaming hot. Frozen meals keep safely for months.

A use-by date is about safety: don't eat food after it. A best-before date is about quality: food is usually still safe if stored properly. Store greens with a paper towel, bread in the freezer and herbs in water. Put older items at the front, and turn wilting vegetables into soups, fried rice or frittatas.

sections.key: Start small: plan four dinners, check the fridge, shop from a list, and review what worked.
sections.b:
Don't try to plan every meal on day one. Pick one planning time, such as Sunday morning, and plan four dinners. Include one batch-cook meal for leftovers and one quick meal for your busiest night. Check the fridge first, write the list, shop once.

At the end of the week, notice what got eaten, what got wasted and what felt like too much effort, then adjust. Keep your plans; after a month you'll have a rotation you can reuse. The Australian Dietary Guidelines recommend plenty of vegetables, and a handy rule of thumb is to fill about half your dinner plate with vegetables or salad.

quiz.q: What should you do before choosing meals for the week?
o: Buy your favourite ingredients first
Check your calendar and what you already have
Pick the most complicated recipes you know
Order takeaway for the first few nights
quiz.e: Good plans start with reality: how busy the week is and what you already have.

quiz.q: What does the 'cook once, eat twice' approach mean?
o: Cooking every single meal twice for flavour
Doubling a recipe and eating it twice in one day
Using one meal's ingredients as the base for another
Reheating food as many times as possible
quiz.e: Overlapping ingredients and planned leftovers save time and use everything up.

quiz.q: Why should you compare unit prices at the supermarket?
o: They show which foods are healthiest
They are always the same across brands
Specials are always the best value
The larger pack isn't always cheaper
quiz.e: The price per kilogram or per 100 grams makes true comparisons possible.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a use-by and a best-before date?
o: Use-by is about safety; best-before is about quality
Use-by is about quality; best-before is about safety
They mean exactly the same thing
Best-before is only for frozen food
quiz.e: Mixing these up is a common reason good food is thrown out.

quiz.q: What is a good way to begin meal planning?
o: Plan every meal for a month straight away
Plan four dinners, check the fridge and write a list
Buy in bulk and decide what to cook later
Avoid leftovers and cook fresh every night
quiz.e: Small, flexible plans are easier to keep, and a review at week's end helps you adjust.

LESSONS.push: Why twenty minutes of planning on Sunday can change your whole week of dinners.

LESSONS.title: CPR: how to save a life
LESSONS.hook: When someone's heart stops, the next few minutes decide everything. Anyone can help, and doing something is always better than doing nothing.

sections.key: In cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping, survival falls with every minute without CPR, and the Australian action plan is DRSABCD.
sections.b:
A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle; the person is usually awake and in pain. Cardiac arrest is different: the heart's rhythm fails and it stops pumping, and the person collapses and stops breathing normally. Brain damage starts within minutes, and survival falls with every minute without CPR. In Australia only around one in ten people survive an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but prompt CPR and defibrillation by bystanders improve those odds greatly.

The ANZCOR action plan is DRSABCD. Check Danger. Check Response. Send for help: call Triple Zero (000), use speaker, and send someone for a defibrillator. Open the Airway. Check Breathing for up to 10 seconds. Start CPR. Attach a Defibrillator when it arrives.

sections.key: If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, including occasional gasps, start CPR.
sections.b:
One big reason bystanders hesitate is uncertainty about breathing. In the first minutes of cardiac arrest, many people make slow, irregular gasping or snoring sounds, called agonal breathing. It can look like breathing, but it isn't effective, and it is a sign of cardiac arrest.

ANZCOR guidance is clear: if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Don't waste time searching for a pulse; it is unreliable even for trained people. If you start CPR on someone who turns out not to need it, the risk of harm is low. The risk of waiting is far higher.

sections.key: Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about a third of its depth at 100 to 120 a minute, with 30 compressions to 2 breaths or compressions alone.
sections.b:
Kneel beside the person, on their back on a firm surface. Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone, other hand on top, arms straight. Press down about one third of the chest depth and let it fully rise. Aim for 100 to 120 compressions a minute; the beat of 'Stayin' Alive' is about right. Ribs may crack. Keep going: a broken rib heals, but a stopped heart doesn't restart on its own.

The standard ratio is 30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths. Tilt the head back, lift the chin, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs and blow for about a second, watching the chest rise. If you are untrained, unable or unwilling to give breaths, ANZCOR advises continuous compressions alone.

sections.key: Anyone can use an AED by following its voice prompts, and CPR on children and infants follows the same plan, adjusted for size.
sections.b:
An automated external defibrillator, or AED, analyses the heart's rhythm and delivers a shock only if it detects a rhythm that can be corrected. You don't need training: switch it on and follow the spoken instructions. Expose the chest, dry it if wet, stick the pads where pictured and stand clear when told. Resume CPR immediately afterwards. AEDs are found in shopping centres, gyms, sporting clubs and workplaces, and using one within minutes can dramatically increase survival.

For a child, use the heel of one or two hands; for an infant under one, two fingers. Press about one third of the chest depth. Use paediatric pads if available, otherwise adult pads. If others are there, swap every two minutes or so, and continue until the person responds, paramedics take over or you can't go on.

sections.key: Doing CPR is always better than doing nothing, and the Triple Zero operator will guide you.
sections.b:
Many people worry they will do it wrong or be sued. Someone in cardiac arrest has no effective circulation, so your CPR can only improve their chances. Good Samaritan laws in the Australian states and territories generally protect people who help in good faith.

If you are unsure, call Triple Zero (000): the operator will talk you through each step. Once the person starts breathing normally, place them in the recovery position and watch them closely. This lesson is general information, not a substitute for training. A first aid course, ideally refreshed every year for CPR, gives you hands-on practice and the confidence to act.

quiz.q: How does cardiac arrest differ from a heart attack?
o: Arrest stops the heart pumping; an attack blocks blood supply
They are the same condition with two names
An attack stops the heart; arrest blocks blood flow
Cardiac arrest only affects older people
quiz.e: A heart attack can trigger cardiac arrest, but arrest means the person collapses and needs CPR immediately.

quiz.q: An unresponsive person makes occasional slow gasps. What should you do?
o: Wait to see if the breathing improves
Start CPR, because gasping is not normal breathing
Search carefully for a pulse first
Leave them on their side and monitor
quiz.e: Agonal breathing is a sign of cardiac arrest, not effective breathing.

quiz.q: If you are untrained or unwilling to give rescue breaths, what does ANZCOR advise?
o: Do nothing until paramedics arrive
Give breaths only
Give continuous chest compressions alone
Press very gently on the chest
quiz.e: Hands-only CPR still moves oxygen that is already in the blood.

quiz.q: Do you need training to use an AED?
o: Yes, only first aiders are allowed
Yes, a certificate is required by law
No, but you must guess where the pads go
No, you turn it on and follow its spoken instructions
quiz.e: AEDs are designed for anyone to use and will not shock someone who does not need it.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't fear of doing it wrong stop you from starting CPR?
o: Your CPR can only improve the person's chances
Hospitals fix any mistakes made later
Mistakes with CPR are never possible
The law requires you to act every time
quiz.e: Doing something is always better than doing nothing, and the Triple Zero operator will guide you.

LESSONS.push: Gasping isn't breathing, and knowing the difference can save a life.

LESSONS.title: Bites and stings in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Australia has some of the world's most venomous animals, yet deaths are rare. Good first aid is a big part of why.

sections.key: For a suspected snakebite, call Triple Zero, bandage the whole limb firmly and keep the person completely still.
sections.b:
Australia has many of the world's most venomous snakes, including brown snakes, tiger snakes and taipans, yet snakebite deaths average only a few a year. Fast first aid and antivenom are why. Many bites are painless and leave little to see, so treat any suspected bite seriously.

Call Triple Zero (000). Venom travels mostly through the lymphatic system, which muscle movement drives, so keep the person lying still. Apply a pressure immobilisation bandage, a technique developed in Australia: bandage firmly over the bite, then up the whole limb from the fingers or toes, as snugly as for a sprain. Splint the limb and leave the bandage on. Don't wash the bite, as venom on the skin helps hospitals identify the snake. Never cut, suck or use a tourniquet.

sections.key: Funnel-web, blue-ringed octopus and cone shell injuries need a pressure bandage, but redback and most other spider bites need a cold pack.
sections.b:
Funnel-web spiders, found mainly along the east coast including Sydney, have life-threatening venom, especially the males. No deaths have been recorded since antivenom arrived in 1981, but that relies on good first aid. Treat a bite from a large black spider there like a snakebite: call 000, apply a pressure immobilisation bandage and keep the person still. The same goes for blue-ringed octopus bites, which can stop breathing, and cone shell stings. Be ready to give rescue breaths or CPR.

Redbacks are different. Their bite causes spreading pain, sweating and nausea, but no deaths have occurred since antivenom arrived in the 1950s. Pressure worsens the pain, so wash the area, apply a cold pack and seek medical advice. Use the same for huntsman and white-tail bites.

sections.key: Bluebottle stings need hot water, but tropical box jellyfish and Irukandji stings need vinegar, a call to Triple Zero and readiness for CPR.
sections.b:
Bluebottles wash up on beaches after onshore winds. Their stings are very painful but rarely dangerous. Pick off any tentacles with your fingers, rinse with seawater (not fresh), then soak the area in hot water, as hot as the person can comfortably tolerate, for about 20 minutes. Use a cold pack if you have no hot water. Skip the vinegar.

Box jellyfish stings are among the world's most dangerous and can stop the heart within minutes.
