Irukandji jellyfish can be as small as a fingernail; the sting may feel mild, then about half an hour later cause severe back pain, vomiting and high blood pressure. For any tropical sting, call 000, pour vinegar over it for at least 30 seconds and be ready to start CPR. Don't rub it or use fresh water.

sections.key: Remove a bee sting fast, use a cold pack for most insect stings, and freeze ticks rather than squeezing them.
sections.b:
A honeybee leaves its barbed sting in your skin, still pumping venom. Speed matters more than technique, so scrape it sideways with a fingernail or pull it out, then apply a cold pack.

Wasps and ants, such as jack jumpers, leave no sting behind. Wash the area and use a cold pack.

For ticks, Australian allergy experts advise 'freeze it, don't squeeze it'. Kill the tick where it sits with a freezing spray, such as one containing ether, then let it drop off or remove it carefully. Squeezing or pulling a live tick can inject more allergen.

sections.key: If someone has trouble breathing, throat or tongue swelling or collapses after a sting, lay them flat, give adrenaline and call Triple Zero.
sections.b:
Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapid allergic reaction and can be fatal. In Australia, stings from bees and jack jumper ants are a common cause. Warning signs include difficult or noisy breathing, a swollen tongue, a tight throat, a hoarse voice, wheezing or persistent coughing, dizziness or collapse. Young children may look pale and floppy.

Lay the person flat. Don't let them stand or walk, though they can sit if breathing is hard. Give an adrenaline autoinjector into the outer mid-thigh and call Triple Zero (000). If in doubt, give adrenaline. This is general information, so a first aid course is strongly recommended.

quiz.q: How should a pressure immobilisation bandage be applied for a snakebite?
o: Only a tight tourniquet above the bite
Firmly over the bite, then up the whole limb, then splint it
A small plaster over the bite after washing it
Loosely around the bite, removed every few minutes
quiz.e: Bandage over the bite, then up the entire limb as snugly as for a sprain, and splint it.

quiz.q: What is the recommended first aid for a redback spider bite?
o: A pressure immobilisation bandage
A tourniquet above the bite
Soaking it in hot water
A cold pack and medical advice
quiz.e: Pressure makes redback pain worse, so wash the area, use a cold pack and seek advice.

quiz.q: After removing tentacles and rinsing with seawater, how should a bluebottle sting be treated?
o: Pour vinegar over it
Soak it in hot water for about 20 minutes
Rub it with sand
Wrap it in a pressure bandage
quiz.e: Hot water, as hot as can be comfortably tolerated, for about 20 minutes is recommended. Vinegar is for tropical jellyfish.

quiz.q: What is the advice for removing a tick?
o: Squeeze it out with tweezers
Pull it off as quickly as possible
Freeze it, don't squeeze it
Cover it in vinegar and wait
quiz.e: Squeezing or pulling a live tick can inject more allergen, so kill it in place with a freezing spray.

quiz.q: Someone stung by a bee has a swollen tongue and noisy breathing. What should you do?
o: Walk them to the car and drive to a GP
Give them a cold drink and wait
Remove the sting and watch for an hour
Lay them flat, give an adrenaline autoinjector and call Triple Zero
quiz.e: These are signs of anaphylaxis, a medical emergency. Adrenaline and Triple Zero (000) come first.

LESSONS.push: One Australian bite needs a bandage, another a cold pack. Which is which?

LESSONS.title: Water safety
LESSONS.hook: Drowning rarely looks like the movies: no splashing, no shouting. Knowing what it really looks like could save someone you love.

sections.key: Several hundred people drown in Australia each year, mostly men, and rivers, creeks and lakes are often the deadliest places, not beaches.
sections.b:
Royal Life Saving Australia's annual reports typically record several hundred drowning deaths a year, plus many non-fatal drownings that can leave lasting brain injury. Around four in five people who drown are male.

Many assume beaches are the biggest danger, but rivers, creeks and lakes are often the leading location, particularly in regional areas. There are no lifeguards there, and snags, cold water and strong currents stay hidden. Children under five are most at risk in and around home swimming pools. Most drownings are preventable with the right knowledge, supervision and choices.

sections.key: Swim between the red and yellow flags, and remember that a rip often looks like the calmest part of the water.
sections.b:
The red and yellow flags mark the area lifesavers have chosen as safest that day and are actively watching. Swimming outside them, or at unpatrolled beaches, greatly raises the risk. Check the signs and ask a lifesaver if unsure. Apps and websites such as Beachsafe list patrolled beaches.

Rip currents are strong channels of water flowing away from shore, and are widely cited as killing more people than sharks, floods and bushfires combined. They often look calm. Look for deeper, darker water, a gap where waves aren't breaking, rippled water among smoother patches, sandy or foamy water flowing out, or debris moving seaward. Watch from high on the beach for a few minutes. If you can't tell, swim between the flags.

sections.key: If caught in a rip, stay calm, float, raise an arm for help, and swim parallel to shore or towards breaking waves if you can.
sections.b:
If you are caught in a rip, don't panic or exhaust yourself swimming straight back against it. Relax and float to save energy; many rips circulate and may carry you back towards shallow water. Raise one arm and wave. That is the signal lifesavers look for.

If you are a capable swimmer, swim parallel to the beach or towards the breaking waves, which usually push you back to shore.

If you see someone else caught in a rip, call Triple Zero (000) and alert a lifesaver. Don't go in yourself unless you are trained. Throw them something that floats, such as a boogie board or esky.

sections.key: Drowning is silent, so actively supervise young children within arm's reach and fence pools properly.
sections.b:
Real drowning rarely involves splashing and shouting. A person who is drowning is fighting for air and often can't call out or wave. Look for a head low in the water, mouth at water level, glassy eyes, an upright body with little leg movement, and arms pressing down on the water. Children can slip under silently in seconds, even near adults. If someone doesn't answer, act immediately.

Royal Life Saving's Keep Watch program says: supervise, restrict access, build water awareness and learn to resuscitate. Keep young children within arm's reach of an adult who is actively watching, not on their phone. Fence pools, with self-closing, self-latching gates. Empty buckets, baths and paddling pools, as toddlers can drown in a few centimetres of water.

sections.key: Wear a lifejacket, never fish alone, avoid alcohol around water and know your own limits.
sections.b:
Rock fishing is one of Australia's most dangerous recreational activities, because large 'king waves' can sweep people off rocks with little warning. Wear a lifejacket; in some high-risk New South Wales areas it is compulsory. Never fish alone, tell someone your plans, check the swell and tide, watch the spot for at least 20 minutes first, and never turn your back on the ocean. Lifejackets matter on boats, kayaks and paddleboards too.

Alcohol is a factor in a significant share of adult drownings. It impairs judgement and balance and encourages risky choices. Avoid it before and during swimming, boating or fishing, and don't swim alone. Be honest about your ability, and never dive into water of unknown depth.

quiz.q: Which type of location is often the leading site of drowning deaths in Australia?
o: Patrolled surf beaches
Rivers, creeks and lakes
Heated indoor pools
Coastal rock pools
quiz.e: Inland waterways have no lifeguards and hide hazards such as snags, cold water and strong currents.

quiz.q: Which of these can be a sign of a rip current?
o: Large waves breaking consistently
Clear, shallow water over sand
A darker, calmer-looking gap where waves aren't breaking
Waves breaking evenly across the whole beach
quiz.e: Rips often look deceptively calm, deeper and darker, with fewer breaking waves.

quiz.q: What should you do first if you are caught in a rip?
o: Swim as hard as you can straight back to shore
Dive to the bottom and push off
Take off your clothes to swim faster
Stay calm, float and raise an arm to signal for help
quiz.e: Floating conserves energy and signalling brings help. Swim parallel to shore if you can.

quiz.q: What does drowning usually look like?
o: Quiet, with the head low and mouth at water level
Loud shouting and splashing
Waving both arms above the head
Swimming quickly towards shore
quiz.e: People who are drowning usually can't call out or wave, which makes it easy to miss.

quiz.q: Which of these is recommended for rock fishing?
o: Fishing alone so you can concentrate
Wearing heavy waders and boots
Wearing a lifejacket and never turning your back on the ocean
Fishing at high tide in big swell for better catches
quiz.e: Lifejackets save lives in rock fishing, and large waves can arrive without warning.

LESSONS.push: Real drowning is silent. Learn what it looks like before you need to.

LESSONS.title: Bushfire safety
LESSONS.hook: Bushfires are part of the Australian landscape. The people who survive them are usually the ones who planned before the smoke appeared.

sections.key: Anyone who lives, works or travels near bush or grass is at risk, and the Fire Danger Rating tells you how dangerous a fire would be.
sections.b:
Bushfires can start anywhere there is dry vegetation, including grassland, farmland and the edges of suburbs. The main season is usually summer and autumn in southern Australia, and winter and spring in the north. Heat, low humidity, strong wind and dry fuel drive fires, and a grass fire can outrun a person.

Since September 2022, every state and territory uses the Australian Fire Danger Rating System, which shows how dangerous a fire would be if one started. Moderate means plan and prepare. High means prepare to act. Extreme means take action now to protect life and property. Catastrophic means for your survival, leave bush fire risk areas. Check your district daily in fire season.

sections.key: Bushfire warnings run from Advice to Watch and Act to Emergency Warning, but you may get none, so never rely on one source.
sections.b:
Once a fire starts, the Australian Warning System has three levels. Advice means a fire has started but there is no immediate danger. Watch and Act means conditions are changing and you need to take action. Emergency Warning means you are in danger and must act immediately.

You may not receive a warning at all, and conditions can change faster than warnings can be issued. If you see or smell smoke and feel threatened, act on your plan.

Use your state fire service website or app, such as Hazards Near Me in NSW or VicEmergency. ABC local radio is an official broadcaster, so keep a battery radio in case power fails. Emergency Alert sends calls and texts. Social media can be wrong.

sections.key: Leaving early, well before a fire threatens, is the safest option, and a written plan tells you when and where to go.
sections.b:
Every household in a bushfire risk area should have a written survival plan. State fire services provide free templates. Decide what will trigger you to leave, such as a rating or warning level, where you will go, which routes you will take, and what to do about pets and livestock. Pack medications, documents, water and chargers. Check on elderly neighbours. Practise the plan together.

Leaving early is the safest choice: before a fire starts, or well before it reaches you, not when you can see flames. Late evacuation is extremely dangerous, as roads can be blocked and smoke makes driving nearly impossible. Of the 173 people who died on Black Saturday in 2009, many had left late or sheltered in homes that could not protect them.

sections.key: Most homes are lost to embers, so clear gutters, cut grass, move flammable items away and seal gaps.
sections.b:
Most homes lost in bushfires are ignited by embers, which can travel kilometres ahead of the fire front, rather than by the flames themselves. Preparation reduces that risk.

Before the season, clean leaves from gutters, mow grass short and trim branches overhanging the roof. Move firewood, doormats, mulch and gas bottles away from the house. Seal gaps under roofing, eaves and doors, and fit metal mesh screens to windows and vents. Keep hoses long enough to reach all around the house.

A well-prepared home is also safer for neighbours and firefighters, even if you plan to leave. Your state fire service can advise on what suits your property.

sections.key: If trapped, shelter from radiant heat: in a car, park in a clear area, stay inside and get low under a woollen blanket.
sections.b:
Radiant heat is the biggest killer in a bushfire, so shelter from it. Wear long clothing of natural fibres such as wool or cotton, sturdy boots, and cover your nose and mouth.

If you are trapped in a car, park away from trees and long grass, ideally in a clear area, with headlights and hazard lights on. Close the windows and vents, stay in the car and get down below window level. Cover yourself with a woollen blanket until the fire front passes, and drink water if you can.

Some areas have designated Neighbourhood Safer Places, but treat them as a last resort. In any emergency, call Triple Zero (000).

quiz.q: What does a Catastrophic fire danger rating tell you to do?
o: Plan and prepare
Prepare to act
Stay home and defend your property
For your survival, leave bush fire risk areas
quiz.e: Catastrophic is the highest rating, and the advice is to leave high-risk areas.

quiz.q: What does a 'Watch and Act' warning mean?
o: There is no fire in your area
The fire is out and you can return
Conditions are changing and you need to take action
Only people on the fire edge need to act
quiz.e: Watch and Act is the middle level. Emergency Warning is the highest.

quiz.q: According to fire services, what is the safest option in a bushfire?
o: Waiting until you see flames before leaving
Sheltering in a swimming pool
Driving towards the fire to check it
Leaving early, well before the fire arrives
quiz.e: Late evacuation is very dangerous because of smoke, blocked roads and fire.

quiz.q: What causes most homes to catch fire in bushfires?
o: Lightning strikes
Embers carried ahead of the fire
Direct flame contact from the fire front only
Electrical faults
quiz.e: Embers can travel kilometres ahead of the fire and ignite gutters, gaps and flammable material.

quiz.q: If you are trapped in a car during a bushfire, what should you do?
o: Get out and run through the smoke
Keep driving towards the flames to get through quickly
Open the windows to let smoke out
Park in a clear area, stay in the car, get low and cover yourself with a woollen blanket
quiz.e: The car body offers shelter from radiant heat while the fire front passes.

LESSONS.push: Most homes lost to bushfire aren't first lit by the fire front. What lights them?

LESSONS.title: The continents
LESSONS.hook: Ask how many continents there are and the answer depends on where you went to school. Even the shape of the world on your wall is a compromise.

sections.key: A continent is a large landmass, but where one ends is partly human convention, so the count ranges from seven to four.
sections.b:
Continents are not neatly separated by oceans. Africa joins Asia at the Isthmus of Suez, and North and South America meet at Panama. The list is an agreed way of dividing land, and traditions differ.

Australian schools teach seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. Much of Latin America teaches the Americas as one, making six. Some geographers join Europe and Asia as Eurasia, because no ocean divides them. The five Olympic rings stand for the inhabited continents, leaving out Antarctica. Join Africa to Eurasia as Afro-Eurasia and you have four.

The Europe–Asia line is conventionally drawn along the Urals, the Caucasus and the Bosphorus. Istanbul straddles it, though geologically Europe sits on the same plate as most of Asia.

sections.key: Asia is the largest and most populous continent, and Australia is the smallest and flattest.
sections.b:
Asia covers about 44 million square kilometres, roughly 30% of Earth's land, and holds about 4.8 billion people, close to 60% of humanity (2024). Africa is second in area, at about 30 million square kilometres, and has the fastest-growing population, about 1.5 billion (2024).

Antarctica, at about 14 million square kilometres, is larger than Europe or Australia but has no permanent residents, only a few thousand researchers in summer. It also has the highest average elevation, because it is covered in ice.

Australia is the smallest continent, at about 7.7 million square kilometres. It is also the flattest, with an average elevation of only about 330 metres.

sections.key: The Australian continent includes New Guinea and Tasmania, while nearby Zealandia is a mostly submerged continent of about 5 million square kilometres.
sections.b:
The continent of Australia, sometimes called Sahul, is the landmass on the Australian continental shelf: the mainland, Tasmania and New Guinea. In the last ice age, when sea levels were far lower, dry land joined them and people walked between them. Oceania is a broader region that adds the Pacific islands of Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia. New Zealand belongs to Oceania, not the Australian continent.

In 2017, geologists made the case that a mostly submerged landmass to the south-west, Zealandia (Te Riu-a-Māui), is a continent. It covers about 5 million square kilometres, but roughly 94% lies under the sea. New Zealand and New Caledonia are its highest parts. Not every geographer lists it, but many now accept it.

sections.key: Continents ride on tectonic plates that move a few centimetres a year and have joined and split apart many times.
sections.b:
The continents are not fixed. They ride on tectonic plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Around 300 million years ago most land was joined in the supercontinent Pangaea, which later broke apart. Australia was part of its southern half, Gondwana, with Antarctica, Africa, South America and India. Zealandia broke away from Gondwana from around 85 million years ago.

Australia separated from Antarctica within the last 50 million years or so, and has drifted north ever since, at about 7 centimetres a year. That adds up: Australia's official coordinate system was updated in 2017, shifting positions by about 1.8 metres so maps line up with GPS.

sections.key: Flat maps must distort the round Earth, and the Mercator projection keeps shapes but hugely inflates areas near the poles.
sections.b:
You cannot flatten a sphere without stretching it, so every world map distorts something. The familiar Mercator projection, designed in 1569 by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator for sailors, shows a constant compass bearing as a straight line.

The price is that areas balloon towards the poles. Greenland looks about as big as Africa, yet Africa is roughly 14 times larger. Australia looks smaller than it is next to Europe.

Equal-area maps, such as the Gall-Peters projection, show true sizes but squash shapes. Compromise projections like the Winkel tripel balance the errors. For true proportions, use a globe, or compare countries with an online true-size tool.

quiz.q: Why do different countries teach different numbers of continents?
o: Some continents have sunk in recent centuries
Continents are defined partly by convention, not only by nature
The United Nations changes the list every decade
Only seven landmasses sit on continental crust
quiz.e: Whether the Americas, or Europe and Asia, count as one continent or two is a matter of tradition.

quiz.q: Which continent is the smallest?
o: Europe
Antarctica
South America
Australia
quiz.e: At about 7.7 million square kilometres, Australia is the smallest continent, and also the flattest.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of the Australian continent but not the country of Australia?
o: New Zealand
Fiji
New Guinea
New Caledonia
quiz.e: New Guinea sits on the same continental shelf and was joined to the mainland by land during the last ice age.

quiz.q: How fast do continents move?
o: A few metres a year, fast enough to see
A few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow
They stay fixed, but sea levels change
A few millimetres a century
quiz.e: Plate movement is slow, but over millions of years it joins and splits the continents.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of the Mercator projection?
o: It makes compass bearings curved
It cannot show the Southern Hemisphere
It greatly exaggerates the size of land near the poles
It squashes the shapes of all countries
quiz.e: Mercator keeps local shapes and straight bearings but inflates areas towards the poles, so Greenland looks as big as Africa.

LESSONS.push: How many continents are there? The honest answer depends on where you went to school.

LESSONS.title: Rivers and mountains
LESSONS.hook: The world's highest peak has seashells at its summit, and nobody can quite agree which river is the longest. Welcome to the restless shape of the land.

sections.key: The Nile is usually listed as longest at about 6,650 km, but the answer depends on where you say a river starts and ends.
sections.b:
Most reference books list the Nile as the longest river, at about 6,650 kilometres. The Amazon is usually given as about 6,400, but some researchers, including Brazilian scientists in 2007, argue it is longer, up to about 7,000 kilometres. The question is genuinely unsettled.

Every measurement involves a judgement. Which headwater stream is the true source: the longest, the biggest or the traditional one? Where does a wide estuary end? Rivers also meander, so a more detailed map traces more bends and a longer river. Published lengths can differ by hundreds of kilometres. The Yangtze, about 6,300, usually ranks third.

On volume there is no contest: the Amazon carries about a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers deliver to the oceans.

sections.key: The Murray, about 2,500 km long, is Australia's longest river, and its basin covers about one-seventh of the continent.
sections.b:
The Murray River, about 2,500 kilometres long, is Australia's longest. It rises in the Australian Alps, forms much of the border between New South Wales and Victoria, and reaches the sea in South Australia. With the Darling, Murrumbidgee and other tributaries, it drains the Murray–Darling Basin: about a million square kilometres across four states and the ACT, roughly one-seventh of Australia. The basin is the heart of the nation's irrigated farming.

It is also fragile. Australian rivers are highly variable, and heavy water use plus drought left the Murray mouth needing regular dredging from the early 2000s. The 2012 Basin Plan aims to share water between farms, towns and the environment.

sections.key: Most great ranges form where tectonic plates collide, and Everest is still rising as India pushes into Asia.
sections.b:
Plate tectonics builds most mountains. When two continents collide, neither sinks easily, so the crust crumples into fold mountains like the Himalayas and the Alps. Where an ocean plate dives beneath a continent, melting rock feeds volcanic chains such as the Andes. Other mountains are single volcanoes, like Kilimanjaro, or blocks of crust lifted along faults. Meanwhile rain, ice, wind and gravity wear rock down, so young ranges are tall and jagged and old ones low and rounded.

Mount Everest is Earth's highest point above sea level, measured in 2020 at 8,848.86 metres. The Himalayas began rising about 50 million years ago when India hit Asia, and still rise a few millimetres a year. Limestone near the summit holds fossils of sea creatures from an ancient ocean floor.

sections.key: Everest is highest above sea level, but Mauna Kea is tallest base to peak and Chimborazo's summit is farthest from Earth's centre.
sections.b:
Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, is known as Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibet. Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer, made the first confirmed ascent on 29 May 1953.

But there are other ways to rank mountains. Mauna Kea in Hawai'i rises only about 4,200 metres above the sea, yet measured from its base on the ocean floor it stands over 10,000 metres, taller than Everest. Earth bulges at the equator, so the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador, about 6,260 metres high, is the surface point farthest from Earth's centre, roughly 2 kilometres farther out than Everest's peak.

K2, at about 8,600 metres, is the second highest and widely regarded as a much deadlier climb.

sections.key: Kosciuszko is the mainland's highest peak, Mawson Peak on Heard Island is higher, and the Great Dividing Range runs over 3,500 km.
sections.b:
Mount Kosciuszko in New South Wales, at 2,228 metres, is the highest mainland peak. It is modest by world standards, because Australia is old and tectonically quiet and its mountains have eroded for hundreds of millions of years. In summer it is an easy walk from the Thredbo chairlift. The Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki climbed there in 1840 and named it after Tadeusz Kościuszko. Mawson Peak, an active volcano on remote Heard Island, an Australian external territory, is higher at about 2,745 metres.

The Great Dividing Range, a chain of ranges and plateaus over 3,500 kilometres long from Cape York to the Grampians, shapes the east. Short, fast rivers drain to the Pacific, while inland rivers flow west towards the Murray–Darling or Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre. It also casts a rain shadow over the dry interior.

quiz.q: Why is it disputed whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer?
o: The Nile has dried up in places
Results depend on where the source and mouth are judged to be
Nobody has travelled the whole Amazon
The Amazon is measured in miles and the Nile in kilometres
quiz.e: Choosing different headwater streams and estuary end points changes the result by hundreds of kilometres.

quiz.q: What is Australia's longest river?
o: The Darling
The Murrumbidgee
The Murray
The Fitzroy
quiz.e: At about 2,500 kilometres, the Murray is Australia's longest river.

quiz.q: Why are there marine fossils near the top of Everest?
o: Birds carried shells up the mountain
The rock formed on an ancient sea floor and was pushed up by colliding plates
Early climbers left them as offerings
Sea levels were once 8 kilometres higher
quiz.e: India's collision with Asia lifted old ocean-floor limestone into the Himalayas.

quiz.q: Why is Chimborazo's summit the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre?
o: It is the tallest mountain above sea level
It rises highest from the ocean floor
Earth bulges at the equator, where Chimborazo stands
It sits on the thickest part of the crust
quiz.e: Earth's equatorial bulge puts Chimborazo's summit about 2 kilometres farther out than Everest's.

quiz.q: What is the highest mountain on Australian territory outside Antarctica?
o: Mount Kosciuszko
Mawson Peak on Heard Island
Mount Townsend
Mount Bogong
quiz.e: Mawson Peak, about 2,745 metres, is higher than Kosciuszko's 2,228 metres.

LESSONS.push: Which river is longest is still disputed. So is which mountain is highest.

LESSONS.title: Deserts
LESSONS.hook: The biggest desert on Earth is covered in ice. Deserts are defined by thirst, not heat, and they are far more alive than they look.

sections.key: A desert is defined by very low rainfall, not temperature, which is why Antarctica is the world's largest desert.
sections.b:
Geographers define deserts by dryness, not heat. A common rule of thumb is less than about 250 millimetres of rain or snow a year, though a better measure compares rainfall with how much water could evaporate. Slightly wetter land, around 250 to 500 millimetres, is semi-arid. Together, arid and semi-arid land covers roughly a third of Earth's land. With little moisture or cloud to trap heat, desert nights can be cold even after scorching days.

By this definition the largest desert is Antarctica, about 14 million square kilometres. Much of its interior receives less than 50 millimetres of precipitation a year, as melted water. The ice is kilometres thick because snow almost never melts. The Arctic ranks second. The McMurdo Dry Valleys, largely free of ice, resemble Mars.

sections.key: Most deserts form under sinking dry air, in rain shadows, far from the sea or beside cold ocean currents.
sections.b:
Several forces make deserts. The biggest is global air circulation: warm, moist air rises near the equator, drops its rain, then sinks as dry air around 30 degrees north and south. That belt holds the Sahara, the Arabian, the Kalahari and much of inland Australia. Rain shadows form where mountains wring moisture from air on one side, as in Patagonia. Some deserts, like the Gobi, are too far from the sea for moist air to reach. The Atacama in Chile and the Namib in southern Africa lie beside cold ocean currents that chill the air and stop rain clouds forming.

Climate can change. The Sahara, the largest hot desert at about 9 million square kilometres, was green between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, with lakes, hippos and crocodiles.

sections.key: Australia is the driest inhabited continent, with ten named deserts covering about 18% of the mainland and about 70% arid or semi-arid.
sections.b:
Geoscience Australia lists ten named deserts covering about 18% of the mainland, and around 70% of the continent is arid or semi-arid. The largest is the Great Victoria Desert, spanning Western Australia and South Australia. Others include the Great Sandy, Tanami, Gibson and Simpson.

The Simpson Desert is known for its long, parallel red sand dunes, some running well over 100 kilometres. Much of the interior drains towards Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre, Australia's lowest point at about 15 metres below sea level. The lake is usually a salt crust, filling completely only a few times a century. When it does, huge numbers of waterbirds arrive to breed.

sections.key: Desert plants and animals survive by storing water, avoiding heat and responding fast to rare rain, and people have lived there for tens of thousands of years.
sections.b:
Cacti and many succulents store water in thick stems or leaves. Australia's spinifex forms tough hummocks that shelter small animals. After rare heavy rain, dormant seeds flower and finish their life cycle in weeks. The thorny devil, a small Australian lizard, has grooves between its scales that draw water by capillary action to its mouth, so it can drink from damp sand or dew. Many desert animals are active only at night. Camel humps hold fat, not water; camels simply tolerate dehydration and conserve water extremely well.

Aboriginal peoples, including the many language groups of the Western Desert, have lived in arid country for tens of thousands of years. Survival depended on knowledge of rock holes, soaks and seasonal plants, passed on through song, story and ceremony.

sections.key: In outback Australia, carry far more water than you think you need, tell someone your plans and stay with your vehicle if stranded.
sections.b:
Australia's deserts are beautiful and increasingly visited, but they punish poor preparation. Fuel and water can be hundreds of kilometres apart, phone coverage disappears quickly and summer temperatures can pass 45 degrees.

Carry far more water than you expect to need, commonly several litres per person per day plus extra for emergencies. Check road conditions, since dirt roads close after rain, and some remote tracks need permits, including to cross Aboriginal land. Tell someone your route and expected arrival. Carry a personal locator beacon or satellite device.

If you break down, stay with your vehicle. It gives shade and is far easier for searchers to spot than a person walking.

quiz.q: What mainly defines a desert?
o: Very high temperatures
Sand dunes covering most of the ground
Very low precipitation compared with evaporation
Having no plants at all
quiz.e: Deserts are defined by dryness. A common rule of thumb is under about 250 mm of precipitation a year.

quiz.q: Why is the Atacama Desert so dry?
o: It sits exactly on the equator
A cold ocean current chills the air and stops rain clouds forming
It is at the centre of a large continent
It is covered by ice all year
quiz.e: Cold currents off Chile chill the air and stop rain clouds forming.

quiz.q: Which best describes Australia's dryness?
o: About 70% of the continent is arid or semi-arid
Deserts cover about half of the mainland
Only the central outback is dry
Almost all rain falls in the interior
quiz.e: Australia is the driest inhabited continent, with about 70% arid or semi-arid land.

quiz.q: How does the thorny devil get water?
o: It stores water in a hump
It digs wells with its claws
It never needs to drink
Grooves between its scales draw water to its mouth
quiz.e: Capillary grooves channel moisture from damp sand or dew to its mouth.

quiz.q: If your car breaks down in remote desert, what is the standard advice?
o: Walk to the nearest town at night
Leave a note and follow the road
Stay with the vehicle
Split up to search for help faster
quiz.e: A vehicle gives shade and is far easier for searchers to see than a person on foot.

LESSONS.push: The world's largest desert is not hot, and it is not in Africa.

LESSONS.title: Borders
LESSONS.hook: There is an island that changes countries every six months and a town where the border runs through people's living rooms. Borders are human inventions, and it shows.

sections.key: Borders are human agreements, from rivers and survey lines to colonial deals made far from the land.
sections.b:
No border exists in nature. Each is a human agreement, or disagreement, drawn onto the land. Some follow physical features, like the Pyrenees between France and Spain. Rivers make obvious lines but can shift course. Others follow latitude or longitude, such as much of the Canada–United States border, the world's longest, at almost 9,000 kilometres.

Some of the most consequential borders were drawn far away. In the late 19th century, European powers competed to claim Africa, and the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 set rules for it. Many resulting borders were straight lines that cut across ethnic groups or bundled rivals together. Britain and France also divided much of the former Ottoman Empire. Most new countries kept their colonial borders at independence, as redrawing them risked endless conflict.

sections.key: Australian state borders mostly follow survey lines, and a surveying error still shapes the South Australia–Victoria border.
sections.b:
Colonial officials drew Australia's internal borders mostly along lines of longitude and latitude. Western Australia's eastern border follows the 129th meridian, which is why it runs dead straight through the desert.

The South Australia–Victoria border was meant to follow the 141st meridian, but the survey of the 1840s ended up a few kilometres too far west. South Australia sued, and in 1914 the Privy Council in London ruled that the marked line stood, so the error remains.

Borders that usually go unnoticed can suddenly matter. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021, several states closed their borders to travellers from other states.

sections.key: Enclaves, shared islands and disputed territories show how messy borders get, and why maps can disagree.
sections.b:
In Baarle, small Belgian and Dutch enclaves are scattered through each other, and the line runs through some houses. Pheasant Island, in a river between France and Spain, switches rule every six months under a treaty from 1659. Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City are each entirely surrounded by a single other country. Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (United States) lie a few kilometres apart but across the International Date Line, so their clocks differ by almost a day.

Many places are claimed by more than one government. Kashmir has been contested since 1947 and is administered by India, Pakistan and China. Most of Western Sahara is controlled by Morocco, but its status is unresolved at the UN. Many countries require official maps to show their own claims, so one border can look different on different maps.

sections.key: Under the UN law of the sea, a country controls a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea and a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone.
sections.b:
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, agreed in 1982, sets the main offshore zones. A territorial sea reaches 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometres) from the coast and is treated much like land. Beyond it, the exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, stretches to 200 nautical miles (about 370 kilometres). It gives rights over fishing, oil, gas and minerals, though other ships may pass freely. Where coasts are closer than 400 nautical miles, neighbours must negotiate a line.

Australia has one of the world's largest EEZs, around 8 million square kilometres, bigger than the mainland. The 1978 Torres Strait Treaty lets traditional inhabitants of Papua New Guinea and the islands move within a protected zone. In 2018 Australia and Timor-Leste signed a treaty setting a permanent boundary in the Timor Sea.

sections.key: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, including Australia's claim to about 42%, but the Antarctic Treaty sets these claims aside.
sections.b:
Antarctica is the one continent without agreed borders. Seven countries claim slices: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom. Australia's claim, the Australian Antarctic Territory, covers about 42% of the continent, the largest of all. Some claims overlap, and most countries recognise none of them.

The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 put the issue on ice. It neither accepts nor rejects the claims, bans military activity, and reserves the continent for peaceful science. A later protocol also bans mining. It is a rare case of rival nations agreeing to share a whole continent, and it has held for more than 60 years.

quiz.q: Why are many African borders drawn as straight lines?
o: They follow natural ridgelines
They follow ancient kingdoms
European powers drew them on maps with little regard for the people living there
African nations chose them at independence
quiz.e: Colonial powers drew many lines from afar, and most new countries kept them at independence.

quiz.q: Why is the South Australia–Victoria border not exactly on the 141st meridian?
o: A surveying error in the 1840s was upheld by the Privy Council
Victoria bought the land in 1901
It follows the Murray River
It was moved after COVID-19
quiz.e: The surveyed line ended up a few kilometres west, and in 1914 the Privy Council ruled that it stood.

quiz.q: Why can two maps of the same disputed border look different?
o: Mapmakers disagree about scale
Many countries require official maps to show their own claims
Borders move each year
Only some maps use satellite data
quiz.e: A fair description states who controls an area, who claims it and what international bodies have said.

quiz.q: How far does a country's exclusive economic zone extend?
o: 12 nautical miles
24 nautical miles
1,000 nautical miles
200 nautical miles
quiz.e: The EEZ reaches 200 nautical miles, about 370 kilometres, giving rights over resources like fish and gas.

quiz.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty do about territorial claims?
o: Divides the continent equally
Gives all of Antarctica to the United Nations
Sets the claims aside without accepting or rejecting them
Recognises only Australia's claim
quiz.e: The 1959 treaty freezes the claims and reserves Antarctica for peaceful science.

LESSONS.push: An island that changes country twice a year. Borders get stranger from there.

LESSONS.title: Cities
LESSONS.hook: For almost all of human history most people lived in the countryside. That changed only within the last couple of decades, and Australia got there long before most.

sections.key: More than half of humanity now lives in urban areas, a milestone reached only around 2007.
sections.b:
The first cities appeared in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, more than 5,000 years ago; Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people. Yet for most of history cities were small islands in a rural world. Around 1800, commonly estimated at under 10% of people lived in towns and cities. Industrialisation pulled workers from farms to factories.

The United Nations estimates that around 2007 the world became majority urban for the first time, and projects that about two-thirds of people will live in urban areas by 2050. Most future growth is expected in Asia and Africa.

Such figures depend on definitions. Some countries count any settlement of a few thousand as urban; others set the bar much higher.

sections.key: City size depends on where you draw the boundary, so rankings differ, and megacities now cluster in Asia and Africa.
sections.b:
A city can be measured three ways: the core municipality, the built-up urban area, or the wider metropolitan region of commuters. The City of Sydney council area has about 200,000 residents, while Greater Sydney has more than 5 million. The UN and other agencies now use a standard method based on population density on satellite-derived grids, which can rank cities differently from national statistics.

A megacity has 10 million or more people. In 1950 only New York and Tokyo qualified; today there are more than 30. For decades the UN ranked greater Tokyo first, at around 37 million. A 2025 UN report using the newer definition placed Jakarta first, with Dhaka and Tokyo close behind, and noted Tokyo's population has begun to shrink. Most of the biggest, fastest-growing cities are now in Asia and Africa.

sections.key: Cities start at harbours, river crossings and resources, then keep growing because businesses and workers benefit from being close together.
sections.b:
Geography explains most city locations. Rivers and harbours provide water, transport and trade. London grew at the lowest point where the Thames could easily be bridged. Resources matter too: Australia's gold rushes built Ballarat, Bendigo and later Kalgoorlie. Once established, a city tends to keep growing because firms, workers and customers gain from being close. Economists call this agglomeration.

Some cities are created by decision. When the colonies federated in 1901, Sydney and Melbourne were rivals, so the Constitution required the capital to be in New South Wales but at least 100 miles from Sydney. The Canberra site was chosen in 1908, an international competition was won by Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, and Parliament moved there from Melbourne in 1927. Brasília (1960) and Abuja (1991) were also planned capitals.

sections.key: About 86% of Australians live in urban areas and around two-thirds live in the capital cities.
sections.b:
Despite the outback image, Australia is one of the most urbanised countries on Earth. About 86% of people live in urban areas, and roughly two-thirds live in the eight capital cities, according to recent ABS figures. Sydney and Melbourne each have more than 5 million people (2023), while Brisbane and Perth have over 2 million.

Most Australians also live near the sea, with commonly cited estimates of around 85% within 50 kilometres of the coast. This reflects history and climate: colonial settlement began at ports, and the dry interior supports few people. Few other countries concentrate so much of their population in so few big cities.

sections.key: Cities bring housing pressure, heat and informal settlements, but concentrate jobs, ideas and services, and well-planned density can be greener per person.
sections.b:
Rapid urban growth brings real problems. Housing costs rise as people compete for land near jobs, a familiar story in Sydney and Melbourne. Sprawl lengthens commutes. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight and release it at night, so cities can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, an effect called the urban heat island, especially noticeable in Western Sydney. In many lower-income countries, UN-Habitat estimates around a billion people live in slums or informal settlements.

Still, people keep moving to cities for jobs, wages, universities, hospitals and culture. Density helps the environment too: public transport is viable, and residents of compact cities often drive less. When comparing cities, look past rankings to commute times, housing costs, green space and services.

quiz.q: Roughly when did more than half of the world's people first live in urban areas?
o: Around 1850
Around 1950
Around 2007
It has not happened yet
quiz.e: The UN estimates the world became majority urban around 2007.

quiz.q: Why do lists of the world's biggest cities often disagree?
o: Some cities refuse to hold censuses
Populations change every week
Only capital cities are counted
Countries and agencies draw city boundaries in different ways
quiz.e: Whether you count the core, the built-up area or the wider metro region changes the numbers dramatically.

quiz.q: What is agglomeration?
o: The benefit businesses and workers gain from clustering together
The merging of two local councils
The spread of suburbs into farmland
A type of city planning law
quiz.e: Being close to customers, suppliers and workers makes firms more productive, so big cities tend to keep growing.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of Australians live in urban areas?
o: About 50%
About 65%
About 86%
About 99%
quiz.e: Despite the outback image, Australia is one of the world's most urbanised countries, with about two-thirds in the capital cities.

quiz.q: What is the urban heat island effect?
o: Heatwaves that only affect islands
Cities being warmer than surrounding countryside
Heat released by power stations
A cooling breeze from the coast
quiz.e: Roads, roofs and buildings absorb heat and release it at night, keeping cities warmer.

LESSONS.push: Around 2007, humanity crossed a line it had never crossed before.

LESSONS.title: World population
LESSONS.hook: It took all of human history to reach one billion people, and just over a decade to go from seven billion to eight. Now the world is quietly changing direction.

sections.key: The world passed 8 billion in 2022 after taking until about 1804 to reach its first billion, and growth is now slowing.
sections.b:
The United Nations marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world reached 8 billion, an estimate rather than a count. The first billion took until about 1804. The second came around 1927, the third in 1960, and then a billion every 12 to 14 years: 4 billion in 1974, 5 in 1987, 6 in 1999 and 7 in 2011. This was not mainly because people had more children. Far fewer people died young, thanks to clean water, sanitation, vaccines, antibiotics and more reliable food, while birth rates took time to fall.

Growth peaked at a little over 2% a year in the 1960s and fell below 1% around 2020. The UN's 2024 projections show a peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s. Projections are not certainties, and other groups expect an earlier, lower peak.

sections.key: Replacement fertility is about 2.1 children per woman, and falling death rates, education, cities and contraception push birth rates below it.
sections.b:
The total fertility rate is roughly the average number of children a woman has in her lifetime. About 2.1 keeps a population stable in the long run, a level called replacement. In the 1960s the global average was around 5. Today it is about 2.3, and most people live in countries below replacement. Australia's rate was about 1.5 in 2023, a record low. South Korea's fell to 0.72, among the lowest ever recorded. Niger's is around six.

Demographers call the pattern the demographic transition. Death rates fall first, so population surges, then birth rates follow. When most children survive, parents have fewer; education and paid work give women more choices; city life makes children costlier; and contraception makes smaller families possible. Europe took over a century; South Korea and Iran, a few decades.

sections.key: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023, and almost everywhere the share of older people is rising.
sections.b:
In 2023, UN estimates showed India overtaking China as the most populous country, each with about 1.4 billion people. China's population began falling in 2022 after decades of low fertility, including the one-child policy from 1980 to 2015. Japan has been shrinking since around 2010. Fast-growing Africa is projected to hold about a quarter of humanity by 2050.

Longer lives and fewer births also mean an older world. Global life expectancy is about 73 years, up from about 46 in 1950. Nearly 30% of Japanese people are 65 or over, with a median age near 49. Niger's median age is about 15. More older people means fewer workers per retiree and higher health costs, which is one reason Australia built compulsory superannuation.

sections.key: About 300 million people live outside their country of birth, and in Australia about 30% of residents were born overseas.
sections.b:
Migration is the third driver of population change, alongside births and deaths. The United Nations estimated about 304 million international migrants in 2024, around 3.7% of the world's people. Most move for work, family or study, while tens of millions more have been forced from home by conflict or disaster.

Australia is one of the most migration-shaped countries on Earth. About 30% of residents were born overseas (2023), with England, India, China and New Zealand the most common birthplaces. Around half of Australians were born overseas or have a parent who was. In most recent years, net overseas migration has added more people than natural increase.

sections.key: Treat projections as scenarios, check the year and source, and be wary of both 'overpopulation' and 'population collapse' alarm.
sections.b:
Population debates attract bold predictions. In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that population would always outrun food. In 1968 Paul Ehrlich's The Population Bomb forecast mass famines in the 1970s. Farm productivity rose faster than either expected, though hunger has not disappeared. Today some warn instead of population collapse.

A few habits help. Check the year and source of any figure, since estimates are revised regularly. Treat projections as scenarios. Remember that impact depends on consumption as well as headcount, because a person in a rich country typically uses far more resources than one in a poor country. And watch slow trends, like ageing, that shape budgets for decades.

quiz.q: What mainly caused the rapid rise in world population over the past two centuries?
o: People having many more children than before
Far fewer people dying young
Migration between continents
Longer pregnancies
quiz.e: Clean water, sanitation, vaccines and better food cut death rates while birth rates took time to fall.

quiz.q: Which of these is a well-established driver of falling birth rates?
o: Colder climates
Bigger houses
Lower life expectancy
More children surviving to adulthood
quiz.e: When most children survive, parents tend to have fewer, especially as education and city living spread.

quiz.q: Which country became the world's most populous in 2023, according to UN estimates?
o: China
United States
India
Indonesia
quiz.e: India overtook China, each having about 1.4 billion people, while China's population began to fall.

quiz.q: About what share of Australia's residents were born overseas (2023)?
o: About 5%
About 30%
About 60%
About 75%
quiz.e: Roughly 30% of Australians were born overseas, and net overseas migration often adds more people than natural increase.

quiz.q: What is a sound way to judge a bold population claim?
o: Check the year and source, and treat projections as scenarios
Trust it if it comes from a famous author
Assume the latest forecast is always right
Judge it by headcount alone, ignoring consumption
quiz.e: Estimates are revised regularly, and impact depends on consumption as well as the number of people.

LESSONS.push: The world's population will probably stop growing within this century. Why?

LESSONS.title: How democracy works
LESSONS.hook: Rule by the people sounds simple. For most of history it was rare, fragile and limited. Here's how it grew, and what actually keeps it alive.

sections.key: Democracy means citizens hold ultimate power, either deciding directly or electing representatives, and its roots reach well beyond Athens.
sections.b:
Democracy comes from the Greek demos, the people, and kratos, power. Authority comes from citizens, not a monarch, priesthood or military. In a direct democracy citizens vote on decisions themselves. In a representative democracy they elect people to decide for them, and can remove them at the next election. Almost every democracy today is mainly representative, with some direct elements.

Athens is the best-known early example, but not the only one. Ancient Indian texts describe republics such as the Vajji confederacy, where councils of clan leaders debated and voted around the 500s BC, though only an elite took part. In Iceland, Norse settlers founded the Althing in 930, often called one of the world's oldest surviving parliaments. In two small Swiss cantons, citizens still vote on laws by raising their hands.

sections.key: Representative government grew through Rome, medieval parliaments and revolutions, and the vote widened only slowly.
sections.b:
After Athens, rule by the people largely faded for centuries, but pieces survived. The Roman Republic elected magistrates and had a Senate, though wealthy families dominated. In England, Magna Carta in 1215 established that even the king was bound by law, and parliaments gradually won control over taxation. A civil war and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 left Parliament stronger than the monarch. This Westminster model later shaped Australia, Canada and New Zealand.

Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke argued that governments get legitimacy from the consent of the governed. The American Revolution of 1776 and French Revolution of 1789 placed this at the centre. Early electorates were small, often limited to propertied men. Over the next century and a half the vote widened to working men, women and groups excluded by race. Universal suffrage is surprisingly recent.

sections.key: The Australian colonies were early pioneers, with paid MPs, the world's first Labour government and the first woman elected to an Australian parliament.
sections.b:
The Australian colonies were busy laboratories of democracy. In 1870 Victoria began paying members of parliament, so working men, not just the wealthy, could afford to serve. In 1899 Queensland's Anderson Dawson became premier of what is usually described as the world's first Labour government, though it lasted only about a week.

Tasmania trialled the Hare-Clark system of proportional representation in Hobart and Launceston in the 1890s and adopted it statewide in 1909. It is still used there and in the ACT. And in 1921 Edith Cowan won a seat in Western Australia, becoming the first woman elected to an Australian parliament.

sections.key: Referendums and citizen initiatives let voters decide some questions directly, as in Switzerland and in Australian constitutional change.
sections.b:
Pure direct democracy is impractical for a nation of millions, but elements survive. Switzerland is the best-known example: citizens vote on national questions several times a year, and can force a vote on a new law by gathering enough signatures. Many US states let citizens put proposals on the ballot.

In Australia, the main direct element is the constitutional referendum: the Constitution can only be changed if voters approve.

Supporters say direct votes give people real ownership of big decisions. Critics warn that complex issues can be reduced to slogans and that turnout and information vary.

sections.key: Free elections alone aren't enough: democracy needs the rule of law, a free press, minority protections and peaceful handovers, plus engaged citizens.
sections.b:
Holding elections doesn't guarantee a working democracy. Elections must be free and fair, run by an independent body, with secret ballots and real choice. The rule of law means everyone, including leaders, answers to the same laws through independent courts. A free press and free speech let citizens learn what government does and criticise it without fear. Minority protections stop the majority overriding others' basic rights. And losers must accept the result.

Churchill told Parliament in 1947 that it had been said democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others tried. It can be slow and frustrating, but it lets mistakes be corrected and leaders replaced without violence. Citizens keep it alive by voting thoughtfully, checking political claims, contacting their local member and respecting those who vote differently.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between direct and representative democracy?
o: Direct democracy has no elections at all
Representative democracy has no parliament
In direct democracy citizens vote on decisions themselves; in representative democracy they elect others to decide
Direct democracy is run by a monarch
quiz.e: Most modern democracies are mainly representative, with some direct elements.

quiz.q: Why is universal suffrage described as surprisingly recent?
o: Early electorates were small, often limited to propertied men, and widened only over generations
Ancient Athens gave every adult a vote
Magna Carta created equal voting rights
The French Revolution gave every adult a vote
quiz.e: The vote widened slowly to working men, women and groups excluded by race over about a century and a half.

quiz.q: Why did Victoria begin paying members of parliament in 1870?
o: To attract candidates from overseas
To reward long-serving members
To stop wealthy members taking bribes
So working men, not just the wealthy, could afford to serve
quiz.e: Paying MPs opened parliament to people without private wealth.

quiz.q: What is the main direct-democracy element in Australia's national system?
o: Citizen-initiated laws
Referendums to change the Constitution
Electing judges
Choosing ministers by lottery
quiz.e: The Constitution can only be changed if voters approve at a referendum.

quiz.q: Which of these is a pillar of a working democracy beyond elections?
o: A single official news source
Leaders being above the law
A free press
Banning opposition parties
quiz.e: A free press lets citizens learn what government is doing and criticise it.

LESSONS.push: Holding elections does not make a country a democracy. What else is needed?

LESSONS.title: Left, right and the big political ideas
LESSONS.hook: Why do we say 'left' and 'right'? The answer involves a French assembly hall in 1789, and the ideas that grew from it still shape every election.

sections.key: Left and right come from the French Assembly of 1789 and now loosely describe views on equality, the economy and the pace of change.
sections.b:
The words left and right began in France in 1789, in the early months of the Revolution. In the National Assembly, members who wanted to keep strong powers for the king, such as a royal veto over laws, sat to the right of the presiding officer. Those who wanted more radical change sat to the left. The seating habit stuck.

Today the labels are shorthand for several questions bundled together. On economics, the left generally favours more government action to reduce inequality, through taxes, welfare and public services. The right generally favours lower taxes, freer markets and more reliance on individual effort. On social questions, the left is often linked with faster change and the right with preserving tradition. The bundles don't always hold together, and the labels shift between countries and eras.

sections.key: Liberalism puts individual rights and consent of the governed at the centre, while conservatism trusts tradition and gradual change.
sections.b:
Liberalism grew from Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke, who argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that government rests on consent. Classical liberals stressed free markets, free speech and limited government. Social liberals later argued that real freedom also needs education, health care and a safety net.

Conservatism is often traced to Edmund Burke's 1790 warning against tearing down institutions for abstract theory. Conservatives hold that customs, families and long-standing institutions carry accumulated wisdom, so change should be careful and gradual. Critics say this can defend unfair arrangements simply because they are old.

Beware the word 'liberal': in the United States it signals the centre-left, but Australia's Liberal Party sits on the centre-right.

sections.key: Socialism seeks equality through collective ownership, while libertarianism seeks maximum individual liberty under a minimal state.
sections.b:
Socialism emerged in the 1800s in response to the harsh conditions of the Industrial Revolution. Socialists argue that wealth is produced collectively, so key industries should be owned or controlled by the public and shared more equally. Communist states built one-party, centrally planned systems. Democratic socialists instead seek change through elections, with strong unions, public services and welfare inside a market economy. Critics point to communist failures and weakened incentives.

Libertarians want people free to live as they choose, so long as they don't harm others, under the smallest possible state. That mixes free markets, which sounds right-wing, with personal freedoms, which can sound left-wing. Critics say a minimal state would leave the vulnerable unprotected and struggle with shared problems like pollution.

sections.key: Two-axis models separate economic views from views on personal freedom, but even they simplify reality.
sections.b:
Because one line mixes up too many questions, some people use two axes. The horizontal axis measures economic views, from more state control on the left to more free market on the right. The vertical axis measures personal freedom, from authoritarian (favouring strong state control of behaviour) to libertarian (favouring minimal control). American libertarian David Nolan drew an early version, and the online Political Compass quiz made the idea widely known.

Even two axes simplify reality. Environmentalism, nationalism and populism cut across these lines in different ways, and political scientists still debate how best to map beliefs.

sections.key: Understanding the strongest version of opposing views sharpens your own thinking and makes political debate less exhausting.
sections.b:
Every major political tradition contains serious thinkers responding to real problems. Liberty, fairness, stability and security all matter, and people weigh them differently. A useful habit is to describe an opposing view so well that its supporters would agree with your summary, sometimes called steelmanning.

Be wary of labels used as insults, and check whether a claim about 'the other side' describes its mainstream or its fringe. Most people's views are a mix, and they change over a lifetime. Understanding the ideas, rather than just the teams, makes political debate more useful.

quiz.q: On economic questions, what does the left generally favour?
o: Lower taxes and lighter regulation
Keeping institutions exactly as they are
More government action to reduce inequality, through taxes and public services
Relying mainly on private enterprise and individual effort
quiz.e: The left generally wants government to do more to reduce inequality, while the right leans towards markets and individual effort.

quiz.q: Which idea is most central to liberalism?
o: Individual rights and government by consent
Rule by a hereditary monarch
Public ownership of all industry
Preserving every tradition unchanged
quiz.e: Liberalism grew from the idea that people have natural rights and that government rests on the consent of the governed.

quiz.q: Which combination best describes libertarianism?
o: High taxes and strict social rules
Central planning and a single party
Strong tradition and a powerful state
Free markets and broad personal freedoms under a minimal state
quiz.e: Libertarians want the smallest possible state in both economic and personal life, which cuts across the usual left-right line.

quiz.q: What does the vertical axis of the political compass measure?
o: Economic views from left to right
Authoritarian versus libertarian views on personal freedom
Urban versus rural voting patterns
Support for change versus tradition
quiz.e: The second axis separates economic views from views on how much the state should control personal behaviour.

quiz.q: What is the point of 'steelmanning' an opposing view?
o: Finding its weakest argument to defeat it
Persuading supporters to give up their view
Describing it so well that its own supporters would agree
Avoiding discussion of it altogether
quiz.e: Stating an opposing view at its strongest improves your own thinking and makes debate more useful.

LESSONS.push: A French seating plan from 1789 still shapes how we talk about elections.

LESSONS.title: How Australia's Parliament works
LESSONS.hook: Two chambers, a Prime Minister who isn't mentioned in the Constitution, and a Governor-General with rarely used powers. Here's how laws really get made in Canberra.

sections.key: Australia's government must keep the confidence of the House, and the Prime Minister and cabinet rest on convention, not the Constitution.
sections.b:
Australia's system is based on the British Westminster model, with a federal twist borrowed from the United States, which is why it is nicknamed 'Washminster'. Its defining feature is responsible government: ministers sit in Parliament, answer questions in daily Question Time, and stay in office only while they keep the confidence of the lower house.

Surprisingly, the Constitution doesn't mention the Prime Minister or the cabinet. Both rest on conventions inherited from Britain. The PM leads the party or coalition with majority support in the House, is chosen by that party rather than by voters, and can be replaced mid-term if the party changes leader. Senior ministers form the cabinet, which decides in confidence. Under cabinet solidarity, ministers must publicly back its decisions or resign.

sections.key: The House of about 150 members decides who governs, while the 76 senators review legislation, with 12 for each state.
sections.b:
The House of Representatives has about 150 members, each representing one electorate of, on average, more than 100,000 voters. Terms last up to three years. The party or coalition with a majority forms government, and the largest group outside it is the Opposition, which scrutinises the government.

The Senate has 76 senators: 12 from each state regardless of population, and two each from the ACT and Northern Territory. Equal state representation was a condition of the smaller colonies joining federation. State senators serve six-year terms, with half elected every three years. Proportional representation means minor parties often hold the balance of power. The Senate reviews and amends bills and investigates government through committees. It cannot introduce tax bills or amend certain money bills, but it can reject them.

sections.key: A bill must pass both houses and receive Royal Assent, and a double dissolution can break a deadlock with the Senate.
sections.b:
A proposed law is called a bill. Most come from ministers, though any member can introduce one. In each house it is introduced at first reading, debated at second reading, examined clause by clause and voted on at third reading. Both houses must pass it in identical form. The Governor-General then gives Royal Assent, and it becomes an Act.

Governments often lack a Senate majority, so they negotiate with crossbenchers. If the Senate twice rejects a bill, at least three months apart, section 57 of the Constitution allows a double dissolution: both houses are dissolved and every seat is contested. If the new Parliament still disagrees, a joint sitting can decide. These are rare. The latest double dissolution was in 2016, and 1974 produced the only joint sitting.

sections.key: The Governor-General has wide formal powers but almost always acts on ministers' advice, keeping reserve powers for a crisis.
sections.b:
Australia is a constitutional monarchy. The King of Australia is represented by the Governor-General, who is appointed by the monarch on the Prime Minister's advice. On paper the powers look huge: summoning and dissolving Parliament, assenting to laws and commanding the defence force. By convention, though, the Governor-General almost always acts on ministers' advice.

A small set of reserve powers can be used independently in a crisis. The most famous use came in 1975, when Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissed Prime Minister Gough Whitlam during a budget deadlock, a decision still debated today. Each state also has its own governor.

sections.key: Australia has federal, state and local government, and councils exist only because state laws create them.
sections.b:
Australia has three tiers of government. Each state has its own parliament, led by a Premier, and handles areas like schools, hospitals, police and roads. All state parliaments have two houses except Queensland's, which abolished its upper house in 1922. The ACT and Northern Territory have single-house assemblies led by Chief Ministers.

The third tier is local government. More than 500 councils run services such as rubbish collection, local roads, libraries and planning approvals. Councils aren't recognised in the federal Constitution; state laws create them. Knowing which level handles what tells you whether to contact your councillor, your state MP or your federal member.

quiz.q: Where does the role of Prime Minister come from?
o: Section 1 of the Constitution
A referendum held in 1975
Convention, not the Constitution's text
A direct national vote for the leader
quiz.e: The Constitution doesn't mention the Prime Minister or cabinet; both rest on unwritten conventions inherited from Britain.

quiz.q: Why does every state have 12 senators regardless of population?
o: Equal representation was a condition of the smaller colonies joining federation
The High Court ruled that population-based seats were unfair
Larger states volunteered to give up Senate seats
The number was set by the first Prime Minister
quiz.e: Equal state representation in the Senate was the price of getting the smaller colonies to join the federation.

quiz.q: What can break a deadlock when the Senate repeatedly blocks a House bill?
o: A ruling by the Governor-General alone
A vote of the state premiers
A decision by the High Court
A double dissolution election
quiz.e: Section 57 lets the government dissolve both houses and take the deadlock to voters, after the Senate twice blocks a bill.

quiz.q: How does the Governor-General normally use the formal powers of the office?
o: Independently, overruling ministers when they see fit
On the advice of ministers, keeping reserve powers for a crisis
Only with the approval of the monarch in London
By vote of the High Court
quiz.e: By convention the Governor-General almost always follows ministers' advice, with independent reserve powers used only in a crisis.

quiz.q: How are local councils created?
o: By the federal Constitution itself
By a decree of the Governor-General
By state laws, not the Constitution
By a vote of the Senate
quiz.e: Councils depend on state legislation, which is why they sit as the third tier beneath state and federal government.

LESSONS.push: Australia's Prime Minister isn't in the Constitution. So where does the job come from?

LESSONS.title: How voting works in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Australia gave the world the secret ballot, makes voting compulsory, and counts your vote more than once. Here's what happens to your ballot after it drops in the box.

sections.key: Voting in federal elections has been compulsory since 1924, and turnout is usually around 90%.
sections.b:
Australia is one of a small number of democracies where voting is compulsory. Enrolment became compulsory in 1911 and voting in 1924, first applying at the 1925 election. Turnout at the 1922 election had fallen below 60%. Since then it has usually been around 90% or more.

Strictly, the legal duty is to attend a polling place, have your name marked off, and put your ballot paper in the box. Because the ballot is secret, nobody checks how, or whether, you filled it in. People who don't vote without a valid reason receive a modest fine. Supporters say compulsion gives governments a mandate from everyone. Critics argue that voting should be a free choice.

sections.key: A House candidate needs more than 50% of formal votes, and preferences pass votes from excluded candidates to later choices.
sections.b:
For the House of Representatives, Australia uses full preferential voting, introduced federally in 1918. You number every box in order of preference: 1 for your favourite, 2 for your next choice, and so on. A ballot not filled in correctly is informal and doesn't count.

To win a seat, a candidate needs more than 50% of formal votes. If nobody has this after first preferences, the candidate with the fewest votes is excluded and each of their ballots passes to the next preference marked. This repeats until someone crosses 50%. Say A has 44%, B 41% and C 15%. If two-thirds of C's voters put B second, B gains 10% and wins with 51%. So you can back a minor candidate without 'wasting' your vote.

sections.key: Senators are elected by proportional representation, so candidates need a quota of votes rather than a majority.
sections.b:
The Senate ballot paper is large, divided by a thick black line. Above the line, you number at least six party or group boxes. Below the line, you number at least twelve individual candidates. These rules have applied since 2016.

Senators are elected by proportional representation using the single transferable vote. At a normal half-Senate election, six senators are elected per state, and each needs a quota of about 14.3% of the votes. Candidates who pass the quota have their surplus votes passed on at reduced value, and low candidates are excluded. This helps smaller parties win seats in proportion to their support.

sections.key: An independent commission runs federal elections, and the secret ballot, first used in Victoria and South Australia in 1856, protects voters from pressure.
sections.b:
Federal elections are run by the Australian Electoral Commission, an independent statutory authority established in 1984. It keeps the electoral roll, counts the votes and regulates donation disclosure. It also oversees redistributions, redrawing boundaries so seats in a state have roughly equal numbers of voters. Independent committees, not politicians, draw them. States and territories have their own commissions.

Before the 1850s, voting in Britain and its colonies was often public, which made bribery and intimidation easy. In 1856 Victoria and South Australia introduced the secret ballot: official, government-printed papers listing all candidates, marked privately. Britain adopted it in 1872. American states took it up from the late 1880s and called it the 'Australian ballot'.

sections.key: Keep your enrolment current, follow the ballot instructions exactly, and remember that how-to-vote cards are only suggestions.
sections.b:
Australian citizens aged 18 and over must enrol, and 16 and 17 year olds can enrol early. Enrol or update your address with the AEC, usually online, whenever you move. Federal elections are held on a Saturday. You can vote at any polling place in your state or territory, vote early at a pre-polling centre, or apply for a postal vote. Polling places are often schools and halls, where sausage sizzles are a tradition.

Before election day, read about the candidates, not just the parties. Follow the ballot instructions carefully, because a missing or repeated number can make a House vote informal. How-to-vote cards are only suggestions; number the boxes however you choose. Your vote is secret, and nobody can require you to reveal it.

quiz.q: What does the law actually require of a voter at a federal election?
o: Voting for one of the two major parties
Attending, being marked off the roll and lodging a ballot paper
Showing an official how you filled in the ballot
Proving afterwards which candidate you chose
quiz.e: The duty is to attend and lodge a ballot paper; because voting is secret, nobody checks how you filled it in.

quiz.q: What happens when no House candidate has more than 50% after first preferences?
o: A new election is held for that seat
The Governor-General chooses between the leaders
The lowest candidate is excluded and their votes pass on
The two leading candidates share the seat for the term
quiz.e: Exclusions and transfers continue until one candidate has a majority, so a vote for a minor candidate isn't wasted.

quiz.q: At a half-Senate election, what does a candidate need to win a seat?
o: A quota of about 14.3% of the votes
More than 50% of the votes
The most first preferences in the state
Support from both major parties
quiz.e: With six seats per state, proportional representation sets a quota of about one-seventh of the vote, which lets smaller parties win seats.

quiz.q: What problem did the secret ballot address?
o: Low turnout at elections across the colonies
Votes being miscounted by returning officers
Too few people being enrolled to vote
Public voting, which allowed bribery and intimidation
quiz.e: Marking a ballot privately protects voters from pressure by employers, landlords, officials or anyone else.

quiz.q: What should you do if a how-to-vote card differs from your own preferences?
o: Follow the card, since it sets the required order
Number the boxes as you choose; cards are only suggestions
Leave the ballot blank so nobody is misled
Ask the party to approve your changes first
quiz.e: How-to-vote cards are only suggestions from parties; your numbering is your own choice.

LESSONS.push: Your vote can be counted more than once. Here's how that decides a seat.

LESSONS.title: Human rights: where they come from
LESSONS.hook: In 1948, after the horrors of the Second World War, the world's nations agreed on a list of rights belonging to every person. Here's what's in it, and how Australia protects rights without a bill of rights.

sections.key: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted on 10 December 1948, set out rights that belong to every person simply because they are human.
sections.b:
Human rights are the basic freedoms that belong to every person, regardless of nationality, sex, race or religion. The idea has deep roots. Magna Carta limited a king's power in 1215, Enlightenment thinkers wrote of natural rights, and France in 1789 and the United States in 1791 put rights into law. But the idea that rights apply to all humanity, as an international concern, took shape after 1945.
