A UN commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt drafted a common standard. Australia sat on the eight-country drafting committee, and H.V. Evatt was President of the General Assembly when the Universal Declaration was adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948, by 48 votes to none with eight abstentions. Its first article: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'

sections.key: The 1948 Declaration was not a binding treaty, but the UN turned its principles into binding covenants in 1966.
sections.b:
The Universal Declaration was not a treaty, so it didn't directly bind countries in law. It was a statement of shared aims, though it has become enormously influential and has shaped many constitutions and laws.

To turn its principles into binding obligations, the UN adopted two major treaties in 1966: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Together with the Declaration, they are often called the International Bill of Human Rights. Other treaties followed on specific issues, including racial discrimination, discrimination against women, torture, children's rights and disability.

sections.key: Civil and political rights protect people from abuse of state power, while economic, social and cultural rights cover needs like work, health and education.
sections.b:
Civil and political rights mainly protect people from the misuse of state power and guarantee participation in public life. They include the right to life, a fair trial, freedom of expression, religion and assembly, privacy, and the right to vote. Many can be limited in certain circumstances, for example to protect public safety or the rights of others, but some, such as the ban on torture, are treated as absolute.

Economic, social and cultural rights cover fair work, joining a union, social security, adequate food and housing, health and education. Because these depend on resources, countries must achieve them progressively. Some argue they are as fundamental as civil rights, since freedom means little without food or schooling. Others see them as policy goals for elected governments rather than rights for courts to enforce.

sections.key: Australia has no national bill of rights; it protects rights through the Constitution, common law, statutes and parliamentary scrutiny.
sections.b:
Australia is often described as the only Western democracy without a national bill or charter of rights. Instead, rights are protected in several ways. The Constitution contains a few express rights and an implied freedom of political communication. The common law presumes Parliament doesn't intend to override basic freedoms unless it says so clearly.

Federal laws ban discrimination on grounds including race (1975), sex (1984), disability (1992) and age (2004), and the Australian Human Rights Commission handles complaints. Since 2012, new federal bills must carry a statement on their compatibility with human rights, reviewed by a parliamentary committee. The ACT, Victoria and Queensland have their own human rights Acts.

sections.key: Australians disagree about a national bill of rights, and anyone facing discrimination can complain to the Australian Human Rights Commission or a state body.
sections.b:
Supporters of a national bill of rights say current protections have gaps, that ordinary laws can be changed by any Parliament, and that a clear list would help vulnerable people. Critics say elected Parliaments, not unelected judges, should balance rights, and that Australia already protects rights well. A middle path is the Victorian model, where courts can declare laws inconsistent with rights but Parliament has the final say.

If you face discrimination at work, in housing, in education or from services, you can complain to the Australian Human Rights Commission or a state body. In 1994, in Toonen v Australia, the UN Human Rights Committee found Tasmania's laws criminalising homosexual acts breached the right to privacy, and federal law changed soon after. For advice on your situation, see a lawyer or community legal centre.

quiz.q: What idea lies at the heart of the 1948 Universal Declaration?
o: Rights are granted by each government to its citizens
Rights apply only to citizens of UN member states
Rights belong to every person simply because they are human
Rights depend on a country's laws and customs
quiz.e: The Declaration holds that rights are universal, belonging to everyone regardless of nationality, sex, race or religion.

quiz.q: How do the 1966 covenants differ from the 1948 Declaration?
o: They are binding treaties that turn its principles into legal obligations
They are non-binding statements of shared aims
They replace it with a shorter list of rights
They apply only to wealthy countries
quiz.e: The Declaration was a statement of aims, so the UN adopted binding covenants to make its principles enforceable obligations.

quiz.q: Which right is treated as absolute and cannot be limited?
o: Freedom of assembly
Freedom of expression
Freedom from torture
The right to privacy
quiz.e: Many civil rights can be limited, for example to protect public safety, but the ban on torture is treated as absolute.

quiz.q: Which statement about rights protection in Australia is correct?
o: It has a national bill of rights dating from 1901
It has no bill of rights but protects rights through several laws
It has never signed a human rights treaty
Rights are protected only by the state governments
quiz.e: Australia lacks a national bill of rights but protects rights through several overlapping laws and processes.

quiz.q: What is a common argument against a national bill of rights?
o: It would remove rights already in the Constitution
It would make existing discrimination laws invalid overnight
It would transfer control of rights to state governments
It would shift power from Parliament to unelected judges
quiz.e: Critics say elected, accountable Parliaments should balance competing rights, rather than judges.

LESSONS.push: Australia helped write the world's human rights list, yet has no bill of rights.

LESSONS.title: The United Nations
LESSONS.hook: Born from the ashes of the Second World War, the UN has 193 members, a veto that can freeze it, and agencies that helped wipe out smallpox. Here's how it works and why it divides opinion.

sections.key: The UN was founded in 1945 to prevent another world war after the League of Nations failed, and now has 193 members.
sections.b:
The United Nations was created as the Second World War ended, to prevent another global war. Its predecessor, the League of Nations, founded in 1920, had failed to stop aggression in the 1930s, partly because major powers were absent or left.

Delegates from 50 countries signed the UN Charter in San Francisco on 26 June 1945, and Poland soon became the 51st founding member. The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, now marked as United Nations Day. Australia was a founding member, and its delegation, led by H.V. Evatt, pushed for a stronger voice for smaller and middle powers. Membership has grown to 193 countries, with headquarters in New York.

sections.key: The UN has six principal organs, and in the General Assembly every member has one vote, but most resolutions are only recommendations.
sections.b:
The Charter created six principal organs: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice in The Hague, the Secretariat, and the Trusteeship Council, suspended in 1994 after its last territory, Palau, became independent. The Secretariat is the UN's staff, led by the Secretary-General, who serves a five-year term.

The General Assembly is the most representative body. All 193 members sit in it, with one vote each, whether China or tiny Tuvalu. It meets from September in New York, debates global issues, approves the budget and elects the Council's non-permanent members. Important questions need a two-thirds majority. But most of its resolutions are recommendations, not binding law, so they carry moral and political weight rather than legal force.

sections.key: Five permanent members of the Security Council can each block any substantive resolution with a veto.
sections.b:
The Security Council is the UN's most powerful body. It has 15 members: five permanent members (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) and ten elected for two-year terms. Its decisions on threats to peace can be binding on all members, and it can impose sanctions or authorise military force.

Each permanent member has a veto: a single 'no' vote blocks any substantive resolution. The veto was the price of getting the great powers to join. It has been used many times, most often by the Soviet Union or Russia and by the United States, and has often left the Council deadlocked. At San Francisco, Australia argued against the full scope of the veto, without success.

sections.key: UN agencies work on health, children, refugees and culture, while peacekeepers lent by member states have had mixed results.
sections.b:
Much of the UN's work happens through agencies. The World Health Organization coordinated the campaign that eradicated smallpox, declared in 1980. UNICEF supports children's health, nutrition and education. UNHCR protects people forced from their homes. The World Food Programme, which won the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize, delivers food aid in crises. UNESCO runs the World Heritage list, which includes the Great Barrier Reef, Uluru-Kata Tjuta and the Sydney Opera House.

Peacekeeping isn't mentioned in the Charter; it developed through practice. Australians were among the first UN military observers, in Indonesia in 1947. Peacekeepers, the 'blue helmets', are troops and police lent by member states to monitor ceasefires and protect civilians. There have been successes, but also grave failures, notably Rwanda in 1994 and Srebrenica in 1995.

sections.key: Supporters value the UN as a global forum and aid provider, while critics point to deadlock, bureaucracy and a power structure frozen in 1945.
sections.b:
Supporters argue the UN has helped avoid a third world war, given every nation a voice, delivered aid to millions, and set shared standards from human rights to aviation. It gives rivals a place to keep talking. Critics say the veto lets any permanent member block action even during atrocities, that the Council reflects the power of 1945 rather than today, that the organisation can be slow and bureaucratic, and that one-country-one-vote gives tiny and huge nations equal weight. Reform is hard because changing the Charter needs the permanent members' agreement.

Australia held the Council's first presidency in 1946 and has served several terms as an elected member. Tens of thousands of Australian personnel have served in UN and UN-authorised missions, including Cyprus, Cambodia and East Timor.

quiz.q: Why was the UN created at the end of the Second World War?
o: To replace national governments with a single world government
To manage trade and tariffs between countries
To prevent another global war after the League failed
To rebuild the cities damaged in the war
quiz.e: The League of Nations had failed to stop 1930s aggression, so the UN was built to prevent another world war.

quiz.q: What is the legal weight of most General Assembly resolutions?
o: They are recommendations, not binding law
They bind every member that voted for them
They bind only the five permanent members
They become law once the Secretary-General signs
quiz.e: Each member has one vote, but most Assembly resolutions are recommendations rather than binding law.

quiz.q: What can a single permanent member of the Security Council do?
o: Expel another member state
Appoint the Secretary-General alone
Override the General Assembly
Block any substantive resolution with its veto
quiz.e: The veto was the price of getting great powers to join, and it can leave the Council deadlocked.

quiz.q: Who supplies the troops and police for UN peacekeeping missions?
o: A permanent standing UN army
Member states, which lend them to the UN
Private security companies hired by the Secretariat
Only the five permanent Security Council members
quiz.e: Blue helmets are troops and police lent by member states to monitor ceasefires and protect civilians.

quiz.q: What is a common criticism of the Security Council?
o: It has no power to impose sanctions
Its permanent membership reflects the world of 1945, not today
It meets only once a decade
It gives every member state a permanent seat
quiz.e: Critics say the Council's structure reflects the power balance of 1945, and reform needs the permanent members' consent.

LESSONS.push: One 'no' vote from any of five nations can stop the UN Security Council. Why?

LESSONS.title: Engines: turning fire into motion
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, all power came from muscle, wind and water. Then people learned to turn fire into motion, and the world sped up.

sections.key: Before engines, work ran on muscle, wind and water, and the first practical steam engine of 1712 was built to pump water from flooded mines.
sections.b:
For most of history, work was done by the muscles of people and animals, helped by wind and flowing water. Both depended on where rivers ran and which way the wind blew. Hero of Alexandria described a steam-spun ball, the aeolipile, in the first century AD, but it was a curiosity. Turning heat into useful motion took another 1,600 years, and the push came from flooded mines.

Thomas Savery patented a steam pump in 1698, but it was limited and failure-prone. In 1712 Devon ironmonger Thomas Newcomen built a working engine near Dudley. Steam filled a cylinder, then a cold spray condensed it, creating a partial vacuum. Air pressure pushed the piston down to work a pump beam. Newcomen engines were slow and burned huge amounts of coal, but hundreds were built.

sections.key: James Watt didn't invent the steam engine; his separate condenser made it far more efficient.
sections.b:
James Watt is often called the inventor of the steam engine, but he improved an existing one. In 1765, after repairing a model Newcomen engine at the University of Glasgow, he realised it wasted most of its fuel reheating a cylinder that was cooled on every stroke.

His fix was a separate condenser, so the cylinder could stay hot. Watt and his partner Matthew Boulton sold engines that used roughly a quarter of the coal of a Newcomen engine. Watt later adapted engines to turn wheels, and coined 'horsepower' to market them. The popular tale of a boiling kettle inspiring him is a legend.

sections.key: Steam power freed factories from rivers and drove the railways and steamships that shrank journeys from days to hours.
sections.b:
Steam became a driving force of the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain around the 1760s. Factories no longer had to sit beside rivers, so they grew in towns near coal and workers. In 1804 Richard Trevithick ran the first steam locomotive on rails, in Wales. In 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first intercity line worked entirely by steam locomotives. Steamships soon crossed oceans regardless of the wind.

Australia's first steam railway opened in Melbourne in 1854, running from Flinders Street to Sandridge, now Port Melbourne. Journeys that once took days shrank to hours.

sections.key: Internal combustion engines burn fuel inside the cylinder, and Henry Ford made cars affordable rather than inventing them.
sections.b:
A steam engine burns fuel outside the cylinder to boil water. An internal combustion engine burns fuel inside it, so it can be much smaller and lighter for the same power. Etienne Lenoir built a working gas engine in France around 1860. In 1876 Nicolaus Otto built a successful four-stroke engine (intake, compression, power, exhaust), a cycle most car engines still use. In the 1890s Rudolf Diesel developed an engine that ignites fuel simply by squeezing air until it is very hot.

Karl Benz built the first practical petrol car in 1885, patented in 1886. In 1888 his wife Bertha drove it about 100 kilometres to visit her mother, proving it worked on real roads. Henry Ford did not invent the car. His contribution was making it cheap: the Model T in 1908, and his moving assembly line from 1913.

sections.key: Electric motors are far more efficient than fuel engines, and engines were built step by step by many people, not lone geniuses.
sections.b:
Electric motors turn electricity into motion using magnetism. In 1821 Michael Faraday showed that a current-carrying wire could rotate around a magnet, the principle behind every motor. In the late 1880s Nikola Tesla and, independently, Galileo Ferraris developed the AC induction motor, still the workhorse of industry. Electric cars were fairly common around 1900 before cheap petrol won out. Electric motors turn around 90% of their energy into motion, while petrol engines manage roughly 20 to 35%.

Big inventions are rarely one person's flash of genius. Newcomen built on Savery, Watt on Newcomen, and Benz and Diesel on Lenoir and Otto. Names stick to whoever made an idea practical or profitable. Engines also brought air pollution and the rise in carbon dioxide behind climate change.

quiz.q: What problem drove the invention of the first practical steam engines?
o: Ships becoming too heavy to sail
Deep mines filling with water
Factories running short of waterwheels
Railways needing faster locomotives
quiz.e: English mines went deeper and flooded, so Newcomen's engine was built to pump the water out.

quiz.q: What did Watt's separate condenser improve?
o: It let engines drive ships across oceans
It made engines cheaper to build from wood
It kept the cylinder hot, saving coal
It removed the need for a boiler
quiz.e: Keeping the cylinder hot meant far less fuel was wasted, so Watt's engines used roughly a quarter of the coal.

quiz.q: How did steam power change where factories could be built?
o: They had to move into forests for timber
They moved underground beside the mines
They had to be built beside railway stations
They no longer had to sit beside rivers
quiz.e: Without the need for water power, factories could grow in towns near coal and workers.

quiz.q: What was Henry Ford's main contribution to motoring?
o: Making cars affordable through mass production
Building the first petrol car
Inventing the four-stroke engine
Inventing the diesel engine
quiz.e: Ford didn't invent the car; the Model T and his moving assembly line made it cheap.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of their energy do electric motors turn into motion?
o: About 25%
About 50%
About 90%
About 10%
quiz.e: Electric motors turn around 90% of their energy into motion, against roughly 20 to 35% for petrol engines.

LESSONS.push: The steam engine's inventor wasn't James Watt. Here's what he really did.

LESSONS.title: Electric light
LESSONS.hook: Before electric light, nights were dim, smoky and a real fire risk. The story of the light bulb involves many hands, not one lone genius.

sections.key: Night light came from flames until inventors found a filament that could glow for long in a good vacuum.
sections.b:
For thousands of years, light after sunset came from flames: wood fires, candles and oil lamps. It was dim, smoky and costly, and house fires were a constant danger. Whale oil, kerosene lamps and coal gas improved things. Sydney's streets were first gas-lit in 1841, supplied by the Australian Gas Light Company, whose name survives as AGL.

Electric light began with the arc lamp. In the early 1800s Humphry Davy showed that electricity leaping between two carbon rods made a brilliant glow, but arc lamps were too harsh and hot for living rooms. The alternative was incandescence: a thin filament heated until it glows. Oxygen left in the bulb destroyed early filaments. The challenge was a lasting filament, in a good vacuum, cheap enough to mass-produce.

sections.key: Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison both reached practical bulbs around 1879, but Edison's greatest contribution was the whole electrical system.
sections.b:
The popular story says Thomas Edison invented the light bulb in 1879. In truth he and English chemist Joseph Swan reached practical carbon-filament bulbs at about the same time, both building on decades of earlier work. After a British patent dispute they joined forces in 1883 as 'Ediswan'.

Edison's real gift was the system around the bulb. A bulb is useless without power, so his team designed generators, underground cables, switches, fuses and meters to bill customers. In September 1882 his Pearl Street Station in New York began supplying paying customers. At his Menlo Park laboratory, staff tested thousands of materials systematically, a model for team-based research and development.

sections.key: Alternating current beat Edison's direct current because transformers let it travel long distances cheaply.
sections.b:
Edison's system used direct current (DC), which flows one way and, at the low voltages of the day, couldn't travel much more than a kilometre or two. Alternating current (AC) rapidly reverses direction and can be stepped up to high voltage by transformers for long-distance transmission, then stepped down for homes. George Westinghouse championed AC, licensing Nikola Tesla's motor patents in 1888. Edison's side stressed AC's dangers in a bitter public battle. AC won because it was cheaper to distribute.

The Tesla versus Edison legend is more mixed than hero versus villain. Many people shaped AC power. Tesla's story of being cheated of a $50,000 bonus comes from his own account and can't be confirmed. And Edison didn't personally kill Topsy the elephant in 1903; a film company bearing his name recorded it.

sections.key: Tamworth became the first Australian town with electric street lighting in 1888, and AC grids later spread across the country.
sections.b:
AC's victory was sealed in the 1890s, when a Westinghouse system lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and, from 1896, carried power from Niagara Falls to Buffalo. In Australia, Tamworth in New South Wales became the first town to light its streets with electricity, in 1888, earning the nickname 'City of Light'.

Over the following decades, local power stations were joined into larger grids, and the east coast grid is now one of the longest interconnected power systems in the world. DC has made a comeback for special jobs: the Basslink cable under Bass Strait uses high-voltage DC.

sections.key: LED bulbs, made possible by the bright blue LED of the early 1990s, use far less energy than old incandescent bulbs.
sections.b:
Old incandescent bulbs wasted most of their energy, around 90%, as heat. Australia began phasing most of them out in 2009, one of the first countries to do so.

The next leap was the light-emitting diode. Nick Holonyak built the first visible, red LED in 1962, but white light needed a bright blue LED. Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura achieved it in the early 1990s, earning the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. LED bulbs use roughly 75 to 80% less energy than incandescent ones and last many times longer, so replacing any remaining old bulbs is an easy way to trim a power bill.

quiz.q: Why did early incandescent filaments burn out so quickly?
o: The glass cracked as it heated
Oxygen left in the bulb destroyed the thin filament
Gas lighting interfered with the current
No material could carry an electric current
quiz.e: A lasting filament needed a good vacuum, because leftover oxygen destroyed early filaments.

quiz.q: What was Edison's biggest contribution to electric lighting?
o: The carbon arc lamp
Alternating current power
A complete electrical supply system
The first LED bulb
quiz.e: Edison's team built generators, cables, fuses and meters, making the bulb useful to paying customers.

quiz.q: Why did alternating current win out over direct current?
o: It was safer than DC at every voltage
Edison came to prefer it in his own plants
It worked better with existing gas lighting
Transformers let it travel far cheaply at high voltage
quiz.e: AC can be stepped up for long-distance transmission and stepped down for homes, making it cheaper to distribute.

quiz.q: Which was the first Australian town to light its streets with electricity, in 1888?
o: Tamworth
Ballarat
Hobart
Broken Hill
quiz.e: Tamworth's electric street lighting earned it the nickname 'City of Light'.

quiz.q: How do LED bulbs compare with old incandescent bulbs?
o: They use about half the energy but burn out sooner
They waste around 90% of their energy as heat
They use roughly 75 to 80% less energy and last far longer
They use the same energy but give brighter light
quiz.e: Incandescent bulbs waste most of their energy as heat, while LEDs use far less and last many times longer.

LESSONS.push: Edison didn't invent the light bulb alone. The fuller story is more interesting.

LESSONS.title: Telephone and radio
LESSONS.hook: In 1850 news from London took months to reach Australia. Within one lifetime, voices crossed the world in a fraction of a second.

sections.key: The telegraph sent coded messages almost instantly, and the Overland Telegraph Line connected Australia to Britain in 1872.
sections.b:
The telegraph was the first electrical communication system. Cooke and Wheatstone patented a practical version in Britain in 1837, and Samuel Morse, with Alfred Vail, developed a simpler system and the dot-and-dash Morse code. In 1844 Morse sent 'What hath God wrought' from Washington to Baltimore. A lasting Atlantic cable followed in 1866, after an 1858 cable failed within weeks.

News from Britain once came to Australia by ship and could take two months or more. In 1872 the Overland Telegraph Line, built under Charles Todd, ran about 3,200 kilometres from Adelaide to Darwin and linked to an undersea cable from Java, connecting Australia to London. Messages arrived within hours. The line crossed the Country of many Aboriginal nations, with lasting effects on the people there. Alice Springs grew around one of its stations.

sections.key: Bell won the 1876 telephone patent, but Elisha Gray and Antonio Meucci have serious claims, and telephones spread through exchanges.
sections.b:
Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish-born teacher of deaf students, received a US telephone patent in March 1876. Days later he reportedly called to his assistant, 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.' Credit remains disputed. Elisha Gray filed on a similar design at the patent office the same day. Antonio Meucci built voice-transmitting devices years earlier but couldn't afford to keep up his patent notice, and in 2002 the US House of Representatives honoured his work. Many contributed; Bell won the legal battles.

A telephone is only useful if it connects, so networks grew around exchanges. Human operators, very often women, connected calls by hand on switchboards. Automatic exchanges appeared in the 1890s. Melbourne opened an exchange in 1880, and by the late 20th century nearly every Australian home had a landline.

sections.key: Radio built on Maxwell and Hertz, and Marconi made wireless telegraphy practical, but credit is shared.
sections.b:
Radio rests on science from the 1860s, when James Clerk Maxwell predicted invisible electromagnetic waves, and the late 1880s, when Heinrich Hertz proved they existed. From 1895, Guglielmo Marconi turned this into practical wireless telegraphy, sending Morse code over ever greater distances. In 1901 he claimed a signal across the Atlantic, though some historians doubt it was truly heard.

Others made key contributions, including Oliver Lodge, Jagadish Chandra Bose, Alexander Popov, Karl Ferdinand Braun and Nikola Tesla. Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Braun. A 1943 US Supreme Court ruling struck down some of Marconi's patent claims, but named no single inventor of radio.

sections.key: The first direct wireless messages from Britain reached Sydney in 1918, and radio then connected the outback.
sections.b:
On 22 September 1918, Australia received its first direct wireless messages from Britain. A message from Prime Minister Billy Hughes, who was then in Britain, was sent from Marconi's station in Wales and picked up roughly 17,000 kilometres away by Ernest Fisk at his home in Wahroonga, Sydney. Fisk went on to lead the company AWA.

Regular broadcasting began in 1923, and radio soon became the nation's shared living room, bringing news, sport and serials. In the outback, Alfred Traeger's pedal-powered radio, from 1929, let remote stations call the Flying Doctor, and later made the School of the Air possible.

sections.key: Mobile phones merged radio and telephone, and communication inventions were collective efforts that reshaped how people live.
sections.b:
On 3 April 1973, Motorola engineer Martin Cooper made the first call from a handheld mobile phone on a New York street. His prototype weighed around a kilogram and offered only about half an hour of talk time. Australia's first mobile network, an analogue service run by Telecom Australia, launched in 1987. Digital networks followed in the 1990s, bringing text messaging, and smartphones from 2007 put the internet in our pockets.

Morse, Bell and Marconi are famous because they made ideas practical, won patents and built companies, not because they worked alone. When a single name is attached to an invention, ask who else was working on the same problem. Each leap changed society: the telegraph cut news times from months to hours, radio created mass audiences, and mobiles made people reachable almost anywhere.

quiz.q: How did the Overland Telegraph Line change Australia's links with Britain?
o: It carried the first mobile calls
It replaced ships for carrying all mail
Messages that took weeks by ship now arrived within hours
It connected Sydney to Melbourne for the first time
quiz.e: The line from Adelaide to Darwin linked to an undersea cable, connecting Australia to London by wire.

quiz.q: Why is credit for the telephone disputed?
o: Bell never received a patent
Elisha Gray and Antonio Meucci worked on similar devices
The first telephone was built in Australia
Bell copied a design by Marconi
quiz.e: Gray filed on a similar design the same day, and Meucci had built voice devices years earlier; Bell won the legal battles.

quiz.q: Which statement about Marconi is most accurate?
o: He discovered electromagnetic waves
He invented the telephone and radio
A court named him the sole inventor of radio
He made wireless practical, building on others
quiz.e: Marconi built on Maxwell and Hertz and worked alongside others, so credit for radio is shared.

quiz.q: How did Alfred Traeger's pedal radio help the outback?
o: It let remote stations call the Flying Doctor
It carried the first messages from Britain
It replaced the Overland Telegraph Line
It brought live sport to cities
quiz.e: The pedal-powered radio connected isolated stations to medical help and later made the School of the Air possible.

quiz.q: What does the history of communication inventions suggest about credit?
o: Single inventors usually worked alone
The famous names usually made ideas practical while many others contributed
Patents always went to the person who had the idea first
Governments usually invented the technologies
quiz.e: Morse, Bell and Marconi are famous for making ideas practical, but many people worked on the same problems.

LESSONS.push: News from London once took two months to reach Australia. Then one wire changed that.

LESSONS.title: The story of flight
LESSONS.hook: People dreamed of flying for thousands of years. Then, in just 25 years, they went from a 12-second hop to crossing the Pacific.

sections.key: The path to powered flight ran through Cayley's four forces, Lilienthal's gliders and Lawrence Hargrave's box kite.
sections.b:
People long dreamed of flying. The first humans actually to fly went up in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon in 1783, but balloons go wherever the wind takes them. Around 1800, English engineer George Cayley identified the four forces of flight: lift, drag, thrust and weight. A fixed wing could provide lift while something else provided thrust, and in 1853 one of his gliders carried a man across a small valley.

In the 1890s Otto Lilienthal made around 2,000 glider flights, inspiring others, before dying in a crash in 1896. In Sydney, Lawrence Hargrave invented the strong, stable box kite in 1893. In 1894 four of them lifted him about five metres at Stanwell Park. He shared his work freely rather than patenting it, and it influenced early European aeroplanes. He featured on the old paper $20 note.

sections.key: The Wright brothers' breakthrough was controlling an aircraft in three dimensions, which gave them the first sustained powered flights in 1903.
sections.b:
On 17 December 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew about 37 metres in 12 seconds. Later that day Wilbur flew about 260 metres in 59 seconds.

Their key insight was control. The brothers, bicycle makers from Ohio, realised a flying machine had to be steered in three dimensions, so they twisted, or warped, the wings to roll the aircraft, alongside a rudder and elevator. They built their own wind tunnel to test wing shapes, and with mechanic Charlie Taylor built a light petrol engine. Rival claims exist, notably for Brazil's Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew publicly in Paris in 1906, but most historians credit the Wrights.

sections.key: Wings create lift by turning air downward, and the popular idea that air must meet up behind the wing is a myth.
sections.b:
A common explanation says air over the curved top of a wing must travel further, so it speeds up to 'meet' the air underneath at the back. This equal-transit-time idea is a myth. Nothing forces the air to meet up, and in fact air over the top arrives well before the air underneath.

What really happens is that the wing, tilted slightly into the airflow, turns a large mass of air downward. Pushing air down pushes the wing up, as Newton's third law describes. The same flow creates lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below. Both descriptions are true at once, which is why planes can even fly upside down.

sections.key: Australians shaped early aviation: the Smith brothers flew England to Australia in 1919, and Qantas began in outback Queensland in 1920.
sections.b:
In 1919 brothers Ross and Keith Smith, with mechanics Wally Shiers and Jim Bennett, flew a Vickers Vimy from England to Darwin in about 28 days, winning a 10,000-pound government prize. In 1928 Charles Kingsford Smith and Charles Ulm, with American crew Harry Lyon and James Warner, made the first flight across the Pacific, from California to Brisbane. Kingsford Smith also made the first Tasman crossing that year, and disappeared over the Andaman Sea in 1935.

In November 1920, Hudson Fysh, Paul McGinness and Fergus McMaster founded Qantas at Winton, Queensland, and it began airmail flights between Charleville and Cloncurry in 1922. Aircraft cut outback journeys from days to hours. In 1928 the first Flying Doctor flight used an aircraft leased from Qantas.

sections.key: Jet engines made long-distance flight routine, and flying is extremely safe because every accident is investigated and its lessons shared.
sections.b:
Propeller aircraft have limits on speed and altitude. In the 1930s Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany independently developed the jet engine, which sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and blasts the exhaust out the back. The first jet airliner, the de Havilland Comet, entered service in 1952, but crashes caused by metal fatigue taught hard lessons. Boeing's 707 from 1958 and 747 from 1970 made long-haul flying ordinary, and in 2018 Qantas launched non-stop flights between Perth and London.

Commercial air travel is now one of the safest ways to travel, largely because accidents are investigated in detail and the lessons shared worldwide, helped by the cockpit flight recorder developed in Australia. The cost is significant greenhouse gas emissions, and cleaner fuels are an active area of research.

quiz.q: What did George Cayley realise about how an aeroplane could work?
o: Flapping wings are the only way to create lift
Lift and thrust must come from the same surface
Balloons are the only practical way to carry a person
A fixed wing can provide lift while something else provides thrust
quiz.e: Separating lift from thrust gave the scientific foundation for aeroplanes.

quiz.q: What was the Wright brothers' key insight?
o: Using a jet engine
Launching from a mountain top
Controlling the aircraft in three dimensions
Building a balloon-plane hybrid
quiz.e: They twisted the wings to roll the aircraft and added a rudder and elevator, so a pilot could steer in three dimensions.

quiz.q: Why is the 'equal transit time' explanation of lift wrong?
o: Air has no reason to meet up, and arrives earlier on top
Wings don't involve air pressure at all
Air under the wing always travels faster
Lift comes only from the engine thrust
quiz.e: Wings tilted into the airflow turn air downward, which pushes the wing up.

quiz.q: How did early aircraft change life in the outback?
o: They made roads and railways unnecessary
They cut journeys from days to hours
They were too costly to use outside cities
They replaced the post office entirely
quiz.e: Qantas began in outback Queensland, where aircraft shortened journeys, carried airmail and supported the Flying Doctor.

quiz.q: Why is commercial flying so safe today?
o: Aircraft no longer have parts that wear out
Planes now fly only in good weather
Every accident is investigated and its lessons are shared worldwide
Flight routes avoid all busy airspace
quiz.e: Detailed investigation and shared lessons, along with tools like flight recorders, have steadily made flying safer.

LESSONS.push: The usual explanation of how wings lift a plane is wrong. Here's the real one.

LESSONS.title: Genuinely Australian inventions
LESSONS.hook: From flight recorders to the tech inside Wi-Fi, some of the world's most useful ideas have Australian fingerprints. Here is what is truly ours, and what is shared.

sections.key: David Warren's flight recorder was new because it captured cockpit voices as well as instrument data.
sections.b:
In 1953 and 1954, a series of de Havilland Comet jet crashes left investigators puzzled. David Warren, a scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories in Melbourne, realised that a recording of the crew's voices and instrument readings would help explain future crashes. By 1958 he had a working prototype that stored hours of cockpit sound and flight data.

Simpler instrument-only recorders were being developed elsewhere, but Warren's combination of voices and data was new. Australia became one of the first countries to require cockpit voice recorders, in the 1960s. Despite the name, 'black boxes' are painted bright orange so they are easier to find.

sections.key: Australians improved existing ideas: grey-scale ultrasound showed soft tissue, and Graeme Clark's multi-channel cochlear implant conveyed speech more clearly.
sections.b:
Medical ultrasound builds pictures from sound echoes. Scottish doctor Ian Donald pioneered its use in pregnancy in the 1950s, but at the Ultrasonics Institute in Sydney, George Kossoff and David Robinson's team developed grey-scale imaging in the early 1970s. Earlier scans showed mostly stark outlines; grey-scale revealed shades of soft tissue. Australian company Ausonics commercialised it, and it became standard worldwide.

A cochlear implant bypasses the damaged inner ear and stimulates the hearing nerve with electrical signals. Single-channel implants already existed, so Graeme Clark didn't invent the idea. His Melbourne team's achievement was a multi-channel implant that conveyed speech far more clearly. The first patient, Rod Saunders, received one in 1978. Cochlear Limited commercialised it in the 1980s, and it has become one of the world's leading hearing implant makers.

sections.key: Dr Fiona Wood and Marie Stoner developed a way to spray a patient's own skin cells onto burns to help new skin grow.
sections.b:
Severe burns heal slowly, and large skin grafts can leave heavy scarring. In the 1990s in Perth, plastic surgeon Dr Fiona Wood and scientist Marie Stoner developed a way to spray a patient's own skin cells onto a wound to help new skin grow.

Early versions grew the cells in a laboratory first. The later ReCell device processes a small sample of healthy skin into a cell suspension during the operation itself. Wood led the burns team at Royal Perth Hospital that treated many survivors of the 2002 Bali bombings, and she was named Australian of the Year in 2005.

sections.key: Australian invention usually means solving a key part of a problem: CSIRO patented a technique behind fast Wi-Fi, and Google Maps began in a Sydney start-up.
sections.b:
Australia didn't invent Wi-Fi outright, but the true story is still impressive. In the early 1990s a CSIRO team including radio astronomer John O'Sullivan tackled a stubborn problem: indoors, radio signals bounce off walls and the echoes smear fast data together. Using mathematics from radio astronomy, they developed a way around it, with a US patent granted in 1996. It became part of widely used Wi-Fi standards, 802.11a and 802.11g, and earned CSIRO hundreds of millions of dollars in licensing settlements.

Google Maps began as Where 2 Technologies, a Sydney start-up founded by Danish-born brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen with Noel Gordon and Stephen Ma. Google bought it in 2004 and launched Maps in 2005, with much early development done in Sydney. When you read that something was 'invented in Australia', ask which part, and who else helped.

sections.key: The Hills Hoist improved on earlier rotary clotheslines, and Australia issued the world's first polymer banknote in 1988.
sections.b:
In 1945 Lance Hill, in Adelaide, built a rotary clothesline with a winding crank to raise and lower it. Demand led him to start a business with his brother-in-law Harold Ling. Hill did not invent the rotary clothesline: earlier designs had been patented in Australia, including by Gilbert Toyne decades before. His success came from a sturdy, adjustable design and post-war mass production.

Soon after decimal currency arrived in 1966, forgers produced convincing fake $10 notes. The Reserve Bank and CSIRO spent about two decades developing banknotes on polymer, a plastic film. The first, a commemorative $10 note, was issued in 1988, and by 1996 Australia had a full set. A clear window is very hard to copy, and the notes last several times longer than paper; dozens of countries now use polymer.

quiz.q: What was new about David Warren's flight recorder?
o: It was the first device painted orange
It recorded cockpit voices as well as instrument data
It sent data by satellite
It could fly the plane automatically
quiz.e: Recording voices alongside instrument data gave investigators a fuller picture of what happened in a crash.

quiz.q: What made Graeme Clark's cochlear implant a real advance?
o: It was the first implant of any kind
It replaced the need for a hearing nerve
It was a multi-channel design that conveyed speech far more clearly
It worked by amplifying sound in the outer ear
quiz.e: Single-channel implants already existed; Clark's multi-channel version carried speech much more clearly.

quiz.q: How does spray-on skin help burns heal?
o: It replaces skin with a synthetic plastic film
It sprays the patient's own skin cells onto the wound to help new skin grow
It numbs the burn so grafts are never needed
It sprays donor skin from another person onto the wound
quiz.e: Using a patient's own cells helps new skin grow and avoids heavy scarring from large grafts.

quiz.q: Which best describes CSIRO's role in Wi-Fi?
o: It patented a technique for fast indoor wireless
It invented all of Wi-Fi entirely on its own
It played no part in any Wi-Fi standard
It invented the internet that Wi-Fi connects to
quiz.e: CSIRO solved the problem of indoor signal echoes, a key part of Wi-Fi rather than the whole of it.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Hills Hoist is accurate?
o: It was the world's first rotary clothesline
It was designed by CSIRO
It was invented in Sydney in 1888
It improved on earlier rotary clothesline designs
quiz.e: Earlier rotary clotheslines had been patented; Hill's success came from a sturdy, adjustable design and mass production.

LESSONS.push: Australia didn't invent Wi-Fi, exactly. What it did invent is more interesting.

LESSONS.title: Risk and return
LESSONS.hook: There is no such thing as a high return with no risk. Understanding why is the first real lesson of investing.

sections.key: Investments that can earn higher returns usually come with a higher chance of losses along the way.
sections.b:
The risk-return trade-off is the closest thing investing has to a law of nature. Money in a government-guaranteed bank account is very unlikely to lose value in dollar terms, so it pays a modest interest rate. Shares in companies can fall sharply, so investors demand the prospect of a higher long-run return to hold them.

If an asset offered high returns with no risk, everyone would buy it until its price rose and its future return shrank. That is why any offer of 'high returns, no risk' should set off alarm bells.

sections.key: In investing, risk means uncertainty: the chance that results differ from what you expected, including losing money.
sections.b:
Most people think of risk as losing money, and that matters. Professionals use a broader meaning: uncertainty about outcomes. A term deposit paying 4% has little uncertainty. A share fund might return 25% one year and lose 15% the next.

That swing is volatility: how widely and how often a price moves. Cash barely moves. The main Australian share index fell roughly half between late 2007 and early 2009, and more than a third in about a month in early 2020. Both times it recovered, but anyone forced to sell near the bottom locked in heavy losses.

sections.key: The main asset classes, from lower to higher expected risk and return, are cash, bonds, property and shares.
sections.b:
Investments are grouped into asset classes that behave in broadly similar ways. Cash, such as savings accounts and term deposits, is the most stable but usually earns the least. Fixed interest, mainly bonds, pays regular interest and tends to be steadier than shares.

Property can deliver rent and capital growth but is lumpy, costly to buy and sell, and can fall in value. Shares, Australian and international, have historically delivered the highest long-run returns of the main classes, with the biggest swings. Cash and bonds are often called defensive assets; property and shares are growth assets.

sections.key: Longer time horizons let you ride out volatility, and your risk should fit both your nerves and your finances.
sections.b:
Your time horizon is how long until you need the money. Over ten or twenty years, diversified share portfolios have historically been far more likely to end up ahead, though that is a pattern from the past, not a guarantee. Money for a house deposit in two years usually belongs somewhere stable. Money you won't touch for decades, like much of your super, can generally afford more growth assets.

Two more limits apply. Risk tolerance is emotional: can you watch your balance drop 30% without panicking? Risk capacity is financial: could you afford that drop? A nervous young worker has high capacity; a brave retiree drawing on savings has less.

sections.key: What matters is your return after inflation, so match each pot of money to its purpose and timeframe.
sections.b:
A 5% return sounds decent, but if prices rise 4%, your real return is only about 1%, and after tax it may be near zero. So cash is not truly risk-free over long periods. Australia's Reserve Bank targets inflation of 2-3% on average, which roughly halves the value of a dollar every 25 to 35 years.

Think in buckets. Emergency money belongs in cash, and short-term goals suit cash or conservative options. Long-term money, like super, can usually lean towards growth. Check which option your fund has you in. This is general information, not personal advice; speak to a licensed financial adviser, and see ASIC's Moneysmart for free guidance.

quiz.q: Why don't low-risk investments usually offer high returns?
o: Because banks are required by law to cap all returns
Because investors would buy them until prices rose and returns shrank
Because low-risk investments are taxed at a higher rate
Because governments set the return on every investment
quiz.e: If an asset offered high returns with no risk, demand would push its price up and its future return down.

quiz.q: What does risk mean to professional investors?
o: Only the chance of losing everything
Uncertainty about outcomes, including results differing from expectations
The fees charged by a fund
The tax paid on gains
quiz.e: Risk is broader than loss: it covers any uncertainty about what you will actually get.

quiz.q: Which of these is usually classed as a defensive asset?
o: Australian shares
International shares
Investment property
Bonds
quiz.e: Cash and bonds are defensive assets; shares and property are growth assets.

quiz.q: What is the difference between risk tolerance and risk capacity?
o: They mean exactly the same thing
Tolerance is emotional comfort with swings; capacity is how much loss you can afford
Tolerance applies to shares; capacity applies to property
Capacity is set by your bank; tolerance by the government
quiz.e: You need to consider both how you will feel and what you can actually afford to lose.

quiz.q: Why is keeping everything in cash not truly risk-free over decades?
o: Banks charge a fee on every deposit
Inflation can steadily erode its buying power
Cash cannot be withdrawn
Cash is not covered by any rules
quiz.e: Real returns matter: if prices rise faster than your interest, your money buys less each year.

LESSONS.push: Why a promise of high returns with no risk should always make you pause.

LESSONS.title: Bonds explained
LESSONS.hook: Governments and companies borrow trillions of dollars from investors. Bonds are how, and they quietly shape your super and your mortgage.

sections.key: A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays you interest and returns your money at a set date.
sections.b:
When you buy a bond, you are lending money. The borrower, called the issuer, promises to pay regular interest, known as the coupon, and to repay the original amount, called the face value, on a set maturity date. A five-year bond with a $100 face value and a 4% coupon pays $4 a year, usually in instalments, then returns the $100 at the end.

Shares make you a part-owner of a company; bonds make you a lender. Lenders get paid before shareholders, which is part of why bonds are generally less risky.

sections.key: Government bonds are among the safest investments; corporate bonds pay more because default is more likely.
sections.b:
The Australian Government borrows by issuing Treasury bonds through the Australian Office of Financial Management, and states borrow through agencies such as NSW Treasury Corporation. A national government that borrows in its own currency can tax and has a central bank, so the chance it fails to repay is considered very low. Australia has held a AAA credit rating from all three major agencies for many years.

Companies can fail, so investors want extra interest to cover credit risk, the chance of default. Bonds rated BBB- or above are investment grade. Lower-rated 'junk' bonds pay more because the risk is genuinely higher. A higher rate is a price for extra risk, not a free bonus.

sections.key: When interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall; when rates fall, existing bond prices rise.
sections.b:
Bonds can be sold before maturity, and their prices change. Imagine you hold a bond paying 3% a year. Then interest rates rise and new bonds pay 5%. Nobody will pay full price for your 3% bond when they can get 5% elsewhere, so its market price falls until its effective return, called its yield, matches the new rate. The reverse happens when rates fall.

This see-saw is the most important idea in bond investing. The longer a bond has left until maturity, the more its price moves when rates change.

sections.key: Bonds are not risk-free: rising rates and inflation can cut their value, as 2022 showed.
sections.b:
Bonds are called defensive, but they can lose value. In 2022, central banks raised interest rates quickly to fight high inflation. Because bond prices fall when rates rise, many bond funds lost money, in some markets in their worst year in generations. Unusually, shares fell at the same time, so balanced portfolios had few places to hide.

Inflation is another danger: a fixed 3% coupon buys less each year if prices rise 6%. If you hold a high-quality bond to maturity, though, you still receive the face value back.

Term deposits differ. An Australian bank deposit is covered by the Financial Claims Scheme up to $250,000 per person per institution and doesn't fluctuate. A bond sells for whatever it fetches that day, and bond funds never mature, so their value moves with rates.

sections.key: Bonds are held for stability, income and cushioning share falls, and you probably already own some through super.
sections.b:
Most diversified portfolios, including many super options, hold shares and bonds. Bonds provide predictable income and usually swing far less than shares. High-quality government bonds have often held their value or risen during share crashes, though 2022 showed this isn't guaranteed. Older investors, and anyone needing money within a few years, typically hold more bonds and cash.

Check your fund's split between growth and defensive assets. When rates rise, the bond portion may dip, but new bonds pay better yields. Be cautious of offers promising well above market rates; that return reflects extra risk. This is general information only. See a licensed financial adviser for personal advice, and Moneysmart for independent guides.

quiz.q: What are you doing when you buy a bond?
o: Buying part-ownership of a company
Opening a bank savings account
Lending money to the issuer in return for interest
Buying a share of a property trust
quiz.e: Bondholders are lenders; shareholders are owners.

quiz.q: Why do corporate bonds usually pay more than government bonds?
o: Companies are required to pay more by law
Investors want compensation for the higher risk of default
Corporate bonds never mature
Corporate bonds are tax-free
quiz.e: The extra interest compensates for credit risk.

quiz.q: If interest rates rise, what typically happens to the price of an existing bond?
o: It rises, because its coupon looks more valuable
It stays the same until maturity
It doubles in value
It falls, because new bonds pay more
quiz.e: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

quiz.q: Why was 2022 a bad year for many bond investors?
o: Most governments defaulted
Interest rates rose quickly, pushing bond prices down
Bonds were banned in several countries
Interest rates fell to zero
quiz.e: Rapid rate rises to fight inflation caused large falls in bond prices.

quiz.q: What is the main role of bonds in a diversified portfolio?
o: To deliver the highest possible long-run returns
To avoid all tax
To guarantee a profit every year
To provide stability and income and cushion share market falls
quiz.e: Bonds usually swing less than shares and provide income, though they are not risk-free.

LESSONS.push: A safe investment lost money in 2022. Here is the see-saw behind it.

LESSONS.title: Diversification
LESSONS.hook: It's sometimes called the only free lunch in investing: a way to reduce risk without necessarily giving up return.

sections.key: Diversification means spreading your money across many investments so no single failure can sink you.
sections.b:
The old saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' is the heart of diversification. If you invest everything in one company and it collapses, you can lose everything. Spread the same money across 200 companies, and one collapse costs you only a small slice. Even household names can go bust or shrink dramatically.

Diversification doesn't prevent losses when the whole market falls. But it greatly reduces the damage from any one bad bet, which is the kind of loss that is hardest to recover from.

sections.key: Investments that don't move together offset each other, and correlation measures how much they move in step.
sections.b:
Investments don't all move together. If one company is hit by a scandal, another may be having a great year. Combine many different assets and their ups and downs partly offset each other, so the portfolio swings less than its parts. Harry Markowitz formalised this in 1952, later earning a Nobel Prize, and the line that diversification is 'the only free lunch in finance' is often attributed to him.

Correlation runs from +1 to -1. At +1 two investments move in lockstep, so holding both adds no diversification. Zero means unrelated; negative means one tends to rise when the other falls. One catch: in severe crises, correlations between risky assets often rise, just when you want them low.

sections.key: Asset allocation, the mix of shares, bonds, property and cash, is the broadest and most important diversification.
sections.b:
The biggest decision in most portfolios is the mix of asset classes, often called asset allocation. Shares offer growth but can fall sharply. Bonds and cash are steadier and have often held up better when shares slump. Property behaves differently again.

A 'balanced' super option might hold roughly two-thirds in growth assets and the rest in defensive assets, although definitions vary between funds. Many researchers argue that asset allocation explains most of the ups and downs in a diversified portfolio over time, more than which individual shares are picked.

sections.key: The Australian share market is dominated by banks and miners, so global shares add industries and economies it lacks.
sections.b:
Our share market is unusually lopsided. Financials, especially the big banks, and materials, especially miners, make up a large share of the main index. Technology and healthcare are much smaller than in global markets. Owning four big banks gives little diversification, because they tend to move together. An investor with only Australian shares is heavily exposed to banks, iron ore and the housing market.

Australia is only around 2% of global share markets, yet many Australians hold mostly local shares. This home bias is partly familiarity and partly franking credits. Global shares bring new industries, economies and currency risk: when the Australian dollar rises, overseas investments are worth less in local terms. Some funds 'hedge' to reduce this.

sections.key: Real diversification means checking what you actually own, since employer shares and overlapping funds hide concentration.
sections.b:
Enron, the US energy company, collapsed in 2001. Many employees had much of their retirement savings in its shares, so they lost their jobs and savings together. Your job, home and super may also depend on the same local economy.

Another trap is 'diworsification': ten funds that all hold the same large companies look diversified but aren't. Check what lies under the labels, and look for one company, sector, country or property making up most of your wealth.

A broad index fund or diversified super option can hold hundreds or thousands of investments at low cost. Diversification reduces risk but cannot eliminate it. This is general information only; see a licensed adviser, and Moneysmart for independent tools.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of diversification?
o: To guarantee profits every year
To avoid paying tax on investments
To reduce the damage any single bad investment can cause
To make returns as high as possible regardless of risk
quiz.e: Spreading money widely limits the impact of any one failure.

quiz.q: Which correlation between two investments provides the least diversification benefit?
quiz.e: A correlation of +1 means they move in lockstep, so holding both adds no diversification.

quiz.q: What does asset allocation mean?
o: Choosing which individual shares to buy
The mix of asset classes such as shares, bonds, property and cash
Timing the market
Splitting money across banks
quiz.e: The mix of asset classes is often the biggest driver of a portfolio's ups and downs.

quiz.q: Why does owning only Australian shares leave you concentrated?
o: The market is dominated by a few sectors, mainly banks and miners
Australian shares cannot be sold
Australia has no technology companies
Local shares carry no franking credits
quiz.e: Banks and miners make up a large share of the main index, and global shares add other industries.

quiz.q: What lesson does the Enron collapse teach?
o: Energy companies should always be avoided
Bonds are riskier than shares
Index funds are unsafe
Holding lots of your employer's shares concentrates your risk
quiz.e: Employees lost both jobs and savings because their money was concentrated in the same company.

LESSONS.push: The only free lunch in investing, and why most portfolios aren't eating it.

LESSONS.title: Property investing in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Australians love bricks and mortar. Here is how investment property actually makes, and loses, money.

sections.key: Residential property is the biggest store of household wealth in Australia, but an investment property is a business decision.
sections.b:
Residential real estate is the largest single component of Australian household wealth, worth far more in total than the Australian share market. Around two million Australians own at least one investment property, according to tax statistics, and most own just one.

Its appeal is easy to see: it is tangible, familiar and can be bought largely with borrowed money. But an investment property is a business decision, not a home, and it should be judged on its numbers, costs and risks like any other investment.

sections.key: Property earns through rent and capital growth, but many costs can eat much of the rent.
sections.b:
Rental yield is annual rent divided by price. A $750,000 unit rented for $600 a week earns about $31,200 a year, a gross yield of roughly 4.2%. Net yield subtracts costs and is always lower. The second return is capital growth, which is never guaranteed and varies by location and period. Yields in many cities have been modest, so investors have leaned on growth.

Costs add up. Stamp duty, a state purchase tax, can run to tens of thousands of dollars. Then come legal and inspection costs, loan interest, rates, landlord insurance, strata fees, repairs, management fees and, in some states, land tax, plus vacancies. Selling brings agent fees and possibly capital gains tax. A property can rise in value and still disappoint.

sections.key: Borrowing to invest, called gearing, magnifies both gains and losses on the money you put in.
sections.b:
Most property investors borrow, often most of the purchase price. This is gearing, or leverage. Suppose you buy a $600,000 property with a $120,000 deposit and a loan for the rest. If the property rises 10%, it gains $60,000, which is 50% of your own money. If it falls 10%, you lose $60,000, half your deposit, and still owe the full loan.

Leverage magnifies outcomes in both directions. You must also keep making repayments whether or not the property is tenanted, and if interest rates rise, those repayments can climb quickly.

sections.key: Negative gearing and capital gains tax rules are changing from July 2027, so check current rules before relying on any tax benefit.
sections.b:
A property is positively geared when rent exceeds costs, including interest, and negatively geared when costs exceed rent. That loss has generally been deductible against other income, such as wages. Legislation passed in June 2026 narrows this: from 1 July 2027, losses on established homes bought after 7:30 pm AEST on 12 May 2026 can only be offset against residential property income and gains. Earlier purchases and new builds keep the old treatment. A deduction only recovers part of a loss.

Capital gains tax applies when you sell an investment property. The 50% discount for assets held over 12 months is being replaced from 1 July 2027 by indexing the cost base for inflation, with a 30% minimum tax; gains built up before then keep the discount. Use ATO guidance and a registered tax agent.

sections.key: A single property is a concentrated, illiquid bet funded with debt, so stress-test the numbers before buying.
sections.b:
Property prices can fall, as they have in some Australian cities and in mining towns after booms faded. One property often represents a huge share of an investor's wealth: one asset, one suburb, one market. It is illiquid, since selling takes weeks or months and costs a lot. Rate rises, a long vacancy or a major repair can strain your budget.

Calculate net yield using realistic costs, not brochure figures. Could you cope with rates two or three percentage points higher, or three months without rent? Be wary of spruikers and 'free' property packages that earn developer commissions; ASIC has warned about them. This is general information only. Speak with a licensed adviser and registered tax agent, and see Moneysmart.

quiz.q: What is the best way to view an investment property?
o: As a home that happens to earn rent
As a guaranteed path to wealth
As a business decision judged on numbers, costs and risks
As a tax-free asset
quiz.e: An investment property should be assessed like any other investment.

quiz.q: A property costs $500,000 and earns $20,000 a year in rent. What is its gross rental yield?
quiz.e: Gross yield is annual rent divided by price: $20,000 / $500,000 = 4%.

quiz.q: What does gearing do to an investor's returns?
o: Eliminates risk completely
Magnifies both gains and losses on the investor's own money
Guarantees capital growth
Removes the need to repay the loan
quiz.e: Borrowing amplifies outcomes in both directions.

quiz.q: When is a property negatively geared?
o: When its value falls
When it has no loan
When its costs, including interest, exceed its rental income
When it is sold at a loss
quiz.e: Costs exceed rent. The loss has generally been deductible, though this is restricted from July 2027 for established homes bought after 12 May 2026, and it is still a loss.

quiz.q: Why is a single investment property considered a concentrated investment?
o: Because a large share of wealth sits in one illiquid asset in one location
Because it is guaranteed to rise in value
Because it is tax-free
Because it can be sold instantly
quiz.e: One property ties much of your wealth to a single asset and local market.

LESSONS.push: A property can rise in value and still lose you money. Here is how.

LESSONS.title: Costly investing mistakes
LESSONS.hook: The biggest threat to most investors isn't the market. It's their own behaviour, and the people who exploit it.

sections.key: Many investing losses come from predictable behaviour: fear, greed, overconfidence and following the crowd.
sections.b:
Investing is simple in principle but hard in practice, because human instincts work against it. We feel losses more strongly than equal gains, a pattern called loss aversion. We are overconfident in our own judgement, and we copy others. Behavioural finance, shaped by researchers such as Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky and Richard Thaler, studies how these biases lead people to buy high, sell low and trade too often. Knowing the traps in advance is the best defence.

Another trap is paying too much. A share price already reflects what investors expect, so even a company that keeps succeeding can disappoint those who bought at the top. Ask not only 'Is this a good company?' but 'What am I paying for it?'

sections.key: A wonderful business can still be a disappointing investment if you pay too much for its shares.
sections.b:
Microsoft is a famous example. Its business kept growing strongly after the dot-com boom, yet its share price didn't regain its December 1999 peak until 2016, almost 17 years later. Buyers at the top had paid in advance for years of success.

The reverse happens too: dull, unloved companies sometimes reward investors because so little was expected of them. It's natural to assume brilliant, fast-growing companies guarantee good returns. But expectations are already in the price, and sky-high expectations leave little room for reward.

sections.key: Selling in a crash locks in losses, and chasing whatever has soared often means buying near the peak.
sections.b:
In March 2020, as COVID-19 spread, share markets plunged, and some Australians switched their super from growth options to cash near the bottom. Markets recovered strongly within months, but those who switched had locked in their losses and missed much of the rebound. A fall is a paper loss until you sell. Decisions made in fear are rarely good ones, and a written plan made before a crash helps you stay calm.

Fear of missing out pushes people in after an investment has already soared. By the time something is famous for its gains, much of the rise may be over. The US Nasdaq index fell by roughly three-quarters from its 2000 peak to its 2002 low. Tips from friends, forums and influencers rarely come with accountability.

sections.key: Crypto hype and borrowing to invest can wipe out savings, as Bitcoin's falls and Storm Financial showed.
sections.b:
Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin have made some early buyers very rich, which fuels the hype. But prices have been extraordinarily volatile. Bitcoin has fallen more than 70% from its peak several times, including in 2022, when the exchange FTX collapsed and customers' funds were frozen. Crypto is speculative, with no earnings or rent behind it. Only invest what you could afford to lose entirely.

A margin loan lets you borrow to buy shares, using them as security. If prices fall far enough, you get a margin call: add cash quickly, or the lender sells your shares, usually near the bottom. Townsville-based Storm Financial encouraged clients, often near retirement, to borrow against their homes and take margin loans on top. When markets crashed in 2008, savings were wiped out, some lost their homes, and the firm collapsed in early 2009.

sections.key: Returns that are high and suspiciously steady signal a scam, and a simple plan is the best protection.
sections.b:
Real investments go up and down. A classic scam sign is returns that are high and smooth. A Ponzi scheme, named after Charles Ponzi, who promised Boston investors 50% returns in 45 days in 1920, pays earlier investors with money from newer ones. It collapses when new money dries up. Bernie Madoff reported steady gains of around 1% a month for decades before his scheme collapsed in 2008, with paper losses of about US$65 billion. Search ASIC's Moneysmart investor alert list, and report suspicions to Scamwatch.

Good investing is boring. Set goals, diversify, keep costs low, automate contributions and check occasionally, not daily. This is general information only; see a licensed adviser, and Moneysmart.

quiz.q: What is loss aversion?
o: Refusing to ever invest in shares
Feeling losses more strongly than equal gains
A tax rule for capital losses
A type of insurance for investments
quiz.e: Loss aversion means the pain of a loss outweighs the pleasure of an equal gain, which can drive poor decisions.

quiz.q: Microsoft's business kept growing after 1999. Why did its shares take until 2016 to regain their 1999 peak?
o: The company nearly went bankrupt
Its shares stopped trading for years
It paid no tax
Investors had paid a very high price for expected future success
quiz.e: A great company can be a poor investment if you pay too much for it.

quiz.q: What does panic selling during a crash typically do?
o: Guarantees you avoid all losses
Turns a temporary paper loss into a permanent one
Increases your future returns
Has no effect on long-term outcomes
quiz.e: Selling locks in the loss and can mean missing the recovery.

quiz.q: What is a margin call?
o: A reminder to pay your broker's annual fee
A phone call offering a hot share tip
A tax bill on share profits
A lender's demand for more cash, or it sells your shares, after prices fall
quiz.e: Margin calls often force investors to sell near the bottom of a fall.

quiz.q: Which is a major warning sign of an investment scam?
o: Returns that vary from year to year
Guaranteed high returns with little risk
A published product disclosure statement
An Australian Financial Services licence
quiz.e: Legitimate investments can't guarantee high returns without risk.

LESSONS.push: Even a brilliant company can be a poor investment. Here is why.

LESSONS.title: Where language came from
LESSONS.hook: Every human society ever found has had a full, complex language. How that ability began is one of the hardest puzzles in science, and the clues are hiding in the words we still use.

sections.key: Spoken language leaves no fossils, so its origins must be pieced together from indirect clues.
sections.b:
Speech vanishes the moment it is spoken, and writing was only invented around 5,000 years ago, in Mesopotamia and Egypt. By then, humans had almost certainly been talking for tens of thousands of years or more. So scientists reason from skeletons, genes, tools, art and the languages alive today.

The question attracted so much wild speculation that in 1866 the Linguistic Society of Paris banned papers on it. It returned as serious science only in recent decades, drawing on biology, archaeology and linguistics together.

sections.key: Estimates for when language began range widely, and clues from bones and genes offer hints, not answers.
sections.b:
Anatomically modern humans appeared in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago. Some researchers argue full language arrived late, perhaps 50,000 to 100,000 years ago, pointing to a flowering of art and symbolic objects. Others think it developed earlier and more gradually. There is no consensus. Every living human population has language of comparable complexity, which suggests the capacity existed before our ancestors spread out of Africa.

Speech needs fine control of breathing, tongue and larynx. A Neanderthal hyoid bone found at Kebara Cave in Israel in 1983 looks very like ours, hinting at some capacity for speech, though this is argued over. The gene FOXP2, linked in 2001 to speech problems in one British family, was hyped as 'the language gene'. It is one of many genes involved, and Neanderthals shared our version.

sections.key: Nicaraguan Sign Language and creoles show children building full grammar from limited input.
sections.b:
One of the best windows into language origins opened in Nicaragua in the late 1970s and 1980s. Deaf children brought together in new schools, most with no shared sign language, began creating their own. Younger children who joined later made it richer and more regular, and it grew into a full language with its own grammar, now called Nicaraguan Sign Language.

Something similar happens with creoles, which grow when children turn a rough trading 'pidgin' into a complete native language. These cases suggest humans are strongly primed to build grammar.

sections.key: Related languages descend from common ancestors, such as Proto-Indo-European, which links English to Hindi and Persian.
sections.b:
Languages change constantly, and when groups separate, their speech drifts apart. Latin split into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian over roughly 1,500 years. Languages sharing an ancestor form a family. Linguists recognise well over a hundred, plus 'isolates' like Basque. Big families include Sino-Tibetan, Niger-Congo (over 1,500 languages), Austronesian (Madagascar to Easter Island) and Pama-Nyungan, covering most of mainland Australia.

In 1786, Sir William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, noted that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were so alike they must share a source. That source, Proto-Indo-European, was never written down, yet its descendants are the first language of nearly half the world, including English, Spanish, Hindi, Bengali, Russian and Persian. Many scholars place it on the steppes north of the Black Sea about 6,000 years ago; a rival theory says Anatolia, in modern Turkey.

sections.key: Regular sound changes let linguists reconstruct vanished languages, and every language is equally capable of complexity.
sections.b:
Linguists rebuild lost languages by lining up related words and working out regular sound changes. Jacob Grimm, one of the fairy-tale brothers, described a famous set in Germanic languages. Latin 'p' became English 'f': pater and father, pes and foot. Latin 't' became 'th': tres and three. Latin 'c' (a 'k' sound) became 'h': centum and hundred, cornu and horn. Patterns like these let scholars reconstruct Proto-Indo-European words for mother, father, daughter, snow and wolf.

There are no 'primitive' languages: every known language can express abstract ideas, and many small ones have grammar more intricate than English. Be sceptical of confident claims about exactly when or how language began. We have strong clues, competing theories and much to learn.

quiz.q: Why is the origin of language so hard to study?
o: Early languages were all written in lost scripts
Speech leaves no fossils, and writing is only about 5,000 years old
Scientists have never studied it
Only one ancient language survives
quiz.e: Speech vanishes instantly, so researchers rely on indirect clues from bones, genes, archaeology and living languages.

quiz.q: What is the best description of the FOXP2 gene?
o: The single gene responsible for language
A gene found only in modern humans
A gene that controls hearing
One of many genes involved in speech and language
quiz.e: FOXP2 affects speech when damaged, but it is one of many genes involved, and Neanderthals shared our version.

quiz.q: What do Nicaraguan Sign Language and creoles suggest about humans?
o: Children can only learn languages from adults
Writing is needed for grammar to develop
Humans are strongly primed to build grammar
Sign languages are simpler than spoken ones
quiz.e: Children given limited input built full languages with their own grammar.

quiz.q: What does the existence of Proto-Indo-European tell us?
o: Languages as different as English and Hindi share a common ancestor
English descends directly from Sanskrit
All the world's languages share one ancestor
It was written on clay tablets
quiz.e: Regular similarities between languages can reveal an unwritten common source.

quiz.q: Grimm's law explains why Latin 'pater' corresponds to which English word?
o: Patter
Parent
Father
Pastor
quiz.e: In Germanic languages, an ancestral 'p' regularly became 'f', giving father, foot and fish.

LESSONS.push: Nobody recorded the first words ever spoken. Here is how we trace them anyway.

LESSONS.title: Where words come from
LESSONS.hook: 'Nice' once meant foolish, 'silly' once meant blessed, and 'muscle' means little mouse. Every word has a backstory, and the true ones are often stranger than the myths.

sections.key: Etymology traces how words' forms and meanings have changed, and meanings can drift or even flip.
sections.b:
Etymology, from Greek words meaning 'the study of true meaning', traces words back through time by comparing old manuscripts, dictionaries and related languages.
