The Oxford English Dictionary, begun in 1857 and completed in 1928, pioneered printing dated quotations showing each word's earliest known uses. A word's origin doesn't fix its meaning today, but it often explains odd spellings and hidden connections.

Meanings rarely stay still. 'Nice' comes from Latin nescius, ignorant, and in Middle English meant foolish before drifting through 'fussy' and 'precise' to 'pleasant'. 'Silly' went the other way: Old English sælig meant happy or blessed, then innocent, pitiable, then foolish. 'Awful' once meant inspiring awe. Linguists call these shifts amelioration and pejoration.

sections.key: Many words contain forgotten images, like 'muscle' (little mouse) and 'disaster' (bad star).
sections.b:
Plenty of words hide little pictures. 'Muscle' comes from Latin musculus, 'little mouse', perhaps because a flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin. 'Disaster' comes via Italian from 'bad star', reflecting an old belief that the planets shaped events. 'Daisy' comes from Old English dæges ēage, 'day's eye', because the flower opens at dawn and closes at dusk.

'Clue' was once 'clew', a ball of thread, like the one Theseus used to escape the labyrinth. 'Robot' comes from Czech robota, forced labour, popularised by Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.

sections.key: Some words changed shape because speakers misheard where one word ended and the next began.
sections.b:
Sometimes words change because of how we split up speech. In Middle English, 'a napron' was heard as 'an apron', and the 'n' slid across; the old form survives in 'napkin'. 'A nadder' became 'an adder', and 'a noumpere' became 'an umpire'. It can go the other way too: 'an ewt' became 'a newt', and 'an ekename', meaning an additional name, became 'a nickname'.

Linguists call this rebracketing. It's a reminder that language lives in the ear first and on the page second. Girl is another surprise: in Middle English it could mean a young person of either sex.

sections.key: Neat origin stories like 'posh' meaning 'port out, starboard home' are often invented after the fact.
sections.b:
Catchy word origins spread fast, and many are false. 'Posh' supposedly stands for 'port out, starboard home', the shady cabins on voyages to India, but no tickets stamped this way have ever been found. There's no evidence that 'rule of thumb' came from a law about beating wives, and 'sincere' doesn't come from sine cera, 'without wax'. Most words older than the 20th century didn't begin as acronyms.

The claim that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, giving us 'salary', is also unproven, though the word is linked to Latin sal, salt. Good dictionaries flag uncertain origins.

sections.key: Australian English borrowed hundreds of Aboriginal words, and 'kangaroo' does not mean 'I don't understand'.
sections.b:
Australian English has borrowed several hundred words from Aboriginal languages, mostly for animals, plants and places. Early loans came from the Sydney language, often called Dharug: dingo, wallaby, wombat and koala (from gula). 'Galah' comes from Yuwaalaraay and Gamilaraay, 'yabby' from Wemba Wemba. Many place names, from Parramatta to Wagga Wagga, are Aboriginal too, though some meanings are disputed.

A popular story says 'kangaroo' means 'I don't understand'. It's a myth. In 1770, while the Endeavour was repaired near present-day Cooktown, the crew recorded gangurru from Guugu Yimithirr speakers. In the 1970s, linguist John Haviland confirmed it names a large kangaroo. When the word reached Sydney, locals didn't recognise it.

To check origins, use the Macquarie Dictionary or Online Etymology Dictionary, and trust notes saying 'origin uncertain'.

quiz.q: What did 'silly' originally mean in Old English?
o: Foolish
Small
Blessed or happy
Angry
quiz.e: Old English sælig meant happy or blessed; the meaning slid towards foolish over centuries.

quiz.q: What does 'muscle' literally mean in Latin?
o: Strong arm
Little mouse
Moving flesh
Iron rope
quiz.e: Musculus means little mouse, perhaps from the look of a muscle moving under the skin.

quiz.q: How did 'a napron' become 'an apron'?
o: A spelling reform in 1900
It was borrowed from French
Speakers misheard where one word ended and the next began
Printers made a typo
quiz.e: This is rebracketing: the 'n' moved from the noun to the article, as with adder and umpire.

quiz.q: What is true about the claim that 'posh' stands for 'port out, starboard home'?
o: It is a folk etymology with no supporting evidence
It is confirmed by old tickets
It was coined by Queen Victoria
It comes from an Aboriginal word
quiz.e: No tickets stamped 'POSH' have been found; the acronym story is almost certainly invented.

quiz.q: What is the truth about the word 'kangaroo'?
o: It means 'I don't understand' in Guugu Yimithirr
It is a name Sydney locals gave the animal
It comes from gangurru, a Guugu Yimithirr word for a large kangaroo
It was invented by Captain Cook's crew
quiz.e: The 'I don't understand' story is a myth; the word was recorded in 1770 and confirmed by linguist John Haviland.

LESSONS.push: A word you use daily once meant foolish. Which one, and how did it change?

LESSONS.title: The world's languages
LESSONS.hook: Humans speak around 7,000 languages, yet half of us speak one of just a couple of dozen. Many of the rest, including most of Australia's own, are at risk of falling silent.

sections.key: There are roughly 7,000 living languages, but half the world's people speak one of about two dozen.
sections.b:
Linguists count roughly 7,000 living languages, including a few hundred sign languages. The figure depends on where you draw the line between a language and a dialect, which is often as much about politics as linguistics; a famous quip says 'a language is a dialect with an army and navy'.

Languages are shared very unevenly. More than half the world's people speak one of only about two dozen, while thousands have fewer than 10,000 speakers each. English leads in total speakers (roughly 1.5 billion), followed by Mandarin, Hindi and Spanish. Mandarin has the most native speakers, then Spanish and English. Rankings shift with how varieties are grouped, so treat lists as approximate.

sections.key: Language diversity clusters in surprising places, with Papua New Guinea home to about 840 languages.
sections.b:
Papua New Guinea, with a relatively small population, has around 840 languages, more than any other country and over a tenth of the world's total. Indonesia and Nigeria each have several hundred. Rugged mountains, islands, rainforest and a long history of small, independent communities help languages multiply. Much of Europe has relatively few.

Some languages have features English speakers find astonishing, such as tones that change meaning, or words that pack a whole sentence into one.

sections.key: Around 40% of the world's languages are endangered, usually because children no longer learn them at home.
sections.b:
Around 40% of the world's languages are considered endangered, usually because children are no longer learning them at home. Pressure comes from bigger languages used in schools, jobs, government and media, and in many places from past policies that punished people for speaking their own language.

When the last speakers die, a language becomes 'sleeping' or extinct, and with it can go knowledge of local plants, animals, history, law and ways of seeing the world. Estimates of how fast languages are being lost vary, but the trend is clear.

sections.key: More than 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages were spoken in 1788, but only about 12 are now strongly learned by children.
sections.b:
When the British arrived in 1788, Australia was one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth. More than 250 distinct languages were spoken, with many dialects. In the Torres Strait, Meriam Mir and Kala Lagaw Ya are traditional, and the creole Yumplatok is widely spoken. Across the north, the creole Kriol is the first language of thousands of Aboriginal people.

Colonisation brought dispossession and, for decades, policies that discouraged or banned Aboriginal languages in missions and schools. The 2020 National Indigenous Languages Report, based on a 2019 survey, found about 120 traditional languages still spoken, but only around 12 learned by children as a first language. Strong ones include Warlpiri and Pitjantjatjara. In the 2021 Census, about 77,000 people spoke an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander language at home.

sections.key: Sleeping languages can be revived, and Aboriginal languages belong to their communities.
sections.b:
Languages no longer spoken are often called 'sleeping', not dead, because they can be woken. Hebrew, used for centuries mainly in religious study, became an everyday language again from the late 1800s. Māori language nests (Te Kōhanga Reo, from 1982) and Welsh revival have had real success. In Australia, Kaurna, the language of the Adelaide Plains, is being revived partly from records made by German missionaries around 1840. Wiradjuri, Dharug and others are taught in communities, schools and universities.

These languages belong to their communities, who decide how they are shared. Look for programs run or endorsed by local language centres, learn the name of the Country where you live, and follow community guidance on restricted words, names or songs. The UN has declared 2022-2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.

quiz.q: About how many living languages are there in the world?
o: About 700
About 2,000
About 7,000
About 70,000
quiz.e: Linguists count roughly 7,000, depending on where the line between language and dialect is drawn.

quiz.q: Which country has the most languages?
o: India
Papua New Guinea
China
Australia
quiz.e: Papua New Guinea has around 840 languages, more than a tenth of the world's total.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the world's languages are considered endangered?
o: About 5%
About 20%
About 90%
About 40%
quiz.e: Around 40% are endangered, usually because children are no longer learning them.

quiz.q: What did the 2020 National Indigenous Languages Report find?
o: About 12 traditional languages are still learned by children as a first language
All traditional languages are still strongly spoken
No traditional languages remain
About 250 are learned by children
quiz.e: Of about 120 traditional languages still spoken, only around 12 were being learned by children as a first language.

quiz.q: What does it mean to call a language 'sleeping' rather than dead?
o: It is spoken only at night
It can be revived, as with Kaurna in Adelaide
It has no written records
It has never been spoken
quiz.e: Sleeping languages can be woken using elders' knowledge and old records.

LESSONS.push: Half the world speaks about two dozen languages. What about the other 7,000?

LESSONS.title: Grammar myths
LESSONS.hook: You were probably told never to split an infinitive or end a sentence with a preposition. Neither rule was ever part of English grammar. Here's where they came from, and what actually matters.

sections.key: Descriptive grammar records how people really use language; prescriptive grammar tells people how they should.
sections.b:
Descriptive grammar observes how fluent speakers actually use a language, the way a biologist describes an animal. By that standard, native speakers rarely make mistakes in everyday speech. Prescriptive grammar sets out how people ought to write or speak, usually in formal settings.

Some prescriptive rules are genuinely useful conventions. Others were invented by 18th and 19th-century writers who admired Latin, and teachers have repeated them ever since, even though great writers have ignored them for centuries.

sections.key: The bans on split infinitives and final prepositions come from Latin, not English grammar.
sections.b:
An infinitive is the 'to' form of a verb. Splitting it means putting a word in between: 'to boldly go'. The rule against this became popular in the 19th century, partly because a Latin infinitive is a single word and can't be split. English isn't Latin, and writers since the Middle Ages have split infinitives. Sometimes it reads better: 'to more than double sales' is clearer than any alternative.

The ban on ending a sentence with a preposition is often traced to John Dryden, who in 1672 criticised Ben Jonson for it, again under Latin's influence. In English it's natural; 'To whom are you talking?' sounds stiff. The joke 'This is the sort of English up with which I will not put' is attributed to Churchill, but there's no good evidence he said it.

sections.key: 'Literally' as an intensifier, 'less' for countable things, singular 'they' and starting with 'And' are all long-established.
sections.b:
Using 'literally' to mean 'very much' goes back to at least the 1700s and appears in Dickens, Twain and Fitzgerald. Major dictionaries record it, noting some people object. Words meaning 'truly' often become intensifiers: 'very' comes from an old French word for 'true'. In writing where precision matters, though, the figurative use can confuse.

The rule that 'less' suits uncountable things and 'fewer' countable ones seems to begin with Robert Baker in 1770, who said he merely preferred it. English speakers had used 'less' with countable nouns for about a thousand years. Singular 'they', as in 'Someone left their umbrella', dates to the 1300s and appears in Shakespeare and Jane Austen. Starting a sentence with 'And' or 'But' is fine; the King James Bible does it constantly.

sections.key: Double negatives are non-standard in formal English, but not illogical.
sections.b:
'I didn't do nothing' is often called illogical, as if two negatives must cancel out. But language isn't arithmetic. Many languages, including Spanish, Italian and Russian, routinely stack negatives for emphasis, and Chaucer and Shakespeare did it in English too. Everyone understands what the speaker means.

The double negative became non-standard in written English over several centuries, and it now signals informal speech. So the real reason to avoid it in a job application is social, not logical: it sounds casual to many readers.

sections.key: Keep conventions that prevent ambiguity, and match your register to your audience.
sections.b:
Some conventions genuinely help readers. Apostrophes distinguish 'its' from 'it's'. Commas change meaning: 'Let's eat, Grandma' versus 'Let's eat Grandma'. Dangling modifiers confuse: 'Walking to work, the rain soaked me' suggests the rain was walking. Subject-verb agreement helps readers track who does what. The test for any rule: does following it make your meaning clearer?

Linguists talk about register, the style that suits a situation. A text to friends, a eulogy, a contract and a job application call for different choices. Formal writing has conventions worth knowing, because some readers judge them. But correcting everyday speech mostly signals status, not logic. Aim for clarity and suitability.

quiz.q: What does descriptive grammar do?
o: Tells people how they should speak
Translates Latin into English
Records how people actually use language
Bans informal speech
quiz.e: Descriptive grammar observes real usage, while prescriptive grammar sets rules for how people ought to use language.

quiz.q: What is often given as the reason for the rule against split infinitives?
o: It prevents ambiguity
Latin infinitives are single words and can't be split
Shakespeare invented it
It was required by law
quiz.e: The rule is modelled on Latin, but English infinitives are two words and have been split for centuries.

quiz.q: What is true about 'literally' used as an intensifier?
o: It first appeared in the 2000s
No dictionary records it
Only Australians use it
It has been used this way since at least the 1700s
quiz.e: Dickens, Twain and Fitzgerald used it; dictionaries record it, often noting that some people object.

quiz.q: Why is the double negative best avoided in a job application?
o: It is mathematically wrong
It is illegal in formal writing
It sounds casual to many readers
It confuses everyone
quiz.e: Double negatives aren't illogical; they signal informal speech, which is a social reason to avoid them.

quiz.q: Which kind of grammar rule is most worth following?
o: Never start a sentence with 'But'
Rules that prevent ambiguity, like careful punctuation
Never split an infinitive
Never end a sentence with a preposition
quiz.e: Conventions that prevent misunderstanding, such as apostrophes and clear modifiers, genuinely help readers.

LESSONS.push: Two grammar rules you were taught at school never belonged to English.

LESSONS.title: How to write clearly
LESSONS.hook: Clear writing isn't a talent you're born with. It's a handful of habits anyone can learn, and they'll make your emails, reports and messages easier to read and harder to ignore.

sections.key: Clear writing starts with a clear main point, stated first for busy readers.
sections.b:
Most muddled writing comes from muddled thinking. Before writing anything important, try to state your main point in one or two plain sentences, as if explaining it to a friend. If you can't, you're not ready. Then ask who your reader is, what they know and what you want them to do.

Many of us were taught to build up to a conclusion, like a school essay. But busy readers skim and may never reach your last paragraph. Lead with the decision, request or key finding. 'Can you approve the budget by Friday?' beats three paragraphs of background. Journalists call this the inverted pyramid; the military says 'bottom line up front'. Clear subject lines and headings do the same job.

sections.key: Short, familiar words and sentences averaging 15 to 20 words are easier to read and more convincing.
sections.b:
Write 'use' rather than 'utilise', 'start' rather than 'commence', 'about' rather than 'in relation to', and 'help' rather than 'facilitate'. Jargon has its place when every reader shares it, but it shuts others out. Plain language isn't dumbing down. The Australian Government Style Manual recommends it, and studies of legal and medical documents show plain versions are understood better, even by experts.

Long sentences force readers to hold too much in their heads. Plain-language guides commonly suggest an average of around 15 to 20 words, one main idea each. Mix lengths to avoid sounding choppy. When a sentence passes about 30 words, split it, often at an 'and', 'which' or 'however'. Shorter paragraphs help, especially on phones.

sections.key: Active voice makes clear who did what, while passive voice can hide responsibility.
sections.b:
In the active voice, the doer comes first: 'The committee approved the plan.' In the passive, the action comes first and the doer may vanish: 'The plan was approved.' Active sentences are usually shorter, clearer and more direct.

The passive can conveniently hide responsibility, as in the classic non-apology 'Mistakes were made.' But the passive isn't a crime. It's useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in 'The bridge was built in 1932', or when you want to focus on what happened.

sections.key: Delete words that add nothing, and turn 'zombie nouns' back into verbs.
sections.b:
Clutter creeps in everywhere: 'at this point in time' means 'now', 'due to the fact that' means 'because', and 'in order to' is usually just 'to'. Words like 'very', 'really' and 'basically' rarely add much.

Another problem is nominalisation, which the writing scholar Helen Sword calls 'zombie nouns': verbs turned into heavy nouns. 'We made a decision to conduct a review' becomes 'We decided to review'. William Strunk's advice, first published in 1918, still holds: 'Omit needless words.'

sections.key: Orwell's rules and a patient edit, read aloud, turn drafts into clear writing.
sections.b:
In his 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language', George Orwell argued that vague, inflated language helps people hide bad ideas. His six rules: avoid familiar metaphors, prefer short words, cut any word you can, use the active over the passive, avoid jargon and foreign phrases when an everyday equivalent exists, and break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.

Almost no one writes clearly in a first draft. Blaise Pascal apologised in 1656 for a long letter because he hadn't had time to make it shorter. Leave a gap between drafting and editing, even an hour. Read aloud to catch clumsy sentences and missing words. Check your point is up front, cut what doesn't earn its place, and ask whether your reader will know what to do next.

quiz.q: What does 'bottom line up front' mean for your writing?
o: Put the key point or request first
Save the conclusion for the end
Use a bold heading
Include a budget table
quiz.e: Busy readers skim, so lead with the decision, request or key finding, then add detail.

quiz.q: What average sentence length do plain-language guides commonly suggest?
o: 5 to 8 words
35 to 40 words
15 to 20 words
There is no guidance
quiz.e: Around 15 to 20 words on average, with variety, keeps writing clear without sounding choppy.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the active voice?
o: Mistakes were made.
The plan was approved.
The report has been finalised.
The committee approved the plan.
quiz.e: In the active voice the doer comes first, making clear who did what.

quiz.q: What is a 'zombie noun'?
o: A made-up word
A verb turned into a heavy noun, like 'make a decision'
An outdated slang term
A noun used as an insult
quiz.e: Helen Sword's term for nominalisations; 'make a decision' is clearer as 'decide'.

quiz.q: What is the best way to improve a first draft?
o: Send it quickly while the ideas are fresh
Add longer words to sound professional
Leave a gap, read it aloud and cut what doesn't earn its place
Avoid the active voice
quiz.e: Editing with fresh eyes and reading aloud reveals clumsy sentences and clutter.

LESSONS.push: Why clear writing is rewriting, and the five-minute test that proves it.

LESSONS.title: How Australian law works
LESSONS.hook: Every day you live inside a system of rules built over 800 years, from English judges to the High Court in Canberra. Here's how it actually fits together.

sections.key: Australian law comes from parliaments (legislation) and judges' decisions (common law), and judges follow precedent.
sections.b:
Australian law has two main sources. Legislation is Acts passed by the Commonwealth, state and territory parliaments, such as road rules or the Fair Work Act. Common law is the body of principles built up by judges deciding cases over centuries, inherited from England in 1788. Where the two clash, legislation generally wins, because parliament can override the common law within the limits of the Constitution.

The common law runs on precedent. The core reasoning in a decision becomes a rule that lower courts in the same system must follow in similar cases. That makes law predictable, yet lets it evolve. Donoghue v Stevenson (1932), a Scottish case about a snail in a ginger beer bottle, shaped the law of negligence across the common law world, including Australia.

sections.key: Each state and territory makes most everyday laws and runs its own court ladder, alongside the Commonwealth.
sections.b:
Australia is a federation, so there is no single set of laws. The Commonwealth makes laws on national subjects like tax, defence, immigration and trade. The six states, and the ACT and Northern Territory, make most everyday laws, including most crimes, driving, property, schools and hospitals. That is why penalties, or the rules for renting a home, can differ between Sydney and Perth.

Courts form a ladder. Local or Magistrates Courts handle most criminal cases and smaller civil claims. District Courts (the County Court in Victoria) hear more serious crimes and larger claims. Supreme Courts hear the gravest cases, such as murder, plus appeals. Federal courts include the Federal Court and the Federal Circuit and Family Court.

sections.key: Criminal cases are brought by the state and need proof beyond reasonable doubt; civil cases need only the balance of probabilities.
sections.b:
In a criminal case, the state prosecutes someone for breaking the law, which is why cases are named like R v Smith, with R for the Crown. Penalties include fines, community orders and prison. The prosecution must prove every element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt. The accused is presumed innocent and doesn't have to prove anything.

In a civil case, one party, the plaintiff, sues another, the defendant, usually for money called damages. The standard is lower: the balance of probabilities, meaning more likely than not. One event, such as a car crash, can lead to both kinds of case.

sections.key: Trials are adversarial, with a neutral judge, and serious criminal cases are usually decided by a jury of 12 ordinary citizens.
sections.b:
Australian trials are adversarial: two sides present their cases while the judge acts as a neutral umpire. Accused people generally have a right to silence, so refusing to answer police questions usually can't be used as evidence of guilt, though some laws create exceptions. In Dietrich v The Queen (1992), the High Court held that a serious trial may be delayed if an accused who can't afford a lawyer would otherwise face an unfair trial.

Serious criminal trials are usually heard by a jury, typically 12 people chosen at random from the electoral roll. The jury decides the facts and guilt. The judge rules on the law and sets the sentence. Jury deliberations must stay secret. Under section 80 of the Constitution, a jury verdict for a serious Commonwealth offence must be unanimous. Juries are rare in civil cases.

sections.key: The High Court is Australia's final court of appeal, and free legal help is available if you need it.
sections.b:
The High Court of Australia, created by the Constitution and first sitting in 1903, sits at the top. Its seven justices, based in Canberra, decide appeals from every other court and settle disputes about the Constitution. Appeals usually need special leave, so only important cases are heard. Since the Australia Act 1986, no appeals can go to Britain's Privy Council. Its decisions can reshape the nation: in Mabo (1992), it rejected the idea that Australia was 'terra nullius'.

This lesson is general information only. If you have a legal problem, Legal Aid and community legal centres offer free or low-cost help, and a lawyer can advise on your situation.

quiz.q: What does the principle of precedent require of a lower court?
o: Follow earlier decisions of higher courts in the same system in similar cases
Ignore earlier cases and apply only the current legislation
Reverse any decision made by a court in another state
Apply the law of the colony as it stood in 1788
quiz.e: Precedent makes law predictable because lower courts follow the reasoning of higher courts.

quiz.q: Why can the penalty for the same offence differ between Sydney and Perth?
o: The Commonwealth sets different penalties for each capital city
Local councils write the criminal law for their area
Each state and territory makes its own laws on most everyday matters
Federal courts adjust penalties by city size
quiz.e: Because Australia is a federation, states and territories make most crime, driving and property laws.

quiz.q: How does the standard of proof differ between criminal and civil cases?
o: Both need proof beyond reasonable doubt
Criminal needs proof beyond reasonable doubt; civil needs the balance of probabilities
Civil needs proof beyond reasonable doubt; criminal needs the balance of probabilities
Criminal cases need only a majority of the evidence
quiz.e: The state must meet a higher standard to convict someone than a plaintiff must to win damages.

quiz.q: What is the jury's role in a serious criminal trial?
o: Decide the law and the sentence
Question the witnesses on the judge's behalf
Advise the prosecution on which charges to lay
Decide the facts and whether the accused is guilty
quiz.e: Juries decide the facts and guilt, while the judge rules on law and sets the sentence.

quiz.q: What is the High Court's place in the Australian system?
o: It hears most traffic and minor criminal cases
It appeals decisions to the Privy Council in Britain
It hears appeals from other courts and settles constitutional disputes
It makes the laws that state parliaments must pass
quiz.e: As the final court of appeal, the High Court sits at the top and interprets the Constitution.

LESSONS.push: You live inside rules that began with English judges 800 years ago.

LESSONS.title: The Australian Constitution
LESSONS.hook: A document written by colonial delegates in the 1890s still decides who can make which laws, and only the voters can change it.

sections.key: The Constitution united six colonies in 1901 and divides law-making power between the Commonwealth and the states.
sections.b:
Before 1901, Australia was six British colonies with their own parliaments, tariffs and even railway gauges. Through the 1890s, delegates met at conventions to draft a federal constitution. Unusually for the time, voters approved it at colonial referendums, and the British Parliament passed it as the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900. The Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901. The Constitution is short, around 128 sections, and freely available online.

Federation meant dividing power. Section 51 lists about 40 subjects for Commonwealth laws, including defence, taxation, trade between states, marriage, immigration, currency and postal services. Everything unlisted stays with the states, which run police, schools, hospitals and most criminal law. If a valid Commonwealth law conflicts with a state law, section 109 makes the state law invalid to the extent of the inconsistency.

sections.key: The Constitution creates Parliament, the executive and the courts, with the Senate protecting smaller states.
sections.b:
The Constitution is organised into chapters. Chapter I creates the Parliament: the King, represented by the Governor-General, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Chapter II covers the executive government, which puts laws into action. Chapter III establishes the High Court and other federal courts. Australia is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy.

The Senate gives each original state the same number of senators regardless of population, 12 each since 1984, protecting smaller states. The House of Representatives is based on population, and the party or coalition that controls it forms government.

sections.key: The balance has shifted towards the Commonwealth through High Court rulings and its control over tax and conditional funding.
sections.b:
The founders expected the states to stay powerful, but the balance has shifted. In the Engineers' Case of 1920, the High Court began reading Commonwealth powers broadly. During World War II, the Commonwealth took over income tax, the High Court upheld the scheme, and that is why income tax is now collected federally.

Section 96 lets the Commonwealth give states money on conditions, so it can shape areas like schools and hospitals that it doesn't directly control. The gap between who raises the money and who spends it is called vertical fiscal imbalance, and it drives constant federal and state negotiation.

sections.key: Australia's legislature and executive are linked, but judicial power is strictly separate, which keeps courts independent.
sections.b:
The Constitution separates three arms of government: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets and applies them. In Australia, the legislature and executive are closely linked, because ministers must sit in parliament and answer to it. This is called responsible government.

The separation of judicial power is much stricter. In the Boilermakers' Case (1956), the High Court held that federal courts can exercise only judicial power, and bodies that aren't courts can't exercise it. This protects judges' independence, so courts can rule against the government of the day without fear.

sections.key: Only a referendum with a double majority can change the Constitution, and most of your rights sit outside it.
sections.b:
Under section 128, the Constitution changes only by referendum. A change needs a double majority: a majority of voters nationally and a majority in at least four of the six states. Territory votes count towards the national total only. Only eight of 45 proposals since 1901 have succeeded. In 1967, over 90% voted to count Aboriginal people in the census; the 1999 republic and 2023 Voice proposals failed.

There is no national bill of rights. The Constitution has few express rights, such as jury trial for serious Commonwealth offences and 'just terms' for acquired property. In 1992 the High Court found an implied freedom of political communication, not a general free speech right. Most protections come from ordinary laws, which parliament can change. Read the official Yes and No cases before voting. This is general information only.

quiz.q: What happens to a state law that conflicts with a valid Commonwealth law?
o: The Commonwealth law is invalid in that state
Both laws apply, and each state chooses which to enforce
The state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency
The High Court must rewrite both laws
quiz.e: Section 109 makes the Commonwealth law prevail over an inconsistent state law.

quiz.q: Why does the Senate give each original state the same number of senators?
o: To match each state's share of the national population
To stop populous states dominating and to protect smaller states
To give the governing party control of both houses
To let the Governor-General choose the Senate's members
quiz.e: Equal Senate representation protects smaller states, while the House is based on population.

quiz.q: How can the Commonwealth shape schools and hospitals it doesn't directly control?
o: By taking over state police forces
By banning states from raising any taxes
By appointing state premiers directly
By giving states money on conditions under section 96
quiz.e: Conditional grants let the Commonwealth influence areas that the states run.

quiz.q: Why does the strict separation of judicial power matter?
o: It stops ministers from sitting in parliament
It gives judges the power to write new laws
It lets courts rule against the government of the day without fear
It allows any government body to act as a court
quiz.e: Keeping judicial power with courts protects judges' independence from government.

quiz.q: What does a referendum need to succeed in changing the Constitution?
o: A national majority and a majority in at least four of six states
A simple majority of voters nationally and nothing more
A majority in the House of Representatives only
Unanimous agreement from all six states
quiz.e: The double majority is a high bar, which is why few proposals have been carried.

LESSONS.push: Only eight of 45 attempts to change this document have ever worked.

LESSONS.title: Contracts: the deals you make every day
LESSONS.hook: Your morning coffee, your phone plan and your job are all contracts. Knowing how they work helps you avoid nasty surprises.

sections.key: A contract is an agreement the law will enforce, and it needs a clear offer matched by acceptance.
sections.b:
A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce. You make them constantly: buying a coffee, tapping onto public transport, signing up for a streaming service, accepting a job or leasing a flat. In Australia, contract law comes mainly from judge-made common law, with legislation like the Australian Consumer Law layered on top to protect consumers.

Every contract starts with an offer: a clear promise to be bound on certain terms. Goods on a shelf and most advertisements are usually only an 'invitation to treat', which is why a shop usually isn't obliged to sell a wrongly priced item, although misleading pricing can breach consumer law. Acceptance must match the offer. 'I'll take it for $50 less' is a counter-offer, which rejects the original.

sections.key: A binding contract generally needs something exchanged, an intention to be legally bound, capacity and reasonably certain terms.
sections.b:
Courts generally look for offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, capacity and reasonably certain terms. Consideration means each side gives or promises something: you pay, the café hands over coffee. So a bare promise of a gift usually can't be enforced. It needn't be fair: selling a car for one dollar can be valid, though a court may check for pressure or deception. A deed can bind without consideration.

Business deals are presumed to be legally binding; family and social arrangements, like cooking dinner for a friend, are presumed not to be. Under-18s can often escape contracts, with exceptions such as necessities, and rules vary by state. Someone lacking mental capacity may also be able to avoid a contract.

sections.key: Most contracts can be verbal, but writing key terms protects you, and some contracts must be in writing.
sections.b:
A common myth is that a contract must be written and signed. Most can be verbal, or formed through emails, texts or clicking 'I agree' online. The problem with verbal contracts is proof: in a dispute, it's your word against theirs. Some contracts must be in writing to be enforceable, notably contracts for the sale of land and certain consumer credit contracts.

For anything important, like building work, a loan to a friend or a business arrangement, put the key terms in writing. Include the price, what's being delivered, deadlines and what happens if things go wrong.

sections.key: The usual remedy for breach is damages that put you where you'd have been, not a punishment for the other side.
sections.b:
Failing to do what a contract requires is a breach. The usual remedy is damages: money to put you in the position you'd have been in had the contract been performed, not to punish the other side. For a serious breach, such as breaking an essential term, the innocent party may be able to end the contract. Occasionally a court orders actual performance, called specific performance, mostly for unique things like land.

Contracts can also be set aside for misrepresentation, duress or unconscionable conduct. Time limits apply to claims, commonly six years in many states.

sections.key: Unfair standard-form terms can be voided, and cooling-off periods exist only where a law or contract creates them.
sections.b:
In take-it-or-leave-it contracts, like phone plans, the Australian Consumer Law protects against unfair terms: those causing a significant imbalance that aren't reasonably necessary to protect the business, such as letting only one side change the price. A court can void it, and since November 2023 relying on unfair terms is also illegal.

Many people believe every contract has a cooling-off period. It doesn't: those rights exist only where a law or the contract creates them. Unsolicited sales, such as door-to-door, carry 10 business days under the Australian Consumer Law. Residential property buyers usually get a few days, such as five business days in NSW, but not at auction. Never sign under pressure. This is general information only; for big contracts, see a lawyer or Legal Aid.

quiz.q: Why isn't a shop usually obliged to sell an item that was wrongly priced?
o: Shops are exempt from the Australian Consumer Law
A shelf price is usually an invitation to treat, not a binding offer
Customers accept an offer only by speaking to staff
Prices on shelves are always legally binding offers
quiz.e: Shelf goods are an invitation for you to make an offer, so the shop can decline.

quiz.q: Why can a simple promise of a gift usually not be enforced?
o: Gifts are illegal without a written deed
Promises between friends are always unlawful
The gift must be of equal value to be valid
The other person has given nothing in return, so there is no consideration
quiz.e: Consideration means each side gives or promises something in exchange.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of relying on a verbal contract?
o: Verbal contracts are never legally valid
Verbal contracts cannot include a price
Proving what was agreed becomes your word against theirs
They can only last for one day
quiz.e: Most contracts can be verbal, but writing key terms gives you proof if a dispute arises.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of damages for breach of contract?
o: To put you where you'd have been if the contract had been performed
To punish the other party for the breach
To force the other party to apologise
To cancel every contract the parties have
quiz.e: Damages compensate the loss rather than punish the person who breached.

quiz.q: When does a cooling-off period apply to a contract?
o: Automatically for every contract you sign
Only for contracts signed in a shop
Only where a law or the contract itself creates one
Only when you ask the seller in writing
quiz.e: There is no general cooling-off right, so check before you sign.

LESSONS.push: You made several contracts before breakfast, and the law may enforce them.

LESSONS.title: Your rights as a consumer
LESSONS.hook: 'No refunds' signs, 'take it up with the manufacturer', 'the warranty's expired'. Australian consumer law says otherwise more often than you think.

sections.key: The Australian Consumer Law gives the same protections in every state and territory, enforced by the ACCC and state agencies.
sections.b:
Since 1 January 2011, one national law, the Australian Consumer Law, has protected consumers across Australia. It sits in a schedule to the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and applies the same way in every state and territory. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) enforces it, together with agencies such as NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria.

It covers consumer guarantees, product safety, misleading conduct, unfair contract terms, unsolicited selling and more. You are generally a consumer if you buy goods or services normally used for personal or household purposes, or anything costing up to $100,000.

sections.key: Consumer guarantees apply automatically, and your remedy depends on whether a failure is major or minor.
sections.b:
Consumer guarantees apply automatically, whatever the receipt or store policy says, and businesses can't exclude them. Goods must be of acceptable quality (safe, durable, free from defects) for a reasonable time, fit for any purpose you told the seller about, and match their description. Services need due care and skill and must be delivered in reasonable time. A $2,000 fridge should last far longer than a $20 kettle.

For a major failure, such as an unsafe item or one you wouldn't have bought knowing the problem, you can choose a refund or replacement, or keep it and claim compensation. For a minor failure, the business can choose to repair, replace or refund. If it refuses or takes too long, you can get it fixed elsewhere and claim reasonable costs.

sections.key: You have no right to a refund for changing your mind, but 'no refunds' signs can't remove your rights when goods are faulty.
sections.b:
You have no legal right to a refund just because you changed your mind; that's store policy. But 'no refunds' signs are misleading if they suggest you have no rights when goods are faulty. The retailer can't send you to the manufacturer. Proof of purchase can be a bank statement or online order, not only the receipt. Sale items are covered too, unless the defect was pointed out before you bought.

A manufacturer's warranty is a promise on top of your guarantees, not a replacement. Guarantees can continue after the warranty ends if a product fails sooner than expected. Before buying an extended warranty, ask what it offers beyond the law.

sections.key: Misleading pricing and conduct are banned, and scams share warning signs: urgency, odd payment methods and requests for access.
sections.b:
The law bans misleading or deceptive conduct in trade. That includes false claims about quality or origin, fake 'was' prices that inflate a discount, and fine print that contradicts the headline offer. Businesses must generally show a single total price including compulsory fees, not hide charges until the end (drip pricing). Large supermarkets must show unit prices, such as price per 100 grams. Exploiting someone who clearly doesn't understand a deal (unconscionable conduct) is also prohibited.

Scams include fake parcel texts, calls impersonating banks or police, investment schemes and romance scams. Warning signs are pressure to act now, unusual payments like gift cards or crypto, and requests for personal details or remote access. Call back on a number you find yourself. If you've lost money, contact your bank, then report to Scamwatch. IDCARE offers free support.

sections.key: Complain to the business first with proof and a named remedy, then escalate to fair trading, an ombudsman or a tribunal.
sections.b:
Start with the business. Gather your proof of purchase, photos and messages, explain the problem, and say which remedy you want under the consumer guarantees. Putting it in writing creates a record.

If that fails, contact your state or territory fair trading agency, which can give advice and may help negotiate. Industry ombudsmen handle specific sectors for free, such as the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, energy and water ombudsmen, and the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. For money claims, state tribunals like NCAT or VCAT are cheaper than courts. Legal Aid and community legal centres can also help. This lesson is general information only.

quiz.q: Who enforces the Australian Consumer Law?
o: Only the High Court
Each store's own complaints department
A separate commission in each suburb
The ACCC together with state and territory fair trading agencies
quiz.e: One national law is enforced by the ACCC and state and territory agencies.

quiz.q: What can you choose if a product has a major failure?
o: Only a repair, at the seller's choice of method
Nothing at all, once you have taken it home
A refund or replacement, or keep it and claim compensation
A store credit note valid for the same shop
quiz.e: For major failures the choice of remedy is yours; for minor ones the business chooses.

quiz.q: Does a 'no refunds' sign remove your rights if goods are faulty?
o: No, you keep your consumer guarantee rights
Yes, if the sign is clearly displayed at the counter
Yes, but only when the faulty item was on sale
Yes, once you have left the shop with the goods
quiz.e: Signs can't override the guarantees, and faulty sale items are covered too.

quiz.q: Which is a common warning sign of a scam?
o: A call-back number that you found yourself
A written receipt sent after the payment
Pressure to act immediately and payment by gift cards or crypto
A request to compare unit prices in a shop
quiz.e: Urgency and unusual payment methods are classic scam signs, so verify by calling back independently.

quiz.q: What should you do first when something goes wrong with a purchase?
o: Go straight to a tribunal to start a claim
Contact the business with proof and the remedy you want
Post a complaint online and wait for a reply
Buy an extended warranty to cover the problem
quiz.e: Start with the business, then escalate to fair trading, an ombudsman or a tribunal.

LESSONS.push: 'No refunds' signs are often wrong. Here's what the law actually says.

LESSONS.title: Your rights at work
LESSONS.hook: Minimum pay, leave, a safe workplace and protection from unfair sacking aren't favours from your boss. For most Australian workers, they're the law.

sections.key: The Fair Work Act covers most employees, with the Commission setting minimums and the Ombudsman enforcing them.
sections.b:
Most Australian employees are covered by the national system under the Fair Work Act 2009. It covers nearly all private-sector workers, though some state public servants and local government workers, and many employees of sole traders and partnerships in WA, fall under state systems.

Two bodies do the heavy lifting. The Fair Work Commission is the independent tribunal that sets minimum wages and awards and hears disputes such as unfair dismissal claims. The Fair Work Ombudsman gives free advice, helps resolve pay disputes and can take employers to court.

sections.key: The National Employment Standards set a floor of conditions, and awards set minimum pay that can't be undercut.
sections.b:
The National Employment Standards (NES) are a safety net that no award, agreement or contract can undercut. They include a maximum of 38 ordinary hours a week for full-time staff, four weeks of paid annual leave (pro rata for part-timers), paid personal and carer's leave, compassionate leave, paid family and domestic violence leave, unpaid parental leave, long service leave, public holidays, and notice and redundancy pay. Some employees can also request flexible working.

The Fair Work Commission reviews the national minimum wage yearly, usually from 1 July. Most workers are also covered by a modern award setting pay and conditions, including penalty rates, overtime and breaks. Enterprise agreements must leave employees better off overall. Employers must pay superannuation and give you a payslip within one working day of payday.

sections.key: Casuals trade paid leave for a higher hourly rate, and can ask to become permanent if their work is regular and ongoing.
sections.b:
Employees can be full-time, part-time, casual or fixed-term. Permanent employees get paid leave and more job security. Casual employees have no firm advance commitment to ongoing work and usually receive a casual loading instead of paid annual and personal leave, commonly 25% under awards. Casuals still get some protections, including unpaid carer's leave and, after enough regular service, the right to claim unfair dismissal.

Since 2024, casuals who believe their work has become regular and ongoing can, after a qualifying period, notify their employer that they want to become permanent. Being wrongly labelled a contractor, called sham contracting, is illegal.

sections.key: Unfair dismissal claims have strict conditions and a 21-day deadline, and discrimination and harassment at work are unlawful.
sections.b:
If you are dismissed in a way that is harsh, unjust or unreasonable, you may be able to claim unfair dismissal. You usually need at least six months' service, or 12 months at an employer with fewer than 15 employees, and some high earners are excluded. A genuine redundancy isn't unfair dismissal. The deadline is strict: generally 21 days. Separately, general protections laws prohibit dismissal because you exercised a workplace right, such as making a complaint or taking leave.

Federal laws make it unlawful to treat workers unfairly because of protected attributes such as race, sex, disability or age, and states have similar laws. Sexual harassment is unlawful, and since late 2022 employers must take reasonable steps to prevent it. Complaints can go to the Australian Human Rights Commission or a state body; the Fair Work Commission deals with bullying.

sections.key: Employers must keep workers safe, including psychologically, and keeping records is the best way to protect your pay.
sections.b:
Work health and safety laws are made by each state and territory. Most use harmonised model laws; Victoria has its own similar law. The business must ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers, including psychological hazards like bullying and excessive workloads. Workers must take reasonable care too. You can often cease work that poses a serious risk, and workers' compensation usually covers medical costs and lost wages.

Protect your rights by keeping payslips, rosters, your contract and notes of hours, because underpayment is common and often accidental. Check your pay with the Fair Work Ombudsman's tools and raise concerns in writing. Since 2025, intentional underpayment has been a federal crime. This is general information only; community legal centres, Legal Aid and employment lawyers can advise.

quiz.q: What does the Fair Work Commission do?
o: Provides free advice and prosecutes employers in court
Collects superannuation from employers
Sets minimum wages and awards and hears disputes like unfair dismissal
Writes each state's safety laws
quiz.e: The Commission is the independent tribunal; the Ombudsman gives advice and enforces.

quiz.q: What does the National Employment Standards safety net mean for your contract?
o: Your contract can't provide less than the NES
Your contract can replace the NES if you sign it
The NES only apply to casual staff
The NES override any better entitlement you have
quiz.e: The NES are a floor, so no award, agreement or contract can go below them.

quiz.q: Why do casual employees usually receive a casual loading?
o: It replaces their superannuation
It is a bonus for working weekends
It is paid instead of annual and personal leave
It makes them ineligible for permanent work
quiz.e: The higher hourly rate, commonly 25%, compensates for the leave casuals don't get.

quiz.q: What is the usual deadline for lodging an unfair dismissal claim?
o: Six months from dismissal
21 days from when the dismissal takes effect
Twelve months from dismissal
Whenever you find new evidence
quiz.e: The deadline is strict, so act quickly after a dismissal.

quiz.q: Why should you keep payslips, rosters and notes of hours?
o: The law requires employees to submit them monthly
They replace the need for a contract
Employers can't keep their own records
Underpayment is common, and records let you check and prove your pay
quiz.e: Good records let you spot underpayment and support a claim if needed.

LESSONS.push: Some of your work rights can't be signed away, even in your own contract.

LESSONS.title: Percentages without the panic
LESSONS.hook: Percentages decide your pay rise, your loan rate and whether a sale is really a bargain. A few simple rules make them easy.

sections.key: A percentage is a number out of 100, so you find it by converting to a decimal and multiplying.
sections.b:
Percent comes from the Latin per centum, 'for each hundred'. So 15% means 15 out of every 100, or 15/100, or 0.15. To find a percentage, convert to a decimal and multiply: 15% of $80 is 0.15 × 80, which is $12.

A handy quirk is that x% of y always equals y% of x. So 8% of 50 is the same as 50% of 8, which is obviously 4. Choosing the easier direction often turns a fiddly sum into an instant one.

sections.key: Percentage change is divided by the starting value, and percentage points are not the same as percent.
sections.b:
Percentage change tells you how big a move was compared with where it started: (new minus old) divided by old, times 100. If petrol rises from $1.80 to $2.07, the rise is 27 cents, and 0.27 ÷ 1.80 is 0.15, so prices rose 15%. Always divide by the starting value, not the ending one.

When the measure is itself a percentage, two kinds of change get mixed up. Unemployment going from 4% to 4.5% rose by half a percentage point, but by 12.5% relative to where it started. People quote whichever sounds more dramatic. The RBA moves the cash rate in basis points, hundredths of a percentage point, so '25 basis points' is a quarter of a point, say 3.60% to 3.85%.

sections.key: Work out what you pay rather than what you save, and remember GST is one eleventh of a GST-inclusive price.
sections.b:
The fastest way to apply a discount is to work out what you pay. With 30% off, you pay 70%, so a $120 jacket costs 0.7 × 120, which is $84. Stacked discounts don't add up: '20% off, plus an extra 10% at the register' means paying 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so the discount is 28%, not 30%. On a $500 item that is $360, not $350. 'Up to 70% off' usually means only a few items get the full 70%.

Australia's GST has been 10% since 1 July 2000. Some things are GST-free, such as most basic food, many medical services and approved education courses. To add GST, multiply by 1.1: $200 becomes $220. Going backwards, GST in a $55 price is one eleventh of the total, $5, not $5.50.

sections.key: To undo a percentage, divide rather than subtract, and losses need bigger gains to recover.
sections.b:
If a jacket costs $84 after a 30% discount, the original isn't $84 plus 30%. The sale price was 0.7 times the original, so divide: $84 ÷ 0.7 is $120.

The same idea explains why ups and downs don't cancel. If a $100 share price rises 50% to $150, then falls 50%, it drops to $75, a net loss of 25%. After a 20% fall you need a 25% rise to get back to where you started, and after a 50% fall you need 100%. Investors who forget this underestimate the damage of big losses.

sections.key: Ask for absolute numbers behind a relative change, and use 10% as a building block for quick estimates.
sections.b:
Accurate percentages can still mislead. If a risk rises from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000, a headline can say it 'doubled', yet that is one extra case per 10,000 people. Ask for the absolute numbers. Compare bases too: 50% of a small group can be fewer people than 10% of a large one. And don't average percentages directly: a 10% return on $1,000 and a 30% return on $100 earn $130 on $1,100, about 12%, not 20%.

Most everyday percentages build from 10%. Move the decimal one place left: 10% of $64 is $6.40. Halve it for 5% ($3.20), add them for 15% ($9.60), double it for 20% ($12.80). For 1%, move two places, handy for card surcharges. These habits help you check a bill or pay rise in seconds.

quiz.q: What is the quickest way to find 8% of 50?
o: Find 50% of 8, which is 4
Add 8 to 50 and halve it
Divide 50 by 8
Multiply 8 by 50 and halve it
quiz.e: x% of y equals y% of x, so choose whichever direction is easier.

quiz.q: Unemployment rises from 4% to 4.5%. How is this best described?
o: A 0.5% relative rise and nothing more
A 4.5% rise on the old rate
Half a percentage point, or a 12.5% relative rise
A 50% rise on the old rate
quiz.e: The simple difference is percentage points, while the relative change divides by the starting value.

quiz.q: A $55 price includes GST. How much of it is GST?
o: $5.50, ten percent of the total
$5, one eleventh of the total
$10, one fifth of the total
$4.50, ten percent of the base price
quiz.e: GST is 10% of the pre-GST price, so it is one eleventh of the GST-inclusive total.

quiz.q: After a 50% fall in value, what gain is needed to recover fully?
quiz.e: Losses need bigger gains to recover because the gain applies to a smaller base.

quiz.q: A headline says a risk has 'doubled'. What should you ask for?
o: The newspaper's circulation figures
The average of the two percentages
The absolute numbers, such as extra cases per 10,000
The date the study was published
quiz.e: A doubling of a tiny risk can still be a very small absolute change.

LESSONS.push: Two sales of 20% and 10% off don't add up to 30%. Here's the sum.

LESSONS.title: Mental maths tricks
LESSONS.hook: You don't need to be 'a maths person' to add up a bill in your head. You just need a handful of shortcuts that professionals quietly use.

sections.key: Break numbers into friendly pieces, or round to a convenient number and adjust.
sections.b:
Nobody really calculates 47 + 38 digit by digit in their head. They break numbers into friendlier pieces. Add tens and ones separately: 40 + 30 is 70, 7 + 8 is 15, total 85. Or lean on a round number: 47 + 40 is 87, then take away the extra 2. Working left to right, biggest parts first, gives a rough answer immediately that you can refine.

Rounding and adjusting suits prices like $4.95. Six items at $4.95 are six at $5, which is $30, minus 6 × 5 cents, which is 30 cents: $29.70. Likewise 99 × 7 is 100 × 7 minus 7, which is 693, and 198 + 245 is 200 + 245 minus 2, which is 443.

sections.key: Multiply by 5 by halving 10 times, by 9 by taking one lot from 10 times, and by 11 by adding the number to 10 times itself.
sections.b:
Five is half of ten, so multiply by 10 and halve: 68 × 5 is 680 halved, 340. The same extends to 25, a quarter of 100: 36 × 25 is 3,600 divided by four, 900. That suits money.

Nine is one less than ten, so multiply by 10 and subtract one lot: 47 × 9 is 470 minus 47, which is 423. In the nine times table, digits add to 9 and the tens digit is one less than the multiplier, so 9 × 7 is 63.

For 11, multiply by 10 and add the number once: 11 × 36 is 360 + 36 = 396. Two-digit shortcut: put the digit sum in the middle. For 78, 7 + 8 is 15, so write 5 in the middle and carry 1: 858.

sections.key: To square a number ending in 5, multiply its tens digit by the next whole number and write 25 on the end.
sections.b:
To square a two-digit number ending in 5, take the tens digit, multiply it by the next whole number up, then write 25 on the end. For 35 × 35: 3 × 4 is 12, so the answer is 1,225. For 85 × 85: 8 × 9 is 72, giving 7,225.

It works because 35 is 30 plus 5, and when you multiply it out the pieces always combine this way. It also helps with neighbours: 45 × 45 is 2,025, so 45 × 46 is simply 2,025 plus 45, or 2,070. And it makes quick work of areas: a block 25 metres by 25 metres is 2 × 3, so 625 square metres.

sections.key: Take the friendly part first when dividing, and double one number while halving the other to land on round figures.
sections.b:
When a $243 bill is split four ways, don't attack 243 directly. Take the friendly part first: $240 ÷ 4 is $60. Then share the remaining $3: 3 ÷ 4 is 75 cents. Everyone pays $60.75. For $186 among six people, 180 ÷ 6 is 30 and 6 ÷ 6 is 1, so it is $31 each.

A related trick is doubling and halving. Halving one number and doubling the other leaves a product unchanged. So 16 × 25 becomes 8 × 50, then 4 × 100, which is 400. Look for the version that lands on a round number.

sections.key: Round to simple numbers for a rough answer first, so you can spot when an exact result is wrong.
sections.b:
Before calculating carefully, get a rough answer. Round each number to something simple and see where the answer should land. At the supermarket, items costing $3.49, $5.99, $2.10 and $7.85 round to about 3.5, 6, 2 and 8, roughly $19.50. The exact total is $19.43. If the register says $29.43, you know instantly something is wrong.

Estimation also catches your own slips, such as a decimal point in the wrong place, which can make an answer ten times too big. Like any skill, mental maths gets faster with practice, so try it on receipts, recipes and fuel stops.

quiz.q: How would you work out six items at $4.95 quickly?
o: Multiply 4 by 6 and then add 95
Add $4.95 to itself six times, digit by digit
Treat them as six at $5, then subtract 30 cents
Round each to $6 and subtract $1 at the end
quiz.e: Round to a friendly number, then correct for the amount you added.

quiz.q: What is a quick way to multiply 36 by 25?
o: Multiply 36 by 5 twice and add them
Find 36 × 100 and divide by four
Double 36 and add 25
Halve 36 and multiply by 50
quiz.e: Twenty-five is a quarter of 100, so multiply by 100 and divide by four.

quiz.q: How do you square 65 using the trick for numbers ending in 5?
o: Multiply 6 by 5 to get 30, then write 25
Multiply 6 by 6 to get 36, then write 25
Add 6 and 5 and write 25
Multiply 6 by 7 to get 42, then write 25 to make 4,225
quiz.e: Tens digit times the next whole number, then 25 on the end.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of doubling one number and halving the other?
o: The product doubles each time
It removes the need to multiply
The product stays the same but may become easier to compute
It only works for money amounts
quiz.e: Doubling and halving keeps the product unchanged while aiming for round numbers.

quiz.q: Why estimate before calculating exactly?
o: It lets you spot wildly wrong answers, like a misplaced decimal
It guarantees that your answer is exact
It replaces the need to ever check a receipt
It works only for supermarket totals
quiz.e: A rough answer gives you a sense check against slips.

LESSONS.push: Professionals multiply by 5 by halving 10. More shortcuts worth knowing.

LESSONS.title: Making sense of big numbers
LESSONS.hook: A million seconds is under two weeks. A billion seconds is over 31 years. Our brains blur the gap, and that matters every time you read a headline.

sections.key: Each of million, billion and trillion is a thousand times the one before, which our brains tend to blur.
sections.b:
Each of these words is a thousand times the one before. A million is 1,000,000. A billion is a thousand millions. A trillion is a thousand billions, a 1 followed by twelve zeros. Because the words sound similar, people treat them as neighbours, but a billion is a thousand times a million.

British usage once called a million million a 'billion' (the long scale). The UK officially adopted the short scale in 1974, and Australia uses it too.

Time makes the gap felt. A day has 86,400 seconds, so a million seconds is about 11.6 days. A billion seconds is about 31.7 years. A trillion seconds is roughly 31,700 years, back to the last ice age, before farming, writing or cities.

sections.key: Translate big sums into daily spending or per-person amounts to judge whether they are large or small.
sections.b:
Imagine spending $1,000 every day. A million dollars would last 1,000 days, roughly two years and nine months. A billion dollars would last a million days, about 2,700 years.

Dividing national figures by population also helps. Australia has roughly 27 million people (mid-2020s), so a $1 billion government scheme works out to about $37 per person, while $1 trillion would be about $37,000 each. Dividing by population turns abstract numbers into something you can judge: is this a lot, or not much at all?

sections.key: Scientific notation writes very large or small numbers as a number from 1 to 10 times a power of ten.
sections.b:
Scientists handle huge and tiny numbers with scientific notation: a number between 1 and 10, multiplied by a power of ten. The power tells you how many places to move the decimal point. The speed of light, about 300,000,000 metres per second, is 3 × 10⁸. Earth is about 4.5 × 10⁹ years old. Tiny numbers use negative powers: a hydrogen atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ metres across, a ten-billionth of a metre.

It also makes calculation easier. To multiply, multiply the front numbers and add the powers: (2 × 10³) × (3 × 10⁴) is 6 × 10⁷.

sections.key: Logarithmic scales and ratios show that small-looking differences can be huge and that relative change often matters most.
sections.b:
Each power of ten is an order of magnitude, so 'three orders of magnitude' means about 1,000 times bigger. Several scales are logarithmic, where each step multiplies. Every extra 10 decibels means ten times the sound intensity, so a 90-decibel lawnmower has about 1,000 times the intensity of a 60-decibel conversation. Star brightness works backwards: five magnitudes brighter looks 100 times brighter, and smaller numbers mean brighter stars.

This means thinking in ratios. A $10,000 pay rise is life-changing on $40,000 and modest on $400,000. Going from 1,000 to 2,000 followers is the same doubling as 1 million to 2 million. Young children, and adults without formal schooling, tend to space numbers in a compressed, roughly logarithmic way. Ask how big a change is in absolute terms, and relative to where it started.

sections.key: Give big numbers a scale, and use rough Fermi estimates to test whether a claim is plausible.
sections.b:
Physicist Enrico Fermi was famous for rough but surprisingly good estimates. At the first atomic bomb test in 1945 he dropped scraps of paper, watched how far the blast moved them, and estimated the yield at about 10 kilotons; later analysis put it at roughly twice that. Try one: hairdressers in a city of five million. About one haircut every two months is 30 million a year. At eight a day for 240 days, each does about 2,000. So around 15,000 hairdressers. Errors often partly cancel.

Headline numbers need a scale. Divide by population or by 365, and compare with the relevant total: a $500 million cut matters differently against a $2 billion budget than a $600 billion one. Check whether it's millions or billions, a common reporting error.

quiz.q: Roughly how long is a billion seconds?
o: About 11.6 days
About 31.7 years
About 31,700 years
About 3 months
quiz.e: A million seconds is under two weeks, while a billion is over 31 years.

quiz.q: What does dividing a national figure by population achieve?
o: It converts it to scientific notation
It shows the exact cost to taxpayers over time
It removes the need to check the source
It turns an abstract sum into a per-person amount you can judge
quiz.e: Per-person figures give a sense of scale, such as $37 each for $1 billion.

quiz.q: How do you multiply two numbers in scientific notation?
o: Add the front numbers and multiply the powers
Multiply both the front numbers and the powers
Multiply the front numbers and add the powers of ten
Add both the front numbers and the powers

quiz.q: Why does a 90-decibel lawnmower carry far more sound than a 60-decibel conversation?
o: Each 10 decibels is ten times the intensity, so 30 more is about 1,000 times
Decibels add up evenly, so it's one and a half times
Lawnmowers use a different scale
It is three times louder because 90 is three times 30
quiz.e: Logarithmic scales multiply with each step, so small-looking numbers hide huge differences.

quiz.q: What makes a Fermi estimate useful?
o: It always gives a precise, exact answer
It needs precise data for every single step
Rough guesses can land close because errors often partly cancel
It works only for questions about population
quiz.e: Quick estimates test whether a claim is plausible or wildly off.

LESSONS.push: A billion seconds is a very different length of time from a million.

LESSONS.title: Famous ideas in maths
LESSONS.hook: Pi, zero, prime numbers and infinity: a handful of ideas that took humanity thousands of years to work out, and a few popular myths about them.

sections.key: Pi is the endless ratio of a circle's circumference to its width, and the Fibonacci pattern appears in nature through efficient packing.
sections.b:
Measure around any circle, divide by the distance across, and you always get pi, about 3.14159. Around 1650 BCE, the Egyptian Rhind Papyrus used a method that gives about 3.16. In 1761 Johann Lambert proved pi is irrational: its digits go on forever without repeating. Computers have calculated over 100 trillion digits, but NASA engineers say about 15 decimal places is plenty for navigating the solar system.

Fibonacci's sequence starts 1, 1, then adds the last two: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55. Leonardo of Pisa used it in 1202 in a rabbit-breeding puzzle, though Indian scholars described it centuries earlier. Sunflower seed spirals often come in consecutive Fibonacci numbers, such as 34 and 55. It's a result of efficient packing, not magic.

sections.key: Treating zero as a real number came from India, and dividing by zero remains undefined.
sections.b:
Zero seems obvious now, but it was a hard-won idea. The Babylonians used a placeholder symbol for an empty position, and the Maya independently developed a zero for their calendars. Treating zero as a number in its own right, something you can add, subtract and multiply, came from India. In 628 CE Brahmagupta wrote rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers.

The Indian place-value system spread through the Islamic world and reached Europe partly through Fibonacci's Liber Abaci in 1202. One rule still stands: dividing by zero is undefined, because no answer makes sense.

sections.key: Primes are the building blocks of whole numbers, there are infinitely many, and encryption relies on their difficulty to find.
sections.b:
A prime can be divided evenly only by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. Two is the only even prime. Every whole number above 1 is either prime or can be built by multiplying primes in exactly one way, making primes the building blocks of arithmetic. Around 300 BCE Euclid proved there are infinitely many.

Primes also protect your online banking. Encryption methods such as RSA rely on the fact that multiplying two huge primes is easy, but working backwards to find them is extraordinarily hard. The largest known prime, found in 2024, has over 41 million digits.

sections.key: Pythagoras' theorem was known long before Pythagoras, and the golden ratio's reputation in art and nature is mostly myth.
sections.b:
In any right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the longest side. A 3-4-5 triangle works, because 9 + 16 is 25. It is named after Pythagoras (about 570 to 495 BCE), but Babylonian tablets such as Plimpton 322, from around 1800 BCE, show it was known earlier. Builders still check corners with a 3-4-5 triangle.

The golden ratio, about 1.618, is (1 + √5) ÷ 2. Ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers approach it, and it appears in a regular pentagon. But claims that the Parthenon, Great Pyramid or Mona Lisa were designed around it mostly come from picking points that fit. A nautilus shell is a spiral, but not a golden one. Studies on preferring golden rectangles are mixed. Le Corbusier did use it deliberately.

sections.key: Infinity behaves strangely, and ideas pursued for their own sake often turn out to be hugely useful later.
sections.b:
Infinity is a concept rather than a reachable number, and it behaves strangely. In Hilbert's Hotel, with infinitely many full rooms, a new guest arrives and everyone moves up one room, freeing room 1. There are exactly as many even numbers as whole numbers, since you can pair them off: 1 with 2, 2 with 4. In the late 1800s Georg Cantor proved something stranger: the infinity of all decimal numbers is larger than the infinity of whole numbers.

Is maths invented, like chess, or discovered, like a continent? People still disagree. But ideas pursued for their own sake often prove useful. Primes were a curiosity for over 2,000 years before securing the internet. Imaginary numbers, once seen as a trick, are essential in electrical engineering and quantum physics. In 1960 Eugene Wigner called this 'the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics'.

quiz.q: Why do sunflower seed spirals often follow Fibonacci numbers?
o: The plant counts the numbers on purpose
It is a coincidence of petal count
Fibonacci planted the first sunflowers
It is a result of efficient packing as the plant grows
quiz.e: The pattern comes from efficient packing, not magic.

quiz.q: What was the key step India added to the idea of zero?
o: Using a placeholder for an empty position
Using zero only in calendars
Treating zero as a number you can add, subtract and multiply
Rejecting negative numbers
quiz.e: Placeholders existed earlier, but treating zero as a true number came from India.

quiz.q: Why do primes matter for online security?
o: Multiplying huge primes is easy, but recovering them is extremely hard
Primes are easy to guess from short passwords
Primes can be divided evenly by any number
Every encryption key is made from an even prime
quiz.e: RSA relies on this one-way difficulty.

quiz.q: What is the best summary of the golden ratio in art and nature?
o: It was used to design the Parthenon and the Mona Lisa
It appears exactly in the spiral of a nautilus shell
It has interesting properties, but many claims about it are myths
It is exactly 1.5 and is found in all great art
quiz.e: Many claims rest on after-the-fact measurements that happen to fit.

quiz.q: What does Hilbert's Hotel show about infinity?
o: An infinite hotel can never be full
A full hotel with infinite rooms can still fit a new guest
Infinity is the largest whole number
Adding a guest always removes one
quiz.e: Infinity behaves strangely: everyone shifts up one room and room 1 is free.

LESSONS.push: Pythagoras may not have proved his own theorem. What else is misattributed in maths?

LESSONS.title: Germ theory: the idea that saved millions
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, doctors blamed disease on bad air. Then a handful of stubborn scientists proved that invisible living things were to blame.

sections.key: For centuries disease was blamed on foul air, which pointed people at smell rather than the real cause.
sections.b:
For centuries, the leading explanation for epidemics was miasma: foul, poisonous air rising from rubbish, swamps and sewage. Malaria literally comes from the Italian for 'bad air'. The theory wasn't entirely foolish. Filthy places really were more dangerous, and cleaning up cities did reduce disease. But it pointed people at the smell rather than the cause.

Doctors went from post-mortems to childbirth without washing, and nobody suspected that the real killers were too small to see.

sections.key: Microbes were seen in the 1670s, but proving they cause disease needed careful experiments.
sections.b:
In the 1670s, Dutch cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground tiny, powerful lenses and looked at pond water, rainwater and scrapings from his own teeth. He saw swarms of moving 'animalcules' and became the first person to describe bacteria.

Yet for almost 200 years few connected them with illness. Many scientists believed microbes arose spontaneously from decaying matter, so they seemed a result of rot, not a cause of sickness. In the 1860s Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long, swan-shaped necks. Air could get in, but dust and microbes were trapped. The broth stayed clear while the neck was intact; tilt the flask so broth touched the dust, and it quickly spoiled. This helped overturn spontaneous generation.

sections.key: Semmelweis and Snow showed that handwashing and clean water cut deaths, before anyone fully understood why.
sections.b:
In 1847, Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed far more mothers died of childbed fever in a Vienna maternity ward run by doctors and students than in the midwives' ward. When a colleague died after cutting himself during an autopsy, with similar symptoms, Semmelweis suspected doctors carried 'cadaverous particles' from corpses. He made staff wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths fell to around 1 to 2%. Colleagues rejected his ideas, and he died in an asylum in 1865.

In 1854 cholera hit Soho, London. John Snow suspected contaminated water, mapped the deaths and found them clustered around a Broad Street pump. Nearby brewery workers, who drank beer, were largely spared. The pump handle was removed and the outbreak, already waning, ended. His work is often called the birth of modern epidemiology.

sections.key: Pasteur and Koch turned germ theory into proof by linking specific microbes to specific diseases.
sections.b:
Pasteur showed that microbes spoil wine and milk, giving us pasteurisation, which uses gentle heat to kill them. Later he developed vaccines, including one for rabies in 1885.

German doctor Robert Koch turned germ theory into hard proof. In 1876 he showed that a specific bacterium caused anthrax in animals. In 1882 he identified the bacterium behind tuberculosis, then one of Europe's biggest killers, and soon afterwards the cause of cholera. Koch's postulates set a logical test: the germ should be found in every case of the disease, grown in pure culture, cause the disease in a healthy host, and be recovered again. His techniques, such as growing bacteria on solid plates, are still used.

sections.key: Antiseptic surgery and handwashing for about 20 seconds with soap remain frontline defences against infection.
sections.b:
