quiz.e: Loki is clever and spiteful, getting the gods into trouble and sometimes out of it.

quiz.q: What is unusual about Ragnarök?
o: The gods know in advance that they will die
Humans fight alongside the gods
It is a battle that the gods win easily
It never ends in the myths
quiz.e: Norse gods face a prophesied end, though a new green world rises afterwards.

LESSONS.push: Norse gods knew they would die, and we still name our weekdays after them.

LESSONS.title: Egypt's gods and the journey after death
LESSONS.hook: For well over a thousand years, Egyptians believed your heart would be weighed against a feather when you died. What happened next depended on how you'd lived.

sections.key: Ancient Egyptian religion lasted about 3,000 years, with hundreds of gods whose roles shifted and merged over time.
sections.b:
Ancient Egyptian religion was not one fixed system. Over roughly 3,000 years it included hundreds of gods, many tied to particular towns, whose roles shifted and merged. The sun god Ra, for example, was later combined with Amun of Thebes as Amun-Ra. Gods were often shown with animal heads to signal their qualities: jackal-headed Anubis watched over the dead, and ibis-headed Thoth was god of writing and wisdom.

Our sources include the Pyramid Texts, carved inside royal pyramids from around 2400 BC and among the oldest religious writings known, plus later coffin inscriptions, papyri and temple walls.

sections.key: Egyptians told of the world rising from primeval waters, with the sun god Ra crossing the sky by day and the underworld by night.
sections.b:
Egyptian creation stories begin with Nun, dark, endless waters. From them rose a mound of land, just as fields emerged each year when the Nile flood went down. In a version from Heliopolis, the creator god Atum produced Shu (air) and Tefnut (moisture), whose children were Geb (earth) and Nut (sky).

The sun god Ra was central to daily life. By day he sailed across the sky in a boat. By night he journeyed through the underworld, fighting the chaos serpent Apep, to be reborn each dawn. Pharaohs called themselves the 'son of Ra'.

sections.key: Osiris was murdered by his jealous brother Set, restored by Isis and avenged by their son Horus, whom each pharaoh embodied.
sections.b:
The most important Egyptian myth concerns Osiris, a wise king who taught people farming and law. His brother Set, god of storms, deserts and disorder, was jealous. The Greek writer Plutarch, around AD 100, gives the fullest telling: Set tricked Osiris into a beautifully made chest, slammed the lid and threw it into the Nile, then cut the body up and scattered it.

Isis, Osiris's wife and sister, searched Egypt for the pieces and, with Nephthys and Anubis, put him back together, in effect making the first mummy. Osiris became ruler of the dead. Their son Horus, raised in hiding in the Nile Delta marshes, fought Set for the throne and lost an eye, which was restored. The Eye of Horus became a popular protective amulet, and each living pharaoh was identified with Horus.

sections.key: Egyptians believed a person had several parts, including the ka and ba, and needed a preserved body to live on after death.
sections.b:
Egyptians saw a person as made of several parts. The ka was the life force, which needed food and drink offerings even after death. The ba, often shown as a bird with a human head, could move between the tomb and the world. Your name and your shadow mattered too.

For these to survive, the body had to be preserved. The goal was to become an akh, a transfigured spirit, and reach the Field of Reeds, an ideal version of Egypt with perfect harvests. Small servant figures called shabtis were buried with the dead to do farm work for them there.

sections.key: In the judgement of the dead the heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, and the heart of a wrongdoer was devoured by Ammit.
sections.b:
The dead faced judgement in the Hall of Two Truths, pictured in the Book of the Dead. The deceased first declared the wrongs they had not committed. Anubis then placed their heart on a scale against a feather representing Maat, goddess of truth, justice and cosmic order, while Thoth recorded the result. A heart weighed down by wrongdoing was eaten by Ammit, part crocodile, part lion and part hippopotamus. A balanced heart meant the person could join Osiris.

That is why mummification left the heart in place, with a heart scarab spell begging it not to testify against its owner. The brain was discarded, as thinking was thought to happen in the heart. A priest then performed the Opening of the Mouth, so the dead could breathe, eat and speak again.

quiz.q: What best describes ancient Egyptian religion?
o: One fixed system with a single creed
A system with hundreds of gods whose roles shifted and merged over time
A belief in a single sun god alone
A religion that lasted only a few centuries
quiz.e: Over roughly 3,000 years its gods changed, and some merged, as Ra and Amun did.

quiz.q: What did Ra do each night, according to Egyptian belief?
o: Slept inside a pyramid
Became the moon
Journeyed through the underworld, fighting the serpent Apep
Weighed the hearts of the dead
quiz.e: Ra's nightly journey ended in rebirth at every dawn.

quiz.q: What did the Eye of Horus become?
o: A popular protective amulet
The symbol of Set
A unit of weight
The name of the sun boat
quiz.e: Horus's restored eye symbolised protection and healing.

quiz.q: What was the ka in Egyptian belief?
o: The preserved body itself
A bird-shaped spirit that left the tomb
The life force that needed offerings after death
The final judge of the dead
quiz.e: The ka needed food and drink even after death, which is why offerings were left.

quiz.q: Why was the heart usually left inside the body during mummification?
o: It was too delicate to remove
It would be needed at the judgement of the dead
It was believed to be where thinking happened, so the brain was kept
It had to be fed by the ba
quiz.e: The heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, so it stayed with the body.

LESSONS.push: Your heart is weighed against a feather. Ancient Egyptians had a plan for that.

LESSONS.title: The five zones of the ocean
LESSONS.hook: Most of the living space on Earth is dark, cold and crushing, and we have seen almost none of it.

sections.key: The ocean covers about 71% of Earth, averages about 3,700 metres deep and is divided into five zones by sunlight.
sections.b:
The ocean covers about 71% of Earth's surface and holds around 97% of its water. Its average depth is roughly 3,700 metres, and because life exists at every depth, the ocean makes up the vast majority of the living space on the planet.

Scientists divide the water column into layers based mainly on how much sunlight reaches them. From top to bottom they are the sunlight, twilight, midnight, abyssal and hadal zones. Each has its own conditions, and the animals in each are shaped by the challenges of light, food, cold and pressure.

sections.key: Phytoplankton in the top 200 metres make about half of Earth's oxygen, and below that many animals migrate up each night.
sections.b:
The sunlight zone runs from the surface to about 200 metres. It is the only layer with enough light for photosynthesis, so tiny drifting plants called phytoplankton grow here. They produce roughly half of the oxygen made on Earth each year and form the base of almost every ocean food chain. This warm zone holds coral reefs, kelp forests, tuna, turtles, dolphins and most fisheries.

Between about 200 and 1,000 metres lies the twilight zone, with faint blue light but too little for plants. Lanternfish, small squid and krill relatives have large eyes and make their own light. Each night vast numbers swim up to feed in darkness, then sink at dawn to hide. This is often described as the largest migration on Earth by numbers of animals.

sections.key: Below 1,000 metres there is no sunlight, the water is near freezing and food arrives mostly as marine snow.
sections.b:
From about 1,000 to 4,000 metres is the midnight zone. No sunlight reaches it at all; the only light comes from animals themselves. Temperatures sit around 2 to 4 degrees Celsius.

With no plants, food mostly arrives as 'marine snow', a slow drift of dead plankton, droppings and other debris from above, plus the occasional carcass. Animals here tend to be slow-moving and energy-saving, with big mouths and stretchy stomachs to make the most of rare meals. Sperm whales dive into this zone to hunt squid.

sections.key: The abyssal plains lie below 4,000 metres, the hadal zone exists only in trenches, and the deepest point is about 11,000 metres.
sections.b:
Below about 4,000 metres is the abyssal zone, named from a Greek word meaning 'bottomless'. Much of it is flat, muddy seafloor called the abyssal plain, covering a huge part of the planet. The deepest layer, the hadal zone, named after Hades, exists only in ocean trenches below about 6,000 metres.

The deepest known point is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, in the western Pacific, at roughly 11,000 metres. Surprisingly, life is found even there, including amphipods, sea cucumbers and microbes.

sections.key: Pressure rises by about one atmosphere every 10 metres, and only about a quarter of the seafloor is mapped in detail.
sections.b:
Water is heavy. For every 10 metres you descend, pressure increases by roughly one atmosphere. At 1,000 metres it is about 100 times surface pressure; in the Challenger Deep it is more than 1,000 times, roughly the weight of a small car on every square centimetre. Deep-sea animals cope because they lack air-filled spaces that would be crushed, and their proteins and cell membranes work under pressure.

We have seen little of it. By the mid-2020s, efforts such as Seabed 2030 had mapped roughly a quarter of the seafloor in high resolution, and the share seen directly is well under one per cent. The ocean has absorbed about 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases and roughly a quarter of human carbon dioxide emissions, and new deep-sea species are described every year.

quiz.q: What mainly defines the ocean's five zones?
o: The temperature of the surface
How much sunlight reaches each layer
The kinds of fish living in them
How far each layer is from land
quiz.e: Scientists divide the water column mainly by how much sunlight reaches each layer.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the oxygen produced on Earth each year comes from ocean phytoplankton?
o: About 5%
Almost all of it
None, they only consume oxygen
About half
quiz.e: Phytoplankton in the sunlight zone produce roughly half of the oxygen made on Earth each year.

quiz.q: What is 'marine snow'?
o: Ice that forms on the seafloor
White coral sand
A drift of dead plankton and debris sinking from above
Foam from breaking waves
quiz.e: Marine snow is sinking organic debris and a key food source in the dark zones.

quiz.q: Where is the deepest known point in the ocean?
o: The Great Australian Bight
The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench
The middle of the Atlantic
Under the Antarctic ice
quiz.e: The Challenger Deep, in the western Pacific's Mariana Trench, is roughly 11,000 metres deep.

quiz.q: About how much does water pressure increase for every 10 metres of depth?
o: One atmosphere
Ten atmospheres
A hundred atmospheres
It stays the same
quiz.e: Pressure rises about one atmosphere per 10 metres, so the deepest trench is over 1,000 atmospheres.

LESSONS.push: Most of Earth's living space is dark and crushing, and we've seen almost none of it.

LESSONS.title: Ocean currents: the planet's conveyor belt
LESSONS.hook: Rivers larger than any on land flow through the sea, carrying heat, food, plastic and even Nemo's dad.

sections.key: Ocean currents are steady flows of water that move heat, nutrients and life around the globe, and the largest dwarf any river.
sections.b:
An ocean current is a steady, directional flow of seawater. Some are shallow and fast, others deep and slow, and the largest carry far more water than all the rivers on land combined. The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which loops around Antarctica from west to east, moves over 100 times the flow of all the world's rivers put together.

Currents shift heat from the tropics towards the poles, shape the climate of whole continents, carry larvae and nutrients that feed fisheries, and decide where floating things end up, from seeds to shipwreck debris.

sections.key: Surface currents are driven by wind and Earth's rotation, while deep currents are driven by temperature and saltiness over about 1,000 years.
sections.b:
Currents in the upper few hundred metres are driven mainly by wind. Steady winds such as the trade winds drag the surface water along. Because Earth spins, moving water is deflected by the Coriolis effect: to the left in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern. Continents then block and redirect the flow. Before engines, knowing the currents could shave weeks off a voyage.

Deep currents work differently. Around Antarctica and in the far North Atlantic, seawater becomes cold and salty, partly because forming sea ice leaves salt behind. That dense water sinks and creeps along the ocean floor, and elsewhere water rises to replace it. This thermohaline circulation links all the oceans in a 'global conveyor belt', and a parcel of water can take around 1,000 years to complete the loop.

sections.key: The Gulf Stream and its wider system help keep north-west Europe mild, and scientists debate how much it is slowing.
sections.b:
The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico up the east coast of North America and across the Atlantic. With prevailing winds, the wider current system it belongs to gives Britain and north-west Europe milder winters than places at the same latitude in Canada.

This system, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, may be weakening as melting ice adds fresh water that is less likely to sink. How much it has slowed, and whether it could approach a tipping point this century, is actively debated among scientists.

sections.key: The East Australian Current carries warm water south along the east coast, and the Leeuwin Current does the same unusually down Western Australia.
sections.b:
The East Australian Current is the one the turtles ride in the 2003 film Finding Nemo. It flows south from the Coral Sea along Queensland and New South Wales, carrying warm water and tropical fish larvae, which is why reef fish sometimes turn up around Sydney in late summer. Much of it peels away eastwards, forming swirling eddies. As the climate warms, it has pushed further south, contributing to warming off Tasmania that has helped shrink its giant kelp forests dramatically.

Most currents on the western side of continents carry cold water towards the equator. Western Australia is an exception. The Leeuwin Current carries warm, low-nutrient tropical water south along the WA coast and around Cape Leeuwin. It helps explain why corals grow at Ningaloo and at the Houtman Abrolhos Islands off Geraldton.

sections.key: Gyres collect floating plastic into scattered garbage patches, and currents shape Australian weather, fishing and swimming safety.
sections.b:
Where major currents connect, they form enormous rotating gyres, five main ones in the subtropical oceans. Floating debris collects towards their calm centres. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is not a solid island of rubbish but a vast area of scattered plastic, mostly small fragments, with discarded fishing gear making up much of its weight. In 1992, thousands of bath toys lost from a ship helped scientists track these currents.

Currents shape daily life too. Shifts in Pacific currents and winds drive El Niño and La Niña, which influence droughts, floods and bushfire seasons in eastern Australia. Upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water supports rich fishing grounds. Rip currents are a leading cause of coastal drowning in Australia: if caught, stay calm, float and signal for help rather than fighting the flow.

quiz.q: Why do ocean currents matter to the planet?
o: They move heat, nutrients and life around the globe
They make the sea level rise and fall each day
They keep the ocean salt content constant
They create all the world's tides
quiz.e: Currents shift heat towards the poles, shape climates and feed fisheries.

quiz.q: What makes deep water sink to drive the global conveyor belt?
o: It is warmer than surface water
Whales push it down
It is cold and salty, and therefore dense
Rain falls on it
quiz.e: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks, driving the slow thermohaline circulation.

quiz.q: Why might the Atlantic overturning circulation be weakening?
o: Melting ice adds fresh water that is less likely to sink
Winds over the Atlantic have stopped
The water there is getting saltier
The Gulf Stream has dried up
quiz.e: Fresh meltwater is less dense and sinks poorly, though scientists debate how much it has slowed.

quiz.q: Why is the Leeuwin Current unusual?
o: It is the fastest current on Earth
It carries warm water south along a western coastline
It flows only in winter
It is made of fresh water
quiz.e: Most currents along western coastlines are cold and flow towards the equator; the Leeuwin is warm and flows south.

quiz.q: What is the Great Pacific Garbage Patch actually like?
o: A solid island you can walk on
A single sunken ship
A vast area of scattered, mostly small plastic pieces
An oil slick
quiz.e: It is a diffuse area of floating plastic, much of it small fragments and fishing gear, collected by a gyre.

LESSONS.push: Rivers larger than any on land flow through the sea. Where do they take us?

LESSONS.title: Life in the deep sea
LESSONS.hook: In total darkness, near-boiling vents feed giant worms, fish carry their own lanterns, and a few humans have visited the very bottom.

sections.key: The deep sea is dark, cold and under immense pressure, yet it is full of life that scientists once thought could not exist.
sections.b:
Below about 200 metres, sunlight fades, and below 1,000 metres it disappears entirely. The water is near freezing and the pressure is immense. For a long time, scientists assumed such a place would be almost lifeless. In the 1870s, the British research ship HMS Challenger dredged the deep seafloor during a voyage around the world and brought up thousands of previously unknown species.

Today we know the deep sea is home to an astonishing variety of animals and microbes, many still undescribed, living in ways that seem alien to us.

sections.key: Hydrothermal vents support life that runs on chemical energy, including giant tube worms that have no mouth or gut.
sections.b:
In 1977, scientists in the submersible Alvin near the Galápagos Islands found hot springs on the seafloor, surrounded by crowded communities of life. At these hydrothermal vents, seawater seeps into the crust, is heated by magma and gushes out loaded with minerals. Black smokers blast out water hotter than 350 degrees Celsius, kept from boiling by the enormous pressure. Bacteria here get energy from chemicals such as hydrogen sulphide, a process called chemosynthesis.

The giant tube worm can grow up to about two metres, with a red plume sticking out of a white tube. As an adult it has no mouth or gut. Billions of bacteria inside it turn vent chemicals into food. Some scientists think life on Earth may have begun at vents, one of several competing ideas.

sections.key: Most deep-sea animals make their own light, called bioluminescence, to hunt, hide and communicate, and anglerfish use it as a lure.
sections.b:
In the dark ocean, making your own light is normal. Studies suggest around three-quarters of animals in the deep water column are bioluminescent, using a chemical reaction or glowing bacteria. Most of it is blue, because blue light travels furthest through seawater. Animals use light to lure prey, startle predators, find mates and hide: some fish glow faintly on their bellies to match the dim light from above and erase their silhouette. A few dragonfish produce red light that most deep-sea animals cannot see, like a private torch.

The female anglerfish dangles a lure of light-producing bacteria, then swallows prey with needle-like teeth. In some species, tiny males bite on and fuse to her permanently.

sections.key: Crewed dives to the Challenger Deep began in 1960 and remain rare, so most exploration is now done by robots.
sections.b:
The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is roughly 11,000 metres deep, enough to swallow Mount Everest with more than two kilometres of water to spare. In 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy officer Don Walsh reached the bottom in the bathyscaphe Trieste. Nobody returned until 2012, when James Cameron made a solo dive in Deepsea Challenger, a submersible designed and built in Sydney. Since 2019, Victor Vescovo's submersible has made repeated dives.

Crewed dives are expensive and risky, so most exploration uses robots. Tethered remotely operated vehicles carry cameras and arms, autonomous vehicles map the seafloor, and baited 'landers' float back up. In 2022, a team led by scientists from the University of Western Australia filmed a snailfish at about 8,300 metres off Japan, the deepest fish ever recorded.

sections.key: The deep sea stores carbon and holds valuable minerals, and scientists warn seabed mining could do lasting damage.
sections.b:
The deep ocean is not just a curiosity. It stores enormous amounts of carbon, helping regulate the climate, and its organisms have produced enzymes and compounds used in medicine and research.

It also holds metal-rich rocks called polymetallic nodules, containing cobalt, nickel and manganese used in batteries. Companies want to mine them, but many scientists warn that deep-sea ecosystems grow and recover extremely slowly, over decades to millions of years, and that we understand them too poorly to judge the damage. Whether and how to allow deep-sea mining is one of the big ocean debates of this decade.

quiz.q: What did the HMS Challenger voyage in the 1870s show about the deep sea?
o: That it is full of previously unknown species
That it is almost completely lifeless
That it is warmer than the surface
That it has no pressure
quiz.e: The expedition's dredging proved the deep seafloor teems with life, contrary to earlier assumptions.

quiz.q: How does an adult giant tube worm get food?
o: It filters plankton with its mouth
It hunts small crabs
Bacteria living inside its body make food from vent chemicals
It absorbs sunlight
quiz.e: Adult giant tube worms have no mouth or gut and depend on internal bacteria.

quiz.q: Why is most deep-sea bioluminescence blue?
o: Animals cannot make other colours
Blue light travels furthest through seawater
It reflects the sky
Blue is the colour of all marine bacteria
quiz.e: Blue light penetrates water best, so it is the most useful colour in the deep.

quiz.q: Why is most deep-sea exploration now done by robots?
o: Crewed dives are expensive and risky
Humans are too large for the trenches
Robots can reach the surface faster
The law forbids crewed dives
quiz.e: Remotely operated and autonomous vehicles can explore for long periods without risking people.

quiz.q: What is a major concern about deep-sea mining?
o: It would drain the ocean
The metals are worthless
It is already banned everywhere
Deep-sea ecosystems recover very slowly and are poorly understood
quiz.e: Scientists warn that slow-growing, poorly studied deep-sea ecosystems could be lastingly damaged.

LESSONS.push: In total darkness, worms with no mouth thrive beside near-boiling vents.

LESSONS.title: Sharks: fear versus facts
LESSONS.hook: Sharks are older than trees, come in more than 500 species and are far more at risk from us than we are from them.

sections.key: Sharks have existed for over 400 million years, longer than trees, and come in more than 500 species of every kind of size.
sections.b:
Sharks appeared more than 400 million years ago, earlier than trees, which evolved roughly 385 million years ago, and long before dinosaurs. They have survived several mass extinctions. Their skeletons are made of cartilage, the flexible material in your nose and ears, which is why fossil sharks are mostly known from teeth. Sharks replace their teeth throughout life, sometimes thousands over a lifetime. The extinct megalodon, which died out around 3.6 million years ago, may have reached 15 metres or more.

There are over 500 known species, and most look nothing like the movie villain. The dwarf lanternshark is about 20 centimetres long and glows in the deep sea. Wobbegongs lie camouflaged on Australian reefs like shaggy rugs.

sections.key: The whale shark is the largest fish and eats plankton, and the Greenland shark may live for centuries.
sections.b:
The whale shark, the largest fish in the world, can exceed 12 metres yet feeds on plankton. Each year it gathers at Ningaloo Reef in WA.

The Greenland shark grows so slowly that a 2016 study estimated some live for several centuries, possibly around 400 years, making it the longest-lived known vertebrate.

Sharks also reproduce differently from most fish, which scatter huge numbers of tiny eggs. Sharks produce a few large, well-developed young, and fertilisation happens inside the female. Some species lay eggs in tough cases; the Port Jackson shark wedges its corkscrew-shaped egg cases into rocky crevices. Many give birth to live pups, and hammerheads and bull sharks nourish their young through a placenta-like connection.

sections.key: In grey nurse sharks the first embryo in each uterus eats its siblings, so a litter is usually just two pups.
sections.b:
The grey nurse shark goes further than most. In each of the mother's two uteri, the first embryo to develop eats its smaller siblings and spare eggs. A litter is usually just two pups, born every second year, and the pups get no parental care once born. They must fend for themselves from day one.

This slow, low-numbers way of reproducing is why many sharks struggle to recover when their numbers fall. Sharks that produce only a few young, mature late and grow slowly cannot quickly replace the animals that are lost.

sections.key: Unprovoked shark bites are rare, but humans kill an estimated 100 million sharks a year and many species are threatened.
sections.b:
Shark bites are frightening and heavily reported, but rare. Worldwide, researchers typically record around 50 to 80 confirmed unprovoked bites a year, with fatalities usually in single figures. In Australia, a few people die from shark bites in a typical year, while well over a hundred drown along the coast. Only a handful of species cause most serious bites, chiefly the white, tiger and bull shark.

The danger runs the other way. A widely cited 2013 study estimated that humans kill around 100 million sharks a year, through fishing, bycatch and the fin trade. A major 2021 study found oceanic sharks and rays had fallen by about 70% since 1970, and around a third of shark and ray species are now threatened. The east coast grey nurse shark is listed as critically endangered.

sections.key: Sharks keep ocean ecosystems balanced, and you can cut your small risk by swimming at patrolled beaches and avoiding dawn, dusk and murky water.
sections.b:
As predators and scavengers, sharks shape whole ecosystems. When large sharks disappear, effects ripple down the food chain, sometimes letting prey overgraze seagrass or reefs. Tiger sharks are thought to help protect seagrass in Shark Bay, WA, by keeping grazing turtles and dugongs on the move.

Australia uses nets, baited drumlines, drones, tagging and alert apps, and which mix works best is debated, partly because nets also catch turtles, dolphins and harmless sharks. You can lower your own risk: swim at patrolled beaches between the flags, avoid dawn, dusk and murky water, and stay clear of baitfish, birds and people fishing. Rips are the far bigger danger.

quiz.q: Which of these appeared on Earth first?
o: Sharks
Trees
Dinosaurs
Flowering plants
quiz.e: Sharks appeared over 400 million years ago, before trees and long before dinosaurs.

quiz.q: What does the whale shark mainly eat?
o: Seals
Other sharks
Seagrass
Plankton
quiz.e: The world's largest fish is a filter feeder, eating plankton; it visits Ningaloo Reef each year.

quiz.q: Why does a grey nurse shark usually give birth to only two pups?
o: It mates only once in its life
The first embryo in each uterus eats its developing siblings
It lays its eggs in rock crevices
Its pups are born fully grown
quiz.e: Each of the mother's two uteri usually produces just one surviving pup.

quiz.q: Roughly how many sharks do humans kill each year, according to a widely cited estimate?
o: About 1,000
About 100,000
About 10 billion
About 100 million
quiz.e: A 2013 study estimated around 100 million sharks are killed each year, so sharks have far more to fear from us.

quiz.q: How can the loss of large sharks harm an ocean ecosystem?
o: Prey can overgraze seagrass or reef communities
Turtles and dugongs disappear at once
The water becomes too salty for fish
Plankton stops growing
quiz.e: As predators, sharks help keep ecosystems balanced, and losing them can ripple down the food chain.

LESSONS.push: Sharks are older than trees. The real danger runs the other way.

LESSONS.title: Whales: giants of the sea
LESSONS.hook: The largest animal that has ever lived swims in our oceans, and humpbacks pass Australia's coast every winter singing songs that change each year.

sections.key: Whales are mammals that evolved from land animals about 50 million years ago, and their closest living relatives are hippos.
sections.b:
Whales breathe air, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and feed them milk. They evolved from four-legged land mammals roughly 50 million years ago, and fossils such as Pakicetus, a wolf-sized animal from what is now Pakistan, show early stages. Their front limbs became flippers, their back legs shrank to tiny internal bones and their nostrils moved to the top of the head as blowholes. DNA studies show their closest living relatives are hippopotamuses.

Whales, dolphins and porpoises together are called cetaceans, in two groups. Baleen whales, such as blue, humpback and southern right whales, have hundreds of keratin plates (like your fingernails) in the upper jaw to strain krill from water, and two blowholes. Toothed whales, including sperm whales, orcas and dolphins, have one blowhole, hunt individual prey and mostly use echolocation.

sections.key: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived, and the sperm whale has the largest brain of any animal.
sections.b:
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, larger than any dinosaur found so far. It can reach around 30 metres and well over 100 tonnes, and its heart alone can weigh around 180 kilograms. Pygmy blue whales feed in Australian waters, including off Perth and in the Bonney Upwelling off South Australia and Victoria.

The sperm whale has the largest brain of any animal and dives to depths of over a kilometre to hunt squid. Some bowhead whales in the Arctic are thought to live for more than 200 years.

sections.key: Humpbacks migrate each year between Antarctica and warm breeding waters off Queensland and the Kimberley, singing songs that spread between populations.
sections.b:
Humpback whales travel each year between feeding grounds in Antarctic waters and breeding grounds in the tropics, one of the longest mammal migrations. One Australian population travels up the east coast to waters inside and near the Great Barrier Reef; the other heads up the west coast to the Kimberley. The northern migration runs roughly May to August, and the return south, often with calves, from about August to November. 

Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs, mostly on the breeding grounds. All males in a population sing roughly the same song, which slowly changes. Researchers found new songs can sweep east across the South Pacific, from eastern Australia to French Polynesia, within a year or two, a kind of cultural transmission rare outside humans.

sections.key: Commercial whaling nearly wiped out Australian humpbacks, but protection let them recover and they left the threatened list in 2022.
sections.b:
Whaling was one of colonial Australia's earliest export industries, from the early 1800s. By the early 1960s the east coast population had collapsed to perhaps a few hundred animals, and the east coast stations closed in 1962. Australia's last whaling station, at Cheynes Beach near Albany in WA, closed in 1978.

The International Whaling Commission agreed a moratorium on commercial whaling in 1982, effective from 1986. Protected from hunting, the east coast humpbacks now number in the tens of thousands, and in 2022 they were removed from the national threatened list. Other species, such as blue whales, remain far below their pre-whaling numbers.

sections.key: Keep legal distances from whales, and report stranded or entangled whales to authorities instead of trying to free them.
sections.b:
Australia is one of the best places in the world to watch whales, from shore, boats or planes. To protect them, there are legal approach distances. Vessels must generally stay at least 100 metres away, with larger distances for mothers with calves in many states, and swimmers, jet skis and drones have their own limits. Rules vary slightly by state, so check before heading out.

If you see a stranded, injured or entangled whale, do not try to free it yourself. Call your state's wildlife or marine rescue hotline, as entangled whales can be extremely dangerous.

quiz.q: What are the closest living relatives of whales?
o: Seals
Hippopotamuses
Sharks
Elephants
quiz.e: DNA studies show whales' closest living relatives are hippos.

quiz.q: What is notable about the blue whale?
o: It has the largest brain of any animal
It is larger than any dinosaur found so far
It has teeth to hunt squid
It lives for more than 200 years
quiz.e: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived.

quiz.q: What is unusual about humpback whale songs?
o: Only females sing
Every whale sings a completely different song
Songs change over time and spread between populations
They sing only when feeding
quiz.e: Songs evolve and can spread eastward across the South Pacific, a form of cultural transmission.

quiz.q: What helped Australian humpback whales recover?
o: Protection from commercial hunting
Fewer predators in the Southern Ocean
Changes in their migration route
Captive breeding programs
quiz.e: After whaling ended, east coast humpbacks rebounded to tens of thousands.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see an entangled whale?
o: Try to cut it free yourself
Call your state's wildlife or marine rescue hotline
Swim alongside to calm it
Ignore it, as it will free itself
quiz.e: Entangled whales can be extremely dangerous, so leave rescue to trained responders.

LESSONS.push: Humpbacks sing songs that sweep across an ocean and change every year.

LESSONS.title: The Great Barrier Reef
LESSONS.hook: The largest structure built by living things on Earth is made by animals smaller than your fingernail, and it is under more pressure than ever.

sections.key: Corals are colonies of tiny animals that build limestone skeletons, and algae living inside them provide most of their food and colour.
sections.b:
Coral may look like rock or plants, but it is made of animals. Each coral is a colony of thousands of tiny polyps, related to jellyfish and sea anemones. Each polyp has stinging tentacles for catching plankton at night and builds a hard cup of limestone beneath itself. Over generations, colonies grow on the skeletons of those before them, creating reefs large enough to be seen from space.

Reef-building corals have a secret partner: microscopic algae called zooxanthellae that live in their tissues. They photosynthesise and share sugars, supplying most of the coral's energy (often cited as up to about 90%) and much of its colour. In return they get shelter and nutrients. This is why reefs grow in clear, sunlit, shallow water.

sections.key: The reef stretches about 2,300 km, is made of around 3,000 reefs, and has grown for hundreds of thousands of years.
sections.b:
The Great Barrier Reef stretches roughly 2,300 kilometres along the Queensland coast, from the Torres Strait to near Bundaberg, and its marine park covers an area larger than Italy. It is around 3,000 individual reefs and hundreds of islands and cays. It supports over 400 kinds of hard coral, more than 1,500 species of fish, six of the world's seven marine turtle species, dugongs, sharks and thousands of molluscs. Every spring, a few nights after a full moon, many corals spawn at once.

Reefs have grown along this coast for hundreds of thousands of years. The living reef began forming around 8,000 years ago, as rising seas flooded the shelf after the last ice age. More than 70 Traditional Owner groups hold ongoing connections to its sea country.

sections.key: When water stays too warm for too long, corals expel their algae, turn white and may die.
sections.b:
When sea temperatures stay just one or two degrees above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the coral-algae partnership breaks down. The coral expels its algae and turns white, revealing its skeleton through clear tissue. This is bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, and if temperatures fall soon enough they can regain their algae and recover. If heat stress is severe or prolonged, they starve and die.

The reef had mass bleaching in 1998 and 2002, then in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, with 2016 and 2017 killing a large share of shallow-water corals.

sections.key: Climate change is the biggest threat to the reef, alongside poor water quality, crown-of-thorns starfish and cyclones.
sections.b:
Scientists and the reef's managers agree climate change is the greatest threat, through marine heatwaves that cause bleaching and ocean acidification, which makes it harder for corals to build skeletons. Other pressures add up. Runoff from farms and land clearing carries sediment and fertiliser that cloud the water and can fuel outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish, which eat coral. Stronger cyclones smash reefs apart.

Recovery takes years, often a decade or more for slow-growing corals, and the gaps between events have been getting shorter. Parts of the reef have recovered well between events, but that resilience is being tested.

sections.key: The reef has been a marine park since 1975 and World Heritage listed since 1981, and visitors help most by visiting responsibly and backing climate action.
sections.b:
The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park was created in 1975, following public campaigns against oil drilling and mining on the reef. In 1981 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List. In 2004 the park was rezoned so about a third became green zones where fishing and collecting are banned, one of the largest such networks in the world. UNESCO has several times considered listing the reef as 'in danger', which Australian governments have argued against. In 1770, James Cook's Endeavour ran aground on it near present-day Cooktown.

Visiting well helps. Choose eco-certified operators, never touch or stand on coral, follow zoning rules and take all rubbish home. Some sunscreen ingredients can harm coral in lab studies, though their real-world impact is debated and small next to warming. The biggest help is cutting emissions and improving water quality.

quiz.q: What are corals?
o: Plants
Rocks
A type of seaweed
Colonies of tiny animals called polyps
quiz.e: Corals are colonies of polyps, animals related to jellyfish and anemones.

quiz.q: What is the Great Barrier Reef actually made of?
o: One continuous wall of coral
Around 3,000 individual reefs and hundreds of islands
A single huge coral colony
Mostly sand and rock
quiz.e: The reef is a vast system of about 3,000 reefs, stretching roughly 2,300 kilometres.

quiz.q: What happens during coral bleaching?
o: Coral is painted by sunlight
Coral grows faster than normal
Heat-stressed coral expels its algae and turns white
Sand covers the reef
quiz.e: Prolonged heat breaks the coral-algae partnership; corals can recover if temperatures fall in time.

quiz.q: What do experts identify as the biggest threat to the reef?
o: Climate change
Tourist boats
Sharks
Overfishing of turtles
quiz.e: Climate change, through marine heatwaves and acidification, is the greatest threat.

quiz.q: What is the effect of the green zones created in 2004?
o: Fishing and collecting are banned in about a third of the park
They allow free access to every reef
They ban all tourism on the reef
They protect only the islands, not the reef
quiz.e: The rezoning created one of the world's largest networks of no-take areas.

LESSONS.push: The largest structure built by living things is made by animals smaller than a fingernail.

LESSONS.title: Aristotle's rhetoric: ethos, pathos, logos
LESSONS.hook: Every ad you scroll past and every speech that moves you is using tools Aristotle catalogued about 2,300 years ago.

sections.key: Aristotle's Rhetoric was the first systematic study of persuasion, built on three modes of proof: ethos (character), pathos (emotion) and logos (reasoning).
sections.b:
In Athens in the 300s BC, citizens argued their own court cases and voted directly in the assembly, so speaking well was a survival skill. Paid teachers called sophists taught it, and critics like Plato worried they made the weaker argument look stronger. Aristotle took a different approach. In his Rhetoric, he studied persuasion the way a scientist studies animals, defining it as seeing the available means of persuasion in any case.

He named three modes of proof: ethos, pathos and logos. Good persuasion usually combines them. Perfect logic from someone we distrust falls flat, and pure emotion fades once the feeling wears off.

sections.key: Ethos is trust built through wisdom, character and goodwill, while pathos stirs emotion so that people feel the stakes.
sections.b:
Ethos is the speaker's credibility. Aristotle said we trust speakers who show practical wisdom, good character and goodwill towards us. These are perceptions a speaker builds. A tradie mentioning 20 years on the tools, a politician rolling up their sleeves at a flood site, or someone admitting a weakness are all building ethos. It can also be borrowed, which is why companies pay celebrities to endorse products.

Pathos is stirring emotions such as fear, pity, anger or hope, because people judge differently when they feel differently. It becomes a problem only when emotion replaces reasons. Australia's graphic cigarette-pack warnings, required since 2006 and enlarged under 2012 plain packaging laws, make the risk feel real.

sections.key: Logos is persuasion by reasoning, and many everyday arguments are enthymemes that leave a premise unstated.
sections.b:
Logos covers facts, examples, statistics and logical steps. Aristotle noticed that everyday arguments rarely spell out every premise. He called these shortened arguments enthymemes. 'Buy this car, it has a five-star safety rating' leaves out the premise 'you want a safe car', which the audience fills in themselves.

That participation is part of what makes enthymemes persuasive. It also makes them a good place to hide weak assumptions. When you hear a punchy argument, try saying the missing premise out loud and ask whether you actually agree with it.

sections.key: Persuasion works best when it suits the moment (kairos) and the purpose of the speech: deliberative, forensic or epideictic.
sections.b:
Kairos is often added to Aristotle's three. It is a broader Greek idea, linked to earlier teachers such as Gorgias, meaning the right message at the right moment. Home insurance pitches land differently the week after a storm, and a barbecue joke can sink a eulogy. That is why sunscreen ads peak in summer and gym ads flood January.

Aristotle also sorted speeches by purpose. Deliberative speeches argue about the future, such as a budget pitch. Forensic speeches argue about the past, as in court. Epideictic speeches praise or blame in the present: eulogies, toasts and award speeches. Knowing which you are giving helps you choose your tools.

sections.key: Asking who is speaking, what you are made to feel, what is claimed and why now helps you judge a message instead of just reacting to it.
sections.b:
Try this on the next ad or speech you meet. Ethos: who is speaking, and is the credibility earned or borrowed? Pathos: what am I being made to feel, and does the feeling match the facts? Logos: what is the actual claim, what evidence supports it, and what premise is unstated? Kairos: why is this reaching me now?

You will find most effective messages lean on one mode more than the others. The skill cuts both ways. It makes you harder to fool, and it makes you a clearer, fairer speaker yourself.

quiz.q: Why does good persuasion usually combine ethos, pathos and logos?
o: Perfect logic from a distrusted speaker falls flat, and pure emotion fades
Audiences prefer long speeches with many techniques
Each mode only works when the others are absent
Greek law required all three in court
quiz.e: Trust, feeling and reasoning each cover a weakness in the others.

quiz.q: Which qualities make an audience trust a speaker, according to Aristotle?
o: Volume, speed and humour
Wealth, fame and good looks
Practical wisdom, good character and goodwill towards the audience
Facts, figures and charts
quiz.e: Ethos rests on seeming wise, good and on the audience's side.

quiz.q: Why can an enthymeme hide weak assumptions?
o: It always contains false statistics
The audience fills in an unstated premise without checking it
It relies only on emotion
It is too long to follow
quiz.e: Saying the missing premise out loud lets you test whether you agree with it.

quiz.q: A budget pitch at work looks to the future. Which kind of speech is it?
o: Forensic
Epideictic
Ceremonial
Deliberative
quiz.e: Deliberative speeches argue about future choices, so they need costs and benefits.

quiz.q: What is the best use of ethos, pathos and logos when you meet an ad?
o: Ignore the message if it uses emotion
Ask what is claimed, what you are made to feel and why it reaches you now
Trust any speaker who sounds confident
Count how many facts it contains
quiz.e: Naming the modes lets you judge a message instead of just reacting to it.

LESSONS.push: Every ad you scroll past borrows from a toolkit written 2,300 years ago.

LESSONS.title: Why stories persuade
LESSONS.hook: Facts tell, stories sell. There's real psychology behind why a good story can change a mind that statistics couldn't.

sections.key: People remember and pass on information more easily when it comes as a story, because a story gives facts a shape.
sections.b:
Long before writing, people passed on knowledge through stories: where the water was, which plants were dangerous, who could be trusted. Aboriginal Australians have kept oral traditions going for many thousands of years, and some researchers argue certain stories preserve memories of real events such as rising seas.

A story gives information a shape: someone wanted something, something got in the way, and something changed. That shape makes facts easier to remember and repeat. Psychologists note that a list of facts is quickly forgotten, while the same facts inside a narrative tend to stick.

sections.key: When we are absorbed in a story we counter-argue less, so stories can shift attitudes quietly and mislead as easily as they inform.
sections.b:
In 2000, psychologists Melanie Green and Timothy Brock described 'narrative transportation': the feeling of being carried away into a story. People who were more absorbed were more likely to adopt beliefs consistent with the story, and less likely to pick holes in it. Given a list of arguments, we naturally counter-argue. Following a character, we are busy wondering what happens next.

That lowered guard is why a single dramatic anecdote can outweigh solid data. As an audience, ask whether a story is typical or just vivid, and what the numbers say.

sections.key: The identifiable victim effect means people give more to help one named person than to help a statistic.
sections.b:
In a well-known 2007 study, Deborah Small, George Loewenstein and Paul Slovic asked people to donate to a charity. Some read about Rokia, a seven-year-old girl from Mali facing hunger. Others read statistics about millions of people facing food shortages in Africa. The Rokia group gave significantly more. Strikingly, adding the statistics to Rokia's story reduced donations.

This 'identifiable victim effect' explains why charities lead with one person's story. It is also a reminder that our compassion doesn't scale well with numbers, which matters when big problems are at stake.

sections.key: Every classic story structure runs on conflict, and a 2016 analysis of 1,327 novels found six core emotional arcs.
sections.b:
In 1863, German writer Gustav Freytag described a pattern in plays now called Freytag's pyramid: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Screenwriters often simplify it to three acts. The engine in every version is conflict. 'I went to the shop and bought milk' isn't a story; 'the shop was closed and the baby was screaming' starts to become one.

Kurt Vonnegut liked to graph a hero's fortune over time. In 2016, University of Vermont researchers tracked the emotional tone of 1,327 novels and found six core arcs: rags to riches, tragedy, man in a hole, Icarus, Cinderella and Oedipus. Icarus, Oedipus and a double 'man in a hole' were among the most downloaded.

sections.key: In persuasive stories the audience is the hero and you are the guide, and the story should open the door while evidence holds it open.
sections.b:
A common mistake is casting your company as the hero. Audiences care most about their own problems. Marketers reframe the hero's journey so the customer is the hero and the brand is the wise guide, like Obi-Wan Kenobi. A bank ad showing a young couple collecting the keys to their first home follows this pattern.

At work, try situation, complication, resolution: here's where we are, here's what went wrong, here's what to do. A two-minute story about one real customer can win more support than twenty slides of data. Use the story to open the door and the evidence to hold it open.

quiz.q: Why do facts inside a story tend to stick better than a list of facts?
o: Stories are always shorter than lists
A story gives information a shape of want, obstacle and change
People are forced to repeat stories aloud
Lists contain too many numbers
quiz.e: The narrative shape makes facts easier to remember and pass on.

quiz.q: Why can an absorbing story change attitudes quietly?
o: Absorbed listeners counter-argue less
It contains stronger evidence than data
Listeners memorise every detail
It always ends with a call to action
quiz.e: Following a character leaves less mental room for picking holes in the message.

quiz.q: What happened in the Rokia study when statistics were added to her story?
o: Donations rose sharply
Nothing changed
Donations fell
People refused to read it
quiz.e: Numbers dampened the emotional pull of one identifiable person.

quiz.q: What is the engine of every classic story structure?
o: A happy ending
A moral lesson
A talking animal
Conflict, where a character faces obstacles
quiz.e: Without a problem, there is no reason to keep listening.

quiz.q: In a persuasive business story, who should usually be the hero?
o: The CEO
The audience or customer
The company
A competitor
quiz.e: The audience cares most about its own problems, so the brand works best as the guide.

LESSONS.push: A seven-year-old girl raised more than a million people could. Why?

LESSONS.title: What makes a great speech
LESSONS.hook: A two-minute address at a cemetery, a hot August afternoon in Washington, a park in Redfern. Why some speeches outlive the people who gave them.

sections.key: Lincoln's 270-word Gettysburg Address and Churchill's blunt 1940 speeches show that short, honest words can carry great weight.
sections.b:
On 19 November 1863, Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a military cemetery at Gettysburg, months after one of the bloodiest battles of the American Civil War. The main speaker, Edward Everett, talked for about two hours. Lincoln spoke for two minutes, roughly 270 words, reaching back to 1776 and framing the war as a test of whether a nation built on equality could survive.

In May and June 1940, new Prime Minister Winston Churchill offered the Commons 'blood, toil, tears and sweat' and called Dunkirk a colossal military disaster. His repeated 'we shall fight' is anaphora: repeating the opening words of successive phrases to build momentum.

sections.key: King's 1963 'I Have a Dream' speech turned an abstract demand for civil rights into vivid pictures of a fairer future.
sections.b:
On 28 August 1963, around 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Martin Luther King Jr began with a prepared text, using the metaphor of America handing Black citizens a bad cheque marked 'insufficient funds'.

Partway through, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson reportedly called out for him to tell them about the dream. King moved into a passage he had used in earlier sermons. The repeated line 'I have a dream' replaced an abstract demand with concrete pictures of a fairer future, blending biblical cadence with American ideals.

sections.key: Keating's 1992 Redfern speech used 'we' to own the dispossession of Aboriginal people, and Gillard's 2012 speech spread worldwide.
sections.b:
On 10 December 1992, Prime Minister Paul Keating spoke in Redfern Park, Sydney, six months after the High Court's Mabo decision. The speech, largely written by Don Watson, said plainly that non-Indigenous Australians had taken the land, brought the diseases and taken the children from their mothers. Its power came from 'we': rather than blaming a distant past, it asked listeners to imagine these things done to them.

On 9 October 2012, Prime Minister Julia Gillard answered Tony Abbott in a roughly 15-minute speech, largely from notes, refusing to be lectured about sexism and misogyny by him. Opinion in Australia was divided, but the video spread globally, and the Macquarie Dictionary soon broadened its definition of misogyny.

sections.key: Great speeches use repetition, rhythm, contrast and concrete images, and they are written for the ear rather than the eye.
sections.b:
Look across these speeches and patterns appear. Repetition: 'we shall fight', 'I have a dream'. Groups of three, like Lincoln's government 'of the people, by the people, for the people'. Contrast, setting what is against what could be. Concrete images: a bounced cheque, beaches and streets, children taken from their mothers.

Speechwriters also write for the ear: short sentences, strong verbs and deliberate pauses. Many of these devices were catalogued by ancient Greek and Roman teachers of rhetoric, which is why a speech from 1863 and one from 2012 can feel related.

sections.key: A great speech names what the audience already feels at a moment of crisis or change, and you can borrow its lessons: be brief, concrete and honest.
sections.b:
None of these speeches worked in a vacuum. Lincoln spoke amid a war whose purpose people questioned. Churchill spoke when invasion seemed possible. King spoke at the height of the civil rights movement. Keating spoke just after Mabo overturned the legal fiction of terra nullius. Gillard spoke after months of heated debate about her treatment as the first female prime minister. The Greeks called this kairos: the right words at the right moment.

The same lessons work at a wedding, a team meeting or a funeral. Be brief. Build around one memorable line or image. Acknowledge hard truths. Speak to what the room feels. Practise aloud.

quiz.q: Repeating 'we shall fight' at the start of successive phrases is an example of what?
o: Irony
Understatement
Alliteration
Anaphora
quiz.e: Anaphora repeats opening words to build momentum.

quiz.q: What did the repeated 'I have a dream' line achieve?
o: It made the speech more formal
It turned an abstract demand into concrete pictures of a fairer future
It replaced the prepared text entirely
It avoided mentioning civil rights
quiz.e: Repetition plus vivid images made the demand easy to picture and remember.

quiz.q: What made Keating's Redfern speech distinctive?
o: It was delivered in parliament
It announced an election
It used 'we' to take responsibility for dispossession
It was only one minute long
quiz.e: Using 'we' asked listeners to imagine these things done to them.

quiz.q: Which techniques do great speeches commonly share?
o: Using 'we' to take responsibility
It was delivered in parliament
It announced an election
It was only one minute long
quiz.e: Repetition, rhythm, contrast and vivid images make speeches memorable when heard.

quiz.q: What does the Greek idea of kairos say about great speeches?
o: Right words meet a moment of change
Only long speeches matter
The speaker outweighs the audience
Timing is irrelevant to logic
quiz.e: A great speech names what an audience already feels and gives it direction.

LESSONS.push: A two-minute speech outshone a two-hour one. What did it do differently?

LESSONS.title: How to argue well
LESSONS.hook: Most arguments are two people defending their egos. Here's how to have the kind where someone actually learns something.

sections.key: The goal of a good argument is to find out what is true, not to beat the other person.
sections.b:
Many of us treat arguments like sport: points scored, opponents defeated. But if you 'win' while being wrong, you lose the chance to learn. Writer Julia Galef calls the alternative the scout mindset: the aim is to see things as they are, rather than to defend a position like a soldier defending territory.

In practice, this means going in curious. Ask yourself: what would I expect to see if I were wrong? What does this person know that I don't? The best arguments leave both people understanding more.

sections.key: Restate the other side's view in its strongest form, and note agreements and lessons, before you criticise it.
sections.b:
A strawman is a weak caricature that is easy to knock down: 'So you think we should just let criminals go free?' A steelman is the strongest, most charitable form of the argument. It shows the other person you have heard them, and it tests your own view properly. A good check is whether they would say, 'Yes, that's exactly what I think.'

Philosopher Daniel Dennett popularised rules he attributed to game theorist Anatol Rapoport. First, restate their position so fairly they wish they had put it that way. Second, list points of agreement. Third, mention what you learned. Only then criticise. It changes the temperature of a disagreement.

sections.key: Attack ideas rather than people, and remember that the person making a claim carries the burden of proof.
sections.b:
In Getting to Yes (1981), Roger Fisher and William Ury advised separating the people from the problem. 'That plan will blow the budget' targets the idea. 'You always come up with hopeless plans' targets the person, and guarantees defensiveness. Dismissing an argument because of who made it is the ad hominem fallacy. Paul Graham's 'hierarchy of disagreement' puts name-calling at the bottom and refuting the central point at the top.

Confidence, repetition and volume prove nothing. The claimant must support the claim, and not all evidence is equal: an anecdote is weaker than a large study. Ask 'how do you know?' of your own beliefs too.

sections.key: Conceding good points builds credibility, and changing your mind in small steps in response to evidence is a strength.
sections.b:
Many people fear that admitting any point weakens their case. Usually the opposite is true. Saying 'you're right about the cost' shows fairness and makes your other points more credible. People also tend to return concessions, as they return favours. You can give ground on details without abandoning your core view.

Research around 2010 suggested a 'backfire effect', where corrections made people believe more strongly. Later, larger studies found this is rare: most people shift a little when shown good evidence. Philip Tetlock found the most accurate forecasters update in small steps. Think in degrees: 'I'm now 60% sure instead of 90%' is an honest change of mind.

sections.key: Ask questions, check your understanding, find the real point of disagreement and pause when emotions run too high.
sections.b:
Next time a disagreement starts, try a few habits. Ask questions before making statements: 'What makes you think that?' Summarise their view and check you have it right. Look for the specific point where you actually disagree, as it is often narrower than it first seemed. Concede what is fair, and keep your tone about the idea.

Also recognise when emotions are too high for good thinking. 'Let's pick this up tomorrow' is not surrender. Online arguments with strangers rarely change minds; a calm, private conversation with someone who trusts you often does. If neither of you can name evidence that would change your mind, you may be arguing about values, not facts.

quiz.q: What does the 'scout mindset' aim for in an argument?
o: Defending your position as firmly as possible
Seeing things as they are, even if you turn out to be wrong
Finding the quickest way to end the argument
Collecting points against your opponent
quiz.e: A scout wants an accurate map, not a victory.

quiz.q: Why is steelmanning more useful than strawmanning?
o: It makes the other side look foolish
It shortens the argument
It tests your own view against the strongest opposing case
It avoids having to listen
quiz.e: If your position only beats the weak version, it hasn't really won.

quiz.q: Why is 'You always come up with hopeless plans' a poor way to disagree?
o: It attacks the person rather than the idea, which provokes defensiveness
It uses too much evidence
It focuses on the budget
It concedes too much
quiz.e: Keep criticism on the idea, not the person.

quiz.q: What did later research find about the 'backfire effect'?
o: It happens almost every time
It only affects experts
It is rare, and most people shift a little given good evidence
It was proven in every country
quiz.e: Corrections usually work at least somewhat, especially in small steps.

quiz.q: What is a sensible response when an argument gets too heated?
o: Raise your voice to be heard
Pause it, for example 'Let's pick this up tomorrow'
Switch to arguing online
Concede everything
quiz.e: Pausing is not surrender, because emotion crowds out good thinking.

LESSONS.push: Most arguments are won by the wrong person. How do you win the real one?

LESSONS.title: Body language: fact and fiction
LESSONS.hook: Crossed arms mean defensive, looking away means lying, and 93% of communication is non-verbal. Most of that is wrong.

sections.key: The claim that 93% of communication is non-verbal misreads narrow 1960s experiments, and words carry most of the content.
sections.b:
You may have heard that only 7% of communication is words, 38% tone of voice and 55% body language. It comes from experiments by psychologist Albert Mehrabian in 1967. But his studies were narrow: listeners heard single words and judged whether the speaker liked or disliked someone, when words and tone clashed. Mehrabian has said his findings don't apply to communication in general.

If 93% of meaning were non-verbal, you could follow a foreign-language film without subtitles. Body language matters, but words carry most of the content.

sections.key: Body language gives clues, not verdicts: read clusters of signals against a person's baseline, and in context.
sections.b:
Non-verbal signals carry real information. A slumped posture, a tight jaw or a warm smile can hint at how someone feels. But a single signal is ambiguous: crossed arms might mean defensiveness, or that the room is cold. Experts suggest reading clusters of signals and comparing them with the person's normal baseline. A usually chatty colleague going quiet tells you more than a naturally reserved person being quiet.

Some findings are more solid. An open posture, facing the person with relaxed shoulders, is seen as warmer. People who get along often mirror each other, though deliberate copying can backfire if noticed.

sections.key: People detect lies only about 54% of the time, and avoiding eye contact is not a reliable sign of lying.
sections.b:
A 2006 review of over 200 studies by Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo found people correctly identify lies and truths only about 54% of the time, barely better than a coin toss. Police officers do little better. There is no reliable 'Pinocchio's nose'. Nervousness and fidgeting show up in anxious truth-tellers too, and practised liars can appear calm.

A 2006 international survey found 'liars avoid eye contact' was the most common lie-detection belief across dozens of countries. Yet gaze aversion is not a reliable sign of lying, and some liars hold more eye contact. Looking up and to one side revealing a lie, an idea from neuro-linguistic programming, has not held up in tests. Focusing on the content of what someone says, such as consistency and checkable detail, works better.

sections.key: Early claims that 'power poses' change hormones failed to replicate, and any effect on feelings appears small.
sections.b:
In 2010, researchers Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that holding expansive 'power poses' for two minutes raised testosterone, lowered cortisol and increased risk-taking. Cuddy's 2012 TED talk on it became one of the most-watched ever.

But a larger 2015 study failed to find the hormone or behaviour effects, and in 2016 Carney said she no longer believed the effects were real. Researchers still debate whether posture has small effects on how powerful people say they feel. Standing tall won't hurt you, but it is not a proven hormonal hack.

sections.key: Comfortable eye contact varies by person and culture, so treat body language as a prompt to ask, never as proof of honesty.
sections.b:
In many Western settings, moderate eye contact signals attention, while staring feels aggressive. One 2016 study found preferred mutual gaze averaged roughly three seconds, with wide individual differences. In many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, avoiding direct eye contact, particularly with elders, can show respect rather than evasion. Similar norms exist in parts of Asia. Misreading this has caused real harm in classrooms, job interviews and courtrooms.

So treat body language as a question, not an answer. If a friend goes quiet, check in: 'You seem unsure, what's on your mind?' In high-stakes settings like hiring, be wary of confident claims about reading people. For your own presence, put the phone away and give genuine attention.

quiz.q: Why is the claim that 93% of communication is non-verbal misleading?
o: It came from narrow experiments on judging liking from single words
It was proven in every language
It only applies to written messages
Nobody has ever tested it
quiz.e: Mehrabian has said his findings don't apply to communication in general.

quiz.q: What is the best way to read someone's body language?
o: Focus on a single gesture such as crossed arms
Read clusters of signals against their normal baseline and the context
Assume it reveals their true thoughts
Ignore it completely
quiz.e: One signal is ambiguous, but patterns and context give better clues.

quiz.q: Roughly how accurately do people detect lies, according to a large review?
o: About 90%
About 75%
About 20%
About 54%
quiz.e: That is only slightly better than chance.

quiz.q: What happened when researchers tested the hormone effects of power posing?
o: A larger study failed to find them
They were confirmed and doubled
They appeared only in athletes
The effects were found to be permanent
quiz.e: One original author later said she no longer believed the effects were real.

quiz.q: In many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, what can less direct eye contact signal?
o: Dishonesty
Boredom
Respect
Anger
quiz.e: Eye contact norms vary by culture, so it is not a universal measure of honesty.

LESSONS.push: Crossed arms, shifty eyes, a power pose. Which of these tells is real?

LESSONS.title: Renting in Australia
LESSONS.hook: About a third of Australian households rent. Knowing a few rules can save you hundreds of dollars and a lot of stress.

sections.key: Tenancy law is set by each state and territory, so check your local rules and apply with a strong, safe application.
sections.b:
Roughly a third of Australian households rent. There is no single national tenancy law: each state and territory has its own act, agency and rules, updated regularly. Notice periods, bond limits and repair rules differ. Bookmark your local body, such as NSW Fair Trading, Consumer Affairs Victoria, the Residential Tenancies Authority in Queensland, Consumer and Business Services in South Australia or Consumer Protection in Western Australia.

A strong application includes photo ID, proof of income, references and a rental ledger. First-timers can offer character references or a guarantor. Be alert to scams that ask for money before you have inspected, and check your state's rules on bidding above the advertised rent.

sections.key: Your bond is usually capped at about four weeks' rent and held by a government authority, and the condition report is your best protection for getting it back.
sections.b:
A bond is a security deposit covering unpaid rent or damage. It is commonly capped at about four weeks' rent, with exceptions for high-rent properties. In most places the landlord must lodge it with a government body, such as the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority in Victoria. The landlord can't simply keep it: it is returned unless both parties agree otherwise or a tribunal decides.

At the start, you should receive a condition report describing each room. Don't sign it blindly. Note every mark, stain and fault, and return it with comments within the deadline, usually a few days. Take dated photos or video and keep copies. At the end, the property is compared against this report.

sections.key: Tenants are entitled to privacy, limited rent rises and a home meeting minimum standards, and must pay rent and look after the property.
sections.b:
You are entitled to quiet enjoyment, meaning reasonable peace and privacy. Landlords generally must give written notice before entering, and only for set reasons. In most states rent can only rise once every 12 months, with written notice of about two months. Your duties include paying rent on time, keeping the place reasonably clean and reporting damage promptly. Fair wear and tear, like worn carpet from normal use, isn't your cost.

Landlords must keep the property in reasonable repair, and several states set minimum standards, such as being weatherproof, with working locks, lighting, ventilation, a working kitchen and bathroom and bedroom privacy coverings. If repairs stall, don't stop paying rent. Apply to your state's tribunal instead.

sections.key: Give proper written notice, expect a break fee if you leave a fixed term early, and attend the final inspection.
sections.b:
A fixed-term lease runs for a set period, often 6 or 12 months. A periodic lease rolls on with no end date. To leave, you must give written notice, with required periods varying by state.

Leaving a fixed-term lease early usually means paying a break fee or covering rent until a new tenant is found, depending on your state. Landlords must also give proper notice and, in several states, can no longer end leases without a valid reason.

Before you go, clean thoroughly, compare the property with the condition report and attend the final inspection.

sections.key: Free tenant advice services and state tribunals exist to resolve disputes, and good records win them.
sections.b:
Most disputes can be solved by calm, written communication. If that fails, each state has a tribunal that hears tenancy disputes cheaply, such as NCAT in NSW, VCAT in Victoria or QCAT in Queensland. Free advice is available from services like the Tenants' Union of NSW, Tenants Victoria and Tenants Queensland.

Keep every email, receipt and photo. Records win disputes. Tenancy laws change often, so check your state's official website for current rules. This lesson is general information only: for your specific situation, talk to a tenant advice service or a lawyer.

quiz.q: Who sets most tenancy rules in Australia?
o: The federal government
Local councils
Real estate agents
Each state and territory
quiz.e: Each state and territory has its own tenancy law, so check your local rules.

quiz.q: Why is the condition report so important?
o: It records the property's state at move-in, protecting your bond
It sets the weekly rent
It lists your neighbours
It is only needed for pets
quiz.e: Noting every mark with dated photos stops existing damage becoming a bond deduction.

quiz.q: What should you generally do if a landlord won't fix repairs?
o: Stop paying rent
Move out without notice
Apply to your state's tribunal
Fix everything and deduct it from rent
quiz.e: Withholding rent can put you in breach, whereas a tribunal can order repairs.

quiz.q: What does leaving a fixed-term lease early usually involve?
o: Nothing, since notice is optional
Losing the right to any bond
A fine from the tribunal
Paying a break fee or covering rent until a new tenant is found
quiz.e: Give proper written notice and expect costs if you leave before the term ends.

quiz.q: Why should you keep every email, receipt and photo in a tenancy?
o: Records win disputes
Landlords require them yearly
They reduce your rent
Tribunals only accept photos
quiz.e: Good records are your best evidence if a dispute reaches a tribunal.

LESSONS.push: A few renting rules can save you hundreds of dollars. Do you know them?

LESSONS.title: Dinosaurs: rulers of the Mesozoic
LESSONS.hook: They dominated the land for over 150 million years, left giant footprints in outback Queensland, and one branch of the family still visits your backyard.

sections.key: Dinosaurs are a specific group of land reptiles that walked with legs straight under the body, and they lived through the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous until 66 million years ago.
sections.b:
Richard Owen coined 'dinosaur', meaning 'terrible lizard', in 1842. Scientifically, dinosaurs are reptiles that walked with their legs held straight beneath the body, not sprawled to the side like a lizard. That rules out pterosaurs (flying reptiles), marine reptiles such as plesiosaurs and mosasaurs, and the sail-backed Dimetrodon, which was closer to mammal ancestors.

They lived through the Mesozoic Era. The Triassic (252 to 201 million years ago) saw the first small dinosaurs around 230 million years ago. The Jurassic brought giant sauropods and Stegosaurus. The Cretaceous, ending 66 million years ago, gave us Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops. T. rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.

sections.key: Dinosaurs split into lizard-hipped and bird-hipped branches, and real sizes ranged from turkey-sized Velociraptor to sauropods of 30 metres or more.
sections.b:
Since the 1880s, scientists have sorted dinosaurs by hip shape. The lizard-hipped saurischians include meat-eating theropods like Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptor, and huge plant-eating sauropods like Brachiosaurus. The bird-hipped ornithischians were plant-eaters such as Triceratops, Stegosaurus and duck-billed hadrosaurs. Confusingly, birds evolved from the lizard-hipped branch. Some researchers propose redrawing this tree, but museums still use the two-branch system.

T. rex reached about 12 metres and perhaps 8 tonnes. Argentinosaurus may have been 30 metres or more and 60 tonnes, though estimates vary. The real Velociraptor, from Mongolia, was turkey-sized and feathered. More than 1,000 non-bird species have been named.

sections.key: Birds evolved from small feathered theropod dinosaurs, so scientists classify them as living dinosaurs.
sections.b:
In 1861, quarry workers in Germany found Archaeopteryx, a roughly 150-million-year-old animal with feathered wings but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. It hinted at a link between dinosaurs and birds.

Since the 1990s, discoveries in north-eastern China have revealed dozens of feathered dinosaurs, many unable to fly. Birds share wishbones, hollow bones and egg-brooding behaviour with theropods like Velociraptor. Scientists now agree that birds are a branch of the dinosaur family tree. That makes the magpie on your fence, and the emu and cassowary, living dinosaurs.

sections.key: Central-west Queensland holds Australia's richest dinosaur record, and Victorian fossils show dinosaurs once lived inside the polar circle.
sections.b:
Australian fossils are rarer than North America's, but discoveries keep coming. Around Winton, rocks about 95 million years old have yielded the sauropods Diamantinasaurus and Savannasaurus and the predator Australovenator, nicknamed 'Banjo'. In 2021, scientists described Australotitan from near Eromanga, estimated at 25 to 30 metres long. Muttaburrasaurus and the armoured Kunbarrasaurus are Queensland finds too.

At Lark Quarry, more than 3,000 small footprints were long read as a stampede, though some researchers now argue the dinosaurs were wading. In Victoria, Dinosaur Cove yielded Leaellynasaura. About 110 million years ago, Australia was joined to Antarctica, inside the polar circle, so these dinosaurs coped with months of winter darkness.

sections.key: Humans never met non-bird dinosaurs, most dinosaurs were not giants, and they were active animals, not failures.
sections.b:
Popular culture gets a lot wrong. Humans and non-bird dinosaurs never met: the last of them died about 66 million years before our species appeared. Most dinosaurs were not giants; many were dog-sized or smaller. The old image of sluggish, cold-blooded creatures dragging their tails has been replaced by active, fast-growing animals, many with feathers, though their metabolism is still researched.

Nor were they failures. Dinosaurs thrived for more than 150 million years and, through birds, are still here. Next time you visit a museum, look for feathers, posture and scale, and you will see how far the science has moved.

quiz.q: Which of these was a true dinosaur?
o: Pterodactylus, a pterosaur
A plesiosaur
Triceratops
Dimetrodon
quiz.e: Pterosaurs, plesiosaurs and Dimetrodon were prehistoric reptiles or relatives, but not dinosaurs.

quiz.q: What was the real Velociraptor like?
o: Human-sized and scaly
Roughly turkey-sized and feathered
A 12-metre predator
A flying reptile
quiz.e: The Mongolian Velociraptor was small and feathered, unlike its film version.

quiz.q: Why do scientists call birds living dinosaurs?
o: They lay eggs
They have scaly legs
They lived in the Jurassic
They evolved from feathered theropod dinosaurs
quiz.e: Birds are a branch of the theropod dinosaur family tree.

quiz.q: What does the Victorian fossil evidence show about dinosaurs?
o: Dinosaurs coped with months of winter darkness near the South Pole
They lived only in warm swamps
They were absent from Australia
They avoided coastal areas
quiz.e: About 110 million years ago Australia sat inside the polar circle, joined to Antarctica.

quiz.q: Which statement about dinosaurs is true?
