o: Humans lived alongside them
Most were enormous
Most species were sluggish
They thrived for over 150 million years, and birds are still here
quiz.e: Dinosaurs were long-lived and varied, and birds are their living branch.

LESSONS.push: The magpie on your fence belongs to a family that ruled for 150 million years.

LESSONS.title: The day the dinosaurs died
LESSONS.hook: Sixty-six million years ago, a rock about 10 kilometres wide slammed into Mexico. Within a short time, around three-quarters of species on Earth were gone.

sections.key: About 66 million years ago a mass extinction ended the Cretaceous, and a worldwide iridium layer pointed to an asteroid.
sections.b:
Geologists long noticed a sharp line in the rock record at the end of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago. Below it are dinosaurs, ammonites and marine reptiles; above it, they are gone. Around three-quarters of species vanished, including every non-bird dinosaur, the pterosaurs and sea reptiles like mosasaurs. It is the most recent of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions.

In 1980, Luis Alvarez, his son Walter, Frank Asaro and Helen Michel found unusually high iridium in the boundary clay near Gubbio, Italy. It is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. The spike appeared in Denmark, New Zealand and elsewhere, pointing to an asteroid about 10 kilometres wide. Many geologists remained sceptical.

sections.key: The Chicxulub crater, about 180 kilometres wide and buried beneath Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, confirmed the impact.
sections.b:
The missing piece was a crater. In the late 1970s, geophysicists working for Mexico's state oil company had noticed a giant buried ring structure. In 1991, researchers linked it to the extinction. Named after the nearby town of Chicxulub, the crater is about 180 kilometres across, mostly hidden under younger rock and the Gulf of Mexico sea floor. Dating shows it formed right at the boundary.

Evidence piled up: 'shocked' quartz grains that form only under extreme pressure, glassy spherules of melted rock, and jumbled tsunami deposits around the Gulf. In 2016, an expedition drilled into the crater's peak ring.

sections.key: The impact's biggest killer was probably an impact winter, as soot, sulfur and dust blocked sunlight and collapsed food chains, though Indian volcanic eruptions may also have played a role.
sections.b:
The asteroid released far more energy than all the world's nuclear weapons combined. Nearby came huge tsunamis and earthquakes, and falling molten debris likely ignited widespread fires. The biggest killer was probably what followed. The target rocks were rich in sulfur, and the blast lofted sulfur aerosols, soot and dust into the atmosphere. This blocked sunlight, cooled the planet for years and shut down much of photosynthesis. When plants and plankton failed, food chains collapsed from the bottom up.

At the same time, eruptions in India built the Deccan Traps, releasing carbon dioxide and sulfur gases. Their role is contested, though most researchers see the asteroid as the main trigger.

sections.key: Survivors were mostly small animals that could shelter and eat varied food, and their descendants, including mammals, then diversified.
sections.b:
Survival was not random. On land, almost nothing larger than about 25 kilograms is thought to have made it. Small animals needed less food, bred quickly and could shelter in burrows or water. Crocodiles, turtles and frogs fared relatively well, likely because their food webs relied on dead plant matter. Some ground-dwelling birds did better than tree-dwellers because forests were devastated. In the oceans, ammonites vanished, while sharks and many fish survived.

Mammals, mostly small and nocturnal for over 100 million years, spread into empty roles. Within about 10 million years they had produced early horses, primates and whale ancestors. Our existence owes something to a very bad day.

sections.key: Asteroids the size of Chicxulub's strike only about once every 100 million years, and in 2022 NASA's DART mission showed we can nudge an asteroid's orbit.
sections.b:
Asteroids of Chicxulub's size are thought to hit Earth roughly once every 100 million years or so, so the risk in any lifetime is tiny. Astronomers have found the great majority of near-Earth asteroids larger than a kilometre, and none are known to be on a collision course.

Smaller objects are more common: the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor in Russia injured over 1,000 people, mostly from shattered glass. In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into a small asteroid called Dimorphos and shortened its orbit around a larger companion by about 32 minutes. For the first time, a species has shown it can deflect an asteroid.

quiz.q: Why was iridium in the boundary layer such an important clue?
o: It is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids
It only comes from volcanoes
It is found in dinosaur bones
It shows the climate was warm
quiz.e: High iridium found worldwide pointed to an extraterrestrial source.

quiz.q: What supported the Chicxulub crater as the impact site?
o: Its location in western Australia
Shocked quartz, glassy spherules and tsunami deposits dated to the boundary
Its small size
A lack of any rock evidence
quiz.e: The crater formed right at the boundary and carries signs of extreme pressure.

quiz.q: What was probably the biggest killer after the impact?
o: Direct hits from the asteroid
Rising sea levels
Blocked sunlight that collapsed food chains
Disease
quiz.e: Soot, sulfur and dust cooled the planet and shut down photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Which animals tended to survive the extinction?
o: Large plant-eating dinosaurs
Small animals, and freshwater species like crocodiles and turtles
Ammonites
Pterosaurs
quiz.e: Small size, shelter and food webs based on dead matter helped survivors.

quiz.q: What did NASA's 2022 DART mission demonstrate?
o: Asteroids can be seen only with large telescopes
A species can deflect an asteroid's orbit
Chicxulub-size impacts occur every year
Asteroid impacts can never be prevented
quiz.e: DART shortened the orbit of Dimorphos by about 32 minutes.

LESSONS.push: A rock about 10 kilometres wide changed life on Earth. Why did mammals win?

LESSONS.title: Ice Age giants and Australia's megafauna
LESSONS.hook: Rhino-sized wombat relatives, a marsupial 'lion' and a goanna the length of a car once roamed Australia. So where did they all go?

sections.key: Megafauna are large animals, usually over about 45 kilograms, and the Ice Age Northern Hemisphere had woolly mammoths, giant deer and sabre-toothed cats.
sections.b:
Megafauna simply means 'big animals', often defined as over about 45 kilograms. The term usually refers to the giants of the Pleistocene, the epoch of repeated ice ages from about 2.6 million to roughly 11,700 years ago. In the last 50,000 years or so, a large share of them disappeared. Unlike dinosaurs, they lived alongside humans, which makes their fate one of science's most debated questions.

Across Europe, Asia and North America lived woolly mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses and cave bears. The giant deer Megaloceros had antlers spanning up to about 3.5 metres. Sabre-toothed cats such as Smilodon hunted in the Americas. Early humans painted many of these animals at Chauvet and Lascaux in France.

sections.key: Australia's megafauna were giant marsupials, led by rhinoceros-sized Diprotodon and the powerful predator Thylacoleo, plus Megalania, a giant goanna.
sections.b:
Australia's megafauna were dominated by giant marsupials. Diprotodon, a distant relative of wombats, was the largest marsupial ever, roughly rhinoceros-sized and up to about 2.7 tonnes. Dozens of skeletons came from the dry bed of Lake Callabonna in South Australia, where animals likely became trapped in mud. Procoptodon goliah was a short-faced kangaroo about 2 metres tall.

Thylacoleo, the 'marsupial lion', was not a cat but a relative of wombats and koalas. Weighing roughly 100 kilograms or more, it had blade-like cheek teeth, a hooked thumb claw and one of the most powerful bites for its body size. Megalania (Varanus priscus), a giant goanna, may have reached 4 to 7 metres, though estimates vary.

sections.key: Genyornis was a heavy flightless bird more closely related to ducks and geese than emus, and its story shows how carefully evidence must be read.
sections.b:
Genyornis newtoni stood about 2 metres tall and weighed perhaps 200 kilograms or more, far heavier than an emu. Despite appearances, it belonged to an extinct group called dromornithids, or mihirungs, whose closest living relatives are ducks and geese, not emus. Its 'thunder bird' relatives had lived in Australia for millions of years.

Scientists argued over burnt eggshell fragments, around 50,000 years old, that seemed to show early people cooking Genyornis eggs. A 2016 study proposed they came from a giant megapode instead, but a 2022 analysis of ancient proteins in the shells confirmed they belonged to Genyornis. It shows how carefully evidence must be read.

sections.key: Humans, climate change or a combination may have caused megafauna extinctions, and large, slow-breeding animals on islands often vanished soon after people arrived.
sections.b:
Most of Australia's megafauna seem to have gone by roughly 40,000 years ago, after people arrived at least 50,000 years ago. One view blames hunting, even at low levels, tipping slow-breeding giants into decline, plus burning that changed habitats. Another points to a drier, more variable climate. Many researchers now favour a combination, varying by species and place. Dating fossils this old is hard, which keeps the debate alive.

Island cases are clearer. New Zealand's moa, some standing over 2 metres tall, became extinct within roughly 200 years of Polynesian settlement around 1300 AD. Madagascar lost its giant elephant birds after people arrived. Africa, where humans evolved, kept more of its megafauna.

sections.key: Naracoorte Caves and Riversleigh are World Heritage fossil sites, and megafauna remind us that large, slow-breeding animals are vulnerable to rapid change.
sections.b:
You can see Australia's megafauna up close. The Naracoorte Caves in South Australia and the Riversleigh fossil fields in north-west Queensland were jointly World Heritage-listed in 1994 as the Australian Fossil Mammal Sites. At Naracoorte, animals fell through openings into the caves over hundreds of thousands of years, preserving an extraordinary record, and a reconstructed Thylacoleo stands among the fossils. Museums across Australia display Diprotodon skeletons and casts.

There is a lesson for today too. Large, slow-breeding animals are especially vulnerable to rapid change, whether from hunting, habitat loss or a shifting climate.

quiz.q: Why is the fate of Ice Age megafauna so debated, unlike that of the dinosaurs?
o: They lived alongside humans
They survived in Africa only
They were all marsupials
They were too small to leave fossils
quiz.e: Because people were around, humans become a possible cause of their disappearance.

quiz.q: What was Thylacoleo, the 'marsupial lion'?
o: A giant cat from Africa
A relative of wombats and koalas that became a powerful predator
A large flightless bird
A relative of the thylacine
quiz.e: Despite its name it was a marsupial relative of wombats and koalas, with a very powerful bite.

quiz.q: Genyornis's closest living relatives are thought to be which animals?
o: Emus
Cassowaries
Ducks and geese
Eagles
quiz.e: Genyornis was a dromornithid, a group related to ducks and geese rather than emus.

quiz.q: What is the current scientific view on why Australia's megafauna disappeared?
o: Still debated: humans, climate or a combination
Definitely an asteroid impact
Definitely only climate change
Disease brought by dingoes
quiz.e: Many researchers favour a combination of human impacts and climate, and the debate continues.

quiz.q: What lesson do megafauna offer for today?
o: Large animals adapt quickly to any change
Extinctions only happen during ice ages
Large, slow-breeding animals are especially vulnerable to rapid change
Fossils reveal little about living species
quiz.e: Slow breeders cannot recover quickly from hunting, habitat loss or climate shifts.

LESSONS.push: A goanna as long as a car once lived here. Where did the giants go?

LESSONS.title: A tour of the solar system
LESSONS.hook: One star, eight planets, five recognised dwarf planets and countless icy leftovers, all born from a collapsing cloud 4.6 billion years ago.

sections.key: The solar system formed 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud, and the frost line explains why small rocky planets sit inside and giants outside.
sections.b:
About 4.6 billion years ago, part of a giant cloud of gas and dust collapsed under its own gravity. Most of it fell to the centre and became hot and dense enough for nuclear fusion: the Sun. The rest flattened into a spinning disc, where dust stuck into pebbles, then boulders, then planets. That is why the planets orbit in roughly the same plane and direction. The Sun holds about 99.8% of the system's mass.

Close to the young Sun it was too hot for ices, so only rock and metal clumped into small planets. Beyond the frost line, ice was plentiful, so cores grew big enough to pull in huge amounts of gas, forming the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and the ice giants Uranus and Neptune.

sections.key: Venus is the hottest planet, Saturn would float in water, and Jupiter outweighs all the other planets combined.
sections.b:
Mercury is the smallest planet, swinging from about 430°C by day to around minus 180°C at night. Venus is hotter, about 465°C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat. It spins backwards so slowly that its day is longer than its year. Mars has ancient river valleys and Olympus Mons, a volcano about 22 kilometres high, roughly two and a half times the height of Everest.

Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets together, and its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth. Saturn's density is low enough that it would float in a big enough bathtub. Uranus is tipped about 98 degrees, probably from an ancient collision. Neptune has winds around 2,000 km/h.

sections.key: If the Sun were the height of a door, Earth would be a 5-cent coin about 215 metres away, showing the solar system is mostly empty space.
sections.b:
Space diagrams mislead because they can't show true distances. Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun, and sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Shrink the Sun to the height of a front door and Earth becomes a 5-cent coin roughly 215 metres away. Jupiter would be about a kilometre off, and Neptune over 6 kilometres.

Voyager 1, launched in 1977 and the most distant human-made object, is now more than 160 times Earth's distance from the Sun. Canberra's Deep Space Communication Complex is the only station able to command Voyager 2.

sections.key: The asteroid belt and Kuiper Belt hold leftover bodies, and Pluto became a dwarf planet in 2006 because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
sections.b:
Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, whose combined mass is only a few per cent of our Moon's. Jupiter's gravity likely stopped it forming a planet. It is mostly empty space, and spacecraft cross it easily. Beyond Neptune, about 30 to 50 times Earth's distance from the Sun, is the Kuiper Belt of icy bodies, including Pluto. The Oort Cloud is thought to supply long-period comets, though it has never been directly observed.

Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930, and an 11-year-old English schoolgirl, Venetia Burney, suggested its name. After astronomers found Eris in 2005, a definition was needed. In 2006 the IAU ruled a planet must orbit the Sun, be nearly round and have cleared its orbital neighbourhood. Pluto fails the third test. Some scientists still disagree.

sections.key: Five planets are visible to the naked eye: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
sections.b:
You don't need a telescope to start exploring. Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn are all visible to the naked eye. Venus is often the brightest point in the sky after the Moon, appearing as the 'evening star' after sunset or the 'morning star' before dawn.

Planets usually shine steadily while stars twinkle, and they follow roughly the same path as the Sun and Moon. Ordinary binoculars reveal Jupiter's four largest moons, first seen by Galileo in 1610. A free stargazing app will show which planets are up tonight from anywhere in Australia, and dark country skies make the view far better.

quiz.q: Why are the inner planets rocky and the outer ones giants?
o: The outer planets are older
The Sun pushed gas outwards after the planets formed
Beyond the frost line ice was plentiful, so large cores gathered gas
The inner planets lost their rings
quiz.e: Cold outer regions had abundant ice, so cores grew big enough to capture gas.

quiz.q: Which is the hottest planet?
o: Venus
Mercury
Mars
Jupiter
quiz.e: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, reaching about 465°C.

quiz.q: Which of these planets can you see with the naked eye?
o: Uranus
Saturn
Neptune
None without a telescope
quiz.e: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn are all visible without a telescope.

quiz.q: If the Sun were shrunk to the height of a front door, what would Earth be?
o: A basketball on the doorstep
A 5-cent coin about 215 metres away
A grain of sand 20 kilometres away
A tennis ball 10 metres away
quiz.e: Neptune would be over 6 kilometres away; the solar system is mostly empty space.

quiz.q: Why was Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006?
o: It is not round
It doesn't orbit the Sun
It hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood
It was found to be a moon of Neptune
quiz.e: Pluto shares its region of the Kuiper Belt with many other icy bodies.

LESSONS.push: Shrink the Sun to a door and Earth is a coin far down the street.

LESSONS.title: Galaxies and the Milky Way
LESSONS.hook: On a dark night in outback Australia you can see our own galaxy's glowing core overhead, and two other galaxies with the naked eye.

sections.key: The Milky Way is a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across, holding perhaps 100 to 400 billion stars.
sections.b:
The Milky Way is a vast system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity. It is a barred spiral: a central bar of stars inside a flat disc with spiral arms, all wrapped in a faint halo of old stars. It spans roughly 100,000 light-years and holds perhaps 100 to 400 billion stars.

The Sun sits in a minor arm, the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the centre. We orbit at about 800,000 km/h, yet one lap takes around 230 million years. At the centre lies a supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, about 4 million times the Sun's mass. Because we live inside the disc, we see it edge-on, as a milky band. "Galaxy" comes from the Greek for milk.

sections.key: From Australia, the bright galactic core rides high on winter evenings, and two neighbouring galaxies are visible to the naked eye.
sections.b:
Australians have one of the best views of our galaxy. Its brightest part, towards Sagittarius and Scorpius, rides high overhead on winter evenings. Many Aboriginal cultures trace figures in the dark dust lanes, not just the stars. The Emu in the Sky has its head in the dark Coalsack beside the Southern Cross, and its body along the Milky Way. For many groups its position is linked to the emu breeding season, though stories differ between Nations.

Look south on a dark night and you may spot the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, dwarf galaxies about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away. Aboriginal people knew them for thousands of years before Magellan's crew recorded them. For the best view, try a dark site such as Warrumbungle National Park.

sections.key: Galaxies are broadly sorted into spirals, ellipticals, lenticulars and irregulars.
sections.b:
In the 1920s, astronomer Edwin Hubble sorted galaxies by shape, and his scheme is still broadly used.

Spiral galaxies, like ours, have flat discs with arms where new stars form, and many have a central bar. Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of mostly older stars with little gas for new ones; the largest known galaxies are giant ellipticals. Lenticular galaxies sit in between, with a disc but no clear arms. Irregular galaxies have no tidy shape, often because gravity from neighbours has pulled them around.

Collisions between galaxies are common over cosmic time, and they can transform one type into another.

sections.key: The Milky Way grew by swallowing smaller galaxies, and it is on course to meet Andromeda.
sections.b:
Big galaxies grow by merging with smaller ones. The Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, found in 1994, is being stretched into streams of stars by our gravity right now. Data from the Gaia spacecraft showed that a sizeable galaxy, nicknamed the Gaia Sausage, crashed into ours 8 to 11 billion years ago. Many astronomers suspect Omega Centauri, a star cluster easily seen from Australia, is the leftover core of another victim. Even so, stars almost never hit one another, because the gaps between them are so vast.

Our Local Group holds dozens of galaxies. Its largest, Andromeda, is about 2.5 million light-years away and approaching at about 110 km/s. A 2025 study put the odds of a merger in the next several billion years near 50-50. Andromeda is visible to the naked eye from the north of Australia.

sections.key: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter, suggesting invisible dark matter makes up about 85% of all matter.
sections.b:
In the 1970s, astronomer Vera Rubin and colleagues measured how fast stars orbit in spiral galaxies. Stars far from the centre moved just as fast as those closer in, far faster than the visible matter's gravity could hold. Something unseen was adding gravity.

Astronomers call it dark matter. It seems to make up about 85% of all matter in the universe, forming huge halos around galaxies. Nobody yet knows what it is, and a minority of physicists explore modified gravity instead.

Every galaxy you see in the night sky is only the visible part of something much larger. Let your eyes adjust for 20 minutes under a dark sky and look for yourself.

quiz.q: Why do we see the Milky Way as a band across the sky?
o: The Sun sits at its centre, so stars surround us evenly
We live inside its flat disc and look along it edge-on
It is a thin ring of dust circling the Sun
It is a nearby galaxy that we view from outside
quiz.e: We are inside the disc, so looking along it shows a dense band of stars.

quiz.q: What forms the body of the Emu in the Sky seen by many Aboriginal cultures?
o: The faint glow of the Magellanic Clouds
A curved line of bright stars in Scorpius
The Southern Cross and its two pointers
Dark dust lanes along the Milky Way
quiz.e: Many Aboriginal cultures read figures in the dark dust lanes, not only in the stars.

quiz.q: Which type of galaxy is made mostly of older stars, with little gas to form new ones?
o: Elliptical
Spiral
Irregular
Barred spiral
quiz.e: Ellipticals are smooth and gas-poor, so few new stars form in them.

quiz.q: Why do stars almost never collide when two galaxies merge?
o: Gravity pushes stars away from each other
Dark matter shields each star from impact
The gaps between stars are enormous
Stars move too slowly to meet
quiz.e: Stars are so far apart that galaxies can pass through each other with few direct hits.

quiz.q: What did the fast orbits of stars far from galactic centres suggest?
o: Unseen matter is adding extra gravity
Galaxies are much younger than thought
Black holes drive the outer stars
Spiral arms spin faster than the core
quiz.e: Visible matter could not supply enough gravity, pointing to dark matter.

LESSONS.push: Two other galaxies are visible to the naked eye from Australia. Can you find them?

LESSONS.title: Exoplanets: worlds beyond the Sun
LESSONS.hook: Thirty-odd years ago we knew of no planets around other stars like the Sun. Now we know of more than 6,000, and some might be able to hold liquid water.

sections.key: The first exoplanets were confirmed in the 1990s, and more than 6,000 are known today.
sections.b:
An exoplanet is any planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. For centuries people wondered whether they existed, but they were too faint and too close to their bright stars to see.

In 1992 astronomers confirmed planets orbiting a pulsar, the dead core of an exploded star. In 1995 Swiss astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b around a Sun-like star, earning the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. It was a surprise: a giant like Jupiter circling its star every four days.

By 2025 the count of confirmed exoplanets passed 6,000, and it keeps climbing.

sections.key: Planets reveal themselves by dimming their star as they pass in front, or by making it wobble.
sections.b:
Most known exoplanets were found by the transit method. When a planet crosses its star, it blocks a tiny fraction of the light: about 1% for a Jupiter-sized planet, and one part in 10,000 for an Earth-sized one. The dip reveals the planet's size, and the time between dips gives its orbit. Only planets aligned edge-on to us transit, so many more go unseen. Astronomers use statistics to account for them.

The wobble method works because a planet and its star circle a shared centre of mass. The star moves slightly towards us, then away, stretching and squeezing its light by the Doppler effect. This found 51 Pegasi b and hundreds more, and it gives the planet's mass. Combined with a transit, mass reveals density: rocky, watery or gassy.

sections.key: Space telescopes showed that planets are common and can now sample the air of distant worlds.
sections.b:
NASA's Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, stared at one patch of sky containing about 150,000 stars. By 2018 it had found more than 2,600 confirmed planets, and showed that planets are common, likely outnumbering stars in our galaxy. Its successor, TESS, launched in 2018, scans most of the sky for planets around bright, nearby stars that are easier to study.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, can analyse starlight filtering through a planet's atmosphere. In 2022 it clearly detected carbon dioxide on a hot giant called WASP-39b.

Bigger telescopes are coming, including the Giant Magellan Telescope, with Australian partners. Citizen science projects such as Planet Hunters also let volunteers spot transits in real data.

sections.key: Exoplanets include scorching hot Jupiters, planets with two suns, and sizes our solar system lacks.
sections.b:
Exoplanets have overturned expectations. Hot Jupiters are gas giants orbiting so close to their stars that their years last only days. Kepler-16b orbits two stars, so it would have two suns in its sky, like Tatooine in Star Wars.

The most common planets found so far are super-Earths and sub-Neptunes, sizes between Earth and Neptune that our solar system lacks entirely.

The TRAPPIST-1 system, about 40 light-years away, has seven roughly Earth-sized planets, some in the habitable zone. The nearest known exoplanet, Proxima Centauri b, circles the closest star to the Sun, 4.2 light-years away. Even so, at the speed of the Voyager probes it would take over 70,000 years to reach.

sections.key: The habitable zone is where liquid water could exist, but no sign of life beyond Earth has been confirmed.
sections.b:
Life as we know it needs liquid water, so astronomers look in a star's habitable zone: not too hot, not too cold for surface water. Around a dim red dwarf the zone sits very close in; around a bright star, far out. It is a starting point, not a verdict. Venus lies near the Sun's inner edge but is scorching, and Mars near the outer edge is frozen and dry.

To search for life, astronomers study atmospheres for biosignatures, such as oxygen alongside methane, which shouldn't linger together unless replenished. Claims need extreme care. In 2025 a team reported a possible hint of a life-linked sulphur compound on K2-18b, but other scientists found the evidence weak. So far, there is no confirmed evidence of life beyond Earth.

quiz.q: What was surprising about 51 Pegasi b, the first planet found around a Sun-like star?
o: A Jupiter-like giant orbiting in four days
It was an Earth-sized rocky world
It orbited a dead star
It had two suns in its sky
quiz.e: A giant planet so close to its star was unexpected and changed ideas about how planetary systems form.

quiz.q: What does the transit method measure?
o: The planet's mass from its pull on the star
The dip in starlight as a planet crosses
The planet's temperature from its colour
The star's age from its flicker
quiz.e: The dip shows the planet's size, and the gaps between dips show its orbit.

quiz.q: What can the James Webb Space Telescope do that earlier planet hunters could not?
o: Count planets across the whole sky at once
Photograph planet surfaces directly
Analyse starlight passing through a planet's atmosphere
Watch for transits in about 150,000 stars
quiz.e: Webb reads the gases in a planet's air from the starlight that filters through it.

quiz.q: Which kind of planet is most common among those found so far, yet absent from our solar system?
o: Hot Jupiters
Super-Earths and sub-Neptunes
Planets with two suns
Rocky planets smaller than Mars
quiz.e: Planets between Earth and Neptune in size are common elsewhere but missing from our own system.

quiz.q: Why does being in the habitable zone not guarantee life?
o: Only red dwarfs have such zones
Liquid water cannot exist in any zone
The zone moves too quickly to matter
Atmosphere matters: Venus is scorching and Mars is frozen
quiz.e: The zone is only a starting point; a planet's atmosphere decides whether water stays liquid.

LESSONS.push: Thirty years ago we knew of no planets around Sun-like stars. Now we know thousands.

LESSONS.title: The world's religions
LESSONS.hook: Around three in four people on Earth identify with a religion. Knowing the basics of what they believe helps you understand your neighbours, the news and much of history.

sections.key: Most religions share beliefs about ultimate reality, a moral code, rituals and community, but differ on God, the afterlife and how to live.
sections.b:
Religions differ enormously, yet scholars notice common threads. Most offer an account of ultimate reality, whether one God, many gods, or an impersonal truth. Most teach a way to live, with ideas of right and wrong, compassion and duty. Most have rituals such as prayer, festivals and ceremonies for birth, marriage and death, and most build communities. For many adherents, religion is a whole way of life, shaping food, clothing, family and the calendar.

The differences matter just as much. Judaism, Christianity and Islam teach one God and are called Abrahamic. Hinduism includes many deities, which many Hindus see as forms of one reality. Buddhism does not centre on a creator God. Some traditions teach resurrection and judgement, others rebirth. Each has wide internal diversity, so ask individuals what they believe.

sections.key: Christianity (about 2.3 billion) and Islam (about 2 billion) are the largest religions, followed by Hinduism (about 1.2 billion).
sections.b:
Counting believers is difficult, so these figures are rounded estimates, drawn mainly from large Pew Research Center surveys. Around three in four people identify with a religion.

Christianity is the largest, with roughly 2.3 billion people, nearly three in ten. Islam follows with about 2 billion. Hinduism has about 1.2 billion, most in India. Buddhism has several hundred million, depending on how it is counted. Judaism is much smaller, about 15 million, but deeply influential.

Around 1.9 billion people describe themselves as having no religion, many in China, though that group includes people with spiritual beliefs.

sections.key: Sikhism, Jainism, Shinto, Taoism, the Baha'i Faith and many Indigenous traditions also shape billions of lives.
sections.b:
Beyond the five largest, many other traditions matter.

Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab region around 500 years ago, has about 25 to 30 million followers. It teaches devotion to one God, equality and service. Jainism, from India, emphasises non-violence towards all living things. Shinto in Japan honours kami, spirits found in nature and ancestors. Taoism and Confucianism have shaped Chinese culture for over 2,000 years. The Baha'i Faith, founded in the 1800s, teaches the unity of religions.

Countless Indigenous traditions around the world connect spirituality to land and ancestors.

sections.key: Aboriginal spirituality, often called the Dreaming, links ancestral beings, Country, law and kinship, and many people today also practise Christianity.
sections.b:
Aboriginal traditions are among the oldest continuous belief systems on Earth. English speakers often call them the Dreaming, though each language group has its own words, such as Tjukurpa in parts of Central Australia. Ancestral beings shaped the land, animals and laws, and remain present in Country. Stories, songs, dances and art carry this knowledge, sometimes along songlines. Beliefs vary between hundreds of nations, and some knowledge is sacred and restricted, so that protocol deserves respect.

Torres Strait Islander spirituality is tied to the sea, the stars and totemic clan relationships. Christian missions spread from the 1800s, sometimes as part of harmful government policies, and today many people combine faith with traditional beliefs. On 1 July, Torres Strait Islanders mark the Coming of the Light, the arrival of missionaries on Erub (Darnley Island) in 1871.

sections.key: At the 2021 Census about 44% of Australians identified as Christian and about 39% reported no religion, so ask rather than assume.
sections.b:
The Census religion question is optional, but it gives a long-term picture. In 1966, fewer than 1% of Australians reported no religion. By 2021 it was about 39%, up from 30% in 2016. Christianity remained the largest group at about 44%, led by Catholics (about 20%) and Anglicans (about 10%). Islam (about 3%), Hinduism (almost 3%) and Buddhism (over 2%) followed, with Hinduism adding the most followers, largely through migration. The 2026 Census will show whether these trends continue.

A few habits help. Ask rather than assume, because believers practise differently. Use the names communities use for themselves. Wishing a colleague a happy Diwali, Eid or Hanukkah is usually welcome. Curiosity and respect open more doors than debate.

quiz.q: Which statement about religions is accurate?
o: Each tradition is uniform, so one believer speaks for all
They all teach belief in a single creator God
Most offer an account of reality, a way to live, rituals and community
They share no common features
quiz.e: Religions differ widely, yet most combine beliefs, a moral code, rituals and community.

quiz.q: Why are religious population figures given as rounded estimates?
o: Counting believers is difficult and relies on surveys
Governments keep the true numbers secret
Religions refuse to record their members
Most people belong to more than one religion
quiz.e: Belief is hard to measure, so figures come from large surveys and are approximate.

quiz.q: What does Jainism particularly emphasise?
o: Equality and service to others
Non-violence towards all living things
Honouring spirits in nature and ancestors
The unity of all religions
quiz.e: Jainism, from India, is known for non-violence towards every living being.

quiz.q: Why should outsiders respect protocol around some Aboriginal knowledge?
o: All Aboriginal beliefs are identical across Australia
It has never been written or spoken in English
Only churches may share spiritual stories
Some knowledge is sacred and restricted to the right people
quiz.e: Beliefs vary between nations, and some knowledge is shared only with those entitled to it.

quiz.q: What is a good habit when talking about someone's religion?
o: Ask what they believe rather than assume
Assume all followers practise the same way
Avoid learning about their festivals
Debate their beliefs to understand them
quiz.e: Believers within one tradition practise differently, so asking works better than assuming.

LESSONS.push: Three in four people hold a religion. Do you know what your neighbour's festival means?

LESSONS.title: Hinduism
LESSONS.hook: The world's third-largest religion has no single founder, no single holy book and no single creed, yet it has shaped the lives of over a billion people for thousands of years.

sections.key: Hinduism has no single founder and grew over thousands of years into a family of related traditions.
sections.b:
Hinduism is often described as the world's oldest living major religion. It has no single founder or date of origin. It grew over thousands of years in South Asia, drawing on the Vedic culture of northern India, whose earliest hymns date to roughly 1500 to 1200 BCE, and on many local traditions. The word Hindu came from outsiders naming people who lived beyond the Indus River. Many Hindus call their tradition Sanatana Dharma, the eternal way.

It is less a single system than a family of traditions. Some Hindus focus devotion on Vishnu, others on Shiva, others on the Goddess (Devi or Shakti). Practice varies by region, language, caste background and family custom. About 1.2 billion Hindus live today, roughly 95% in India.

sections.key: Hindus see an eternal self (Atman) within each being, and four ideas guide life: dharma, karma, samsara and moksha.
sections.b:
Brahman is the ultimate reality underlying everything. Each living being has an Atman, an eternal self or soul. Hindu schools understand the relationship differently. Advaita Vedanta teaches that Atman and Brahman are ultimately one. Devotional schools see the soul as distinct from God, yet deeply connected through love.

Four ideas are key. Dharma is duty or right living, and it differs by stage of life and role. Karma is action, and Hindus believe actions have consequences shaping this life and future ones. Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth. Moksha is liberation from that cycle, the ultimate goal.

Classical texts also name four aims of life: dharma, artha (prosperity), kama (pleasure and love) and moksha. A full life balances all of them.

sections.key: Hindus honour many deities, often seen as different faces of one divine reality.
sections.b:
Hindu worship includes many deities. Vishnu, the preserver, is believed to descend to Earth in forms called avatars, most famously Rama and Krishna. Shiva is associated with destruction and renewal, meditation and dance. Devi appears in many forms, including Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, Parvati and the warrior goddess Durga. Ganesha, with his elephant head, is the remover of obstacles and is often worshipped before new beginnings.

Many Hindus see these deities as different faces of one divine reality. A family may have a favourite deity at home.

sections.key: Key Hindu texts include the Vedas, Upanishads, Ramayana, Mahabharata and the Bhagavad Gita.
sections.b:
Hinduism has a vast body of sacred writing, much of it in Sanskrit.

The Vedas are the oldest, collections of hymns and ritual knowledge passed down orally for centuries before being written. The Upanishads explore philosophical questions about Brahman and Atman.

Two great epics are beloved across South Asia. The Ramayana tells the story of Prince Rama. The Mahabharata is one of the longest poems ever composed, at around 100,000 verses. Within it sits the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between Krishna and the warrior Arjuna about duty and devotion.

sections.key: Hindus worship through puja at home and in temples, and mark festivals like Diwali; in Australia, Hinduism is among the fastest-growing religions.
sections.b:
Worship, called puja, takes place at a home shrine or temple. It often involves offering flowers, food, light and incense before a sacred image called a murti. Diwali, the festival of lights, usually falls in October or November and celebrates light over darkness and good over evil. Families light oil lamps, share sweets and honour Lakshmi. Holi, in spring, is famous for coloured powder. Navaratri honours the Goddess over nine nights. Pilgrimage to sites like Varanasi on the Ganges is also important.

In Australia, Hinduism rose to almost 3% of the population at the 2021 Census, largely through migration from India, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Fiji. It added more followers than any other religion between 2016 and 2021. At temples, visitors usually remove shoes and dress modestly. If invited to a celebration, accept any sweets offered.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes Hinduism's origins?
o: It was founded by one teacher at a known date
It was founded in Europe and spread to Asia
It grew over millennia with no single founder
It began as a branch of Buddhism
quiz.e: Hinduism grew gradually from Vedic culture and many local traditions, not from a single founder.

quiz.q: What is moksha?
o: The duty that fits your role in life
Liberation from the cycle of rebirth
The consequences of past actions
The eternal self within each being
quiz.e: Moksha is the ultimate goal: freedom from samsara, the cycle of birth, death and rebirth.

quiz.q: How do many Hindus understand their many deities?
o: As rival gods competing for worship
As ancient stories without religious meaning
As different faces of one divine reality
As gods of separate nations
quiz.e: Many Hindus see Vishnu, Shiva, Devi and others as different forms of one reality.

quiz.q: What is the Bhagavad Gita?
o: A collection of the oldest hymns, passed down orally
A dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna about duty and devotion
An epic telling the story of Prince Rama
A philosophical text about Brahman and Atman
quiz.e: The Gita sits inside the Mahabharata and focuses on duty and devotion.

quiz.q: What does Diwali celebrate?
o: The arrival of spring and coloured powder
Nine nights of devotion to the Goddess
The victory of light over darkness and good over evil
A pilgrimage along the Ganges
quiz.e: Diwali, the festival of lights, celebrates light over darkness with lamps and sweets.

LESSONS.push: No founder, no single holy book, and still over a billion followers. How does that work?

LESSONS.title: Judaism
LESSONS.hook: One of the world's oldest monotheistic religions, with only about 15 million adherents, yet its ideas helped shape both Christianity and Islam.

sections.key: Jews believe God made a covenant with Abraham's descendants, and they remember the Exodus from Egypt every year.
sections.b:
Judaism traces its story to Abraham, who according to the Hebrew Bible left Mesopotamia in response to God's call, perhaps around 4,000 years ago by traditional reckoning. Jews believe God made a covenant, a binding agreement, with him: his descendants would be God's people and be faithful to God. It passed to his son Isaac and grandson Jacob, also called Israel, whose twelve sons became ancestors of the twelve tribes. Covenant is central to Jewish life.

The central story of Jewish memory is the Exodus. According to the Torah, the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt until Moses led them to freedom. At Mount Sinai, God gave Moses the Torah, including the Ten Commandments. Historians debate how these events relate to the archaeological record, but Jews have retold the story every year for millennia.

sections.key: Jews believe in one God and follow the commandments of the Torah, valuing study, questioning and ethical action.
sections.b:
Torah means teaching. Narrowly, it is the first five books of the Bible, handwritten on scrolls and read in synagogues. The full Hebrew Bible is the Tanakh: Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). The Talmud, compiled between about 200 and 500 CE, records rabbinic debate and law. Study is itself worship.

Judaism centres on belief in one God. The Shema, recited morning and evening, begins: Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One. Tradition counts 613 commandments, or mitzvot, covering worship, ethics, food (kashrut) and daily life. Judaism stresses ethical action, including justice and charity, more than doctrine about the afterlife.

sections.key: Shabbat is a weekly day of rest from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall, and festivals mark the Jewish year.
sections.b:
Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday, recalling that God rested on the seventh day of creation. It begins with candles and a family meal with blessings over wine and braided challah bread. Observant Jews refrain from work, which traditionally includes cooking, driving and using electrical devices. Others mark the day more simply.

The calendar is lunisolar: lunar months, with a leap month to keep festivals in season. Rosh Hashanah, the new year, begins ten High Holy Days that end with Yom Kippur, a day of fasting and prayer. Passover retells the Exodus at a ritual meal, the Seder. Hanukkah recalls the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the second century BCE. At 13, boys celebrate a Bar Mitzvah, and girls in many communities a Bat Mitzvah at 12 or 13.

sections.key: Jewish history includes exile, diaspora and the Holocaust, and today's branches range from Orthodox to Progressive.
sections.b:
The Babylonians destroyed the First Temple in 586 BCE, and the Romans destroyed the Second in 70 CE. After that most Jews lived in the diaspora, scattered across many lands. Communities developed distinct cultures, such as Ashkenazi in Europe and Sephardi and Mizrahi in the Mediterranean and Middle East.

Persecution recurred over centuries, culminating in the Holocaust, in which about six million Jews were murdered.

Today the main branches include Orthodox, Conservative and Reform, which is called Progressive in Australia. A rabbi, a teacher of Jewish law and tradition, often leads prayer and study. Many Jews are secular but culturally Jewish.

sections.key: About 100,000 Australians are Jewish, a community present since the First Fleet.
sections.b:
Jews have been in Australia since 1788, when a small number of Jewish convicts arrived on the First Fleet. Today about 100,000 Australians identify as Jewish, mostly in Melbourne and Sydney, including many Holocaust survivors and their descendants.

Notable Jewish Australians include General Sir John Monash, a commander in the First World War, and Sir Isaac Isaacs, the first Australian-born Governor-General.

If you are invited to a Shabbat dinner or Seder, bring flowers or kosher wine, and ask your host about customs. Hosts usually welcome curiosity shown with respect.

quiz.q: What does the idea of the covenant mean in Judaism?
o: A binding relationship with mutual duties
A set of food laws
A prayer recited each morning
A pilgrimage to Jerusalem
quiz.e: The covenant is a relationship between God and the Jewish people with duties on both sides.

quiz.q: What does the Shema declare?
o: That the Torah was given at Mount Sinai
That God is one
That the Sabbath is holy
That the Temple will be rebuilt
quiz.e: The Shema, recited morning and evening, affirms that the Lord is One.

quiz.q: Why does the Jewish calendar add a leap month?
o: To make Shabbat fall on Saturday
To lengthen the High Holy Days
To match the Roman calendar
To keep festivals in their seasons
quiz.e: A lunisolar calendar needs an extra month so lunar months stay aligned with the seasons.

quiz.q: What is the term for Jews living scattered across many lands after the Roman destruction of the Second Temple?
o: Exodus
Covenant
Diaspora
Kashrut
quiz.e: After 70 CE most Jews lived in the diaspora and developed distinct cultures there.

quiz.q: How long have Jewish people lived in Australia?
o: Since the gold rushes of the 1850s
Since the First Fleet in 1788
Only since the Second World War
Since Federation in 1901
quiz.e: Jewish convicts arrived on the First Fleet, so the community dates to the colony's beginning.

LESSONS.push: One of the world's smallest major faiths helped shape two of its largest. How?

LESSONS.title: Buddhism
LESSONS.hook: A prince walked away from his palace to understand why people suffer. The path he taught now guides hundreds of millions, and its meditation practices have spread far beyond it.

sections.key: Siddhartha Gautama gave up a life of luxury, found the Middle Way and became the Buddha, the awakened one.
sections.b:
Buddhism began with Siddhartha Gautama, born into a ruling family at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal. His dates are debated, but many scholars place his life in the fifth century BCE. According to tradition, he grew up sheltered in luxury until he saw four sights: an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering holy man. Shaken by ageing, sickness and death, he left his palace, his wife and his young son at about 29 to seek a way beyond suffering.

For several years he practised extreme self-denial, fasting until close to death, but found no understanding. He concluded the answer lay in a Middle Way between indulgence and harsh asceticism. Buddhists believe that, meditating under a tree at Bodh Gaya, he attained enlightenment and became the Buddha, the awakened one. He taught for about 45 years.

sections.key: Life involves suffering caused by craving; suffering can end, and the Eightfold Path is the way.
sections.b:
The Buddha's first teaching, given at Sarnath, set out the Four Noble Truths. First, life involves dukkha, often translated as suffering but also meaning dissatisfaction or unease. Second, dukkha arises from craving and attachment: wanting things to be other than they are. Third, suffering can end; this ending is nirvana. Fourth, a path leads to it. Buddhists often compare this to a doctor's approach: identify the illness, find its cause, confirm there is a cure, and prescribe the treatment.

The Noble Eightfold Path groups into three areas. Wisdom: right view and right intention. Ethical conduct: right speech, action and livelihood. Mental discipline: right effort, mindfulness and concentration. "Right" means wise or skilful, not rule-bound. Like strands of a rope, the strands work together.

sections.key: Buddhists teach impermanence, non-self, karma and rebirth, and many do not centre their practice on a creator God.
sections.b:
Several ideas run through Buddhist teaching. Anicca, impermanence, holds that everything changes. Anatta, non-self, teaches that there is no fixed, unchanging self, only a flow of experiences. Karma means that intentional actions shape future experience, and rebirth occurs in a cycle called samsara, which ends with nirvana.

Buddhism does not centre on a creator God, though many Buddhists honour buddhas, bodhisattvas and other beings. Buddhists take refuge in the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dharma (his teaching) and the Sangha (the community). Many lay Buddhists also follow five precepts: avoiding killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech and intoxicants.

sections.key: Buddhism has three main traditions, and meditation is central to many of them.
sections.b:
Buddhism spread across Asia in three broad traditions. Theravada, the way of the elders, is found mainly in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, and draws on scriptures in Pali. Mahayana, the great vehicle, spread through China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam and emphasises the bodhisattva, who seeks enlightenment for all beings. Zen and Pure Land are Mahayana schools. Vajrayana, found in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia, uses ritual, chanting and visualisation; the Dalai Lama is its best-known figure.

Meditation is central to many forms, though not every Buddhist meditates regularly. Samatha steadies the mind, often by focusing on the breath. Vipassana observes thoughts and sensations to see their impermanence. Since the 1970s, secular mindfulness programs inspired partly by Buddhism have spread into hospitals, schools and workplaces.

sections.key: About 2.4% of Australians identified as Buddhist at the 2021 Census, and temples welcome respectful visitors.
sections.b:
About 2.4% of Australians identified as Buddhist at the 2021 Census, many with roots in Vietnam, China, Sri Lanka, Thailand and other Asian countries, along with many Australian-born converts.

Nan Tien Temple near Wollongong is one of the largest Buddhist temples in the Southern Hemisphere and welcomes visitors. At any temple, remove your shoes, dress modestly, avoid pointing your feet at Buddha images, and ask before taking photos.

Many temples offer free introductory meditation classes, a good way to learn from practitioners directly.

quiz.q: Why did Siddhartha abandon extreme self-denial?
o: He wished to return to palace life
It did not bring understanding, so he chose a Middle Way
Other teachers forbade fasting
He had already reached nirvana
quiz.e: Neither indulgence nor harsh asceticism brought insight, so he taught a path between them.

quiz.q: What does the Second Noble Truth say causes dukkha?
o: Ignorance of the scriptures
Lack of wealth
Craving and attachment
The wrath of the gods
quiz.e: Dukkha arises from craving: wanting things to be other than they are.

quiz.q: What does the idea of anatta, or non-self, teach?
o: The soul passes unchanged between lives
The self is only an illusion of the body
Everything changes constantly
There is no fixed, unchanging self, only a flow of experiences
quiz.e: Anatta says what we call the self is a changing stream of experiences.

quiz.q: What is the aim of vipassana meditation?
o: To observe thoughts and sensations and see their impermanence
To steady the mind by focusing on the breath
To chant the Buddha's name
To visualise deities
quiz.e: Vipassana, or insight practice, looks at experience to understand how it changes.

quiz.q: What is a respectful way to behave when visiting a Buddhist temple?
o: Wear shoes and take photos freely
Point your feet at the Buddha image
Remove shoes, dress modestly
Skip the introductory classes
quiz.e: Shoes off, modest dress and asking before photos show respect for the space.

LESSONS.push: A prince left a palace to ask one question. Its answer still guides millions.

LESSONS.title: Christianity
LESSONS.hook: The world's largest religion began with a Jewish teacher in a small Roman province. Two thousand years later, it shapes the calendar, laws and holidays of countries like Australia.

sections.key: Jesus was a Jewish teacher in Roman-ruled Judea who taught love of God and neighbour; Christians believe he rose from the dead.
sections.b:
Christianity centres on Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher in Galilee and Judea, then under Roman rule. He was probably born around 4 BCE and was crucified in Jerusalem around 30 CE under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. Most historians agree he existed, taught, gathered followers and was crucified. Christians believe more: that he is the Son of God and the Messiah, and rose from the dead three days later. "Christ" comes from the Greek for anointed one, translating the Hebrew Messiah.

According to the Gospels, Jesus taught that people should love God with all their heart and their neighbour as themselves. He taught through parables, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son. The Sermon on the Mount includes the Beatitudes and the Lord's Prayer. He welcomed outsiders and healed the sick.

sections.key: Most Christians believe in one God as a Trinity, that Jesus is God made human, and that salvation comes through him.
sections.b:
The Bible has two main parts. The Old Testament largely matches the Hebrew Bible. The New Testament has 27 books written in Greek, including four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, letters (many by Paul) and Revelation. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include some additional Old Testament books. It has been translated into more languages than any other book.

Most Christians believe in one God who exists as a Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. They believe God became human in Jesus, the incarnation, and that through his death and resurrection people can be reconciled with God and receive eternal life, called salvation. Many churches summarise their beliefs in the Nicene Creed, agreed in 325 CE. Most practise baptism and Holy Communion, sharing bread and wine in memory of Jesus.

sections.key: Christianity grew from a persecuted minority into a world faith, and split into Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant branches.
sections.b:
After Jesus's death, apostles such as Peter and Paul spread the message across the Roman Empire. Early Christians were a small, sometimes persecuted minority. Emperor Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE, and in 380 it became the empire's official religion. Armenia (around 301) and the Ethiopian kingdom of Aksum (330s) had already adopted it. Today most Christians live outside Europe, with large growing numbers in Africa and Latin America.

In 1054, tensions between Rome and Constantinople separated the Catholic Church, led by the Pope, from the Eastern Orthodox churches. In 1517, Martin Luther's criticisms helped spark the Protestant Reformation, producing Lutheran, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist and many other churches. Catholics, with over a billion members, are about half of all Christians.

sections.key: Christmas celebrates Jesus's birth, while Easter, the most important Christian festival, celebrates his resurrection.
sections.b:
Christmas, on 25 December, celebrates the birth of Jesus. Many Orthodox Christians celebrate on 7 January because they follow the older Julian calendar.

For Christians, Easter is the most important festival. It is preceded by Lent, a season of about 40 days of reflection and often fasting. Holy Week includes Good Friday, remembering Jesus's crucifixion, and ends with Easter Sunday, celebrating his resurrection.

Easter's date moves each year, falling on a Sunday between late March and late April, based on the spring full moon in the northern hemisphere.

sections.key: About 44% of Australians identified as Christian in 2021, with Catholics the largest group at about 20%.
sections.b:
Christianity arrived with the First Fleet in 1788, whose chaplain, Richard Johnson, was Anglican. Irish convict and settler families made Catholicism a major force. In the 2021 Census Catholics were the largest group at about 20%, followed by Anglicans at about 10%. Overall, about 44% of Australians identified as Christian, down from much higher levels in earlier decades.

The Uniting Church formed in 1977 from Methodist, Congregational and most Presbyterian churches. Mary MacKillop, canonised in 2010, is Australia's first saint. Church-run schools, hospitals and charities remain significant.

quiz.q: What do most historians agree about Jesus?
o: He was born in Rome
He rose from the dead
He existed, taught and was crucified
He wrote the Gospels
quiz.e: Historians agree on his life and crucifixion; belief in the resurrection is a matter of Christian faith.

quiz.q: What does the Trinity mean to most Christians?
o: Three separate gods
One God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit
Three stages in Jesus's life
Three parts of the Bible
quiz.e: The Trinity is the belief in one God who exists as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

quiz.q: What began the Protestant Reformation in 1517?
o: The fall of the Roman Empire
A dispute over the date of Easter
The split between Rome and Constantinople
Criticisms of church practices, led by Martin Luther
quiz.e: Luther's criticisms led to Lutheran, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist and other Protestant churches.

quiz.q: Why does the date of Easter change each year?
o: It is based on the spring full moon
It follows the birthday of Jesus
It is set by each country's government
It falls 40 days after Christmas
quiz.e: Easter falls on a Sunday set by the spring full moon, so it moves between late March and late April.

quiz.q: Which Christian group was the largest in Australia at the 2021 Census?
o: Anglicans
The Uniting Church
Orthodox Christians
Catholics
quiz.e: Catholics, at about 20%, edged out Anglicans at about 10% as Australia's largest Christian group.

LESSONS.push: It began with one teacher in a Roman province. Why does it still set our calendar?

LESSONS.title: Islam
LESSONS.hook: About one in four people on Earth is Muslim. The largest Muslim nation is not in the Middle East, and Muslims first reached Australia's shores long before the cameleers.

sections.key: Islam means submission to the one God, and Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad.
sections.b:
The Arabic word Islam means submission to the will of God. Allah is simply the Arabic word for God. The central belief is tawhid, the oneness of God. Muslims believe God sent many prophets, including Adam, Abraham (Ibrahim), Moses (Musa) and Jesus (Isa), and that Muhammad was the last.

Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE and became a respected merchant. Muslims believe that around 610 he received the first revelation through the angel Jibril (Gabriel). After opposition in Mecca, he and his followers moved to Medina in 622, a journey called the Hijra that starts the Islamic calendar. He died in 632.

The Qur'an, revealed over about 23 years, has 114 chapters, called surahs. The Arabic original is the true Qur'an; translations are interpretations. Many Muslims memorise it all, earning the title hafiz.

sections.key: The Five Pillars are the declaration of faith, prayer, charity, fasting in Ramadan and pilgrimage to Mecca.
sections.b:
Muslim practice rests on five pillars. Shahada is the declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Salat is prayer five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca. Zakat is giving to those in need, commonly 2.5% of savings above a set threshold each year. Sawm is fasting from dawn to sunset in Ramadan. Hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca, which every adult Muslim who is able should make at least once.

Ramadan is the ninth month of the lunar calendar. The lunar year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan moves earlier each year. Children, the sick, travellers and pregnant women may be exempt. Each evening the fast is broken with a shared meal, iftar. Eid al-Fitr, a joyful festival, ends the month.

sections.key: Most Muslims are Sunni, about a fifth are Arab, and Indonesia has the largest Muslim population.
sections.b:
After Muhammad's death, his followers disagreed over who should lead. Those who became Sunni accepted Abu Bakr, a close companion, as the first caliph. Those who became Shia believed leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants. Shia Muslims mourn the death of Ali's son Husayn at Karbala in 680 each year at Ashura. Today about 85 to 90% of Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 15% Shia, the majority in Iran and Iraq. Sufism, a mystical tradition, is found within both.

Only about one in five Muslims is Arab. Indonesia has the largest Muslim population of any country, followed by Pakistan, India and Bangladesh.

sections.key: During the Islamic Golden Age, scholars advanced algebra, optics, medicine and astronomy.
sections.b:
From about the eighth to the thirteenth centuries, scholars in the Islamic world made major advances. In Baghdad, the House of Wisdom gathered and translated Greek, Persian and Indian works.

Al-Khwarizmi wrote a founding text on algebra, a word that comes from Arabic, and his name gave us "algorithm". Ibn al-Haytham used experiments to study light and vision. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was taught in European universities for centuries.

The numerals we use today, first developed in India, reached Europe largely through Arabic texts, and many stars still carry Arabic names.

sections.key: Muslims have been connected with Australia since Makassan trepangers and the cameleers, and about 3% of Australians were Muslim in 2021.
sections.b:
Contact with Australia is old. From at least the 1700s, Makassan sailors from Sulawesi, many of them Muslim, visited northern Australia to harvest trepang, or sea cucumber, trading with the Yolngu of Arnhem Land.

From the 1860s, cameleers, known as Afghans though many came from British India, opened up the outback and built some of Australia's first mosques. The Ghan train is named after them.

At the 2021 Census, about 3% of Australians were Muslim.

quiz.q: What does the word Islam mean?
o: Peace between nations
Submission to the will of God
The final revelation
Pilgrimage to Mecca
quiz.e: Islam means submission to God's will, and a Muslim is one who submits.

quiz.q: Why does Ramadan fall earlier each year?
o: The fast shortens each year
It is moved to match the seasons
The lunar year is about 11 days shorter
Hajj dates shift it
quiz.e: The Islamic calendar follows the moon, so Ramadan drifts about 11 days earlier annually.

quiz.q: Which statement about Muslims around the world is accurate?
o: Most Muslims are Arab
Most Muslims are Shia
Iran has the largest Muslim population
Only about one in five Muslims is Arab
quiz.e: Muslim communities span the globe, with Indonesia the largest, and Arabs are a minority.

quiz.q: How did Arabic scholarship influence the modern world?
o: It carried our numerals to Europe
It invented writing
It built the first universities in Greece
It replaced Latin in science
quiz.e: Indian-developed numerals reached Europe largely through Arabic texts, alongside advances in algebra, optics and medicine.

quiz.q: Who were the Makassan visitors to northern Australia?
o: Cameleers who opened the outback
Sulawesi sailors who harvested trepang
Pearl divers from Japan
Gold rush miners from China
quiz.e: Makassan trepangers, many of them Muslim, visited northern Australia from at least the 1700s.

LESSONS.push: Muslims visited Australia long before the cameleers. Who came first, and why?

LESSONS.title: How rockets work
LESSONS.hook: A rocket doesn't push against the air. It throws mass out the back so fast that the rest of it has no choice but to go forward.

sections.key: Rockets work by Newton's third law: they throw gas backwards, so the rocket goes forwards, even in a vacuum.
sections.b:
Every rocket relies on Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Burning propellant makes hot gas at enormous pressure, and the nozzle forces it out the back at several kilometres per second. Pushing that mass backwards pushes the rocket forwards. A garden hose kicks in your hand, and a balloon zips around the room, for the same reason.

A common myth is that rockets push against the air, so they couldn't work in space. They work slightly better in a vacuum, because no air pressure resists the exhaust. What they do need is oxygen to burn their fuel, so they carry their own oxidiser. Common pairings are refined kerosene with liquid oxygen, and liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. Solid boosters mix fuel and oxidiser into a rubbery solid.

sections.key: A rocket is mostly propellant, so it drops empty tanks in stages to avoid carrying dead weight.
sections.b:
Getting to space is so demanding that a rocket is mostly a flying fuel tank. Typically 85 to 90% of a large rocket's lift-off mass is propellant, and the payload is often only a few per cent. A Falcon 9 weighs about 550 tonnes at lift-off but carries at most around 23 tonnes to low orbit, roughly 4%. Every extra kilogram of fuel also has to be lifted, which needs yet more fuel.

Carrying empty tanks wastes energy, so most rockets are built in stages. The large first stage does the heavy lifting through the thick lower atmosphere, then shuts down and falls away. A smaller second stage pushes a much lighter vehicle onwards, and some rockets add a third. Staging is the practical answer to the harsh arithmetic of the rocket equation.

sections.key: Staying in low orbit means travelling sideways at about 7.8 km/s, roughly 28,000 km/h.
sections.b:
Reaching space is surprisingly easy: the commonly used boundary, the Kármán line, is only about 100 kilometres up. Staying there is the hard part.

An object in orbit is constantly falling towards Earth, but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. In low Earth orbit that takes about 7.8 kilometres per second, roughly 28,000 km/h.

That is why rockets lean over soon after launch and spend most of their effort gaining sideways speed rather than height. Launching eastwards also borrows a boost from Earth's own rotation.

sections.key: Rocket theory and flight date back to Tsiolkovsky and Goddard, and reusable boosters have since cut launch costs.
sections.b:
The Chinese used gunpowder rockets in war by the 1200s. Around 1903 the Russian schoolteacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published the equation linking a rocket's speed to its exhaust speed and fuel load. In 1926 American physicist Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket in Massachusetts; it flew for about two and a half seconds. Germany's V-2 of World War II, the first large guided ballistic missile, later helped both the US and Soviet space programs.

For most of the space age, rockets were thrown away after one use, like building a new airliner for every flight. The Space Shuttle (1981 to 2011) was partly reusable but slow and costly to refurbish. In December 2015 SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 first stage upright, and it now routinely reflies boosters, some more than 30 times.

sections.key: Woomera in South Australia launched WRESAT, Australia's first satellite, in 1967.
sections.b:
Australia has a real place in rocket history. From 1947 the vast Woomera range in outback South Australia was used by Britain and Australia to test missiles and research rockets.

In November 1967 WRESAT, Australia's first satellite, was launched from Woomera on a modified American rocket, putting Australia among the first few nations with a satellite in orbit.

The Australian Space Agency was set up in 2018, and several Australian companies are developing launch vehicles and satellites. Across the Tasman, Rocket Lab launches small satellites from New Zealand's Mahia Peninsula. Next time you see a launch, you'll know it's Newton doing the work.

quiz.q: Why can a rocket work in the vacuum of space?
o: It pushes against faint traces of air
It pushes gas backwards and gets pushed forwards in reply
It uses Earth's gravity to pull it upward
It floats on the solar wind
quiz.e: Thrust comes from throwing exhaust backwards, so no air is needed to push against.

quiz.q: Why do most rockets drop stages as they climb?
o: To reduce noise during launch
To signal the crew that they are in orbit
To shed empty tanks and dead weight
To cool the engines
quiz.e: Dropping dead weight lets the remaining engines accelerate a much lighter vehicle.

quiz.q: Why is staying in orbit harder than reaching space?
o: There is too little oxygen up there
The Kármán line moves higher over time
Gravity switches off above 100 km
You must travel sideways at about 7.8 km/s
quiz.e: Orbit means falling around Earth, which needs enormous sideways speed, not just height.

quiz.q: What has reusable boosters changed about spaceflight?
o: Launches have become cheaper
Rockets no longer need fuel
Orbit speeds are slower
Stages are no longer needed
quiz.e: Landing and reflying boosters avoids discarding an expensive rocket after every flight.

quiz.q: What was WRESAT?
o: A British missile test range
A rocket engine built at Woomera
Australia's first satellite, launched in 1967
The Australian Space Agency's headquarters
quiz.e: WRESAT launched from Woomera in 1967 and made Australia one of the first nations with a satellite.

LESSONS.push: A rocket doesn't push against the air. So what does it push against?

LESSONS.title: The Space Race
LESSONS.hook: In 1957 a metal ball the size of a beach ball started beeping overhead, and two superpowers began racing to the Moon.

sections.key: The Space Race grew from Cold War rivalry and missile technology, starting with Sputnik 1 in 1957.
sections.b:
After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rivals in the Cold War, a long standoff that stopped short of direct war. Space became a stage for that contest. Each side wanted to prove its system produced better science, and the stakes were military as well as symbolic: a rocket that could orbit a satellite could also carry a nuclear warhead across the world.

On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite. It was a polished metal sphere about 58 centimetres across, weighing roughly 84 kilograms. It simply transmitted a beeping radio signal, audible about every 96 minutes. The launch shocked Americans, who had assumed they were ahead. A month later Sputnik 2 carried a dog named Laika, the first animal to orbit Earth; she did not survive.

sections.key: The Soviets claimed early firsts, including Gagarin as the first human in space in 1961.
sections.b:
The Soviets kept claiming the headlines. Luna 2 reached the Moon's surface in 1959. On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin, a 27-year-old air force pilot, became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1. He orbited Earth once in about 108 minutes, then ejected during descent and parachuted down, as designed. His cry of "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!") became famous. He died in a jet training crash in 1968, aged 34.

In June 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, spending almost three days in orbit. On 18 March 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk from Voskhod 2. His suit ballooned so much that he had to let air out to squeeze back inside.

sections.key: The US launched Explorer 1 and created NASA in 1958, then sent astronauts to orbit.
sections.b:
The US answered quickly. On 31 January 1958 it launched Explorer 1, whose instruments detected the Van Allen radiation belts, bands of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field. Later that year the government created NASA to run a civilian space program. Sputnik also prompted major new US spending on science and maths education.

Alan Shepard became the first American in space on 5 May 1961, on a 15-minute suborbital hop. In February 1962 John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth, circling it three times. As his capsule passed over Western Australia, the people of Perth switched on their lights, earning it the nickname "City of Light".

sections.key: In 1961 President Kennedy committed the US to landing on the Moon before the decade ended, and Gemini practised the skills needed.
sections.b:
Stung by Gagarin's flight, President John F. Kennedy told Congress in May 1961 that America should land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the decade was out. In 1962 in Texas he added: "We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard." The goal gave the race a clear finish line. At its peak, Apollo employed roughly 400,000 people across government and industry.

Astronauts first had to master untried skills. The US Gemini program, flying two-person crews in 1965 and 1966, practised spacewalks, flights of up to two weeks, and the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit. Meanwhile the Soviet program lost its brilliant chief designer, Sergei Korolev, who died in 1966.

sections.key: The US won the Moon race in 1969, and by 1975 the rivals were shaking hands in orbit.
sections.b:
The race had real costs. In January 1967 a fire during a ground test of Apollo 1 killed three astronauts, and months later cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died when the parachute of Soyuz 1 failed. The Soviets' giant N1 Moon rocket failed all four of its launch attempts.

In July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, effectively settling the race. By 1975 the mood had shifted. In the Apollo-Soyuz mission, American and Soviet crews docked and shook hands in orbit. That spirit later grew into the International Space Station.

quiz.q: Why did Sputnik alarm Americans beyond its beeping signal?
o: It carried a nuclear weapon
Satellite rockets could also carry warheads
It could be seen from every city
It had been launched without warning
quiz.e: Space technology grew out of missile programs, so a satellite launch signalled military capability.

quiz.q: What did Gagarin's 1961 flight on Vostok 1 achieve?
o: The first spacewalk
The first Moon landing
The first woman in orbit
The first human in space
quiz.e: Gagarin orbited Earth once, becoming the first person in space.

quiz.q: What did Explorer 1 detect?
o: The Van Allen radiation belts
Water on the Moon
Sputnik's radio signal
The solar wind
quiz.e: Explorer 1's instruments found bands of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field.

quiz.q: What did the Gemini program practise for the Moon missions?
o: Landing on the Moon
Designing the N1 rocket
Spacewalks, long flights and docking
Launching satellites
quiz.e: Gemini tested the skills Apollo would need, including the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit.

quiz.q: What did the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz mission show?
o: That the Soviets had won the race
That the Moon landing had failed
That Apollo 1 was safe
That rivals could cooperate in orbit
quiz.e: After the race, rivals docked and shook hands in orbit, a spirit that led to the International Space Station.

LESSONS.push: A beeping metal ball in 1957 launched a race. How did it end in a handshake?

LESSONS.title: Apollo and the Moon landing
LESSONS.hook: In July 1969 about 600 million people watched two men walk on the Moon, and those pictures reached the world through a dish in a sheep paddock in New South Wales.

sections.key: Apollo 11 put Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon on 20 July 1969 (US time) using a small lander, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit.
sections.b:
Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July 1969 with Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. NASA used a plan called lunar orbit rendezvous. Collins stayed in orbit in the command module, Columbia, while a light, spidery lander called Eagle carried the other two down to the Sea of Tranquillity. That was 20 July in US time and 21 July in Australia.

The landing was tense. Computer alarms flashed, and Armstrong steered past a boulder field by hand, with less than a minute of fuel to spare by some estimates. Hours later he said, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' Aldrin followed about 20 minutes later. The pair walked for roughly two and a half hours.

sections.key: The Saturn V rocket made Apollo possible, and six missions landed 12 men on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.
sections.b:
Getting there took the Saturn V, a three-stage rocket about 110 metres tall. Its five first-stage engines burned roughly 13 tonnes of propellant every second. It flew 13 times between 1967 and 1973 and never lost a crew. Only the small command module came home; Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July.

Apollo 12 landed in November 1969, beside an older robotic probe. Apollo 13 never landed: an oxygen tank exploded, and the crew survived by using the lunar module as a lifeboat. The last three landings carried a battery-powered buggy, the Lunar Roving Vehicle. In all, six missions landed and 12 men walked on the Moon. Apollo 17 left in December 1972, and no one has been back since.

sections.key: Australian stations, including the Parkes radio telescope, brought the Moonwalk pictures to the world.
sections.b:
Because Earth was turning, the Moon was above Australia when Armstrong stepped out, so Australian stations did vital work. The first TV images came through the Honeysuckle Creek tracking station near Canberra. Minutes later, the CSIRO's 64-metre radio telescope at Parkes, in central-west New South Wales, took over and supplied the clearer pictures for most of the moonwalk.
