Strong gusts of wind buffeted the dish, beyond its normal safe limits, but staff kept it tracking. The story inspired the 2000 Australian film The Dish.

sections.key: Apollo's rocks, instruments and reflectors still serve science, and the evidence that the landings happened is overwhelming.
sections.b:
The six landings brought back about 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, still studied by scientists around the world, including in Australia. In 2022 scientists opened an Apollo 17 sample that had stayed vacuum-sealed since 1972. Seismometers showed the Moon has moonquakes. When Apollo 12 crashed its discarded lander stage into the surface, the Moon rang for nearly an hour, like a bell, because the dry, cold rock barely dampens vibrations.

Conspiracy theories say the landings were faked. Yet around 400,000 people worked on Apollo, and the Soviet Union, which tracked the missions and had every reason to expose a hoax, never disputed them. The laser mirrors left behind still work, and NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed the landing sites, even the astronauts' footpaths.

sections.key: Artemis is taking humans back towards the Moon, aiming for the south pole, where ice could supply water, oxygen and rocket fuel.
sections.b:
After five decades, humans are going back. NASA's Artemis programme is named after Apollo's twin sister in Greek mythology. Artemis I flew uncrewed around the Moon in late 2022. In April 2026, Artemis II sent four astronauts, including a Canadian, around the Moon and back without landing.

Later missions aim to land astronauts near the lunar south pole. Permanently shadowed craters there may hold water ice that could supply drinking water, oxygen and even rocket fuel. China has also announced plans to land astronauts by 2030.

When you look at the Moon, you're looking at a place humans have walked.

quiz.q: What was the 'lunar orbit rendezvous' plan used for Apollo 11?
o: The whole spacecraft landed and lifted off together
One astronaut stayed in orbit while a light lander took two down
Two spacecraft joined together on the Moon's surface
A robot landed first and prepared the site for the crew
quiz.e: Using a small lander for the descent meant only a light craft had to land and lift off again.

quiz.q: How did the Apollo 13 crew survive after an oxygen tank exploded?
o: They landed on the Moon and waited for rescue
They turned back using only the damaged command module
They used the lunar module as a lifeboat
They docked with another spacecraft in orbit
quiz.e: Apollo 13 never landed; the crew improvised, using the lunar module as a lifeboat on the way home.

quiz.q: Why were Australian stations vital to the Moonwalk broadcast?
o: Earth's rotation put the Moon above Australia at that moment
Australia built the cameras the astronauts used
The Moon can only be tracked from the southern hemisphere
Australian engineers designed the lunar module
quiz.e: As Earth turned, the Moon was over Australia, so Honeysuckle Creek and Parkes caught the TV signal.

quiz.q: Why is the Soviet Union's silence strong evidence that the landings were real?
o: It had no way of tracking the missions
It had agreed to keep the missions secret
It was not interested in the space race
It tracked the missions and had every reason to expose a hoax
quiz.e: A rival that watched Apollo closely would have exposed any fake, but it never disputed the landings.

quiz.q: Why are future missions aiming for the Moon's south pole?
o: Permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice
The ground there is flatter than anywhere else
It is always in sunlight
It is the closest point to Earth
quiz.e: Water ice could supply drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel for future crews.

LESSONS.push: A dish in a sheep paddock showed the world the Moon. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: The International Space Station
LESSONS.hook: Right now, about 400 kilometres above you, people are eating, sleeping and doing experiments while circling Earth every hour and a half.

sections.key: The ISS orbits about 400 km up at 28,000 km/h and has been continuously crewed since November 2000.
sections.b:
The International Space Station is a large, crewed laboratory about 400 kilometres up, roughly the distance from Perth to Albany, but straight up. It travels at about 28,000 km/h and circles Earth every 90 minutes, so the crew sees about 16 sunrises and sunsets a day.

The first module launched in November 1998, and people have lived aboard continuously since 2 November 2000. A whole generation has grown up without a day when humans weren't living in space. You can see the station yourself, shortly after dusk or before dawn: a bright, steady point of light gliding across the sky, without flashing like a plane. NASA's free Spot the Station service tells you when.

sections.key: Five space agencies built the ISS in orbit, piece by piece, over more than a decade.
sections.b:
The station was too big to launch in one go. Over more than a decade, US Space Shuttles and Russian rockets carried up the pieces, and astronauts bolted them together during hundreds of hours of spacewalks. The finished structure is about 109 metres across, roughly a football field, and weighs around 420,000 kilograms. Huge solar arrays supply its electricity. It is often described as the most expensive object ever built, at well over US$100 billion.

Five agencies run it: NASA, Roscosmos, the European Space Agency, Japan's JAXA and the Canadian Space Agency. Russia provides key modules and propulsion, Japan built the Kibo laboratory, Europe the Columbus lab and Canada the robotic arm, Canadarm2. Astronauts from more than 20 countries have visited, including Adelaide-born Andy Thomas.

sections.key: Astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth, not because gravity is missing.
sections.b:
At the station's height, Earth's gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are in continuous free fall, falling around Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it. Scientists call this microgravity. Water forms wobbling spheres, flames burn as round blue balls and dropped tools drift away.

A typical crew is about seven people. They sleep in small cabins, zipped into sleeping bags fixed to the wall. Water is precious: the station recycles moisture from air, washing and even urine, and in 2023 NASA reported about 98% water recovery. Food comes in pouches, with tortillas popular because they don't make crumbs. Toilets use airflow instead of gravity. The Cupola, a seven-windowed dome, is made for photographing Earth.

sections.key: Long spaceflight changes eyes, blood and genes, but NASA's Twins Study found most changes faded within months.
sections.b:
Weaker bones and muscles are only the start. Many astronauts on long missions develop swelling at the back of the eye and a slight flattening of the eyeball, a condition NASA calls spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome, and some need stronger glasses afterwards. Blood volume drops in orbit, so returning crew can feel faint when they first stand up. Radiation doses are far higher than on the ground.

In NASA's Twins Study, astronaut Scott Kelly spent almost a year on the station while his identical twin, Mark, stayed on Earth. Researchers found changes in Scott's gene activity, gut bacteria and immune system, most of which returned to normal within months. Findings like these help plan trips to Mars.

sections.key: The ISS is mainly a laboratory where microgravity reveals what gravity hides, and it is due to retire around 2030.
sections.b:
Thousands of experiments have run aboard. Microgravity lets scientists study things that gravity masks on Earth. Protein crystals can grow larger and more orderly, helping researchers understand molecules targeted by medicines. Flames, fluids and new materials behave differently, which improves models used on the ground. Crews have grown lettuce, chillies and flowers, and ate lettuce grown on the station in 2015. The Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, a particle detector on the outside, searches cosmic rays for clues about dark matter.

The ageing ISS is due to retire around 2030 and be steered into a remote part of the Pacific Ocean. Commercial stations are being developed, and China already operates its own, Tiangong.

quiz.q: Why does the ISS crew see about 16 sunrises and sunsets a day?
o: The station is far brighter than Earth's surface
Earth spins much faster at that height
The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes
The Sun rises more often in space
quiz.e: At 28,000 km/h the station completes an orbit roughly every 90 minutes, passing through day and night each time.

quiz.q: How was the ISS built?
o: In orbit, over more than a decade, from pieces carried up by shuttles and rockets
On Earth as one unit, then launched in a single flight
By robots alone, without astronauts
On the Moon, then moved into orbit
quiz.e: It was too big to launch whole, so astronauts assembled it in space during many spacewalks.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts on the ISS float?
o: Gravity is almost zero at that height
The station's engines push them upward
Air inside the station is very thin
They and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth
quiz.e: Gravity is still about 90% as strong; free fall around the planet creates the floating effect.

quiz.q: What did NASA's Twins Study find about Scott Kelly's year in space?
o: His body changed permanently
Many changes in gene activity, gut bacteria and immunity returned to normal within months
His identical twin on Earth changed more
Nothing about his body changed at all
quiz.e: Space changes the body in many ways, but most of the changes in the Twins Study faded after his return.

quiz.q: Why run experiments in microgravity?
o: Rockets can only carry small experiments
Experiments are cheaper in space than on Earth
It shows effects that gravity masks on Earth, such as larger, more orderly protein crystals
Space has no radiation to interfere
quiz.e: Without gravity masking them, crystals, flames and fluids behave differently, giving scientists new insights.

LESSONS.push: It circles Earth every 90 minutes, and you can watch it pass overhead.

LESSONS.title: Telescopes: our eyes on the universe
LESSONS.hook: In 1610 a hand-made tube of lenses showed Galileo moons circling Jupiter. Today a mirror a million and a half kilometres away sees galaxies born soon after the Big Bang.

sections.key: Galileo's telescope showed Jupiter's moons and the Moon's craters, supporting the idea that planets orbit the Sun.
sections.b: The telescope was invented in the Netherlands around 1608, and within a year the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei had built his own, eventually reaching about 20 times magnification. Pointing it at the sky, he found mountains and craters on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way, and in January 1610 four moons orbiting Jupiter. He later saw that Venus shows phases like the Moon. These observations challenged the old belief that everything circled Earth and supported the idea that the planets orbit the Sun.

sections.key: A telescope's power comes from its light-collecting area, and astronomers fight Earth's blurring air with high sites and adaptive optics.
sections.b:
The key feature of a telescope isn't magnification but light-collecting area. A bigger lens or mirror gathers more light, revealing fainter objects and finer detail. Large lenses sag and blur colours, so in 1668 Isaac Newton built a reflecting telescope with a curved mirror. Almost every big research telescope today is a reflector, with mirrors of 8 to 10 metres and 25 to 40 metres under construction.

Earth's atmosphere is a nuisance. Moving air makes stars twinkle and blurs detail, and water vapour blocks some wavelengths. So major observatories sit on high, dry sites like Mauna Kea in Hawaii and Chile's Atacama Desert. Siding Spring Observatory near Coonabarabran, New South Wales, hosts the 3.9-metre Anglo-Australian Telescope. Adaptive optics, deformable mirrors that change shape hundreds of times a second, cancel out the blur.

sections.key: Hubble and Webb work above Earth's atmosphere, measuring the universe's age and seeing its earliest galaxies.
sections.b:
The Hubble Space Telescope launched in April 1990 aboard Space Shuttle Discovery and orbits about 540 kilometres up, above the blurring air. Its 2.4-metre mirror was ground slightly the wrong shape, so early images were fuzzy, until astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993. Its Deep Field images revealed thousands of galaxies in tiny patches of sky, and its measurements helped pin the universe's age at about 13.8 billion years and show that its expansion is accelerating.

The James Webb Space Telescope launched on 25 December 2021. Its 6.5-metre mirror, made of 18 gold-coated hexagonal segments, unfolded in space. Webb observes mainly in infrared, which passes through dust and reveals very distant galaxies whose light has been stretched by the universe's expansion. It orbits about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, shaded by a tennis-court-sized sunshield that keeps it extremely cold.

sections.key: Radio telescopes reveal what visible light can't, and Australia leads the field from Parkes to the Square Kilometre Array.
sections.b:
Visible light is only a small slice of what the universe sends us. In the 1930s the engineer Karl Jansky discovered radio waves coming from the Milky Way, launching radio astronomy. The CSIRO's 64-metre Parkes dish, opened in 1961 and also known as Murriyang in Wiradjuri, helped pinpoint the first identified quasar, has discovered a large share of known pulsars, and revealed the first fast radio burst, a mysterious millisecond flash.

The Square Kilometre Array will be the world's largest radio telescope, split between two sites with very little radio interference. SKA-Low is being built in Western Australia's Murchison region, on the traditional lands of the Wajarri Yamaji people, with around 131,000 antennas shaped like small metal Christmas trees. SKA-Mid, with about 200 dishes, is in South Africa's Karoo. Scientists hope it will study the first stars and galaxies and test theories of gravity.

sections.key: You can follow in Galileo's footsteps with binoculars, dark skies and 20 minutes of patience.
sections.b:
You don't need expensive gear to follow in Galileo's footsteps. A decent pair of binoculars shows craters on the Moon, Jupiter's four largest moons as tiny points, and star clusters like the Jewel Box in the Southern Cross. Get away from city lights and give your eyes 20 minutes to adjust to the dark. Free apps can identify what you're seeing.

Australia's southern skies are superb, and the Magellanic Clouds, two neighbouring galaxies, are visible to the naked eye. Many public observatories and astronomy clubs run affordable viewing nights.

quiz.q: What did Galileo's observations of Jupiter's moons and Venus's phases challenge?
o: The idea that the Moon has craters
The old belief that everything circled Earth
The idea that stars are far away
The belief that the Milky Way is a cloud
quiz.e: Moons circling Jupiter and Venus showing phases supported the idea that planets orbit the Sun.

quiz.q: Why do major observatories sit on high, dry mountains?
o: Mountains are closer to the Moon
The ground there is magnetic
They get less atmospheric blurring and water vapour
Cities ban telescopes at low altitude
quiz.e: Less, drier air above the telescope means a sharper view of the sky.

quiz.q: Why does the James Webb Space Telescope observe mainly in infrared?
o: Infrared light is brighter than visible light
Infrared passes through dust and shows distant galaxies whose light has been stretched
Its mirror cannot reflect visible light
Infrared is easier to focus
quiz.e: Expansion stretches distant light into longer wavelengths, which Webb is built to catch.

quiz.q: Why is SKA-Low being built in Western Australia's Murchison region?
o: The site has very little radio interference
It is close to major cities
It already had a large telescope
The ground there is very flat and wet
quiz.e: Radio telescopes pick up faint signals, so they need quiet, remote locations.

quiz.q: What can ordinary binoculars show you of Jupiter?
o: Its rings and surface storms in fine detail
Nothing, because Jupiter is too faint
Its surface craters
Its four largest moons as tiny points
quiz.e: Binoculars are enough to see the same four moons Galileo spotted in 1610.

LESSONS.push: A mirror 1.5 million kilometres away is reading light older than Earth.

LESSONS.title: Mars: the red frontier
LESSONS.hook: Mars once had rivers and lakes. Today it's a freezing desert patrolled by robots, and the most likely next destination for human footprints.

sections.key: Mars is about half Earth's width with 38% of its gravity, a day almost like ours, and a rusty red surface.
sections.b: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and about half Earth's diameter. Its surface gravity is about 38% of ours, so a 70-kilogram person would feel like they weighed about 27 kilograms. A Martian day, called a sol, lasts about 24 hours and 40 minutes, remarkably close to our own, but a Martian year takes 687 Earth days. Its red colour comes from iron oxide, essentially rust, in its dust and rocks. It has two small, lumpy moons, Phobos and Deimos, which may be captured asteroids.

sections.key: Mars has thin, cold air and no magnetic shield, yet it holds the largest known volcano and a canyon nearly as long as Australia is wide.
sections.b:
Mars is harsh. Its air pressure is less than 1% of Earth's, and it is mostly carbon dioxide, too thin to breathe or to keep liquid water stable for long. The average temperature is around −60°C, though a summer afternoon near the equator can briefly rise above 0°C. With no global magnetic field, harmful radiation reaches the ground. Dust storms are common, and some grow to cover almost the whole planet.

Olympus Mons, the largest known volcano, is about 22 kilometres high, two and a half times Mount Everest. Valles Marineris stretches about 4,000 kilometres, nearly as long as Australia is wide, and plunges up to 7 kilometres deep. Lower gravity and no moving tectonic plates let volcanoes grow for ages over the same hot spots.

sections.key: Robots have studied Mars since the 1960s, and Curiosity and Perseverance have shown it once held a lake and river delta.
sections.b:
Many early Mars missions failed. Mariner 4 sent back the first close-up photos in 1965, showing a cratered surface. The Viking landers tested soil for life in 1976, with results most scientists read as inconclusive. In 2004 the rovers Spirit and Opportunity were planned to last about 90 sols; Opportunity worked for more than 14 years and drove over 45 kilometres before a dust storm ended it in 2018.

Curiosity, car-sized and nuclear-powered, landed in Gale Crater in 2012 using a rocket-powered 'sky crane'. It confirmed the crater once held a lake that could have supported microbes. Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, an ancient river delta, in 2021 and has collected rock samples in sealed tubes, but NASA's Mars Sample Return programme lost its funding in early 2026, so no mission is approved to bring them home. Its helicopter Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet.

sections.key: Mars once had flowing water, but today most of it is frozen at the poles and underground.
sections.b:
Orbiters and rovers have found dried riverbeds, ancient deltas, lakebed sediments and minerals that only form in water, strong evidence that liquid water flowed on Mars billions of years ago. The planet may have had a thicker atmosphere then, before much of it was stripped into space.

Today, most of its water is frozen. The polar caps contain water ice topped seasonally by carbon dioxide frost, and ice lies buried beneath large areas of the surface. In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander scraped up and confirmed water ice. Whether small amounts of liquid water exist today is still debated.

sections.key: A human trip to Mars is limited by launch windows, radiation and distance, so planners want to make fuel and oxygen on site.
sections.b:
Earth and Mars line up favourably about every 26 months, so launch windows are limited. A trip takes around six to nine months each way, and crews would likely wait a year or more for the planets to realign, making a round mission two to three years. Radio messages take 3 to 22 minutes each way, so real-time help from Earth isn't possible. The biggest challenges include radiation, landing heavy loads in thin air, toxic perchlorate salts in the soil and the strain of isolation.

Carrying everything from Earth would be impossibly expensive, so planners want to 'live off the land'. Perseverance's toaster-sized MOXIE experiment made oxygen from Martian carbon dioxide. Buried ice could provide water and, combined with carbon dioxide, methane rocket fuel. Timelines have repeatedly slipped, and most experts expect a first landing to be at least a decade away.

quiz.q: Why is Mars red?
o: Its dust and rocks contain iron oxide, or rust
Its atmosphere glows red in sunlight
Its oceans dried up and left red salt
It is very close to the Sun
quiz.e: Iron oxide in Martian dust and rock gives the planet its rusty colour.

quiz.q: Why could Martian volcanoes grow so large?
o: Mars has stronger gravity than Earth
Lower gravity and no moving plates let them grow over the same hot spots
The atmosphere there is very thick
The Sun heats the surface more strongly
quiz.e: With no moving tectonic plates, a volcano can keep building over one hot spot for ages.

quiz.q: What did the Curiosity rover confirm about Gale Crater?
o: It is still full of liquid water
It was formed by an asteroid strike only recently
It once held a lake that could have supported microbes
It contains proof of past animal life
quiz.e: Curiosity found that ancient Mars had conditions that could have supported microbes.

quiz.q: Where is most of Mars's water today?
o: Flowing in rivers across the equator
Frozen in polar caps and buried ice
Spread through the air as thick clouds
In large open lakes
quiz.e: Mars once had flowing water, but today it is mostly ice.

quiz.q: What does 'living off the land' mean for Mars missions?
o: Growing all crew food from Earth seeds
Landing near cities built by robots
Making water, oxygen and fuel from Martian resources
Sending crews home each season
quiz.e: Using local carbon dioxide and ice would cut the huge cost of hauling supplies from Earth.

LESSONS.push: A day on Mars is almost the same length as ours. A year is not.

LESSONS.title: How computers actually work
LESSONS.hook: Every photo, message and game on your devices comes down to billions of tiny switches flicking on and off, billions of times a second.

sections.key: Every computer is built from billions of tiny on/off switches, now transistors made from silicon.
sections.b:
Strip away the screen and software, and a computer stores and changes patterns of on and off. Each tiny switch is a 1 (on) or a 0 (off). One switch can't do much, but billions, wired together and flipped in sequence, can add numbers, draw pictures and play music.

Early computers used bulky vacuum tubes. ENIAC, finished in 1945, used about 17,000 and weighed around 27 tonnes. Australia's first computer, CSIRAC, built in Sydney in 1949 and now held by Melbourne Museum, was one of the earliest stored-program computers. In 1947 Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley at Bell Labs built the first transistor: a tiny solid-state switch, far smaller, cooler and more reliable than a tube. Today's are made from silicon, found in ordinary sand, which gave Silicon Valley its name.

sections.key: Transistors wired into logic gates make simple decisions, and combining gates builds every calculation a computer performs.
sections.b:
A handful of transistors wired together makes a logic gate, a circuit that takes on/off inputs and produces an output by a fixed rule. An AND gate outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1. An OR gate outputs 1 if either input is 1. A NOT gate flips its input.

The maths behind this was worked out by the English mathematician George Boole in the 1850s, long before electronics existed. Combine enough gates and you can build a circuit that adds two numbers, then one that multiplies, compares and remembers. Every calculation your device performs is built from these tiny decisions.

sections.key: The CPU repeats a simple fetch, decode and execute loop billions of times a second, and shrinking transistors made it faster.
sections.b:
The central processing unit, or CPU, carries out instructions in a relentless loop: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode it, execute it, repeat. Each is tiny, like 'add these two numbers'. The trick is speed. A 3 gigahertz CPU ticks through about 3 billion cycles a second, and modern chips have several cores working side by side.

In 1965 Gordon Moore, later a co-founder of Intel, noticed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling at a steady rate, later revised to about every two years. Moore's law isn't a law of physics, but it held for decades and drove computers from room-sized machines to pocket devices. Top chips now hold tens of billions of transistors. Progress is slowing as parts approach atomic scales, so engineers also gain speed through smarter designs and specialised chips.

sections.key: RAM is fast, temporary workspace that empties when power is lost; storage is the larger, slower, permanent filing cabinet.
sections.b:
The CPU keeps what it's working on right now in random-access memory, or RAM. Think of it as a workbench: fast to reach, but limited in size and cleared at the end of the day. RAM is volatile, losing everything when power is cut, which is why unsaved work disappears in a blackout. When you open an app, it's copied into RAM. If RAM fills up, the computer shuffles data back and forth and everything slows down.

Storage is the long-term filing cabinet. Older computers used hard disk drives, which store data magnetically on spinning platters. Most modern laptops and all smartphones use solid-state drives (SSDs), which use flash memory chips with no moving parts, so they are faster, quieter and tougher. Storage is far larger than RAM but slower. When people say a phone has '256 gigabytes', they mean its storage.

sections.key: Knowing the parts helps you choose upgrades: RAM for sluggishness, storage for space, and a restart to clear clutter.
sections.b:
If a computer feels sluggish with many tabs open, more RAM often helps more than a faster CPU. If you keep running out of room for photos, you need more storage, or a cloud backup. An SSD is one of the best upgrades for an older computer still running a hard drive.

Restarting a device genuinely helps, because it clears RAM of clutter from programs that didn't tidy up after themselves.

Most of all, remember that behind every 'smart' device is a very fast, very obedient machine following simple instructions written by people.

quiz.q: Why did transistors replace vacuum tubes?
o: They were louder and easier to repair
They were much smaller, cooler and more reliable
They used glowing filaments to store data
They could only be made in Australia
quiz.e: A solid-state switch controlled by electricity itself needs no filament and is smaller, cooler and more reliable.

quiz.q: What does an AND logic gate output?
o: 1 if either input is 1
The opposite of its input
0 whenever the inputs differ
1 only if both inputs are 1
quiz.e: Logic gates apply fixed rules to on/off inputs, and combining them builds every calculation.

quiz.q: What does a CPU do in its constant loop?
o: Fetches, decodes and executes instructions
Stores files and deletes old data
Draws the screen and plays sound only
Waits for the user to type
quiz.e: Programs feel clever because millions of simple steps happen faster than you can blink.

quiz.q: Why does unsaved work disappear in a blackout?
o: Storage drives wipe themselves
The CPU runs out of instructions
RAM is volatile and loses its contents without power
Apps cannot run offline
quiz.e: RAM only holds data while powered; saving writes it to permanent storage.

quiz.q: A computer is sluggish with many tabs open. Which upgrade most likely helps?
o: A larger screen
More RAM
A faster internet plan only
More storage for photos
quiz.e: Open tabs fill RAM; when it runs out, the computer shuffles data around and slows down.

LESSONS.push: Tens of billions of switches sit in your pocket. Here's how they add up.

LESSONS.title: Binary: the language of computers
LESSONS.hook: With just two digits, 0 and 1, computers store every word you've typed, every song you've streamed and every photo you've taken.

sections.key: Computers use binary because telling on from off is reliable, and binary counting works like decimal with only two digits.
sections.b:
We count in base ten, probably because we have ten fingers. Computers count in base two, using only 0 and 1. The reason is practical: transistors are switches, and it's easy and reliable to tell 'on' from 'off', but hard to tell ten voltage levels apart amid electrical noise. Gottfried Leibniz described binary arithmetic in 1703, centuries before electronic computers.

In decimal, each column is worth ten times the one to its right. In binary, each is worth twice: ones, twos, fours, eights. So 1011 means one eight, no fours, one two and one one: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Counting goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101. The logic is identical to decimal, just with fewer digits. Hence the old joke: there are 10 kinds of people, those who understand binary and those who don't.

sections.key: Computers store letters as numbers: a bit is one binary digit, a byte is eight bits, and codes like ASCII and Unicode map numbers to characters.
sections.b:
A single binary digit is a bit. One bit can only say yes or no. Eight bits make a byte, which can represent 256 values, from 00000000 to 11111111, or 0 to 255.

Computers don't store letters, they store numbers that stand for letters. In the 1960s, the ASCII standard assigned numbers to 128 characters: capital A is 65, which is 01000001 in binary, lowercase a is 97, and a space is 32. ASCII only covered English, so Unicode was created to include the world's writing systems. It now defines more than 150,000 characters, from Chinese and Arabic to emoji. When you text a smiley face, you're sending a code number that your friend's phone looks up and draws. A garbled message appears when two systems disagree about the code.

sections.key: Photos and sound become numbers too: pixels store red, green and blue values, and sound is measured thousands of times a second.
sections.b:
A digital photo is a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels. Each pixel's colour is stored as three numbers, for red, green and blue light, each from 0 to 255. That is one byte per colour, giving about 16.7 million colours. Pure red is 255, 0, 0; white is 255, 255, 255. A 12-megapixel photo would take roughly 36 megabytes stored raw. JPEG shrinks files by discarding detail your eye is unlikely to notice, which is why saving the same photo again and again slowly degrades it.

Sound is a wave of changing air pressure. A microphone turns it into an electrical signal, and the computer measures that signal at regular intervals, called sampling. Audio CDs take 44,100 samples a second, each a 16-bit number. MP3 and streaming formats remove sounds humans can barely hear, cutting file sizes by around 90%.

sections.key: Programs are numbers stored in memory like any other data, so one machine can run any software without rewiring.
sections.b:
Perhaps the most important idea in computing is that instructions themselves are numbers. A program is a long list of binary codes the processor recognises, such as 'add', 'compare' or 'jump'. Programmers rarely write raw binary: they write in languages like Python or JavaScript, and special software translates it into machine code.

Storing programs in memory alongside data, an idea from the 1940s associated with John von Neumann and others, means a computer can run completely different software without being rewired. The same laptop can be a typewriter, a cinema or a calculator, depending on which numbers it's running.

sections.key: Binary thinking helps with internet speeds, storage and file quality, and reminds you that computers shuffle numbers, not meaning.
sections.b:
Internet speeds are usually quoted in megabits per second, so divide by eight to estimate megabytes: 100 Mbps is about 12.5 megabytes a second. A kilobyte is about a thousand bytes, a megabyte a million, a gigabyte a billion, though some systems count in powers of two, so a kilobyte can mean 1,024 bytes.

When a phone warns that storage is full, videos, especially 4K ones, are usually the biggest culprits, since they are thousands of images per minute plus sound. Compressed photos look blotchy when zoomed in, and 'high quality' files take longer to send.

Binary is a reminder that computers don't understand meaning: they shuffle numbers. The meaning comes from the people who designed the codes, and from you.

quiz.q: Why do computers use binary rather than base ten?
o: Binary is the only system that can store text
It is easier to program than decimal
It was invented for electronic computers
Telling on from off is easy and reliable, while ten voltage levels are not
quiz.e: Two states stay robust despite electrical noise, which is why transistor switches suit binary.

quiz.q: How does a computer store the letter 'A'?
o: As a number code, such as 65 in ASCII
As a small picture of the letter
As a sound wave
As a pair of switches that spell it out
quiz.e: Computers store numbers that stand for characters, and your device looks up and draws the matching symbol.

quiz.q: How is the colour of a pixel usually stored?
o: As a single number from 0 to 9
As a short sound clip
As the name of the colour
As three numbers for red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255
quiz.e: Mixing three values from 0 to 255 gives about 16.7 million possible colours.

quiz.q: What does it mean that instructions are numbers too?
o: Programs can only run once
One machine can run completely different software without being rewired
Computers understand English commands directly
Programmers must write everything in binary
quiz.e: Because programs sit in memory like data, the same laptop can be a typewriter, a cinema or a calculator.

quiz.q: Your internet plan is 100 Mbps. Roughly how many megabytes per second is that?
quiz.e: Megabits divide by eight to give megabytes, so 100 Mbps is about 12.5 MB per second.

LESSONS.push: Every song you stream is just numbers. Here's how sound becomes digits.

LESSONS.title: What's inside your smartphone
LESSONS.hook: The phone in your pocket holds more computing power than the machines that guided astronauts to the Moon, plus a dozen sensors you probably never think about.

sections.key: A smartphone packs a processor, memory, radios and sensors into one slab, and far outpowers the Apollo guidance computer.
sections.b:
A modern smartphone is a complete computer squeezed into a slab about 8 millimetres thick. Its heart is a system-on-a-chip, a single piece of silicon that combines the main processor, a graphics processor, memory controllers, image processing and, increasingly, specialised circuits for artificial intelligence. Squeezing it all together saves space and power. Around it sit RAM, flash storage, radios, cameras, speakers, a battery and a screen.

The Apollo Guidance Computer that helped land astronauts on the Moon in 1969 had only about 4 kilobytes of working memory. A typical phone today is many thousands of times more powerful.

sections.key: Your phone senses movement, rotation, direction, air pressure and light, and its touchscreen reads the electrical field of your finger.
sections.b:
An accelerometer measures movement and gravity, which is how the screen rotates and your steps are estimated. A gyroscope detects rotation. A magnetometer senses Earth's magnetic field and acts as a compass. A proximity sensor turns off the screen at your ear, and an ambient light sensor adjusts brightness. A barometer measures air pressure and helps estimate which floor you're on. Combined with satellite positioning, these let maps track you smoothly.

Most touchscreens are capacitive: beneath the glass is a fine grid of conductors carrying a small charge. Your body conducts electricity, so a nearby finger disturbs the field and the phone calculates where. The grid senses many points at once, allowing pinch and zoom. Ordinary gloves don't work because fabric doesn't conduct, and water droplets also disturb the field.

sections.key: Phone cameras make up for tiny sensors with software that merges several frames into one better photo.
sections.b: Phone camera sensors are tiny compared with those in professional cameras, so they capture less light. Manufacturers compensate with computational photography. When you press the shutter, the phone often captures several frames in quick succession, some darker and some brighter, then aligns and merges them to reduce blur, rescue shadows and keep bright skies from washing out. Portrait mode uses depth information to blur the background artificially, and night modes stack many exposures. Multiple lenses offer wide, standard and zoom views. Much of a good phone photo is created by software decisions, not just by the lens.

sections.key: Your phone talks to towers, routers, earbuds, payment terminals and satellites using several separate radios.
sections.b:
When you make a call or load a web page, your phone sends radio signals to the nearest mobile tower. Networks divide the landscape into cells, each served by an antenna, hence 'cellular'. As you move, your phone is handed from cell to cell without dropping the connection. Each generation, from 3G to 4G to 5G, has brought more speed and capacity. Australia's major carriers switched off their 3G networks around 2024, retiring some older phones.

Wi-Fi connects to your router, and Bluetooth links to earbuds, watches and cars. Near-field communication (NFC) works within a few centimetres: when you tap to pay, your phone sends a one-time code, not your actual card number. A satellite receiver picks up GPS signals to work out your location, and some recent phones can send emergency texts to satellites where there's no mobile coverage.

sections.key: Lithium-ion batteries wear faster with heat, and simple habits keep your phone secure and long-lived.
sections.b:
Phones run on lithium-ion batteries, which store a lot of energy for their weight. Their development earned John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Charging moves lithium ions one way; using the phone moves them back. Over time, chemical wear means the battery holds less charge, often noticeably after two or three years. Heat speeds that wear, so avoid leaving a phone in a hot car. Many phones offer optimised charging that pauses around 80%.

Install updates promptly, because they fix security holes. Avoid running the battery completely flat. Use a case and screen protector, a screen lock, and check which apps can use your location, camera and microphone. When you retire a phone, back it up, erase it and recycle it through a program like MobileMuster.

quiz.q: What is a system-on-a-chip?
o: A tiny screen built into the glass
A removable memory card
A single piece of silicon combining the processor, graphics, memory controllers and more
A separate chip used only for calls
quiz.e: Combining parts on one chip saves space and power in a slim phone.

quiz.q: Why don't ordinary gloves work on a touchscreen?
o: The screen only responds to heat
Gloves are too thick for sensors
The glass blocks fabric
Fabric doesn't conduct electricity, so the screen can't sense your finger
quiz.e: Touchscreens detect how a conductive finger disturbs an electrical field.

quiz.q: How do phone cameras make up for their small sensors?
o: By merging several frames in software
By using a much larger flash
By slowing the shutter to minutes
By saving only black-and-white images
quiz.e: Computational photography blends multiple exposures to reduce blur and rescue shadows.

quiz.q: Why is tap-to-pay safer than reading out your card number?
o: It uses Wi-Fi instead of NFC
It works from several metres away
Your phone sends a one-time code instead of your real card number
It does not need a PIN or lock
quiz.e: The terminal never receives your actual card number, only a code that works once.

quiz.q: What speeds up the wear on a phone battery?
o: Using it for video calls
Heat, such as being left in a hot car
Installing updates
Using Wi-Fi
quiz.e: Chemical wear accelerates with heat, so keep phones cool.

LESSONS.push: Your phone senses motion, air pressure and magnetism. Most of us never notice.

LESSONS.title: Passwords, passkeys and staying locked
LESSONS.hook: Billions of stolen passwords circulate online, and if you reuse yours, one leak can open every door you have.

sections.key: Reusing passwords and choosing short, predictable ones lets criminals turn one breach into many.
sections.b:
The single biggest password mistake is reuse. Websites get breached all the time, and stolen email and password pairs are traded in huge lists. Criminals then run automated attacks called credential stuffing, trying those pairs on banks, email providers and shopping sites. If you used the same password for an old forum and your email, the forum's breach hands them your email too, and email is the master key for resetting almost everything else.

Criminals also guess billions of combinations against stolen databases, starting with '123456', 'password', names, sports teams, keyboard patterns and dictionary words with a number on the end. Swapping letters for symbols, like 'P@ssw0rd', fools almost nobody, because tools try those substitutions automatically. What really slows attackers is length. Each extra character multiplies the combinations, so advice has shifted from complexity to length.

sections.key: A long passphrase of random words is strong and memorable, and a reputable password manager protects the rest.
sections.b:
A passphrase strings several random words together, such as 'crystal onion clay pretzel'. It is long, so hard to crack, yet easier to remember than a jumble of symbols. The Australian Cyber Security Centre recommends four or more random words. Random is key: lyrics, quotes and your children's names are predictable. Use passphrases for what you must type from memory: your computer login, phone and password manager.

Reputable password managers encrypt your vault on your own device, using a key derived from your master passphrase, so the company stores only data it can't read. This was tested in 2022 when criminals stole LastPass vault backups: well-protected vaults stayed locked, but weak master passwords left people exposed. Choose a strong, unique master passphrase, turn on multi-factor authentication, and set up recovery options.

sections.key: Security questions are a back door, because their answers are often public or guessable.
sections.b:
Many accounts let you reset a password by answering questions like your mother's maiden name or your first pet, which can quietly undo all your careful password work. The answers are often public or guessable. In 2015 Google researchers found an attacker had nearly a one-in-five chance of guessing English speakers' answer to 'What is your favourite food?' in a single try. The answer was pizza. Around 40% of users also couldn't remember their own answers when needed.

Inventing an answer only helps if it's truly random, because people often pick the same predictable fakes. Treat each answer like a password: generate a random one and save it in your password manager.

sections.key: Passkeys replace passwords with a private key that stays on your device, so there is nothing to steal, reuse or hand to a fake site.
sections.b:
Passkeys are a newer technology designed to replace passwords, backed by Apple, Google, Microsoft and the FIDO Alliance. When you create one, your device makes a matching pair of cryptographic keys. The website stores the public key; the private key stays protected on your devices and is never shared.

To sign in, you just unlock your device with your face, fingerprint or PIN. Because there is no password to type, there's nothing to steal in a breach and nothing to reuse. A fake website can't trick you either, since the passkey only works with the real site. Where it's offered, it's worth using.

sections.key: Check whether you have been breached, then secure your email first, because it unlocks everything else.
sections.b:
Have I Been Pwned, a free service created by Australian security researcher Troy Hunt, shows whether your email has appeared in known breaches. Many password managers also warn about reused, weak or leaked passwords. If you're caught up in one, change that password immediately, plus any account where you reused it, and turn on multi-factor authentication. Watch for scam messages using leaked details. If identity documents were exposed, IDCARE, Australia's national identity and cyber support service, offers free help.

You don't have to fix everything at once. Start with your main email: a unique passphrase and multi-factor authentication. Then do banking, myGov and social media. Let a password manager replace old passwords gradually, switch to passkeys where offered, keep recovery codes safe offline and update your devices. Attackers prefer easy targets and will move on.

quiz.q: Why is reusing a password so risky?
o: Websites delete passwords that are reused
Reused passwords are always short
A breach at one site lets criminals try the same details on other accounts
Browsers cannot save reused passwords
quiz.e: Credential stuffing turns one leak into access to many accounts, and email is the master key.

quiz.q: What makes a passphrase a good choice?
o: Several random words make it long and hard to crack but easy to remember
A famous quote with symbols swapped in
A short word with a number on the end
Your pet's name with a capital letter
quiz.e: Length matters most, and random words stay memorable while avoiding predictable patterns.

quiz.q: Why are security questions a weak point?
o: They are always printed on your card
Websites never ask them
They only work for old accounts
Answers like your favourite food are often public or easy to guess
quiz.e: A guessable answer can undo a strong password, so treat each answer like a password.

quiz.q: Why can't a fake website steal a passkey?
o: Passkeys are written on your device screen
The passkey only works with the real site
Passkeys expire every few minutes
Fake sites cannot load on phones
quiz.e: The private key never leaves your device and is tied to the genuine website.

quiz.q: Which account should you secure first?
o: Your streaming account
An old gaming forum
Your main email, because it resets everything else
Your social media profile photos
quiz.e: Whoever controls your email can reset passwords for almost all your other accounts.

LESSONS.push: Swapping an 'a' for '@' fools almost no one. What actually protects you?

LESSONS.title: Phishing: don't take the bait
LESSONS.hook: Most cyber attacks don't start with genius hackers breaking code. They start with a message that convinces a real person to click.

sections.key: Phishing tricks people into acting by pretending to be someone trusted, through email, text, phone, social media and QR codes.
sections.b:
Phishing is when criminals pretend to be someone you trust, such as your bank, a delivery company, the tax office or your boss, to trick you into clicking a link, opening an attachment, handing over details or sending money. The name comes from fishing: cast enough bait and someone will bite. It began in the 1990s and remains one of the most common ways attacks begin, because fooling a person is often easier than breaking security technology.

It has spread beyond email. Scam texts (smishing) claim a parcel is waiting or a toll is unpaid. Phone scams (vishing) use a live voice, sometimes a spoofed caller ID. Fake QR codes can lead to lookalike payment pages. Scammers increasingly use AI to write flawless messages or imitate voices. Spear phishing is tailored to one person using details found online.

sections.key: Phishing works by creating pressure, so urgency itself is a warning sign, though the absence of red flags doesn't prove safety.
sections.b:
Phishing messages push emotional buttons. Urgency: 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours.' Fear: 'You owe unpaid tax.' Curiosity: 'Is this you in this photo?' Greed: 'Claim your refund.' Authority: a message that seems to come from a manager or police. All aim at getting you to act before careful thinking catches up.

Common red flags include a sender that doesn't quite match the organisation, links to odd web addresses like 'mybank-secure-login.co', unexpected attachments, a generic greeting, and any request for passwords, one-time codes, card details or remote access. On a computer, hover over a link to preview its real destination. But modern scams can look polished, use your name and appear in genuine message threads, so no red flags doesn't mean safe.

sections.key: In business email compromise, criminals fake or hack an email to redirect payments, so always confirm changed bank details by phone.
sections.b:
Businesses are prime targets for business email compromise. Criminals hack or imitate a supplier's email account, then say their bank details have changed. The next invoice gets paid into the scammer's account. Others pose as a senior manager urgently asking staff to transfer money or buy gift cards. Home buyers are targeted too, with fake emails from 'conveyancers' giving new account details for a deposit.

The defence is simple but must be firm: always verify any change of bank details by phoning the person on a number you already have, never the one in the email.

sections.key: The best defence is to verify independently, using a number or website you already trust, never the one in the message.
sections.b:
The single most useful habit is to verify independently. If a message claims to be from your bank, don't click its link or call its number. Open your banking app, type the bank's address into your browser yourself, or phone the number on the back of your card. The same goes for the tax office, myGov, delivery companies and toll roads.

If a friend or relative messages from a new number asking for money, call them on their old number. Genuine organisations won't mind you checking. The ACCC's Scamwatch sums it up as three steps: stop, check, protect.

sections.key: If you fall for a scam, act quickly, contact your bank, secure your accounts and report it.
sections.b:
Act quickly and don't be embarrassed; smart people are caught every day. If you gave out card or bank details or sent money, call your bank immediately on its official number, as it may be able to stop payments. If you entered a password, change it straight away, along with any account using the same one, and turn on multi-factor authentication. If you installed software or gave remote access, disconnect from the internet and get trusted help. IDCARE offers free support for identity theft, and the Australian Cyber Security Hotline, 1300 CYBER1, can advise.

Report scams to Scamwatch (scamwatch.gov.au), run by the ACCC, and cybercrime through ReportCyber (cyber.gov.au), run by the ASD's Australian Cyber Security Centre. Also tell the organisation being impersonated. Even a report that doesn't recover your money can stop the scam reaching someone else.

quiz.q: Why does phishing remain so common?
o: Security technology cannot be updated
Only large companies are ever targeted
Fooling a person is often easier than breaking security technology
It is legal in many countries
quiz.e: Attackers target human attention because people are often the easiest way in.

quiz.q: What do phishing messages try to make you do?
o: Think carefully and compare options
Act quickly before careful thinking catches up
Wait several days for a reply
Share the message with friends first
quiz.e: Pressure is the warning sign: urgency, fear and curiosity aim to rush you.

quiz.q: A supplier emails to say their bank details have changed. What should you do?
o: Pay the next invoice as normal
Reply to the email asking if it is true
Check the email's signature
Phone them on a number you already have
quiz.e: Verifying by a known number stops business email compromise payments reaching scammers.

quiz.q: A text claims to be from your bank. What is the safest response?
o: Open your banking app or type the bank's address yourself
Click the link to check your account
Reply asking for proof
Call the number in the text
quiz.e: Verify independently using contact details you already trust.

quiz.q: You entered your password on a fake site. What should you do first?
o: Wait to see if anything happens
Change it and any account that uses the same one, and turn on multi-factor authentication
Delete the email only
Restart your computer
quiz.e: Fast action limits the damage, and multi-factor authentication adds a second barrier.

LESSONS.push: Many cyber attacks need no genius hacker, only one moment of your attention.

LESSONS.title: Your data and your privacy
LESSONS.hook: Every tap, search and purchase leaves a trace. Here's who collects it, what happened when big companies lost it, and what rights you have.

sections.key: Free services earn money from advertising, so detailed data about you has commercial value, collected through many kinds of tracking.
sections.b:
Many popular online services are free because they make money largely by selling advertising, and ads are worth more when targeted. That makes knowledge of your age, location, interests, habits and purchases valuable. 'If you're not paying for the product, you are the product' is a simplification, since data also improves services and fights fraud, but 'free' usually involves a trade.

Tracking takes many forms. Third-party cookies, placed by advertisers, can follow you across sites. Tracking pixels, tiny invisible images, report when you open an email or page. Apps may collect your location, contacts and usage. Device fingerprinting identifies you from your device's settings, even without cookies. Loyalty cards link purchases to you, and data brokers trade information to build profiles. Combined, these pieces can reveal a surprising amount about your life.

sections.key: The 2022 Optus and Medibank breaches exposed millions of Australians' data and showed why storing less matters.
sections.b:
In September 2022, Optus revealed a cyber attack that exposed personal information of around 10 million current and former customers, among the largest breaches in Australian history. Details included names, dates of birth, addresses, and for many, driver's licence or passport numbers. Millions had to replace identity documents. It sparked debate about why companies keep so much data, sometimes about customers who left years earlier, and helped drive tougher privacy penalties later that year.

In October 2022, health insurer Medibank was hit, affecting about 9.7 million current and former customers, including health claims for many. Medibank refused to pay the ransom, in line with government advice, and the criminals published some data. In 2024 the government imposed cyber sanctions on a Russian man it identified as responsible. Health information can be exploited, so storing less, and protecting it well, matters.

sections.h: The Privacy Act and your rights
sections.key: The Privacy Act sets rules for handling personal information and gives you rights to access, correct and complain.
sections.b:
Australia's main law is the Privacy Act 1988, with 13 Australian Privacy Principles covering how personal information is collected, used, stored, disclosed and secured. It applies to federal agencies and most businesses and not-for-profits with annual turnover above $3 million, plus some smaller ones such as health providers. States have their own laws for their agencies. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) oversees it, and it was updated in 2022 and 2024.

You generally have the right to know why information is collected and how it will be used, to ask for access and corrections, to avoid identifying yourself where practical, and to opt out of direct marketing. Since 2018 the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme has required organisations to notify you and the OAIC of breaches likely to cause serious harm. If unhappy, complain to the organisation first, then the OAIC.

sections.key: You can reduce tracking with a few settings, and data you never hand over can't be leaked.
sections.b:
You can reduce tracking without going off the grid. On your phone, review which apps can access your location, contacts, camera and microphone, and switch off anything unnecessary. iPhones let you ask apps not to track you across other apps; Android has similar ad privacy settings. In your browser, block third-party cookies or use a privacy-focused browser.

Check social media privacy settings, and think twice before posting your birthday, address or holiday dates publicly. When a form asks for information, ask whether it's really needed. Data you never hand over can't be leaked, sold or misused later.

sections.key: After a breach, read the notice, secure your accounts, replace exposed documents and watch for follow-up scams.
sections.b:
If you're told your data was caught in a breach, read the notice carefully to see exactly what was exposed. Change affected passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication. If identity documents were exposed, follow advice about replacing them; some agencies can issue new licence numbers.

Consider a free credit ban through Australia's credit reporting bodies if you're worried about identity fraud, and watch bank statements closely. Be wary of follow-up scam messages using your leaked details. IDCARE provides free support.

This is general information only: for a specific legal problem, talk to a lawyer or community legal centre.

quiz.q: Why do free online services collect detailed data about you?
o: To make the service slower
Because law requires every user profile to be public
Targeted advertising is worth more, so your data has commercial value
To delete it after a day
quiz.e: Advertising pays for free services, and ads are worth more when aimed at the right people.

quiz.q: What debate did the Optus breach spark?
o: Whether phone plans should be cheaper
Why companies keep so much data, even about former customers
Whether customers should store their own data
Whether passports should be digital
quiz.e: Holding less data, for less time, reduces what can be stolen.

quiz.q: What does the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme require?
o: Covered organisations must notify you and the OAIC of breaches likely to cause serious harm
Customers must report their own breaches
Breaches must be kept confidential
Only government agencies must disclose breaches
quiz.e: Since 2018, covered organisations have had to tell people when a breach is likely to cause serious harm.

quiz.q: Why does handing over less information protect you?
o: Companies cannot sell small amounts of data
Forms will not accept it
Any data you give is deleted after a year
Data you never hand over can't be leaked, sold or misused later
quiz.e: The simplest protection is to ask whether a form really needs the information.

quiz.q: What should you do first after being told your data was in a breach?
o: Ignore it unless money is taken
Read the notice, change affected passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication
Delete all your accounts
Reply to any message that mentions it
quiz.e: Knowing exactly what was exposed guides the steps that protect you.

LESSONS.push: Small traces add up to a detailed picture of your life. Here's how.

LESSONS.title: Hacking: myth and reality
LESSONS.hook: Forget the hoodie in a dark room typing green code. Real hacking is often slower, stranger and much more human than the movies suggest.

sections.key: The word 'hacker' began as praise for clever tinkering, and hat colours now separate permission from crime.
sections.b:
The word 'hacker' began as praise. In the late 1950s and 1960s, members of a model railway club at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology used 'hack' for a clever, playful technical solution. Only in the 1980s, as computers spread and break-ins made headlines, did it come to mean someone who enters systems without permission.

Security people now borrow hat colours from old Western films. White hats test systems with permission and help fix weaknesses; many are penetration testers, paid to attack an organisation's defences before criminals do. Black hats break in illegally for money, data, disruption or bragging rights. Grey hats probe without permission but report the flaw rather than exploit it. Even then, unauthorised access to a computer is a crime in Australia under Commonwealth and state laws.

sections.key: Most attacks exploit known weaknesses such as unpatched software and reused passwords, and they come from opportunists, criminal gangs and state-linked groups.
sections.b:
Real attacks are rarely feats of genius. Criminals use automated tools to scan the internet for computers running outdated software with publicly known flaws, then exploit the ones that haven't been patched. Others use leaked passwords, cloud storage left open to the world, or accounts without multi-factor authentication. A 'zero-day' is a flaw the software maker doesn't know about, so no fix exists. These are rare and valuable, and mostly used by well-resourced groups, including some linked to governments.

Attackers range from opportunists with ready-made tools, to organised gangs, to state-linked groups pursuing espionage or disruption, to hacktivists with political aims. The Australian Signals Directorate defends against serious cyber threats and publishes an annual cyber threat report.

sections.key: Social engineering manipulates people rather than machines, so training people to pause and verify matters.
sections.b:
Often the easiest way into a system is through a person. Social engineering means manipulating people into handing over access or information. Examples include a phishing email, a phone call pretending to be IT support, a fake courier who tailgates staff through a secure door, or a USB stick left in a car park labelled 'salaries'.

The American hacker Kevin Mitnick, once among the FBI's most wanted, became famous for talking his way into systems rather than cracking code. He later worked as a security consultant. Technology can't fully fix this problem, which is why training people to pause and verify matters so much.

sections.key: Ransomware locks or steals an organisation's data and demands payment, and paying guarantees nothing.
sections.b:
Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts an organisation's files, then demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, for the key. Many gangs also steal data first and threaten to publish it, called double extortion. Some operate like businesses, with specialists, customer support for paying victims, and affiliates who rent their ransomware.

In 2017 the WannaCry attack spread worldwide within days and disrupted parts of Britain's National Health Service. Hospitals, councils, schools and businesses of all sizes are targets. Paying guarantees nothing and funds further crime, so governments generally advise against it. Since 2025, larger Australian businesses must report ransom payments to the government. Offline backups are the best defence.

sections.key: Basic habits block most attacks, and bug bounty programs turn ethical hackers into a legitimate line of defence.
sections.b:
The good news is that most attacks target easy weaknesses, so basic hygiene defeats many of them. Keep devices and apps updated, use unique passwords or passkeys, turn on multi-factor authentication, and keep a backup that isn't permanently connected. Be sceptical of unexpected messages and verify requests independently.

Companies also invite hackers to help. Bug bounty programs reward anyone who finds a security flaw and reports it privately, so it can be fixed before criminals find it. Netscape ran one of the first in 1995, and payouts for serious flaws can now reach tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars. If hacking fascinates you, learn legally through capture-the-flag competitions, practice labs and TAFE or university courses.

quiz.q: What makes a hacker a 'white hat'?
o: They test systems with permission and help fix weaknesses
They break in but never take anything
They only attack large governments
They work alone and never get paid
quiz.e: White hats hack with permission to improve security, which separates them from black hats who break in illegally.

quiz.q: What do most real cyber attacks exploit?
o: Brand-new flaws that nobody has discovered
Known weaknesses such as unpatched software and reused passwords
Brilliant custom code written by lone geniuses
Physical damage to computer hardware
quiz.e: Most attackers look for an easy way in, so basic habits like updating and unique passwords block a lot of them.

quiz.q: Why is social engineering so effective?
o: It relies on rare zero-day flaws
It needs very expensive equipment
It targets people, whom technology can't fully protect
It only works against large banks
quiz.e: Manipulating a person is often easier than cracking code, which is why training people to pause and verify matters.

quiz.q: Why do governments generally advise against paying a ransom?
o: Payment is illegal in every country
Payment guarantees nothing and funds further crime
Hackers always delete the data once paid
Insurance never covers the cost
quiz.e: Paying doesn't guarantee recovery and rewards criminals, so offline backups are the better defence.

quiz.q: Why keep a backup that isn't permanently connected?
o: It uses less electricity
It runs faster than a connected backup
Ransomware can't reach it
It stops phishing emails arriving
quiz.e: An offline backup stays out of ransomware's reach, so you can recover without paying.

LESSONS.push: Most break-ins don't need genius. Find out what they do need.

LESSONS.title: The Mechanical Turk: a chess machine with a secret
LESSONS.hook: For over 80 years, a turbaned automaton beat chess players across Europe and America. The truth inside its cabinet still echoes through modern AI.

sections.key: In 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen unveiled a chess-playing 'machine', and its demonstrations were staged to convince people nothing was hidden.
sections.b:
In 1770 the engineer Wolfgang von Kempelen presented a chess-playing 'machine' to Empress Maria Theresa's court in Vienna. A life-sized figure in Ottoman-style robes and a turban sat behind a large wooden cabinet with a chessboard on top. Its mechanical arm grasped pieces and moved them, and it shook its head at illegal moves. It usually won. Kempelen seemed slightly embarrassed by the fame and reportedly kept it packed away for years.

Before each game, the operator opened the cabinet doors one at a time, shining a candle through a tangle of cogs and levers, and lifted the robes to show more machinery. The whirring was mostly for effect. Never seeing everything at once, onlookers felt sure nothing was hidden.

sections.key: A strong human chess player hid inside the cabinet, using a sliding seat, magnets and levers to play.
sections.b:
The secret was simple and daring: a skilled chess player was hidden inside. A moving seat let him slide along as each door opened, keeping him behind panels and fake machinery. Each piece on the board carried a magnet that tugged a small metal marker, so he could follow the game. He planned moves on his own small pegboard and steered the Turk's arm with levers. A candle gave light, and smoke escaped through the figure's turban.

Over the decades, a series of strong players worked as operators, cramped and sweating in the dark. The theatre worked: people left certain the machine held only machinery, exactly as intended.

sections.key: The Turk toured for decades, sceptics such as Edgar Allan Poe argued a human was hidden inside, and a fire destroyed it in 1854.
sections.b:
In the 1780s the Turk toured Europe, and accounts say it played Benjamin Franklin in Paris. After Kempelen died in 1804, the showman Johann Nepomuk Maelzel, who also promoted the metronome, bought it. Stories say it played Napoleon in 1809, though some tales were embroidered, so hold them loosely. Maelzel took it to the United States in 1826, drawing large paying crowds.

Not everyone was fooled. In 1836 Edgar Allan Poe argued in an essay that a person must be concealed inside, noting that a true machine would win every game while the Turk sometimes lost. Some of his other reasoning was wrong. The Turk burned in a Philadelphia museum in 1854, and only then did a son of its last owner publish the secret.

sections.key: Amazon Mechanical Turk, launched in 2005, openly pays people to do tasks that computers find hard.
sections.b:
The Turk's name came back in 2005, when Amazon launched Amazon Mechanical Turk. It lets businesses post small online tasks that are easy for people but hard for computers, such as describing a photo, checking whether two products are the same or transcribing a blurry receipt. Thousands of workers around the world complete them for small payments.

Amazon called the idea 'artificial artificial intelligence'. Like the original Turk, it looks like a computer doing the work, but humans are quietly inside. Platforms like this became a major source of the labelled data that later trained machine learning systems, including image recognisers.

sections.key: Much of today's AI still depends on hidden human labour, so it pays to ask who or what is really doing the work.
sections.b:
The Turk's lesson is still relevant. Modern AI systems learn from huge amounts of data that people have created, sorted and labelled, often low-paid workers in many countries. Humans also rate chatbot answers to teach them which responses are helpful, and moderate the disturbing content that filters miss. Some start-ups have been caught presenting services as automated while staff did much of the work behind the scenes.

None of this means AI is fake. It means the line between machine and human effort is often blurrier than it looks. Like eighteenth century audiences, we tend to see intelligence where clever presentation invites us to.

quiz.q: Why did the operator open the cabinet doors one at a time before each game?
o: To let the hidden player stretch his legs
To cool the clockwork before play began
To convince onlookers the cabinet held only machinery
To let the opponent inspect the chess pieces
quiz.e: The ritual was theatre: showing the inside piece by piece made people believe they had seen everything.

quiz.q: How did the hidden player follow the game on the board?
o: Each piece carried a magnet that tugged a marker he could see
He watched through a small mirror in the turban
An assistant called out every move
He listened to the clicking of the gears
quiz.e: Magnets and levers let a human follow and steer the game while staying out of sight.

quiz.q: What was Poe's sharp point about the Turk?
o: Its arm moved too smoothly for clockwork
A true machine would win every game, yet it sometimes lost
It never made illegal moves
Its cabinet was too small to hold machinery
quiz.e: A genuine machine would not lose at random, which hinted that a fallible human was playing.

quiz.q: Why did Amazon call its service 'artificial artificial intelligence'?
o: It looks like a computer doing the work, but humans quietly do it
It uses two layers of neural networks
It copies the way a chess machine thinks
It replaces human workers with software
quiz.e: Like the original Turk, the service hides human effort behind something that looks automated.

quiz.q: What does the Turk's story teach about modern AI?
o: AI systems are mostly fake
AI never needs human input once built
Chess is the best test of intelligence
Much AI depends on hidden human labour, so it pays to ask who is doing the work
quiz.e: Humans label data, rate answers and moderate content, so machine and human effort blur together.

LESSONS.push: For 80 years a chess 'machine' beat all comers. Its secret still echoes in AI.

LESSONS.title: Where the word ‘robot’ came from
LESSONS.hook: The word ‘robot’ is barely a century old. It was born in a Czech play about manufactured workers who rise up against their makers.

sections.key: The word 'robot' comes from the Czech 'robota', meaning forced labour, and first appeared in Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.
sections.b:
In 1920 the Czech writer Karel Čapek published R.U.R., short for Rossum's Universal Robots. It premiered in Prague in January 1921 and soon played in New York, London and beyond, carrying a new word into dozens of languages. The play is set in a factory on a remote island that mass-produces cheap, tireless, obedient artificial workers. Humans grow idle, the robots rebel, and almost all of humanity is wiped out.

Čapek credited his brother Josef with the word. Karel had considered 'labori', from Latin, but found it too bookish. Josef suggested 'roboti', from the Czech 'robota', meaning drudgery or forced labour, historically the unpaid work serfs owed their landlords. The name hinted at exploitation from the start.

sections.key: Čapek's original robots were made of synthetic organic material, closer to androids than to metal machines.
sections.b:
If you picture R.U.R.'s robots as clanking metal figures, you are picturing a later idea. Čapek's robots were assembled from an artificial organic material, a kind of synthetic protoplasm, mixed in vats and shaped into bodies. They looked almost human and were built in factories like any other product. In modern terms they resemble biological androids more than mechanical machines.

The metal man came mostly from later films, magazine covers and toys of the 1920s and 1930s, such as the gleaming robot in Fritz Lang's 1927 film Metropolis. Over time, 'robot' came to mean any machine that senses, decides and acts in the world.

sections.key: People built lifelike moving machines long before anyone called them robots, but those machines could not sense or respond to the world.
sections.b:
The dream is ancient. Greek myths described bronze guardians like Talos, said to patrol the island of Crete. In the first century AD, Hero of Alexandria wrote about devices driven by water, air and weights, including self-opening temple doors. In 1206 the engineer Ismail al-Jazari, working in what is now Turkey, described water-powered automata, including a band of mechanical musicians.

In eighteenth century Switzerland, Pierre Jaquet-Droz and his collaborators built 'The Writer', a doll-sized boy who dips a quill in ink and writes a programmable message. It still works and is displayed in a museum in Neuchâtel. These were marvels of clockwork, though none could sense or respond to the world.

sections.key: Isaac Asimov imagined robots with built-in safety rules, and his stories show how hard it is to turn values into rules.
sections.b:
In the 1940s the American writer Isaac Asimov grew tired of stories where robots always turned on their creators. In his 1942 story 'Runaround' he set out the Three Laws of Robotics. A robot must not harm a human or, through inaction, allow one to come to harm. It must obey human orders unless that conflicts with the first law. And it must protect itself unless that conflicts with the first two.

Asimov also coined the word 'robotics'. Many of his best stories are about the laws failing in unexpected ways, an early insight into how hard it is to turn values into rules.

sections.key: The first factory robot arrived in 1961, and Čapek's questions about labour, control and who benefits still shape debates about AI.
sections.b:
Real robots arrived in factories, not living rooms. In 1961 the Unimate, built from George Devol's patented programmable arm and promoted by Joseph Engelberger, began work at a General Motors plant in New Jersey, lifting and stacking hot die-cast metal. It was just a heavy arm bolted to the floor, but it could be reprogrammed. Today millions of industrial robots weld, paint, pack and assemble, mostly in controlled environments.

Čapek's themes remain. What happens when machines do the work? Who profits? Could created beings deserve rights? Many researchers think the robot-uprising template distorts public thinking, since real AI risks are more often errors, bias, misuse and economic disruption. Technology is also about the people who build and own it.

quiz.q: Where does the word 'robot' come from?
o: A Latin word meaning 'to build'
A Czech word for drudgery or forced labour
A Greek word for 'moving statue'
An old German word for 'iron man'
quiz.e: 'Robota' meant forced labour, so the name carried a hint of exploitation from the start.

quiz.q: How did Čapek's original robots differ from the popular image of a robot?
o: They were made of steel plates
They were powered by clockwork
They were made of synthetic organic material, closer to androids
They were invisible machines in a factory
quiz.e: The metal robot came from later films and toys; Čapek's creatures were artificial flesh.

quiz.q: What did early automata such as 'The Writer' lack that real robots have?
o: The ability to sense and respond to the world
Any moving parts at all
A shape that resembled a person
A way of being displayed in public
quiz.e: Clockwork automata followed fixed mechanisms, while robots sense, decide and act.

quiz.q: What do many of Asimov's stories about the Three Laws reveal?
o: That robots can never be built safely
How hard it is to turn values into rules
That humans should avoid obeying robots
That machines will always rebel
quiz.e: The laws often fail in unexpected ways, which shows how difficult it is to capture values in simple rules.

quiz.q: Why do many researchers think the robot-uprising story distorts thinking about AI?
o: Real AI risks are more often errors, bias, misuse and economic disruption
AI systems cannot make mistakes
Robots are too expensive to build
Uprisings are impossible in factories
quiz.e: Realistic risks are less dramatic than rebellious machines, but they matter more to real people.

LESSONS.push: The word 'robot' is barely a century old, and it meant something grim.

LESSONS.title: Will machines take our jobs? What history says
LESSONS.hook: People have feared that machines would make human work obsolete for over 200 years. The real story is more surprising, and more uncomfortable, than either side admits.

sections.key: The Luddites objected to machines being used to cut wages, and their hardship shows new technology can leave particular people worse off for a generation.
sections.b:
In 1811 groups of skilled English textile workers began smashing machinery at night, signing letters as the mythical 'General Ludd'. The movement lasted until 1816. The government sent thousands of soldiers, made machine-breaking a capital crime in 1812, and hanged or transported many Luddites, some to Australia. 'Luddite' is now an insult for someone who hates technology, but historians call that unfair. The Luddites objected to machines being used to cut wages, employ unskilled labour and produce shoddier goods.
