Their suffering was real. Hand-loom weavers, once well paid, saw wages collapse over decades as power looms took over. Historians still debate how quickly ordinary living standards rose in the Industrial Revolution.

sections.key: Machines replaced most farm work, yet people moved into new kinds of jobs as cheaper food left more money to spend elsewhere.
sections.b:
Consider farming. Around 1900, roughly two in five American workers worked on farms, and the share in Australia was also large. Today it is a small fraction in both countries, thanks to tractors, harvesters, fertilisers and better crops.

A farmer in 1900 might have predicted mass unemployment. Instead, people moved into factories, offices, shops, schools and hospitals, doing jobs that had barely existed before. Rising productivity made food cheaper, which left people with more money for other things, which created demand for new kinds of work. Over the long run, this pattern has repeated again and again.

sections.key: Economists warn against assuming there is a fixed amount of work, though history is no guarantee that everything will work out.
sections.b:
A common mistake in automation debates is the lump of labour fallacy: the idea that an economy has a fixed amount of work, so if machines do more, there is less for people. History suggests otherwise. When technology makes something cheaper, people often buy more of it, and the savings get spent elsewhere. New technologies also create entirely new industries, from car repair to web design. Avoiding the fallacy doesn't guarantee a good outcome. It just means 'machines do more, so humans do less' is too simple.

In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes popularised the phrase 'technological unemployment', yet predicted his grandchildren might work around 15 hours a week. Neither arrived.

sections.key: Automation usually changes the tasks within jobs before it removes jobs, and the effects can play out unexpectedly over decades.
sections.b:
Automated teller machines spread through banks from the 1970s, and it seemed obvious that human tellers would vanish. Yet the economist James Bessen found that in the United States, teller jobs held up and even grew for decades. Cheaper branches meant banks opened more of them, and tellers shifted towards customer service and selling financial products. Teller numbers did eventually fall, mainly as online and mobile banking spread.

Many economists think of a job as a bundle of tasks. Technology automates some and can make the rest more valuable. Spreadsheets automated a great deal of calculation, yet accountants and analysts grew in number as their time shifted to interpreting numbers and advising people.

sections.key: AI reaches into thinking work, economists disagree about how this time will unfold, and how society handles the transition matters enormously.
sections.b:
Past waves of automation mostly replaced muscle and routine tasks. AI can now draft text, write code, summarise documents and analyse images, reaching into work that once seemed safely human. Some economists expect the familiar pattern: disruption, then new jobs and higher living standards. Others worry the change could be faster and broader, giving workers less time to adapt, or could concentrate gains among a few companies. Honest forecasters admit deep uncertainty.

What history does teach clearly is that how a society handles the transition matters enormously, through education, retraining, safety nets and who shares in the gains. The Luddites' real question, who benefits from new machines, has never gone away.

quiz.q: What were the Luddites mainly protesting?
o: Machines being used to cut wages and replace skilled work with cheaper goods
The invention of all machinery
Government taxes on textile exports
Competition from overseas craftspeople
quiz.e: The Luddites weren't against machines as such; they objected to how machines were used against workers.

quiz.q: Why did cheaper food from rising farm productivity help create new jobs?
o: Farmers were forced to retrain as soldiers
People had more money to spend on other things, creating demand for new work
Food exports replaced factory production
Governments hired former farm workers
quiz.e: Savings from productivity get spent elsewhere, which creates demand for new kinds of work.

quiz.q: What is the lump of labour fallacy?
o: The belief that wages never change
The idea that new technology always creates jobs
The belief that all workers are equally skilled
The mistaken idea that there is a fixed amount of work, so machines leave less for people
quiz.e: The amount of work isn't fixed, because cheaper goods and new industries create new demand.

quiz.q: What did the ATM story show about automation?
o: It usually changes the tasks within jobs before it removes jobs
Machines never affect employment
Bank tellers vanished within a few years
Customers prefer talking to machines
quiz.e: Tellers shifted towards customer service, and job numbers fell only later as online banking spread.

quiz.q: What does history teach clearly about automation?
o: New technology leaves every worker better off
How a society manages the transition matters enormously
Workers can safely ignore new technology
AI will repeat the past exactly
quiz.e: Education, retraining, safety nets and who shares the gains shape who benefits from new machines.

LESSONS.push: The Luddites weren't against machines. Find out what they actually wanted.

LESSONS.title: How spam filters learned to fight junk mail
LESSONS.hook: Every day, filters quietly throw away enormous amounts of junk email before you ever see it. Their story is one of the first great victories of everyday machine learning.

sections.key: Unsolicited mass messages have been profitable since 1978 because sending a million emails costs almost nothing.
sections.b:
On 3 May 1978, Gary Thuerk, a marketing manager at Digital Equipment Corporation, sent a message to several hundred users of ARPANET, the network that grew into the internet, inviting them to presentations of new computers. The network was meant for government and research use, and the reaction was swift and angry. Thuerk later said it led to some sales, which is why unsolicited mass email never went away. When email reached the public in the 1990s, sending a million messages cost almost nothing, so a tiny response rate could still turn a profit.

The name comes from a 1970 Monty Python sketch where Vikings chant 'Spam, Spam, Spam' until nothing else can be heard. A 1994 case, when two lawyers advertised to thousands of Usenet groups at once, brought the word wider attention.

sections.key: Hand-written rules were easy to dodge, so filters learned to score mail using probability.
sections.b:
The first defence was a list of rules: block 'make money fast', block all capitals, block known senders. Spammers adapted almost instantly by misspelling words, swapping letters for numbers, hiding text in images and changing addresses. Rigid rules also caught innocent mail, such as a doctor's email mentioning a medicine name.

In 2002 the programmer Paul Graham's essay 'A Plan for Spam' popularised a filter based on Bayesian probability. It studies emails already sorted into spam and genuine mail, and for each word works out how much more often it appears in one pile. A new email is scored by combining its most telling words: 'winner' pushes towards spam, a colleague's name the other way. It learns from your own mail.

sections.key: Each time you mark a message as spam or not spam, you give the filter a labelled example to learn from.
sections.b:
Spam filtering is a classic case of supervised machine learning: learning from examples labelled with the right answer. When you click 'report spam' or rescue a message from the junk folder, you supply those labels. Large providers combine signals from vast numbers of users, so a scam campaign reported by early recipients can be blocked for everyone else quickly.

Modern filters look far beyond words. They check where a message came from, how that sender has behaved before, whether links lead to known scam sites, and whether the email passes technical checks proving it came from the domain it claims, using standards called SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

sections.key: A filter must balance catching junk against wrongly hiding real email, and cutting one kind of error usually raises the other.
sections.b:
Every filter makes two kinds of mistakes. A false negative lets spam into your inbox, which is annoying. A false positive sends a real message to the junk folder, which can be far worse if it is a job offer, a bill or a message from a friend.

Filters can be tuned to be stricter or more relaxed, but reducing one kind of error usually increases the other. Most providers lean towards letting a little spam through rather than losing genuine mail. That is why it is worth checking your junk folder occasionally, especially when you are waiting for something important, such as a booking confirmation or a password reset.

sections.key: Spam and phishing keep evolving, so filters are only one layer and your own caution is the last one.
sections.b:
Spammers and filter builders are locked in an arms race. As filters improved, many criminals moved to phishing, crafting emails that impersonate banks, delivery companies or government agencies to steal passwords and money. Some now use AI to write fluent, personalised messages without the spelling mistakes that once gave scams away.

Laws help too. Australia's Spam Act 2003, enforced by the Australian Communications and Media Authority, requires commercial messages to have consent, identify the sender and include a way to unsubscribe. But no filter is perfect. The best final layer is you: slow down, check the sender, and never click a link in an unexpected message asking you to log in or pay.

quiz.q: Why did unsolicited mass email never go away?
o: Email providers refused to block it
Sending millions of messages costs almost nothing, so a tiny response rate can still profit
It was required for government networks
Most people enjoy receiving advertisements
quiz.e: Near-zero cost means even a very low response rate can make spam worthwhile.

quiz.q: Why do learning filters beat hand-written rules?
o: They never make mistakes
They only block messages from known senders
They need no examples to work
They learn from sorted examples and keep up as spammers change tactics
quiz.e: Rules are easily dodged, while a filter that learns from examples can adapt as the junk changes.

quiz.q: What do you do when you click 'report spam'?
o: Supply a label that helps train the filter
Delete the sender from the internet
Change the filter's rules by hand
Tell the sender to stop emailing
quiz.e: Your report is a labelled example, and providers combine many users' labels to protect everyone.

quiz.q: Why do providers usually lean towards letting a little spam through?
o: Spam is harmless to everyone
Blocking spam is illegal
A wrongly hidden real message, such as a job offer or bill, can be far worse
Stricter filters cost too much electricity
quiz.e: False positives can hide important mail, so providers accept some false negatives.

quiz.q: What is the best final defence against phishing?
o: Replying to the sender to confirm
Relying only on the spam filter
Clicking the link to check where it leads
Slowing down, checking the sender and not clicking links in unexpected messages
quiz.e: No filter is perfect, so careful habits are the last and strongest layer of protection.

LESSONS.push: Filters hide most junk mail, but they make one costly mistake.

LESSONS.title: Clever Hans and the AI that learned the wrong lesson
LESSONS.hook: A horse that seemed to do maths, and computers that seemed to diagnose disease, turned out to be solving a different problem altogether. Here's how AI can be right for the wrong reasons.

sections.key: Clever Hans seemed to do maths but was really reading unconscious cues from the people around him.
sections.b:
In early 1900s Berlin, the retired schoolteacher Wilhelm von Osten toured with his horse, Hans. Ask Hans to add five and three and he tapped his hoof eight times. He seemed to handle fractions, dates and even spelling, and von Osten genuinely believed his horse could think. In 1904 a commission of experts found no sign of deliberate trickery.

Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst ran careful experiments. When the questioner did not know the answer, or Hans could not see them, his accuracy collapsed. Hans was not counting. He was reading tiny, unconscious changes in posture and expression that told him when to stop tapping.

sections.key: Shortcut learning is when an AI uses an accidental pattern in its data to get right answers without learning the real thing.
sections.b:
Clever Hans had learned something impressive, just not what people thought. Machine learning systems do the same. A model uses whatever patterns help it get right answers on its training examples, whether or not they are the ones we intended. If an accidental feature lines up with the answers, the model may latch on, because that is often easier than learning the real thing. Researchers call this shortcut learning. Unlike specification gaming, it happens even when the goal is sensible.

In 2016 researchers deliberately trained a wolf-versus-husky classifier on photos where only the wolves had snow behind them. It did well, but a highlighting tool showed it was largely looking at the snow. High accuracy alone doesn't show what a system has learned.

sections.key: Medical AI has learned hospital and pen-mark shortcuts, while the famous tank-and-weather story is probably a myth.
sections.b:
In a 2018 study, deep learning models trained on chest X-rays could identify which hospital an image came from, using clues such as markings and equipment. Because some hospitals had sicker patients, the hospital itself helped predict disease, and the models did worse on X-rays from elsewhere. In 2019 dermatologists reported that a skin cancer classifier was more likely to call a mole cancerous if it had been marked with a surgical skin marker, which doctors often draw on suspicious spots. The systems had partly learned doctors' habits, not the disease.

A famous tale of a tank-spotting network that really detected cloudy weather is probably a myth: researchers have found no solid evidence it happened. We no longer need it, as documented examples are plentiful.

sections.key: Testing on genuinely new data and asking what a model is looking at can reveal hidden shortcuts.
sections.b:
Pfungst exposed Clever Hans by changing the conditions: he hid the questioner and used questions nobody in the room knew the answer to. AI researchers use similar tricks. The most important is testing a model on data from different sources than it was trained on, such as X-rays from another hospital or photos from another country. If performance drops sharply, a shortcut may be to blame.

Researchers also use tools that highlight which parts of an input influenced a decision, and they deliberately alter images or text to see whether irrelevant changes flip the answer. Collecting more varied training data, where accidental patterns no longer line up with the answers, makes shortcuts harder to learn.

sections.key: When an AI seems brilliant, ask what exactly it was tested on and what else could explain its success.
sections.b:
The deepest lesson of Clever Hans is about us, not the horse. Von Osten was honest, and the experts who first examined Hans were not fools. They simply did not ask what else might explain the results.

A 2021 review of dozens of published AI models for diagnosing COVID-19 from chest scans found none ready for clinical use, with many suffering from flaws such as biased or mismatched data. Impressive accuracy figures can hide a narrow trick. Whenever you hear that an AI can detect something remarkable, think like Pfungst: what exactly was it tested on, and could it be picking up on something other than what we think?

quiz.q: How did Pfungst show that Hans wasn't really counting?
o: He weighed the horse before each show
He asked Hans harder arithmetic questions
He trained a second horse to compare results
Hans's accuracy collapsed when the questioner didn't know the answer or Hans couldn't see them
quiz.e: Hans relied on unconscious cues from people, so removing those cues removed his accuracy.

quiz.q: What is shortcut learning?
o: A model using an accidental pattern in its data instead of the real signal
A model finishing training faster than expected
A model copying answers from another model
A model ignoring data it does not recognise
quiz.e: Models take the easiest pattern that predicts the answer, even when it is not the one we intended.

quiz.q: Why did the X-ray models perform worse at other hospitals?
o: The new X-rays were lower quality
They had partly learned hospital-specific clues that did not carry over
They were trained on too many images
Doctors at other hospitals disagreed with them
quiz.e: Because the hospital helped predict disease, the models leaned on clues that failed elsewhere.

quiz.q: What is a good way to expose a hidden shortcut?
o: Retest on the same photos several times
Make the model larger
Test on data from different sources than the training data
Ask the model to explain itself in words
quiz.e: A sharp performance drop on genuinely new data suggests the model relied on a shortcut.

quiz.q: What should you ask when an AI seems to do something remarkable?
o: Who built it, and how large is the company
What exactly was it tested on, and could something else explain its success
How fast does it produce answers
Whether it works on a phone
quiz.e: Impressive accuracy can hide a narrow trick, so check what the test really measured.

LESSONS.push: A horse that 'did maths' shows how AI can be right for the wrong reasons.

LESSONS.title: How computers learned to understand speech
LESSONS.hook: Talking to a phone feels effortless now, but getting a machine to hear words took seventy years of clever engineering. Here is how ‘wreck a nice beach’ became ‘recognise speech’.

sections.key: Spoken words run together, vary between speakers and sound alike, so machines first turn sound into a picture called a spectrogram.
sections.b:
Spoken words feel separate, but the sound is mostly a continuous stream with no clear gaps. Each speech sound, or phoneme, changes shape depending on its neighbours, called coarticulation. Accents, speed, mood, noise and microphone quality add more variation, and different phrases can sound almost identical: 'recognise speech' and 'wreck a nice beach'. People resolve these puzzles using knowledge of language and context. A computer starts with only a fast-changing series of air pressure measurements, sampled thousands of times a second.

A key first step is slicing the audio into tiny overlapping pieces and measuring the energy at each frequency. Side by side, these form a spectrogram, a picture with time running left to right and pitch bottom to top. Vowels show as bands, and 's' as high-frequency fuzz.

sections.key: Early recognisers matched whole-word templates, but from the 1970s probability-based models beat hand-written rules.
sections.b:
In 1952 Bell Laboratories built Audrey, which recognised spoken digits from zero to nine, mostly from a voice it had been tuned for. In 1962 IBM showed the Shoebox at the Seattle World's Fair. It understood 16 words, including digits and commands like 'plus' and 'minus', and did simple sums. These machines matched whole-word sound patterns against stored templates, which could never scale to everyday conversation.

In the 1970s the US defence research agency DARPA funded a speech understanding programme, and Carnegie Mellon's Harpy handled about a thousand words. Researchers at IBM and elsewhere then championed hidden Markov models, which calculate probabilities for phonemes and for which word follows another. With enough recorded speech, statistics beat expert rules and dominated for about three decades.

sections.key: Dictation software arrived in the 1990s, and deep neural networks made voice assistants practical around 2010 to 2012.
sections.b:
In 1997 Dragon Systems released Dragon NaturallySpeaking, one of the first products to let ordinary people dictate continuous speech on a home computer without pausing between words. It needed training on your voice and a quiet room, and accuracy still frustrated many users, but it was a milestone, especially for people unable to type easily.

The next leap came around 2010 to 2012, when university and technology teams showed that deep neural networks could cut error rates substantially. Combined with huge amounts of recorded speech and cloud computing, this made smartphone voice assistants and automatic video captions practical for millions of people.

sections.key: Smart speakers listen locally for a short wake word and only then record and send audio elsewhere.
sections.b:
A common worry is that smart speakers constantly record everything. In normal operation they work in two stages. A small, low-power model on the device itself listens continuously, but only for a short wake word, such as the assistant's name. Only when it thinks it has heard that phrase does the device start recording your request and, typically, send it to powerful computers elsewhere for full recognition.

The wake word detector is deliberately simple, so it sometimes triggers by mistake on similar sounds, accidentally capturing snippets of conversation. Most devices let you review and delete recordings and mute the microphone, which is worth knowing if privacy matters to you.

sections.key: Speech recognition works better for some accents, ages and voices than others because systems learn from the recordings they are trained on.
sections.b:
Speech systems learn from the recordings they are trained on. If those recordings mostly feature certain accents, the systems work best for people who sound like that. Studies have found commercial systems making noticeably more errors for some groups, including speakers of particular dialects, people with strong regional or non-native accents, children, older adults and people with speech impairments.

This matters more as voice becomes a way to access services, from banking to medical transcription. Developers are collecting more diverse speech data and letting systems adapt to individual voices, but equal accuracy for everyone remains an unfinished job.

quiz.q: Why is speech so hard for computers to recognise?
o: Words are recorded too slowly
Sound arrives as separate, clearly spaced words
Words run together, vary between speakers and can sound alike
Microphones can't measure air pressure
quiz.e: Speech is a continuous, variable stream, and people rely on context that computers must learn.

quiz.q: Why did the statistical approach beat hand-written rules?
o: Given enough recorded speech, probabilities proved more reliable than expert rules
Statistics needed no recorded speech
Rules could only handle digits
Statistical models ran on tiny devices
quiz.e: Models that calculate probabilities from lots of data handled real speech better than rules written by experts.

quiz.q: What made smartphone voice assistants practical around 2010 to 2012?
o: Smaller microphones
Deep neural networks, huge amounts of recorded speech and cloud computing
Bigger spectrogram pictures
Faster typing keyboards
quiz.e: Deep networks cut error rates, and data plus cloud computing delivered them to millions of phones.

quiz.q: What does a smart speaker do before sending audio anywhere?
o: It records every conversation in the room
It asks you to press a button
It transcribes everything locally
A small on-device model listens only for a short wake word
quiz.e: Full recording and recognition begin only after the device thinks it heard the wake word.

quiz.q: Why does speech recognition work worse for some speakers?
o: Some people speak too quietly
Systems learn from training recordings, so they suit the voices that dominate them
Voices of older people are illegal to record
Microphones only detect certain accents
quiz.e: Less representative training data means more errors for groups who are underrepresented in it.

LESSONS.push: How 'recognise speech' once sounded like 'wreck a nice beach' to a machine.

LESSONS.title: How AI learns: walking downhill in the fog
LESSONS.hook: Behind almost every modern AI lies one surprisingly simple idea: take a small step in the direction that makes your mistakes smaller, then repeat it billions of times.

sections.key: Gradient descent trains a model by repeatedly stepping in the direction that shrinks its loss, the number measuring its mistakes.
sections.b:
Imagine standing on a mountainside in dense fog. You can't see the valley, but you want the lowest point. So you feel the slope underfoot, step in the steepest downhill direction, and repeat. This is gradient descent, the method used to train nearly all modern neural networks. The mountain represents how wrong the model is, and each position is a different setting of its internal numbers.

To measure 'wrong', a model needs a loss function. For house prices, it compares each prediction with the real price and combines the errors into one number. For a language model, the loss measures how surprised it was by the actual next word. The model becomes very good at whatever the loss measures, which isn't always exactly what we want.

sections.key: The gradient tells you, for every parameter at once, which way to turn it to change the loss, so training turns each one slightly downhill.
sections.b: A neural network is controlled by parameters, also called weights, which you can picture as knobs. A small model might have thousands; the largest today have billions or more. Each combination of settings gives a different loss. The gradient, a tool from calculus, tells you for every knob at once which way to turn it, and how strongly, to increase the loss fastest. So you turn every knob a little the opposite way, lowering the loss slightly. The French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy described the method in 1847, long before computers. What changed was the scale.

sections.key: The learning rate sets the size of each step, and a value too small or too large can ruin training.
sections.b: How far should you step each time? The learning rate controls it. Too small, and training crawls. Too large, and you overshoot the valley, leap up the opposite slope and may bounce around wildly or even climb higher, like taking giant strides on that foggy mountain. Engineers spend a lot of effort tuning it. A common practice is to start with larger steps and gradually shrink them, so the model can settle into a good spot.

sections.key: Training works in practice despite rough loss landscapes, and small random batches make each step fast.
sections.b:
Real loss landscapes are full of dips, ridges, plateaus and saddle points, which slope down in some directions and up in others. In theory you could be trapped in a local minimum, a hollow far above the true lowest point. In practice, very large networks seem to train well anyway: with millions of dimensions there is usually some direction still leading down, and many low points are roughly equally good. Why it works so reliably is still being researched.

Checking every training example before each step would be painfully slow. So training uses stochastic gradient descent: each step estimates the slope from a small random batch, perhaps a few hundred examples. The path wobbles, but steps are quick, and the wobble can help avoid getting stuck.

sections.key: Backpropagation efficiently works out how much each weight contributed to the error, and gradient descent then takes the step.
sections.b:
In a deep network with many layers, how do you work out how each of millions of weights contributed to the final error? Backpropagation starts with the error at the output and works backwards, layer by layer, using the chain rule from calculus to share out responsibility for the mistake.

Several people developed versions of the idea, but a 1986 paper by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams made it widely known for training neural networks. Backpropagation calculates the slope; gradient descent takes the step. Repeated over enormous datasets, with clever variations, they are the engine of today's deep learning.

quiz.q: What does the loss function do?
o: It turns the model's errors into a single number that training tries to shrink
It sets how many examples are in each batch
It decides how many layers a network has
It stores the model's final answers
quiz.e: Training needs one number measuring how wrong the model is, so it knows whether a step helped.

quiz.q: What does the gradient tell you about a model's parameters?
o: How many parameters the model needs
Which way and how strongly each one affects the loss, so it can be nudged downhill
Which training examples to delete
How long training will take
quiz.e: The gradient points uphill for every parameter at once, so stepping the opposite way lowers the loss.

quiz.q: What can happen if the learning rate is too large?
o: Training becomes slow but safe
The loss function stops working
The model memorises its data perfectly
Steps overshoot the valley and training may bounce around or get worse
quiz.e: Giant strides can jump straight over the low point, so step size must be tuned.

quiz.q: Why does training use small random batches?
o: Estimating the slope from a batch is far faster than checking every example
Batches make the slope exactly accurate
Random batches remove the need for a loss
Large datasets cannot be stored
quiz.e: Noisy but quick steps add up to steady improvement, and the wobble can even help avoid getting stuck.

quiz.q: How do backpropagation and gradient descent work together?
o: Backpropagation picks the learning rate
Gradient descent calculates the slope and backpropagation takes the step
Backpropagation calculates the slope and gradient descent takes the step
They are two names for the same step
quiz.e: Backpropagation works out each weight's share of the error, and gradient descent uses it to adjust the weights.

LESSONS.push: Modern AI learns by one simple move, repeated billions of times. Think fog.

LESSONS.title: Words as maps: how AI captures meaning
LESSONS.hook: Computers only understand numbers. So how can a machine know that ‘puppy’ is close to ‘dog’ and far from ‘spreadsheet’? The answer is to give every word a place on a giant map.

sections.key: Words used in similar contexts have similar meanings, so giving words arbitrary ID numbers tells a computer nothing.
sections.b:
In 1957 the linguist J. R. Firth wrote: 'You shall know a word by the company it keeps.' You can learn a lot about a word from its neighbours. Meet 'wombok' in 'the wombok was crisp and fresh' and 'she chopped the wombok for the stir-fry', and you'd guess it's a vegetable. 'Coffee' and 'tea' both appear near 'cup', 'hot' and 'morning'.

Computers need numbers, but the simplest scheme, numbering each word, fails. 'Aardvark' is 1, 'abacus' is 2, and the numbers carry no meaning: to such a system 'cat' and 'kitten' are as unrelated as 'cat' and 'carburettor'. Better to give related words related numbers, so what a model learns about 'dog' transfers to 'puppy'.

sections.key: An embedding gives each word a list of numbers that places it on a learned map, where related words sit close together.
sections.b:
The solution is an embedding: a list of numbers, often a few hundred long, acting as coordinates that place each word on an enormous map. An ordinary map needs two numbers; an embedding uses hundreds of dimensions we can't picture, but the mathematics works the same way. 'Sydney', 'Melbourne' and 'Brisbane' cluster in one region, 'happy', 'glad' and 'cheerful' in another. People don't choose the positions. The model learns them from huge amounts of text.

In 2013 a Google team led by Tomas Mikolov released word2vec. Directions on the map seemed to carry meaning: 'king' minus 'man' plus 'woman' landed nearest 'queen'. The famous examples were somewhat selected, and the arithmetic is less neat in general, but meaning had been captured in geometry.

sections.key: Embeddings absorb the stereotypes in the text they learn from, which matters when they are used in real decisions.
sections.b:
Because embeddings learn from human writing, they also learn human prejudices. In 2016 researchers showed that word2vec embeddings trained on news articles completed analogies such as 'man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker'. In 2017 another team found that embeddings reproduced many associations measured in psychological tests of human bias, linking some names, genders and groups with pleasant or unpleasant words.

The embeddings weren't programmed to be biased; they faithfully mapped the patterns in their text. This matters because embeddings sit inside search engines, recruitment tools and recommendation systems, where such associations can quietly shape real decisions. Researchers have developed methods to measure and reduce these effects.

sections.key: Modern models create contextual embeddings, recalculating a word's position for each sentence it appears in.
sections.b:
The original embeddings gave each word one fixed position. But 'bank' means something different in 'river bank' and 'bank loan', and 'bat' could be an animal or cricket gear. One point has to blur these together.

From around 2018, new models, soon dominated by the transformer design, began producing contextual embeddings, where a word's position is recalculated for each sentence using every surrounding word. Today's chatbots work this way. Text is broken into pieces called tokens, each starting with an embedding, and many layers then refine them, mixing in context until the model has a rich representation of the whole passage.

sections.key: Embeddings now represent sentences, images, songs and products, powering search by meaning and recommendations.
sections.b:
The embedding idea spread far beyond single words. Whole sentences and documents can be embedded, so a search engine can find pages matching the meaning of your question even if they share no exact words with it. Songs, products and films can be embedded based on who enjoys them, helping recommendation systems suggest similar items.

Some systems embed images and text into the same shared space, so a photo of a beach lands near the words 'sand and waves', letting you search your photo library by description. Whenever an app finds things that are 'similar' in a way that feels like understanding, there is a good chance it is measuring distances on a learned map.

quiz.q: Why is numbering words 1, 2, 3 a poor way to give them to a computer?
o: The numbers become too large to store
Computers cannot read numbers in order
The numbers carry no information about meaning or similarity
Numbers cannot represent rare words
quiz.e: With arbitrary IDs, 'cat' and 'kitten' look as unrelated as 'cat' and 'carburettor'.

quiz.q: What does an embedding do?
o: Translates a word into another language
Counts how often a word appears in a book
Replaces each word with its dictionary definition
Places each word as a point on a learned map, with related words close together
quiz.e: Positions are learned from text, so words used in similar contexts end up near each other.

quiz.q: Why do embeddings reproduce stereotypes?
o: Engineers deliberately add them
They learn from human writing, which contains those patterns
They only use old books
They cannot tell names from other words
quiz.e: Embeddings faithfully map the patterns in their text, including human prejudices.

quiz.q: How do contextual embeddings differ from the original ones?
o: A word's position is recalculated for each sentence using the surrounding words
They give every word the same position
They work only for single words
They remove tokens from the text
quiz.e: This lets the model separate meanings such as a river bank and a bank loan.

quiz.q: How can embeddings help a search engine?
o: By storing every page word for word
By ranking pages purely by length
By finding pages that match the meaning of your question even without shared words
By blocking unusual searches
quiz.e: Because meaning becomes distance on a map, similar ideas can be found even when the wording differs.

LESSONS.push: To an AI, 'puppy' sits near 'dog' on a map. Here's how words get a place.

LESSONS.title: Expert systems: when AI ran on rules
LESSONS.hook: In the 1980s, the future of AI was supposed to be computers stuffed with the knowledge of human experts. Businesses spent fortunes on it. Then the boom went bust.

sections.key: Expert systems captured a specialist's knowledge as if-then rules, and their power came from specialised knowledge rather than general reasoning.
sections.b:
In the 1960s and 1970s, researchers such as Edward Feigenbaum at Stanford argued for dropping general problem-solvers and focusing on deep knowledge of one narrow field. Interview human experts, write what they know as hundreds or thousands of rules, such as 'if the patient has a fever and a stiff neck, consider meningitis', and let an inference engine chain the rules together. These programs became known as expert systems.

An early success was DENDRAL, begun at Stanford in 1965 with Feigenbaum, geneticist Joshua Lederberg and chemist Carl Djerassi. It helped chemists work back from the fragments of mass spectrometry to a molecule's structure, ranking possible structures. Some results appeared in scientific papers. Its lesson: power came less from clever general reasoning than from specialised knowledge.

sections.key: MYCIN matched specialists at advising on blood infections and could show its reasoning, yet it was never used on real patients.
sections.b:
In the 1970s Edward Shortliffe and colleagues at Stanford built MYCIN, which identified bacteria causing serious blood infections and recommended antibiotics. Several hundred rules carried 'certainty factors', since medical evidence is rarely clear-cut. In a formal evaluation, experts rated its advice as good as or better than that of infectious disease specialists. Yet it was never used in hospitals, because of slow question sessions, the computers of the day and unresolved questions of responsibility if it was wrong.

Its strength was transparency. Asked why it wanted to know something, MYCIN showed the rule it was applying; asked how it reached a conclusion, it listed the chain of rules. Modern neural networks are far harder to interpret, so explainable AI researchers try to recover some of that clarity for medicine, lending and law.

sections.key: In the 1980s expert systems left the laboratory, and one called XCON saved its company tens of millions of dollars a year.
sections.b:
By the early 1980s, expert systems had left the laboratory. A famous example was XCON, developed with Carnegie Mellon University for Digital Equipment Corporation. It configured complex computer orders, working out which cables, cabinets and components a customer's system needed, a job that had produced costly errors. XCON grew to thousands of rules, and the company estimated it saved tens of millions of dollars a year.

Such successes sparked a boom. Companies set up AI departments, start-ups sold specialised hardware and software, and in 1982 Japan launched its ambitious Fifth Generation Computer project, prompting rival government programmes in Britain, Europe and the United States.

sections.key: Getting expert knowledge into rules was slow and fragile, and the resulting systems failed badly outside their narrow domain.
sections.b:
The trouble was getting knowledge in. Experts often cannot fully explain what they do, because much of their skill is intuition built over years. Interviewing them and turning their answers into rules was painstaking, a problem Feigenbaum called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. Systems also became hard to maintain, since a new rule could clash with existing ones in unexpected ways.

And they were brittle. Step slightly outside the narrow domain, or give them a situation their rules did not anticipate, and they could fail badly, with no common sense to fall back on. A medical rule system knew nothing about the world beyond its rules, not even that patients are people.

sections.key: The expert systems market crashed in the late 1980s, but rule-based software lives on and machine learning rose partly in response.
sections.b:
By the late 1980s, expectations had run far ahead of results. The market for specialised AI computers collapsed around 1987, as ordinary desktop machines became powerful enough to do the job more cheaply. Funding was cut, companies folded, and the field entered what became known as the second AI winter.

Yet expert systems never disappeared. Rule-based software still checks insurance claims, flags suspicious bank transactions, calculates tax and guides call centre staff, though rarely under the AI label. Machine learning rose partly as an answer to the knowledge bottleneck: rather than asking experts to write down rules, let computers learn patterns directly from data.

quiz.q: Where did a system like DENDRAL get its power?
o: From clever general reasoning about any problem
From a very fast computer
From specialised knowledge packed into it
From learning on millions of examples
quiz.e: Expert systems showed that deep knowledge of one narrow field could beat general reasoning.

quiz.q: What was a key strength of expert systems like MYCIN?
o: They could show the chain of rules behind a conclusion
They could learn new rules by themselves
They worked well outside their field
They never needed a doctor's input
quiz.e: Explicit rules let users check the reasoning step by step and spot faulty logic.

quiz.q: What did XCON do for Digital Equipment Corporation?
o: It designed new computer chips
It trained sales staff
It configured complex computer orders, saving the company tens of millions of dollars a year
It diagnosed faults in customers' machines
quiz.e: Real business success like XCON helped spark the 1980s expert systems boom.

quiz.q: Why were expert systems called brittle?
o: Their hardware broke easily
Outside their narrow domain they could fail badly, with no common sense to fall back on
They ran too slowly to be useful
Experts refused to use them
quiz.e: Rules covered only what had been anticipated, so unexpected situations caused failures.

quiz.q: How did the expert systems story help shape machine learning?
o: Machine learning copied their rule lists
Experts proved that learning from data was impossible
Rule-based software was banned in banks
Machine learning rose partly as an answer to the knowledge bottleneck, learning patterns from data
quiz.e: Rather than asking experts to write rules, researchers let computers learn patterns directly from data.

LESSONS.push: In the 1980s, firms spent fortunes bottling human expertise. Then the boom went bust.

LESSONS.title: The bitter lesson: why scale keeps winning
LESSONS.hook: For seventy years, researchers have tried to make AI smarter by teaching it what humans know. Again and again, they were beaten by simpler methods with more computing power. One famous essay asked what that means.

sections.key: Sutton argued that general methods which scale with computation eventually beat methods built on human knowledge.
sections.b:
In March 2019, Rich Sutton, a pioneer of reinforcement learning, published a short essay called ‘The Bitter Lesson’. His claim: looking back over decades of AI research, general methods that make the most of computation, chiefly search and learning, win by a large margin in the end.

Researchers kept building in their own understanding, such as how chess masters think or how language works. It helped in the short term and felt satisfying. But it plateaued, and was overtaken by methods that simply scaled up. That is why the lesson is ‘bitter’: it suggests much of that careful effort is wasted. Sutton later shared the Turing Award, computing’s highest honour, with Andrew Barto.

sections.key: Methods that improve with more computation keep gaining almost automatically, and their gains follow predictable curves.
sections.b:
The engine behind the lesson is the long fall in the cost of computation. For decades the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubled every couple of years, a trend known as Moore’s law, and specialised AI chips have added more. A method that improves with more computation gets better almost automatically. One built on hand-crafted human knowledge improves only as fast as people can write that knowledge down.

Scaling can even be forecast. In 2020, OpenAI researchers reported that a language model’s error falls along a smooth power-law curve as size, data and computation grow. In 2022, DeepMind’s Chinchilla work showed many large models had too little data for their size.

sections.key: In chess and Go, raw search and self-play eventually beat approaches built on human expertise.
sections.b:
Chess was the first clear example. Many researchers hoped to win by capturing how grandmasters understand the board. Instead, IBM’s Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 largely through enormous search, examining huge numbers of positions per second, combined with expert-tuned evaluation.

Go repeated the story with a twist. In 2016, DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, having learned partly from human games and partly from playing itself. The following year, AlphaGo Zero learned purely from self-play, given nothing but the rules, and became stronger still. Human knowledge had been a helpful crutch that was eventually not needed.

sections.key: In speech and vision, systems that learned from data and computation overtook ones built on expert-designed knowledge.
sections.b:
The same pattern played out elsewhere. Early speech recognition tried to apply linguistic knowledge about how words and sounds work. From the 1970s, statistical methods that learned probabilities from recorded speech pulled ahead, and deep neural networks took over in the 2010s.

In computer vision, researchers spent years hand-designing features, carefully engineered methods for detecting edges, corners and textures. Then in 2012, a deep network that learned its own features from over a million labelled images beat them decisively. Each time, the experts’ knowledge was genuine and hard-won. It just mattered less than a general learning method with enough data and computation.

sections.key: Critics say scale alone has limits, and whether it will keep delivering is still hotly debated.
sections.b:
The bitter lesson has thoughtful critics. Successful methods do contain human insight: convolutional networks for vision build in the idea that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears in an image, and that idea came from people.

There are practical limits too. High-quality data is finite, and training ever larger models consumes vast amounts of money, electricity and chips. Some researchers argue that current systems still struggle with reliable reasoning, learning from few examples and understanding the physical world, and that new ideas, not just more scale, will be needed. Even so, the past decade’s biggest leaps came less from elegant theories of intelligence than from learning methods scaled to a size earlier generations could barely imagine.

quiz.q: What is the main claim of Sutton’s ‘Bitter Lesson’ essay?
o: General methods that scale with computation tend to win in the long run
Expert knowledge should always be built into AI systems first
AI progress depends mainly on cleverly designed algorithms
Search methods are better than learning methods in every field
quiz.e: Over decades, methods that make the most of growing computation overtook those built on human understanding.

quiz.q: Why does a method that scales with computation have a long-term advantage?
o: It improves almost automatically as computing gets cheaper and faster
It needs far less data than hand-crafted systems
It copies human reasoning more accurately over time
It avoids any need for large amounts of electricity
quiz.e: Falling computing costs compound over decades, while hand-written knowledge grows only as fast as people can write it down.

quiz.q: What did AlphaGo Zero show about human knowledge in Go?
o: It learned purely from self-play and became stronger than earlier versions
It needed a larger library of human games to improve
It could only win when experts tuned its evaluation
It played best when copying famous human strategies
quiz.e: Without any human games, self-play alone produced a stronger player, so human knowledge was not essential.

quiz.q: What happened in computer vision around 2012?
o: A deep network that learned its own features beat hand-designed ones
Engineers perfected hand-designed edge and corner detectors
Speech methods were adapted to recognise images
Researchers abandoned large labelled image sets
quiz.e: Learning features from a million labelled images outperformed years of expert feature engineering.

quiz.q: Which is a criticism of relying on scale alone?
o: High-quality data is finite and huge models cost vast resources
Larger models always get worse at reasoning tasks
Human insight plays no part in successful methods
Computing power has stopped getting cheaper entirely
quiz.e: Data limits, costs and gaps in reasoning are why some researchers think new ideas are needed too.

LESSONS.push: For seventy years, clever AI lost to brute force. What does that tell us?

LESSONS.title: The Rosetta Stone: cracking the code of the pharaohs
LESSONS.hook: For fourteen centuries nobody on Earth could read an Egyptian hieroglyph. Then a broken slab of stone and a stubborn young Frenchman changed everything.

sections.key: The Rosetta Stone carried one decree in three scripts, so readable Greek could unlock the unreadable Egyptian.
sections.b:
In July 1799, during Napoleon’s invasion of Egypt, French soldiers rebuilding a fort near Rashid (Rosetta) in the Nile Delta noticed a dark block covered in writing. It was a broken slab of granodiorite, a little over a metre tall, with three bands of text.

The text was an ordinary decree from priests at Memphis in 196 BC, praising the young king Ptolemy V. What mattered was the format: hieroglyphs, Demotic (the everyday cursive script) and ancient Greek. Scholars could read Greek, so it could act as a crib for the other two. The British took the stone in 1801 under the terms of surrender, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

sections.key: Hieroglyphs stayed unreadable for centuries because scholars wrongly assumed they were mystical symbols, not sounds.
sections.b:
Hieroglyphs were used for over three thousand years, but as Egypt became part of the Greek, Roman and Christian world, fewer people learnt them. The last known inscription was carved at the temple of Philae in AD 394, and the knowledge vanished.

For centuries, European scholars believed each picture stood for a deep idea. In the seventeenth century, Athanasius Kircher published elaborate translations that were pure invention. That assumption was the real barrier. While people looked for hidden philosophy in every owl and reed, they could not see that many signs simply spelt out sounds, like letters. Even with the Greek crib, cracking the code took more than twenty years.

sections.key: Matching royal names in oval cartouches to the Greek text revealed that hieroglyphs could spell sounds.
sections.b:
Some hieroglyphs were enclosed in an oval ring, now called a cartouche. Scholars suspected these held royal names. In the 1810s, the English polymath Thomas Young, a physicist and doctor, showed that one cartouche matched the name Ptolemy in the Greek text, and he identified several sounds correctly. But he believed sound signs were used mainly for foreign names.

Then a second inscription helped. An obelisk from Philae carried the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra, which share the letters p, t, o and l. Where the same signs appeared in the same positions in both cartouches, that was strong evidence of an alphabet-like system.

sections.key: Champollion proved in 1822 that sound signs were used throughout the script, even for native Egyptian names.
sections.b:
Jean-François Champollion, a French linguist, had studied languages obsessively since boyhood, including Coptic, the late form of Egyptian still used in Christian church services. In 1822, he studied cartouches copied from temples such as Abu Simbel. One began with a sun disc. In Coptic, the word for sun was ‘re’. It ended with signs he already read as ‘s’, and between them was a sign he linked to the Coptic word for birth, ‘mise’.

Together they spelt Ramesses, a truly Egyptian pharaoh, not a Greek one. Sound signs were used throughout the script. A family story says he rushed to his brother’s office, cried that he had done it, and collapsed.

sections.key: Hieroglyphs mix sound signs and whole-word signs, with silent determinatives and no written vowels.
sections.b:
Champollion announced his results in a famous letter in September 1822, and the decades that followed confirmed and refined them. Hieroglyphic writing proved to be a clever mixture. Some signs stand for a single consonant, some for two or three consonants together, and some for a whole word.

Many words end with a silent sign called a determinative, which tells the reader what kind of thing is meant. A pair of walking legs might mark a verb of movement, while a seated man marks a person. Vowels were usually not written, which is why scholars still argue over how names were pronounced. Once the system was understood, temple walls, tomb paintings and papyri could finally speak again.

quiz.q: Why was the Rosetta Stone so valuable to scholars?
o: The same decree appeared in Greek, which they could already read
It contained a long history of the pharaohs
It was the oldest known example of hieroglyphs
It explained the rules of Egyptian grammar directly
quiz.e: Because the three texts said the same thing, the known Greek could serve as a crib for the other two scripts.

quiz.q: What was the main barrier to reading hieroglyphs for centuries?
o: Scholars assumed the signs were mystical symbols, not sounds
No example of the script survived anywhere in Egypt
The signs were too faint to copy accurately
Greek scholars refused to study the script
quiz.e: Looking for hidden philosophy in every picture stopped people noticing that many signs spelt out sounds.

quiz.q: What did comparing the Ptolemy and Cleopatra cartouches suggest?
o: The script had an alphabet-like system of sound signs
Cartouches only ever held names of gods
Every sign stood for one whole word
Greek names were written in a different script
quiz.e: The same signs appeared in the same positions in shared letters, which pointed to signs for sounds.

quiz.q: Why did the name Ramesses matter for Champollion’s breakthrough?
o: It showed sound signs were used for native Egyptian names too
It proved the Greek text was a faithful translation
It was the first name found on the stone itself
It showed Coptic had nothing to do with Egyptian
quiz.e: A purely Egyptian name spelt with sound signs showed the principle applied throughout the script, not just to foreign names.

quiz.q: What does a determinative do in hieroglyphic writing?
o: It is a silent sign showing what kind of thing a word means
It marks the vowels that the writer left out
It stands for two or three consonants together
It shows the end of a royal name
quiz.e: Determinatives give meaning clues, such as a seated man for a person, without being pronounced.

LESSONS.push: For fourteen centuries no one could read Egyptian. A broken slab changed that.

LESSONS.title: 1066: the year England changed hands
LESSONS.hook: In a single autumn, England's king fought two invasions, marched hundreds of kilometres and died on a ridge in Sussex. The country that came out the other side would never be the same.

sections.key: When Edward the Confessor died childless in 1066, three men claimed the English throne.
sections.b:
Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 without children and with no obvious heir. The English council quickly chose Harold Godwinson, the richest and most powerful earl in the kingdom, and he was crowned the very next day.

Two other men believed the crown was theirs. William, Duke of Normandy, a distant relative of Edward, claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn an oath to support him. Across the North Sea, Harald Hardrada, King of Norway and one of the most famous warriors of his age, claimed it through an older agreement between earlier kings. Both began preparing invasions, and Harold had to guard a long coastline without knowing who would strike first.

sections.key: Harold beat the Norwegians in the north, but three days later William landed in the south.
sections.b:
Harold spent the summer waiting for William on the south coast, but the Normans were held in port by unfavourable winds. In September, with supplies low, Harold sent much of his army home.

Almost immediately, Harald Hardrada landed in the north with a large fleet, joined by Harold’s exiled brother, Tostig. They defeated the northern earls at Fulford on 20 September. Harold marched north astonishingly fast and surprised the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. It was a crushing victory: Hardrada and Tostig were both killed, and the age of great Viking invasions of England is often said to end there. Three days later, on 28 September, William’s army landed at Pevensey in Sussex.

sections.key: At Hastings the English shield wall held all day, until the line thinned and Harold fell.
sections.b:
Harold raced south again and took up a strong position on a ridge about ten kilometres from Hastings, where the town of Battle stands today. His soldiers formed a shield wall, a dense line of overlapping shields bristling with spears and long-handled Dane axes. William’s army combined archers, heavy infantry and mounted knights.

All day on 14 October the Normans attacked uphill, and all day the wall held. A rumour spread that William was dead, and he reportedly lifted his helmet to show his men his face. Norman accounts describe retreats, some panicked and some possibly feigned, that lured English soldiers off the ridge to be cut down. By evening Harold was dead, along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine, and the remaining army collapsed.

sections.key: The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery that tells the story of 1066, and what it shows of Harold’s death is debated.
sections.b:
The Bayeux Tapestry is not technically a tapestry. Tapestries are woven; this is embroidery, with coloured woollen threads stitched onto strips of linen. It is around seventy metres long and half a metre tall, and tells the story like a comic strip. It was likely commissioned by Bishop Odo, William’s half-brother, and many historians think English embroiderers made it. It shows over six hundred people, horses, ships, Halley’s Comet and a few rude figures in the margins. Its final section is lost.

The famous image of Harold’s death, a figure grasping an arrow near his eye, is debated. It may be Harold, or the man beside him cut down by a knight, or both. The tapestry was also restored in the nineteenth century, which may have altered the arrow.

sections.key: The Conquest replaced England’s ruling class, reshaped its landscape and left its mark on the English language.
sections.b:
William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, but conquest took years. Rebellions in the north were met with the Harrying of the North in 1069 and 1070, a campaign of deliberate destruction that caused famine across a huge region.

Within a generation, almost every great English landholder had been replaced by a Norman or other Frenchman. Castles of earth and timber, then stone, appeared across the country, including the Tower of London. At Christmas 1085, William ordered the Domesday Book, an extraordinary survey of who owned what across most of England. French became the language of the court for centuries, which is why English has paired words: cow and beef, pig and pork, sheep and mutton.

quiz.q: Why was the English throne contested in 1066?
o: Edward the Confessor died childless, and three men claimed the crown
Harold Godwinson had no support among the English council
The crown had already been promised to Norway by treaty
Edward left a will naming William of Normandy king
quiz.e: With no obvious heir, Harold, William and Hardrada each claimed the throne.

quiz.q: Why was Harold’s position so difficult in September 1066?
o: He had to fight a northern invasion, then face William in the south
He had disbanded his whole army before Hardrada landed
William had already captured London by then
His brother Tostig had joined the Normans
quiz.e: Harold’s victory at Stamford Bridge came only days before William landed at Pevensey, leaving his army exhausted.

quiz.q: How did the Normans finally break the English line at Hastings?
o: Retreats, some possibly feigned, drew soldiers off the ridge
A surprise night attack on the English camp
Heavy cavalry charged straight through the shield wall
William’s archers destroyed the line from afar
quiz.e: The shield wall held all day, but men lured downhill could be cut off, and the line slowly thinned.

quiz.q: Why is the Bayeux Tapestry not strictly a tapestry?
o: It is embroidery stitched onto linen, not woven
It is painted on long strips of cloth
It was made in Normandy by monks
It is far too short to count as one
quiz.e: Tapestries are woven, while this work is stitched with woollen thread onto linen.

quiz.q: Why does English have pairs like cow and beef, or pig and pork?
o: French became the language of the court for centuries after 1066
Latin replaced English in all farming terms
Norman farmers invented new animal breeds
Domesday clerks renamed foods for tax records
quiz.e: The Norman ruling class spoke French, so English kept both words, often one for the animal and one for the meat.

LESSONS.push: In one autumn, England’s king fought two invasions. How did it end?

LESSONS.title: Cleopatra: the last pharaoh
LESSONS.hook: She has been painted as a seductress for two thousand years, mostly by her enemies. The real Cleopatra was a scholar-queen fighting to keep her country alive.

sections.key: Cleopatra belonged to a Greek-speaking dynasty founded by one of Alexander the Great’s generals.
sections.b:
Cleopatra VII was born in 69 BC, but her family story begins with Alexander the Great. After Alexander died, one of his generals, Ptolemy, took control of Egypt and founded a dynasty. For nearly three hundred years the Ptolemies ruled from Alexandria, the glittering Greek city on the Mediterranean coast. They presented themselves to Egyptians as pharaohs, but they spoke Greek and often married their own siblings to keep power in the family.

Here is a perspective worth sitting with: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. To her, the pyramids were already ancient monuments, more than two thousand years old.

sections.key: Ancient sources describe Cleopatra as charming, multilingual and politically skilled, not as a famous beauty.
sections.b:
Hollywood made Cleopatra a famous beauty, but the ancient evidence points elsewhere. The Greek writer Plutarch, who drew on earlier sources, said her beauty was not in itself incomparable, but her presence was captivating, her conversation charming and her voice delightful.

He reported that she spoke many languages and could talk to foreign envoys without interpreters. According to Plutarch, she was the first of her dynasty to bother learning Egyptian, the language of the people she ruled. Her coins show a strong hooked nose and a firm chin, though coin portraits were also political images. Educated in Alexandria, one of the great centres of learning in the ancient world, she ruled as a skilled, calculating politician.

sections.key: Cleopatra won back her throne by allying with Julius Caesar.
sections.b:
Cleopatra came to power around 51 BC as co-ruler with her younger brother, Ptolemy XIII, but his advisers soon drove her out. She raised an army, and the siblings were at war when Julius Caesar arrived in Alexandria in 48 BC, chasing his Roman rival Pompey.

Cleopatra needed to reach Caesar without being caught by her brother’s men. Plutarch says she was smuggled into the palace by boat at dusk, hidden inside a bag for bedding, the origin of the later legend about a carpet. Caesar took her side. After months of fighting in the city, Ptolemy XIII drowned while fleeing, and Cleopatra was restored to the throne. She later bore a son, Ptolemy Caesar, nicknamed Caesarion.

sections.key: Cleopatra’s partnership with Mark Antony ended in defeat at the Battle of Actium in 31 BC.
sections.b:
Cleopatra was in Rome when Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC, and she quickly returned to Egypt. Mark Antony now controlled Rome’s eastern provinces. In 41 BC he summoned her to Tarsus, in modern Turkey. Plutarch describes her arriving on a barge with a gilded stern, purple sails and silver oars, dressed as the goddess Aphrodite. Whatever the exact details, it was political theatre, and it worked. They became partners in power and in private, and she had three children with him.

In 34 BC, Antony handed territories to Cleopatra and her children, and his rival Octavian used this as proof that Antony had betrayed Rome to a foreign queen. At the naval Battle of Actium in 31 BC, their fleet was beaten.

sections.key: Cleopatra’s enemies shaped her image, but she spent her reign trying to keep Egypt independent.
sections.b:
A year after Actium, Octavian’s armies closed in on Alexandria. Antony, believing Cleopatra was already dead, stabbed himself. Cleopatra died in August 30 BC, aged thirty-nine, rather than be paraded through Rome as a captive. The famous story says an asp, smuggled to her in a basket of figs, bit her. Yet even Plutarch admitted nobody knew the truth, and some historians think poison is more likely. Caesarion was later killed on Octavian’s orders.

Egypt became a Roman province, ending three thousand years of pharaohs. Because Octavian won, his version dominated, and Roman poets painted Cleopatra as a drunken, power-hungry foreigner. Historians today see a ruler who used money, diplomacy and alliances to keep Egypt independent. Her tomb has never been found.

quiz.q: What was the background of the dynasty Cleopatra belonged to?
o: Greek-speaking rulers from Alexander’s general
Native Egyptian priests who seized power
Roman governors appointed by the Senate
Phoenician merchants who ruled from Carthage
quiz.e: The Ptolemies were Greek rulers who presented themselves to Egyptians as pharaohs.

quiz.q: What does the ancient evidence suggest was Cleopatra’s real strength?
o: Her intelligence, charm and languages
Her reputation as the most beautiful woman alive
Her skill as a general leading armies in battle
Her habit of ruling without any allies
quiz.e: Plutarch stressed her captivating presence, conversation and languages rather than her looks.

quiz.q: Why did Cleopatra ally with Julius Caesar?
o: She needed him to help her regain the throne from her brother
He had promised to make Egypt a Roman province
Her brother had asked her to negotiate for him
She wanted Rome to protect Alexandria from Antony
quiz.e: Ousted by her brother’s advisers, she gained a powerful ally, and Caesar took her side.

quiz.q: Why did Antony’s gift of territories hurt him politically?
o: Octavian used it to argue Antony had betrayed Rome to a foreign queen
It made Cleopatra Rome’s official ruler
It drained Egypt of money and soldiers
Antony’s own army refused to support it
quiz.e: Octavian turned the ceremony in Alexandria into propaganda against Antony in Rome.

quiz.q: Why is the popular image of Cleopatra so unreliable?
o: Octavian won, so his hostile version of her dominated
No ancient writer ever mentioned her
Her own writings were widely believed fakes
She was invented by later playwrights
quiz.e: The victors told the story, so later writers inherited a picture shaped by her enemies.

LESSONS.push: Cleopatra’s famous looks may be the least reliable part of her story.

LESSONS.title: The real life of a medieval knight
LESSONS.hook: Forget cranes lifting clanking men onto horses. Real knights were trained athletes, expensive to equip, and often far less chivalrous than the stories suggest.

sections.key: Knighthood was earned through years of service, usually starting as a page at around seven.
sections.b:
Becoming a knight was not a matter of simply buying a sword. In the classic pattern, a boy from a noble family was sent at around seven to serve in another lord’s household as a page. He learnt manners, riding, basic weapon handling and how to serve at table.

At around fourteen he became a squire, attached to a knight whose armour he cleaned, whose horses he tended and whom he followed onto the battlefield. If he proved himself, he might be dubbed a knight around twenty-one, sometimes in a solemn ceremony and sometimes in a hurry on the eve of battle. Ages varied a great deal, but the idea was constant: knighthood was earned through years of service.

sections.key: A knight was costly military equipment, so lords supported knights with land.
sections.b:
A knight was in many ways a very expensive piece of military equipment. He needed armour, a sword, a lance, a shield, squires and servants, and above all horses. The finest warhorses, called destriers, were specially bred and trained for the noise and violence of battle, and could cost many times the price of an ordinary horse. He also needed riding horses for travel and pack horses for baggage.

This is why knights were usually supported by land. In return for military service, a lord granted them estates whose peasants produced the income. The cost was so heavy that, by the 1200s, the English crown was ordering qualified landowners to become knights, and many paid fines to avoid it.

sections.key: Armour was lighter than the myth suggests, and painted shield designs identified knights in battle.
sections.b:
Films show knights hoisted onto horses by cranes, helpless if they fell. That is a myth, popularised in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. A complete suit of plate armour, at its peak in the 1400s, typically weighed twenty to twenty-five kilograms, less than many modern soldiers carry. Because the weight was spread across the body, a fit man could run, mount a horse and get up after a fall. The real cost was stamina: experiments with volunteers in replica armour found walking and running took roughly twice the energy.

Full-face helmets from the twelfth century made knights hard to identify, so they painted bold designs on shields and on the cloth surcoats worn over armour, hence ‘coat of arms’. These became hereditary, tracked by heralds. Many modern logos still borrow the look.

sections.key: Tournaments began as near-real war and became a route to fortune and fame.
sections.b:
Tournaments started in the eleventh and twelfth centuries as something close to real war. Teams of knights charged each other across open countryside in a mêlée, capturing opponents and holding them for ransom. People were injured and killed, and the Church repeatedly condemned them.

For a skilled but landless knight, though, they were a path to fortune. William Marshal, an English knight of the late twelfth century, reportedly captured hundreds of opponents and rose to become one of the most powerful men in England. Later tournaments became more organised and theatrical, with jousting, in which two knights charged each other with lances, often separated by a barrier. Champions became celebrities, and spectators watched from decorated stands.

sections.key: Chivalry mostly applied between knights, while ordinary people often suffered cruelty.
sections.b:
Chivalry described an ideal knight: brave, loyal to his lord, generous, courteous and devoted to the Church. Poets and romances about King Arthur and his knights spread these values, and many knights took them seriously. Rules of conduct also had practical benefits, since a captured noble was usually worth more alive, for ransom, than dead.

But chivalry mostly applied between knights. Ordinary soldiers and peasants often received no such mercy. Medieval armies regularly practised the chevauchée, a raid that deliberately burned villages and crops to ruin an enemy’s economy. The gap between the ideal and reality was obvious even at the time, and many medieval writers criticised knights for their cruelty and greed.

quiz.q: How did a boy typically become a knight in the classic pattern?
o: Years of service as a page, then a squire
Inheriting the title automatically at birth
Buying a sword and armour at around fourteen
Passing a written exam set by the king
quiz.e: Knighthood was earned through long service in another lord’s household, not simply bought.

quiz.q: Why were knights usually supported with land?
o: Their armour, horses and servants were very costly
Land was the only thing the crown could pay with
Peasants refused to serve under landless knights
Knights were forbidden to earn money any other way
quiz.e: Estates, worked by peasants, produced the income needed to pay for the knight’s equipment.

quiz.q: What does modern evidence show about knights in plate armour?
o: They could run, mount horses and rise after a fall
They needed cranes to be lifted onto horses
They could barely walk because of its weight
They wore it only for ceremonies
quiz.e: A suit weighed about twenty to twenty-five kilograms, spread across the body, so a fit man could move freely.

quiz.q: Why did tournaments appeal to a skilled but landless knight?
o: Capturing opponents for ransom could bring wealth and status
Winning gave automatic ownership of an estate
The Church rewarded the best fighters
They were the only way to be knighted
quiz.e: Ransom from captured knights, as in William Marshal’s career, could make a fortune.

quiz.q: How did chivalry work in practice?
o: It mostly applied between knights, not to peasants
It protected every person in a war zone, whatever their rank
It forbade all raids on enemy farmland and villages
It was never taken seriously by any knight at all
quiz.e: Courtesy was reserved for fellow nobles, while raids like the chevauchée devastated ordinary communities.

LESSONS.push: Medieval knights weren’t helpless in armour. What was the real cost?

LESSONS.title: Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot
LESSONS.hook: He was a minor king who died as a teenager. That is exactly why his tomb survived, and why its discovery in 1922 stunned the world.

sections.key: Tutankhamun was a minor king who restored Egypt’s old gods and died at about eighteen or nineteen.
sections.b:
Tutankhamun ruled Egypt for only about nine or ten years in the fourteenth century BC, coming to the throne at around eight or nine. His father was very probably Akhenaten, the pharaoh who abandoned Egypt’s traditional gods to worship a single sun disc, the Aten. The boy was originally named Tutankhaten, meaning living image of the Aten.

Early in his reign, guided by powerful advisers, the court restored the old gods, and his name was changed to Tutankhamun, honouring the god Amun. He died at around eighteen or nineteen. To later Egyptians, he was a footnote, and later kings even left his name off official lists.

sections.key: After years of fruitless digging, Howard Carter found Tutankhamun’s tomb in November 1922.
sections.b:
By the early twentieth century, most archaeologists believed the Valley of the Kings had given up all its secrets. Howard Carter, an English archaeologist, disagreed. Small finds bearing Tutankhamun’s name convinced him that the king’s tomb was still out there. His sponsor, the fifth Earl of Carnarvon, was ready to stop paying by 1922, but Carter persuaded him to fund one final season.

On 4 November 1922, workers uncovered a stone step cut into the bedrock, leading to a sealed doorway. On 26 November, Carter made a small hole and held up a candle. Asked whether he could see anything, he later recalled replying that he could see wonderful things: gilded couches, statues, chests and chariots, in a room no one had entered for over three thousand years.

sections.key: Robbers entered the tomb, but it was soon resealed and forgotten, so most of its contents survived.
sections.b:
Tutankhamun’s tomb was not untouched. Evidence showed that robbers broke in at least once, and probably twice, soon after the burial. They took small, easily carried valuables such as oils and metal objects before officials found the break-in, tidied up and resealed it.

Then luck intervened. Flood debris and the rubble and huts of workers digging later tombs, including that of Ramesses VI, buried the entrance, and it was forgotten. The tomb itself was small, possibly a private tomb adapted in a hurry after his unexpected death. Yet it held over five thousand objects, and recording, conserving and removing them took Carter and his team about a decade.

sections.key: Everyday objects in the tomb reveal as much about Egyptian royal life as the gold does.
sections.b:
The best known treasure is the funerary mask, made of gold inlaid with glass and semi-precious stones and weighing about ten kilograms. The king’s body lay inside three nested coffins, the innermost of solid gold and weighing over a hundred kilograms, enclosed within a stone sarcophagus and four gilded wooden shrines.

But many of the most revealing objects were ordinary: chariots, bows, walking sticks, board games, linen underwear, sandals, jars of food and wine, and a lock of hair that belonged to his grandmother, Queen Tiye. There were even two tiny mummified daughters, stillborn babies buried with their father. Together these objects let historians see an Egyptian royal life in unusual detail.

sections.key: The pharaoh’s curse was a newspaper invention, and how Tutankhamun died is still unresolved.
sections.b:
In April 1923, just months after the opening, Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo. A mosquito bite, which he had accidentally nicked while shaving, became infected. Newspapers competing for stories spread the idea of a pharaoh’s curse, and novelists such as Arthur Conan Doyle encouraged it.

No curse inscription was found in the tomb. Howard Carter, who spent the most time inside, lived until 1939. Later studies comparing people present at the opening with others found no sign that they died earlier. How Tutankhamun himself died is still debated. Scans and DNA studies have pointed to a broken leg, a foot deformity and evidence of malaria, but no single cause is agreed.

quiz.q: What changed in Egyptian religion early in Tutankhamun’s reign?
o: The court restored the traditional gods abandoned by Akhenaten
A single sun disc was made the only god
Amun was removed from official worship
Egypt adopted gods from neighbouring lands
quiz.e: His name changed from Tutankhaten to Tutankhamun as worship of Amun and the old gods returned.

quiz.q: What kept Carter searching despite years without results?
o: Small finds bearing the king’s name
A map left behind by an earlier explorer
Carnarvon’s promise of unlimited funds
Records placing the tomb under Ramesses VI
quiz.e: Those small finds convinced him the king’s tomb was still in the Valley of the Kings.

quiz.q: Why did most of the treasure survive in the tomb?
