o: The entrance was buried and forgotten
Robbers never found the burial chamber at all
Priests removed the most valuable items first
It was hidden deep inside a great pyramid
quiz.e: Robbers took only small items, and later rubble covered the entrance, so the tomb stayed hidden for over three thousand years.

quiz.q: Why did ordinary objects in the tomb matter to historians?
o: They revealed everyday royal life in unusual detail
They proved the gold was not genuine
They were more valuable than the gold items
They showed the tomb had been robbed
quiz.e: Chariots, games, sandals and food jars show how an Egyptian king lived, not just how he was buried.

quiz.q: What does the evidence say about the pharaoh’s curse?
o: No curse was found, and those present at the opening did not die earlier
Carter and all his team died within a year
A curse inscription sat above the entrance
Carnarvon died from an ancient poison
quiz.e: Carnarvon died of an infection, Carter lived until 1939, and studies found no unusual early deaths.

LESSONS.push: A minor king’s tomb survived 3,000 years. Its obscurity was the secret.

LESSONS.title: Hannibal: the general who crossed the Alps
LESSONS.hook: He marched elephants over the Alps and destroyed Roman armies one after another. So why did Rome, not Hannibal, win the war?

sections.key: Carthage’s Barca family wanted revenge after Rome won the First Punic War, and Hannibal inherited that aim.
sections.b:
In the third century BC, Rome, a rising land power that controlled most of Italy, faced Carthage, a wealthy trading city founded by Phoenicians in what is now Tunisia. The Romans called Carthaginians Poeni, hence the Punic Wars. In the first, from 264 to 241 BC, Rome, which had barely had a navy, built fleets almost from scratch and won. Carthage lost Sicily and paid a huge indemnity.

Hamilcar Barca then conquered territory in Spain. His son Hannibal grew up in military camps there. Ancient historians tell how the nine-year-old swore at an altar never to be a friend of Rome. He took command at about twenty-six in 221 BC, and in 218 BC the Second Punic War began.

sections.key: Hannibal attacked overland through the Alps, arriving in Italy with a fraction of his army.
sections.b:
Rome controlled the sea, so Hannibal attacked overland, which no one expected. In 218 BC he led his army from Spain across the Pyrenees, through southern Gaul and over the Rhône, with war elephants ferried on rafts. Late in the year, he crossed the Alps.

The journey took about fifteen days in the mountains, through snow, landslides and ambushes by local tribes. Polybius, who wrote within living memory and claimed to have walked the route, says Hannibal reached Italy with about twenty thousand infantry and six thousand cavalry, a fraction of the force that had left Spain. Most of the elephants died soon after. Which pass he used is still debated.

sections.key: At Cannae, Hannibal’s weak centre drew the Romans into an encirclement that destroyed their army.
sections.b:
Hannibal defeated the Romans at the Trebia in 218 BC, then ambushed an army in fog beside Lake Trasimene in 217. Rome responded under Quintus Fabius Maximus, who avoided pitched battle and shadowed Hannibal, earning the nickname Cunctator, the delayer. Frustrated Romans abandoned that approach.

In 216 BC at Cannae, a huge Roman army attacked. Hannibal placed his weakest troops in the centre, which bent backwards under pressure as planned, drawing the Romans in. His heavy infantry then closed in from both sides while his cavalry struck from behind. The Romans were surrounded and slaughtered. Ancient sources give fifty thousand or more dead, and military academies still study the battle.

sections.key: Rome survived Cannae because its allies mostly stayed loyal and Hannibal lacked the means to take the city.
sections.b:
After Cannae, many expected Rome to surrender. It did not. The Senate refused to discuss peace, raised new legions, and returned to Fabius’s careful strategy. Hannibal hoped Rome’s Italian allies would desert in large numbers. Some, including Capua, did, but most of central Italy stayed loyal and kept supplying men and money.

Hannibal lacked siege equipment and reinforcements to attack Rome, and Carthage sent him little help. He stayed in Italy about fifteen years, undefeated in major battle yet unable to finish the war. Meanwhile a brilliant young Roman general, Publius Cornelius Scipio, conquered Carthaginian Spain and invaded North Africa, forcing Carthage to recall Hannibal to defend his home city.

sections.key: Scipio beat Hannibal at Zama in 202 BC, and Rome later destroyed Carthage, though not by sowing it with salt.
sections.b:
In 202 BC, Scipio and Hannibal met at Zama in North Africa. Scipio had learnt from his enemy, opening lanes in his lines for Hannibal’s charging elephants to pass through harmlessly, and his cavalry won the day. Carthage surrendered, gave up its fleet and overseas empire, and paid heavy tribute. Scipio was honoured with the name Africanus.

Hannibal led Carthage’s government for a time, then fled into exile in the East, and around 183 BC took poison rather than be handed to the Romans. In the Third Punic War, Rome besieged and destroyed Carthage in 146 BC. The popular story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt, however, appears to be a modern invention.

quiz.q: Why did the Barca family want another war with Rome?
o: Carthage lost Sicily and paid a huge indemnity
Rome had destroyed Carthage’s capital city
Carthage had been denied access to Spain
Rome had killed Hannibal’s father in battle
quiz.e: Defeat in the First Punic War left Carthage humiliated, which fuelled the desire for revenge.

quiz.q: Why was Hannibal’s route over the Alps surprising?
o: Rome controlled the sea and expected no overland attack
It was the shortest road from Spain to Rome
Roman armies had been defending the passes
The Alps were not yet considered difficult
quiz.e: Since Rome held the sea, an attack through the Alps was unexpected, though it cost him much of his army.

quiz.q: How did Hannibal win at Cannae?
o: His centre gave way, drawing Romans into an encirclement
He attacked the Roman camp at night
His elephants broke the Roman line
He ambushed the Romans in fog
quiz.e: The weak centre bent back as planned, and infantry and cavalry closed around the Romans.

quiz.q: Why did Rome survive after Cannae?
o: Most allies stayed loyal and Hannibal lacked help
Carthage signed a peace treaty immediately
The Alps blocked Hannibal’s retreat
Rome had beaten Hannibal’s army soon after
quiz.e: Rome refused peace, its allies kept supplying men, and Hannibal could not attack the city itself.

quiz.q: What does the story of salting Carthage’s fields show?
o: Popular history often includes appealing stories with no ancient evidence
Rome systematically poisoned all conquered farmland
Carthage’s soil was naturally too salty to farm
Scipio ordered the salting after Zama
quiz.e: The salt story appears to be a modern invention, not something the ancient sources record.

LESSONS.push: Hannibal won battle after battle yet lost the war. What went wrong?

LESSONS.title: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War
LESSONS.hook: A teenage peasant girl from a village in eastern France told a prince that God had sent her to save his kingdom. Astonishingly, she very nearly did.

sections.key: By the 1420s France was close to defeat, with English and Burgundian forces holding Paris and the north.
sections.b:
The Hundred Years' War actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long truces. At its heart was inheritance: English kings, descended from French nobility, held lands in France and claimed the French crown itself. England won famous victories at Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356 and Agincourt in 1415, where Henry V’s outnumbered army, with its longbowmen, defeated a much larger French force.

By the 1420s, France was in desperate trouble. The Duke of Burgundy had sided with England, and the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 declared that the English king would inherit the throne, disinheriting the French heir, Charles, known as the Dauphin. Paris and much of the north were under English and Burgundian control.

sections.key: Joan, an illiterate farmer’s daughter, convinced the cautious Dauphin by passing weeks of questioning.
sections.b:
Joan was born around 1412 in Domrémy, in north-eastern France, to a farming family. She could not read or write. From about thirteen, she later said, she heard voices and saw saints, especially Michael, Catherine and Margaret, who told her to go to the Dauphin, drive out the English and see him crowned.

In early 1429, at around seventeen, she persuaded a local garrison commander to give her an escort, cut her hair short and rode in men’s clothing to the Dauphin’s court at Chinon. Charles was cautious: she could be a saint, a fraud or an agent of the devil. Churchmen at Poitiers questioned her for weeks and found nothing wrong in her faith or conduct. The situation was desperate enough to take a chance.

sections.key: Joan’s presence broke the siege of Orléans and led to Charles being crowned at Reims.
sections.b:
Orléans, the key to southern France, had been under English siege since late 1428. Charles gave Joan armour, a banner and a place with an army bringing supplies. She arrived at the end of April 1429. She did not formally command, but her presence electrified soldiers and townspeople, and she pushed for bold attacks. She was wounded by an arrow between neck and shoulder but returned to the fight. On 8 May the English abandoned the siege.

More victories followed, including Patay in June. Joan then urged Charles to make the dangerous journey to Reims, the traditional site where French kings were crowned. On 17 July 1429 he was crowned Charles VII, with Joan standing nearby holding her banner.

sections.key: Joan was captured in 1430, abandoned by Charles and tried for heresy by a Church court allied with the English.
sections.b:
After the coronation, Joan’s fortunes turned. An attack on Paris failed, and the king grew more interested in negotiation than war. In May 1430, while defending Compiègne, she was pulled from her horse and captured by Burgundian soldiers, who sold her to the English. There is no evidence that Charles made any serious attempt to rescue her.

In 1431 she was tried for heresy in Rouen by a Church court led by Pierre Cauchon, a bishop allied with the English. They needed her condemned, since that would suggest Charles had been crowned with the devil’s help. The records show an illiterate young woman answering trick questions from learned men with remarkable sharpness and courage.

sections.key: Joan was executed in 1431, but a retrial cleared her in 1456 and she became a saint in 1920.
sections.b:
One major charge was that she wore men’s clothing, which her accusers treated as a sin against divine law. Under pressure she signed a statement renouncing her claims and agreed to wear women’s dress, but days later she resumed men’s clothing, and the court declared her a relapsed heretic. On 30 May 1431, in the market square of Rouen, she was burned at the stake. She was about nineteen.

Within a generation, the war she had helped turn ended, as French armies took back Normandy and Gascony. By 1453, England held only Calais. A retrial authorised by the Pope declared the original verdict null in 1456. Joan was made a saint in 1920 and is a patron saint of France.

quiz.q: What did the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 declare?
o: The English king would inherit the French throne instead of the Dauphin
France would be divided between Burgundy and England
Charles would be crowned at Reims
The war would end with a lasting peace
quiz.e: It disinherited the Dauphin Charles, leaving France in desperate trouble.

quiz.q: Why did Charles have Joan examined before trusting her?
o: A woman claiming divine orders could be a saint, a fraud or a danger
Church law banned women from joining armies
Burgundy had warned him she was a spy
He had already decided she was a heretic
quiz.e: Backing the wrong claimant would be disastrous, so churchmen tested her faith and conduct for weeks.

quiz.q: What was Joan’s main effect at Orléans?
o: Her presence inspired the army to bold attacks that broke the siege
She formally commanded the whole French army
She negotiated peace with the English
She ended the siege by diplomacy alone
quiz.e: Though not in formal command, she pushed commanders to attack, and the English left on 8 May 1429.

quiz.q: Why did the English want Joan condemned as a heretic?
o: It would suggest Charles had been crowned with the devil’s help
It would make Burgundy join their side
It would stop her from raising a new army
It would let them seize Orléans again
quiz.e: Discrediting Joan undermined the legitimacy of Charles’s coronation.

quiz.q: What happened after Joan’s execution?
o: A retrial cleared her, and she became a saint
Charles was never recognised as king
England kept all of its French lands
The Pope fully upheld the original verdict
quiz.e: A retrial overturned the 1431 verdict in 1456, and she was canonised in 1920.

LESSONS.push: A teenage farm girl turned a lost war. What happened next surprises many.

LESSONS.title: Hadrian's Wall: life on the edge of an empire
LESSONS.hook: For nearly three hundred years, soldiers from across the Roman world guarded a stone wall in the rain of northern Britain. The letters they left behind are astonishingly human.

sections.key: Hadrian chose to consolidate the empire, and his soldiers built a fortified wall of milecastles, forts and ditches across northern Britain.
sections.b:
Hadrian became emperor in AD 117, when the empire was at its largest. Rather than keep conquering, he consolidated, and around AD 122 he visited Britain. Construction began soon after. The wall ran about 118 kilometres, from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway, built mainly by the three legions stationed in Britain.

It was more than a line of stone. The eastern part was stone up to about three metres thick; the western section began as turf and was later rebuilt in stone. Every Roman mile (about 1.5 kilometres) stood a small fort called a milecastle with a gateway, and two turrets lay between each pair. A ditch ran in front, an earthwork called the vallum behind, and around fifteen larger forts, such as Housesteads, were added.

sections.key: The wall was probably less a barrier against invasion than a way to control movement, tax trade and display Roman power.
sections.b:
It is tempting to see the wall as a barrier against invading hordes. His biography, written centuries later, says Hadrian built it to separate the Romans from the barbarians. But most historians think its purpose was more complicated. Soldiers did not usually fight from the top of walls; they fought in the open, and the many gateways suggest people were expected to pass through, under supervision.

Its main jobs were probably controlling who crossed, collecting customs duties, preventing small-scale raids and cattle rustling, and watching the tribes to the north. It was also a statement: a massive stone barrier from coast to coast announced the power of Rome. Historians still debate how much each purpose mattered.

sections.key: Auxiliary troops recruited from across the empire garrisoned the wall, making the frontier remarkably multicultural.
sections.b:
The legionaries who built the wall mostly moved elsewhere once it was finished. It was garrisoned by auxiliaries, soldiers recruited from the empire’s provinces who became Roman citizens after their service. Inscriptions show units from what are now Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Spain and beyond. At Arbeia, in modern South Shields, there was even a unit of bargemen from the Tigris river in Mesopotamia.

A tombstone found there was set up by Barates, a man from Palmyra in Syria, for his wife Regina, a freed slave from the British Catuvellauni tribe. It carries an inscription in Latin and a line in Palmyrene Aramaic. The northern frontier was one of the most multicultural places in Roman Britain.

sections.key: The Vindolanda tablets are wooden letters and records that bring the everyday lives of Roman soldiers to life.
sections.b:
Just south of the wall lies Vindolanda, a fort that predates Hadrian’s Wall. From 1973, archaeologists there led by Robin Birley began finding thin wooden tablets, preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free soil, covered in ink handwriting from around AD 100. They include duty reports, supply lists and private letters.

One soldier is sent socks, sandals and two pairs of underpants. Another note dismissively calls the locals Brittunculi, little Britons. The most famous is a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, the wife of the fort’s commander. A scribe wrote most of it, but a few warm lines at the end appear to be in Claudia’s own hand, among the earliest known examples of Latin handwriting by a woman.

sections.key: Hadrian’s Wall does not mark the England–Scotland border; it lies wholly within England.
sections.b:
A common myth is that Hadrian’s Wall marks the border between England and Scotland. It does not. The whole wall lies within England, and in places the modern border is up to about a hundred kilometres to the north.

Around AD 142, Hadrian’s successor Antoninus Pius pushed further into what is now Scotland and built the turf Antonine Wall, but it was abandoned within about twenty years and the army returned to Hadrian’s line. The wall was garrisoned until Roman rule in Britain ended in the early fifth century. Afterwards, much of its stone was taken to build farms, churches and roads. Even so, long stretches still stand, and since 1987 it has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

quiz.q: What is Hadrian’s Wall best described as?
o: A wall with milecastles, turrets, ditches and forts
A single stone barrier with no gates at all
A line of watchtowers built along the coast
A pair of forts at each end joined by a road
quiz.e: The wall was part of a larger frontier system with regular milecastles, turrets, forts, a ditch and the vallum.

quiz.q: Why do historians doubt it was only a defensive barrier?
o: Its many gateways let people cross under supervision
It was built without any soldiers to guard it
It stopped well short of the coast at both ends
It was never connected to any forts or roads
quiz.e: Gateways, customs duties and watching the tribes suggest control of movement mattered as much as defence.

quiz.q: Who garrisoned the wall after its construction?
o: Auxiliaries recruited from across the empire
Local Britons drafted from the northern tribes
Citizens of Italy sent out from Rome
The three legions that had built it
quiz.e: Auxiliaries from places like Belgium, Spain and Syria served there and became citizens afterwards.

quiz.q: What makes the Vindolanda tablets so valuable?
o: They preserve ordinary soldiers’ everyday letters
They list every Roman soldier who served in Britain
They are the oldest Roman writing ever found
They explain exactly how the wall was designed
quiz.e: Handwritten notes about socks, duty rosters and birthday invitations show everyday life on the frontier.

quiz.q: How does Hadrian’s Wall relate to the modern England–Scotland border?
o: It lies wholly in England, well south of the border
It follows the modern border almost exactly
Half of the wall stands inside Scotland today
It was built along the modern border on purpose
quiz.e: The border is not the wall, which sits wholly within England.

LESSONS.push: Hadrian’s Wall isn’t the border with Scotland. So what was it really for?

LESSONS.title: Myths about the Middle Ages
LESSONS.hook: Flat Earth, no baths, and everyone dead by thirty. Much of what people think they know about medieval life was invented or exaggerated centuries later.

sections.key: Educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was a sphere; the flat Earth story mostly arose in the 1800s.
sections.b:
One of the most persistent ideas about the Middle Ages is that people believed the Earth was flat, and that Columbus had to prove otherwise. In fact, educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was a sphere. Ancient Greek scholars had shown this, and writers such as the English monk Bede in the eighth century took it for granted. A thirteenth-century astronomy textbook, De sphaera, taught a spherical Earth in universities for centuries. Kings were even shown holding an orb, a globe symbolising their rule.

The argument over Columbus’s voyage was about the size of the Earth, and his critics were right that it was larger than he claimed. The flat Earth myth spread mostly in the 1800s.

sections.key: Low average life expectancy reflected high infant mortality, not early old age.
sections.b:
You may have heard that medieval people lived to around thirty. Estimates of average life expectancy at birth in that range are plausible, but averages can mislead. A huge share of children died in infancy or early childhood from disease, and these deaths pulled the average down sharply.

If a family had one child who died as a baby and another who lived to sixty, their average is about thirty, yet no one died at thirty. People who survived childhood had a reasonable chance of reaching their fifties or sixties, and some lived much longer. Old people were a normal part of medieval communities. Dangers for adults were real, including childbirth, plague, war and accidents, but thirty was not old age.

sections.key: Medieval people washed regularly and drank water, not only beer and wine.
sections.b:
Medieval people did not have modern plumbing, but they were not indifferent to dirt. Washing hands before and after meals was expected etiquette, people washed their faces and bodies with water from basins, and soap was made and sold across Europe. Many towns had public bathhouses, often called stews in England. These became associated with prostitution, and many closed in the sixteenth century, partly because of fears that they spread disease, including syphilis.

The claim that people drank beer because all water was deadly is also exaggerated. They preferred clean springs, wells and rivers, and towns built fountains and pipes. Medical writings sometimes recommended water. Ale was popular because it was cheap, calorie-rich and enjoyable, and much everyday ale was fairly weak.

sections.key: Chastity belts and mass witch burnings were mostly inventions or products of later eras, not the Middle Ages.
sections.b:
The image of a crusading knight locking his wife into an iron chastity belt is a favourite of comedies and tourist museums. Historians find almost no reliable evidence for it. The earliest mentions are a handful of fifteenth-century references, several seemingly jokes about jealous husbands. Many belts once displayed in museums are eighteenth- or nineteenth-century creations. Wearing one for long would cause serious infections.

Witch hunts are also often placed in the Middle Ages. In fact, the large-scale hunts mostly came in the early modern period, peaking roughly between 1560 and 1630. Earlier, an early medieval Church text, the Canon Episcopi, treated witches flying at night as an illusion. Belief in organised, devil-worshipping witches grew in the fifteenth century, helped by the Malleus Maleficarum of 1486 and the printing press. Estimates suggest forty to sixty thousand executions, many by hanging.

sections.key: The ‘Dark Ages’ label is outdated: the medieval centuries brought universities, cathedrals, clocks and more.
sections.b:
In the fourteenth century, the Italian scholar Petrarch helped popularise the idea that the centuries after Rome’s fall were a time of darkness compared with classical antiquity. The label stuck, but most historians now avoid it. The early medieval period does have fewer written sources in some regions, which makes it darker to us in the sense of being harder to see.

But the medieval centuries also produced the first European universities, such as Bologna, Paris and Oxford, soaring Gothic cathedrals, mechanical clocks, eyeglasses and the spread of windmills. Monasteries copied and preserved many classical texts. Meanwhile, scholars in the Islamic world, Byzantium and China were making major advances. The Middle Ages were not a pause in history.

quiz.q: What was the real argument about Columbus’s voyage?
o: The size of the Earth, not its shape
Whether the Earth was flat or round
Whether the Atlantic had any land at all
Whether ships could survive a long voyage
quiz.e: Educated people knew the Earth was round; Columbus’s critics were right that it was larger than he claimed.

quiz.q: Why does a medieval life expectancy of about thirty mislead?
o: High infant mortality pulled the average down
Most adults died of plague before thirty
Records only covered the poorest people
Adults then aged much faster
quiz.e: Those who survived childhood could reach their fifties or sixties, so thirty was not old age.

quiz.q: Why was ale so popular in the Middle Ages?
o: It was cheap, nourishing and enjoyable
Water was banned by the Church
Clean springs and wells did not exist
Ale was always stronger than wine
quiz.e: People drank water too, but ale gave cheap energy for hard work and was widely enjoyed.

quiz.q: The large-scale European witch hunts belong mainly to which era?
o: The early modern period, after the Middle Ages
The early Middle Ages, after Rome’s fall
The age of the Crusades in the 1100s
The nineteenth century and the Industrial Age
quiz.e: Earlier Church texts were sceptical of witches’ powers; the mass trials came later.

quiz.q: Why do most historians avoid the term ‘Dark Ages’?
o: The era produced universities, cathedrals and clocks
No written records survive from the whole period
Europe was cut off from changes in other regions
It only describes the centuries after the year 1500
quiz.e: The label reflects scarce sources in some regions, not an absence of achievement.

LESSONS.push: Most of what you think you know about medieval life is wrong. Start here.

LESSONS.title: The Library of Alexandria: what really happened
LESSONS.hook: It is the most famous lost library in history, supposedly destroyed in a single catastrophic fire. The truth is slower, stranger and more of a warning.

sections.key: The Ptolemies founded the Library in the early third century BC, inside a royal research institute called the Mouseion.
sections.b: After Alexander the Great died, his general Ptolemy took Egypt and made Alexandria his capital. Early in the third century BC, Ptolemy I or his son Ptolemy II founded the Mouseion, a temple to the Muses that worked as a research institute, and with it the Library. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to outshine Athens as the centre of Greek culture, so they paid scholars to live, work and dine together at royal expense. The aim was bold: collect every important book written in Greek, plus translations of works from other cultures. A later tradition says the Hebrew scriptures were first translated into Greek there, producing the Septuagint.

sections.key: The Library collected aggressively, but nobody knows its true size, since ancient estimates run from about forty thousand to seven hundred thousand scrolls.
sections.b:
The physician Galen, writing centuries later, told two stories. Ships arriving in the harbour were searched for books, which were copied; the owners received the copies and the Library kept the originals. And Ptolemy III borrowed the official Athenian texts of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, left fifteen talents of silver as a deposit, then kept the originals and forfeited the money. These tales may be exaggerated.

The size is just as uncertain. Ancient writers give figures from about forty thousand to seven hundred thousand scrolls, often long after the fact, and duplicates and multi-scroll works muddle any count. Its main rival was Pergamon, in modern Turkey.

sections.key: The Library mattered most for its scholars, who measured the Earth, catalogued literature and edited Homer.
sections.b: Eratosthenes, one of its chief librarians, estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the angle of the Sun's shadow at Alexandria and at Syene, far to the south, on the same day. His result was remarkably close to the true value, though historians debate how close because his units of length are uncertain. The poet Callimachus compiled the Pinakes, a huge catalogue of Greek authors and works, often called an ancestor of the library catalogue. Zenodotus and Aristarchus produced careful editions of Homer by comparing different copies to remove errors. Alexandria also became a great centre of medicine, mathematics and astronomy.

sections.key: Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BC burned some books, but sources disagree on what was lost, and scholarship in Alexandria carried on afterwards.
sections.b: The most famous story of the Library's destruction involves Julius Caesar. In 48 BC, besieged in Alexandria during the civil war involving Cleopatra and her brother, Caesar set fire to ships in the harbour. Several ancient writers say the blaze spread and burned books, and Seneca mentions forty thousand lost. But the sources disagree about what burned. Some historians think the fire mainly destroyed warehouses near the docks holding scrolls awaiting export or cataloguing, not the Library itself. What is clear is that scholarly life continued. The geographer Strabo worked in the city a couple of decades later and wrote about the Mouseion, without mentioning a destroyed library.

sections.key: The Library most likely faded over centuries through purges, war, lost funding and rotting papyrus, not one great fire.
sections.b:
As early as 145 BC, Ptolemy VIII expelled many intellectuals, including the head librarian Aristarchus. Under Roman rule royal patronage vanished, and in the AD 270s fighting under Aurelian devastated the palace quarter where the Library probably stood. A quieter enemy was damp coastal air, which rotted fragile papyrus scrolls unless they were recopied. A library that loses its funding and staff loses its books without any fire.

Later writers blamed convenient villains. The AD 391 destruction of the Serapeum, and the murder of Hypatia in 415, did not destroy the Library. The tale of Caliph Umar burning books in 642 first appears over five centuries later, and most historians reject it.

quiz.q: What was the Ptolemies' ambitious aim for the Library?
o: To store only royal tax records and legal documents
To copy every book held in Athens and then close it
To collect every important Greek book, plus translations of other cultures' works
To keep foreign writings out of Greek scholarship
quiz.e: The Library aimed to gather all significant Greek writing and translations, supported by scholars paid to work in the Mouseion.

quiz.q: Why should ancient figures for the Library's size be treated with caution?
o: They vary widely and were written long afterwards by people who could not check
They were all recorded by Roman tax officials
They count only the books taken from ships
They come from a single source that was proven forged
quiz.e: Estimates range from about 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls, and duplicates and multi-scroll works make any count unreliable.

quiz.q: How did Eratosthenes estimate the circumference of the Earth?
o: By timing how long a ship took to sail around the Mediterranean
By comparing the Sun's shadow angles at Alexandria and Syene on the same day
By measuring the height of the Great Pyramid at noon
By counting the steps between Alexandria and Athens
quiz.e: Different shadow angles at two distant places on the same day let him calculate the curve of the Earth.

quiz.q: What do historians conclude about Caesar's fire in 48 BC?
o: It destroyed the whole Library and ended scholarship there
It burned only the Serapeum in the south of the city
It was set deliberately to destroy Greek books
Sources disagree about what burned, and scholarship in Alexandria continued afterwards
quiz.e: The fire may have hit dockside warehouses, and Strabo later described the Mouseion without noting any ruined library.

quiz.q: What most likely ended the Library?
o: A long decline through purges, war, lost funding and decaying papyrus
A single fire started by Caliph Umar in 642
An earthquake that buried the palace quarter
A decree closing it after Hypatia's death
quiz.e: Knowledge usually dies through neglect, and the evidence points to centuries of decline rather than one dramatic ending.

LESSONS.push: The most famous library fire in history may never have destroyed the library.

LESSONS.title: The day the Mona Lisa vanished
LESSONS.hook: In 1911 a handyman walked out of the Louvre with the world's most famous painting under his smock. Strangely, the theft is a big part of why it became so famous.

sections.key: The Mona Lisa was stolen on Monday 21 August 1911, when the Louvre was closed for cleaning and workmen moved freely.
sections.b: Mondays were cleaning days at the Louvre. The galleries were shut and workmen wandered the halls. On the morning of 21 August 1911, a man in a white workman's smock lifted Leonardo da Vinci's portrait off its hooks in the Salon Carré. The painting is small, about 77 by 53 centimetres, and painted on a thin poplar panel rather than canvas. The thief carried it to a service stairwell, removed the heavy frame and protective glass box, and slipped the panel under his clothing. Accounts differ on whether he hid in a storeroom overnight or arrived that morning among the staff. Either way, he walked out into the Paris streets and nobody stopped him.

sections.key: The empty wall went unremarked for more than a day because paintings were often taken away for photography, and the search then chased the wrong suspects.
sections.b:
The next morning, the painter Louis Béroud arrived to sketch and found four iron pegs where the Mona Lisa should have been. Guards assumed the museum's photographers had taken it, which happened regularly. Only when Béroud pressed them did the truth sink in. The Louvre closed for a week and the director lost his job.

Police followed strange trails. The poet Guillaume Apollinaire was jailed for several days because an acquaintance had earlier stolen ancient statuettes from the Louvre that Picasso had ended up with. Picasso was questioned too. Both were cleared. The real thief had been interviewed early, at his lodgings, and aroused no suspicion.

sections.key: The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, a craftsman who knew the Louvre and kept the painting in a trunk in his Paris room for more than two years.
sections.b:
Vincenzo Peruggia was an Italian craftsman who had worked at the Louvre and helped install the very glass cases meant to protect its paintings. He knew the building, and the staff knew him. For more than two years he kept the Mona Lisa in a trunk with a false bottom in his Paris room.

In late 1913 he wrote to Alfredo Geri, an art dealer in Florence, offering to return the painting to Italy. Geri arranged a hotel meeting with Giovanni Poggi, director of the Uffizi Gallery. After examining the panel and checking the Louvre's markings on its back, they alerted police, and Peruggia was arrested.

sections.key: Peruggia claimed patriotism, but his belief that Napoleon had looted the painting was wrong, and he had also asked for money.
sections.b:
At his trial in Florence, Peruggia argued that he had acted out of patriotism. He believed, wrongly, that Napoleon had looted the painting from Italy. In fact Leonardo took it to France himself, and it entered the French royal collection long before Napoleon was born.

Peruggia's story struck a chord with many Italians, and he received a fairly light sentence of a little over a year, of which he served only about seven months. Historians note that he had also asked for money, so his motives were probably mixed. Before going home, the painting was displayed in Florence, Rome and Milan to enormous crowds. It returned to the Louvre in early 1914.

sections.key: The theft turned a respected masterpiece into the most famous painting in the world.
sections.b:
Before 1911, the Mona Lisa was admired by art lovers, but it was not obviously the most famous painting on Earth. The theft changed that. For two years the story ran in newspapers worldwide, and photographs of the portrait were printed again and again. Visitors even queued at the Louvre to stare at the empty space on the wall. When the painting came back, it returned as a celebrity.

Art historians often call the theft a turning point, alongside Leonardo's reputation and the picture's remarkable technique, such as the soft, smoky blending called sfumato. Today it sits behind protective glass and is seen by millions of visitors every year.

quiz.q: Why could the thief move so freely through the Louvre?
o: It was a public holiday and the guards were away
It was a Monday, when the galleries were closed and workmen were about
The museum was being emptied for a move
He had been given a key by the director
quiz.e: Cleaning day meant closed galleries and workmen in smocks, so a man in a smock drew no attention.

quiz.q: Why did guards not raise the alarm straight away?
o: They assumed the museum's photographers had taken the painting away
They believed it had been sent for restoration
They thought it had been lent to another museum
They were told it had been sold
quiz.e: Paintings were routinely moved for photography, so an empty wall looked normal for more than a day.

quiz.q: How did Peruggia's insider knowledge help him?
o: He had designed the Louvre's alarm system
He was a guard on duty that morning
He had studied under Leonardo's descendants
He had worked at the Louvre, knew the building, and the staff knew him
quiz.e: Familiarity let him blend in and avoid suspicion, even when police interviewed him early on.

quiz.q: What was wrong with Peruggia's claim that he was returning the painting to Italy?
o: It had been painted in Paris to begin with
It had been given to France by Italy's king
Leonardo himself took it to France, long before Napoleon was born
It was never Italian property in the first place
quiz.e: Napoleon never looted it; it entered the French royal collection centuries earlier, and Peruggia had also asked for money.

quiz.q: How did the theft affect the painting's reputation?
o: It was proven a forgery and fell from favour
Two years of worldwide news coverage made it a global celebrity
It lost value because it had been damaged
It stayed as little known as before
quiz.e: Constant press coverage turned a respected masterpiece into the world's most famous painting.

LESSONS.push: A thief walked out of the Louvre with its most famous painting. It made it more famous.

LESSONS.title: The Bayeux Tapestry: 1066 in wool
LESSONS.hook: A strip of linen nearly 70 metres long tells the story of the Norman conquest of England like a medieval comic strip. And technically, it isn't even a tapestry.

sections.key: The Bayeux Tapestry is actually an embroidery: coloured wool stitched onto linen, not woven on a loom.
sections.b: A true tapestry has its picture woven into the cloth on a loom. The Bayeux Tapestry was made differently. Its images were stitched with coloured woollen yarn onto a long band of plain linen, which makes it an embroidery. It is roughly 68 metres long but only about half a metre tall, made from several pieces of linen joined together. The embroiderers used a handful of colours, mainly reds, yellows, greens and blues, yet created hundreds of people, horses, ships, buildings and animals. Short Latin captions run above the scenes. Read from left to right, it unfolds like a film reel, which is why it is often called the world's oldest comic strip.

sections.key: It was probably commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conqueror's half-brother, and stitched by English embroiderers in the 1070s.
sections.b:
No document records who ordered it, but most historians think it was Odo, Bishop of Bayeux and half-brother of William the Conqueror. Odo appears prominently in the scenes, and Bayeux Cathedral was consecrated in 1077, a likely occasion for such a gift.

Strangely for a French treasure, it was probably made in England. The style of the drawings and some of the spelling in the captions suggest English craftspeople, possibly in Canterbury, which was famous for its needlework. So the story of England's conquest may have been stitched by the conquered themselves, working for one of the new Norman rulers.

sections.key: The story is told from the winners' side: Harold swears an oath to William, so the Normans can brand him an oath breaker.
sections.b:
The embroidery opens with the old king, Edward the Confessor, and his powerful nobleman Harold Godwinson. Harold sails to France, is captured, and ends up at the court of William, Duke of Normandy. He even joins William on a campaign in Brittany. Then comes the key scene: Harold swears an oath with his hands on holy relics.

The embroidery does not spell out the promise, but Norman sources claimed he swore to support William's claim to the English throne. When Edward died in January 1066 and Harold took the crown himself, the Normans could present him as an oath breaker. The tapestry tells the story from the winners' point of view.

sections.key: The embroidery shows Halley's Comet as an omen, then the everyday logistics of building and launching an invasion fleet.
sections.b:
Soon after Harold is crowned, people point up at a star with flaming tails. This is Halley's Comet, which really did appear in the spring of 1066 and was widely seen as an omen.

The embroidery then shows something history books often skip: the logistics of invasion. Trees are felled, ships are built, and men carry armour, swords, spears and barrels of wine down to the boats. Horses are loaded and the fleet crosses the Channel. Once landed, the Normans build a fort and cook a feast. These everyday scenes are priceless to historians, offering rare pictures of eleventh century clothing, weapons, tools, ships and food.

sections.key: The tapestry ends with the Battle of Hastings in 1066, and has survived nine centuries of fires, revolutions and wars.
sections.b:
The battle scenes are crowded and violent. Norman cavalry charge English soldiers in a shield wall on a hill. At one point William lifts his helmet to show he is still alive. Then comes Harold's death, though historians still debate which figure is Harold, and some think the arrow in the eye was altered in nineteenth century restoration. The final section is missing.

The first written record is an inventory of 1476, when it hung in Bayeux Cathedral. During the French Revolution it was nearly cut up to cover wagons, until a local official saved it. Napoleon displayed it while planning his own invasion of England. In 1944 it was moved to the Louvre for safekeeping, and today it is kept in Bayeux under low light.

quiz.q: Why is the Bayeux Tapestry technically not a tapestry?
o: It is painted in dye on a plain linen sheet
It is embroidered with wool on linen rather than woven on a loom
It is printed onto silk using wooden blocks
It is too long to count as a single work
quiz.e: A true tapestry is woven into the cloth, while this work is stitched onto it.

quiz.q: Where was the embroidery most likely made?
o: In Normandy, by monks in Bayeux Cathedral
In Rome, by craftspeople serving the Pope
In England, probably by English needleworkers working for a Norman patron
In Flanders, by weavers working for Harold
quiz.e: The drawing style and the spelling in the captions suggest English craftspeople, perhaps in Canterbury.

quiz.q: Why does Harold's oath matter to the story as told?
o: It lets the Normans portray Harold as an oath breaker when he takes the throne
It proves Harold had been crowned in Normandy
It shows William promised England to Harold
It explains why Edward left England in 1066
quiz.e: The embroidery presents events from the winners' viewpoint, with Harold's broken promise as the justification for invasion.

quiz.q: Why do historians value the scenes of building ships and loading supplies?
o: They prove the invasion fleet was never delayed
They show which battles William won in France
They record the names of every Norman soldier
They give rare pictures of eleventh century clothing, tools, ships and food
quiz.e: These everyday scenes show how an invasion was really organised and what ordinary things looked like.

quiz.q: What do historians still debate about the death scene?
o: Whether Harold was ever actually crowned king in London
Which figure is Harold, and whether the arrow was altered later
Whether the battle took place in the year 1066
Which side won the Battle of Hastings in the end
quiz.e: Even the most famous scene is uncertain, partly because of nineteenth century restoration work.

LESSONS.push: It is called a tapestry, but it isn't one. And the conquered may have made it.

LESSONS.title: How the movies began
LESSONS.hook: A bet about a galloping horse, a peephole machine and a café screening in Paris led to the most popular art form of the twentieth century. And one of the first feature films was Australian.

sections.key: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed a running horse in sequence, showing that all four hooves leave the ground, tucked under the body.
sections.b: For centuries, painters showed galloping horses with legs stretched out front and back like a rocking horse. Nobody could see fast enough to know. In California, the businessman Leland Stanford hired the photographer Eadweard Muybridge to find out whether all four hooves ever left the ground at once. In 1878, Muybridge set up a row of cameras along a track, triggered one after another as the horse raced past. The pictures showed that the hooves did leave the ground, but when they were tucked under the body, not stretched out. Muybridge then put his sequences on a spinning disc and projected them, so audiences watched the horse appear to run. Moving pictures had begun.

sections.key: Film is a row of still photographs shown fast enough that the brain's motion detection blends them into smooth movement.
sections.b:
A film strip is a long row of photographs, each slightly different from the last. Shown quickly enough, the brain stops seeing separate pictures and perceives smooth movement. This was long explained by persistence of vision, the idea that each image lingers on the retina. Most researchers now think that is incomplete. The illusion mainly comes from how the visual system detects motion, filling in movement between closely spaced images, an effect psychologists call apparent motion.

Early silent films ran at varied speeds, often around 16 to 20 frames per second. When sound arrived in the late 1920s, 24 frames per second became the standard, and it is still common today.

sections.key: Edison sold films for one viewer at a time, while the Lumière brothers projected them to a paying crowd in Paris in 1895.
sections.b:
Thomas Edison's laboratory, with much of the work done by his assistant William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, used flexible celluloid film with holes punched along the edges. Their Kinetoscope, shown to the public in 1894, was a wooden cabinet with a viewing hole. One customer at a time peered in at a film lasting less than a minute: a strongman flexing, dancers, a sneeze. Edison thought individual viewing would be more profitable, which let rivals take the lead in projection.

In France, Auguste and Louis Lumière built the Cinématographe, a light, hand-cranked machine that could film, print and project. On 28 December 1895, beneath the Grand Café in Paris, they showed short scenes from life to a paying audience. The tale of viewers fleeing their train film has little reliable evidence.

sections.key: Filmmakers learned tricks and editing, and by 1906 Australia's The Story of the Kelly Gang had become the first feature-length story film.
sections.b:
Georges Méliès, a Paris stage magician, discovered that stopping the camera, changing something and restarting could make people vanish. His 1902 film A Trip to the Moon became one of early cinema's most famous images. In 1903, Edwin S. Porter's The Great Train Robbery told an action story across separate scenes, and audiences learned to accept cuts.

In 1906, a Melbourne team including the Tait family filmed the bushranger Ned Kelly's story. The Story of the Kelly Gang ran about an hour, far longer than almost anything before, and is widely considered the first feature-length narrative film. Most of it is lost, since early nitrate film was fragile and flammable. Fragments restored by the National Film and Sound Archive joined UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007.

sections.key: Synchronised sound in the late 1920s transformed cinema within a few years, ending careers but opening new forms.
sections.b:
Silent films were rarely silent. Cinemas hired pianists, organists or whole orchestras, and some used narrators or sound effects. But recording dialogue that matched the actors' lips was hard. In 1927 Warner Bros released The Jazz Singer, with synchronised songs and a few spoken lines. Audiences were thrilled, and within a few years most studios had switched to sound.

The change was brutal for some. Actors whose voices did not suit the microphone lost careers, cinema musicians lost jobs, and cameras were temporarily trapped in soundproof booths. Yet sound also opened new forms, such as the musical. In barely three decades, moving pictures had gone from scientific curiosity to global art.

quiz.q: What did Muybridge's photographs reveal about galloping horses?
o: The hooves never all leave the ground together
All four hooves leave the ground, but when tucked under the body
The legs stretch out front and back, as painters showed
Only the back legs ever leave the ground
quiz.e: The sequence showed the hooves airborne with legs gathered beneath the horse, not stretched out like a rocking horse.

quiz.q: Why do still frames appear to move when shown quickly?
o: The images physically blend together on the screen
The eye stores every frame for a full second
The brain's motion detection fills in movement between closely spaced images
The projector bends the light between frames
quiz.e: Apparent motion, not simple persistence of vision, mainly explains the illusion.

quiz.q: Why did Edison's Kinetoscope lose ground to the Lumière brothers' machine?
o: It served one viewer at a time, while rivals projected to crowds
It could only show images that did not move
It cost far more than any projector to run
It could not use celluloid film
quiz.e: Edison favoured individual viewing, which let rivals take the lead in projection for audiences.

quiz.q: Why is The Story of the Kelly Gang famous?
o: It was the first film to use recorded dialogue
It was the first film shown in a theatre
It was the first film made in colour
It is widely regarded as the first feature-length narrative film
quiz.e: At about an hour long in 1906, it was far longer than earlier films and toured several countries.

quiz.q: What was the effect of sound arriving in the late 1920s?
o: Audiences preferred silent films and sound faded
Most studios switched within a few years, ending some careers and creating the musical
Cinemas kept showing silent films because sound proved too costly
It changed cinema only slowly, over several decades
quiz.e: Sound transformed the industry quickly, costing some actors and musicians their work while opening new forms.

LESSONS.push: A bet about a galloping horse helped start cinema. One early feature was Australian.

LESSONS.title: Frida Kahlo: painting her own reality
LESSONS.hook: A teenage bus crash left her in pain for life. From her bed, with a mirror above her, Frida Kahlo began painting the face that would become one of the most recognised in art.

sections.key: Frida Kahlo was born in 1907 near Mexico City, survived polio, and planned to study medicine, not art.
sections.b:
Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, then a village on the edge of Mexico City. Her father was a photographer of German origin and her mother was Mexican. Later she often gave her birth year as 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began, linking herself to the birth of modern Mexico.

At about six she caught polio, which left her right leg thinner than the left. Bright and rebellious, she was admitted in 1922 as one of a small number of girls at the elite National Preparatory School, planning to study medicine. Art was not yet her ambition.

sections.key: A 1925 bus crash left her with lifelong pain, and while recovering in bed she began painting self-portraits using a mirror.
sections.b:
On 17 September 1925, the bus Frida was riding in collided with a streetcar in Mexico City. She was eighteen. A metal handrail pierced her body, and she fractured her spine, pelvis, collarbone, ribs and right leg. Doctors doubted she would survive. She did, but she spent months in bed and lived with pain for the rest of her life, undergoing many operations.

During her recovery, her mother had a special easel made so she could paint lying down, and a mirror fitted above her bed. With her own reflection as the most available subject, she began painting self-portraits. Medicine gave way to art.

sections.key: Her stormy marriage to the muralist Diego Rivera shaped her life, and the couple moved among artists, writers and revolutionaries.
sections.b:
In 1928 Frida showed her paintings to Diego Rivera, already Mexico's most famous painter and a leader of the mural movement, which covered public walls with scenes of Mexican history and workers' lives. He encouraged her, and they married in 1929. He was about twenty years older and much larger, and her parents reportedly compared the match to an elephant marrying a dove.

Both had many affairs, and Rivera's affair with Frida's sister Cristina hurt her deeply. They divorced in 1939 and remarried in 1940. They travelled to the United States, where Rivera painted murals, and their circle included artists, writers and political figures, among them the exiled Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky.

sections.key: Kahlo painted her pain and identity in about 55 self-portraits, and rejected the Surrealist label because she painted her reality, not dreams.
sections.b:
Kahlo made around 55 self-portraits, more than a third of her known paintings. She kept her joined eyebrows and faint moustache, and often wore traditional Tehuana dresses from southern Mexico, celebrating Indigenous culture. Her small, detailed works drew on folk art and devotional paintings called retablos, and were frank about pain, miscarriage, surgery and heartbreak. In The Two Fridas (1939), two versions of herself sit hand in hand, their exposed hearts joined by a single vein.

The Surrealist leader André Breton visited in 1938 and arranged a Paris exhibition in 1939. The Louvre bought her self-portrait The Frame, making her the first twentieth century Mexican artist in its collection. Yet she said she did not paint dreams but her own reality.

sections.key: Kahlo attended her first Mexican solo show from her bed, died in 1954, and became a global icon decades later.
sections.b:
Her health worsened in the 1940s and 1950s. She wore supportive corsets, some of which she painted on, and had several spinal operations. In 1953 part of her right leg was amputated because of gangrene. That year she had her first solo exhibition in Mexico. Told by doctors not to attend, she arrived by ambulance and received guests lying on her four poster bed, which was installed in the gallery. She died at the Blue House on 13 July 1954, aged 47.

In life she was often seen as Rivera's wife. From the 1970s feminist art historians, Mexican American artists and a 1983 biography broadened her audience. In 2021 Diego and I sold for about 35 million US dollars, then a record for a Latin American artist.

quiz.q: What did Kahlo originally plan to study?
o: Medicine
Painting
Photography
Architecture
quiz.e: Art was not yet her ambition when she entered the National Preparatory School planning a medical career.

quiz.q: How did Kahlo begin painting self-portraits?
o: As a student, copying her father's photographs
While travelling in the United States with Rivera
While bedridden after her accident, using a mirror fitted above her bed
As a teacher, using her students as models
quiz.e: Her own reflection was the most available subject during months of recovery.

quiz.q: Who was Diego Rivera?
o: A French critic who arranged her Paris show
Mexico's most famous muralist, whom she married in 1929
Her art teacher at the National Preparatory School
A Russian revolutionary exiled in Mexico
quiz.e: Rivera was already celebrated when she showed him her work, and their marriage was central to her life.

quiz.q: How did Kahlo respond to being called a Surrealist?
o: She rejected it, saying she painted her own reality, not dreams
She embraced it and joined their Paris group
She said she had never heard of the movement
She agreed but only for her early works
quiz.e: Her strange images, like roots growing from her body, expressed real experiences of pain and identity.

quiz.q: How did Kahlo attend her first solo exhibition in Mexico in 1953?
o: She sent a letter and stayed away on medical advice
She attended on crutches once her leg had healed
She opened it by video from her home
She arrived by ambulance and received guests from her bed
quiz.e: Against her doctors' advice, she was carried in on her four poster bed and greeted guests lying down.

LESSONS.push: A mirror above a hospital bed changed the course of one woman's life and art.

LESSONS.title: Michelangelo and the Sistine Chapel ceiling
LESSONS.hook: A sculptor who didn't want the job spent four years painting a chapel ceiling twenty metres above the floor. He didn't do it lying on his back, either.

sections.key: Pope Julius II hired Michelangelo, who saw himself as a sculptor, to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling in 1508.
sections.b: In 1508, Michelangelo Buonarroti was in his early thirties and already famous for his marble David in Florence and his Pietà in Rome. He thought of himself first as a sculptor. Pope Julius II, a forceful and warlike pope, had hired him to carve a grand tomb, but then turned to decorating the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, built by his uncle, Pope Sixtus IV. Michelangelo had little experience of fresco and accepted reluctantly. The walls already held frescoes by leading painters such as Botticelli and Perugino. The ceiling, painted as a starry sky, was about to be transformed.

sections.key: Fresco means painting on wet plaster, so the artist must finish each section before it dries.
sections.b: Fresco means fresh in Italian. The painter applies pigments mixed with water onto wet lime plaster. As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction locks the colour into the wall, making it extremely durable. The catch is speed. Each day only as much plaster as could be painted before it set was laid. These daily patches are called giornate, from the Italian for a day's work. Mistakes could not be painted over; the plaster had to be chipped away and redone. Michelangelo's team transferred his designs to the plaster using full-size drawings called cartoons, either by pricking holes along the lines or by pressing them into the soft surface.

sections.key: Michelangelo painted standing on a scaffold with his head tilted back, helped by assistants, not lying flat and alone.
sections.b:
A popular image shows Michelangelo lying on his back for years, paint dripping onto his face. In reality, he designed a wooden scaffold that bridged the chapel just below the ceiling, leaving the floor free for services. He and his assistants worked standing, heads tilted back and arms raised.

It was still punishing. Michelangelo wrote a comic poem, with a little sketch in the margin, complaining about his aching neck, bent back and the paint dripping onto his face. Nor did he work entirely alone, as another myth claims. Assistants ground pigments, prepared plaster and helped with some painting, although he painted the great majority of the figures himself.

sections.key: The ceiling tells nine Genesis scenes, including the famous Creation of Adam, though the hidden brain theory has no evidence behind it.
sections.b:
The ceiling is about 40 metres long and 13 metres wide, with more than 300 figures. Down the centre run nine scenes from Genesis, from God separating light from darkness to the story of Noah. Around them sit huge prophets and sibyls, prophetesses from the classical world, and muscular nude youths called ignudi on painted architecture that only looks three-dimensional. Michelangelo painted the scenes in reverse story order, starting near the entrance with Noah, and his figures grew larger as he went.

In The Creation of Adam, fingertips almost meet. Some writers say the shape around God resembles a brain, hidden by Michelangelo the anatomist, but there is no evidence he intended it.

sections.key: Michelangelo returned to paint The Last Judgment, and a 1980 to 1994 restoration revealed that his colours were bright, not dark.
sections.b:
The ceiling was unveiled in 1512 and stunned everyone who saw it. More than two decades later, Michelangelo painted The Last Judgment across the wall behind the altar, working from 1536 to 1541. Christ raises the saved while the damned tumble towards hell. Some church officials were scandalised by the nudity, and after his death Daniele da Volterra was hired to paint drapery over figures, earning the nickname Il Braghettone, the breeches maker.

For centuries, candle and incense smoke and old varnish darkened the ceiling. A Vatican restoration from 1980 to 1994 revealed vivid pinks, greens, oranges and blues. It was controversial, with some critics arguing that final touches were lost. The chapel still hosts the conclave that elects a pope.

quiz.q: How did Michelangelo see himself when he accepted the commission?
o: As an architect, with years of fresco work
Primarily as a sculptor, with little fresco experience
As a poet who painted occasionally
As a fresco master chosen for his skill
quiz.e: He accepted the ceiling reluctantly because sculpture, not painting, was his main art.

quiz.q: Why did fresco painters work in daily sections called giornate?
o: Each section needed a different pope's approval
The pigments faded if mixed for longer than a day
The scaffold could reach only a small area at a time
Paint must be applied before the plaster dries, locking in the colour
quiz.e: Colour sets into wet plaster as it dries, so each day's patch had to be finished before it hardened.

quiz.q: How did Michelangelo actually paint the ceiling?
o: Standing on a scaffold he designed, with his head tilted back
Lying on his back on a platform
Suspended in a sling from the roof
From the chapel floor using a long brush
quiz.e: The lying-down image is a myth; the work was still punishing for his neck and back.

quiz.q: What is the status of the idea that a brain is hidden in The Creation of Adam?
o: Proven by his notes on anatomy
Confirmed by the Vatican after restoration
A modern reading with no evidence Michelangelo intended it
Recorded in his poem about the ceiling
quiz.e: Michelangelo had studied anatomy, but there is no evidence he hid a brain deliberately.

quiz.q: What did the 1980 to 1994 restoration reveal?
o: Bright colours that had been hidden under centuries of soot and varnish
That the ceiling had originally been painted gold
That most figures were painted by assistants
That the ceiling was painted on canvas
quiz.e: Candle smoke and old varnish had made the colours look sombre, so vivid pinks and blues surprised everyone.

LESSONS.push: Michelangelo did not paint the Sistine ceiling the way the legend says.

LESSONS.title: The Stradivarius mystery
LESSONS.hook: Violins made in a small Italian town three centuries ago sell for millions of dollars. But when top players are blindfolded, can they actually tell the difference?

sections.key: Antonio Stradivari worked in Cremona into his early nineties, and his instruments from about 1700 to 1720 are called his golden period.
sections.b: Cremona, in northern Italy, was the heart of violin making for generations. The Amati family established the craft there in the 1500s, and the Guarneri family also worked in town. Antonio Stradivari was born around 1644 and may have trained with Nicolò Amati. He worked for an extraordinary length of time, making violins, violas, cellos, guitars and harps until he died in 1737, in his early nineties. Estimates suggest he made a thousand or more instruments, and roughly 650 are thought to survive, though the numbers are approximate. Experts generally regard instruments from about 1700 to 1720 as his golden period, when his designs were most refined.

sections.key: A violin's sound comes from its whole wooden body, and theories about Stradivari's secret, from cold-climate wood to chemicals, remain unproven.
sections.b:
A string alone makes little sound. Its vibrations pass through the bridge into the body, a thin spruce top and maple back, which amplifies and shapes the tone. Tiny differences in wood density, thickness and varnish change which frequencies are boosted.

People have long hunted for a lost secret. One theory points to the Maunder Minimum, a period of low solar activity in the Little Ice Age, when slow-growing trees may have produced unusually dense wood. Other research suggests the wood was treated with minerals or chemicals, perhaps against woodworm. None is proven, and many experts think Stradivari's skill matters more than any single ingredient.

sections.key: In controlled blind tests, experienced violinists could not reliably tell Stradivari violins from good new ones.
sections.b: From 2010, the French acoustics researcher Claudia Fritz and American violin maker Joseph Curtin ran careful experiments. In the first, published in 2012, experienced violinists wore modified welder's goggles so they could not see which instrument they were playing. They tried violins by Stradivari and Guarneri alongside high quality new ones. Players could not reliably tell old from new, and the most preferred instrument was a new one. A larger 2014 follow-up with leading soloists found similar results, and later concert hall tests found listeners often thought the new violins projected better. These studies do not prove old violins are poor, only that their superiority is far less obvious than legend suggests.

sections.key: Old Italian violins keep their value through rarity, history and the effect of belief, not sound alone.
sections.b:
If blindfolded players struggle to pick them, why do Stradivari violins stay so valuable? They are rare historical objects, like Old Master paintings, and their price reflects scarcity, craftsmanship and provenance as much as sound. Many have names and long histories, passing through the hands of famous musicians.

Some violinists argue that lab tests cannot capture what it feels like to live with an instrument for years, learning its responses in large halls. Belief may play a part too. Knowing you are playing a three hundred year old masterpiece can change how you play and how listeners hear. Researchers still debate how much of the magic is acoustic and how much is psychological.

sections.key: Top Stradivari violins sell for millions, so most are owned by foundations and loaned to players.
sections.b:
In 2011, the Stradivari known as the Lady Blunt sold for about 15.9 million US dollars, with the proceeds going to relief efforts after the earthquake and tsunami in Japan. Few working musicians could ever afford such prices, so many of the finest instruments are owned by banks, foundations, governments or wealthy collectors, who lend them to talented performers. In Australia, for example, some leading players perform on historic Italian instruments on loan.

A few are kept almost unplayed in museums, such as the Messiah violin at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, prized partly because it looks nearly new. Most are still played, which many musicians feel is what they were made for.

quiz.q: Roughly when is Stradivari's golden period usually dated?
o: About 1560 to 1580
About 1650 to 1660
About 1700 to 1720
About 1730 to 1737
quiz.e: Instruments from these years are generally regarded as his most refined.

quiz.q: What does the 'Little Ice Age' theory propose?
o: Cold weather made the varnish harder and shinier
Slow-growing trees in a cool period gave unusually dense, even wood
Frozen rivers let wood be shipped faster to Cremona
Low sunlight changed the pitch of the strings
quiz.e: It is one unproven idea, and many experts think the maker's skill matters more.

quiz.q: What did the blind tests of Fritz and Curtin find?
o: Players could not reliably tell old Italian violins from good new ones
Players always picked the Stradivari correctly
Audiences preferred old violins in concert halls
Players could tell only by smelling the varnish
quiz.e: Experienced violinists often preferred a new instrument, so the old violins' advantage is far less clear than legend suggests.

quiz.q: Why do Stradivari violins stay so valuable despite the tests?
o: Modern violins cannot be played in large halls
They are made of a wood that no longer exists
Rarity, history and belief add value beyond sound alone
The tests were later withdrawn as invalid
quiz.e: Their price reflects scarcity, craftsmanship and provenance, and belief may change how they are played and heard.

quiz.q: Why are many top Stradivari instruments loaned to performers?
o: They sound best when passed between many players
Most musicians cannot afford their multi-million-dollar prices
Owners are required by law to lend them out
Their makers' wills forbade private ownership
quiz.e: Foundations, banks and collectors own many of them and lend them to talented players.

LESSONS.push: When top violinists play blindfolded, can they pick the multi-million-dollar violin?

LESSONS.title: The night The Rite of Spring caused an uproar
LESSONS.hook: In Paris in 1913, a new ballet about an ancient sacrifice provoked jeers, shouting and scuffles in the audience. Within a year, its music was being cheered.

sections.key: The Rite of Spring was a Ballets Russes work about ancient pagan rituals, ending with a young woman dancing herself to death.
sections.b:
Before the First World War, Europe's most exciting dance company was the Ballets Russes, run by the Russian impresario Sergei Diaghilev. His star dancer was Vaslav Nijinsky, and his young composer was Igor Stravinsky, who had already scored hits in Paris with The Firebird (1910) and Petrushka (1911). With the painter Nicholas Roerich, Stravinsky devised a ballet about pagan rituals in prehistoric Russia, with Nijinsky as choreographer.

The Rite of Spring has no conventional plot. Tribes celebrate spring with dances, and a young woman is chosen for sacrifice. In the Sacrificial Dance she dances in a frenzy until she dies. It premiered on 29 May 1913 at the new Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris.

sections.key: Stravinsky's score used a very high opening bassoon, harsh repeated chords and unpredictable rhythms to create something savage and new.
sections.b:
The music opens with a bassoon playing a folk-like melody so high in its range that many listeners could not identify the instrument. Soon the orchestra builds layers of overlapping tunes. Then comes a famous passage where strings hammer the same harsh chord again and again, with accents falling in unpredictable places, so the listener cannot settle into a regular beat. Elsewhere the time signature changes almost every bar.

Stravinsky used a very large orchestra, with extra woodwinds, brass and percussion. Many melodies were based on or inspired by Russian folk tunes, but they were reshaped into something entirely new and startling.

sections.key: Nijinsky's choreography rejected ballet's grace for stamping, hunched, inward-turned movements.
sections.b:
Classical ballet prized elegance: turned-out feet, lifted bodies and the illusion of weightlessness. Nijinsky did the opposite. His dancers turned their toes inwards, hunched their shoulders, jumped heavily, landed with a thud and stamped in rhythmic groups. Roerich's costumes were heavy, colourful smocks inspired by old Russian peasant dress. To many in the audience it looked ugly or even ridiculous, and to others daringly modern.

The dancers found the shifting rhythms extremely hard to follow. Nijinsky's choreography was performed only a handful of times and then largely lost, until it was reconstructed for the Joffrey Ballet in 1987 from notes, drawings and memories.

sections.key: The premiere was interrupted by laughter, shouting and arguments, but the legend of a full-scale riot has probably grown in the retelling.
sections.b:
Soon after the curtain rose, parts of the audience began to laugh, whistle and jeer, while others shouted back in defence of the work. The noise grew so loud that the dancers struggled to hear the orchestra, and Nijinsky stood on a chair in the wings shouting the counts to them. Stravinsky left his seat and went backstage.

Exactly what happened is hard to pin down. Many famous descriptions were written years or decades later and contradict each other. Some describe fist fights and objects being thrown, and stories circulated of police being called. Historians agree there was a real uproar, but caution that the legend of a full-scale riot has probably grown.

sections.key: Heard without the dancers in 1914, The Rite of Spring was a triumph and became a cornerstone of twentieth century music.
sections.b:
The ballet was performed only a few more times in 1913. But in April 1914 the music was played as a concert piece in Paris without dancers, and this time it was a triumph, with Stravinsky reportedly carried from the hall on admirers' shoulders. Freed from the startling choreography, audiences could focus on the score's raw power.

The Rite became one of the most influential works of the century, shaping later classical music, jazz and film scores. In 1940, Walt Disney used it in the film Fantasia, set to scenes of the early Earth and dinosaurs. Today it is a regular part of orchestral programmes, and dozens of choreographers have created their own versions of the ballet.

quiz.q: What happens in the ballet's final scene?
o: Rival tribes sign a peace and celebrate the harvest
A prince breaks a spell and marries a swan
An elder is crowned king of the spring tribes
A chosen young woman dances in a frenzy until she dies
quiz.e: The ballet has no conventional plot; it ends with a sacrifice meant to bring back spring.

quiz.q: Why did the opening of the score puzzle listeners?
o: It began with a solo played on the wrong instrument
A bassoon played so high that many could not recognise the instrument
It was played entirely off stage in silence
It started with a choir singing in Latin
quiz.e: The unusual high register was one of many surprises in a score of harsh chords and shifting rhythms.

quiz.q: How did Nijinsky's choreography differ from classical ballet?
o: It used heavy stamping, hunched shoulders and inward-turned toes
It used graceful leaps and a floating, weightless style
It had dancers speak and sing rather than move
It copied the steps of a traditional Russian folk dance
quiz.e: Instead of elegance and apparent weightlessness, he chose heavy, inward, primal movement.

quiz.q: What do historians say about the famous 'riot' at the premiere?
o: There was no disturbance and the audience applauded
The police stopped the show and arrested the composer
There was a real uproar, but many accounts came later and the legend has grown
It was a full riot, confirmed by all accounts
quiz.e: Accounts written years later contradict each other, so the exact violence is uncertain.

quiz.q: How was the music received when played as a concert piece in 1914?
o: It caused another uproar and was withdrawn
It was a triumph, without the startling choreography
It was ignored by critics and audiences
It was received politely but forgotten quickly
quiz.e: Without the dance, audiences could focus on the score's power, and it became a classic.

LESSONS.push: A ballet premiere in 1913 caused an uproar. A year later, the same music was cheered.

LESSONS.title: The Bauhaus: the school that designed the modern world
LESSONS.hook: A German art school lasted only fourteen years before the Nazis shut it down. Yet its ideas are in your kitchen chairs, your fonts and the buildings you walk past every day.

sections.key: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in 1919 to unite art and craft, so students learned both principles and hands-on skills.
sections.b: In 1919, just after the First World War, the architect Walter Gropius founded a school in Weimar, Germany, by merging an art academy with a school of arts and crafts. He called it the Staatliches Bauhaus, roughly meaning state house of building. Gropius believed the old split between fine artists and craftspeople was harmful. Painters looked down on furniture makers, while industry churned out poorly designed products. At the Bauhaus, students learned artistic principles and hands-on skills in workshops for metal, wood, textiles, pottery, printing and more. The long-term goal was building, bringing all the arts together. Germany was poor and divided, and the school hoped to help shape a better society.

sections.key: Every student began with a preliminary course that stripped away old habits and explored materials, shape and colour.
sections.b: New students first took the preliminary course, developed by Johannes Itten and later run by László Moholy-Nagy and Josef Albers. The aim was to unlearn old academic habits and experiment directly with materials. Students explored the textures of wood, glass, paper and metal, studied contrasts of light and dark, and built structures from folded paper. Albers later became famous for his studies of how colours change depending on their neighbours. The painters Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky taught theories of form and colour. It was one of the most remarkable teaching staffs ever gathered.

sections.key: Bauhaus workshops designed simple objects for industry, but women who were promised equality were steered towards weaving.
sections.b:
The school shifted from handcraft towards designing prototypes for industry. Marianne Brandt designed teapots and lamps. Marcel Breuer designed a tubular steel armchair in the mid 1920s, later called the Wassily chair, inspired by the steel tubes of his bicycle. Herbert Bayer designed clean lower case typefaces. Many Bauhaus designs are still made today.

The school officially welcomed women, and in its first year more women than men applied. Leaders worried, and many women were pushed towards weaving. They turned that limitation into an achievement: under Gunta Stölzl, the first female master, the weaving workshop became one of the most commercially successful, and Anni Albers developed new textiles. Brandt broke into metalwork.

sections.key: Pressure from conservative politicians, then the Nazis, forced the Bauhaus from Weimar to Dessau and Berlin, and closed it in 1933.
sections.b:
Conservative politicians in Weimar saw the Bauhaus as foreign, left-wing and a waste of public money, and cut its funding. In 1925 it moved to Dessau, where Gropius designed an icon of modern architecture, completed in 1926: a glass curtain wall, flat roofs and linked wings. Gropius stepped down in 1928, followed by Hannes Meyer and, from 1930, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. The Weimar and Dessau buildings are now UNESCO World Heritage sites.
