This matters in pregnancy. If an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby, she can make antibodies that attack the red cells of that baby or a later one, a condition called haemolytic disease of the newborn. Since the late 1960s, injections of anti-D antibodies have prevented most cases.

sections.key: O negative red cells suit almost anyone, but there are over 40 blood group systems, and blood type does not shape personality.
sections.b:
Type O negative red cells carry no A, B or D antigens, so a recipient's antibodies have nothing to attack. That is why emergency teams rely on O negative when there is no time to test. AB positive people can receive red cells of any type, and for plasma the rules flip: AB plasma has no ABO antibodies and suits anyone. Hospitals still crossmatch whenever they can.

Researchers have identified more than 40 blood group systems, so rare combinations sometimes need specially matched donors. In Australia roughly four in ten people are O positive, fewer than one in ten O negative, and about one per cent AB negative. Careful large studies find no meaningful link between blood type and personality, despite the popular idea in Japan.

quiz.q: Why were early transfusions so unpredictable?
o: Doctors used needles that were too thick
Nobody knew that blood comes in incompatible types
Patients always rejected animal blood
Blood spoiled before it could be given
quiz.e: The hidden incompatibility between blood types explained why one transfusion saved a life and the next killed.

quiz.q: What did Landsteiner's mixing experiments reveal?
o: All human blood is identical
Blood always clots in a test tube
Some blood mixtures made red cells clump, revealing distinct groups
Serum is toxic to red cells
quiz.e: The clumping pattern let him sort people into groups, which explained the old transfusion disasters.

quiz.q: Why does a person with type A blood react badly to type B red cells?
o: Their plasma contains anti-B antibodies that attack the cells
Type B cells are too large to circulate
Type A blood lacks the platelets to cope
Type B cells carry no antigens at all
quiz.e: Plasma carries antibodies against the antigens you lack, and they attack incompatible cells.

quiz.q: What problem did anti-D injections largely prevent?
o: Blood clots after surgery
Iron deficiency in pregnancy
Allergic reactions to plasma
Haemolytic disease of the newborn
quiz.e: Anti-D injections stop an Rh-negative mother from making antibodies against an Rh-positive baby's red cells.

quiz.q: Why is O negative blood used when there is no time to test?
o: It clots faster than other types
Its red cells lack A, B and D antigens, so there is little to attack
It carries extra oxygen
It is the most common type in Australia
quiz.e: With no A, B or D antigens, O negative red cells rarely trigger a reaction in the recipient.

LESSONS.push: A few test tubes in Vienna explained why giving blood once killed patients.

LESSONS.title: How a cut heals
LESSONS.hook: Slice your finger and your body launches a carefully timed rescue operation, from emergency plugging to months of quiet rebuilding.

sections.key: Within seconds of a cut, blood vessels tighten and platelets and fibrin plug the hole, forming a clot that dries into a scab.
sections.b:
The moment skin is cut, damaged blood vessels tighten to reduce blood flow. Tiny cell fragments called platelets touch the exposed tissue and become sticky. They clump into a soft plug and release chemicals that call in more platelets.

At the same time a chain of clotting proteins switches on, step by step, until fibrinogen is converted into long strands of fibrin. These strands weave through the plug like a net, trapping red cells and turning liquid blood into a solid clot. As the surface dries out, it becomes the familiar crusty scab.

sections.key: Redness, heat, swelling and pain are signs that your immune cells have arrived to clean the wound.
sections.b:
Around two thousand years ago the Roman writer Celsus described the four classic signs of inflammation: redness, heat, swelling and pain. They do not mean something is going wrong. Damaged cells release chemical alarms that widen nearby blood vessels, bringing extra blood that makes the area red and warm. Leakier vessel walls let fluid and immune cells seep into the tissue, causing swelling.

Within hours, white blood cells called neutrophils arrive to kill bacteria. Macrophages follow, large cells that swallow debris, dead cells and germs. They also signal the next wave of repair cells to start work, which makes them the managers of healing.

sections.key: Over days, fibroblasts lay down collagen, new capillaries sprout and skin cells crawl across to close the wound.
sections.b:
After a few days the wound enters its building phase. Cells called fibroblasts move in and make collagen, the tough protein that gives skin its strength. New capillaries sprout to supply oxygen and nutrients. Together they form granulation tissue, the pink, slightly bumpy surface you may see in a healing graze.

Meanwhile, skin cells at the edges multiply and crawl across the gap, sliding under the scab until they meet in the middle. Some fibroblasts turn into cells that contract, gently pulling the wound edges closer. Once the new skin is complete, the scab is no longer needed and falls away.

sections.key: Scars keep remodelling for a year or more, but never fully match the original skin.
sections.b:
The final phase is the slowest. The first collagen is laid down hastily. Over following months the body breaks it down and replaces it with stronger, better organised fibres. A scar that looked red and raised often fades and flattens over a year or more.

Even so, scar tissue never becomes perfect skin. It typically regains at most around 80 per cent of the original strength, and it usually lacks hair follicles and sweat glands. Curiously, researchers have found that wounds in early foetuses can heal without any scar at all. Understanding how is a long-standing goal of wound research.

sections.key: Keep small cuts clean and covered, and know that smoking, diabetes, poor nutrition and infection slow repair.
sections.b:
Many of us were told to let cuts breathe. In 1962 British researcher George Winter tested this on pigs, whose skin is similar to ours. Shallow wounds covered with plastic film healed considerably faster than wounds left in the air. A dry scab is a barrier that new skin cells must tunnel under, while a moist surface lets them glide across. So clean small cuts gently and keep them covered.

Healing needs blood supply, oxygen and raw materials. Smoking narrows blood vessels, diabetes can damage circulation, and collagen needs protein and vitamin C. Healing also slows with age. Seek medical help for wounds that are deep, gaping, very dirty, caused by animal bites, or showing spreading infection. For severe bleeding, apply firm pressure and call 000.

quiz.q: What forms the net of strands that turns liquid blood into a clot?
o: Collagen
Keratin
Haemoglobin
Fibrin
quiz.e: Fibrinogen is converted into fibrin strands, which weave through the platelet plug and trap red cells.

quiz.q: Why does an injured area become red and warm?
o: Bacteria produce heat as they grow
Nearby blood vessels widen and bring in extra blood
Nerves overheat from pain signals
The scab traps body heat
quiz.e: Inflammation is the immune response at work, not a sign that healing has failed.

quiz.q: Which cells make the collagen that rebuilds the wound?
o: Neutrophils
Platelets
Fibroblasts
Macrophages
quiz.e: Fibroblasts produce collagen, which forms granulation tissue and gives the new skin its strength.

quiz.q: How does a mature scar compare with the original skin?
o: It is weaker and usually lacks hair follicles
It is stronger than the original
It is identical once fully healed
It gains extra sweat glands
quiz.e: Scar tissue regains at most about 80 per cent of the original strength and lacks follicles and sweat glands.

quiz.q: What did George Winter's 1962 pig experiment suggest for small cuts?
o: Wounds heal fastest in direct sunlight
Scabs speed up healing
Clean, covered, moist wounds heal faster than exposed ones
Covering wounds usually causes infection
quiz.e: A moist, covered wound lets new skin cells glide across, while a dry scab forces them to tunnel.

LESSONS.push: Leaving a cut open to the air feels sensible. A 1962 experiment on pigs says otherwise.

LESSONS.title: Your teeth: the hardest part of you
LESSONS.hook: Your teeth are coated in the toughest material your body makes, yet a bag of lollies can slowly dissolve it. Here is how they work and how to keep them.

sections.key: Enamel is the hardest substance in the body, but it has no living cells, so lost enamel cannot regrow.
sections.b:
A tooth is built like a fortress. The outer layer of the crown is enamel, the hardest substance in the human body. It is about 96 per cent mineral, mostly crystals of a calcium phosphate called hydroxyapatite. Beneath it lies dentine, softer and full of microscopic tubes, which is why a worn or cracked tooth can feel sensitive to cold.

At the centre is the pulp, a soft core of nerves and blood vessels that keeps the tooth alive. Tiny fibres called the periodontal ligament anchor the root into the jawbone. Enamel has one great weakness: it contains no living cells, so once it is lost the body cannot grow it back.

sections.key: Humans get only two sets of teeth, 20 baby teeth then 32 adult teeth, which must last a lifetime.
sections.b:
Like most mammals, we get two sets of teeth. Children have 20 baby teeth, which usually start appearing at around six months, while the adult teeth are already forming deep in the jaw. From about age six the baby teeth loosen and fall out as permanent teeth push up from below.

A full adult set has 32 teeth: incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding. The last four molars, the wisdom teeth, usually arrive between the late teens and mid twenties, if they arrive at all. Unlike sharks, which replace teeth throughout their lives, we get no third set.

sections.key: Mouth bacteria turn sugar into acid that dissolves enamel, so how often you eat sugar matters more than how much.
sections.b:
Your mouth is home to hundreds of species of bacteria, living in a sticky film called plaque. Some, including Streptococcus mutans, feed on sugars and release acid as waste. When a tooth surface becomes acidic enough, roughly below a pH of 5.5, minerals begin to dissolve out of the enamel.

Saliva fights back. It neutralises acid and supplies calcium and phosphate that can rebuild early damage. Trouble starts when attacks come too often for saliva to keep up. That is why how often you eat sugar matters more than the total amount. Sipping soft drink all afternoon is harder on teeth than having one with lunch.

sections.key: Fluoride's protective power was discovered through brown-stained teeth that rarely decayed, and it helps enamel resist acid.
sections.b:
In the early 1900s a young dentist named Frederick McKay moved to Colorado Springs and noticed many locals had brown-stained teeth. Over years he found those teeth were strangely resistant to decay, and the cause was eventually traced to naturally high fluoride in the water. Researchers then worked out that a much lower level could reduce decay without staining.

In 1945 Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to add fluoride to its water deliberately. In Australia, the Tasmanian town of Beaconsfield led the way in 1953. Fluoride helps enamel rebuild into a form called fluorapatite, which resists acid better than the original.

sections.key: Plaque left along the gumline can lead to gum disease and tooth loss, so brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and clean between teeth.
sections.b:
Healthy teeth can still be lost if the gums and bone fail. Plaque left along the gumline causes gingivitis: redness, swelling and bleeding when you brush. At this stage good cleaning reverses it. Left in place, plaque hardens into tartar, which a toothbrush cannot remove. Ongoing inflammation can progress to periodontitis, where pockets form and the supporting bone is gradually destroyed, so teeth loosen and may fall out. Gum disease has been linked with diabetes and heart disease, though how much one causes the other is still studied.

People have cleaned teeth for thousands of years, from chew sticks to hog-hair brushes, and nylon bristles arrived in 1938. Australian dental authorities recommend brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth, and spitting rather than rinsing so some fluoride stays on the enamel.

quiz.q: Why can't the body repair enamel that has been lost?
o: Enamel is made of protein
Enamel is replaced every year
Enamel contains no living cells
Enamel has no minerals
quiz.e: Enamel is non-living mineral, so once it is lost the body cannot regrow it.

quiz.q: How many teeth are in a full adult set?
quiz.e: Humans get 20 baby teeth and then 32 adult teeth, with no third set.

quiz.q: Why is sipping a sugary drink all afternoon worse than having it with a meal?
o: Sugar becomes more acidic over time
Repeated acid attacks give saliva no time to repair enamel
Saliva stops flowing after meals
It stains the teeth brown
quiz.e: The frequency of sugar exposure matters because saliva needs gaps between acid attacks to rebuild enamel.

quiz.q: What clue led to the discovery of fluoride's benefits?
o: Teeth that glowed under ultraviolet light
Children who never lost baby teeth
Sailors whose teeth fell out
Brown-stained teeth that rarely decayed
quiz.e: Naturally fluoridated water produced stained but decay-resistant teeth, which showed fluoride protects enamel.

quiz.q: What is true of gingivitis?
o: It always leads to tooth loss
It can be reversed with good cleaning
It is caused by fluoride
It only affects baby teeth
quiz.e: Early gum disease reverses with good cleaning, but untreated plaque can progress to periodontitis.

LESSONS.push: Your teeth are coated in the hardest thing you make, and it can never regrow.

LESSONS.title: How your voice works
LESSONS.hook: Every word you speak begins as a buzz from two tiny folds of tissue in your throat. The rest is shaped by your body like a musical instrument.

sections.key: Your voice is made in the larynx, where two vocal folds sit across the airway and vibrate when you speak.
sections.b:
Sitting at the top of your windpipe is the larynx, or voice box, a structure of cartilage, muscle and ligament. The bump at the front of the neck, the Adam's apple, is part of its largest cartilage and tends to stick out more in men.

Stretched across the airway are two vocal folds. They are often called vocal cords, but they are not strings. Each is a layered band of muscle and ligament covered in soft, moist membrane. When you breathe, the folds swing apart to let air through. When you swallow, they snap shut, helping stop food and drink going down the wrong way. When you speak, they come together and vibrate.

sections.key: Air from the lungs makes the vocal folds open and shut hundreds of times a second, and tighter folds give higher pitch.
sections.b:
To make sound, muscles bring the vocal folds together. Air pushed up from the lungs builds pressure beneath them until it forces them apart and a puff escapes. The folds spring back together, helped by their own elasticity and the pressure drop as air rushes between them, and the cycle repeats.

It happens remarkably fast. A typical adult man's speaking voice vibrates at around 100 to 120 cycles per second, and a typical woman's at around 200. Tighter, thinner folds vibrate faster and make higher notes, which is how you change pitch. Push more air through and the sound gets louder. On its own, though, this buzz sounds nothing like speech.

sections.key: Your throat, mouth and nose shape the raw buzz into speech, which is why you can whisper without vibrating your vocal folds.
sections.b:
The raw buzz travels up through the throat, mouth and nose, which together form the vocal tract. Like a guitar's body, this space strengthens some frequencies and weakens others. By moving your tongue, lips, jaw and soft palate you change its shape, and with it the sound. Vowels depend mainly on tongue and lip position: say "ee" then "oo" and feel the difference. Consonants come from briefly blocking or narrowing airflow with the lips, teeth or tongue.

Whispering shows the two systems working separately. Your vocal folds do not vibrate at all, yet you still form clear words using the air rushing through your mouth.

sections.key: Puberty, hormones and ageing reshape the larynx, which is why voices deepen, crack and change across life.
sections.b:
Children of both sexes have similar voices because their larynxes are similar in size. At puberty, testosterone makes the larynx grow and the vocal folds lengthen and thicken, especially in boys. Longer, heavier folds vibrate more slowly, and many male voices drop by around an octave. During the change a voice may crack unpredictably as the muscles adjust to a rapidly changing instrument.

Girls' voices deepen too, but only slightly. Voices keep changing throughout life. In older age, vocal folds can thin and lose some muscle, making a voice weaker or breathier. Hormonal changes around menopause can also lower a woman's voice a little.

sections.key: Your recorded voice sounds odd because you normally hear yourself through bone, and lasting hoarseness needs a doctor.
sections.b:
Most people wince at a recording of their own voice. Others hear you only through the air, but you also hear yourself through the bones of your skull. Bone conduction carries low frequencies well, so the voice in your head sounds deeper and fuller. A recording captures only the airborne version, which is much closer to what others hear.

Because the folds collide many times a second, heavy use takes a toll. Teachers, singers, coaches and call centre workers are most at risk of voice problems, including swelling or small callus-like growths called vocal nodules. Rest a sore voice, avoid habitual shouting, stay hydrated and do not smoke. Whispering is not necessarily restful. Hoarseness from a cold usually settles within a week or two, but if it lasts more than about three weeks, see a doctor.

quiz.q: What do the vocal folds do when you swallow?
o: Vibrate rapidly
Stretch to their longest
Close to help protect the airway
Swing wide open
quiz.e: Closing the folds helps stop food and drink going down the wrong way.

quiz.q: How do you raise the pitch of your voice?
o: Push much more air through
Tighten and thin the vocal folds
Open your mouth wider
Breathe through your nose
quiz.e: Tighter, thinner folds vibrate faster, producing higher notes, while more air mainly adds volume.

quiz.q: What does whispering show about how speech is made?
o: It uses only the nose
It needs no airflow
Words can be formed without the vocal folds vibrating
The folds vibrate fastest
quiz.e: Whispering separates the buzz from the shaping: the vocal tract alone forms clear words.

quiz.q: Why do many male voices drop at puberty?
o: Testosterone makes the vocal folds longer and thicker
The lungs grow larger
The tongue becomes heavier
The nose lengthens
quiz.e: Longer, heavier folds vibrate more slowly, producing a lower voice.

quiz.q: Why does your voice sound deeper to you than on a recording?
o: Microphones remove low notes
Recordings speed up speech
Your ears are tuned to high sounds
You also hear it through the bones of your skull
quiz.e: Bone conduction adds low frequencies that a recording, and everyone else, does not hear.

LESSONS.push: Your own recorded voice sounds wrong to you. It is actually the accurate one.

LESSONS.title: Water and thirst: how much do you really need?
LESSONS.hook: Eight glasses a day sounds like ancient wisdom, but its origins are murkier than you might think. Your body has a far better guide built in.

sections.key: Water makes up roughly half to 60 per cent of an adult's body weight and underlies almost every process in the body.
sections.b:
Water is the most abundant substance in your body. In a typical adult it makes up roughly 50 to 60 per cent of body weight, and in newborn babies around 75 per cent. People with more muscle tend to carry more water, because muscle holds more than fat does.

About two thirds sits inside your cells, and the rest bathes the spaces between cells or flows as blood plasma. Water dissolves nutrients, carries waste to the kidneys, cushions joints and the brain, and spreads heat around the body. Almost every chemical reaction that keeps you alive happens in it, which is why your body guards its water levels so carefully.

sections.key: You lose water constantly through urine, sweat and breath, and food supplies roughly a fifth of what you take in.
sections.b:
Even on a quiet day you are always losing water. Most leaves as urine, but a surprising amount escapes unnoticed as sweat evaporating from your skin and as vapour in every breath. More is lost in faeces. A sedentary adult in a mild climate typically loses around two and a half litres a day, and far more during hard exercise or hot weather.

Water comes in from drinks, from food, and in a small amount from the chemical reactions that burn fuel in your cells. Food matters more than many people realise. Fruit, vegetables, soups, rice and pasta are full of water, and food can supply roughly a fifth of a typical intake.

sections.key: There is no good evidence that everyone needs eight glasses of plain water a day, and all drinks count.
sections.b:
The rule of eight glasses a day is repeated everywhere, yet nobody has found solid scientific evidence behind it. One often-cited origin is a 1945 recommendation from a United States nutrition board of about two and a half litres of water a day for adults. The same advice noted that most of this is already in prepared foods, a detail that was quietly forgotten.

Australian guidelines suggest typical fluid intakes from drinks of around 2.6 litres for men and 2.1 litres for women, but these are averages for healthy people, not targets everyone must hit. Tea, coffee, milk and other drinks all count. The mild diuretic effect of caffeine is small in regular drinkers.

sections.key: Your brain tracks how concentrated your blood is and adjusts thirst and urine to match, so thirst and pale urine are a reliable guide.
sections.b:
Deep in the brain, the hypothalamus holds sensors that track how concentrated your blood is. When you lose water, the blood becomes slightly saltier and these sensors respond in two ways. They make you feel thirsty, and they prompt the pituitary gland to release antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin.

This hormone tells the kidneys to reabsorb more water, so urine becomes smaller in volume and darker. When you drink plenty, the hormone falls and the kidneys release more dilute urine. The system responds to changes of only a few per cent. For most healthy people, drinking when thirsty and noticing pale straw-coloured urine is a reliable guide.

sections.key: Older adults, babies and people working in heat are prone to dehydration, but drinking far more than you need can dangerously dilute blood sodium.
sections.b:
Thirst works well for most healthy adults, but it weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without feeling thirsty. Babies and young children lose fluid quickly through fever, vomiting or diarrhoea and cannot fetch a drink. Hard work in Australian summer heat can sweat out more than a litre an hour. Early signs include thirst, dark urine, headache, tiredness and dizziness. Heat stroke is an emergency: if someone in the heat is confused or collapses, call 000 and start cooling them.

Drinking too much is also risky. If fluid arrives faster than your kidneys can remove it, blood sodium becomes diluted (hyponatraemia) and brain cells can swell. A 2005 study found around one in eight Boston Marathon runners had low blood sodium at the finish. Many sports doctors now advise drinking to thirst.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of an adult's body weight is water?
o: 10 to 20 per cent
About 30 per cent
50 to 60 per cent
80 to 90 per cent
quiz.e: Water makes up roughly half to 60 per cent of an adult's weight, and more of a newborn's.

quiz.q: Which source of water do people often overlook?
o: Air absorbed through the skin
Food such as fruit, vegetables and soups
Water stored in the bones
Breathing in through the nose
quiz.e: Food can supply roughly a fifth of a typical water intake.

quiz.q: What detail of the 1945 recommendation was later forgotten?
o: It applied only to children
It was meant for soldiers only
It recommended 20 glasses a day
Most of the water is already in prepared foods
quiz.e: The famous advice never meant eight glasses of plain water, since much of our water comes from food.

quiz.q: What does antidiuretic hormone do when you are low on water?
o: It tells the kidneys to keep more water
It makes you sweat more
It speeds up breathing
It raises blood sugar
quiz.e: The kidneys reabsorb more water, so urine becomes smaller in volume and darker.

quiz.q: What is the danger of drinking far more water than you need?
o: Blood sugar rises sharply
Blood sodium becomes dangerously diluted
The kidneys stop making urine
The blood becomes too concentrated
quiz.e: Excess water dilutes blood sodium, which can swell brain cells, so drinking to thirst is usually safer.

LESSONS.push: Eight glasses a day is everywhere, yet nobody can show where it came from.

LESSONS.title: Fever: why your body turns up the heat
LESSONS.hook: A fever is not your body losing control of its temperature. It is a deliberate decision, and one that animals have been making for hundreds of millions of years.

sections.key: In a fever the brain deliberately raises its target temperature, which is why you shiver and feel cold as it rises.
sections.b:
Your body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain that works like a thermostat. During an infection, immune cells release signalling molecules, including cytokines such as interleukin 1 and interleukin 6. These trigger a substance called prostaglandin E2, which raises the hypothalamus's set point.

Suddenly your normal temperature feels too cold. You shiver, your skin turns pale as blood vessels narrow to save heat, and you reach for a blanket, all to warm up to the new target. When the fever breaks and the set point drops, the opposite happens: you feel hot, flush and sweat heavily.

sections.key: Normal body temperature is a range that shifts through the day, and 37 degrees is only an approximate average.
sections.b:
The figure of 37 degrees Celsius traces largely to German physician Carl Wunderlich, who in 1868 published an analysis of a huge number of armpit readings. His work helped make the thermometer a standard medical tool. Modern measurements suggest the average is often a little lower, commonly around 36.5 to 36.8 degrees, depending on the person and where it is measured.

Your temperature also follows your body clock, usually lowest in the early morning and highest in the late afternoon or evening. Age, activity and, for women, the menstrual cycle shift it too. Some researchers have found evidence that average temperatures have drifted down since Wunderlich's day.

sections.key: Cold-blooded animals give themselves a fever by seeking warmth, which suggests fever is ancient and useful.
sections.b:
In the 1970s physiologist Matthew Kluger studied desert iguanas, which cannot make their own body heat and control temperature by moving between warm and cool spots. When infected with bacteria, the lizards chose warmer places, raising their temperature by around two degrees, a so-called behavioural fever. Lizards kept at cooler temperatures were much more likely to die.

Similar behaviour has since been seen in fish, insects and other animals. Because fever appears across so many branches of the animal kingdom, and costs a lot of energy, most scientists conclude it evolved because it helps fight infection. A costly trait that useless would probably have been lost long ago.

sections.key: Higher temperatures speed up parts of the immune system and make life harder for some germs.
sections.b:
Fever seems to help in several ways. Many immune processes run faster when warm, including the movement of white blood cells and the production of some defensive molecules. Some bacteria and viruses multiply less efficiently in warmer surroundings, and the body also restricts the iron many bacteria need to grow.

History offers a grim illustration. In 1917 Austrian psychiatrist Julius Wagner-Jauregg deliberately infected patients with neurosyphilis, then an incurable brain infection, with malaria to induce high fevers. Some improved, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1927. The treatment was dangerous and was abandoned once penicillin arrived, but it showed that fever could attack a disease.

sections.key: A fever is regulated by the brain, whereas heat stroke is the body failing to shed heat, and some fevers need urgent care.
sections.b:
In a fever the brain has raised its set point and the body still regulates around it, so infection fevers rarely climb much above about 41 degrees. In heat stroke the set point is unchanged: the body absorbs or makes heat faster than it can lose it, and temperature keeps rising. Fever medicines act on the set point, so they do not treat heat stroke. It is an emergency: call 000 and start cooling the person.

Most fevers pass within a few days, and medicines mainly improve comfort, so follow the label or ask a pharmacist. Get urgent help for a baby under three months with fever, or for anyone with a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when pressed, trouble breathing, severe drowsiness or confusion. Call 000 if a febrile seizure lasts more than five minutes.

quiz.q: Why does a person with a rising fever shiver and feel cold?
o: Their blood has lost heat to the infection
The brain has raised its target temperature
The infection has damaged their nerves
Their muscles are too weak to stay warm
quiz.e: The raised set point makes normal body temperature feel too cold, so the body works to warm up.

quiz.q: What do modern measurements say about normal body temperature?
o: It is exactly 37 degrees for everyone
It never changes during the day
It is always highest in the morning
It is a range, often a little below 37 degrees
quiz.e: Normal temperature varies by person, time of day and measurement site, and 37 degrees is only an old average.

quiz.q: What did the desert iguana experiments suggest about fever?
o: Infected lizards sought warmth, and cooler lizards died more often
Lizards cannot get infections
Fever kills cold-blooded animals
Lizards cool down when infected
quiz.e: Fever across the animal kingdom, even self-induced, suggests it is an ancient and useful defence.

quiz.q: How does a higher temperature help fight infection?
o: It destroys all bacteria instantly
It switches off the immune system to save energy
It makes blood vessels leak iron
It speeds up some immune processes and hinders some germs
quiz.e: Warmth boosts parts of the immune response and makes conditions harder for some microbes.

quiz.q: Why don't fever-reducing medicines treat heat stroke?
o: They only work on children
Heat stroke is not caused by a raised set point
They make heat stroke worse
Heat stroke involves a low temperature
quiz.e: Heat stroke is the body failing to shed heat, so it needs urgent cooling and a call to 000.

LESSONS.push: A fever is not your body losing control. It is closer to the opposite.

LESSONS.title: Reflexes: when your spine decides first
LESSONS.hook: Touch a hot pan and your hand is gone before you feel the pain. That split-second move is made without your brain's permission.

sections.key: The idea that the body can react automatically goes back to Descartes, and we now know many reflexes are handled by the spinal cord.
sections.b:
René Descartes' Treatise of Man, published in 1664 after his death, included a famous drawing of a boy with his foot near a fire. Descartes imagined that heat tugged on tiny threads in the nerves, opening valves in the brain that sent spirits to the muscles to pull the foot away. The details were wrong, but the core idea was striking: some actions might happen mechanically, like clockwork, without any conscious choice.

Over the following centuries, scientists found that many automatic responses do not even need the brain. They are handled lower down, in the spinal cord, by circuits we now call reflex arcs.

sections.key: The knee jerk is a simple reflex in which a stretch sensor connects directly to a motor neuron in the spinal cord.
sections.b:
When a doctor taps the tendon below your kneecap, your lower leg kicks forward. In 1875 two German neurologists, Wilhelm Erb and Carl Westphal, independently described this reflex, and it has been tested ever since.

The tap briefly stretches the quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh. Stretch sensors in the muscle, called muscle spindles, fire signals along a sensory nerve into the spinal cord. There, the sensory neuron connects directly to a motor neuron, which sends a command straight back, telling the muscle to contract. With only one connection in the chain, it is a monosynaptic reflex. In everyday life it helps keep you upright.

sections.key: Every reflex arc has a receptor, a sensory neuron, a processing step, a motor neuron and a muscle or gland, and muscles work in coordinated pairs.
sections.b:
A reflex arc has five basic parts. A receptor detects a change such as stretch, heat or pressure. A sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord or brainstem. A processing step links it to an outgoing motor neuron, sometimes through extra cells called interneurons. Finally a muscle or gland responds.

British physiologist Charles Sherrington spent decades mapping these circuits and coined the word synapse for the gap between nerve cells. He showed that reflexes coordinate muscles in pairs. When the quadriceps contracts in the knee jerk, signals simultaneously relax the hamstrings behind the thigh so they do not fight the movement. Sherrington shared the 1932 Nobel Prize.

sections.key: The withdrawal reflex pulls you away from harm and stiffens your other leg, often before you feel any pain.
sections.b:
Step on a sharp object and your foot lifts before you have time to think. This withdrawal reflex is more complex than the knee jerk. It uses several interneurons in the spinal cord to activate a group of muscles that pull the limb away.

At the same moment, a linked circuit called the crossed extensor reflex stiffens your other leg so it can take your weight and you do not topple. Signals also travel up to the brain, which is why you then feel the pain, look down and perhaps say something unprintable. The reflex circuit is short and conscious pain takes longer to form, so the movement often comes first.

sections.key: Reflexes take tens of milliseconds, far quicker than conscious reactions, and newborn reflexes help doctors check development.
sections.b:
Newborn reflexes fade within months as the brain's higher regions take control. Stroke a cheek and the baby turns to feed; touch a palm and they grip; sense a fall and they fling out their arms. In 1896 Joseph Babinski described how stroking the sole makes the big toe curl down in healthy adults. If it points up and the toes fan out, it can signal damage to nerve pathways from the brain.

A spinal reflex takes only a few tens of milliseconds. A conscious reaction to something you see takes around a fifth to a quarter of a second. In sprinting, a runner who reacts within a tenth of a second of the gun has false started, because a genuine response cannot reliably be that fast. Catching a ball feels like a reflex but is learned.

quiz.q: What do scientists now know about many automatic responses?
o: They are controlled only by the heart
They are handled by the spinal cord without needing the brain
They are always learned in childhood
They depend on the eyes
quiz.e: Reflex arcs in the spinal cord handle many automatic responses without involving the brain.

quiz.q: In the knee-jerk reflex, what does the sensory neuron connect to in the spinal cord?
o: A long chain of brain cells
The heart's pacemaker
A motor neuron directly
The bones of the knee
quiz.e: Only one connection links the sensor to the motor neuron, which makes the knee jerk monosynaptic and very fast.

quiz.q: What happens to the hamstrings when the quadriceps contracts in the knee jerk?
o: They contract too
They are cut off from the brain
They shorten and stiffen
They relax so they do not oppose the movement
quiz.e: Reflexes coordinate muscles in pairs so that opposing muscles do not fight each other.

quiz.q: What does the crossed extensor reflex do when you step on something sharp?
o: It stiffens the other leg to support your weight
It makes you feel the pain sooner
It lifts both feet at once
It slows your heart rate
quiz.e: It keeps you balanced while the injured foot withdraws, often before you feel pain.

quiz.q: Why is a sprinter who reacts within a tenth of a second counted as false starting?
o: Reflexes are banned in athletics
A genuine response cannot reliably be that fast
The gun's sound takes longer to arrive
It gives other runners a disadvantage
quiz.e: Conscious reactions take around a fifth of a second or more, so anything much faster is treated as anticipation.

LESSONS.push: Touch something hot and your hand moves before you feel it. Who decided?

LESSONS.title: The lymphatic system: your hidden drainage network
LESSONS.hook: Alongside your blood vessels runs a second network that most people barely know exists. Without it, you would swell up like a balloon.

sections.key: Fluid constantly leaks out of your capillaries, and the lymphatic system collects it and returns it to the blood.
sections.b:
Your smallest blood vessels, the capillaries, are deliberately leaky. As blood flows through, pressure pushes plasma into the tissues, carrying oxygen and nutrients to cells. Most of it seeps back, but not all. Each day several litres are left among the cells. If nothing collected it, your tissues would swell and your blood volume would steadily fall.

That is the job of the lymphatic system, a network of thin-walled vessels that begin as tiny dead-end tubes woven among the tissues. They soak up the excess fluid, now called lymph, along with proteins, debris and sometimes germs, and carry it back towards the bloodstream.

sections.key: Lymph is moved by muscle movement, breathing and one-way valves rather than by a heart.
sections.b:
Blood has the heart to push it around, but lymph has no central pump. Lymphatic vessels contain one-way valves, like those in veins, that stop fluid flowing backwards. The walls of larger vessels can contract rhythmically, and each time nearby muscles squeeze, or your chest rises and falls as you breathe, lymph is nudged further along.

Most of it eventually drains through the thoracic duct into large veins near the left collarbone, rejoining the blood. This helps explain why ankles often swell after hours of sitting still on a long flight. With the leg muscles inactive, fluid moves along more slowly, and gravity lets it pool in the feet.

sections.key: Hundreds of lymph nodes filter lymph and act as meeting points where immune cells encounter signs of infection.
sections.b:
Along the lymphatic vessels sit lymph nodes, small bean-shaped structures found in clusters in places such as the neck, armpits and groin. Estimates vary, but a typical adult has several hundred. As lymph passes through, the nodes filter out debris and microbes. They are also packed with lymphocytes, the immune cells that recognise specific invaders.

Because fluid from every tissue flows through them, nodes act as checkpoints where immune cells meet evidence of infection. When they detect a threat, lymphocytes multiply rapidly, which is why the glands in your neck can swell and become tender during a sore throat. The tonsils, spleen and thymus are also part of the wider lymphatic family.

sections.key: Dietary fat enters the body through lymphatic vessels called lacteals, which an Italian anatomist first spotted in a dog in 1622.
sections.b:
In 1622 Italian anatomist Gaspare Aselli, dissecting a recently fed dog, noticed thin white threads across its intestines. Cutting one released a milky fluid. He called them lacteals, from the Latin for milk. Decades later Jean Pecquet traced the fluid to the thoracic duct, and in the 1650s Olaus Rudbeck and Thomas Bartholin described the wider lymphatic network.

Aselli's vessels had a real purpose. Most nutrients go straight into blood vessels leading to the liver, but fats are packaged into large particles called chylomicrons that enter the lacteals instead. After a fatty meal, gut lymph turns cloudy and white. This fat-rich fluid travels up the thoracic duct and enters the bloodstream near the collarbone, reaching the body before it passes through the liver.

sections.key: Damage to lymph vessels causes long-lasting swelling called lymphoedema, and even the brain turned out to have lymphatic vessels.
sections.b:
When lymphatic vessels are blocked or damaged, fluid builds up as lymphoedema, a persistent swelling often in an arm or leg. In Australia and similar countries a common cause is cancer treatment, because surgery or radiation may damage lymph nodes. Cancers can spread via lymph vessels, so surgeons often check the first node a tumour drains into, called the sentinel node. In parts of the tropics, mosquito-borne parasitic worms cause lymphatic filariasis, which in severe cases brings enormous swelling called elephantiasis.

Textbooks long taught that the brain had no lymphatic vessels. In 2015 two teams, one in the United States and one in Finland, independently reported them in the meninges, the membranes wrapping the brain. They appear to drain fluid, waste and immune cells towards nodes in the neck. Their role in disease remains uncertain.

quiz.q: Why does the body need a lymphatic system?
o: To pump blood when the heart rests
To make red blood cells
To collect fluid that leaks from capillaries and return it to the blood
To carry oxygen to the brain
quiz.e: Without lymphatic drainage, leaked fluid would pool in tissues and blood volume would fall.

quiz.q: What moves lymph through the body?
o: A small heart in the chest
Muscle movement, breathing and one-way valves
The kidneys
Gravity alone
quiz.e: With no central pump, squeezing muscles, breathing and valves keep lymph flowing one way.

quiz.q: Why can glands in your neck swell during a throat infection?
o: Fat collects in the neck
The thyroid becomes infected
Blood vessels burst
Immune cells in the lymph nodes multiply to fight it
quiz.e: Lymph nodes are checkpoints where lymphocytes multiply when they detect a threat.

quiz.q: How does fat from a meal first enter circulation?
o: Through lacteals in the lymphatic system
Directly into the liver's blood supply
Through the stomach wall
Through the skin
quiz.e: Fat particles are too large for blood capillaries, so they travel in the lymph before joining the blood.

quiz.q: What did researchers report in 2015?
o: The brain has no lymphatic vessels
Lymph nodes make blood
Lymphatic vessels exist in the membranes around the brain
The thoracic duct has a twin
quiz.e: The discovery overturned textbook teaching and may help explain how the brain clears waste.

LESSONS.push: You have a second circulation with no pump, and the brain's was missed for centuries.

LESSONS.title: Evolution's leftovers: goosebumps, tailbones and the appendix
LESSONS.hook: Your body carries traces of ancestors who had fur, tails and much bigger jaws. Some leftovers have found new jobs; others are just along for the ride.

sections.key: A vestigial structure has lost its original function, or much of it, but it is not necessarily useless.
sections.b:
In The Descent of Man, published in 1871, Charles Darwin pointed to what he called rudimentary organs as evidence that humans share ancestry with other animals. These were parts that seemed shrunken or purposeless in us but were fully functional in other species.

The modern term is vestigial. It is often misunderstood as meaning completely useless. Biologists use it more carefully: a vestigial structure has lost its original function, or much of it, though it may have gained a new one. In the late 1800s some anatomists drew up long lists of supposedly useless organs. Some items on those lists, such as the thymus, later proved essential.

sections.key: Goosebumps fluff up fur to insulate and look bigger, which helps furry mammals but does little for us.
sections.b:
When you are cold or deeply moved by music, tiny muscles at the base of your hair follicles contract, pulling hairs upright and raising little bumps. Each of these arrector pili muscles attaches to a single hair.

In heavily furred mammals the same reflex fluffs up the coat, trapping a thicker layer of insulating air. It also makes an animal look bigger, which is why a frightened or angry cat puffs up. Humans have lost most of our body fur, so the reflex achieves very little warmth or intimidation. These muscles may still play a supporting role in hair growth, but the visible goosebump is largely a leftover.

sections.key: Every human embryo briefly has a tail, and the coccyx that remains still anchors important muscles.
sections.b:
At the base of your spine sits the coccyx, or tailbone, made of several small fused vertebrae. It is what remains of the tail carried by our primate ancestors, and apes such as chimpanzees and gorillas lack an external tail too. Human embryos make the connection vivid. Around the fourth to sixth week of development an embryo has a distinct tail with more vertebrae than an adult keeps. Later the tail stops growing and its extra cells are removed.

Yet the coccyx is not useless. It anchors muscles, tendons and ligaments of the pelvic floor, and bears some of your weight when you lean back to sit.

sections.key: Once dismissed as useless, the appendix appears to support the immune system and may shelter helpful gut bacteria.
sections.b:
Darwin suggested the appendix was a shrunken remnant of a larger organ that helped ancestral primates digest leaves. For over a century it was treated as a useless troublemaker, famous mainly for appendicitis, which can be life-threatening if the organ bursts.

The picture has changed. The appendix is rich in lymphoid tissue, involved in immune defence. Researchers have also proposed that it acts as a safe house for beneficial gut bacteria, helping repopulate the intestine after an illness such as severe diarrhoea. Comparative studies suggest an appendix has evolved independently many times in different mammals, which hints at some advantage. Even so, people who have it removed live normal, healthy lives.

sections.key: Wisdom teeth often don't fit because human jaws shrank, and some people lack muscles such as the palmaris longus without any loss.
sections.b:
Our ancestors had larger jaws and chewed tougher food. Human jaws became smaller over hundreds of thousands of years, a change many researchers link to cooking and softer diets. Teeth shrank less, so wisdom teeth often find no room and can stay trapped (impaction), causing pain or infection. A significant minority of people never develop one or more at all.

Touch your thumb to your little finger and flex your wrist: many people see a thin cord rise at the inner wrist. That is the palmaris longus tendon. Roughly one in seven people, varying between populations, lack it in one or both arms, with no noticeable loss of grip strength. Small ear muscles, used by some animals to swivel their ears, survive too, and a few humans can still wiggle theirs.

quiz.q: What do biologists mean by a vestigial structure?
o: One that is always completely useless
One that has lost its original function, or much of it
One that only appears in embryos
One that grows larger with age
quiz.e: Vestigial means reduced or changed in function, and such a part may still have a new job.

quiz.q: What do goosebumps do for furry mammals?
o: Make their skin waterproof
Help them sweat
Help them hear better
Fluff up the fur for insulation and to look bigger
quiz.e: The reflex traps insulating air and makes an animal look larger, but does little in mostly hairless humans.

quiz.q: What useful job does the coccyx still do?
o: It produces blood cells
It anchors muscles and ligaments of the pelvic floor
It controls balance
It protects the kidneys
quiz.e: The tailbone is a remnant of a tail, but it supports the pelvic floor and bears weight when sitting.

quiz.q: What role have researchers proposed for the appendix?
o: A safe house for beneficial gut bacteria
Digesting cellulose in humans
Storing fat
Making digestive enzymes
quiz.e: The appendix is rich in immune tissue and may help restock gut bacteria after illness.

quiz.q: Why do wisdom teeth often have no room to arrive?
o: Modern teeth grow faster than before
Wisdom teeth are larger than other molars
Human jaws have become smaller while teeth shrank less
Baby teeth fail to fall out
quiz.e: Smaller jaws, linked to cooking and softer diets, leave too little space for the third molars.

LESSONS.push: Your body carries a tail, a spare muscle and a gut organ once thought useless.

LESSONS.title: What cancer really is
LESSONS.hook: Cancer is not one disease but hundreds, all sharing a single rebellion: cells that stop following the body's rules. Understanding that rebellion has transformed treatment.

sections.key: Cancer is hundreds of diseases united by cells that divide without control and invade other tissues.
sections.b:
Cancer is not a modern disease. The Edwin Smith Papyrus, an Egyptian medical text from around 1600 BCE, describes bulging masses in the breast and says there is no treatment. Tumours have also been found in ancient mummies and skeletons. The Greek physician Hippocrates used the word karkinos, meaning crab, perhaps because swollen veins around some tumours looked like a crab's legs. The Romans translated it into the Latin word cancer.

Today we know it is not one disease but hundreds, varying by tissue and by the genes involved. What unites them is cells that divide without control and can invade other tissues.

sections.key: Cancer begins when mutations damage genes that drive cell growth or genes that restrain it.
sections.b:
Healthy cells divide only when they receive the right signals, and stop when they should. Genes govern this. Proto-oncogenes act like accelerators; when mutated, they can become oncogenes, like an accelerator stuck to the floor. Tumour suppressor genes act like brakes. The most famous, TP53, is called the guardian of the genome because it can halt division or order a damaged cell to destroy itself. It is mutated in around half of all cancers. Elephants, with far more cells than us but no more cancer (a puzzle called Peto's paradox), carry many extra copies of it.

In 1971 Alfred Knudson, studying a childhood eye cancer, proposed that both copies of a tumour suppressor gene usually need to be knocked out: the two-hit hypothesis.

sections.key: Cancer cells gradually acquire shared abilities, including escaping the normal limit on how often a cell can divide.
sections.b:
In 2000 Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg argued that cancers share acquired abilities: making their own growth signals, ignoring stop signals, avoiding programmed cell death, dividing indefinitely, building blood vessels, and invading and spreading. In 2011 they added reprogramming energy use and evading the immune system. No single mutation provides all of these. A cell gathers them over years or decades.

Take dividing indefinitely. In the early 1960s Leonard Hayflick showed normal human cells divide only about 40 to 60 times, partly because protective chromosome caps called telomeres shorten each time. Many cancer cells switch on telomerase, an enzyme that rebuilds the caps. HeLa cells, taken in 1951 from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge or consent, are still dividing and helped develop the polio vaccine.

sections.key: Mutations build up with age and cause cancer, and a tumour evolves, which is why it can resist treatment.
sections.b:
Every cell division carries a small chance of copying errors, and outside factors damage DNA too. Mutations accumulate over a lifetime, the main reason cancer becomes more common with age. Established causes include tobacco smoke (linked to many cancers, not only lung cancer), ultraviolet radiation (behind most skin cancers, a serious issue in sunny Australia), alcohol, and viruses such as human papillomavirus.

A tumour is not a uniform mass. Its cells keep mutating, so one tumour holds many genetically different groups. This is natural selection inside one person: a cell that grows faster or resists a drug leaves more descendants. A therapy may shrink a tumour, then a resistant group regrows, so doctors often combine treatments. Most cancer deaths are caused by tumours that have spread, or metastasised.

sections.key: Treatments now include drugs that target specific mutations or unleash the immune system, and prevention matters too.
sections.b:
Surgery, radiation and chemotherapy remain central, but newer approaches build on understanding how cancer works. Targeted therapies block the specific molecules a cancer depends on. Imatinib, approved in 2001, transformed the outlook for a blood cancer called chronic myeloid leukaemia. Immunotherapy releases the brakes cancers use to hide from immune cells, and James Allison and Tasuku Honjo shared the 2018 Nobel Prize for the discoveries behind these checkpoint drugs.

Prevention matters too. Australia's human papillomavirus vaccination program and cervical screening have put the country on track to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem, and national screening programs also look for early breast and bowel cancers.

quiz.q: What does the word 'cancer' describe today?
o: Hundreds of diseases sharing uncontrolled cell division
One disease that behaves the same in every tissue
A modern illness caused by industrial life
An infection that spreads between people
quiz.e: Cancers differ by tissue and genes, but all involve cells that divide without control and can invade other tissues.

quiz.q: What happens when a tumour suppressor gene such as TP53 is damaged?
o: A key brake on cell division is lost
Cells divide faster than before in healthy tissue only
The immune system is switched off completely
Telomeres grow longer in every cell
quiz.e: Tumour suppressor genes act like brakes, so losing them lets damaged cells keep dividing.

quiz.q: How do many cancer cells avoid the normal limit on cell divisions?
o: They rebuild their telomeres using telomerase
They stop making any new proteins
They avoid ever being exposed to oxygen
They copy their DNA without any errors
quiz.e: Switching on telomerase rebuilds the protective caps, letting cancer cells divide far beyond the normal limit.

quiz.q: Why can a cancer return after a drug first shrinks the tumour?
o: A resistant group of cells survives and regrows
The drug turns healthy cells into cancer cells
Tumours always contain identical cells that adapt together
The body forgets how to fight the drug
quiz.e: A tumour evolves, so cells that happen to resist a therapy survive and multiply.

quiz.q: What do immunotherapy checkpoint drugs do?
o: Release the brakes cancers use to hide from immune cells
Block the one molecule every cancer depends on
Remove tumours by cutting out whole organs
Replace damaged genes in every cell
quiz.e: Checkpoint drugs let the immune system recognise and attack cancer cells that had been hiding from it.

LESSONS.push: Cancer is hundreds of diseases. What single rebellion links them all?

LESSONS.title: New Coke: the taste test that backfired
LESSONS.hook: In 1985 Coca-Cola replaced its famous recipe with one that beat the old drink in blind taste tests. Within three months the company was begging forgiveness.

sections.key: Coca-Cola changed its recipe because blind taste tests, including its own, showed people preferred sweeter drinks.
sections.b:
By the early 1980s Coca-Cola's share of the American soft drink market had been sliding for years while Pepsi gained. Pepsi targeted younger drinkers and, from 1975, ran the Pepsi Challenge: shoppers sipped from two unmarked cups, and on camera they often picked Pepsi. Coca-Cola's own blind tests gave the same uncomfortable answer.

Under chief executive Roberto Goizueta, the company did the unthinkable and reformulated a recipe treated as almost sacred for nearly a century. In the secret Project Kansas, it put a sweeter, smoother cola through about 200,000 taste tests. It beat both old Coke and Pepsi. On 23 April 1985, Coca-Cola announced that the old formula was retired.

sections.key: Customers reacted not as tasters but as people who had lost something that belonged to them.
sections.b:
The reaction caught the company off guard. Phone lines at its Atlanta headquarters were flooded with thousands of angry calls, and sacks of letters arrived from people who felt betrayed. Some customers stockpiled cases of the original. In Seattle, Gay Mullins started the Old Cola Drinkers of America and won wide media coverage. Comedians and columnists piled on.

Much of the anger was not about flavour at all. Many complainers had never compared the two drinks carefully. They were upset that something tied to childhood, family and national identity had been taken away without anyone asking them first.

sections.key: Taste tests measured which drink people preferred in a sip, not what the brand meant to them.
sections.b:
The flaw in the research is easy to see in hindsight. Blind tests asked a narrow question: which liquid do you prefer right now, in a small sip? They never asked how people would feel if the old drink disappeared for good.

One popular explanation is that sweeter drinks tend to win quick sip tests even when people would not choose them for a whole can, though how much that mattered here is still argued about. Some of the company's own focus groups hinted at trouble, as a minority reacted angrily to the idea of losing the original, but the strength of that feeling was underestimated. Customers buy meaning and habit as well as features.

sections.key: Coca-Cola reversed course publicly after just 79 days, and the original formula came back as Coca-Cola Classic.
sections.b:
By early July the company had seen enough. On 11 July 1985, 79 days after the launch, it announced the original formula would return as Coca-Cola Classic, and the news led television bulletins across the country.

Company president Donald Keough told reporters that some critics would say Coca-Cola had made a marketing mistake, some cynics would say it had planned the whole thing, and the truth was that it was not that dumb and not that smart. For a while both drinks were sold side by side. Classic comfortably outsold its replacement. New Coke was later renamed Coke II and lingered in a few markets for years before quietly disappearing.

sections.key: A brand's value lives partly in customers' heads, and admitting a mistake fast can limit the damage.
sections.b:
Was New Coke a disaster? In the short term it was an embarrassment, but there is an odd twist. The uproar reminded Americans how attached they were to the original, and after Classic returned, Coca-Cola's sales recovered and its lead over Pepsi strengthened. The company did not plan this. It did one thing well: once it understood its mistake, it reversed quickly and publicly instead of defending the decision for years.

Business schools still teach the case. Data can be precise and still answer the wrong question. Loyal customers can feel ownership of a product they do not legally own. And humility, shown early, is often cheaper than stubbornness.

quiz.q: Why did Coca-Cola decide to change its recipe?
o: Blind tests showed many people preferred sweeter rivals
Its original formula had become too expensive to make
Regulators had banned an ingredient in the old drink
Customers had been asking for a sweeter cola
quiz.e: Its share was sliding and blind tests, including its own, kept favouring a sweeter taste.

quiz.q: What was much of the anger over New Coke really about?
o: Losing something tied to childhood and identity without being asked
A noticeably higher price at the shop
Poor advertising for the new drink
A sharp drop in the quality of the cans
quiz.e: Many angry customers had never compared the drinks carefully; they resented losing a familiar part of their lives.

quiz.q: What did the blind taste tests fail to measure?
o: How people would feel if the old drink vanished
Which drink people preferred in a single sip
Whether the new drink was sweeter than Pepsi
How many people took part in the testing
quiz.e: A sip test answers a narrow question about taste and misses what a brand means to its customers.

quiz.q: What did Coca-Cola do once it understood its mistake?
o: Brought back the original quickly and publicly
Defended the new formula for several more years
Quietly removed the original from every market
Replaced the new drink with a third formula
quiz.e: Reversing within 79 days, in the open, limited the damage.

quiz.q: What can the New Coke case teach about data?
o: Precise data can still answer the wrong question
More tests always remove the need for judgement
Taste is the only thing customers value
Data should be ignored when customers complain
quiz.e: The tests were precise, but they measured a sip rather than the meaning of the brand.

LESSONS.push: The new recipe won 200,000 taste tests. So why did it fail within months?

LESSONS.title: The Tylenol murders and the art of crisis response
LESSONS.hook: In 1982 seven people in Chicago died after taking poisoned painkillers. How one company responded became the textbook example of handling a crisis.

sections.key: In 1982 someone laced Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules with cyanide and returned them to shop shelves.
sections.b:
On 29 September 1982 a twelve-year-old girl in a Chicago suburb took an Extra-Strength Tylenol capsule for a cold and died within hours. Over the next few days six more people in the Chicago area died the same way, including three members of one family.

Investigators found the link: capsules of Tylenol, the best-selling painkiller in the United States, had been filled with potassium cyanide. The bottles had come from different factories, which suggested the poison was not added during manufacturing. Someone appeared to have taken bottles from shops, tampered with them and returned them to the shelves. Panic spread across the country, and copycat tampering incidents followed.

sections.key: Johnson and Johnson recalled about 31 million bottles nationwide, at a cost of around 100 million US dollars.
sections.b:
Tylenol was made by McNeil Consumer Products, a subsidiary of Johnson and Johnson, and held roughly a third of the American market for over-the-counter painkillers. Almost overnight that share collapsed, reportedly to under ten per cent. Experts predicted the brand would never recover, and some advised retiring the name.

The company had not caused the crime, and the tampering seemed limited to one region. A narrow, legalistic response would have been cheaper. Led by chairman James Burke, it chose the expensive path. It worked with police, the Food and Drug Administration and the media, warned the public not to take any Tylenol capsules, and recalled around 31 million bottles nationwide. Burke said the company's credo, written in the 1940s and putting customers first, guided its decisions.

sections.key: Tylenol returned in tamper-evident packaging, which soon became standard across the industry.
sections.b:
The company did not stop at the recall. Within about two months it relaunched Tylenol capsules in triple-sealed packaging: a glued box, a plastic seal around the neck and a foil seal over the mouth of the bottle. These did not make tampering impossible, but they made it much easier to see. Sales representatives visited doctors and pharmacists, and discount coupons helped win customers back.

In 1983 the United States passed a federal law making tampering with consumer products a crime, and tamper-evident seals spread across food, drink and medicine. The foil seal you peel off a new jar today is partly a legacy of the 1982 poisonings.

sections.key: Nobody has ever been charged with the murders, and the case shows that crises can start outside a company's control.
sections.b:
The criminal side never found closure. A man named James Lewis sent Johnson and Johnson a letter demanding one million dollars to stop the killings. He was convicted of extortion and spent years in prison, but he was never charged with the poisonings and always denied them. He died in 2023. Investigators reopened the case several times and tested new evidence as forensic science improved, yet the murders remain officially unsolved. For the families, that means decades without answers.

For business, it is a reminder that some crises begin entirely outside a company's control. The only thing it truly controls is how it responds.

sections.key: Speed, honesty and visible concern for people tend to rebuild trust better than defensiveness.
sections.b:
Within about a year Tylenol had regained much of its lost market share, a recovery few experts thought possible. The case is still taught as a model of crisis management, although some scholars note the company was helped by being an obvious victim rather than a culprit.

Several principles stand out. Act fast, even before you have every fact. Put public safety ahead of short-term profit, and be seen doing so. Communicate openly with authorities and the media rather than hiding. Fix the underlying weakness so the problem cannot easily happen again. Companies that later stumbled in a crisis were often criticised for doing the opposite: delaying, minimising and protecting themselves first.

quiz.q: What suggested the poison was not added at the factory?
o: The affected bottles came from different factories
Every bottle came from a single batch
The capsules were found only in one shop
The poison could not survive manufacturing
quiz.e: Poisoned bottles from several factories pointed to tampering after they reached the shops.

quiz.q: Why was Johnson and Johnson's recall considered so significant?
o: It recalled capsules nationwide despite poisonings only near Chicago
It recalled only the bottles found to be poisoned
It waited for the court case before acting
It blamed shops and kept selling the product
quiz.e: Choosing the costly path, putting public safety ahead of profit, became the model for crisis response.

quiz.q: What lasting change came from the poisonings?
o: Tamper-evident seals became standard on consumer products
Painkillers were banned from sale in shops
Capsules replaced tablets across the industry
Shops began keeping medicine behind locked glass
quiz.e: Triple-sealed packaging and a new federal law spread tamper-evident seals across many products.

quiz.q: What does the unsolved case show about crises?
o: Some begin outside a company's control, so the response is what it controls
A company is always to blame for its own crises
A crisis ends once someone is convicted
Unsolved crimes harm a brand more than solved ones
quiz.e: The company could not control the crime, but it could control how it responded.

quiz.q: Which approach does the Tylenol case recommend in a crisis?
o: Act fast and communicate openly, putting people first
Wait for every fact and stay silent until then
Protect the balance sheet before anything else
Minimise the problem to calm customers
quiz.e: Speed, honesty and visible concern for people rebuilt trust far better than defensiveness would have.

LESSONS.push: A poisoning that cost a company millions created the seal on your jar.

LESSONS.title: Double-entry bookkeeping: the Renaissance idea behind every business
LESSONS.hook: A friar who was friends with Leonardo da Vinci wrote down a method that still sits beneath every company's accounts, from corner cafes to global giants.

sections.key: Double-entry bookkeeping evolved among Italian merchants and was described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494.
sections.b:
Picture a merchant in fourteenth-century Genoa, Florence or Venice. He buys wool on credit, ships cloth to distant ports, borrows from partners and lends to customers. A simple list of money in and out no longer shows whether he is making a profit, who owes him and whom he owes. Italian merchants and bankers gradually developed a cleverer method. Surviving account books show it in use by at least the 1300s, and houses like the Medici bank relied on it. Nobody knows who invented it.

In 1494 the friar and mathematician Luca Pacioli, a friend of Leonardo da Vinci, published a huge textbook in Venice with a section on merchants' bookkeeping. Printing spread it across Europe. He described the system rather than inventing it, stressing careful daily records and books that balance.

sections.key: Each transaction is recorded in at least two accounts, so the books always balance and errors show up.
sections.b:
The core idea is simple and powerful. Every business transaction affects at least two things, so you record it twice. Suppose a small business buys a delivery van for 20,000 dollars in cash. It gains a van but loses the same amount of cash. Both changes are written down. If it instead borrows 20,000 dollars from a bank, it gains cash and also gains a debt to repay.

Recording both sides means nothing slips through the cracks. Money never just appears or vanishes in the books; it always comes from somewhere and goes somewhere. This also creates a built-in error check, because if the two sides do not match, a mistake has been made.

sections.key: Assets always equal liabilities plus equity, because everything a business has was funded by borrowing or by its owners.
sections.b:
Double-entry rests on one balancing rule, the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity. Assets are what the business owns or controls, such as cash, stock, equipment and money customers owe it. Liabilities are what it owes others, such as loans and unpaid bills. Equity is what is left for the owners, including the money they put in and the profits kept in the business.

The equation says that everything a business has was funded either by borrowing or by its owners. Because every transaction is recorded on both sides, the equation stays true after each one. The balance sheet, one of a company's main financial reports, is this equation set out in detail.

sections.key: Debits and credits simply mean the left and right sides of an account, not good and bad.
sections.b:
The words debit and credit confuse almost everyone at first, because in daily life a credit sounds good and a debit sounds bad. In bookkeeping they just mean the left side and the right side of an account. By convention, debits increase assets and expenses, while credits increase liabilities, equity and income. Every transaction must have equal debits and credits.

This explains why your bank statement seems backwards. When you deposit money, the bank records a credit to your account, because from the bank's point of view your money is something it owes you, a liability. The language is written from the perspective of whoever keeps the books.

sections.key: Double-entry lets owners, lenders and investors trust and compare a business's numbers.
sections.b:
More than five centuries after Pacioli, accounting software still runs on double-entry under the surface. When an app shows a profit figure, a balance sheet or an amount owing for tax, it builds those reports from paired entries.

The method made larger, more complex businesses possible, because owners could track performance without personally watching every coin. It also let outsiders such as banks and investors judge a business from its accounts. Some historians argue it helped shape modern capitalism itself, though that bigger claim is debated. The German writer Goethe had a character call it one of the finest inventions of the human mind. For anyone starting a business, understanding it is a genuine superpower.

quiz.q: What did Pacioli's 1494 book do for bookkeeping?
o: Spread an existing merchant method across Europe
Invented double-entry from scratch
Replaced it with a simpler single list
Banned merchants from lending to customers
quiz.e: Pacioli described a system merchants already used, and the printing press carried it far and wide.

quiz.q: A business borrows 20,000 dollars from a bank. How does double-entry record it?
o: Cash rises and a debt to repay is also recorded
Only the cash received is recorded
Profit rises by 20,000 dollars
The loan is recorded only when it is repaid
quiz.e: Every transaction affects two things, so both the new cash and the new debt are written down.

quiz.q: What does the accounting equation say?
o: Assets equal liabilities plus equity
Profit equals revenue plus liabilities
Equity equals assets plus liabilities
Assets equal cash minus debts owed
quiz.e: Everything a business owns was funded either by borrowing or by its owners.

quiz.q: What do debit and credit actually mean in bookkeeping?
o: The left and right sides of an account
Money gained and money lost
Good news and bad news for the owner
Money owed to you and money you owe
quiz.e: They are positions in the books, not judgements, which is why a deposit is a credit on the bank's records.

quiz.q: Why does double-entry still matter today?
o: Outsiders can trust and judge a business from its accounts
It avoids the need for any tax reporting
It guarantees a business will make a profit
It removes the need for balance sheets
quiz.e: Paired entries make reports reliable, so owners, banks and investors can compare numbers.

LESSONS.push: A friar who knew Leonardo wrote down the rule every set of accounts obeys.

LESSONS.title: The Post-it Note: a failed glue and a choir bookmark
LESSONS.hook: One of the world's best-known office products began as a glue that did not stick properly. It took a scientist's persistence and a singer's frustration to see its value.

sections.key: Spencer Silver's weak, reusable adhesive looked like a failure but became the basis of the Post-it Note.
sections.b:
The company behind the Post-it Note turns setbacks into products. It began in 1902 as the Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Company, set up to mine what the founders believed was valuable corundum. The rock was poor quality, so the company moved into sandpaper, then masking tape and Scotch tape. Since the late 1940s, technical staff have also been able to spend a share of their time, often described as fifteen per cent, on projects of their own choosing.

In 1968 3M chemist Spencer Silver tried to make a very strong adhesive and made an odd one instead. It gripped lightly, so objects could be stuck down, peeled away and reused with little residue. Silver was convinced it was special, but could not say what it was for.

sections.key: Art Fry needed bookmarks that would stay put in his hymn book without damaging it.
sections.b:
The breakthrough came from a colleague's annoyance. Art Fry, a 3M product development engineer, sang in his church choir in Minnesota. He marked hymns with scraps of paper, which kept falling out. Around 1974 he remembered Spencer Silver's light adhesive and realised it could make the perfect bookmark: it would stay in place but peel off without tearing the page.

He began coating paper with the glue and experimenting. Soon he noticed an even bigger use. When he wrote a note on a sticky bookmark and stuck it on a report for a colleague, it worked as a message that stayed attached without damaging the document underneath.

sections.key: Early test sales flopped until people were given free samples and tried the notes for themselves.
sections.b:
Even with a working product, success was not guaranteed. In 1977 3M test marketed the notes in four American cities as Press 'n Peel, and sales were disappointing. Customers had never seen anything like it and could not imagine why they needed it.

Instead of giving up, the company changed tactics. In 1978 it flooded Boise, Idaho, with free samples, an effort later nicknamed the Boise Blitz. Once office workers actually used the notes, they wanted more, and a large majority of those surveyed said they would buy them. Renamed Post-it Notes, the product launched across the United States in 1980 and in other countries soon after. Today it is sold in well over a hundred countries.

sections.key: The famous canary yellow came from scrap paper that happened to be nearby, not from careful design.
sections.b:
Many famous product features are carefully designed. The colour of the Post-it Note was not. According to the company's own telling, the team working on early versions used scrap paper that happened to be yellow, borrowed from a neighbouring laboratory. The colour stuck, in more ways than one, and canary yellow became the signature.

It also proved practical, because a bright yellow square stands out on a desk, a computer screen or a page of black and white text. Today the notes come in a rainbow of colours, sizes and shapes, but yellow remains the shade most people picture. Not every successful choice in business comes from planning.

sections.key: Innovation needs both a technology and someone who finds the right problem, and trying a product can persuade better than advertising.
sections.b:
The Post-it story shows how innovation often really works. It was not a single flash of genius. It needed a technology nobody had a use for, a scientist stubborn enough to keep promoting it, a colleague with a real everyday problem, and a company culture that allowed time for side projects.

It also shows a marketing truth: a genuinely new product can fail if customers cannot picture using it, and letting people try it can be more persuasive than any advertisement. Silver and Fry both received recognition for the invention, and Post-it Notes are now among the most recognisable office products ever made.

quiz.q: Why did Spencer Silver's adhesive seem like a failure at first?
o: It was weak, though it could be reused cleanly
It was too strong to remove from surfaces
It dissolved quickly in water
It could only be used on aircraft
quiz.e: It missed the goal of a very strong glue, but its light, clean grip later proved valuable.

quiz.q: What turned the weak adhesive into a product idea?
o: A colleague wanted bookmarks that would not fall out or tear
A customer asked for stronger office glue
A competitor launched a similar adhesive
A government contract for removable labels
quiz.e: A real everyday problem matched a technology that had been looking for a use.

quiz.q: What turned weak early sales around?
o: Giving out free samples so people could try the notes
Cutting the price in four test cities
Running television advertisements nationwide
Changing the notes to a stronger adhesive
quiz.e: Customers could not imagine needing the product until they used it.

quiz.q: Why are Post-it Notes yellow?
o: The team happened to use yellow scrap paper
Market research showed yellow sold best
Yellow was the cheapest dye available
Yellow matched the company's logo
quiz.e: The colour came from paper at hand and then proved practical because it stands out.
