quiz.e: Archaeologists working on the HS2 rail project identified his coffin by its lead breastplate.

LESSONS.title: Zheng He and the treasure fleets
LESSONS.hook: Decades before Columbus, a Chinese admiral led some of the largest fleets the world had ever seen across the Indian Ocean. Then China stopped sending them.

sections.key: Zheng He was a Muslim boy from Yunnan who was captured, served a Ming prince and rose to command vast fleets.
sections.b: Zheng He was born around 1371 in Yunnan, in southwest China, into a Muslim family originally named Ma. His father and grandfather had reportedly made the pilgrimage to Mecca. When Ming armies conquered Yunnan, the boy was captured, castrated, as was common for captive boys entering royal service, and sent to serve in the household of a prince, Zhu Di. He grew into a tall, capable soldier and adviser and helped Zhu Di win a bloody civil war to seize the throne in 1402. Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor, one of the most ambitious rulers in Chinese history. He rewarded his loyal eunuch with a new surname, Zheng, and later gave him command of an enterprise on a scale the world had rarely seen.

sections.key: Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He led seven expeditions across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean.
sections.b: The first voyage set out in 1405. Chinese records describe a fleet of over 300 ships carrying around 27,000 people: sailors, soldiers, interpreters, doctors, craftsmen and officials. Over seven voyages, ending in 1433, the fleets visited ports across what are now Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Sri Lanka, then pressed on to India's Calicut, a hub of the spice trade, and Hormuz at the entrance to the Persian Gulf. Later voyages sent detachments to Arabia and down the coast of East Africa, to places such as Mogadishu and Malindi. Some crew visited Mecca. The fleets sailed with the monsoon winds, which reverse with the seasons across the Indian Ocean, so the timing of each voyage followed a reliable rhythm.

sections.h: How big were the treasure ships?
sections.key: Old records describe ships over 120 metres long, but historians and engineers debate whether that is realistic.
sections.b: The largest vessels in the fleet were called treasure ships. A later Ming source gives their size in a way that works out at roughly 120 to 140 metres long, which would make them some of the biggest wooden ships ever built, many times longer than Columbus's Santa Maria. Some historians accept these figures, pointing to a huge rudder post found at a Nanjing shipyard site. Many others are sceptical. Wooden hulls of that length tend to flex and leak, and later texts may have exaggerated. A common middle view is that the biggest ships were perhaps around 60 to 75 metres long, still enormous for their day. What nobody disputes is that the fleets as a whole were vast and impressively organised.

sections.key: The voyages mainly displayed Ming power and drew rulers into China's tribute system, though force was sometimes used.
sections.b: The fleets did not set out to found colonies. Their main purpose was to show the might and wealth of the new emperor, gather tribute, and bring foreign rulers into the Chinese system in which they acknowledged the emperor's supremacy and received generous gifts and trade in return. Envoys from dozens of states came back with the fleets to visit the Ming court. That does not mean the voyages were entirely peaceful. The soldiers on board fought on several occasions, including against a pirate leader near Palembang in Sumatra and in a conflict in Sri Lanka, where a local king was captured and taken to China. Zheng He's fleets were floating diplomacy backed by an unmistakable threat of force.

sections.key: In 1414 a giraffe from East Africa arrived in China and was celebrated as a mythical qilin.
sections.b: One of the most charming results of the voyages was a giraffe. In 1414, envoys from Bengal brought one to China; it had originally come from Malindi on the East African coast. Courtiers declared it a qilin, a gentle creature from Chinese legend whose appearance was said to signal a wise and virtuous ruler. A court painting shows the giraffe led by a handler, along with a poem of praise for the emperor. More animals followed in later years, including zebras, ostriches and oryx. For the Yongle Emperor, whose seizure of power had been violent and controversial, there was obvious political value in having heaven's approval walk into the palace on four very long legs.

sections.key: After the 1430s the Ming court turned away from great ocean voyages, for reasons historians still debate.
sections.b: Zheng He probably died around 1433, during or soon after the seventh voyage, and he may have been buried at sea. No fleet on that scale ever sailed again. Historians point to several reasons. The voyages were extremely expensive, and the court faced costly pressures on land, especially from Mongol forces on the northern frontier and the building of the new capital at Beijing. Confucian officials were often hostile to the powerful palace eunuchs who ran the voyages, and saw them as a wasteful vanity. Later Ming governments also restricted private overseas trade for long periods. A story claims that officials deliberately destroyed the voyage records, though how much was lost and why is still debated. Either way, China's great age of ocean expeditions closed.

sections.key: Zheng He did not reach America, but he is honoured today across Asia as a symbol of seafaring and cultural exchange.
sections.b: Zheng He's story has attracted some wild claims. A popular book published in 2002 argued that his fleets discovered America and sailed around the world in 1421. Historians have firmly rejected this, as there is no credible evidence for it in Chinese or other records, or in archaeology. The real story needs no exaggeration. Around Southeast Asia, temples and shrines remember him, including in Malacca, Semarang and Surabaya, and he is a respected figure among both Chinese and Muslim communities. In modern China he has become a symbol of peaceful maritime exchange. It is worth remembering the contrast he offers. Decades before Portuguese ships reached India, Chinese fleets had crossed the same ocean, and then chose not to come back.

quiz.q: How did Zheng He come to serve the Ming court?
o: He was a merchant who bought a position
He was captured as a boy and placed in the household of a prince
He was the son of the emperor
He won a naval examination
quiz.e: Captured when Ming armies took Yunnan, he served Zhu Di, who became the Yongle Emperor.

quiz.q: Which of these places did Zheng He's fleets reach?
o: The Caribbean
Madagascar's west coast
Hormuz and the East African coast
Japan's northern islands
quiz.e: The fleets sailed to India, Hormuz and later to East African ports like Mogadishu and Malindi.

quiz.q: What is the debate about the treasure ships?
o: Whether they really were up to 120 metres or more long
Whether they were made of iron
Whether they used sails
Whether they carried soldiers
quiz.e: Old records imply huge sizes, but many historians and engineers think the largest were closer to 60 to 75 metres.

quiz.q: Why was the giraffe's arrival politically useful to the emperor?
o: It proved China could conquer Africa
It was used to pay a debt
It was a gift to Mongol leaders
It was hailed as a qilin, a sign of a virtuous ruler
quiz.e: Courtiers linked it to the legendary qilin, implying heaven approved of the emperor's reign.

quiz.q: What do historians say about the claim that Zheng He discovered America in 1421?
o: It is well documented
There is no credible evidence for it
It is proven by a map in Beijing
It was confirmed by DNA studies
quiz.e: The claim has been firmly rejected because no reliable records or archaeology support it.

LESSONS.title: How railways invented time zones
LESSONS.hook: Once every town set its clocks by its own sun. Then trains arrived, timetables turned into chaos, and the world had to agree on what time it was.

sections.h: When every town had its own noon
sections.key: Before railways, towns kept local solar time, so clocks differed from place to place.
sections.b: For most of history, time was local. Noon was when the Sun stood highest in the sky, and because the Earth turns, that moment arrives slightly later the further west you go. Each town set its clocks by its own sun, often checked with a sundial and kept by a church or town hall clock. The differences were real but small: in England, Bristol's clocks ran about ten minutes behind London's. When the fastest way to travel was by horse, nobody cared. A coach journey took so long that a few minutes' disagreement between towns made no practical difference. Watches were expensive anyway, and most people lived by bells, daylight and habit rather than precise minutes.

sections.key: Fast trains and timetables made dozens of local times confusing and even dangerous.
sections.b: Railways changed the scale of the problem. Suddenly people could cover in hours what once took days, and timetables needed to be precise to the minute. If each station ran on its own local time, a timetable became a puzzle, and passengers missed connections. Worse, on single track lines, where trains travelling in opposite directions had to pass at set places, confusion over time could cause collisions. The telegraph made a solution possible, because a time signal could now be sent along wires almost instantly. Railway companies became, in effect, the keepers of the clock. They began running their whole networks on a single standard time, whatever the sundial in a particular town might say.

sections.key: British railways adopted Greenwich time in the 1840s, and it became the legal time across Great Britain in 1880.
sections.b: In Britain, the Great Western Railway began using London time across its network in 1840. Other companies followed, and by around 1848 most British railways had adopted Greenwich Mean Time, based on observations at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich. People called it railway time. Not everyone was happy. Some towns kept two times for a while, and a few public clocks were given two minute hands, one showing local time and one showing London time. Gradually, as people came to depend on trains, the rest of daily life followed the railway clock. In 1880 Parliament made Greenwich Mean Time the legal standard across Great Britain. A local idea of time had given way to a national one.

sections.key: On 18 November 1883, North American railways switched from dozens of local times to a handful of time zones.
sections.b: North America faced a far bigger problem. The United States spans so much longitude that railways were using dozens of different times, and a big station might display several clocks at once. On 18 November 1883, the railways of the United States and Canada switched to a system of standard time zones, each roughly an hour apart. In many towns, clocks were reset at noon, so people experienced noon twice that day, once by the old local time and once by the new standard time. That is why it is remembered as the day of two noons. The change was organised by the railways, not the government. The United States did not make time zones official in federal law until 1918.

sections.key: In 1884 an international conference chose Greenwich as the prime meridian, the starting line for world longitude.
sections.b: Standard zones need a starting point. In 1884 delegates from about twenty five countries met in Washington DC for the International Meridian Conference. They chose the meridian passing through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich as zero degrees longitude. Practical reasons favoured it, as most of the world's shipping already used charts based on Greenwich. The Canadian railway engineer Sandford Fleming was one of the great champions of a worldwide system of time based on a single meridian. Not everyone agreed. France abstained in the vote and kept using the Paris meridian for its own purposes for decades. The conference did not actually impose time zones around the world, but it gave countries a shared reference to build their own on.

sections.key: The Australian colonies adopted standard time in 1895, and South Australia later moved to a half-hour zone.
sections.b: In Australia, each colony had kept its own local time, and travellers crossing borders by train faced the same headaches as everyone else. In 1895 the colonies agreed on standard times based on Greenwich: Eastern, Central and Western. South Australia first chose nine hours ahead of Greenwich, but in 1899 it moved to nine and a half hours, a choice that has been debated ever since. The Northern Territory, then administered by South Australia, followed. Half-hour zones like this are unusual but not unique: India uses one, and Nepal goes further with a quarter-hour offset. Daylight saving complicates the picture today. Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory don't use it, so in summer the mainland runs on five different times.

sections.key: Modern civil time is based on atomic clocks, while time zones remain a mix of geography and politics.
sections.b: Greenwich Mean Time has largely been replaced as the world's reference by Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, which is kept by a network of highly accurate atomic clocks. Because the Earth's spin is slightly irregular, leap seconds have occasionally been added to keep UTC close to the Sun, but in 2022 international scientists voted to stop adding them by 2035. Time zones themselves are decided by governments, and politics often beats geography. China, which spans the width of five standard zones, uses just one official time, so in its far west the Sun can rise very late by the clock. Spain sits mostly west of Greenwich but uses Central European Time. The railway engineers' solution still governs every phone and laptop.

quiz.q: What determined the time in a town before standard time?
o: The nearest railway station
The position of the Sun, so each town had its own local time
A national clock in the capital
Royal decree
quiz.e: Noon was when the Sun was highest, so towns east and west of each other kept slightly different times.

quiz.q: Which invention made a single standard time practical across a network?
o: The steam engine
The sundial
The telegraph
The pendulum clock
quiz.e: The telegraph could carry a time signal along wires almost instantly.

quiz.q: Why is 18 November 1883 called ‘the day of two noons’?
o: Clocks were reset at noon, so many towns had noon twice
There was a solar eclipse
The Sun rose twice in the Arctic
Two different calendars were in use
quiz.e: When North American railways switched to standard zones, many towns reset their clocks at local noon.

quiz.q: What did the 1884 International Meridian Conference decide?
o: That every country must use GMT
That time zones should be exactly one hour apart worldwide
That France would host the prime meridian
That longitude zero would run through Greenwich
quiz.e: It chose Greenwich as the prime meridian; countries still set their own time zones.

quiz.q: Which change did South Australia make in 1899?
o: It adopted daylight saving
It moved to a half-hour zone, nine and a half hours ahead of Greenwich
It joined Eastern Standard Time
It abolished standard time
quiz.e: SA first chose nine hours ahead of Greenwich, then shifted to nine and a half in 1899.

LESSONS.title: Lewis and Clark: across a continent
LESSONS.hook: In 1804 a small army party set out to cross North America to the Pacific and back. They found no easy river route, but they mapped a continent and depended on the people who already lived there.

sections.key: After the Louisiana Purchase, President Jefferson sent an expedition to explore the west and look for a water route to the Pacific.
sections.b: In 1803 the United States bought the vast Louisiana Territory from France, roughly doubling the size of the young country, for about fifteen million dollars. President Thomas Jefferson had already been planning an expedition into the west, and now it had added urgency. He wanted to know what the land held, from plants and animals to rivers and mountains, and to make contact with the Native nations who lived there. Above all, he hoped to find a practical water route, by river and a short overland carry, linking the Missouri to the Pacific. Many still dreamed of a Northwest Passage across the continent. To lead the effort he chose his personal secretary, an army captain named Meriwether Lewis.

sections.key: Lewis chose William Clark as co-leader, and their party of soldiers, boatmen and others left near St Louis in May 1804.
sections.b: Lewis asked his former army comrade William Clark to share command, and the two worked as genuine equals, although the army officially ranked Clark lower. Lewis spent months preparing, studying botany, astronomy and medicine and buying supplies, from rifles and gunpowder to scientific instruments and thousands of gifts for Native leaders. The expedition, known as the Corps of Discovery, included about thirty to forty soldiers and boatmen, with numbers changing along the way. Among them was York, an enslaved man owned by Clark, and Lewis's large Newfoundland dog, Seaman. In May 1804 the party set off up the Missouri River from their winter camp near St Louis, in a keelboat and two smaller boats, rowing, poling and hauling against the current.

sections.key: The Corps spent its first winter among the Mandan and Hidatsa, where it hired Charbonneau and Sacagawea.
sections.b: By late 1804 the expedition had travelled well over two thousand kilometres up the Missouri to the villages of the Mandan and Hidatsa people, in what is now North Dakota. These were busy trading towns of earth lodges, and the Corps built a small fort nearby to survive a bitterly cold winter. Only one member of the party died on the entire journey, Sergeant Charles Floyd, in August 1804, probably of a burst appendix. At the Mandan villages the captains hired a French-Canadian trader, Toussaint Charbonneau, as an interpreter. One of his wives was Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman who had been captured by Hidatsa raiders as a girl. In February 1805 she gave birth to a son, Jean Baptiste, who travelled the rest of the way as a baby.

sections.key: Sacagawea was not the expedition's guide, but her skills and presence mattered enormously.
sections.b: Sacagawea is often pictured leading the Corps across the mountains, pointing the way. The truth is more interesting. She was not hired as a guide and did not know most of the route. Her value lay elsewhere. She spoke Shoshone, the language of the people from whom the expedition badly needed horses, and she recognised landmarks in her home region, such as Beaverhead Rock in what is now south-western Montana. Clark noted that a woman travelling with the party signalled peaceful intentions to the nations they met, because war parties did not travel that way. In August 1805 the Corps met a Shoshone band whose chief, Cameahwait, turned out to be Sacagawea's brother. The meeting helped secure the horses they needed to cross the mountains.

sections.key: The Rocky Mountains proved far wider and harder than expected, and the Corps nearly starved crossing them.
sections.b: The expedition's first great obstacle was the Great Falls of the Missouri, where it took about a month to carry boats and supplies around a series of waterfalls. Then came the Rockies. Jefferson had hoped for a short portage between rivers, but the mountains were range after range. In September 1805 the Corps crossed the Bitterroot Mountains along a steep trail in early snow, with little game to hunt. They were reduced to eating candles and some of their horses. Starving and sick, they came down into the lands of the Nez Perce, who fed them and helped them build canoes. The crossing ended the dream of an easy water route across the continent.

sections.key: The Corps reached the Pacific in November 1805, and everyone, including York and Sacagawea, voted on where to winter.
sections.b: The Corps paddled down the Snake and Columbia rivers and in November 1805 reached the Pacific coast, where Clark wrote of the ocean in his journal with famously creative spelling. They had to decide where to spend the winter, and the captains put the question to the whole party. York's view and Sacagawea's were recorded alongside the soldiers', an extraordinary moment for an enslaved man and a Native woman in that era, though it changed nothing about their status afterwards. They built Fort Clatsop, near today's Astoria in Oregon, and endured a wet, miserable winter, with rain recorded on most days. In March 1806 they started for home. The return journey included a deadly clash with Blackfeet warriors, the only fight of the journey in which people were killed.

sections.key: The Corps returned in 1806 with maps and descriptions of many species, but its legacy for Native nations was painful.
sections.b: The Corps arrived back in St Louis in September 1806, after more than two years away, to a public that had largely given them up for dead. Their journals and Clark's maps transformed knowledge of the west, and they described well over a hundred animals and plants new to science, including the grizzly bear, prairie dog and western species of trout. But the expedition also opened the way for fur traders, settlers and the US government, and over the following century Native nations along the route lost much of their land and many lives. The fates of the travellers were mixed. Lewis died from gunshot wounds in 1809, most likely suicide. Clark did not free York for around a decade. Sacagawea is thought to have died young, around 1812, though some Shoshone traditions say she lived into old age.

quiz.q: What did Jefferson most hope the expedition would find?
o: Gold in the Rocky Mountains
A practical water route to the Pacific
The source of the Mississippi
A site for a new capital
quiz.e: He hoped rivers and a short overland carry would link the Missouri to the Pacific.

quiz.q: How many members of the Corps died during the expedition?
o: One
About half
Twelve
None
quiz.e: Sergeant Charles Floyd died in 1804, probably of appendicitis; he was the only death.

quiz.q: What was Sacagawea's most important role?
o: She was the official guide for the whole route
She commanded the boats
She interpreted Shoshone, recognised landmarks near her homeland, and signalled peaceful intent
She drew the expedition's maps
quiz.e: She was not the guide, but her language skills, local knowledge and presence were vital.

quiz.q: Who helped the starving Corps after they crossed the Bitterroot Mountains?
o: The Mandan
The Blackfeet
French fur traders
The Nez Perce
quiz.e: The Nez Perce fed them and helped them build canoes for the journey down to the Pacific.

quiz.q: What was remarkable about the vote on where to winter in 1805?
o: It was decided by the President
York and Sacagawea had their views recorded alongside the soldiers'
Only the captains voted
They voted to sail home by sea
quiz.e: An enslaved man and a Native woman were included, though their status did not change afterwards.

LESSONS.title: Into the Challenger Deep
LESSONS.hook: The deepest point in the ocean lies nearly 11 kilometres down, under pressure that could crush a submarine. Two men first reached it in 1960 in a craft held up by petrol.

sections.key: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is the deepest known point in Earth's oceans, nearly 11 kilometres down.
sections.b: In the western Pacific, east of the Philippines and south west of Guam, lies the Mariana Trench, a curved scar on the seafloor more than 2,500 kilometres long. It forms where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. At its southern end is the Challenger Deep, the deepest known place in the world's oceans. Estimates of its depth vary slightly between surveys, but it is close to 11,000 metres, or about 10,900 metres by most recent measurements. Put Mount Everest at the bottom, and its summit would still sit more than two kilometres underwater. The trench is named after HMS Challenger, a British ship whose round-the-world scientific voyage in the 1870s took a sounding there, and a later survey ship of the same name pinpointed the deep in 1951.

sections.key: At the bottom, water pressure is more than a thousand times that at the surface.
sections.b: Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly another atmosphere of pressure. At the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the pressure is more than a thousand times what we feel at sea level, roughly equivalent to more than a tonne pressing on every square centimetre. An ordinary submarine would be crushed long before it got there. Any vessel carrying people needs a cabin that can resist this squeeze, which in practice means a thick, strong sphere, since a sphere spreads pressure evenly. The trouble is that such a sphere is extremely heavy and sinks like a stone. The question for engineers was not only how to get down, but how to float back up again.

sections.key: Auguste Piccard's bathyscaphe used a huge float filled with petrol to provide buoyancy at extreme depths.
sections.b: The solution came from the Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard, who had already flown balloons into the stratosphere. He realised the same principle could work in water. His bathyscaphe, meaning ‘deep boat’, was essentially an underwater balloon. A large float filled with petrol was attached above a small, thick steel crew sphere. Petrol is lighter than water and compresses very little, so it keeps providing lift even under enormous pressure. To descend, the craft carried tonnes of iron pellets as ballast, held in place by electromagnets. To come back up, the crew released the pellets and the petrol float carried them to the surface. Piccard and his son Jacques built the bathyscaphe Trieste in Italy in the 1950s, and the US Navy later bought it.

sections.key: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh became the first people to reach the bottom of the Challenger Deep.
sections.b: On 23 January 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy lieutenant Don Walsh squeezed into the Trieste's cramped sphere, only about two metres across inside, and began their descent. It took nearly five hours. Partway down, they heard a loud crack, and later found that an outer window had fractured, though the inner structure held. Finally they settled onto the seabed, nearly 11 kilometres down. They spent only around twenty minutes on the bottom. Their landing stirred up a cloud of fine sediment that made photographs impossible. Piccard reported seeing a flatfish through the porthole, but many biologists now doubt this, since fish are not thought to survive at that depth. The ascent took over three hours, and both men returned to a hero's welcome.

sections.key: After 1960 no one returned to the Challenger Deep in person for more than fifty years.
sections.b: It seems astonishing, but after the Trieste's dive, no human went back to the bottom of the Challenger Deep for fifty-two years. Ocean science moved on in other directions. Robotic and uncrewed vehicles, such as Japan's Kaikō in the 1990s, reached the deep and collected samples. Crewed submersibles like the American Alvin explored hydrothermal vents and shipwrecks at more modest depths. Money and attention also flowed to the Space Race, and it was often said that more people had walked on the Moon than had visited the deepest ocean. That remained true until 2012. The deep sea is still far less explored than most people realise, and much of the world's seafloor has not been mapped in high detail.

sections.key: In 2012 James Cameron made the first solo dive to the bottom in a sub built largely in Australia.
sections.b: On 26 March 2012, the filmmaker and explorer James Cameron dived alone to the Challenger Deep in Deepsea Challenger, a vertical, torpedo-like submersible. The vessel was designed and built mostly in Sydney by a team that included the Australian engineer Ron Allum, who helped develop new lightweight syntactic foam, a material packed with tiny hollow glass spheres, that could provide buoyancy at full ocean depth instead of a giant petrol float. Cameron's descent took about two and a half hours, and he spent around three hours at the bottom filming and collecting samples. A hydraulic fault cut his time short. He described the seabed as a lunar-like, desolate landscape. The submersible was later donated to the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in the United States.

sections.key: Since 2019, a reusable submersible has carried many people to the bottom, including the first woman.
sections.b: In 2019 the American explorer Victor Vescovo began repeated dives in the Limiting Factor, a titanium-hulled submersible designed to reach the bottom of any ocean again and again. On his Five Deeps Expedition, he reached the deepest points of all five oceans. Over the following years the craft took a number of people to the Challenger Deep. In June 2020, Kathryn Sullivan, a former NASA astronaut who had been the first American woman to walk in space, became the first woman to reach it. Dives have also brought sobering news, as researchers have reported plastic debris and human-made pollutants even in the deepest trenches. The bottom of the world is no longer out of reach, and neither, it turns out, is our rubbish.

quiz.q: Roughly how deep is the Challenger Deep?
o: About 4,000 metres
About 11,000 metres
About 8,800 metres
About 20,000 metres
quiz.e: Most recent surveys put it close to 11,000 metres, deeper than Everest is tall.

quiz.q: Why did the Trieste use a float full of petrol?
o: Petrol was used to fuel the engines on the seabed
It made the craft heavier for the descent
Petrol is lighter than water and barely compresses, so it provides lift at great depth
It protected the crew from cold
quiz.e: Like a balloon in air, the petrol float kept providing buoyancy even under huge pressure.

quiz.q: Why could Piccard and Walsh take no photographs at the bottom?
o: Their camera froze
It was forbidden by the Navy
They forgot the camera
Their landing stirred up a cloud of sediment
quiz.e: The fine silt clouded the water around the porthole during their short stay.

quiz.q: What was special about Deepsea Challenger?
o: It was built largely in Sydney and carried the first solo dive to the bottom
It was the first submarine to use petrol
It was uncrewed
It was the first craft to reach the trench in the 1950s
quiz.e: James Cameron dived alone in 2012 in a sub designed and built mostly in Sydney.

quiz.q: Who was the first woman to reach the Challenger Deep?
o: Sylvia Earle
Kathryn Sullivan
Jacques Piccard's daughter
Amelia Earhart
quiz.e: Former astronaut Kathryn Sullivan made the dive in June 2020 aboard the Limiting Factor.

LESSONS.title: Scurvy: the cure that kept getting lost
LESSONS.hook: For centuries a disease killed more sailors than storms and battles. The cure was found, forgotten and found again, and the final answer turned on a lucky choice of guinea pig.

sections.key: Scurvy killed huge numbers of sailors on long voyages during the age of sail.
sections.b: When ships began making long ocean voyages, a terrible disease followed them. After a couple of months on a diet of salted meat and ship's biscuit, sailors became exhausted and depressed. Their gums swelled, turned spongy and bled, and teeth loosened. Bruises appeared without cause, old wounds reopened and long-healed fractures could come apart. Without treatment, scurvy ended in death. Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in the 1490s lost many men to it. During George Anson's voyage around the world in the 1740s, around 1,900 men set out and only a few hundred came home, with disease, especially scurvy, causing far more deaths than enemy action. Estimates of scurvy's total toll vary, but it ranks among the deadliest hazards of the age of sail.

sections.key: Without vitamin C, the body cannot properly build collagen, the protein that holds tissues together.
sections.b: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, or ascorbic acid. Most animals make their own vitamin C, but humans, other apes and monkeys, guinea pigs and some bats and birds cannot, because the gene for the final enzyme in the process stopped working in their ancestors. We must get it from food. Vitamin C is a helper for enzymes that finish building collagen, the strong, rope-like protein in skin, blood vessels, gums, bones and scar tissue. Without it, newly made collagen is weak and unstable. Tiny blood vessels leak, causing bleeding gums and bruising, and wounds cannot knit. Because the body slowly replaces its collagen over time, even scars that healed years earlier can break down.

sections.key: In 1747 James Lind ran one of the first controlled clinical trials, and citrus was the clear winner.
sections.b: In 1747 the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind, serving on HMS Salisbury, chose twelve sailors with scurvy whose cases were as similar as possible. He divided them into six pairs and gave each pair a different remedy on top of the same basic diet: cider, a weak sulphuric acid mixture called elixir of vitriol, vinegar, seawater, a paste of spices and garlic, or two oranges and a lemon each day. The men given citrus improved dramatically, one being fit for duty within about a week. Cider showed modest benefit, and the rest did little. It was a tiny trial, but its design of comparing treatments side by side in similar patients makes it a landmark in the history of medicine.

sections.key: Lind didn't see citrus as a unique cure, and his preserved juice lost much of its power.
sections.b: Lind's result did not end scurvy. In his 1753 treatise, he presented citrus as one useful measure among many, alongside ideas about damp air and digestion, rather than as a specific cure. He also recommended preserving juice by heating it into a concentrated ‘rob’ for long voyages. Vitamin C is fragile and breaks down with heat, so this concentrate was far weaker than fresh fruit. Others promoted alternatives that sounded scientific but worked poorly, such as malt wort. James Cook's voyages became famous for low scurvy deaths, yet he credited several remedies, including sauerkraut, and his real success probably came from his constant hunt for fresh food ashore. Lind's experiment was strong evidence, but nobody yet understood what made citrus special.

sections.key: The Royal Navy issued lemon juice from 1795, but a later switch to limes helped scurvy return.
sections.b: Pushed by the physician Gilbert Blane and others, the Royal Navy began issuing lemon juice to all sailors in 1795, usually mixed into the daily grog. Scurvy largely vanished from the fleet, a real advantage during the long blockades of the Napoleonic Wars. Then the cure was quietly undermined. In the mid nineteenth century the navy shifted to cheaper limes, often from British colonies in the West Indies. Limes contain considerably less vitamin C than lemons, and processing the juice could destroy more. On long Arctic expeditions in the 1870s, scurvy struck sailors who had been taking their lime juice, leading many experts to wrongly conclude citrus did not work after all. British sailors, meanwhile, had acquired a lasting nickname, limeys.

sections.h: Wrong theories and a lucky guinea pig
sections.key: In 1907 Norwegian researchers produced scurvy in guinea pigs, one of the few animals that, like us, can't make vitamin C.
sections.b: By the late nineteenth century, scurvy was misunderstood again. Some doctors blamed bacterial infection or poisons in spoiled tinned meat. Polar explorers noticed that fresh meat seemed to prevent scurvy, which was true, since fresh meat and especially organ meats contain some vitamin C, but it muddied the citrus story. The breakthrough came in 1907. Two Norwegian scientists, Axel Holst and Theodor Frølich, were studying beriberi and fed guinea pigs a grain-only diet. Instead of beriberi, the animals developed scurvy. It was a stroke of luck: had they used rats or mice, which make their own vitamin C, they would have seen nothing. Now scurvy could be studied in the lab, and researchers could test which foods prevented it.

sections.key: By the early 1930s vitamin C had been isolated, identified and synthesised, earning two Nobel Prizes in 1937.
sections.b: Researchers used guinea pigs to measure how much anti-scurvy power different foods held, and the hunt for the active substance began. The Hungarian scientist Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated a compound he called hexuronic acid in the late 1920s, and in the early 1930s, working with Joseph Svirbely, he showed it prevented scurvy. The American chemist Charles Glen King's group reported similar findings at about the same time. The compound was renamed ascorbic acid, meaning ‘against scurvy’. In 1933 the British chemist Norman Haworth worked out its structure and helped synthesise it, and Tadeus Reichstein developed a method later used for mass production. In 1937 Szent-Györgyi won the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine, and Haworth shared the chemistry prize.

sections.key: Scurvy is now rare but still occurs, usually in people with very restricted diets.
sections.b: With vitamin C cheap and plentiful in fruit and vegetables, scurvy is rare in wealthy countries, but it has not disappeared. Doctors still see cases in people whose diets are severely limited, such as some older people living alone, people with alcohol dependence or certain eating disorders, and occasionally children with very selective eating. Because it is now unusual, it can be missed, as bleeding gums and bruising have many causes. Treatment with vitamin C, guided by a doctor, usually brings rapid improvement. Scurvy's story carries a lasting lesson. Lind found strong evidence in 1747, yet confusion, cost-cutting and wrong theories meant sailors died for more than a century afterwards. A cure is only as good as our understanding of why it works.

quiz.q: Why can a lack of vitamin C reopen old wounds?
o: Vitamin C fights infection in scars
Collagen is constantly replaced, and without vitamin C the new collagen is weak
It causes bones to dissolve
It lowers blood pressure
quiz.e: Vitamin C helps enzymes finish building collagen, so replacement collagen in old scars becomes unstable.

quiz.q: What made Lind's 1747 study a landmark?
o: It used thousands of sailors
It proved vitamins exist
It compared different treatments side by side in similar patients
It was the first use of lemons at sea
quiz.e: Its controlled design of comparing remedies in matched pairs is why it is celebrated.

quiz.q: Why did Lind's ‘rob’ of boiled juice disappoint?
o: Heating destroyed much of the vitamin C
It was too sour to drink
It spoiled within days
Sailors refused it
quiz.e: Vitamin C breaks down with heat, so the concentrate was much weaker than fresh fruit.

quiz.q: Why did scurvy return on some later voyages despite a citrus ration?
o: Sailors stopped drinking grog
Lemons were banned
Ships stopped carrying fresh water
The navy switched to limes, which contain less vitamin C, and processing destroyed more
quiz.e: The lime juice ration was weaker, and Arctic expeditions in the 1870s suffered scurvy as a result.

quiz.q: Why was the choice of guinea pigs in 1907 so lucky?
o: Guinea pigs eat only citrus
Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C
Guinea pigs never get beriberi
They live for many decades
quiz.e: Rats or mice make vitamin C, so they would not have developed scurvy on the same diet.

LESSONS.title: Salt: the rock that built civilisations
LESSONS.hook: Empires taxed it, armies guarded it and whole cities grew rich on it. The humble white crystal on your table has one of the biggest stories in food.

sections.h: A mineral we cannot live without
sections.key: Our bodies need sodium to work, which is why people and animals have always gone looking for salt.
sections.b: Salt is mostly sodium chloride, and the sodium in it is essential. Your nerves use sodium to fire signals, your muscles need it to contract, and your kidneys use it to manage the balance of water in your body. Hunter-gatherers eating plenty of meat got enough sodium from their food, but once people settled down to farm grain, they needed extra. Animals feel the same pull, which is why grazing animals wear tracks to natural salt licks. Many ancient roads and settlements grew up along these routes. The irony of modern life is that the problem has flipped: most Australians now eat more salt than health authorities recommend, and most of it comes hidden in processed foods such as bread, sauces and processed meats.

sections.key: Salt has been mined underground, boiled from springs and dried from sea water for thousands of years.
sections.b: There are three classic ways to get salt. The first is mining rock salt, the remains of ancient seas that dried out and were buried. At Hallstatt in the Austrian Alps, people have mined salt since the Bronze Age, and the region was rich enough that archaeologists named a whole early European culture after it. The second is boiling brine from salty springs, a method used across Europe and China. The third is solar evaporation: letting the sun and wind dry sea water in shallow ponds. Australia is a major producer this way, with huge salt fields on the Western Australian coast near Dampier, where dazzling white stockpiles are shipped to Asia, mostly for industry rather than dinner tables.

sections.h: China's deep wells and state monopoly
sections.key: Chinese engineers drilled astonishingly deep brine wells, and the state turned salt into a vital source of revenue.
sections.b: In Sichuan, Chinese workers developed percussion drilling, using heavy bits on bamboo cables to punch narrow wells deep into the ground to reach brine. Over centuries the technique improved until, in 1835, the Shenhai well at Zigong passed 1,000 metres deep, an extraordinary feat before modern machinery. The same region tapped natural gas from the wells and used it to fuel the fires that boiled the brine. Salt was also big business for the state. Under the Han dynasty in 117 BC, the government took control of salt and iron production. A famous court debate in 81 BC, recorded as the Discourses on Salt and Iron, argued over whether the state should profit from such necessities, a question about monopolies and taxes that still sounds modern.

sections.key: Because everyone needs salt, governments taxed it heavily, and those taxes became symbols of injustice.
sections.b: A tax on salt is hard to dodge, which made it tempting for rulers and hated by everyone else. In France, the gabelle salt tax lasted for centuries and was wildly uneven: some regions paid many times more than others, and people in some areas were required to buy a minimum amount of salt each year. Smuggling flourished, and smugglers were punished harshly. The gabelle became one of the grievances of the French Revolution and was abolished in 1790. In British India, a salt monopoly and tax gave Mahatma Gandhi a perfect symbol. In 1930 he walked to the sea at Dandi and picked up natural salt in defiance of the law, a simple act that drew the world's attention to the campaign for independence.

sections.key: The word salary is linked to the Latin for salt, but the story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is not well supported.
sections.b: You may have heard that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, and that this is where the word salary comes from. The word part is real: salary comes from the Latin salarium, which is related to sal, meaning salt. Rome also had a famous road called the Via Salaria, the Salt Road, leading to salt works near the Tiber's mouth. But historians have found no clear ancient evidence that soldiers were routinely paid in salt itself. Salarium may have meant an allowance connected to buying salt, or the link may be older and murkier. The honest answer is that nobody is sure. It is a good reminder that a story can be attached to a true word origin and still be mostly guesswork.

sections.key: Salt preserves food by drawing water out of it, leaving too little free water for most microbes to grow.
sections.b: Before refrigeration, salt was one of the main ways to keep food from rotting. It works through osmosis. When salt surrounds food, water is pulled out of the food's cells and out of any bacteria present, and the remaining water is so tightly bound up with dissolved salt that most microbes cannot use it. That is how salted cod, cured ham, anchovies and corned beef were made. Salt cod became a huge international trade, and it is still a beloved ingredient in Portugal, Spain and the Caribbean. Salt also controls fermentation. In sauerkraut, kimchi and pickles, the right amount of salt holds back spoilage organisms while letting helpful lactic acid bacteria do their sour, flavourful work.

sections.key: Nearly all cooking salts are chemically similar; the differences that matter most are crystal size and added iodine.
sections.b: Sea salt, rock salt, pink Himalayan salt and table salt are all overwhelmingly sodium chloride. Trace minerals give some salts a tint, but in the amounts you eat they make little nutritional difference. What really changes is the crystal. Big flakes dissolve slowly and crunch on top of food, while fine salt packs densely, so a teaspoon of fine salt is noticeably saltier than a teaspoon of flakes. That is why recipes that just say ‘a teaspoon of salt’ can come out differently. Iodine is the other big difference. Iodine deficiency can cause goitre and affect brain development, so many countries add it to salt. Since 2009, Australian bakers have been required to use iodised salt in most bread, a quiet public health measure.

quiz.q: Why did farming communities need to seek out extra salt?
o: Grain-based diets supply less sodium than meat-rich ones
Farm work makes salt evaporate from the body
Salt was needed to grow wheat
Animals refused to graze without it
quiz.e: Hunters got sodium from meat, but diets built on grain needed additional salt, so salt sources became precious.

quiz.q: What did engineers achieve at the Shenhai well in Zigong in 1835?
o: The first underground salt mine
A brine well more than 1,000 metres deep
The first solar salt pond
A salt-powered steam engine
quiz.e: Using percussion drilling on bamboo cables, Sichuan workers reached more than 1,000 metres long before modern drilling rigs.

quiz.q: What was the gabelle?
o: A Roman salt road
A Chinese salt monopoly
A hated French salt tax
A type of salt cod
quiz.e: The gabelle was France's salt tax, unequal from region to region and abolished in 1790 during the Revolution.

quiz.q: What is the most accurate thing to say about the word ‘salary’?
o: It proves Roman soldiers were paid in salt
It comes from Latin and is linked to salt, but the payment story is unproven
It has no connection to salt
It comes from the Via Salaria road tax
quiz.e: Salarium is related to sal, salt, but there is no clear ancient evidence that soldiers were routinely paid in salt.

quiz.q: How does salt stop food from spoiling?
o: It kills all bacteria instantly on contact
It pulls water out, leaving too little free water for most microbes
It seals the surface of the food
It changes the food's protein into sugar
quiz.e: Through osmosis, salt draws out water and binds what remains, so most spoilage microbes cannot grow.

LESSONS.title: Bananas: the fruit of clones
LESSONS.hook: The banana in your lunchbox is almost certainly a genetic copy of nearly every other banana in the shop. That makes it cheap, convenient and surprisingly fragile.

sections.h: Not a tree, and technically a berry
sections.key: The banana plant is a giant herb with a ‘trunk’ made of leaves, and its fruit is botanically a berry.
sections.b: A banana plantation looks like a forest, but banana plants are not trees. They have no wood at all. What looks like a trunk is a pseudostem, made of tightly wrapped leaf bases, and the true stem stays mostly underground as a fleshy corm. Some banana plants grow taller than a house, which makes them among the largest herbaceous plants in the world. Each pseudostem flowers once, produces one large bunch of fruit and then dies back, while new shoots called suckers grow up from the base to replace it. Botanically, the banana fruit counts as a berry, because it develops from a single flower's ovary and has its seeds inside the flesh. Strawberries, confusingly, do not count as true berries.

sections.key: Bananas were first cultivated in New Guinea and South-East Asia thousands of years ago, then spread across the tropics.
sections.b: Wild bananas grow across South-East Asia and the western Pacific. Archaeological evidence from Kuk Swamp in the highlands of Papua New Guinea suggests people were cultivating bananas there around 7,000 years ago, among the earliest farming anywhere. Over thousands of years, bananas were carried by traders and migrants to India, across the Indian Ocean to Africa and through the Pacific islands. They reached the Americas after European contact, in the early sixteenth century. Today hundreds of varieties are grown. Sweet dessert bananas are eaten raw, while starchy plantains and cooking bananas are boiled, fried or mashed like potatoes. In parts of East Africa, such as Uganda, cooking bananas are a daily staple food rather than a snack.

sections.key: Cultivated bananas are seedless and sterile, so every new plant is grown from a piece of its parent: a clone.
sections.b: Wild bananas are full of hard seeds, so many that the fruit is barely worth eating. The bananas we eat come from rare natural plants that ended up with three sets of chromosomes instead of the usual two. That odd genetics makes them sterile, so they develop soft, sweet fruit without proper seeds. The tiny dark specks in the middle of a banana are the undeveloped remains of seeds. Because these plants cannot breed normally, farmers multiply them by planting suckers or cuttings from existing plants, and today often by growing plantlets in laboratories from tissue. Every new plant is genetically identical to its parent. In effect, a whole plantation, and even a whole industry, can be one plant copied millions of times.

sections.key: The world's main export banana, the Gros Michel, was nearly wiped out by a soil disease in the twentieth century.
sections.b: Until the mid-twentieth century, the banana sold in Western shops was mostly a variety called Gros Michel, or Big Mike. It was large, creamy and had a thick skin that survived long shipping journeys well. Many people who tasted both say it had a richer flavour than today's supermarket banana. But Gros Michel was vulnerable to Panama disease, a wilt caused by a soil fungus, Fusarium, that blocks the plant's water-carrying vessels. Because every Gros Michel plant was a clone, none had resistance, and the fungus can survive in soil for decades. Plantations across Central America and the Caribbean were devastated, and growers kept clearing new land. By the 1960s, the export industry had switched to a resistant variety: the Cavendish.

sections.key: The Cavendish banana is named after an English duke whose gardener grew it in a greenhouse in the 1830s.
sections.b: The Cavendish has a surprisingly English story. In the 1830s, a banana plant from southern China was grown in the hothouses at Chatsworth House in Derbyshire, the estate of William Cavendish, the sixth Duke of Devonshire. His head gardener, Joseph Paxton, a self-taught horticulturalist who later designed the Crystal Palace for London's Great Exhibition, coaxed it into fruit and named it after his employer. Plants from Chatsworth were sent around the world, including to Pacific islands, and the variety spread. When Panama disease ruined the Gros Michel, the Cavendish turned out to resist that strain of the fungus. It was more delicate to ship, so exporters changed to packing bananas in boxes. Today Cavendish bananas dominate the world's banana export trade.

sections.key: Bananas are picked green and ripen as starch turns to sugar, a process driven by the gas ethylene.
sections.b: Bananas destined for shops are harvested while hard and green, because ripe fruit bruises easily and would spoil on the journey. Like apples, tomatoes and avocados, bananas are climacteric fruit, meaning they keep ripening after picking. The trigger is ethylene, a simple gas that the fruit produces itself. Distributors place green bananas in ripening rooms and add a little ethylene to start them off evenly. As a banana ripens, its starch is converted into sugars, the flesh softens and the green chlorophyll in the skin breaks down, revealing yellow pigments. Brown sugar spots show it is very ripe. Putting bananas in a paper bag with an apple traps ethylene and speeds ripening, while refrigeration blackens the skin but leaves the flesh fine.

sections.key: Powerful American fruit companies held enormous influence in Central America, inspiring the phrase ‘banana republic’.
sections.b: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, American companies built a vast banana trade in Central America and the Caribbean. The largest, the United Fruit Company, owned huge plantations, railways, ports and ships, and wielded great influence over several governments. In 1904 the American writer O. Henry used the phrase ‘banana republic’ in his book Cabbages and Kings to describe an unstable country dominated by foreign business interests. Real events matched the image. In 1928 Colombian troops fired on striking banana workers in what became known as the Banana Massacre; the death toll is still disputed. In 1954, a CIA-backed coup overthrew Guatemala's elected government, whose land reforms had threatened United Fruit's holdings. The term now describes any corrupt, unstable state.

sections.key: Australia grows its own bananas, mostly in north Queensland, and protects them with strict biosecurity.
sections.b: Most of Australia's bananas are grown in far north Queensland, especially around Tully and Innisfail, with smaller crops in northern New South Wales, Western Australia and the Northern Territory. Cavendish makes up most of the crop, while the small, sweet Lady Finger is a local favourite. Because Australia is free of many banana pests and diseases, fresh bananas are not imported, which is why cyclones that flatten Queensland plantations, such as Larry in 2006 and Yasi in 2011, have sent prices soaring. The biggest threat is a new strain of Panama disease, Tropical Race 4, which attacks Cavendish too. It was found in the Northern Territory in the late 1990s and in Queensland in 2015, where growers fight to contain it with strict farm hygiene.

quiz.q: What is the ‘trunk’ of a banana plant actually made of?
o: Soft wood
Tightly wrapped leaf bases
Hollow bamboo-like stems
Roots that grow upwards
quiz.e: The pseudostem is formed from overlapping leaf bases; banana plants have no wood and are giant herbs.

quiz.q: Why is every Cavendish banana plant genetically identical?
o: They are genetically engineered in labs
Seedless, sterile bananas are propagated from suckers or tissue of a parent plant
All bananas come from one seed bank
Bees pollinate them from a single flower
quiz.e: Because cultivated bananas are sterile, new plants are grown from pieces of existing ones, making them clones.

quiz.q: What caused the collapse of the Gros Michel banana trade?
o: A cyclone in Central America
Panama disease, a soil fungus to which the cloned plants had no resistance
Consumers preferred smaller bananas
A ban on banana imports
quiz.e: Fusarium wilt spread through genetically identical plantations, forcing a switch to the resistant Cavendish.

quiz.q: What makes green bananas ripen?
o: Exposure to sunlight
Ethylene gas, which the fruit produces and which ripening rooms add
Cold storage
Washing them in water
quiz.e: Bananas are climacteric fruit; ethylene triggers starch to turn into sugar and the skin to turn yellow.

quiz.q: Why do cyclones in Queensland cause big jumps in Australian banana prices?
o: Bananas are only grown in winter
Fresh bananas are not imported, so local crop losses cut supply
Cyclones spread Panama disease to shops
Supermarkets raise prices to fund repairs
quiz.e: Strict biosecurity means fresh bananas are not imported, so damage to north Queensland farms shrinks supply sharply.

LESSONS.title: The potato: from the Andes to everywhere
LESSONS.hook: A knobbly tuber from the high Andes fed empires, sparked suspicion in Europe, and became one of the world's most important foods.

sections.key: Potatoes were domesticated in the Andes of South America thousands of years ago, near Lake Titicaca.
sections.b: Wild potatoes grow across the Americas, but the potato we eat was domesticated in the Andes, in the region of southern Peru and northern Bolivia around Lake Titicaca. Estimates for when this happened range from about 7,000 to 10,000 years ago. Andean farmers had a remarkable challenge: growing food at altitudes of more than 3,000 metres, with frosts, thin air and short seasons. Over generations they bred thousands of varieties, in colours from purple and red to gold and near black, each suited to particular soils, heights and uses. Many of these traditional varieties are still grown by Andean communities, and the International Potato Center in Lima, Peru, keeps a huge collection of them as insurance for the future.

sections.key: Andean peoples invented a way to freeze-dry potatoes using cold nights, sunny days and their own feet.
sections.b: Fresh potatoes rot, which is a problem if you want to store food for lean years. Andean peoples solved this with chuño. Potatoes are spread out on the ground in the dry winter, where they freeze at night under clear, cold skies and thaw in the strong high-altitude sun during the day. After several cycles, people tread on them to squeeze out the water. The result is a light, hard, dried potato that can last for years. It is, in effect, freeze-drying, invented centuries before the modern laboratory version. The Inca state stored large amounts of chuño and other foods in roadside warehouses, helping to feed armies, workers and communities in hard times.

sections.key: Spanish conquerors encountered the potato in the 1530s, and it reached Europe within a few decades.
sections.b: Spanish soldiers met the potato during their conquest of the Inca Empire in the 1530s. By the later sixteenth century, potatoes had crossed the Atlantic, with records from the Canary Islands and Spain in the 1560s and 1570s. At first, Europeans were wary. The potato belongs to the nightshade family, alongside deadly nightshade, and its leaves and green parts really do contain toxic compounds called glycoalkaloids, including solanine. Some people thought potatoes caused disease, and they were unfamiliar to cooks used to grain and bread. Gradually, though, farmers noticed something powerful: potatoes produced far more calories per hectare than wheat or rye, grew in poor soils and cool climates, and could stay safely in the ground until needed.

sections.key: In France, Antoine-Augustin Parmentier championed the potato after eating it as a prisoner of war.
sections.b: Antoine-Augustin Parmentier was a French army pharmacist who was captured by the Prussians during the Seven Years' War. As a prisoner, he was fed potatoes, and he survived well on them. Back in France he became the potato's tireless promoter, especially after famines made the need for new food sources obvious. In 1772 the Paris Faculty of Medicine declared potatoes fit to eat. Parmentier hosted potato dinners for important guests and won royal support. A famous story says he had a field of potatoes guarded by soldiers during the day but not at night, so curious locals would steal the ‘valuable’ crop. That tale may have been embellished over time, but French cooks still honour him: dishes named Parmentier contain potato.

sections.key: Heavy dependence on one potato variety left Ireland exposed when blight struck in 1845.
sections.b: By the 1840s, a large share of Ireland's rural poor relied on potatoes for most of their food. Many grew a single high-yielding variety, the Lumper, which meant the crop was genetically very uniform. In 1845 a disease called late blight, caused by a fungus-like organism named Phytophthora infestans, swept in and turned potatoes black and rotten in the ground. The blight returned in following years. Roughly a million people died of starvation and disease, and more than a million emigrated, many to North America, Britain and Australia. Political choices made the disaster worse: food continued to be exported from Ireland, and relief was inadequate. The famine is a lasting lesson about the danger of depending on a single crop.

sections.key: Potatoes are now grown worldwide, with China and India the largest producers.
sections.b: From its Andean home, the potato spread across Europe, Asia and Africa, and is now among the most important food crops on Earth. As of the mid-2020s, China grows the most potatoes, followed by India. Potatoes give more food per hectare than most grains and need less water, which makes them valuable as populations grow and climates change. They are also more nutritious than their reputation suggests. A potato provides energy as starch, along with fibre, potassium and a useful amount of vitamin C, much of it close to the skin. It is usually what we do to potatoes, such as deep frying and adding lots of salt, butter and cream, that makes them less healthy, rather than the potato itself.

sections.key: Starchy and waxy potatoes behave differently, and green potatoes should be trimmed or thrown away.
sections.b: Potatoes fall into two broad camps. Floury or starchy varieties, such as russets, break apart when cooked and make fluffy mash, roast potatoes and chips. Waxy varieties, such as kipflers and many small new potatoes, hold their shape and suit salads and boiling. The difference comes down to the starch content and how the cells hold together. Store potatoes somewhere cool, dark and dry. Light makes them turn green, as they produce chlorophyll, and alongside it they can make more glycoalkaloids, which taste bitter and can cause illness in large amounts. Cut away green patches and sprouts generously, and throw out potatoes that are very green or taste bitter. Keeping them away from light is the simplest fix.

quiz.q: Where was the potato first domesticated?
o: Mexico
The Andes around Lake Titicaca
Ireland
The Amazon basin
quiz.e: Domesticated potatoes come from the Andes of southern Peru and northern Bolivia, thousands of years ago.

quiz.q: How is traditional chuño made?
o: By smoking potatoes over fire
By boiling and mashing them
By repeated freezing and thawing, then squeezing out water
By burying them in salt
quiz.e: Freezing nights and sunny days, plus trampling to remove water, produce a freeze-dried potato that lasts for years.

quiz.q: Why was Ireland so vulnerable to potato blight in the 1840s?
o: Potatoes were a new crop there
Many poor families relied heavily on one uniform variety, the Lumper
Ireland had banned other crops
The climate was too dry for potatoes
quiz.e: Dependence on a single genetically uniform variety meant blight could wipe out crops across the country.

quiz.q: What is true about the story of Parmentier's guarded potato field?
o: It is documented in court records
It is a popular tale that may have been embellished
It happened in Ireland
The guards were Prussian prisoners
quiz.e: Parmentier really did promote potatoes, but the guarded field story is a famous tale that may have grown in the telling.

quiz.q: What should you do with a potato that has turned green?
o: Eat it, green means extra vitamins
Cut away green parts generously, and discard it if very green or bitter
Store it in sunlight to fix it
Boil it longer to remove all toxins
quiz.e: Greening signals more glycoalkaloids; trim green parts and discard very green or bitter potatoes.

LESSONS.title: Rice: the grain that feeds billions
LESSONS.hook: Billions of people eat rice every day. Its story runs from ancient Chinese wetlands to a ‘miracle rice’ and paddies in the New South Wales Riverina.

sections.key: Asian rice was domesticated in China thousands of years ago, and African rice was domesticated separately in West Africa.
sections.b: Most of the rice we eat is Asian rice, Oryza sativa. Archaeological and genetic evidence points to domestication in the Yangtze River region of China, beginning roughly 9,000 years ago, though researchers still debate how the different main types, japonica and indica, arose and spread. Over time, farmers selected plants whose grains stayed on the stalk rather than scattering, making harvest easier. Remarkably, people in West Africa independently domesticated a different species, African rice, Oryza glaberrima, in the inland delta of the Niger River, around 3,000 years ago. African rice is hardy and still grown, though Asian rice has largely replaced it. Today rice is a staple food for billions of people, especially across Asia.

sections.key: Rice is one of the few grain crops that can grow in standing water, which helps farmers control weeds.
sections.b: Rice does not actually need to be underwater to grow, but it tolerates flooding far better than most plants. It has internal air channels that carry oxygen from the leaves down to the roots, which lets it thrive in waterlogged soil where competing weeds struggle. Farmers worked out long ago that flooding a field was a powerful way to control weeds and pests. Building paddies took enormous effort, from levelled fields with earth banks to the spectacular terraces carved into hillsides in the Philippines, Indonesia and southern China. One downside is that flooded soils, without oxygen, are home to microbes that produce methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Farmers are trialling methods such as alternate wetting and drying to cut emissions.

sections.h: The secret of sticky and fluffy
sections.key: The texture of cooked rice depends mainly on two starches, amylose and amylopectin.
sections.b: Rice starch comes in two main forms. Amylose is a straight-chain molecule, and rices high in it, such as many long-grain varieties, cook up firmer with separate grains. Amylopectin is highly branched, and it makes rice soft and sticky. Japanese short-grain rice has relatively little amylose, which is why it clumps nicely for sushi. Arborio and similar risotto rices release creamy starch when stirred. So-called glutinous or sticky rice, used in Thai and Lao cooking, is almost entirely amylopectin. Despite the name, it contains no gluten; ‘glutinous’ simply means glue-like. Basmati and jasmine are both fragrant, but jasmine tends to be softer and slightly stickier. Rinsing rice removes surface starch and gives looser grains.

sections.h: White rice and a Nobel Prize
sections.key: Polishing rice removes vitamins in the bran, and studying the resulting disease led to the discovery of vitamins.
sections.b: Brown rice still has its bran and germ, which contain fibre, oils, minerals and B vitamins. White rice has them polished away, making it quicker to cook and longer lasting, but less nutritious. In the late nineteenth century, as steam-powered mills spread polished rice across Asia, a disease called beriberi became widespread, causing nerve damage, weakness and heart failure. In the Dutch East Indies, now Indonesia, the physician Christiaan Eijkman noticed in the 1890s that chickens fed polished rice developed similar symptoms, and recovered when given unpolished rice. His work helped reveal that tiny amounts of certain substances in food are essential. The missing substance turned out to be thiamine, vitamin B1, and Eijkman shared the 1929 Nobel Prize.

sections.key: A short, high-yielding variety released in 1966 helped transform food supplies across Asia.
sections.b: In the 1960s, many experts feared mass famine in Asia as populations grew faster than harvests. At the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, plant breeders crossed a tall Indonesian variety with a dwarf variety from Taiwan. The result, released in 1966 and called IR8, had short, stiff stems. Older tall varieties tended to fall over when fertilised heavily, but IR8 could carry heavy heads of grain without collapsing, and it often yielded far more. It became known as ‘miracle rice’ and was a key part of the Green Revolution. Yields rose dramatically in countries such as India and the Philippines. The revolution had costs too, including heavier use of fertiliser, pesticides and water, and the loss of many traditional varieties.

sections.key: Australia grows rice mainly in the Riverina of New South Wales, with very high yields but a heavy dependence on water.
sections.b: Rice has been grown commercially in Australia for about a century, mostly in the Riverina and Murray regions of southern New South Wales, with irrigation water from the Murrumbidgee and Murray rivers. Australian rice growers achieve some of the highest yields per hectare in the world, and the industry has bred varieties suited to local conditions, including types that use less water. Because rice needs so much water, the size of each year's crop swings dramatically with drought and water allocations. In very dry years production has collapsed to a tiny fraction of normal. That makes rice a lightning rod in debates about how Australia should share water among farms, towns and rivers.

sections.key: Rice can be cooked many ways, but leftovers must be cooled quickly because of a spore-forming bacterium.
sections.b: There are two classic methods for cooking rice. The absorption method uses a measured amount of water that the grains soak up completely, while the boiling method cooks rice in plenty of water that is drained away, like pasta. Automatic electric rice cookers, popularised in Japan from the mid-1950s, switch off or to warm when the water has gone. Whatever the method, leftovers need care. Rice can carry spores of Bacillus cereus, which survive cooking. If cooked rice sits warm for hours, the spores can grow and make toxins that reheating will not destroy, causing vomiting. Cool leftover rice quickly, refrigerate it within a couple of hours, eat it within a day or so and reheat it until steaming hot.

quiz.q: Which statement about the origins of rice is correct?
o: All rice comes from one domestication in India
Asian rice came from China, and African rice was domesticated separately in West Africa
Rice was first grown in Australia
Rice was domesticated in Europe and spread east
quiz.e: Asian rice began in the Yangtze region, while African rice was independently domesticated in the Niger delta.

quiz.q: Why did farmers flood rice paddies?
o: Rice cannot grow without being underwater
Flooding controls weeds that cannot tolerate waterlogged soil
It adds salt to the soil
It keeps birds away
quiz.e: Rice tolerates flooding thanks to internal air channels, while most competing weeds do not.

quiz.q: Why is glutinous rice sticky?
o: It contains gluten
It is almost entirely amylopectin starch
It is rinsed in sugar water
It is high in amylose
quiz.e: Glutinous rice is nearly all branched amylopectin; ‘glutinous’ means glue-like and it contains no gluten.

quiz.q: What did Christiaan Eijkman's work on polished rice help reveal?
o: That rice causes allergies
That foods contain essential micronutrients, later identified as vitamins
That rice should be boiled longer
How to make rice grow faster
quiz.e: Beriberi in chickens fed polished rice led towards the discovery of thiamine, vitamin B1.

quiz.q: Why should leftover rice be cooled and refrigerated quickly?
o: It loses its flavour after an hour
Bacillus cereus spores can grow and make heat-resistant toxins
It absorbs fridge smells
Warm rice turns into sugar
quiz.e: Spores survive cooking; if rice sits warm, they can produce toxins that reheating does not destroy.

LESSONS.title: Pots and pans: what your cookware is doing
LESSONS.hook: Cast iron, stainless steel, non-stick and copper each handle heat differently. Know their personalities and your cooking gets easier overnight.

sections.h: Two jobs: spreading and holding heat
sections.key: Good cookware needs to spread heat evenly and hold enough heat that food does not cool the pan too much.
sections.b: A pan has two main heat jobs. The first is conducting heat sideways from the burner so the whole base is evenly hot, avoiding a scorching ring in the middle and cool edges. Metals vary hugely here. Copper conducts heat roughly twenty-five times better than stainless steel, and aluminium is not far behind copper. The second job is storing heat. A thick, heavy pan holds more energy, so when you drop in a cold steak, the pan's temperature does not crash and you still get a good sear. Cast iron is a poor conductor but a great heat store. No single material does everything perfectly, which is why cooks tend to collect a few different pans for different tasks.

sections.key: Cast iron is slow to heat but holds heat superbly, and its seasoning is a layer of oil baked into a hard coating.
sections.b: Cast iron pans are heavy, nearly indestructible and can last for generations. They heat slowly and unevenly, so it pays to preheat them gently for several minutes. Once hot, they hold heat beautifully, which makes them ideal for searing meat, frying and baking cornbread or pizza. Their famous seasoning is not grime. When thin layers of oil are heated past their smoke point, the oil polymerises, linking into a hard, slick coating bonded to the metal. A popular myth says you must never use detergent on cast iron. Modern dishwashing liquid is mild and will not strip well-polymerised seasoning, although soaking or a dishwasher can cause rust. Dry the pan straight away and wipe on a little oil.

sections.key: Stainless steel is tough and non-reactive, and the best pans hide an aluminium or copper core for even heating.
sections.b: Stainless steel does not rust easily, does not react with acidic foods like tomato or wine, and can go from stovetop to oven. On its own, though, it is a poor conductor of heat. Good stainless pans are therefore clad: they sandwich a layer of aluminium or copper between stainless steel, either just in the base or right up the sides. Food sticks to stainless when the pan is not hot enough, because proteins bond to the metal. A handy test is to flick in a drop of water. If it skitters around as a bead instead of sizzling away, the pan is hot, thanks to the Leidenfrost effect, where a cushion of steam holds the droplet up. Then add oil and food.

sections.key: The slippery coating on non-stick pans comes from a plastic discovered by accident in 1938.
sections.b: In 1938 a chemist named Roy Plunkett, working for DuPont in the United States, was experimenting with refrigerant gases. One cylinder seemed empty, but when it was cut open, it contained a waxy white solid. The gas had polymerised into polytetrafluoroethylene, or PTFE, a material so slippery and unreactive that almost nothing sticks to it. DuPont sold it as Teflon, and it was used in industry and the military before reaching kitchens. In the 1950s a French engineer, Marc Grégoire, found a way to bond PTFE to aluminium, reportedly at his wife Colette's suggestion, and the Tefal company was born. Non-stick pans made cooking eggs, pancakes and delicate fish dramatically easier, and they spread around the world.

sections.key: PTFE is stable at normal cooking temperatures, but an empty pan overheated on high can release harmful fumes.
sections.b: At ordinary cooking temperatures PTFE is very inert and passes through the body unchanged if tiny flakes are swallowed. The concern is overheating. Above roughly 260 degrees Celsius, the coating starts to break down and release fumes that can cause flu-like symptoms in people, sometimes called polymer fume fever. Pet birds are far more sensitive, and these fumes can kill them. An empty non-stick pan left on a high burner can reach those temperatures within minutes. So cook on low to medium heat, never preheat it empty on high and replace pans when the coating is badly scratched or flaking. A chemical once used in manufacturing PTFE, called PFOA, raised health and environmental concerns and has been phased out by major manufacturers.

sections.key: Carbon steel is the chef's lighter cast iron, copper is fast and responsive, and aluminium is light and cheap.
sections.b: Carbon steel is close to cast iron in chemistry but is rolled thinner, so it heats faster and is much lighter. Woks, French omelette pans and crepe pans are often carbon steel, and like cast iron they are seasoned. Copper is the most responsive metal, heating and cooling almost instantly as you adjust the flame, which is why pastry cooks love it for sugar work and sauces. Copper reacts with some foods, so most copper pans are lined with tin or stainless steel. Plain aluminium is light, cheap and a good conductor, but it reacts with acidic and alkaline foods and dents easily. Hard-anodised aluminium has a toughened surface layer that is harder and less reactive.

sections.h: Induction and choosing what to buy
sections.key: Induction cooktops only work with magnetic pans, and a few well-chosen pieces beat a big matching set.
sections.b: Induction cooktops do not heat up a coil or flame. Instead, a rapidly changing magnetic field makes electric currents flow inside the base of the pan itself, so the pan becomes the heat source. That only works with magnetic metals such as cast iron, carbon steel and many stainless steels. Plain aluminium, copper and glass will not work unless they have a magnetic base. A quick test is to see whether a fridge magnet sticks firmly to the bottom. When building a kitchen, a few good pieces usually beat a large boxed set: a heavy frying pan in cast iron or carbon steel, a non-stick pan for eggs, a clad stainless saucepan and a big pot for stock and pasta cover most cooking.

quiz.q: Why does a heavy pan sear a cold steak better than a thin one?
o: It is non-stick
It stores more heat, so its temperature does not crash
It conducts heat faster than copper
It contains less iron
quiz.e: Thick, heavy pans hold more heat energy, so adding cold food does not drop the temperature as much.

quiz.q: What is the seasoning on a cast iron pan?
o: Leftover grease and food residue
Oil polymerised by heat into a hard coating
A factory-applied Teflon layer
Rust that has been polished
quiz.e: Heating thin layers of oil past their smoke point links them into a hard, slick polymer bonded to the iron.

quiz.q: How was PTFE, the non-stick coating, discovered?
o: By a French cook looking for a better pan
By accident, when a gas cylinder polymerised into a white solid
By NASA for spacecraft
By heating cast iron with oil
quiz.e: In 1938 Roy Plunkett found a seemingly empty gas cylinder contained a slippery white solid: PTFE.

quiz.q: What is the main safety rule for non-stick pans?
o: Never use them for eggs
Do not overheat them empty on high heat
Always wash them in a dishwasher
Only use metal utensils
quiz.e: Above roughly 260°C, PTFE breaks down into harmful fumes, especially dangerous to pet birds.

quiz.q: How can you check whether a pan will work on an induction cooktop?
o: See whether it is heavy
See whether a magnet sticks to its base
Check that it is shiny
Fill it with water and look for bubbles
quiz.e: Induction relies on magnetism to make currents flow in the pan, so the base must be magnetic.

LESSONS.title: Sugar: a sweet substance with a bitter past
