Should Germany include German-speaking Austria and its many non-German peoples, or leave Austria out? And the parliament had no army or money of its own. In 1849 it finally offered the crown of a united Germany to Frederick William IV of Prussia. He refused to accept a crown offered by an elected assembly rather than by fellow princes. The parliament soon dissolved, and its remnant was dispersed by troops.

sections.key: Divisions among revolutionaries and the loyalty of armies allowed the old rulers to strike back.
sections.b: The revolutions of 1848 failed for several connected reasons. Middle class liberals wanted constitutions and order, while workers wanted jobs and social change, and the two soon feared each other. In Paris, the closure of the national workshops sparked the bloody June Days uprising, crushed by the army with thousands killed. Nationalities quarrelled too: Hungarians demanded freedom from Austria while denying it to Croats and Romanians within Hungary. Above all, the armies mostly stayed loyal to their monarchs. In late 1848 Austrian troops retook Vienna, and the young Franz Joseph became emperor. In 1849 Russian troops helped Austria crush Hungary. In France, voters elected Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte president, and in 1851 he seized power and soon declared himself emperor.

sections.key: Although the revolutions were defeated, some major changes lasted.
sections.b: It is tempting to call 1848 the turning point where history failed to turn, but some changes endured. In the Austrian Empire, peasants were freed from compulsory labour owed to landlords, the remnants of serfdom, and this reform was never reversed. Prussia kept a constitution and parliament, although a limited one. Denmark became a constitutional monarchy in 1849, the Netherlands adopted a more liberal constitution in 1848, and Switzerland adopted a federal constitution that laid the foundations of its modern state. Piedmont-Sardinia kept its constitution and later led the unification of Italy. The year also showed rulers that ignoring public opinion was dangerous, and they increasingly used nationalism for their own purposes, as Bismarck later did in Germany.

sections.key: Defeated revolutionaries spread their ideas across the world, while new political movements took shape.
sections.b: Many revolutionaries fled into exile. Thousands of Germans, known as Forty-Eighters, emigrated to the United States, where many became journalists, politicians and soldiers, and some later fought for the Union in the American Civil War. In Britain, the Chartist movement for working-class voting rights held a huge meeting in London in April 1848, but it fizzled out without revolution. Coincidentally, The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels was published in February 1848, just as the revolutions began, though it had little influence on events that year. Its later impact was enormous. For historians, 1848 remains a fascinating case study in how revolutions spread quickly, why unity is so hard to keep, and why winning a crowd is not the same as winning a state.

quiz.q: What economic troubles helped trigger the revolutions?
o: A gold rush
Crop failures, high food prices and a financial crisis
A sudden boom in wages
The end of the slave trade
quiz.e: Potato blight and poor harvests drove up food prices in the mid 1840s, followed by financial crisis and unemployment in 1847.

quiz.q: What did France's new Second Republic introduce in 1848?
o: Voting rights for all adult men
A new monarchy
Votes for women
A ban on newspapers
quiz.e: The provisional government declared a republic, introduced universal male suffrage and abolished slavery in French colonies.

quiz.q: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail to unite Germany?
o: It voted against unity
It had no army or money, and Prussia's king refused its crown
France invaded Frankfurt
It was never elected
quiz.e: Without power of its own, the parliament depended on princes, and Frederick William IV refused a crown offered by an elected assembly.

quiz.q: Which factor most helped the old rulers regain control?
o: The armies mostly stayed loyal to their monarchs
The revolutionaries won every battle
Britain invaded Europe
Railways stopped working
quiz.e: Loyal armies, along with divisions between liberals, workers and rival nationalities, allowed monarchs to crush the uprisings.

quiz.q: Which change in the Austrian Empire outlasted the revolutions?
o: A republic
The end of compulsory peasant labour for landlords
Independence for Hungary
Votes for all
quiz.e: The abolition of the remnants of serfdom in the Austrian Empire was never reversed, even after the revolutions were defeated.

LESSONS.title: Australia's Vietnam War
LESSONS.hook: It was Australia's longest war of the twentieth century and its most divisive. Young men were chosen for it by a lottery of birthdays, and many came home to silence.

sections.key: Fear of communism spreading through Asia, and the wish to keep the United States close, drew Australia in.
sections.b: After the Second World War, Australian leaders worried about the rise of communism in Asia, especially after the communist victory in China in 1949 and the Korean War. A popular idea, the domino theory, held that if one country fell to communism its neighbours would follow, one after another, until the threat reached Australia's doorstep. Vietnam had been divided in 1954 into a communist North and a non-communist South, and an insurgency was growing in the South, supported by the North. Australia also wanted to strengthen its alliance with the United States, formalised in the ANZUS treaty of 1951, as Britain's power in the region faded. In 1962 the Menzies government sent a small team of thirty military advisers to South Vietnam.

sections.key: In 1965 Australia committed combat troops, and later a task force based at Nui Dat.
sections.b: The advisers of the Australian Army Training Team Vietnam, known as the Team, trained South Vietnamese troops and became some of the most decorated Australian units of the war. In April 1965 Prime Minister Robert Menzies announced that an infantry battalion would be sent, saying South Vietnam had requested help, a claim later questioned by historians. The battalion served alongside American forces. From 1966 Australia ran its own 1st Australian Task Force, based at Nui Dat in Phuoc Tuy province, south-east of Saigon. There the army focused on patrolling the jungle and villages to cut the insurgents off from local support. Australian troops became known for slow, patient, careful patrolling, partly learned from earlier experience in Malaya, rather than heavy firepower.

sections.key: National service selected twenty-year-old men by drawing birth dates, and conscripts could be sent to Vietnam.
sections.b: In 1964 the government introduced a new scheme of national service. Twenty-year-old men had to register, and a lottery drew birth dates from a barrel. If your birthday was drawn, you could be called up for two years of military service. From 1965 the law allowed these conscripts, often called nashos, to be sent overseas, including to Vietnam. Around 15,000 national servicemen served there, and some of them were killed. The randomness troubled many Australians. A young man's future, and perhaps his life, could depend on whether a marble bearing his birth date came out of a barrel. Some refused to register or to serve, and a few were jailed. The ballot made the war deeply personal for families across the country.

sections.key: In August 1966, a single company of Australians fought a much larger enemy force in a rubber plantation.
sections.b: On 18 August 1966, D Company of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, about 105 men, was patrolling near Nui Dat in a rubber plantation called Long Tan. In a tropical downpour they ran into a far larger force of Viet Cong and North Vietnamese troops. For several hours the Australians, along with three New Zealand artillery observers, fought off repeated attacks, helped by intense artillery fire from the base and an ammunition drop by helicopter. As darkness fell, armoured personnel carriers arrived and the attackers withdrew. Eighteen Australians were killed. Enemy losses were far higher, though exact numbers are disputed. The Battle of Long Tan became the best-known Australian action of the war, and 18 August is now marked as Vietnam Veterans Day.

sections.key: As the war dragged on, opposition grew into some of the largest protests in Australian history.
sections.b: At first many Australians supported the war, but doubts grew as it dragged on without victory, particularly after the Tet Offensive of 1968 showed the enemy was far from beaten. Television brought images of the fighting into lounge rooms. Groups such as Save Our Sons, formed by mothers of possible conscripts, campaigned against the ballot. In May 1970 the Moratorium marches brought huge crowds into city streets around Australia. In Melbourne, led by Labor politician Jim Cairns, crowds were estimated at between 70,000 and 100,000 people, filling the city centre. Supporters of the war saw protesters as disloyal, and many protesters saw the government as sending young men to die for an unwinnable cause. The divide split families, churches and friendships.

sections.key: Australian combat troops withdrew in 1971, and the Whitlam government ended conscription in 1972.
sections.b: As the United States began reducing its forces, Australia followed. The task force left Phuoc Tuy in late 1971, and the last advisers left soon after. In December 1972 the newly elected Whitlam Labor government ended conscription, freed men jailed for refusing to serve and withdrew the remaining personnel. Altogether, almost 60,000 Australians served in Vietnam, and around 520 died, with thousands wounded. For the Vietnamese, the cost was vastly greater. Estimates of Vietnamese deaths during the war vary widely, but most run into the millions, civilians and soldiers alike. In April 1975, North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon and the country was reunified under communist rule. Australia later resettled tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees.

sections.key: Many veterans returned to indifference or hostility, and recognition came only years later.
sections.b: Unlike soldiers returning from the world wars, most Vietnam veterans came home individually or in small groups, often flying in quietly, and were expected to slip back into ordinary life. Some were abused by protesters, while some older veterans' organisations were slow to welcome them. Many struggled with what is now recognised as post-traumatic stress, and concerns grew about the health effects of chemical defoliants such as Agent Orange, investigated by a Royal Commission in the 1980s. Recognition came slowly. In October 1987, tens of thousands of Vietnam veterans marched through Sydney in a Welcome Home parade, an emotional moment for many. A national memorial was dedicated in Canberra in 1992. The war's lessons about alliances, conscription and public trust are still debated today.

quiz.q: What was the domino theory?
o: A plan to build railways in Asia
The idea that if one country fell to communism its neighbours would follow
A strategy for winning elections
A theory about economic growth
quiz.e: The domino theory held that communism would spread from country to country, a fear that drove Australian involvement.

quiz.q: How were national servicemen selected?
o: By exam results
By height and weight
By a ballot of birth dates
By volunteering only
quiz.e: Birth dates were drawn from a barrel, and twenty-year-old men whose birthdays were chosen could be conscripted.

quiz.q: Why is 18 August marked as Vietnam Veterans Day?
o: It is the date of the fall of Saigon
It is the anniversary of the Battle of Long Tan
It is the day conscription ended
It is when the first advisers arrived
quiz.e: On 18 August 1966, D Company 6RAR fought the Battle of Long Tan, now the best-known Australian action of the war.

quiz.q: What were the Moratorium marches of 1970?
o: Victory parades
Huge protests against the war
Recruitment drives
Marches for refugees
quiz.e: The May 1970 Moratorium marches brought enormous crowds into Australian cities to oppose the war and conscription.

quiz.q: When did Vietnam veterans receive a national Welcome Home parade in Sydney?
quiz.e: The Welcome Home parade in October 1987 came many years after most veterans had returned quietly to civilian life.

LESSONS.title: Apartheid: rise and fall
LESSONS.hook: For more than four decades, South Africa's laws sorted every person by race and decided where they could live, work, love and vote. Then, against most predictions, the system was dismantled without the all-out civil war many had feared.

sections.key: Racial discrimination in South Africa long predated apartheid, which made it total and systematic.
sections.b: South Africa's black majority had faced discrimination for centuries under Dutch and then British colonial rule. When the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, most black South Africans were denied the vote. The Natives Land Act of 1913 restricted black land ownership to a small fraction of the country, and pass laws controlled where black people could travel and work. In 1912, educated black leaders founded the organisation that became the African National Congress, or ANC, to fight for rights. The word apartheid, meaning apart or separateness in Afrikaans, came into political use in the 1940s. It described a plan to push segregation much further, turning a patchwork of discriminatory practices into a complete legal system governing every part of life.

sections.key: After 1948 the National Party passed laws classifying everyone by race and separating them by law.
sections.b: In 1948 the National Party, drawing its support mainly from white Afrikaners, won the election and began building apartheid. The Population Registration Act of 1950 classified every South African into racial groups, broadly white, coloured, Indian and black African, with officials sometimes deciding a person's category through humiliating tests. Marriage and sexual relationships across racial lines were banned. The Group Areas Act assigned separate residential areas to each group, and whole communities, such as District Six in Cape Town and Sophiatown in Johannesburg, were bulldozed and their residents forcibly moved. Separate and unequal schools, hospitals, beaches, buses and even park benches followed. Bantu Education was designed to prepare black children for lives as labourers. Pass laws required black adults to carry identity documents everywhere.

sections.key: Apartheid's planners tried to strip black South Africans of citizenship by assigning them to separate ‘homelands’.
sections.b: The most ambitious part of apartheid was the homeland system. The government divided black South Africans into ethnic groups and assigned each to a territory, or Bantustan, often scattered fragments of poor land. The aim was to declare these homelands independent, so that black people would become citizens of them rather than of South Africa, leaving a white-ruled state with no black citizens at all. Four homelands, including Transkei, were declared independent, though almost no other country recognised them. Millions of people were forcibly moved to these areas in the 1960s and 1970s, often to places with few jobs or services. Black workers who needed jobs in cities became migrants in their own country, living in hostels far from their families.

sections.key: Peaceful protest was met with bullets and bans, pushing the resistance towards armed struggle.
sections.b: Through the 1950s the ANC and its allies led mass nonviolent campaigns, and in 1955 adopted the Freedom Charter, declaring that South Africa belonged to all who lived in it. On 21 March 1960 at Sharpeville, police opened fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws, killing 69 people, many shot in the back. The government banned the ANC and other groups. Leaders including Nelson Mandela concluded that peaceful protest alone was failing, and in 1961 an armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, began a sabotage campaign. In 1964, after the Rivonia trial, Mandela and others were sentenced to life imprisonment, and many were sent to Robben Island. Inside South Africa, open opposition was largely silenced for more than a decade.

sections.key: School students rising up in 1976 began a wave of resistance that never fully stopped.
sections.b: On 16 June 1976, thousands of school students in Soweto, near Johannesburg, marched against a rule forcing them to be taught some subjects in Afrikaans, a language many saw as the language of their oppressors. Police opened fire. A photograph of the dying twelve-year-old Hector Pieterson, carried by another student, travelled around the world. Unrest spread across the country, and hundreds of people were killed in the months that followed. The Black Consciousness movement, led by Steve Biko, urged black South Africans to reject feelings of inferiority. Biko died in police custody in 1977 after severe beatings. In the 1980s township protests, strikes and boycotts grew, and the government declared states of emergency, detaining many thousands of people without trial.

sections.key: Sanctions and boycotts isolated South Africa, and sporting bans hit white South Africans hard.
sections.b: International pressure grew steadily. The United Nations condemned apartheid, and many countries imposed trade, arms and financial sanctions, especially in the 1980s. Banks refused new loans and companies pulled out, damaging an already struggling economy. Sport mattered deeply to many white South Africans, and sporting boycotts struck at their sense of belonging in the world. South Africa was excluded from the Olympics for decades. In Australia, a 1971 tour by South Africa's Springbok rugby team sparked large protests and clashes, and later governments of both major parties took strong anti-apartheid positions in the Commonwealth. Historians debate how much sanctions themselves forced change, compared with internal resistance and economic decline, but together they made apartheid increasingly costly to keep.

sections.key: In 1990 the government unbanned the ANC and released Mandela, opening tense negotiations.
sections.b: By the late 1980s, many in the government realised apartheid could not survive. On 2 February 1990, President F. W. de Klerk announced to parliament that the ANC and other banned organisations would be legalised. Nine days later, on 11 February, Nelson Mandela walked out of prison after 27 years. Negotiations over a new constitution followed, interrupted by violence that killed thousands of people, including clashes between the ANC and the Inkatha Freedom Party and attacks by those trying to wreck the talks. In 1993 the assassination of popular ANC leader Chris Hani brought the country close to the brink, but Mandela's appeal for calm held. That year Mandela and de Klerk were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

sections.key: South Africa's first fully democratic election brought Mandela to the presidency.
sections.b: On 27 April 1994, South Africans of every race voted together for the first time. Millions of people queued for hours, sometimes in lines stretching for kilometres, many casting the first vote of their lives. The ANC won about 62 per cent of the vote, and on 10 May Mandela was inaugurated as president, leading a government of national unity that included de Klerk as a deputy president. A new constitution, adopted in 1996, included one of the world's most extensive bills of rights. The country set up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to hear testimony about the crimes of the apartheid years. The legal system of apartheid was gone, though its economic legacy of deep inequality remains a major challenge today.

quiz.q: What did the Population Registration Act of 1950 do?
o: Gave everyone the vote
Classified every South African into a racial group
Created the national census of farms
Ended pass laws
quiz.e: The Act classified every person by race, the foundation on which all other apartheid laws rested.

quiz.q: What was the goal of the homeland system?
o: To give black South Africans more farmland
To strip black South Africans of South African citizenship
To build new cities for all races
To prepare for a world war
quiz.e: Planners hoped to make black people citizens of nominally independent homelands, leaving white-ruled South Africa without black citizens.

quiz.q: What happened at Sharpeville on 21 March 1960?
o: Mandela was released
Police killed 69 people protesting the pass laws
The first democratic election was held
The ANC was founded
quiz.e: Police fired on protesters at Sharpeville, killing 69, after which the government banned the ANC.

quiz.q: What sparked the Soweto uprising of 1976?
o: Rising bread prices
A rule forcing students to be taught some subjects in Afrikaans
A rugby match
The death of Mandela
quiz.e: Students marched against compulsory Afrikaans teaching, and police fired on them, sparking unrest across the country.

quiz.q: When did South Africa hold its first fully democratic election?
quiz.e: On 27 April 1994, South Africans of all races voted together for the first time, and Mandela became president.

LESSONS.title: Mao's China: the Great Leap and the Cultural Revolution
LESSONS.hook: Mao Zedong set out to transform China into a modern socialist power within a generation. Two of his campaigns caused one of the deadliest famines in history and a decade of political terror.

sections.key: In 1949 the Communists won China's civil war and set out to remake society from top to bottom.
sections.b: On 1 October 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing, after the Communist Party won a long civil war against Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, who retreated to Taiwan. China had endured decades of foreign invasion, warlords and civil war, and many Chinese welcomed peace and the promise of national strength. The new government moved fast. Land reform in the early 1950s took land from landlords and gave it to peasants, but it was carried out through mass ‘struggle sessions’ in which landlords were publicly denounced, and many were killed. Estimates of deaths in land reform and related campaigns range from several hundred thousand to several million. Private businesses were nationalised, and a Soviet-style planned economy began to take shape.

sections.key: Mao invited open criticism in 1956 and 1957, then punished hundreds of thousands who spoke up.
sections.b: In 1956 Mao encouraged intellectuals to speak freely with the slogan ‘let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend’. After hesitation, criticism poured in, attacking officials, the party's privileges and even its right to rule. Mao abruptly reversed course. In 1957 he launched the Anti-Rightist Campaign, and roughly 550,000 people, many of them teachers, writers, scientists and engineers, were labelled ‘rightists’. Many lost their jobs and were sent to labour camps or the countryside for years. Historians still debate whether Mao planned the trap from the start or reacted to criticism that went further than he expected. Either way, the lesson was clear to everyone: honest criticism was dangerous. That silence would have disastrous consequences in the years ahead.

sections.key: From 1958, Mao tried to make China an industrial power almost overnight through mass mobilisation.
sections.b: In 1958 Mao launched the Great Leap Forward, aiming to overtake Britain in steel production within about fifteen years and to prove that mass enthusiasm could beat Soviet-style caution. Hundreds of millions of peasants were organised into vast people's communes, where private plots were abolished and families ate in communal canteens. Millions of small backyard furnaces were built to make steel, consuming pots, pans and tools, while much of what they produced was useless. Farmers were pulled from fields to work on furnaces and dams. Pseudo-scientific farming methods such as very close planting and deep ploughing were imposed. A campaign against the Four Pests killed huge numbers of sparrows, and crop-eating insects flourished, adding to the harm.

sections.key: Inflated harvest reports led the state to seize grain that farmers needed to survive.
sections.b: Local officials, terrified of being labelled rightists, reported fantastic harvests that never existed. The state then took a share of grain based on those false figures, leaving many villages with little or nothing to eat, while China continued to export grain. In 1959, at a party conference at Lushan, Defence Minister Peng Dehuai privately criticised the Leap in a letter to Mao. Mao denounced and purged him, and the campaign was pushed even harder. The result was a catastrophic famine between 1959 and 1961. Estimates of excess deaths vary widely, from around fifteen million to more than forty million, with many demographers putting the figure at around thirty million. It is among the deadliest famines in recorded history, and largely caused by policy.

sections.key: Pragmatic leaders repaired the damage, but Mao feared the revolution was losing its way.
sections.b: By the early 1960s, other leaders, especially head of state Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, quietly reversed many Leap policies. They allowed private plots and markets again and used material incentives, and food production slowly recovered. Mao stepped back from day-to-day economic management but grew suspicious. He believed the party was becoming a new privileged elite, and that the Soviet Union, which he now regarded as having betrayed true communism, showed how a revolution could decay. He also resented the loss of his own authority. Meanwhile his image was being built into a cult of personality, helped by Defence Minister Lin Biao, whose army published Quotations from Chairman Mao, the famous Little Red Book, in the mid 1960s.

sections.key: In 1966 Mao unleashed millions of young Red Guards against party officials, teachers and tradition.
sections.b: In 1966 Mao launched the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, calling on young people to attack ‘bourgeois’ influences within the party and society. Students formed groups of Red Guards. At huge rallies in Tiananmen Square, millions waved the Little Red Book and cheered Mao. Red Guards humiliated, beat and sometimes killed teachers, officials and neighbours accused of being class enemies. They ransacked homes, burned books and smashed temples and historic sites as part of a campaign against the ‘Four Olds’: old customs, culture, habits and ideas. Liu Shaoqi was purged and died in custody in 1969. Deng Xiaoping was sent to work in a tractor factory. Rival Red Guard factions fought each other, sometimes with weapons, and the army had to restore order.

sections.key: Millions of urban youths were sent to the countryside, and political violence continued for a decade.
sections.b: From 1968, with the Red Guards out of control, Mao sent millions of young urban people, an estimated sixteen to seventeen million over the following years, ‘up to the mountains and down to the countryside’ to learn from peasants. Many lost their education and spent years in harsh rural poverty, an experience that shaped a whole generation, including China's later leader Xi Jinping. Political turmoil continued. In 1971 Lin Biao, by then Mao's chosen successor, died in a plane crash in Mongolia, after apparently fleeing China following a failed plot, though the details remain murky. Estimates of the number of people killed during the Cultural Revolution vary widely, from hundreds of thousands to two million or more, with many millions more persecuted.

sections.key: Mao's successors arrested his radical allies, turned to reform and gave a carefully limited verdict on his rule.
sections.b: Mao died on 9 September 1976. Within a month, the radical leaders known as the Gang of Four, including his widow Jiang Qing, were arrested. By the late 1970s Deng Xiaoping had emerged as China's paramount leader and launched the reforms that opened China's economy to markets and the world. In 1981 the Communist Party issued an official resolution that called the Cultural Revolution a catastrophe responsible for the most severe setbacks since 1949, and acknowledged Mao's mistakes. Yet it insisted his contributions outweighed his errors, and his portrait still hangs over Tiananmen Square. Open research into these years remains restricted in China, and archives are hard to access, which is why historians' estimates of the human toll still vary so much.

quiz.q: What happened after the Hundred Flowers campaign invited criticism?
o: The critics were rewarded with promotions
Hundreds of thousands were labelled rightists and punished
China held free elections
Mao resigned
quiz.e: Mao reversed course with the Anti-Rightist Campaign of 1957, branding around 550,000 people rightists and teaching everyone that criticism was dangerous.

quiz.q: Why did the state take so much grain during the Great Leap Forward?
o: Farmers volunteered it for export
Procurement was based on hugely inflated harvest reports
There was a record harvest
The Soviet Union demanded it all
quiz.e: Officials afraid of punishment reported fantastic harvests, and the state took grain based on those false figures, leaving villages starving.

quiz.q: Which statement best reflects estimates of the Great Leap famine death toll?
o: Fewer than one million
Estimates range widely, from about fifteen to more than forty million
Exactly ten million, according to official records
No one died of famine
quiz.e: Historians and demographers disagree, but estimates range from about fifteen to more than forty million, with many around thirty million.

quiz.q: What were the ‘Four Olds’ that Red Guards attacked?
o: Four elderly party leaders
Old customs, culture, habits and ideas
Four ancient cities
Old weapons, tools, coins and books
quiz.e: Red Guards targeted old customs, culture, habits and ideas, destroying temples, books and historic sites.

quiz.q: What did the Communist Party's 1981 resolution conclude about Mao?
o: He made no mistakes
The Cultural Revolution was a catastrophe, but Mao's contributions outweighed his errors
He should be removed from all memorials
The Great Leap was a success
quiz.e: The resolution condemned the Cultural Revolution and acknowledged Mao's mistakes, while maintaining that his contributions were greater.

LESSONS.title: Backing up: never lose your photos again
LESSONS.hook: In 1998, a single mistyped command wiped out most of Pixar's Toy Story 2. What saved the film was a backup nobody knew existed.

sections.key: Even experts lose data, and the copy that saves you is often the one you didn't plan.
sections.b: In 1998, partway through making Toy Story 2, someone at Pixar ran a command that began deleting the film's files. Characters, sets and animation disappeared from the shared drives as staff watched. Worse, the studio's regular backups turned out not to have been working properly. The film was rescued because Galyn Susman, a technical director working from home after having a baby, had a fairly recent copy of the project on her home computer. The machine was carefully wrapped and driven back to the studio, and most of the work was restored. The story is told and retold in technology circles for a simple reason: if a world-class studio can come that close to disaster, so can your phone full of family photos.

sections.key: Files are lost to hardware failure, theft, accidents, malware and simple human error.
sections.b: Data rarely vanishes in dramatic ways. A phone is dropped in the surf, a laptop is stolen from a car, a hard drive quietly fails after a few years, or you delete a folder while tidying up and empty the bin. Fires, floods and break-ins take computers and the backup drive sitting right beside them. Then there is malicious software, especially ransomware, which scrambles your files and demands payment to unlock them. Storage is also less permanent than it feels. Every drive eventually fails, and cheap USB sticks and memory cards can corrupt without warning. The question is never whether something will go wrong with a device you own, but whether you will lose anything when it does.

sections.key: Keep three copies of what matters, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy kept offsite.
sections.b: The most widely quoted rule of thumb, popularised by photographer Peter Krogh, is 3-2-1. Keep at least three copies of anything important: the original plus two backups. Store them on at least two different kinds of storage, such as your computer's internal drive and an external drive, so a single type of failure cannot take them all. And keep at least one copy offsite, somewhere physically separate, so a fire, flood or burglary at home leaves something behind. Today the offsite copy is usually a cloud backup service, but a drive kept at a relative's house or your workplace also counts. The rule is not magic, but it forces you to think about every way your data could be destroyed at once.

sections.key: A syncing service copies your mistakes everywhere, instantly, unless it also keeps old versions.
sections.b: Many people assume their files are safe because they live in iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox. These services are wonderful, but most of them are built mainly to sync: to keep the same files identical across all your devices. That means if you delete a folder, or overwrite a document with the wrong version, the change can spread to every device within seconds. A true backup is a separate copy that your everyday mistakes cannot reach. Many sync services do keep deleted files and older versions for a limited time, which helps, so it is worth learning how long yours keeps them and how to restore them. Treat sync as convenience, and make sure something else is your safety net.

sections.key: Keep at least one backup disconnected, so malware on your computer cannot reach it.
sections.b: Ransomware is software that encrypts your files so you cannot open them, then demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, for the key. Paying is no guarantee you will get your files back, and it funds the criminals. The best defence is a recent backup the malware cannot touch. If your external drive is permanently plugged in, ransomware can encrypt it along with everything else. So many experts suggest keeping a backup drive unplugged except while a backup is running, or using a cloud service that keeps older versions you can roll back to. The Australian Cyber Security Centre lists regular backups among its essential strategies for protecting computers, alongside keeping software updated. A good backup turns a catastrophe into an inconvenience.

sections.key: Your phone is probably your most valuable store of memories, so make sure it backs itself up.
sections.b: For many people, the irreplaceable files are not documents but photos and videos of children, travels and people who are no longer here. Most of those now live on a phone, which is easy to lose, drop or break. Both iPhones and Android phones can back up automatically to the cloud, but the free storage is often small, and once it fills up, backups can silently stop. Check your phone's settings to see when it last backed up successfully. Paying a few dollars a month for more storage is cheap insurance. For extra safety, periodically download your photo library to a computer or external drive as well, so your memories do not depend on a single company or a single account login.

sections.key: A backup you have never restored from is only a hope, so practise getting files back.
sections.b: Pixar's backups were running, or so everyone thought, until the day they were needed. The lesson is that a backup only matters if you can restore from it. Every few months, pick a random file or photo and try to recover it from each backup. Open it and check it actually works. Make sure you know your cloud account password and have your two-factor authentication sorted, because many people discover their backup is locked behind a login they cannot remember on the very day their phone is lost. If you use backup software, read its reports for errors. Ten minutes of testing tells you whether you really have three copies or only believe you do.

sections.key: The backup that runs by itself is the one that actually happens.
sections.b: Good intentions are a poor backup plan, because nobody remembers to copy files by hand every week. Set things up once so they run on their own. Turn on automatic phone backups. Use your computer's built-in tool, such as Time Machine on a Mac or File History on Windows, with an external drive. Add a cloud backup service for the offsite copy. Then put a reminder in your calendar every few months to check it is all still working and to test a restore. Start with whatever matters most: photos, important documents, tax records and anything you would grieve to lose. You do not need a perfect system on day one. Any backup is infinitely better than none.

quiz.q: What saved most of the Toy Story 2 files after they were accidentally deleted?
o: The studio's automated nightly backups
A copy on a staff member's home computer
Rebuilding the files from printed storyboards
A recovery service that scanned the deleted drives
quiz.e: Pixar's regular backups had not been working properly. A technical director working from home had a recent copy on her own computer, which was used to restore most of the film.

quiz.q: In the 3-2-1 rule, what does the 1 stand for?
o: One backup made each day
One copy stored offsite
One password protecting everything
One external hard drive
quiz.e: The rule is three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one copy offsite, so a fire, flood or theft at home cannot destroy them all.

quiz.q: Why is a syncing service like a shared cloud folder not a complete backup on its own?
o: It only works on Wi-Fi
It cannot store photos
Deletions and mistakes can be copied to every device
It deletes files after a year
quiz.e: Sync keeps files identical everywhere, so an accidental deletion or overwrite can spread instantly. Some services keep old versions for a while, which helps, but a separate backup is safer.

quiz.q: What is a good way to protect a backup from ransomware?
o: Keep the backup drive plugged in at all times
Keep at least one backup disconnected or versioned
Store backups in the same folder as the originals
Pay the ransom quickly
quiz.e: Ransomware can encrypt any drive it can reach. An unplugged drive, or a cloud backup with older versions, gives you a clean copy to restore.

quiz.q: Why should you occasionally test restoring a file?
o: To prove the backup really works when you need it
Because backups expire after testing
Testing makes backups faster
It is required by law
quiz.e: Many people discover their backups were failing only when disaster strikes. Restoring a sample file confirms the system, and your login, actually work.

LESSONS.title: Six knots worth knowing
LESSONS.hook: Most people know one knot and use it for everything. Sailors, climbers and truckies know better, and a handful of knots will cover almost anything you need.

sections.key: Knowing a few simple terms makes any knot instruction far easier to follow.
sections.b: Knot instructions use a small vocabulary. The working end is the end you are moving to tie the knot. The standing part is the rest of the rope, often the part under load. A bight is a U-shaped fold in the rope, and a loop is a bight where the rope crosses itself. Strictly speaking, knot enthusiasts distinguish a hitch, which ties a rope to an object such as a post or ring, from a bend, which joins two ropes. It also helps to know that almost every knot weakens a rope, often substantially, because the tight curves concentrate stress. That is why the right knot matters, and why anything involving climbing, lifting people or heavy loads needs proper training and gear.

sections.key: The reef knot is ideal for tying bandages and parcels, but it is unreliable for joining two ropes under load.
sections.b: The reef knot, also called the square knot, is the one many people learned at school: right over left, then left over right. Done correctly, it lies flat and neat, which is why it has long been used for tying bandages, slings and parcels. Get the second step the same way round as the first and you have tied a granny knot, which slips easily. The reef knot's big weakness is that it can spill or capsize when used to join two ropes that are pulled hard, especially if they differ in thickness or stiffness. Knot experts have warned about this for generations. For joining two ropes under strain, a sheet bend is far more secure, though harder to remember at first.

sections.key: The bowline makes a fixed loop that will not slip, and it stays easy to untie even after heavy loading.
sections.b: Pronounced ‘boh-lin’, the bowline has been called the king of knots. It forms a loop at the end of a rope that does not tighten or slide, which makes it useful for tying a rope around a tree, a post or even, in a rescue, a person. Generations of children have learned it with a little story: make a small loop in the standing part, then the rabbit (the working end) comes up out of the hole, goes around the back of the tree, and goes back down the hole. Pull it tight. One great virtue is that after taking a heavy load, a bowline can still be loosened by pushing the collar. Its weakness is that it can work loose when not under load, so climbers usually prefer a figure-eight loop.

sections.key: The clove hitch quickly ties a rope to a post and is easy to adjust, but it can slip if the post turns.
sections.b: The clove hitch is two turns around a pole, with the second crossing over the first and the end tucked under itself. It is fast to tie, easy to adjust and easy to undo, which is why it is used to secure fenders on boats, start lashings when building with poles, and tie off tent lines and garden stakes. It can also be dropped over the top of a post as two loops, which is handy when you need to tie up quickly. However, the clove hitch is not a set-and-forget knot. If the post rotates, or if the load keeps changing direction, it can gradually work itself loose. For a long-term or critical tie, add a couple of half hitches or choose a sturdier knot.

sections.h: Round turn and two half hitches
sections.key: Wrapping the rope fully around the object first takes the strain, so you can tie off even under load.
sections.b: If you need to tie a rope to a ring, rail or post and it is already under tension, perhaps from a boat drifting away, this is the knot. First pass the rope around the object twice, which is the round turn. The friction of those two wraps holds most of the load, giving you time to finish. Then take the working end around the standing part and through itself to make a half hitch, and repeat to make a second one in the same direction. The finished knot is strong, secure and can be untied without too much fuss, even after a strain. Boaties use it for mooring, and it is just as handy for tying a hammock, a tarp or a load to a fixed point.

sections.key: A figure eight at the end of a rope stops it slipping through a hole, pulley or your hand.
sections.b: The simplest useful knot of all is the stopper, tied at the end of a rope to stop it escaping. The overhand knot works, but it can jam tight and be very hard to undo. The figure-eight is better: make a loop, pass the end around the standing part, then back through the loop so the rope traces a figure eight. It is bulkier, so it is less likely to pull through, and it is easier to untie afterwards. Sailors put stopper knots at the ends of lines so they cannot run out through pulleys. Around the home it is useful on drawstrings, swing ropes and clotheslines. The same shape, threaded back along itself, forms the figure-eight loop that climbers rely on.

sections.key: The trucker's hitch acts like a simple pulley, letting you pull a load down tight on a trailer or roof rack.
sections.b: Anyone who has watched a load shift on a trailer will appreciate the trucker's hitch. You make a fixed loop partway along the rope, pass the working end around an anchor point such as a tie-down hook, then back up through the loop. Pulling on the end now works like a simple pulley system, giving a mechanical advantage that is theoretically about three to one, though friction reduces it. That lets you tension the rope far more than you could by pulling alone. Once it is tight, pinch it in place and secure the end with two half hitches. It is a favourite of farmers, campers and anyone moving house with a trailer. Always check loads again after a few kilometres, as ropes settle.

sections.key: Knots are learned by the hands, not the eyes, so practise until you can tie them without thinking.
sections.b: Reading about knots is a little like reading about swimming. The knowledge only sticks once you have done it many times. Keep a short length of rope near the couch and tie each knot while watching television until you can do it without looking. Then practise in awkward conditions: with the rope behind a post, in the dark, or with cold hands. That is when you will actually need it, while a tarp flaps in a storm or a boat drifts from the jetty. Animated knot websites and apps let you watch each step slowly. Start with the bowline, the clove hitch and the round turn with two half hitches. Those three alone will handle most everyday jobs.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of the reef knot?
o: It is very hard to untie
It can spill when joining two ropes under load
It only works on thin string
It cannot lie flat
quiz.e: The reef knot is great for bandages and parcels, but used to join two ropes under strain, especially different ones, it can capsize and come apart.

quiz.q: Why is the bowline so useful?
o: It tightens around whatever it holds
It forms a fixed loop that will not slip and stays easy to untie
It joins two ropes of different thickness
It never loosens, even without load
quiz.e: The bowline gives a loop that holds its size and can be untied after loading. Its weakness is that it can work loose when not under load.

quiz.q: When can a clove hitch work itself loose?
o: When it is tied on a fixed post
When the rope is wet
When the post rotates or the load keeps changing direction
Only when tied in nylon rope
quiz.e: The clove hitch is quick and adjustable but not secure on a rotating post or with a shifting load, so add half hitches for anything critical.

quiz.q: In a round turn and two half hitches, what does the round turn do?
o: Its friction takes the strain while you finish the knot
It makes the knot easier to untie later
It stops the rope fraying
It doubles the rope's breaking strength
quiz.e: Two full wraps around the object create enough friction to hold most of the load, giving you time to tie the half hitches.

quiz.q: Why can a trucker's hitch pull a load tighter than a simple knot?
o: It uses a slip knot that grips harder
It works like a pulley, giving mechanical advantage
It uses two ropes instead of one
The rope stretches more
quiz.e: Looping the rope back through a fixed loop creates a simple pulley, theoretically about three to one before friction, so you can tension the rope strongly.

LESSONS.title: Mending clothes: buttons, seams and holes
LESSONS.hook: A missing button or a split seam sends a lot of good clothing to landfill. Ten minutes with a needle and thread can save it.

sections.key: Mending was once an everyday skill, and it is making a comeback for reasons of cost and waste.
sections.b: During the Second World War, clothing in Britain was rationed, and in 1943 the government published a booklet called Make Do and Mend. It taught people to darn socks, patch elbows, turn old garments into new ones and make clothes last as long as possible. For most of history, that attitude was simply normal. Clothes were expensive, and people repaired them again and again. Today clothing is cheap, and huge quantities end up in landfill, often for faults that would take minutes to fix. Mending is coming back, partly to save money, partly to reduce waste and partly because many people find it calming. The basic skills are simple, and you do not need a sewing machine to learn them.

sections.key: A few needles, some thread, pins, small scissors and a seam ripper will handle most repairs.
sections.b: You can build a useful mending kit in a small tin. Include a packet of hand-sewing needles in assorted sizes, a few reels of thread in black, white, navy, grey and beige, and some pins. Add small sharp scissors, a few safety pins and spare buttons. Many garments come with a spare button sewn inside or in a little bag on the tag, so keep those together. A seam ripper, a small hooked tool for cutting stitches, is cheap and makes unpicking easy. A thimble protects your fingertip when pushing through thick fabric, and a needle threader helps tired eyes. Polyester or all-purpose thread suits most jobs. Match colours as closely as you can, choosing slightly darker if unsure, because it tends to show less.

sections.key: Use a comfortable length of thread, doubled for strength, with a secure knot at the end.
sections.b: Cut a length of thread about as long as your arm. Much longer and it tangles. Cut it cleanly at an angle, which makes it easier to thread, then pass it through the eye of the needle. For buttons and other jobs that take strain, pull the thread through until both ends meet and knot them together, so you sew with a double strand. For finer work, a single strand with a knot at one end is neater. A simple way to knot is to wrap the end around your fingertip a couple of times, roll it off between finger and thumb, and pull the twist down into a small knot. When you finish, make a few small stitches in the same spot to lock everything in place.

sections.key: Leave a little slack under the button and wrap it to form a shank, so it can sit neatly in the buttonhole.
sections.b: Mark where the button goes by looking for the old holes or lining it up with its buttonhole. Start from the back of the fabric so the knot is hidden. Bring the needle up through one hole of the button and down through the opposite one, and repeat several times. Here is the trick most people miss: lay a toothpick or matchstick across the top of the button and sew over it. When you remove it, the button will have a little slack. Bring the needle up between the button and the fabric, then wind the thread tightly around those stitches a few times. This forms a shank, which lets the button sit on top of the buttonhole without puckering. Finish at the back with several locking stitches.

sections.key: A split seam is usually the easiest repair of all, because you are simply rejoining the original stitch line.
sections.b: A seam that has come apart, perhaps under an arm or along the side of a pair of trousers, is often the quickest fix in mending. Turn the garment inside out and pin the two edges together along the old stitch line. Start a little before the gap, where the original stitching is still sound, and sew along the line with a backstitch. You bring the needle up a short way ahead, then go back down at the end of the previous stitch, creating a strong, continuous line that looks almost like machine sewing. Carry on a little past the gap and lock off. For seams that can only be reached from the outside, a ladder stitch pulls the edges together and becomes almost invisible.

sections.key: A slip stitch or blind hem catches only a thread or two of the outer fabric, so it barely shows.
sections.b: When a hem comes down, fold it back along its original crease and pin it. The aim is to sew it so that almost nothing shows on the outside. With a slip stitch, you hide most of the thread inside the fold of the hem, then pick up just one or two threads of the main fabric with each stitch before slipping back inside the fold. Keep the stitches small and not too tight, or the fabric will pucker. For a fast, temporary fix, iron-on hemming tape bonds the hem in place with heat and no sewing at all, though it may not survive many washes. It is also useful for shortening trousers when you have no time to sew.

sections.key: Darning weaves new threads across a hole, and visible mending turns the repair into decoration.
sections.b: Darning is how socks and knitwear were traditionally repaired. You stretch the area over something rounded, such as a darning mushroom or even a light bulb, then sew rows of thread across the hole and weave more threads through them at right angles, creating a small patch of new fabric. For woven clothes like jeans, a patch on the inside or outside works well. Many menders now celebrate their repairs rather than hiding them. Sashiko, a Japanese stitching tradition whose name means roughly ‘little stabs’, uses rows of small running stitches, often white on indigo, to reinforce worn cloth. Patched and repatched Japanese textiles called boro, once a sign of poverty, are now admired as art.

sections.key: Many zip problems can be fixed with graphite, soap or a gentle squeeze of pliers.
sections.b: Zips cause a lot of unnecessary clothing deaths. If a zip sticks, rub a graphite pencil, a bar of soap or a little candle wax along the teeth, then work the slider gently back and forth. If the teeth keep separating behind the slider, the slider has often widened with wear. Squeezing its sides very gently with pliers, a little at a time, can make it grip again. If a pull tab snaps off, a small key ring or paperclip makes a serviceable replacement. Some repairs, such as replacing a whole zip in a coat, are fiddly enough that a tailor or alterations shop is worth the money. Knowing which jobs to do yourself and which to pay for is part of the skill.

quiz.q: What was Make Do and Mend?
o: A 1943 British wartime booklet on making clothes last
A Japanese school of embroidery
A modern recycling brand
An Australian sewing competition
quiz.e: During wartime clothes rationing, the British government published Make Do and Mend to teach people to repair and reuse their clothes.

quiz.q: Why lay a toothpick across a button while sewing it on?
o: To keep the needle straight
To leave slack for a thread shank so it sits well
To stop the thread knotting
To hold the button in place while you sew
quiz.e: The toothpick leaves slack, which you wrap with thread to form a shank. That lets the button sit neatly through the buttonhole without puckering.

quiz.q: Which stitch gives a strong, continuous line for repairing a split seam?
o: Backstitch
Tacking stitch
Blanket stitch
Cross stitch
quiz.e: Backstitch goes back to meet the end of the previous stitch each time, creating a strong, unbroken line that resembles machine stitching.

quiz.q: What does darning involve?
o: Gluing a patch over a hole
Weaving new threads across a hole to rebuild fabric
Ironing the edges of a hole together
Cutting out the damaged area
quiz.e: Darning lays rows of thread across a hole and weaves more threads through them at right angles, effectively creating new fabric.

quiz.q: A zip's teeth keep separating behind the slider. What is a common fix?
o: Replace the whole garment
Gently squeeze the slider with pliers
Cut off the bottom stop
Wash it on hot
quiz.e: Worn sliders often spread slightly. A gentle squeeze with pliers, a little at a time, can help it grip the teeth again.

LESSONS.title: The emergency department: how it really works
LESSONS.hook: Why does someone who arrived after you get seen first? The answer goes back to Napoleon's battlefields, and understanding it makes a hospital visit far less frustrating.

sections.key: Triage, the system of treating the sickest first, has its roots in Napoleonic battlefield medicine.
sections.b: For much of history, wounded soldiers were treated according to rank, or not treated at all until the fighting ended. Dominique-Jean Larrey, a surgeon in Napoleon's armies, changed that. He introduced light, fast horse-drawn ‘flying ambulances’ to reach the wounded during battle, and he insisted that the most dangerously injured be treated first, whatever their rank or even their side. The word triage comes from the French trier, meaning to sort. The idea spread through military medicine and, in the twentieth century, into civilian hospitals. The principle is the same today. An emergency department is not a queue. It is a sorting system designed to make sure the person most likely to die without help is seen first.

sections.key: Your first stop is a brief assessment by an experienced nurse, who decides how urgently you need care.
sections.b: When you arrive at an Australian emergency department, you will usually speak first with a triage nurse. In a couple of minutes they ask what has happened, check key signs such as breathing and pulse, and look for danger. They are not diagnosing you. They are deciding how long you can safely wait. Be clear and specific: when the problem started, how severe it is, what medicines you take and any important conditions you have. Do not exaggerate, but do not play things down either. Triage nurses are highly experienced at spotting serious illness, and they rely on what you tell them. After triage you may be sent to the waiting room, or straight through to a treatment area.

sections.key: Every patient is given one of five categories, each with a maximum recommended time to be seen.
sections.b: Australian and New Zealand emergency departments use the Australasian Triage Scale, which has been in place in various forms since the 1990s. It has five categories. Category 1 is immediately life-threatening, such as cardiac arrest, and should be seen immediately. Category 2 should be seen within 10 minutes, for example severe chest pain or serious breathing difficulty. Category 3 within 30 minutes, Category 4 within an hour and Category 5 within two hours, for less urgent problems such as a minor wound. These are the maximum times within which assessment and treatment should begin, not how long the whole visit takes. Hospitals report how often they meet these targets, and busy departments sometimes fall short, especially in the lower categories.

sections.key: Long waits usually mean sicker people have arrived or the hospital's wards are full.
sections.b: Waiting rooms can be maddening, especially when you can see people being called ahead of you. Usually it means someone more urgent has come in, perhaps by ambulance through a different door. Arriving by ambulance, by the way, does not jump the queue. Ambulance patients are triaged too, and a less urgent ambulance patient may wait in the same waiting room. Another major cause of delay is called access block. When patients who need admission cannot move up to a ward because no beds are free, they stay in emergency, occupying cubicles and staff time. That is why waits often reflect pressure across the whole hospital rather than slow work in the department itself.

sections.key: Call 000 for emergencies, and use a GP, pharmacist or urgent care clinic for problems that are not.
sections.b: Some situations always warrant Triple Zero (000) or the emergency department: chest pain, difficulty breathing, signs of stroke such as a drooping face or slurred speech, severe bleeding, a serious head injury, seizures, severe burns or someone who is unconscious or unresponsive. If in doubt, call 000. For problems that need attention but are not life-threatening, such as a sprain, minor cut or ear infection, a GP, after-hours GP or urgent care clinic may see you faster. Pharmacists can advise on many minor illnesses, and nurse-staffed health advice lines can help you decide where to go. Choosing the right place is not just good for you. It keeps the emergency department free for the people who truly need it.

sections.h: What to bring and how to help
sections.key: Bring your medication list and Medicare card, and tell staff straight away if things get worse.
sections.b: If you can, bring your Medicare card, a list of your medicines and allergies, and details of your doctor and any major conditions. A phone charger, water and something to read make long waits easier, though ask staff before you eat or drink, as you may need surgery or tests. Having a friend or family member with you helps: they can listen, remember what doctors said and speak up for you. Most importantly, if your condition changes while you wait, such as worse pain, new symptoms or feeling faint, tell the triage nurse straight away. You can be reassessed and moved up. Staff would far rather hear from you than discover a deterioration late.

sections.key: Public hospital emergency care is free for Medicare-eligible patients, but ambulance costs vary by state.
sections.b: If you are eligible for Medicare, treatment as a public patient in a public hospital emergency department costs nothing. Ambulances are a different story. Some states and territories cover their own residents, while others can charge substantial fees unless you have ambulance cover through a state subscription scheme or private health insurance. It is worth checking your situation before you ever need one, though cost should never stop you calling 000 in an emergency. When you are discharged, ask for a copy of your discharge summary, make sure you understand any new medicines and warning signs to watch for, and book a follow-up with your GP. The emergency department fixes the crisis. Your GP handles what comes after.

quiz.q: What does the word triage come from?
o: A Latin word for wound
A French word meaning to sort
The name of a famous nurse
A Greek word for urgent
quiz.e: Triage comes from the French trier, to sort. Napoleon's surgeon Dominique-Jean Larrey pioneered treating the most urgently wounded first.

quiz.q: Under the Australasian Triage Scale, a Category 2 patient should be seen within
o: 2 hours
1 hour
30 minutes
10 minutes
quiz.e: Category 1 is immediate, Category 2 within 10 minutes, Category 3 within 30, Category 4 within 60 and Category 5 within 120 minutes.

quiz.q: Does arriving by ambulance guarantee you will be seen faster?
o: Yes, ambulance patients always go first
No, ambulance patients are triaged by urgency too
Only after midnight
Only if you have private health insurance
quiz.e: Everyone is triaged on how urgent their condition is. A less urgent ambulance patient may still wait in the waiting room.

quiz.q: What is access block?
o: When the waiting room is locked overnight
When admitted patients stay in emergency because ward beds are full
When an ambulance cannot reach a hospital
When triage nurses are on a break
quiz.e: Access block happens when patients who need admission cannot move to a ward, so they occupy emergency beds and slow the whole department.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel worse while waiting to be seen?
o: Wait quietly for your turn
Leave and come back later
Tell the triage nurse straight away
Search your symptoms online first
quiz.e: If your condition changes, tell the triage nurse immediately. You can be reassessed and given a more urgent category.

LESSONS.title: Small talk that isn't so small
LESSONS.hook: Most of us avoid chatting with strangers because we expect it to be awkward. Experiments suggest we have badly misjudged both them and ourselves.

sections.key: People predicted talking to a stranger would be unpleasant, but those who did it enjoyed their commute more.
sections.b: In a well-known study published in 2014, psychologists Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder approached commuters on trains and buses in Chicago. Some were asked to strike up a conversation with a stranger, some to keep to themselves, and others to commute as usual. Beforehand, people predicted that talking to a stranger would be the least pleasant option. Afterwards, those who had chatted reported the most positive journeys. Commuters also assumed other people would not want to talk, yet those approached were generally happy to. The researchers concluded that many of us wrongly avoid conversation, missing small but real pleasures because of mistaken expectations. Similar findings have since appeared in other settings and countries, though the effects are modest rather than life-changing.

sections.key: After a conversation, people tend to underestimate how much the other person liked them.
sections.b: A 2018 study led by Erica Boothby asked strangers to chat and then rate both how much they liked their partner and how much they thought their partner liked them. Again and again, people underestimated how much they were liked. The researchers called it the liking gap. It seems to happen because we replay our own awkward moments and harsh self-criticism, while the other person was paying attention to the conversation as a whole and found us perfectly pleasant. The gap appeared in lab conversations, among new university housemates and in workshops with members of the public. If you leave a chat thinking you were boring, the evidence suggests the other person very probably did not see it that way.

sections.key: Brief, friendly exchanges with acquaintances and strangers can lift your mood and sense of belonging.
sections.b: Close friends and family are central to wellbeing, but casual connections count too. Psychologist Gillian Sandstrom, with Elizabeth Dunn, found that people tended to feel happier on days when they had more interactions with weak ties, such as classmates, neighbours and the person who makes their coffee. In another study, customers asked to have a genuine, friendly exchange with a barista left in a better mood than those told to be as efficient as possible. Weak ties also bring practical benefits. Sociologist Mark Granovetter's classic research suggested that new opportunities, including jobs, often come through acquaintances rather than close friends, because they move in different circles and hear about different things.

sections.key: The easiest opener is a friendly comment or question about something you are both experiencing.
sections.b: Most people overthink the first sentence. You do not need wit, just a door. The simplest opener is about your shared situation: the weather, the queue, the event, the food or the dog sitting at your feet. ‘Have you been to one of these before?’ or ‘How do you know the host?’ works at almost any gathering. Open questions, which cannot be answered with a yes or no, give the other person room to talk. A popular memory aid is FORD: family, occupation, recreation and dreams, four broad topics most people enjoy discussing. Read the cues, though. Someone with headphones on and eyes on a book may not want company, and that is fine too.

sections.key: Asking follow-up questions makes people like you more, because it shows you were really listening.
sections.b: A 2017 study by researchers at Harvard, led by Karen Huang, analysed thousands of conversations, including those from speed dating events. People who asked more questions were better liked, and one kind mattered most: follow-up questions, which build on what the other person has just said. If someone mentions they have just come back from Tasmania, ‘What was the highlight?’ shows you heard them, in a way that switching to your own holiday does not. Follow-ups signal attention, interest and care, which are what most of us want from a conversation. The research also found that people tend to ask fewer questions than would be ideal, perhaps because they are busy planning what to say next.

sections.key: People enjoy deeper conversations with strangers more than they expect to.
sections.b: Small talk is a warm-up, not a destination. Research by Michael Kardas, Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, published in 2022, found that people expected deep conversations with strangers to feel more awkward and less enjoyable than they actually were. Participants who answered more personal, meaningful questions with a stranger consistently reported feeling more connected than they had predicted. You do not need to leap to intimate subjects. Simply moving from ‘What do you do?’ to ‘What do you enjoy most about it?’ or ‘How did you end up doing that?’ invites a real answer. Offering something genuine about yourself in return helps the other person feel safe going further.

sections.key: Conversations rarely end when both people want them to, so a warm, clear exit is a kindness.
sections.b: Ending a conversation can feel harder than starting one. A 2021 study led by Adam Mastroianni asked people how long they had wanted their conversations to last, and found that conversations almost never ended when both people wanted them to. Often both wanted to stop earlier, or one wanted more and the other less, and neither could tell. So a graceful exit is helpful. Summarise something from the chat, thank them and give a reason, even a simple one: ‘I'll let you get back to your evening. It was great hearing about the trip.’ If you would like to meet again, say so specifically. A clean, warm ending leaves both people with a good final impression.

quiz.q: In Epley and Schroeder's commuter study, how did people who talked to strangers feel afterwards?
o: More stressed than expected
More positive than those who kept to themselves
Exactly as they had predicted
Embarrassed and keen to avoid it again
quiz.e: Commuters expected talking to a stranger to be unpleasant, but those who did it reported the most positive journeys.

quiz.q: What is the liking gap?
o: Liking people less as you get to know them
Underestimating how much a conversation partner liked you
The difference between online and in-person friends
Liking people who are similar to you
quiz.e: After conversations, people consistently underestimate how much the other person liked them, often because they dwell on their own awkward moments.

quiz.q: According to Granovetter's research, why are acquaintances useful for finding jobs?
o: They are more honest than close friends
They move in different circles and hear about different opportunities
They are usually managers
They are more willing to lend money
quiz.e: Weak ties connect you to networks beyond your own, so they often pass on information and opportunities your close friends would not hear about.

quiz.q: Which type of question was most linked to being liked in Huang's research?
o: Questions about the weather
Follow-up questions building on what the person said
Questions about yourself
Yes or no questions
quiz.e: Follow-up questions show you were listening and interested, and people who asked more of them were better liked.

quiz.q: What did Mastroianni's study find about how conversations end?
o: They usually end exactly when both people want
They rarely end when both people want them to
They always run too short
Women always end them first
quiz.e: Conversations almost never ended when both people wanted, and people could not tell what their partner wanted, which is why a clear, warm exit helps.

LESSONS.title: Flat battery, flat tyre: getting yourself going
LESSONS.hook: The two most common reasons cars get stuck are a dead battery and a flat tyre. Both are fixable by the roadside, if you know the order of things and put safety first.

sections.key: Get well off the road, turn on your hazard lights and only do the job yourself if it is genuinely safe.
sections.b: Before you touch a jack or a jumper lead, think about traffic, which is the biggest danger at any roadside breakdown. Pull off as far from moving cars as you can, onto firm, level ground if possible, and turn on your hazard lights. Put the handbrake on and switch off the engine. If you are on a busy highway or freeway, on a bend or in poor light, it is often safer for everyone to get out on the side away from traffic, stand well back behind a barrier if there is one, and call roadside assistance instead of attempting the job. If anyone is injured, there is a fire or fuel leak, or you are in danger, call Triple Zero (000).

sections.key: Lights left on, short trips, age and heat are common reasons a battery fails to start the car.
sections.b: A flat battery usually announces itself when you turn the key or press the start button: a rapid clicking, a slow, laboured crank, or nothing at all, often with dim dashboard lights. Common causes include leaving headlights or interior lights on, many short trips that never fully recharge the battery, and the car sitting unused for weeks. Age matters too. Car batteries typically last a few years, and Australian heat tends to shorten their life. If the engine cranks strongly but will not start, the battery is probably not the problem. Before jump-starting, look at the battery. If it is cracked, leaking, bulging or smells strongly of rotten eggs, do not jump it. Call for help.

sections.key: Connect positive to positive, then negative to a bare metal point on the flat car, away from the battery.
sections.b: First check both cars' owner's manuals, as some have special jump points or warnings. Park the cars close but not touching, switch off both engines, and make sure the two batteries are the same voltage, which is 12 volts in almost all ordinary cars. Then connect the leads in this order. Red clamp to the positive terminal of the flat battery. Other red clamp to the positive terminal of the good battery. Black clamp to the negative terminal of the good battery. The last black clamp goes not on the flat battery, but on a bare, unpainted metal point on the flat car's engine or body, away from the battery. Batteries can give off hydrogen gas, and this keeps any final spark away from it.

sections.key: Run the donor car for a few minutes, start the flat car, then remove the leads in reverse order.
sections.b: With the leads connected, start the donor car and let it run for a few minutes to put some charge into the flat battery. Then try to start the stranded car. If it does not start after a few short attempts, stop and wait, as repeated long cranking can overheat the starter motor. Once it is running, remove the leads in exactly the reverse order: black from the metal point, black from the good battery, red from the good battery, then red from the formerly flat one. Do not let the clamps touch each other while any are still attached. Then drive the car for a decent stretch, rather than switching it straight off, and have the battery tested soon. A battery that went flat once may be on its way out.

sections.h: Jump starter packs and modern cars
sections.key: Portable lithium jump starters let you start a car alone, but hybrids and EVs need their manual's instructions.
sections.b: You do not always need a second car. Compact lithium jump starter packs, about the size of a thick book, can start most petrol cars and many diesels without help, and they fit easily in a glovebox. Keep one charged, as they slowly lose power while sitting unused. Modern cars bring some complications. Many have the battery hidden in the boot or under a seat, with separate jump points under the bonnet. Hybrid and electric vehicles have a small 12-volt battery that powers the electronics, and if it goes flat the car will not switch on. They can often be jump-started, but manufacturers have specific procedures and some warn against using them to jump other cars. Always follow the manual.

sections.key: Stop promptly, secure the car, and loosen the wheel nuts while the wheel is still on the ground.
sections.b: If you feel a tyre deflating, with the car pulling to one side or a flapping sound, slow down gently and pull over as soon as it is safe. Driving on a flat quickly ruins the tyre and can damage the wheel. Once you are stopped safely, find the spare, jack, wheel brace and, if your car has them, the locking wheel nut key. On a slope, put something heavy against the wheel diagonally opposite the flat to stop the car rolling. Now, before lifting the car, use the brace to loosen each wheel nut about half a turn, usually anticlockwise. With the tyre still on the ground, the wheel cannot spin while you strain, and you get far better leverage.

sections.key: Jack only at the marked jacking point, never put any part of your body under the car, and tighten nuts in a star pattern.
sections.b: Position the jack at the jacking point shown in the owner's manual, usually a reinforced section of the sill near the wheel. Raise the car just until the flat tyre is clear of the ground. Never put any part of your body under a car held up only by a jack. Remove the nuts, keeping them together, pull off the wheel and fit the spare. Screw the nuts on by hand, then snug them with the brace, working in a star or criss-cross pattern so the wheel sits evenly. Lower the car, then do the final tightening, again in a star pattern. Many tyre shops recommend having the nuts checked again after a short distance, as they can settle.

sections.key: A space-saver spare is for getting you to a tyre shop, at reduced speed, not for everyday driving.
sections.b: Many cars now carry a space-saver spare, a narrow temporary wheel that saves boot space and weight. It is designed to get you to a tyre shop, not to drive on for weeks. Most carry a sticker or moulded label with a maximum speed, often 80 kilometres per hour, and they reduce braking and cornering grip, so drive gently. Some newer cars have no spare at all, just a tyre repair kit with a sealant and small compressor. These can fix small punctures in the tread, such as from a nail, but not cuts in the sidewall or major damage. Find out what your car carries before you need it, and practise once at home. A calm driveway lesson beats a first attempt on a highway at night.

quiz.q: You get a flat on a busy freeway with little room beside the lane. What is usually the safest choice?
o: Change the tyre quickly on the traffic side
Get well clear of traffic and call roadside assistance
Keep driving to the next exit no matter how far
Stand behind the car to warn drivers
quiz.e: Traffic is the biggest roadside danger. If changing the tyre would put you close to moving cars, get to safety and call for help instead.

quiz.q: Where should the final black jumper lead clamp be attached?
o: The negative terminal of the flat battery
Bare unpainted metal on the flat car, away from its battery
The positive terminal of the good battery
Any plastic part of the engine cover
quiz.e: Connecting the last clamp to bare metal away from the battery keeps any spark away from hydrogen gas the battery may release.

quiz.q: Which sign suggests a battery should NOT be jump-started?
o: The engine clicks when you try to start it
The dashboard lights are dim
The battery case is cracked or bulging
The car has been parked for a week
quiz.e: A cracked, leaking or swollen battery is damaged and could be dangerous. Do not jump it; call for help.

quiz.q: Why loosen the wheel nuts before jacking up the car?
o: The jack will not work otherwise
With the tyre on the ground, the wheel will not spin as you turn the brace
It lets air out of the tyre
It is a legal requirement
quiz.e: Loosening the nuts with the wheel on the ground stops it spinning and gives you leverage. Then jack the car and remove them.

quiz.q: What is a space-saver spare intended for?
o: Permanent use until the next service
Getting you to a tyre shop at reduced speed
Towing heavy trailers
Driving in wet conditions only
quiz.e: Space-savers are temporary wheels, usually with a maximum speed on a label, and they reduce grip. Replace them with a proper tyre soon.

LESSONS.title: Reading a map and compass
