Both copied a Latin sign system
quiz.e: Clerc came to America with Thomas Gallaudet in 1817, and French signs blended with local signing to form ASL.

quiz.q: What does the Martha's Vineyard story suggest?
o: Deafness was cured there
When a community shares sign language, deafness is far less disabling
Sign languages cannot survive on islands
Hearing people cannot learn to sign
quiz.e: Because many hearing islanders signed, deaf residents took part fully in community life.

quiz.q: What did the 1880 Milan congress decide?
o: To make sign language compulsory in schools
To favour speech-only teaching and exclude sign language
To create one universal sign language
To close deaf schools
quiz.e: The mostly hearing delegates voted for oralism, leading to decades of bans on signing in classrooms.

quiz.q: Which sign language is Auslan most closely related to?
o: American Sign Language
French Sign Language
British Sign Language
Japanese Sign Language
quiz.e: Auslan descends mainly from BSL, and together with New Zealand Sign Language forms one language family.

LESSONS.title: What your eyes and brain do when you read
LESSONS.hook: Reading feels smooth and effortless, but your eyes are jumping, stopping and skipping all the time. And your brain is using circuits that evolved for something else.

sections.h: A new trick for an old brain
sections.key: Writing is too recent for evolution to have produced a reading brain.
sections.b: Humans have been speaking for at least tens of thousands of years, probably far longer, but writing was invented only around 5,000 years ago, and mass literacy is barely a few centuries old. That is far too recent for evolution to have produced a brain built for reading. So how do we do it? The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene has proposed a theory called neuronal recycling. Learning to read repurposes brain circuits that originally evolved for other jobs, such as recognising objects and faces, and links them to the brain's language areas. In children learning to read, brain scans show a region on the underside of the left hemisphere becoming increasingly tuned to written letters and words.

sections.key: A specific region becomes specialised for recognising written words.
sections.b: That region is often called the visual word form area, sitting in the left fusiform gyrus, near areas that respond to faces and objects. In skilled readers it responds strongly to letters and words in a familiar script, and much less to unfamiliar symbols. It helps us recognise a word whether it is written in capitals, lower case or different fonts, an impressive feat of pattern recognition. Damage to this area, for example from a stroke, can cause a condition in which a person can still write but struggles to read back what they have just written. Research also suggests that learning to read changes the brain in other ways, including how it processes spoken sounds, which partly explains why reading and phonics are so closely linked.

sections.h: Your eyes jump, they don't glide
sections.key: Reading is a rapid series of jumps and pauses, not a smooth sweep.
sections.b: If you watch someone's eyes as they read, you will see they do not move smoothly along the line. They make quick jumps called saccades, separated by brief pauses called fixations. In English, a typical fixation lasts roughly a quarter of a second, and a typical jump covers around seven to nine letters. During the jump itself, you take in almost no useful visual information; the brain stitches the pauses together so that reading feels continuous. Readers skip many short, predictable words, such as the and of, and land more often on longer content words. About one jump in ten or so goes backwards, as the reader checks something. Researchers study all this with eye trackers, which record exactly where and when the eyes stop.

sections.key: You only see clearly a few letters at a time, and the window points in your reading direction.
sections.b: Sharp vision covers only a tiny part of what your eyes see, so at each fixation you can identify only a handful of letters clearly. Clever experiments, in which text on a screen changes depending on where the reader is looking, have measured this window. For English readers it extends roughly three or four letters to the left of the fixation point and about fourteen or fifteen to the right, because that is where the next words are. For readers of Hebrew, which runs right to left, the window is reversed. Information from the edge of the window helps the brain plan the next jump and get a head start on the next word. Reading, in short, is constant prediction.

sections.key: Research shows that reading much faster usually means understanding much less.
sections.b: Typical silent reading speeds for adults are roughly 200 to 300 words per minute, varying with the text and the reader. Speed reading courses have long promised thousands of words per minute, often by claiming you can stop hearing words in your head or take in whole lines at a glance. A major 2016 review of the research, with the eye-movement scientist Keith Rayner as lead author, concluded that these claims do not hold up. The limiting factor is not the eyes but the brain's speed in recognising words and understanding language. Pushing much faster forces a trade-off: comprehension drops. Speed reading techniques are essentially skimming, which is a useful skill for finding information but not a shortcut to deep understanding. Becoming a faster reader comes mainly from reading more.

sections.key: A famous internet text about jumbled words was not based on Cambridge research and only partly true.
sections.b: You may have seen a message claiming that, according to research at Cambridge University, it doesn't matter what order the letters in a word are, as long as the first and last letters are right. Matt Davis, a scientist at a Cambridge brain research unit, investigated and found no such study at Cambridge. The text is readable partly because of how it was written: many words are short and unscrambled, function words are intact, and the jumbled letters are often close to their correct positions. Scrambling longer words more thoroughly makes text much harder to read, and research shows jumbled letters still slow readers down noticeably. The meme does capture something real, though: the brain uses context and letter identity flexibly, not strictly one letter after another.

sections.key: A famous story suggests silent reading was once rare, but historians are more cautious.
sections.b: In his Confessions, written around 400 CE, Saint Augustine described his surprise at seeing Bishop Ambrose of Milan reading silently, his eyes moving over the page while his voice was still. This passage was long taken as proof that almost everyone in the ancient world read aloud. Reading aloud was certainly common, partly because ancient texts were often written without spaces between words, which made them harder to read silently. But historians now point to other ancient sources showing silent reading was known, and argue Augustine's surprise may have had other causes. What is clearer is that word spacing, which spread in European manuscripts during the early Middle Ages, made silent, private reading easier and much more widespread.

quiz.q: What does the neuronal recycling theory propose?
o: Reading uses brain circuits that evolved for other tasks
Humans evolved a reading gene 5,000 years ago
Neurons are replaced each time we learn a word
Reading uses only the right hemisphere
quiz.e: Writing is too recent for evolution to shape, so reading repurposes circuits such as those for recognising objects.

quiz.q: What are saccades?
o: Brief pauses on a word
Quick jumps of the eyes between fixations
Backward reading of a whole page
Spoken mistakes while reading aloud
quiz.e: Saccades are the rapid jumps between fixations. We take in almost no useful information during the jump itself.

quiz.q: Why does an English reader's attention window extend further to the right?
o: The right eye is usually stronger
That is where the upcoming words are
Letters on the left are smaller
It is a random quirk
quiz.e: The window points in the direction of reading, which is why it is reversed for readers of Hebrew.

quiz.q: What did a major 2016 review conclude about speed reading?
o: It triples comprehension
Big gains in speed generally cost comprehension
It works only for children
It is impossible to read faster than 100 words per minute
quiz.e: The bottleneck is language processing in the brain, so going much faster mostly means understanding less.

quiz.q: What did a Cambridge scientist find about the scrambled letters meme?
o: It was based on a famous Cambridge study
There was no such Cambridge study, and the claim is only partly true
It was written by a Cambridge professor in 1903
It applies only to English
quiz.e: Matt Davis found no such study. Scrambled text is readable only under certain conditions and still slows readers down.

LESSONS.title: Banned books: the trials that changed what we can read
LESSONS.hook: Popes, customs officers and courts have all tried to stop people reading certain books. Again and again, the ban made the book more famous.

sections.key: For four centuries the Catholic Church kept an official list of forbidden books.
sections.b: In 1559, under Pope Paul IV, the Catholic Church published the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the Index of Prohibited Books. Catholics were forbidden to read or own listed works without permission. The Index grew out of anxiety about the printing press and the Protestant Reformation, which spread new ideas faster than authorities could control them. Over time it included works by figures such as the astronomer Galileo, the philosopher René Descartes and many others whose ideas were judged dangerous to faith or morals. Galileo's Dialogue, which defended the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, stayed on the list for around two centuries. The final edition appeared in 1948, and the Index was formally abolished in 1966, ending its legal force.

sections.key: James Joyce's novel was banned in the United States until a landmark 1933 ruling.
sections.b: James Joyce's Ulysses, set in Dublin over a single day in 1904, broke many rules of the novel, including frank descriptions of sex and the body. When episodes appeared in an American magazine, The Little Review, the editors were prosecuted for obscenity in 1921 and fined. No publisher in Britain or America would take the full book, so it was published in Paris in 1922 by Sylvia Beach, owner of the bookshop Shakespeare and Company. Copies were smuggled into other countries and seized by customs. In 1933 the publisher Random House deliberately arranged for a copy to be seized to provoke a test case. Judge John M. Woolsey ruled that the book, read as a whole, was not obscene, and it was legally published in the United States in 1934.

sections.key: A famous 1960 trial in Britain opened the door to frank literature.
sections.b: D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover, about an affair between an aristocrat's wife and a gamekeeper, was privately printed in Florence in 1928 and banned in Britain in its full form for decades. In 1959 a new British law allowed a book's literary merit to be considered as a defence against obscenity. Penguin Books tested it in 1960 by announcing a cheap, unabridged paperback, and was prosecuted. The defence called around 35 witnesses, including novelists, critics and clergy, to argue for the book's value. The chief prosecutor famously asked the jury whether it was a book they would want their wives or servants to read, a question that made the prosecution seem hopelessly out of touch. The jury acquitted Penguin, and the paperback sold millions of copies within months.

sections.key: For much of the twentieth century, Australia had one of the strictest censorship regimes in the Western world.
sections.b: Australian censorship was run largely through customs, which seized imported books at the border, alongside state obscenity laws. For decades the list of banned titles was itself kept confidential for long periods, so readers often did not know what they were missing. Works by authors such as James Joyce, D. H. Lawrence and many others were banned at various times, as were political works judged subversive. Lady Chatterley's Lover remained banned in Australia for several years after the British trial. Pressure for change grew through the 1960s. In 1970, Penguin Australia secretly printed Philip Roth's banned novel Portnoy's Complaint locally and distributed it, provoking prosecutions in several states. Around the same time, the federal customs minister Don Chipp began dramatically loosening the system, moving toward a classification approach.

sections.key: Censorship has sometimes gone far beyond bans to violence against books and authors.
sections.b: On 10 May 1933, Nazi-organised students in Berlin and other German cities burnt tens of thousands of books by Jewish, left-wing and other authors deemed un-German. More than a century earlier the German poet Heinrich Heine, whose own works were among those burnt, had written in a play that where books are burnt, people will eventually be burnt too. In 1989 Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Khomeini, issued a fatwa calling for the death of Salman Rushdie over his novel The Satanic Verses, which many Muslims considered blasphemous. Rushdie spent years in hiding. His Japanese translator, Hitoshi Igarashi, was murdered in 1991, and others connected to the book were attacked. In 2022, Rushdie himself was stabbed at a public lecture in New York state and lost the sight of one eye.

sections.key: Banning a book often draws more attention to it than it would otherwise receive.
sections.b: Censors face a stubborn problem: forbidding a book advertises it. The Lady Chatterley trial turned a little-read novel into a bestseller, and Ulysses gained a glamorous reputation partly because readers had to smuggle it. Today, book bans more often take the form of challenges to books in school and public libraries, where parents or groups ask for titles to be removed. Organisations such as the American Library Association track these challenges, which in recent years have frequently targeted books about race, gender and sexuality. People still argue about where the line falls between protecting children and restricting ideas. Many libraries celebrate an annual Banned Books Week, inviting readers to discover the books others tried to keep from them, and to decide for themselves.

quiz.q: When was the Catholic Church's Index of Prohibited Books abolished?
quiz.e: First published in 1559, the Index had its final edition in 1948 and was abolished in 1966.

quiz.q: How did Ulysses become legal in the United States?
o: Joyce removed the controversial chapters
A judge ruled in 1933 that, read as a whole, it was not obscene
The president pardoned it
It was reclassified as a medical text
quiz.e: Random House arranged a test case, and Judge John M. Woolsey ruled in the book's favour.

quiz.q: What change in British law made the Lady Chatterley trial possible?
o: Abolition of all censorship
A 1959 law allowing literary merit as a defence
A ban on Penguin Books
A law requiring juries to read every book
quiz.e: The Obscene Publications Act 1959 allowed literary merit to be considered, which Penguin tested in 1960.

quiz.q: What did Penguin Australia do with Portnoy's Complaint in 1970?
o: Refused to sell it
Secretly printed and distributed it in defiance of the ban
Published a censored version
Sent copies back to America
quiz.e: Penguin Australia printed it locally and distributed it, provoking prosecutions and adding pressure for reform.

quiz.q: What is a common effect of banning a book?
o: It is quickly forgotten
It often attracts more attention and readers
It becomes illegal everywhere
Its author stops writing
quiz.e: Bans tend to advertise books; the Lady Chatterley trial turned the novel into a bestseller.

LESSONS.title: Does your language shape how you think?
LESSONS.hook: Do Inuit really have hundreds of words for snow? Does a language without left and right change how you see the world? The truth is stranger and more subtle than the myths.

sections.key: Benjamin Lee Whorf argued that the structure of a language shapes the way its speakers think.
sections.b: Benjamin Lee Whorf was a chemical engineer who worked for a fire insurance company in Connecticut, and studied linguistics in his spare time, partly under the anthropologist Edward Sapir. In his job he noticed that workers were careless near drums labelled empty, even though empty petrol drums can be full of explosive vapour. The word empty, he suggested, was shaping their behaviour. In the 1930s he went further, arguing that languages carve up reality differently and that speakers of very different languages think about the world in fundamentally different ways. This became known as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, though neither man ever stated it as a formal hypothesis, and the label was applied by others after their deaths.

sections.key: Linguists distinguish between language determining thought and merely influencing it.
sections.b: It helps to separate two claims. The strong version, sometimes called linguistic determinism, says language sets the limits of thought: if your language has no word for something, you cannot think about it. The weak version, linguistic relativity, says language nudges what you notice, remember and pay attention to, without imprisoning you. The strong version is almost certainly false. People can think about things they have no words for, babies and animals reason without language, and we constantly invent new words for new ideas, which would be impossible if words had to come first. Translation, while imperfect, is always possible to a meaningful degree. The live scientific question is about the weak version: how much, and in what ways, does language nudge thought?

sections.key: Claims about Hopi time and Inuit snow words became cautionary tales.
sections.b: Whorf claimed the Hopi language of Arizona had no words or grammatical forms referring to time as we understand it, so Hopi speakers saw the world differently. In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki published a large study documenting extensive time expressions in Hopi, including words for days, seasons and units of time. Then there is the claim that Inuit have dozens or hundreds of words for snow. It grew from a modest remark by the anthropologist Franz Boas, who mentioned four distinct root words, and was exaggerated with each retelling. Linguists Laura Martin and Geoffrey Pullum debunked the inflation in the 1980s. Inuit languages build long words from many parts, so counting words is misleading, and English has plenty of snow words too.

sections.h: The language without left or right
sections.key: Speakers of some Aboriginal languages use compass directions for everything, and track direction constantly.
sections.b: Some of the strongest evidence for linguistic relativity comes from Australia. In Guugu Yimithirr, from the Cape York region of Queensland, speakers do not use words like left, right, in front or behind to describe where things are. Instead they use cardinal directions, roughly north, south, east and west, even at small scales: there is an ant on your northern leg. Research by the linguists John Haviland and Stephen Levinson found that speakers kept remarkably accurate track of direction at all times, even indoors or after travelling, because their language demands it. In experiments where people turned around and recreated arrangements of objects, speakers of such languages tended to preserve compass direction, while English and Dutch speakers preserved left and right.

sections.key: Language can speed up colour discrimination and may be needed for exact counting.
sections.b: Russian has two basic colour terms for what English calls blue: goluboy for lighter blues and siniy for darker blues. In a 2007 study, Russian speakers were slightly faster at telling apart two shades when they fell on different sides of that boundary, while English speakers showed no such advantage. The effect disappeared when participants had to repeat numbers silently at the same time, suggesting language was actively involved. Numbers offer a more dramatic case. The Pirahã people of the Amazon have no words for exact numbers, only terms meaning roughly small and larger amounts. In several experiments they matched small sets accurately but struggled with exact quantities beyond about three, though results varied with the task. Researchers concluded that number words may be a cognitive tool for exact quantities.

sections.key: How we picture time can follow the direction of writing or the words we use for it.
sections.b: Asked to arrange pictures showing a sequence, such as a person ageing, English speakers tend to lay them out from left to right, while speakers of Hebrew and Arabic, written right to left, often go right to left. Research by Lera Boroditsky and Alice Gaby with Kuuk Thaayorre speakers, from Pormpuraaw on Cape York, found they tended to arrange time from east to west, whichever way they were facing, like the sun's path. In the Aymara language of the Andes, the word for the past is linked to the front and the future to the back: you can see what has already happened, while the future is unseen behind you. Speakers' gestures match, pointing forward for the past. These findings show how flexible human thinking about time can be.

sections.key: Language nudges thought in measurable ways, but some celebrated findings have not held up.
sections.b: Most researchers now accept a modest form of linguistic relativity. Language does not trap anyone's mind, but it guides attention, makes some distinctions easier to notice and remember, and provides tools, like number words, that extend what we can do. Caution is still essential. Some well-publicised findings, such as experiments suggesting that grammatical gender changes how people describe objects, have proved difficult to replicate, and other claims linking grammar to behaviours like saving money remain contested. Critics such as the psychologist Steven Pinker argue that thought largely runs on something deeper than any particular language. Learning another language, then, may not rewire your mind, but it can show you distinctions you never noticed, and a different way of standing in the world.

quiz.q: What observation from Whorf's insurance work inspired his thinking?
o: Workers ignored fire alarms written in English
Workers were careless around drums labelled empty that were full of vapour
Fires were more common in bilingual factories
Workers misread the word flammable
quiz.e: He suggested the word 'empty' shaped behaviour, even though the drums held explosive vapour.

quiz.q: Which version of the Sapir-Whorf idea is almost certainly false?
o: The weak version, that language nudges attention
The strong version, that language sets the limits of thought
Both are proven true
Neither has been tested
quiz.e: People think about things they lack words for and invent new words, so language cannot strictly limit thought.

quiz.q: What happened to the claim that Inuit have hundreds of words for snow?
o: It was confirmed by Franz Boas
It was an exaggeration of a modest remark, debunked by linguists
It was found to apply only to Hopi
It was proved in a 2007 experiment
quiz.e: Boas mentioned four roots; retellings inflated it, and Laura Martin and Geoffrey Pullum exposed the myth.

quiz.q: How do Guugu Yimithirr speakers usually describe where things are?
o: Using left and right
Using compass directions such as north and east
By counting steps
By naming nearby landmarks only
quiz.e: They use cardinal directions even at small scales, and research found they track direction with remarkable accuracy.

quiz.q: What did the Pirahã number studies suggest?
o: Pirahã speakers cannot see small sets of objects
Exact number words may be a tool needed for exact quantities
Counting is innate in all humans
Pirahã has the largest number vocabulary in the world
quiz.e: Without exact number words, Pirahã speakers struggled to match exact quantities above about three.

LESSONS.title: The pigeonhole principle: the simplest idea that proves surprising things
LESSONS.hook: If you have more pigeons than holes, some hole holds two pigeons. That is the whole idea, and it can prove that two people in Sydney have exactly the same number of hairs.

sections.key: If more items go into fewer boxes, at least one box must hold more than one item.
sections.b: Imagine ten pigeons flying home to nine pigeonholes. However they arrange themselves, at least one hole must end up with two birds. There is no clever trick, no probability and no calculation involved. It simply cannot be otherwise. This is the pigeonhole principle, and it may be the most obvious statement in all of mathematics. Yet mathematicians love it, because it lets you prove that something must exist without ever finding it. You do not need to know which hole is crowded, only that one is. The German mathematician Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet used the idea in the 1830s and 1840s, and in German it became known as the Schubfachprinzip, the drawer principle. The English name is thought to refer to the small compartments in old desks and mail sorters rather than to actual birds.

sections.key: Count the possible categories, add one, and a match is guaranteed.
sections.b: Here is the principle at its most practical. Your drawer holds a jumble of black socks and grey socks, the power is out, and you need a matching pair. How many socks must you grab to be certain? The answer is three. There are only two colours, so two socks might be one of each, but a third sock has to match one of them. The colours are the pigeonholes and the socks are the pigeons. The same thinking works for anything. With 367 people in a room, at least two must share a birthday, because there are only 366 possible dates, counting 29 February. Notice the difference between certainty and likelihood. A shared birthday becomes likely with just 23 people, but only 367 makes it a guarantee.

sections.key: Sometimes the principle proves a fact that sounds impossible to check.
sections.b: A typical human head has somewhere around 100,000 hairs, and estimates usually range up to about 150,000. Nobody has anything close to a million. Now consider Sydney, home to more than five million people. Make a pigeonhole for every possible hair count, from zero for the completely bald up to one million, giving just over a million holes. Then place each Sydneysider in the hole matching their exact number of hairs. There are far more people than holes, so at least two residents must have precisely the same number of hairs on their heads. In fact, the principle guarantees that some hair count is shared by at least five people. Nobody could ever find them by counting, yet we know for certain that they exist.

sections.key: Spread n items across k boxes and some box must hold at least n divided by k, rounded up.
sections.b: The principle has a stronger version, which tells you not just that some box is shared but how crowded it must be. Suppose 100 people attend a conference and are each born on one of the seven days of the week. Divide 100 by 7 and you get about 14.3, so at least one weekday must be the birthday of 15 or more of them. The rule is to divide the number of items by the number of boxes and round up. With 10 pigeons and 3 holes, some hole has at least 4. This version is how you can prove that among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month, and among any 25, at least three were.

sections.key: At any gathering, at least two people have shaken the same number of hands.
sections.b: Here is a lovely puzzle. At a party, people shake hands with some of the other guests but never with themselves or twice with the same person. Prove that two guests have shaken exactly the same number of hands. Say there are 20 guests. Each person's count could be anything from 0 to 19, which looks like 20 possible values for 20 people, just enough to all be different. But look closer. If someone shook nobody's hand, then nobody can have shaken all 19 other hands. So the values 0 and 19 cannot both appear. That leaves only 19 usable pigeonholes for 20 guests, and two people must share a count. The trick is a common one: first show there are fewer real options than there appear to be.

sections.h: Why no app can shrink every file
sections.key: Counting alone proves that perfect lossless compression of every possible file is impossible.
sections.b: The pigeonhole principle sets hard limits in computing. Compression software such as zip shrinks files and later restores them exactly. Could a cleverer program shrink every possible file, even by a single bit? Counting says no. There are 1,024 different files that are exactly 10 bits long, but only 1,023 different files that are shorter, including the empty one. If every 10-bit file were squeezed into something shorter, two of them would have to share the same compressed version, and the program could not know which original to restore. So any lossless method that shrinks some files must leave others the same size or make them bigger. Real compression works because everyday files, like text and photos, are full of patterns, while truly random data cannot be squeezed.

sections.key: When something feels like it must happen, ask whether you can count the boxes.
sections.b: The principle teaches a habit of mind. Many claims that sound mysterious become clear once you ask how many possibilities there are and how many things must fit into them. It explains why hash functions, which turn any amount of data into a short fingerprint, must sometimes give two different inputs the same fingerprint, so security depends on making such collisions extraordinarily hard to find rather than impossible. It explains why a short PIN can only have so many combinations. It also guards against faulty reasoning, because the principle guarantees only that a match exists, not where it is or how many there are. Professional mathematicians use far more sophisticated versions in number theory and combinatorics, but each one starts with the same simple picture of crowded pigeonholes.

quiz.q: You have only black and grey socks in a dark drawer. How many must you take to be sure of a matching pair?
o: Two
Three
Four
Five
quiz.e: With only two colours, two socks could differ, but a third must match one of them.

quiz.q: Why must two Sydney residents have exactly the same number of hairs?
o: Hair counts are inherited
There are more residents than possible hair counts
Most people have exactly 100,000 hairs
Hairdressers have counted them
quiz.e: With just over a million possible hair counts and more than five million people, some count must be shared.

quiz.q: If 10 pigeons go into 3 holes, what is the most you can say for certain?
o: Every hole has 3 pigeons
One hole is empty
Some hole has at least 4 pigeons
Some hole has exactly 5 pigeons
quiz.e: 10 divided by 3 is about 3.3, which rounds up to 4, so at least one hole must hold 4 or more.

quiz.q: In the handshake puzzle with 20 guests, why are there really only 19 possible counts?
o: Nobody can shake 19 hands
Counts of 0 and 19 cannot both occur
Everyone shakes at least one hand
Handshakes always come in pairs of 10
quiz.e: If someone shook nobody's hand, nobody can have shaken everyone's, so only 19 values are available for 20 people.

quiz.q: What does the pigeonhole principle prove about compression?
o: All files can be shrunk by half
No method can shrink every possible file without loss
Photos cannot be compressed
Compression always loses data
quiz.e: There are fewer shorter files than longer ones, so some files would have to share a compressed form.

LESSONS.title: The clever maths hiding in A4 paper
LESSONS.hook: Fold an A4 sheet in half and you get a smaller sheet of exactly the same shape. That is no accident: it rests on a single number, the square root of 2.

sections.key: Most rectangles change shape when you cut them in half.
sections.b: Take an ordinary rectangle and cut it in half across its long side. Usually the two halves have a different shape from the original. A square cut in half becomes two long, thin strips. A sheet twice as long as it is wide becomes two squares. This is a nuisance for printers, publishers and office workers, because a page designed for one size will not shrink neatly onto the next size down. Margins end up lopsided and enlarged copies leave gaps. The question is whether there is a rectangle that keeps its exact proportions every time you halve it. There is, and only one shape works. Most of the world now uses it every day without giving it a second thought, every time someone loads a printer or slips a letter into an envelope.

sections.key: A sheet whose long side is about 1.414 times its short side keeps its shape when halved.
sections.b: Call the short side 1 and the long side r. When you fold the sheet in half, the old short side becomes the new long side, and the new short side is r divided by 2. For the shape to stay the same, the ratio of long to short must be unchanged, so r divided by 1 must equal 1 divided by r over 2. Rearranged, that means r squared equals 2, so r is the square root of 2, about 1.414. Check it with A4, which measures 210 by 297 millimetres. Divide 297 by 210 and you get 1.414, almost exactly the square root of 2. Fold it in half and you get A5, 148 by 210 millimetres, with the very same proportions.

sections.key: A0 has an area of one square metre, and every A size is half the one before.
sections.b: The A series begins with A0, a sheet with an area of one square metre and sides in the ratio of the square root of 2. Its measurements are 841 by 1,189 millimetres, which multiply to 999,949 square millimetres, as close to one square metre as whole millimetres allow. Halve A0 and you get A1. Halve that for A2, then A3, then A4, which is one sixteenth of a square metre. This gives a neat bonus for anyone posting letters. Paper weight is sold in grams per square metre, so a standard 80 gram office sheet of A4 weighs one sixteenth of 80 grams, which is exactly 5 grams. Count the pages in an envelope and you can estimate its weight before you reach the post office.

sections.h: A German idea, two centuries in the making
sections.key: The idea was suggested in the 1780s, used in revolutionary France and standardised in Germany in 1922.
sections.b: In 1786 the German scientist and writer Georg Christoph Lichtenberg noted in a letter that a sheet with sides in the ratio of the square root of 2 could be halved again and again without changing shape. A few years later, revolutionary France, busy rationalising everything from weights to calendars, used the same ratio for some official paper sizes in a 1798 law on stamp duty. The idea then faded until the German engineer Walter Porstmann built a full system around it, starting from one square metre. Germany adopted his standard, DIN 476, in 1922. Other countries followed over the decades, and in 1975 it became the international standard ISO 216. Australia uses it, as do most nations, but the United States and Canada mostly stick with older inch-based sizes such as Letter.

sections.key: The 141% and 71% buttons on a copier are the square root of 2 and its reciprocal.
sections.b: Look at the zoom buttons on an office photocopier and you may see two strange-looking settings: 141% and 71%. They are the square root of 2 in disguise. To enlarge an A4 page so it fills an A3 sheet, the area must double, so each side must grow by a factor of the square root of 2, which is about 1.414, or 141%. To shrink A4 down to A5, each side shrinks by 1 divided by the square root of 2, about 0.707, or 71%. Because every sheet in the series has the same shape, the copy fits perfectly with no awkward white strip down one side. Two A4 pages placed side by side also shrink exactly onto one A4 sheet, which is how booklets and handouts are made.

sections.key: B and C sizes fill the gaps, and C envelopes are designed to hold A sheets.
sections.b: The system has two companion series. B sizes sit between A sizes. B4, for example, measures 250 by 353 millimetres, larger than A4 but smaller than A3, and each side is the geometric mean of its neighbours, found by multiplying them and taking the square root. B sizes are used for posters, passports and some books. The C series, mostly used for envelopes, sits between the A and B sizes, so a C envelope is just a little larger than the matching A sheet. A C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet flat, while a C5 envelope takes A4 folded once in half. The popular DL envelope, 110 by 220 millimetres, is made for an A4 sheet folded into thirds. A whole family of sizes fits together because of one number.

sections.key: The golden ratio is famous, but the square root of 2 is the ratio that actually runs the office.
sections.b: People often assume that elegant rectangles must follow the golden ratio, about 1.618, which is said to appear in art and architecture, though many of those claims are exaggerated. The golden rectangle has its own neat trick: cut a square off one end and the remaining piece is another golden rectangle. That is beautiful mathematics, but it is not what you need for paper. When you fold a sheet, you halve it rather than trim off a square, and only the square root of 2 survives halving. Compare US Letter, 8.5 by 11 inches, with a ratio of about 1.29. Fold it in half and the shape changes noticeably. A4 is a quiet reminder that a simple equation, solved properly, can make countless everyday jobs a little easier.

quiz.q: What is the ratio of the long side to the short side of A4 paper?
o: About 1.29
About 1.414
About 1.618
Exactly 1.5
quiz.e: 297 divided by 210 is about 1.414, the square root of 2, the only ratio that survives halving.

quiz.q: Why does a standard 80 gram sheet of A4 weigh about 5 grams?
o: A4 is one sixteenth of a square metre
A4 is one tenth of a square metre
Paper is sold by the sheet
Each A size is one third of the last
quiz.e: A0 is one square metre and A4 is A0 halved four times, so it weighs one sixteenth of 80 grams.

quiz.q: Who built the full A-series system that Germany adopted in 1922?
o: Isaac Newton
Walter Porstmann
Leonhard Euler
Carl Gauss
quiz.e: Walter Porstmann's DIN 476 standard later became the international standard ISO 216.

quiz.q: Why does a photocopier use 141% to enlarge A4 onto A3?
o: A3 is 41% longer than A4 on one side only
Doubling the area means multiplying each side by the square root of 2
It is a marketing convention
A3 is 141% heavier
quiz.e: A3 has twice the area of A4, so each side grows by about 1.414, which is 141%.

quiz.q: Which envelope holds an A4 sheet without folding?
o: C5
DL
C4
B6
quiz.e: C sizes are slightly larger than the matching A size, so C4 holds A4 flat, while C5 takes A4 folded once.

LESSONS.title: Every shuffle is history: the astonishing size of 52!
LESSONS.hook: Shuffle a pack of cards properly and you have almost certainly created an order that no one in history has ever held. The maths behind that claim is simple and staggering.

sections.key: The number of ways to arrange things is found by multiplying down from the total.
sections.b: How many ways can you arrange three books on a shelf? Any of the three can go first, either of the remaining two can go second, and the last one fills the final spot. That is 3 × 2 × 1, which makes 6 arrangements. With four books it is 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, or 24. This multiplying-down pattern is called a factorial and is written with an exclamation mark, so 4! means 24. The notation was introduced by the French mathematician Christian Kramp in 1808, and it suits the numbers, because factorials grow at an exclamation-worthy pace. Ten books can be arranged in 3,628,800 different ways. A shelf of twenty books has more than two quintillion possible orders.

sections.key: A standard deck can be ordered in about 8 × 10 to the power of 67 ways.
sections.b: Now apply the idea to a pack of 52 playing cards. The top card can be any of 52, the next any of the remaining 51, and so on down to the last card. Multiply them all together and you get 52!, a number roughly 8 followed by 67 zeros. Written out, it is 68 digits long, beginning 8065. That number is hard to imagine, so try this. Suppose every one of the eight billion people alive today had been shuffling a deck once every second since the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago. Together they would have produced roughly 3.5 × 10 to the power of 27 shuffled decks. That sounds like a lot, but it is less than a billionth of a billionth of a billionth of all possible orders.

sections.key: A properly shuffled deck is very likely in an order never seen before.
sections.b: Because the number of possible orders dwarfs the number of shuffles that have ever taken place, a well-shuffled deck is almost certainly unique in history. The odds that it matches any earlier shuffle, anywhere, are vanishingly small. There is an important catch hidden in the word ‘well’. A brand-new pack comes out of the box in a set order, and a couple of lazy shuffles leave much of that order intact. Decks shuffled badly are far more likely to repeat known patterns. Casinos take shuffling seriously for exactly this reason. The claim of uniqueness is about thoroughly randomised decks, where every one of those 52! orders is equally likely, not about a pack someone has given one quick riffle.

sections.key: Mathematicians showed that about seven riffle shuffles are needed to mix a deck well.
sections.b: So how many shuffles does it take? In 1992 the mathematicians Dave Bayer and Persi Diaconis published a famous analysis of the riffle shuffle, where you split the deck in two and let the halves fall together. They showed that the deck stays noticeably ordered for the first few shuffles, then becomes well mixed quite suddenly, at around seven shuffles. Beyond that, extra shuffles add little. Diaconis is an unusual figure in maths. He left home as a teenager to travel as a magician and only later became a celebrated professor of statistics. Other shuffling styles are much weaker. The overhand shuffle, where small clumps of cards are slid from one hand to the other, mixes so slowly that one analysis suggested it would take thousands of shuffles to randomise a deck.

sections.key: Eight perfect riffle shuffles return a deck to exactly its starting order.
sections.b: A perfect shuffle is not random at all. Skilled magicians can cut a deck into two exact halves of 26 and interleave them perfectly, one card from each side in turn. In the version called the out-shuffle, the top card stays on top. Do this once and the deck looks mixed. Keep going, and something surprising happens. After exactly eight perfect out-shuffles, a 52-card deck returns to its original order. Magicians use the predictability of perfect shuffles to make a pack look thoroughly mixed while secretly knowing where every card is. The lesson for everyone else is that mixing depends on randomness. A shuffle that is too precise is really just a permutation, a fixed rearrangement, and doing a fixed rearrangement enough times can bring you back to where you began.

sections.key: When order does not matter, you divide out the repeats, which gives combinations.
sections.b: Sometimes order does not matter. A five-card poker hand is the same hand whatever order you pick the cards up in. To count hands, start with 52 × 51 × 50 × 49 × 48 ordered ways to deal five cards, then divide by 5!, the 120 ways of rearranging the same five cards. That gives 2,598,960 possible poker hands. The same idea measures lotteries. A game where you choose 6 numbers from 45 has 8,145,060 possible combinations, so a single entry has about a one in eight million chance of the top prize. Counting like this is called combinatorics. It sounds abstract, but it tells you plainly how long the odds are, and why it is unwise to treat a lottery ticket as a plan rather than a bit of entertainment.

sections.key: Huge numbers of combinations are what make good passwords and encryption keys hard to guess.
sections.b: The explosive growth of possibilities is not just a party fact; it protects you every day. A four-digit PIN has only 10,000 possibilities, which is why banks lock a card after a few wrong guesses. A long password made of several random words has vastly more, because each extra word multiplies the total. Modern encryption relies on keys chosen from so many possibilities that trying them all would take longer than the age of the universe, even with enormous computing power. The same principle that makes a shuffled deck unique makes a properly chosen key unguessable. There is a practical takeaway: when you want something to be hard to guess, length and genuine randomness matter far more than clever substitutions, like swapping the letter o for a zero.

quiz.q: What does 4! equal?
quiz.e: 4! means 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, which is 24.

quiz.q: Roughly how many ways can a 52-card deck be ordered?
o: About 52 million
About 8 × 10 to the power of 67
About 2.6 million
About 10 to the power of 12
quiz.e: 52! is about 8 followed by 67 zeros, a 68-digit number.

quiz.q: According to Bayer and Diaconis, about how many riffle shuffles mix a deck well?
o: Three
Seven
Twenty
Fifty-two
quiz.e: The deck stays noticeably ordered for a few shuffles, then becomes well mixed at around seven.

quiz.q: What happens after eight perfect out-shuffles of a 52-card deck?
o: It is fully random
It is in reverse order
It returns to its original order
The top card moves to the bottom
quiz.e: A perfect shuffle is a fixed rearrangement, and eight of them bring a 52-card deck back to the start.

quiz.q: Why do you divide by 5! when counting poker hands?
o: To remove suits
Because the order of the five cards does not matter
To allow for jokers
Because only five players can play
quiz.e: The same five cards can be picked up in 120 orders, so dividing by 5! counts each hand once.

LESSONS.title: The averaging trap: when rates don't add up
LESSONS.hook: Drive somewhere at 60 km/h and back at 40, and your average speed is not 50. Averages of rates fool almost everyone, and the mistake shows up in fuel bills, class sizes and bus stops.

sections.key: Averaging two speeds over equal distances does not give the average speed.
sections.b: You drive 60 kilometres to visit a friend at a steady 60 km/h, then crawl home through roadworks at 40 km/h. What was your average speed? Nearly everyone says 50 km/h, but that is wrong. The trip there took one hour. The trip home took an hour and a half, because 60 kilometres at 40 km/h is 1.5 hours. You covered 120 kilometres in 2.5 hours, which is 48 km/h. The slow leg drags the average down more than the fast leg lifts it, because you spend longer travelling slowly. Average speed is always total distance divided by total time. The moment you average the speeds themselves, you quietly give the fast leg and the slow leg equal weight, even though you spent far more time on the slow one.

sections.key: Some average-speed targets cannot be reached no matter how fast you go.
sections.b: This trap leads to a famous brain teaser. A cyclist rides one kilometre up a steep hill at 30 km/h and wants to average 60 km/h over the full two-kilometre trip, up and back down. How fast must she go downhill? Intuition suggests 90 km/h, to balance out the 30. But to average 60 km/h over two kilometres, the whole trip must take two minutes. The climb alone, one kilometre at 30 km/h, has already used up those two minutes. She would need to come down in no time at all, which means travelling infinitely fast. The target is impossible. Puzzles like this show why it pays to translate rates back into the real quantities behind them, such as distances and times, before doing any averaging at all.

sections.key: For equal distances at different speeds, the right average is called the harmonic mean.
sections.b: There is a proper tool for this job. For two speeds over equal distances, the correct average is the harmonic mean: divide 2 by the sum of the reciprocals of the speeds. For 60 and 40 km/h, the reciprocals are 1/60 and 1/40, which add to 1/24. Two divided by 1/24 is 48, matching the earlier answer. The harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the ordinary average, and it leans towards the smaller number. It appears whenever you average rates over a fixed amount of something, such as kilometres per hour over fixed distances or price per item over a fixed budget. A simpler rule of thumb is enough for most people: if in doubt, add up the totals and divide, rather than averaging the rates.

sections.key: Litres per 100 kilometres shows real savings far more honestly than kilometres per litre.
sections.b: In 2008 the researchers Richard Larrick and Jack Soll published a study in the journal Science about what they called the ‘MPG illusion’. Americans measure fuel economy in miles per gallon, and people assume that a bigger improvement in that number saves more fuel. Australia mostly uses litres per 100 kilometres, which avoids the trap. Compare two upgrades. Replacing a thirsty car that uses 20 litres per 100 kilometres with one using 15 saves 5 litres every 100 kilometres. Replacing an efficient car that uses 6 litres with one using 4 saves only 2 litres. In kilometres per litre, the first upgrade goes from 5 to about 6.7, while the second leaps from about 16.7 to 25. The second looks far more impressive, yet the first saves more than twice as much fuel.

sections.key: The average class size and the class size the average student experiences are different numbers.
sections.b: Imagine a small college with just two classes, one of 10 students and one of 90. The college can truthfully report an average class size of 50. Now ask each student how big their class is. The 10 students in the small class answer 10, but the 90 in the large class answer 90. Average those 100 answers and you get 82. Both numbers are correct, but they measure different things. Most students are in the crowded class, so the typical student experience is far more cramped than the official average. The same effect means that, on average, people's friends have more friends than they do, a result called the friendship paradox. Popular people appear in many friend lists, so they are overrepresented when you look at anyone's friends.

sections.key: If you arrive at random, you are more likely to land in a long gap between buses.
sections.b: Buses on your route come on average every 10 minutes, so you might expect to wait about 5 minutes. But buses often bunch up. Suppose the gaps alternate between 5 minutes and 15 minutes. That still averages 10, but if you arrive at a random moment, you are three times as likely to land in a 15-minute gap as a 5-minute one, simply because it lasts three times as long. Your expected wait works out to 6.25 minutes, longer than the 5 minutes you would wait if the buses were perfectly regular. Statisticians call this the inspection paradox. Whenever you sample something by stumbling into it, whether a gap between buses, a queue or a class, longer and bigger things are more likely to be the ones you find.

sections.key: Before averaging anything, ask what is being counted and whose point of view it is.
sections.b: These traps share a cause: an average is only meaningful if you know what it is an average of. A few questions protect you. First, are you averaging rates? If so, go back to the totals, such as distance and time, or fuel and kilometres, and divide those instead. Second, who is doing the counting? An average across classes, buses or businesses can differ wildly from the average experienced by the people inside them. Third, would a different unit tell a different story? Kilometres per litre and litres per 100 kilometres carry identical information, but one makes savings easy to see. None of this requires advanced maths, just the patience to ask what lies behind the number before you trust it to describe your own life.

quiz.q: You drive 60 km at 60 km/h and return the same 60 km at 40 km/h. What is your average speed?
o: 50 km/h
48 km/h
52 km/h
45 km/h
quiz.e: 120 km in 2.5 hours is 48 km/h, because you spend more time on the slow leg.

quiz.q: A cyclist climbs 1 km at 30 km/h. Why can she never average 60 km/h over the 2 km round trip?
o: The hill is too steep
The climb alone uses up all the time allowed
Bicycles have a speed limit
Downhill speed cannot exceed 90 km/h
quiz.e: Averaging 60 km/h over 2 km allows two minutes, and the climb has already taken two minutes.

quiz.q: Which car swap saves more fuel over 100 km?
o: From 6 to 4 litres per 100 km
From 20 to 15 litres per 100 km
Both save the same
It depends on the price of petrol
quiz.e: Going from 20 to 15 saves 5 litres per 100 km, compared with only 2 litres for the other swap.

quiz.q: A college has one class of 10 and one of 90. What average class size do its students experience?
quiz.e: 10 students report 10 and 90 report 90, which averages to 82 across all 100 students.

quiz.q: Why do randomly arriving passengers tend to wait longer when buses bunch up?
o: Drivers slow down
They are more likely to arrive during a long gap
Timetables are wrong
Buses skip stops
quiz.e: Long gaps take up more of the clock, so a random arrival is more likely to fall in one.

LESSONS.title: The doomsday rule: find the weekday of any date in your head
LESSONS.hook: A mathematician named John Conway could tell you the day of the week for any date in history in a couple of seconds. His method is easy to learn, and it starts with 4 April.

sections.h: A party trick with a grim name
sections.key: Every year, a set of easy-to-remember dates all fall on the same day of the week.
sections.b: In the early 1970s the British mathematician John Horton Conway, famous for inventing the Game of Life, devised a way to work out the weekday of any date mentally. He built on an earlier method by Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, who was also a mathematician. Conway's trick rests on a striking fact. In any given year, a whole collection of memorable dates always land on the same weekday. Conway called that weekday the year's ‘doomsday’. The name sounds ominous, but it means nothing sinister, just the anchor day for that year. Once you know a year's doomsday and remember the anchor dates, finding the weekday of any other date in that year takes only a little counting forwards or backwards.

sections.key: 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10 and 12/12 always share a weekday, along with a few others.
sections.b: Here are the dates that always fall on the doomsday. First the even months, which are easy: 4 April, 6 June, 8 August, 10 October and 12 December, or 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10 and 12/12. For the odd months, a popular American mnemonic is ‘I work 9 to 5 at 7-Eleven’. That gives 9 May and 5 September, plus 11 July and 7 November. Australians writing dates day first can simply remember that the pairs swap. The last day of February is always a doomsday, as is 14 March, celebrated as Pi Day in the United States. For January, use 3 January in ordinary years and 4 January in leap years. In 2026, every one of these dates is a Saturday.

sections.key: Find the nearest anchor date, then step by weeks and count the remaining days.
sections.b: Now put the anchors to work. In 2026 the doomsday is Saturday. What day is Christmas? The nearest anchor is 12 December, a Saturday. Add a week and 19 December is also Saturday, then 26 December is too. Christmas, the day before, is a Friday. What about Australia Day, 26 January 2026? In an ordinary year, 3 January is a doomsday, so it is Saturday. Then 10, 17, 24 and 31 January are Saturdays, so 26 January is a Monday. With a little practice you jump to the nearest anchor and count only a few days. Because the anchors are spread through the year, no date is ever more than a couple of weeks from one, so even awkward dates take just a moment.

sections.key: Each year the doomsday moves forward one day, or two after a leap day.
sections.b: Doomsdays shift in a predictable way. A normal year has 365 days, which is 52 weeks and one day, so the doomsday moves forward by one weekday. A leap year has an extra day, so the jump after 29 February is two. In 2026 the doomsday is Saturday. In 2027 it moves to Sunday. Then 2028 is a leap year, so its doomsday jumps two places to Tuesday, because 29 February 2028 falls before 4 April and pushes everything along. To handle any year in a century, start from a known anchor. For the 1900s it is Wednesday and for the 2000s it is Tuesday. Add the number of years past the century, plus the number of leap years in that stretch, and count forward that many weekdays, ignoring complete weeks.

sections.h: A worked example: the Moon landing
sections.key: Working out a date from 1969 takes three quick steps.
sections.b: Let us test the method on a famous date. Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969, by American time. The anchor for the 1900s is Wednesday. The year is 69 years into the century, and in that time there were 17 leap years, since 69 divided by 4 is 17 with some left over. Add them: 69 plus 17 makes 86. Remove complete weeks: 86 divided by 7 is 12 weeks with 2 left over. Count two days on from Wednesday and the doomsday for 1969 is Friday. Now the anchor for July is 11 July, so that was a Friday, and so was 18 July. That makes 20 July a Sunday. In eastern Australia, the clocks were well into the next day, so viewers here watched on Monday 21 July.

sections.key: The calendar's rules make it repeat exactly every 400 years.
sections.b: The doomsday method works because the calendar follows fixed rules. Most countries use the Gregorian calendar, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 and adopted gradually around the world. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which are only leap years if divisible by 400. So 1900 was not a leap year but 2000 was. These rules create a cycle of 400 years containing 146,097 days, which happens to be exactly 20,871 weeks. That means the calendar repeats perfectly every 400 years, with every date on the same weekday as four centuries earlier. A quirky consequence is that, across that cycle, the 13th of the month falls on a Friday slightly more often than on any other day of the week.

sections.key: Speed comes from repetition, and the payoff is a deeper feel for how the calendar works.
sections.b: Conway became remarkably fast at the method and reportedly had his computer quiz him with random dates when he logged in, timing his answers. He died in April 2020, during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, but the method remains popular with puzzle fans and memory competitors. To learn it, start small. Learn the current year's doomsday and the anchor dates, then check yourself against a calendar using birthdays and holidays. Once that feels easy, add the year-to-year shift, and later the century anchors. Beyond the party trick, the method teaches a useful idea from mathematics called modular arithmetic, which is the arithmetic of remainders. Weekdays cycle every seven, just as hours on a clock cycle every twelve, and many real-world patterns run in such repeating loops.

quiz.q: Which of these dates always falls on the same weekday as 4 April in the same year?
o: 1 May
6 June
25 December
1 January
quiz.e: 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10 and 12/12 always share the year's doomsday.

quiz.q: If 12 December 2026 is a Saturday, what day is 25 December 2026?
o: Thursday
Friday
Saturday
Sunday
quiz.e: 19 and 26 December are also Saturdays, so 25 December is the day before, a Friday.

quiz.q: The doomsday for 2027 is Sunday. Why is the doomsday for 2028 Tuesday rather than Monday?
o: 2028 is a leap year
2027 is a leap year
Doomsdays always jump two days
The calendar resets every decade
quiz.e: 29 February 2028 adds an extra day before the anchor dates, so the doomsday jumps two places.

quiz.q: Which of these years was not a leap year?
quiz.e: Century years are leap years only if divisible by 400, so 1900 was not but 2000 was.

quiz.q: What branch of maths does the doomsday rule rely on?
o: Calculus
Modular arithmetic, the arithmetic of remainders
Geometry
Statistics
quiz.e: Weekdays repeat every seven days, so the method works with remainders after dividing by 7.

LESSONS.title: Logarithms: the invention that turned multiplying into adding
LESSONS.hook: In 1614 a Scottish nobleman published tables that saved astronomers years of drudgery. For the next 350 years, his idea sat in the pocket of every engineer as the slide rule.

sections.key: Before calculators, multiplying large numbers by hand was slow and full of errors.
sections.b: Picture an astronomer around 1600, working out the orbit of a planet. Each step requires multiplying and dividing long numbers, often with seven or more digits, and a single slip ruins weeks of work. Navigators plotting positions at sea and surveyors mapping land faced the same burden. Adding two large numbers is quick and fairly safe, but multiplying them by hand means many rows of partial products and a lot of carrying. Mathematicians had long wondered whether there was a way to turn hard multiplication into easy addition. A clue came from patterns in powers. Since 2 × 2 × 2 is 8 and 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 is 16, multiplying 8 by 16 means adding the counts of twos, 3 plus 4, to get 7 twos, which is 128.

sections.key: Napier published the first tables of logarithms in 1614 after about twenty years of work.
sections.b: John Napier was a Scottish landowner, the Laird of Merchiston near Edinburgh, who also wrote a fiercely argued book on the biblical Book of Revelation. Mathematics was his passion, and he spent around two decades developing what he called logarithms, a word he built from Greek roots meaning ratio and number. In 1614 he published them in a Latin book usually known by its short title, the Descriptio, short for a description of the wonderful rule of logarithms. The book contained tables pairing numbers with their logarithms. To multiply two numbers, you looked up their logarithms, added them, and looked up which number had that total as its logarithm. Napier's version was not quite the logarithm used today, but the essential trick, turning multiplication into addition, was there.

sections.key: A logarithm answers the question: what power do I raise the base to, to get this number?
sections.b: The modern idea is easiest with base 10. The logarithm of 100 is 2, because 10 squared is 100. The logarithm of 1,000 is 3. In-between numbers have in-between logarithms. The logarithm of 2 is about 0.301, and the logarithm of 8 is about 0.903. Now watch the magic. Add those two logarithms and you get about 1.204. Look up which number has a logarithm of 1.204 and the answer is 16, which is exactly 2 × 8. Multiplication has become addition, and division becomes subtraction. Raising a number to a power becomes simple multiplication, and finding a square root becomes halving. With a good book of tables, a calculation that once took an hour could be done in minutes, with far less room for mistakes.

sections.key: Henry Briggs travelled to Scotland to meet Napier and went on to produce practical base 10 tables.
sections.b: Napier's book thrilled the English mathematician Henry Briggs, a professor in London, who travelled to Scotland in 1615 to meet him. The two agreed that logarithms would be far more convenient if they were based on 10, so that the logarithm of 10 was 1 and of 100 was 2. Napier died in 1617, and Briggs carried out the enormous labour of calculating the new tables by hand, publishing them in stages, including a large volume in 1624 covering numbers up to 20,000 and from 90,000 to 100,000. Others filled the gap soon after. These common logarithms became a standard tool. Students were still using printed books of log tables in classrooms, including in Australia, until electronic calculators became cheap and common in the 1970s.

sections.key: Logarithms arrived just in time to help Johannes Kepler finish his great planetary tables.
sections.b: One of the first scientists to seize on the new tool was the German astronomer Johannes Kepler. He had already worked out that planets move in ellipses, but turning that insight into tables predicting planetary positions years ahead required staggering amounts of arithmetic. Kepler studied Napier's work, wrote his own account of how logarithms worked and used them in completing the Rudolphine Tables, published in 1627. Those tables predicted planetary positions far more accurately than anything before them, and they helped persuade astronomers that Kepler's ideas, and the Sun-centred picture of the solar system, were correct. Kepler even dedicated a book to Napier, not knowing at first that Napier had died. Logarithms did not create the scientific revolution, but they made its endless calculations bearable.

sections.key: Placing two logarithmic scales side by side turned multiplication into sliding a ruler.
sections.b: Soon after Napier, the English mathematician Edmund Gunter drew a ruler marked with a logarithmic scale, so that distances along it represented logarithms. Using dividers, users could add lengths and so multiply numbers. In the 1620s and 1630s, the clergyman William Oughtred had the clever idea of sliding two such scales against each other, which did the adding automatically. This was the slide rule. Over the following centuries it became the engineer's constant companion. Slide rules helped design bridges, ships, aircraft and the rockets of the space age, and engineers on NASA's Apollo program used them. A good slide rule gave answers to about three significant figures, which is accurate enough for most engineering. Pocket electronic calculators replaced them almost overnight in the 1970s, ending three and a half centuries of service.

sections.key: Logarithms still describe how we measure sound, earthquakes, acidity and growth.
sections.b: Calculators made log tables obsolete, but logarithms themselves are everywhere. They are the natural way to handle quantities that span huge ranges or grow by multiplying. The decibel scale for sound is logarithmic, so every 10 decibels means ten times the sound intensity. Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic too, as is the pH scale for acidity, where each step is a tenfold change. In finance and biology, logarithms help describe compound growth and halving. Your own senses seem to work in a roughly logarithmic way, noticing proportional changes rather than absolute ones, so an extra candle brightens a dark room far more than a sunny one. The idea Napier spent twenty years refining still shapes how scientists see the world, long after its original purpose disappeared.

quiz.q: Using powers of 2, why does 8 × 16 equal 128?
o: 8 plus 16 is 24
3 twos plus 4 twos makes 7 twos, and 2 to the power of 7 is 128
Both numbers are even
16 divided by 8 is 2
quiz.e: 8 is 2 to the power of 3 and 16 is 2 to the power of 4, so adding the powers gives 2 to the power of 7.

quiz.q: In what year did John Napier publish his tables of logarithms?
quiz.e: Napier published his Descriptio in 1614 after about twenty years of work.

quiz.q: If the logarithm of 2 is about 0.301 and the logarithm of 8 is about 0.903, what number has a logarithm of about 1.204?
quiz.e: Adding logarithms multiplies the numbers, so the answer is 2 × 8, which is 16.

quiz.q: What change did Henry Briggs and Napier agree on?
o: Using base 10 for logarithms
Writing tables in English
Using logarithms for addition only
Replacing tables with machines
quiz.e: Base 10 logarithms made the logarithm of 10 equal 1, which was far more convenient for calculation.

quiz.q: How does a slide rule multiply numbers?
o: By counting beads
By sliding two logarithmic scales so their lengths add
By using gears
By storing answers in a table
quiz.e: Lengths along the scales represent logarithms, and adding them multiplies the numbers.

LESSONS.title: Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge
LESSONS.hook: A largely self-taught clerk in Madras posted pages of strange formulas to a famous English mathematician. They were so astonishing that they changed both men's lives.

sections.h: A boy and a borrowed book
sections.key: Ramanujan taught himself advanced mathematics, largely from a single dense book of results.
sections.b: Srinivasa Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 in Erode, in southern India, and grew up in the town of Kumbakonam. As a teenager he came across a book by George Shoobridge Carr, a summary of several thousand mathematical results, mostly given without proofs. Ramanujan worked through it on his own, filling notebooks with his own discoveries. His obsession had a cost. He won a scholarship to college but neglected his other subjects, failed his exams and lost the scholarship. For several years he lived in poverty, working on mathematics with little guidance. Eventually, with the help of supporters who recognised his talent, he found a job as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust in 1912, which gave him a small wage and time to keep working.

sections.key: In 1913 Ramanujan wrote to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, enclosing pages of extraordinary results.
sections.b: In January 1913 Ramanujan wrote to Godfrey Harold Hardy, one of the leading mathematicians in England, at Trinity College, Cambridge. He enclosed pages packed with formulas, many of them about infinite series and fractions, offered without proof. Hardy received many letters from cranks, and at first he was tempted to dismiss it. But as he and his colleague John Littlewood studied the pages, they realised they were looking at something remarkable. Some results were already known, a few were wrong, but many were new and astonishing. Hardy later wrote that some of the formulas must be true, because if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them. He set about bringing Ramanujan to Cambridge, though travelling overseas raised difficult questions for a devout Brahmin.

sections.key: Ramanujan arrived in 1914 and produced brilliant work, but struggled with cold, food and illness.
sections.b: Ramanujan sailed for England in 1914, arriving shortly before the outbreak of the First World War. He and Hardy formed one of the great partnerships in mathematical history, although they were very different people. Hardy insisted on rigorous proofs, while Ramanujan seemed to arrive at results by intuition, sometimes saying they came to him from the goddess Namagiri, his family deity. Hardy had to teach him the discipline of proof without crushing his originality. Life in wartime Cambridge was hard for him. He was a strict vegetarian, wartime food was scarce, the climate was cold and he was far from his family. Even so, his output was extraordinary, and in 1918 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, one of the first Indians to receive that honour.

sections.key: Ramanujan saw at once that 1729 is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two ways.
sections.b: The most famous story about Ramanujan comes from Hardy himself. Visiting his friend in hospital, Hardy mentioned that he had arrived in taxi number 1729, which he thought a rather dull number. Ramanujan replied that, on the contrary, it was very interesting. It is the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways. Check it: 1 cubed is 1 and 12 cubed is 1,728, which add to 1,729. Also, 9 cubed is 729 and 10 cubed is 1,000, which add to 1,729 as well. Numbers with this property are now called taxicab numbers in honour of the story. It captures something real about Ramanujan, who seemed to know individual numbers the way other people know old friends.

sections.key: Ramanujan and Hardy found a formula to estimate how many ways a number can be split into sums.
sections.b: One of their greatest achievements concerns partitions, the number of ways to write a whole number as a sum of positive whole numbers. The number 4 has five partitions: 4, 3 plus 1, 2 plus 2, 2 plus 1 plus 1, and 1 plus 1 plus 1 plus 1. The counts explode as numbers grow. The number 200 has 3,972,999,029,388 partitions, a figure the mathematician Percy MacMahon worked out painstakingly by hand. Hardy and Ramanujan found a formula that estimated such values with astonishing accuracy, and it was later refined into an exact formula. Ramanujan also spotted hidden patterns. The partition counts of 4, 9, 14, 19, 24 and so on, every fifth number, are always divisible by 5. Those counts begin 5, 30, 135, 490 and 1,575.

sections.key: Ramanujan fell seriously ill, returned to India in 1919 and died the following year, aged 32.
sections.b: By 1917 Ramanujan was seriously ill, and he spent long periods in hospitals and nursing homes in England. At the time doctors suspected tuberculosis, but historians and doctors still debate the cause, and some later studies have suggested a liver infection called amoebiasis. In 1919 he returned to India, weak but still working, and produced new ideas about strange functions he called mock theta functions. He died on 26 April 1920, aged just 32. His notebooks have kept mathematicians busy ever since. In 1976 the American mathematician George Andrews found a bundle of his later papers, now called the ‘lost notebook’, in the library of Trinity College. Researchers spent decades proving the results it contained, and some of his ideas have since found uses in modern physics.

sections.key: His formulas still help calculate pi and inspire research, and India celebrates his birthday.
sections.b: Ramanujan's influence reaches well beyond pure mathematics. In 1914 he published remarkably fast formulas for calculating pi, and in the 1980s computer scientists used one of his series to compute pi to millions of digits. Since 2012 India has celebrated his birthday, 22 December, as National Mathematics Day. His life has been told in Robert Kanigel's 1991 biography The Man Who Knew Infinity, later made into a film. His story is also a warning about lost talent. He was discovered partly by luck, through supporters in India and a single letter that happened to reach the right reader. Hardy, looking back, rated Ramanujan's natural genius above anyone he had known, and wondered how much more he might have achieved with an earlier, fuller education.

quiz.q: Why did Ramanujan lose his college scholarship?
o: He refused to study maths
He neglected his other subjects and failed exams
He moved to England
He was accused of copying
quiz.e: His passion for mathematics led him to neglect other subjects, and he failed his exams.

quiz.q: What did Hardy say about some of Ramanujan's formulas?
o: They were obviously copied
They must be true because no one could have imagined them otherwise
They were all already known
They were too simple to matter
quiz.e: Hardy felt some results were so strange that nobody could have invented them unless they were true.

quiz.q: Which pair of cube sums shows why 1729 is special?
quiz.e: 1729 equals 1 cubed plus 12 cubed and also 9 cubed plus 10 cubed.

quiz.q: How many partitions does the number 4 have?
o: Four
Five
Six
Eight
quiz.e: 4, 3+1, 2+2, 2+1+1 and 1+1+1+1 make five partitions.

quiz.q: What was found in the library of Trinity College in 1976?
o: Ramanujan's original letter to Hardy
The ‘lost notebook’ of his later work
A portrait of Ramanujan
Napier's tables
quiz.e: George Andrews discovered Ramanujan's later papers, now called the lost notebook.

LESSONS.title: I cut, you choose: the maths of fair sharing
LESSONS.hook: Two children and one cake have a perfect solution that is thousands of years old. Add more children and mathematicians needed until 2016 to finish the job.

sections.key: One person divides and the other chooses, so neither has reason to complain.
sections.b: Two siblings, one slice of cake, and an argument brewing. The classic solution is simple: one cuts, the other chooses. The cutter has every reason to make the two pieces equal in their own eyes, because they will get whichever piece is left. The chooser can then take the piece they prefer. Neither can reasonably complain. The idea is ancient. In the Book of Genesis, Abraham proposes dividing the land between himself and his nephew Lot and lets Lot choose which part to take. Mathematicians admire divide-and-choose because it works even when people value things differently. One sibling may care about the icing and the other about the size. Nobody needs to agree on what fair means, and nobody needs to trust anybody else's judgement.

sections.key: A share can be proportional, meaning at least your fair fraction, or envy-free, meaning you prefer it to anyone else's.
sections.b: Mathematicians who study fair division separate two ideas. A division is proportional if each of n people receives what they consider at least one nth of the total. A division is envy-free if nobody would rather swap their share for someone else's. With two people, these are the same thing: if you think your piece is at least half, you cannot prefer the other half. With three or more, they come apart. You might think your piece is a fair third, yet feel that someone else got a better piece than you did. Envy-free is the stronger and more satisfying standard, because it removes resentment entirely. It is also much harder to achieve, which is why even the three-person cake puzzled mathematicians until around 1960.

sections.key: A simple method guarantees everyone at least a fair share, but it does not prevent envy.
sections.b: In the 1940s the Polish mathematician Hugo Steinhaus and his colleagues Stefan Banach and Bronisław Knaster studied how to share fairly among many people. One of their methods is called the last diminisher. The first person cuts a slice they consider a fair share. The slice is passed around, and anyone who thinks it is too big may trim it down. The last person to touch the slice takes it. Everyone else continues with the rest of the cake. Each person can always guarantee themselves at least their fair fraction by trimming whenever a slice looks too generous. The method is proportional, but it is not envy-free. Someone might still believe that a later slice, cut from the remainder, was bigger and better than their own.

sections.key: In about 1960, two mathematicians independently found an envy-free method for three people.
sections.b: Around 1960, John Selfridge and John Conway, the mathematician behind the Game of Life, each found an envy-free method for three people. Neither published at first, so it spread by word of mouth and is now called the Selfridge–Conway procedure. Roughly, it works like this. The first person cuts the cake into three pieces they consider equal. The second person may trim the biggest piece to tie with the second biggest, setting the trimmings aside. Then the third person picks first, the second picks next and must take the trimmed piece if it is still available, and the first person takes what remains. A clever second round shares out the trimmings in a similar way. At the end, nobody prefers anyone else's total. It takes at most five cuts.

sections.key: Envy-free methods for any number of people were found in 1995, and a bounded one only in 2016.
sections.b: For four or more people, the problem became notoriously difficult.
