In 1995 the political scientist Steven Brams and the mathematician Alan Taylor published an envy-free procedure for any number of people. But it had a strange flaw. For some cakes and some preferences, the number of cuts it needed had no upper limit, so you could not say in advance when it would finish. Finding a method guaranteed to end within a fixed number of steps remained an open problem until 2016, when the computer scientists Haris Aziz and Simon Mackenzie found one. Their method always finishes, but the number of steps it may need is so astronomically large that nobody would use it at a party. The result is a proof that fairness is possible, not a practical recipe.

sections.key: Fair division maths can set rents for rooms of different quality so that no housemate envies another.
sections.b: Fair division is not just about cake. Housemates sharing a place with a big sunny room, a small room and a room near the noisy road face the same problem in reverse: they must divide a rent bill as well as rooms. In 1999 the mathematician Francis Su published a method, building on work by others, that uses a result called Sperner's lemma to show that there is always a way to set the rents so that each person prefers their own room at its price. Online tools based on these ideas now help people split rent, share chores and divide shared costs. Chores are a reminder that fairness flips when the thing being shared is unpleasant. With dirty jobs, the chooser picks the smallest burden, and the cutter adjusts accordingly.

sections.h: Fairness at the bottom of the sea
sections.key: An international treaty uses a version of divide-and-choose to share deep-sea mining sites.
sections.b: The most surprising use of divide-and-choose may be in international law. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, agreed in 1982, a company or country wanting to mine minerals from the deep seabed beyond national borders proposes an area large enough for two mining operations, split into two parts of similar estimated value. The International Seabed Authority then chooses one of the parts to reserve for future mining by the Authority itself or by developing countries, and the applicant may work the other. The applicant has every reason to divide fairly, just like the child cutting the cake. It is a striking example of a nursery rule turned into a tool of diplomacy, and it shows that good mechanisms, rather than trust or goodwill, can make sharing work.

quiz.q: Why does ‘I cut, you choose’ encourage the cutter to be fair?
o: The cutter goes first
The cutter gets whichever piece is left
The chooser checks the sizes
A referee measures the pieces
quiz.e: Because the chooser picks first, the cutter's best strategy is to make both pieces equal in their own eyes.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a division to be envy-free?
o: Everyone gets exactly the same size
Nobody would rather have someone else's share
Everyone gets at least one nth
The pieces are all cut by one person
quiz.e: Envy-free means each person prefers, or is happy with, their own share over anyone else's.

quiz.q: What is a weakness of the last diminisher method?
o: It never finishes
It does not guarantee anyone a fair share
Someone may still envy a share given out later
It only works for two people
quiz.e: It is proportional, guaranteeing a fair fraction, but it does not prevent envy.

quiz.q: What did Aziz and Mackenzie achieve in 2016?
o: The first two-person method
A bounded envy-free method for any number of people
A method using only one cut
Proof that fair division is impossible
quiz.e: Their method always finishes within a fixed number of steps, though that number is astronomically large.

quiz.q: In deep-sea mining under the Law of the Sea, who chooses which part of the area is reserved?
o: The applicant
The International Seabed Authority
The nearest coastal country
A random lottery
quiz.e: The applicant divides the area in two and the Authority chooses one part to reserve.

LESSONS.title: The maths of queues: why lines get long so suddenly
LESSONS.hook: A café that is busy most of the time can run smoothly, then a few extra customers turn it into a long wait. Queueing theory explains why, and how to fix it.

sections.key: Queueing theory began in 1909 with Agner Erlang's work on telephone exchanges.
sections.b: In the early 1900s telephone companies faced an expensive puzzle. Every call needed a line through the exchange. Too few lines and callers heard a busy signal; too many and costly equipment sat idle. Agner Krarup Erlang, a Danish mathematician working for the Copenhagen Telephone Company, tackled the problem with probability. In 1909 he published a paper on telephone conversations and probability, followed by further work that let engineers calculate how many lines they needed for a given level of service. His work founded queueing theory, the mathematics of waiting. A unit of telephone traffic, the erlang, is still named after him. The same maths now runs call centres, hospital emergency departments, supermarket checkouts, traffic lights and the computer servers that handle internet requests.

sections.key: Queues form even when there is enough capacity on average, because arrivals bunch up.
sections.b: Suppose a coffee cart can serve 30 customers an hour and, on average, 24 arrive each hour. You might think there would never be a queue, since the barista has spare capacity. In reality, customers do not arrive at neat, evenly spaced intervals. Some minutes bring nobody; then three people turn up together. Service times vary too, because one person wants a flat white and the next orders five complicated drinks. When several customers arrive close together, a queue forms, and the time the barista spends idle during quiet moments cannot be saved up for later. Lost idle time is gone for good. This is the key insight of queueing theory. Variability, not just the average workload, is what creates waiting, and waiting can build up even when a system looks comfortably under capacity.

sections.key: As a system gets close to full capacity, waiting times shoot up dramatically.
sections.b: Queueing models reveal a striking curve. In a classic model of a single server with random arrivals and random service times, the average wait in the queue depends on utilisation, the fraction of time the server is busy. At 50 per cent utilisation, the average wait equals about one typical service time. At 80 per cent it is four service times. At 90 per cent it is nine, and at 95 per cent it is nineteen. Plotted on a graph, the line stays fairly flat, then bends sharply upward like a hockey stick. That is why a café can cope well for most of the morning, then suddenly be swamped when just a few extra customers arrive. It is also why a system run at nearly full capacity, with no slack, is fragile.

sections.key: A single queue feeding several servers usually beats separate lines for each server.
sections.b: Think of a supermarket with a separate line at every checkout. You pick one, and the person in front has a problem with a price, while the line beside you races ahead. Now think of a bank or airport using one snaking queue that feeds several counters, with the person at the front going to whichever counter frees up first. The average wait is usually shorter with a single queue, and, just as importantly, the waits are far more even. Nobody gets stuck behind one slow transaction while other servers sit idle. Mathematicians call this the benefit of pooling. Separate lines can still make sense when space is tight or when express lanes help speed up small purchases, but pooling is one of the most reliable lessons of queueing theory.

sections.key: The average number in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each spends there.
sections.b: One of the most useful results in the field is beautifully simple. Little's law, proved by the American researcher John Little in 1961, says that the average number of items in a stable system equals the rate at which they arrive multiplied by the average time each one stays. If a café gets 20 customers an hour and each stays for half an hour, then on average 20 × 0.5, or 10 customers are inside at any moment. The law works almost regardless of the details. It applies to customers in shops, patients in a hospital ward, cars on a motorway or tasks waiting on a computer. Managers use it in reverse, too. Knowing how many people are typically present and how fast they arrive tells you how long each one is staying.

sections.key: The experience of waiting depends on psychology as much as on the clock.
sections.b: Queueing maths measures minutes, but people judge waits by how they feel. In 1985 the business researcher David Maister wrote an influential essay on the psychology of waiting lines. Among his principles were that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, that uncertain waits feel longer than known ones, and that unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones. Unfair waits, such as watching someone push in, feel longer than fair ones. This explains many familiar features of modern life. Theme parks post estimated waiting times at the start of a line. Apps show your position in a call queue or how far away your rideshare is. Businesses place screens and menus where people queue. None of this shortens the wait, but it can make it feel noticeably more bearable.

sections.key: Leave slack, reduce variability and pool resources, whether you run a shop or a calendar.
sections.b: Queueing theory offers practical advice well beyond shops. Planning your own week works like a queue. If your schedule is packed at 95 per cent of your available time, any small delay causes knock-on chaos, just as the hockey-stick curve predicts. Leaving some slack is not laziness; it is what keeps the whole system flowing. Reducing variability helps too. Booking appointments, staggering arrivals and preparing for predictable busy periods all smooth out the bunching that creates queues. Pooling shared resources, such as one shared inbox for a team rather than separate ones, spreads work more evenly. And when you are the one waiting, it helps to remember that a long line is rarely about one slow person. It is usually mathematics at work.

quiz.q: Who founded queueing theory with work on telephone exchanges?
o: Alan Turing
Agner Krarup Erlang
John Napier
Florence Nightingale
quiz.e: Erlang, working for the Copenhagen Telephone Company, published his first work on the subject in 1909.

quiz.q: Why can a queue form even when a server has spare capacity on average?
o: Customers are always slow
Arrivals and service times vary, and idle time cannot be saved
Averages are calculated wrongly
Servers always slow down
quiz.e: Randomness bunches arrivals together, and time lost being idle in quiet moments is gone for good.

quiz.q: In the classic single-server model, how does the average wait at 90% utilisation compare with 50%?
o: About the same
About twice as long
About nine times as long
About half as long
quiz.e: The wait is about one service time at 50% and about nine service times at 90%.

quiz.q: A clinic sees 6 patients an hour, each staying 2 hours on average. By Little's law, how many are there on average?
quiz.e: Little's law multiplies the arrival rate by the time in the system: 6 × 2 = 12.

quiz.q: According to David Maister, which of these makes a wait feel longer?
o: Being told the reason for it
Having something to do
Seeing it as unfair
Knowing how long it will be
quiz.e: Maister argued that unfair waits, like seeing someone push in, feel longer, while explained, occupied and known waits feel shorter.

LESSONS.title: Calculus without fear: the maths of change
LESSONS.hook: Calculus has a fearsome reputation, but its two big ideas can be grasped with a speedometer and an odometer. Its invention also sparked one of the bitterest feuds in science.

sections.key: Calculus answers how fast something is changing and how much has built up over time.
sections.b: Strip away the symbols and calculus asks two questions. First, how fast is something changing at this exact moment? Second, if you know how fast something is changing, how much has it added up to over time? Every car carries a picture of both ideas. The speedometer shows how fast your distance is changing right now. The odometer adds up all those changing speeds into a total distance travelled. The first idea is called differentiation, and its result is a derivative. The second is integration, and its result is an integral. These two operations sit at the heart of physics, engineering, economics and biology, anywhere things change smoothly. The genius of calculus is that it handles constant change, where ordinary arithmetic only works with fixed values.

sections.key: Ancient Greek paradoxes showed that thinking about infinitely small steps is genuinely tricky.
sections.b: The ideas behind calculus troubled thinkers long before anyone named it. Around the fifth century BCE, the Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea devised paradoxes about motion. In one, the swift Achilles can never catch a tortoise with a head start, because each time he reaches where the tortoise was, it has moved a little further on. In another, a moving arrow is at rest at every instant, so how can it move at all? Zeno's puzzles exposed a real difficulty: how can an infinite number of steps add up to a finite result? Today we can answer him. Add a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on forever, and the total gets ever closer to exactly 1. An infinite sum can have a finite value.

sections.key: Archimedes found areas and volumes by squeezing shapes between ever-finer approximations.
sections.b: In the third century BCE, Archimedes of Syracuse came remarkably close to integral calculus. To find the area of a circle, he trapped it between polygons drawn inside and outside it, then doubled the number of sides again and again. With 96-sided polygons, he showed that pi lies between 223/71 and 22/7, which is between about 3.1408 and 3.1429. His approach, now called the method of exhaustion, squeezed an unknown quantity between approximations that could be made as close as you liked. He used similar reasoning to find the area under a curve called a parabola and the volume of a sphere, which he was so proud of that he wanted a sphere and cylinder carved on his tomb. What he lacked was a general method that worked for every problem.

sections.h: Newton, Leibniz and a bitter feud
sections.key: Newton and Leibniz each invented calculus independently, then their supporters fought over who came first.
sections.b: In the mid-1660s, while Cambridge was closed by plague, the young Isaac Newton developed what he called the method of fluxions, but he kept it largely to himself for years. In Germany, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed his own version in the 1670s and published first, in 1684. A bitter priority dispute followed, with Newton's supporters accusing Leibniz of plagiarism. In 1712 the Royal Society, of which Newton was president, issued a report that ruled in Newton's favour. Newton himself secretly drafted much of it. Historians now agree that the two men invented calculus independently. Leibniz's notation, such as dy/dx for a derivative and the long S symbol for an integral, proved clearer and won out, while British mathematicians, sticking loyally to Newton's dots, fell behind continental Europe for a century.

sections.key: A derivative finds the speed at an instant by measuring change over ever-shorter intervals.
sections.b: Drop a ball, and the distance it falls in metres is about 4.9 multiplied by the time in seconds squared, ignoring air resistance. How fast is it moving at exactly one second? Speed is distance divided by time, but at a single instant no time passes. So take short intervals. From 1 to 1.1 seconds, the ball falls from 4.9 metres to about 5.93, an average speed of 10.29 metres per second. From 1 to 1.01 seconds, the average is about 9.85. As the interval shrinks towards zero, the average speed closes in on exactly 9.8 metres per second. That limit is the derivative. On a graph, it is the slope of the curve at a single point, found by zooming in until the curve looks like a straight line.

sections.key: An integral adds up countless thin slices to find a total, such as distance or area.
sections.b: Integration runs the other way. If you drive at a steady 60 km/h for two hours, you travel 120 kilometres. On a graph of speed against time, that is the area of a rectangle, 60 high and 2 wide. But real driving involves constantly changing speed, so the graph is a wavy line. To find the distance, slice the area under it into thin vertical strips, each almost a rectangle, and add them up. The thinner the strips, the better the answer, and in the limit of infinitely thin strips, you get the exact area, which is the integral. This is Archimedes' squeezing idea made general. Engineers use integrals to find the total force on a dam wall, the volume of a fuel tank or the energy used over a day.

sections.key: Differentiation and integration are opposites, which turns hard area problems into easy ones.
sections.b: The deepest discovery of calculus is that its two halves undo each other. If you integrate a speed to get distance, then differentiate that distance, you get the speed back. This link is called the fundamental theorem of calculus, and Newton and Leibniz each grasped it. Earlier mathematicians, including Isaac Barrow, Newton's teacher at Cambridge, had glimpsed the connection, but the two founders turned it into a working method. Its power is enormous. Instead of slicing an area into thousands of strips, you can often find a formula whose derivative is the curve you care about, and the area follows almost instantly. Problems that once took Archimedes' genius became routine exercises. This single connection is why calculus spread so quickly through science in the following century.

sections.key: Calculus worked for over a century before mathematicians fully explained why.
sections.b: Early calculus had an embarrassing weakness. Newton and Leibniz reasoned with quantities that were infinitely small yet not quite zero, which critics found hard to swallow. In 1734 the Irish philosopher George Berkeley mocked these vanishing quantities as ‘ghosts of departed quantities’. Calculus kept producing correct answers in astronomy and engineering, but its foundations were shaky. In the nineteenth century, mathematicians including Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Karl Weierstrass rebuilt the subject on the idea of a limit, defined precisely without any mysterious infinitesimals. Their definitions answered Zeno at last. Today calculus underpins weather forecasting, rocket trajectories, medical scanners, economic models and the training of artificial intelligence systems, which adjust millions of settings by following derivatives downhill towards smaller errors. The maths of change runs much of the modern world.

quiz.q: In a car, which instrument is a picture of integration?
o: The speedometer
The odometer
The fuel gauge
The rev counter
quiz.e: The odometer adds up changing speeds over time into a total distance, which is what an integral does.

quiz.q: What did Archimedes prove about pi using 96-sided polygons?
o: It equals exactly 22/7
It lies between 223/71 and 22/7
It equals 3
It is a whole number
quiz.e: Squeezing the circle between inner and outer polygons showed pi lies between about 3.1408 and 3.1429.

quiz.q: Who secretly drafted much of the 1712 Royal Society report on the calculus dispute?
o: Leibniz
Newton
Berkeley
Archimedes
quiz.e: Newton was president of the Royal Society and drafted much of the report that ruled in his own favour.

quiz.q: A falling ball's distance is 4.9 × t squared. What is its speed at exactly 1 second?
quiz.e: Average speeds over shrinking intervals close in on 9.8 m/s, which is the derivative at 1 second.

quiz.q: What does the fundamental theorem of calculus say?
o: Every curve is a straight line
Differentiation and integration undo each other
Infinitely small quantities are zero
Calculus only works for circles
quiz.e: Integrating then differentiating gets you back where you started, linking the two halves of calculus.

LESSONS.title: Dollar Bill and the day Australia went decimal
LESSONS.hook: On one Monday in 1966, a whole nation swapped pounds, shillings and pence for dollars and cents. Almost nobody wanted it called the dollar at first.

sections.key: Before 1966 Australians did their sums in a system based on twelves and twenties.
sections.b: For most of its history Australia counted money the British way. A pound was worth 20 shillings, and each shilling was worth 12 pence, so a pound held 240 pennies. Prices were written in a clumsy shorthand such as £2 7s 6d, and adding up a shopping bill meant constant carrying of twelves and twenties. Australia had issued its own pound since 1910, but the arithmetic was inherited from medieval England. By the 1950s businesses, banks and schools were complaining. Children spent hours learning to convert pence into shillings, and the new adding machines and early computers suited tens far better. Many countries had long since gone decimal, and a government committee set up in 1959 recommended Australia follow.

sections.key: The government's first choice of name, the ‘royal’, was so unpopular it was quietly dropped.
sections.b: Choosing a name proved harder than doing the maths. The public sent in thousands of suggestions, from the austral and the kanga to the emu and the ming, a cheeky nod to Prime Minister Robert Menzies' nickname. In 1963 the government announced that the new unit would be called the royal. The reaction was swift and scornful. Newspapers mocked it, and many people felt it sounded old-fashioned for a young country building its own identity. Within months the government backed down and settled on the dollar, a name already used in the United States, Canada and elsewhere, and short enough to say easily. The fuss is a reminder that money is not just maths. It carries national pride.

sections.key: The switch happened on a single day, backed by a huge public education campaign.
sections.b: The changeover was set for Monday 14 February 1966, nicknamed C-Day. To prepare people, the Decimal Currency Board ran one of the biggest public information campaigns Australia had seen. Its star was a cartoon character called Dollar Bill, and a catchy jingle sung to the tune of the bush ballad ‘Click Go the Shears’ explained the change on radio and television. The conversion rule was simple: ten shillings became one dollar, so one pound became two dollars. Banks closed briefly beforehand to prepare, and thousands of cash registers and machines had to be converted or replaced. Old and new money circulated side by side for a while, with shopkeepers giving change in decimal currency to drain the old coins from circulation.

sections.key: The new coins carried Australian wildlife, a design that has lasted for decades.
sections.b: The coin designs came from Stuart Devlin, a young Australian designer who later became a famous silversmith in London. Instead of kings and coats of arms on every coin, he chose native animals. The one cent showed a feathertail glider, the two cent a frilled-neck lizard, the five cent an echidna, the ten cent a lyrebird and the twenty cent a platypus. The fifty cent carried the national coat of arms. The monarch stayed on the other side, as is still the custom. These designs became so familiar that they have stayed largely unchanged through many decades, even as portraits of the monarch were updated. For many Australians, the platypus on the twenty is as recognisable as any flag.

sections.h: The coin worth more than its face
sections.key: The first round fifty cent coin contained so much silver it was worth melting down.
sections.b: One coin did not last long. The original 1966 fifty cent piece was round and made of 80 per cent silver. That seemed reasonable at first, but the world price of silver climbed during the 1960s, and soon the metal inside the coin was worth more than fifty cents. People began hoarding them rather than spending them, a textbook case of what economists call Gresham's law: when two kinds of money circulate, the one with more valuable content tends to disappear into drawers, leaving the cheaper one in use. The government withdrew the round coin and in 1969 introduced the distinctive twelve-sided fifty cent piece, made of copper and nickel, which is still in use today.

sections.key: Australia kept innovating, pioneering polymer banknotes and later scrapping its smallest coins.
sections.b: The story did not stop in 1966. In 1988, for the bicentenary of European settlement, the Reserve Bank issued a ten dollar note printed on plastic polymer instead of paper. It was developed in Australia, partly to defeat counterfeiters, since a clear window and other features were very hard to copy. By 1996 Australia had become the first country with a full series of polymer notes, and the technology has since spread to many countries. Meanwhile inflation slowly shrank the value of small coins. In 1992 the one and two cent coins were withdrawn, and cash totals have been rounded to the nearest five cents ever since. Card payments, of course, are still charged to the exact cent.

quiz.q: Under the old system, how many pence made up one pound?
quiz.e: A pound held 20 shillings and each shilling held 12 pence, so a pound was 240 pence.

quiz.q: What name did the government first announce for the new currency in 1963?
o: The royal
The austral
The emu
The sterling
quiz.e: The government announced the royal, but public mockery led it to switch to the dollar.

quiz.q: What was the conversion rule on C-Day?
o: One pound became one dollar
Ten shillings became one dollar
One shilling became one dollar
One penny became one cent
quiz.e: Ten shillings equalled one dollar, so one pound became two dollars.

quiz.q: Why did the round 1966 fifty cent coin disappear from circulation?
o: It was too easy to forge
It was too heavy to carry
Its silver came to be worth more than fifty cents
It showed the wrong monarch
quiz.e: Rising silver prices meant the metal was worth more than the face value, so people hoarded the coins, an example of Gresham's law.

quiz.q: What happened to Australia's one and two cent coins in 1992?
o: They were made of polymer
They were withdrawn and cash totals rounded to five cents
They were redesigned with new animals
They became collectors' gold coins
quiz.e: The coins were withdrawn and cash totals have since been rounded to the nearest five cents.

LESSONS.title: Why the Aussie dollar rises and falls
LESSONS.hook: In 2001 an Australian dollar bought less than 50 US cents. A decade later it bought more than a US dollar. Here is what moves a currency.

sections.key: An exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another.
sections.b: When you hear that the Australian dollar is ‘at 65 US cents’, it means one Australian dollar can be swapped for 65 American cents. An exchange rate is a price, and like other prices it is set by supply and demand. Every day, importers, exporters, tourists, investors and banks buy and sell currencies, and the trading in currency markets is enormous, measured in trillions of US dollars a day worldwide. If more people want Australian dollars, perhaps to buy Australian iron ore or Australian bonds, the price rises. If more people want to sell them, it falls. The Australian dollar is one of the most heavily traded currencies in the world, often nicknamed the Aussie.

sections.key: Australia let its currency float freely in December 1983, one of the biggest economic reforms in its history.
sections.b: It was not always this way. For decades Australia's currency was pegged, first to the British pound, then to the US dollar, and from 1974 to a basket of currencies that officials adjusted. The government and Reserve Bank effectively decided the rate, and strict controls limited how much money could flow in or out of the country. Defending the peg became increasingly difficult as money sloshed around the world. In December 1983 the Hawke government, with Treasurer Paul Keating, floated the dollar and removed most exchange controls, letting the market set the price. It was a dramatic shift. Since then the Reserve Bank has only occasionally stepped into the market, usually during periods of severe disorder.

sections.key: The Aussie dollar often moves with the prices of the minerals and farm goods Australia exports.
sections.b: Australia sells huge quantities of iron ore, coal, gas, gold, wheat and beef to the world. When those commodity prices climb, foreign buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for them, and the currency tends to rise. That is why traders call the Aussie a commodity currency. The mining boom of the 2000s is the clearest example. China's rapid industrialisation drove up demand for Australian iron ore and coal, and the dollar climbed from a low of under 48 US cents in 2001 to above parity, more than one US dollar, in late 2010, peaking in 2011. When commodity prices later fell, the dollar fell with them. The link is not perfect, but it is strong enough to watch.

sections.key: Higher interest rates can attract investors, pushing a currency up.
sections.b: Commodities are only part of the story. Investors constantly move money around the world looking for the best return. If Australian interest rates are higher than those in the United States or Japan, investors can earn more by holding Australian dollar deposits or bonds, so they buy Australian dollars to do it. This tends to push the currency up. One famous strategy, the carry trade, involves borrowing in a low interest currency, such as the Japanese yen for much of recent history, and investing in a higher interest one. It can be profitable for years and then unwind suddenly when markets panic. That is one reason the Aussie often falls sharply during global crises, as nervous investors rush to safer currencies.

sections.key: A strong dollar helps importers and travellers, while a weak one helps exporters and tourism.
sections.b: Whether a high dollar is good news depends on who you are. When the Aussie is strong, overseas holidays are cheaper, imported cars and electronics cost less, and Australians can buy foreign shares more cheaply. But exporters suffer, because their goods become more expensive for foreign buyers, and local manufacturers struggle to compete against cheaper imports. Universities and tourism operators also feel it, since Australia becomes a pricier place to study or visit. A weak dollar flips these effects. Overseas trips hurt, but farmers, miners and tour operators gain. This is why the exchange rate works as a kind of shock absorber for the economy, cushioning the blow when commodity prices or global conditions change.

sections.key: Comparing burger prices is a playful way to ask whether a currency is overvalued.
sections.b: If a currency is fairly priced, the same basket of goods should cost roughly the same everywhere once you convert the money. Economists call this idea purchasing power parity. In 1986 The Economist magazine turned it into a light-hearted gauge called the Big Mac index, comparing the price of the burger in different countries. If a Big Mac costs much more in Switzerland than in the United States after conversion, the Swiss franc looks overvalued by burger logic. The index is deliberately simple, since local wages, rents and taxes all affect burger prices. But it captures a real idea. In the long run exchange rates tend to drift towards levels that make prices broadly comparable, even if they stray widely in the short term.

quiz.q: What is an exchange rate?
o: A tax on foreign travel
The price of one currency in terms of another
The interest rate set by the central bank
A fixed rate set by the United Nations
quiz.e: An exchange rate is a price, set by supply and demand for currencies.

quiz.q: What happened to the Australian dollar in December 1983?
o: It was pegged to the US dollar
It replaced the pound
It was floated and the market set its price
It was linked to the price of gold
quiz.e: The Hawke government, with Treasurer Paul Keating, floated the dollar and removed most exchange controls.

quiz.q: Why is the Aussie called a commodity currency?
o: It often moves with the prices of the resources Australia exports
It is backed by gold reserves
It can only be used to buy commodities
It is made of metal
quiz.e: When prices for iron ore, coal and other exports rise, demand for Australian dollars rises too.

quiz.q: How can higher Australian interest rates affect the dollar?
o: They always weaken it
They have no effect
They can attract foreign investors, pushing the dollar up
They force the dollar back to parity
quiz.e: Investors seeking better returns buy Australian dollars to hold higher yielding deposits and bonds.

quiz.q: Who generally benefits from a weak Australian dollar?
o: Australians holidaying overseas
Exporters and tourism operators
Importers of foreign cars
People buying foreign shares
quiz.e: A weak dollar makes Australian goods and holidays cheaper for foreigners, helping exporters and tourism.

LESSONS.title: Bank runs: when everyone wants their money at once
LESSONS.hook: Your bank does not keep your savings in a vault. Usually that is fine. When everyone turns up at once, it can be catastrophic.

sections.key: Banks lend out most of the money deposited with them, keeping only a fraction on hand.
sections.b: When you deposit money in a bank, it does not sit in a box with your name on it. Banks take deposits that customers can withdraw at any moment and use them to fund loans that will not be repaid for years, such as mortgages and business loans. They keep only a small portion as cash and reserves, betting, sensibly, that not everyone will want their money on the same day. This arrangement is the heart of banking and it is genuinely useful, turning idle savings into homes and businesses. But it creates a built-in fragility. A bank can be perfectly sound, with good loans that will be repaid, and still be unable to hand everyone their money back immediately.

sections.key: A run can topple a healthy bank simply because people fear it will fall.
sections.b: Imagine a rumour spreads that your bank is in trouble. Even if you think the rumour is false, you have a problem. If other people believe it and withdraw their money, the bank may run out of cash, and those who wait could lose out. So the rational move is to join the queue. Everyone reasons the same way, and the fear becomes reality. Economists Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig described this trap in a famous 1983 model, showing how a bank run can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. Their work helped earn them a share of the 2022 Nobel Prize in economics, alongside Ben Bernanke, who studied how bank failures deepened the Great Depression.

sections.key: Australia suffered one of history's great banking crises after a property bubble burst.
sections.b: Australia knows this story well. In the 1880s Melbourne boomed on gold wealth and borrowed British money, and land prices soared in a speculative frenzy. Dozens of building societies and land banks lent freely against property. When the bubble burst at the end of the decade, borrowers defaulted and many of these institutions collapsed. In 1893 the crisis reached the major banks. Depositors rushed to withdraw their money, and many of the colonies' major banks suspended payments within a few weeks. Some reopened after being reorganised, but savings were frozen or lost and the colonies plunged into a deep depression that lasted for much of the decade. Melbourne took years to recover.

sections.key: Banks fight runs by explaining that the money is safe, just tied up in loans.
sections.b: The classic film It's a Wonderful Life, released in 1946, contains one of the clearest explanations of a bank run ever filmed. When panicked customers crowd into George Bailey's building and loan company demanding their savings, he explains that their money is not in a safe. It is in Joe's house and the Kennedys' house, lent out so neighbours could buy homes. If everyone insists on withdrawing at once, the whole community suffers. Bailey calms the crowd by asking each person to take only what they need. Real banks rely on something similar but more powerful: a central bank willing to lend them cash against good assets in an emergency, acting as a lender of last resort.

sections.key: Governments now insure deposits so that ordinary savers have no reason to run.
sections.b: The most effective cure for bank runs has been deposit insurance. After thousands of American banks failed in the early 1930s, the United States created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 1933, promising savers they would get their money back up to a limit. With that guarantee in place, there was little reason to panic, and large-scale runs became rare. Australia introduced its Financial Claims Scheme during the global financial crisis in 2008. As of the mid-2020s it protects deposits up to 250,000 dollars per account holder at each authorised bank, building society or credit union. Because the guarantee exists, the need to use it is far less likely. Confidence itself is the protection.

sections.key: Modern runs can happen in hours, driven by phones and social media.
sections.b: Runs have not disappeared. In September 2007 queues formed outside branches of Britain's Northern Rock, one of the first visible signs of the global financial crisis and the first run on a British bank in well over a century. In March 2023 California's Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in a run of startling speed. Many of its customers were tech firms with deposits far above the insured limit, and as worries spread through group chats and social media, they tried to pull tens of billions of dollars in a single day using banking apps. There were no queues outside, just a flood of online transfers. The bank was closed by regulators within roughly two days, showing how quickly modern panic can spread.

quiz.q: Why can a sound bank still be unable to pay all depositors at once?
o: It keeps all deposits in gold
Most deposits have been lent out in long-term loans
Banks are not allowed to hold cash
Deposits are held by the government
quiz.e: Banks lend most deposits as long-term loans and keep only a fraction available as cash.

quiz.q: What did Diamond and Dybvig show about bank runs?
o: They only happen to badly run banks
They can be self-fulfilling, toppling even healthy banks
They are caused by high interest rates
They cannot happen once a country has a central bank
quiz.e: Their 1983 model showed that fear of a run can rationally cause one, even at a sound bank.

quiz.q: In It's a Wonderful Life, where does George Bailey say the depositors' money is?
o: In a vault in New York
Invested in gold
Lent out in their neighbours' homes
Spent on staff wages
quiz.e: He explains the money is lent out to neighbours for their houses, not sitting in a safe.

quiz.q: What does Australia's Financial Claims Scheme do?
o: Guarantees deposits up to a limit at authorised institutions
Sets the cash rate
Insures shares against market falls
Lends money to first home buyers
quiz.e: It protects deposits, as of the mid-2020s up to 250,000 dollars per account holder at each authorised institution.

quiz.q: What made the 2023 run on Silicon Valley Bank unusual?
o: It happened over several years
It involved only paper cheques
It was extraordinarily fast, driven by online transfers and social media
It was stopped by deposit insurance alone
quiz.e: Customers tried to pull tens of billions of dollars in a day using apps, with panic spreading online.

LESSONS.title: The Medici: the bankers who built a Renaissance
LESSONS.hook: A family of Florentine money-changers became bankers to the Pope, patrons of genius and rulers of a city. Their tricks still shape finance today.

sections.key: Banking in Renaissance Italy began with money-changers working at benches in the street.
sections.b: In the 1300s Italian cities such as Florence, Venice and Genoa were the trading hubs of Europe, awash with coins from dozens of different states. Merchants needed someone to weigh, test and swap these coins, and to move money safely across long distances. Money-changers set up at tables, and the Italian word for such a bench, banco, gave us the word bank. A banker who could not pay was said to be banca rotta, a broken bench, the root of our word bankrupt. In 1397 Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Medici Bank in Florence. Within a few decades it would become the most powerful bank in Europe.

sections.key: The Medici grew rich by managing the finances of the Catholic Church.
sections.b: The Medici's greatest client was the papacy. The Church collected revenues from all over Christian Europe, from England to Poland, and needed a way to move that money to Rome without carting chests of silver across the Alps. The Medici, with their network of trusted agents, could do it. For long stretches of the 1400s they served as the main bankers to the Pope, a relationship that brought enormous profits and political influence. Their Rome branch was often the most profitable in the company. The connection lasted well beyond the bank itself. In the following century two members of the family became popes themselves, Leo X and Clement VII, a sign of how deeply the family had woven itself into the Church.

sections.key: The Church banned charging interest, so bankers earned it through currency exchange instead.
sections.b: There was an awkward problem. The Church condemned usury, which in that era meant charging interest on a loan, as a sin. So how could a bank make money? The answer was the bill of exchange. A merchant in Florence might hand over florins and receive a document payable months later in another currency, say in Bruges or London. The rates used at each end were set so that the banker made a profit, but on paper the deal was an exchange of currencies, not a loan. Theologians argued over whether this was acceptable, and the risk of exchange rate movements gave bankers a defence. In practice, interest was hidden inside the exchange.

sections.key: The Medici ran a network of semi-independent branches across Europe, an early model for modern firms.
sections.b: At its height the Medici Bank had branches in Rome, Venice, Milan, Geneva, Avignon, Bruges and London, among other places. Each was run by a branch manager who often held a share in the profits, giving him a reason to work hard, while the family in Florence kept overall control. Branches were set up as separate partnerships, which meant a disaster in one city would not automatically drag down the rest. The Medici and other Italian merchants kept careful accounts using double-entry bookkeeping, recording every transaction as both a debit and a credit so errors stood out. The method was spreading among Italian traders by the 1300s, and the friar Luca Pacioli described it in print in 1494.

sections.key: Medici wealth funded some of the greatest art and architecture of the Renaissance.
sections.b: Giovanni's son Cosimo de' Medici used the bank's fortune to become the unofficial ruler of Florence from 1434, steering politics through allies rather than holding a crown. He was also a generous patron. He funded churches, the library of the monastery of San Marco and artists such as Donatello, and supported scholars who translated ancient Greek philosophy. His grandson Lorenzo, known as Lorenzo the Magnificent, continued the tradition, and the young Michelangelo spent time in his household. Part of this giving was genuine love of learning and beauty. Part of it was likely an attempt to win public support, and perhaps to ease consciences troubled by the Church's teaching on wealth. Either way, Florence was transformed.

sections.key: Bad loans to rulers and weaker management brought the bank down by 1494.
sections.b: Under Lorenzo, who was more interested in politics and poetry than ledgers, the bank weakened. Some branch managers made reckless loans to princes, who were powerful, unpredictable and hard to sue. The London branch lent heavily to King Edward IV during the Wars of the Roses and suffered heavy losses. The Bruges branch, under Tommaso Portinari, lent to Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, who was killed in battle in 1477. One by one, branches closed. In 1494, when the Medici were driven out of Florence, the bank collapsed. The lesson echoes through financial history: lending to the mighty can feel safe until the mighty decide, or are unable, to pay.

quiz.q: Where does the word ‘bank’ come from?
o: The Latin word for gold
The Italian word banco, meaning bench
The name of a German banking family
The banks of the river Arno
quiz.e: Money-changers worked at benches, banco in Italian, which gave us bank, and banca rotta gave us bankrupt.

quiz.q: Who was the Medici Bank's most important client for much of the 1400s?
o: The King of France
The papacy
The Ottoman Sultan
The Venetian navy
quiz.e: The Medici served as main bankers to the Pope, moving Church revenues across Europe.

quiz.q: How did bankers earn a return despite the Church's ban on usury?
o: By building profits into bills of exchange between currencies
By charging entry fees to churches
By selling indulgences
By ignoring the ban openly
quiz.e: Bills of exchange were framed as currency swaps, with profit built into the exchange rates.

quiz.q: Why were Medici branches set up as separate partnerships?
o: To avoid all taxes
So a disaster in one branch would not automatically sink the others
Because the Pope required it
So each branch could issue its own coins
quiz.e: Separate partnerships limited the damage a failure in one city could do to the rest.

quiz.q: What helped bring down the Medici Bank?
o: A Florentine stock market crash
The invention of paper money
Risky loans to rulers such as Edward IV and Charles the Bold
A ban on double-entry bookkeeping
quiz.e: Large loans to powerful rulers went bad, and the bank collapsed in 1494 when the Medici were expelled from Florence.

LESSONS.title: Behavioural economics: why we're not rational with money
LESSONS.hook: Traditional economics imagined people as cool calculators. Then psychologists started running experiments, and the calculators turned out to be human.

sections.key: Classic economic models assumed people weigh every option logically to get the best outcome.
sections.b: For much of the twentieth century, economic theory leaned on a convenient character sometimes nicknamed Homo economicus. This imaginary person knows what they want, calculates costs and benefits precisely, never gets tired or tempted, and always chooses the option that serves them best. The assumption made the maths workable, and it still explains a great deal about how markets behave. But anyone who has bought something on impulse, kept a gym membership they never use or put off saving for retirement knows real people are different. Behavioural economics grew from the idea of testing how people actually decide, using experiments borrowed from psychology, and then building those findings back into economics.

sections.key: Losing something tends to hurt more than gaining the same thing feels good.
sections.b: In 1979 psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published prospect theory, which described how people really evaluate risky choices. One of its central ideas is loss aversion. In many experiments, the pain of losing 100 dollars outweighs the pleasure of winning 100 dollars, often by something like twice as much, though estimates vary and some researchers argue the effect is smaller or depends on the situation. Loss aversion helps explain why investors hang on to falling shares, hoping to avoid admitting a loss, and why ‘don't miss out’ marketing works so well. Kahneman was awarded the Nobel Prize in economics in 2002. Tversky had died in 1996, and the prize is not given posthumously.

sections.key: We treat money differently depending on where it came from or what we have labelled it for.
sections.b: In theory a dollar is a dollar. In practice we sort money into mental jars. Economist Richard Thaler called this mental accounting. Someone might carry credit card debt at a high interest rate while keeping savings in a holiday fund earning far less, because the holiday money feels untouchable. A tax refund or a win at the races often gets spent more freely than wages, as if it were not quite real money. Mental accounting is not always bad. Labelling money for bills or emergencies can be a useful way to stop yourself overspending. But it can also lead to choices that cost money, so it helps to ask occasionally whether your jars still make sense together.

sections.key: People tend to value things more simply because they own them.
sections.b: In a well-known study published in 1990, Kahneman, Thaler and Jack Knetsch handed coffee mugs to half the students in a class. Those who received mugs were asked what price they would sell for, and those without were asked what they would pay. In theory the two groups should have valued the mugs similarly. Instead, owners typically demanded around twice as much as buyers were willing to pay. This is the endowment effect. It helps explain why people overprice their own homes and cars when selling, and why free trial offers work: once something feels like yours, giving it up feels like a loss. Later research has debated how strong the effect is in different settings.

sections.key: We tend to grab rewards now and push costs into the future, even against our own plans.
sections.b: Ask people whether they would prefer 100 dollars in a year or 110 dollars in a year and a week, and most will wait the extra week. Ask whether they want 100 dollars today or 110 dollars next week, and many grab the money now. The gap is the same, but the present has a special pull. Economists call this present bias. It shows up in spending, saving, diets and procrastination, and it explains why buy now, pay later deals are so tempting. The future self who has to pay feels like a stranger. One response is to make good choices automatic, so your present self does not have to win the argument every time.

sections.key: Small changes to how choices are presented can change behaviour, without banning anything.
sections.b: If people are predictably irrational, can choices be designed to help them? In their 2008 book Nudge, Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein argued that defaults matter enormously. If workers are automatically enrolled in a retirement plan and must opt out, far more end up saving than if they must opt in. Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed a scheme called Save More Tomorrow, in which workers commit in advance to saving part of future pay rises, sidestepping both present bias and loss aversion. Thaler received the Nobel Prize in 2017. Australia's compulsory superannuation, introduced in 1992, goes further than a nudge, since employers must contribute, but it rests on a similar insight about how hard saving is.

quiz.q: What is loss aversion?
o: Avoiding all investments
Feeling losses more strongly than equal gains
Preferring to save rather than spend
Fear of losing a wallet
quiz.e: In many experiments losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains please, though estimates vary.

quiz.q: Someone keeps a holiday fund while paying high interest on a credit card. Which idea does this illustrate?
o: Mental accounting
The endowment effect
Inflation
Gresham's law
quiz.e: Treating money as separate jars, rather than as interchangeable, is mental accounting.

quiz.q: In the mug experiment, what did owners of the mugs tend to do?
o: Give them away for free
Ask about the same price buyers offered
Demand around twice what buyers would pay
Refuse to answer
quiz.e: Owners valued the mugs more simply because they owned them, the endowment effect.

quiz.q: Why do buy now, pay later deals appeal so strongly?
o: They are always the cheapest option
Present bias makes immediate rewards feel more important than future costs
They improve credit scores
They are required by law
quiz.e: Present bias pulls us towards rewards now while the future cost feels distant.

quiz.q: What did Thaler and Sunstein argue about defaults?
o: They have little effect
Automatic enrolment with an opt-out greatly increases saving
People should always be forced to choose
Defaults should be banned
quiz.e: When saving is the default, far more people end up saving than when they must opt in.

LESSONS.title: The gold standard and the end of Bretton Woods
LESSONS.hook: For generations, money was promised to be as good as gold. Then on a Sunday night in 1971, an American president broke the link with a television address.

sections.key: Under the gold standard a currency could be swapped for a fixed amount of gold.
sections.b: For much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the world's major currencies were tied to gold. Under the gold standard a government promised that its paper money could be exchanged for a fixed weight of gold on demand. Britain led the way. Its pound was effectively linked to gold from the early 1700s, partly thanks to a gold price set in 1717 while Isaac Newton was Master of the Mint, and formally from 1821. By the 1870s Germany, the United States and many others had joined. Because each currency was fixed to gold, they were fixed to each other too, making international trade and lending more predictable. The classical gold standard lasted until the First World War.

sections.key: Gold kept money stable but tied governments' hands during downturns.
sections.b: The gold standard had a strong appeal. A government could not simply print money to pay its bills, because it had to hold enough gold to back its promises, so long-run inflation stayed low. But this discipline came at a cost. The money supply depended on how much gold a country held, not on what the economy needed. When gold flowed out, a country often had to raise interest rates and squeeze its economy, even in a slump. Prices could fall for years, making debts harder to repay. The system also depended on new gold discoveries. Gold rushes in California, Australia and South Africa expanded the world's money supply in ways that had nothing to do with economic policy.

sections.key: Countries that abandoned gold earlier generally recovered from the Depression sooner.
sections.b: After the First World War, countries tried to rebuild the gold standard. In 1925 Britain, with Winston Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, returned to gold at the pre-war rate, which most economists now agree overvalued the pound and hurt British industry. John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a pamphlet called The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill. When the Great Depression struck, the gold standard helped spread deflation from country to country, as central banks raised rates to defend their gold. Britain left gold in 1931 and the United States effectively devalued in 1933. Research by economic historians, including Barry Eichengreen and Ben Bernanke, found that countries leaving gold earlier tended to recover faster.

sections.key: Allied nations designed a new system with the US dollar at its centre, linked to gold.
sections.b: In July 1944, while the Second World War still raged, delegates from 44 Allied nations met at a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. Led by Keynes for Britain and Harry Dexter White for the United States, they designed a new monetary order to avoid the chaos of the 1930s. Under the Bretton Woods system, other currencies were pegged to the US dollar, and the dollar was convertible into gold at 35 dollars an ounce, but only for foreign governments and central banks, not ordinary citizens. Countries could adjust their pegs in serious circumstances. The conference also created the International Monetary Fund and what became the World Bank, both still central to the global economy today.

sections.key: The system needed ever more dollars abroad, which slowly undermined faith in the gold promise.
sections.b: Bretton Woods carried a hidden contradiction, identified by economist Robert Triffin around 1960. The world needed a growing supply of dollars to finance expanding trade, and those dollars could only come from the United States spending, investing and lending abroad. But the more dollars piled up overseas, the less likely it was that America held enough gold to honour them all. Through the 1960s, war spending in Vietnam and domestic programmes widened the gap. Foreign governments, notably France under Charles de Gaulle, began converting dollars into gold, and American gold reserves shrank. By the end of the decade, there were far more dollars held abroad than the gold in American vaults could cover at 35 dollars an ounce.

sections.key: In August 1971 the US suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, ending the gold link for good.
sections.b: On Sunday 15 August 1971, President Richard Nixon went on television and announced that the United States would temporarily stop converting dollars into gold for foreign governments. He also imposed wage and price controls and a surcharge on imports. The suspension was never lifted. Attempts to patch together new fixed rates collapsed, and by 1973 the major currencies were floating against each other. Since then, the world's money has been fiat money, valuable because governments declare it legal tender and people trust it, not because it can be exchanged for metal. Some still call for a return to gold, but most economists argue that the flexibility to respond to crises is worth the loss of the golden anchor.

quiz.q: Under a gold standard, what could you do with paper money?
o: Exchange it for a fixed amount of gold
Use it only within one city
Exchange it for shares
Nothing beyond buying goods
quiz.e: The government promised paper money could be converted into a fixed weight of gold.

quiz.q: What did economic historians find about countries that left gold early in the Great Depression?
o: They suffered longer depressions
They tended to recover sooner
They were invaded
They saw no difference
quiz.e: Leaving gold freed countries to ease monetary policy, and early leavers generally recovered faster.

quiz.q: Under Bretton Woods, who could convert US dollars into gold at 35 dollars an ounce?
o: Any American citizen
Foreign governments and central banks
Only the IMF
Nobody
quiz.e: Convertibility was available to foreign governments and central banks, not ordinary citizens.

quiz.q: What was the Triffin dilemma?
o: Gold was too heavy to transport
The world needed more dollars abroad, which eroded confidence in their gold backing
The IMF could not agree on a president
Exchange rates changed every day
quiz.e: The growing pile of overseas dollars made the gold promise less and less credible.

quiz.q: What did President Nixon announce on 15 August 1971?
o: A return to the gold standard
A new currency
A suspension of dollar convertibility into gold
The founding of the IMF
quiz.e: The Nixon shock suspended convertibility, and by 1973 major currencies were floating.

LESSONS.title: The global financial crisis of 2008
LESSONS.hook: It began with American home loans that should never have been made. Within months, some of the world's biggest banks were failing and governments were scrambling to stop a second Great Depression.

sections.h: A housing boom built on credit
sections.key: In the early 2000s US house prices soared, fuelled by easy loans to risky borrowers.
sections.b: In the early 2000s American house prices rose rapidly for years. Interest rates were low after the dot-com crash, and lenders competed fiercely for business. Many began offering subprime mortgages to borrowers with weak credit histories, sometimes with little checking of income at all, and often with low introductory rates that would jump later. The thinking was that rising house prices would bail everyone out. If a borrower struggled, they could refinance or sell at a profit. Buyers, lenders and investors all assumed prices would keep climbing, or at least would not fall across the whole country at once. When prices peaked around 2006 and began to fall, that assumption collapsed, and defaults began to climb.

sections.key: Mortgages were bundled into complex securities and sold around the world.
sections.b: Many lenders did not keep the loans they made. Instead, banks bundled thousands of mortgages into securities and sold them to investors, a process called securitisation. These were then repackaged again into more complex products, such as collateralised debt obligations, which split the income into layers of different risk. Credit rating agencies gave many of the top layers their highest AAA rating, signalling they were extremely safe. Pension funds, banks and councils around the world bought them. Because lenders could sell the loans on, some had less reason to care whether borrowers could repay. And because the products were so complex, few investors truly understood how much risk they held, or where it really sat.

sections.key: Banks had borrowed heavily, so small losses could wipe them out.
sections.b: The danger was magnified by leverage. Many investment banks had borrowed large sums relative to their own capital, often around thirty dollars or more for every dollar of their own, and much of that borrowing was short term. When mortgage securities lost value, a bank's thin cushion of capital could vanish quickly. Lenders grew nervous and refused to roll over loans, and banks stopped trusting each other. In March 2008 the investment bank Bear Stearns was rescued through a sale to JPMorgan Chase with support from the US Federal Reserve. Then, in September, came the shock that turned a crisis into a panic. The authorities chose not to rescue Lehman Brothers, a 158-year-old investment bank.

sections.key: Lehman Brothers' collapse triggered a global panic and frozen credit markets.
sections.b: On 15 September 2008 Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, the largest in US history, with assets of more than 600 billion dollars. Within days the insurance giant AIG, which had sold enormous amounts of protection against mortgage defaults, needed a massive government rescue. A large money market fund that held Lehman debt ‘broke the buck’, falling below one dollar a share, sparking runs on similar funds. Lending between banks almost seized up around the world, and companies struggled to borrow even for routine needs. Share markets plunged. Governments and central banks responded with unprecedented measures, including the 700 billion dollar US rescue program known as TARP, emergency lending and guarantees to stop a total collapse of the financial system.

sections.key: Fast stimulus, sharp rate cuts, sound banks and Chinese demand helped Australia avoid a recession.
sections.b: Australia came through the crisis better than almost any other advanced economy. Several factors helped. Its big banks had less exposure to American subprime securities and were closely supervised. The Reserve Bank cut the cash rate rapidly, from 7.25 per cent in September 2008 to 3 per cent by April 2009. The government guaranteed bank deposits and wholesale funding, and spent heavily on stimulus, including cash payments to households and a large school building program. Meanwhile China launched its own enormous stimulus, keeping demand for Australian iron ore and coal strong. The economy shrank in only one quarter, at the end of 2008, so it avoided the technical definition of a recession, two consecutive quarters of decline.

sections.key: The crisis led to tougher bank rules and years of low interest rates and slow growth.
sections.b: Elsewhere, the damage lasted years. Millions of Americans lost their homes, unemployment in the United States reached around 10 per cent, and parts of Europe slid into a debt crisis from 2010, with Greece the most severe case. Central banks cut interest rates to near zero and began buying bonds on a vast scale. Regulators responded with new rules. The international Basel III standards required banks to hold more and better quality capital and more liquid assets, and the US passed the Dodd-Frank Act in 2010. Debate continues over whether these reforms went far enough, and over the fairness of rescuing banks while many ordinary people bore the costs. The crisis also fuelled lasting public anger at finance.

quiz.q: What were subprime mortgages?
o: Loans only for commercial property
Home loans to borrowers with weak credit histories
Mortgages guaranteed by the government
Loans with no interest
quiz.e: Subprime loans went to riskier borrowers, often with teaser rates that later rose.

quiz.q: What is securitisation?
o: Hiring security guards for banks
Bundling loans into securities sold to investors
Insuring deposits
Raising interest rates
quiz.e: Banks bundled mortgages into securities and sold them, spreading the risk worldwide.

quiz.q: Why did leverage make banks so vulnerable?
o: They had no customers
Heavy borrowing meant a small fall in asset values could wipe out their capital
It forced them to hold gold
It made their shares too expensive
quiz.e: With thin capital and large borrowings, modest losses could make a bank insolvent.

quiz.q: What happened on 15 September 2008?
o: Bear Stearns was sold
Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy
TARP was repaid
The Basel III rules took effect
quiz.e: Lehman's bankruptcy, the largest in US history, turned the crisis into a global panic.

quiz.q: Which of these helped Australia avoid recession during the crisis?
o: Raising interest rates sharply
Large exposure to US subprime securities
Rapid rate cuts, government stimulus and strong Chinese demand
Leaving the gold standard
quiz.e: Fast rate cuts, stimulus, sound banks and China's demand for resources all helped.

LESSONS.title: The market for lemons: when sellers know more than buyers
LESSONS.hook: A short paper about dodgy used cars was rejected by several journals. It went on to win a Nobel Prize and explain why some markets break down.

sections.key: In 1970 George Akerlof showed what happens when sellers know far more than buyers.
sections.b: In the United States a defective car is called a lemon, while a good one is sometimes called a peach. In 1970 a young economist named George Akerlof published a paper titled The Market for Lemons, using used cars to explore a simple but powerful idea. The seller of a used car knows its history: whether it has been in a flood, burns oil or was thrashed by its owner. The buyer usually does not. Economists call this asymmetric information, where one side of a deal knows much more than the other. Akerlof asked what happens to a market when buyers cannot tell good products from bad ones. The answer was surprisingly gloomy.

sections.key: If buyers cannot tell good from bad, good sellers may leave and the market shrinks.
sections.b: Imagine buyers know that some used cars are peaches and some are lemons, but cannot tell which is which. Sensibly, they will only offer an average price. To the owner of a genuine peach, that average is too low, so many of them decide not to sell. That leaves a higher share of lemons on the market. Buyers notice and lower their offers further, which drives out even more good cars. In the extreme, the market can collapse until only lemons remain, or no trade happens at all, even though many buyers would have happily paid a fair price for a good car. Bad quality, in effect, drives out good.

sections.key: Akerlof's paper was turned down several times before becoming a classic.
sections.b: The paper had a rocky start. Akerlof later recounted that it was rejected by several leading journals, with reviewers suggesting it was too trivial or, alternatively, that if it were correct, economics would be different. It was eventually published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 1970. Over time it became one of the most cited papers in the field, because the idea applied far beyond cars. In 2001 Akerlof shared the Nobel Prize in economics with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz, who had developed related ideas about how markets cope with hidden information. Together their work helped launch the economics of information, which now underpins thinking about insurance, lending and online trade.

sections.key: People who expect to claim are keener to buy insurance, which can push premiums up.
sections.b: Insurance shows the lemons problem in reverse. The buyer of health insurance often knows more about their own health than the insurer does. If premiums are set at an average level, people who expect to need lots of care find the deal attractive, while healthy people may decide it is not worth it. As the healthy leave, the insured pool gets sicker and more expensive, premiums rise and still more healthy people drop out. This spiral is called adverse selection. Australia's Lifetime Health Cover, introduced in 2000, tackles it by adding a loading to private hospital cover premiums for people who first take out cover later in life, from their early thirties on, encouraging people to join while they are young and healthy.

sections.key: Markets fight back with warranties, credentials and checks that reveal hidden quality.
sections.b: Markets are not helpless. Michael Spence showed how the informed side can send a signal, an action that is costly for low-quality sellers to fake. A dealer who offers a long warranty on a used car is signalling confidence, since honouring it on a lemon would be expensive. Spence's best-known example was education: a degree may signal persistence and ability to employers, whatever its direct usefulness. Stiglitz showed how the less informed side can screen, for instance by offering a menu of insurance policies with different excesses so that customers reveal their own risk by what they choose. Brand reputations, independent inspections and vehicle history reports all perform the same job, making hidden quality visible.

sections.key: From online reviews to consumer law, much of modern commerce exists to solve information gaps.
sections.b: Once you see the lemons problem, it pops up everywhere. Online marketplaces rely on ratings and reviews so strangers can trust each other, and fake reviews are damaging precisely because they poison those signals. Lenders check credit histories because borrowers know more about their own finances. Employers ask for references. Consumer protection laws, including statutory guarantees that goods must be of acceptable quality, give buyers some assurance and reduce the advantage of sellers who hide defects. Akerlof's insight was that missing information is not a minor detail. It can stop a market working at all. Much of the machinery of modern commerce, from warranties to watchdogs, exists to close that gap.

quiz.q: What is asymmetric information?
o: When prices are different in two countries
When one side of a deal knows much more than the other
When both sides share all information
When information is protected by copyright
quiz.e: Akerlof used used cars, where sellers know more than buyers, to illustrate asymmetric information.

quiz.q: In Akerlof's model, why might good cars disappear from the market?
o: Buyers prefer lemons
Average prices are too low for owners of good cars, so they stop selling
The government bans them
Good cars are always exported
quiz.e: When buyers only offer average prices, owners of good cars withdraw, leaving more lemons.

quiz.q: What is adverse selection in insurance?
o: Insurers choosing only healthy customers
People most likely to claim being keenest to buy cover, pushing premiums up
Choosing the wrong policy by mistake
A ban on insurance for young people
quiz.e: As healthy people drop out, the pool gets riskier and premiums rise, a spiral called adverse selection.

quiz.q: Why can a long warranty work as a signal?
o: It is required by law
It would be very costly for a seller of a bad car to honour
It lowers the car's price
It hides the car's history
quiz.e: A signal works because it is costly to fake, so offering it suggests genuine quality.

quiz.q: Who shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in economics with Akerlof?
o: Keynes and Hayek
Kahneman and Thaler
Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz
Diamond and Dybvig
quiz.e: Spence and Stiglitz developed related ideas about signalling and screening under hidden information.

LESSONS.title: Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured
LESSONS.hook: Is the gap between rich and poor growing? The answer depends on what you measure, and economists have been arguing about it for more than a century.

sections.key: Income is what flows in each year; wealth is what you own, and it is usually far more unequal.
sections.b: Talk about inequality often blurs two different things. Income is the money that comes in over a period, from wages, business profits, interest, rent or government payments. Wealth is the stock of what you own minus what you owe: a house, superannuation, shares, savings and a car, less any mortgage or debts. A young doctor might have a high income but little wealth, while a retired farmer could have modest income and substantial wealth in land. Across almost every country, wealth is distributed far more unequally than income. Wealth builds up over a lifetime, earns its own returns and can be passed on to the next generation, so differences tend to compound over time.

sections.h: The Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient
sections.key: A single number from 0 to 1 summarises how unequally income or wealth is shared.
sections.b: In 1905 the American economist Max Lorenz proposed a neat way to picture inequality. Line everyone up from poorest to richest and plot what share of total income the bottom 10 per cent, 20 per cent and so on receive. If everyone earned the same, the line would be perfectly straight. The more it sags, the more unequal the society. In 1912 the Italian statistician Corrado Gini turned this into a single number. A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality, everyone has the same, and 1 means one person has everything. Most developed countries have income Gini figures somewhere between roughly 0.25 and 0.40, and wealth figures that are considerably higher.

sections.key: Vilfredo Pareto noticed that wealth tends to concentrate in similar ways across very different societies.
sections.b: Around 1900 the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto studied tax and property records from several countries and centuries. He noticed that the distribution of income and wealth at the top followed a similar mathematical pattern again and again, with a small share of people holding a large share of the total. The popular 80/20 rule was later named after him, although that rule of thumb is far looser than his actual mathematics. Pareto's pattern, now called a power law, still describes the top of wealth distributions surprisingly well, and it means averages can be misleading when a few people hold so much.

sections.key: When a few people are very rich, the average can paint a misleadingly rosy picture.
sections.b: If a billionaire walks into a pub, the average wealth of the drinkers suddenly soars, yet nobody else is any richer. This is why economists often prefer the median, the person exactly in the middle when everyone is lined up, to the mean, or average. In unequal societies the mean income sits well above the median, because a small group of high earners pulls it up. Statisticians also compare ratios, such as the income of someone at the 90th percentile with someone at the 10th. Another common approach is to track the share of total income going to the top 1 per cent. Each measure highlights a different part of the picture, so careful analysts look at several.

sections.h: Kuznets, Piketty and the great debate
sections.key: Economists disagree about whether growth naturally narrows or widens inequality.
sections.b: In 1955 economist Simon Kuznets suggested that inequality rises as countries industrialise and then falls as they mature, an idea pictured as an upside-down U, the Kuznets curve. For a while the mid-twentieth century seemed to prove him right, as gaps narrowed in many rich countries. Then, from around 1980, top income shares rose again in the United States, Britain and elsewhere. In 2013 French economist Thomas Piketty published Capital in the Twenty-First Century, arguing that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of the economy, wealth tends to concentrate. His book became a surprise bestseller and drew strong criticism, with economists still debating his data, his theory and his proposed wealth taxes.

sections.h: Mobility: can you climb the ladder?
sections.key: How easily people move up or down the income ladder matters as much as the gap itself.
sections.b: A snapshot of inequality does not say whether the same people stay at the top or bottom. Economic mobility asks how strongly your income as an adult is linked to your parents' income. Research led by economist Miles Corak found that countries with higher inequality tend to have lower mobility between generations, a link dubbed the Great Gatsby curve by Alan Krueger in 2012. The relationship is a correlation, and researchers debate what drives it, from education and housing to social networks. Measured mobility in Australia has generally been found to be higher than in the United States, though comparing countries is tricky. Many people care less about gaps themselves than about whether the ladder is climbable.

quiz.q: Why is wealth usually more unequal than income?
o: Wealth is not taxed
It builds up over lifetimes, earns returns and can be inherited
Income is fixed by law
Wealth only includes cash
quiz.e: Wealth accumulates and compounds across lifetimes and generations, so gaps widen over time.

quiz.q: What does a Gini coefficient of 0 mean?
o: One person has everything
The data are missing
Everyone has exactly the same
The economy is not growing
quiz.e: 0 is perfect equality and 1 means one person holds everything.

quiz.q: Why do economists often prefer the median to the mean when measuring typical income?
o: The median is easier to calculate
A few very high earners can pull the mean well above what a typical person earns
The mean is illegal to publish
The median always rises faster
quiz.e: The median shows the person in the middle, unaffected by extreme incomes at the top.

quiz.q: What did Thomas Piketty argue in Capital in the Twenty-First Century?
o: Inequality always falls as economies grow
When returns on capital exceed economic growth, wealth tends to concentrate
Money should be backed by gold
Inequality cannot be measured
quiz.e: Piketty argued that when the return on capital exceeds growth, wealth concentrates, a view still debated.

quiz.q: What does the Great Gatsby curve describe?
o: Rising house prices in New York
A link between higher inequality and lower mobility across generations
The spending habits of the very rich
The shape of the Lorenz curve
quiz.e: Countries with more inequality tend to have less mobility between parents' and children's incomes.

LESSONS.title: Quantitative easing: what central banks do when rates hit zero
LESSONS.hook: When interest rates can fall no further, central banks reach for a stranger tool: creating money to buy bonds. Australia tried it in 2020, with mixed results.

sections.key: Central banks normally steer the economy with short-term interest rates, but those can only fall so far.
