sections.b: In ordinary times a central bank like the Reserve Bank of Australia manages the economy mainly through its cash rate, the overnight interest rate at which banks lend to each other. Cutting it makes borrowing cheaper and encourages spending and investment. But there is a floor. Once rates approach zero, cutting further becomes difficult, because people and banks could simply hold cash, which pays nothing but never charges you either. Economists call this the zero lower bound. Some central banks in Europe and Japan pushed slightly negative rates, but not by much. When a severe downturn hits and rates are already near zero, central banks need other tools. Quantitative easing, usually shortened to QE, is the best known.

sections.key: A central bank creates new reserves and uses them to buy bonds, pushing down longer-term interest rates.
sections.b: Under QE a central bank buys large amounts of financial assets, mainly government bonds, from banks and investors. It pays for them by creating new central bank reserves, electronic money held in the accounts that commercial banks keep at the central bank. No banknotes are printed, despite the popular phrase. The purchases push up bond prices, and because bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, longer-term interest rates fall. Lower long-term rates feed through to mortgages and business loans. Sellers of bonds receive cash they may invest in other assets such as corporate bonds or shares, an effect known as portfolio rebalancing. QE also signals that the central bank intends to keep rates low for a long time.

sections.key: Japan pioneered QE in 2001, and other major central banks adopted it after 2008.
sections.b: Japan was the first to try modern QE. After its asset bubble burst in the early 1990s, the country endured years of weak growth and falling prices. In 2001 the Bank of Japan began buying government bonds to expand bank reserves, a program that ran until 2006 and was later revived on a much larger scale. The global financial crisis made QE mainstream. From late 2008 the US Federal Reserve bought trillions of dollars of government bonds and mortgage-backed securities over several rounds, and the Bank of England began its own program in 2009. The European Central Bank launched large-scale bond buying in 2015. What began as an emergency experiment became a standard part of the toolkit.

sections.key: During the pandemic the RBA cut rates to near zero, targeted bond yields and bought bonds for the first time.
sections.b: Australia avoided QE during the global financial crisis because its interest rates were well above zero. The pandemic changed that. In March 2020 the Reserve Bank cut the cash rate to 0.25 per cent and introduced a target for the yield on three-year government bonds, also 0.25 per cent, promising to buy whatever was needed to hold it there. It also offered banks cheap three-year funding through a Term Funding Facility. In November 2020 it cut the cash rate and yield target to 0.1 per cent and announced a Bond Purchase Program of 100 billion dollars, later extended. Over the following year and a half, purchases under that program eventually totalled roughly 280 billion dollars.

sections.key: Australia's yield target was abandoned abruptly in 2021, damaging the RBA's credibility.
sections.b: Yield control is not new. The US Federal Reserve capped government bond yields during and after the Second World War until 1951, and the Bank of Japan adopted a version in 2016. Australia's target, though, ended awkwardly. As the economy recovered faster than expected in 2021 and inflation began to rise, markets bet that rates would rise sooner than the RBA had suggested. In late October 2021 the bank stopped defending the target, and in early November formally abandoned it. Many borrowers had taken the bank's earlier guidance that rates would likely stay low until 2024 at face value. The bank's own review in 2022 acknowledged that the disorderly exit had damaged its reputation.

sections.h: Did QE work, and at what cost?
sections.key: QE probably helped in crises, but its effects are hard to measure and its side effects are debated.
sections.b: Most central bank research concludes that QE lowered long-term interest rates and helped stabilise markets during crises, especially when markets were in turmoil. Measuring its effect on jobs and growth is much harder, because nobody can rerun history without it. Critics raise several concerns. By pushing up the prices of bonds, shares and property, QE may have widened wealth gaps, since those assets are mostly owned by people who are already wealthy. It can blur the line between monetary policy and government financing. And when interest rates later rose, central banks faced large losses on the bonds they held. The RBA reported negative equity after its losses in 2022, though central banks can keep operating normally in that situation.

quiz.q: What is the zero lower bound?
o: The minimum wage
The limit on how far interest rates can usefully be cut
The lowest possible exchange rate
A legal limit on government debt
quiz.e: Once rates are near zero, further cuts are difficult because people can hold cash instead.

quiz.q: How does a central bank pay for bonds under QE?
o: By printing large quantities of banknotes
By raising taxes
By creating new central bank reserves electronically
By selling gold
quiz.e: QE is funded with newly created reserves held by commercial banks at the central bank.

quiz.q: Which central bank pioneered modern QE in 2001?
o: The Bank of Japan
The Reserve Bank of Australia
The European Central Bank
The Bank of England
quiz.e: Japan began buying bonds to expand reserves in 2001 after years of weak growth and falling prices.

quiz.q: What did the RBA target in March 2020 besides the cash rate?
o: The price of iron ore
The exchange rate with the US dollar
The yield on three-year government bonds
House prices
quiz.e: The RBA set a 0.25 per cent target for three-year government bond yields.

quiz.q: Which is a common criticism of QE?
o: It always causes hyperinflation
It may widen wealth gaps by lifting asset prices
It lowers bond prices
It cannot be used by central banks
quiz.e: Higher prices for shares, bonds and property mainly benefit people who already own those assets.

LESSONS.title: Cane toads: the pest that conquered the north
LESSONS.hook: In 1935 a hundred-odd toads were shipped to Queensland to save the sugar crop. They ignored the beetles they were meant to eat and set off across a continent.

sections.key: Cane toads were brought to Australia in 1935 to control beetles damaging sugar cane.
sections.b: In the early 1930s Queensland's sugar industry had a problem. Grubs of native cane beetles were chewing the roots of the crop, and farmers wanted a weapon. The cane toad, a large, hardy amphibian native to Central and South America, had a reputation for eating pests in plantations elsewhere. In June 1935, 102 toads were brought from Hawaii to a sugar experiment station at Gordonvale, near Cairns. They bred rapidly in captivity, and within months more than two thousand young toads were released around the cane fields of north Queensland. Some scientists of the day warned that releasing an untested predator was reckless. Their warnings were brushed aside. It is now one of the most famous examples of biological control going badly wrong.

sections.key: The toads could not reach the beetles, so they ate almost everything else instead.
sections.b: The plan had a basic flaw. Adult cane beetles spend much of their time up on the tall cane stalks, and their grubs live underground among the roots. Cane toads are heavy, ground-dwelling hunters that cannot climb, and they had little reason to stay in the fields at all. Cane farms offered thin cover and patchy water, while the surrounding countryside offered insects, frogs, small mammals, pet food and almost anything else that would fit in a toad's mouth. There is no good evidence that the toads ever made a meaningful dent in beetle numbers. Farmers eventually turned to chemical pesticides instead. Meanwhile the toads simply kept doing what they do best: eating, breeding and moving on to new ground.

sections.key: Huge clutches of eggs, a tough body and a lack of natural enemies let cane toads spread fast.
sections.b: Cane toads have almost every trait an invader could want. A single female can lay tens of thousands of eggs in one clutch, wrapped in long strings of jelly in still water. Tadpoles develop quickly, and adults tolerate heat, drought and a wide range of habitats, from wetlands to suburban backyards. In their native range, diseases, parasites and predators that have evolved alongside them keep numbers in check. In Australia almost none of those controls existed. Toads spread south into New South Wales and west across the Northern Territory, reaching Western Australia's Kimberley by the late 2000s. They now occupy well over a million square kilometres of northern and eastern Australia, and the western front is still moving.

sections.key: Toads at the invasion front have evolved to move faster, speeding up the spread.
sections.b: When scientists measured the toad invasion, they found something surprising: it was accelerating. In the early decades the front advanced around ten kilometres a year. By the 2000s, toads in the Northern Territory were pushing forward at more than five times that rate. Biologist Rick Shine and his colleagues discovered why. The toads leading the charge had longer legs than those in older populations, and they travelled further each night in straighter lines. The reason is simple selection. The fastest toads arrive first at new ground, where there is plenty of food and few competitors, and they breed with other fast toads. Generation after generation, the front became a population of athletes. It is one of the clearest examples of evolution happening within living memory.

sections.key: Cane toad toxin kills many native predators that have never evolved to cope with it.
sections.b: The real damage comes from the toad's defences. Large glands behind its head, called parotoid glands, hold a poison made of chemicals called bufadienolides, which attack the heart. Every life stage is toxic, including eggs and tadpoles. Predators in the toads' native range have had millions of years to adapt, but Australian predators had never met a toad. Goannas, freshwater crocodiles, northern quolls, some snakes and pet dogs die after biting or swallowing one. When the toad front reaches a new area, populations of some goanna species can crash dramatically. Yet not every native animal is defeated. Some birds, such as crows and kites, learned to flip toads over and eat the safer innards, and native water rats have been seen doing something similar.

sections.key: Rather than eradicate toads, scientists now try to reduce harm and teach predators to avoid them.
sections.b: Nobody has found a way to remove cane toads from Australia, so the focus has shifted to limiting the damage. One clever idea uses the toads' own biology. Researchers found that cane toad tadpoles are strongly attracted to a chemical from toad toxin, because they hunt and eat newly laid toad eggs. Traps baited with that chemical can catch huge numbers of tadpoles while leaving native tadpoles largely alone. Another approach is taste aversion training. Northern quolls and goannas have been fed small toads or toad sausages that make them sick but do not kill them, so they learn to avoid toads before the main invasion arrives. If you catch toads at home, wildlife authorities recommend humane methods, such as cooling them in a fridge and then freezing them.

quiz.q: Why were cane toads brought to Queensland in 1935?
o: To control beetles damaging sugar cane
To control mosquitoes
As exotic pets
To feed native crocodiles
quiz.e: The toads were meant to eat cane beetles, whose grubs were damaging the roots of the sugar crop.

quiz.q: Why did the toads fail to control the beetles?
o: The beetles were poisonous to them
The toads hibernated through beetle season
They could not climb to the adult beetles, and the grubs lived underground
Farmers killed the toads before they could breed
quiz.e: Adult beetles live up on the cane stalks and their grubs are underground, out of reach of a heavy ground-dwelling toad.

quiz.q: Why are toads at the invasion front faster than toads in older populations?
o: They eat a better diet
Warmer weather makes them faster
They are a different species
The fastest toads reach new ground first and breed with each other
quiz.e: Selection favours speed at the front: the fastest arrive first and breed together, so each generation there runs faster.

quiz.q: Where is most of a cane toad's poison stored?
o: In its skin colour
In parotoid glands behind its head
In its tongue
Only in its eggs
quiz.e: The parotoid glands behind the head hold bufadienolide toxins, although every life stage of the toad is toxic.

quiz.q: How do the tadpole traps used against cane toads work?
o: They use bright lights
They poison the whole waterway
They use a lure made from toad toxin, which attracts cane toad tadpoles
They play the sound of male toads calling
quiz.e: Cane toad tadpoles are drawn to a toxin chemical because they hunt toad eggs, so it lures them while largely sparing native tadpoles.

LESSONS.title: Living light: the glow of bioluminescence
LESSONS.hook: In the darkest places on Earth, animals make their own light. They use it to hunt, hide, flirt and even call the police on their attackers.

sections.key: Bioluminescence is light produced by a chemical reaction inside a living thing.
sections.b: Bioluminescence is cold light made by life. In most cases a molecule called a luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped along by an enzyme called a luciferase, and the energy released comes out as a photon rather than as heat. The names come from Lucifer, an old Latin word meaning light-bringer. Different groups of living things have evolved their own versions of these chemicals, which tells scientists that the ability to glow has arisen independently many dozens of times. Some animals make the light themselves. Others, such as many deep-sea fish, house colonies of glowing bacteria in special organs and feed them in return for their light. Either way, the result is remarkably efficient, with very little energy wasted as heat.

sections.key: Most bioluminescent species live in the sea, where it is a common way of life.
sections.b: On land, glowing creatures feel like a rare treat. In the ocean they are everywhere. When researchers surveyed animals in the deep waters off California, they found that roughly three-quarters of the animals they observed could make light. Jellyfish, squid, shrimps, worms and fish all glow. Most marine light is blue or blue-green, because those colours travel furthest through sea water, while reds fade out within the first few metres. Many deep-sea animals cannot even see red light. One group of dragonfish exploits this beautifully. They produce red light from organs near their eyes and can see it themselves, which gives them a private searchlight to spot prey that has no idea it is being illuminated.

sections.key: Some animals glow on their bellies to erase their own shadows, a trick called counter-illumination.
sections.b: In the twilight zone of the ocean, faint light filters down from above. Any animal swimming there casts a dark silhouette that predators below can spot. Many fish, squid and shrimps solve this by lighting up their undersides to match the dim glow overhead, so their outline disappears. This is called counter-illumination. Hatchetfish do it with rows of light organs along their bellies. The Hawaiian bobtail squid does it with bacteria. The squid grows a light organ that it fills with glowing bacteria called Vibrio fischeri, and each morning it expels most of them before regrowing the colony. The animal can even adjust the brightness to match moonlight. It is invisibility achieved by adding light, rather than taking it away.

sections.key: Light can be used as bait, as a warning, or to confuse a predator.
sections.b: The deep-sea anglerfish dangles a glowing lure from a modified fin spine on its head, lit by bacteria, and swallows whatever comes to investigate. Light is also used for defence. Some tiny plankton flash when disturbed, and biologists have proposed a burglar alarm idea: the flash may attract larger predators that attack whatever is attacking the plankton. Certain jellyfish give off pinwheels of light when grabbed, which may serve the same purpose. Other animals use light like a smoke screen. Some deep-sea shrimps and squid squirt out clouds of glowing fluid instead of dark ink, and the vampire squid can release sticky, glowing mucus. A predator lunging at the bright cloud may miss the animal slipping away into the darkness.

sections.key: On land, glowing insects use light to find mates or to trap food.
sections.b: Fireflies are actually beetles, and their flashes are a courtship language. Males flash species-specific patterns as they fly, and females answer from the ground with their own timed signal. Some females take advantage of this. In North America, females of the firefly genus Photuris can mimic the replies of another genus, luring in eager males and eating them. Australia and New Zealand have a very different light show. The glow-worms in caves and damp gullies, such as those at Springbrook in Queensland or Waitomo in New Zealand, are not worms at all but the larvae of fungus gnats. They hang sticky silk threads from the ceiling and glow blue to attract small flying insects, which become trapped and are reeled in.

sections.key: Glowing plankton light up beaches, and glowing proteins have transformed biology.
sections.b: Sometimes the glow comes to the shore. Tiny single-celled plankton called dinoflagellates flash when disturbed, so breaking waves, paddling feet and kayak strokes can light up in electric blue. Beaches in Tasmania, Jervis Bay and many places overseas occasionally put on this display. Some fungi glow too, including Australia's ghost fungus, which shines a faint green on rotting wood at night. Scientists have borrowed nature's lights for their own work. Firefly luciferase is used in laboratories to detect chemical activity, and a green fluorescent protein from a jellyfish became a revolutionary tool for tagging cells and genes. Its discovery and development earned the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A glow first noticed in the sea now helps researchers watch diseases develop.

quiz.q: What usually produces the light in bioluminescence?
o: A chemical reaction involving a luciferin, oxygen and a luciferase
Heat from the animal's body
Electricity stored in the skin
Reflected moonlight
quiz.e: A luciferin reacts with oxygen, helped by the enzyme luciferase, releasing energy as light rather than heat.

quiz.q: Why is most light in the sea blue or blue-green?
o: Animals cannot make other colours
Salt turns light blue
Blue light scares predators
Those colours travel furthest through sea water
quiz.e: Blue and blue-green light travel furthest in sea water, while red fades within the first few metres.

quiz.q: What is counter-illumination?
o: Flashing to warn others of danger
Glowing on the underside to hide your silhouette from below
Using light to attract mates
Squirting glowing ink
quiz.e: By matching the faint light from above, an animal's shadow disappears to predators looking up.

quiz.q: What are the glow-worms of Australian and New Zealand caves?
o: Earthworms with glowing skin
Firefly larvae
Larvae of fungus gnats
A type of glowing snail
quiz.e: They are fungus gnat larvae that glow to lure small insects into sticky silk threads.

quiz.q: What causes the glowing waves seen on some beaches?
o: Tiny plankton called dinoflagellates that flash when disturbed
Radioactive minerals
Phosphorus washing off rocks
Jellyfish stings
quiz.e: Dinoflagellates flash when the water is disturbed, so waves and footsteps light up blue.

LESSONS.title: Elephants: memory, matriarchs and the meaning of death
LESSONS.hook: Elephants live in families led by wise old females, talk in rumbles too low for us to hear, and pay strange attention to their dead.

sections.key: There are three living elephant species: African savanna, African forest and Asian elephants.
sections.b: Most of us grew up learning about two kinds of elephant, African and Asian. Genetic studies have shown that Africa actually holds two distinct species. The African savanna elephant is the largest land animal alive, with big males reaching around four metres at the shoulder and weighing six tonnes or more. The African forest elephant is smaller, with straighter, downward-pointing tusks, and lives in the rainforests of central and west Africa. The two lineages split long ago, and in 2021 the International Union for Conservation of Nature began assessing them separately. The Asian elephant is a different branch again, more closely related to the extinct woolly mammoth than to either African species. It has smaller ears and a domed head with two bumps.

sections.key: Elephant families are led by an older female whose experience can mean life or death.
sections.b: Elephant society is built around females. A family group is usually made up of related mothers, daughters, sisters and their young, led by an older female called the matriarch. Young males leave as they reach adolescence, often in their early to mid teens, and live more solitary lives or join loose groups of other males. Research in Kenya's Amboseli National Park showed why the matriarch matters. Families led by older females were better at telling the calls of familiar elephants from strangers, and responded more appropriately to the roars of lions, reacting most strongly to the more dangerous ones. Older matriarchs also remember routes to water during drought. When poaching kills these leaders, families lose a lifetime of knowledge that cannot easily be replaced.

sections.key: Elephants communicate with deep rumbles, some below the range of human hearing.
sections.b: Elephants trumpet, but much of their conversation is far quieter to our ears. They use deep rumbles, part of which fall into infrasound, frequencies too low for humans to hear. These low sounds travel well over long distances, helping scattered groups keep in touch and males find females ready to mate. Researchers have also found evidence that elephants can detect vibrations travelling through the ground. Their feet and trunks are packed with sensitive nerve endings, and elephants sometimes freeze, lean forward and press a foot down as if listening. The trunk itself is a marvel: a boneless organ of muscle that can pluck a single blade of grass, suck up litres of water or lift a heavy log, and it carries an extraordinary sense of smell.

sections.key: Elephants grow slowly, eat constantly and carry their young for nearly two years.
sections.b: Being an elephant means eating almost all the time. An adult may spend most of the day feeding and can eat well over a hundred kilograms of grass, leaves, bark and fruit, much of which passes through only partly digested. Pregnancy lasts around 22 months, the longest of any land mammal, and the calf is born weighing around a hundred kilograms. It will rely on its mother and her relatives for years, with aunts and older sisters helping to look after it. Elephants can live into their sixties or beyond in the wild. Their size and appetite make them ecosystem engineers. They dig waterholes, open up thick bush and, in the case of forest elephants, spread the seeds of many trees in their dung.

sections.key: Elephants show unusual interest in the bones and bodies of other elephants.
sections.b: Field researchers have long reported that elephants behave strangely around their dead. They may stop, touch a body with their trunks and feet, stand quietly beside it or return to it over several days. Experiments in Amboseli found that elephants showed far more interest in elephant skulls and ivory than in the skulls of other large animals or in pieces of wood. Mothers have been seen carrying or staying close to dead calves. Whether this amounts to grief as humans feel it is still debated, and careful scientists avoid claiming too much. What is clear is that death does not go unnoticed. The old story of elephant graveyards, where elephants go to die, is a myth, though bones can gather near water where weak animals linger.

sections.key: Elephants pass a mirror test, and poaching has even shaped their evolution.
sections.b: Elephants are among the few animals that seem to recognise themselves in a mirror. In 2006 an Asian elephant named Happy at the Bronx Zoo repeatedly touched a painted mark on her head that she could only see in her reflection. Elephants also cooperate on tasks, use branches to swat flies and remember individuals for years. Sadly, humans have shaped them too. Ivory poaching targets animals with tusks, and in Mozambique's Gorongosa National Park heavy poaching during the civil war from 1977 to 1992 left a population with a far higher share of tuskless females. Genetic research published in 2021 confirmed that this was evolution driven by hunting. It is a sobering reminder of how quickly human pressure can change a species.

quiz.q: How many living species of elephant are generally recognised today?
o: Three
Two
Four
One
quiz.e: African savanna, African forest and Asian elephants are now treated as three distinct species.

quiz.q: What did research in Amboseli show about older matriarchs?
o: They are more aggressive to all visitors
They leave the family once they are old
Their families respond more appropriately to threats like lions
They stop communicating with others
quiz.e: Families led by older matriarchs were better at judging which calls and lion roars were genuinely dangerous.

quiz.q: What is infrasound?
o: Sound that only travels underwater
A high-pitched alarm call
Echolocation clicks
Sound too low in frequency for humans to hear
quiz.e: Infrasound is below the range of human hearing, and part of elephants' rumbles fall into it, carrying over long distances.

quiz.q: What is true of the so-called elephant graveyards?
o: They are well-documented sites elephants walk to before dying
They are a myth, though bones may gather near water
They are protected by law in Kenya
They are only used by Asian elephants
quiz.e: There are no special graveyards; bones may accumulate near water where weak animals linger.

quiz.q: Why does Gorongosa National Park have many tuskless female elephants?
o: A disease destroyed their tusks
They were bred that way in zoos
Heavy ivory poaching favoured tuskless animals, driving evolution
Tusks fall off in hot climates
quiz.e: Poaching during the civil war killed tusked elephants, so tuskless ones survived to breed, and genetic work confirmed the shift.

LESSONS.title: Emperor penguins: fathers of the Antarctic winter
LESSONS.hook: While every other bird flees the Antarctic winter, emperor penguins walk into it to breed. The fathers then stand in the dark for two months with an egg on their feet.

sections.key: Emperor penguins are the largest penguins and the only animals that breed on Antarctic sea ice in winter.
sections.b: Emperor penguins stand a little over a metre tall and can weigh more than 30 kilograms when well fed, making them the largest of all living penguins. They live only around Antarctica and spend most of their lives at sea, hunting fish, krill and squid. What makes them unique is their timing. Most Antarctic animals breed in the brief summer, when food is plentiful and temperatures are mild. Emperors do the opposite. As autumn arrives, they march, waddle and toboggan on their bellies across the sea ice to traditional breeding sites, sometimes many kilometres from open water. There, in the coldest, darkest season on the planet, they court, pair up and raise their single chick.

sections.key: The female lays one egg and passes it to the male, then heads to sea to feed.
sections.b: After courtship, around May or June, the female lays a single large egg. She has already fasted for weeks and is depleted, so she must return to the ocean to feed. First, though, the egg must be transferred to her partner, and this is a delicate moment. If the egg rolls onto the ice for more than a short time, it can freeze and the embryo dies. The pair carefully nudge it from her feet to his. The male then balances it on top of his own feet and covers it with a warm, feathered fold of skin called a brood pouch. The female sets off on a long trek back to the open sea, leaving him to guard the egg alone.

sections.key: Male emperors incubate the egg for about two months while eating nothing.
sections.b: For roughly 65 days the male stands with the egg on his feet, through the polar night, in temperatures that can fall below minus 40 degrees Celsius and winds that howl across the ice. He eats nothing during this time. Counting the weeks of courtship before the egg arrived, a male may go without food for around four months, losing a large share of his body weight. He survives by burning the fat he built up at sea and by conserving every scrap of energy, moving as little as possible. It is one of the most extreme fasts of any bird. If his partner is delayed, he can even produce a nourishing secretion from his throat to give the newly hatched chick a first meal.

sections.key: Thousands of penguins huddle together and slowly shuffle so everyone takes a turn in the warmth.
sections.b: Alone, a male emperor would struggle to survive the winter. Together they manage it. In the worst weather, males press tightly into huddles that can contain thousands of birds. Inside a dense huddle the temperature can climb above 30 degrees Celsius, so warm that birds sometimes need to break away to cool down. Huddles are not static. Researchers filming colonies have found that the birds shuffle in small, coordinated steps, sending slow waves through the group, so that the huddle gradually moves and reorganises. Birds on the windy edge work their way inwards while others drift outwards. The result is a remarkably fair system, in which no single bird stays in the warm centre or on the freezing edge for too long.

sections.h: The worst journey in the world
sections.key: Explorers once risked their lives to collect emperor eggs in the middle of winter.
sections.b: The emperors' winter breeding was so mysterious that scientists once took terrible risks to study it. In 1911, during Robert Falcon Scott's Antarctic expedition, three men, Edward Wilson, Henry Bowers and Apsley Cherry-Garrard, set out in the winter darkness to reach the emperor colony at Cape Crozier. They hoped the embryos would reveal clues to how birds evolved from reptiles. In temperatures that dropped below minus 50 degrees Celsius, they man-hauled sledges for weeks, lost their tent in a blizzard and nearly died. They returned with three eggs. Wilson and Bowers later perished with Scott on the return from the South Pole. Cherry-Garrard told the story in his classic book The Worst Journey in the World.

sections.h: Counted from space, threatened by warming
sections.key: Satellites now count emperor colonies, and shrinking sea ice is their greatest threat.
sections.b: Emperor colonies are remote and hard to reach, so scientists now find many of them from space. The birds leave large brown stains of guano on the white ice, visible in satellite images, and high-resolution pictures can even be used to estimate numbers. Surveys like this have revealed colonies no one knew existed. The same technology shows the danger the species faces. Emperors need stable sea ice that lasts from autumn until their chicks grow waterproof feathers in summer. In 2022, early sea ice break-up in one region of west Antarctica led to the likely loss of almost all chicks in several colonies. Because sea ice is shrinking as the climate warms, many scientists warn that emperor numbers could fall steeply this century.

quiz.q: What makes emperor penguins' breeding unusual?
o: They breed on Antarctic sea ice during winter
They breed only on rocky islands
They lay their eggs in the water
They breed every five years
quiz.e: Emperors are unique in breeding through the Antarctic winter on sea ice, rather than in summer.

quiz.q: What happens to the egg after it is laid?
o: The female keeps it in a nest of stones
It is buried in snow
Both parents take turns daily
It is carefully passed to the male, who keeps it on his feet
quiz.e: The pair transfer it to the male, who balances it on his feet under a brood pouch while the female feeds at sea.

quiz.q: About how long does the male incubate the egg?
o: Two weeks
About two months
Six months
Ten days
quiz.e: The male incubates for roughly 65 days without eating, on top of the weeks he has already fasted.

quiz.q: How do huddles stay fair to all the birds?
o: The strongest stay in the middle
Females push males out
Birds shuffle in coordinated steps, so positions slowly rotate
Huddles only form for a few minutes
quiz.e: Small coordinated movements send waves through the huddle, so birds move between the edge and the warm centre.

quiz.q: How do scientists find emperor colonies from space?
o: By spotting guano stains on the ice in satellite images
By tracking radio collars
By detecting their body heat
By listening for their calls
quiz.e: Brown guano stains stand out on white ice, letting satellites locate colonies and help estimate numbers.

LESSONS.title: Hibernation: the art of switching off
LESSONS.hook: Some animals survive hard times by turning their bodies almost all the way down. A few cool themselves to below freezing and still wake up.

sections.key: Hibernation is a controlled shutdown of the body's metabolism, not simply deep sleep.
sections.b: We often say an animal is sleeping through winter, but hibernation is something quite different. A hibernating animal deliberately lowers its metabolism, the rate at which its body burns energy, to a tiny fraction of normal. Its body temperature drops, its heart slows and its breathing becomes slow and irregular. A hibernating ground squirrel's heart, for example, may slow from hundreds of beats a minute to just a handful. Biologists call this state torpor. Hibernation is long torpor lasting weeks or months, used to survive seasons when food is scarce and keeping warm would be expensive. The key point is control. A hibernator is not simply going cold. Its body is actively managing the shutdown and can bring itself back again.

sections.key: Many small animals drop into short bouts of torpor overnight or for a few days.
sections.b: Not every animal shuts down for months. Many small birds and mammals use daily torpor, a shorter, shallower version. Hummingbirds are a famous example. They burn energy so fast while feeding that a cold night without food could kill them, so some species let their body temperature fall sharply overnight, then warm up at dawn. Australia has many champions of this strategy. Small marsupials such as dunnarts and some possums and gliders can enter torpor when food runs short or the weather turns cold. Many of Australia's microbats do the same. Torpor lets these animals pause their energy spending without needing to store enough fat for a whole winter. In a land of unpredictable droughts and cold snaps, flexibility is a powerful advantage.

sections.key: Arctic ground squirrels cool their bodies to below zero without freezing solid.
sections.b: The Arctic ground squirrel of Alaska and northern Canada holds a remarkable record. During hibernation its body temperature can fall below zero degrees Celsius, to almost minus three degrees, the lowest core temperature measured in a mammal. Its body fluids do not freeze, because they are supercooled, staying liquid below the usual freezing point. Even so, the squirrel cannot simply stay that way all winter. Like most small hibernators, it wakes up every week or few, rewarming its body to normal temperature for a short time before dropping again. These arousals burn a large share of its stored energy, and scientists still debate exactly why they are needed, suggesting reasons such as resetting the immune system or restoring the brain.

sections.key: Bears stay quite warm in winter but go months without eating, drinking or passing waste.
sections.b: Bears were once said not to be true hibernators, because their body temperature drops only a few degrees. Today most biologists accept them as hibernators of a special kind. A black bear or brown bear in its den slows its metabolism dramatically while staying relatively warm, which helps a mother give birth and nurse tiny cubs in mid-winter. The most astonishing part is what bears do without. They can go for months without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating. Their bodies recycle waste products into new protein, and they lose surprisingly little bone or muscle despite lying still for so long. Medical researchers study bears closely, hoping to learn lessons that could help bedridden patients or people with kidney disease.

sections.key: Echidnas and the mountain pygmy possum are among Australia's true hibernators.
sections.b: Australia might not seem like hibernation country, but some of its animals do it. Short-beaked echidnas in cooler regions, such as Tasmania and the alpine high country, can hibernate for several months, letting their body temperature fall close to that of the soil around them. The mountain pygmy possum, a small, endangered marsupial found only in the alpine areas of Victoria and New South Wales, hibernates for months beneath the winter snowpack, living among boulder fields. It feasts in spring and summer on Bogong moths, which migrate to the mountains, and builds up fat for the long sleep. Fewer moths in recent years has worried researchers, because the possums depend on that rich food supply to survive winter.

sections.key: Hibernation turns up in unexpected animals and may one day help medicine.
sections.b: Hibernation has surprised scientists more than once. In 1946 naturalist Edmund Jaeger found a common poorwill, a North American nightbird, torpid in a rock crevice in winter, showing that at least one bird could hibernate. In 2004 researchers reported that the fat-tailed dwarf lemur of Madagascar hibernates for months in tree holes, making it the first primate known to do so. These discoveries have sparked serious medical interest. If doctors could safely slow a human's metabolism, it might protect organs during surgery, buy time for trauma or stroke patients, or one day help astronauts on very long journeys. For now that remains research, not reality. Hibernators remind us that bodies can be far more flexible than we assume.

quiz.q: What best describes hibernation?
o: A controlled, long-lasting drop in metabolism and body temperature
A very deep, ordinary sleep
Fainting caused by cold
Simply staying in a burrow
quiz.e: Hibernation is long-lasting torpor, an actively controlled shutdown of metabolism, not just deep sleep.

quiz.q: Why do hummingbirds use daily torpor?
o: To avoid predators
To migrate faster
To save energy on cold nights without food
To digest nectar
quiz.e: Their energy use is so high that a cold night without food could kill them, so they cool down overnight to save energy.

quiz.q: What is remarkable about the Arctic ground squirrel?
o: It never wakes during winter
It hibernates in water
It hibernates for two years
Its body can cool to below zero degrees Celsius without freezing
quiz.e: Its body fluids stay supercooled below zero, the lowest core temperature recorded in a mammal.

quiz.q: What can hibernating bears go without for months?
o: Breathing
Eating, drinking, urinating and defecating
A heartbeat
Any change in body temperature
quiz.e: Bears go months without food, water or passing waste, recycling waste products into protein.

quiz.q: Where does the mountain pygmy possum hibernate?
o: In hollow eucalypts on the coast
In desert sand dunes
Beneath the winter snow in alpine boulder fields
In caves with bats
quiz.e: It lives in the alpine areas of Victoria and New South Wales and hibernates under the snowpack among boulders.

LESSONS.title: The wolves of Yellowstone
LESSONS.hook: When wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, they became the centre of one of ecology's most famous stories. The truth is messier, and more interesting.

sections.key: Some species have effects on their ecosystem far larger than their numbers suggest.
sections.b: In the 1960s American ecologist Robert Paine ran a simple experiment on the rocky shore of Washington State. He repeatedly removed a predatory sea star from one stretch of rocks and left a neighbouring stretch alone. Without the sea star, mussels took over, crowding out many other species, and the diversity of the shore collapsed. Paine called such a species a keystone, after the stone at the top of an arch that holds the rest in place. The idea that predators can control the structure of whole ecosystems, through a chain of effects called a trophic cascade, became hugely influential. Sea otters were found to protect kelp forests by eating sea urchins. Wolves in Yellowstone would become the most famous test case of all.

sections.key: By the 1920s wolves had been deliberately wiped out of Yellowstone National Park.
sections.b: Yellowstone, established in 1872, was the world's first national park, but early managers saw wolves as vermin. Wolves killed livestock on surrounding ranches and preyed on elk and deer, which visitors liked to see. Government hunters shot, trapped and poisoned them, even inside the park. By the mid-1920s, wolves had been eliminated from Yellowstone. Over the following decades, elk numbers rose, and park managers grew concerned about heavy browsing of young aspen, willow and cottonwood trees. At times rangers culled elk themselves. Meanwhile attitudes to predators were changing. Ecologists argued that a park without its top predator was incomplete, and after the wolf was listed as endangered, plans to bring it back gained momentum despite fierce opposition from many ranchers.

sections.key: In 1995 and 1996, wolves captured in Canada were released into Yellowstone.
sections.b: In January 1995, the first grey wolves caught in Alberta were carried into Yellowstone and held in acclimation pens before release. Over 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves from Canada were set free in the park, and more were released in central Idaho. The wolves thrived. Packs formed, pups were born and the population grew quickly, with the number living inside the park settling at roughly one hundred in most years since. Wolves became one of Yellowstone's biggest attractions, and people now travel from around the world to watch them in the Lamar Valley. Scientists radio-collared many animals, making Yellowstone's wolves among the most closely studied large predators on Earth and giving researchers decades of data on what happens when a top predator returns.

sections.key: A popular account says wolves restored trees, beavers and even the shape of rivers.
sections.b: As the wolves settled in, elk numbers on the park's northern range fell sharply, from around 19,000 in the mid-1990s to a fraction of that within two decades. Some researchers reported that willows and aspens were growing taller in places, and beaver colonies increased. A powerful story took shape. Wolves, it was said, not only ate elk but frightened them away from exposed valleys and riverbanks, a landscape of fear. Released from browsing, trees recovered, beavers returned, songbirds followed and even riverbanks stabilised. A short online video in 2014, How Wolves Change Rivers, spread this story to many millions of viewers. It is a beautiful narrative of nature healing itself, and parts of it are supported by real evidence.

sections.key: The strength of Yellowstone's trophic cascade is still debated by researchers.
sections.b: Many ecologists think the popular story is too tidy. Elk declined for several reasons at once, including predation by cougars and bears as well as wolves, hunting by people outside the park and drought. Some studies found that elk did not avoid risky places as strongly as the landscape of fear idea suggested, and that aspen often failed to recover even where wolves were common. Other work found that willow recovery was patchy and modest. One important reason is that when beavers vanished, their dams collapsed, streams cut deeper channels and the water table dropped. Willows on those drier banks struggle regardless of how many elk are around. Researchers still disagree on how much of Yellowstone's change can truly be credited to wolves.

sections.key: Wolves clearly changed Yellowstone, but ecosystems rarely follow a simple chain of cause and effect.
sections.b: Some effects of the wolves are well established. Their kills provide carcasses that feed ravens, eagles, magpies, bears and coyotes through the winter, and wolves have reshaped the behaviour and numbers of other predators. Elk herds are now smaller and behave differently. What remains contested is how far those changes flowed down to trees, rivers and the wider landscape. The debate is not a failure of science but an example of it working, as researchers test an appealing idea against messy data. The broader lesson is valuable. Removing a top predator can change an ecosystem for a century, and putting it back does not simply rewind the clock. Some damage, like the loss of beaver dams, takes its own path to repair.

quiz.q: What did Robert Paine's sea star experiment show?
o: Removing a single predator can collapse the diversity of a whole community
Sea stars are endangered
Mussels eat sea stars
Predators have little effect on ecosystems
quiz.e: Without the sea star, mussels took over and many species disappeared, giving rise to the keystone species idea.

quiz.q: Why were wolves removed from Yellowstone?
o: They were dying of disease
They migrated north naturally
They were moved to zoos for breeding
They were seen as vermin that killed livestock and game
quiz.e: Early managers and hunters deliberately killed wolves as pests, eliminating them by the mid-1920s.

quiz.q: Where did the wolves released into Yellowstone in 1995 and 1996 come from?
o: Alaska
Canada
Mexico
Europe
quiz.e: Thirty-one wolves captured in Canada were released into the park over 1995 and 1996.

quiz.q: What is the 'landscape of fear' idea?
o: That visitors fear wolves
That wolves avoid humans
That elk avoid risky places where wolves hunt, letting plants recover there
That rivers flood when wolves are present
quiz.e: The idea is that fear of wolves changes where elk feed, easing browsing pressure on exposed valleys and riverbanks.

quiz.q: Why have some willows struggled to recover even with fewer elk?
o: Loss of beaver dams lowered the water table and dried out stream banks
Wolves eat willows
Too much rain
Tourists trampled them
quiz.e: Without beaver dams, streams cut deeper and the water table dropped, making banks too dry for willows to thrive.

LESSONS.title: Spider silk: nature's super-material
LESSONS.hook: Weight for weight, some spider silk is stronger than steel and tougher than Kevlar. Spiders make it at room temperature from water and protein, and we still cannot copy it properly.

sections.key: Spider silk is a protein stored as liquid and turned into solid thread as it is pulled out.
sections.b: Every spider makes silk, even species that never build a web. Silk is made of proteins called spidroins, produced in glands inside the abdomen and stored as a thick liquid. As the spider draws it out through tiny nozzles called spinnerets, the liquid passes along a narrowing duct. Changes in acidity and water content, combined with the stretching force of pulling, cause the protein molecules to line up and lock together into a solid fibre. Remarkably, the spider usually pulls the silk out with its legs or by its own weight as it drops, rather than squirting it. The whole process happens at normal temperature, using water as the solvent, while human factories making strong fibres often need high heat and harsh chemicals.

sections.key: A single orb-weaving spider can make several different silks for different jobs.
sections.b: Orb-weaving spiders, the ones that build classic wheel-shaped webs, are the master chemists. A single spider can have up to seven types of silk glands, each producing a different material. Dragline silk, used for the web's frame and the safety line a spider trails behind it, is extremely strong. The sticky capture spiral is made from a much stretchier silk coated with glue droplets, so that a fast-flying insect is caught and slowed rather than bouncing off. Other silks are used to wrap prey, to cement threads to surfaces and to build protective cases for eggs. Each one has its own balance of strength and stretch. Together they make a web that is light, cheap to build and surprisingly good at absorbing impacts.

sections.key: Dragline silk combines strength and stretch, making it exceptionally tough for its weight.
sections.b: The claim that spider silk is stronger than steel is often repeated, so it is worth being precise. Steel and high-quality dragline silk have broadly similar strength per thickness, but silk is far lighter, so weight for weight silk comes out ahead. Its real superpower, however, is toughness, the amount of energy a material can absorb before breaking. Because dragline silk can both resist pulling and stretch a good deal, it absorbs more energy than Kevlar, the fibre used in protective vests. The toughest silk known comes from Darwin's bark spider of Madagascar, described in 2010. It builds enormous webs over rivers, anchored by bridge lines that can stretch around 25 metres across the water, the largest orb webs known.

sections.key: Young spiders and some adults travel huge distances by floating on silk threads.
sections.b: Silk lets spiders do something surprising: fly. In a behaviour called ballooning, a spider climbs to a high point, raises its abdomen and releases fine threads into the air until it lifts off. Spiders have been found drifting thousands of metres up and landing on ships far out at sea, which helps explain how they are among the first animals to colonise new islands. For a long time scientists assumed ballooning depended only on wind. Research published in 2018 showed that spiders also respond to the natural electric field in the atmosphere, which can provide some lift to the charged silk. In parts of Australia, mass ballooning occasionally blankets paddocks in shimmering silk, a phenomenon sometimes nicknamed angel hair.

sections.h: A cape made by a million spiders
sections.key: Spider silk can be woven, but harvesting it is painstaking because spiders cannot be farmed like silkworms.
sections.b: People have long dreamed of spider silk cloth, but there is a problem. Spiders are territorial and often cannibalistic, so they cannot be packed together like silkworms. A famous project in Madagascar showed what it takes. Textile maker Simon Peers and designer Nicholas Godley had workers collect more than a million golden orb-weaver spiders over several years, gently draw silk from each one using a hand-cranked device, then return them to the wild. The resulting naturally golden textiles, including a cape displayed at London's Victoria and Albert Museum in 2012, are among the rarest fabrics in the world. Long before that, fine spider silk was used as crosshairs in optical instruments such as telescope and gun sights, because it was thin, strong and even.

sections.key: Engineers have produced spider silk proteins in other organisms, but matching the real thing remains difficult.
sections.b: Since spiders cannot be farmed, scientists have tried to make spider silk without them. Researchers have inserted spider silk genes into bacteria, yeast, silkworms and plants, and in one well-known project, into goats whose milk contained silk proteins. Making the protein turns out to be the easier half of the problem. Spinning it into fibre as good as a spider's has proven very hard, because the spider's duct performs its chemistry and stretching with remarkable precision. Some companies have launched products using artificial silk proteins, but none yet matches natural dragline silk at large scale. Possible future uses include medical sutures, artificial ligaments, lightweight protective gear and biodegradable materials. For now, the humble garden spider still out-engineers the laboratory.

quiz.q: How does liquid silk protein become solid thread?
o: Chemical changes in the duct plus the pulling force line up the proteins
It is heated inside the spider
It dries in sunlight
It reacts with the air like glue
quiz.e: Changes in acidity and water, combined with stretching as it is drawn out, make the proteins lock into a solid fibre.

quiz.q: Why is the capture spiral of an orb web made from stretchy silk?
o: It is cheaper to make
It reflects ultraviolet light
So insects are caught and slowed rather than bouncing off
It lasts longer in rain
quiz.e: Stretchy silk with glue droplets absorbs the impact of a fast insect so it sticks instead of breaking free.

quiz.q: What is the main superpower of dragline silk compared with Kevlar?
o: Heat resistance
It is magnetic
It never stretches
Toughness: it absorbs more energy before breaking
quiz.e: Silk combines strength and stretch, so it absorbs more energy than Kevlar before breaking.

quiz.q: What did 2018 research add to our understanding of ballooning?
o: Spiders flap their legs to fly
Spiders can respond to the atmosphere's electric field, which can help lift them
Only adult spiders balloon
Ballooning happens only at night
quiz.e: Researchers showed spiders sense electric fields that can provide lift, not just wind.

quiz.q: Why can't spiders be farmed like silkworms?
o: They die in captivity within hours
Their silk is poisonous
They are territorial and often cannibalistic
It is illegal everywhere
quiz.e: Crowded spiders attack and eat each other, so silk must be collected from individual spiders by hand.

LESSONS.title: Termite mounds: cities without architects
LESSONS.hook: Millions of tiny, mostly blind insects build towers taller than a person, without plans or a boss. The way those towers breathe has even fooled scientists.

sections.key: Termites are relatives of cockroaches that live in highly organised colonies.
sections.b: Australians often call termites white ants, but they are not ants at all. Genetic studies show they are a specialised group of cockroaches that became social. Like ants and bees, they live in colonies with a strict division of labour. A king and queen found the colony and produce the offspring, workers gather food and build, and soldiers defend the nest, some with huge jaws, others with snouts that squirt sticky chemicals. Unlike ants, termite workers include both males and females, and young termites grow gradually rather than passing through a pupa stage. In large colonies of some African species, the queen's abdomen swells to an enormous size, and she may lay thousands of eggs a day for years.

sections.key: Termites live on wood and grass, which they digest with help from microbes.
sections.b: Termites have a talent few animals share: they can live on wood, dead grass and other tough plant material. Cellulose, the main ingredient of plant cell walls, is very hard to break down. Termites manage it with help from partners in their guts, including bacteria and, in some groups, single-celled organisms that digest the fibres. Some African and Asian termites go further and farm. Species of Macrotermes carry chewed plant material into chambers inside their mounds, where they grow a special fungus on it, then eat the fungus and partly digested material. By recycling dead plant matter, termites play a role in hot, dry ecosystems similar to that of earthworms in cooler, wetter ones, returning nutrients to the soil and loosening it.

sections.key: Mounds emerge from simple rules followed by individual termites, a process called stigmergy.
sections.b: No termite knows what the finished mound will look like. Most workers are blind, and none is in charge. So how do they build such complex structures? In the 1950s French biologist Pierre-Paul Grassé proposed an idea he called stigmergy. Each insect responds to the work already done around it. A termite drops a mud pellet laced with a scent, and that scent makes other termites more likely to drop their pellets in the same spot. Small piles grow into pillars, pillars bend towards each other and arches form. Local cues such as humidity, airflow and carbon dioxide also guide where they dig and build. The grand structure emerges from millions of tiny decisions, with no plan anywhere in the colony.

sections.h: Compass mounds of the Top End
sections.key: In the Northern Territory, magnetic termites build flat mounds aligned north to south.
sections.b: Some of the world's most striking mounds are in northern Australia. In Litchfield National Park, near Darwin, fields of thin, slab-like mounds stand like gravestones, all aligned roughly north to south. They are built by so-called magnetic termites. The name refers to the alignment, which looks as if the termites were using a compass. Their broad faces catch the gentle morning and late-afternoon sun, while the thin edge faces the fierce midday sun, which helps keep the mound's temperature more stable through the day. Experiments have suggested the termites can sense the Earth's magnetic field. Nearby, the giant cathedral mounds of other termite species can tower several metres high, among the largest structures built by any animal apart from humans.

sections.key: Mounds were long thought to work like chimneys, but research shows a more complex, lung-like system.
sections.b: A big colony uses lots of oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and heat, so its mound must exchange air with the outside. For decades the textbook explanation was a kind of chimney: warm air from the colony rises up a central shaft and is drawn out, pulling fresh air in. Later work, notably by physiologist J. Scott Turner and colleagues, found that this was too simple. Many mounds are closed structures with porous walls, more like a lung than a chimney. Research has shown that daily temperature swings, with the mound's outer walls heating and cooling faster than its core, drive air to circulate through its channels, while wind gusts also help push gases through the walls. Scientists are still refining the details.

sections.key: A building in Zimbabwe borrowed ideas from termite mounds to save energy.
sections.b: Termite mounds have long fascinated architects. The best-known example is the Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe, a large office and shopping complex completed in 1996. Architect Mick Pearce, working with engineers, designed it to stay cool without conventional air conditioning, using thick heavy walls that store heat, fans that move cool night air through the building and chimneys that release warm air. It uses far less energy for cooling than comparable buildings. There is an irony here: the design drew on the chimney model of termite ventilation, which biologists have since revised. Nature still holds plenty of lessons, though. In Brazil, scientists reported in 2018 a vast field of termite mounds covering an area around the size of Great Britain, some estimated to be about four thousand years old.

quiz.q: What are termites most closely related to?
o: Cockroaches
Ants
Bees
Beetles
quiz.e: Despite the nickname white ants, genetic studies show termites are social cockroaches.

quiz.q: How do Macrotermes termites get food from plant material?
o: They catch insects that eat the plants
They store honey
They drink sap from roots
They farm a fungus on chewed plant material inside the mound
quiz.e: They bring plant material into fungus chambers, grow a special fungus and then eat it.

quiz.q: What is stigmergy?
o: A queen termite giving building orders
Individuals responding to work already done, so structure emerges without a plan
A type of termite poison
The chemical that hardens mud
quiz.e: Each termite reacts to cues like scented mud pellets, and the mound emerges from millions of local decisions.

quiz.q: Why are magnetic termite mounds aligned north to south?
o: To follow underground water
To block prevailing winds
To catch gentle morning and evening sun while presenting a thin edge to the midday sun
To mark colony borders
quiz.e: The alignment helps keep the mound's temperature more stable by limiting midday heating.

quiz.q: How does current research suggest many termite mounds ventilate?
o: Through daily temperature swings and wind driving air through porous walls, more like a lung
Like a simple chimney with a constant updraft
Termites fan air with their wings
They do not need ventilation
quiz.e: Work by Turner and others showed mounds act more like lungs, with daily heating and cooling plus wind moving air.

LESSONS.title: Island evolution: giants, dwarfs and the dodo
LESSONS.hook: Strand animals on an island and strange things happen. Elephants shrink, rats grow huge and birds forget how to fly.

sections.key: Islands isolate living things, letting evolution run off in unusual directions.
sections.b: Islands have taught biologists more about evolution than almost any other place. When a few plants or animals reach a remote island by drifting, flying or being blown off course, they find themselves cut off from their relatives, often with few competitors and no large predators. Over many generations they can change dramatically. Charles Darwin's visit to the Galapagos Islands in 1835 helped shape his thinking, and Alfred Russel Wallace developed similar ideas while exploring the islands of the Malay Archipelago. Because islands are small, separate and often young, scientists can compare populations on neighbouring islands like repeated experiments. Patterns appear again and again around the world, from the Mediterranean to the Pacific, suggesting that island life pushes evolution in some predictable ways.

sections.key: Galapagos finches show how one ancestor can split into many species, and how beaks change fast.
sections.b: The finches of the Galapagos are the classic example of adaptive radiation, in which one ancestral species spreads into many forms that suit different ways of life. Over the past two million years or so, the descendants of a single colonising group evolved into more than a dozen species with beaks shaped for crushing seeds, probing cactus flowers, catching insects or even drinking the blood of seabirds. Biologists Peter and Rosemary Grant studied the finches of the tiny island of Daphne Major for decades. After a severe drought in 1977, when only large, hard seeds remained, birds with bigger beaks survived better, and the next generation had measurably larger beaks on average. Evolution, they showed, could be seen and measured within a few years.

sections.key: On islands, large animals often shrink while small animals often grow larger.
sections.b: Biologists have noticed a broad tendency nicknamed the island rule. Large mammals stranded on islands often become smaller over generations, perhaps because food is limited and there are fewer predators to outgrow. Small animals such as rodents often become larger, perhaps because they no longer need to hide from predators and face less competition. The fossil record is full of examples. Dwarf elephants, some about the size of a large pig, once lived on Mediterranean islands including Sicily, Malta and Crete. On the Indonesian island of Flores, there were dwarf relatives of elephants alongside giant rats. The rule is a tendency rather than a law, and scientists still debate how consistent it is, but the examples are striking.

sections.key: A small human species lived on Flores, and its origins are still debated.
sections.b: In 2003 researchers excavating Liang Bua cave on Flores found the skeleton of an adult human relative who stood about a metre tall. The species was named Homo floresiensis and quickly nicknamed the hobbit. Its brain was about the size of a chimpanzee's, yet stone tools were found in the same cave layers. Later work dated the skeletal remains to between roughly 100,000 and 60,000 years ago. How the hobbits came to be so small is still debated. One idea is that they descended from Homo erectus and shrank under island conditions, like the island's elephants. Another is that they came from an older, already small-bodied lineage. Either way, Flores shows that human evolution, too, was shaped by islands.

sections.key: Without predators, island birds often lose flight, which leaves them defenceless when people arrive.
sections.b: Flying is expensive. It requires big muscles and a light, demanding body. On islands without ground predators, many birds evolved to give it up. The dodo of Mauritius was a large, flightless relative of pigeons, whose closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon. New Zealand, with no native land mammals other than bats, became a kingdom of birds, including the giant moa, the kiwi and the kakapo, a heavy, flightless, nocturnal parrot. Losing flight was a sensible adaptation until humans arrived with rats, cats, pigs and hunting. The dodo was gone within a century of Dutch sailors landing in 1598, with the last widely accepted sighting in 1662. The moa vanished within a few centuries of people reaching New Zealand.

sections.key: Islands hold a large share of the world's recent extinctions, and also its best rescue stories.
sections.b: Island species often evolve without defences against newcomers, so they are especially vulnerable. Most recorded animal extinctions in the past five centuries have been island species, many caused by introduced rats, cats and other invaders. Australia has a famous case. On Lord Howe Island, a large, flightless stick insect disappeared after black rats came ashore from a shipwreck in 1918. Decades later, in 2001, researchers found a tiny surviving population on Ball's Pyramid, a sheer volcanic spire in the ocean nearby. Captive breeding programs have since raised many more. In 2019 a major operation began to eradicate rodents from Lord Howe, opening the possibility of returning the insect home. Islands show both how easily species are lost and how they can be saved.

quiz.q: What did Peter and Rosemary Grant observe after the 1977 drought on Daphne Major?
o: The next generation had larger beaks on average
All finches died
Finches stopped breeding for ten years
Beaks became smaller
quiz.e: With only large, hard seeds left, bigger-beaked birds survived better and passed on larger beaks.

quiz.q: According to the island rule, what tends to happen to large mammals on islands?
o: They grow larger
They become flightless
They become smaller over generations
They stay exactly the same
quiz.e: Large mammals often shrink on islands, as seen in the dwarf elephants of the Mediterranean and Flores.

quiz.q: Which statement about Homo floresiensis is accurate?
o: It was a modern human with a disease
Its small size is fully explained and agreed upon
It lived on Madagascar
It was about a metre tall, and scientists still debate how it became so small
quiz.e: The species stood about a metre tall, and its origins, whether through island dwarfing or an older small lineage, are still debated.

quiz.q: What was the dodo's closest living relative?
o: The emu
The Nicobar pigeon
The kakapo
The kiwi
quiz.e: The dodo was a giant, flightless pigeon, and its closest living relative is the Nicobar pigeon.

quiz.q: Where was the Lord Howe Island stick insect rediscovered?
o: In a museum drawer
In Tasmania
On Ball's Pyramid, a volcanic spire near Lord Howe
In New Zealand
quiz.e: In 2001 a tiny population was found clinging on at Ball's Pyramid, decades after rats wiped it out on Lord Howe.

LESSONS.title: Symbiosis: the partnerships that built life
LESSONS.hook: Every cell in your body contains descendants of ancient bacteria. Life on Earth is less a war of all against all than a tangle of deals, partnerships and double-crosses.

sections.key: Symbiosis means close, long-term living together, from mutual benefit to outright parasitism.
sections.b: In 1879 the German botanist Anton de Bary used the word symbiosis to describe different organisms living together. Biologists today usually divide such relationships by who benefits. In mutualism both partners gain, as when bees pollinate flowers while collecting nectar. In commensalism one partner benefits while the other is barely affected, such as barnacles riding on a whale. In parasitism one partner gains at the other's expense. These categories are useful, but nature rarely respects neat boxes. A relationship can shift with conditions, becoming beneficial in one setting and harmful in another, and partners are always under pressure to take a little more than they give. Symbiosis is best seen as a spectrum of bargains, constantly renegotiated through evolution.

sections.key: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria that were engulfed long ago.
sections.b: The most important partnership in the history of life happened well over a billion years ago. A single-celled organism took in a bacterium, and instead of digesting it, the two came to depend on each other. That bacterium became the mitochondrion, the structure that powers our cells using oxygen. Later, an early cell took in a photosynthetic bacterium, which became the chloroplast in plants and algae. In the 1960s American biologist Lynn Margulis championed this idea, called endosymbiosis, against widespread scepticism. The evidence is now overwhelming. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own small circular DNA, like bacteria, their own bacteria-like ribosomes and double membranes, and they divide by splitting in two. Complex life, including us, is a partnership at its core.

sections.key: Lichens and reef-building corals are partnerships between very different organisms.
sections.b: A lichen looks like a single organism, but it is a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, either an alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus provides structure and shelter, and the partner makes food from sunlight. Together they can colonise bare rock, tree bark and frozen tundra where neither could live alone. In 2016 researchers revealed that many lichens also contain a yeast, a third partner that had gone unnoticed for over a century of study. Reef-building corals have a similar arrangement. Their cells house microscopic algae that photosynthesise and pass much of their food to the coral. When water becomes too hot, the partnership breaks down and the coral expels the algae, turning white in what is known as coral bleaching.

sections.key: Figs and fig wasps depend on each other entirely in one of nature's tightest partnerships.
sections.b: A fig is not really a fruit at first but an enclosed cluster of tiny flowers turned inwards. Only one creature can pollinate them: a tiny fig wasp, usually specialised to one or a few fig species. A female wasp squeezes in through a narrow opening at the tip of the fig, often losing her wings in the process. Inside, she pollinates some flowers and lays eggs in others, then dies. Her offspring develop in the fig, mate, and the females emerge carrying pollen to find a new fig. Neither partner can reproduce without the other, and the relationship is thought to be tens of millions of years old. With hundreds of fig species worldwide, figs feed many rainforest animals, making this partnership vital far beyond itself.

sections.key: Partnerships invite cheating, and nature has many cheats and mimics.
sections.b: On coral reefs, the bluestreak cleaner wrasse runs cleaning stations where larger fish, including predators, line up to have parasites and dead skin removed. The client gets cleaned, and the wrasse gets a meal. But cleaners would often prefer to nibble the client's protective mucus, which is a form of cheating. Clients respond by chasing cheats or swimming away to another station, and research has shown that cleaners behave better when other fish are watching, as though their reputation matters. There are also outright fakes. A species of sabre-toothed blenny closely mimics the cleaner's colour and dance, then darts in to bite chunks out of unsuspecting fish. Every successful partnership creates an opening for someone to exploit it.

sections.key: In parts of Africa, honeyguide birds and human honey hunters cooperate.
sections.b: One of the most remarkable partnerships involves our own species. In parts of Africa, a bird called the greater honeyguide leads people to wild bees' nests. The bird cannot easily break into a hive, but it can eat the wax left behind once humans have opened it. Honey hunters among the Yao people of northern Mozambique summon honeyguides with a special trilling call. A study published in 2016 showed that honeyguides responded to this traditional call far more than to other sounds, and that people who used it were much more likely to be led to a nest. Later research found that honeyguides in different regions respond best to the local human call. It is a genuine two-way relationship between a wild animal and people.

sections.key: Symbiotic microbes shape our health, and one is being used to fight dengue fever.
sections.b: Each of us carries trillions of bacteria, mostly in the gut. You may have heard that bacteria outnumber your own cells ten to one. That figure is a myth based on a rough old estimate; a 2016 study concluded the ratio is closer to one to one. These microbes still matter, helping to digest food, train the immune system and fend off harmful germs. Symbiotic microbes can also be put to work. A bacterium called Wolbachia lives inside many insect species. Researchers found that when it is introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, it reduces their ability to transmit viruses such as dengue. The World Mosquito Program, which began in Australia, released Wolbachia mosquitoes in north Queensland, where local dengue outbreaks have since become very rare.

quiz.q: In which kind of symbiosis do both partners benefit?
o: Mutualism
Parasitism
Commensalism
Predation
quiz.e: Mutualism benefits both partners, like bees and flowers; commensalism helps one without much effect on the other.

quiz.q: Which evidence supports the idea that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria?
o: They are found only in plants
They are made of cellulose
They can live outside cells today
They have their own circular DNA and divide by splitting
quiz.e: Mitochondria carry their own small circular DNA, bacteria-like ribosomes and double membranes, and divide by splitting in two.

quiz.q: What happens to a coral during bleaching?
o: It grows a white shell
It expels the algae that live in its cells
It is covered in sand
It begins to photosynthesise itself
quiz.e: When water is too hot, the coral-algae partnership breaks down and the coral expels its algae, turning white.

quiz.q: What do sabre-toothed blennies do?
o: They clean parasites from larger fish
They pollinate sea grass
They mimic cleaner wrasse, then bite chunks out of fish
They guard coral from predators
quiz.e: The blenny looks and moves like a cleaner wrasse but bites its victims instead of cleaning them.

quiz.q: What is true of the claim that bacteria outnumber human cells ten to one?
o: It is a myth; recent estimates put the ratio closer to one to one
It is accurate
The ratio is actually a hundred to one
Humans have no bacteria in the gut
quiz.e: A 2016 study estimated roughly equal numbers of bacterial and human cells, debunking the old ten-to-one figure.

LESSONS.title: The ring of Gyges: would you be good if no one could see?
LESSONS.hook: A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible, and within days he has seduced a queen and murdered a king. Plato used the story to ask the most uncomfortable question in ethics.

sections.key: Plato’s Republic tells of a shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility and uses it to seize a kingdom.
sections.b: Early in Plato’s Republic, written around 375 BC, a young man named Glaucon tells a story. A shepherd called Gyges is tending his flock in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, when an earthquake splits the ground. Climbing down into the chasm, he finds a hollow bronze horse with little doors in its side. Inside lies the body of a giant, wearing nothing but a gold ring. Gyges takes it. Later, sitting with other shepherds, he idly turns the ring’s setting towards his palm and discovers that he has vanished. Turning it back makes him visible again. He wastes no time. He gets himself sent to the palace as a messenger, seduces the queen, kills the king with her help and takes the throne.

sections.key: Glaucon argues that people are only good because they fear being caught.
sections.b: Glaucon, who was in real life one of Plato’s older brothers, tells the story to make a point. Imagine, he says, two such rings: one given to a just man and one to an unjust man. He bets that both would end up behaving the same way, taking whatever they wanted, slipping into houses and doing as they pleased. No one, he suggests, is so iron willed that they would keep their hands off other people’s property when they could take it with no risk at all. If that is right, then justice is not something we value for itself. It is a compromise. We agree not to harm each other only because we are afraid of being harmed, and we act fairly only because we might be seen.

sections.key: Glaucon sharpens the test by stripping the just person of every reward.
sections.b: Glaucon then pushes further. Picture the most perfectly unjust person, he says, someone so skilled at wrongdoing that they enjoy a spotless reputation for goodness. They grow rich, marry well and are admired by all. Now picture the most perfectly just person, but give them a reputation for wickedness. They are whipped, imprisoned and finally executed, all while remaining honest to the end. Which life is better? Glaucon’s brother Adeimantus joins in, pointing out that parents and poets praise justice mostly for the good name and rewards it brings, not for itself. The brothers ask Socrates to prove that being just is better for the person who is just, even when every outside reward has been stripped away.

sections.key: Plato’s reply is that justice is a kind of health of the soul.
sections.b: Answering the challenge takes up most of the rest of the Republic. Socrates argues that the soul has three parts: reason, which seeks truth; spirit, which feels pride, anger and honour; and appetite, which craves food, sex and money. In a just person, reason rules, spirit supports it, and appetite is kept in its place. In an unjust person, the parts are at war, and appetite or ambition takes control. The unjust ruler with the magic ring, on this view, is not free at all. He is a slave to cravings that can never be satisfied, restless, suspicious and alone. Justice, Plato concludes, is to the soul what health is to the body, and no amount of wealth makes up for a sick soul.

sections.key: A different and older version of the Gyges story appears in the historian Herodotus.
sections.b: Gyges may have been a real person. A king of Lydia by that name ruled in the 7th century BC and founded a dynasty that later included the famously wealthy Croesus. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, tells a very different tale of how he came to power.
