sections.key: Henry Molaison had severe epilepsy that medicines of the day could not control.
sections.b: Henry Molaison was born in 1926 in Connecticut. As a child he began having seizures, and by his twenties they had become so frequent and severe that he could barely work or live normally. Some accounts link the epilepsy to a bicycle accident when he was young, though the cause was never certain, and there was a family history of epilepsy too. Anti seizure drugs did not help enough. In 1953, aged 27, he was referred to the neurosurgeon William Beecher Scoville, who believed that removing a region deep in the temporal lobes might stop the seizures. Experimental brain surgery was more common and less cautious in that era, and Henry and his family agreed to the operation.

sections.key: Scoville removed tissue from both sides of the brain, including most of the hippocampus.
sections.b: Scoville removed parts of the medial temporal lobe on both sides of Henry's brain. This included most of a curled structure called the hippocampus, along with the amygdala and nearby tissue. In one sense the operation worked: Henry's seizures became much less severe. But the cost became clear almost immediately. He could not remember the hospital staff he saw every day. He could not find his way to the bathroom. He would read the same magazine repeatedly with fresh interest. His intelligence, his personality, his language and much of his memory of his earlier life were intact. What he had lost was the ability to turn new experiences into lasting memories. Scoville later warned other surgeons never to repeat the procedure on both sides.

sections.key: Milner showed that memory depends on specific brain structures, not the whole brain equally.
sections.b: From 1955, a young psychologist from Montreal named Brenda Milner began testing Henry. In 1957 she and Scoville published a paper describing his case, and it overturned a common belief of the time: that memory was spread evenly across the brain, so that no single area was essential. Henry's case showed that the hippocampus and its neighbours were crucial for forming new long term memories of facts and events. Yet it also showed they were not the store where old memories lived, because Henry could recall much of his childhood. To protect his privacy, he was known in hundreds of scientific papers only by his initials, H.M. Few people outside research knew his name until he died.

sections.key: Henry could learn new skills without remembering that he had ever practised them.
sections.b: Milner's most famous experiment asked Henry to trace a star shape while seeing his hand and the paper only in a mirror, an awkward task that almost everyone finds frustrating at first. Over three days of practice, Henry got steadily better, just like anyone else. But each day he insisted he had never done the task before, and he was surprised at how well he did it. This was a profound result. It showed that there is more than one kind of memory. Remembering facts and events, called declarative memory, depended on the structures Henry had lost. Learning skills and habits, called procedural memory, relied on other brain systems that were still working.

sections.key: Henry's short term memory worked, so he could hold a conversation as long as nothing distracted him.
sections.b: Henry could repeat a list of numbers or keep a thought in mind for a short while, so long as he kept rehearsing it. His short term or working memory was largely normal. He could follow a conversation and be polite and witty. But once his attention shifted, the information was gone. The neuroscientist Suzanne Corkin, who studied him for over four decades, said he never learned to recognise her, although he sometimes had a vague sense she was familiar. Over the years a few scraps did stick. He could draw a rough floor plan of a house he moved into after the surgery, and he picked up fragments of later events. But almost every day began, in effect, in the 1950s.

sections.key: Henry was usually calm and good humoured, and he knew in a general way that his memory was poor.
sections.b: What was it like to be Henry? He seemed to understand, in a general way, that he had trouble remembering. He once said that every day was alone in itself, whatever enjoyment he had and whatever sorrow. He was often described as gentle, patient and fond of crossword puzzles, which drew on vocabulary he had learned before the operation. When he was told of a death in his family, he grieved, but the grief could return as fresh news. He lived with his parents and later in a care home, and took part in research willingly for most of his life. Many scientists who worked with him have written of their gratitude and of the ethical questions his case raises about consent.

sections.h: A brain shared with the world
sections.key: After Henry died in 2008, his brain was sliced into thousands of thin sections and made available to researchers.
sections.b: Henry Molaison died in December 2008, aged 82. With consent arranged years earlier, his brain was preserved, scanned and then, in 2009, cut into 2,401 extremely thin slices at the University of California, San Diego, in a procedure streamed online. The slices were digitised so that researchers anywhere could examine exactly what had been removed and what remained. His legacy is enormous. Modern ideas about the different types of memory, the role of the hippocampus, and how memories are consolidated all trace back to him. He never remembered any of the scientists who studied him, but generations of students now learn his name. It is a strange and moving kind of immortality for a man who lived in the present.

quiz.q: What was the main thing Henry lost after his 1953 operation?
o: His intelligence and language
Memories of his childhood
The ability to form new long term memories
His ability to recognise faces from before 1953
quiz.e: His intelligence, language and many older memories survived. What he lost was the ability to lay down new lasting memories of facts and events.

quiz.q: What common belief did Henry's case challenge?
o: That memory is spread evenly across the whole brain
That the brain has two hemispheres
That epilepsy cannot be treated
That short term memory exists
quiz.e: Henry showed that specific structures, especially the hippocampus, are crucial for forming new memories, contradicting the idea that memory had no special location.

quiz.q: What did the mirror drawing experiment reveal?
o: Henry could not improve at any new task
Skills can be learned without any memory of practising them
Henry remembered each practice session clearly
Mirror tasks damage memory
quiz.e: Henry improved over three days yet denied ever doing the task. Skill learning (procedural memory) works through different systems from memory for events.

quiz.q: Why could Henry hold a conversation?
o: His long term memory recovered after a year
Someone repeated everything for him
His short term memory was largely normal while he stayed focused
He read from prepared notes
quiz.e: His working memory functioned, so he could hold information briefly while rehearsing it; it vanished once his attention shifted.

quiz.q: What happened to Henry's brain after he died?
o: It was buried with him
It was cut into thousands of thin slices and digitised for research
It was kept secret by one laboratory
It was found to be completely normal
quiz.e: In 2009 it was sliced into 2,401 sections and digitised so researchers worldwide could study exactly what had been removed.

LESSONS.title: Split brain: two minds in one head?
LESSONS.hook: When surgeons cut the bridge between the brain's two halves, patients seemed perfectly normal. Then clever experiments revealed that each half could know things the other did not.

sections.key: The corpus callosum is a thick band of around 200 million nerve fibres linking the brain's two halves.
sections.b: Your brain has two cerebral hemispheres, left and right, which look like near mirror images. They are joined by several bundles of fibres, the largest of which is the corpus callosum, a band containing roughly 200 million nerve fibres. It lets the two halves share information constantly. Each hemisphere mainly handles the opposite side of the body: the left hemisphere controls the right hand and receives information from the right side of what you see, and the right hemisphere does the reverse. In most people, the left hemisphere also does most of the work of producing speech. These facts sound dry, but put them together with one unusual operation and you get some of the strangest findings in all of psychology.

sections.key: From the 1940s, surgeons cut the corpus callosum to stop severe seizures spreading across the brain.
sections.b: Some forms of epilepsy involve electrical storms that start in one area and sweep across both hemispheres. In the 1940s and again in the 1960s, surgeons tried cutting the corpus callosum in patients whose seizures could not be controlled any other way. The idea was to stop a seizure in one half from spreading to the other. For many patients it helped. More surprising was how ordinary they seemed afterwards. They could talk, walk, joke and go back to daily life. Early observers concluded that the corpus callosum might not do very much at all. It took careful laboratory testing to show that something extraordinary had changed beneath the calm surface.

sections.key: By sending information to only one hemisphere, researchers revealed that each side could know things alone.
sections.b: In the 1960s the neurobiologist Roger Sperry and his student Michael Gazzaniga, working at Caltech, designed a clever test. A patient stared at a dot in the centre of a screen while a word or picture was flashed briefly to the left or right of it, too quickly for the eyes to move. An image on the right went only to the left hemisphere, and the patient could easily name it. An image on the left went only to the right hemisphere, and the patient typically said they had seen nothing. Yet if asked to reach behind a screen with the left hand, controlled by the right hemisphere, they could pick out the very object shown. One half knew; the half that did the talking did not.

sections.key: The research showed real differences between the hemispheres, though the popular ‘left brain, right brain’ idea goes much too far.
sections.b: The experiments suggested that the left hemisphere usually dominates language and the right hemisphere is often better at some spatial tasks, such as arranging blocks into a pattern or recognising faces. Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work. But the findings were later stretched into a popular myth: that people are either ‘left brained’ logical types or ‘right brained’ creative types. There is no good evidence for this. A large brain imaging study published in 2013 found no sign that individuals have a stronger left or right side overall. In a healthy brain, almost every complex activity, including creativity and logic, draws on both hemispheres working together through the corpus callosum.

sections.key: When the speaking hemisphere lacked information, it confidently invented an explanation.
sections.b: Gazzaniga's most famous demonstration involved a patient known as P.S. His left hemisphere was shown a chicken's claw, and his right hemisphere was shown a snowy scene. He was then asked to choose matching pictures from a set. His right hand picked a chicken, which made sense. His left hand picked a shovel, which matched the snow. When asked why, his speaking left hemisphere, which had never seen the snow, did not hesitate. It said, in effect, that the chicken claw goes with the chicken, and you need a shovel to clean out the chicken shed. The answer was fluent, confident and completely made up. The patient was not lying. He believed it.

sections.h: The interpreter in all of us
sections.key: Gazzaniga argued that the left hemisphere constantly builds stories to explain our behaviour, even without the facts.
sections.b: From experiments like this, Gazzaniga proposed that the left hemisphere houses what he called an ‘interpreter’: a system that keeps weaving our actions, feelings and perceptions into a coherent story. In split brain patients its guesses are exposed because the other half's information is cut off. But the idea reaches far beyond them. Many studies show that ordinary people, too, often give confident reasons for choices that were actually influenced by things they never noticed. We do not simply observe our own minds from the inside. To a surprising degree, we explain ourselves after the fact, just as we would explain someone else, and we rarely feel the difference between knowing and guessing.

sections.key: Whether a split brain patient has one consciousness or two is still debated.
sections.b: The deepest question is philosophical. If each hemisphere can perceive, decide and act without the other knowing, is a split brain patient one person or two? Some early reports described occasional conflict between the hands, such as one hand doing up buttons while the other undid them, though such episodes seem to be rare and mostly occur soon after surgery. In 2017 a Dutch led team reported that two patients could respond accurately to images on either side using either hand, and argued that consciousness may stay unified even when perception is split. Others dispute that interpretation. Today the operation is performed far less often because better treatments exist, so researchers have fewer patients to learn from.

quiz.q: In most people, which hemisphere controls the right hand and does most of the work of speech?
o: The right hemisphere
The left hemisphere
Both equally
Neither; it is the corpus callosum
quiz.e: Each hemisphere mostly controls the opposite side of the body, and in most people the left hemisphere is dominant for language.

quiz.q: A split brain patient is flashed a picture on the left side of the screen. What typically happens?
o: They name it immediately
They say they saw nothing, but their left hand can pick out the object
They see it twice
They cannot use either hand
quiz.e: The image goes only to the right hemisphere, which usually cannot speak, yet controls the left hand and can identify the object by touch.

quiz.q: What does the evidence say about ‘left brained’ and ‘right brained’ personality types?
o: They are well established
Only creative people are right brained
There is no good evidence that people are dominated by one side overall
Left brained people are better at maths
quiz.e: Hemispheres do specialise in some tasks, but a large imaging study found no sign that individuals rely mainly on one side overall.

quiz.q: In the chicken and shovel demonstration, why did the patient's explanation involve a chicken shed?
o: The speaking hemisphere never saw the snow, so it invented a reason
He had worked on a chicken farm
The researcher suggested it
His right hemisphere was talking
quiz.e: The left hemisphere saw only the claw and had no access to the snow scene, so it confidently made up an explanation for the shovel.

quiz.q: What is Gazzaniga's ‘interpreter’?
o: A translator who helped the patients
A left hemisphere system that builds explanations for our behaviour, even without the facts
A part of the right hemisphere that recognises faces
A device used to flash images
quiz.e: The interpreter weaves a coherent story about what we do and feel, and split brain studies exposed how readily it guesses.

LESSONS.title: Learned helplessness, and the twist fifty years later
LESSONS.hook: A famous experiment seemed to show that animals could learn to give up. Half a century on, the scientist who made it famous admitted they had got it backwards.

sections.key: In the 1960s, dogs that had experienced unavoidable shocks often failed to escape when escape became possible.
sections.b: In 1967 two young researchers at the University of Pennsylvania, Martin Seligman and Steven Maier, published experiments that would become famous. Dogs were placed in harnesses and given mild but unpleasant electric shocks. Some could stop the shocks by pressing a panel with their heads. Others received exactly the same shocks but had no way of stopping them. Later, all the dogs were put in a box divided by a low barrier, where they could escape a shock simply by jumping across. Most dogs that had controlled the earlier shocks, or had no shocks at all, quickly learned to jump. But most of the dogs that had faced inescapable shocks lay down and whimpered, making little attempt to escape.

sections.key: Seligman and Maier concluded the dogs had learned that nothing they did mattered.
sections.b: The researchers called this learned helplessness. Their explanation was that the dogs in the inescapable group had learned something during the first phase: that their actions had no effect on what happened to them. They then carried that expectation into the new situation, even though escape was now easy. The key was not the pain itself, since both groups of shocked dogs received identical shocks. It was the lack of control. Today experiments like these would face much tougher ethical scrutiny, and they are uncomfortable to read about. But at the time they offered a striking idea, because they suggested that passivity and hopelessness might be learned, and so perhaps could be unlearned.

sections.key: Researchers found similar effects in humans and proposed helplessness as a model for depression.
sections.b: Studies with people soon followed, using milder discomforts such as unpleasant noise or unsolvable puzzles. Participants who had faced a noise they could not switch off were often slower to discover how to stop it later, when a simple solution existed. Seligman proposed that learned helplessness could help explain depression, in which people often feel that nothing they do will make a difference, lose motivation and stop trying. The idea was enormously influential. It shaped how psychologists thought about poverty, abusive relationships, schooling and workplace stress. It also gave many people a vocabulary for their own experience: the sense of having tried and failed so often that trying no longer seemed worth it.

sections.h: It depends how you explain it
sections.key: A 1978 revision argued that what matters is how people explain their failures to themselves.
sections.b: There was a problem. Not everyone who faced uncontrollable events became helpless. In 1978 Seligman and colleagues revised the theory to focus on how people explain bad events. People most at risk of helplessness tended to see setbacks as permanent (‘this will always happen’), pervasive (‘this ruins everything’) and personal (‘it is entirely my fault’). People who saw the same setbacks as temporary, limited and partly due to circumstances bounced back more readily. This ‘explanatory style’ research led Seligman towards what he called learned optimism and, later, the positive psychology movement. It also fed into cognitive therapies that help people notice and question their automatic explanations.

sections.key: In 2016, Maier and Seligman concluded that passivity is the default, and what animals actually learn is control.
sections.b: After decades of research, Steven Maier, by then a neuroscientist, traced the brain circuits behind the original effect. In 2016 he and Seligman published a paper looking back at fifty years of work, and they reported that the original theory had the mechanism backwards. Passivity in the face of prolonged bad events is not learned at all. It is the brain's default response, driven by activity in a deep brainstem region called the dorsal raphe nucleus. What can be learned is control. When an animal discovers that its actions work, a region of the prefrontal cortex detects this and switches off the default passivity. In other words, it is not helplessness we learn, but hope.

sections.key: Experiences of control can protect against future stress, a finding with practical uses.
sections.b: This reversal is more than a technical footnote. Maier's experiments in rats found that animals that first experienced controllable stress were later more resilient, even when facing stress they could not control. The experience of mastery seemed to leave a lasting protective effect, at least in those studies. The findings are mainly from animals, so care is needed in applying them to people. Still, they fit well with human research suggesting that a sense of agency matters for wellbeing. It suggests that the best defence against hopelessness may not be avoiding hardship altogether, but building up genuine experiences of effort paying off, so that the brain has evidence that what we do can make a difference.

sections.key: Learned helplessness remains a powerful idea, but its story shows how science corrects itself.
sections.b: The phrase learned helplessness is now part of everyday language, and the basic observation has held up well: repeated uncontrollable setbacks can sap motivation. What changed was the explanation of why. That makes this a fine example of science working properly, with the original scientists themselves revising their own famous theory when better evidence arrived. For everyday life, the practical message is encouraging. If giving up is the default, then small, achievable wins are not trivial. Breaking a big problem into manageable steps, noticing what you can influence, and questioning explanations that are permanent, pervasive and personal are all ways of teaching the brain, again and again, that effort matters.

quiz.q: In the original experiments, what was the key difference between the two groups of shocked dogs?
o: One group received stronger shocks
One group could stop the shocks and the other could not
One group was older
One group had been trained to jump
quiz.e: Both groups received identical shocks; the difference was control. That is what made the result so striking.

quiz.q: According to the 1978 revision, which explanations of a setback put people most at risk?
o: Temporary, limited and situational
Permanent, pervasive and personal
Funny, shared and minor
Unexpected, rare and external
quiz.e: Seeing setbacks as lasting, all encompassing and wholly your own fault was linked to helplessness; the opposite style supported resilience.

quiz.q: What did Maier and Seligman conclude in 2016?
o: The original dogs were faking
Helplessness is learned in the prefrontal cortex
Passivity is the default response, and what is learned is control
The effect never existed
quiz.e: The brain's default under prolonged stress is passivity; detecting control allows the prefrontal cortex to switch that default off.

quiz.q: What did Maier's rat studies suggest about prior experience of controllable stress?
o: It made later stress worse
It had no effect
It seemed to make animals more resilient to later stress
It erased all memory of stress
quiz.e: Mastery experiences appeared to leave a protective effect, though findings in animals must be applied to people with care.

quiz.q: Which human condition did Seligman propose learned helplessness could help explain?
o: Depression
Colour blindness
Short sightedness
Allergies
quiz.e: Feeling that nothing you do makes a difference, and losing motivation as a result, is common in depression.

LESSONS.title: Earworms: why songs get stuck in your head
LESSONS.hook: Almost everyone has had a few seconds of a song loop endlessly in their mind. Researchers have studied which tunes stick, why, and what actually helps get rid of them.

sections.key: An earworm is a short piece of music that replays in the mind without you choosing it.
sections.b: The word earworm is a translation of the German Ohrwurm, and psychologists also call it involuntary musical imagery. It is usually not a whole song but a fragment, often the chorus or a catchy hook, that repeats on a loop. It is extremely common. In large surveys, around nine in ten people say they get earworms at least once a week, and many report them daily. Most are mildly annoying or even pleasant, and they tend to fade within minutes or hours. Earworms are not the same as hearing music that seems to come from outside your head, which is rare and worth mentioning to a doctor. An earworm feels like your own inner voice humming.

sections.key: Recent or repeated listening is the most common trigger, but memories and moods can start one too.
sections.b: The most obvious trigger is hearing a song recently, especially more than once. That is why a tune from an advertisement, a shop or a child's television show can haunt you for the rest of the day. But earworms can also be cued by memory: a word, a place or a person connected with a song can set it going, even when you have not heard it for years. People report more earworms when they are tired, stressed or doing tasks that need little thought, such as walking, showering or doing chores. Those who listen to a lot of music, and people with musical training, tend to report earworms more often.

sections.h: The anatomy of a sticky tune
sections.key: Songs that become earworms tend to be fairly fast, with a familiar shape plus something unusual.
sections.b: In 2016 a team led by Kelly Jakubowski, then at Goldsmiths, University of London, analysed reports from around 3,000 people about the songs that most often got stuck in their heads. Compared with similarly popular songs that rarely stuck, the earworms tended to have faster tempos and melodies with a fairly common overall shape, the kind of rising and falling pattern found in many nursery rhymes. But they also tended to have something distinctive, such as unusual leaps between notes or repeated phrases. The most frequently named songs included Lady Gaga's ‘Bad Romance’ and Kylie Minogue's well named ‘Can't Get You Out of My Head’. Familiar enough to be easy, unusual enough to grab attention.

sections.key: Earworms seem linked to the brain's habit of replaying unfinished patterns, though the exact cause is still unknown.
sections.b: No one is entirely sure why earworms happen. One idea is that musical memories are especially easy to rehearse, because melody and rhythm bind them together, and the brain's auditory regions can replay them like a short recording. Another is that the mind returns to things that feel incomplete. This links to the Zeigarnik effect, named after the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik, who reported in the 1920s that people remembered interrupted tasks better than completed ones. However, later attempts to repeat her findings have given mixed results, so it is best seen as a hypothesis. What is clear is that earworms thrive when the mind is idle and wandering, and fade when it is fully occupied.

sections.key: Trying hard not to think of a song may keep it going.
sections.b: Many people try to banish an earworm by force of will. The trouble is that deliberately suppressing a thought can make it more likely to return, a pattern the psychologist Daniel Wegner explored in his famous ‘white bear’ studies, in which people asked not to think about a white bear kept thinking about it. With earworms, the more you check whether the song is gone, the more you remind yourself of it. Researchers who have surveyed earworm sufferers find that people use all sorts of strategies, from singing a different song to simply waiting. Often, accepting the earworm and letting your attention move on to something else works as well as anything.

sections.key: Chewing gum and moderately demanding tasks have some evidence behind them.
sections.b: A few strategies have been tested. In a 2015 study at the University of Reading, people who chewed gum after hearing catchy songs reported fewer intrusive thoughts of those songs than people who did not. The likely reason is that chewing ties up some of the same mental machinery used to imagine speaking or singing to yourself. Other research suggests that a moderately challenging task, such as an anagram or a sudoku, can crowd out an earworm. The key word is moderately: tasks that are too easy leave room for the song, while tasks that are too hard make the mind wander. Some people swear by listening to the whole song through, to give it an ending, but evidence for that is thinner.

sections.key: Earworms may be a side effect of a memory system built to rehearse and keep sound patterns.
sections.b: Earworms can be annoying, but they hint at something remarkable. Before writing, much of human culture was carried in songs, chants and rhymes, precisely because melody and rhythm make words easier to remember. Advertisers exploit the same quirk with jingles, and teachers use it with songs for the alphabet or times tables. The brain's tendency to replay sound patterns, even uninvited, may simply be the flip side of a powerful system for learning and keeping them. For most people earworms are harmless. If intrusive music or thoughts become constant and distressing, though, it is worth talking to a GP, as occasionally it can be part of a broader issue such as obsessive compulsive disorder.

quiz.q: Roughly how common are earworms, according to large surveys?
o: Only musicians get them
About one in ten people get them weekly
Around nine in ten people get them at least weekly
They happen to everyone every hour
quiz.e: Surveys find that around nine in ten people experience an earworm at least once a week, making them one of the most common quirks of the mind.

quiz.q: What features did the 2016 Goldsmiths study link to sticky songs?
o: Slow tempos and entirely unpredictable melodies
Faster tempos, a common melodic shape and something distinctive
Long songs with no chorus
Songs with no lyrics only
quiz.e: Earworms tended to be fairly fast with familiar melodic contours, plus unusual leaps or repetitions that grab attention.

quiz.q: What is the current status of the Zeigarnik effect?
o: It is one of the best replicated findings in psychology
Later attempts to repeat it have given mixed results
It was proven fraudulent
It only applies to music
quiz.e: Zeigarnik's 1920s finding that unfinished tasks are better remembered has not reliably replicated, so linking it to earworms is a hypothesis.

quiz.q: Why can trying hard to suppress an earworm backfire?
o: Suppressing thoughts can make them more likely to return
It damages hearing
It makes the song speed up
It only works on weekends
quiz.e: As Wegner's ‘white bear’ studies showed, actively suppressing a thought and checking whether it is gone tends to keep it alive.

quiz.q: Why might chewing gum reduce earworms?
o: Sugar blocks memory
Chewing uses some of the same mental machinery as imagining singing or speaking
It makes the ears ring
It speeds up the song until it ends
quiz.e: Chewing seems to interfere with the inner rehearsal that keeps a tune looping, which is why gum chewers reported fewer intrusive songs.

LESSONS.title: Sleep paralysis: the demon on your chest
LESSONS.hook: You wake in the dark, unable to move, and you are certain someone is in the room. For centuries people blamed witches and demons. The real explanation lies in a brief mix-up between sleep and waking.

sections.key: Sleep paralysis is being awake but temporarily unable to move, often with vivid hallucinations.
sections.b: Sleep paralysis usually happens just as you are falling asleep or waking up. You are aware of your surroundings, your eyes can usually open, but you cannot move your arms, legs or head, and you may struggle to speak or cry out. Episodes typically last from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, though they can feel much longer. On their own the paralysis would be unsettling enough. What makes many episodes truly frightening is what often comes with them: a powerful sense that something or someone is in the room, a feeling of pressure on the chest, and sometimes vivid sights, sounds or the sensation of being touched. Then it ends, and you can move again.

sections.key: Estimates vary, but one large review suggested roughly 8 per cent of people have experienced it at least once.
sections.b: Because people rarely talk about it, many who experience sleep paralysis assume they are alone, or worry that they are losing their mind. In fact it is common. A widely cited 2011 review by Brian Sharpless and Jacques Barber pooled dozens of studies and estimated that about 8 per cent of the general population have had at least one episode, with much higher rates among students and among people with some psychiatric conditions. Other estimates vary, partly because definitions and survey questions differ. Most people who experience it have only occasional episodes. For a smaller group it happens often, and for them it can become a source of dread around bedtime.

sections.key: The paralysis is the normal muscle shutdown of dream sleep, lingering while you are partly awake.
sections.b: The explanation lies in rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, the stage when most vivid dreaming happens. During REM sleep, the brain actively switches off most of the body's voluntary muscles, leaving only the eyes and breathing muscles working. This is a protective feature, because it stops you acting out your dreams. Normally the switch flips back the moment you wake. In sleep paralysis, the transition goes slightly wrong. Your conscious mind comes online while the muscle shutdown of REM sleep is still in force. You are, in effect, partly awake and partly still in a dreaming state, which is why the experience can feel so real and so strange.

sections.key: Dream imagery leaking into waking awareness explains the sense of a menacing presence.
sections.b: If part of your brain is still in dream mode, dream imagery can spill into what you perceive with your eyes open. That is why people see shadowy figures, hear footsteps or voices, or feel hands upon them. The sense of threat may be sharpened because the brain's alarm systems are active during REM sleep. The feeling of weight on the chest probably has a simpler partial cause. In REM sleep breathing is controlled automatically and tends to be shallow, and when you try to take a deep breath deliberately, you can't, which may be felt as something pressing down. Your brain, searching for an explanation for being trapped and frightened, readily supplies a sinister one.

sections.key: Cultures around the world have their own names and stories for sleep paralysis.
sections.b: Because the experience is so similar everywhere, many cultures have developed their own explanations. In parts of Newfoundland it has been called being ‘hagged’, after an old hag believed to sit on sleepers' chests. In Japan it is known as kanashibari, meaning something like ‘bound in metal’. Medieval Europeans spoke of demons that pressed on sleepers at night, and the word nightmare originally referred to a ‘mare’, a spirit believed to sit on people as they slept. Henry Fuseli's famous 1781 painting The Nightmare shows a demon crouched on a sleeping woman's chest. Some researchers have even suggested that certain reports of alien abductions may be sleep paralysis interpreted through modern ideas.

sections.key: Sleep deprivation, irregular hours and stress are among the most common triggers.
sections.b: Research has linked sleep paralysis to several factors. Perhaps the most important are not getting enough sleep and having an irregular sleep schedule, which is one reason shift workers, new parents, students during exams and long haul travellers can be more prone to it. Stress and anxiety appear to increase the risk, and it is more common among people with post traumatic stress disorder. Some studies suggest sleeping on your back may make episodes more likely, though the evidence is limited. Frequent sleep paralysis can also be one feature of narcolepsy, a sleep disorder that causes overwhelming daytime sleepiness. For most people, though, an occasional episode is simply a harmless glitch.

sections.key: Knowing what is happening, staying calm and keeping regular sleep habits all help.
sections.b: Simply understanding sleep paralysis can take away much of its power. Many people find that reminding themselves ‘this is sleep paralysis, it is harmless and it will pass’ makes episodes far less frightening. Some people find that focusing on slow breathing, or trying to move something small such as a finger or toe, helps break the spell, although evidence for specific techniques is limited. Over the longer term, the most useful steps are getting enough sleep and keeping a regular sleep routine where possible. If episodes are frequent or distressing, or come with extreme sleepiness during the day, it is worth talking to a GP, who may refer you to a sleep specialist.

quiz.q: What causes the paralysis itself?
o: A blocked blood vessel in the neck
The muscle shutdown of REM sleep continuing while you are partly awake
Low blood sugar during the night
An evil spirit, according to sleep scientists
quiz.e: During REM sleep the brain switches off most voluntary muscles. In sleep paralysis that shutdown lingers after awareness returns.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the general population did a 2011 review estimate had experienced at least one episode?
o: Less than 1 per cent
About 8 per cent
About 50 per cent
Nearly everyone
quiz.e: Sharpless and Barber's review estimated about 8 per cent, with higher rates among students and some psychiatric groups.

quiz.q: Why might sleep paralysis come with a sense of pressure on the chest?
o: Dream imagery and shallow, automatic REM breathing that you can't deepen at will
Someone is really sitting there
Your heart has stopped
It is caused by a heavy blanket
quiz.e: Breathing in REM sleep is shallow and automatic, and trying to breathe deeply when you can't may be felt as weight pressing down.

quiz.q: What did the word ‘nightmare’ originally refer to?
o: A horse that ran at night
A spirit believed to sit on sleepers
A type of bad dinner
A dark painting
quiz.e: A ‘mare’ was a spirit believed to press on people as they slept, an older explanation for what we now call sleep paralysis.

quiz.q: Which of these is most strongly linked to sleep paralysis?
o: Eating cheese at dinner
Too little or irregular sleep
Living near the coast
Drinking water before bed
quiz.e: Sleep deprivation and irregular schedules, common in shift workers and students, are among the most consistent risk factors.

LESSONS.title: Why time flies, and why it drags
LESSONS.hook: An hour in a dentist's waiting room crawls, while a week on holiday vanishes. Yet looking back, the holiday feels longer. Your sense of time is not a clock. It is a story your brain tells.

sections.key: The brain has no single organ for sensing time; it estimates time from many signals.
sections.b: We have eyes for light and ears for sound, but there is no dedicated sense organ for time. Instead, the brain builds a sense of duration from many sources: the rhythms of neural activity, how much attention we pay to time passing, our emotional state, and how many new events we take in. Several brain regions are involved, including networks that help with timing movements and with judging short intervals. This is one reason our sense of time is so flexible. For short intervals of a second or less, people are surprisingly precise. For longer stretches, our judgements are easily pushed around by what we are doing and feeling.

sections.key: When we pay attention to time passing, it seems to slow down.
sections.b: Psychologists distinguish between judging time while it passes, called prospective timing, and judging it afterwards, called retrospective timing. When you are waiting for something, such as a kettle to boil or a phone call, your attention keeps returning to the passage of time, and each check makes the interval seem longer. That is the grain of truth in the saying that a watched pot never boils. When you are absorbed in something, little attention is left for tracking time, and it seems to fly. Emotions also play a part. Fear and anxiety can stretch our sense of time, while enjoyable focus tends to shrink it.

sections.key: A holiday flies by while it happens but feels long in memory, because it is full of new experiences.
sections.b: Here is the puzzle. A week of new sights on holiday seems to rush past, yet when you look back, it feels longer than a routine week at work. The psychologist and broadcaster Claudia Hammond named this the holiday paradox. The likely explanation is that, looking back, we judge durations partly by how many distinct memories we have from that period. A holiday packed with novel experiences leaves many memories, so it seems long in hindsight. A routine week leaves few distinct memories, and blurs into its neighbours. The reverse happens with boredom: a dull afternoon drags while you live through it, then shrinks to almost nothing in memory.

sections.h: Does time really slow in a crisis?
sections.key: In a famous experiment, people in free fall judged their fall as longer but could not see faster.
sections.b: Many people describe car crashes or falls as happening in slow motion. In a 2007 study, the neuroscientist David Eagleman and colleagues tested this by having volunteers fall backwards about 31 metres into a safety net at a Texas amusement park. Afterwards, they estimated that their own fall had lasted roughly a third longer than the falls they watched others take. But while falling, each volunteer watched a special wrist display that flashed numbers slightly too fast to read under normal conditions. If time had really slowed for them, they should have been able to read the numbers. They could not. The researchers concluded that frightening moments are not perceived in slow motion, but remembered in rich detail, which makes them feel longer afterwards.

sections.key: When you first glance at a clock, the second hand can seem to freeze for longer than a second.
sections.b: Have you ever looked at an analogue clock and felt that the second hand paused before it started moving again? This illusion is called chronostasis. It happens because each time your eyes jump to a new spot, your brain briefly suppresses the blurred view during the movement, then appears to fill the gap with the image you land on. In effect, it backdates your view of the clock. A 2001 study by Kielan Yarrow and colleagues found that people judged the first moment after an eye movement as lasting longer than it really did. The effect is small, but it is a neat reminder that perception is constantly being edited before it reaches you.

sections.key: Many people feel time passes faster as they age, though the evidence is more mixed than the saying suggests.
sections.b: A common complaint of adulthood is that the years seem to rush by. One popular explanation is that each year is a smaller fraction of your life, so it feels shorter, though this is hard to test. A more research friendly idea links back to the holiday paradox: childhood and youth are full of firsts, while adult life often settles into routine, leaving fewer distinctive memories per year. Surveys do find that older people often say the last decade went quickly. But studies asking about the past week or month show weaker age differences than you might expect, so the feeling seems to apply mostly to long stretches of time looked back upon.

sections.key: Novelty and variety are the best tools for making life feel longer in memory.
sections.b: If remembered time depends on distinct memories, there are practical ways to make life feel fuller. Breaking routines with small changes, such as a new walking route, a different weekend activity or learning a skill, gives the memory more distinct markers to hold onto. Travel, even locally, can do the same. Paying deliberate attention, such as noticing details or taking a few minutes at the end of a day to recall what happened, may also help experiences stick. None of this makes the clock tick slower. But since our sense of how long we have lived is built from memories rather than minutes, filling time with variety is the closest thing we have to stretching it.

quiz.q: How does the brain sense the passing of time?
o: Through a dedicated time sense organ in the ear
By combining many signals such as attention, emotion and new events
By counting heartbeats only
It doesn't sense time at all
quiz.e: There is no single time organ; the brain estimates duration from neural rhythms, attention, emotion and the events we take in.

quiz.q: What explains the holiday paradox?
o: Holidays are always longer than work weeks
Novel experiences create many distinct memories, so the holiday seems long looking back
Sunlight slows down the body clock
We sleep more on holiday
quiz.e: In hindsight we judge duration partly by how many distinct memories a period holds, and holidays are packed with new ones.

quiz.q: What did the 2007 free fall experiment find?
o: Volunteers could read numbers that were normally too fast to see
Time genuinely slows during fear
Volunteers remembered their fall as longer but could not see the fast numbers
Volunteers felt their fall was shorter than it was
quiz.e: Their perception did not speed up; the frightening moment was simply remembered in rich detail, which made it seem longer afterwards.

quiz.q: What is chronostasis?
o: A sleep disorder
The illusion that a clock's second hand freezes when you first look at it
A fear of clocks
A loss of the sense of time after injury
quiz.e: After an eye movement the brain fills the gap with the new image, making the first moment you see seem longer than it was.

quiz.q: Which approach is most likely to make a period of life feel longer in memory?
o: Repeating the same routine every day
Adding novelty and variety
Checking the time more often
Sleeping more
quiz.e: Distinct new experiences give memory more markers to hold onto, so the period seems fuller and longer in hindsight.

LESSONS.title: Why you can't tickle yourself
LESSONS.hook: Try it now: tickle the sole of your own foot. Almost nothing. The reason reveals one of the brain's cleverest tricks, a system that predicts the future a fraction of a second ahead.

sections.key: People have puzzled over self tickling for more than two thousand years.
sections.b: The question is old. A collection of ancient Greek writings known as the Problems, traditionally attributed to Aristotle, asks why a person cannot tickle themselves. Charles Darwin also noticed that tickling depends on the touch being unexpected. Most of us know this from experience. Someone else running a feather across your foot, or poking your ribs, can reduce you to helpless laughter. Doing exactly the same thing yourself, with the same pressure in the same place, produces little more than a dull touch. Since the skin receives much the same stimulation either way, the difference must lie in the brain. In the late 1990s, neuroscientists worked out what it was.

sections.key: Scientists distinguish a light, itchy tickle from the heavy kind that makes people laugh.
sections.b: In 1897 the American psychologists Granville Stanley Hall and Arthur Allin described two different sensations we call tickling. One is a light, feathery touch that causes an itchy, crawling feeling, like an insect walking on your skin. It was later named knismesis. The other is the heavier, probing touch to places such as the ribs, armpits and feet that makes people squirm and laugh, called gargalesis. Interestingly, people can sometimes give themselves the light, itchy kind, but the laughter producing kind almost always needs another person. Tickling is also strongly social. Children who are tickled by someone they trust usually laugh, while the same touch from a stranger can feel threatening rather than funny.

sections.key: Whenever you move, your brain predicts the sensations that movement will cause.
sections.b: Every time your brain sends a command to your muscles, it also makes a copy of that command, sometimes called an efference copy. Using this copy, the brain predicts what you should feel as a result. When the actual sensations arrive, they are compared with the prediction. Anything that matches is treated as expected and turned down in intensity. Anything that does not match stands out. This system is constantly at work. It helps you tell the difference between touching something and being touched, and it lets your brain focus on surprising events in the world rather than on the predictable consequences of your own actions. When you try to tickle yourself, your brain knows exactly what is coming.

sections.key: Experiments with a robot showed that adding a small delay made self tickling feel more ticklish.
sections.b: In the late 1990s Sarah Jayne Blakemore, Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith at University College London tested this idea with a clever device. Participants moved a handle with one hand, and a robot copied the movement, stroking a piece of soft foam across the palm of their other hand. When the robot copied the movement exactly and instantly, it did not feel very ticklish. But when the researchers added a delay of a fraction of a second, or changed the direction of the stroke, participants rated the sensation as increasingly ticklish. With a delay of around 200 milliseconds, it felt nearly as ticklish as a touch from outside. The more the sensation failed to match the prediction, the stronger it felt.

sections.key: Because we feel our own force less, people tend to push back harder than they were pushed.
sections.b: This prediction system has a curious side effect. In a 2003 study published in Science, pairs of volunteers took turns pressing on each other's finger, each told to press back with exactly the same force they had just felt. Neither intended to escalate, yet the force rose sharply round after round, by roughly 40 per cent each turn. Because each person felt their own press as weaker than it really was, they pushed harder to match what they had received. The researchers suggested this may help explain why physical scuffles, such as children's tit for tat shoving, so often escalate. Each side genuinely feels it is only responding in kind.

sections.key: Some research suggests people who hear voices can tickle themselves more effectively.
sections.b: If the brain fails to predict the consequences of its own actions properly, self produced sensations might feel as though they come from outside. Researchers have explored whether this could help explain some symptoms of schizophrenia, such as hearing one's own inner speech as an external voice, or feeling that one's actions are controlled by someone else. A study by Blakemore and colleagues published in 2000 found that people who experienced these symptoms rated self tickling as more intense than other participants did. This is an active area of research and the full picture is complex. But it offers a striking possibility: that the sense of being the author of your own actions depends on accurate predictions.

sections.key: The inability to tickle yourself is a small sign of a brain that constantly separates self from world.
sections.b: It is easy to dismiss tickling as trivial, but the failure to tickle yourself points to something deep. Your brain is not passively receiving information from the senses. It is constantly predicting what it will feel, and using those predictions to sort sensations into those caused by you and those caused by the world. That sorting is so automatic that we never notice it, except in odd moments like this one. Many neuroscientists now see prediction as one of the brain's core jobs, involved in everything from catching a ball to understanding speech. So next time you try, and fail, to tickle yourself, you are watching that prediction machine quietly doing its work.

quiz.q: What does the brain use to predict the sensations caused by your own movements?
o: A copy of the motor command, sometimes called an efference copy
Signals from the stomach
A memory of being tickled as a child
The sense of smell
quiz.e: The brain copies each command it sends to the muscles and uses it to predict, and so dampen, the sensations that follow.

quiz.q: In the tickling robot experiment, what made self tickling feel more ticklish?
o: Making the foam softer
Adding a short delay or changing the stroke's direction
Asking participants to close their eyes
Using both hands at once
quiz.e: Delays or changed directions made the sensation mismatch the brain's prediction, so it was dampened less and felt more ticklish.

quiz.q: What is gargalesis?
o: A light, itchy tickle like an insect
The heavier tickling that makes people laugh
A fear of being tickled
A skin condition
quiz.e: Gargalesis is the heavy, laughter producing kind, which almost always needs another person; knismesis is the light, itchy kind.

quiz.q: Why did the force escalate in the finger pressing study?
o: Participants were trying to win
Each person felt their own press as weaker, so they pressed harder to match
The equipment was faulty
The second person was always stronger
quiz.e: Self generated force is perceived as weaker, so each person overshot while genuinely believing they were matching what they received.

quiz.q: What did a 2000 study find in people who experienced symptoms such as hearing voices?
o: They could not feel touch at all
They rated self tickling as more intense than other participants did
They were immune to all tickling
They could tickle others more effectively
quiz.e: This supports the idea that some symptoms may involve problems predicting the results of one's own actions, though the picture is complex.

LESSONS.title: Phantom limbs: feeling a hand that isn't there
LESSONS.hook: Most people who lose a limb continue to feel it, sometimes for decades. The phantom can itch, clench and ache, and it has taught scientists that the body you feel is a model built by the brain.

sections.key: After amputation, most people continue to feel the missing limb.
sections.b: Doctors have recorded the phenomenon for centuries. The sixteenth century French surgeon Ambroise Paré described soldiers complaining of pain in limbs that had been removed. The term ‘phantom limb’ was coined in 1871 by the American neurologist Silas Weir Mitchell, who had treated many amputees from the American Civil War. Studies since then suggest that most amputees, by many estimates well over half, experience phantom sensations at some point. The phantom can feel warm or cold, itchy or tingling. It can seem to move, gesture or grip. Some people instinctively reach out with a phantom hand to catch a falling object or answer the phone. Phantoms are not limited to limbs, and have been reported after the loss of a breast, a tooth or other body parts.

sections.key: Phantom limb pain is common and can be severe, but it is real pain, not imagination.
sections.b: For many people the phantom is mostly a strange but tolerable presence. For a large number, though, it hurts. Estimates of how many amputees experience phantom pain vary widely between studies, but it is a common problem. The pain can be burning, stabbing or cramping, and some people describe a phantom hand clenched so tightly that the fingernails seem to dig into the palm. For a long time such reports were sometimes dismissed as psychological in the dismissive sense of the word, as though patients were imagining things. Today the pain is understood to be fully real, generated by changes in the nervous system. In fact, all pain is produced by the brain, which is precisely why it can be felt in a limb that no longer exists.

sections.key: The brain contains a map of the body, and it does not simply go blank when a limb is lost.
sections.b: In the 1930s and 1940s the Canadian neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield stimulated the surface of patients' brains during surgery and found that touch sensations from different body parts were mapped in an orderly strip across a region called the somatosensory cortex. This map is often drawn as a distorted little figure, the ‘homunculus’, with enormous hands and lips because those areas are so sensitive. The map has some odd neighbours. The area for the hand, for example, sits right beside the area for the face. When a limb is amputated, its region of the map loses its normal input, but the brain cells there are still alive. That fact turned out to matter a great deal.

sections.key: Touching an amputee's face could trigger sensations in his phantom hand.
sections.b: In the early 1990s the neuroscientist V. S. Ramachandran, working in California, tested a young man who had lost his arm. While the man's eyes were closed, Ramachandran stroked different parts of his body with a cotton bud. When he touched the cheek, the man reported feeling it on his cheek and also on his missing thumb. Touches to other spots on the face mapped onto other phantom fingers. Ramachandran proposed that, deprived of its usual input, the brain's hand area had been invaded by signals from the neighbouring face area. Brain imaging studies supported the idea that body maps reorganise after amputation, though researchers still debate how exactly this reorganisation relates to phantom pain.

sections.key: A cheap box with a mirror could sometimes relieve a clenched or painful phantom.
sections.b: Ramachandran then had an inventive idea. Some patients felt their phantom was frozen in a painful position. What if the brain could be shown the limb moving? In the mid 1990s he built a simple box with a vertical mirror in the middle. A patient placed their intact arm on one side and looked into the mirror, so the reflection appeared exactly where the missing arm should be. When they moved the real hand, it looked as though the phantom was moving too. Some patients reported that the phantom suddenly felt as though it moved, and that cramping eased. The approach became known as mirror therapy, and it is now used in some rehabilitation settings, often alongside other treatments.

sections.key: Mirror therapy helps some people, but trials are small and results are mixed.
sections.b: Mirror therapy captured public imagination because it is so cheap and so elegant. The scientific picture is more modest. Clinical trials have generally been small, and systematic reviews describe the overall quality of evidence as limited, with benefits that vary a lot between people. Some patients find it very helpful, others feel little change. Researchers, including the Australian pain scientist Lorimer Moseley, have developed related approaches such as graded motor imagery, which works through stages like recognising left and right limbs in pictures, imagining movements and then mirror work. Phantom pain is usually managed with a combination of approaches by a medical team, and anyone experiencing it should seek specialist advice.

sections.key: Phantoms reveal that the body you feel is a construction of the brain, which can be fooled even without amputation.
sections.b: Phantom limbs reveal something true of everyone. You do not feel your body directly. You feel the brain's model of it, built from touch, vision, the sense of where your limbs are, and expectations. In the famous rubber hand illusion, first reported in 1998 by Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen, a person's real hand is hidden while a fake rubber hand sits in view. When both are stroked at the same time with a brush, many people begin to feel the touch on the rubber hand, and some even flinch when it is threatened. Seen in this light, a phantom is the brain's body model carrying on after the body itself has changed.

quiz.q: Who coined the term ‘phantom limb’?
o: Ambroise Paré in the 1500s
Silas Weir Mitchell in 1871
Wilder Penfield in the 1940s
V. S. Ramachandran in the 1990s
quiz.e: Paré described the phenomenon centuries earlier, but the term was coined by Mitchell after treating amputees from the American Civil War.

quiz.q: Why does the face matter in the story of phantom limbs?
o: The face controls the arms
In the brain's body map, the hand area sits next to the face area
The face is where phantom pain is usually felt
Penfield studied only facial nerves
quiz.e: Because the hand and face areas are neighbours, the face's signals may invade the deprived hand area after amputation.

quiz.q: How does the mirror box work?
o: It shines light on the stump
A reflection of the intact limb makes it look as if the phantom is moving
It records nerve signals
It hides both limbs from view
quiz.e: Seeing the reflected intact limb in the missing limb's place gives the brain visual evidence that the phantom moves.

quiz.q: What is the fairest summary of the evidence for mirror therapy?
o: It cures all phantom pain
It has been proven useless
It helps some people, but trials are small and results mixed
It works only on legs
quiz.e: Systematic reviews describe limited evidence; some patients benefit greatly and others little, so it is often one part of a broader treatment.

quiz.q: What does the rubber hand illusion show?
o: Rubber is a good conductor of touch
The brain's sense of the body can be fooled by matching sight and touch
Only amputees can feel phantom sensations
Hands are less sensitive than feet
quiz.e: Synchronised stroking leads many people to feel touch on a fake hand, showing that the felt body is a model the brain builds.

LESSONS.title: Stockholm syndrome: the story behind a famous label
LESSONS.hook: In 1973 four bank hostages in Sweden seemed to side with their captors, and a new psychological condition was born. But the hostages' own account of those six days tells a different story.

sections.key: In August 1973 a bank robbery in central Stockholm turned into a six day hostage siege.
sections.b: On the morning of 23 August 1973, a man named Jan-Erik Olsson walked into a branch of Kreditbanken on Norrmalmstorg square in central Stockholm, fired a gun and took bank staff hostage. Among his demands was that a well known criminal, Clark Olofsson, be brought from prison to join him, and the authorities agreed. For six days the two men held four employees, three women and one man, in the bank's vault. The siege became a national media event in Sweden, broadcast and reported intensely. It ended on 28 August when police pumped tear gas into the vault. The robbers surrendered, and none of the hostages was seriously physically injured.

sections.key: During and after the siege, the hostages seemed more afraid of the police than of their captors.
sections.b: What puzzled observers was how the hostages behaved. They seemed to fear the police more than the robbers. One hostage, Kristin Enmark, spoke by phone with the Swedish Prime Minister, Olof Palme, and pleaded to be allowed to leave with the robbers, saying she trusted them and feared the police would get them killed. After their release, the hostages reportedly showed some sympathy for their captors, and some stayed in contact with Olofsson in later years. To many outsiders this looked bizarre, even irrational. Why would anyone feel safer with armed men who had taken them prisoner than with the officers trying to rescue them?

sections.key: The term emerged from psychiatrist Nils Bejerot, who advised police during the siege.
sections.b: The Swedish psychiatrist and criminologist Nils Bejerot advised the police during the siege. He suggested that the hostages' attitude was a psychological reaction caused by their captivity, and the idea spread through the media as ‘Norrmalmstorg syndrome’, soon known abroad as Stockholm syndrome. In the popular version, captives become emotionally attached to their captors and even take their side. The label gained enormous fame the following year with the kidnapping of the American heiress Patty Hearst, who later took part in a bank robbery with her kidnappers. At her 1976 trial, the defence argued she had been coerced and brainwashed. She was convicted, but her sentence was later commuted and she was eventually pardoned.

sections.h: Kristin Enmark's side of the story
sections.key: Enmark argued that her reaction was a rational response to a dangerous police operation.
sections.b: Kristin Enmark has given her own account in interviews and a memoir. She has said that during the siege the police seemed willing to risk the hostages' lives, and that the robbers, whatever their crimes, were the people physically present who could keep them safe minute by minute. In that light, trying to stay on good terms with them, and fearing a chaotic police assault, looks less like a disorder and more like a survival strategy. Notably, Bejerot never interviewed her before giving his opinion, and she had publicly criticised the police handling of the siege. Critics have argued that the label conveniently shifted attention from the authorities' decisions to the supposed psychology of a young woman.

sections.key: Stockholm syndrome is not a recognised psychiatric diagnosis and has little research behind it.
sections.b: Despite its fame, Stockholm syndrome does not appear in the major psychiatric diagnostic manuals, the DSM and the ICD. There are no agreed diagnostic criteria, and researchers who have reviewed the literature have found remarkably little systematic evidence for it. Much of what is written about it relies on a handful of famous cases and media reports. Studies of hostage situations suggest that strong positive bonds with captors are uncommon. This does not mean that captives never feel complicated emotions towards the people holding them. But it does mean the popular idea of a well defined syndrome, in which victims are reliably ‘converted’ to their captors' side, rests on a thin and shaky foundation.

sections.key: Being agreeable to someone who holds power over you is often a sensible strategy.
sections.b: Many researchers and clinicians now prefer to describe what people do in captivity as survival strategies. Being compliant, friendly and calm towards someone who controls whether you live or die can reduce the chances of violence. Seeing the captor as a human being, and wanting them to see you as one, may make you safer. Small kindnesses from a captor, such as being allowed to go to the toilet or not being harmed, can produce real feelings of gratitude in a person under extreme stress. These reactions make sense in context. Calling them a syndrome risks implying that the victim's mind has malfunctioned, when it may in fact have been working hard to keep them alive.

sections.key: The term is widely used for abusive relationships, which critics say can blame victims.
sections.b: Today the phrase Stockholm syndrome is often used for people who stay in or defend abusive relationships, or for anyone who seems to side with those who mistreat them. Critics, including researchers who work with survivors of domestic and family violence, argue this can be harmful. It can suggest that victims are irrational or complicit, rather than recognising the fear, isolation, financial pressure and danger that often make leaving extremely difficult. Understanding those pressures matters far more than a catchy label. In Australia, anyone in immediate danger should call 000, and support for family violence is available through 1800RESPECT, the national counselling service, on 1800 737 732.

quiz.q: How many hostages were held in the Norrmalmstorg vault?
o: One
Four
Twelve
Twenty
quiz.e: Four bank employees, three women and one man, were held for six days in August 1973.

quiz.q: Who is credited with the idea behind the label?
o: Kristin Enmark
Clark Olofsson
Nils Bejerot
Olof Palme
quiz.e: Psychiatrist Nils Bejerot, who advised police, attributed the hostages' attitude to their captivity; the media spread it as Norrmalmstorg, later Stockholm, syndrome.

quiz.q: How did Kristin Enmark explain her behaviour during the siege?
o: She had fallen in love with a robber
She saw it as a rational response, fearing the police operation could get the hostages killed
She said she had been hypnotised
She claimed she remembered nothing
quiz.e: Enmark argued that staying on good terms with the captors and fearing a chaotic assault was a survival strategy, not a disorder.

quiz.q: What is the status of Stockholm syndrome in the major diagnostic manuals?
o: It is a core diagnosis in the DSM
It is not a recognised diagnosis in the DSM or ICD
It was added in 2013
It appears only in the ICD
quiz.e: It has no agreed criteria, does not appear in either manual, and has little systematic research behind it.

quiz.q: Why do critics worry about applying the label to abusive relationships?
o: It is too technical
It can suggest victims are irrational or complicit, overlooking fear and practical barriers
It only applies to bank robberies
It encourages people to call the police
quiz.e: Critics argue the label pathologises victims rather than recognising the real dangers and pressures that make leaving hard.

LESSONS.title: Choking: back blows and chest thrusts
LESSONS.hook: Most people picture the Heimlich manoeuvre. Australian first aid guidelines teach something different, and the reason is a surprising story about evidence.

sections.key: Severe choking is often quiet, because a blocked airway leaves no air to shout with.
sections.b: Choking happens when food or an object lodges in the airway and stops air reaching the lungs. Movies make it loud and dramatic, but a person with a fully blocked airway usually cannot speak, cough or breathe. They may clutch at their throat, look panicked, and their lips and face may turn blue or grey. Without air, the brain is starved of oxygen within minutes, so the response needs to be fast. Choking is a risk at every age. Toddlers explore the world with their mouths, and grapes, nuts, popcorn and hard lollies are common culprits. Older adults are at risk too, especially when swallowing has become weaker after a stroke or with conditions such as dementia. Meat is a classic cause in adults.

sections.key: If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing and stay with them.
sections.b: The simplest way to judge how serious choking is: can the person cough effectively? A strong, noisy cough means air is still moving, and coughing is the body's own best tool for clearing the airway. In that case, encourage them to keep coughing, and do not slap their back or give them water while they are coughing well. Stay with them and watch closely, because a partial blockage can become a complete one. If the cough does not clear the object, call Triple Zero (000). A weak, silent or ineffective cough, difficulty breathing, or an inability to speak are signs of a severe blockage. That is when you need to act and call for help at the same time.

sections.key: For severe choking, bend the person forward and give up to five sharp blows between the shoulder blades.
sections.b: Under Australian guidelines from the Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation, known as ANZCOR, the first step for a conscious adult or child with severe choking is back blows. Call 000, or have someone else call. Then stand slightly behind the person, support their chest with one hand and bend them well forward, so gravity helps rather than hinders. With the heel of your other hand, give a sharp blow between the shoulder blades. Check after each blow to see whether the object has come out, rather than automatically delivering all five. The aim is a sudden jolt that loosens the blockage, along with gravity, so it falls forward out of the mouth instead of being driven deeper.

sections.key: If back blows fail, give up to five chest thrusts, then keep alternating the two.
sections.b: If five back blows have not cleared the airway, switch to chest thrusts. Support the person's back with one hand and place the heel of your other hand on the lower half of the breastbone, the same spot used for CPR compressions. Push in sharply. Chest thrusts are slower and sharper than CPR compressions, and each one is designed to squeeze a burst of air out of the lungs, like a cough you are creating for them. Check after each thrust. If the blockage still has not cleared after five, go back to five back blows, then five chest thrusts, and keep alternating until the object comes out, help arrives, or the person becomes unresponsive.

sections.key: Australian guidelines do not recommend abdominal thrusts, though some other countries still teach them.
sections.b: In 1974 the American surgeon Henry Heimlich popularised abdominal thrusts: standing behind a choking person and pulling sharply inwards and upwards under the ribs. The technique became world famous, and it is still taught in the United States and the United Kingdom, usually after back blows. Australian and New Zealand guidelines take a different view. ANZCOR's airway guideline states that abdominal thrusts are not recommended, pointing to reports of life-threatening complications such as injuries to internal organs, and concluding that back blows and chest thrusts work with a low risk of harm. Countries weigh the same limited evidence differently. If you live in Australia, learn the local method, and do not worry that you have forgotten something by not using the Heimlich.

sections.key: Infants are held head-down along your thigh or forearm for back blows and chest thrusts.
sections.b: Babies under a year old are too small and fragile for adult techniques. For an infant with severe choking, call 000 and position the baby face down and head-down along your thigh or forearm, supporting the head and jaw. Give up to five back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking after each one. If that fails, turn the baby onto their back, still head-down, and give up to five chest thrusts using two fingers on the lower half of the breastbone. Keep alternating. Prevention matters enormously: cut grapes and cherry tomatoes lengthways into quarters for small children, avoid whole nuts for under fives, and make sure children sit down while eating.

sections.key: If a choking person becomes unresponsive, call 000 and start CPR.
sections.b: If a choking person becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally, lay them on their back, make sure Triple Zero has been called, and start CPR following DRSABCD. Chest compressions themselves create pressure inside the chest that may help push the object out. Before giving rescue breaths, look in the mouth. If you can see something, you can try to remove it, but guidelines advise against blind finger sweeps, where you poke around without seeing anything, because they can push an object further in. Even if the object comes out and the person seems completely fine, they should still be checked by a doctor, as chest thrusts and the choking itself can cause injuries that are not obvious straight away.

quiz.q: A person is choking but coughing loudly and forcefully. What should you do?
o: Give five back blows immediately
Encourage them to keep coughing and stay with them
Give them a glass of water
Start chest compressions
quiz.e: A strong cough means air is moving, and coughing is the best way to clear the airway. Watch closely in case it gets worse.

quiz.q: Under Australian guidelines, what is the first technique for a conscious adult with severe choking?
o: Abdominal thrusts
Blind finger sweeps
Up to five back blows with the person bent forward
Lying them flat on their back
quiz.e: ANZCOR guidelines start with back blows, with the person bent well forward so gravity helps.

quiz.q: Where are chest thrusts given?
o: On the lower half of the breastbone
Just below the belly button
On the upper back
On the side of the ribs
quiz.e: Chest thrusts use the same spot as CPR compressions but are slower and sharper.

quiz.q: Why do Australian guidelines not recommend abdominal thrusts?
o: They are too hard to learn
They only work on children
They were never tested
There are reports of life-threatening complications, and back blows and chest thrusts work with low risk of harm
quiz.e: ANZCOR cites serious complications reported with abdominal thrusts, including the Heimlich manoeuvre.

quiz.q: A choking person becomes unresponsive. What should you do?
o: Keep giving back blows while they lie on the floor
Make sure 000 has been called and start CPR
Do blind finger sweeps until you find the object
Sit them up and wait
quiz.e: Start CPR following DRSABCD. Compressions may also help dislodge the object.

LESSONS.title: Stopping severe bleeding
LESSONS.hook: A person can lose a dangerous amount of blood in minutes. The most powerful tool for stopping it is something everyone already owns: their hands.

sections.key: Severe bleeding can become life-threatening faster than an ambulance can arrive.
sections.b: An adult body holds roughly five litres of blood. Losing a large share of that quickly starves the brain and organs of oxygen, and a wound to a major blood vessel in the arm, leg, neck or groin can bleed heavily enough to become life-threatening within minutes. Paramedics are fast, but not always fast enough, which is why the person standing next to the injured one matters most. Bleeding is life-threatening if blood is spurting or pulsing, flowing steadily, pooling on the ground, or soaking through clothing and bandages. First check for danger to yourself, then call Triple Zero (000), or ask someone else to call while you act. Put the phone on speaker so the operator can coach you.

sections.key: Firm, direct pressure on the wound is the quickest and most effective way to control bleeding.
sections.b: Australian first aid guidelines are clear: direct pressure is usually the quickest and most effective way to stop bleeding. Put a pad, such as a folded cloth, gauze or a clean T-shirt, directly on the wound and press down hard with both hands. If nothing is available, use your bare hands and worry about cleanliness later; infection can be treated in hospital, but blood loss cannot be undone. Lean in and use your body weight. Keep the pressure steady rather than lifting it to check every few seconds, because each peek can let a fragile clot break. If you have gloves, wear them, but do not waste precious time hunting for them while the person bleeds.

sections.key: If blood soaks through, leave the first pad in place and put another on top.
sections.b: A common instinct is to peel away a blood-soaked dressing and replace it with a fresh one. Resist it. Removing the first pad can tear away the clot forming underneath and start the bleeding again. Instead, place a second pad over the first and bind it firmly with a bandage, or simply keep pressing. Help the person lie down, especially if the bleeding is from a leg or is severe, and keep the injured part still. Lying down reduces the risk of fainting and helps blood reach the brain. If you need to free your hands for something else, a firmly tied bandage over the pads can hold pressure in place while you deal with other problems.

sections.key: Never pull out an embedded object; pad around it and press on the pads instead.
sections.b: If a knife, a shard of glass or a piece of metal is stuck in a wound, leave it where it is. It may be plugging the hole and holding back the bleeding, and pulling it out can cause sudden, severe blood loss and further damage. Instead, build padding around the object, so it is supported and cannot move, and apply pressure on the pads either side of it rather than on the object itself. This is called indirect pressure. Call 000 and keep the person as still as possible. The same principle applies to something like a fence paling or a stick: hospital teams have the equipment, imaging and blood supplies to remove it safely.

sections.key: For life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure cannot stop, a tourniquet can save a life if you are trained to use one.
