sections.b: A tourniquet is a tight band placed around an arm or leg, above a wound, to cut off blood flow to the limb. Old first aid courses taught people to fear them, but experience from military medicine, including wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, showed they save lives in catastrophic limb bleeding. Australian guidelines now say a tourniquet should be used for life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot control, if one is available and the first aider is trained. It goes a short distance above the wound, about five centimetres unless the product's instructions say otherwise, not over a joint or the wound itself, and is tightened until the bleeding stops. Note the time it was applied and tell paramedics, and never loosen it yourself once it is on.

sections.key: Pale, clammy skin, a fast pulse and confusion can signal shock; keep the person lying down and warm.
sections.b: Even once bleeding is controlled, the body may struggle to cope with what it has lost. Shock is a dangerous drop in blood flow to the organs. Signs include pale, cold and clammy skin, a rapid, weak pulse, fast breathing, thirst, anxiety, confusion and drowsiness. Keep the person lying down, reassure them, and cover them with a blanket or jacket to stop heat loss, because the body cannot afford to spend energy keeping warm. Do not give them anything to eat or drink, since they may need surgery. Keep monitoring their breathing and responsiveness. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR and keep going until help arrives.

sections.key: Most bleeding is minor: for a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose.
sections.b: Most bleeding we see in daily life is not dangerous. For small cuts, rinse the wound with clean water, press with a clean cloth until it stops, and cover it with a dressing. Watch over the following days for signs of infection, such as spreading redness, swelling, heat or pus. For a nosebleed, the old advice to tilt the head back is wrong, because blood then runs down the throat and can cause vomiting. Instead, sit up, lean forward and firmly pinch the soft part of the nose, just below the bony bridge, for at least ten minutes without letting go to check. Seek medical help if a nosebleed will not stop or followed a blow to the head.

quiz.q: What is usually the quickest and most effective way to control severe bleeding?
o: Raising the limb above the head
Firm, direct pressure on the wound
Pouring cold water on it
Applying a tourniquet to every wound
quiz.e: Direct pressure is the first and most effective step, using a pad or even bare hands.

quiz.q: Blood soaks through the pad you are pressing on. What should you do?
o: Remove it and replace it with a clean one
Stop pressing to see where the bleeding is coming from
Leave it in place and add another pad on top
Wash the wound with water
quiz.e: Removing the first pad can tear away a forming clot.

quiz.q: A piece of glass is stuck in a wound. What should you do?
o: Leave it in, pad around it and press on the pads
Pull it out quickly
Push it in further to stop the bleeding
Wrap a bandage tightly over the glass itself
quiz.e: The object may be plugging the wound, so use indirect pressure around it.

quiz.q: When do Australian guidelines say a tourniquet should be used?
o: For any cut on a limb
Instead of calling 000
Only on the neck
For life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure cannot control, if available and trained
quiz.e: Tourniquets save lives in catastrophic limb bleeding; note the time and leave it on.

quiz.q: What is the right first aid for a nosebleed?
o: Tilt the head back
Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
Lie flat on the back
Blow the nose hard
quiz.e: Leaning forward stops blood running down the throat, and steady pinching lets it clot.

LESSONS.title: Seizures: what to do and what not to do
LESSONS.hook: Watching someone have a seizure is frightening, and the most famous piece of advice about it is completely wrong. The right response is calm, simple and mostly about keeping them safe.

sections.key: A seizure is a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
sections.b: The brain runs on electrical signals passed between billions of nerve cells. During a seizure, a sudden burst of abnormal, synchronised activity disrupts that traffic. What happens next depends on where in the brain it starts and how far it spreads. Epilepsy is a condition in which a person has a tendency to have recurring seizures, but seizures can also be triggered by other things: a high fever in young children, a head injury, very low blood sugar, alcohol withdrawal, some drugs, or an illness affecting the brain. Seizures are more common than many people think, and many people will witness one at some point. That makes basic seizure first aid worth knowing, whether at home, at work or on public transport.

sections.h: Not every seizure looks the same
sections.key: Some seizures cause convulsions, while others look like staring, confusion or odd repeated movements.
sections.b: The type most people picture is a tonic-clonic seizure, once called a grand mal. The person may cry out, stiffen, fall, and then jerk rhythmically, sometimes with noisy breathing, drooling, or loss of bladder control. Most stop on their own within a few minutes. But many seizures look nothing like this. In a focal seizure, a person may seem dazed, pluck at their clothes, smack their lips, wander aimlessly or not respond properly, while staying on their feet. An absence seizure, most common in children, can look like a few seconds of blank staring and is easily mistaken for daydreaming. Someone having one of these quieter seizures may be misjudged as drunk or rude, when they actually need patience and protection.

sections.key: Note the time, move dangers away and cushion the head; don't restrain the person.
sections.b: When someone has a convulsive seizure, stay with them and stay calm. Check the time on your phone straight away, because how long the seizure lasts is one of the most important things to know. Move hard or sharp objects out of the way and put something soft, such as a folded jacket, under their head. Loosen anything tight around their neck if you can do it safely. Do not try to hold them down or stop the movements; restraint can injure both of you and will not end the seizure. Do not move them unless they are in danger, such as near traffic, water, stairs or a fire. Ask onlookers to give them space and privacy.

sections.key: Never put anything in a person's mouth during a seizure; it is impossible to swallow your tongue.
sections.b: For generations, people were told to force something between the teeth of a person having a seizure, supposedly to stop them swallowing their tongue. This is a myth, and a harmful one. The tongue is anchored to the floor of the mouth and cannot be swallowed. Pushing a spoon, wallet or fingers into the mouth can break teeth, injure the jaw, cause choking on broken fragments, and get your fingers badly bitten. A person may bite their tongue or cheek during a seizure, which can bleed, but this usually heals and is far less dangerous than what well-meaning bystanders cause. Likewise, do not give anything to eat or drink until they are fully awake and able to swallow.

sections.key: Once the movements stop, roll the person onto their side and stay with them while they recover.
sections.b: When the convulsions end, gently roll the person onto their side into the recovery position. This helps keep the airway clear and lets saliva or vomit drain from the mouth. Check that their breathing is returning to normal. Recovery takes time. It is common for a person to be confused, drowsy, embarrassed or upset for some minutes, or even longer, after a seizure. Speak calmly, tell them where they are and what happened, and stay until they are fully alert. Many people with epilepsy carry an identification card or wear a medical bracelet, and some have a seizure management plan, which may tell you what is usual for them and when to call for help.

sections.key: Call an ambulance if a seizure lasts over five minutes, repeats, happens in water, or causes injury or breathing trouble.
sections.b: Many people with known epilepsy do not need an ambulance for a typical, short seizure. But Epilepsy Action Australia advises calling Triple Zero (000) if the seizure lasts more than five minutes, if another seizure follows before the person has recovered, or if they do not wake up afterwards. Call too if the person is injured, has trouble breathing, is pregnant or diabetic, if the seizure happened in water, or if it is their first seizure. And call if you are unsure what to do. Any seizure in water is an emergency because of the risk of drowning, even if the person seems fine afterwards. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR.

sections.key: Febrile seizures in young children are frightening but usually harmless; seek medical help the first time.
sections.b: Some young children, usually between about six months and six years old, have a seizure when they have a high fever. These are called febrile convulsions. For a parent, watching their child stiffen and jerk can be terrifying, but most febrile convulsions stop within a few minutes and do not cause lasting harm. The child does not usually go on to develop epilepsy. The first aid is the same: stay calm, time it, keep the child safe on a soft surface on their side, and do not put anything in their mouth. Call 000 if it lasts more than five minutes or the child has trouble breathing, and have a doctor check a child after their first febrile convulsion to look for the cause of the fever.

quiz.q: What might a focal or absence seizure look like?
o: Always violent jerking of the whole body
Blank staring, confusion or repeated movements like lip smacking
Sudden sneezing
Fast, loud speech
quiz.e: Many seizures are quiet and can be mistaken for daydreaming, drunkenness or rudeness.

quiz.q: Why should you check the time when a seizure starts?
o: Because how long it lasts determines whether to call 000
So you can tell the person later how bored you were
Because seizures always stop after one minute
It doesn't matter
quiz.e: A seizure lasting more than five minutes needs an ambulance.

quiz.q: Should you put something in the person's mouth to stop them swallowing their tongue?
o: Yes, a spoon is ideal
Yes, but only your fingers
Only a soft cloth
No: the tongue can't be swallowed and objects can cause serious injury
quiz.e: This is a harmful myth. Keep everything out of the mouth.

quiz.q: What should you do once the jerking movements stop?
o: Give them a glass of water
Make them stand up and walk
Roll them onto their side and stay with them
Leave them to sleep alone
quiz.e: The recovery position helps keep the airway clear while they recover.

quiz.q: Which situation calls for an ambulance?
o: A seizure that happens in water
A seizure in a person with known epilepsy that lasts one minute and stops
The person feels tired afterwards
The person is embarrassed
quiz.e: Seizures in water are always an emergency because of the risk of drowning.

LESSONS.title: Electricity: the danger you can't see
LESSONS.hook: Electricity gives no warning: no smell, no sound, nothing to see. A few simple rules, and one small switch in your meter box, stand between ordinary life and a fatal shock.

sections.key: Electric current through the body can stop the heart and cause deep burns that look small from outside.
sections.b: When electricity finds a path through the body, it can do harm in several ways. Current crossing the chest can throw the heart into a chaotic rhythm called ventricular fibrillation, in which it quivers instead of pumping, which is cardiac arrest. Current can also make muscles contract so strongly that a person cannot let go of what they are holding. And as it passes through tissue, electricity generates heat, causing burns along its path. The entry and exit wounds on the skin can look small, while muscles, nerves and blood vessels inside are badly damaged. That is why anyone who has had a significant electric shock or an electrical burn should be checked by a doctor, even if they feel fine.

sections.key: A safety switch, or RCD, cuts the power in a fraction of a second when current leaks to earth.
sections.b: A residual current device, usually called a safety switch in Australia, is one of the great quiet lifesavers of modern homes. It constantly compares the current flowing out along the active wire with the current coming back along the neutral wire. If they do not match, some current is leaking somewhere, possibly through a person, and the switch cuts the power within a fraction of a second, fast enough to greatly reduce the risk of death. Safety switches are different from circuit breakers and fuses, which mainly protect wiring from overloading. Newer homes are required to have them, but many older homes have them on only some circuits, or none. Most have a test button that is worth pressing regularly.

sections.key: In Australia, electrical wiring work must be done by a licensed electrician.
sections.b: Across Australia, it is illegal for an unlicensed person to do electrical wiring work, such as installing power points, replacing light switches or running new cables. That rule exists because faulty wiring can kill, sometimes years later and sometimes someone else entirely, such as a future tenant or a tradesperson. A loose connection can also start a fire inside a wall. At home, the safe habits are simple. Do not use appliances with frayed or damaged cords. Do not overload power boards or daisy-chain them together. Keep electrical appliances away from water and never touch switches with wet hands. Do not try to fish toast out of a plugged-in toaster with a knife. And if a switch or power point feels warm or smells of burning, get it checked.

sections.key: Stay at least eight metres away from fallen powerlines and treat every line as live.
sections.b: After storms, crashes and bushfires, powerlines can end up on the ground, on fences, on cars or in trees. Treat every fallen line as live, even if it is not sparking or humming, because it may still be energised or could be re-energised automatically. Electricity distributors advise staying at least eight metres away, about two car lengths, and keeping others back too. Electricity can travel through wet ground, puddles, fences and metal, so you do not need to touch the line itself to be hurt. If someone is injured or there is a fire, call Triple Zero (000). Otherwise, report it to your local electricity distributor, whose emergency number is usually printed on your power bill.

sections.h: If a line falls on your car
sections.key: Stay inside the vehicle unless it is on fire; if you must get out, jump clear without touching the car and ground together.
sections.b: If a powerline falls onto your car, the safest place is usually inside it. The current may be flowing through the body of the car into the ground, and you are protected as long as you do not form a path between the car and the earth. Stay put, call 000, and warn anyone approaching to keep away. If you must leave because of fire, open the door, and jump well clear with your feet together, making sure no part of your body touches the car and the ground at the same time. Then move away with small shuffling or hopping steps, keeping your feet close together, because the voltage in the ground changes with distance from the contact point.

sections.key: Never touch someone in contact with electricity; switch off the power first.
sections.b: If you see someone being electrocuted, your instinct will be to grab them. Don't. If they are still in contact with the source, the current can flow into you as well, and then there are two casualties. First, switch off the power at the switchboard or the wall, or unplug the appliance if you can do so safely. For powerlines and high voltage, do not approach at all: call 000 and wait for the electricity company to make it safe. Once the power is off, check the person using DRSABCD, start CPR if they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, and send someone for a defibrillator. Cool any electrical burns with cool running water for twenty minutes.

sections.key: Overhead powerlines are a major hazard when using ladders, tall machinery, boat masts and tipper trucks.
sections.b: Many serious electrical accidents happen outdoors, when someone accidentally brings a tall object into contact with overhead powerlines. A painter on an aluminium ladder, a farmer raising an auger or tipper tray, a sailor launching a boat with its mast up, or a young person climbing a tree or a train carriage can all be killed by a line they never noticed. Electricity can also jump, or arc, across a gap to an object that comes close enough, without direct contact. The simple habit is to look up before you raise anything tall, carry long objects horizontally, and plan routes on farms and worksites around powerlines. Never climb power poles, transmission towers or the roofs of trains.

quiz.q: Why should someone who had a significant shock see a doctor even if they feel fine?
o: Because shocks always cause broken bones
Because the current may have damaged tissue inside or affected the heart
Because they will need a tetanus injection
They don't need to
quiz.e: Internal damage can be far worse than small skin burns suggest.

quiz.q: What does a safety switch (RCD) do?
o: Cuts the power within a fraction of a second when current leaks
Stops power bills going up
Boosts power during storms
Only protects against lightning
quiz.e: It compares outgoing and returning current and cuts power if they don't match.

quiz.q: How far should you stay from a fallen powerline?
o: Half a metre
One metre
At least eight metres
It's safe if the line isn't sparking
quiz.e: Distributors advise at least eight metres, about two car lengths, and to treat every line as live.

quiz.q: A powerline has fallen on your car and there is no fire. What should you do?
o: Get out and run
Touch the door handle to test it
Stay inside, call 000 and warn people to keep away
Drive over the line
quiz.e: Inside the car you are protected as long as you don't form a path to the ground.

quiz.q: Someone is still touching a live appliance. What should you do first?
o: Pull them away by the arm
Throw water on them
Start CPR immediately
Switch off the power at the switchboard or unplug it if safe
quiz.e: Touching them while the power is on could make you a second casualty.

LESSONS.title: Poisons at home: one number to remember
LESSONS.hook: Most poisonings happen not in labs or crime novels but in ordinary kitchens, bathrooms and handbags. Knowing one phone number, and one danger hiding in your remote control, could save a child's life.

sections.key: Most poisonings are accidents at home, and children under five are especially at risk.
sections.b: Poisoning sounds like something from a detective story, but the reality is far more ordinary. Most cases are accidents in the home. Young children, especially those under five, are particularly vulnerable because they explore with their mouths, copy adults and move fast. A child can climb onto a bench, open a handbag or find a dropped tablet in seconds. Common culprits include medicines, both prescription and over the counter, cleaning products, dishwasher and laundry detergent pods, essential oils, cosmetics, garden chemicals and some plants. Adults are poisoned too, often through medication mix-ups, such as taking a double dose by mistake, or through chemicals stored in the wrong containers. The good news is that a few habits prevent most of it.

sections.key: The Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 gives expert advice any time, day or night, across Australia.
sections.b: Australia has a national phone number for poisoning advice: 13 11 26, the Poisons Information Centre. It is answered around the clock, every day of the year, from anywhere in the country. Specialists can tell you whether a substance and amount is likely to be harmful, what to do right now, and whether the person needs to go to hospital. Many calls end with the reassuring news that nothing more needs to be done. It is worth saving the number in your phone and putting it on the fridge. But if the person has collapsed, is having a seizure, is having trouble breathing, or is very drowsy, do not call the Poisons line first. Call Triple Zero (000) for an ambulance.

sections.key: Do not induce vomiting or give anything to eat or drink unless an expert tells you to.
sections.b: Old remedies for poisoning included making the person vomit with salt water, mustard or syrup of ipecac, or giving them milk. Modern advice is to do none of these unless told to by the Poisons Information Centre or a doctor. Vomiting can cause further harm, especially with corrosive substances such as drain cleaner, which burn on the way down and can burn again on the way back up, or with petroleum products like kerosene, which can be inhaled into the lungs. If something is in the mouth, have them spit it out and wipe the mouth. For chemicals on skin or in eyes, rinse with plenty of running water. Keep the container so you can tell the experts exactly what it was.

sections.key: Swallowed button batteries can burn through tissue within hours; get emergency help straight away.
sections.b: Small, coin-shaped lithium batteries are everywhere: in car keys, remote controls, kitchen scales, thermometers, toys and greeting cards that play music. If a child swallows one and it lodges in the oesophagus, the tube to the stomach, the battery reacts with saliva and body fluids and produces a strongly alkaline chemical that can burn through tissue, sometimes within two hours. The damage can reach major blood vessels. Children have died in Australia this way. Symptoms may be vague or absent at first, so do not wait for them. If you suspect a child has swallowed or put a button battery in their nose or ear, call 000 or go straight to a hospital emergency department, and call 13 11 26 for advice.

sections.key: Deaths of Australian children led to mandatory button battery safety standards.
sections.b: In 2013, a four-year-old Queensland girl, Summer Steer, died after swallowing a button battery that no one knew she had found. Her death, and others, led to campaigns by families, doctors and consumer groups. In 2022, Australia introduced mandatory safety standards, enforced by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. Products containing button batteries must have secure battery compartments that young children cannot easily open, batteries must be sold in child-resistant packaging, and warnings are required. Australia was among the first countries in the world to introduce mandatory rules of this kind. Even so, older products, cheap imports and spare batteries lying in drawers remain a risk, so store them up high and dispose of used ones safely.

sections.key: Store medicines and chemicals up high, locked away, and always in their original containers.
sections.b: Most poisonings can be prevented with storage. Keep medicines, including vitamins and pain relievers, in a locked or child-resistant cupboard at least 1.5 metres off the ground, not in handbags, on bedside tables or in bowls on the kitchen bench. Put them away straight after use, including while you answer the door. Never store chemicals in drink bottles or food containers, a classic cause of accidental poisoning in adults as well as children. Keep products in their original containers with their labels. Visiting grandparents and guests may carry medicines in their bags, so ask them to keep bags out of reach. And give medicines with the lights on, reading the label, to avoid dose mix-ups.

sections.key: Never eat wild mushrooms unless an expert has identified them; deadly species grow in Australia.
sections.b: Some of the most dangerous poisons are natural. The death cap mushroom, Amanita phalloides, was introduced to Australia and grows in places such as Canberra and Melbourne, often under oak trees. It can look similar to edible mushrooms, cooking does not destroy its toxins, and eating even part of one can cause liver failure. Symptoms are often delayed for many hours, which can give false reassurance. The safest rule is never to eat a mushroom picked from the wild unless an expert has identified it with certainty. Some common garden plants are toxic too, such as oleander. If someone has eaten an unknown mushroom or plant, call 13 11 26 straight away, even if they feel well, and keep a sample.

quiz.q: What is the national Poisons Information Centre number in Australia?
o: 000 only
quiz.e: 13 11 26 is answered 24 hours a day, every day. Call 000 if the person collapses or struggles to breathe.

quiz.q: Someone has swallowed drain cleaner. Should you make them vomit?
o: Yes, with salt water
Yes, by giving them milk first
No: vomiting can cause more harm; get expert advice immediately
Only if they feel sick
quiz.e: Corrosive substances can burn again on the way back up. Don't induce vomiting unless told to.

quiz.q: Why are swallowed button batteries so dangerous?
o: They are sharp
They can produce a chemical reaction that burns through tissue within hours
They are always radioactive
They make children sleepy
quiz.e: A lodged battery can cause severe internal burns, so get emergency help straight away.

quiz.q: Which storage habit is most risky?
o: Keeping medicines in a locked cupboard
Keeping chemicals in their original labelled containers
Putting medicines away right after use
Storing chemicals in an old drink bottle
quiz.e: Chemicals in drink bottles are easily mistaken for a drink, by adults as well as children.

quiz.q: What makes the death cap mushroom particularly dangerous?
o: Its toxins survive cooking and symptoms can be delayed for hours
It only grows overseas
It tastes bitter so people spit it out
It only affects children
quiz.e: Delayed symptoms can give false reassurance while the liver is being damaged.

LESSONS.title: Carbon monoxide: the invisible killer
LESSONS.hook: It has no colour, no smell and no taste, and its symptoms feel like the flu. Here is how an ordinary heater can quietly poison a home, and how to stop it.

sections.key: The deaths of two boys in Shepparton in 2010 changed how Australia thinks about gas heaters.
sections.b: In May 2010, two brothers, Chase and Tyler Robinson, aged eight and six, died in their sleep at their rented home in Shepparton, Victoria. The cause was carbon monoxide from a faulty gas heater. Nothing had seemed wrong. There was no smoke, no strange smell and no alarm, because the home had no carbon monoxide detector. A coronial inquest examined who was responsible for maintaining the heater and how to stop it happening again. Their mother, Vanessa Robinson, became a prominent campaigner for gas heater safety, and the case helped bring changes, including Victoria's requirement for regular gas safety checks in rental homes. Their story is a painful reminder that the most dangerous hazards are sometimes the ones we cannot sense at all.

sections.key: Carbon monoxide grabs onto haemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen, starving the body of oxygen.
sections.b: Carbon monoxide is a gas made when fuels such as gas, wood, charcoal, petrol or diesel burn without enough oxygen. Its danger lies in the blood. Red blood cells carry oxygen using a protein called haemoglobin. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin roughly two hundred times more strongly than oxygen does, so even small amounts in the air steadily push oxygen out of the blood. The brain and heart, which need the most oxygen, suffer first. Because the gas is colourless, odourless and tasteless, people breathe it without any idea they are being poisoned. At high levels it can cause unconsciousness and death within minutes. At lower levels over hours or days it can cause lasting damage to the brain and heart.

sections.key: Headache, dizziness, nausea and tiredness can easily be mistaken for the flu.
sections.b: The early signs of carbon monoxide poisoning are frustratingly ordinary: headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, tiredness, weakness, shortness of breath and confusion. People often assume they have the flu, a migraine or a stomach bug. Some clues point to carbon monoxide instead. Several people in the house, or pets, feel sick at the same time. Symptoms are worse at home, or when a heater or appliance is running, and improve when you go outside or leave for the day. People who are asleep or have been drinking may not notice symptoms before losing consciousness, which is why poisoning at night is especially dangerous. Babies, older people, pregnant women and people with heart or lung disease are particularly vulnerable.

sections.key: Faulty or poorly ventilated gas heaters and fuel-burning devices used indoors cause most cases.
sections.b: In Australian homes, a major source is gas space heaters, especially older or poorly maintained ones. An open-flued heater draws air from the room and is meant to send fumes outside through a flue, but a blocked or faulty flue, or strong exhaust fans pulling air the wrong way, can spill carbon monoxide back inside. Unflued gas heaters release their fumes straight into the room and need good ventilation. Other causes are tragically common: using a barbecue, a camping stove, an outdoor patio heater or charcoal indoors or in a tent, caravan or garage, running a generator inside or near an open window, or leaving a car engine running in a closed garage. None of these should ever be used in an enclosed space.

sections.key: Have gas heaters serviced regularly by a licensed gasfitter and keep rooms ventilated.
sections.b: Gas heaters should be serviced by a licensed gasfitter, generally at least every two years, or as the manufacturer recommends. A carbon monoxide test checks whether the heater is spilling fumes, especially when exhaust fans are running. Warning signs of a faulty appliance include a yellow or orange flame instead of a crisp blue one, soot or staining around the heater, or a stale, stuffy feel in the room. Never block vents, and do not leave gas heaters running overnight in bedrooms unless the manufacturer says it is safe. If you rent, ask the landlord when the heater was last checked. And never bring outdoor equipment such as barbecues or patio heaters inside, even briefly on a cold night.

sections.key: A carbon monoxide alarm is a useful extra layer of protection, but it does not replace servicing.
sections.b: Smoke alarms do not detect carbon monoxide. A separate carbon monoxide alarm, available from hardware stores, sounds a warning when levels rise, giving you the chance to get out before you are overcome. Place it according to the manufacturer's instructions, typically in rooms with fuel-burning appliances and near sleeping areas, and test it regularly. Some combined smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are also available. Carbon monoxide alarms are not yet required in most Australian homes, but safety regulators encourage them, especially for homes with gas heating. An alarm is a backstop, not a substitute for regular servicing. And if one sounds, take it seriously, even if no one feels unwell yet.

sections.key: Get everyone into fresh air, turn off the appliance if safe, and call 000.
sections.b: If you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning, act fast. Get everyone, including pets, out of the building and into fresh air. If it is safe and quick to do so, turn off the suspected appliance and open doors and windows on your way out, but do not delay leaving. Call Triple Zero (000). If anyone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR once you are in a safe place. Do not go back inside until the appliance has been checked by a licensed gasfitter and the source found. In hospital, people are treated with high-concentration oxygen, which speeds up the removal of carbon monoxide from the blood. Even people who recover quickly should be medically assessed.

quiz.q: Why is carbon monoxide so dangerous to the body?
o: It burns the lungs
It binds to haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen
It thickens the blood
It causes an allergic reaction
quiz.e: Carbon monoxide pushes oxygen out of the blood, starving the brain and heart.

quiz.q: Which clue suggests carbon monoxide rather than the flu?
o: Symptoms improve when you leave the house
A runny nose
A sore throat
Only one person is unwell
quiz.e: Several people or pets unwell, and symptoms that ease away from home, are warning signs.

quiz.q: Which of these is safe?
o: Using a barbecue in the garage on a cold night
Running a generator in the laundry
Using a camping stove inside a tent
Running a barbecue outdoors in the open air
quiz.e: Fuel-burning equipment like barbecues, stoves and generators belongs outdoors only.

quiz.q: Which flame colour on a gas heater can signal a problem?
o: A crisp blue flame
A yellow or orange flame
No visible flame on an electric heater
A steady flame
quiz.e: A yellow or orange flame, soot or staining can mean incomplete burning and carbon monoxide.

quiz.q: What should you do first if you suspect carbon monoxide poisoning?
o: Get everyone into fresh air and call 000
Open a window and go back to bed
Wait to see if symptoms improve
Turn the heater up
quiz.e: Fresh air and an ambulance come first; the source must be checked before returning.

LESSONS.title: Croc country: staying safe in the north
LESSONS.hook: Northern Australia is home to the largest reptile on Earth, an ambush hunter that has been perfecting its technique for millions of years. The rules for living alongside it are simple, and they work.

sections.key: The saltwater crocodile is the world's largest living reptile and a patient ambush hunter.
sections.b: The estuarine or saltwater crocodile, Crocodylus porosus, is the largest living reptile on the planet. Large males can grow beyond five metres long and weigh many hundreds of kilograms, while females are considerably smaller. In Australia, salties live across the tropical north, from the Kimberley in Western Australia through the Northern Territory to Queensland, where they are found down the east coast into central Queensland. They are ambush predators. A crocodile can lie almost completely submerged, with only its eyes and nostrils showing, and wait for a long time for an animal to come close to the water's edge. Then it lunges with astonishing speed. Australia's other species, the freshwater crocodile, is smaller and far less dangerous, though it can still bite.

sections.key: After heavy hunting, legal protection from around the early 1970s allowed crocodile numbers to recover strongly.
sections.b: In the decades after the Second World War, saltwater crocodiles were hunted intensively for their skins, and populations crashed in many areas. Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Queensland introduced protection between about 1970 and 1974. Since then, numbers have bounced back strongly, especially in the Northern Territory, where the wild population is estimated at around one hundred thousand. It is one of conservation's great success stories, but it has a consequence. More crocodiles, and larger ones, now share rivers, beaches and boat ramps with growing numbers of residents and tourists. Fatal attacks remain rare in Australia, typically around one or two a year, but nearly all involve people who were in or right beside the water.

sections.key: Saltwater crocodiles live in rivers, billabongs, swamps and beaches, sometimes far inland.
sections.b: The name saltwater crocodile is misleading. Salties live in tidal rivers, mangroves and estuaries, but also in freshwater billabongs, swamps, waterholes and rivers far from the coast. They also swim along the coast and can turn up on popular beaches and around islands. A waterhole that looks clear and inviting, with no warning sign, may still hold a crocodile. Crocodiles are also hard to spot. Muddy water, reflections and their camouflage mean even locals can miss a large animal a few metres away. Wildlife authorities therefore give one simple rule: in croc country, assume any body of water may contain crocodiles, whether or not there is a sign, and do not swim unless you are certain it is safe.

sections.key: Never swim in croc country, stay back from the water's edge and never feed crocodiles.
sections.b: Queensland's CrocWise guidance, and similar advice from the Northern Territory and Western Australia, sets out habits that dramatically reduce risk. Obey warning signs, but never assume water without signs is safe. Do not swim, paddle or wade where crocodiles may live. Stand a few metres back from the water's edge when fishing, and never stand on overhanging logs or branches. Do not clean fish or leave fish scraps, bait or food near the water, at boat ramps or at campsites, because they attract crocodiles. Never feed crocodiles; animals that associate people with food become bolder and more dangerous. Be extra alert at night and during the breeding season, roughly September to April, when crocodiles are more active and territorial.

sections.key: Camp at least 50 metres from the water and keep arms and legs inside the boat.
sections.b: Campers in croc country should set up at least fifty metres from the water's edge and at least two metres above the high water mark, according to CrocWise guidance. Collect water with a bucket from a distance rather than wading in, and do not prepare food, wash dishes or do other chores at the water's edge or on sloping banks. Crocodiles are creatures of habit and can learn people's routines, so avoid using the same spot at the water's edge every day. In boats, do not dangle arms or legs over the side, and do not lean out to free a snagged lure. Small boats such as canoes and kayaks are not recommended in crocodile habitat. If you fall in, get out as quickly as possible.

sections.key: Zigzag running is a myth; the real danger is at and in the water, not on land.
sections.b: One popular piece of folklore says that if a crocodile chases you, you should run in a zigzag, because crocodiles cannot turn quickly. Experts regard this as a myth. Crocodiles can move fast over short distances on land, but they rarely chase people away from the water. The real risk is the sudden lunge from the water at someone standing on the bank, wading or swimming. The best advice is simply to keep your distance in the first place. Another dangerous myth is that crocodiles are only in remote wilderness. In fact they are regularly seen in waterways near towns such as Darwin, Cairns and Townsville, which is why wildlife authorities run removal programs in busy areas.

sections.key: Report crocodile sightings to wildlife authorities and call 000 in an emergency.
sections.b: Each state and territory with crocodiles has a way to report sightings, and doing so helps wildlife officers decide whether a crocodile poses a risk and needs to be removed. Check the current reporting method for the area you are visiting, as it may be a phone line or an online form. Report crocodiles that behave aggressively, approach people or boats, or turn up in towns or popular swimming spots. If someone is attacked or injured, call Triple Zero (000) immediately. Do not put yourself in danger by entering the water. Once the person is out of the water and safe, control bleeding with firm, direct pressure, keep them warm and lying down, and follow DRSABCD until help arrives.

quiz.q: Which statement about the saltwater crocodile is correct?
o: It is the world's largest living reptile
It only lives in the open ocean
It is smaller than the freshwater crocodile
It is found in southern Australia
quiz.e: Large males can exceed five metres, making it the largest living reptile.

quiz.q: Why have saltwater crocodile numbers increased in Australia?
o: They were introduced from Asia
Legal protection after heavy hunting allowed populations to recover
Climate change created new rivers
Farms released them
quiz.e: Protection introduced in the early 1970s allowed a strong recovery.

quiz.q: A clear waterhole in croc country has no warning sign. What should you assume?
o: It is definitely safe
Only freshwater crocodiles could be there
It may contain crocodiles; don't swim unless certain it is safe
Crocodiles avoid clear water
quiz.e: Salties live in billabongs and waterholes far inland, and signs can't cover every location.

quiz.q: According to CrocWise guidance, how far from the water's edge should you camp?
o: At least 5 metres
At least 50 metres
At least 500 metres
Distance doesn't matter
quiz.e: Camp at least 50 metres from the edge and 2 metres above the high water mark.

quiz.q: What is the truth about running in a zigzag from a crocodile?
o: It's essential advice
It only works on wet ground
It works for freshwater crocodiles only
It's a myth; the real danger is at and in the water
quiz.e: Crocodiles rarely chase people far from the water. Keep your distance from the edge.

LESSONS.title: Cold water and hypothermia
LESSONS.hook: People who die in cold water often never get cold enough to freeze. The first minute is the most dangerous, and the instinct to swim hard can be exactly the wrong one.

sections.h: Not just a cold place problem
sections.key: Hypothermia happens in Australia, from Tasmanian summers to winter rock fishing and alpine walks.
sections.b: It is easy to think of hypothermia as something that happens to polar explorers. Yet in Australia, people regularly get into trouble in cold conditions: bushwalkers in Tasmania caught by sudden storms, even in summer, skiers and hikers in the Australian Alps, rock fishers swept into winter seas, and kayakers and boaters who capsize in cold rivers and lakes. Water is the great accelerator. It draws heat from the body far faster than air at the same temperature. Wind and wet clothing do something similar on land. Combine rain, wind, tiredness and inadequate clothing, and a person can become dangerously cold on a day when the air temperature seems mild, especially in the mountains, where weather can change within an hour.

sections.key: Sudden immersion triggers a gasp and rapid breathing that can cause drowning within the first minute.
sections.b: When a person suddenly falls into cold water, the shock of cold on the skin triggers an involuntary gasp, followed by rapid, uncontrollable breathing, a racing heart and a spike in blood pressure. This cold shock response peaks in the first minute or so. It is extremely dangerous: if your head is underwater during that first gasp, you can inhale water and drown almost immediately, long before your body has had time to cool. The racing heart and blood pressure can also trigger heart problems in people at risk. This is why many cold water deaths happen close to shore or a boat, and why even strong swimmers can drown quickly after falling into cold water unexpectedly.

sections.key: If you fall into cold water, fight the urge to swim hard; float on your back until your breathing settles.
sections.b: The instinct after falling in is to thrash and swim hard for safety. But swimming and panicking during cold shock makes it harder to control your breathing and increases the risk of inhaling water. Water safety organisations, including the Royal National Lifeboat Institution in Britain, now teach a simple message: float first. Lean back, spread your arms and legs, and keep your face out of the water, moving your hands gently if needed, until the gasping and fast breathing settle, typically within a minute or two. Then you can think clearly about what to do: signal for help, grab something that floats, or swim to safety if it is close. A lifejacket makes all of this far easier.

sections.key: A useful rule of thumb: about a minute to control breathing, ten minutes of useful movement, an hour before unconsciousness.
sections.b: The Canadian physiologist Gordon Giesbrecht popularised a rule of thumb for cold water called 1-10-1. You have roughly one minute to get your breathing under control after the cold shock. You then have roughly ten minutes of meaningful movement before the cold makes your muscles and nerves in the arms and legs too weak to swim or hold on. And it may take around an hour or more for true hypothermia to cause unconsciousness, longer with a lifejacket and warm clothing. The numbers are approximate and vary with water temperature, body size and clothing, but the message is powerful. Do not panic, use those first ten minutes wisely, and if you cannot get out, focus on staying afloat.

sections.key: Shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech and confusion are warning signs; severe cases may stop shivering.
sections.b: Hypothermia means the body's core temperature has dropped below about 35 degrees Celsius, from a normal of around 37. Early signs include intense shivering, cold and pale skin, and fumbling hands. As it worsens, people develop what some instructors call the umbles: they stumble, mumble, fumble and grumble. Speech slurs, movements become clumsy, and thinking becomes slow and confused, so a person may make poor decisions or deny anything is wrong. In severe hypothermia, shivering may actually stop, which is a dangerous sign rather than a good one. The person may become drowsy, have a slow pulse and breathing, and eventually lose consciousness. Because judgement fades early, companions need to watch each other closely.

sections.key: Get the person out of the cold, remove wet clothing, insulate them gently and call 000.
sections.b: Call Triple Zero (000) for anyone with more than mild hypothermia. Move the person out of the wind, rain or water to a warmer, sheltered place, and handle them gently, because a very cold heart can be sensitive to rough movement. Remove wet clothing and replace it with dry layers, or wrap them in blankets, sleeping bags or a space blanket, including the head and neck. Insulate them from the cold ground. If they are fully alert and able to swallow, warm sweet drinks can help, but never give alcohol. Do not rub their limbs or put them in a hot bath. If they become unresponsive and stop breathing normally, start CPR. Very cold people have sometimes been successfully resuscitated after long periods.

sections.key: If someone is in trouble in the water, help from land if you can; don't become a second victim.
sections.b: Each year, people drown trying to rescue others, often family members, including children and dogs. The safest approach is reach or throw, don't go. Call 000. Then try to reach the person from a safe position with a pole, branch, rope or towel, lying down on the bank to keep your balance, or throw them something that floats, such as a lifebuoy, an esky, a bodyboard or a ball. Tell them to float on their back and keep calm. Only trained rescuers with proper equipment should enter the water, especially cold or fast flowing water. Prevention is simpler: wear a lifejacket when boating or rock fishing, dress in layers, check the forecast and tell someone where you are going.

quiz.q: What makes the first minute in cold water so dangerous?
o: Hypothermia sets in immediately
An involuntary gasp and rapid breathing can cause you to inhale water
Your muscles freeze solid
Cold water is heavier
quiz.e: The cold shock response can cause drowning before the body has cooled at all.

quiz.q: What is the best first action after falling into cold water?
o: Swim as hard as possible to shore
Take off your lifejacket
Shout continuously
Float on your back until your breathing settles
quiz.e: Floating first helps you get through cold shock without inhaling water.

quiz.q: In the 1-10-1 rule, what does the ten stand for?
o: About ten minutes of meaningful movement before arms and legs weaken
Ten seconds before drowning
Ten degrees Celsius water
Ten hours until hypothermia
quiz.e: Use that time wisely to get out or secure something that floats.

quiz.q: A very cold person has stopped shivering and is confused and drowsy. What does this suggest?
o: They have warmed up
They are just tired
Severe hypothermia, which is dangerous
They have mild dehydration
quiz.e: Shivering can stop as hypothermia worsens, which is a warning sign.

quiz.q: Which is a correct hypothermia first aid step?
o: Rub their arms and legs vigorously
Give them a shot of alcohol to warm up
Put them straight into a hot bath
Remove wet clothing and wrap them in dry, insulating layers
quiz.e: Handle gently, insulate and call 000. Never give alcohol or rub the limbs.

LESSONS.title: First on the scene of a car crash
LESSONS.hook: One day you may be the first person to arrive at a crash. What you do in the first few minutes, starting with protecting yourself, can decide how many people go home.

sections.key: Park safely well clear of the crash and switch on your hazard lights before doing anything else.
sections.b: The instinct when you see a crash is to rush straight to the wreckage. But the scene is often dangerous: traffic is still moving, drivers are distracted, and visibility may be poor. Rescuers are sometimes struck by other vehicles. So start by making yourself safe. Slow down and park well clear of the crash, ideally off the road, so your car does not become part of the problem. Turn on your hazard lights. If it is dark, wear something bright or use a torch, and if you have a reflective triangle, set it up well back from the scene. Keep children and passengers in your car or well away from the road. Then assess the scene before approaching.

sections.key: Call Triple Zero, give an exact location and describe what you see.
sections.b: Call Triple Zero (000) as early as possible, or ask a bystander to call while you check on people. The operator will ask which service you need, usually ambulance, police and possibly fire. The most important information is where you are. Look for road names, cross streets, kilometre markers, landmarks or the direction of travel. The free Emergency+ app, developed by Australia's emergency services, displays your GPS coordinates on screen so you can read them out. Then describe the crash: how many vehicles, how many people injured, whether anyone is trapped, unconscious or bleeding badly, and whether there is fuel leaking, smoke or fire. Stay on the line; the operator can guide you through first aid.

sections.key: Watch for fuel, fire, traffic, fallen powerlines and unstable vehicles before approaching.
sections.b: Before approaching, look around for dangers. Is there spilt fuel, smoke or fire? Are there fallen powerlines, which could make the vehicle and ground around it dangerous? Is the car unstable, on its side or on a slope? Is traffic still flowing past? If it is safe, ask the occupants to turn off the ignition, or reach in and turn it off yourself if you can do so without risk, and make sure nobody smokes nearby. Do not approach a vehicle with powerlines on it; stay at least eight metres away and warn others. Electric and hybrid vehicles can carry high voltage components, so leave anything other than basic first aid to emergency crews. If you cannot make it safe, stay back and wait.

sections.h: Don't move them unless you must
sections.key: Leave injured people where they are unless there is immediate danger, such as fire or traffic.
sections.b: People in a crash may have injuries to the neck or spine that you cannot see. Unnecessary movement could make them worse. So, as a general rule, leave injured people where they are, keep them still, and support their head if they are conscious and you can do it comfortably. Talk to them, reassure them and tell them help is coming. Ask them not to move their head. The exception is immediate danger: fire, rising water, or the risk of being struck by traffic. In those cases, getting the person out of danger is more important than the risk of a spinal injury. If you have to move someone, try to keep their head, neck and body aligned, with help from others if possible.

sections.key: An unconscious person's airway takes priority over a possible spinal injury.
sections.b: If a person is unresponsive, the biggest immediate threat is often their airway. An unconscious person lying on their back, or slumped forward in a car seat, can have their airway blocked by their tongue, blood or vomit. Australian resuscitation guidelines are clear that keeping the airway open takes priority over the possibility of a spinal injury. Follow DRSABCD. If the person is breathing normally but unconscious, carefully support their airway, and if you need to, roll them onto their side, keeping head and neck as aligned as you can. If they are not breathing normally, they will need CPR, which generally means getting them onto their back on a firm surface, with help from others.

sections.key: Leave a motorcyclist's helmet on unless it must come off to manage their airway or breathing.
sections.b: Motorcycle crashes raise a specific question: should you take the helmet off? The general first aid advice is to leave it on. The helmet may be supporting a neck injury, and removing it incorrectly could cause harm. If the rider is conscious and breathing, lift or open the visor so they can breathe easily, talk to them and keep them still. The helmet only needs to come off if it is preventing you from managing their airway or breathing, for example if they are vomiting or need CPR. Ideally, two people do this: one supports the head and neck from below while the other gently spreads the helmet sides and eases it off. Many first aid courses practise this skill.

sections.key: Drivers involved must stop and help; witnesses should stay to give police an account.
sections.b: Australian road rules require drivers involved in a crash to stop, give whatever help they can to anyone injured, and exchange details, and in many circumstances the crash must be reported to police. Witnesses are not usually obliged to stay, but your account can be valuable, so if you can, wait and speak to police, or leave your contact details. While you wait, keep checking injured people, cover them to keep them warm, and do not give them food or drink. Afterwards, it is normal to feel shaken, even if you did everything right. Talking to someone you trust, or a support service, can help. Doing a first aid course is the best way to feel ready for a day like this.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you arrive at a crash?
o: Run straight to the vehicles
Park safely well clear and turn on your hazard lights
Take photos for social media
Move the crashed cars off the road
quiz.e: Protecting yourself stops you becoming another casualty.

quiz.q: What does the Emergency+ app help you do?
o: Book a tow truck
Contact your insurer
Show your GPS location so you can tell the 000 operator
Switch off the crashed car
quiz.e: Giving an exact location helps emergency services reach you quickly.

quiz.q: When should you move an injured person at a crash?
o: Always, so they are comfortable
Only if there is immediate danger, such as fire or traffic
Only if they ask to sit up
Never, even if the car is on fire
quiz.e: Unnecessary movement could worsen a spinal injury, but immediate danger comes first.

quiz.q: An unconscious crash victim's airway is at risk. What takes priority?
o: Keeping the airway open, even if a spinal injury is possible
Leaving them exactly as they are
Removing their shoes
Giving them water
quiz.e: Australian guidelines put the airway ahead of a possible spinal injury.

quiz.q: When should a motorcyclist's helmet be removed?
o: Always, straight away
Only by the rider's family
Never under any circumstances
Only if it prevents managing their airway or breathing
quiz.e: Otherwise leave it on, lift the visor and keep the rider still.

LESSONS.title: How people really behave in disasters
LESSONS.hook: We imagine stampedes and mass panic. Decades of research tell a stranger story: in a crisis, the real danger is often that people stay calm, slow and polite for far too long.

sections.key: Disaster researchers have found that mass panic is rare; people usually behave calmly and help each other.
sections.b: Films love to show crowds screaming and trampling each other when disaster strikes. Real disasters rarely look like that. From the 1950s onwards, sociologists studying fires, floods, earthquakes and bombings, including the American researcher Enrico Quarantelli and the Disaster Research Center he co-founded, found that true mass panic, meaning wild, selfish flight, is uncommon. Most people stay surprisingly orderly. Strangers help strangers, families stick together, and survivors are usually the first rescuers, pulling neighbours from rubble long before professionals arrive. Fatal crowd crushes do occur, but investigations typically point to overcrowding and poor crowd management rather than people losing their minds. The persistent belief in panic can do harm, by making authorities reluctant to share frightening information quickly.

sections.key: Our brains tend to interpret new danger as normal, which delays action.
sections.b: If panic is not the main problem, what is? Researchers point to something quieter: delay. When an alarm sounds or smoke appears, our first instinct is often to explain it away. It is probably a drill, a false alarm, burnt toast. This tendency, sometimes called normalcy bias, makes sense most of the time, because most alarms really are false. Our brains are built to expect tomorrow to look like today. But in a genuine emergency, the minutes spent assuming everything is fine can be the minutes that matter most. People in burning buildings have finished meals, completed emails and waited for lifts. The warning signs were there; they were simply interpreted as normal.

sections.key: Before acting, people seek information and look to others, a process researchers call milling.
sections.b: Even when people accept that something is wrong, they rarely act straight away. Instead they search for information and check what others think. They phone family, ask colleagues, look out the window and scan social media. Researchers call this milling. It is deeply human, because we are social animals who look to the group to decide what is happening. But it can be deadly when everyone waits for everyone else. If no one moves, each person reads the calm around them as evidence that there is no danger. Studies of the World Trade Center evacuation on 11 September 2001 found that many survivors delayed leaving to make calls, gather belongings or seek more information.

sections.key: Under extreme stress, some people freeze, unable to think or act.
sections.b: A third response is freezing. Under sudden, overwhelming stress, some people become stuck, unable to decide or move. This is not cowardice; it reflects the brain struggling to process an unfamiliar situation quickly enough. Survivors of plane crashes and shipwrecks have described fellow passengers sitting motionless as fire or water approached. The British psychologist John Leach, who studied survival behaviour, has suggested that only a minority of people respond quickly and effectively in a sudden crisis, while most are bewildered for a time and a small minority behave in counterproductive ways. Exact proportions are debated, but the pattern is widely recognised. The practical lesson is that people who freeze often respond well to clear, loud, simple instructions from someone else.

sections.key: Rehearsal is the best antidote; the brain under stress falls back on what it has practised.
sections.b: The most famous example of preparation paying off is Rick Rescorla, a former soldier who became head of security for the financial firm Morgan Stanley at the World Trade Center. After the 1993 bombing of the towers, he became convinced the buildings would be attacked again, and he made the company's staff practise evacuation drills regularly, walking down the stairwells, despite grumbling from busy employees. On 11 September 2001, when the North Tower was hit, Rescorla ignored advice to stay put and ordered his people out of the South Tower. Almost all of the firm's roughly 2,700 staff there survived. Rescorla went back inside to help others and was killed when the tower collapsed.

sections.key: In plane evacuations, people who stop for luggage slow everyone down.
sections.b: Aircraft are designed to be evacuated within about ninety seconds, but that assumes people move at once and carry nothing. Investigators of real evacuations have repeatedly found passengers stopping to retrieve bags from overhead lockers, blocking aisles while fire spreads. A striking counterexample came on 2 January 2024 at Tokyo's Haneda Airport, when a Japan Airlines Airbus A350 collided with a coast guard aircraft on the runway and burst into flames. All 379 people on the airliner escaped, a result widely credited to the crew's training and to passengers who largely followed instructions and left their belongings behind. Tragically, five of the six crew on the smaller coast guard plane were killed. Your phone and bag can be replaced.

sections.key: Know your exits, decide in advance what you'll do, and act early on warnings.
sections.b: The research points to a few habits that can help. When you enter a hotel, theatre, plane or new workplace, notice the nearest exits, and count the rows or doors to them, because smoke can make it hard to see. Make decisions in advance, while calm. For example, decide that if a fire alarm sounds, you will leave immediately, or that on a severe bushfire day you will leave early rather than wait and see. Practise household fire escape plans. When a warning comes, treat it as real until proven otherwise; an unnecessary evacuation costs little, while a late one can cost everything. And in a crisis, be the person who says, clearly and calmly, we need to go now.

quiz.q: What have disaster researchers found about mass panic?
o: It is the main cause of deaths in disasters
It is rare; most people behave calmly and help each other
It happens in every fire
It only happens at night
quiz.e: Studies since the 1950s have found orderly, helpful behaviour is far more common than panic.

quiz.q: What is normalcy bias?
o: The tendency to interpret warning signs of danger as normal, which delays action
A fear of normal situations
The belief that disasters happen to others
A bias towards running away
quiz.e: Because most alarms are false, people often assume a real one is too.

quiz.q: Why can milling be dangerous?
o: It makes people run in circles
It wastes food supplies
Everyone waits for others to act, and calm around them looks like proof of safety
It causes stampedes
quiz.e: Seeking information and checking with others is human, but it delays evacuation.

quiz.q: What did Rick Rescorla do that saved lives on 11 September 2001?
o: Built a new staircase
Told staff to stay at their desks
Called the fire brigade first
Made staff practise evacuation drills regularly and ordered them out
quiz.e: Rehearsal meant staff knew what to do, and almost all of the firm's people in the South Tower survived.

quiz.q: What lesson does the Haneda Airport evacuation in 2024 reinforce?
o: Take your carry-on bag with you
Wait for the plane to stop burning
Follow crew instructions and leave belongings behind
Use the exit you boarded through
quiz.e: All 379 people on the airliner escaped, credited largely to crew training and passengers following instructions.

LESSONS.title: Solid, liquid, gas … and stranger things
LESSONS.hook: School taught us three states of matter. Nature has more, including one that fills the stars and one that was only made in a lab in 1995.

sections.key: Whether something is solid, liquid or gas depends on how freely its particles move.
sections.b: Everything around you is made of atoms and molecules that never stop moving. In a solid, they are locked into fixed positions and can only vibrate on the spot, which is why a brick keeps its shape. In a liquid, the particles are still packed closely together, but they can slide past one another, so water takes the shape of whatever holds it. In a gas, the particles fly about freely, bouncing off each other and the walls of their container, with mostly empty space between them. The molecules in the air you are breathing right now are travelling at roughly 500 metres per second, faster than a passenger jet, colliding with each other billions of times every second.

sections.key: Melting, boiling and sublimation all happen when particles gain or lose enough energy to break free.
sections.b: Heat a solid and its particles vibrate harder until they break out of their fixed places and the solid melts. Keep heating and some escape the liquid altogether as a gas. A curious detail is that while ice is melting, its temperature stays at 0°C. The energy goes into breaking the bonds holding the particles in place rather than making them move faster. The boiling point also depends on the air pressure above. Water boils at 100°C at sea level, but on the summit of Mount Everest it boils at only around 70°C, which makes a decent cup of tea surprisingly hard. Some substances skip the liquid stage entirely. Dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, turns straight into gas, a change called sublimation.

sections.key: Glass is an amorphous solid, and the idea that old windows have slowly sagged is a myth.
sections.b: Glass is odd. Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's rather than arranged in a neat crystal, yet it is rigid like a solid. Scientists call this an amorphous solid. A popular story says glass is really a very slow liquid, and that old church windows are thicker at the bottom because the glass has flowed downwards over centuries. It isn't true. Old window glass was made by spinning or blowing, which produced panes of uneven thickness, and glaziers often fitted the thicker edge at the bottom, though not always. Calculations suggest that glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag visibly. Roman glassware from two thousand years ago has kept its shape perfectly well.

sections.key: Some substances that seem solid are actually extraordinarily slow liquids, and an Australian experiment proves it.
sections.b: If you want a material that truly flows while looking solid, try pitch, a tar-like substance that shatters when you hit it with a hammer. In 1927, Professor Thomas Parnell at the University of Queensland heated some pitch, poured it into a sealed glass funnel and, three years later, cut the funnel's stem open. Then everyone waited. The pitch flows, but so slowly that a single drop takes the best part of a decade to form and fall. Fewer than a dozen drops have fallen since the experiment began, and a camera set up to catch one in 2000 famously failed at the crucial moment. It is recognised as one of the longest running laboratory experiments in the world, and it still sits in a cabinet in Brisbane today.

sections.key: Heat a gas enough and its atoms are torn apart into a glowing soup of charged particles.
sections.b: Push a gas to extreme temperatures and the collisions become violent enough to knock electrons off their atoms. The result is plasma, a mix of free electrons and positively charged ions. Because its particles carry electric charge, plasma behaves very differently from an ordinary gas. It conducts electricity and responds strongly to magnetic fields. Plasma can seem exotic, but you have seen plenty of it. Lightning bolts, the glow inside a neon sign and the shimmering curtains of an aurora are all plasma. So is the Sun, and so is every other star. That means that, although plasma is rare in everyday life on Earth, most of the ordinary visible matter in the universe is thought to exist in this state.

sections.key: At temperatures just above absolute zero, thousands of atoms can merge into a single quantum blob.
sections.b: In the 1920s, the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose and Albert Einstein predicted something remarkable. If you cooled certain atoms close enough to absolute zero, the coldest temperature possible, they would stop behaving as separate particles and fall into the same quantum state, acting as one giant wave. For seventy years nobody could get anything cold enough to test it. Then, in 1995, Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman in Colorado used lasers and magnetic traps to cool rubidium atoms to around 170 billionths of a degree above absolute zero. A Bose–Einstein condensate appeared. They shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics with Wolfgang Ketterle, who made one independently. Physicists now use these condensates to study quantum behaviour on a scale almost large enough to see.

sections.key: Many everyday materials refuse to fit neatly into one box.
sections.b: Mix cornflour with water and you get oobleck, a goo that pours like a liquid but turns firm when you punch it or run across it. Scientists call it a non-Newtonian fluid, because its thickness changes with the force applied. Liquid crystals are another in-between. Their rod-shaped molecules flow like a liquid but line up in an orderly way like a crystal, and turning them with electric fields is how many screens control light. Sand and grain can pour through a funnel like water, yet hold up a person standing on a beach. These borderline cases are a useful reminder that solid, liquid and gas are labels people invented, while nature is under no obligation to follow them.

quiz.q: In which state can particles slide past each other while staying packed closely together?
o: Solid
Liquid
Gas
Plasma
quiz.e: Liquid particles are close together but free to slide, which is why liquids take the shape of their container.

quiz.q: Why does water boil at a lower temperature on top of Mount Everest?
o: The water is purer there
The air pressure is much lower
It is colder at altitude
There is less oxygen in the water
quiz.e: Boiling point depends on the pressure above the liquid; less pressure means water boils at only around 70°C.

quiz.q: Why are some old window panes thicker at the bottom?
o: Glass slowly flows downwards
Gravity compresses glass over time
The panes were made unevenly and often fitted thick edge down
Rainwater deposits minerals on them
quiz.e: Old glassmaking produced uneven panes. Glass at room temperature would take longer than the age of the universe to sag visibly.

quiz.q: What is plasma?
o: A gas so hot its atoms are split into electrons and ions
A very thick liquid
A solid with no crystal structure
A gas cooled close to absolute zero
quiz.e: Extreme heat strips electrons from atoms, creating the charged soup found in lightning, neon signs and stars.

quiz.q: What happens in a Bose–Einstein condensate?
o: Atoms split into quarks
Atoms freeze into a perfect crystal
Atoms turn directly into plasma
Atoms act together as a single quantum wave
quiz.e: Cooled to billionths of a degree above absolute zero, the atoms fall into the same quantum state and behave as one.

LESSONS.title: Air pressure: the weight of the sky
LESSONS.hook: Right now the air is pressing on you with the weight of about ten tonnes on every square metre. Here's why you don't notice, and how people first worked it out.

sections.h: Living at the bottom of an ocean of air
sections.key: Air has weight, and the whole atmosphere above you is pushing down.
sections.b: Air feels like nothing, but it is made of real molecules with real mass, and there are many kilometres of it stacked above your head. At sea level, the weight of that column of air presses on every surface with a force of roughly ten tonnes per square metre. Scientists measure it as about 101 kilopascals. So why aren't we flattened? Because air pressure pushes in every direction at once, not just downward, and the fluids and air inside your body push back outward with equal force. Everything is balanced. You only notice air pressure when that balance is suddenly upset, for example when your ears pop in a lift, or when a sealed packet of chips puffs up on a flight.

sections.key: In 1643 an Italian scientist balanced the atmosphere against a column of mercury and invented the barometer.
sections.b: In the early 1600s, well diggers and engineers knew a frustrating fact. Suction pumps could not raise water more than about ten metres, no matter how well they were built. Evangelista Torricelli, a former assistant to Galileo, suspected the answer was the weight of the air. In 1643 he filled a long glass tube with mercury, which is about 13.6 times denser than water, covered the open end and turned it upside down into a dish of mercury. The column dropped until it stood about 76 centimetres high, leaving an empty space at the top. The weight of the air pressing on the dish was holding the mercury up. Torricelli had made the first barometer, and he noticed the height changed slightly from day to day.

sections.key: Carrying a barometer up a mountain proved that air pressure comes from the air above us.
sections.b: The French thinker Blaise Pascal reasoned that if the atmosphere really had weight, there should be less of it pressing down at the top of a mountain. In 1648 he persuaded his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, to test the idea on the Puy de Dôme, a volcanic peak in central France. Périer set up mercury tubes at the bottom, left one there with a watcher, and carried another to the summit, about a kilometre higher. At the top, the mercury column was several centimetres shorter. Coming down, it rose again. It was a beautifully simple experiment, and it settled the question. Today the unit of pressure, the pascal, honours him, and aircraft altimeters still work by measuring this same fall in pressure with height.

sections.key: In the 1650s a German mayor showed the astonishing force of air pressure using two metal hemispheres.
sections.b: Otto von Guericke, a scientist and mayor of the city of Magdeburg, built one of the first air pumps around 1650. He then staged a famous demonstration. He fitted two copper hemispheres about half a metre across together, with nothing but a greased rim between them, and pumped out the air from inside. With no air pushing outwards from within, the atmosphere outside clamped the halves together. Accounts describe two teams of horses straining in opposite directions and failing to pull the sphere apart. When von Guericke opened a valve and let air back in, the halves simply fell open. The point was profound. What held the hemispheres together was not some mysterious pull from the vacuum, but the ordinary air outside pushing in.

sections.key: When you drink through a straw, you don't pull the drink up; the atmosphere pushes it.
sections.b: It feels like sucking pulls things towards you, but a vacuum cannot pull anything. When you drink through a straw, you lower the air pressure inside your mouth. The normal air pressure pressing down on the surface of the drink is now greater than the pressure inside the straw, so the drink is pushed up into your mouth. Suction cups work the same way. Squash out the air beneath them and the atmosphere outside holds them firmly against the tiles. This also explains the old pump puzzle. Even a perfect vacuum can only let the atmosphere push water up about ten metres, because that is how tall a column of water the weight of the air can balance. Deeper mines needed pumps that pushed from below.

sections.key: Air pressure shapes the weather, the way we cook and how aircraft keep us alive.
sections.b: Air pressure changes from place to place, and those differences drive the weather. Regions of high pressure usually bring sinking air and settled, clear skies, while low pressure brings rising air, cloud and often rain. Wind is air moving from higher pressure towards lower, which is why the curved lines on a weather map, called isobars, are so useful. Pressure also changes how we cook. A pressure cooker traps steam, raising the pressure inside so water boils at around 120°C and food cooks much faster. And at the cruising height of an airliner, the outside air is far too thin to breathe for long. Cabins are pressurised to a level similar to being on a mountain a couple of kilometres high.

quiz.q: Why aren't we crushed by air pressure?
o: Air is too light to matter
Air pressure pushes in all directions and our bodies push back equally
Gravity cancels it out
Our skin is strong enough to resist it
quiz.e: The pressure is balanced inside and out. We only notice it when that balance changes quickly.

quiz.q: What did Torricelli's experiment show?
o: Air has no weight
Mercury evaporates in a vacuum
The weight of the air can hold up a column of mercury
Water is denser than mercury
quiz.e: The atmosphere pressing on the dish held the mercury column at about 76 centimetres, creating the first barometer.

quiz.q: What happened to the mercury column at the top of the Puy de Dôme?
o: It was shorter, because there was less air above
It was taller, because the air was colder
It stayed exactly the same
It froze solid
quiz.e: Less air above means less pressure, so the column fell by several centimetres.

quiz.q: What really held von Guericke's hemispheres together?
o: Magnetism
A pull from the vacuum inside
Glue on the rim
Air pressure outside pushing in
quiz.e: With the air removed from inside, nothing pushed outward, so the outside atmosphere clamped the halves together.

quiz.q: What actually moves a drink up a straw?
o: Your mouth pulling it
The vacuum attracting it
Air pressure pushing down on the drink's surface
Surface tension
quiz.e: Lowering the pressure in your mouth lets the higher outside air pressure push the drink up.

LESSONS.title: Viruses: life's tiny hijackers
LESSONS.hook: They can't eat, grow or reproduce on their own, yet they outnumber the stars in the observable universe and have left their fingerprints all over your DNA.

sections.key: A virus is little more than genetic instructions wrapped in a protective coat.
sections.b: A virus is astonishingly simple. At its core is a short set of genetic instructions, written in either DNA or RNA. Around that is a protein shell called a capsid, and some viruses, including the flu and coronaviruses, wrap themselves in an extra fatty envelope stolen from the last cell they infected. That is more or less it. A virus has no machinery to make energy, no way to build proteins and no means of copying itself. Viruses are also tiny. Most are far smaller than bacteria, typically measured in tens to hundreds of nanometres, where a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. They were impossible to see until electron microscopes produced the first clear images in the late 1930s.

sections.h: The germ that slipped through the filter
sections.key: Viruses were discovered in the 1890s because they were too small to be caught by filters that trapped bacteria.
sections.b: In 1892, the Russian scientist Dmitri Ivanovsky was studying a disease that left tobacco leaves blotchy and mottled. He squeezed sap from sick plants and passed it through a fine porcelain filter designed to trap bacteria. To his surprise, the filtered sap could still infect healthy plants. A few years later, in 1898, the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck repeated the work and concluded that something entirely new was at play, an infectious agent much smaller than any bacterium that could only multiply inside living cells. He used the Latin word virus, meaning poison or slimy liquid, to describe it. The culprit, tobacco mosaic virus, became the first virus ever identified, and decades later one of the first ever photographed.

sections.key: A virus breaks into a cell, takes over its machinery and turns it into a virus factory.
