sections.b: Each virus carries proteins on its surface that fit particular receptors on the outside of particular cells, a little like a key fitting a lock. That is why many viruses are choosy. The virus that causes COVID-19, for example, uses its spike protein to latch onto a receptor called ACE2. Once attached, the virus gets inside and releases its genetic instructions. The cell, unable to tell the difference, starts reading them as if they were its own, building viral proteins and copying the viral genes. New viruses are assembled inside, then burst out or bud from the cell's surface, ready to infect its neighbours. A single infected cell can release thousands of new virus particles before it dies or is destroyed.

sections.key: Scientists still argue about whether viruses count as living things.
sections.b: Outside a cell, a virus is inert. It doesn't eat, breathe, grow or respond to anything, and some can sit on a surface like a speck of dust. Many textbook definitions of life require an organism to carry out its own metabolism and reproduce by itself, and viruses fail both tests. Yet inside a cell they multiply furiously, and they clearly evolve by natural selection, the hallmark of living systems. Their genes mutate, and the versions best at spreading come to dominate, which is why new flu vaccines are needed most years. Some biologists describe viruses as being on the edge of life, while others argue they deserve a branch of their own. There is no single agreed answer, and the debate remains lively.

sections.key: Most viruses on Earth infect bacteria, and some viruses are bigger than bacteria.
sections.b: When we think of viruses, we think of human illness, but the vast majority infect bacteria instead. These are called bacteriophages, meaning bacteria eaters, and many look like tiny lunar landers, with a head and spidery legs that inject their DNA into a bacterium. Scientists estimate that there are around ten million trillion trillion viruses on Earth, a number far larger than the count of stars in the observable universe. Most float in the oceans, where they kill a large share of marine bacteria every day, releasing nutrients that feed other life. Then there are the giants. Mimivirus, identified in 2003 inside amoebae, was so large that researchers had first mistaken it for a bacterium. It even carries genes once thought unique to cellular life.

sections.key: Around eight per cent of your DNA is the leftover remains of ancient viral infections.
sections.b: Some viruses, called retroviruses, insert their genes directly into the DNA of the cells they infect. HIV is a retrovirus. Over millions of years, retroviruses occasionally infected egg or sperm cells of our ancestors, and when that happened their genes could be passed on to every future generation. Today, roughly eight per cent of the human genome is made up of these viral fossils, far more than the small fraction that codes for our proteins. Most are broken and silent. A few, though, have been put to work. A gene called syncytin, which originally came from a retrovirus, helps form a key layer of the placenta. In a very real sense, part of the process that lets humans be born came from a virus.

sections.key: Antibiotics don't work on viruses, so we rely on the immune system, vaccines and antiviral drugs.
sections.b: Antibiotics kill bacteria by attacking structures that bacteria have and our cells don't, such as their cell walls. Viruses have none of these structures and hide inside our own cells, so antibiotics do nothing against a cold or the flu. Taking them for a viral infection only helps breed resistant bacteria. Instead, our bodies rely on the immune system, which learns to recognise a virus and remember it. Vaccines train that memory safely in advance, and they have achieved remarkable things. Smallpox, a viral disease that killed hundreds of millions of people in the twentieth century alone, was declared eradicated in 1980 after a worldwide vaccination campaign. Antiviral drugs also exist, working by jamming particular steps in a virus's life cycle.

quiz.q: What is a virus basically made of?
o: A complete cell with a nucleus
Genetic material inside a protein coat
A tiny bacterium
A chain of sugar molecules
quiz.e: A virus is genetic instructions wrapped in a capsid, sometimes with an extra fatty envelope.

quiz.q: How were viruses first detected in the 1890s?
o: They glowed under ultraviolet light
They were seen through a light microscope
Filtered sap that trapped bacteria could still cause disease
They were grown in a dish of jelly
quiz.e: Ivanovsky and Beijerinck found that tobacco mosaic disease passed through filters fine enough to catch bacteria.

quiz.q: Why do many viruses only infect certain kinds of cells?
o: Their surface proteins must fit specific receptors
They can only survive at certain temperatures
They are attracted by colour
They need cells of a certain size
quiz.e: Like a key in a lock, a virus's surface proteins must match receptors on the target cell.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the human genome comes from ancient retroviruses?
o: Less than 0.1 per cent
About half
None
Around 8 per cent
quiz.e: Retroviruses that infected our ancestors' egg and sperm cells left viral genes we still carry.

quiz.q: Why won't antibiotics cure the flu?
o: The flu is too mild
Viruses lack the structures antibiotics attack and hide inside our cells
Flu viruses are too large
Antibiotics only work on fungi
quiz.e: Antibiotics target bacterial features like cell walls. Viruses have none and use our own cells to multiply.

LESSONS.title: Why things float
LESSONS.hook: A steel ship weighing tens of thousands of tonnes floats, yet a small pebble sinks. The explanation goes back to a Greek genius, and possibly a bath.

sections.key: The famous ‘Eureka!’ story is probably more legend than history.
sections.b: The tale goes like this. King Hiero II of Syracuse suspected his goldsmith had mixed cheaper silver into a gold crown. He asked the mathematician Archimedes to find out without damaging it. Stepping into a bath, Archimedes noticed the water rise, realised he could measure the crown's volume by the water it displaced, and ran through the streets shouting ‘Eureka!’, meaning ‘I have found it!’. The trouble is that the story was written down by the Roman architect Vitruvius around two centuries after Archimedes died, and some historians doubt it. Galileo later pointed out that the overflow method would be too imprecise for a crown, and suggested Archimedes more likely used a balance and his own principle of buoyancy. Either way, the principle itself is real and enormously useful.

sections.key: Anything in a fluid is pushed upwards by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
sections.b: Archimedes wrote a treatise called On Floating Bodies, and its central idea is now known as Archimedes' principle. When an object sits in water, it pushes some of that water out of the way. The surrounding water pushes back, creating an upward force called buoyancy. The size of that force equals the weight of the water displaced. If the object weighs less than the water it can displace, it floats. If it weighs more, it sinks, though it will still feel lighter, which is why you can lift a friend easily in a swimming pool. The principle works for any fluid, liquid or gas. It explains why a log bobs on a river, and why a helium balloon rises through the heavier air around it.

sections.key: Shape matters: a hull spreads its weight over a large volume of displaced water.
sections.b: Steel is about eight times denser than water, so a solid block of it sinks instantly. Hammer that same steel into the shape of a bowl, though, and it can float. The trick is that a hull encloses a huge volume of air. When the ship settles into the water, it pushes aside a large amount of water, and it keeps sinking lower until the weight of the water it has displaced exactly equals the ship's own weight. At that point, it floats. This is also why a ship sits lower when loaded with cargo, because it has to push aside more water to balance its extra weight. Punch a hole in the hull and let water replace the air, and the balance is lost.

sections.key: A simple painted mark on the side of ships stopped owners from dangerously overloading them.
sections.b: In nineteenth century Britain, some ship owners overloaded old, overinsured vessels so heavily that they sank, sometimes with their crews. Sailors called them coffin ships. A member of parliament named Samuel Plimsoll campaigned furiously against the practice, and the Merchant Shipping Act of 1876 made load line markings compulsory on British ships. The Plimsoll line, as it became known, shows how deep a ship may safely sit in the water. Modern versions have several marks, because buoyancy depends on the water itself. Fresh water is less dense than seawater, and warm water is less dense than cold, so a ship floats slightly lower in a tropical river than in a cold northern sea. The markings allow for each situation.

sections.h: Salt water and the Dead Sea
sections.key: The denser the liquid, the easier it is to float.
sections.b: You float more easily in the ocean than in a swimming pool, because dissolved salt makes seawater denser, so each litre you displace weighs more and pushes up harder. You can see this at home. An egg sinks in a glass of tap water but floats if you stir in enough salt. The most famous example is the Dead Sea, on the border of Israel, Jordan and the West Bank. Its water is several times saltier than the ocean, so dense that swimmers bob on the surface as if lying on a lilo, and it is hard to swim normally at all. Your own body is close to the density of water, which is why a deep breath, filling your lungs with air, helps you float.

sections.key: Controlling buoyancy lets machines and animals rise and sink at will.
sections.b: A submarine floats on the surface until it opens its ballast tanks and lets seawater in. Heavier now, it sinks. To rise again, it uses compressed air to blow the water back out. Many bony fish manage the same trick with a swim bladder, a gas-filled sac they can inflate or deflate to hover at a chosen depth without constantly swimming. Buoyancy works in air too. Heating air makes it expand and become less dense, so a balloon full of hot air is pushed upward by the cooler, denser air around it. On 21 November 1783, a hot air balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers carried two men across Paris, in the first free flight with people on board. Archimedes' principle had taken humans into the sky.

quiz.q: Why do some historians doubt the famous ‘Eureka!’ story?
o: Archimedes never lived in Syracuse
It was written down about two centuries after his death
Baths didn't exist in ancient Greece
Gold crowns were never made in that era
quiz.e: The story comes from Vitruvius, writing long after Archimedes, and Galileo argued the method was too imprecise.

quiz.q: According to Archimedes' principle, the upward force on a floating object equals what?
o: The object's volume
The depth of the water
The weight of the fluid it displaces
The object's surface area
quiz.e: Buoyancy equals the weight of the displaced fluid, so an object floats if it weighs less than the fluid it can push aside.

quiz.q: Why can a steel ship float when a steel block sinks?
o: Its hull encloses lots of air and displaces a large volume of water
Ship steel is lighter than normal steel
The engines hold it up
Salt water is denser than steel
quiz.e: The hull's shape lets it displace water weighing as much as the whole ship.

quiz.q: Why does a ship's load line have several marks?
o: For different cargoes
For different times of day
For different crew sizes
Because water density changes with saltiness and temperature
quiz.e: Ships float lower in fresh or warm water, so the safe loading depth depends on where the ship is sailing.

quiz.q: How does a submarine dive?
o: By pointing its nose down and driving
By letting seawater into its ballast tanks
By pumping air into its tanks
By heating its hull
quiz.e: Flooding the ballast tanks makes the submarine heavier than the water it displaces, so it sinks.

LESSONS.title: Static electricity: sparks from nowhere
LESSONS.hook: That zap from a car door or a supermarket trolley is the same force that gave electricity its name, and it runs the printer in your office.

sections.h: Amber and the birth of a word
sections.key: The word electricity comes from the Greek for amber, which crackles with static when rubbed.
sections.b: Ancient Greeks noticed something odd about amber, the golden fossilised tree resin. Rub it with fur or wool and it would attract bits of straw, feathers and dust. Tradition credits the philosopher Thales of Miletus, around 600 BC, with describing this, though nothing he wrote survives. The Greek word for amber was elektron. Almost two thousand years later, in 1600, the English physician William Gilbert published a book on magnetism in which he showed that many other materials, like glass and sulphur, behaved the same way. He described them with the new Latin word electricus, meaning like amber. From that root came the English word electricity, so every power point in your home carries a quiet echo of a lump of ancient resin.

sections.key: Rubbing two materials together moves electrons from one to the other, leaving both charged.
sections.b: Atoms contain positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons, normally in balance. When two different materials touch and rub, electrons can transfer from one surface to the other. The material that gains electrons ends up with a negative charge, and the one that loses them becomes positive. Scientists rank materials in a list called the triboelectric series according to how readily they gain or lose electrons, so rubbing a balloon on your hair leaves the balloon negative and your hair positive. Opposite charges attract and like charges repel, which is why each of your hair strands, all carrying the same charge, tries to push away from the others. Surprisingly, physicists still do not fully understand the details of exactly how charge moves during contact, and it remains an active research question.

sections.key: Static shocks happen when built-up charge suddenly jumps to a conductor, and they're worse in dry weather.
sections.b: Walking across carpet in rubber-soled shoes, or sliding across a car seat, can build up a charge on your body of several thousand volts. Nothing happens until you reach for something metal, like a door handle. Then the charge jumps across the gap in a tiny spark, and you feel the zap. Despite the high voltage, the shock is harmless because the amount of charge is tiny and the current lasts only a fraction of a second. Shocks are far more common in dry conditions, such as cold winter days or air-conditioned offices. In humid air, a thin film of moisture on surfaces lets charge leak away gradually before it can build up. A simple trick is to touch metal with a key first, so the spark jumps from the key instead.

sections.h: Balloons, walls and hair on end
sections.key: A charged object can attract a neutral one by rearranging the charges inside it.
sections.b: Rub a balloon on your jumper and it will stick to a wall. That seems strange, because the wall has no overall charge. The explanation is called induction. The negative balloon pushes the electrons in the wall's surface slightly away and draws the positive charges a little closer. Because the nearby positive charges are closer than the repelled negative ones, the attraction wins, and the balloon clings. A Van de Graaff generator, invented by the American physicist Robert Van de Graaff in 1929, uses a moving rubber belt to pile charge onto a metal dome. Place your hand on one at a science museum and your body fills with charge too. Every hair on your head carries the same charge, so they repel one another and stand straight up.

sections.key: Photocopiers, laser printers and pollution filters all run on static electricity.
sections.b: In 1938, an American patent lawyer and inventor named Chester Carlson, tired of copying documents by hand, made the first dry copy using static electricity in a makeshift lab in Queens, New York. His process, later called xerography, took years to find a backer, but it became the basis of the photocopier and the laser printer. Inside, light is used to create a pattern of electric charge on a drum, powdery toner sticks only to the charged areas, and heat fuses it onto paper. Static also cleans the air. Electrostatic precipitators, developed in the early twentieth century, give smoke particles in chimneys a charge so they are drawn onto collecting plates. Car makers use the same idea to spray paint evenly onto charged car bodies.

sections.key: A tiny spark can ignite fuel vapour or dust, and can quietly destroy electronics.
sections.b: Most static shocks are just annoying, but a spark in the wrong place can cause a fire. Petrol gives off flammable vapour, and fuel stations warn people not to get back into their car while refuelling, because sliding across the seat can build up charge that may spark at the nozzle. Touching the metal body of the car before handling the nozzle helps discharge you safely. If a fire does start, move away and call 000. Fine dust from flour, sugar or grain can also explode if a spark ignites a dense cloud of it, which is why factories and silos manage static carefully. Electronics are vulnerable too. A discharge too small for you to feel can still damage a microchip, so technicians often wear grounding wrist straps.

quiz.q: Where does the word ‘electricity’ come from?
o: The Latin for lightning
The Greek word for amber
The name of an inventor
The Greek word for spark
quiz.e: Rubbed amber attracts light objects, and the Greek for amber, elektron, gave us the word.

quiz.q: What happens when you rub a balloon on your hair?
o: Protons move from your hair to the balloon
The balloon becomes magnetic
Electrons transfer, leaving the balloon negative and your hair positive
Heat makes the balloon sticky
quiz.e: Rubbing moves electrons between surfaces, giving the two materials opposite charges.

quiz.q: Why are static shocks more common in dry weather?
o: Moisture in humid air lets charge leak away before it builds up
Dry air contains more electrons
Carpets are thicker in winter
Metal conducts better when cold
quiz.e: A thin film of moisture on surfaces drains away charge gradually in humid conditions.

quiz.q: How does a charged balloon stick to a neutral wall?
o: The wall is always positively charged
Air pressure holds it there
The balloon becomes slightly sticky
Its charge rearranges charges in the wall's surface, creating attraction
quiz.e: Induction pulls opposite charges closer and pushes like charges away, so attraction wins.

quiz.q: Which everyday machine grew out of Chester Carlson's 1938 invention?
o: The microwave oven
The photocopier
The television
The electric kettle
quiz.e: Carlson's xerography used static charge to make toner stick in the right places, the basis of photocopiers and laser printers.

LESSONS.title: Plastics: the miracle material
LESSONS.hook: Plastics went from a Victorian curiosity to something found in the deepest ocean trench in barely a century. It's a story of long molecules, lucky accidents and an unsolved problem.

sections.key: Plastics are polymers: enormous molecules built from thousands of small repeating units.
sections.b: The word polymer comes from Greek for ‘many parts’. A polymer is a giant molecule made by linking small building blocks, called monomers, into long chains, often thousands of units long. Polyethylene, the plastic in shopping bags and milk bottles, is simply the small molecule ethylene joined end to end over and over. Nature was making polymers long before chemists. Silk, rubber, wool, the cellulose in wood and paper, and even your own DNA are all polymers. What makes synthetic plastics so useful is that chemists can tune them. By choosing different monomers, chain lengths and the way chains link to each other, they can make materials that are soft or rigid, clear or coloured, stretchy or tough, able to suit almost any purpose.

sections.key: The plastic age began in the 1800s, and the first fully synthetic plastic arrived in 1907.
sections.b: The earliest plastics were made by chemically changing natural materials. In 1862, the English inventor Alexander Parkes displayed Parkesine, made from plant cellulose, at the International Exhibition in London. In the United States, John Wesley Hyatt developed celluloid around 1870, and the story goes that he was partly inspired by a search for a substitute for ivory in billiard balls. Celluloid later became the basis of early photographic and movie film, though it was dangerously flammable. The real turning point came in 1907, when the Belgian-born chemist Leo Baekeland, working in New York, created Bakelite from phenol and formaldehyde. It was the first plastic made entirely from synthetic ingredients. Hard, heat resistant and electrically insulating, it was soon used in radios, telephones and electrical fittings.

sections.key: Several of the most important plastics were discovered by mistake, then made famous by World War II.
sections.b: In 1933, chemists Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson at the British company ICI were experimenting with gases under high pressure when they found a waxy white solid in their vessel. It was polyethylene. Making it reliably took years, but it arrived just in time to insulate the cables of wartime radar systems. In 1938, Roy Plunkett at DuPont in the United States opened a cylinder of refrigerant gas that seemed empty and found a slippery white powder inside. It became PTFE, sold as Teflon. Meanwhile his colleague Wallace Carothers had invented nylon, and nylon stockings caused a sensation when they went on sale in 1940. Soon afterwards, nylon was diverted to parachutes and ropes for the war effort.

sections.key: Some plastics melt and can be reshaped, while others set permanently.
sections.b: Plastics fall into two broad families. Thermoplastics are made of long chains that are tangled together but not tied to each other. Heat them and the chains can slide past one another, so the plastic softens and can be moulded again. Polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC and the PET used in drink bottles are all thermoplastics, which is what makes them possible to recycle by melting. Thermosets are different. As they set, their chains form chemical cross-links, binding everything into one rigid network. Once made, they cannot be melted down. Heat them too far and they char instead. Bakelite, epoxy glues and the resin in fibreglass are thermosets. Their toughness is exactly what makes them useful, and also what makes them so hard to recycle.

sections.key: The number inside the triangle tells you what a plastic is made of, not that it will be recycled.
sections.b: Turn over a plastic container and you will usually find a number from 1 to 7 inside a triangle of arrows. These resin identification codes were introduced in the United States in 1988 to help recyclers sort different plastics. Number 1 is PET, used for soft drink bottles. Number 2 is high-density polyethylene, common in milk bottles. Number 5 is polypropylene, used for many takeaway containers, and number 7 is a catch-all for everything else. The arrows have caused a lot of confusion, because they look like a recycling promise. They are not. Whether an item can actually be recycled depends on the facilities and markets available locally, which is why kerbside rules vary between councils. Checking your council's guidelines beats guessing.

sections.key: Plastic is cheap to make and slow to break down, and only a small share is ever recycled.
sections.b: Global plastic production has grown from almost nothing in 1950 to roughly 400 million tonnes a year by the 2020s. A widely cited 2017 study estimated that of all the plastic waste ever generated up to 2015, only around 9 per cent had been recycled, with the rest burned, buried in landfill or left in the environment. Part of the problem is chemistry. The same strong carbon chains that make plastics durable mean few microbes can digest them, so most plastics do not biodegrade in any useful timeframe. Instead, sunlight and waves slowly break them into smaller and smaller fragments. Recycling also has limits, because each time many plastics are melted and reprocessed, their chains get shorter and the material gets weaker.

sections.key: Tiny plastic fragments are now found almost everywhere, and scientists are still working out what that means.
sections.b: Pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres are called microplastics. Some are made small, like the microbeads once common in face scrubs, while most come from larger items breaking down, from tyres wearing on roads, and from synthetic fibres shed by clothes in the wash. They have been found in Arctic snow, on remote mountaintops and in the deepest part of the ocean, the Mariana Trench. Studies have also detected microplastics in human blood and organs. What that means for health is genuinely uncertain. Researchers are still developing reliable ways to measure such tiny particles and to work out whether, and at what levels, they cause harm. It is an active area of research, and early headlines should be read with care.

quiz.q: What is a polymer?
o: A metal alloy
A long chain of repeating small molecules
A single very heavy atom
A mixture of oil and water
quiz.e: Polymers are giant molecules built by linking many small monomers together, like beads on a chain.

quiz.q: What made Bakelite a milestone in 1907?
o: It was the first biodegradable plastic
It was the first clear plastic
It was the first plastic made entirely from synthetic ingredients
It was the first plastic used for film
quiz.e: Earlier plastics like Parkesine and celluloid were modified natural materials. Bakelite was fully synthetic.

quiz.q: How was polyethylene discovered?
o: By accident, during high-pressure experiments at ICI in 1933
During a search for parachute material
By Leo Baekeland in New York
While trying to make artificial silk
quiz.e: Fawcett and Gibson found a waxy solid in their vessel, and the new plastic later insulated wartime radar cables.

quiz.q: Why are thermosets hard to recycle?
o: They dissolve in water
They are too light to collect
They are made from natural rubber
Their chains are cross-linked, so they can't be melted and reshaped
quiz.e: Cross-links lock thermosets into a rigid network, so heating chars them instead of melting them.

quiz.q: What does the number in the triangle on plastic packaging tell you?
o: The type of plastic it is made from
That it will definitely be recycled
How many times it has been recycled
How long it takes to break down
quiz.e: Resin identification codes identify the plastic type. Whether it is recycled depends on local facilities.

LESSONS.title: Measuring the world: the metric story
LESSONS.hook: Revolutionaries once set out to measure the planet to define the metre. Today a metre, a second and a kilogram are fixed by the laws of nature themselves.

sections.key: Before the metric system, units changed from town to town, and confusion made cheating easy.
sections.b: In eighteenth century France, there was no single foot, pound or bushel. Units of length, weight and volume varied from region to region and even from market to market, with many bearing the same name but meaning different amounts. Merchants, landlords and tax collectors could exploit the confusion, and ordinary people often felt cheated. When the French Revolution swept away the old order in 1789, reformers wanted measurement swept away with it. They dreamed of a rational system based on nature rather than the length of some king's foot, a system that belonged to no single nation. A motto often associated with the project captures the ambition, describing it as a system for all times and all peoples. What they built became the metric system.

sections.key: The original metre was meant to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
sections.b: In 1791, the French Academy of Sciences decided that the new unit of length, the metre, would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the line of longitude through Paris. Someone had to measure it. From 1792, two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, spent around seven years surveying the stretch between Dunkirk and Barcelona, using careful triangulation from church towers and hilltops, often in the chaos of revolution and war. Méchain was tormented by a small inconsistency in his own measurements that he kept secret. In the end, because of small errors and the Earth's not-quite-perfect shape, the official metre came out about 0.2 millimetres shorter than intended. It was close enough, and it stuck.

sections.key: Metric units link to each other neatly and scale up and down in powers of ten.
sections.b: The genius of the metric system is that its units connect. A litre is the volume of a cube ten centimetres on each side. The kilogram was originally defined as the mass of one litre of water. Everything scales by tens, so converting is just a matter of moving a decimal point, and prefixes like kilo, centi and milli work the same way for every unit. Temperature joined in too. The Celsius scale puts 0 at the freezing point of water and 100 at its boiling point, although its inventor, the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius, originally set it up the other way around in 1742, with 100 for freezing and 0 for boiling. The scale was flipped into its familiar form shortly after his death.

sections.key: For 130 years, the world's kilogram was a single metal cylinder kept near Paris.
sections.b: In 1875, seventeen nations signed the Metre Convention, setting up an international bureau to look after the system. In 1889, a new standard kilogram was adopted: a small cylinder of platinum and iridium, about 39 millimetres tall, kept in a vault at Sèvres near Paris under three nested glass bell jars. It was known as Le Grand K, and by definition it weighed exactly one kilogram. Copies were sent to countries around the world and occasionally brought back for comparison. Over the decades, a troubling pattern emerged. The copies and the original drifted apart by tens of micrograms, roughly the weight of a grain of sand. Nobody could say which had changed, because the original was, by definition, always exactly one kilogram.

sections.key: Since 2019, all the base units of measurement have been tied to fixed constants of nature.
sections.b: Scientists steadily replaced metal objects with constants that never change. In 1967, the second was redefined as exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation from a caesium atom, the basis of atomic clocks. In 1983, the metre became the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second, so the speed of light now has an exact value by definition. The kilogram was the last to go. On 20 May 2019, it was redefined using the Planck constant, a fundamental number from quantum physics, measured with extraordinary precision using devices called Kibble balances. Le Grand K was retired. In principle, any well-equipped laboratory anywhere in the universe could now reproduce a kilogram without ever travelling to Paris.

sections.key: Australia switched to metric in the 1970s, though a few old units linger.
sections.b: Australia moved to decimal currency in 1966, and the Metric Conversion Act of 1970 set the country on course to change its measurements too. Over the following decade, temperatures, distances, weights and volumes all changed over. One of the most visible moments came on 1 July 1974, when road signs across the country switched from miles to kilometres. Today most of the world uses metric for daily life, with the United States the best-known exception. Still, older units hang on in Australia in surprising places. Television and phone screens are usually sold by their size in inches, tyre pressures are often given in pounds per square inch, and many people still describe a newborn baby's weight, or their own height, in imperial units.

sections.key: Mixing units has crashed a spacecraft and nearly brought down an airliner.
sections.b: In 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter reached Mars and vanished. Investigators found that software from one team produced thruster data in imperial pound-force seconds, while another team's software expected metric newton-seconds. The tiny repeated error steered the probe far too close to the planet, where it was destroyed. Sixteen years earlier, in 1983, an Air Canada Boeing 767 ran out of fuel at cruising height, partly because a fuel calculation had mixed up pounds and kilograms during the airline's switch to metric. The aircraft was carrying far less fuel than the crew believed. The pilots glided the powerless jet to a disused airbase at Gimli, in Manitoba, and everyone on board survived. It became known as the Gimli Glider.

quiz.q: How was the metre originally defined?
o: The length of a king's arm
One ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator
The distance light travels in one second
The length of a pendulum swinging once per second
quiz.e: The French Academy chose a natural standard, and Delambre and Méchain surveyed from Dunkirk to Barcelona to measure it.

quiz.q: How did Anders Celsius originally set up his temperature scale?
o: With 0 for body temperature
With 32 for freezing
With 100 for freezing and 0 for boiling
With 0 at absolute zero
quiz.e: His original scale was upside down and was reversed into the familiar form after his death.

quiz.q: What was the problem with Le Grand K?
o: It was stolen in 1911
It rusted
It was too heavy to move
It and its copies slowly drifted apart in mass
quiz.e: Comparisons showed differences of tens of micrograms, and nobody could tell which ones had changed.

quiz.q: What is the kilogram now defined by?
o: The Planck constant
A litre of pure water
A new silicon sphere
The mass of a caesium atom
quiz.e: Since 20 May 2019, the kilogram has been fixed by the Planck constant, measured using Kibble balances.

quiz.q: Why was the Mars Climate Orbiter lost?
o: It was hit by a meteor
Software mixed imperial and metric units
Its solar panels failed
Its fuel froze
quiz.e: One team's software used pound-force seconds while another expected newton-seconds, sending the probe too close to Mars.

LESSONS.title: Chaos and the butterfly effect
LESSONS.hook: A weather scientist rounded off a number and went to get a coffee. When he came back, he had discovered why the future can never be fully predicted.

sections.key: For centuries, many scientists believed that perfect knowledge would allow perfect prediction.
sections.b: After Isaac Newton showed that simple laws could explain the motions of the planets, the universe began to look like a vast and precise machine. In 1814, the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace described an imaginary intellect that knew the position of every particle and every force acting on them. For such a being, he wrote, nothing would be uncertain, and the future would be laid out as clearly as the past. Later writers called this imagined mind Laplace's demon. The idea was not foolish. Astronomers really could predict eclipses centuries ahead. It seemed that the only obstacle to predicting anything, including the weather, was gathering enough data and doing enough calculation. That confidence lasted until the twentieth century.

sections.key: In 1961 a tiny rounding of a number transformed a computer weather forecast.
sections.b: Edward Lorenz was a meteorologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who had built a simple weather model on an early computer. In 1961, wanting to look at one run again more closely, he restarted it partway through, typing in numbers from an earlier printout. The printout had rounded the numbers to three decimal places, so instead of 0.506127 he entered 0.506. The difference was tiny, about one part in four thousand. He went to get a coffee while the slow machine worked. When he returned, the new forecast had tracked the old one for a while, then drifted further and further away, until the two bore no resemblance at all. Lorenz realised this was not a fault in the computer. It was a property of the weather.

sections.key: The famous image was a question, not a claim that insects cause storms.
sections.b: Lorenz published his findings in 1963, but they reached a wide audience after a talk he gave in 1972. Its title, reportedly suggested by a fellow meteorologist when Lorenz had not supplied one, asked: ‘Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?’ The phrase stuck and became known as the butterfly effect. It is often misunderstood. Lorenz was not saying that butterflies control the weather. His point was that in some systems, differences far too small to measure can grow until they completely change the outcome, which makes long-range prediction impossible in practice. By coincidence, a plot of his equations traces a looping shape that looks rather like a pair of butterfly wings.

sections.key: A chaotic system follows exact rules, yet its long-term behaviour is unpredictable.
sections.b: Scientists use the word chaos in a specific way. A chaotic system is deterministic, meaning the same starting point always produces exactly the same result. There is no randomness in the rules. The catch is what mathematicians call sensitive dependence on initial conditions. Tiny differences at the start do not stay tiny; they grow, roughly doubling again and again, until they swamp everything. Since we can never measure anything perfectly, our predictions eventually fail. A double pendulum, which is simply one pendulum hanging from the end of another, shows this beautifully. Release it twice from what looks like the same position and the two swings will soon follow completely different, wild paths. The rules are simple; the behaviour is anything but.

sections.key: Hints of chaos appeared in the 1880s, in a famous error about the solar system.
sections.b: Lorenz was not the first to stumble on chaos. In the 1880s, King Oscar II of Sweden offered a prize for anyone who could prove the solar system was stable over the long run. The French mathematician Henri Poincaré studied a simplified version, three bodies moving under each other's gravity, and won in 1889. Then, as his paper was being prepared for publication, a serious error was found. Correcting it, Poincaré realised that the three-body problem could behave in extraordinarily tangled ways, with tiny changes leading to vastly different orbits. The printed copies had to be recalled and destroyed, reportedly at a cost greater than the prize money. His corrected work is now seen as an early glimpse of chaos theory.

sections.key: Chaos sets limits on prediction, but it doesn't make forecasting useless.
sections.b: Chaos explains why weather forecasts are reliable for a few days, useful for about a week, and of little value beyond about two weeks. Forecasters now deal with this honestly through ensembles, running a model many times with slightly different starting conditions. If the runs agree, confidence is high; if they spread out, the outlook is uncertain. Chaos turns up widely elsewhere too. In 1976, the Australian-born scientist Robert May showed that a very simple equation for animal populations could swing from steady numbers to wild, chaotic booms and busts. Even the orbits of the planets are thought to be chaotic over tens of millions of years. Laplace's demon would need infinitely precise data, and nature never provides that.

quiz.q: What did ‘Laplace's demon’ represent?
o: A being who could predict everything from perfect knowledge of the present
A flaw in Newton's laws
A random force in nature
An early computer
quiz.e: Laplace imagined that knowing every particle and force would make the future completely predictable.

quiz.q: What triggered Lorenz's discovery in 1961?
o: A broken thermometer
A storm that his model missed
Entering a number rounded to three decimal places
A power cut
quiz.e: Typing 0.506 instead of 0.506127 caused his forecast to diverge completely over time.

quiz.q: What was Lorenz's real point about the butterfly?
o: Insects control global weather
Tiny, unmeasurable differences can grow to change outcomes entirely
Tornadoes start in Brazil
Weather is completely random
quiz.e: The image illustrates sensitive dependence: small differences make long-range prediction impossible in practice.

quiz.q: Which statement about chaotic systems is correct?
o: They follow no rules
They are always random
They only occur in weather
They follow exact rules but are unpredictable in the long term
quiz.e: Chaotic systems are deterministic, but tiny errors in starting conditions grow until predictions fail.

quiz.q: How do forecasters deal with chaos?
o: They only forecast one day ahead
They run a model many times with slightly different starting conditions
They rely on historical averages only
They ignore small measurement errors
quiz.e: Ensemble forecasting shows how confident a forecast is by how much the runs agree or spread apart.

LESSONS.title: Carbon: the element of everything
LESSONS.hook: The same atom makes a diamond, a pencil, a soccer-ball-shaped molecule and most of you. Carbon's secret is its talent for holding hands.

sections.key: Carbon can form four strong bonds, letting it build chains, rings and endless complex molecules.
sections.b: Each carbon atom has four electrons available for bonding, so it can link with up to four other atoms at once. Crucially, it bonds strongly with other carbon atoms, forming long chains, branches and rings that act as frameworks for other elements to hang from. This flexibility is why carbon is the backbone of the molecules of life, including proteins, fats, sugars and DNA. The chemistry of carbon compounds is so vast that it has its own branch, organic chemistry, covering many millions of known substances. Carbon is common, too. After hydrogen, helium and oxygen, it is the fourth most abundant element in the universe by mass, and by mass it makes up around a fifth of your body.

sections.key: Carbon is made inside stars, and a scientist predicted how before it was proven.
sections.b: The Big Bang produced almost no carbon. It is forged inside stars, where three helium nuclei fuse into one carbon nucleus. In the early 1950s, the British astronomer Fred Hoyle realised there was a problem: by the known physics, this reaction should be far too rare to make the amount of carbon we see. He reasoned that since carbon obviously exists, carbon nuclei must have a particular energy state that made the reaction much more likely. In 1953 he persuaded sceptical experimental physicists at Caltech to look for it, and they found it close to where he had predicted. The carbon in your cells was made this way in stars that lived and died long before the Sun formed.

sections.key: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; only the arrangement of atoms differs.
sections.b: In diamond, every carbon atom is locked to four neighbours in a rigid three-dimensional framework, which makes it the hardest natural material known. Natural diamonds form deep in the Earth's mantle, typically well over a hundred kilometres down, under enormous heat and pressure, and are carried up in rare volcanic eruptions. In graphite, carbon atoms bond to three neighbours in flat sheets of hexagons, stacked like pages in a book. The sheets are held together only weakly, so they slide easily, making graphite soft and slippery. Surprisingly, at the Earth's surface graphite is the more stable form. Diamonds are technically on their way to becoming graphite, but the change is so incredibly slow that in practice it never happens.

sections.h: There's no lead in a pencil
sections.key: Pencil ‘lead’ is graphite, named after a centuries-old mistake.
sections.b: In the sixteenth century, a remarkably pure deposit of graphite was found at Borrowdale in England's Lake District. People didn't know what it was. Because it left grey marks and looked a bit like lead ore, it was called black lead or plumbago, from the Latin for lead. Shepherds reportedly used it to mark their sheep, and it was soon being cut into sticks for writing and drawing. The deposit was so valuable that it was guarded, and the name stuck long after chemists showed in the late 1700s that the material was a form of carbon. Modern pencil ‘lead’ is graphite mixed with clay, and the ratio sets its hardness. More clay gives a harder, lighter H pencil, while more graphite gives a softer, darker B pencil.

sections.key: In 1985 scientists discovered a hollow cage of 60 carbon atoms, shaped exactly like a soccer ball.
sections.b: For a long time, diamond and graphite were the only well-known pure forms of carbon. Then, in 1985, Harold Kroto from Britain and Robert Curl and Richard Smalley from Rice University in Texas, working with their students, blasted graphite with a laser and found a surprisingly stable molecule made of exactly 60 carbon atoms. Its structure turned out to be a hollow sphere of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, the same pattern as a classic soccer ball. They named it buckminsterfullerene, after the American architect Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes it resembled, and it soon picked up the nickname buckyball. The three senior scientists shared the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Buckyballs have since been detected in clouds of gas and dust in space.

sections.key: A single layer of carbon atoms was first isolated using ordinary sticky tape.
sections.b: Graphene is a single sheet of graphite, just one atom thick. Physicists long doubted such a thin sheet could be isolated in a stable form. In 2004, at the University of Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov did it in an almost comically simple way. They pressed sticky tape onto graphite, peeled it off, and kept splitting the flakes with fresh tape until some were just one atom thick. Graphene turned out to be extraordinary: incredibly strong for its weight, flexible, nearly transparent and an excellent conductor of electricity and heat. Geim and Novoselov won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics. Geim also holds an Ig Nobel Prize, awarded in 2000 for using powerful magnets to levitate a live frog, making him a rare winner of both.

sections.key: Carbon cycles constantly between air, oceans, rocks and living things.
sections.b: The carbon atoms in your body have been on a very long journey. Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air and use sunlight to build it into sugars. Animals eat the plants, and both release carbon dioxide again as they breathe and decay. The oceans absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide, and over millions of years carbon is locked away in limestone and other rocks, then slowly returned by volcanoes. Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient living things, carbon that was buried and stored for millions of years. Burning them releases that carbon back into the air far faster than natural processes can remove it, which is the main reason carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are rising.

quiz.q: Why is carbon so good at building complex molecules?
o: It is the heaviest common element
It can form four bonds, including strong bonds with other carbon atoms
It is a metal
It never reacts with other elements
quiz.e: Four bonds and strong carbon to carbon links let it form chains, rings and branching frameworks.

quiz.q: What did Fred Hoyle predict in 1953?
o: That diamonds form in space
A special energy state of carbon nuclei that lets stars make carbon
The existence of graphene
That carbon was made in the Big Bang
quiz.e: Since carbon exists, Hoyle reasoned the nucleus must have a state that makes its formation in stars possible.

quiz.q: What is the difference between diamond and graphite?
o: Diamond contains oxygen
Graphite contains lead
Only the arrangement of the carbon atoms
Diamond is made of heavier carbon atoms
quiz.e: Both are pure carbon. Diamond is a rigid 3D framework; graphite is sliding flat sheets.

quiz.q: What shape is a buckminsterfullerene molecule?
o: A hollow cage of pentagons and hexagons like a soccer ball
A flat sheet one atom thick
A long straight chain
A pyramid
quiz.e: C60 is a sphere of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, named after Buckminster Fuller's geodesic domes.

quiz.q: How was graphene first isolated in 2004?
o: Using a particle accelerator
By burning diamonds
By crushing pencils in a blender
By peeling graphite repeatedly with sticky tape
quiz.e: Geim and Novoselov split graphite flakes with tape until some were a single atom thick, earning a Nobel Prize.

LESSONS.title: Antimatter: the universe's missing twin
LESSONS.hook: For every particle there is a mirror-image twin with the opposite charge. When they meet, both vanish in a flash of pure energy. So why is the universe made almost entirely of one kind?

sections.key: In 1928, Paul Dirac's equation for the electron predicted a particle nobody had seen.
sections.b: The British physicist Paul Dirac was famously quiet and precise, and in 1928 he produced one of the most elegant equations in physics. He combined quantum mechanics with Einstein's special relativity to describe the electron moving at high speed. The equation worked beautifully, but it had a strange feature. Just as the square root of four can be plus two or minus two, Dirac's equation allowed solutions that seemed to describe electrons with negative energy. Rather than discard them, Dirac took them seriously. After some false starts, in 1931 he proposed that they pointed to a new particle, with the same mass as an electron but a positive electric charge. Mathematics had predicted a form of matter no one had ever detected.

sections.key: In 1932 Carl Anderson spotted the antielectron in tracks left by cosmic rays.
sections.b: Carl Anderson, a young physicist at Caltech, was studying cosmic rays, high-energy particles that rain down from space. He used a cloud chamber, a device filled with vapour in which charged particles leave trails of droplets, placed inside a strong magnet. A magnetic field bends positive and negative particles in opposite directions. To tell which way particles were travelling, Anderson put a lead plate across the chamber, since a particle loses energy passing through it and curves more tightly afterwards. In 1932 he photographed a track that curved like an electron's, but the wrong way. It was a particle with an electron's mass and a positive charge. He called it the positron, and shared the 1936 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery.

sections.key: When matter meets its antimatter twin, their entire mass turns into energy.
sections.b: Every type of particle has an antiparticle with the same mass but opposite charge and some other opposite properties. Electrons have positrons, protons have antiprotons, and so on. When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate, and their mass is converted into energy, usually as high-energy gamma rays, following Einstein's famous E = mc². This is the most complete conversion of mass into energy known. Nuclear fission and fusion turn only a tiny fraction of their fuel's mass into energy, less than one per cent. Annihilation converts all of it. The process also runs the other way. A sufficiently energetic gamma ray passing near an atomic nucleus can turn into an electron and a positron, a process called pair production, creating matter out of energy.

sections.key: Physicists have made antiprotons, then anti-atoms, and trapped them in magnetic bottles.
sections.b: The antiproton was created in 1955 at the Bevatron accelerator in Berkeley, California, by a team led by Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain, who won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. The next goal was to put an antiproton and a positron together to make antihydrogen, the simplest anti-atom. Researchers at CERN, near Geneva, first did this in 1995, producing just a handful of atoms that annihilated almost instantly. Holding them is the hard part, because antimatter touching the walls of any container is destroyed. In 2010, CERN's ALPHA experiment trapped antihydrogen atoms in a carefully shaped magnetic field, and soon held some for around a quarter of an hour. In 2023, ALPHA confirmed that antihydrogen falls under gravity, just like ordinary matter.

sections.key: Antimatter is not just in physics labs; it's used in medicine and occurs in nature.
sections.b: Some radioactive atoms decay by emitting positrons, and medicine puts this to work in PET scans, short for positron emission tomography. A patient is given a substance, often a form of sugar tagged with radioactive fluorine. Busy tissues, such as some tumours, take up more of it. Each positron it emits travels a tiny distance before meeting an electron and annihilating, sending out two gamma rays in almost exactly opposite directions. Rings of detectors catch both and trace back where they came from, building up a map of activity inside the body. Positrons also appear naturally. A very small fraction of decays of potassium-40, found in bananas and in your own body, produce them, and some thunderstorms have been observed producing bursts of antimatter.

sections.key: Antimatter powers starships in science fiction, but making it costs vastly more energy than it releases.
sections.b: Because annihilation converts mass entirely into energy, antimatter is often imagined as the perfect fuel. The reality is sobering. Antiparticles have to be made in particle accelerators, one collision at a time, and the process is staggeringly inefficient, consuming far more energy than the antimatter could ever give back. Storing it is also extremely difficult, since it must be kept in a vacuum and suspended in magnetic fields so it never touches anything. CERN has noted that if all the antimatter it has ever made were annihilated at once, the energy would light a single household light bulb for only a few minutes. Antimatter weapons and engines remain firmly in the realm of fiction. For now, antimatter is a tool for understanding nature, not powering it.

sections.key: The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, yet almost none of the antimatter remains.
sections.b: Here is the deepest puzzle. According to our best theories, the Big Bang should have produced matter and antimatter in equal amounts. If so, they should have annihilated each other completely, leaving a universe filled with nothing but light. Instead, there are galaxies, stars and people, all made of matter. Somehow, a small excess of matter survived, often estimated at roughly one extra particle for every billion matter and antimatter pairs. In 1967, the Soviet physicist Andrei Sakharov set out the conditions needed for such an imbalance. Experiments since 1964 have found that some particles and their antiparticles do behave slightly differently, but the differences measured so far are far too small to explain it. Why anything exists at all remains unsolved.

quiz.q: How was antimatter first predicted?
o: From cosmic ray photographs
From Dirac's equation combining quantum mechanics and relativity
From observations of the Sun
From Einstein's theory of gravity
quiz.e: Dirac's 1928 equation allowed solutions that, by 1931, he interpreted as a new positively charged particle.

quiz.q: How did Carl Anderson know his particle was positively charged?
o: It glowed red in the cloud chamber
It was heavier than an electron
Its track curved the opposite way to an electron's in a magnetic field
It was attracted to the lead plate
quiz.e: The magnet bent its track like an electron's but in the opposite direction, and the lead plate showed which way it was travelling.

quiz.q: How does annihilation compare with nuclear fission?
o: Annihilation converts all the mass into energy; fission converts less than one per cent
They release the same energy
Fission is far more efficient
Annihilation releases no energy
quiz.e: When matter meets antimatter, their whole mass becomes energy, the most complete conversion known.

quiz.q: How does a PET scan use antimatter?
o: It fires antiprotons into the body
It stores antimatter in the scanner
It turns body tissue into antimatter
It detects the paired gamma rays from positrons annihilating with electrons
quiz.e: Positrons from a radioactive tracer annihilate with electrons, and detectors trace the opposite-pointing gamma rays back to their source.

quiz.q: What is the matter–antimatter mystery?
o: Why antimatter falls upward
Why the universe is made almost entirely of matter when equal amounts should have formed
Why positrons are heavier than electrons
Why antimatter can't be made in labs
quiz.e: A small excess of matter somehow survived the Big Bang, and known effects are far too small to explain it.

LESSONS.title: The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born
LESSONS.hook: A woman in a Scottish café sipped a ginger beer and claimed she found a rotting snail in it. Her lawsuit changed the law for almost everyone in the English-speaking world.

sections.key: A ruined drink in 1928 led to one of the most famous court cases ever decided.
sections.b: On the evening of 26 August 1928, May Donoghue met a friend at the Wellmeadow Café in Paisley, near Glasgow. Her friend bought her an ice cream float, made with ginger beer from a dark, opaque glass bottle. Mrs Donoghue drank some of it. When the rest was poured out, she later said, the decomposed remains of a snail slid into her glass. She claimed the sight, and what she had already swallowed, made her ill with shock and gastroenteritis. Nobody could see through the bottle, so nobody could have spotted the snail beforehand. It sounds like a small, unpleasant accident. Yet the question it raised would travel all the way to the highest court in Britain and reshape the law for nearly a century.

sections.key: Mrs Donoghue had no contract with anyone, so the old law seemed to leave her with no remedy.
sections.b: At the time, if a faulty product hurt you, your main legal route was usually to sue the person who sold it to you for breaching your contract. But Mrs Donoghue had not bought the drink. Her friend had, so she had no contract with the café owner. The café owner had not made the drink or sealed the bottle either. The obvious target was the manufacturer, David Stevenson, whose name was on the bottle. The trouble was that she had no contract with him at all. Earlier cases suggested that a manufacturer owed nothing to a stranger who consumed its goods, except in a few special situations, such as inherently dangerous items. On the law as many understood it, she had nowhere to go.

sections.h: All the way to the Lords
sections.key: The House of Lords decided only whether she had a case in law, not whether there really was a snail.
sections.b: Mrs Donoghue had little money, and she was allowed to sue as a pauper, which meant she did not have to pay the usual court costs. Her lawyer, Walter Leechman, took on the manufacturer. The case reached the House of Lords, then Britain's highest court, which gave its decision in May 1932. Importantly, the judges were not deciding whether a snail had really been in the bottle. They were answering a preliminary question: assuming everything she said was true, did the law give her a claim? By a narrow majority of three to two, the Lords said yes. A manufacturer who sells products in a form meant to reach the consumer unchanged owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care.

sections.key: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle became the foundation of the modern law of negligence.
sections.b: The most famous judgment came from Lord Atkin, who reached for a Bible story. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, a lawyer asks Jesus, ‘Who is my neighbour?’ Atkin gave a legal answer. You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour. And your neighbour, in law, is anyone so closely and directly affected by what you do that you ought to have them in mind. This was a broad principle rather than a narrow rule about ginger beer. It suggested that a general duty of care could exist between strangers, wherever harm was foreseeable and the relationship close enough. Lawyers call this the neighbour principle, and it is still taught to almost every first year law student.

sections.key: To win a negligence claim you generally need a duty of care, a breach of that duty and harm caused by the breach.
sections.b: Donoghue v Stevenson gave shape to negligence, the area of law dealing with careless harm. In broad terms, a person suing for negligence must show three things. First, the other side owed them a duty of care. Second, the other side breached that duty by falling below the standard of a reasonable person in their position. Third, the breach actually caused them harm of a kind the law recognises. These ideas now sit behind claims about car crashes, medical mistakes, slippery supermarket floors and unsafe buildings. Courts have spent decades refining where duties begin and end, because a duty that stretched forever would make everyone liable for everything. Many places, including Australian states, have also passed laws limiting some claims and damages.

sections.h: The case that went around the world
sections.key: Courts across the common law world, including Australia, adopted the principle within a few years.
sections.b: A Scottish decision about a Paisley café could easily have stayed local. Instead, it spread quickly. In the mid 1930s, an Australian case reached the Privy Council in London, then the final court of appeal for Australia. Dr Richard Grant had developed severe dermatitis from woollen underwear made by Australian Knitting Mills, which contained irritating chemicals left over from manufacturing. Relying on the principle from Donoghue v Stevenson, the Privy Council found the manufacturer liable. Courts in Canada, New Zealand and elsewhere followed similar paths. Later, governments built consumer protection laws on top of these foundations, giving people statutory rights against makers of unsafe goods. The snail had travelled a very long way from Scotland.

sections.key: No court ever decided whether the snail existed, because the case settled out of court.
sections.b: Here is the twist. After the House of Lords ruled that Mrs Donoghue had a claim, the case was supposed to return to the Scottish courts for a trial on the facts. But David Stevenson died before that could happen, and the claim was settled out of court. So no judge ever ruled on whether there really was a snail in the bottle. Some sceptics have wondered about it ever since. In a sense it does not matter. The case is remembered not for its facts but for its principle. Today a memorial marks the site of the old café in Paisley, and lawyers from around the world have visited it to pay tribute to a woman, a bottle and a possibly imaginary snail.

quiz.q: Why couldn't Mrs Donoghue simply sue for breach of contract?
o: Contracts were not enforceable in Scotland
Her friend bought the drink, so she had no contract with anyone
The café had closed down
The bottle had no label
quiz.e: She had not bought the ginger beer herself, so she had no contract with the café or the manufacturer.

quiz.q: What did the House of Lords actually decide in 1932?
o: That a snail was definitely in the bottle
That the café owner must go to prison
That, if her story was true, she had a valid claim in law
That ginger beer should be sold in clear bottles
quiz.e: The Lords answered a preliminary legal question, assuming her facts were true, and ruled 3 to 2 that a duty of care existed.

quiz.q: In Lord Atkin's neighbour principle, who counts as your ‘neighbour’?
o: Anyone so closely and directly affected by your actions that you ought to have them in mind
Only people who live next door
Only people you have a contract with
Only members of your family
quiz.e: Atkin's legal neighbour is anyone closely and directly affected by your acts, whose harm you could reasonably foresee.

quiz.q: Which three elements does a negligence claim generally need?
o: Intent, motive and opportunity
A contract, a signature and a witness
An offer, acceptance and payment
A duty of care, a breach of that duty and harm caused by it
quiz.e: Negligence broadly requires a duty, a breach of the expected standard of care, and harm caused by that breach.

quiz.q: Why did no court ever rule on whether the snail existed?
o: The bottle was lost
The manufacturer died and the case was settled out of court
Mrs Donoghue dropped the case
Snails could not be used as evidence
quiz.e: David Stevenson died before the trial on the facts, and the claim was settled, so the snail was never proven or disproven.

LESSONS.title: Habeas corpus: the right not to simply vanish
LESSONS.hook: Two Latin words protect you from being locked away without reason. They have stood up to kings, slave owners and presidents.

sections.key: Habeas corpus is a court order demanding that a jailer justify why a person is being held.
sections.b: Habeas corpus is Latin for ‘you shall have the body’. It is the name of a writ, a formal order from a court, directed at whoever is holding a prisoner, whether a jailer, a soldier or a government official. The writ commands them to bring the person before the court and show a lawful reason for the detention. If they cannot, the judge can order the prisoner released. The idea is simple but powerful. It does not decide whether someone is guilty. It asks a more basic question: is there any legal authority to hold this person at all? That makes it a check on power itself. Without it, a government could make people disappear into cells with no charge, no trial and no end date.

sections.key: The writ grew out of medieval English courts and the promise in Magna Carta of no imprisonment without lawful judgment.
sections.b: Habeas corpus did not appear in a single moment. Versions of the writ existed in English courts by the 1200s, at first mostly as a tool for bringing people to court rather than for freeing them. Over time, judges began using it to examine whether detentions were lawful. It drew strength from a famous promise in Magna Carta of 1215: that no free man would be imprisoned except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land. That promise was often broken in practice, but it became a powerful ideal. Over the following centuries, as courts and Parliament wrestled with the Crown over who held power, habeas corpus slowly became the practical tool for turning that ideal into reality.

sections.key: Clashes with Charles I and later kings led Parliament to strengthen the writ in the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679.
sections.b: In 1627, King Charles I jailed several knights who refused to pay a forced loan he had demanded without Parliament's consent. They sought habeas corpus, but the jailer's only answer was that they were held by the king's special command. The court refused to release them. Outrage over the Five Knights' Case helped produce the Petition of Right in 1628, which declared such imprisonment unlawful. Arguments continued for decades, and in 1679 Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act, which set deadlines and penalties to stop officials dodging the writ. According to an account by Bishop Gilbert Burnet, the act squeaked through the House of Lords only because a very large lord was jokingly counted as ten votes. Historians treat that story with caution.

sections.key: In 1772 an English court used habeas corpus to stop an enslaved man being shipped away by force.
sections.b: One of the most dramatic uses of the writ came in 1772. James Somerset had been enslaved in Virginia and brought to England by Charles Stewart, a customs official. Somerset escaped, was recaptured and was put aboard a ship bound for Jamaica, where he would be sold. Supporters, including the campaigner Granville Sharp, sought habeas corpus. The case came before Lord Mansfield, the senior judge of the King's Bench. Mansfield ruled that there was no law in England allowing a master to force Somerset out of the country, and he was freed. The decision did not abolish slavery, which continued in British colonies for decades, but it was widely celebrated and became a landmark in the long struggle against slavery.

sections.key: In emergencies governments have suspended habeas corpus, and those moments have always been controversial.
sections.b: Because habeas corpus limits government power, governments under pressure have sometimes tried to switch it off. Britain's Parliament suspended it several times, for example in the 1790s amid fears of revolution spreading from France. The framers of the United States Constitution included the writ but allowed suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety required it. In 1861, at the start of the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln suspended it in some areas. Chief Justice Roger Taney argued in the Merryman case that only Congress had that power, and Lincoln largely ignored him. Congress later authorised suspension. Ever since, lawyers and historians have debated how far emergencies justify setting aside this ancient safeguard.

sections.key: Habeas corpus remains part of the legal toolkit in Australia and across the common law world.
sections.b: English colonists carried habeas corpus around the world, and it remains part of the law in countries including Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India and the United States. In Australia, superior courts such as the state Supreme Courts and the High Court can issue it. In practice, many detentions are now reviewed through other routes, such as bail hearings, appeals and judicial review, so the old writ is used less often than its fame suggests. But it still matters most when other protections fail. It has been invoked over immigration detention, mental health detention and wartime imprisonment. Its enduring message is that power must always answer one question in court: by what lawful authority is this person being held?

quiz.q: What does a writ of habeas corpus require?
o: That a prisoner be found guilty or innocent immediately
That the person holding a prisoner bring them to court and justify the detention
That a prisoner be given a lawyer
That a trial be held before a jury
quiz.e: The writ orders the jailer to produce the prisoner and show a lawful reason for holding them.

quiz.q: Which 1215 document promised no imprisonment except by lawful judgment or the law of the land?
o: The Bill of Rights
The Petition of Right
Magna Carta
The Habeas Corpus Act
quiz.e: Magna Carta's promise became an ideal that habeas corpus later helped put into practice.

quiz.q: What did the Five Knights' Case of 1627 help produce?
o: The Petition of Right of 1628
The abolition of the monarchy
The first jury trial
The United States Constitution
quiz.e: When the court refused to release the knights, Parliament responded with the Petition of Right.

quiz.q: What did Lord Mansfield decide in James Somerset's case?
o: That slavery was abolished across the British Empire
That Somerset must be returned to Virginia
That Somerset should be sold in England instead
That no English law allowed Somerset to be forcibly removed from the country
quiz.e: Mansfield freed Somerset, though slavery continued in British colonies for decades afterwards.

quiz.q: When does the US Constitution allow habeas corpus to be suspended?
o: Whenever the President wishes
During rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it
During any election year
Never under any circumstances
quiz.e: The Constitution permits suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion, as Lincoln's actions in 1861 tested.

LESSONS.title: The 1967 referendum: what it really changed
LESSONS.hook: More than 90 per cent of Australians voted Yes in 1967, the biggest win in referendum history. Yet many people still believe it did things it never did.

sections.key: On 27 May 1967 Australians voted overwhelmingly to change the Constitution regarding Aboriginal people.
sections.b: Changing Australia's Constitution is notoriously hard. A proposal must pass Parliament and then win a double majority: a majority of voters nationally, and majorities in at least four of the six states. Only a handful of the more than 40 proposals put to the people have ever passed. On 27 May 1967 one question about Aboriginal people won about 91 per cent of the national vote and carried every state. No referendum before or since has come close. The result is remembered as a turning point in Australian history, and the date now marks the start of National Reconciliation Week. But to understand why it mattered, it helps to know exactly which words were removed, and also what the vote did not do.

sections.key: The referendum deleted a phrase from the race power and removed section 127 entirely.
sections.b: The 1901 Constitution mentioned Aboriginal people only twice, and both times to exclude them. Section 51, which lists the subjects the federal Parliament can make laws about, gave it power over ‘the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State’, for whom special laws were deemed necessary. That left laws about Aboriginal people to the states. Section 127 said that in reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, or of a state, ‘aboriginal natives shall not be counted’. The 1967 referendum removed the words ‘other than the aboriginal race in any State’ from section 51, and deleted section 127 altogether. Those two changes were the entire legal effect of the vote.

sections.h: Myth one: the right to vote
sections.key: The referendum did not give Aboriginal people the vote; that had already happened through ordinary laws.
sections.b: One of the most common beliefs about 1967 is that it gave Aboriginal people the right to vote. It did not. Voting rights are set mainly by ordinary laws passed by parliaments, not by the Constitution. Some Aboriginal people had been able to vote in a few colonies since the 1850s and 1890s, although many were later excluded. The Commonwealth Electoral Act was amended in 1962 to give all Aboriginal people the right to vote in federal elections. The states moved at different speeds, and Queensland was the last to grant state voting rights, in 1965. So by the time of the referendum, Aboriginal Australians could already vote everywhere, even though many still faced real barriers in practice.

sections.h: Myth two: citizenship and ‘flora and fauna’
sections.key: The vote did not create citizenship, and there was never a law classifying Aboriginal people as flora and fauna.
sections.b: Another myth is that the referendum made Aboriginal people citizens. Australian citizenship was created in 1949, and Aboriginal people born in Australia were covered by it, although in practice many were still denied rights through state laws controlling where they lived, worked and married. A third persistent myth says Aboriginal people were managed under a ‘Flora and Fauna Act’ until 1967. Historians and fact checkers have found no such law, at federal or state level. The myth probably spread because it captured how dehumanising the real treatment felt, but it is not accurate. Correcting these myths does not shrink the referendum's importance. It shows that its power was partly symbolic, and partly about which government held responsibility.

sections.key: A decade of grassroots activism by Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal campaigners built the case for Yes.
sections.b: The referendum did not come from nowhere. Through the late 1950s and 1960s, groups such as the Federal Council for the Advancement of Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders gathered petitions, held meetings and lobbied politicians. Faith Bandler, an activist of South Sea Islander heritage, was one of the campaign's best known leaders, alongside Aboriginal figures such as Joe McGinness and many others. Events like the 1965 Freedom Ride through country New South Wales, led by Charles Perkins and university students, exposed segregation in pools, pubs and cinemas. By the time Parliament put the question, it had support from across the major parties, and there was no organised No case. That unusual unity helps explain the record result.

sections.key: The referendum gave the federal Parliament power to make laws for Aboriginal people, opening a new era of national policy.
sections.b: Removing the exclusion from section 51 meant the Commonwealth, not just the states, could now make laws specifically for Aboriginal people. Over the following years, the federal government created new agencies and programs, and in 1976 Parliament passed the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act. The deletion of section 127 meant Aboriginal people would be included in official population counts. Yet the change was neutral on its face. The race power lets the Commonwealth make laws about people of any race, and courts have since debated whether those laws must be for a group's benefit. Many campaigners felt that real progress came more slowly than the 1967 euphoria promised. Even so, the vote remains a landmark of national goodwill.

quiz.q: What is the ‘double majority’ needed to change Australia's Constitution?
o: Both houses of Parliament voting twice
A national majority of voters plus majorities in at least four of the six states
Two thirds of all voters
A majority in every state and territory
quiz.e: A proposal needs a majority nationally and a majority in at least four states.

quiz.q: What did section 127, deleted in 1967, say?
o: That Aboriginal people could not vote
That Aboriginal people could not own land
That Aboriginal people were not citizens
That Aboriginal natives should not be counted in reckoning the population
quiz.e: Section 127 excluded Aboriginal people from official population counts, and the referendum removed it.

quiz.q: When did all Aboriginal people gain the right to vote in federal elections?
quiz.e: An amendment to the Commonwealth Electoral Act in 1962 gave the federal vote, five years before the referendum.

quiz.q: What did historians find about the supposed ‘Flora and Fauna Act’?
o: It was repealed by the referendum
It applied only in Queensland
No such law ever existed
It was replaced by the Citizenship Act
quiz.e: No federal or state law classified Aboriginal people as flora and fauna, though the myth reflected real mistreatment.

quiz.q: What was the main legal effect of changing section 51?
o: It abolished state governments
It created Australian citizenship
It granted land rights automatically
It allowed the federal Parliament to make laws specifically for Aboriginal people
quiz.e: Removing the exclusion gave the Commonwealth power to legislate for Aboriginal people, not only the states.

LESSONS.title: Gerrymandering: winning by drawing the lines
LESSONS.hook: You can lose the popular vote and still win the election, if someone has drawn the map cleverly enough. Meet the strange art of the gerrymander.

sections.key: The word comes from an 1812 cartoon mocking a district shaped like a monster.
sections.b: In 1812, the Massachusetts legislature redrew the boundaries of its state senate districts. The new map was designed to help the governing party, and Governor Elbridge Gerry signed it into law. One district north of Boston snaked around in such a strange, twisting shape that critics said it looked like a salamander.
