sections.b: When it was discovered, Pluto was assumed to be roughly Earth-sized, since it was supposed to be disturbing Neptune's orbit. Each new measurement shrank it. In 1978 astronomers discovered its largest moon, Charon, which allowed them to calculate Pluto's mass precisely, and it turned out to be tiny: only about a fifth of the mass of our Moon. Pluto is about 2,380 kilometres across, narrower than Australia is wide. Charon is about half Pluto's diameter, so large that the two swing around a shared point in the space between them. Pluto's orbit is also odd. It is stretched and tilted, and between 1979 and 1999 it actually came closer to the Sun than Neptune.

sections.key: From 1992 astronomers found many icy worlds beyond Neptune, including Eris, which is more massive than Pluto.
sections.b: In 1992 astronomers found another small icy body beyond Neptune, the first known member of what is now called the Kuiper Belt. Hundreds, then thousands more followed. Pluto, it became clear, was not a lonely ninth planet but one of the largest members of a vast belt of frozen leftovers. The crisis came in 2005, when a team led by Mike Brown announced Eris, a distant world first thought to be larger than Pluto. Later measurements showed Eris is very slightly smaller in diameter but about a quarter more massive. Either way, astronomers faced a choice. If Pluto was a planet, Eris had to be one too, and possibly dozens more. The solar system needed a proper definition.

sections.key: The International Astronomical Union defined a planet with three tests, and Pluto failed the third.
sections.b: In August 2006, at its meeting in Prague, the International Astronomical Union voted on the first formal definition of a planet. A planet must orbit the Sun, must have enough mass for gravity to pull it into a roughly round shape, and must have 'cleared the neighbourhood' around its orbit, meaning it dominates its path gravitationally. Pluto passes the first two tests but fails the third, because it shares its region with countless Kuiper Belt objects. It was placed in a new category, dwarf planet, alongside Eris and the largest asteroid, Ceres. Haumea and Makemake were added later. The decision was controversial. Some planetary scientists still argue for a definition based on a body's own properties, not its surroundings.

sections.key: In 2015 New Horizons revealed Pluto to be a surprisingly active world with glaciers, mountains and a giant heart-shaped plain.
sections.b: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft launched in January 2006, months before the vote, and flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015 after a journey of nine and a half years. Expectations were modest: perhaps an old, cratered ball of ice. Instead it revealed a world of startling variety. A huge pale heart-shaped region, named Tombaugh Regio, contains a smooth plain of nitrogen ice called Sputnik Planitia, so young it has almost no craters, slowly churning and flowing like glaciers. There are mountains of water ice several kilometres high and a thin, hazy blue atmosphere. Aboard the spacecraft was a small portion of Clyde Tombaugh's ashes, carried past the world he had discovered 85 years earlier. Dwarf planet or not, Pluto proved fascinating.

quiz.q: How did Clyde Tombaugh discover Pluto?
o: With a radio telescope
By comparing photographs to find a moving dot
From calculations alone
Using a space probe
quiz.e: Tombaugh used a blink comparator to flick between photographs taken nights apart, spotting a dot that moved against the stars.

quiz.q: Who suggested the name Pluto?
o: Percival Lowell
Walt Disney
Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old from Oxford
Clyde Tombaugh
quiz.e: Venetia Burney suggested the name; staff liked it partly because its first letters honoured Percival Lowell.

quiz.q: What allowed astronomers to measure Pluto's mass precisely?
o: The discovery of its moon Charon in 1978
Landing a probe on it
Its eclipse of Neptune
The 2006 vote
quiz.e: Charon's orbit revealed how strongly Pluto pulls on it, giving Pluto's mass: only about a fifth of our Moon's.

quiz.q: Which test of the 2006 planet definition does Pluto fail?
o: Orbiting the Sun
Being round
Clearing the neighbourhood around its orbit
Having a moon
quiz.e: Pluto orbits the Sun and is round, but it shares its region with many Kuiper Belt objects, so it hasn't cleared its neighbourhood.

quiz.q: What is Sputnik Planitia?
o: A crater on Charon
A young plain of nitrogen ice inside Pluto's 'heart'
A Soviet probe sent to Pluto
A ring around Pluto
quiz.e: Sputnik Planitia is a vast, young, slowly flowing plain of nitrogen ice within the heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio.

LESSONS.title: Jupiter and Saturn: the giants
LESSONS.hook: Jupiter could swallow every other planet with room to spare, and Saturn is light enough, in a sense, to float. Meet the two kings of the solar system.

sections.key: Jupiter has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined.
sections.b: Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth and roughly 318 times more massive. Put all the other planets together and Jupiter still outweighs them more than twice over. Despite its size, it spins faster than any other planet, completing a day in just under 10 hours, which makes it visibly flattened at the poles. When Galileo pointed his telescope at it in January 1610, he saw four small points of light that changed position night after night. They were moons circling Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. It was powerful evidence that not everything in the heavens orbits Earth, and it helped undermine the old Earth-centred view of the universe. Ganymede is larger than the planet Mercury.

sections.key: Jupiter would need roughly 80 times more mass to become even the smallest true star.
sections.b: Jupiter is often called a 'failed star' because it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium, like the Sun. The label is misleading. To ignite hydrogen fusion in its core, an object needs roughly 80 times Jupiter's mass. Jupiter was never close. It does give off a little more heat than it receives from the Sun, left over from its formation and slow contraction, but it does not shine by fusion. Its interior is extraordinary all the same. Under crushing pressure deep inside, hydrogen is thought to become an electrically conducting fluid known as metallic hydrogen. Swirling currents in that fluid probably generate Jupiter's enormous magnetic field, the strongest of any planet, which traps radiation that is lethal to unshielded spacecraft electronics.

sections.key: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has lasted for at least about two centuries.
sections.b: Jupiter's colourful stripes are bands of cloud, driven by powerful jet streams flowing east and west. Its most famous feature is the Great Red Spot, a high-pressure storm system that spins anticlockwise and is wider than Earth. Astronomers have continuously tracked it since at least the 1830s. Giovanni Cassini described a spot in 1665, but historians are unsure whether it was the same storm. The Great Red Spot has been shrinking over the past century and has become rounder, though it is still enormous. NASA's Juno spacecraft, orbiting Jupiter since 2016, has measured that the storm reaches hundreds of kilometres down into the atmosphere. Nobody is quite sure why it has lasted so long or what gives it its reddish colour.

sections.key: Saturn's rings are mostly water ice, stretching hundreds of thousands of kilometres yet typically only tens of metres thick.
sections.b: Saturn's rings are made of countless pieces of ice, from tiny grains to chunks as big as a house, each orbiting the planet like a miniature moon. The main rings span roughly 280,000 kilometres, about three quarters of the distance from Earth to the Moon, yet in many places they are only about ten metres thick. Scaled down to the width of a sheet of paper, they would be far thinner than the paper itself. Galileo saw them in 1610 but his telescope was too blurry to make sense of them; he thought Saturn had 'ears'. Christiaan Huygens worked out in the 1650s that they were a ring. Scientists still debate whether the rings formed with Saturn or are much younger, perhaps from a shattered moon.

sections.key: Saturn's average density is lower than water's, the only planet of which that is true.
sections.b: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium and has an average density of about 0.7 grams per cubic centimetre, less than water's 1.0. That gives rise to a famous claim: drop Saturn into a big enough bathtub and it would float. It is a fun way to picture how light the planet is for its size, though the thought experiment falls apart quickly, since Saturn has no solid surface and such a vast body of water would collapse into a planet of its own. Saturn's low density and fast spin, about ten and a half hours per day, make it the most flattened planet. At its north pole sits a bizarre six-sided jet stream, a hexagon wider than Earth, first spotted by Voyager.

sections.key: The Cassini spacecraft studied Saturn for 13 years before deliberately diving into the planet in 2017.
sections.b: The Cassini–Huygens mission, a partnership between NASA, the European Space Agency and the Italian Space Agency, arrived at Saturn in 2004. Its Huygens probe parachuted onto Titan in January 2005, the most distant landing ever made, revealing riverbeds and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. Cassini also discovered jets of water vapour spraying from the small moon Enceladus, evidence of a hidden ocean. By 2017 the spacecraft was almost out of fuel. To avoid any risk of it crashing into, and contaminating, a moon that might host life, controllers steered it through the gap between Saturn and its rings 22 times, then sent it plunging into Saturn's atmosphere on 15 September 2017. It transmitted data until the very end.

quiz.q: Why is calling Jupiter a 'failed star' misleading?
o: It is made of rock
It would need roughly 80 times more mass to fuse hydrogen
It is colder than Earth
It once was a star
quiz.e: Fusion requires about 80 times Jupiter's mass, so Jupiter was never close to becoming a star.

quiz.q: What did Galileo see around Jupiter in 1610?
o: Rings
Four moons orbiting it
The Great Red Spot
Volcanoes on Io
quiz.e: Galileo saw four moons circling Jupiter, showing that not everything in the sky orbits Earth.

quiz.q: What is the Great Red Spot?
o: A volcano
A crater
A giant storm wider than Earth
A shadow cast by a moon
quiz.e: It is a long-lived anticlockwise storm wider than Earth, tracked continuously since at least the 1830s.

quiz.q: What are Saturn's rings mainly made of?
o: Gas
Water ice
Molten rock
Metal dust
quiz.e: The rings are countless pieces of water ice, from tiny grains to house-sized chunks.

quiz.q: Why was Cassini deliberately crashed into Saturn?
o: To measure the impact
To avoid contaminating moons that might host life
Because it lost contact
To test a new engine
quiz.e: With fuel running low, controllers sent it into Saturn so it could never crash into and contaminate moons like Enceladus or Titan.

LESSONS.title: Planetary defence: dodging asteroids
LESSONS.hook: The dinosaurs had no space program. We do, and in 2022 humanity knocked an asteroid off course for the very first time.

sections.key: Small space rocks strike Earth all the time, and every so often a big one causes real damage.
sections.b: Tonnes of space dust and small rocks fall on Earth every day, mostly burning up harmlessly as shooting stars. Larger impacts are rarer but very real. About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly ten kilometres wide struck near what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, and the resulting global catastrophe wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs. Impacts on that scale are thought to happen only every hundred million years or so. Smaller ones are far more frequent and can still devastate a city or region. The good news is that, of all natural disasters, an asteroid impact is the only one we can, in principle, see coming years ahead and prevent entirely. That is the job of planetary defence.

sections.key: Two airbursts over Russia, in 1908 and 2013, show what relatively small asteroids can do.
sections.b: On 30 June 1908, something exploded in the air above the Tunguska region of Siberia. It flattened an estimated 80 million trees across about 2,000 square kilometres of forest. Most scientists think it was a stony asteroid or comet fragment perhaps 50 to 60 metres across that blew apart before reaching the ground. Because the area was so remote, very few people were hurt. On 15 February 2013, a rock about 20 metres wide burst over the city of Chelyabinsk in Russia, captured by countless dashboard cameras. Its blast wave arrived well after the flash, shattering windows across the city, and around 1,500 people were injured, mostly by flying glass.

sections.key: After a very bright flash in the sky, stay away from windows because the shockwave can arrive minutes later.
sections.b: Chelyabinsk taught a practical lesson. The fireball was brighter than the Sun for a moment, and many people ran to their windows to see what was happening. Sound and pressure waves travel far more slowly than light, so the blast arrived a minute or more after the flash, smashing glass into curious faces. Experts now suggest that if you ever see an exceptionally bright fireball, you should treat it a little like lightning and wait for the boom: move away from windows and take cover until the shockwave has passed. Such events are extremely rare, and most fireballs are harmless. If anyone is injured, call 000 in Australia. Meteorites that land are almost never hot or dangerous to touch.

sections.key: Survey telescopes have found the great majority of the largest near-Earth asteroids, and none is on a collision course.
sections.b: Since the 1990s, telescopes have been systematically scanning the sky for near-Earth objects, asteroids and comets whose orbits bring them close to ours. Surveys such as Catalina, Pan-STARRS and ATLAS photograph the sky night after night, looking for moving dots, and astronomers then calculate each object's orbit for decades ahead. Scientists believe more than 90 percent of near-Earth asteroids larger than a kilometre wide, the kind that could cause global disaster, have now been found, and none poses a known threat for at least the next century. Smaller objects, still big enough to destroy a city, are far less complete. New facilities, including the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile and planned space telescopes, are expected to find many more.

sections.key: New asteroids sometimes show a small impact chance that disappears as their orbits are measured more precisely.
sections.b: When an asteroid is first spotted, its path is uncertain, a little like predicting a thrown ball's landing spot from a split-second glimpse. Sometimes Earth falls inside the early range of possibilities, so the impact odds look worrying, then drop to zero as more observations come in. In 2004 the asteroid Apophis, about 340 metres wide, briefly showed a chance of hitting Earth in 2029 of nearly 3 percent. Further tracking ruled out any impact in 2029 and for at least the next century. Instead, on 13 April 2029 it will pass within about 32,000 kilometres of Earth, closer than many communications satellites, and may be visible to the naked eye from parts of the world. In early 2025, another asteroid, 2024 YR4, followed a similar pattern before being ruled out.

sections.key: In 2022 NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into an asteroid and measurably changed its orbit.
sections.b: Finding a dangerous asteroid is only half the problem; we also need a way to move it. The simplest idea is a kinetic impactor: hit it hard with a spacecraft, years in advance, so a tiny change in speed grows into a miss by the time it reaches Earth. NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test, or DART, tried this on a harmless target. Dimorphos is a small moonlet, about 160 metres wide, orbiting a larger asteroid called Didymos. On 26 September 2022, DART slammed into it at over 20,000 kilometres per hour. Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos had taken about 11 hours and 55 minutes; afterwards it was about 32 minutes shorter, far more than the minimum mission goal. The European Space Agency's Hera mission is following up.

quiz.q: What was the Chelyabinsk event of 2013?
o: A nuclear test
An asteroid about 20 metres wide exploding in the air
A comet hitting the ground
A meteorite landing in a lake
quiz.e: A roughly 20-metre rock burst in the atmosphere over Chelyabinsk; its blast wave injured around 1,500 people, mostly with broken glass.

quiz.q: If you see an extremely bright fireball, what is sensible advice?
o: Rush to the window to watch
Move away from windows until any shockwave passes
Go outside and look for the meteorite immediately
Turn off all electricity
quiz.e: The blast wave travels much slower than light and can arrive a minute or more later, so staying away from windows protects you from flying glass.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of near-Earth asteroids over one kilometre wide have been found?
o: About 10 percent
About half
More than 90 percent
None so far
quiz.e: Surveys have found more than 90 percent of the kilometre-plus near-Earth asteroids, and none is known to threaten Earth for at least a century.

quiz.q: What will Apophis do on 13 April 2029?
o: Hit the Pacific Ocean
Pass within about 32,000 kilometres of Earth
Collide with the Moon
Break apart near Mars
quiz.e: Apophis will pass closer than many communications satellites, but further tracking ruled out an impact.

quiz.q: What did the DART mission achieve?
o: It landed people on an asteroid
It changed the orbit of the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos
It destroyed a dangerous asteroid
It brought back asteroid samples
quiz.e: DART's impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by about 32 minutes, proving a kinetic impactor can deflect an asteroid.

LESSONS.title: Australia's place in space
LESSONS.hook: A sheep paddock dish carried Apollo 11's moonwalk to the world, and a quiet desert range launched a satellite in 1967. Australia's space story is bigger than most people know.

sections.key: After World War II, Britain and Australia built a huge rocket testing range at Woomera in South Australia.
sections.b: In 1947, Britain and Australia agreed to set up a long-range weapons testing site in the remote outback of South Australia. The town of Woomera, named after an Aboriginal spear-throwing tool, grew up to support it. The range stretched for well over a thousand kilometres across the desert, giving room to fire rockets and missiles far from populated areas. Through the 1950s and 1960s, thousands of scientists, engineers and military staff worked there on British missile and rocket programs. The site's remoteness also raised serious issues: British nuclear tests at nearby Maralinga and Emu Field in the 1950s exposed Aboriginal people and service personnel to radiation, a legacy later examined by a Royal Commission in the 1980s.

sections.key: On 29 November 1967 Australia launched its first satellite, WRESAT, from Woomera.
sections.b: In the mid-1960s, the United States had a spare Redstone rocket left over from a research program and offered it to Australia. Scientists at the Weapons Research Establishment in Salisbury, South Australia, then designed and built a small satellite in under a year. Named WRESAT, it was launched from Woomera on 29 November 1967, making Australia one of the first handful of nations to launch a satellite from its own territory. The cone-shaped spacecraft measured the Sun's radiation and the upper atmosphere, transmitting for about five days before its batteries ran out, then burned up on re-entry in January 1968. In 1971 Britain also launched its only satellite on a British rocket, Prospero, from Woomera.

sections.key: The 64-metre Parkes radio telescope helped carry television of the Apollo 11 moonwalk to hundreds of millions of viewers.
sections.b: The Parkes radio telescope opened in 1961 among the sheep paddocks of central western New South Wales, its 64-metre dish among the most advanced in the world. In July 1969, when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon, the Moon was high over Australia. The first minutes of television were received by NASA's Honeysuckle Creek station near Canberra, which captured Armstrong climbing down the ladder. Parkes then took over and supplied the pictures for most of the rest of the roughly two-and-a-half-hour moonwalk, despite strong winds that pushed the dish close to its safety limits. The 2000 Australian film The Dish dramatised the story, with some liberties. In 2020 the telescope was also given the Wiradjuri name Murriyang.

sections.key: Canberra hosts one of NASA's three Deep Space Network stations, which talk to spacecraft across the solar system.
sections.b: To stay in touch with distant spacecraft as Earth rotates, NASA built three tracking stations spaced roughly a third of the way around the globe: Goldstone in California, Madrid in Spain, and Tidbinbilla near Canberra. At any moment at least one can see a given spacecraft. The Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex, operated on NASA's behalf by Australia's national science agency CSIRO, has helped communicate with missions such as Voyager, the Mars rovers and New Horizons. Parkes too has made discoveries of its own. In 2007, astronomers searching its archived data found the first known fast radio burst, a millisecond flash of radio waves from far beyond our galaxy, opening up an entirely new field of astronomy.

sections.key: When NASA's Skylab space station fell on Western Australia in 1979, the local shire jokingly fined NASA for littering.
sections.b: Skylab, America's first space station, re-entered the atmosphere in July 1979, earlier than planned, and broke up over the Indian Ocean and southern Western Australia. Pieces of debris rained down around the town of Esperance and across the Nullarbor, though no one was hurt. The Shire of Esperance issued NASA a light-hearted 400-dollar fine for littering. A San Francisco newspaper offered a 10,000-dollar prize for the first piece of Skylab delivered to its office, which was claimed by a 17-year-old from Esperance, Stan Thornton, who flew to the United States with fragments. The fine itself went unpaid for 30 years until a Californian radio host raised the money from listeners and paid it in 2009.

sections.key: Several Australian-born astronauts have flown with NASA, and Australia now has its own national space agency.
sections.b: Australia's first person in space was Paul Scully-Power, an Australian-born oceanographer who flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger in 1984 as a payload specialist. Adelaide-born engineer Andy Thomas became a NASA astronaut and flew four missions, including a long stay aboard the Russian Mir space station in 1998. Other astronauts with Australian roots have followed. In 2024 Katherine Bennell-Pegg became the first astronaut to graduate from training under the Australian flag, completing the European Space Agency's basic astronaut training. Australia also established its own Australian Space Agency in 2018. And its deserts remain useful: in 2010 and 2020, Japanese Hayabusa capsules carrying samples from asteroids parachuted down near Woomera, bringing pieces of other worlds to Australian soil.

quiz.q: Why was Woomera chosen as a rocket range?
o: It was close to Sydney
Its remote outback location gave space to fire rockets safely
It was the coldest place in Australia
It had an existing airport for jets
quiz.e: Woomera's vast, sparsely populated desert allowed rockets and missiles to be fired far from towns.

quiz.q: What was WRESAT?
o: A radio telescope
Australia's first satellite, launched in 1967
A British rocket
A NASA tracking station
quiz.e: WRESAT was built in South Australia and launched from Woomera on 29 November 1967 on a spare American Redstone rocket.

quiz.q: What role did Parkes play in the Apollo 11 broadcast?
o: It sent the first command to land
It supplied TV pictures for most of the moonwalk after Honeysuckle Creek's first minutes
It recorded the astronauts' heart rates
It tracked the Saturn V launch
quiz.e: Honeysuckle Creek caught Armstrong's first steps, then Parkes took over and provided most of the broadcast.

quiz.q: What did astronomers find in archived Parkes data in 2007?
o: The first exoplanet
The first known fast radio burst
Pluto's moon Charon
A new comet
quiz.e: The first known fast radio burst, a brief flash of radio waves from far beyond the Milky Way, was found in Parkes data.

quiz.q: How did the Shire of Esperance respond to Skylab debris landing in 1979?
o: It sued the United States
It issued NASA a joke 400-dollar littering fine
It built a museum and charged NASA entry
It banned future space stations
quiz.e: The shire fined NASA 400 dollars for littering; a radio host finally paid it in 2009.

LESSONS.title: Reading starlight: what stars are made of
LESSONS.hook: In 1835 a famous philosopher declared that we could never know what the stars are made of. Within a few decades, scientists were doing exactly that, using rainbows.

sections.key: In 1835 Auguste Comte named the chemistry of the stars as something humans could never know.
sections.b: The French philosopher Auguste Comte, founder of positivism, wanted science to stick to what could actually be observed. In 1835 he offered an example of knowledge forever beyond reach: we could study the shapes, distances and motions of the stars, but never their chemical composition, since no one could visit them or take a sample. It seemed a reasonable claim. Chemistry meant handling substances in a laboratory, and the stars were unreachably far away. Yet within about 25 years, scientists had found a way to identify elements in the Sun from Earth. Comte's prediction is now often quoted as a warning that 'impossible' can be a dangerous word. The key had already been found, in a ray of sunlight split by glass.

sections.key: Joseph von Fraunhofer found hundreds of mysterious dark lines crossing the Sun's spectrum.
sections.b: Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a glass prism splits white sunlight into a rainbow of colours, a spectrum. For more than a century nobody looked very closely. Then in 1814, Joseph von Fraunhofer, a brilliant German glassmaker and optician who had survived being buried in the collapse of his workshop as a boy, built instruments precise enough to magnify the spectrum. He found it was crossed by hundreds of thin dark lines, as if certain exact colours were missing. He carefully mapped around 570 of them and labelled the strongest with letters, a system still used today. He did not know what caused them. That puzzle remained unsolved for over 40 years, until two scientists in Heidelberg cracked it.

sections.key: Kirchhoff and Bunsen showed that each chemical element absorbs and emits its own unique set of colours.
sections.b: In Heidelberg around 1859, the physicist Gustav Kirchhoff and the chemist Robert Bunsen, whose name lives on in the laboratory gas burner, heated different substances in a flame and studied their light through a prism. Each element produced its own distinct set of bright coloured lines, like a fingerprint or barcode. Sodium, for example, glowed with a pair of yellow lines at exactly the position of two of Fraunhofer's dark lines in sunlight. Kirchhoff realised that cooler gas in the Sun's outer layers absorbs those same precise colours from the light passing through. Dark lines in starlight therefore reveal which elements are present. Using this method, the pair even discovered two new elements on Earth, caesium and rubidium.

sections.h: An element found in the Sun first
sections.key: Helium was identified in the Sun's spectrum in 1868, decades before it was found on Earth.
sections.b: During a total solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers studying the Sun's glowing outer layers saw a bright yellow line that matched no known element. The French astronomer Jules Janssen observed it from India, and the English astronomer Norman Lockyer studied it soon afterwards. Lockyer, working with the chemist Edward Frankland, concluded it belonged to a new element and named it helium, after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun. Many chemists were sceptical of an element known only from a distant star. Then in 1895 the Scottish chemist William Ramsay detected the same spectral line from gas released by a uranium mineral. Helium, the second most common element in the universe, had first been discovered 150 million kilometres away.

sections.key: In 1925 Cecilia Payne showed that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium, overturning expert opinion.
sections.b: In the early 1900s astronomers assumed stars had roughly the same chemical make-up as Earth's crust, rich in heavier elements like iron. Cecilia Payne, a young British astronomer who had moved to Harvard because women had few prospects in astronomy in England, applied new atomic physics to stellar spectra. Her 1925 doctoral thesis concluded that stars are overwhelmingly made of hydrogen and helium, in vastly greater amounts than anyone expected. The senior astronomer Henry Norris Russell persuaded her to describe the result as almost certainly not real. A few years later Russell reached the same conclusion himself. Payne was right: hydrogen and helium make up about 98 percent of the ordinary matter in stars. Her thesis is now considered among astronomy's most important.

sections.key: A star's spectrum also reveals its temperature and whether it is moving towards or away from us.
sections.b: Spectra hold far more than a list of ingredients. A star's colour reveals its surface temperature: red stars are relatively cool, around 3,000°C, while blue-white stars can exceed 20,000°C. In the early 1900s, Annie Jump Cannon at Harvard classified hundreds of thousands of stars by their spectra into the sequence O, B, A, F, G, K and M, from hottest to coolest, which astronomers still use. Spectra also reveal motion through the Doppler effect. Light from an object moving away is stretched towards the red end, while light from one approaching is squeezed towards blue. Measuring these tiny shifts showed that distant galaxies are rushing away from us, the evidence for an expanding universe, and still helps detect planets around other stars.

quiz.q: What did Auguste Comte claim in 1835?
o: Stars are made of fire
We could never know the chemical composition of stars
The Sun is mostly hydrogen
Light travels instantly
quiz.e: Comte said star chemistry was forever unknowable; spectroscopy proved him wrong within a few decades.

quiz.q: What did Fraunhofer discover in the Sun's spectrum?
o: A new colour beyond violet
Hundreds of thin dark lines
That sunlight has no red
That the Sun was cooling
quiz.e: Fraunhofer mapped around 570 dark lines crossing the solar spectrum, though he didn't know their cause.

quiz.q: What did Kirchhoff and Bunsen realise about the dark lines?
o: They were caused by Earth's atmosphere only
Each element absorbs its own unique set of colours
They were flaws in glass prisms
They showed the Sun's rotation
quiz.e: Each element has a distinctive set of spectral lines, so dark lines in starlight reveal which elements are present.

quiz.q: Where was helium first detected?
o: In a uranium mine
In the Sun's spectrum
In the ocean
In a meteorite
quiz.e: Helium was identified in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 and only found on Earth in 1895.

quiz.q: What did Cecilia Payne's 1925 thesis show?
o: Stars are mostly iron
Stars are mostly hydrogen and helium
The universe is expanding
Stars have the same make-up as Earth's crust
quiz.e: Payne showed stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium; a senior astronomer doubted it but later agreed.

LESSONS.title: Dark matter and dark energy
LESSONS.hook: Everything we have ever seen, every star, planet and person, makes up only about 5 percent of the universe. The rest is a mystery with a name but no explanation.

sections.key: In 1933 Fritz Zwicky found that galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved far too fast for the visible matter to hold them together.
sections.b: The Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky, working at Caltech, was known as brilliant and abrasive in equal measure. In 1933 he measured the speeds of galaxies in the Coma Cluster, a huge swarm of galaxies hundreds of millions of light-years away. They were moving so fast that the cluster should have flown apart long ago, unless it contained far more mass than its visible light suggested. Zwicky called the hidden material 'dunkle Materie', German for dark matter. His estimate of how much was missing was much larger than modern figures, partly because distances to galaxies were badly underestimated then, but the basic puzzle was real. For decades, though, most astronomers paid little attention, treating it as an oddity likely to be explained away.

sections.key: In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford showed that stars at the edges of galaxies orbit far too fast.
sections.b: In a solar system, outer planets orbit more slowly than inner ones because most of the mass sits in the centre. Neptune crawls compared with Mercury. Astronomers expected the same pattern in spiral galaxies, whose light is concentrated in a bright central bulge. In the 1970s, American astronomer Vera Rubin and her colleague Kent Ford measured the orbital speeds of stars and gas across spiral galaxies, including Andromeda. The outer regions were not slowing down. Their speeds stayed roughly flat far beyond where the visible stars thinned out. The simplest explanation was that each galaxy sits inside a vast, invisible halo of extra mass. Combined with radio observations by others, this work turned dark matter from a curiosity into a central problem of astronomy.

sections.key: Gravitational lensing and colliding galaxy clusters reveal where dark matter is, even though it gives off no light.
sections.b: Dark matter does not shine, absorb or reflect light, as far as we can tell, but it does have gravity, and gravity bends light. Massive clusters of galaxies act like giant, warped lenses, distorting the images of more distant galaxies behind them into arcs and smears. By measuring that distortion, astronomers can map where the mass actually is. A famous example is the Bullet Cluster, two galaxy clusters that collided. In 2006 researchers showed that most of the ordinary matter, in the form of hot gas, had been slowed and piled up in the middle, while most of the mass, revealed by lensing, had passed straight through. This was widely seen as strong evidence that dark matter is a real substance, separate from ordinary matter.

sections.key: Dark matter is thought to be an unknown type of particle, but decades of searching have not yet found it.
sections.b: Dark matter is not simply dim stars, dust or black holes; observations rule out ordinary matter making up more than a small fraction of it. Most physicists think it is a kind of particle not included in the standard model of particle physics, one that barely interacts with anything except through gravity. Candidates have included weakly interacting massive particles, nicknamed WIMPs, and extremely light particles called axions. Experiments deep underground, shielded from cosmic rays, wait for the rare moment a dark matter particle might bump into an atom. Australia's Stawell Underground Physics Laboratory, built in a Victorian gold mine, hosts one such experiment. So far, no search has made a confirmed detection, and a minority of scientists argue that gravity itself may need modifying instead.

sections.key: In 1998 two teams discovered that the expansion of the universe is speeding up, not slowing down.
sections.b: Since the 1920s, astronomers had known the universe is expanding. The natural assumption was that gravity would gradually slow that expansion. In the 1990s, two competing teams set out to measure the slowdown using Type Ia supernovae, exploding white dwarfs that shine with a predictable peak brightness and so act as cosmic distance markers. One team was led by Saul Perlmutter in the United States; the other, the High-Z Supernova Search Team, was led by Brian Schmidt at the Australian National University's Mount Stromlo Observatory, with Adam Riess making key analyses. In 1998 both reached the same startling result: distant supernovae were fainter than expected, meaning the expansion is accelerating. The three shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.key: Whatever drives the acceleration is called dark energy, and it makes up roughly two thirds of the universe.
sections.b: Something seems to be pushing space apart. Physicists call it dark energy, a name for the effect rather than an explanation. The leading idea is that empty space itself carries a small, constant energy, which behaves like the cosmological constant Einstein once added to his equations and later abandoned. Yet when physicists try to calculate the energy of empty space from quantum theory, they get an answer wildly larger than what is observed, one of the biggest mismatches in science. Combining measurements of the cosmic microwave background, galaxies and supernovae, the universe's budget appears to be about 68 percent dark energy, about 27 percent dark matter and only about 5 percent ordinary matter, the stuff of stars, planets and people.

sections.key: Recent surveys hint dark energy might be changing over time, which would reshape ideas about the universe's fate.
sections.b: If dark energy stays constant, the expansion will keep accelerating forever. Distant galaxies will eventually recede beyond our view, leaving a cold, dark and lonely future billions of years from now. But nobody knows whether it is constant. In 2024 and 2025, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument, which maps millions of galaxies from an observatory in Arizona, reported hints that dark energy may be weakening over time. The results are intriguing but not yet conclusive, and more data from it and from new space telescopes such as Europe's Euclid are expected to test them. It is a humbling position: after centuries of astronomy, we can measure the universe with great precision yet still cannot say what most of it is.

quiz.q: What led Fritz Zwicky to propose dark matter in 1933?
o: Galaxies in the Coma Cluster were moving too fast for their visible mass
He saw a black hole
Stars disappeared from photographs
The Sun's orbit was irregular
quiz.e: The Coma Cluster's galaxies moved so fast that the cluster needed much more mass than could be seen to hold together.

quiz.q: What did Vera Rubin and Kent Ford find about spiral galaxies?
o: Their outer stars orbit far slower than expected
Their outer stars orbit about as fast as inner ones, implying hidden mass
They contain no gas
They are all shrinking
quiz.e: Rotation speeds stayed roughly flat far from the centre, suggesting each galaxy sits within a halo of unseen matter.

quiz.q: Why is the Bullet Cluster considered strong evidence for dark matter?
o: It glows in dark matter light
Lensing showed most of its mass separated from the hot gas after a collision
It contains no galaxies
It is moving faster than light
quiz.e: After the collision, the hot gas piled up in the middle while most of the mass, mapped by lensing, passed through, separating the two.

quiz.q: What did the 1998 supernova studies reveal?
o: The universe is shrinking
The expansion of the universe is accelerating
Supernovae are all the same distance away
Dark matter is made of neutrinos
quiz.e: Distant Type Ia supernovae were fainter than expected, showing the expansion is speeding up. Brian Schmidt of the ANU shared the Nobel Prize for this.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the universe is ordinary matter?
o: About 68 percent
About 27 percent
About 50 percent
About 5 percent
quiz.e: Ordinary matter is only about 5 percent; dark matter is about 27 percent and dark energy about 68 percent.

LESSONS.title: Barcodes and QR codes: reading the stripes
LESSONS.hook: Lines drawn in beach sand, a pack of chewing gum in Ohio and a Japanese board game all helped create the codes you scan every day.

sections.key: The barcode began as an idea for speeding up grocery checkouts in the late 1940s.
sections.b: In 1948, the head of an American food chain reportedly asked a dean at the Drexel Institute of Technology in Philadelphia whether checkouts could be automated. A graduate student, Bernard Silver, overheard and told his friend Norman Joseph Woodland. Woodland later recalled that the breakthrough came on a Miami beach. Thinking of the Morse code he had learned as a Boy Scout, he pushed his fingers into the sand and dragged them towards himself, turning dots and dashes into thin and thick lines. The pair filed a patent in 1949, granted in 1952, which included a circular 'bullseye' version that could be read from any direction. But nothing could yet read it cheaply. Practical barcodes had to wait more than two decades for lasers and microchips.

sections.h: A pack of gum makes history
sections.key: The first product scanned with a modern barcode at a checkout was a pack of Juicy Fruit gum in 1974.
sections.b: In the early 1970s American grocers agreed on a single standard, the Universal Product Code, or UPC. The winning design came from IBM, where Woodland was then working, and used straight vertical bars rather than a bullseye, which tended to smudge on fast printing presses. On 26 June 1974, at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, a cashier scanned a ten-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum, and the age of the scanner began. Take-up was slow at first, because shops needed expensive scanners and manufacturers had to print codes on everything. Once enough products carried them, the benefits snowballed: faster queues, fewer pricing errors and detailed data on exactly what sold and when. Europe soon adopted a compatible 13-digit system, which Australia uses too.

sections.key: A scanner measures reflected light, and the widths of the dark and light bars encode the digits.
sections.b: A barcode is really a message written in light and shadow. The scanner shines light across the stripes, traditionally a red laser, although many modern scanners use a small camera instead. Black bars absorb most of the light and white spaces reflect it, so a sensor sees a rapidly changing pattern of bright and dark. Each digit is represented by a particular combination of bar and space widths. Guard patterns at the start, middle and end tell the scanner where the code begins and help it work out whether it is reading the code forwards or upside down. The number itself rarely contains the price. It identifies the product, and the shop's computer looks up the current price in its own database. That is why a price change does not mean relabelling every item.

sections.key: The QR code was invented in 1994 at Denso Wave to track car parts, inspired partly by the game of Go.
sections.b: An ordinary barcode holds only a short number, and in busy Japanese car factories workers were scanning many of them for every box of parts. At Denso Wave, then a division of the car-parts maker Denso, engineer Masahiro Hara led a small team to design something better. Hara has said the idea came to him while playing Go, whose black and white stones on a grid suggested storing information in two dimensions rather than one. Released in 1994, the Quick Response code could hold thousands of characters, including Japanese kanji. The team's hardest puzzle was making it instantly recognisable among the clutter of printed text. They studied printed material to find a shape that almost never appears by chance, and settled on the nested squares now sitting in three corners of every QR code.

sections.key: QR codes use clever error correction, so they can still be read even when part of them is missing.
sections.b: Those three large squares are called finder patterns. Wherever the code sits in a camera image, and at whatever angle, the scanner spots them and works out which way is up. Smaller patterns help it correct for curves and tilt. The rest of the grid holds the data plus extra information for error correction, based on mathematics published by Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon in 1960, the same family of methods used on CDs and in communication with distant spacecraft. Whoever creates a QR code can choose one of four levels of protection. At the highest, roughly 30 per cent of the code can be dirty, torn or covered and the message can still be recovered. That is why some QR codes have a logo printed right over their middle and still scan perfectly.

sections.h: Free to use, and easy to abuse
sections.key: Denso Wave chose not to enforce its patent, which helped QR codes spread, but they can also hide scams.
sections.b: Denso Wave held a patent on the QR code but announced it would not exercise it for codes following the published standard, so anyone could create and read them for free. That decision, plus smartphone cameras that could scan codes without a special app, turned QR codes into everyday objects. Australians scanned them millions of times to check in to venues during the COVID-19 pandemic, and they now appear on menus, parking meters and bills. The flip side is that a QR code is just a link you cannot read with your own eyes. Scammers stick fake codes over real ones or send them by email, leading to sites designed to steal card details or passwords. Check the web address before entering anything, and be wary of any code printed on a sticker.

quiz.q: According to Norman Woodland's own account, what inspired the barcode?
o: The keys of a piano
Morse code dots and dashes, drawn out in sand
The rings of a tree
Railway tracks seen from above
quiz.e: Woodland recalled dragging his fingers through beach sand, stretching Morse code's dots and dashes into thin and thick lines.

quiz.q: What was the first item scanned with a UPC barcode at a supermarket checkout in 1974?
o: A can of soup
A loaf of bread
A ten-pack of Juicy Fruit gum
A bottle of milk
quiz.e: A cashier in Troy, Ohio, scanned a ten-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum on 26 June 1974.

quiz.q: Why doesn't a shop have to relabel products when it changes a price?
o: The barcode only identifies the product; the price is looked up in the shop's database
Scanners ignore price information
Prices are printed in invisible ink
Barcodes update themselves wirelessly
quiz.e: The number in the barcode names the product, and the shop's computer supplies whatever the current price is.

quiz.q: What was the QR code originally designed to do?
o: Replace credit cards
Track parts in car factories
Store music
Sort mail in post offices
quiz.e: Denso Wave created it in 1994 to speed up the tracking of car parts, packing far more data than a barcode.

quiz.q: Why can a QR code with a logo over its centre still scan?
o: The logo is ignored by cameras
Only the corners contain data
Error correction lets the message be rebuilt even when part of the code is missing
The logo itself contains the data
quiz.e: Reed-Solomon error correction adds redundancy, so at the highest level about 30 per cent of the code can be lost.

LESSONS.title: Y2K: the disaster that didn't happen
LESSONS.hook: As 1999 drew to a close, the world braced for computers to think it was 1900. Midnight came and almost nothing broke. Was it all hype, or one of history's great quiet successes?

sections.key: Early programmers stored years as two digits to save scarce and expensive memory.
sections.b: In the 1960s and 1970s, computer memory and storage were astonishingly expensive, and a standard punch card had only 80 columns. Programmers saved space wherever they could, and one obvious shortcut was writing years as two digits: 68 instead of 1968. Everyone knew what it meant. Few expected their programs to still be running decades later, yet many were. Banking, payroll, airline and government systems had been built in layers on top of old code, often written in languages such as COBOL, and the originals were rarely replaced. By the 1990s, vast amounts of software assumed every year began with 19. When the calendar ticked over to 2000, the year 00 might be read as 1900. The problem became known as Y2K, short for Year 2000.

sections.key: A two-digit year breaks any calculation that compares or subtracts dates across the century boundary.
sections.b: The fear was never that computers would explode. It was arithmetic. If a system calculates someone's age by subtracting their birth year from the current year, 00 minus 65 gives minus 65. Interest on a loan, the expiry date of a credit card, whether a warranty had lapsed, which records were old enough to delete: all relied on comparing dates. A computer sorting records might place the year 2000 before 1999. Some problems appeared years before the deadline, as systems began handling future dates such as card expiries and long-term contracts. There was a lesser-known complication too. Some programs failed to treat 2000 as a leap year, because the rule is fiddly: century years are normally not leap years, unless they are divisible by 400. The year 2000 was one.

sections.key: The worry extended beyond office computers to chips embedded in equipment, though most turned out not to care about dates.
sections.b: Office computers were only part of the concern. Tiny processors were embedded in lifts, power stations, medical devices, factory controllers and building security systems, and nobody had a complete list of which ones tracked the date. Testing them was slow and costly. In practice, most embedded chips did not use calendar dates at all, or used them in harmless ways, but organisations could not know that without checking. That uncertainty is part of what made Y2K so unsettling. The fear was not one failure but many failures arriving at the same moment around the world, in systems connected to one another. Supply chains, utilities and banks all depend on each other, and a cascade of small faults could, in theory, have grown into something much bigger.

sections.key: Governments and businesses spent hundreds of billions of dollars checking and fixing code.
sections.b: Through the late 1990s, armies of programmers combed through old code, line by line, and retired COBOL programmers found themselves in demand again. Common fixes included expanding years to four digits, or 'windowing', where a program treats two-digit years below a cut-off, say 50, as 20xx and the rest as 19xx. Estimates of the worldwide cost vary widely, but are often put at somewhere between 300 and 600 billion US dollars. Australia, like many countries, ran national awareness and readiness programs, and governments set up command centres to monitor the changeover. Some critics argued that much of the money went to overcautious consultants. Others pointed out that the work also cleaned up and documented ageing systems that badly needed attention anyway.

sections.key: When 2000 arrived, failures were few and minor, and Australia was among the first places to find out.
sections.b: Because of time zones, the Pacific and Australia reached midnight many hours before Europe and North America, and the world watched them for early signs of trouble. None came on a large scale. There were glitches. Some websites displayed the year as 19100, because of how certain programs added 1900 to the year, and a few ticketing and payment machines misbehaved. In Japan, some monitoring equipment at nuclear power plants reported errors, without any danger to safety. In the United States, a military satellite intelligence system had several hours of problems. Most faults were fixed quickly and passed almost unnoticed. Within days, some of the newspapers that had warned of chaos were running stories asking whether the whole thing had been a beat-up.

sections.key: When prevention works, it can look as though there was never a problem in the first place.
sections.b: Y2K is a classic example of what is sometimes called the preparedness paradox. Fix a problem before it bites, and the absence of disaster can make the warning look silly. Experts still debate how bad things would have been without the effort. Some countries that spent relatively little also had few problems, partly because they relied less on old computer systems. Yet many people who did the work insist they found and fixed serious faults that would have caused real damage. Date bugs have not gone away, either. Many systems count time as seconds since 1 January 1970, and where that count is stored as a 32-bit number it will overflow on 19 January 2038. Much software has already been updated, but somewhere, quietly, the next deadline is ticking.

quiz.q: Why did early programs store years as two digits?
o: It was required by law
To save scarce and expensive memory and storage
Computers could not count past 99
To make dates easier to read aloud
quiz.e: Memory and storage were costly, so dropping the '19' saved space across millions of records.

quiz.q: Why was the year 2000 a tricky leap year for some software?
o: It was the first leap year ever recorded
Century years are usually not leap years, but those divisible by 400 are
It had two extra days
Leap years were abolished in 1999
quiz.e: The rule skips most century years, but 2000 is divisible by 400, so it was a leap year and some programs got it wrong.

quiz.q: What was 'windowing'?
o: Replacing old computers with new ones
Running backup systems in parallel
Treating two-digit years below a cut-off as 20xx and the rest as 19xx
Shutting down systems over New Year
quiz.e: Windowing was a cheaper fix than rewriting every date, interpreting two-digit years according to a chosen cut-off.

quiz.q: What odd year appeared on some websites on 1 January 2000?
quiz.e: Some programs added 1900 to a year counter that had reached 100 and then printed '19' in front of it.

quiz.q: What is the preparedness paradox?
o: Preparing too much always causes problems
Successful prevention can make the original warning look exaggerated
Nobody can prepare for computer failures
Prepared people panic more
quiz.e: Because the work prevented most failures, the lack of disaster led some to conclude the danger was never real.

LESSONS.title: How a search engine finds anything
LESSONS.hook: Type a few words and, in a fraction of a second, the right page appears out of billions. It is not searching the internet when you press Enter. It did that long before.

sections.key: The early web grew so fast that finding anything on it became a serious problem.
sections.b: When the World Wide Web opened to the public in the early 1990s, there were only a handful of websites, and people kept lists of them. Within a few years there were millions of pages, written by anyone, linked in every direction, with no central catalogue. Early helpers took two approaches. Yahoo began in 1994 as a hand-built directory, with people sorting sites into categories, rather like a library. Others, such as AltaVista, used software to read pages automatically and match the words you typed. Directories could not keep up with the web's explosive growth, and simple word-matching was easily fooled: a page that repeated a word hundreds of times could jump to the top. Search needed a better way to judge which pages were actually worth showing.

sections.key: Search engines send out programs called crawlers that follow links from page to page and download what they find.
sections.b: Behind every search engine is a crawler, sometimes called a spider or a bot. It starts with a list of known web addresses, downloads each page, notes every link on it, and adds those new addresses to its list. Repeated endlessly, this lets a crawler explore much of the public web, though never all of it. Pages behind logins, private databases and sites that ask not to be crawled are left out. A website can put a small file called robots.txt on its server telling crawlers what they may visit, a convention dating back to 1994 that relies largely on good manners. Popular pages are revisited often, sometimes many times a day, while obscure ones may be checked only occasionally, so results can briefly lag behind reality.

sections.key: Instead of searching the web when you type, a search engine looks things up in a giant prepared index, like the one at the back of a book.
sections.b: A common assumption is that a search engine scans the internet the moment you press Enter. It doesn't; that would take far too long. Instead it has already built an index, organised a little like the index at the back of a textbook. For every word, it stores a list of the pages that contain it, along with details such as where on the page the word appears. When you search for 'koala habitat', the engine pulls up the list for each word and finds pages that appear on both. Computer scientists call this an inverted index. Google's is spread across huge numbers of computers in data centres around the world and runs to well over a hundred million gigabytes, which is why answers return in a fraction of a second.

sections.key: Google's founders ranked pages by the links pointing to them, treating each link as a kind of vote.
sections.b: In 1996, two Stanford PhD students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, began a research project nicknamed BackRub. Their insight came from academic publishing, where an important paper is one that many other papers cite. They treated a link from one web page to another as a citation. A page linked to by lots of other pages was probably useful, and a link from an important page counted for more than a link from an obscure one. They called the measure PageRank, a pun on Page's surname. Their search engine, launched as a company called Google in 1998, took its name from 'googol', the number 1 followed by 100 zeros, with a change of spelling. Its results were noticeably better than its rivals', and within a few years it dominated web search.

sections.key: Modern search ranking blends many signals, including meaning, quality, freshness and your location.
sections.b: PageRank still matters, but it is now one ingredient among many. Search engines try to work out what you meant, not just what you typed, so a search for 'how tall is Uluru' can surface a page that says 'Uluru rises 348 metres above the plain'. They consider how recent a page is, whether it works well on phones, the language you use and where you are searching from, which is why 'pizza near me' gives different answers in Perth and in Hobart. Increasingly, machine learning models help interpret meaning. Exactly how the signals are combined is a closely guarded secret, partly for competitive reasons and partly to stop people gaming the system. A whole industry, search engine optimisation, exists to help websites climb the rankings.

sections.key: Most search engines are free to use because they earn money from advertising matched to what you are looking for.
sections.b: Running a search engine costs a fortune, yet you pay nothing to use one. The money comes mainly from advertising. When you search for 'running shoes', advertisers compete in an automated auction, run in a split second, for the chance to show you a link, and they typically pay only when someone clicks. A search is a powerful moment for advertisers, because you are telling the engine exactly what you want right now. This business model has been enormously profitable, and it explains a few things worth knowing. Sponsored results often appear above ordinary ones, marked with a small label. Search engines also learn from what people click. It pays to notice the difference between an ad and a result, and to remember that the top link is not automatically the best one.

quiz.q: Why did hand-built web directories like early Yahoo struggle?
o: They charged users to search
They could not keep up with how fast the web was growing
They only worked in English
They were banned by governments
quiz.e: People sorting sites by hand simply could not keep pace with millions of new pages.

quiz.q: What is robots.txt?
o: A virus that attacks search engines
A list of the world's robots
A file where a website tells crawlers what they may visit
The code inside a search box
quiz.e: Dating from 1994, it is a polite convention that well-behaved crawlers follow.

quiz.q: What actually happens when you press Enter on a search?
o: The engine looks up your words in an index it built earlier
The engine visits every website live
Your computer downloads the whole web
A person finds the answer for you
quiz.e: Searching the live web would be far too slow, so engines consult a huge inverted index prepared in advance.

quiz.q: What was the key idea behind PageRank?
o: Ranking pages by how often they repeat a word
Ranking pages alphabetically
Ranking pages by how new they are
Treating links from other pages as votes, with important pages' votes counting more
quiz.e: Borrowed from academic citations, it treated links as signs that a page was worth reading.

quiz.q: How do most search engines make their money?
o: Selling search results to governments
Advertising matched to what people search for
Charging websites to be crawled
Subscription fees from users
quiz.e: Advertisers bid to appear for particular searches, usually paying when someone clicks.

LESSONS.title: How a mobile call finds you
LESSONS.hook: Your phone is a radio, quietly chatting with towers you never notice. Here is how a call reaches you, even on a moving train.

sections.h: A phone is a two-way radio
sections.key: Mobile phones send and receive radio waves, talking to a nearby base station rather than directly to each other.
sections.b: When you call a friend across the street, your two phones do not talk directly. Your phone sends radio signals to the nearest base station, usually a set of antennas on a tower, rooftop or pole. From there the call travels over cables and optical fibre through the operator's network, and back out to whichever base station is near your friend. Radio is only the first and last link in the chain. Phones transmit at fairly low power to save battery, so networks need base stations spread across the landscape, often only a few hundred metres apart in busy city areas. The central problem engineers had to solve was how to let millions of people share a limited range of radio frequencies at the same time without drowning each other out.

sections.key: Dividing the land into small cells lets the same radio frequencies be reused again and again.
sections.b: The answer, proposed at Bell Labs in 1947 by engineers Douglas Ring and W. Rae Young, was to divide an area into small zones called cells, each with its own base station. Neighbouring cells use different frequencies, but cells far enough apart can reuse the same ones without interfering. Planners often draw them as a honeycomb of hexagons, although real cells are messy shapes bent by hills and buildings. The clever part is that capacity grows as cells shrink. A busy city centre may have many small cells, while a rural area may be covered by a few large ones. This is why the technology is called cellular, and why Americans call their phones cell phones. The idea took decades to become practical, waiting on electronics able to manage it.

sections.key: As you travel, the network passes your call from one cell to the next, usually without you noticing.
sections.b: Cells only work if a call can survive moving between them. Your phone constantly measures the strength of signals from nearby base stations and reports back. As you drive away from one tower and towards another, the network decides when to switch and moves your call to the new cell in a fraction of a second. This is called handover. On a fast train it can happen every minute or so. When there is no neighbouring cell to take over, as on a remote highway, the call drops. Even when you are not on a call, an idle phone checks in from time to time, so the network knows roughly which group of cells you are in. That is how an incoming call knows where to find you.

sections.key: Your SIM securely proves to the network who you are, using a secret key that never leaves the chip.
sections.b: The little SIM card, or its built-in digital version, the eSIM, is a tiny secure computer. It stores an identity number linked to your account and a secret key that is designed never to leave the chip. When your phone connects, the network sends a random challenge. The SIM combines it with the secret key to produce an answer, and the network, which holds a copy of the same key, checks the result. If it matches, you are in. This lets the network bill the right person and makes it hard to impersonate someone else's phone. Older analogue phones had no such protection: their calls could be overheard with a radio scanner and their identities copied, or cloned, to run up bills on someone else's account.

sections.key: Each mobile generation brought a big change, from analogue voice to texting to fast mobile internet.
sections.b: The first generation, 1G, arrived in the 1980s and carried voice as analogue radio signals; Australia's first cellular network opened in 1987. 2G, in the early 1990s, went digital, which improved security and made room for text messages. The first text was sent on 3 December 1992, when engineer Neil Papworth typed 'Merry Christmas' from a computer to a colleague's phone in Britain. Messages were capped at 160 characters, a limit that shaped how a generation wrote. 3G, from the early 2000s, made mobile internet practical, and 4G, from around 2010, made video streaming and apps routine. 5G adds higher speeds and shorter delays, partly by using higher frequencies with a shorter range, which means many more small cells.

sections.key: Older networks are shut down to free up radio spectrum, which is why old phones can stop working.
sections.b: Radio spectrum is limited, so operators periodically switch off old networks to reuse their frequencies for newer, more efficient ones. Australia closed its analogue network in 2000, its 2G networks during the 2010s, and its 3G networks in 2023 and 2024. Some older phones that relied on 3G for voice calls suddenly could not call anyone, including emergency services. If you or an older relative are unsure whether a phone still works properly, your provider can check it. In an emergency, call 000 from any mobile. If your own network has no coverage but another network does, your emergency call can be carried on that other network. The number 112 also works from mobiles, but 000 remains Australia's main emergency number.

quiz.q: Why are mobile networks divided into many small cells?
o: So that phones can talk directly to each other
So the same frequencies can be reused in cells far enough apart
To make towers cheaper to paint
Because radio only travels in hexagons
quiz.e: Reusing frequencies across non-neighbouring cells lets millions of people share limited spectrum.

quiz.q: What is 'handover'?
o: Passing your phone to someone else
Switching from mobile data to Wi-Fi
Moving an ongoing call from one cell to the next as you travel
Transferring your number to a new provider
quiz.e: The network switches your call to a stronger base station, usually in a fraction of a second.

quiz.q: How does a SIM prove your identity to the network?
o: By sending your name and address
By answering a random challenge using a secret key stored on the chip
By sharing your fingerprint
By sending a photo of the phone's owner
quiz.e: Both the SIM and the network hold the same key, so a correct answer proves the SIM is genuine.

quiz.q: What did the first text message, sent in 1992, say?
o: Hello world
Merry Christmas
Can you hear me?
Happy New Year
quiz.e: Engineer Neil Papworth sent 'Merry Christmas' to a colleague's phone on 3 December 1992.

quiz.q: Why do operators switch off older networks such as 3G?
o: Old networks are illegal
To free up limited radio spectrum for newer, more efficient technology
Because phone towers wear out every ten years
To force people to change providers
quiz.e: Spectrum is scarce, so old networks are retired and their frequencies reused for 4G and 5G.

LESSONS.title: How screens make pictures
LESSONS.hook: Everything on your screen, from a sunset photo to this sentence, is built from millions of tiny lights in just three colours.

sections.key: A screen is a grid of pixels, short for picture elements, each set to its own colour many times a second.
sections.b: Look at a screen through a magnifying glass, or through a drop of water on a phone, and the illusion falls apart. The smooth image is really a grid of tiny dots called pixels, short for picture elements. A 4K television has 3840 pixels across and 2160 down, more than eight million in all. Each pixel shows one colour at a time, and the screen's electronics update every pixel many times per second. Your eyes and brain blend the grid into a continuous picture and the rapid updates into smooth motion. The closer together the pixels are packed, the sharper the image looks. A modern phone fits several hundred pixels into every inch, so densely that at normal viewing distance the individual dots are invisible.

sections.key: Each pixel mixes red, green and blue light, and your eyes blend them into the full range of colours.
sections.b: Each pixel is usually made of three smaller subpixels: one red, one green and one blue. By varying their brightness, a screen can produce millions of colours. Red and green light together look yellow, all three at full strength look white, and all three off look black. This is additive colour mixing, the opposite of mixing paints, where adding more colours makes things darker. It works because of the way our eyes are built. The retina has three types of cone cells, most sensitive to long, medium and short wavelengths of light. A screen does not reproduce the real light coming off a lemon, only a mix of red, green and blue that stimulates our cones in the same proportions. Animals with different eyes would likely see our screens quite differently.

sections.key: An LCD screen shines a constant backlight through liquid crystals that act as tiny adjustable shutters.
sections.b: Most computer monitors and many televisions use liquid crystal displays, or LCDs. Behind the panel is a backlight, today usually made of LEDs, that shines white light the whole time. In front of it sit two polarising filters, set at angles to each other, with a thin layer of liquid crystal in between. Liquid crystals are substances whose molecules can flow like a liquid yet line up in an orderly way, like a crystal. A small voltage twists or untwists them, changing how much light makes it through the second filter. Each subpixel has its own colour filter and its own tiny transistor to control it. The weakness is that the backlight stays on behind everything, so dark scenes can look slightly grey rather than truly black.

sections.key: In an OLED screen every subpixel makes its own light, so a black pixel can simply switch off.
sections.b: OLED stands for organic light-emitting diode. Here there is no backlight. Each subpixel is a thin sandwich of carbon-based materials that glow when an electric current passes through them. To show black, a pixel simply turns off, giving deep blacks and striking contrast, and it can save battery on phones when much of the screen is dark. OLED panels can also be thinner and even flexible, which is what makes folding phones possible. The trade-offs are cost and ageing. The organic materials slowly lose brightness with use, and blue ones fade fastest. If the same image stays on screen for very long periods, such as a news ticker or a game's scoreboard, it can leave a faint permanent ghost, known as burn-in. Manufacturers fight it with tricks such as subtly shifting the image.

sections.key: Screens redraw the whole image many times a second, and this refresh rate is measured in hertz.
sections.b: A screen never shows true motion. It shows a rapid series of still images, each slightly different, like a flipbook. The number of times it redraws each second is the refresh rate, measured in hertz. Many screens refresh 60 times a second, while newer phones, gaming monitors and televisions reach 120 hertz or more, which makes scrolling and fast games feel noticeably smoother. Films are traditionally shot at only 24 frames per second, so a screen often shows each frame of a movie more than once. Some phones change their refresh rate on the fly, dropping as low as one hertz for a still image to save battery, then jumping back up as soon as you start to scroll. The faster your finger moves, the more those extra frames matter.

sections.key: Beyond a certain pixel density, extra resolution makes little visible difference at normal viewing distances.
sections.b: More pixels are not always better. Whether you can see the difference depends on pixel size, screen size and how far away you are. The human eye can only resolve detail down to a certain fineness, and once pixels are smaller than that at your viewing distance, adding more brings little visible gain. Apple built its 'Retina' marketing in 2010 around exactly this idea: pixels too small to pick out individually at a typical viewing distance. It also explains why, for most people watching from the couch, an 8K television offers only a modest improvement over 4K. Other qualities, such as contrast, brightness, colour accuracy and how cleanly the screen handles fast motion, often matter more to how good a picture actually looks.

quiz.q: What does the word 'pixel' stand for?
o: Picture element
Pixel light
Photo cell
Primary exel
quiz.e: Pixel is short for picture element, the smallest dot a screen controls individually.

quiz.q: On a screen, what do red and green light combine to make?
o: Brown
Yellow
Purple
Black
quiz.e: Screens use additive mixing of light, where red plus green looks yellow, unlike mixing paints.

quiz.q: Why can dark scenes look slightly grey on an LCD?
o: The pixels are too large
The liquid crystals glow faintly
The backlight stays on behind every pixel, and some leaks through
The screen refreshes too slowly
quiz.e: LCDs block a constant backlight, and the crystals can never block it completely.

quiz.q: What is burn-in on an OLED screen?
o: The screen overheating
A faint permanent ghost left by an image shown for very long periods
A cracked display
Colours becoming too bright
quiz.e: The organic materials age with use, so pixels showing the same image for ages wear unevenly.

quiz.q: What does a 120 hertz refresh rate mean?
o: The screen uses 120 watts
The screen has 120 colours
The screen redraws its image 120 times per second
The screen lasts 120 months
quiz.e: Hertz means times per second, so the image is updated 120 times each second for smoother motion.

LESSONS.title: The transistor: the switch that changed everything
LESSONS.hook: In 1947 two physicists built a clumsy contraption of gold foil, plastic and germanium. Its descendants now number in the billions inside your phone.

sections.key: Before transistors, electronics relied on vacuum tubes, which were hot, bulky and failed often.
sections.b: In the first half of the twentieth century, electronics meant vacuum tubes, known in Australia and Britain as valves. These glass bulbs could amplify a signal or switch a current on and off, making radio, television and the first electronic computers possible. But they were bulky and power hungry, they ran hot, and their filaments burned out like light globes. ENIAC, an American computer completed in 1945, used around 17,500 of them, filled a large room and drew about 150 kilowatts of power. Tubes failed regularly, and finding the dead one took time. The American telephone giant AT&T had a particular interest in something better, because its network relied on huge numbers of tubes and mechanical switches. Its research arm, Bell Labs, went looking for a solid replacement.

sections.key: In December 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain demonstrated the first working transistor.
sections.b: Bell Labs assembled a team to study semiconductors, materials such as germanium and silicon that conduct electricity better than an insulator but worse than a metal. In December 1947, physicists John Bardeen and Walter Brattain pressed two closely spaced gold contacts onto a slab of germanium and found that a small current through one could control a larger current through the other. The device amplified a signal. They demonstrated it to Bell Labs managers on 23 December. It was an awkward-looking thing, held together with a plastic wedge and a spring, but it worked. Their group leader, William Shockley, was reportedly frustrated not to have been directly involved, and within weeks he had worked out a sturdier design, the junction transistor, which became the basis for practical devices.

sections.key: A transistor is a tiny electrically controlled switch, and switches are all a computer needs to calculate.
sections.b: A transistor does two related jobs. It can amplify, turning a weak signal into a stronger copy, which made pocket transistor radios possible. And it can act as a switch with no moving parts, where a small voltage on one terminal turns a larger current on or off. That second job is the foundation of computing. Computers represent information as on and off, one and zero. Combine a few transistors and you get logic gates, circuits whose output is on only if both inputs are on, or if either is. Combine gates and you can add numbers, compare them and store them. Because transistors can switch billions of times per second while using very little power, enormous numbers of them can work together on a single chip.

sections.key: The inventors shared a Nobel Prize, but Shockley's difficult management helped spark the birth of Silicon Valley.
sections.b: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. By then Shockley had left Bell Labs and set up the Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory in Mountain View, California, hiring brilliant young scientists. His management proved so suspicious and erratic that in 1957 eight of them walked out together. They became known as the 'traitorous eight'. With backing from an industrial company, they founded Fairchild Semiconductor, which became a seedbed for the region later nicknamed Silicon Valley. Two of the eight, Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore, went on to found Intel in 1968. Bardeen, meanwhile, won a second Nobel Prize in Physics in 1972, for helping explain superconductivity, and remains the only person to have won that prize twice.

sections.h: Putting it all on one chip
sections.key: The integrated circuit, invented independently by Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce, put many components on a single piece of material.
sections.b: Early transistors were separate components, soldered by hand into circuits. As designs grew more complex, the wiring itself became the problem, a challenge engineers called the tyranny of numbers. In 1958, Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built a working circuit with its components formed in a single piece of germanium. Months later, Robert Noyce at Fairchild proposed a more practical approach in silicon, building on the flat 'planar' process developed by his colleague Jean Hoerni, which let components and their connections be made together, rather like printing. Both men are credited as inventors of the integrated circuit. Kilby received a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for it; Noyce had died in 1990. The microchip turned electronics from a craft into something closer to mass printing.

sections.key: Gordon Moore predicted in 1965 that the number of transistors on a chip would keep doubling, and for decades he was right.
