sections.b: In 1965 Gordon Moore, then at Fairchild, wrote a magazine article observing that the number of components on a chip had been doubling every year, and predicted the trend would continue for at least a decade. In 1975 he revised the pace to roughly every two years. This became known as Moore's law, though it is an observation about engineering and economics rather than a law of nature. It held up remarkably well for about half a century, partly because the industry treated it as a target to hit. Modern chips contain tens of billions of transistors, each far smaller than a bacterium. Progress has slowed as some parts of transistors shrink to just a few atoms thick, and engineers now debate how much longer the trend can continue.

quiz.q: What was the main problem with vacuum tubes?
o: They could only be made in Japan
They were bulky, ran hot, used lots of power and burned out
They could not amplify signals
They only worked underwater
quiz.e: Tubes did the job, but machines like ENIAC needed thousands of them, with huge power use and frequent failures.

quiz.q: Who demonstrated the first working transistor in December 1947?
o: Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla
Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore
John Bardeen and Walter Brattain
Jack Kilby and Jean Hoerni
quiz.e: Bardeen and Brattain's point-contact transistor was shown to Bell Labs managers on 23 December 1947.

quiz.q: Why is a transistor's ability to act as a switch so important for computers?
o: Switches make computers quieter
Computers represent information as on and off, and switches combine into logic gates
Switches stop computers overheating
It lets computers connect to the internet
quiz.e: On-off switches build logic gates, and gates build circuits that add, compare and store numbers.

quiz.q: What did the 'traitorous eight' found after leaving Shockley?
o: Bell Labs
IBM
Texas Instruments
Fairchild Semiconductor
quiz.e: Fairchild became a seedbed of Silicon Valley, and two of its founders later started Intel.

quiz.q: What is Moore's law?
o: A law of physics about electricity
An observation that the number of transistors on chips roughly doubles every two years
A rule that computers must halve in price yearly
A law banning chips smaller than a virus
quiz.e: It began as Gordon Moore's 1965 observation and became an industry target, not a law of nature.

LESSONS.title: How your phone camera takes a photo
LESSONS.hook: A phone camera's lens is smaller than a pea, yet it can rival cameras costing thousands of dollars. The secret is less about glass and more about software.

sections.key: A camera sensor is a grid of millions of light-sensitive sites that turn light into electric charge.
sections.b: Where film cameras used chemistry, a digital camera uses an image sensor, a silicon chip covered in millions of tiny light-sensitive sites, often called photosites. Each works a little like a bucket left out in the rain. During an exposure, particles of light called photons strike the silicon and knock electrons loose, and the photosite collects them. Brighter light means more photons and more charge. When the exposure ends, the charge in each bucket is measured and converted into a number. That grid of numbers is the raw material of your photo. Almost all phone cameras use a type of sensor called CMOS, built with the same manufacturing methods as computer chips, which made sensors cheap and power-efficient enough to fit inside phones.

sections.key: Sensors only measure brightness, so a mosaic of coloured filters, the Bayer filter, is used to capture colour.
sections.b: A photosite cannot tell what colour light it receives; it only counts how much. To capture colour, most sensors place a tiny filter over each photosite, letting through only red, green or blue light. The usual arrangement, patented in 1976 by Bryce Bayer, an engineer at Kodak, is a checkerboard pattern with twice as many green filters as red or blue, because our eyes are most sensitive to detail in green light. So each photosite knows about only one colour. Software then estimates the two missing colours at every point by looking at its neighbours, a process called demosaicing. In a sense, two-thirds of the colour information in a typical digital photo is educated guesswork, though the guesses are very good indeed.

sections.key: Tiny sensors collect less light, which makes photos noisy in dim conditions.
sections.b: Phones are thin, so their sensors and lenses must be small. A full-frame professional camera sensor is about 36 by 24 millimetres; most phone sensors are a fraction of that area. A smaller sensor gathers less light overall, and in a dim room each photosite may collect only a small number of photons. Light arrives randomly, so with few photons the counts fluctuate from one photosite to the next, and the image fills with grainy speckles called noise. The electronics add a little noise of their own. This is a physical limit, not a manufacturing fault, and it explains why phone photos used to look so poor indoors and at night. Cramming in more megapixels can make it worse, because each photosite becomes smaller still.

sections.key: Modern phones quietly capture a burst of frames and merge them into a single better image.
sections.b: The breakthrough was computational photography. When you press the shutter, a modern phone has often already been capturing frames continuously, and it combines several of them into one picture. Averaging many frames cancels out much of the random noise, in the same way that averaging many people's guesses tends to cancel out individual errors. Combining shorter and longer exposures lets the phone keep detail in both a bright sky and dark shadows, a technique called high dynamic range, or HDR. Night modes go further, capturing frames over a second or more and aligning them to correct for your shaking hands. All of this happens in moments on dedicated processors. So the photo you see is not a single instant of light, but a carefully assembled composite.

sections.key: Phones also use software to sharpen, smooth, adjust colours and simulate effects such as blurred backgrounds.
sections.b: After merging frames, the phone keeps editing. It adjusts white balance so that a white shirt looks white under orange indoor lighting, sharpens edges, smooths skin and boosts colours to look pleasing. Many phones recognise what is in the scene, such as food, faces or sky, and treat each part differently. Portrait mode imitates the soft background blur of a large camera lens. A phone's tiny lens produces little natural blur, so software estimates how far away each part of the scene is, using two cameras, depth sensors or machine learning, then blurs the background artificially. Look closely at hair or the edges of glasses and you can sometimes spot mistakes. Different brands make different choices, which is why the same scene can look noticeably different on two phones.

sections.key: Because phones interpret scenes so heavily, a photo is part record and part reconstruction.
sections.b: All cameras interpret the world. Film chemistry favoured some colours over others, and photographers have always chosen exposure and framing. But phones push interpretation much further, and the line between capturing and creating has blurred. Some features can erase unwanted people from the background, or combine the best expressions from several shots of a group. A well-known controversy arose in 2023 over phone photos of the Moon, when a tester showed that one brand's processing added lunar detail that was missing from a deliberately blurred original, by drawing on a model trained on what the Moon looks like. Most processing is harmless and simply produces better pictures. Still, a photo from a modern phone is best thought of as the camera's best estimate of a scene, not a perfect copy.

quiz.q: What does each photosite on a camera sensor actually measure?
o: The colour of the light
The distance to the subject
How much light, by collecting electrons knocked loose by photons
The temperature of the scene
quiz.e: Photosites count light like buckets collecting rain; colour has to be added by filters.

quiz.q: Why does the Bayer filter use twice as many green filters as red or blue?
o: Green filters are cheaper
Our eyes are most sensitive to detail in green light
Green light travels faster
Most scenes are mostly green
quiz.e: Bryce Bayer's pattern favours green to match how human vision picks up detail.

quiz.q: Why do photos from small sensors look grainy in dim light?
o: The lens gets dirty in the dark
Few photons arrive, so random variation between photosites shows up as noise
Phones deliberately add grain
Sensors stop working below a certain temperature
quiz.e: With little light, the natural randomness of photon arrival becomes visible as speckled noise.

quiz.q: How does combining many frames improve a phone photo?
o: It makes the file smaller
Averaging frames cancels out much of the random noise
It increases the number of pixels on the sensor
It makes the lens wider
quiz.e: Random noise differs between frames, so averaging them leaves the real image clearer.

quiz.q: How does a phone create portrait mode's blurred background?
o: Its lens is wider than a professional camera's
It estimates depth and blurs the background with software
It takes the photo out of focus on purpose
It uses a special blurry filter over the lens
quiz.e: Small phone lenses give little natural blur, so software maps depth and adds the blur afterwards.

LESSONS.title: How computers store letters and emoji
LESSONS.hook: Computers only understand numbers. So how does a letter, a Chinese character or a laughing-crying face survive the trip from your phone to someone else's?

sections.key: Computers store text by giving every character an agreed number, a system called a character encoding.
sections.b: Inside a computer there are no letters, only binary numbers. To store text, everyone involved must agree on a table that maps each character to a number. Send the number 65 and the receiving computer, using the same table, shows a capital A. Early computers each had their own tables, so text from one machine could turn to gibberish on another. In 1963, American standards bodies published the first version of ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, refined over the following years. It used 7 bits, allowing 128 codes: upper and lower case English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes, such as a 'bell' code that rang a bell on teleprinters. ASCII was a huge success, but it was designed for English and left out most of the world's writing.

sections.key: Rival encodings for other languages led to garbled text, a problem known by the Japanese word mojibake.
sections.b: Computers usually store data in bytes of eight bits, which can hold 256 values, so many systems used the spare 128 slots for accented letters, symbols or other alphabets. The trouble was that different countries and companies filled those slots differently. Greek, Russian, Hebrew and Western European text each had their own versions, and languages such as Chinese and Japanese, with thousands of characters, needed more complex schemes of their own. Open a document using the wrong table and the numbers came out as the wrong characters. Japanese users had a word for the resulting jumble: mojibake, roughly 'character transformation'. Anyone who has seen an apostrophe turn into a string like â€™ on a web page has met the same problem.

sections.key: Unicode set out to give every character in every writing system its own unique number.
sections.b: In the late 1980s, engineers including Joe Becker of Xerox and Lee Collins and Mark Davis of Apple began working on a universal solution. The Unicode Consortium was founded in 1991 and published the first version of the standard that year. Its goal was simple to state and enormous to achieve: one number, called a code point, for every character in every writing system, past and present. Capital A is still 65, to stay compatible with ASCII, and is written in Unicode as U+0041. Unicode now covers well over 150,000 characters across more than 160 scripts, including Arabic, Devanagari, Cherokee, Egyptian hieroglyphs and cuneiform. New characters are added through a formal proposal process, and the standard is updated roughly once a year.

sections.key: UTF-8, sketched in a diner in 1992, became the way most text on the web is stored.
sections.b: Giving characters numbers is only half the job; you also need a way to store those numbers as bytes. One evening in September 1992, computer scientists Ken Thompson and Rob Pike, then working at Bell Labs, sketched a scheme on a placemat in a New Jersey diner. It became UTF-8. Its elegance is that ordinary English text is stored exactly as in ASCII, one byte per character, so old files and programs keep working. Other characters use two, three or four bytes, with bit patterns that clearly mark where each character starts, so software never mistakes part of one character for another. UTF-8 spread steadily, and today the great majority of web pages use it, a quiet but enormous victory for compatibility.

sections.key: Emoji began on Japanese mobile phones in the late 1990s and entered Unicode in 2010.
sections.b: Emoji come from Japan, where the word combines e, meaning picture, and moji, meaning character; its resemblance to the English word 'emotion' is a coincidence. Japanese mobile phones offered picture characters in the late 1990s. A set of 176 simple designs, each 12 by 12 pixels, created by Shigetaka Kurita for NTT Docomo's mobile internet service in 1999, became the most famous early collection and is now held by the Museum of Modern Art in New York, although another carrier had offered picture symbols slightly earlier. Each Japanese carrier used its own codes, so emoji often broke when sent between networks. Pressure from companies including Google and Apple led to emoji being added to Unicode in 2010, which let them spread worldwide.

sections.key: Unicode defines what an emoji means, but each company draws its own version, and some are built from combinations.
sections.b: Unicode assigns each emoji a code point and a name, such as U+1F602, 'face with tears of joy', but it does not dictate the artwork. Apple, Google, Microsoft, Samsung and others draw their own designs, so a message can look subtly different on the recipient's phone. Designs are sometimes redrawn: the pistol emoji, for example, was changed to a toy water gun by most major platforms in the late 2010s. Many emoji are not single characters at all. Skin tones are added by attaching a modifier to a base emoji, and many family and profession emoji are built by joining several emoji with an invisible character called a zero-width joiner. A single small picture on your screen can be made of seven or more code points.

quiz.q: How many different codes did 7-bit ASCII allow?
quiz.e: Seven bits give 2 to the power of 7, or 128, possible codes, enough for English but little else.

quiz.q: What is 'mojibake'?
o: A Japanese emoji set
Garbled text produced when the wrong character encoding is used
A type of computer virus
A font for writing kanji
quiz.e: Reading bytes with the wrong table turns text into a jumble, which Japanese users named mojibake.

quiz.q: What makes UTF-8 so practical?
o: It stores every character in exactly one byte
It only works for English
Plain English text is stored exactly as in ASCII, so old files keep working
It compresses images
quiz.e: UTF-8 is backwards compatible with ASCII while still able to represent every Unicode character.

quiz.q: What does the Japanese word 'emoji' mean?
o: Emotion icon
Picture character
Small face
Mobile message
quiz.e: E means picture and moji means character; the link to 'emotion' is a coincidence.

quiz.q: How are many family and profession emoji created?
o: By joining several emoji with an invisible zero-width joiner
By drawing them by hand on each phone
By sending a photo instead of text
By using a separate app
quiz.e: Several code points glued by zero-width joiners are displayed as a single picture.

LESSONS.title: Open source: the free code running the world
LESSONS.hook: Much of the digital world runs on software written in the open and given away. In 2024, one engineer's curiosity about a half-second delay showed both the strength and the fragility of that system.

sections.key: Open source software shares its source code so anyone can read, change and redistribute it.
sections.b: Software begins as source code, instructions written by people in a programming language. Most commercial programs are distributed only in compiled form, which computers can run but humans can barely read, so the recipe stays secret. Open source software publishes the recipe. Anyone can study how it works, fix it, improve it or build something new from it, under a licence that sets out the rules. Some licences let you do almost anything; others require that if you share a modified version, you must share your changes too. Open source does not necessarily mean nobody is paid. Many developers are employed by companies that rely on the software. But the code itself is shared, and it is everywhere: phones, cars, televisions, routers and the servers behind most websites.

sections.h: A printer that started a movement
sections.key: Richard Stallman launched the free software movement in 1983, arguing that users should control their programs.
sections.b: In computing's early days, researchers shared code freely, but by the late 1970s software was increasingly locked up as a commercial product. Richard Stallman, a programmer at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, later described a formative frustration: a new laser printer kept jamming, and he could not fix the problem in its software because the maker would not share the source code. In 1983 he announced the GNU project, to build a complete operating system made only of free software, and in 1985 he founded the Free Software Foundation. 'Free' meant freedom, not price, which he summed up as free as in free speech, not free beer. His GNU General Public License required shared modifications to stay free, a clever legal twist nicknamed copyleft.

sections.key: In 1991 a Finnish student, Linus Torvalds, started the Linux kernel, which completed a free operating system.
sections.b: By the early 1990s, the GNU project had built many tools but still lacked a finished kernel, the core of an operating system that manages memory, processors and hardware. In August 1991, Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old student at the University of Helsinki, posted a message online saying he was writing a free operating system, adding that it was just a hobby and would not be big and professional like GNU. He released the code, and programmers around the world began sending improvements. Combined with GNU's tools, Linux became a complete free operating system. Torvalds later created Git as well, now the most widely used tool for tracking changes to code. Few hobbies have turned out quite so big and professional.

sections.key: Linux and other open source software now underpin phones, servers, supercomputers and the web.
sections.b: Today Linux is far more widespread than most people realise. Android, the world's most popular phone operating system, is built on the Linux kernel. Linux runs most of the servers behind websites and cloud services, and since 2017 every one of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers on the regularly published TOP500 list has run it. Beyond Linux, open source projects supply web browser engines, databases, programming languages and the encryption libraries that help protect online banking. Companies large and small build on this shared foundation rather than writing everything from scratch, which saves enormous effort. Even firms that once treated open source as a threat came around. Microsoft's chief executive Steve Ballmer called Linux 'a cancer' in 2001; Microsoft later became one of open source's biggest contributors.

sections.key: Critical open source projects are sometimes maintained by tiny, underfunded teams, which creates hidden risks.
sections.b: Shared code has a weakness: everyone uses it, but no one in particular is responsible for it. In 2014 researchers discovered Heartbleed, a serious flaw in OpenSSL, encryption software used by a large share of the web's secure servers. It emerged that the project was run by a handful of people, with only one working on it full time, and received only around 2000 US dollars a year in donations. In 2021 another severe flaw, Log4Shell, turned up in Log4j, a widely used tool for recording what programs do, again maintained largely by volunteers. Each crisis pushed companies and governments to fund critical projects more seriously. A popular web cartoon sums up the worry: modern digital infrastructure balanced on one small project that a lone volunteer has been thanklessly maintaining for years.

sections.h: Half a second that saved the internet
sections.key: In 2024 an engineer noticed a tiny slowdown and uncovered a backdoor planted in widely used open source software.
sections.b: In March 2024, Andres Freund, a Microsoft software engineer who works on the PostgreSQL database, noticed something odd: logging in to a test machine was using more processor time than it should, adding about half a second. Curious, he traced the delay to xz Utils, a small compression tool included in many Linux systems. Someone had hidden a backdoor in it that could have let an attacker take control of affected servers. The culprit, using the name Jia Tan, had spent around two years earning the trust of the project's overstretched volunteer maintainer before gaining the access needed to slip it in. It was caught before reaching the stable versions of major Linux distributions. Who was behind it remains unknown, though many security experts suspect a well-resourced, possibly state-backed group.

quiz.q: What makes software 'open source'?
o: It is always free of charge and written by volunteers
Its source code is published so anyone can read, change and share it under a licence
It has no bugs
It only runs on Linux
quiz.e: Open source is about access to the source code; many contributors are actually paid by companies.

quiz.q: What did Richard Stallman mean by 'free' software?
o: Software that costs nothing
Software with no licence
Freedom for users to run, study, change and share it
Software made by the government
quiz.e: His slogan 'free as in free speech, not free beer' stressed freedom rather than price.

quiz.q: How did Linus Torvalds describe his project in 1991?
o: As the future of all computing
As a commercial rival to Microsoft
As just a hobby that would not be big and professional
As a secret military project
quiz.e: His modest announcement became one of the most widely used pieces of software ever written.

quiz.q: What did the Heartbleed bug reveal about open source?
o: That open source code cannot be trusted at all
That critical projects can depend on tiny, underfunded teams
That encryption is unnecessary
That only companies should write software
quiz.e: OpenSSL protected much of the web but was run by a handful of people on very little money.

quiz.q: What first tipped off Andres Freund to the xz Utils backdoor?
o: A warning from police
An anonymous email
A small, unexpected slowdown when logging in
A virus scanner alert
quiz.e: Logins were using more processor time than they should, adding about half a second, and he investigated.

LESSONS.title: Turing and the problems no computer can solve
LESSONS.hook: Before electronic computers existed, a 23-year-old mathematician proved there are questions no computer, however powerful, will ever be able to answer.

sections.key: In 1928 David Hilbert asked whether a mechanical method could decide whether any mathematical statement was provable.
sections.b: In the early twentieth century, the German mathematician David Hilbert hoped mathematics could be placed on perfectly solid foundations. In 1928 he and Wilhelm Ackermann posed a challenge known by its German name, the Entscheidungsproblem, or 'decision problem'. Could there be a definite step-by-step procedure that, given any statement in formal logic, would decide whether it could be proved? If so, mathematics might in principle be mechanised, its questions settled by following rules rather than by flashes of insight. Then, in 1931, Kurt Gödel showed that any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. But the decision problem was a separate question, and answering it required something nobody yet had: a precise definition of what a 'mechanical procedure' actually is.

sections.key: Turing defined computation by imagining a simple machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape.
sections.b: In 1936 Alan Turing, a 23-year-old fellow of King's College, Cambridge, tackled the problem in a paper titled 'On Computable Numbers'. He began by asking what a human clerk does when calculating with pencil and paper, and stripped it down to its bare essentials. The result was an imaginary device now called a Turing machine: an endless tape divided into squares, a head that can read, write or erase one symbol at a time and move left or right, and a finite table of rules saying what to do next, depending on the symbol it sees and its current state. It sounds absurdly simple. Yet Turing argued convincingly that anything that can be calculated by following a precise procedure can be calculated by a machine like this.

sections.h: One machine to imitate them all
sections.key: Turing showed a single universal machine could carry out any other machine's rules, the idea behind every modern computer.
sections.b: Turing's paper contained a second startling idea. The rule table of any Turing machine could itself be written down as symbols on a tape. So he described a universal machine which, given a description of any other machine plus its input, would simulate it step by step and produce the same result. In other words, one machine could do the work of every machine, provided it was handed the right instructions. That is exactly what a modern computer is. Your laptop does not need different hardware to be a word processor, a game or a calculator; it simply loads a different program. Historians debate how directly Turing's abstract idea influenced the engineers who built the first stored-program computers in the late 1940s, but the concept was there in 1936.

sections.key: The halting problem asks whether a given program will eventually finish or run forever.
sections.b: Anyone who has watched a frozen app knows that programs sometimes get stuck in endless loops. It would be extremely useful to have a perfect checker: a program that could examine any other program and its input and report, in advance, whether it will eventually stop or run forever. For some programs the answer is obvious. A program that counts from one to ten halts; one that says 'repeat forever' does not. Others are fiendishly hard. Consider a program that searches for an even number greater than 2 that is not the sum of two primes, stopping only if it finds one. Whether it ever halts depends on Goldbach's conjecture, an unsolved problem in mathematics since 1742. A perfect halting checker would settle such questions instantly.

sections.key: Turing proved that no general halting checker can exist, using a self-referential trick.
sections.b: Suppose someone claims to have built a perfect checker; call it H. The argument, in the form it is usually taught today, goes like this. Build a new program, call it Contrary, that takes any program, asks H whether that program halts when given its own code as input, and then does the opposite. If H says it halts, Contrary loops forever; if H says it loops, Contrary stops. Now feed Contrary its own code. If H predicts Contrary halts, Contrary loops; if H predicts it loops, Contrary halts. Either way H is wrong, so no such H can exist. Turing used reasoning of this kind to answer Hilbert: no general mechanical procedure can decide every mathematical question. The American logician Alonzo Church reached the same conclusion independently, by a different route, shortly before.

sections.key: Undecidability has practical consequences, such as why no virus scanner or bug checker can ever be perfect.
sections.b: The halting problem is not a quirk of old mathematics; its consequences run right through computing. A later result, Rice's theorem, extends it: no program can perfectly decide, for every possible program, any meaningful property of how that program behaves, such as whether it will ever leak a password. That is why no antivirus software can be guaranteed to catch every possible piece of malicious code, and why tools that check programs for bugs must accept limits. They can miss problems, raise false alarms or give up on some cases. In practice, engineers work around this with time limits, careful restrictions and checkers that are right most of the time. Turing's 1936 insight remains a humbling boundary. Some questions are not merely hard for computers. They are impossible.

quiz.q: What did Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem ask?
o: Whether computers could think
Whether a mechanical procedure could decide if any logical statement is provable
Whether every equation has a solution
Whether infinity exists
quiz.e: Hilbert and Ackermann asked for a step-by-step method that would settle provability for any statement.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of a Turing machine?
o: A keyboard and screen
A network connection
An endless tape, a read-write head and a finite table of rules
Thousands of vacuum tubes
quiz.e: Turing's imaginary machine was deliberately minimal, modelled on a clerk working with pencil and paper.

quiz.q: Why is Turing's universal machine so important?
o: It was the first machine to be built from transistors
It showed one machine could do any other machine's work if given the right instructions
It broke the Enigma code
It proved Goldbach's conjecture
quiz.e: That is the principle of every modern computer: one piece of hardware, endlessly many programs.

quiz.q: What does the halting proof show?
o: That every program eventually stops
That no general program can correctly predict, for every program and input, whether it will halt
That computers are slower than humans
That loops should never be used
quiz.e: Feeding the contrary program its own code forces any claimed perfect checker into a contradiction.

quiz.q: Which practical consequence follows from undecidability?
o: Computers cannot add large numbers
No antivirus program can be guaranteed to catch every possible piece of malicious code
Programs cannot be copied
Internet speeds are limited
quiz.e: Rice's theorem means perfect general analysis of program behaviour is impossible, so real tools accept limits.

LESSONS.title: The illusory truth effect: why repetition feels like proof
LESSONS.hook: Hear something often enough and it starts to feel true, even when you know better. Here's why your brain falls for it, and how to fight back.

sections.key: Simply repeating a statement makes people rate it as more likely to be true.
sections.b: In 1977 the psychologists Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino ran a simple experiment with university students. Over three sessions, two weeks apart, the students read a long list of trivia statements and rated how confident they were that each one was true. Some statements were true and some were false, and they were obscure enough that most people couldn't know for sure. The twist was that some statements appeared in every session, while others were brand new each time. The repeated statements were rated as more and more likely to be true with each session, whether they were actually true or not. Nothing about the evidence had changed. Only familiarity had. The researchers had documented what is now called the illusory truth effect.

sections.key: Familiar ideas are easier for the brain to process, and that ease gets mistaken for accuracy.
sections.b: Why should repetition matter? The leading explanation involves something psychologists call processing fluency. A statement you have met before is quicker and easier to read and understand, because your brain has already done some of the work. That smooth, effortless feeling is normally a decent clue: things we hear often are frequently true, because true things tend to be repeated by many independent sources. So the mind takes a shortcut and treats ease as a sign of accuracy. The trouble is that fluency can come from almost anywhere. Studies have found that statements printed in easier-to-read colours are judged more likely to be true, and that rhyming sayings, such as ‘woes unite foes’, are rated as more accurate than the same ideas phrased without a rhyme.

sections.key: Repetition can nudge belief even in claims that contradict what you already know.
sections.b: It's tempting to think this only works on topics you know nothing about. A 2015 study led by the psychologist Lisa Fazio tested that idea. Participants read statements such as ‘A sari is the name of the short pleated skirt worn by Scots’, which contradicts something most of them knew: that skirt is a kilt. Even so, reading a false statement more than once made people rate it as somewhat more true than they otherwise would. Knowledge helped, but it didn't switch the effect off. People often failed to bring what they knew to mind, relying on the feeling of familiarity instead. Later research has found that the biggest jump in belief tends to come from the second exposure, with smaller gains after that.

sections.h: Fake news and the repeat button
sections.key: Even a single earlier glimpse of a false headline can make it seem more accurate later.
sections.b: In 2018 Gordon Pennycook, Tyrone Cannon and David Rand showed people real fake-news headlines from social media, styled as they would appear in a feed. Later, the headlines people had seen before were rated as more accurate than ones they were seeing for the first time, after just one earlier exposure. Strikingly, the effect still appeared when the headlines had carried a warning label saying they were disputed by fact-checkers. This matters because online platforms are repetition machines. A claim can reach you through a friend's post, a meme, a video and a comment thread in the same afternoon, and each one makes it feel a little more familiar. Advertisers and propagandists have understood the power of repetition for a very long time.

sections.key: Repeating a myth to debunk it can accidentally spread it, so lead with the truth instead.
sections.b: This creates a headache for anyone trying to correct a falsehood. A typical myth-busting article repeats the myth, sometimes in large type, then explains why it's wrong. Readers may later remember the familiar claim and forget the correction. Researchers once worried that corrections might routinely ‘backfire’ and strengthen false beliefs, but later work found this is rare; corrections generally do help. Still, how you correct matters. A widely recommended approach, sometimes called a ‘truth sandwich’, starts with the accurate fact, mentions the myth once and clearly labels it as false, explains why it's wrong, then finishes by repeating the truth. That way the fact, not the myth, is the thing that gets the repetition and becomes familiar.

sections.key: Pausing to ask how you actually know something helps separate familiarity from evidence.
sections.b: You can't stop repetition from affecting you, but you can make it work less well. One useful habit is to notice the feeling of ‘I've heard that before’ and treat it as a cue, not a conclusion. Ask where you heard it, whether the source was reliable, and whether you have ever seen actual evidence. Some studies suggest that prompting people to focus on accuracy, or to think about how they know a claim is true, reduces the effect, especially for claims they have the knowledge to check. It also helps to be careful about what you repeat yourself. Every time you pass on a dubious claim, even as a joke, you add one more exposure to someone else's sense that it's true.

quiz.q: What did the 1977 study find about statements that were repeated across sessions?
o: They were rated as more likely to be true
They were rated as less trustworthy
They were remembered but believed less
They only gained belief if they were actually true
quiz.e: Repeated statements were rated as increasingly likely to be true, whether they were true or false. Only their familiarity had changed.

quiz.q: What is ‘processing fluency’?
o: A measure of how fast someone reads
The ease with which the brain handles information, which can feel like truth
A technique for memorising facts
Being fluent in a second language
quiz.e: Familiar or easy-to-process information feels smooth, and the mind tends to treat that ease as a sign the information is accurate.

quiz.q: In Fazio's 2015 study, what happened when people repeatedly read false statements that contradicted their own knowledge?
o: They rejected them completely
They became sceptical of everything
Repetition still made the statements seem somewhat more true
They permanently forgot the correct fact
quiz.e: Knowledge helped but didn't switch the effect off. People often relied on the feeling of familiarity instead of retrieving what they knew.

quiz.q: What is the ‘truth sandwich’ approach to correcting a myth?
o: Repeat the myth several times so people notice it
Ignore the myth completely
Mock the people who believe it
Start and finish with the fact, mentioning the myth once in between
quiz.e: Leading and ending with the accurate fact means the truth, not the myth, gets the repetition that builds familiarity.

quiz.q: What did Pennycook and colleagues find about fake headlines that carried a ‘disputed’ label?
o: The label made people distrust them permanently
One earlier exposure still made them seem more accurate later
People refused to read them
The label made them twice as believable
quiz.e: Even a single prior exposure raised perceived accuracy, and the effect appeared even when headlines had been flagged as disputed by fact-checkers.

LESSONS.title: Confirmation bias: the puzzle almost everyone gets wrong
LESSONS.hook: Three numbers, one hidden rule, and a mistake that reveals how we all hunt for proof we're right rather than for the truth.

sections.key: In 1960 Peter Wason gave people a simple number puzzle that exposed a deep habit of thought.
sections.b: In 1960 the British psychologist Peter Wason, at University College London, gave volunteers three numbers: 2, 4, 6. He told them the sequence followed a rule he had in mind, and their job was to discover it. They could propose their own sets of three numbers, and he would say whether each one fitted the rule. When they felt sure, they could announce their answer. Most people quickly formed a theory, such as ‘even numbers going up by two’, and then tested it with sets like 8, 10, 12 and 20, 22, 24. Every one of those guesses got a yes. Confident, they announced their rule, and many of them were told they were wrong.

sections.h: Testing to confirm, not to disprove
sections.key: People tested examples that fitted their theory, so they never saw it fail.
sections.b: Wason's actual rule was simply ‘any three numbers in increasing order’. Sets like 1, 2, 3 or 5, 17, 300 would also have earned a yes. The volunteers who failed had not been careless. They had done something very natural: they looked for examples that fitted their idea, rather than examples that might break it. A test like 8, 10, 12 could never show them they were wrong, because it fitted both their theory and the real rule. The people who succeeded tended to try sequences that their own theory said should fail, such as 1, 2, 3 or 3, 10, 50. When one of those came back with a yes, they learnt something important: their theory was too narrow.

sections.key: In Wason's 1966 selection task, most people turn over the wrong cards.
sections.b: Wason's most famous puzzle followed in 1966. Imagine four cards on a table, each with a letter on one side and a number on the other. You can see E, K, 4 and 7. The rule is: ‘If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.’ Which cards must you turn over to check whether the rule is being broken? Most people pick E, and often 4 as well. E is right. But 4 tells you nothing, because the rule says nothing about what must be behind an even number. The card you need is 7: if a vowel is hiding behind it, the rule is broken. In many studies, only around one person in ten, or fewer, chooses correctly.

sections.key: The same logic becomes simple when the puzzle is about catching rule-breakers.
sections.b: Here's the strange part. Researchers later rewrote the puzzle in familiar terms. Imagine you're checking a bar where the rule is: ‘If someone is drinking beer, they must be over 18.’ The four cards show: drinking beer, drinking cola, age 25 and age 16. Which do you check? Almost everyone instantly picks the beer drinker and the 16-year-old, which is logically the same answer as E and 7. Studies by Richard Griggs and James Cox in 1982 found that versions like this are solved far more often than the abstract one. Psychologists still debate why. Some argue our minds are tuned to spot social cheating; others say familiar situations simply make it obvious which cases could break the rule.

sections.key: We tend to seek, notice and remember information that supports what we already believe.
sections.b: Wason's puzzles became classic demonstrations of what is now called confirmation bias: the tendency to search for, interpret and remember information in ways that support what we already think. It shows up far beyond the laboratory. A detective who settles on a suspect early may give extra weight to clues that point their way. Someone convinced a colleague dislikes them reads every short email as proof. Investors can seek out news that flatters the shares they already own. Online, search engines and feeds make it easy to find something that agrees with almost any belief. The bias isn't stupidity. Holding on to a working theory saves effort, and often the theory is right. The danger is that we rarely notice when it isn't.

sections.h: Try to break your own idea
sections.key: The best test of a belief is one that could prove it wrong.
sections.b: The lesson from Wason is practical. When you have a theory, ask: what would I expect to see if I were wrong, and have I looked for it? Scientists build this into their method by designing experiments that could fail. You can do a small version in daily life. Before a big purchase, read the worst reviews, not just the best. Before deciding someone is untrustworthy, list the evidence that points the other way. In a 1984 study, Charles Lord and colleagues found that asking people to deliberately consider the opposite reduced biased judgements more effectively than simply telling them to be fair and unbiased. Testing your ideas like this feels uncomfortable, but it's the quickest route to the truth.

quiz.q: What was the real rule in Wason's 2-4-6 task?
o: Even numbers increasing by two
Numbers that add up to 12
Any three numbers in increasing order
Any three even numbers
quiz.e: The rule was simply any ascending sequence. People rarely discovered it because they only tested sets that fitted their narrower theory.

quiz.q: Why did testing a set like 8, 10, 12 fail to help people?
o: It fitted both their theory and the real rule, so it couldn't show them they were wrong
The numbers were too large
Wason gave misleading answers
It broke the rule
quiz.e: A test that fits every theory you're considering can't tell them apart. Informative tests are ones your theory predicts should fail.

quiz.q: In the card task showing E, K, 4 and 7, which cards must be turned over to check the rule?
o: E and 4
4 and 7
K and 4
E and 7
quiz.e: E could have an odd number behind it, and 7 could have a vowel behind it. Either would break the rule. The 4 card can't break it, whatever is on the back.

quiz.q: Why is the drinking-age version of the card puzzle so interesting?
o: It uses a completely different kind of logic
It has the same logical structure, yet people solve it far more easily
Nobody can solve it
It proves people are better at maths when relaxed
quiz.e: Checking the beer drinker and the 16-year-old is logically identical to checking E and 7, but the familiar social setting makes the answer feel obvious.

quiz.q: According to the 1984 study by Lord and colleagues, what helped reduce biased judgements?
o: Being told to be fair
Reading more evidence that supports your view
Deliberately considering the opposite
Deciding more quickly
quiz.e: Actively imagining how the evidence could point the other way worked better than a general instruction to be unbiased.

LESSONS.title: Outcome bias: why good decisions can end badly
LESSONS.hook: A coach made one of the most criticised calls in sport, and a poker player says we judged it all wrong. Learn to tell a smart choice from a lucky one.

sections.key: When a decision ends in disaster, we tend to assume the decision itself was foolish.
sections.b: In February 2015 the Seattle Seahawks were seconds away from winning the Super Bowl, the biggest game in American football. Trailing the New England Patriots by four points, they had the ball about a metre from the line with 26 seconds left. Most fans expected them to hand it to their powerful running back. Instead, coach Pete Carroll called a pass. It was intercepted by Malcolm Butler, and the Patriots won. Headlines called it one of the worst play calls in the history of the game. Yet a number of analysts argued the call was reasonable: interceptions that close to the line are rare, and an incomplete pass would stop the clock and leave time for more attempts. Had it worked, it might have been praised as clever.

sections.key: Judging a decision only by its result is a mistake poker players call ‘resulting’.
sections.b: The former professional poker player Annie Duke tells the Carroll story in her 2018 book Thinking in Bets. She describes the habit of judging decisions purely by how they turned out using a term from poker: ‘resulting’. In poker it's easy to see the problem. You can play a hand perfectly and still lose because the last card goes against you. You can also make a reckless bet and win. Over thousands of hands, good decisions come out ahead, but any single hand is heavily shaped by luck. Real life works the same way, only with fewer hands and messier information, which makes it much harder to see the difference between a smart choice and a fortunate one.

sections.key: People rate the very same decision as worse when it happens to turn out badly.
sections.b: In 1988 the psychologists Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave volunteers descriptions of decisions made under uncertainty, such as a doctor's choice about whether to go ahead with a risky operation. Everyone received the same information that had been available to the decision-maker at the time. The only thing that changed was the outcome: in some versions the patient lived, and in others the patient died. People rated the decision itself as worse, and the decision-maker as less competent, when the outcome was bad. Yet the choice had been made with exactly the same knowledge, and the outcome added nothing to what the doctor could have known beforehand. Baron and Hershey called this outcome bias.

sections.key: Every outcome mixes decision quality with luck, giving four very different combinations.
sections.b: A helpful way to picture this is a simple grid. A good decision with a good outcome is a deserved success. A good decision with a bad outcome is bad luck. A bad decision with a bad outcome is a predictable failure. And a bad decision with a good outcome is a lucky escape, which may be the most dangerous of all. Think of someone who drives home after too many drinks and arrives safely. The outcome teaches them nothing useful, or worse, teaches them that it was fine. Each lucky escape can make the next risky choice feel safer. Outcome bias collapses these four boxes into two: it worked, so it was right; it failed, so it was wrong.

sections.key: Once we know the result, we overestimate how predictable it was.
sections.b: Outcome bias has a close relative: hindsight bias, the feeling that we ‘knew it all along’. In the 1970s the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff showed that once people learnt how an event turned out, they judged that outcome to have been more predictable than people who hadn't been told. Their memories of what they had predicted earlier also shifted towards what actually happened. Together these biases make the world seem more orderly than it really is. They also make us unfair judges. Workers, doctors, pilots and leaders can be blamed for bad outcomes they could not reasonably have foreseen, while people who took foolish risks and got away with them can be rewarded and promoted.

sections.key: To learn from experience, review how a decision was made, not just how it turned out.
sections.b: The fix is to judge decisions by the process behind them. Ask: what did we know at the time? What options did we consider? Did we think about the risks and how likely they were? Was there information we could reasonably have gathered but didn't? Armies, hospitals and airlines have long used structured reviews after events, and these work best when they examine successes and failures with the same honesty. A simple personal tool is a decision journal. Before an important choice, write down what you expect to happen and why. Later, compare that with what actually happened. Over time you'll see whether your judgement is sound, or whether you've simply been lucky.

quiz.q: Why do some analysts defend Pete Carroll's 2015 Super Bowl call?
o: The pass was actually completed
Interceptions that close to the line are rare, and a pass could save time
The rules required a pass in that situation
The running back was injured
quiz.e: Judged on the information available, the pass had a low chance of interception and helped manage the clock. The bad outcome doesn't by itself prove the decision was bad.

quiz.q: What does ‘resulting’ mean?
o: Judging a decision purely by how it turned out
Recording the score after each game
Making decisions very quickly
Betting only on likely winners
quiz.e: Annie Duke borrowed the poker term to describe confusing the quality of a decision with the quality of its outcome.

quiz.q: In Baron and Hershey's study, what changed between versions of each scenario?
o: The information available to the doctor
The doctor's experience
Only the outcome
The type of operation
quiz.e: Everything the decision-maker knew stayed the same. Only the result changed, yet people judged the decision differently.

quiz.q: Why might a bad decision with a good outcome be especially dangerous?
o: It always leads to punishment
It can teach people that a risky choice was fine
It is impossible to notice
It makes people far too cautious
quiz.e: A lucky escape rewards the risky behaviour, making it feel safer and more likely to be repeated.

quiz.q: What is hindsight bias?
o: Forgetting decisions you made
Planning too far ahead
Trusting experts after a mistake
Seeing an outcome as more predictable once you know it
quiz.e: Fischhoff showed that knowing the result makes it seem more foreseeable, and even shifts our memories of what we predicted.

LESSONS.title: N-rays: the rays only believers could see
LESSONS.hook: In 1903 a respected French physicist discovered a new kind of radiation, and other scientists soon confirmed it. There was just one problem: it didn't exist.

sections.key: After the discovery of X-rays, physicists were primed to find new kinds of radiation.
sections.b: At the end of the 1800s, physics was full of astonishing discoveries. In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen found X-rays, which could pass through flesh and reveal the bones beneath. The next year Henri Becquerel discovered that uranium gave off its own mysterious radiation, and soon Marie and Pierre Curie were isolating new radioactive elements. Invisible rays seemed to be everywhere, waiting to be found. In 1903 René Blondlot, a highly respected physicist at the University of Nancy in France, announced that he had found another kind. He named them N-rays, after his home city. Given everything that had happened in the previous eight years, the claim did not seem outlandish. It seemed like the next exciting chapter.

sections.key: N-rays were detected by tiny changes in brightness that observers judged by eye.
sections.b: Blondlot reported that N-rays were given off by many sources, including certain lamps and heated metals, and some colleagues soon claimed they came from the human body as well. The key detail was how they were detected. N-rays supposedly made a small electric spark or a faintly glowing screen grow slightly brighter. Observers sat in a darkened room and judged these changes with their own eyes. That is a very weak signal to rely on. In dim light, the human eye struggles to judge small differences in brightness, and the tiny flickers that happen anyway are easy to read as meaningful. Even so, other scientists, many of them French, soon reported observations of their own, and a stream of research papers followed.

sections.key: Skilled laboratories outside France tried and failed to reproduce the effect.
sections.b: Not everyone was convinced. Physicists in Germany and Britain, among them some of the most skilled experimenters of the day, set up the apparatus and saw nothing. Supporters had an answer ready: perhaps the sceptics' eyes were not sensitive enough, or they lacked the right technique. This is a warning sign worth remembering. When a result can only be seen by people who already believe in it, and failures are explained away as the observer's fault, the claim has become very difficult to test. A real effect should show up for careful researchers whether or not they hope to find it. The disagreement rumbled on, until a visiting American physicist decided to investigate for himself.

sections.key: In 1904 Robert Wood secretly removed a vital part of the equipment, and the readings carried on.
sections.b: In 1904 the American physicist Robert W. Wood, of Johns Hopkins University, visited Blondlot's laboratory. Blondlot demonstrated how an aluminium prism supposedly spread N-rays out into a spectrum, with readings taken in a darkened room. While the room was dark, Wood quietly removed the prism and kept it out of sight. Blondlot carried on reading out measurements as if nothing had changed. Wood also reported other secret checks in which observers kept seeing effects that should have vanished. He published his account in the scientific journal Nature later that year. Without accusing anyone of dishonesty, the report made it clear that the observations depended on what the observers expected, not on any real rays.

sections.key: Blondlot almost certainly believed what he saw; his perception was guided by his expectations.
sections.b: There is no good evidence that Blondlot set out to deceive anyone. He was an accomplished scientist who had done respected earlier work measuring the speed of electrical waves. What went wrong was more ordinary and more unsettling: he and others genuinely perceived what they expected to perceive. After Wood's report, interest in N-rays faded quickly, especially outside France, though Blondlot is said to have kept believing in them. The episode is now a classic case study in how expectation shapes observation. The chemist Irving Langmuir later popularised the phrase ‘pathological science’ for cases like this, where researchers fool themselves with effects so faint they sit right at the edge of what can be detected.

sections.h: Clever Hans and the cure: blinding
sections.key: Good science guards against expectation by keeping observers from knowing what to expect.
sections.b: A similar lesson had come from a horse. In early 1900s Berlin, a horse called Clever Hans appeared to answer arithmetic questions by tapping his hoof. In 1907 the psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed that Hans was responding to tiny, unconscious cues from the people around him, who tensed and relaxed as he neared the right answer. When the questioner didn't know the answer, or Hans couldn't see them, his skill vanished. The solution to both stories is blinding. In a well-run modern trial, the people measuring results don't know which participants received the treatment. Wood, in effect, ran a blind test. Whenever you can, test a claim in a way that stops the tester's hopes from steering the result.

quiz.q: Why did N-rays seem believable in 1903?
o: They had been predicted decades earlier
They were bright enough to see in daylight
X-rays and radioactivity had recently been discovered
Every laboratory in Europe had detected them
quiz.e: Coming just after X-rays and radioactivity, another invisible ray seemed like a natural next discovery.

quiz.q: How were N-rays supposedly detected?
o: With a Geiger counter
By slight brightening of a spark or glowing screen, judged by eye
By the heat they produced
By the sound they made in a vacuum tube
quiz.e: Observers judged faint changes in brightness in a dark room, a signal easily shaped by expectation and random flicker.

quiz.q: What warning sign appeared when other laboratories couldn't find N-rays?
o: Failures were blamed on the sceptics' eyes or technique
The sceptics refused to try the experiment
The equipment was too expensive to build
The sceptics were not trained physicists
quiz.e: When a claim's failures are always explained away as the observer's fault, it becomes almost impossible to test.

quiz.q: What did Robert Wood do during his 1904 visit?
o: Bribed the laboratory assistants
Proved N-rays came from the sun
Secretly removed the prism, yet the readings carried on
Measured the rays with better instruments
quiz.e: Removing the essential prism should have changed the results. When it didn't, it showed the readings came from expectation.

quiz.q: What does ‘blinding’ mean in an experiment?
o: Running it in complete darkness
Keeping observers unaware of information that could sway their judgement
Hiding the results from the public
Testing only on animals
quiz.e: Blinding stops the hopes and expectations of the people involved from influencing what they see or record.

LESSONS.title: Deduction, induction and abduction: three ways to reason
LESSONS.hook: Sherlock Holmes called it deduction, but he was usually doing something else. Learn the three basic kinds of reasoning, and what each can and can't prove.

sections.h: ‘You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive’
sections.key: Holmes's first meeting with Watson shows reasoning from small clues to a big conclusion.
sections.b: In A Study in Scarlet, published in 1887, Sherlock Holmes shakes hands with Dr John Watson and immediately says, ‘You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.’ Watson is astonished. Later Holmes explains his chain of thought. Here was a gentleman of a medical type with a military air, so probably an army doctor. His face was tanned but his wrists were pale, so he had recently come from the tropics. He looked haggard and held his left arm stiffly, suggesting illness and an injury. Where might an English army doctor recently have suffered such hardship? Afghanistan. Holmes called this the science of deduction. Logicians, though, would say he was mostly doing something different. To see why, we need three kinds of reasoning.

sections.key: In a valid deduction, if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.
sections.b: Deduction moves from general statements to a conclusion that follows necessarily. The classic example: all humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore Socrates is mortal. If both starting statements, called premises, are true, the conclusion cannot be false. That is deduction's great strength: certainty. Its weakness is that the conclusion contains nothing that wasn't already packed inside the premises. Deduction also depends completely on the premises being right. An argument can be perfectly valid in its structure and still reach a false conclusion if a premise is wrong: all birds can fly; penguins are birds; therefore penguins can fly. Logicians call an argument ‘sound’ only when it is valid and its premises are actually true.

sections.key: Induction generalises from experience, which is useful but never completely certain.
sections.b: Induction works the other way, from particular observations to general conclusions. The sun has risen every morning in recorded history, so it will rise tomorrow. Every swan Europeans had ever seen was white, so all swans must be white. Most of our everyday knowledge, and much of science, rests on reasoning like this, and usually it serves us well. But an inductive conclusion can always be overturned by new evidence. In 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh and his crew saw black swans on a river in what is now Western Australia, which became known as the Swan River. A belief backed by countless observations was undone by a single flock of birds.

sections.key: Abduction reasons from evidence to the most likely explanation, as detectives and doctors do.
sections.b: The third kind of reasoning was named abduction by the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce, who developed the idea from the late 1800s into the early 1900s. It starts with a surprising observation and asks what would best explain it. The lawn is wet this morning. Did it rain, did the sprinkler run, or did dew form overnight? You weigh up the clues, perhaps noticing that the footpath is bone dry, which points to the sprinkler. Abduction is also called inference to the best explanation. This is what Holmes was really doing with Watson: choosing the most plausible story to fit the clues. Doctors do the same when they diagnose an illness from symptoms, and mechanics do it when tracing a strange noise in an engine.

sections.key: Abduction can miss alternatives, and a common logical slip treats it like deduction.
sections.b: Abduction is powerful but risky, because the best explanation you can think of may not be the true one. Perhaps Watson was tanned from a holiday and had hurt his arm falling off a horse. The answer is only as good as the range of explanations you consider. A common error is to treat abduction as if it were deduction. ‘If it rained, the lawn would be wet. The lawn is wet. Therefore it rained.’ That feels logical, but it's a known fallacy called affirming the consequent, because other things could have wet the lawn. Induction has its own trap: generalising from too few cases, such as judging a whole city on one rude waiter.

sections.key: Good thinking cycles through explanation, prediction and testing.
sections.b: In practice the three kinds of reasoning work as a team, and science is a good model. A researcher notices something odd and uses abduction to propose a likely explanation, called a hypothesis. They then use deduction to work out what should happen if that explanation is true: if this fertiliser helps plants grow, then plants given it should grow taller than identical plants without it. Finally they gather observations and use induction to judge whether the evidence supports the idea. Then the cycle starts again. You can do the same with everyday puzzles. When you land on an explanation, ask what else could explain the facts, what your idea predicts, and whether you've checked.

quiz.q: Which kind of reasoning was Holmes mostly using when he guessed Watson had been in Afghanistan?
o: Deduction
Abduction
Induction
Pure intuition
quiz.e: Holmes was inferring the most plausible explanation for a set of clues, which is abduction, not a guaranteed deduction.

quiz.q: What makes a deductive argument ‘sound’?
o: It is convincing to most people
It is based on many observations
It is valid and its premises are true
It has a surprising conclusion
quiz.e: A valid argument with a false premise can reach a false conclusion. Soundness requires both correct structure and true premises.

quiz.q: What did the black swans seen in 1697 show about induction?
o: A conclusion based on many observations can be overturned by one new one
Induction is always wrong
Swans migrate to Australia each year
Deduction is more reliable than observation
quiz.e: Countless sightings of white swans didn't prove all swans were white. One new observation was enough to overturn the generalisation.

quiz.q: ‘If it rained, the lawn would be wet. The lawn is wet, so it rained.’ What's wrong with this?
o: Nothing, it is a valid deduction
It assumes rain is rare
It relies on too few observations
It affirms the consequent, ignoring other possible causes
quiz.e: A wet lawn fits rain, but also a sprinkler or dew. Treating a possible explanation as certain is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

quiz.q: In the scientific cycle, what role does deduction usually play?
o: Working out what should happen if a hypothesis is true
Coming up with the first guess
Collecting observations
Replacing the need for evidence
quiz.e: Deduction turns a hypothesis into testable predictions, which observations can then support or undermine.

LESSONS.title: The framing effect: same facts, different choices
LESSONS.hook: Would you choose a treatment with a 90 per cent survival rate? What about one with a 10 per cent death rate? They're identical, yet the wording changes what people choose.

sections.key: Describing the same options as lives saved or lives lost flipped people's choices.
sections.b: In 1981 the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published a now-famous problem. Imagine a disease outbreak expected to kill 600 people. One group of participants chose between two programs. With Program A, 200 people will be saved. With Program B, there's a one-third chance all 600 are saved and a two-thirds chance no-one is saved. Most chose A, the sure thing. A second group got the same choice in different words. With Program C, 400 people will die. With Program D, there's a one-third chance nobody dies and a two-thirds chance all 600 die. Now most chose D, the gamble. Yet A and C describe exactly the same outcome, as do B and D.

sections.h: Gains feel safe, losses invite a gamble
sections.key: People tend to avoid risk when thinking about gains, and take risks to avoid sure losses.
sections.b: The outbreak problem revealed a pattern that Kahneman and Tversky built into their prospect theory. When outcomes are described as gains, such as lives saved, people tend to be cautious and prefer a certain result. When the same outcomes are described as losses, such as deaths, people become more willing to gamble to avoid a sure loss. Part of the reason is loss aversion: losses tend to feel more painful than equivalent gains feel good, with many studies putting the ratio at roughly two to one, though estimates vary. Logically, the wording should make no difference, because the numbers are identical. Psychologically, the frame sets the reference point against which everything else is judged.

sections.key: Even physicians' choices shifted depending on whether outcomes were framed as survival or death.
sections.b: You might hope experts would see through framing. In a 1982 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, Barbara McNeil and colleagues, including Tversky, asked people to choose between surgery and radiation therapy for lung cancer. Surgery carried a higher risk of dying during or soon after treatment, but better long-term survival. When the results were presented as chances of surviving, surgery looked more attractive than when the very same results were described as chances of dying. The effect appeared among patients, among students, and among physicians. Since then, many guides to communicating medical risk have encouraged presenting figures in more than one way, for example giving both survival and death rates together.

sections.key: Labels that highlight the positive side make products seem better, even after tasting them.
sections.b: Framing is everywhere in shopping. In a 1988 study, Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth asked people to evaluate minced beef described either as ‘75 per cent lean’ or ‘25 per cent fat’. It was the same meat, but people rated the ‘lean’ version as better quality and less greasy. Interestingly, the gap shrank when people actually tasted the beef, though it didn't vanish. Marketers know this well. Yoghurt is ‘95 per cent fat free’ rather than ‘5 per cent fat’. A fee might be presented as a ‘discount for paying cash’ instead of a ‘surcharge for paying by card’. None of these descriptions is false. They simply choose which side of the same coin you see first.

sections.key: In politics and news, choosing which aspect of an issue to emphasise can shift opinions.
sections.b: There's a second, broader kind of framing. Instead of describing the same numbers in two ways, it highlights different aspects of an issue. In a 1997 study by Thomas Nelson, Rosalee Clawson and Zoe Oxley, Americans read a news story about a planned rally by the Ku Klux Klan. When the story framed it as a matter of free speech, readers were more tolerant of the rally going ahead than when the same event was framed as a threat to public order. Debates about tax, immigration, crime and climate are full of these frames. Is a policy ‘tax relief’ or a ‘cut to services’? Each phrase invites you to think about one side of the trade-off and quietly forget the other.

sections.key: Restate choices in more than one way and convert percentages into real numbers before deciding.
sections.b: You can't avoid frames, because every description has to start somewhere. But you can learn to notice them. When you face an important choice, deliberately flip the wording: if you're told nine out of ten customers are satisfied, remind yourself that one in ten isn't. If a deal is framed as avoiding a loss, ask how it looks as a plain gain. Turn percentages into concrete counts, such as ‘out of 100 people like me, how many?’ This makes risks much easier to compare. Be especially wary when someone else has chosen the frame for you and stands to gain from your decision. And when you present information to others, giving both frames is often the fairest thing you can do.

quiz.q: In the outbreak problem, why is the switch in people's choices surprising?
o: The programs had genuinely different outcomes
Programs A and C described exactly the same outcome
The second group was given more information
The participants were all doctors
quiz.e: Saving 200 of 600 is the same as 400 dying. Only the wording changed, yet the majority preference reversed.

quiz.q: When outcomes are framed as losses, people tend to:
o: Become more cautious
Choose whichever option is listed first
Become more willing to gamble
Ignore the numbers entirely
quiz.e: Facing a sure loss feels so painful that people often prefer a risky option that might avoid it altogether.

quiz.q: Who was influenced by framing in the 1982 lung cancer study?
o: Only students
Only patients without medical training
Nobody, once the numbers were explained
Patients, students and physicians alike
quiz.e: Physicians were affected too, which is why presenting risks in more than one frame is often recommended.

quiz.q: What happened in the minced beef study when people actually tasted the meat?
o: The framing effect shrank but didn't disappear
The effect became much stronger
People preferred the ‘fat’ label
Tasting made them reject both samples
quiz.e: Direct experience reduced the influence of the label, but the ‘lean’ description still gave the beef an edge.

quiz.q: Which is a good way to defuse a frame?
o: Go with your first reaction
Restate the choice the other way and convert percentages into counts
Only trust positive descriptions
Avoid numbers completely
quiz.e: Seeing both versions and using concrete counts strips away the emotional pull of a single framing.

LESSONS.title: The wisdom of crowds: when many guesses beat experts
LESSONS.hook: In 1906 hundreds of people guessed the weight of an ox. Hardly anyone was spot on, but together they were astonishingly close. Here's why, and when crowds turn foolish.

sections.key: Francis Galton found that a crowd's middle guess was remarkably close to an ox's true weight.
sections.b: In 1906 the scientist Francis Galton visited a livestock fair in Plymouth, England. Visitors could pay a small fee to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and dressed, with prizes for the closest entries. Galton, who was not a great admirer of ordinary people's judgement, collected the 787 legible tickets afterwards and analysed them. The guesses were all over the place. But the middle value, the median, was 1,207 pounds, about 547 kilograms. The actual weight was 1,198 pounds, so the crowd was out by less than one per cent. Later analyses found the average of the guesses was even closer. Galton published the result in Nature in 1907 under the title ‘Vox Populi’, the voice of the people.

sections.key: When people's mistakes are independent, overestimates and underestimates tend to cancel each other out.
sections.b: How can a crowd of non-experts beat almost every individual in it? Each guess contains two parts: some genuine information and some error. One person might overestimate because the ox looks bulky, while another underestimates because they're thinking of a smaller breed. If those errors point in different directions, they tend to cancel out when you average them, while the useful information adds up. The result is an estimate that is often better than most of the individual guesses, and sometimes better than an expert's. But this only works if people bring different knowledge and make their mistakes independently. If everyone shares the same blind spot, averaging simply produces a confident version of the same error.

sections.key: Combining many judgements works in plenty of everyday settings, from quiz shows to forecasts.
sections.b: The idea was popularised by the journalist James Surowiecki in his 2004 book The Wisdom of Crowds. One of his examples came from the quiz show Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? Contestants who were stuck could phone a friend they had chosen for being smart, or poll the studio audience. By Surowiecki's account, the chosen friends gave the right answer about 65 per cent of the time, while the audience's most popular answer was right about 91 per cent of the time. Similar principles underpin many tools today, from averaging the forecasts of several economists to combining many runs of weather models, and the product ratings that pool the experiences of thousands of buyers.

sections.key: Crowds are wise when they are diverse, independent, decentralised and properly combined.
sections.b: Surowiecki argued that wise crowds need four ingredients. Diversity: people should bring different information and perspectives, not all the same views. Independence: each person's judgement should be their own, rather than copied from those around them. Decentralisation: people should be able to draw on local and specialised knowledge. And aggregation: there must be some way of combining all the private judgements into one answer, such as an average, a vote or a market price. Take away any of these and the magic fades. A room of people who all read the same article, or who call out their guesses one after another, is less a crowd of independent minds than one opinion repeated many times.

sections.key: Social influence can make crowds more confident without making them more accurate.
sections.b: Independence is the fragile ingredient. In a 2011 study, Jan Lorenz and colleagues in Switzerland asked groups to estimate factual quantities, such as crime figures, over several rounds. Some groups were shown what the others had guessed before answering again. Seeing others' answers narrowed the range of guesses and made people more confident, but the group's estimates did not become more accurate. The crowd had lost its diversity without gaining any wisdom. On a larger scale, similar dynamics help explain stock market bubbles, fads and panic buying, where people react to each other rather than to independent information. A crowd that copies itself doesn't cancel out its errors. It can amplify them.

sections.key: Averaging two separate guesses of your own can improve your accuracy.
sections.b: You can even borrow the effect for yourself. In 2008 Edward Vul and Harold Pashler asked people to answer factual questions, then unexpectedly asked them to guess again. The average of a person's two guesses was more accurate than either guess alone, and the benefit was larger when the second guess came three weeks later rather than straight away. The delay helped because it made the second guess more independent of the first. Researchers call this the crowd within. A practical version: when you estimate something important, such as how long a job will take, make a guess, then assume your first answer was wrong, think about why, and make a second estimate. Then average the two.

quiz.q: What was striking about the guesses at the Plymouth fair?
o: Most people guessed exactly right
The median guess was within about one per cent of the true weight
The butchers' guesses were by far the best
Nobody guessed within 100 pounds
quiz.e: Individual guesses varied widely, but the middle value of all 787 was only nine pounds off the actual weight.

quiz.q: Why does averaging many guesses work?
o: Independent errors tend to cancel out
Crowds always contain an expert
People guess more carefully in groups
Large numbers are easier to estimate
quiz.e: When errors point in different directions, they offset each other, leaving the shared genuine information.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Surowiecki's conditions for a wise crowd?
o: Diversity
Independence
Aggregation
Unanimity
quiz.e: Wise crowds need diversity, independence, decentralisation and aggregation. Everyone agreeing is not required, and can be a warning sign.

quiz.q: What did Lorenz and colleagues find when people saw others' guesses?
o: Accuracy improved sharply
Guesses spread out more widely
Guesses narrowed and confidence rose, without the group becoming more accurate
People stopped guessing altogether
quiz.e: Social influence reduced diversity and boosted confidence, but didn't improve the collective estimate.

quiz.q: In Vul and Pashler's study, when did a second guess help most?
o: When it was made immediately
When it was made three weeks later
When a friend made it instead
When it copied the first guess
quiz.e: A delay made the second guess more independent of the first, so averaging the two cancelled out more error.

LESSONS.title: Small samples, big surprises: the law of small numbers
LESSONS.hook: The places with the lowest cancer rates and the highest ones share the same surprising feature. Understanding why will change how you read every ranking and review.

sections.key: Both the healthiest and unhealthiest-looking places on a map are often the ones with the fewest people.
sections.b: Imagine a map of the United States showing kidney cancer rates county by county. The counties with the lowest rates are mostly rural and sparsely populated. It's tempting to explain this: fresh air, clean water, active lives, fewer pollutants. Now look at the counties with the highest rates. They are also mostly rural and sparsely populated.
